# TO THOSE ON THE HOLY-NAMED MOUNTAIN
## OF ATHOS
### LEADING THE HESYCHASTIC LIFE <note>The 'hesychastic' life refers to a tradition of prayer and silence (hesychia) focused on inner stillness and the Jesus Prayer.</note>
## TO OUR MOST HOLY FATHERS
### THIS EDITION
### OF THE HOLY PHILOKALIA <note>original: "Φιλοκαλίας"; literally meaning 'Love of the Beautiful,' referring to the beauty of divine virtue.</note>
### IS DEDICATED

->THE PUBLISHER<-

---

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal divider consisting of a central floral or sun-like ornament with scrolling vines and leaves extending to both sides.</image-desc>

To whom else would it have been more just to dedicate this edition of this most divine book of the Holy Neptics <note>original: "Νηπτικῶν"; the 'Neptic' or 'Watchful' Fathers are those who emphasize mental sobriety and vigilance over one's thoughts</note>, which guides one in the heavenly and angel-like way of life and which prescribes and teaches its rules—the Holy *Philokalia*, I say—than to you?

Among you, that most divine way of life—which those who composed the most wise and most spiritual treatises of this Holy Book followed, and for which they became your leaders, guides, and models—is still in its prime and flourishing greatly.

Your mountain, truly named Holy and the mystical garden of the All-Queen and All-Pure Virgin <note>referring to the *Theotokos* or Virgin Mary, who is traditionally considered the patroness of Mount Athos</note>, has brought forth, and still brings forth through the grace of the All-Good God and the unceasing intercessions of the All-Blameless Maiden, thousands of blooming palms and multiplying cedars, like those in Lebanon, in the spirit.

In you, as if in some ark, the precious treasures of Byzantinism <note>original: "Βυζαντινίσμοῦ"; here referring to the cultural, liturgical, and spiritual heritage of the Byzantine Empire preserved after its fall</note> have been preserved intact, and these highly-valued items are 

<column-break/>

admired by all who value aesthetic beauty and are lovers of antiquity, and especially by those who are truly pious and genuine children of the Orthodox Eastern Church.

From among you came the ever-memorable Nikodemos <note>St. Nikodemos the Hagiorite (1749–1809), a prolific monk and scholar who helped compile this collection</note>, who spent his life on the publication of so many holy and God-beloved books, and indeed contributed and laid down no small effort for the present book when he published it along with the Holy Makarios of Corinth <note>St. Makarios of Corinth (1731–1805), the bishop who initiated the compilation of the Philokalia</note>.

And you also brought this edition to light, showing no ordinary eagerness for its reception.

To you, therefore, this edition ought to be dedicated. And to you we dedicate it: as an encouragement for the struggle for greater virtue, as an excellent example and model of an angel-like way of life, and as courage and strength for triumphing over the schemes of the All-Evil Satan. — Pray, then, holy Fathers, for us too, so that God may be merciful to us on the great day of Judgment.

# PREFACE

...to publish the book to the ears of the many as if it were something strange; for he says that a certain danger follows from these things. To him, we briefly strike back in response: that we also, dear companion, did not come to such an undertaking by following our own reasoning, but rather by making use of examples. On one hand, the Holy Scripture commands all the pious without distinction to pray without ceasing, and to have the Lord always before their eyes. It is impious to say that the commands of the Spirit are either forbidden or impossible, according to Basil the Great <note>St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) was a foundational figure in Christian monasticism; his "Longer Rules" are a cornerstone of Eastern ascetic life.</note>. On the other hand, we also have the written tradition of the Fathers. For Gregory the Theologian <note>Also known as Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Father and one of the three "Great Hierarchs" of the Orthodox Church.</note> suggests to all the people under him in common that they should remember God more than they breathe. And the divine Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), the "Golden-Mouthed" Archbishop of Constantinople, famed for his eloquence.</note> sets forth three whole discourses concerning unceasing and noetic prayer <note term="noetic prayer">original: "νοερᾶς προσευχῆς"; this refers to "prayer of the mind" or "prayer of the heart," an internal, wordless communion with God distinct from spoken liturgy.</note>, and in countless other places in his remaining discourses, he exhorts everyone in common to pray at all times. And that wonderful Gregory of Sinai <note>A 14th-century monk who revitalized the practice of the Jesus Prayer on Mount Athos.</note> traveled through various cities teaching such salvation-bringing work. Furthermore, God Himself from above, having sent an Angel through a miracle, sealed such truth by silencing the monk who spoke against it, as is seen at the end of this present book. And why do I need words for this? Since even those living in the world and dwelling in palaces, having such meditation as an uninterrupted task—as we have said—practically confirm this word, and are themselves sufficient to silence those who speak against it. And if some have occasionally been slightly led astray, what is the wonder? They suffered this mostly out of conceit <note>original: "οἰήσεως"; refers to spiritual pride or self-delusion.</note>, according to Gregory of Sinai. But I think the greatest and primary cause of this deviation is this: not accurately following the teaching of the Fathers concerning this work in all things—it is not because of the work itself; heaven forbid! For this work is holy, and through it we rather need to be

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin>
delivered from all delusion. For even the commandment of the Law of God, which was found to lead to life, says Paul, became death to some; but this did not happen because of the commandment—how could it, since it is holy, just, and true? Rather, it was because of the wickedness of those sold under sin. What then because of this? Must we condemn the divine Commandment because of the sin of some? Must we also disregard such salvation-bringing work because of the deviation of some? Not at all; neither that, nor this. Rather, trusting in Him who said, *I am the way and the truth*, we must undertake the work with all humility and a disposition of mourning. For to the one who is delivered from conceit and the desire to please men, even if the entire evil phalanx of demons should break against him, they will not even be able to approach, according to the teaching of the Fathers. Since things are so, and since the Book is presented as entirely blameless from every side for the reasons stated, it would finally be most timely to take into one’s hands that dinner-invitation of Wisdom, and with a high proclamation, to call everyone to the spiritual banquet of this Book; as many as are not "banquet-haters" regarding divine things, nor like those in the Gospels who make excuses about fields, and oxen, and wives <note>A reference to the Parable of the Great Banquet in Luke 14:16–24.</note>. Come then, come! Eat the knowledge-filled bread of wisdom found within it, and drink the wine that gladdens the heart in a noetic way, which transports one away from all things sensible and intelligible alike because of the deification <note term="theosis">original: "θέωσιν"; the process of being united with God's grace and transformed into His likeness.</note> found in ecstasy; and be drunk with a sober drunkenness as you eat. Come, all you who happen to be sharers in the Orthodox calling, Laity and Monks together, you who strive to find the Kingdom of God that is within you, and the treasure hidden in the field of the heart; which is the sweet Jesus Christ. So that, once our mind is freed from its captivity to lower things and its wandering, and the heart is purified of the passions through the...

# PREFACE

...through the unceasing and awesome invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the other cooperating virtues taught in this Book, may you be united with one another, and through yourselves also be united to God—in accordance with the Lord’s petition to the Father, when He says: *that they may be one, as we are one* <note>A reference to the "High Priestly Prayer" of Jesus in John 17:11, 22.</note>. And thus, being united to Him and completely transformed

<column-break/>

by the possession and ecstasy of divine love <note>original: "θείου ἔρωτος"; while "eros" often refers to romantic love, in this mystical context it describes an intense, self-transcending yearning for God.</note>, may you be most abundantly deified <note term="deification">original: "θεωθείητε"; the process of *theosis*, where a person becomes "godlike" by grace, partaking in the divine nature without losing their human identity.</note> in noetic perception <note term="noetic">original: "νοερᾷ"; referring to the "nous," the spiritual "eye" of the heart or the highest faculty of the soul that perceives God directly rather than through logic.</note> and unwavering assurance. May you return to God’s original purpose for humanity, glorifying the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the one most sovereign Godhead. To Whom belongs all glory, honor, and worship unto the ages of ages. Amen.

# PREFACE 3

For indeed, through spiritual and systematic <note>original: "ἐπιστημονικῆς"; used here to mean a methodical or disciplined spiritual practice.</note> labor, together with the possible fulfillment of the commandments and other moral virtues, a warmth is born in the heart through the invocation of the All-Holy Name. From this spiritual energy, the passions are consumed—for "our God is a consuming fire" <note>A reference to Hebrews 12:29.</note>, a fire that consumes all wickedness. Gradually, the mind <note term="nous">original: "νοῦς"; the "eye of the soul" or the faculty of direct spiritual perception, distinct from the discursive reason.</note> and the heart are purified and united with one another. Once these are purified and joined together, the saving commandments are more easily fulfilled; the fruits of the Spirit begin to blossom in the soul, and a whole treasury of good things is abundantly bestowed.

To put it briefly, from this practice, it is possible for us to return more quickly to the perfect grace of the Spirit given to us from the beginning in Holy Baptism. This grace is indeed within us, but like a spark buried in soot <note>original: "αἰθάλη"; the soot or ash of the passions that covers the divine spark.</note>, it has been hidden by the passions. By this method, we may behold it shining forth clearly, be enlightened in our understanding, and consequently be perfected and deified <note term="theosis">original: "θεωθῆναι"; the process of becoming godlike through union with God's grace.</note> in a fitting manner.

Most of the Fathers mention this work sporadically in their writings, as if speaking to those who already know the matter. But some, perhaps foreseeing the ignorance and negligence of our generation regarding this saving study <gloss>*</gloss>, did not hesitate to hand down to us, their children, a detailed explanation of its practical method through certain natural techniques <note term="natural methods">original: "φυσικῶν μεθόδων"; these often involve physical aids to concentration, such as rhythmic breathing or posture, intended to help the mind descend into the heart.</note>, like a paternal inheritance. They honored this practice with many names, calling it the "beginning of every other work pleasing to God," a "treasury of good things," the "purest sign of repentance," and "noetic practice which is the gateway to true contemplation" <note term="theoria">original: "θεωρίας"; the direct vision or experience of God.</note>. By these names, they encourage everyone toward this soul-profiting work. Yet from here, I begin to lament, and my emotion cuts short my speech.

<column-break/>

<insert>2</insert>
For regarding the books that philosophize about such truly Purifying, Illuminating, and Perfecting work—to use the words of the Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian mystical theologian who categorized the spiritual life into these three stages.</note>—and also those other books which are called "Neptic" <note term="neptic">original: "Νηπτικὰ"; from "nipsis," meaning watchfulness, sobriety, or spiritual alertness.</note> by many because they deal with attention and watchfulness: all of these together, acting as necessary means and instruments, aim at the same goal: to deify <note term="theurgy">original: "Θεουργῆσαι"; literally "to work God" or "to make divine," referring to the transformation of the human person by divine grace.</note> man.

However, due to their antiquity and their scarcity—not to mention that they have never been printed—these works have almost vanished. Even where some copies remained, they were moth-eaten and entirely decayed, practically the same as if they had never existed at all. I will add that since most of our people are negligent, being "troubled about many things" <note>A reference to Martha in Luke 10:41.</note>—namely, the bodily and practical virtues—or to speak more truly, spending their whole lives only on the *tools* of the virtues, they somehow, with great ignorance, overlook the "one thing needful": the guarding of the mind and pure prayer. Thus, this brief and sweetest work is in danger of failing entirely. As a result, grace is obscured and extinguished, <margin>The</margin> and with it, our union and deification in God falls away.

(This was, as has been said, the primary and well-pleasing will of God from the beginning. <gloss>*</gloss> It is toward this most purposeful end that God the Word looks: in His creation of us for existence, and in His providence for our well-being and eternal well-being. <gloss>*</gloss> Simply put, this is the goal of everything divinely enacted in both the Old and New Testaments.)

For where previously many people, including those in the world and even Kings themselves living in palaces, daily burdened by ten thousand worries and life's cares, had this one and only work: to pray unceasingly in the heart (as we find many examples in history); now, through negligence and ignorance, this is forgotten not only by those in the world, but even by those <gloss>+</gloss>

# PREFACE

...even for monks themselves who live in quiet solitude, it is a most rare thing—oh, what a loss!—and very difficult to find. Being deprived of this [practice], even though each person struggles as much as they can and endures labors for the sake of virtue, they nevertheless harvest no fruit. This is because without the unceasing remembrance of the Lord, and the resulting purity of heart and mind <note term="nous">original: "νοῦς"; the "eye of the soul" or the faculty of direct spiritual perception.</note> from every evil thing, it is impossible to bear fruit. For He says, "Without me, you can do nothing" <note>John 15:5</note>. And again: "He who remains in me bears much fruit" <note>John 15:5</note>.

From this, I conclude that there is no other reason why those who excel in holiness—those who live even after death—have vanished, and why those being saved in the present time are so few, except for this: that we have neglected this work which leads to deification <note term="theosis">original: "θέωσις"; the process of becoming godlike through union with God's grace.</note>. Someone once said that without the mind being deified, it is not only impossible for a person to be sanctified, but they cannot even be saved. This is a most awe-inspiring thing even to hear, for to be saved and to be deified are the same thing, according to the revelation of those wise in God. Furthermore, and most importantly, we are deprived of the books that guide us toward this goal. Without these, it is among the things that are impossible to achieve the end.

But look! Here is the man who is good and noble in all things, the Christ-loving Lord **John Mavrogordato** <note>A prominent member of the Phanariote Mavrogordatos family who funded the first publication of the Philokalia in 1782.</note>; he who yields to no one in any matter of excellence, as far as generosity, love for the poor, hospitality, and the rest of the choir of virtues are concerned. He is forever set on fire by a divine zeal for the common benefit of all.

This man, inspired by the grace of Christ—who desires all people to be saved and to reach deification—transforms mourning into joy by solving this difficulty. For by setting before the public the Means of Deification, he wholeheartedly—and, so to speak, with hands and feet—assists and cooperates in every way in this part of the pre-

<column-break/>

-eternal counsel of God. Oh, the glory! Bravo to these great deeds! For behold, here are the works that were never before published in former times. Behold, those things that lay in secret, in darkness, and in some corner—ignored, moth-eaten, and tossed aside or scattered here and there. Behold, those works which scientifically guide one toward the purity of heart, watchfulness <note term="nepsis">original: "νῆψις"; a state of spiritual sobriety, alertness, and vigilance over one's thoughts.</note> of the mind, and the restoration of the grace within us—and beyond that, to deification. Having gathered these into one, and sparing no expense at all, he publishes them through the great and shining light of the Printing Press. (For it was necessary, truly necessary, for those things which proclaim divine enlightenment to also be deemed worthy of the light of the press.) And through this, he frees those who know [the path] from the labors of hand-copying, while simultaneously stirring up those who do not know it toward a love of possessing this book—or rather, a love for its practical application. And so you have, O dearest Reader, through the most excellent Lord John, this present spiritual Book, provided without labor and easy to obtain.

> This Book is the storehouse of watchfulness; the guardian of the mind; the mystical school of noetic prayer <note term="noetic prayer">original: "νοερὰ προσευχή"; prayer of the mind or heart, specifically the Jesus Prayer.</note>. This Book is the exceptional pattern of the practical life; the unerring guide of contemplation; the Paradise of the Fathers; the golden chain of the virtues. This Book is the dense conversation with Jesus; the trumpet that calls back grace; and to put it briefly, the very instrument of deification—a thing more desired than ten thousand others, sought and meditated upon for many years, but not found until now.

Therefore, it would be an inescapable debt laid upon you, and owed by every principle of justice, to entreat the Divine with fervent prayers on behalf of the Benefactor and his collaborators, so that they too may achieve the same measure of deification and, as those who labored for this, be the first to enjoy its fruits.

But having reached this point in the discourse, someone might perhaps object, saying that it is not permissible for some of the things in the Bo-

<meta>This page continues the introductory themes from the previous page, moving from the practical scarcity of spiritual texts to a high theological defense of the human purpose: deification. It establishes the "pre-eternal counsel" of God to make man godlike, the interruption of this plan by the devil's envy, and the ultimate restoration of this plan through the Incarnation of the Word.</meta>

# PREFACE
## TO THE PRESENT
# BOOK

God—that blessed Nature, the super-perfect perfection, the Creative Principle of all things good and beautiful, supremely good and supremely beautiful—pre-ordained from eternity His divine purpose to deify <note term="deify">original: "θεῶσαι"; to make godlike or to unite a person with God's own life and grace.</note> man. Having placed this goal within Himself as His primary intent for man from the beginning, He created him at the time He deemed best. Taking the body from matter and placing within it a soul from Himself, He established him as a kind of world—great in the multitude of its powers and excellence—within a small one <note term="microcosm">The author refers to the classical idea of man as a "microcosm" or "small world" that reflects the "macrocosm" of the entire universe.</note>. He made him an observer of visible Creation and an initiate of the intelligible <note term="intelligible">original: "νοουμένης"; referring to the spiritual realm perceived by the mind or "nous" rather than the physical senses.</note>, according to Gregory the Great in Theology <note>St. Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), known as "The Theologian."</note>. For what else was man but truly a statue and a divinely-wrought image full of every grace? Then, giving him the law of the Commandment as a test of his Free Will, God saw fit to leave the rest to him; and, as Sirach says, He left him in the hand of his own counsel <note>Sirach 15:14</note>, to choose what appeared best to him. The prize for keeping the commandment was to receive the substantial grace of deification <note term="theosis">original: "θέωσις"; the process of becoming godlike through union with God.</note>, becoming a god and being enlightened by the purest light for all ages. But alas! Because of the wicked scheme of envy, the originator of evil <note>The Devil</note> did not allow this to be realized. Conceiving envy against both the Creator and the creature, as the Holy Maximus says <note>St. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD), a central figure in the theology of theosis.</note>: against the

<column-break/>

Creator, so that the all-praised power of His Goodness, which deifies man through its activity, might not be revealed; and against the creature, so that man might not appear as a partaker of such supernatural glory through deification. The deceitful one, tricking wretched man with craftiness, prepared him through fair-sounding advice to transgress the deifying commandment. And—alas!—having separated man from divine glory, the rebel thought himself a sort of Olympic victor, as if he could cut off the fulfillment of God’s pre-eternal counsel.

But since, according to the divine oracles, the counsel of God for the deification of human nature "remains forever" <note>Psalm 32:11</note>, and "the thoughts of His heart to all generations"—namely the reasons of Providence and Judgment which extend toward this goal—stand unchangeably in both the present and the future age, according to the explanation of the Holy Maximus. In the last days, through the depths of His mercy, the most divine Word of the Father Himself saw fit to nullify the counsels of the Rulers of Darkness, and to bring into effect the ancient and true counsel He had intended. And so, by the good pleasure of the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, He became incarnate, assuming our whole nature and deifying it; then [He provided] the saving [laws]...

-> # PREFACE <-

...and having granted us His God-working <note>original: "θεουργοὺς"; actions or commandments that perform a divine work in the soul.</note> commandments, and the perfect grace of His All-Holy Spirit through Baptism—sowing it like a divine seed in our hearts—He has given us, according to the divine Evangelist, power. Thus, by living according to His life-giving commandments and spiritual stages of growth, and by preserving the grace within us unquenched through their practice, we might finally bear fruit, and through this grace become children of God and be deified <note term="deification">The process of "theosis," or becoming united with God’s life and character.</note>, reaching the status of a perfect man, the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. For this was, in short, the whole end and conclusion of the entire Economy <note term="economy">original: "οἰκονομίας"; the divine plan or "household management" of God for the salvation of humanity.</note> of the Word toward us. 

But alas! For here it is right to "groan bitterly," according to the divine Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), a famous preacher and Patriarch of Constantinople.</note>. For we who have enjoyed such grace and been deemed worthy of such nobility—so that our soul, being cleansed by the Spirit in Baptism, shines brighter than the sun—have faltered. Since we receive this most god-like radiance as infants, we have (partly through ignorance, but mostly blinded by the moonless night of worldly cares) buried this grace so deeply under our passions that the Spirit of God within us is in danger of being completely extinguished. We have come to suffer almost the same as those who answered Paul by saying: "we have not even heard if there is a Holy Spirit." We have truly become as we were in the beginning, according to the Prophet, when grace did not yet rule over us. 

Woe to our weakness! How malice has destroyed us, along with our improper attachment to the things of the senses. And the truly amazing thing is this: if we happen to hear of grace being active in others, we slander them out of envy, and we do not even believe that there is an "operation of grace" in this present age. What then? The Spirit grants wisdom to the God-wise Fathers, and in addition to universal watchfulness <note term="watchfulness">original: "νήψει" (nepsis); a state of spiritual sobriety, alertness, and attention to one's thoughts.</note>, and total attention and guarding of the mind, He reveals to them a way to

<column-break/>

find grace once again, in a way truly wondrous and highly methodical. This was to pray unceasingly to our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God—not simply, I mean, with the mind and lips alone (for this is obvious to all who choose to be pious, and easy for anyone). Rather, it involves turning the whole mind toward the inner man—which is indeed wondrous—and thus calling upon the All-Holy name of the Lord deep within, even in the very depth of the heart, and seeking mercy from Him. In this, one pays attention to the naked words of the prayer alone, and admitting nothing else at all from within or without, one keeps the intellect entirely formless <note term="formless">original: "ἀσχημάτιστον"; a state of prayer where the mind is free from mental images or sensory imaginations.</note> and beyond time. 

The starting points for this practice, and its "raw material" so to speak, the Fathers took from the teaching of the Lord Himself, who said at one time:

> "The Kingdom of God is within you."

And at another:

> "Hypocrite, cleanse first the inside of the cup and of the dish, and then the outside of them will be clean."

These sayings are understood not in a sensory way, but as referring to our inner man. This is also seen from the Apostle Paul, writing to the Ephesians as follows:

> "For this reason I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ... that He may grant you to be strengthened with power through His Spirit in the inner man, that Christ may dwell through the Spirit in your hearts."

What could be clearer than this testimony? And elsewhere he says:

> "...singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord."

Do you hear? He says "in the heart." Furthermore, the Chief of the Apostles [Peter] confirms this, saying:

> "...until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts."

The Holy Spirit teaches this as a necessity for every pious person in countless other pages of the New Testament, as those who look into them carefully can see. By such...

# BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## OF ANTHONY THE GREAT

---

<image-desc>The first letter "A" of the main text is a decorative drop cap set within an ornate rectangular frame featuring floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

**A**nthony our great Father, the leader of the choir of ascetics <note term="ascetics">original: "ἀσκητῶν"; those who practice strict self-discipline and abstain from worldly pleasures for spiritual growth.</note>, flourished during the reign of Constantine the Great, around the three hundred and thirtieth year from the Birth of God <note>original: "Θεογονίας"; referring to the year 330 AD, calculated from the Nativity of Christ.</note>. He was a contemporary of Athanasius the Great <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD), the Bishop of Alexandria who wrote the famous "Life of Antony."</note>, who also wrote his biography at great length. Having reached the highest peak of virtue and dispassion <note term="dispassion">original: "ἀπαθείας"; a state of being free from disordered passions or emotional disturbances.</note>—even though he was a simple and unlettered man—he possessed as a teacher from above that wisdom of the Spirit which makes wise the fishermen and infants. Being illuminated by this wisdom, he introduced many other sacred and spiritual exhortations pertaining to various subjects, and he gave most wise answers to those who questioned him, full of benefit for the soul, as can be seen in many places within the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* <note>original: "Γεροντικῶν"; a collection of wisdom and anecdotes from the early Christian monastics in Egypt.</note>. In addition to these, the one hundred and seventy chapters contained in this present book, our ever-

<column-break/>

memorable father has left to us. That these are the genuine offspring of his god-like mind is confirmed, among others, by the Holy Martyr Peter of Damascus <note>An 8th-century hesychast writer and saint.</note>. Moreover, the very texture of the phrasing removes every handle of doubt and almost cries out to those who study them carefully that they are contemporary with that sacred antiquity.

It is no wonder, then, if the style of language leans toward a simpler, ancient, and unpolished form of discourse; but this is the wonder: that through such great simplicity, such immense salvation and benefit come to those who read. How much the power of persuasion flourishes in them! How much sweetness drips from them! And in general, how much good character and the exactness of the Gospel way of life <note term="way of life">original: "πολιτείας"; can also mean "citizenship" or "conduct," referring here to living according to the standards of the Kingdom of Heaven.</note> shower down upon us! All those who taste this honey with the spiritual throat of their intellect will surely know the pleasure.

<meta>This page transitions from the general biographical introduction of St. Anthony the Great into the beginning of his "170 Chapters." These chapters represent the core of his ethical and ascetic teachings, focusing on the definition of a truly "rational" human being as one who lives according to virtue rather than mere book-learning.</meta>

## OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS
# ANTHONY THE GREAT
### EXHORTATIONS ON THE CHARACTER OF MEN AND THE GOOD LIFE

---

->In 170 Chapters<-

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' (originally 'O' in Greek) inside a rectangular frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>People are called rational <note term="rational">original: "λογικοὶ" (logikoi); in this context, it refers to those who use their reason to seek God, rather than just those who possess the faculty of speech or logic.</note> in an improper sense. They are not rational because they have learned by heart the sayings and the books of the ancient sages. Rather, the rational ones are those who possess a rational soul and are able to discern what is good and what is evil. They flee from what is wicked and harmful to the soul, while they zealously practice, through careful study, what is good and soul-profiting. These people do such things with great gratitude toward God. Only these should truly be called rational men.

<margin>2.</margin>
The truly rational man has but one pursuit: to obey and to please the God of all things. To this end—and this alone—he trains his own soul: how he might become pleasing to God, giving thanks for His great and magnificent providence <note term="providence">original: "προνοίᾳ" (pronoia); the belief in God's protective care and spiritual direction of the universe.</note> and His governance of all things, regardless of what lot he may fall into during life. For it is absurd to be grateful to doctors who provide us with bitter and unpleasant <unclear>medicine</unclear> <note>original: "φάρμακα" (pharmaka); the OCR notes a smudge here, but the context clearly indicates medicine.</note> for the sake of the body's health, yet to be ungrateful to God for the things that seem difficult to us, failing to recognize that everything happens as it should, both for our own benefit and according to His providence. For the knowledge of God and faith in Him are the salvation and perfection of the soul.

<margin>3.</margin>
We have received from God the greatest and most virtuous powers: self-control, forbearance, temperance, fortitude, patience, and others like them. These have been stationed against us to resist and help us against the difficulties that come from the other side <note>Meaning the temptations or hardships that arise from the world or the devil.</note>. If we exercise these powers and keep them ready at hand, we will no longer consider anything that happens to us to be harsh, or painful, or unbearable. We will realize that all things

<column-break/>

are human <note>That is, common to human experience.</note> and are conquered by the virtues within us. Those who are foolish in soul do not keep this in mind; they do not consider that everything happens for our benefit and as it should, so that our virtues may shine forth and we may be crowned by God.

<margin>4.</margin>
By considering the possession of money and its lavish use to be merely a short-lived illusion, and by knowing that a life of virtue and one pleasing to God is superior to wealth, you will not groan, you will not lament, you will blame no one. Rather, you will give thanks to God for everything, even when you see those worse than yourself relying on words or wealth. For the worst passions of the soul are desire, the seeking of glory, and ignorance.

<margin>5.</margin>
The rational man, observing himself, examines what is fitting and what is beneficial for him—what things truly belong to the soul and are helpful, and what things are foreign to it. In this way, he flees what harms the soul as something foreign, which separates it from immortality <note term="immortality">original: "ἀθανασίας" (athanasias); the state of the soul living forever in union with God.</note>.

<margin>6.</margin>
The more moderately a person lives, the happier they are. This is because they do not worry about many things: servants, laborers, or the possession of livestock. For by nailing ourselves to such things and falling into the difficulties that arise from them, we blame God. Yet death is watered by our own self-chosen desires, and we remain wandering in the darkness of a life of sins, failing to recognize our true selves.

<margin>7.</margin>
One ought not to say that it is impossible for a person to achieve a virtuous life, but rather that it is not easy. Nor is such a thing easily grasped by just anyone. However, those who share in a virtuous life are those among men who are pious and

<summary>This page opens St. Anthony’s '170 Chapters,' defining 'rationality' not as intellectual learning but as the moral ability to discern good from evil. It emphasizes gratitude toward God's providence, even in hardship, and the cultivation of internal virtues to overcome external difficulties.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "170 Chapters" of St. Anthony the Great. Having established the definition of a "rational man" in the previous sections, Anthony now contrasts the "God-loving mind" with the "worldly mind" and begins a series of metaphors comparing the cultivation of virtue to the work of artisans, helmsmen, and charioteers.</meta>

## OF OUR HOLY FATHER 
# ANTHONY THE GREAT

<margin>8.</margin> Those who possess a God-loving mind <note term="mind">original: "νοῦν" (noun/nous); in Orthodox spirituality, the *nous* is the "eye of the soul," the faculty that perceives God directly.</note> are rare. For the "common mind" is worldly and changeable, providing both good and evil thoughts, altering its nature and shifting toward material things. But the God-loving mind is the punisher of wickedness, which arises in men by their own choice through spiritual laziness.

The uneducated and ignorant find these words laughable and do not wish to hear them, because their lack of education is being exposed; they want everyone to be just like themselves. In the same way, those who are dissipated in their life and character strive to make everyone else worse than they are, thinking that they will find safety from blame in the sheer number of the wicked. The weak soul is destroyed and muddied by wickedness, which contains within itself: profligacy, pride, greed, anger, rashness, frenzy, murder, lamentation, envy, grasping, robbery, pain, falsehood, pleasure, sloth, grief, cowardice, disease, hatred, blame, weakness, wandering, ignorance, deceit, and the forgetting of God. Through these and similar things, the wretched soul—which separates itself from God—is punished.

<margin>9.</margin> Those who wish to practice a virtuous, devout, and honorable life should not be judged by a manufactured persona or a false way of living. Instead, just as painters and sculptors are judged by their work, so should they demonstrate their virtuous and God-loving way of life <note term="way of life">original: "πολιτείαν" (politeian); refers to one's entire conduct or "citizenship" in the spiritual life.</note> through their actual deeds. They turn away from all wicked pleasures as if they were traps.

<margin>10.</margin> The man who is rich and high-born is actually miserable in the eyes of the wise if he lacks the education of the soul and a life of virtue. On the other hand, the man who is poor and a slave by status, but is adorned with education and a virtuous life, is truly blessed <note term="blessed">original: "εὐδαίμων" (eudaimon); often translated as "happy," but here implying a soul in a state of grace or well-being.</note>. Just as strangers wander aimlessly on the roads, so too those who do not care for a virtuous life are led astray by their desires and perish.

<margin>11.</margin> A person should be called a "man-maker" if they are able to tame the uneducated so that they fall in love with reason and education. In the same way, those who reform the lives of the dissipated toward a virtuous way of life that is pleasing to God should also be called "man-makers," for they are re-sculpting human beings. For gentleness and self-control are true happiness and a good hope for the souls of men.

<column-break/>

<margin>12.</margin> It is fitting for people to truly and properly practice their character and their way of life. For once this is set right, the things concerning God are easily known. For he who worships God with his whole heart and with faith receives the power from Him to control his anger and desire; for desire and anger are the causes of all evils.

<margin>13.</margin> A "man" is defined as either one who is rational <note term="rational">original: "λογικός" (logikos); meaning one who lives according to the *Logos* or reason.</note>, or one who allows himself to be corrected. He who cannot be corrected is called "inhuman," for this [stubbornness] is characteristic of the inhuman. Such people are to be avoided. For it is not possible for those who live alongside wickedness ever to be counted among the immortals.

<margin>14.</margin> Our rationality, when it is truly present within us, makes us worthy of being called "men." But when we fall away from reason, we differ from the irrational animals only in the shape of our limbs and our voice. Therefore, let the well-disposed man recognize that he is immortal, and he will hate every shameful desire, which is the cause of death for men.

<margin>15.</margin> <margin><gloss>meaning "as" or "like"</gloss></margin> Just as each of the crafts demonstrates its own excellence by shaping the materials available to it—for example, one worker crafts wood, another bronze, another gold and silver—so also you, hearing of the "good life" and the virtuous way of life that pleases God, ought to show that you are truly rational in your soul, and not only in the shape of your body. The soul that is truly rational and God-loving immediately recognizes everything in life; it seeks God's favor with love and thanks Him in truth, directing its every impulse and its entire mind toward Him.

<margin>16.</margin> Just as pilots direct a ship toward a target so they do not strike an underwater rock or a reef, so also those who are zealous for the virtuous life should carefully examine what they must do and what they must avoid. They should consider the true and divine laws to be for their own benefit, cutting off wicked thoughts from the soul.

<margin>17.</margin> Just as pilots and charioteers achieve their goal through practice and care, so also those who care for a right and virtuous life must practice and think about how they might live fittingly and [please] God— <note>The text on this page ends mid-sentence.</note>

<summary>St. Anthony defines the "rational man" not by intellect but by a God-loving soul that chooses virtue over vice. He argues that education and character, rather than wealth or status, are what truly make a person "human."</summary>
<keywords>rationality (logikos), God-loving mind (nous), virtue, vice, education (paideia), immortality, man-maker, self-control</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Exhortations on the Character of Men" by St. Anthony the Great. Following the previous page's discussion on the rarity of the God-loving mind, these chapters (18–32) define true freedom, the priority of actions over words, and the soul's independence from earthly authority.</meta>

->### EXHORTATIONS ON THE CHARACTER OF MEN AND GOOD CONDUCT<-

...living in a seemly manner; for he who wishes, and understands that he is able, by believing, proceeds toward incorruption.

<margin>18.</margin> Let those be considered free by you who are not free by their station in life, but those who are free in their life and character. For one should not truly call "free" those rulers who are wicked or undisciplined, for they are slaves to the passions of matter. Freedom and happiness of the soul consist in genuine purity and contempt for temporal things.

<margin>19.</margin> Remind yourself that you must show who you are without ceasing, but let it be through good conduct <note term="conduct">original: "πολιτείας" (politeias); refers to one's manner of life or citizenship in the kingdom of God.</note> and through the works themselves. For in this way, the sick find and recognize physicians as saviors and benefactors not from their words, but from their deeds.

<margin>20.</margin> The mark of a rational and virtuous soul is found in the gaze, the walk, the voice, the laughter, the occupations, and the company one keeps. For everything is transformed and rearranged toward a more decorous state. Their God-loving mind, acting as a sober gatekeeper, shuts out the entries of evil and shameful thoughts.

<margin>21.</margin> Examine your own circumstances and prove them, realizing that rulers and masters have authority over the body only, but not over the soul; let this be ever ready in your mind. Therefore, if they command murders or anything absurd, unjust, or harmful to the soul, you must not obey them, even if they torture the body. For God created the soul free and self-governing <note term="self-governing">original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion); a technical term in Greek philosophy and theology for free will or moral autonomy.</note>, responsible for its own actions, whether good or evil.

<margin>22.</margin> The rational soul strives to be rid of aimlessness, vanity, arrogance, deceit, envy, robbery, and similar things, which are the works of demons and of an evil will. Everything is set right through persistent diligence and study, at least for the man whose desire does not rush toward base pleasures.

<margin>23.</margin> Those who practice a simple and complete life are both delivered from dangers and have no need of guards. By conquering desire in all things, they easily find the path toward God.

<margin>24.</margin> For rational men, it is not necessary to attend to many conversations, but only to those which are beneficial and guided by the will of God. For in this way, men proceed again toward life and eternal light.

<column-break/>

<margin>25.</margin> Those seeking a virtuous and God-loving life must be rid of conceit and all empty and false reputation, and they must strive for a good correction of their life and mindset. For the God-loving and unchanging mind is an ascent and a path toward God.

<margin>26.</margin> There is no benefit in learning words if the soul lacks the conduct that is well-pleasing and acceptable to God. The cause of all evils is error, deceit, and ignorance of God.

<margin>27.</margin> The study of the most beautiful life and the care of the soul produces good and God-loving men. For he who seeks God finds Him, by conquering desire in all things and not ceasing from prayer. Such a man does not fear demons.

<margin>28.</margin> Those who are deceived by worldly hopes and who know what must be done for the most beautiful life only as far as words go, suffer something similar to those who possess medicines and medical instruments but neither know how to use them nor care to do so. Therefore, regarding the sins committed by us, let us never blame our birth <note>original: "γένεσιν" (genesin); here referring to astrological fate or "the stars."</note> or anyone else, but only ourselves; for if the soul itself chooses to be lazy, it cannot be unconquerable.

<margin>29.</margin> To the one who does not know how to distinguish what is good and what kind of thing is evil, it is not permitted to judge the good and the evil. For a man who knows God is good; but if he is not good, he knows nothing, nor will he ever be known. For the way to the knowledge of God is goodness itself.

<margin>30.</margin> Good and God-loving men rebuke people for evil to their faces when they are present, but they do not slander them when they are absent; nor do they permit those who attempt to speak such things.

<margin>31.</margin> In conversations, let all harshness be absent; for modesty and self-control are able to adorn rational men more than virgins. For the God-loving mind is a light shining around the soul, just as the sun is for the body.

<margin>32.</margin> For each of the passions of the soul that befall you, remember that for those who think rightly and wish to establish their own affairs in necessity and safety, the perishable possession of riches is not considered pleasant, but rather right and true opinions. These are what make them happy...

<summary>This page defines true freedom as moral purity rather than social status and asserts the soul's autonomy over earthly rulers. It emphasizes that virtue must be demonstrated through deeds and that the knowledge of God is inseparable from being a good person.</summary>
<keywords>Freedom, Virtue, Civil Disobedience, God-loving Mind, Self-governance, Discernment, Conduct</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Exhortations on the Character of Men" attributed to St. Anthony the Great. Following the previous page's discussion on the limits of worldly authority over the soul, this section (chapters 33–42) focuses on the internal discipline of the "rational man," the fleeting nature of wealth, and the necessity of persistent practice in virtue.</meta>

->### EXHORTATIONS ON THE CHARACTER OF MEN AND GOOD CONDUCT<-

...wealth is both plundered and seized by those more powerful; but the virtue of the soul is the only possession that is both secure and inviolable, saving those who possess it even after death. For those who think in this way are not swept away by the illusions of wealth and other pleasures.

<margin>33.</margin>
It is not fitting for the unstable and uneducated to test men of renown; a man of renown <note>original: "ἐλλόγιμος" (ellogimos); literally "accounted" or "eminent," here referring to one whose life is illuminated by divine reason.</note> is he who is pleasing to God, who remains silent most of the time, or speaks only a few, necessary things that are pleasing to God.

<margin>34.</margin>
Those who pursue a virtuous and God-loving way of life <term>conduct: "πολιτεία" (politeia); one's manner of living or spiritual citizenship</term> take care for the virtues of the soul as their own personal possession and as an eternal delight. They enjoy temporal things as much as possible, and as God gives and wills, making use of them with all joy and thanksgiving, even if they happen to be quite modest. For eating sumptuously nourishes the material bodies, but the knowledge of God, self-control, goodness, beneficence, piety, and gentleness deify the soul.

<margin>35.</margin>
As many of those in power who compel others to commit absurd and soul-damaging deeds do not hold mastery over the soul, which was created with its own free will. They may bind the body, but not the choice <note>original: "προαίρεσιν" (proairesin); the faculty of moral choice or intention</note>, of which the rational man remains master because of God who created him—who is stronger than every authority, necessity, and every power.

<margin>36.</margin>
Let those who consider the loss of money, children, servants, or any other possession to be a "misfortune" know first that one must be content with what is given by God. And when it is necessary to give them back, do so readily and gratefully, not being troubled by their deprivation—or rather, their return. For having used things that were not their own, they have simply given them back again.

<margin>37.</margin>
It is the work of a good man not to sell his free judgment for the sake of receiving money, even if what is offered happens to be a great deal. For the affairs of this life are like a dream, and wealth possesses illusions that are uncertain and short-lived.

<margin>38.</margin>
Those who are truly human should strive to live in a God-loving and virtuous way so that their virtuous life shines out among other men; just as the purple trim applied

<column-break/>

to white garments serves to decorate them, making them shine and be easily recognized—in this way, they take care for the virtues of the soul with greater security.

<margin>39.</margin>
Wise men must examine their own strength and the preparation of the soul’s virtue within them, and so prepare themselves and stand against the passions they encounter, according to the inherent strength granted to them by nature from God. For against beauty and every soul-damaging desire, there is self-control; against toils and want, there is endurance; against insult and anger, there is forbearance <term>forbearance: "ἀνεξικακία" (anexikakia); the quality of being patient under injury or provocation</term>; and other things similar to these.

<margin>40.</margin>
It is impossible for a man to become good and wise suddenly; it happens through laborious study, conduct, experience, time, practice, and the desire for good work. The good and God-loving man, who knows God in truth, never stops doing everything that pleases God without begrudging. Such men, however, are rarely found.

<margin>41.</margin>
It is not right for those less naturally gifted to despair of themselves and neglect a God-loving and virtuous life, or to despise it as something unreachable and incomprehensible to them. Instead, they should practice according to their strength and take care of themselves. For even if they cannot reach the summit of virtue and salvation, through practice and desire they either become better or at least do not become worse—which is no small benefit to the soul.

<margin>42. <br/> ✛</margin>
Man, according to his rational nature <note>original: "λογικόν" (logikon); referring to the faculty of reason that links humans to the Divine Word/Logos</note>, is joined to that ineffable and divine power; but according to his bodily nature, he has a kinship with the animals. A few men—those who are "perfect" and truly rational—strive to have their mind and kinship directed toward God the Savior, and they demonstrate this through their works and virtuous conduct. But the majority of men, being foolish in soul, have abandoned that divine and immortal adoption and have leaned toward the dead, unfortunate, and short-lived kinship of the body. Thinking of the things of the flesh like irrational animals, and being inflamed by pleasures, they separate themselves from God and...

<summary>This page discusses the invulnerability of the soul's virtue compared to worldly wealth and emphasizes that the rational man’s moral choice cannot be coerced by external authorities. It further explains that spiritual progress requires persistent practice and that humans must choose between their divine kinship through reason or their animal kinship through the flesh.</summary>

### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, ANTHONY THE GREAT

...drag the soul down from the heavens into the abyss, away from its own [divine] wills.

<margin>43.</margin> The rational man <note>original: "λογικὸς ἀνὴρ" (logikos anēr); in this context, it refers to a person whose life is guided by the *Logos* or Divine Reason, rather than mere logic.</note>, keeping in mind his participation and union with the Divine, will never love anything earthly or lowly; instead, he keeps his mind fixed on heavenly and eternal things. He knows that the will of God is the salvation of man, being the cause of all that is good and the source of eternal blessings for humanity.

<margin>44. +</margin> When you find someone who is argumentative and fights against the truth and what is evident, stop the argument and give way to such a person, for his intellect has become petrified <note>original: "ἀπολιθωθέντι" (apolithōthenti); literally "turned to stone," meaning his mind is hardened and unreachable.</note>. For just as the poorest water makes even the finest wines useless, in the same way, bad company corrupts those who are virtuous in both life and mind.

<margin>45.</margin> If we use every effort and every means to avoid physical death, how much more ought we to strive to avoid the death of the soul? For to the one who wishes to be saved, there is no obstacle except for the soul’s own neglect and laziness.

<margin>46.</margin> Those who find it difficult to understand what is beneficial and what is rightly spoken are considered to be in a poor state of health. But as for those who understand the truth yet shamelessly argue against it, their power of reasoning has been killed; their character has become like that of a wild beast. They do not recognize God, nor has their soul been enlightened.

<margin>47.</margin> God brought forth the various kinds of animals for a variety of needs through His Word: some to be eaten, and others for service. But He created man to be a spectator of them and their works, and to be their grateful interpreter. Therefore, men should strive so that they do not die like irrational beasts, having seen nothing and having failed to understand God and His works. One must know that God is all-powerful; nothing stands in opposition to the One who is all-powerful. Rather, out of non-existence, He made and continues to make through His Word all that He wills for the salvation of men.

<margin>48.</margin> Things in heaven are immortal because of the goodness residing in them; but things on earth have become mortal because of the self-chosen <note>original: "αὐθαίρετον" (authaireton); emphasizing that evil is a choice, not a natural necessity.</note> wickedness within them, which comes upon the foolish through their own laziness and their ignorance of God.

<column-break/>

<margin>49.</margin> Death, when understood by men, is immortality; but when it is not understood by the unlearned, it is death. One should not fear this death, but rather the destruction of the soul, which is the ignorance of God. That is the truly terrifying thing for the soul.

<margin>50. +</margin> Wickedness <term>wickedness: "κακία" (kakia); in Greek philosophy and theology, this refers to moral vice or the corruption of one's nature</term> is a passion of matter; therefore, it is not possible for a body to exist without some form of wickedness. But the rational soul, realizing this, shakes off the weight of matter—which is wickedness—and rising up from such a weight, it knows the God of all. It watches over the body as if it were an enemy or a foe, refusing to be persuaded by it. In this way, the soul is crowned by God, having conquered the passions of wickedness and matter.

<margin>51. +</margin> When wickedness is recognized by the soul, it is hated like a most foul-smelling beast; but when it is not recognized, it is loved by the one who is ignorant of it. It holds him captive, making a slave of its own lover. This wretched and miserable person neither sees nor understands what is beneficial for him, but instead thinks he is being adorned by wickedness and rejoices in it.

<margin>52.</margin> The pure soul, being good, is enlightened and shone upon by God; then the mind thinks of good things and gives birth to God-loving words. But when the soul is muddied <note>original: "βορβορωθῇ" (borborōthē); a vivid term meaning to be submerged in filth or mire.</note> by wickedness, God turns away from it—or rather, the soul separates itself from God. Then evil demons enter into the reasoning and suggest unholy deeds to the soul: adulteries, murders, thefts, sacrileges, and the like, which are the works of demons.

<margin>53.</margin> Those who know God are filled with all good intentions and, desiring heavenly things, they despise the things of this life. Such people do not please the many, nor are they pleased by the many. As a result, they are not only hated but also mocked by the many who are foolish. They endure everything in the midst of poverty, knowing that what appears as "evil" to the many is "good" for them. For the one who understands heavenly things believes in God, knowing that all things are the creations of His will. But the one who does not understand never believes that the world is the work of God, or that it came into being for the sake of man’s salvation.

<margin>54.</margin> Those who are filled with wickedness and are drunk with ignorance do not know God.

<summary>This page contains a series of moral and spiritual exhortations focusing on the "rational man" who prioritizes the soul over material concerns. It discusses the origins of evil as a "passion of matter" and emphasizes that the true death to be feared is the ignorance of God.</summary>

### EXHORTATIONS ON THE CHARACTER OF MEN AND GOOD CONDUCT

...for they are not sober in soul. But God is perceived by the mind; and while He is not visible, He is most manifest through visible things, just as the soul is in the body. If it is impossible for a body to exist without a soul, so it is impossible for all visible things and everything that exists to consist without God.

Why was man created? So that, by contemplating the works of God, he might behold Him and glorify the One who created them for man's sake. The mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); the highest faculty of the soul, capable of direct spiritual perception of the Divine.</note> that is beloved by God is an invisible good, granted by God to those who are worthy through a virtuous life <note>original: "χρηστῆς πολιτείας" (chrēstēs politeias); refers to a way of living, a moral "citizenship," or daily conduct.</note>.

<margin>56.</margin> A free person is one who is not enslaved to pleasures, but through wisdom and self-control <note>original: "σωφροσύνης" (sōphrosynēs); often translated as temperance or "soundness of mind."</note> masters the body, and is content with great gratitude for what is given by God, even if it happens to be very modest. For if the God-loving mind and the soul are in harmony, they bring peace to the entire body, even against its will; for when the soul wills it, every bodily movement is extinguished.

<margin>57.</margin> Those who do not love what they currently possess for their existence, but reach for more, enslave themselves to the passions that disturb the soul and impose upon it thoughts and fantasies that these things are bad. Just as tunics that are too long for one's measure hinder those struggling in a race, in the same way, the desire for wealth beyond measure does not allow souls to strive or to be saved.

<margin>58.</margin> Whatever state a person is in against their will and without their desire is a prison and a punishment to them. Therefore, be content with your present circumstances, lest by bearing them ungratefully you punish yourself without realizing it. There is only one way to achieve this: the contempt for worldly things.

<margin>59.</margin> Just as we have the power of sight from God to recognize things seen—what is white and what is the color of black—so Reason has been gifted to us by God to distinguish what is beneficial for the soul. But desire, when torn away from reason, gives birth to pleasure and does not allow the soul to be saved or joined to God.

<margin>60.</margin> Sins are not the things done according to nature, but the evil things done according to choice. Eating is not a sin, but eating without gratitude, decorum, and self-restraint is a sin; for the body must be maintained in life without any evil intent. Neither is it a sin to look purely, but

<column-break/>

to look with envy, pride, and greed; and not to listen peacefully, but with anger; and not to bridle the tongue for gratitude and prayer, but for slander; and not to employ the hands for acts of mercy, but for murders and robberies. And thus each of the members sins, when it works evil instead of good by its own choice, contrary to the will of God.

<margin>61.</margin> If you doubt that each of your actions is watched by God, consider that you, being a human and dust, can think about all kinds of places at the same time; how much more so God, who sees all things as if they were a mustard seed—He who gives life to all and feeds all as He wills?

<margin>62.</margin> When you close the doors of your house and are alone, know that the angel assigned by God to every person is present with you—whom the Greeks call the "personal spirit" <note>original: "οἰκεῖον δαίμονα" (oikeion daimona); here used in the classical sense of a protective guardian spirit or "genius," rather than a "demon" in the modern sense.</note>. This angel is sleepless and cannot be deceived; he is always present with you, seeing everything, and is not hindered by the darkness. Along with him, God is also present in every place. For there is no place or any matter in which God is not, as He is greater than all and encompasses all in His hand.

<margin>63.</margin> If soldiers keep faith with Caesar because they are provided with food by him, how much more should we strive to thank God unceasingly with never-silent mouths, and to please the God who created all things for the sake of man?

<margin>64.</margin> Gratitude toward God and a virtuous life are the "fruit" of man, well-pleasing to God. But just as the fruits of the earth are not brought to perfection in a single hour but through time, rain, and care, in the same way, the fruits of men are made radiant through practice, study, time, endurance, self-restraint, and patience. And if because of these things you ever seem to be pious to some, do not trust yourself as long as you are in the body, and do not think that any of your works please God. For know that it is not easy for a human to keep themselves sinless until the end.

<margin>65.</margin> Nothing is more precious among men than Reason <note>original: "Λόγου" (Logou); this term implies both the spoken word and the divine faculty of rationality.</note>. So powerful is reason that through reason and...

...with thanksgiving we serve God; but by using useless or blasphemous speech, we condemn our own soul. It is the mark of a senseless person to blame his own birth or anyone else for the sins he commits, since he uses evil words or deeds by his own free will <note>original: "αὐτεξουσίως" (autexousiōs); the ability to act by one's own power or choice.</note>.

<margin>66.</margin>
If we strive to heal the passions of the body so as not to be laughed at by those we meet, we must much more necessarily strive to heal the passions <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē); in this context, "passions" refers to disordered emotions or spiritual illnesses like greed, anger, or lust.</note> of the soul. For we are to be judged face-to-face before God, so that we may not be found dishonored or laughable. Since we possess free will, if we desire not to fulfill our cravings for evil deeds, we are able to do so; it is within our power to live in a way that is pleasing to God. No one can ever force us to do something evil against our will. By struggling in this way, we shall be men worthy of God, living like angels in the heavens.

<margin>67.</margin>
If you wish, you are a slave to the passions; if you wish, you are free and will not bow down to them. For God made you with free will. The person who conquers the passions of the flesh is crowned with incorruptibility. If there were no passions, there would be no virtues, nor would there be the crowns granted by God to those among men who are worthy.

<margin>68.</margin>
Those who do not see what is for their own benefit, and who do not recognize what is good, have a blinded soul; their power of discernment has been crippled. Therefore, we should not pay attention to them, so that we do not inevitably fall into the same things ourselves through lack of foresight, like the blind.

<margin>69.</margin>
One must not be angry with those who sin, even if the deeds they commit are crimes worthy of punishment. Instead, we ought to turn those who stumble back to the right path for the sake of justice itself, and punish them if it happens to be necessary, either by our own hand or through others. But one must not be angry or filled with rage, because anger acts only according to passion and not according to judgment and justice. Likewise, one should not approve of those who show mercy when it is uncalled for. Evil people must be punished for the sake of what is good and just, and not because of one's own passion of anger.

<margin>70.</margin>
The only secure and unstealable possession is the soul's own; that is, a virtuous life pleasing to God, and the knowledge <note>original: "γνῶσις" (gnōsis); spiritual insight or experiential knowledge of God.</note> and practice of good deeds. For

<column-break/>

wealth is a blind guide and a foolish counselor; and the person who uses wealth badly and for luxury destroys his own senseless soul.

<margin>71.</margin>
Men ought either to possess nothing extra, or if they do have possessions, they should know for certain that all things in this life are by nature perishable, easily taken away, discarded, or broken; therefore, they should not be troubled by the things that happen to them.

<margin>72.</margin>
Understand that bodily pains are naturally inherent to the body, since it is perishable and material. Therefore, in the face of such sufferings, the educated soul <note>original: "πεπαιδευμένη ψυχή" (pepaideumenē psychē); a soul that has been trained or disciplined in virtue.</note> should put forward endurance and patience with gratitude, and not blame God for why He created the body.

<margin>73.</margin>
Those who compete in the Olympic Games are not crowned for the defeat of just one, or two, or three; rather, they are crowned only when they have defeated everyone who competed against them. In the same way, anyone who wishes to be crowned by God must train his soul in temperance <note>original: "σωφρονεῖν" (sōphronein); to be of sound mind, self-controlled, or moderate.</note>—not only regarding bodily matters, but also regarding profits, theft, envy, food, vanity, insults, death, and all such things.

<margin>74.</margin>
Let us not practice a good and God-loving way of life for the sake of human praise; instead, let us choose the virtuous life for the salvation of the soul. For death is seen daily before our eyes, and human affairs are uncertain.

<margin>75.</margin>
It is in our power to live temperately, but to become rich is not in our power. What then? Should we condemn our own soul for the sake of a short-lived fantasy of wealth, which we do not even have the power to acquire? Are we merely desiring wealth? Oh, how foolishly we run, not knowing that humility comes before all the virtues, just as gluttony and the desire for worldly things come before all the passions.

<margin>76.</margin>
The wise must remember unceasingly that by enduring small and short-lived labors in this life, we enjoy the greatest pleasure and eternal delight after death. Therefore, the person who wrestles with the passions and wishes to be crowned by God, if...

...should fall, let him not become faint-hearted or remain in his fall, despairing of himself. Instead, let him rise again and wrestle <note>The author uses the metaphor of an athletic contest (the "agon"), common in early Christian writing to describe the spiritual life as a struggle for a crown of victory.</note>, and strive to be crowned until his final breath, raising himself up from whatever fall may occur. For bodily labors are the weapons of the virtues and become the salvation of the soul.

<margin>76.</margin>
The circumstances of life cause men, even those worthy athletes, to be crowned by God. Therefore, one must mortify their limbs during life from all worldly things; for a dead man will never worry about any worldly matter.

<margin>78.</margin>
<margin>+</margin>
It is not right for the rational and struggling soul to be immediately trampled down or to shrink back in fear before the passions <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē); disordered impulses or spiritual illnesses.</note> that occur, lest it be mocked as cowardly. For when the soul is disturbed by worldly fantasies, it falls away from what is proper. Our spiritual virtues lead the way to eternal goods, while the self-chosen vices of men become the cause of punishments.

<margin>79.</margin>
A rational man is attacked by the rational senses within him through the passions of the soul. There are five senses of the body: sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch. Through these five senses, the wretched soul is taken captive, falling under its own four passions. These four passions of the soul are vainglory, joy, anger, and cowardice. When a man has acted as a good general through prudence and deliberation, and has mastered and conquered these passions, he is no longer attacked; instead, his soul is at peace, and he is crowned by God as a victor.
<margin>+</margin>

<margin>80.</margin>
Among those found in inns <note>original: "πανδοχείοις" (pandocheiois); a common metaphor in ancient philosophy and Christianity comparing human life to a temporary stay at a traveler's lodge.</note>, some receive beds, while others have no bed and sleep on the floor; nevertheless, they snore just as much as those sleeping on a bed. Having waited out the measure of the night, they all leave the beds of the inn behind in the morning and depart together, carrying only their own belongings. In the same way, all who enter into this life—both those who lived modestly and those who lived in glory and wealth—depart from life as if from an inn. They take nothing with them from the luxury and wealth of life, except only their own deeds, whether good or bad, performed by them during their life.

<column-break/>

<margin>81.</margin>
If you are in a position of superior authority, do not readily threaten anyone with death. Know that by nature you also are subject to death, and that the soul strips off the body like a final garment. Understanding this clearly, practice gentleness, and by doing good, give thanks to God at all times. For he who has no pity has no virtue in himself.

<margin>82.</margin>
To escape death is impossible and unattainable. Knowing this, men who are truly rational, trained in the virtues and in God-loving thought, accept death without groaning, fear, or mourning, considering its inevitability and the release it brings from the evils of this life.

<margin>83.</margin>
<margin>* i.e., discernment.</margin>
Those who have forgotten the honorable life that is pleasing to God, and who do not hold right and God-loving doctrines, should not be hated. Rather, they should be pitied as people who are "crippled" <gloss>*</gloss> in their discernment and blind in their heart and mind. For by accepting evil as good, they perish through ignorance; these thrice-wretched and senseless souls do not recognize God.

<margin>84.</margin>
<margin>+</margin>
Avoid speaking about piety and the right way of life to the masses. I do not say this out of envy, but because I believe you will appear ridiculous to the senseless; for "like rejoices in like." Such words have few listeners—perhaps very few indeed. It is better not to speak unless it is what God wills for the salvation of man.

<margin>85.</margin>
The soul suffers with the body, but the body does not suffer with the soul. For example, when the body is cut, the soul suffers with it; when the body is vigorous and healthy, the passions of the soul rejoice with it. But when the soul thinks, the body does not think along with it; it remains left to itself. For thinking is an experience of the soul, just as are ignorance, pride, unbelief, greed, hatred, envy, anger, indifference, vainglory, honor, discord, and the perception of the good. For such things are enacted through the soul.

<margin>86.</margin>
<margin>+</margin>
When thinking on the things of God, be pious: be free from envy, good, temperate, gentle, generous according to your power, sociable, not quarrelsome, and the like. For this is the soul's secure possession: to please God through...
