...of such things; and to judge no one, nor to say of anyone that "this person is evil" or "he has sinned." Instead, it is better for a person to seek out their own evils and to examine their own way of life <note>original: "πολιτείαν" (politeian); often refers to a monk's regulated way of life or "citizenship" in the kingdom of God.</note> by themselves, to see if it is pleasing to God. For what does it concern us if another is wicked?

<margin>87.</margin>
The person who is true to their nature strives to be pious. Now, a pious person is one who does not desire the things of others. To a human being, all created things are "other" <note>In this philosophical context, "other" refers to everything outside of the soul's true nature as an image of God.</note>. Therefore, such a person despises all things, being an image of God. A person becomes an image of God when they live rightly and in a way pleasing to God; otherwise, <margin>+</margin> it is impossible for this to happen unless the person withdraws from worldly affairs. He who possesses a God-loving mind knows every benefit to the soul and every act of devotion that comes from it. The God-loving man blames no one else for the sins he commits himself; and this is a sign of a soul that is being saved.

<margin>88.</margin>
As many as strive to hold onto temporary possessions by force, and who love the appetite for works of wickedness—ignoring death and the destruction of their own soul—these wretched people do not consider what is for their own benefit. They do not calculate what people suffer after death because of their wickedness.

<margin>89.</margin>
Wickedness is a passion of matter; but God is not the cause of wickedness. He has provided humans with knowledge, understanding, the ability to discern between good and evil, and free will. That which gives birth to the passions of wickedness is the negligence and laziness of men. <margin>+</margin> For God is entirely without blame. By the choice of their own will, the demons became evil, just as the majority of men do.

<margin>90.</margin>
The person who lives together with piety does not allow wickedness to slip into the soul. When wickedness is absent, the soul exists in safety and remains unharmed. Over such people, neither an unlucky demon nor fate has any power. For God delivers them from evils, and they live unharmed, guarded as God-like beings. And if anyone praises such a man, he laughs to himself at those who praise him; and if anyone blames him, he does not offer a defense to those who revile him, nor is he indignant at what is said about him.

<margin>91.</margin>
Evil follows nature, just as rust follows bronze and dirt follows the body.

<column-break/>

But the coppersmith did not make the rust, nor did the parents make the dirt. In the same way, God did not make wickedness. He gave both knowledge and discernment to man so that he might flee from evil, knowing that he is harmed and punished by it. Watch yourself carefully, then, so that if you see someone prospering in power and wealth, you do not call them "blessed," having been deceived by the fantasy of the demon. Instead, let death be immediately before your eyes, and you will never desire anything evil or worldly.

<margin>92.</margin>
Our God granted immortality to those in the heavens, but for those on earth, He created change. To the whole universe, He gifted life and movement—all for the sake of man. Therefore, do not let the worldly fantasy of the demon snatch you away, for he casts evil thoughts into the soul. But immediately, by reflecting on heavenly goods, say to yourself: "If I wish, it is within my power to conquer even this struggle of passion; but I will not conquer if I wish to satisfy my own desire." Practice this, for it is able to save your soul.

<margin>93.</margin>
Life is the union and connection of <margin>x</margin> the mind <note>original: "νοός" (noos); the highest faculty of the human person, often translated as "intellect" or the "eye of the heart" in Orthodox spirituality.</note>, the soul, and the body. Death is not the destruction of these things that were joined together, but the dissolution of their connection. For to God, all things are preserved even after their dissolution.

<margin>94.</margin>
The mind is not the soul, but a gift of God that saves the soul. The mind that is pleasing to God runs ahead and advises the soul to despise temporary, material, and corruptible things, and instead to fall in love with eternal, incorruptible, and immaterial goods. Thus, while a person walks in the body, they contemplate the things in the heavens and the things concerning God through the mind, perceiving and beholding all things. The God-loving mind is the benefactor and the salvation of the human soul.

<margin>95.</margin>
When the soul enters the body, it is immediately darkened by grief and pleasure, and it perishes <note>Here, "perishes" refers to a spiritual death or loss of clarity, rather than a total cessation of existence.</note>. Grief and pleasure are like the "humors" <note>The author uses the medical language of the time, comparing emotions to the bodily fluids (humors) that were believed to control health.</note> of the body. But the God-loving mind, acting in opposition, brings "grief" to the body and saves the soul, acting like a doctor who cuts or burns the flesh to heal the patient.

<margin>96.</margin>
As many souls as are not guided by reason and are not steered by the mind—so that it may choke, restrain, and govern their passions, namely grief and pleasure...

...ness; these souls perish like the irrational animals, for their <term>rational faculty</term> <note>original: "τοῦ λογικοῦ" (tou logikou); the part of the soul capable of reason and logic.</note> is dragged along by the passions, like a charioteer who has been overpowered by his horses.

<margin>88.</margin> The soul exists within the body, and within the soul is the Mind; and within the Mind is Reason. <margin>89.</margin> Because God is generous and good, He made man with <term>free will</term> <note>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion); the innate power of self-determination.</note>, providing him with the ability to please God if he so chooses. What pleases God is for there to be no wickedness in a person. If among men good works and the virtues of a holy and God-loving soul are praised, while shameful and wicked actions are condemned, how much more so is this true for God, who desires the salvation of mankind?

<margin>100.</margin> A person receives good things from God because He is good; indeed, for this reason, man was created by God. But a person draws evil things upon themselves, stemming from their own nature, the wickedness within them, their desires, and their lack of spiritual perception.

<margin>101.</margin> The irrational soul, although it is immortal and the master of the body, becomes a slave to the body through pleasures. It does not realize that the physical delight of the body is harmful to the soul. Lacking perception and acting foolishly, it focuses only on the body's comfort.

<margin>102.</margin> God is good. Man is wicked. There is no evil in heaven, and no true good upon the earth. However, the rational man chooses what is better and recognizes the God of all things. He gives thanks and hymns Him; even before death, he loathes the body and does not allow the wicked senses to fulfill their impulses, knowing their destructive power and their influence.

<margin>105.</margin> Reason is the servant of the Mind. For whatever the Mind wills, Reason interprets and expresses.

<margin>106.</margin> The Mind sees all things, even those in the heavens; nothing overshadows it except for sin. To the pure Mind, nothing is incomprehensible, just as to Reason, nothing is unutterable.

<margin>107.</margin> Because of the body, man is mortal; but because of the Mind and Reason, he is immortal. When you are silent, you perceive; having perceived, you speak. For in silence, the Mind gives birth to the Word. A thankful word offered to God is found to be the salvation of man.

<margin>108.</margin> He who speaks irrational things possesses no Mind, for he speaks without perceiving anything. Rather, consider what is profitable for you to do for the salvation of your soul.

<margin>109.</margin> Speech that possesses Mind and is soul-profiting is a gift from God. God is everywhere and in all things, for He is limitless.

...actions <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the effects of sloth on the soul.</note> of the protection of God, by the vice arising from sloth, is consumed in the matter of the body—just as copper is consumed by rust—and is found to be unsightly and useless for salvation.

<margin>150.</margin>
**God is good, impassible, and unchangeable.** <term>impassible</term> <note>original: "ἀπαθής" (apathes); meaning God is not subject to suffering or shifting emotions like humans are.</note> If someone considers it reasonable and true that God does not change, yet wonders how He rejoices in the good and turns away from the wicked, or how He is "angered" by those who sin yet becomes "merciful" when He is served, it must be said: God neither rejoices nor is He angered. For to rejoice or to be grieved are human passions. Nor is He "served" by gifts, for then He would be overcome by pleasure. It is not right to think the Divine fares well or poorly based on human affairs. Rather, <margin>+</margin> He is good and only bestows benefits, never harming, remaining always the same. But we, by remaining good through our likeness to Him, are joined to God; but by becoming evil through our unlikeness, we are separated from <margin>* perhaps: "through virtue"</margin> God. And by living in * virtue, we hold fast to God; but by becoming evil, we make Him our enemy—not because He is "angry" in an arbitrary way, but because our sins do not allow God to shine within us, instead linking us to punishing demons. If through prayers and good deeds we find a release from sins, we have not "served" or "changed" God; rather, through our actions and our turning back toward the Divine, we heal our own wickedness and once again enjoy God's goodness. Thus, to say that God "turns away" from the wicked is like saying the sun hides itself from those who have lost their sight.

<margin>151.</margin>
**The pious soul knows the God of all.** For piety is nothing else but doing the will of God, which is the knowledge of God: being without envy, self-controlled, gentle, generous according to one's power, communal, non-contentious, and doing all things that are pleasing to the will of God.

<margin>152.</margin>
**The knowledge of God and the fear of Him are the healing of the passions of matter.** <note>The "passions of matter" refers to the chaotic desires associated with the physical body.</note> For when ignorance of God dwells in the soul, the passions remain incurable and rot the soul; it is as if the soul is rotting from a chronic ulcer caused by vice. God is not the cause of this, for He has sent down science and knowledge to mankind.

<margin>155.</margin>
**The crown of incorruptibility, virtue, and the salvation of man is to bear misfortunes cheerfully and with gratitude.** To master anger, the tongue, the belly, and pleasures—this becomes the greatest help to the soul.

<margin>156.</margin>
**That which holds the World together is the Providence of God.** And there is no place destitute of this Providence. <term>Providence</term> <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia); God's purposeful care and governance of the universe.</note> Providence is the self-perfecting Word of God, the shaper of the matter that comes into the world, the creator and craftsman of all things that come to be. For it is not possible for matter to be organized without the discerning power of the Word, who is the image, the mind, the wisdom, and the providence of God.

<margin>164.</margin> A man knows God, and is known by God, if he strives to be inseparable from God at all times. A man becomes inseparable from God when he is good above all things and masters every pleasure; not because he lacks the means to provide them, but through his own will and self-control.

<margin>165.</margin> <margin>+</margin> Do good to the one who wrongs you, and you will have God as a friend. Do not slander your enemy to anyone. Practice love, sobriety, patience, self-control, and the like. For this is the knowledge of God: through humility and such things, the following of God. These works are not of the common sort, but belong to the <term>intellectual soul</term> <note>original: "νοητικῆς ψυχῆς" (noetikēs psychēs); referring to the highest part of the human soul capable of spiritual perception.</note>.

<margin>166.</margin> Because of those who impiously dare to say that plants and herbs have souls <note>A common philosophical debate in antiquity regarding the different levels of life.</note>, I have written this chapter for the simpler ones for their information. Plants have natural life, but they do not have a soul. Man is called a rational animal because he has a mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun)</note> and is capable of receiving knowledge. As for the other animals, those of the earth and the air, there is a voice in them because they have spirit and a soul. All things that grow and decrease are living things, because they live and grow, but they do not all have a soul. There are four differences among living things: Some are immortal and ensouled, such as the Angels. Others have mind, soul, and spirit, like humans. Others have spirit and soul, like the animals. And others have only life, like the plants. Life in plants exists without a soul, spirit, mind, or immortality; but all other things cannot exist without life. Every human soul is clearly always in motion, moving from one place to another.

<column-break/>

<margin>167.</margin> When you receive an imagination of some pleasure, guard yourself, lest you be immediately carried away by it; but delaying a little, remember death, and consider how it is better to be conscious within yourself of having conquered this deception of pleasure.

<margin>168.</margin> Just as passion exists in birth—for whatever is born into life is also corrupted—so also does evil exist within passion. Do not say, then, "God could not cut out evil." For those who say this speak senselessly and foolishly. It was not necessary for God to cut out matter. For these passions belong to matter. But God, for our benefit, cut out evil from men by granting them mind, science, knowledge, and discernment of the good; so that, knowing that we are harmed by evil, we might flee from it. But the foolish man follows after evil and prides himself in it, and as if caught in a net, he struggles while being coiled within it; never being able to look up and see and know God, who made all things for the salvation and <term>deification</term> <note>original: "ἀποθέωσιν" (apotheosin); the process of becoming like God through grace.</note> of man.

<margin>169.</margin> Mortal things envy themselves because they foreknow <unclear>death</unclear>. And immortality comes to the holy soul because it is good; but death happens to the foolish and wretched soul because it is evil.

<margin>170.</margin> When you turn to your own bed with <term>thanksgiving</term> <note>original: "εὐχαρίστως" (eucharistos); the root of the word 'Eucharist,' meaning gratitude.</note>, remembering the benefits and the great providence of God toward yourself, being filled with good thoughts, you shall be greatly gladdened. Then the sleep of your body becomes the sobriety of your soul, and the closing of your eyes becomes a true vision of God; and your silence, being pregnant with the good, gives with all your soul and strength a heartfelt glory to the God of all. For when evil is absent from a man, thanksgiving alone, more than any costly sacrifice, pleases God; to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
# OF ISAIAH THE SOLITARY

Our Holy Father Isaiah the Solitary lived in the year 370 AD, being a contemporary of Abba Macarius the Great. By meditating night and day on the divine Scriptures, and by drawing abundant streams of spiritual wisdom from the wells of salvation, he became the author of many beautiful discourses. These discourses contain various soul-profiting 
<column-break/>
subjects, so much so that an entire book was compiled from them. Having extracted this small work <note>original: "λογίδιον" (logidion); literally a "little word" or short treatise.</note> from those writings, we have presented it here for those who desire to guard their own <term>mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun); in Orthodox spirituality, this refers to the "eye of the heart" or the highest faculty of the soul that perceives God.</note>. It teaches, in a concise way, how one must repel the attacks of intrusive thoughts <note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismōn); these are not just simple thoughts, but the seeds of temptation or mental suggestions.</note>, how to keep the conscience blameless, how to practice secret meditation, and how to skillfully preserve the tripartite nature of the soul <note>The ancient view that the soul consists of three parts: the rational, the spirited (emotions/anger), and the appetitive (desires).</note> in all <term>tranquility</term> <note>original: "ἀταραξίᾳ" (ataraxia); a state of inner stillness and freedom from emotional disturbance.</note>.

### OF THE SAINT
# ISAIAH THE SOLITARY
## ON THE GUARDING OF THE MIND
### 27 Chapters.

<margin>1.</margin>
Anger is a natural property of the mind when directed against the passions. Without such anger, a person cannot achieve <term>purity</term> <note>original: "ἁγνεία" (hagneia); often specifically referring to chastity or a heart free from divided loyalties.</note>, unless he becomes angry at everything sown within him by the enemy. When Jacob <note>This quote is actually attributed to Job 30:1 in the Bible. The text identifies the speaker as Jacob, possibly following a specific patristic tradition or a scribal variation.</note> found them [the enemies/temptations], he rebuked them, saying: "You are dishonored and despised, lacking in every good thing, whom I did not think worthy to be with the dogs of my flocks." He who wishes to reach this natural state of anger must cut off all his own self-will, until he establishes himself in the natural state of the mind.

<margin>2.</margin>
If you are resisting enmity, and you 
<column-break/>
see it weaken and flee from you, do not let your heart rejoice; for the malice of the [evil] spirits is behind them. They prepare a war worse than the first, leaving it behind the city and ordering it not to move. If you resist them by standing against them, they flee from your presence in apparent weakness. But if your heart is exalted because you chased them, and you abandon the "city," some will rise from behind while others stand in front, leaving the wretched soul in their midst with no further refuge. The "city" is prayer; "resistance" <note>original: "ἔνστασις" (enstasis); a firm standing or objection.</note> is the refutation <note>original: "ἀντιλογία" (antilogia); the practice of talking back to or contradicting tempting thoughts using scripture.</note> made in Christ Jesus; and the "foundation" is <term>spiritedness</term> <note>original: "θυμός" (thymos); often translated as 'anger,' here it refers to the soul's energy or righteous indignation used as a defense mechanism against demons.</note>.

# OF HOLY ISAIAH THE ANCHORITE

<margin>3.</margin>
Let us stand, therefore, beloved, in the fear of God, guarding and keeping the practical application of the virtues. Let us not give any offense to our conscience, but let us pay attention to ourselves in the fear of God, until the conscience itself sets itself free along with us, so that a union may be formed between us and it. Thereafter, it shall become our guardian, showing us each thing that we must cut away. But if we do not obey it, it will depart from us and abandon us, and we will fall into the hands of our enemies, who will never let us go again. This is just as our Master taught us, saying: *Be reconciled with your adversary while you are on the way with him*, and so forth <note>A reference to Matthew 5:25. Isaiah interprets the "adversary" in the legal metaphor not as the devil, but as the conscience.</note>. They say that the conscience is the "adversary" because it opposes a person who wishes to follow the will of their flesh. And if a person does not listen to it, the conscience delivers them over to their enemies.

<margin>4.</margin>
If God sees that the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); the highest faculty of the soul, often called the "eye of the heart."</note> has submitted to Him with all its strength, and has no other help but Him alone, He strengthens it, saying: *Fear not, my servant Jacob, O little Israel* <note>Isaiah 41:14</note>. And again: *Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by my name; you are mine. When you pass through the waters, I am with you; and the rivers shall not overwhelm you. And if you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who saves you* <note>Isaiah 43:1-3</note>.

<margin>5.</margin>
Therefore, if the mind hears this assurance, it takes courage against its enemies, saying: *Who is he that contends with me? Let him stand against me. And who is he that judges me? Let him draw near to me. Behold, the Lord is my helper; who shall harm me? Behold, all of you shall grow old like a garment, and be consumed by moths* <note>Isaiah 50:8-9</note>.

<margin>6.</margin>
If your heart has naturally come to hate sin, it has conquered; for it has distanced itself from those things that give birth to sin. Keep the thought of judgment <note>original: "κόλασιν" (kolasin); refers to the trial or punishment in the afterlife.</note> before you, and know that your Helper remains beside you. Do not grieve Him in anything, but weep before Him, saying: "It is Your mercy, O Lord, that redeems me. For it is impossible for me to escape the hands of the enemies without Your help." By paying attention to your heart, He Himself will preserve you from every evil.

<margin>7.</margin>
The monk ought to shut all the

<column-break/>

gates of the soul—that is, the senses—to keep from falling because of them. When the mind sees that it is not being dominated by anything, it prepares itself for immortality, gathering its senses together and making them into one body.

<margin>8.</margin>
If the mind is set free from every hope in the visible world, this is the sign that sin has died within you.

<margin>9.</margin>
If the mind is set free, the "middle wall" <note>original: "μεσότης" (mesotēs); a reference to the barrier of passions or worldly attachment that separates the human soul from God.</note> that stands between itself and God is removed.

<margin>10.</margin>
If the mind is set free from all its enemies and observes the <term>Sabbath</term> <note>In this ascetic context, "keeping the Sabbath" refers to the soul resting from the "work" of the passions and worldly distractions.</note>, it exists in another, new age, contemplating things that are new and incorruptible. For "where the carcass is, there also will the eagles be gathered" <note>Matthew 24:28; here used metaphorically to describe the soul's focus on Christ.</note>.

<margin>11.</margin>
The demons withdraw themselves in craftiness for a time, hoping that the person will relax their heart, thinking they have found rest. Then, they suddenly leap upon the wretched soul and seize it like a little bird. If they prove stronger than the soul, they humble it mercilessly in every kind of sin—sins worse than those the person originally prayed to be forgiven for. Let us stand, therefore, in the fear of God and guard the heart, performing our practical duties and preserving the virtues, which block the malice of our enemies.

<margin>12.</margin>
Our teacher Jesus Christ, knowing their great ruthlessness and having mercy on the human race, commanded us with intensity of heart, saying: *Be ready at every hour, for you do not know at what hour the thief is coming; let him not come and find you sleeping* <note>Matthew 24:42-44</note>. And again: *Take heed, lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that hour come upon you suddenly* <note>Luke 21:34</note>. Stand, therefore, over your heart, watching your senses; and if the remembrance of God dwells in peace with you, you will catch the "thieves" as they try to sneak in. For the one who is strict with their thoughts recognizes those who are about to enter and defile them. These thoughts disturb the mind so that it becomes distracted and idle; but those who recognize their malice remain undisturbed, praying to the Lord.

<margin>13.</margin>
Unless a person hates all the business of this world, they cannot...

### ON THE GUARDING OF THE MIND

...to serve God. What then is the service of God? It is nothing else than that we should have nothing alien in our <term>mind</term> <note>original: "νῷ" (nō); the intellect or "eye of the heart," which Isaiah considers the faculty meant for communion with God.</note> when we pray to Him: no pleasure when we bless Him, no malice when we sing to Him, no hatred when we prefer Him, and no evil jealousy to hinder us when we meditate upon Him and remember Him. For all these dark things are walls surrounding the wretched soul; it cannot purely serve God while it contains these things within itself. They hinder the soul in the air <note>A reference to the "toll-houses" or demonic forces believed to inhabit the air and obstruct the soul's ascent.</note> and do not allow it to meet God, to bless Him in secret, or to be joined to Him in sweetness of heart so that it may be enlightened by Him. Because of this, the mind is always darkened and cannot progress toward God, because it does not take care to cut these things away with knowledge.

<margin>14.</margin> When the mind saves the senses of the soul from the desires of the flesh and brings them across into <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "ἀπαθείᾳ" (apatheia); not a state of being "unfeeling," but a state of being free from the compulsion of the passions.</note>, and separates the soul from the desires of the flesh—then if God sees the shamelessness of the passions, that they rush upon the soul to seize the senses in sin, and the mind cries out to God in secret without ceasing, He sends His help and releases everything at once.

<margin>15.</margin> I entreat you, as long as you are in the body, do not let your heart go free. For just as a farmer cannot trust any of his crops growing in his field—for he does not know what will happen to them until they are locked up in his storehouses—so a person cannot let their heart go free as long as they have breath in their nostrils. And just as a person does not know what passion will meet them until their last breath, so it is not possible for a person to let their heart go free as long as they have breath; but one must always cry out to God for help and His mercy.

<margin>16.</margin> He who does not find help in time of war cannot believe even in peace.

<margin>17.</margin> When, therefore, someone separates themselves from the "left side" <note>An ascetic term referring to sinful impulses, distractions, or demonic influence.</note> and knows accurately all the sins they have committed against God—since one does not see sins unless they are separated from them by a "separation of bitterness"—those who have reached this measure have found weeping, prayer, and shame before

<column-break/>

God, remembering the evil friendships of the passions. Let us struggle, therefore, brothers, according to our strength, and God will work with us according to the multitude of His mercy. And if we have not guarded our hearts as our fathers did, at least let us do what is in our power to keep our bodies sinless as God requires, and let us believe that in the time of the famine that has overtaken us, He will also show mercy to us along with His saints.

<margin>18.</margin> He who has given his heart to seek God in piety, in truth, cannot have the thought that he has pleased God. For as long as his conscience reproves him concerning things that are against nature, he is a stranger to freedom. For as long as there is one who reproves, there is also an accuser; and where there is an accusation, there is no freedom. If, therefore, while praying, you see yourself as having nothing at all of malice accusing you, then you are truly free and have entered into His holy rest according to His will. If you see that the good fruit has grown strong and the weeds of the enemy no longer choke it—and that the enemies have not merely retreated of their own accord through craftiness, pretending no longer to war with your senses—and if the cloud has cast a shadow over the <term>tabernacle</term> <note>Isaiah uses the "tabernacle" (the portable sanctuary of the Israelites) as a metaphor for the human person inhabited by the Spirit.</note>, and the sun has not scorched you by day nor the moon by night; if there is found in you all the preparation of the tabernacle, to set it up and guard it according to the will of God—then a victory has been won for you through God. And then, finally, He Himself will overshadow the tabernacle, because it is His. But as long as there is war, a person is under fear and trembling: to win today or be defeated; to be defeated tomorrow or to win. For the struggle grips the heart. But <term>dispassion</term> is beyond war. For it has received the prize and is no longer anxious about the division of the three parts, because they have reached a state of peace with one another through God. These three are: soul, body, and spirit. When, therefore, these three become one through the energy of the Holy Spirit, they can no longer be separated. Do not, then, consider yourself as having died to sin as long as you are forced by your enemies, whether awake or asleep. For as long as a wretched person is in the arena, they have no grounds for confidence.

<margin>19.</margin> If the mind grows strong and prepares...

### OF SAINT ISAIAH THE ANACHORITE <note>Isaiah the Anachorite, or the Solitary, was a 5th-century ascetic who lived in the Egyptian desert and later near Gaza. His writings are foundational to the "Philokalia," a collection of texts on prayer and holiness.</note>

<warning>Small ink stain in column 2 partially obscuring text in the paragraph marked 26.</warning>

...himself to follow the love that extinguishes all the passions of the body, and will not allow any of those things which are contrary to nature to dominate the heart through its own power; the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); the faculty of the soul that perceives God.</note> resists what is contrary to nature until it separates the soul from those things and restores it to what is according to nature.

<margin>20.</margin> Examine yourself, brother, every day, observing your heart to see what passions are within it in the presence of God; and cast them out of your heart, so that a harsh sentence does not come upon you.

<margin>21.</margin> Pay attention, then, to your heart, brother, and be vigilant against your enemies; for they are cunning in their wickedness. Be persuaded in your heart of this word: that it is impossible for a person to do good while they are doing evil. For this reason, our Savior taught us to be watchful, saying: "For narrow is the gate and difficult is the way that leads to life, and there are few who find it."

<margin>22.</margin> Take heed to yourself, then, lest anything of destruction should separate you from the love of God, and keep a firm hold on your heart. Do not grow despondent, saying: "How shall I guard it, being a sinful man?" For when a person leaves their sins and turns back to God, their repentance gives them a new birth and makes them entirely new.

<margin>23.</margin> Everywhere Holy Scripture, both Old and New, speaks about the guarding of the heart. First, David the Psalmist cries out: "O sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?" <note>Psalm 4:2</note> and again: "Their heart is vain." Concerning those who calculate vanities, he said: "For he said in his heart, I shall not be shaken" <note>Psalm 10:6</note> and again: "For he said in his heart, God has forgotten." There are many other such passages. For the monk ought to understand the purpose of the Scripture—to whom it speaks and when it speaks—and he must continually maintain the struggle of his <term>ascetic practice</term> <note>original: "ἀσκήσεως" (askēseōs); the disciplined training of the monk.</note>. He must watch for the assaults of the adversary, and like a pilot, he must steer through the waves, being guided by grace, not turning aside from the path. Attending to himself alone, he should converse with God in stillness, with wordless thought and a mind free from curiosity.

<margin>24.</margin> For the season demands prayer from us, just as a pilot requires winds, and as storms and tempests require the spirits. We are capable of receiving the assaults of <term>thoughts</term> <note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismōn); often refers to the initial seeds of temptation or mental images that lead to sin.</note>, as well as virtue and vice; and it is said that pious and God-loving reason is the master of the passions.

<column-break/>

It is necessary for us <term>hesychasts</term> <note>original: "ἡσυχασταῖς" (hēsychastais); those who practice "hesychia" or inner stillness/silence, often as hermits.</note> to distinguish and separate virtues and vices with prudence and sobriety. We must know which virtue to practice when brothers and fathers are present, and which to work upon when we are alone; which is the first virtue, and which the second and third. We must know which passion belongs to the soul and which to the body; which virtue is of the soul and which of the body. We must know from which virtue pride strikes the mind, from which vainglory arises, from which anger approaches, and from which gluttony comes. For we ought to purify our thoughts and "every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God."

<margin>25.</margin> The first virtue is <term>freedom from care</term> <note>original: "ἀμεριμνία" (amerimnia); a state of being unburdened by worldly anxieties or attachments.</note>, which is to say, a death toward every person and every thing. From this, desire for God is born. This in turn gives birth to "natural anger," which resists everything attempted by the enemy. Then the fear of God finds a place to dwell in the person, and through that fear, love is made manifest.

<margin>26.</margin> One must overthrow the assault of a thought in the heart through pious rebuttal at the time of prayer, lest we be found speaking to God with our lips while our hearts are calculating unseemly things. For God does not accept a murky or contemptuous prayer from a hesychast. Everywhere Scripture testifies that we must guard the senses of the soul. For if the will of the monk is subject to the law of God, and if his mind governs his subjects according to that law—by "subjects" I mean all the movements of the soul, especially anger and desire—then we have worked virtue and fulfilled righteousness. We direct desire toward God and His will, and anger against the devil and sin. What then is the thing we seek? It is <term>inner meditation</term> <note>original: "κρυπτὴ μελέτη" (kryptē meletē); the "secret" or "hidden" practice of repeating scripture or prayers in the heart.</note>.

<margin>27.</margin> If filth is sown in your heart while you are sitting in your cell, take heed: resist the wickedness so that it does not master you. Strive to remember God, for He is watching you; and the things you are reasoning in your heart are laid bare before Him. Say then to your soul: "If you fear sinners like yourself seeing your sins, how much more should you fear God, who watches over all things?"

<summary>Saint Isaiah provides a guide for monks on "guarding the heart," emphasizing that the mind must actively resist unnatural passions to return to its natural state of communion with God. He outlines a hierarchy of virtues starting with "freedom from care" (amerimnia) and stresses that God sees even the secret thoughts of a solitary in their cell.</summary>

And from this counsel, the fear of God is revealed to your soul; and if you remain with it, you will remain unmoved by the passions; just as it is written: "Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall never be shaken."

## A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
# OF EVAGRIUS THE MONK

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' with floral patterns.</image-desc>Evagrius, that wise and learned man, flourished around the year 380. Having been promoted to the rank of Reader by <note>Saint Basil the Great (330–379 AD) was one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" and a primary architect of Eastern monasticism.</note> Basil the Great, he was later ordained a Deacon by Basil's brother, Gregory of Nyssa. He was educated in the sacred art of speech by <note>Also known as Gregory of Nazianzus, a celebrated orator and theologian.</note> Gregory the Theologian, under whom he served as Archdeacon while Gregory held the oversight of the Church in Constantinople,

<column-break/>

according to Nikephoros Kallistos, in Book 11, Chapter 42 <note>Nikephoros Kallistos Xanthopoulos was a 14th-century Byzantine historian; this reference helps date and verify the biographical claims.</note>. Later, after renouncing worldly affairs, he took up the monastic life. Being subtle in his understanding and extremely skilled at expressing what he perceived, he left behind many and varied writings. Among these are the present "Discourse to those Living in Stillness," and his "Chapters on the Discernment of Passions and Thoughts." Because these works are considered so necessary and beneficial, it was decided they should be included in this book.

# OF EVAGRIUS THE MONK
## A MONASTIC SKETCH
### TEACHING HOW ONE OUGHT TO PRACTICE ASCETICISM AND LIVE IN STILLNESS.

Become like an excellent merchant, testing everything for the sake of stillness; and hold fast to those things that are quiet and useful for this purpose. However, I tell you: love exile. ...[of worldly things] occurs, and creates in you a desire for the tables of those outside. Thinking thus, guard yourself in your giving and receiving. If you choose what is better, and if it is possible for you, cast your care upon another faithful man; so that being cheerful in this way, you will have good and joyful hopes. The way of stillness knows how to give you these useful exhortations.

But sometimes physical weakness occurs, and it may be necessary to eat a second, or a third, or even many times; if so, do not let your **reasoning** <note>original: "λογισμός" (logismos); in Evagrius's psychology, this refers to the mental impulses or "thoughts" that can lead to virtue or vice.</note> be grieved. It is necessary to pray in this way, especially

<column-break/>

because of our wicked enemies. For whenever they see us standing at prayer, they also diligently set themselves against us, suggesting to our minds those things that we ought not to be thinking about or considering at the time of prayer. They do this so that they might lead our mind away captive and make our petition and supplication from prayer idle, vain, and useless. For prayer, petition, and supplication truly become vain and useless when they are not carried out—as was said before—in fear and trembling, with sobriety and watchfulness.

Furthermore, if someone approaching a human king performs their petition with fear, trembling, and sobriety, how much more should one stand in the same way before God, the Master of all things, and Christ, the **King of Kings** and **Lord of Lords**, and likewise offer their supplication and petition? It is very much required. For even the entire intellectual multitude of the Angels and their choir, ministering in fear and glorifying in trembling, send up an unceasing hymn to Him, together with His Father who is without beginning, and the All-Holy and co-eternal Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

### CHAPTERS ON THE DISCERNMENT OF PASSIONS AND THOUGHTS

<margin>1.</margin> Of the demons that oppose the <term>active life</term> <note>original: "πρακτική" (praktike); the first stage of the spiritual life focused on purifying the soul from passions.</note>, those who are entrusted with the appetites of **gluttony** are the first to stand ready for battle, along with those who suggest **greed** to us, and those who call us toward **human glory** <note>Often referred to as "vainglory."</note>. All the others follow behind these and take over those who have been wounded by them. For it is not possible to fall into the hands of the spirit of sexual immorality unless one has first fallen to gluttony. And it is not possible for anger to be stirred up unless one is fighting for food, or money, or glory. And it is not possible to escape the demon of sorrow unless one has suffered the loss of all these things. Nor will anyone escape **pride**, the first

<column-break/>

offspring of the devil, unless they have banished greed, the root of all evils—if indeed *poverty humbles a man*, according to Solomon. <note>Reference to Proverbs 10:4 in the Septuagint version.</note> To put it briefly, it is not possible for a person to fall into the power of a demon unless they have first been wounded by those primary leaders.

For this reason, the devil also brought these three "thoughts" <note>original: "λογισμούς" (logismos).</note> to the Savior: first, urging that the stones become bread; second, promising the whole world if He would fall down and worship him; and third, saying that if He would listen, He would be glorified and suffer nothing from such a great fall. But our Lord, appearing superior to these, commanded the devil to go behind Him, teaching us through these...

### EVAGRIUS THE MONK, A MONASTIC OUTLINE

...as it is impossible to repel the devil without disregarding these three **thoughts**. <note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismoi); in Evagrian spirituality, these are not just random ideas but "tempting impulses" or "seed-thoughts" that lead to sin.</note>

<margin>2.</margin> All demonic thoughts introduce into the soul mental images of things perceived by the senses; the **mind** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); the highest part of the human soul, capable of direct communion with God.</note> is then shaped by these images and carries the forms of those things within itself. From the object itself, the mind can then recognize which demon is approaching. For example, if the face of someone who has harmed or insulted me appears in my mind, it reveals the thought of **resentment** <note>original: "μνησικακίας" (mnesikakia); literally "remembering-evil" or holding a grudge.</note> drawing near. Again, if there is a reminder of money or glory, the one who is troubling us will be clearly identified by the object. It is the same with other thoughts: you will find who is standing by and suggesting them based on the object presented.

I do not say that all memories of such things come from demons, for the mind itself is naturally inclined to bring up images of past events when moved by a person's own will. However, those memories which stir up **anger** or **desire** contrary to nature are demonic. Because of the disturbance of these powers, the mind commits adultery in its thinking and becomes combative; it is unable to receive the vision of God, who gave it its laws. For that divine radiance appears to the **ruling faculty** <term>hegemonikon: the governing or "command" center of the soul</term> during the time of prayer only when it is stripped of the mental images of worldly things.

<margin>3.</margin> A person cannot repel passionate memories unless they take care of their desire and anger. Desire is worn down through fasting, vigils, and sleeping on the ground; anger is tamed through patience, forbearance, forgetting wrongs, and acts of mercy. For almost all demonic thoughts, which cast the mind into ruin and destruction, are composed of these two **passions**. <note>original: "παθῶν" (pathon); disordered or "suffering" states of the soul.</note> It is impossible to overcome these passions unless one completely disregards food, money, and glory—and even one's own body, because of those who often attempt to strike it. 

It is absolutely necessary, then, to imitate those who are in danger at sea and must throw their belongings overboard because of the violence of the winds and the rising waves. But we must be very careful here: let us not throw our belongings overboard just to be seen by men. If we do, we have already received our reward 

<column-break/>

for ourselves. Then another shipwreck, even more difficult than the first, will take us—the spirit of the demon of **vainglory** <note>original: "κενοδοξίας" (kenodoxia); literally "empty glory" or seeking the approval of others.</note> blowing against us. This is why our Lord, in the Gospels, instructs the mind—the "helmsman"—saying: 

> Take care not to perform your acts of mercy before men to be seen by them; otherwise, you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. 

And again: 

> When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites; for they love to pray in the synagogues and on the street corners so that they may be seen by men. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward. 

And when you fast, do not be like the hypocrites, looking gloomy. 

> For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to be fasting to men. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward. 

We must pay attention here to the **Physician of Souls**: observe how he heals anger through mercy, cleanses the mind through prayer, and withers desire through fasting. From these is composed the "New Adam," who is being renewed according to the image of his Creator. In this state, because of **impassivity**, there is no male and female; and because of faith, there is no Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free; but Christ is all and in all.

### ON DREAMS

<margin>4.</margin> We must investigate how the demons shape and form our **ruling faculty** <term>hegemonikon</term> during the fantasies that occur in sleep. Such a thing seems to happen to the mind either through the eyes seeing, or the ears hearing, or some other sense, or from the memory. Memory shapes the ruling faculty by stirring up things that it previously experienced through the body. It seems to me, then, that the demons move the memory to shape the ruling faculty, since the physical organs are held inactive by sleep. 

How they move the memory, we must ask? Perhaps through the passions. This is clear because those who are pure and **impassive** <note>original: "ἀπαθεῖς" (apatheis); those who have reached a state of inner peace and freedom from the pull of disordered passions.</note> no longer suffer anything of this sort. There is also a "simple" movement of the memory caused by the holy powers, through which we meet with and feast with the saints. However, we must note that whatever the soul receives together with the body...

The previous page discussed how the mind is shaped by mental images (idols) of sensory objects and how these images can reveal which "demon" or tempting thought is attacking the monk. ### TEACHING HOW ONE MUST PRACTICE ASCETICISM, AND KEEP STILL
->5<-

...[i]dols, these are moved by the memory outside the body. This is clear from the fact that we often experience this even in our sleep while the body is at rest. For just as it is possible to remember water both when thirsty and when not thirsty, so it is possible to remember gold with **greed** <note>original: "πλεονεξίας" (pleonexias); literally 'wanting more,' the drive for acquisition.</note> and without greed. And so it is with other things. However, to find such differences in these **fantasies** <note>original: "φαντασιῶν" (phantasion); mental images or imaginations that occupy the mind.</note> is a sign of the demons' wicked craft. At the same time, this must also be known: the demons also use external things to create a fantasy; for example, the sound of the waves for those who are sailing.

<margin>5.</margin> Our **anger** <note>original: "θυμός" (thymos); the 'irascible' part of the soul. In this context, it is the energy used for both righteous indignation and sinful rage.</note> contributes greatly to the demons' goal when it is moved contrary to nature, and it becomes most useful for every one of their wicked schemes. Therefore, none of them refrain from disturbing it by night and by day. But when they see it bound by **gentleness**, they immediately release it under "justified" pretexts, so that, having become very sharp, it might serve their beast-like thoughts. For this reason, it is necessary not to provoke it for either just or unjust matters; do not give an "evil sword" to those who suggest these things—something I know many do, catching fire more than they should over small excuses. 

For tell me, why do you fall so quickly into a fight? If indeed you have looked down on food, money, and glory? Why do you feed the "dog," while claiming to possess nothing? <note>Evagrius compares the irascible part of the soul to a guard dog; if the dog is barking at others, it implies the monk is still "guarding" some internal attachment or possession.</note> If he barks and attacks people, it is obvious he possesses something and wishes to guard it. But I am convinced that such a person is far from **pure prayer**, knowing that anger is the destroyer of such prayer. 

In addition to this, I marvel that you have forgotten the saints: David crying out, *Cease from wrath, and forsake anger*; and Ecclesiastes commanding, *Remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh*; and the **Apostle** <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Timothy 2:8.</note> ordering us to lift up holy hands in every time and place, *without anger and doubting*. And why do we not learn from the mystical and ancient custom of men, which chases dogs out of the house at the time of prayer? This hints at the fact that anger must not be present with those

<column-break/>

praying. And *their wine is the anger of dragons*; but the **Nazirites** <note>A group in the Hebrew Bible consecrated to God who abstained from wine and cutting their hair.</note> abstained from wine. 

Regarding the need not to be anxious about clothing or food, I think it is superfluous to write, since the **Savior** himself forbids it in the Gospels: *Do not be anxious for your soul*, he says, *what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or what you shall put on*. For this belongs strictly to the pagans and the unbelievers who reject the providence of the Master and deny the Creator. But for Christians, such a thing is entirely alien, once they have believed that even the *two sparrows sold for a penny* are under the care of the holy angels. 

Nevertheless, this is also a habit of the demons: after impure thoughts, they also throw in thoughts of **anxiety**; so that "Jesus might slip away" <note>An allusion to John 5:13; the presence of Christ is lost when the mind is crowded with worldly worries.</note> because there is a crowd of thoughts in the place of the mind, and the "word" might become unfruitful, being choked by the thoughts of anxiety. Therefore, putting these aside, let us cast our care upon the Lord, being content with what is present; and by practicing a poor life and dress, let us daily strip away the "fathers of **vainglory**." 

If anyone thinks it is shameful to be in poor dress, let him look at Saint Paul, in cold and nakedness, who looked forward to the crown of righteousness. But since the Apostle called this world a "theater" and a "stadium," let us see if it is possible for one who has clothed himself in thoughts of anxiety to run for the **prize of the upward call of God**, or to wrestle against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age. I, for my part, do not know how it could be, being taught by physical experience itself. For such a person will clearly be tripped up by his tunic and dragged down, just as the mind is by thoughts of anxiety; if indeed the word is true which says that the mind stays close to its own treasure: *For where your treasure is*, it says, *there your heart will be also*.

<margin>6.</margin> Of **thoughts** <note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismoi); specifically the intrusive, tempting thoughts that lead to passions.</note>, some cut and some are cut. Evil thoughts cut the good ones, and in turn, evil thoughts are cut by good ones. Therefore, the **Holy Spirit** pays attention to the first thought that is placed, and judges or accepts us according to it. What I mean is this: I have a certain phil[anthropy/love]...

<summary>This page analyzes how anger and anxiety act as demonic distractions that prevent pure prayer. Evagrius uses the metaphors of a guard dog and an athlete's tunic to illustrate how emotional disturbances and worldly worries trip up the mind in its spiritual journey.</summary>

<keywords>anger, thymos, anxiety, merimna, prayer, demons, logismoi, asceticism, St. Paul, gentleness, poverty, mental images</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Evagrius’s psychological analysis of the monk’s inner life. The previous page discussed how the "irascible" part of the soul (anger) is manipulated by demons. Here, he examines how the source and intent of a "thought" (logismos) can be distinguished and how to handle the "wandering" mind that drifts during prayer or meditation.</meta>

# EVAGRIUS THE MONK, A MONASTIC OUTLINE

...a **thought** <note>original: "λογισμὸν" (logismon); for Evagrius, a 'logismos' is more than just a passing idea—it is a suggestive impulse or mental image that can lead toward or away from God.</note> of hospitality, and indeed I have it for the sake of the Lord. But this thought, when the tempter approaches, is "cut" or divided: the tempter suggests practicing hospitality for the sake of **vainglory**. And again, I have a thought of hospitality, but now it is to appear good to other people. Yet this thought too is "cut" when a better thought arrives—one that directs our virtue toward the Lord and compels us not to do these things for the sake of human approval.

<margin>7.</margin>
We have learned through much observation that there is a difference between **angelic thoughts**, **human thoughts**, and **thoughts from demons**. First, angelic thoughts investigate the very natures of things and search out their spiritual "reasons" <note>original: "λόγους" (logous); the underlying divine principles or purposes for which a thing was created.</note>. For example: For what purpose was gold created? Why is it scattered like sand in the lower parts of the earth and found only with great labor and toil? How is it that, once found, it is washed with water and handed over to fire, and thus placed into the hands of craftsmen? These craftsmen then make the lampstand of the Tabernacle, the censer, the ladles, and the bowls—from which the Babylonian King no longer drinks, thanks to the grace of our Savior. Instead, **Cleopas** <note>A reference to the disciple on the Road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35) whose heart "burned" when Jesus explained the scriptures.</note> carries a heart set on fire by these mysteries. 

A demonic thought, however, neither knows nor understands these things. It shamelessly suggests only the acquisition of physical gold, and predicts the luxury and fame that will come from it. 

Finally, the human thought neither seeks to acquire the gold nor investigates what it symbolizes; it merely brings into the mind the bare form of gold, separated from both passion and greed. This same principle applies to all other things, as one practices this rule in a **mystical** <note>original: "μυστικῶς" (mystikos); here meaning 'hidden' or 'inner' spiritual exercise.</note> way.

<margin>8.</margin>
There is a demon called the "Wandering One," who appears to the brothers especially toward dawn. He leads the **mind** <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun); the 'intellect' or 'eye of the soul,' which should ideally be focused on God.</note> from city to city, from village to village, and from house to house—pretending these are simple social visits. The mind then spends a long time conversing with acquaintances and, in doing so, corrupts its own inner state through these encounters. Slowly, the person becomes distant from the knowledge of God and forgets their virtue and their monastic vows. Therefore, it is necessary for

<column-break/>

the **hermit** <note>original: "ἀναχωροῦντα" (anachorounta); one who has withdrawn from the world to practice 'hesychia' or stillness.</note> to watch this demon closely: where he comes from and where he ends up. For he does not make that long circuit around the world by chance or at random; he does it because he wants to ruin the hermit's inner stillness. He wants the mind to be "inflamed" by these thoughts and "intoxicated" by so many imaginary conversations, so that it may immediately fall into the hands of the demon of **sexual immorality**, or **anger**, or **sorrow**—the very demons that most defile the brilliance of the soul's state. 

But if we intend to clearly understand his cunning, let us not speak to him quickly, nor reveal what is happening—how he constructs these encounters in our imagination and how he gradually drives the mind toward "death"—for if he sees he is being watched, he will flee from us. If he flees, we will learn nothing about the things we were eager to study. Instead, for one or two days, let us allow him to finish his "drama" so that, having learned his scheme accurately, we can expose him with a word and put him to flight. 

Since the mind is often clouded during the time of temptation and cannot see exactly what is happening, do this after the demon has departed: sit down and remember in your own heart what happened to you—where you started, where you traveled, in what place you were seized by the spirit of immorality, or sorrow, or anger, and how those things happened in sequence. Study these things and commit them to memory, so that you have the evidence to expose him when he approaches again. Point out the "hidden place" where he was lurking, and you will not follow him anymore. 

In fact, if you wish to drive him to a frenzy, expose him the moment he arrives: name the first "place" you entered in your mind, then the second, then the third. He will be deeply distressed, unable to bear the shame. The proof that you have struck him effectively is that the thought will flee from you; it is impossible for it to remain when it is openly exposed. Once this demon is defeated, a heavy sleep follows, along with a numbness and great coldness of the eyelids, endless yawning, and heavy shoulders. All of these the **Holy Spirit** dissolves through intense prayer.

<margin>9.</margin>
Hatred against the demons is very [useful] to us...

<summary>Evagrius distinguishes between angelic, human, and demonic thoughts using the metaphor of gold, and provides a psychological method for monks to observe and defeat the "Wandering Demon" of distraction.</summary>
<keywords>logismoi, discernment of spirits, wandering mind, distraction, gold metaphor, psychological observation, spiritual warfare, mindfulness, Evagrius Ponticus</keywords>

-># TEACHING HOW TO PRACTICE ASCETICISM AND STILLNESS<-

...contributes to salvation and is suitable for the work of virtue. Yet we are not strong enough to nurture this within ourselves like a good **offspring**; for pleasure-loving spirits <note>original: "πνευμάτων" (pneumatōn); in this context, refers to demonic impulses or "spirits" of temptation.</note> tear it apart, calling the soul back again to its old friendships and habits. But this "friendship"—or rather, this "hard-to-heal gangrene"—is treated by the **Physician of souls** <note>A common title for Christ in early Christian writing.</note> through a period of "abandonment." For He allows us to suffer something fearful by night and by day, until the soul runs back to its original hatred of evil, learning to say to the Lord in the words of **David**: "I hated them with a perfect hatred; they became my enemies" <note>Psalm 139:22. For the monk, "enemies" refers to demonic thoughts, not people.</note>. For he hates his enemies with a "perfect hatred" who sins neither in action nor in **thought** <note>original: "διάνοιαν" (dianoian); the seat of intellect and reflection.</note>. This is the proof of the first and greatest **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias); not a lack of feeling, but a state of inner calm where one is no longer driven by chaotic passions.</note>.

<margin>10.</margin>
But regarding the demon that makes the soul **insensible** <note>original: "ἀναίσθητον" (anaisthēton); a state of spiritual numbness or "hardening of the heart" where one no longer feels the weight of their actions.</note>, what is there to say? For I am afraid even to write about him. I fear how the soul departs from its own proper state during the time of his visit; it strips off the fear of the Lord and all piety. It considers sin as "not sin" and lawlessness as "not lawlessness." It remembers eternal judgment and punishment as if they were **mere words**. It even laughs at the "fiery earthquake." It may confess God with its lips, but it does not understand His commands. You might strike your chest as the soul moves toward sin, but the soul feels nothing. You might speak to it from the **Scriptures**, but it is entirely calloused and does not hear. You might bring up the reproach of other people, yet it takes no account of it. It does not even understand human shame, like a pig that has closed its eyes and burst through a fence. 

The thoughts of **vainglory** <note>original: "κενοδοξίας" (kenodoxias); the prideful desire for human praise.</note>, when they linger, bring on this demon. Indeed, "unless those days were shortened, no flesh would be saved" <note>Matthew 24:22.</note>. This demon rarely visits those who live among the brothers, and the reason is clear: when we see the misfortunes of others—those oppressed by disease, those suffering in prison, or those meeting sudden death—this demon is put to flight. The soul is gradually pricked with **compunction** <note>original: "κατανυσσομένης" (katanyssomenēs); a piercing of the heart that leads to repentance.</note>, comes to sympathy, and the "callousness" built up by the demon is dissolved. We, however, lack these remedies because of our solitude and the scarcity of

<column-break/>

those who are sick among us. It was to put this demon to flight above all that the Lord, in the **Gospels**, commanded us to visit the sick and those in prison. For He says, "I was sick, and you visited me" <note>Matthew 25:36.</note>. 

Nevertheless, you should know this: if a **hermit** <note>original: "ἀναχωρούντων" (anachōrountōn); one who has "withdrawn" to the desert.</note> falls under this demon but does not entertain lustful thoughts or abandon his cell out of **listlessness** <note>original: "ἀκηδίας" (akēdias); acedia, the "noonday demon" of boredom or spiritual apathy.</note>, then he has received endurance and self-control descending from the heavens, and he is blessed to have achieved such dispassion. As for those who profess to practice godliness but choose to live among worldly people, let them beware of this demon. For I am ashamed before men to say or write any more about it.

### ON THE DEMON OF SORROW

<margin>11.</margin>
All the demons teach the soul to love pleasure; only the demon of **Sorrow** <note>original: "λύπης" (lypēs); also translated as sadness or grief.</note> refuses to do this. Instead, it destroys the thoughts that have entered, cutting off every pleasure of the soul and drying it up through grief—for truly, "a sorrowful man's bones are dried up" <note>Proverbs 17:22.</note>. When this demon attacks in moderation, it makes the hermit "proven" or "tested"; for it persuades him to accept nothing of this world and to avoid every pleasure. But when it persists too long, it generates thoughts that advise the soul to "withdraw" <note>A euphemism here for suicide or total despair.</note> or forces it to flee far away. 

This is what the holy **Job** once reflected upon and suffered when he was troubled by this demon. For he says, "I wish I could lay hands on myself, or ask another to do this for me" <note>Job 6:9 or similar apocryphal reading common in the Septuagint tradition.</note>. The symbol of this demon is the **viper**; its nature is given by God’s kindness to destroy the poisons of other beasts, but if it is taken in excess, it destroys the animal itself. **Paul** handed over the lawbreaker in **Corinth** to this demon <note>1 Corinthians 5:5; 2 Corinthians 2:6-7.</note>; which is why he wrote back urgently to the Corinthians, saying, "Confirm your love toward him, lest such a one be swallowed up by excessive sorrow." Yet this spirit, though it afflicts men, knows how to become a mediator of good **repentance** <note>original: "μετανοίας" (metanoias); a change of mind/heart.</note>. This is why the holy **John the Baptist** called those who were stung by this spirit and fled to God "broods of vipers," saying: "Who warned you to flee

<summary>This page describes two spiritual dangers: a demon of "insensibility" that numbs the soul to sin and God's word, and a demon of "sorrow" that can either lead to healthy repentance or destructive despair. Evagrius emphasizes that acts of compassion and endurance in solitude are the primary defenses against these psychological states.</summary>

# EVAGRIUS THE MONK: A MONASTIC OUTLINE

...[to flee] from the coming wrath? Produce, therefore, fruit worthy of repentance, and do not think to say within yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father." <note>A reference to Matthew 3:7-9, where John the Baptist warns those who rely on their lineage rather than their actions.</note> Yet everyone who has imitated Abraham, and has gone out from his land and from his kindred, has himself become stronger than this demon.

<margin>12.</margin>
If anyone has mastered anger, this man has mastered the demons. But if anyone is enslaved to this passion, he is a stranger to the monastic life and a foreigner to the ways of our Savior; for it is said that the Lord himself "teaches the meek his ways." <note>Psalm 25:9.</note> Therefore, the mind of the solitary becomes difficult to catch when it flees to the "plain of meekness." For the demons fear almost no virtue as much as they fear **meekness**. The great Moses possessed this, having been called "meek beyond all men." <note>Numbers 12:3.</note> And the holy David declared it to be worthy of God's remembrance, saying: "Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness." <note>Psalm 132:1.</note> Furthermore, our Savior himself commanded us to become imitators of his own meekness, saying: "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." <note>Matthew 11:29.</note> But if someone abstains from food and drink, yet provokes anger with evil **thoughts** <note>original: "λογισμοῖς" (logismois); in Evagrius’s system, these are not just "thoughts" but "impulses" or "suggestions" from demons.</note>, he is like a ship traveling the open sea that has a demon for a pilot. Therefore, we must attend with all our power to "our dog" <note>An ancient metaphor for the "irascible" or "spirited" part of the soul—the part that gets angry. It should act like a guard dog protecting the soul.</note> and teach it to destroy only the "wolves" and not to devour the "sheep," showing all meekness toward all people.

### CONCERNING VAINGLORY

<margin>13.</margin>
Alone among the **thoughts** <note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismōn)</note>, that of **vainglory** <note>original: "κενοδοξίας" (kenodoxias); the desire for empty praise or human recognition.</note> is complex; it embraces almost the entire world and opens the doors to all the demons, becoming like a wicked traitor to a city. Therefore, it greatly humbles the mind of the solitary, filling him with many words and worldly matters, and ruining his prayers—through which he otherwise strives to heal all the wounds of his soul. All the demons, once they have been defeated, help to increase this thought; and through it, they all again find an entrance into souls, making the "last state worse than the first." <note>Matthew 12:45.</note> From

<column-break/>

this thought is born the thought of **pride** <note>original: "ὑπερηφανίας" (hyperēphanias); for Evagrius, vainglory is seeking praise from others, while pride is thinking one has reached the goal by one's own power.</note>, which shook the "seal of likeness" and the "crown of beauty" from the heavens down to the earth. <note>An allusion to the fall of Lucifer, often associated with the descriptions in Ezekiel 28.</note> But spring away from this and do not linger, so that we do not "betray our life to others and our years to the merciless." <note>Proverbs 5:9.</note> This demon is put to flight by intense prayer and by doing or saying nothing by choice that contributes to cursed vainglory.

<margin>14.</margin>
When the mind of the solitary forgets even a little **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias); the state of being undisturbed by the passions.</note>, it immediately mounts the horse of vainglory and gallops through the cities, becoming drunk on the praise of its own fame. By a divine "stewardship," the spirit of **fornication** <note>original: "πορνείας" (porneias)</note> meets such a person, and locking him in one of the "pigsties," teaches him no longer to leave his bed before reaching perfect health, nor to imitate those sick people who are undisciplined. Such people, still carrying the remains of weakness within themselves, commit themselves to journeys and untimely baths, and so fall back into recurring diseases. Therefore, as we sit in our cells, let us pay attention to ourselves, so that as we progress in virtue, we may become difficult to move toward vice. As we are stirred in **knowledge** <note>original: "γνώσει" (gnōsei)</note>, we receive a multitude of various **contemplations** <note>original: "θεωρημάτων" (theōrēmatōn)</note>; and rising up again, we behold more clearly the light of our Savior.

<margin>15.</margin>
I am not able to write all the villainies of the demons, and I am ashamed to list their evil schemes, fearing the simpler among those who will read this. But regarding the spirit of fornication, hear its cunning. When someone acquires dispassion of the "desiring part" <note>The "concupiscible" part of the soul that deals with physical hunger and sexual desire.</note> and the shameful thoughts become cold, at that moment the demon introduces men and women playing with one another, and makes the solitary a spectator of shameful acts and gestures. But this temptation does not last long; for intense prayer and a very strict diet, along with vigils and the exercise of spiritual contemplations, drive it away like a waterless cloud. There are times, however, when it even touches the flesh, prying it toward an irrational "burning," and this wicked one devises ten thousand other things—which are not necessary to publish or commit to writing. This demon also contributes to such thoughts and...

<summary>Evagrius discusses the vital roles of meekness in conquering demons and warns against the "traitorous" nature of vainglory, which leads to pride and spiritual relapse. He also touches upon the specific demonic temptations of fornication that occur even as a monk progresses toward dispassion.</summary>

# TEACHING HOW ONE OUGHT TO PRACTICE AND BE STILL

...[the movement] of anger directed against the demon. For the demon fears this movement of **anger** most of all when it is stirred up against those "thoughts" <note>original: "λογισμοῖς" (logismois); these are the intrusive, obsessive impulses or demonic suggestions that Evagrius categorizes.</note> that disturb us, for it destroys his mental schemes. This is the meaning of the saying: *Be angry, and do not sin* <note>Psalm 4:4 / Ephesians 4:26.</note>; it is a useful medicine applied to the soul in times of temptation. 

The demon of anger also imitates this; he himself shapes images of parents, friends, or relatives being insulted by unworthy people. By doing this, he stirs the anger of the monk who has withdrawn from the world, provoking him to say something evil or to act against those appearing in his mind. One must pay close attention to these things and quickly snatch the mind away from such mental idols; otherwise, if the mind lingers on them, it will become like a **smoldering brand** during the time of prayer. Those who are prone to anger fall into these temptations most of all, being easily ignited by their impulses. Such people are far from pure prayer and the knowledge of our Savior Jesus Christ.

<margin>16.</margin>
The Lord has handed over the "thoughts" <note>original: "νοήματα" (noêmata); here referring to the mental concepts of worldly things.</note> of this age to the human being, the good shepherd, just as if they were sheep. For it is written: *He gave the thought to every man in his heart,* <note>Cf. Ecclesiastes 3:11.</note> joining to it **desire** and **anger** as helpers. Thus, through anger, he may put to flight the "thoughts of the wolves," and through desire, he may cherish the sheep, even when often buffeted by rains and winds. 

Moreover, He gave a law for how to shepherd the sheep: a "place of green pasture" and "water of rest," a "psaltery," a "lyre," a "rod," and a "staff." <note>References to Psalm 23 and the tools of the spiritual life.</note> From this flock, the shepherd is fed and clothed, and he gathers the "mountain hay." For who, it is said, *shepherds a flock and does not drink of its milk?* <note>1 Corinthians 9:7.</note> 

Therefore, the one who has withdrawn from the world must guard this flock night and day, lest any of the offspring be "torn by wild beasts" or fall into the hands of "robbers." If any such thing should happen in the mountain valley, he must immediately snatch it from the mouth of the "lion" and the "bear." <note>An allusion to David guarding his father’s sheep in 1 Samuel 17:34-35.</note> 

A thought concerning a brother becomes "torn by wild beasts" if it is nurtured within us with **hatred**. A thought concerning a woman is torn if it is turned over within us with **shameful desire**. A thought of silver or gold is torn if it dwells with **greed**. And the thoughts of "holy gifts" <note>spiritual talents or virtues</note> are torn if they are grazed within the mind alongside **vainglory**. The same thing will happen

<column-break/>

with other thoughts if they are stolen by the passions. One must not only keep watch over these things by day, but also guard them while keeping vigil by night. For it happens that even through "shameful and evil fantasies," one may lose his own property. 

This is what was said by the Holy Jacob: *I did not bring to you a sheep torn by wild beasts; I made good what was stolen by day and what was stolen by night. I was consumed by the heat of the day and the frost of the night, and sleep departed from my eyes.* <note>Genesis 31:39-40. Evagrius interprets Jacob's physical labor as an allegory for the monk's mental discipline.</note> 

If "listlessness" <term>akēdia: the "noonday demon" of spiritual exhaustion or boredom</term> should come upon us from our toil, let us run up a little way onto the **Rock of Knowledge** and converse with the "psaltery," striking the strings of the virtues with the knowledge of God. And let us again graze the sheep beneath Mount Sinai, so that the God of our fathers may call us also from the "burning bush" <note>Exodus 3:2-4.</note> and grant us the "words of signs and wonders."

<margin>17.</margin>
Christ raises the rational nature that has been "put to death by vice," doing so through the **contemplation** <term>theoria: spiritual insight into the inner meaning of creation</term> of all the ages. His Father, in turn, raises the soul that has died the "death of Christ" through the **knowledge of Himself**. And this is what was said by Paul: *If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him.* <note>2 Timothy 2:11 or Romans 6:8.</note>

<margin>18.</margin>
When the mind (*nous*) has stripped off the "old man" and put on the "man of grace," then it will see its own state at the time of prayer, resembling **sapphire** or the **color of heaven**. This state is what the Scripture calls the "Place of God," which was seen by the elders on Mount Sinai. <note>Exodus 24:10. Evagrius describes the highest state of prayer as seeing the soul's own light, which is blue like the sky.</note>

<margin>19.</margin>
Among the "unclean demons," some tempt the human being *as a human being*, while others disturb the human being *as an irrational animal*. The first group, when they approach, instill in us thoughts of vainglory, pride, envy, or judgmentalism—things that do not touch any of the irrational animals. But the second group, when they draw near, stir up **anger** or **desire** contrary to nature. For these are "passions" common to us and the irrational animals, though they are hidden by our rational nature. 

Therefore, the Holy Spirit says regarding those thoughts that happen to humans: *I said, "You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High; but you die like men, and fall like one of the princes."* <note>Psalm 82:6-7.</note> But to those who are moved irrationally, what does He say? *Do not become like the horse...* <note>Psalm 32:9. The text cuts off here at "ἵπ-" (hippos, meaning horse).</note>

<summary>Evagrius explains how to redirect anger against demons and uses a detailed shepherd allegory to describe the monk's task of guarding "thoughts" from passions. He also describes the luminous "sapphire" state of the mind during pure prayer and distinguishes between uniquely human sins and animalistic impulses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Evagrius Ponticus’s "Monastic Sketch." The previous page discussed the role of anger and desire as tools for the "shepherd" (the monk) to guard his thoughts.
