### EVAGRIUS THE MONK, A MONASTIC SKETCH

...[like the] horse and the mule, which have no understanding; with bit and bridle bind their jaws, those who do not come near to you <note>Psalm 32:9.</note>. But the soul that sins, it shall die <note>Ezekiel 18:4.</note>. It is clear that while men, as men, die and are buried by men, the irrational creatures, when they are put to death—or rather, when they fall—will be eaten by vultures or ravens. Of these, some of the young ones call upon the Lord, while others are "hatched in blood" <note>This imagery draws from Job 38:41 and Psalm 147:9, where God feeds the young ravens. Evagrius uses this to distinguish between those seeking God and those consumed by violence or passion.</note>. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

<margin>20.</margin> When one of the enemies wounds you by casting a thought at you, and you wish to turn his sword back, as it is written, into his own heart <note>Psalm 37:15.</note>, do as we say: Analyze within yourself the "thought" <note>original: "λογισμόν" (logismon); an intrusive or obsessive impulse.</note> cast by him, whatever it may be. Determine what things it is composed of, and what exactly it is that is distressing the mind. For example, suppose he sends the "thought of greed" <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας" (philargyrias); literally "love of silver."</note>. Divide this thought into: the mind that received it, the mental concept of gold, the gold itself, and the passion of greed. Then ask: which of these is the sin? Is it the mind? But how can that be, since it is the image of God? Is it the mental concept of gold? Who with any sense would ever say that? Is it the gold itself? For what purpose was it created? It follows, then, that the cause of the sin is the fourth element: which is not a thing that exists in its own essence, nor a mental concept of a thing, but a certain misanthropic pleasure born from free will, which compels the mind to make a bad use of God’s creatures. It is this pleasure that the law is trusted to "circumcise." As you investigate these things, the thought will be destroyed, being dissolved into its own underlying theory <note>original: "θεωρίαν" (theorian); here meaning an analytical or spiritual understanding of its components.</note>. The demon will flee from you once your intellect is raised to these heights by this knowledge. 

But if you do not wish to use his own sword against him, but instead desire first to subdue him with your own "sling," then take a stone from your shepherd’s bag and seek its deeper meaning: how is it that angels and demons interact with our world, but we do not interact with their worlds? For we cannot join angels more closely to God, nor do we choose to make demons more impure. And how was

<column-break/>

the "Morning Star" <note>original: "ἑωσφόρος" (heosphoros); the "light-bringer" or Lucifer.</note> who rose at dawn cast down to the earth? He has made the sea like a pot of ointment, and the dark pit of the abyss like a prisoner <note>Imagery likely drawn from the description of Leviathan in Job 41.</note>. He makes the abyss boil like a copper cauldron, throwing everyone into confusion by his malice, wishing to rule over all. Truly, the contemplation of these matters deeply wounds the demon and puts his entire camp to flight. 

However, these things happen only to those who are somewhat purified and who can see to some extent the inner purposes of created things. Those who are still impure do not know the contemplation of these things; and even if they learned them from others, they would not be heard as they "sing the charm," because of the great "dust and noise" stirred up by their passions during the war. For the camp of the "foreigners" <note>original: "ἀλλοφύλων" (allophylon); often used in the Greek Bible for the Philistines, representing the passions/demons.</note> must be silenced entirely so that Goliath alone may meet our David. In the same way, we should use this division of the war and this method of analysis against all impure thoughts.

<margin>21.</margin> Whenever some of the impure thoughts are quickly put to flight, let us seek the reason: why did this happen? Was it because the thing was rare and the material for it hard to find? Or was it because of the **impassibility** <term>original: "ἀπάθειαν" (apatheian); a state of soul where one is no longer dominated by destructive passions or emotional triggers.</term> we possess that the enemy had no power against us? For instance, if a hermit imagines being entrusted with the spiritual governance of a city, he does not linger on this thought—it is recognized as absurd based on what was said before. But if someone is offered a city, even a common one, and he thinks the same way, that person is blessed in his impassibility. This same method of examination will be found useful for all other thoughts as well. 

It is necessary to know these things for our own zeal and strength, so that we may see whether we have crossed the Jordan and are near the "palm trees," or if we are still dwelling in the wilderness and being struck by the foreigners. For the "demon of greed" <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας" (philargyrias).</note> seems to me to be very "shifty" <note>original: "ποικίλος" (poikilos); multifaceted or complex.</note> and ingenious at deception. Often, when he is squeezed by an extreme renunciation of possessions, he immediately pretends to be a steward and a lover of the poor. He welcomes guests who have not yet arrived with great sincerity, and sends "ministries" to others who are in want. He visits the city prisons and pretends to ransom those who are being sold. He even suggests associating with wealthy women...
<meta>The catchword "ἄλ-" indicates the next page begins with "ἄλλαις" (others) or another word starting with "al-".</meta>

<summary>Evagrius describes a logical method for dismantling temptations by breaking them into components (mind, object, and passion). He also explains how the demon of greed disguises itself as false charity to re-attach the monk to worldly concerns.</summary>
<keywords>Evagrius Ponticus, spiritual warfare, logismois, philargyria (greed), apatheia (impassibility), theoria (contemplation), David and Goliath, discernment of thoughts</keywords>

# TEACHING HOW ONE OUGHT TO PRACTICE ASCETICISM AND BE STILL

...to submit to others again, advising those who possess a heavy purse. And having thus deceived the soul little by little, the demon surrounds it with the **thoughts of greed** <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας" (philargyrias); literally "love of silver." In monastic thought, this isn't just wanting money, but the anxiety for future security.</note>, and hands it over to the demon of **vainglory** <note>original: "κενοδοξίας" (kenodoxias); the desire for human praise.</note>. This demon introduces a multitude of people who "glorify the Lord" for the monk’s clever management of resources, and he gradually arranges for people to talk to each other about the **Priesthood** <note>Evagrius warns that the demon of vainglory often tempts monks with the idea of being ordained as a priest or bishop to "do good," which pulls them away from their quiet life.</note>. He predicts the death of the current priest, and suggests that the monk could not escape this office even if he tried ten thousand things. And thus the wretched mind, being bound by these thoughts, fights with those men who do not accept his "future" authority; but to those who do accept it, he readily grants gifts and welcomes them for their gratitude. Some who rebel against him, he hands over to judges and orders them to be exiled from the city. While these thoughts are turning about inside him, immediately the demon of **pride** <note>original: "ὑπερηφανίας" (hyperēphania); the final and most dangerous of the "eight thoughts" in Evagrian psychology.</note> stands by, sending continuous lightning bolts through the air of the cell, and **winged dragons**; and finally, bringing about a loss of one’s senses. But we, praying for the destruction of these thoughts, let us live in poverty with thanksgiving. For we brought nothing into the world, and it is clear that we can carry nothing out. Having food and covering, we shall be content with these; remembering Paul saying, "the love of money is the root of all evils." <note>1 Timothy 6:7–10.</note>

<margin>22.</margin>
All impure thoughts, lingering in us because of the **passions** <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē); disordered desires or emotional attachments that cloud the mind.</note>, lead the mind down to destruction and ruin. For just as the mental image of bread lingers in the hungry man because of hunger, and the image of water in the thirsty man because of thirst; so also the mental images of money, and the shameful thoughts born from excess 

<column-break/>

food, linger because of the passions. But this will likewise be made manifest in the case of the thoughts of vainglory and other mental images. It is not possible for a mind choked by such thoughts to stand before God and be crowned with the **crown of righteousness**. For dragged down by these thoughts, even that thrice-wretched mind in the Gospels refused the "best part" of the knowledge of God; and again, the man bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness had his garment woven from these thoughts; the Caller declared him not worthy of such a wedding <note>Referencing the Parable of the Wedding Feast in Matthew 22:1–14.</note>. Therefore, the **wedding garment** is the **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπάθεια" (apatheia); not "apathy," but a state of inner calm and freedom from being controlled by the passions.</note> of the rational soul that has denied worldly desires. Why it is that thoughts of sensible things corrupt knowledge when they linger was discussed in the *Chapters on Prayer*.

<margin>23.</margin>
Among the demons opposing the **practical life** <note>original: "πρακτικῇ" (praktikē); the stage of ascetic practice and struggle against the passions.</note>, there are three front-runners whom the whole "camp of the aliens" follows. These stand first in the war and call souls toward vice through impure thoughts: those entrusted with the appetites of **gluttony**, those suggesting **greed** to us, and those calling us toward the **glory of men**. Therefore, desiring pure prayer, keep watch over your anger; and loving self-control, master the belly. Do not give bread to your stomach to the point of satiety, and afflict it with water. Keep vigil in prayer, and put resentment far from you. Let the words of the Holy Spirit not fail you, and "knock at the doors" by writing with the hands of virtues. Then the dispassion of the heart will rise for you, and you will see a **star-like mind** <note>original: "νοῦν ἀστεροειδῆ" (noun asteroeidē); a famous Evagrian image describing the mind when it becomes luminous and calm like the stars during prayer.</note> in prayer.

# BY EVAGRIUS THE MONK, A MONASTIC RULE

...protects the body and maintains a steady state of self-control.
<margin>2.</margin> He who has laid hold of knowledge, and harvests the pleasure that comes from it, will no longer be persuaded by the demon of **vainglory** <note>original: "κενοδοξίας" (kenodoxias); the desire for human praise and recognition.</note>, even if that demon offers him all the pleasures of the world. For what could he promise that is greater than **spiritual contemplation**? <note>original: "πνευματικῆς θεωρίας" (pneumatikēs theōrias); the direct "vision" or deep understanding of divine realities.</note> But as long as we have not yet tasted this knowledge, let us zealously work through **the practice** <note>original: "τὴν πρακτικὴν" (tēn praktikēn); the first stage of monastic life focused on purifying the heart through discipline.</note>, showing our aim to God: that we do everything for the sake of knowing Him.
<margin>3.</margin> It is also necessary to set forth the paths of the monks who have gone before us and to guide ourselves by them. For many things were both done and said well by them. Among these, one of them said that a "dryer and steady diet, joined with love, quickly brings the monk into the **harbor of dispassion**." <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias); not "apathy" in the modern sense, but a state of inner peace where one is no longer driven by chaotic passions.</note>
<margin>4.</margin> I visited

<column-break/>

**Saint Macarius** <note>St. Macarius the Great (c. 300–391 AD), one of the most famous "Desert Fathers" of Egypt.</note> at high noon, and being greatly inflamed by thirst, I asked for water to drink. But he said, "Be satisfied with the shadow; for many who are traveling right now, or sailing, are deprived even of this." Then, as I was training myself in thoughts regarding self-control, he said: "Take courage, my child. For in twenty whole years, I have never taken my fill of bread, nor water, nor sleep. Instead, I ate my bread by weight, and drank my water by measure, and leaning a little against the walls, I snatched only a tiny portion of sleep."
<margin>5.</margin> A wandering mind is steadied by reading, vigil, and prayer. A flaming desire is withered by hunger, labor, and withdrawal. A circling anger is calmed by the chanting of psalms, long-suffering, and mercy. For things that are immoderate and untimely are short-lived; they are more harmful than they are helpful.

# A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## OF THE HOLY
### CASSIAN THE ROMAN

Our Holy Father **Cassian the Roman** <note>Known in the West as St. John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD). He lived among the Egyptian monks and later founded monasteries in France.</note> lived during the reign of **Theodosius the Younger** <note>original: "Θεοδοσίου τοῦ μικροῦ" (Theodosiou tou mikrou); literally "Theodosius the Little," the Eastern Roman Emperor from 408 to 450 AD.</note>, around the 431st year after Christ. Of the works he labored upon, the one *On the Eight Thoughts* and the one *On Discernment* were placed here, as they drip with every kind of benefit and grace. The most wise **Photius** <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and famous scholar who reviewed Cassian's works in his book "The Library" (Bibliotheca).</note> also mentions these, saying in his own words in Reading 157, pages 265 and 266: "And the second work is addressed to the same person (namely, Castor), and

<column-break/>

bears the title *On the Eight Thoughts*, dealing with **gluttony, fornication, greed, anger, sorrow, listlessness** <note>original: "ἀκηδίαν" (akēdian); a state of spiritual boredom or "the noonday devil."</note>, **vainglory, and pride**." These words are useful, if anything ever was, to those who choose to take up the ascetic struggle... and a third short treatise was read alongside these... which teaches what **discernment** <note>original: "διάκρισις" (diakrisis); the ability to distinguish between healthy and destructive thoughts.</note> is, and how it is greater than the other virtues, and where it is born from, and how it is mostly a gift from above, and so forth.
The Church also commemorates him on the 29th of February <note>Because his feast falls on a Leap Day, it is often moved to Feb 28 in non-leap years.</note>, honoring him with praises and encomiums.

### BY THE HOLY

# CASSIAN THE ROMAN
<note>St. John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD) was a monk and theologian who traveled to Egypt to learn from the Desert Fathers before founding monasteries in Marseilles, France.</note>

## TO BISHOP CASTOR

### CONCERNING THE EIGHT THOUGHTS OF WICKEDNESS
<note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismon); in monastic literature, these are "intrusive thoughts" or "vices" that tempt the soul.</note>

Having first composed the discourse regarding the organization of Communal Monasteries <note>original: "Κοινοβίων" (Koinobiōn); communities where monks live together under a common rule.</note>, and now once again trusting in your prayers for this present work, we have attempted to write about the eight thoughts of wickedness: I mean **gluttony**, and **fornication**, **avarice** <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας" (philargyrias); literally "love of silver" or money.</note>, **anger**, **sadness**, **acedia** <note>original: "ἀκηδίας" (akēdias); a state of spiritual listlessness or "no-care" often called the "noonday demon."</note>, **vainglory**, and **pride**.

### CONCERNING SELF-CONTROL OF THE STOMACH

Primarily, therefore, we shall speak about **self-control** <note>original: "ἐγκρατείας" (enkrateias); the virtue of temperance or mastery over one's impulses.</note> of the stomach, which is the opposite of gluttony; both the manner of fasts, and the quality and quantity of foods. And these things we will not say from ourselves, but rather what we have received from the **Holy Fathers**. They, therefore, did not hand down a single rule for fasting, nor one way of partaking in food, nor the same measure for everyone. This is because not everyone has the same strength, whether due to age, or due to illness, or due to a more delicate bodily constitution. But they handed down one goal for all: to flee from fullness and to turn away from the satiation of the stomach. They judged that a daily fast was more beneficial and more helpful toward achieving purity than a fast extended over three or four days, or even lasting a week. For he says that a person who extends their fast immoderately often uses food beyond measure afterward. As a result of this, sometimes from the excess of starvation the body grows weak and becomes more sluggish toward spiritual services; while at other times, being weighed down by the multitude of foods, it produces listlessness and laxity in the soul. And again, they judged that

<column-break/>

the eating of vegetables is not suitable for everyone, nor legumes, nor can everyone use a diet of dry bread. They said that one person eating two pounds <note>original: "λίτρας" (litras); the Roman *libra*, roughly 327 grams.</note> of bread might still be hungry, while another eating only one pound, or even six ounces, is fully satisfied. To all, therefore, as was said before, they handed down one limit for self-control: not to be deceived by the filling of the belly, nor to be led away by the pleasure of the throat. For it is not only the different quality of foods, but also the quantity of the amount, that is accustomed to ignite the "fiery darts" of fornication. For with whatever food the stomach is filled, it gives birth to the seed of debauchery. And again, it is not only the intoxication of wine that is accustomed to make the mind drunk; even an excess of water and an overabundance of any food makes the mind heavy and nodding with sleep. For the Sodomites, the cause of their destruction was not intoxication from wine and various foods, but "fullness of bread," according to **the Prophet** <note>A reference to Ezekiel 16:49: "Now this was the sin of your sister Sodom: She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed and unconcerned."</note>. Bodily weakness is not an obstacle to the purity of the heart, provided we give the body what its weakness requires, rather than what its pleasure desires. The use of food is taken only so far as to serve the needs of living, not so much as to be a slave to the impulses of desire. A moderate and reasoned partaking of food maintains the health of the body and does not take away from holiness. An accurate limit and rule of self-control handed down by the Fathers is this: the one eating should stop while the appetite is still present, and not wait for total satiation. And **the Apostle** <note>A reference to St. Paul in Romans 13:14.</note> also, having said, "make no provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts," did not forbid the necessary maintenance of life, but...

<image-desc>Institutional library stamp of the University of Crete (ΠΑΝΕΠΙΣΤΗΜΙΟ ΚΡΗΤΗΣ) in the bottom right corner.</image-desc>

<summary>Saint Cassian introduces the eight primary vices of the monastic life, beginning with a nuanced discussion on gluttony and fasting. He emphasizes that spiritual self-control is not about a one-size-fits-all rule, but about individual moderation and avoiding the "fullness of the stomach" that leads to other sins.</summary>

<meta>This page continues St. John Cassian’s teachings on the eight vices. The previous page ended while discussing that there is no single rule for fasting, as physical needs vary between individuals.</meta>

[page 36]

### OF THE HOLY CASSIAN THE ROMAN

...forbidden pleasure-loving care. Furthermore, for the perfect purity of the soul, the abstinence from food alone is not sufficient, unless the other virtues also cooperate. Therefore, humility—through the obedience of work and the physical exhaustion of the body—contributes greatly to our progress. The avoidance of greed <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας" (philargyrias); literally "love of silver," referring to the hoarding of wealth.</note>, which means not only refusing to have money but even refusing to desire its possession, leads to purity of soul. Avoiding anger, sadness, vainglory, and pride—all these produce the general purity of the soul. However, that specific purity of soul found through self-restraint <note>original: "σωφροσύνης" (sōphrosynēs); a complex term meaning sound-mindedness, temperance, or chastity.</note> is especially achieved through temperance and fasting. For it is impossible for a person with a full stomach to fight the spirit of fornication <note>original: "πνεύματι τῆς πορνείας" (pneumati tēs porneias); in this tradition, vices were often personified as spirits or demons attacking the mind.</note> within their thoughts. Therefore, let our first struggle be to control the stomach and enslave the body, not only through fasting but also through vigils, toil, reading, and by gathering the heart into the fear of Gehenna <note>original: "γεέννης"; a reference to hell or the place of judgment.</note> and the desire for the Kingdom of Heaven.

## CONCERNING THE SPIRIT OF FORNICATION AND THE DESIRE OF THE FLESH

Our second struggle is against the spirit of fornication and the desire of the flesh; a desire which begins to trouble a person from their earliest years. This is a great and difficult struggle, involving a double battle. Because while other vices fight only within the soul, this one is dual, established in both soul and body; for this reason, it is necessary to undertake a double battle. For bodily fasting alone is not sufficient to acquire perfect self-restraint and true purity, unless there is also a crushing of the heart, earnest prayer to God, frequent study of the scriptures, toil, and manual labor—all of which can restrain the unstable impulses of the soul and recall it from shameful fantasies. Above all, humility of soul contributes to this; without which, no one will be able to overcome fornication or any of the other vices. Therefore, it is necessary first to guard the heart with all vigilance from filthy thoughts.

<column-break/>

For from the heart proceed, according to the Lord’s voice, evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, and the rest. Indeed, fasting is commanded for us not only for the affliction of the body, but also for the wakefulness <note>original: "νῆψιν" (nēpsin); spiritual sobriety or "watchfulness," a central concept in Eastern Christian meditation.</note> of the mind; so that the mind may not be darkened by the abundance of food and become unable to guard against intrusive thoughts. Therefore, one must show all diligence not only in bodily fasting, but also in spiritual study; without which, it is impossible to ascend to the height of true chastity and purity. It is proper for us first to cleanse, according to the Lord’s voice, the inside of the cup and the plate, so that the outside may also become clean. For this reason, if we are eager to "compete lawfully" and "be crowned" <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:5, where St. Paul uses athletic metaphors for spiritual life.</note> by defeating the unclean spirit of fornication, let us not trust in our own power or ascetic practice, but in the help of our Master, God. For a person does not stop being attacked by this spirit until they truly believe that they are delivered from this disease and ascend to the height of purity not by their own diligence or toil, but by God’s protection and help. Indeed, this achievement is beyond human nature; in a way, the one who has trampled down the irritations of the flesh and its pleasures exists "outside the body." For this reason, it is impossible for a person (so to speak) to fly up on their own wings to this high and heavenly prize of holiness and become an imitator of angels, unless the grace of God brings them up from the earth and the mire. For by no other virtue are people bound in the flesh made more like the spiritual angels than by self-restraint. For through this, while still living on the earth, they have—as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul's statement in Philippians 3:20.</note> says—their citizenship in the heavens.

<margin>In other manuscripts: "to run towards"</margin>
A sign that we have perfectly acquired this virtue is that the soul* does not pay attention to any image of shameful fantasy during sleep. For even if such a movement is not counted as a sin, it is nevertheless proof that the soul is sick and has not been delivered from the passion. For this reason, the shameful fantasies that happen to us in sleep are an indictment of the preceding...

<summary>Cassian explains that while fasting is essential, it must be paired with humility and other virtues to achieve true purity of soul. He focuses on the "spirit of fornication," describing it as a unique struggle of both body and soul that can only be overcome through divine grace rather than human effort alone.</summary>

# ON THE EIGHT THOUGHTS OF WICKEDNESS

of indifference <note>original: "ῥαθυμίας" (rhathymias); a state of spiritual lethargy or "sloth."</note>, and of the weakness within us we ought to believe; the disease hidden in the secret places of the soul is made manifest by the flow that occurs during the relaxation of sleep. Therefore, the Physician of our souls [Christ] placed the medicine in the secret parts of the soul, saying: *“That whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart”* (Matthew 5:28). He was not so much correcting the curious and lustful eyes as he was the soul established within, which has used the eyes—given by God for good—in an evil way. For this reason, the wise Proverb does not say, "with all vigilance guard your eyes," but rather, *“With all vigilance guard your heart”* (Proverbs 4:23); applying the remedy of vigilance especially to that which uses the eyes for whatever it desires. Therefore, let this 

<margin>* in other [manuscripts]: of cleansing</margin>

be the safeguard of our heart: so that when a memory of a woman arises in our mind, brought up through the devil’s malice—be it of a mother, or a sister, or other devout women—we should quickly cast it out of our heart. We do this so that by dwelling too long on this memory, the deceiver of evils may not use these persons to trip us up and plunge the mind into shameful and harmful thoughts. This follows the command given by God to the first-formed [Adam], which orders us to "guard the head of the serpent" (Genesis 3:15); that is, the very beginnings of harmful thoughts through which the serpent attempts to crawl into our souls. We must act so that by the acceptance of the "head"—which is the first assault of the thought—we do not then accept the rest of the snake's body, which is the consent to the pleasure. And from that point, the serpent would drag the mind down into unlawful action. Instead, it is proper, according to what is written, to "kill all the sinners of the land in the mornings" (Psalm 101:8); that is, to use the light of knowledge to discern and destroy sinful thoughts from the "land," which is our heart, according to the Lord’s teaching. And while the "children of Babylon"—by which I mean evil thoughts—are still infants, we must dash them against the ground and crush them against the "Rock," which is Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). For if they are allowed to grow into "manhood" through our consent, they cannot be conquered without 

<column-break/>

great groaning and labor. In addition to these things said from the Divine Scripture, it is also good to remember the words of the Holy Fathers. It was said by the Holy Basil, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia: "I do not know a woman, and yet I am not a virgin." <note>St. Basil means that although he was celibate, he did not consider himself to have the perfect, unblemished purity of heart required for true spiritual virginity.</note> He recognized that the gift of virginity is achieved not only through physical abstinence from women, but just as much through the holiness and purity of the soul, which is naturally achieved through the fear of God. The Fathers also say this: that we cannot perfectly acquire the virtue of purity <note>original: "ἁγνείας" (hagneias); referring to chastity or ritual/moral purity.</note> unless we first acquire true humility in our heart; nor can we be deemed worthy of true knowledge as long as the passion of fornication is settled in the secret places of the soul. To show the achievement of self-control <note>original: "σωφροσύνης" (sōphrosynēs); sound-mindedness or temperance.</note> from the Apostle as well, let us recall one of his sayings and conclude this discourse: *"Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord"* (Hebrews 12:14). That he is speaking about this [purity] is clear from what he adds: *"lest there be any fornicator or profane person like Esau."* Therefore, as much as the achievement of holiness is heavenly and angelic, it is fought against by even heavier plots from our adversaries. For this reason, we ought to strive not only to practice the restraint of the body, but also contrition of the 

<margin>* in other [manuscripts]: prayers</margin>

heart and frequent * repentance with groaning. This is so that the furnace of our flesh—which the Babylonian King [the devil] kindles every day with the provocations of desire—may be extinguished by the dew of the presence of the Holy Spirit. In addition to these things, a greatest weapon for us in this war is "vigil according to God." For just as the vigilance of the day prepares one for nighttime holiness, so the nighttime vigil according to God paves the way for the soul's purity during the day.

## CONCERNING GREED

Our third struggle is against the spirit of greed <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας" (philargyrias); literally the "love of silver."</note>. This is a foreign vice, recognized as being outside of our nature, finding its starting point in the monk through a lack of faith. For the provocations of the other passions—I mean anger and desire—seem to come from the body...

-> # BY SAINT CASSIAN THE ROMAN <-

to have their starting points; and in a way, as if they were innate, having their beginning from birth. This is why they are conquered only after a long time. But the disease of greed <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας" (philargyrias); literally "love of silver."</note> comes from the outside and can be cut off more easily if it meets with diligence and attention. If neglected, however, it becomes more destructive than the other passions and difficult to cast out. For it is the "root of all evils," according to the Apostle [Paul] (1 Timothy 6:10). Let us consider it this way: the natural movements of the body are seen not only in children, who do not yet have the discernment of good and evil, but even in the smallest nursing infants. Although they have no trace of [sinful] pleasure in themselves, they nonetheless show a natural movement in the flesh. Similarly, the sting of anger is seen in infants when we see them moved against those who have grieved them. I say these things not to blame nature as the cause of sin—God forbid—but to show that while anger and desire were joined to man by the Creator for good, they somehow seem to fall away from the natural use of the body into what is "contrary to nature" through laziness. For the movement of the body was given by the Creator for the procreation of children and the continuation of the race through succession, not for fornication. And the movement of anger has been implanted in us for our salvation, so that we might be angry against wickedness, not so that we might turn into wild beasts against our own kind. Therefore, even if we use these things badly, nature is not "sinful," nor should we blame the Creator—just as we would not blame someone who gave a small iron tool for a necessary and useful purpose if the receiver used it for the service of murder. We have said these things wishing to show that the passion of greed does not have its excuse in nature, but only from a most wicked and corrupt choice <note>original: "προαιρέσεως" (proaireseōs); a technical term for the deliberate moral will or disposition.</note>. For this disease, when it finds the soul lukewarm and lacking faith at the beginning of its renunciation <note>original: "ἀποταγῆς" (apotagēs); the formal act of leaving the world to become a monk.</note>, suggests certain seemingly just and reasonable excuses for the monk to keep something of what he possesses. For it outlines in the monk's mind a long old age and bodily weakness, and that the provisions given by the monastery are not sufficient for comfort—I do not say for the sick, but not even for the healthy—and that there is no worthy care for the sick there, but rather they are completely neglected;

<column-break/>

and how, if he does not have hidden gold, he will die miserably. Finally, it suggests that he cannot remain for long in the monastery because of the weight of the tasks and the strictness of the [spiritual] father. And when it misleads the mind with such thoughts to keep even one denarius, it then persuades him to secretly learn a handicraft <note>original: "ἐργόχειρον" (ergocheiron); manual labor or a craft practiced by a monk to keep the mind focused and sometimes to earn a small living for charity.</note> without the abbot's knowledge, from which he will be able to increase the money he so desires. And thereafter, it deceives the wretched man with uncertain hopes, suggesting profit from the handicraft, and from this, ease and freedom from worry. Entirely given over to the thought of profit, he notices nothing of the opposite: not the madness of anger if he should ever happen to suffer a loss, nor the darkness of sorrow if he should fail in his hope for profit. But as for others the "belly is their god" (Philippians 3:19), so for this man, gold is his god. Therefore, the blessed Apostle, knowing this, called this not only the root of all evils but also "idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). Let us consider, then, how much wickedness this disease drags a person into, such that it even casts them into idolatry. For the greedy man, having turned his mind away from the love of God, loves the images of men engraved in gold. Darkened by these thoughts, the monk continues to grow worse and can no longer have any obedience. Instead, he is resentful, feels he is being treated unfairly, and grumbles at every task, speaking back; and with no reverence preserved, he is carried away like a most stubborn horse toward the cliffs. He is not satisfied with his daily food and protests that he cannot endure these things to the end. He says that God is not only in that place, nor is his own salvation locked up there; and that if he does not leave that monastery, he will perish. And so, having his saved-up money as a co-worker in this corrupt opinion, as if lightened by these "wings," he meditates on his exit from the monastery. Then he answers all commands with pride and harshness, and regarding himself as a stranger and an outsider, if he sees anything in the monastery needing correction, he neglects it, despises it, and blames everything that happens. Then he seeks out excuses through which he might become angry or grieved, so that he does not seem to be leaving without a cause...

<summary>Saint Cassian explains that greed is not a natural instinct but a corrupt choice driven by a lack of faith, leading a monk to hoard money, neglect obedience, and eventually abandon his monastery. He contrasts greed with natural impulses like anger or desire, which are meant for virtuous purposes but can be misused.</summary>

## ON THE EIGHT THOUGHTS OF VICE
### 39

...of the monastery. If he is also able, by whisperings and idle talk, to deceive and cast another out of the monastery, he does not shrink from doing even this, wishing to have a partner in his own fault. Thus inflamed by the fire of his own possessions, the greedy man <note>original: "φιλάργυρος" (philargyros); literally, a lover of silver.</note> will never be able to be at peace in the monastery or live under a rule. When the demon, like a wolf, snatches him from the fold and separates him from the flock, he finds him ready to be devoured; then the demon arranges things so that the very tasks he neglected during the appointed hours in the communal monastery <note>original: "κοινοβίῳ" (koinobio); a monastery where monks live and work together.</note> are now performed in his private cell night and day with great eagerness. He is not allowed to keep the customs of prayer, nor the manner of fasting, nor the rule of vigils; instead, having bound him with the madness of greed, the demon persuades him to direct all his zeal toward manual labor <note>original: "ἐργόχειρον" (ergocheiron); specifically hand-work done by monks to support themselves.</note>.

There are three ways this disease manifests, which the Divine Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers equally forbid: 

1. One way prepares wretched men to acquire and amass those things they did not even possess while living in the world. 
2. Another way causes those who have once renounced their possessions to repent of their decision, suggesting they seek back what they had already offered to God. 
3. A third way, which from the beginning binds the monk with unbelief and lukewarmness, does not allow him to be perfectly freed from worldly things; it plants a fear of poverty and a lack of faith in God's providence, making him a transgressor of the very promises he confessed when renouncing the world.

We find examples of these three ways condemned in Divine Scripture. For **Gehazi** <note>The servant of the prophet Elisha who greedily sought gifts from Naaman (2 Kings 5).</note>, wishing to acquire money he did not previously have, lost the prophetic grace which his teacher intended to leave him as an inheritance; instead of a blessing, he inherited eternal leprosy through the Prophet's curse. And **Judas**, wishing to take money which he had previously cast away to follow Christ, not only slipped into the betrayal of the Master and fell from the choir of the Apostles, but also ended his physical life with a violent death. **Ananias** and **Sapphira**, by keeping back some of what they possessed <note>See Acts 5:1-11.</note>, were punished with death by the Apostolic 

<column-break/>

mouth. **Moses** the great, in the book of Deuteronomy, mystically commands those who promise to renounce the world but still cling to earthly things through the fear of unbelief:

> If there is any man who is fearful and cowardly in heart, let him not go out to war; let him return to his own house, lest he make the hearts of his brothers faint like his own heart. <note>Deuteronomy 20:8.</note>

Is there any testimony safer or clearer than this? Do we not learn from this that those renouncing the world must renounce it perfectly before going out to the spiritual war? We must not make a weak and corrupt beginning that turns others away from Gospel perfection and fills them with cowardice. 

Because the saying in the Divine Scripture—"it is more blessed to give than to receive"—is a holy truth, some interpret it badly to justify their own deception and desire for greed. They misrepresent the meaning of the word and the Lord’s teaching which says:

> If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. <note>Matthew 19:21.</note>

They judge it more "blessed" to maintain power over their own wealth and to give to the needy from their abundance, rather than practicing non-possession <note>original: "ἀκτημοσύνης" (aktemosynes); the monastic ideal of owning absolutely nothing.</note>. Let such people know they have not yet renounced the world, nor have they reached monastic perfection, as long as they are ashamed to take up the poverty of the Apostle for Christ’s sake. They should instead serve themselves and the needy through the work of their own hands, fulfilling the monastic promise in deed, and be glorified with the Apostle. Having scattered their old wealth, let them fight the good fight with **Paul** in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness. 

For if that same Apostle had known that keeping one's former wealth was more necessary for perfection, he would not have looked down upon its value; for he himself says he was a prominent man and a citizen of Rome. And those in Jerusalem who sold their houses and fields and placed the price at the feet of the Apostles would not have done so if they had known that the Apostles judged it "more blessed" to be fed by one's own money rather than by one's own labor...

...and by the offering of the nations. The aforementioned Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> teaches more clearly about these things in his writings to the Romans, saying: "But now I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints, for they were pleased to do so, and they are their debtors." And though he himself was often subjected to chains, prisons, and the exhaustion of travel—and hindered by these things from his usual habit of providing for himself with his own hands—he teaches that he received these necessities from the brothers who came to him from Macedonia, saying: "For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need." And writing to the Philippians: "And you Philippians yourselves know that when I left Macedonia, no church entered into partnership with me in the matter of giving and receiving, except you only. For even in Thessalonica, you sent me help for my needs once and twice." 

Let these greedy men, then, according to their own opinion, consider themselves more blessed than the Apostle, since they provided for his needs out of their own private substance! But no one, unless they had reached the height of folly, would dare to say such a thing. Therefore, if we wish to follow the Gospel command and that whole church which was founded from the beginning upon the Apostles, let us not be persuaded by our own suspicions, nor let us misunderstand what has been well said. Instead, casting aside this lukewarm and faithless opinion, let us take up the strictness of the Gospel. For in this way, we shall be able to follow in the footsteps of the Fathers, never depart from the science of the Cenobium <note>original: "Κοινοβίου" (Koinobiou); the communal life of monks living together.</note>, and truly renounce this world. 

It is good here to remember a saying of a Saint. It is told of Saint Basil, the Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, that he said the following to a certain senator who had renounced the world lukewarmly and held back some of his own money: "You have both lost the senator, and failed to become a monk." We must, therefore, with all diligence, cut out from our soul the root of all evils, which is greed <note>original: "φιλαργυρία" (philargyria); literally, "love of silver."</note>; knowing for certain that as long as the root remains, the branches will easily grow. But to achieve this virtue is difficult unless one lives in a communal monastery; for in such a place, we are free from worry even about our most basic needs.

<column-break/>

Keeping the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira <note>A New Testament couple struck dead for withholding money they promised to the community (Acts 5).</note> before our eyes, let us shudder at the thought of leaving for ourselves anything of our old substance. Likewise, fearing the example of Gehazi <note>The servant of Elisha who was cursed with leprosy for his greed (2 Kings 5).</note>, who was handed over to eternal leprosy because of his greed, let us guard ourselves against amassing money for ourselves which we did not even possess while in the world. Furthermore, considering the death of Judas by hanging, let us fear to take up anything which we once despised when we renounced the world. Above all these things, keeping always before our eyes the uncertainty of death—lest in an hour we do not expect, our Lord should come and find our conscience stained by greed—He will say to us what was said in the Gospel to that rich man: "Fool! This night they require your soul from you; and the things you prepared, whose will they be?"

### ON ANGER

Our fourth struggle is against the spirit of anger <note>original: "ὀργῆς" (orges).</note>; and it is necessary that, with God's help, we cut out its deadly venom from the depths of our soul. For while this spirit lurks in our heart and blinds the eyes of the heart with dark disturbances, we can neither acquire discernment <note>original: "διάκρισιν" (diakrisin); the ability to distinguish between good and evil impulses.</note> of what is profitable, nor find a grasp of spiritual knowledge, nor maintain the perfection of good counsel. We cannot become partakers of true life, nor will our mind be capable of perceiving the contemplation of the divine and true light. For it says: "My eye was troubled by anger." 

Neither shall we become partakers of divine wisdom, even if we are considered very wise in the opinions of everyone; since it is written: "Anger rests in the bosom of fools." Nor can we acquire the saving counsels of discernment, even if we are considered prudent by men; for it is written: "Anger destroys even the prudent." Nor shall we be able to hold the governance of righteousness with a sober heart; for it is written: "The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God." Nor can we acquire that orderliness and decency <note>original: "εὐσχημοσύνην" (euschymosynen); outward grace and proper conduct.</note> praised by all; for it is written: "An angry man is not decent." He, therefore, who wishes to [attain] toward perfect...

...[wishing] to come, and desiring to fight the spiritual struggle lawfully, let him be a stranger to every defect of anger and wrath; and let him hear what the "chosen vessel" <note>original: "σκεῦος τῆς ἐκλογῆς" (skeuos tēs eklogēs); a traditional epithet for St. Paul the Apostle, based on Acts 9:15.</note> commands him: "Let all bitterness," he says, "and anger, and wrath, and clamor, and blasphemy be put away from you, with all malice." <note>Quoting Ephesians 4:31.</note> When he says "all," he leaves us no excuse for anger, whether as necessary or reasonable. Therefore, he who wishes to correct a brother who has stumbled, or to impose a penance upon him, should strive to keep himself untroubled, lest while wishing to heal another, he draws the disease upon himself. To such a person that Gospel saying will be spoken: "Physician, heal yourself"; and again: "Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?" <note>Luke 4:23 and Matthew 7:3.</note> For from whatever cause the movement of anger boils over, it blinds the eyes of the soul, and does not allow it to behold the Sun of Righteousness. <note>A title for Christ, derived from Malachi 4:2.</note> For just as one who places gold or leaden plates over his eyes equally hinders his power of sight—the value of the gold plate making no difference in the resulting blindness—so also, from whatever cause anger is Kindled, whether seemingly reasonable or unreasonable, the power of sight is darkened. We use anger according to its nature only when we move it against passionate and pleasure-loving <term>thoughts</term> <note>original: "λογισμοὺς" (logismous); in monastic literature, these are the intrusive impulses or "seeds" of vice that tempt the soul.</note>. Thus the Prophet teaches us, saying: "Be angry, and do not sin"; <note>Psalm 4:4.</note> that is, move your anger against your own passions and against evil thoughts, and do not sin by carrying out what they suggest. And the following words clearly show this meaning: "For what you say in your hearts," he says, "be moved to compunction upon your beds." That is, when evil thoughts enter your heart, cast them out through anger against them; and after casting them out, finding yourselves as if in a bed of the soul's <term>stillness</term> <note>original: "ἡσυχίας" (hesychias); the state of inner silence and tranquility sought by monks.</note>, you may then be moved to <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "μετάνοιαν" (metanoian); literally a "change of mind."</note>. The blessed Paul agrees with this, using this same testimony and adding: "Let not the sun go down on your anger; neither give place to the devil." <note>Ephesians 4:26-27.</note> That is, do not cause Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, to set in your hearts by

<column-break/>

provoking him through your consent to wicked thoughts, lest by His withdrawal, the devil finds a place in you. Concerning this Sun, God also says through the Prophet: "But for you who fear my name, the Sun of Righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings." <note>Malachi 4:2.</note> But if we take the saying literally, we are not permitted to keep our anger even until the setting of the sun. What then shall we say of those who, through the savagery and madness of a passionate disposition, maintain their anger not only until the setting of this physical sun, but extend it for many days? They remain silent toward one another, no longer expressing it through words, but by their silence toward each other, they increase the poison of <term>rancor</term> <note>original: "μνησικακίας" (mnesikakias); the "remembrance of wrongs" or holding a grudge, considered a particularly deadly spiritual state.</note> to their own destruction. They are ignorant that one must abstain from anger not only in outward action, but also in the mind, lest the intellect be darkened by the gloom of rancor and fall away from the light of knowledge and <term>discernment</term> <note>original: "διακρίσεως" (diakriseōs); the spiritual ability to distinguish between good and evil impulses.</note>, and be deprived of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. For this reason, the Lord also commands in the Gospels to leave the gift at the altar and be reconciled with one's brother; because it is not possible for this gift to be acceptable while wrath and rancor are stored up within us. And the Apostle also teaches us this, saying we should "pray without ceasing" and "in every place lift up holy hands without anger and doubting." <note>1 Thessalonians 5:17 and 1 Timothy 2:8.</note> It follows, then, that we must either never pray—and thus be liable for breaking the apostolic command—or, striving to keep what is commanded, we must do so without anger and rancor. And since we often disregard the fact that our brothers are grieved or troubled, saying that they are grieved through no fault of ours, the Physician of souls, wishing to tear out the excuses of the soul by the roots from the heart, commands that if *we* happen to be grieved against a brother, we must leave the gift and be reconciled; but also, if *he* is grieved against us, whether justly or unjustly, we must heal him through an apology and only then offer the gift. But why should we dwell so long on the Gospel commands, when it is possible...

<meta>This page continues the teachings of St. John Cassian on the vice of anger. Having previously established that anger blinds the spiritual "eyes," he now argues that physical isolation (hermit life) is no cure for a resentful heart, as the root of the passion must be pulled out rather than merely hidden from society.</meta>

### BY SAINT CASSIAN THE ROMAN

...[learn] this from the old law; which, though it seems to have a concession regarding strictness <note>Referring to the Old Testament laws which were sometimes seen as more "external" or less rigorous than the internal requirements of the Gospel.</note>, says: "Do not hate your brother in your heart"; and again, "the ways of those who remember wrongs lead to death." <note>Leviticus 19:17 and Proverbs 12:28 (LXX).</note> Here it not only forbids the outward action, but also punishes the internal thought. Therefore, it is proper for those following the divine laws to struggle with all their might against the spirit of anger, and against the disease stored within us. We should not move our wrath against other people and then seek out the wilderness and solitude, as if the one provoking us to anger were not there; [thinking] that in solitude the virtue of <term>long-suffering</term> <note>original: "μακροθυμίας" (makrothymias); patient endurance or a "large heart" that can bear provocation.</note> will easily be achieved. For it is out of pride, and a refusal to blame ourselves and attribute the causes of our disturbance to our own laziness, that we desire withdrawal from our brothers. For as long as we attribute the causes of our weakness to others, it is impossible for us to reach the perfection of long-suffering. The core of our correction and peace, then, is not achieved through the long-suffering of our neighbor toward us, but from our own forbearance toward our neighbor. When we flee the struggle of long-suffering and seek the desert and solitude, whatever passions we carry there untreated are merely hidden, not erased. For solitude and withdrawal, for those not yet freed from passions, not only know how to preserve these passions but even to cover them up; and it does not allow them to perceive any longer by what passion they are defeated. On the contrary, it suggests to them a fantasy of virtue, and convinces them that they have achieved both long-suffering and humility, as long as there is no one present to irritate and test them. But when some occasion arises that moves and exercises them, immediately those stored-up passions—which were previously hidden—like unbridled horses leaping from their starting stalls, fed by long silence and leisure, drag their own rider more violently and savagely toward destruction. For our passions become more savage within us when they are idle from the exercise provided by [interacting with] people. Even the very shadow of patience and long-suffering, which we seemed to possess in form while mixed with the

<column-break/>

brothers, we lose through the neglect of exercise and through solitude. For just as poisonous beasts, resting quietly in the wilderness and in their own dens, only then show their own madness when they seize upon someone approaching; so also passionate people, being quiet not by a disposition of virtue but by the necessity of the desert, then vomit forth their venom when they catch hold of someone approaching and irritating them. For this reason, for those seeking the perfection of <term>gentleness</term> <note>original: "πραότητος" (praotētos); a state of mildness or meekness.</note>, every effort must be made not only not to be angry with people, but not even with irrational or inanimate things. For I remember, when I lived in the desert, becoming angry at a reed-pen because of its thickness or thinness; and again at wood, when I wanted to cut it and could not do so quickly; and again at a fire-stone <note>A flint used for striking sparks.</note>, when I was in a hurry to strike a fire and the spark did not leap out quickly. Thus anger was so intensified that I would vent it even against senseless objects. If, therefore, we desire to attain the beatitude of the Lord, we ought not only to forbid anger in action, as has been said, but also in thought. For it is not as beneficial to control the mouth in a time of wrath and not utter mad words, as it is to cleanse the heart from the <term>remembrance of wrongs</term> <note>original: "μνησικακίας" (mnēsikakias); often translated as "grudge-bearing" or "resentment."</note>, and not to turn over evil thoughts in one's own mind against a brother. For the Gospel teaching commands that the roots of sins be cut out, just as much as the fruits. For once the root of anger has been cut from the heart, neither hatred nor envy will be brought into action. For "he who hates his brother," it is said, "is a murderer"; <note>1 John 3:15.</note> for he kills him by the disposition of hatred in his mind. The blood of such a person is not poured out by a sword for men to see, but God beholds him slain by the mind and the disposition of hatred. It is He who, not only for deeds but also for thoughts and intentions, gives to each one either crowns or punishments; as He Himself says through the Prophet: "Behold, I am coming to gather their works and their thoughts." <note>Isaiah 66:18.</note> And again the Apostle says: "their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another, on the day when [God] shall judge..." <note>Romans 2:15.</note>

<summary>Cassian explains that anger is an internal disease that cannot be cured by fleeing into solitude; rather, the "root" of resentment must be extracted from the heart. He shares a personal anecdote about getting angry at inanimate objects like pens and stones to show how deep the passion of wrath can run.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discourse on the vice of anger, emphasizing that no provocation justifies wrath. It then introduces the fifth vice, sorrow (lupē), which Cassian describes as a spiritual darkness that leads to despair and isolation.</meta>

# ON THE EIGHT THOUGHTS OF WICKEDNESS
<center>7</center>

...God judges the secrets of men. And the Master Himself, teaching us that it is necessary to put away all anger, says in the Gospels: "Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment." <note>Matthew 5:22. Cassian notes a famous textual variant here; many later manuscripts added "without cause" (eikē), but he argues the older, stricter version is the original intent.</note> For this is how the accurate copies of the manuscripts contain it. The word, "without cause," was added as an insertion. It is obvious that this addition contradicts the intended purpose of the Scripture. For the Lord’s aim is that He wants us to cut off the root and the spark of anger in every way, and not to preserve even a single pretext for anger within ourselves; lest, by appearing to be moved by a "reasonable" cause at the beginning, we later fall into the madness of irrational rage. 

The perfect cure for this disease is this: that we believe that it is never permissible for us to be moved to wrath, whether for "just" or "unjust" reasons. For when the spirit of anger darkens the mind, we will find neither the light of <term>discernment</term> <note>original: "διακρίσεως" (diakriseōs); the ability to distinguish between spirits or moral choices.</note>, nor the steadiness of right counsel, nor the guidance of righteousness. Nor is it possible for our soul to become a temple of the Holy Spirit while the spirit of anger, by darkening our intellect, takes mastery over us. Finally, having the uncertainty of death before our eyes every day, we must guard ourselves from anger. And we must know that there is no benefit in self-control, nor in the renunciation of all material things, nor in fasts and vigils, if we are found liable to judgment while being held captive by anger and hatred.

### ON SORROW

Our fifth struggle is against the spirit of sorrow <note>original: "λύπης" (lupēs); in this context, it refers to a worldly or destructive grief/depression rather than godly repentance.</note>, which darkens the soul, cutting it off from all spiritual contemplation and hindering it from every good work. For whenever this evil spirit seizes the soul and darkens it entirely, it does not allow one to perform prayers with readiness, nor to persevere in the benefit of holy readings. It does not tolerate a person being gentle and compassionate toward the brothers; it creates a hatred toward all the tasks of one's work, and even toward the very profession of the [monastic] life itself. Having thrown all the soul's salvific plans into confusion, and having paralyzed its vigor and perseverance, sorrow makes the soul senseless and frantic, binding it with the thought of

<column-break/>

despair <note>original: "ἀπογνώσεως" (apognōseōs); a total loss of hope in God’s mercy.</note>. Therefore, if our aim is to fight the spiritual struggle and to defeat the spirits of wickedness with God’s help, let us guard our hearts with all watchfulness against the spirit of sorrow. 

For just as a moth eats a garment and a worm eats wood, so sorrow devours the soul of a man. It persuades him to shun every good encounter and does not allow him to receive a word of advice even from his true friends, nor does it permit him to give them a kind or peaceful answer. Instead, having wrapped itself around the entire soul, it fills it with bitterness and <term>listlessness</term> <note>original: "ἀκηδίας" (akēdias); a state of spiritual apathy or "the noonday demon."</note>. Eventually, it suggests that he should flee from other people, as if they were the causes of his disturbance. It does not allow him to recognize that the disease is not on the outside, but is stored up within; it is only revealed when trials come upon us through practice and bring it to light. 

A person will never be harmed by another unless he has the causes of the passions stored within himself. For this reason, God—the Creator of all and the Physician of souls, who alone knows accurately the wounds of the soul—does not command us to abandon the company of men, but to cut off the causes of wickedness within us. We must recognize that the health of the soul is achieved not by separation from people, but by living and practicing virtue among those who are virtuous. 

When, therefore, we abandon the brothers under some "reasonable" pretexts, we have not cut off the occasions for sorrow; we have only exchanged them, for the disease stored within will stir these feelings up again through other circumstances. Therefore, let our entire war be against the internal passions. For once these are cast out of the heart through the grace and cooperation of God, we will easily live—I do not say only with men—but even with wild beasts, according to what was said by the blessed Job: "The wild beasts shall be at peace with you." <note>Job 5:23.</note> Primarily, then, we must struggle against the spirit of sorrow that casts the soul into despair, so that we may drive it from our hearts. For it was this that did not allow Cain to repent after his brother’s murder, nor Judas after the betrayal of the Master...

The text emphasizes that the cure for these passions is internal transformation rather than physical withdrawal from society.</summary>

...sion. Let us practice only that one sorrow: the kind that leads to repentance for our sins, which is joined with a good hope. Concerning this, the Apostle said: "For godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, not to be regretted." <note>2 Corinthians 7:10. Cassian distinguishes between a healthy, transformative sorrow and a destructive, worldly one.</note> For godly sorrow, by nourishing the soul with the hope of repentance, is mixed with joy. Therefore, it makes a person eager and obedient for every good work; it makes them approachable, humble, gentle, and long-suffering, patient in every good labor and in contrition, for it is truly according to God. As a result, the fruits of the Holy Spirit are recognized in that person: namely, joy, love, peace, long-suffering, goodness, faith, and <term>self-control</term> <note>original: "ἐγκράτειαν" (enkrateian); the virtue of mastering one's desires and impulses.</note>. However, from the opposite kind of sorrow, we recognize the fruits of the evil spirit: which are <term>accidie</term> <note>original: "ἀκηδία" (akēdia); a state of listlessness or spiritual apathy often called "the noonday demon."</note>, impatience, anger, hatred, argumentative behavior, despair, and sluggishness in prayer. We ought to avoid this destructive sorrow just as we avoid sexual immorality, greed, anger, and the rest of the passions. This is healed through prayer, hope in God, the study of the divine words, and living among devout people.

### ON ACCIDIE

Our sixth struggle is against the spirit of accidie, which is linked to and works alongside the spirit of sorrow. This is a terrible and heavy demon, always at war with monks. He falls upon the monk at the <term>sixth hour</term> <note>original: "ἕκτην ὥραν" (hektēn hōran); mid-day or noon, when the heat is greatest and the monk's resolve often falters.</note>, instilling in him a sense of exhaustion and chills, and creating a hatred for his very location, for the brothers living with him, for every kind of work, and even for the reading of the Holy Scriptures. It suggests to him thoughts of moving elsewhere—claiming that unless he moves to other places, all his labor and time will be wasted. In addition to all this, it implants a hunger within him at the sixth hour, such as he would not feel after a three-day fast, or a very long journey, or the heaviest labor. Then, it puts thoughts in his mind that he cannot get rid of this sickness and burden in any other way except by constantly going out and visiting the brothers, supposedly for the sake of 

<column-break/>

spiritual benefit or for visiting the sick. When the demon cannot deceive him through these means, he then plunges him into a very heavy sleep; he becomes even more violent and powerful against the monk, and is not overthrown except through prayer, the avoidance of idle talk, the study of the divine words, and patience in temptations. For if the demon does not find him secured by these weapons, he strikes him down with his arrows, proving him to be unstable, making him a wanderer, lazy, and idle. He causes him to go around many monasteries, caring for nothing else except looking for where the best food and drink are to be found. For the mind of the person suffering from accidie imagines nothing else but these distractions. Eventually, because of this, the demon binds him to worldly matters, and little by little lures him with these harmful preoccupations until he drives him out completely from the monastic calling. The divine Apostle, knowing this sickness to be most heavy and wanting to pull it up by the roots from our souls like a wise physician, shows the primary causes from which it is born, saying: "We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks in a <term>disorderly</term> <note>original: "ἀτάκτως" (ataktōs); literally "out of rank" or "irresponsibly." Paul uses this to describe those who refuse to work.</note> manner, and not according to the tradition which you received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us; for we did not behave ourselves in a disorderly way among you; nor did we eat any man’s bread for free; but we worked with labor and toil night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. Not because we do not have authority, but to make ourselves an example for you to follow. For even when we were with you, this we commanded you: that if any would not work, neither should he eat. For we hear that there are some who walk among you in a disorderly way, working not at all, but are busybodies. Now those who are such we command and exhort by our Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread." <note>2 Thessalonians 3:6-12.</note> Let us hear how clearly the Apostle shows us the causes of accidie. For he calls "disorderly" those who do not work, revealing much wickedness in this one word. For the disorderly person is also irreverent and rash in

# ON THE EIGHT THOUGHTS OF VICE

...words, and prone to insults, and thereafter unfit for stillness, and a slave to <term>accidie</term> <note>original: "ἀκηδίας" (akēdias); a state of spiritual apathy, boredom, or listlessness often called "the noonday demon."</note>. He [the Apostle Paul] therefore commands us to withdraw from them—that is, to separate ourselves as if from a plague—and not to follow the tradition they received from us. By this expression, he shows that they are proud and contemptuous, and destroyers of apostolic traditions. And again he says: "We did not eat anyone’s bread for free, but worked with labor and toil night and day." <note>2 Thessalonians 3:8.</note> The teacher of the nations, the herald of the Gospel, the one caught up to the third heaven, who says that the Lord commanded those who proclaim the Gospel to live from the Gospel—he works with labor and toil night and day, so as not to be a burden to anyone. What then should we do, who grow listless in our work and seek bodily rest, we to whom neither the preaching of the Gospel nor the care of the churches has been entrusted, but only the care of our own souls? Then, showing more clearly the harm born of idleness, he adds: "doing no work, but being busybodies." <note>2 Thessalonians 3:11.</note> For from idleness comes meddling, and from meddling, disorder, and from disorder, every vice. Preparing their cure again, he adds: "Now such persons we command... that they work in stillness and eat their own bread." <note>2 Thessalonians 3:12.</note> And he speaks even more severely: "If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat." <note>2 Thessalonians 3:10.</note> The holy Fathers in Egypt, having been educated by these apostolic decrees, do not permit monks to be idle at any time—especially the younger ones—knowing that through the endurance of work they both drive away accidie and provide their own food, while also helping those in need. For they do not work only for their own needs, but also provide for strangers, the poor, and those in prisons from their own labor, believing such benevolence to be a holy sacrifice well-pleasing to God. And the Fathers also say this: that the one who works often fights against a single demon and is afflicted by it; but the idle person is taken captive by ten thousand spirits. In addition to these things, it is good to remember a saying of <term>Abba Moses</term> <note>One of the most famous Desert Fathers, a former bandit who became a master of the spiritual life.</note>, the most proven among the fathers, which he uttered to me

<column-break/>

after I had sat for a short time in the desert. I was troubled by accidie, and I went to him and said that yesterday, being terribly troubled by accidie and becoming very weak, I was not freed from it until I went and visited Abba Paul. In response to this, Abba Moses said to me: "Take heart; you have not freed yourself from it, but rather you have surrendered yourself as a captive and a slave. Know then, that it will fight against you even more heavily as a deserter, unless from now on you strive to overcome it through endurance, prayer, and the work of your hands."

### ON VAINGLORY

Our seventh struggle is against the spirit of <term>vainglory</term> <note>original: "κενοδοξίας" (kenodoxias); the desire for empty praise, or seeking the admiration of others for spiritual achievements.</note>. This is a multiform and very subtle passion, and it is not quickly understood, even by the one being tempted by it. Indeed, the attacks of other passions happen to be more obvious and their battle is somewhat easier, as the soul recognizes the enemy and immediately overthrows it through contradiction and prayer. But the vice of vainglory, being multiform as has been said, is difficult to combat. For it attacks in every pursuit: in voice, in speech, in silence, in work, in vigils, in fasts, in prayer, in reading, in stillness, and in patience. Through all these things, it attempts to strike down the soldier of Christ with its arrows. For instance, whomever it cannot deceive into vainglory through the luxury of clothing, it attempts to tempt through cheap garments. And whomever it could not lift up through honor, it raises to arrogance through the bearing of so-called dishonor. And whomever it could not persuade to be vainglorious through knowledge of words, it lures through silence as if they were "quiet." And whomever it could not persuade to be softened by the luxury of food, it weakens toward praise through fasting. Simply put, every work and every pursuit provides a pretext for battle to this evil demon. Furthermore, it even suggests fantasies of the <term>priesthood</term> <note>original: "κλῆρον" (klēron); literally 'lot' or 'portion', referring to the clergy or ordination.</note>. For I remember a certain elder, while I was staying in <term>Scetis</term> <note>A desert valley in Egypt that became a famous center for early Christian monks.</note>, who went to the cell of a certain brother for the sake of a visit...

# OF SAINT CASSIAN THE ROMAN

...[the elder] who, having approached his door, heard him speaking within. The elder, thinking he was practicing a reading from the Scriptures, stood listening. He realized, however, that the man was losing his mind under the influence of <term>vainglory</term> <note>original: "κενοδοξία" (kenodoxia); literally "empty glory," the desire for human approval or a false reputation for holiness.</note>. He was ordaining himself a Deacon, and granting the dismissal to the <term>catechumens</term> <note>Those receiving instruction in the faith but not yet baptized; in the early liturgy, they were dismissed before the Eucharist began.</note>. When the elder heard these things, he pushed the door and entered. The brother met him, bowed according to custom, and asked if he had been standing at the door for a long time. The elder jokingly replied to him: "I arrived just now, while you were performing the dismissal for the catechumens." When the brother heard this, he fell at the feet of the elder and begged him to pray for him, so that he might be delivered from this delusion. I have mentioned this because I wanted to show to what a state of insensibility this demon brings a person. Therefore, he who wishes to compete perfectly and to truly bind on the crown of righteousness must strive by all means to conquer this multifaceted beast. He should always keep before his eyes the saying of **David**: *The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please men.* <note>Psalm 52:6 (LXX) / 53:5 (Masoretic).</note> And he should do nothing while looking around for the praise of men, but should seek only the reward from God. He must always reject the thoughts that enter his heart and praise him, and he should humble himself before God. For in this way he will be able, with God's help, to be delivered from the spirit of vainglory.

### ON PRIDE

Our eighth struggle is against the spirit of <term>Pride</term> <note>original: "Ὑπερηφανία" (hyperēphania); considered the most dangerous of the vices because it targets those who have already made progress in virtue.</note>. This is the most difficult struggle, and more savage than all the previous ones. It especially wars against the perfect, and attempts to destroy those who have climbed almost to the very height of the virtues. Just like a plague-bearing and destructive disease does not corrupt just one member of the body, but ruins the whole of it, so Pride does not destroy just one part of the soul, but corrupts it entirely. While each of the other passions, even if it disturbs the soul, wars against only the one virtue opposed to it—striving to conquer that alone—it darkens the soul only in part. But the passion of pride

<column-break/>

darkens the soul entirely and leads it to the ultimate fall. To understand what has been said more clearly, let us look at it this way: gluttony strives to destroy self-control; lust, chastity; avarice, poverty; anger, gentleness; and the other forms of vice, their opposite virtues. But the vice of Pride, when it gains mastery over the wretched soul—like some most harsh tyrant who has captured a great and high city—overthrows it entirely and digs it up to its foundations. A witness to this is that **Angel** <note>Lucifer/Satan.</note> who fell from heaven because of pride. Although he was created by God and adorned with every virtue and wisdom, he did not wish to attribute these things to the grace of the Master, but to his own nature. Because of this, he supposed himself to be equal to God. The **Prophet**, rebuking this thought of his, said: *You said in your heart, while sitting on a high mountain: I will set my throne upon the clouds, and I will be like the Most High; but you are a man, and not God.* <note>Cf. Isaiah 14:13-14 and Ezekiel 28:2.</note> And again another **Prophet** says: *Why do you boast in malice, O mighty one?* <note>Psalm 51:3 (LXX) / 52:1 (Masoretic).</note> and the rest of the psalm. Knowing these things, therefore, let us be afraid and guard our hearts with all vigilance from the death-bearing spirit of pride. Let us always say to ourselves the words of the <term>Apostle</term> <note>St. Paul.</note> whenever we achieve some virtue: *Not I, but the grace of God which is with me.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:10.</note> And that which was spoken by the **Lord**: *For without me, you can do nothing.* <note>John 15:5.</note> And that which was spoken by the **Prophet**: *Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain.* <note>Psalm 126:1 (LXX) / 127:1 (Masoretic).</note> And also: *It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.* <note>Romans 9:16.</note> For even if someone is most boiling with eagerness and diligent in their resolve, being bound to flesh and blood, they will not be able to reach perfection except through the mercy of Christ and His grace. For **James** says: *Every good gift is from above.* <note>James 1:17.</note> And the **Apostle Paul**: *For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it, but were exalting yourself as if it were your own?* <note>1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> That salvation comes to us by the grace and mercy of God, that **thief** <note>The Penitent Thief on the cross (Luke 23:39-43).</note> is a true witness; he did not receive the Kingdom of Heaven as a prize for virtue, but by the grace and mercy of God.
