## BY THE SAME HOLY MAN

# TO ABBOT LEONTIUS

### CONCERNING THE HOLY FATHERS IN SCETIS, AND CONCERNING DISCERNMENT, A DISCOURSE FULL OF GREAT BENEFIT.

The debt I promised to the most blessed <term>Pope Castor</term> <note>Castor was the Bishop of Apt in Gaul (modern France). In this period, "Pope" was a respectful title used for various bishops, not exclusively the Bishop of Rome.</note> concerning the account of the lives of the Holy Fathers and their teaching, I have partially paid in my previous writings to him, most holy Leontius—specifically regarding the regulation of <term>cenobitic</term> monasteries <note>Monasteries where monks live in a community, rather than as hermits.</note> and the eight thoughts of vice. Now I have set out to complete it. Since I have learned that the aforementioned high priest has left us and moved to Christ, I considered it necessary to send the remaining parts of the narrative to you, who have succeeded to his virtue and, with God's help, the care of the monastery.

When we arrived in the desert of **Scetis** <note>A famous monastic center in Egypt, now known as Wadi El Natrun.</note>, where the most proven fathers of the monks dwell—I and the holy **Germanus**, who had been my spiritual friend from early youth, in the schools, in military service, and in the monastic life—we saw **Abba Moses**, a holy man shining not only in practical virtues but also in spiritual contemplation. We begged him with tears to speak a word of edification to us, through which we might be able to ascend to perfection. After much pleading, he said:

"Children," he said, "all virtues and pursuits have a certain <term>goal</term> <note>original: "σκοπόν" (skopon); the immediate target one aims at.</note>; those who look toward it and regulate themselves accordingly attain the desired <term>end</term> <note>original: "τέλος" (telos); the ultimate outcome or final destination.</note>. For the farmer, sometimes enduring the sun's flame and sometimes the cold of the frost, works the earth eagerly, having the goal of showing it clear of thorns and weeds; the end, however, is the enjoyment of the fruits. The merchant, not fearing the dangers of the sea or land, gives himself eagerly to his business, having the goal of profit from it; the end is the enjoyment of that profit. The soldier fears neither the dangers of war nor the hardships of living abroad, having the goal of advancement in rank through bravery; the end is the reward from that rank.

<column-break/>

Therefore, our own profession also has a goal and its own end, for which we eagerly endure every toil and labor. For this reason, the hunger of fasts does not wear us down; the toil of vigils delights us; the reading and meditation on the Scriptures happens eagerly; and the labor of work, obedience, the stripping away of all earthly things, and the stay in this desert are performed with pleasure. 

You, who have despised your homeland, family, and the whole world, and have accepted life in a foreign land, and have come to us, rustic and simple men, tell me: what is your goal? And looking toward what end have you done this?"

Answering, we said: "For the sake of the **Kingdom of Heaven**."

To which Abba Moses said: "You have spoken well concerning the end; but what is the goal toward which you look, so that by not turning aside from the straight path, we may be able to reach the Kingdom of the Heavens?"

...of the heavens? You did not say." And when we confessed our ignorance, the old man replied: "The **end** of our profession, as has been said, is the Kingdom of God; but the **goal** is <term>purity of heart</term> <note>original: "καθαρότης τῆς καρδίας" (katharotēs tēs kardias); a state of inner stillness and freedom from distracting passions.</note>, without which it is impossible to reach that end. Therefore, let our mind be fixed on this goal at all times. And if it should ever happen that the heart swerves a little from the straight path, let us immediately lead it back, directing it toward the goal as if by a <term>carpenter’s rule</term> <note>original: "τεκτονικῷ κανόνι" (tektonikō kanoni); a straightedge used by builders to ensure accuracy.</note>. The blessed Apostle Paul, knowing this, says: '*Forgetting those things which are behind and reaching forward to those things which are ahead, I press toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God.*' It is for the sake of this goal, therefore, that we perform all our tasks; for its sake, we despise all things—homeland, family, riches, and the whole world—so that we may acquire purity of heart. If we forget this goal, we must necessarily stumble and wander far astray, like people walking in the dark and straying from the straight path. This has happened to many who, at the beginning of their <term>renunciation</term> <note>original: "ἀποταγῆς" (apotagēs); the formal vow of a monk to leave the secular world.</note>, despised great wealth and the whole world, yet later, over a <term>hoe</term> <note>original: "δικέλλης" (dikellēs); a two-pronged mattock or garden tool.</note>, or a needle, or a reed-pen, or a book, they allow themselves to be stirred to anger and rage. They would not suffer this if they remembered the goal for which they despised all their possessions. For it is for the sake of love for our neighbor that we despise wealth, so that by fighting over it and increasing our disposition toward anger, we do not fall away from love. When, therefore, over small material things, we show that same disposition of anger toward a brother, we have fallen away from our goal, and our renunciation is of no benefit to us. The blessed Apostle knew this when he said: '*Though I give my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.*' From this we learn that perfection does not follow immediately upon the act of stripping oneself or the renunciation of possessions, but only after the attainment of love, the qualities of which the same Apostle describes: '*Love*,' he says, '*is not jealous, is not puffed up, is not provoked to anger, does not envy, does not boast, and thinks no evil.*' All these things constitute purity of heart. It is for this that one must

<column-break/>

do all things: despise money, and gladly endure fasting and vigils, and occupy oneself with reading and psalms. However, one should not, for the sake of these aforementioned practices, neglect love, should it ever happen that some necessary and God-pleasing duty prevents us from our usual fasting or reading. For the gain of fasting is not so great as the loss caused by anger, nor is the benefit of reading as great as the harm caused by showing contempt for a brother or grieving him. For fasts, vigils, the study of the Scriptures, the stripping away of wealth, and the renunciation of the whole world are not perfection itself, as has been said, but **tools of perfection**. Perfection is not found *in* these things, but is acquired *through* them. It is in vain, then, that we boast of our fasting, vigils, poverty, and reading of the Scriptures, when we have not attained love toward God and our neighbor. For he who has attained love has God within himself, and his mind is always with God."

To this, Germanus replied: "And who is able, while bound to this flesh, to keep the mind always with God so as to think of nothing else—not of visiting the sick, nor receiving guests, nor of manual labor, nor the other needs of the body, which are necessary and unavoidable? Finally, how can the human intellect always see the invisible and incomprehensible God and remain inseparable from Him?"

Moses said: "To see God always and to be inseparable from Him in the manner you imagine is impossible for a human being wearing the flesh and joined to weakness. But in another way, it is possible to see God. For the <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "θεωρία" (theoria); the spiritual perception or "vision" of divine truth.</note> of God is understood and perceived in many ways. For God is known not only in His blessed and incomprehensible essence—for this is reserved in the future age for His Saints alone—but He is also known from the majesty and beauty of His creations, and from His daily governance and providence, and from His justice, and from the wonders which He displays in every generation toward His Saints. For when we consider the measureless nature of His power and His sleepless...

<summary>Abba Moses explains that while the Kingdom of Heaven is the ultimate destination, the immediate goal of a monk is "purity of heart." He argues that spiritual disciplines like fasting are merely tools to achieve love, and that God can be "seen" through the beauty of creation and His daily providence.</summary>

# DISCOURSE ON DISCERNMENT.

...His eye, which looks upon the hidden things of the heart and from whom nothing can be hidden; gripped by a trembling in our hearts, we wonder at and worship Him. When we consider that the drops of rain, the sand of the sea, and the stars of heaven are all numbered by Him, we are struck with awe at the greatness of His nature and His wisdom. When we consider His ineffable and indescribable wisdom, His love for mankind, and His incomprehensible patience—which bears the countless failings of those who sin—we glorify Him. When we consider His great love toward us, that even though we had done nothing good, He condescended to become man, though He was God, so that He might save us from error, we are stirred to a longing for Him. When we consider that He Himself conquers our adversary, the devil, within us, and for the sake of our <term>will</term> <note>original: "προαιρέσεως" (proaireseōs); the faculty of moral choice or intention.</note> alone and our turning toward the good, He grants us eternal life, we worship Him. There are also other countless forms of <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "θεωρίαι" (theōriai); spiritual visions or insights gained through prayer and purification.</note> like these which, according to the proportion of our labor and the measure of our purification, spring up within us, through which God is seen and understood.

Then Germanus asked again: "How does this happen? For often, even when we do not wish it, many memories and <term>evil thoughts</term> <note>original: "πονηροὶ λογισμοὶ" (ponēroi logismoi); intrusive, distracting, or sinful thoughts that the desert fathers analyzed as the roots of sin.</note> trouble us. Almost without our knowing, they steal upon us, entering secretly and subtly; so much so that not only are we unable to stop them from coming, but it is even very difficult to recognize them. We wish to learn if it is possible for the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "διάνοιαν" (dianoian); the discursive intellect or faculty of thought.</note> to be entirely free from these things and not be troubled by them at all."

Moses said: "For the mind not to be troubled by these memories is impossible; but to accept them and dwell on them, or to cast them out, is possible for everyone who strives. For just as their coming is not within our power, so their expulsion lies within our authority. The correction of our mind is also within our will and diligence. For when we wisely and continually meditate on the law of God, occupy ourselves with psalms and hymns, devote ourselves to fasts and vigils, and continually remember the things to come—both the Kingdom of Heaven and the <term>Gehenna</term> <note>original: "γεέννης" (geennēs); a reference to the place of spiritual punishment or "hell."</note>

<column-break/>

of fire—and all the works of God, then evil thoughts diminish and find no place. But when we occupy ourselves with worldly cares and fleshly matters, and give ourselves over to vain or idle conversations, then foul thoughts multiply within us. For just as a <term>water-mill</term> <note>original: "μύλον ἐξ ὑδάτων" (mylon ex hydatōn); a common mechanical analogy in ancient literature to describe perpetual motion.</note> moved by water cannot stop its movement, yet it is in the power of the one standing over the mill to grind either wheat or weeds; so also our mind, being always in motion, cannot be idle from thoughts. But it is within our power to give it either spiritual meditation or fleshly labor."

Seeing us marvelling and struck with awe at these things, and seeing that we were disposed toward his words with an insatiable longing, the old man was silent for a short while, and then said: "Since your longing has extended the discourse to such a length, and you are still eager—from which I gather that you truly thirst for the teaching of perfection—I wish to speak to you about the excellent good of <term>discernment</term> <note>original: "διακρίσεως" (diakriseōs); the ability to distinguish between good and evil impulses, often considered the highest practical virtue in monasticism.</note>. Among the other virtues, this one happens to be a kind of citadel and queen. I will show its excellence, its height, and its benefit, not only from our own words but also from the ancient opinions of the Fathers; for the Lord provides grace to those who explain, according to the merit and the longing of the listeners. For it is no small virtue, but one that ranks among the most distinguished gifts of the Holy Spirit. Among these, the Apostle says: '*To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another faith, by the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing; to another the **discernment of spirits**.*' Then, having completed the list of spiritual gifts, he adds: '*But one and the same Spirit works all these things.*'

You see, therefore, that the gift of discernment is not earthly, nor is it small, but it is a very great gift of divine grace. If the monk does not follow it with all his power and diligence, and if he does not acquire the discernment of the spirits that rise up within him with a firm reason, he must necessarily wander as if in the night; not only falling into the most difficult pits of wickedness, but even stumbling on level and straight ground. I remember, for instance, once in...

# OF THE HOLY CASSIAN THE ROMAN

In the years of my youth, while I was in the regions of the Thebaid where the blessed Anthony lived, some Elders gathered to see him and held a discussion with him concerning the perfection of virtue. They asked: "Which of all the virtues is the greatest, and which is able to keep a monk safe from the snares of the devil and his deceit?" Each one then gave an opinion according to the understanding of his own mind. Some said fasting and vigils, because through these the mind is refined and purity is attained, allowing one to approach God more easily. Others said <term>detachment</term> <note>original: "ἀκτημοσύνη" (aktēmosynē); the voluntary poverty and lack of possessions practiced by monks.</note> and the contempt for one's own affairs, because by this the mind is freed from the complex ropes of worldly care, making it easier to approach God. Others chose the virtue of almsgiving, as the Lord says in the Gospels: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me to eat," and so on. When each had spoken in this manner according to his own judgment, suggesting various virtues by which a person might more easily approach God, and after the greater part of the night had passed, consumed by this inquiry, the blessed Anthony spoke last of all. "All these things you have said are both necessary and beneficial to those who seek God and desire to come to Him. But we are not permitted to grant the first prize to these virtues. For we have found many who were worn out by fasts and vigils, and who withdrew themselves into the desert, and who practiced detachment to such an extreme that they did not even leave themselves daily food, and who performed almsgiving to the point that they had nothing left to give—yet after all this, they fell miserably away from virtue and slipped into vice. What was it, then, that caused them to fall from the straight path? In my definition and my opinion, it was nothing else than that they did not possess the gift of <term>discernment</term> <note>original: "διάκρισις" (diakrisis); the spiritual faculty of judgment that avoids extremes and perceives the true source of thoughts.</note>. For this virtue teaches a person to leave behind excess on either side and to walk the royal road."

<column-break/>

"Discernment does not allow one to be robbed from the 'right side' through immoderate self-control, nor to be dragged down to the 'left side' through indifference and sloth. Indeed, discernment is a kind of eye and lamp of the soul, according to that voice from the Gospel which says: 'The lamp of the body is the eye; if therefore your eye is single, your whole body will be light; but if your <margin>evil</margin> eye* is dark, your whole body will be dark.' And so it is: because discernment investigates all the thoughts and actions of a person, it distinguishes and separates every foul thing and anything displeasing to God, and keeps error far from him. One may learn this also from the histories in the Divine Scriptures. For that man Saul, the first entrusted with the kingship of Israel—because he did not have this eye of discernment, his mind was darkened. He did not know how to discern that it was more pleasing to God to obey the command of the Holy Samuel than to offer a sacrifice. From the very things by which he thought he was serving God, he caused offense and was cast out from the kingdom. He would not have suffered this if he had possessed the light of discernment within himself. The Apostle also calls this 'the sun,' according to his saying: 'Let not the sun go down upon your anger.' This is also called the <term>governance</term> <note>original: "κυβέρνησις" (kybernēsis); literally the steering or piloting of a ship.</note> of our life, according to what is written: 'Those who have no governance fall like leaves.' It is called 'counsel' by the Scripture, without which we are taught by the Scripture to do nothing—so much so that we are not even permitted to drink the spiritual wine which gladdens the heart of man without it, as the saying goes: 'Drink wine with counsel.' And again, it says: 'As a city is broken down and without walls, so is a man who does not do all things with counsel.' In this virtue, wisdom, understanding, and perception consist; without these, neither can our inner house be built, nor can spiritual wealth be gathered, as it is said: 'With wisdom a house is built, and with understanding it is set upright, and with prudence the storehouses of wealth are filled.' This is also called 'solid food,' belonging to those who through practice have their senses..."

<summary>Saint Anthony the Great explains to a group of desert elders that discernment (diakrisis) is the highest virtue, as it prevents spiritual pride and extreme asceticism from leading to a fall. Using scriptural metaphors like the "eye of the soul" and "governance," he argues that even good deeds like fasting and poverty fail without this guiding wisdom.</summary>

# DISCOURSE ON DISCERNMENT

...having their senses exercised to discern both good and evil. Through these words, it is clearly demonstrated that no virtue can be established or remain firm until the end without the gift of discernment; for discernment is the mother and the guardian of all virtues. This was the definition and the opinion of Anthony, with which the rest of the Fathers agreed. And so that we may confirm the definition of Saint Anthony with fresh examples from our own times, remember the elder Heron, and the pitiful fall which he suffered just a few days ago before our very eyes. Consider how, through the mockery of the devil, he was cast down from that height of his ascetic life into the depths of death. For we remember him spending fifty years in <term>Scetis</term><note>original: "Σκήτει" (Skete); a famous monastic settlement in the Egyptian desert, a cradle of early Christian monasticism.</note>, practicing great hardship and intense self-control, seeking out the furthest desert and a solitude beyond all others living there. Yet, after so many labors and struggles, he was deceived by the devil and slipped into a most grievous fall, casting all the fathers and brothers in Scetis into inconsolable grief. He would not have suffered this if he had been protected by the virtue of discernment, which would have taught him not to trust his own <term>reasoning</term><note>original: "λογισμῷ" (logismō); refers to one's private thoughts or internal justifications, which monks were warned not to trust without the guidance of an elder.</note>, but to obey the counsel of the fathers and brothers. For he followed his own reasoning to such an extent, pursuing fasting and isolation from men, that he would not even come to the Church for the feast of Holy Pascha (Easter). He did this so that he would not have to meet with the fathers and brothers or eat with them, fearing he might be forced to partake of <gloss>legumes</gloss> or anything else offered at the table, and thus appear to have fallen away from his own personal goal and rule. Having been deceived by his own will for a long time, he eventually welcomed an angel of Satan, worshipping him as an angel of light. He was commanded by this "angel" at midnight to throw himself into a very deep well, so that he might know by experience that he would never again be subject to any danger because of the great virtue and labors for God that he possessed. Without discerning the one who gave this advice with his reason, but being darkened in his intellect, he threw himself into the well at midnight.

<column-break/>

And not long after, the brothers realized what had happened and were barely able, with much labor, to pull him out half-dead. After he was pulled out, he lived for two days and died on the third, leaving the brothers and the priest <term>Paphnutius</term><note>A famous desert father and disciple of Saint Macarius.</note> in inconsolable grief. Paphnutius, moved by great compassion and remembering Heron’s many labors and the numerous years he had endured in the desert, did not exclude him from the memory and the <term>offering</term><note>original: "προσφορᾶς" (prosphoras); the liturgical prayers and Eucharistic offerings made for the departed.</note> for those who have fallen asleep, so that he would not be numbered among those who die a <gloss>violent death</gloss><note>original: "βιαιοθανάτοις" (biaiothanatois); a term often used for those who commit suicide, who were typically denied full Christian burial rites.</note>. 

What shall I say about those two brothers who stayed beyond the desert of the <term>Thebaid</term><note>A region in Upper Egypt, named after Thebes, where many early hermits lived.</note>, where the blessed Anthony once lived? These two, moved by an undiscerning reasoning, decided to travel into the inner desert, which was vast and uninhabited. They judged within themselves that they would not receive food from any human hand, but only that which the Lord would provide for them by a miracle. When they were wandering in the desert and fainting from hunger, they were spotted from afar by the <term>Mazices</term><note>original: "Μάζικες"; a nomadic Berber tribe of North Africa, often feared by monks for their raids.</note>—a tribe that is perhaps the wildest and most cruel of all savage nations. Yet, through divine providence, they changed their natural wildness into kindness and met the monks with bread. One of the two brothers, when discernment came upon him, accepted the bread with joy and thanksgiving. He reasoned that these men, who were so cruel and savage and always delighted in human blood, would never have shown compassion to those who were already fainting and brought them food unless God had moved them. But the other brother refused the food because it was brought to him by men; persisting in his undiscerning plan, he perished from the exhaustion of starvation. Therefore, even though both had made a bad plan at the beginning and followed an irrational and deadly opinion, the one corrected what he had rashly and recklessly decided when discernment entered him. But the other, persisting in his foolish preconception and being found without discernment, brought upon himself the death which the Lord had wished to turn away from him.

And what shall I say about that man whose name I do not wish to mention because he is still alive? He frequently welcomed a demon as an angel...

### OF SAINT CASSIAN THE ROMAN

...receiving revelations through him <note>Referring to the devil disguised as an angel of light.</note>, and continually seeing a lamp-light in his cell. Later, he was commanded by this visitor to offer his own son—who was staying with him in the monastery—as a sacrifice to God, so that by this act he might be deemed worthy of the same honor as the Patriarch Abraham. He was so led astray by this advice that he would have carried out the slaughter of his son in actual deed, had the son not seen him—contrary to his usual habit—sharpening a knife and preparing bonds with which he intended to bind him like a whole burnt offering, and thus secured his safety by flight. 

It would be a long story to relate the deception of that Mesopotamian monk who, after displaying such great self-control and living shut up in a cell for many years, was later so mocked by diabolical revelations and dreams. Despite all his labors and virtues, in which he surpassed all the monks living there, he fell away into <term>Judaism</term><note>In this monastic context, "Judaism" refers to the specific deception of a Christian abandoning their faith for Jewish rites like circumcision under the influence of a "revelation."</note> and circumcision. For the devil, wishing to deceive him, frequently showed him true dreams so that, through these, he might make the error he intended to suggest at the last more easily accepted. 

One night, the devil showed him the crowd of Christians with the Apostles and Martyrs as dark and filled with all shame, wasting away in grief and mourning. Conversely, he showed the crowd of the Jews with Moses and the Prophets shining with a brilliant light, living in joy and cheerfulness. The deceiver then advised him that if he wished to share in the blessedness and joy of the Jewish people, he should receive circumcision; and he, being deceived, did exactly that. 

It is clear, therefore, from all that has been said, that all those mentioned would not have been mocked so piteously and miserably if they had happened to possess the gift of **discernment**. To this, Germanus said: "By both recent examples and the definitions of the ancient fathers, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that discernment is the source, root, head, and bond of all virtues. But in what way can we acquire it, we desire to learn? And how can we recognize the true discernment that comes from God, and that which is falsely named, counterfeit, and diabolical?" Then Abba Moses said: "True discernment is not acquired

<column-break/>

except through true humility, by revealing not only what we do but also what we <term>think</term><note>original: "ἐνθυμούμεθα" (enthumoumetha); the inner deliberations of the mind.</note> to the fathers. We must not trust in any of our own **reasoning**, but follow the words of the elders in everything, believing that to be good which they themselves approve. This practice not only prepares the monk to remain unharmed through true discernment and the right path, but also preserves him safe from all the snares of the devil. For it is impossible for one who regulates his life by the judgment and opinion of those who have gone before him to fall into the deception of demons. 

Even before someone is deemed worthy of the gift of discernment, the very act of manifesting and revealing <term>wicked thoughts</term><note>original: "φαύλας ἐνθυμήσεις" (phaulas enthumēseis).</note> to the fathers withers them and makes them weaker. For just as a snake brought out from a dark hole into the light hastens to flee and disappear, so also do evil <term>thoughts</term><note>original: "λογισμοί" (logismoi); the internal impulses or suggestions that lead to sin.</note>, when made manifest through excellent confession and disclosure, hasten to flee from the person. 

So that you may learn this virtue more accurately and by example, I will relate the deed of Abba Serapion, which he himself used to offer continually to those who visited him for the sake of protection. For he said: 'When I was younger, I lived with my Abba. When we ate, as I rose from the table, driven by the influence of a demon, I would steal a <term>biscuit</term><note>original: "παξαμᾶν" (paxaman); a hard monastic rusk or twice-baked bread.</note> and eat it in secret from my Abba. Since I continued doing this for some time, being mastered by it, I was unable to overcome it. I was judged only by my own conscience, for I was ashamed to tell the elder. 

But it happened by the providence of the loving God that certain brothers came to the elder for the sake of spiritual benefit, and they asked him about their own thoughts. The elder replied that nothing so harms monks and gladdens demons as hiding one's thoughts from spiritual fathers. He also spoke to them about self-control. While these things were being said, I came to myself and, considering that God had revealed my failings to the elder, I was pricked in my heart and began to cry. I pulled the biscuit out from the fold of my garment, which I had wickedly made a habit of stealing, and throwing myself on the ground, I asked for forgiveness...'

# DISCOURSE ON DISCERNMENT

<column-break/>

...of things past; and prayer for the security of things to come. Then the elder said: "O child, your **confession** has set you free, even while I remained silent. And the demon who was wounding you through your silence—because you spoke out regarding your own state—you have now slain. Up until now, you allowed him to lord it over you by neither speaking against him nor rebuking him. From this moment on, he shall no longer have a place in you, having been brought out from your heart into the light."

The elder had not yet finished speaking when, behold, the <term>energy</term><note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia). In this context, it refers to the actual presence or manifestation of the demonic power.</note> appeared like a torch of fire being drawn out of my chest. It filled the house with such a stench that those present thought a great quantity of sulfur was being burned. Then the elder said: "Behold, the Lord has provided the proof of my words and of your liberation through this sign which has occurred." Thus, through this confession, the passion of **gluttony** <note>original: "γαστριμαργία" (gastrimargia), literally "belly-madness."</note> and that diabolical energy departed from me, so much so that I never again felt even a trace of such a desire. 

Behold, therefore, we learn from the words of **Abba Serapion** that we are deemed worthy of the gift of true **discernment** <note>original: "διάκρισις" (diakrisis). This is the primary virtue discussed in this text: the ability to distinguish between divine, natural, and demonic impulses.</note> only when we do not trust the judgment of our own minds, but rather the teaching and tradition of the fathers. Indeed, through no other fault does the devil lead a monk over such precipices as when he persuades him to disregard the admonitions of the fathers and follow his own judgment and will. 

We ought to take examples from human arts and sciences to be educated. For if we are unable to master these things—which we can handle with our hands, see with our eyes, and hear with our ears—on our own, but rather require someone to teach us well and guide us, how foolish is it to think that the **spiritual art**, the most difficult of all arts, does not require a teacher? This art is invisible and hidden, perceived only by purity of heart; a failure in this art brings not a temporary loss, but the destruction of the soul and eternal death.

**Germanus** said: "A pretext of shame and a cloak of harmful 'piety' <note>Germanus is referring to a false sense of reverence or 'pious' fear that prevents a monk from being honest.</note> often arises from the fact that many, having heard the thoughts of the brothers, not only fail to heal them, but even con-

<column-break/>

-demn them and drive them to despair. We ourselves have known this to happen in the regions of Syria. A certain brother disclosed his own thoughts to one of the elders there with all simplicity and truth, shamelessly stripping bare the secrets of his own heart. But as soon as the elder heard him, he began to be indignant and moved against the brother, blaming him for such foul reflections. As a result, many who heard of this were too ashamed to announce their own thoughts to the elders."

**Abba Moses** said: "It is good, as I said before, not to hide one’s own thoughts from the fathers. However, one should not tell them to just anyone, but to **spiritual elders** who possess discernment—not merely those who are gray-haired with age. For many, looking only to age and disclosing their thoughts, have fallen into despair instead of finding a cure, due to the inexperience of those listening. 

There was a certain brother who was very diligent, but was violently troubled by the demon of **fornication**. He went to a certain elder and announced his thoughts to him. But that man, being inexperienced, became indignant and called the brother miserable and unworthy of the **monastic habit** <note>original: "μοναχικὸν σχῆμα" (monachikon schema). The "habit" or "schema" represents the monk's rank and commitment; to be "unworthy" of it is a severe judgment.</note> for even entertaining such thoughts. Hearing this, the brother despaired of himself and, leaving his own place, began to return to the world. 

But by the providence of God, **Abba Apollo**, the most proven of the elders, met him. Seeing him troubled and very gloomy, he asked him: 'Child, what is the cause of such great sadness?' At first, out of great despondency, the brother answered nothing. But later, after being much encouraged by the elder, he revealed his situation, saying: 'Thoughts often trouble me, and I went and told them to such-and-forth elder; according to his word, there is no hope of salvation for me. Having despaired of myself, I am going back into the world.'

When Father Apollo heard these things, he greatly encouraged and admonished the brother, saying: 'Do not be surprised, child, nor despair of yourself. For even I, at such an age and with these gray hairs, am violently troubled by these very thoughts. Do not, therefore, lose heart over such a burning, which is not cured so much by human effort as...'"

<summary>Abba Serapion recounts how confessing a secret sin physically expelled a demon, while Abba Moses warns that monks must seek out discerning, experienced elders—rather than just those old in years—to avoid being driven to despair by harsh judgment.</summary>

# OF SAINT CASSIAN THE ROMAN

...by the loving-kindness of God. "Only grant me today," he said, "and return to your cell." The brother did as he was told. And Abba Apollo, leaving him, went to the cell of the elder who had driven the brother to despair. Standing outside, he entreated God with tears, saying:

> Lord, you who bring temptations for our benefit, transfer the spiritual war of the brother onto this elder, so that through experience in his old age he may learn what he was not taught over many years: how to suffer along with those who are under assault.

As he finished the prayer, he saw an <term>Ethiopian</term><note>original: "αἰθίοπα" (aithiopa). In early monastic literature, demons were often described in this way to symbolize darkness and spiritual "otherness."</note> standing near the cell, shooting arrows at the elder. Wounded by them, the elder immediately began to stagger here and there as if drunk. Unable to endure the pressure, he left his cell and took the very same road toward <term>the world</term><note>original: "ἐπὶ τὸν κόσμον" (epi ton kosmon). In a monastic context, this refers to abandoning the religious life to return to secular society.</note> as the younger man had. But Abba Apollo, perceiving what had happened, met him and said: "Where are you going? What is the cause of this turmoil that possesses you?" Realizing that the Saint knew his condition, the elder said nothing out of shame. Then Abba Apollo said to him:

> Return to your cell, and from now on recognize your own weakness. Consider yourself either ignored by the devil or despised by him, since you were never deemed worthy of a struggle against him. Why do I say struggle? You could not endure even one day of his assault!

This happened to you because, when you received a younger man being warred upon by our common enemy, instead of anointing him for the contest, you cast him into despair. You failed to consider that wise command which says: 

> Deliver those being led away to death, and do not hesitate to ransom those being slain.

Nor did you consider the parable of our Savior, which says: 

> A bruised reed he shall not break, and a smoking wick he shall not quench.

For no one could bear the enemy’s plots, nor quench the fiery boiling of nature, if the grace of God did not guard our human weakness. Therefore, since this <term>saving economy</term><note>original: "σωτηριώδους ταύτης οἰκονομίας" (sōtēriōdous tautēs oikonomias). Here, 'economy' refers to God's purposeful and instructional management of human events.</note> concerning us has been fulfilled, let us beseech God with new prayers to turn aside the lash that was released against you. For he causes pain, and then restores; he strikes, and his hands heal; he humbles and exalts; he brings death and gives life; he brings down to Hades and brings up again.

<column-break/>

Having said these things and prayed, he immediately delivered the elder from the war that had been brought upon him. He exhorted him to ask God to give him "the tongue of the learned," so that he might know at what time it is necessary to speak a word. From all that has been said, then, we learn that no other safe path to salvation will be found except the practice of reporting one's own <term>thoughts</term><note>original: "λογισμούς" (logismous). In ascetic theology, these are not just simple ideas but intrusive spiritual provocations or temptations.</note> to the most discerning of the Fathers, and by them being directed toward virtue, rather than following one's own judgment and criteria. 

For even if one happens to encounter a simpler elder, or a few who are inexperienced, one must not for this reason flee from reporting their thoughts to the most proven Fathers, nor despise the tradition of the ancestors. For the Fathers themselves did not act on their own impulse, but from God and the God-inspired Scriptures. They handed down to later generations the practice of questioning those who have progressed further. This can be learned from many other passages in the God-inspired Scripture, but especially from the history concerning **Saint Samuel**. Though he was dedicated to God by his mother from infancy and deemed worthy of divine conversation, he did not trust his own judgment. Instead, having been called once and twice by God, he ran back to the elder **Eli**, and by his teaching was shaped and guided in how he ought to answer God. Thus, the one whom God himself voted worthy of his call, God willed to be trained by the instruction and direction of the elder—evidently so that he would be led toward humility. 

Even **Paul**, when Christ called him personally and spoke with him, though Christ was able to open his eyes immediately and make known the way of perfection, he referred him to **Ananias**. He commanded him to learn the way of truth from him, saying:

> Arise and go into the city, and there it will be told to you what you must do.

By these examples, he teaches us to follow the guidance of those who have moved ahead, lest the good thing said of Paul be misunderstood and become an example of arrogance for those who come after—each person wanting to be led to the truth by God in a manner similar to Paul, rather than through the Fathers. That these things are indeed this way is possible to learn not only from what has been said...

The text concludes that spiritual safety lies in revealing one's thoughts to experienced elders rather than relying on private judgment, citing Samuel and St. Paul as examples.</summary>

<header>DISCOURSE ON DISCERNMENT.</header>

...not only from what he said, but also from what the Apostle showed by his own deeds, where he writes: "I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter and James, and I laid before them the Gospel which I preach; lest by any means I should be running, or had run, in vain." This he did despite the grace of the Holy Spirit accompanying him through the power of the signs he performed. Who, then, is so proud and arrogant as to follow his own opinion and judgment, when the <term>chosen vessel</term><note>original: "σκεῦος τῆς ἐκλογῆς" (skeuos tēs eklogēs). A traditional title for the Apostle Paul, referencing Acts 9:15.</note> confesses that he needed the counsel of the Apostles who were before him? It is clearly demonstrated through these examples that the Lord reveals the way of perfection to no one except those guided to it by spiritual Fathers, just as He says through the Prophet: "Ask your father, and he will announce it to you; your elders, and they will tell you." Therefore, with all our power and diligence, we ought to acquire the good gift of **discernment** within ourselves; which will be able to keep us unharmed from either extreme. For, as the Fathers say, the extremes on either side are equally harmful: both the excess of fasting and the satiation of the belly; the immoderation of wakefulness and the surfeit of sleep; and all other excesses. Indeed, we have known some who, though not defeated by gluttony, were cast down by immoderate fasting and slipped into the very passion of gluttony because of the weakness resulting from that immoderate fasting. I myself remember once suffering such a thing; I practiced <term>self-restraint</term><note>original: "ἐγκρατευσάμενος" (enkrateusamenos), referring to the ascetic discipline of enkrateia or temperance.</note> to such an extent that I forgot the desire for food; I remained without eating for two or three days and did not desire food at all, unless others prompted me to eat. And again, from my eyes—by the plot of the devil—sleep so departed that for many nights I remained awake, entreating the Lord that I might partake of even a little sleep. I was in greater danger from immoderate starvation and wakefulness than from gluttony and the fullness of sleep. With such and so many teachings did Saint Moses gladden us; so that, having benefited, we might glorify the Lord, who provides such wisdom to those who fear Him. To Him belong honor and power unto the ages. Amen.

# A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER
# MARK THE ASCETIC

---

<image-desc>Ornate drop cap initial 'O' set within a decorative rectangular frame featuring scrollwork and vine motifs.</image-desc>
Our Holy Father Mark the Ascetic flourished around the year four hundred and thirty. He was a disciple of Saint John Chrysostom, according to <term>Nikephoros Kallistos</term><note>original: "Νικηφόρον Κάλλιστον." A 14th-century Byzantine historian known for his "Ecclesiastical History."</note> in Volume 2, Book 14, Chapter 58. He was a contemporary of Saint Nilus and Isidore of

<column-break/>

Pelusium, those renowned Ascetics. Being industrious and having devoted himself to the study of the Divine Scriptures, he composed many discourses full of all kinds of instruction and benefit. Thirty-two of these are mentioned by Nikephoros Kallistos as teaching every path of the ascetic life, though they are not currently found.

<summary>This page concludes the teaching of Abba Moses on the "Golden Mean" of discernment, warning that excessive fasting or wakefulness can be as spiritually dangerous as gluttony. It then begins a biographical sketch of Mark the Ascetic, a 5th-century disciple of John Chrysostom.</summary>

<keywords>discernment, Apostle Paul, spiritual fathers, moderation, fasting, gluttony, insomnia, Abba Moses, Mark the Ascetic, Nikephoros Kallistos, John Chrysostom, asceticism</keywords>

--- Page 66 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the teachings of the Desert Fathers (specifically the discourse on discernment) to the works of Saint Mark the Ascetic. The previous page concluded the biography of Abba Moses and introduced the lineage of spiritual authority that leads to Mark.</meta>

<header>OF THE HOLY MARK THE ASCETIC</header>

Only eight other discourses of his, among those he spoke, are preserved. These are mentioned by Kallistos himself, as well as by the critic Photios in his *Library* <note>original: "Ἀναγνώσει" (Anagnōsei) - literally 'Reading,' referring to the sections of Photios’s massive 9th-century literary review</note>, volume 6, page 268.

Among these, the first discourse—"On the Spiritual Law"—and the third—"On those who think they are justified by works"—are arranged here into brief, concise chapters. The eighth discourse, "To the Monk Nicholas," is also included here, as these are the most useful and relate directly to the spiritual law. His writings are also mentioned by the Holy Martyr Peter Damascene, and by the one among

<column-break/>

the Saints, Gregory of Thessaloniki <note>Gregory Palamas, the 14th-century defender of Hesychasm</note>, as well as Gregory of Sinai, the most holy Patriarch Kallistos, Paul of Evergetis, and many other Fathers. These fathers not only read these works themselves but also strongly encourage us to read them.

The Holy Church of Christ also honors him, celebrating his memory on the 5th of March, proclaiming his ascetic struggles, his wisdom in words, and the grace of miracles given to him from above.

<margin>2.</margin> First, we know that God is the beginning, the middle, and the end of every good thing. Furthermore, it is impossible for good to be put into action or to be truly believed except in Christ Jesus and the Holy Spirit.

13. ->He who prays only with his body and does not yet have spiritual knowledge is like the blind man crying out and saying: "Son of David, have mercy on me."<- <note>A reference to the blind man Bartimaeus in Mark 10:47; "bodily prayer" refers to reciting words without inner mental focus or spiritual insight.</note>

<margin>77.</margin>
From the love of pleasure comes neglect, and from neglect comes forgetfulness. For God has gifted the knowledge of what is beneficial to everyone.

<margin>78.</margin>

<margin>79.</margin>

<margin>80.</margin>

<margin>81.</margin>
The person who possesses a sound understanding but boasts in their ignorance is not only simple in their speech, but also in their knowledge.

<margin>82.</margin>
For just as the wisdom of words is one thing and prudence is another, so also is simplicity of speech one thing and foolishness another.

<margin>83.</margin>
Ignorance of words will not harm a most pious man, just as the wisdom of words does not harm the humble-minded.

<margin>84.</margin>
Do not say, "I do not know what is necessary, and therefore I am blameless for not doing it." For if you did the good things you *did* know, the rest would be revealed to you in sequence, <note>original: "oikeios tropon hen di' henos"</note> understood one by one in their proper order. It does not benefit you

<column-break/>

to know the second things before you have practiced the first. For knowledge "puffs up" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 8:1: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up."</note> because of idleness, but love builds up because it endures all things.

<margin>85.</margin>
Read the words of Holy Scripture through actions, and do not be wordy, being puffed up by mere intellectual concepts.

<margin>86.</margin>
He who abandons action and relies on mere knowledge holds a staff made of reed instead of a double-edged sword; which, in time of war—according to the Scripture—will pierce his hand and enter it, injecting the poison of his own nature before his enemies do.

<margin>87.</margin>
Every thought has a measure and a weight before God. For it is possible to consider the same thing either with passion or with a single-minded purpose.

<margin>88.</margin>
He who has performed a commandment should expect the trial that follows it. For love for Christ is tested by opposing circumstances.

<margin>89.</margin>
Never be contemptuous by neglecting your thoughts. For God is unerring and watches every intent.

<margin>90.</margin>
When you see a thought suggesting human glory to you, know clearly that it is preparing shame for you.

<margin>91.</margin>
The enemy of the spiritual law understands what is just, and seeks only our mental consent. For in this way, he will either make the person under his power liable to the labors of repentance, or if they do not repent, he will cause them pain through involuntary afflictions. Sometimes he even prepares the person to fight against these afflictions, so that their pains are multiplied here, and at their departure from this life, he may prove them faithless because of their lack of patience.

<margin>92.</margin>
Many have resisted the things that happen to them; but apart from prayer and repentance, no one has escaped a terrible fate.

<margin>93.</margin>
Evils gain their power one through another; likewise, good things grow through each other, and they urge those who participate in them to move even further forward.

<margin>94.</margin>
The devil makes small sins seem trivial. For otherwise, he cannot lead a person toward greater evils.

<margin>95.</margin>
The root of shameful desire is human praise, just as the root of self-control is the rebuke of our vices—not only when we hear it, but when we also accept it.

<margin>96.</margin>
He who has renounced the world but still enjoys... <unclear>pleasure?</unclear> has gained no benefit...

...passions. For what he used to do through money, he does even when possessing nothing.

<margin>97. <note>original: "ψζ΄"</note> In another version: "possess."</margin> Again, the self-controlled person, if they acquire money, is a brother to the former in their mind; they share the same mother because of the mental pleasure, but have a different father because of the specific way the <term>passion</term><note>A "passion" in this context is a disordered impulse, like an addiction or an uncontrolled emotion.</note> has changed.

<margin>98.</margin> There is one who cuts off a passion for the sake of a greater indulgence, and he is glorified by those who are ignorant of his true aim. Perhaps he even ignores his own heart, performing deeds that bring no spiritual profit.

<margin>99.</margin> The cause of all vice is <term>vainglory</term><note>kenodoxia: the empty desire for the praise of others</note> and pleasure; he who does not hate these will not strip away his passions.

<margin>100.</margin> The "love of money" is said to be the root of all evils, but it is clear that it is sustained through those other two <insert>vainglory and pleasure</insert>.

<margin>101.</margin> The mind is blinded by these three passions: I mean the love of money, vainglory, and pleasure.

<margin>102.</margin> These are the "three daughters of the leech" according to the Scripture, loved with great affection by their mother, Foolishness. <note>This refers to Proverbs 30:15: "The leech has two daughters, crying, 'Give! Give!'" Mark adds a third to match his triad of vices.</note>

<margin>103.</margin> Knowledge and faith, the natural companions of our nature, have been dulled by nothing else but these three.

<margin>104.</margin> Fury, anger, wars, murders, and all the rest of the catalog of evils have become powerfully strong among men because of them.

<margin>105.</margin> One must hate the love of money, vainglory, and pleasure as if they were the mothers of all vices and the stepmothers of all virtues.

<margin>106.</margin> Because of these, we were commanded "not to love the world, nor the things in the world"; this was not so that we might indiscriminately hate God's creations, but so that we might cut off the opportunities for those three passions.

<margin>107.</margin> "No one," it says, "serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life." <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:4.</note> For he who wants to conquer the passions while remaining entangled is like a man trying to quench a fire with straw.

<margin>108.</margin> He who is angry with his neighbor because of money, or glory, or pleasure, has not yet realized that God administers all things with justice.

<margin>109.</margin> When you hear the Lord saying that "if anyone does not renounce all that they have, they are not worthy of me," do not think only of money; understand it as referring to all the activities of vice.

<margin>110.</margin> He who does not know the truth cannot truly believe. For knowledge, by its nature, precedes faith.

<column-break/>

<margin>111.</margin> Just as God assigned to each visible thing what is fitting for it, so He does for human thoughts—whether we want it or not.

<margin>112.</margin> If someone is clearly sinning and does not repent, yet suffers no hardship until their death, consider their judgment to be without mercy.

<margin>113.</margin> He who prays with understanding endures whatever comes upon him; but he who holds a grudge has not yet prayed purely.

<margin>114.</margin> If you have been deprived of something, or reproached, or driven out by someone, do not look at the present moment, but wait for the future; you will find that it has become the cause of many good things for you, not only in this life but in the age to come.

<margin>115.</margin> Just as bitter wormwood benefits those with a poor appetite, so suffering evil benefits those with a poor character. These "medicines" prepare the former for health and the latter for repentance.

<margin>116. <note>original: "ρισ΄"</note> In another version: "undoubtedly."</margin> If you do not wish to suffer evil, do not wish to do evil. For the one follows the other unalterably. Whatever a person sows, that they shall also reap.

<margin>117.</margin> When we voluntarily sow bad things but reap them involuntarily, we ought to marvel at the justice of God.

<margin>118. <note>original: "ριη΄"</note> In another version: "we ought not to disbelieve."</margin> Because a certain amount of time is set between the sowing and the reaping, we often disbelieve in the reality of the divine reward or punishment.

<margin>119.</margin> Having sinned, do not blame the physical action, but the thought. For if the mind had not run ahead, the body would not have followed.

<margin>120.</margin> Among those who do wrong openly, the one who does evil in secret is more wicked. Therefore, he is punished more severely.

<margin>121.</margin> He who weaves deceits and does evil secretly is a "snake," according to the Scripture, "sitting in wait on the road, biting the heel of the horse." <note>A reference to Genesis 49:17.</note>

<margin>123.</margin> Just as it is impossible to graze sheep and wolves together, it is impossible for one who works deceit against his neighbor to obtain mercy.

<margin>138.</margin> <margin>Perhaps: "Again"</margin> When we cast out every voluntary vice from the mind, then we shall fight against the passions that arise from <term>pre-possession</term><note>prolepsis: the involuntary memory or impulse toward a sin based on past habits.</note>.

<margin>139.</margin> <term>Pre-possession</term> is the involuntary memory of former evils. For the one still struggling, it is hindered from turning into a passion; but for the victor, it is overturned at its very first <term>provocation</term>.

<margin>140.</margin> A <term>provocation</term><note>prosbole: the very first "flicker" of a thought or temptation before it takes shape as an image in the mind.</note> is an imageless movement of the heart, which those who are experienced catch in advance, like a narrow mountain pass.

<margin>142.</margin> Do not say, "I do not want it, but it comes anyway." For even if you do not want the thing itself, you certainly love the causes of that thing.

<margin>10.</margin> Some, having been praised for <term>virtue</term><note>Arete: moral excellence or the habit of doing good.</note>, were overcome, and they thought the pleasure of their <term>vainglory</term><note>Kenodoxia: the desire for empty human praise or a sense of self-importance.</note> was actually spiritual comfort. <margin>11.</margin> Those who, on the pretext of their spiritual struggles, exalt themselves over the more negligent, think they are justified by bodily works. <margin>12.</margin> Apart from the works corresponding to it, knowledge is not yet firm, even if it happens to be true. For in every matter, the work is the confirmation.

<margin>15.</margin> When we openly perform the commandments, we receive what is appropriate from the Lord accordingly, but we are benefited according to the intent of our <term>free will</term><note>Proairesis: the moral choice or internal disposition behind an action.</note>.

<margin>16.</margin> One who wishes to do something but is unable, is as one who has done it in the eyes of God, the Knower of Hearts. This must be understood regarding both good and evil things.

<margin>17.</margin> The mind, apart from the body, performs many good and evil things; but the body, apart from the mind, can perform none of these. For the <term>law of freedom</term><note>Referring to the Gospel or the internal spiritual law that guides the soul beyond mere external rules.</note> is read before the action.

<margin>18.</margin> Some, not doing the commandments, think they believe rightly; others, doing them, expect the Kingdom as a wage that is owed. Both have fallen away from the truth.

<margin>19.</margin> A wage is not owed to servants from a master; nor, on the other hand, do those who do not serve rightly attain freedom.

<margin>20.</margin> If Christ died for us according to the Scriptures, and we no longer live for ourselves but for Him who died for us and rose again, it is clear that we are indebted to serve Him until death. How then can we consider <term>adoption</term><note>Huiothesia: the state of being made a child of God through grace.</note> to be something owed to us?

<margin>21.</margin> Christ is Master by essence and Master by <term>dispensation</term><note>Oikonomia: God's plan for the salvation of humanity through the Incarnation.</note>; for He both created us when we did not exist,

<column-break/>

and when we were dead in sin, He ransomed us through His own Blood, and granted grace to those who believe in this way.

<margin>22.</margin> When you hear the Scripture saying that He will "render to each according to his works," do not think of works worthy of hell or the Kingdom, but that Christ renders to each according to the works of their unbelief or faith in Him; not as one exchanging goods, but as God our Creator and Redeemer.

<margin>23.</margin> Those of us who were deemed worthy of the <term>washing of rebirth</term><note>Loutron paliggenesias: a reference to Holy Baptism (Titus 3:5).</note> do not offer good works for the sake of a reward, but for the preservation of the purity given to us.

<margin>24.</margin> Every good work which we perform through our nature makes us abstain from its opposite, but it cannot produce an increase in holiness apart from grace.

<margin>25.</margin> The temperate man abstains from gluttony; the one who possesses nothing, from greed; the quiet man, from loquacity; the pure, from the love of pleasure; the modest, from fornication; the self-sufficient, from the love of money; the gentle, from disturbance; the humble-minded, from vainglory; the obedient, from contentiousness; the one who accepts rebuke, from hypocrisy. Similarly, the one who prays abstains from hopelessness; the poor, from having many possessions; the confessor, from denial; the martyr, from idolatry. Do you see how every virtue performed until death is nothing other than an abstinence from sin? Now, abstinence from sin is a work of nature, not an exchange for the Kingdom.

<margin>26.</margin> A person barely keeps the things of his own nature, but Christ grants adoption through the Cross.

<margin>27.</margin> There is a partial commandment, and there is another that is comprehensive. For by the partial He commands one to share with the person who has nothing, but by the other He commands one to renounce all their possessions.

<margin>28.</margin> <margin>operation</margin> There is an operation of grace unknown to the infant [in faith]; and there is an operation of malice * that mimics the truth. It is good not to gaze too closely at such things because of the danger of delusion, nor to anathematize them because of the truth; but rather to offer everything to God through hope, for He knows the usefulness of both.

<margin>29.</margin> He who wishes to cross the spiritual sea is patient, humble, watchful, and temperate. If he tries to force his way in without these four, he will trouble his heart, but he will not be able to cross.

<margin>30.</margin> <term>Stillness</term><note>Hesychia: a state of inner quietness, tranquility, and cessation of external distractions for the purpose of prayer.</note> is the cutting off of evils; but if one also adds the four virtues to prayer...

<note>original title: "Mark the Ascetic, On those who think they are justified by works, virtue, knowledge, Christ, grace, commandments"</note>

<summary>This page contains a series of aphorisms emphasizing that while good works are natural to the human soul and necessary for preserving spiritual purity, salvation and "adoption" as children of God are gifts of grace rather than wages earned. Mark the Ascetic warns against both the pride of those who rely on their works and the folly of those who rely on intellectual knowledge without practice.</summary>

# ON THOSE WHO THINK THEY ARE MADE RIGHTEOUS BY WORKS. #

...if it is taken up, nothing is a more direct help toward <term>dispassion</term><note>original: "apatheia." In Eastern Christian thought, this is not a lack of feeling, but a state of being free from the control of destructive passions like anger or greed.</note> than it.

<margin>31.</margin> It is not possible for the <term>mind</term><note>original: "nous." The "eye of the soul" or the faculty used to perceive God.</note> to find <term>stillness</term><note>original: "hesychia." A state of inner quiet and deep prayer.</note> without the body; nor is it possible to break down the "middle wall" between them without stillness and prayer.

<margin>32.</margin> The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. But those who walk by the spirit will not carry out the desires of the flesh.

<margin>33.</margin> No prayer is perfect without <term>noetic invocation</term><note>Prayer that is not just spoken but centered in the deep intellect/heart.</note>. When the thought cries out without distraction, the Lord will listen.

<margin>34.</margin> When the mind prays without distraction, it humbles the heart. And "a broken and humbled heart, God will not despise."

<margin>35.</margin> Prayer is called a virtue, even though it is the mother of the virtues. For it gives birth to them through union with Christ.

<margin>36.</margin> Whatever we do without prayer and good hope turns out later to be harmful and incomplete.

<margin>37.</margin> When you hear that "the last shall be first, and the first shall be last," understand this to refer to those who share in the virtues and those who share in love. For love is the last of the virtues in the order of practice, but it is found to be the first of all in terms of value, showing those virtues born before it to be "last" by comparison.

<margin>38.</margin> If you become listless while praying, or find yourself troubled by many kinds of evil, remember your departure from this life and the harsh punishments. It is better, however, to cling to God through prayer and hope than to focus on external memories, even if they happen to be beneficial.

<margin>39.</margin> None of the virtues alone, by itself, opens our natural door, unless all of them are linked to one another in sequence.

<margin>40.</margin> One who is fed by mere thoughts is not <term>temperate</term><note>Self-controlled or disciplined.</note>. For even if the thoughts are helpful, they are not more helpful than hope.

<margin>41.</margin> Every unrepented sin is a "sin unto death"; regarding such a sin, even if a Saint prays for someone else, he is not heard.

<margin>42.</margin> The person who truly repents does not count their labor as a fair trade against their old sins, but uses that labor to seek God's favor.

<margin>43.</margin> If we are already in debt to perform all the good things our nature is capable of every day, what do we have left to give back to God as payment for our past evils?

<margin>44.</margin> Whatever excellence of virtue we might achieve today, it is a rebuke of our past

<column-break/>

neglect, not a repayment for it.

<margin>45.</margin> The person who is troubled in their mind but physically at rest is like one who is physically troubled but mentally relaxed.

<margin>46.</margin> Voluntary suffering of both kinds—of the mind and the flesh—helps the other. The suffering of the mind helps the flesh, and the suffering of the flesh helps the mind. When they are not in harmony, the struggle becomes more wretched.

<margin>47.</margin> It is a great virtue to endure whatever happens to us and to love a neighbor who hates us, according to the word of the Lord.

<margin>48.</margin> The proof of sincere love is the forgiveness of wrongs. For it was in this way that the Lord loved the world.

<margin>49.</margin> It is impossible to forgive faults from the heart without true knowledge. For such knowledge shows to each person that what happens to them is their own responsibility.

<margin>50.</margin> You will lose nothing of what you give up for the sake of the Lord. For in its own time, it will return to you many times over.

<margin>51.</margin> When the mind forgets the goal of <term>piety</term><note>Eusebeia: a life of devotion and right worship.</note>, then even a visible act of virtue becomes useless.

<margin>52.</margin> If bad advice is harmful to every person, it is much more so to those who have taken up a life of strict discipline.

<margin>53.</margin> Seek wisdom through action regarding the counsel of men and the reward of God. For the spoken word is neither wiser nor more beneficial than practical work.

<margin>54.</margin> Divine help follows labors undertaken for the sake of piety. This must be known through divine law and conscience.

<margin>55.</margin> One person receives a thought and holds onto it without examination. Another receives it and compares it with the truth. One must ask: which of them acted more piously?

<margin>56.</margin> True knowledge consists in the endurance of distressing things and in not blaming other people for one's own misfortunes.

<margin>57.</margin> The one who does good and seeks a reward is serving not God, but his own will.

<margin>58.</margin> It is not possible for a sinner to escape recompense except through repentance appropriate to the fault.

<margin>59.</margin> Some say: "We cannot do good unless we actively receive the grace of the Spirit."

<margin>60.</margin> Those who by their own choice are inclined toward pleasures always dismiss what is within their power as being "unhelpful."

-># OF THE HOLY MARK THE ASCETIC#<-

<margin>61.</margin> <term>Grace</term><note>original: "charis." In this context, it refers to the divine assistance and presence of God given freely to believers.</note> has been given mystically to those baptized in Christ; but it remains active in proportion to how well one fulfills the commandments. Grace never ceases to help us in secret, but it is up to us to do—or not to do—the good according to our strength.

<margin>62.</margin> First, in a manner worthy of God, grace awakens the <term>conscience</term><note>original: "syneidesis." The internal moral compass that Mark views as being "stirred" by divine action.</note>. This is why even evildoers, once they repented, were able to please God.

<margin>63.</margin> Again, grace is hidden within the teaching of one's neighbor. Sometimes it also follows the mind during reading, and through a natural sequence, it teaches the mind its own truth. Therefore, if we do not hide the <term>talent</term><note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25), where a "talent" is a unit of currency representing the gifts or responsibilities God entrusts to humans.</note> of this partial sequence, we shall effectively enter into the joy of the Lord.

<margin>64.</margin> One who seeks the "activities" of the Spirit before practicing the commandments is like a slave bought with silver who, at the very moment he is purchased, demands that his freedom be granted along with the bill of sale.

<margin>65.</margin> He who has discovered that external trials occur through the justice of God, in seeking the Lord, has found knowledge coupled with righteousness.

<margin>66.</margin> If you understand according to the Scripture that the judgments of the Lord are in all the earth, then every event that befalls you will become a teacher of the knowledge of God.

<margin>67.</margin> According to each person's inner disposition, what is owed to them meets them. Only God knows the variety of the appropriate trial that is brought upon us.

<margin>68.</margin> When you suffer some dishonor from men, immediately consider the reward of glory from God that follows; thus, you will be without sorrow or disturbance at the dishonor. When that glory comes, you will be faithful and beyond reproach.

<margin>69.</margin> If you are praised by the multitude by God's permission, do not mix any ostentation into the Lord’s <term>stewardship</term><note>original: "oikonomia." This refers to God's plan or the way He manages the world and human lives.</note>, so that you do not later fall into the opposite state through a change of fortune.

<margin>70.</margin> A seed will not grow without earth and water; and a person will not benefit without voluntary labors and divine assistance.

<margin>71.</margin> It is not possible for rain to fall without a cloud, nor is it possible to please God without a good conscience.

<margin>72.</margin> Do not refuse to learn, even if you happen to be very wise. For God’s stewardship is more profitable than our own wisdom.

<margin>73.</margin> When the heart is moved by some pleasure from the place of

<column-break/>

<term>love of labor</term><note>original: "philoponia." A technical term for the ascetic's love of the "toil" required for spiritual growth, such as fasting or long vigils.</note>, then, like a very heavy stone sliding down a slope, it becomes difficult to restrain.

<margin>74.</margin> Just as an inexperienced calf, running after green pastures, ends up at a precipice, so the soul is found to be led astray little by little by <term>thoughts</term><note>original: "logismoi." In ascetic literature, these are specifically tempting or intrusive thoughts that pull the mind away from God.</note>.

<margin>75.</margin> When the mind acts manfully in the Lord and pulls the soul away from long-standing habits, then the heart is punished as if by executioners, being pulled this way and that by the mind and by the <term>passion</term><note>original: "pathos." An uncontrolled impulse or ingrained vice.</note>.

<margin>76.</margin> Just as those sailing the sea in hope of gain gladly endure the sun's scorching heat, so those who hate vice love correction. For the former opposes the winds, and the latter opposes the passions.

<margin>77.</margin> Just as "flight in winter or on the Sabbath" <note>A reference to Matthew 24:20.</note> causes pain to the flesh and desecration to the soul, so does the uprising of passions in an aged body and a consecrated soul.

<margin>78.</margin> No one is so good and merciful as the Lord; but even He does not forgive the one who does not repent.

<margin>79.</margin> Many of us feel sorrow for our sins, yet we gladly accept the causes of those sins.

<margin>80.</margin> A mole crawling under the earth, being blind, cannot see the stars; and he who does not have faith concerning temporary things cannot believe in eternal ones.

<margin>81.</margin> True knowledge—a grace before grace—has been gifted to men by God; above all, it teaches those who share in it to have faith in the Giver.

<margin>82.</margin> When a sinful soul does not accept the trials that come upon it, then the Angels say of it: "We healed Babylon, but she was not healed." <note>A reference to Jeremiah 51:9, often interpreted by the Church Fathers as the soul's refusal of spiritual medicine.</note>

<margin>83.</margin> A mind that forgets true knowledge fights for things that are harmful as if they were beneficial to men.

<margin>84.</margin> Just as fire cannot remain in water, so a foul thought cannot stay in a God-loving heart. For every God-lover is also a lover of labor, and voluntary labor is by nature the enemy of pleasure.

<margin>85.</margin> A passion that has gained a foothold in action through the will later rises up violently against the participant, even when they do not want it.

<margin>86.</margin> We love the causes of involuntary thoughts, and because of this, they come upon us; in the case of voluntary thoughts, we clearly love the deeds themselves as well.
