->### ON THOSE WHO THINK THEY ARE JUSTIFIED BY WORKS ###<-

<margin>87.</margin> <term>Conceit</term><note>original: "Oiesis." A sense of self-importance or an inflated opinion of one's own righteousness.</note> and arrogance are the causes of blasphemy. Love of money and vain glory are the causes of heartlessness and hypocrisy.

<margin>88.</margin> When the devil sees that the <term>mind</term><note>original: "nous." In Eastern Christian thought, this refers to the "eye of the heart" or the highest faculty of the human person that perceives God.</note> has prayed from the heart, he then brings great and crafty temptations. For he does not wish to destroy small virtues with great attacks.

<margin>89.</margin> A lingering <term>thought</term><note>original: "logismos." Often refers to intrusive or obsessive thoughts that lead to temptation.</note> reveals a person's <term>attachment</term><note>original: "prospatheia." A passionate or biased inclination toward something worldly.</note>. But a thought that is quickly destroyed signifies an internal war and opposition to evil.

<margin>90.</margin> There are three mental states into which the mind enters through change: according to nature, above nature, and against nature. When it enters the state **according to nature**, it finds itself to be the cause of its own evil thoughts; it then confesses its sins to God, recognizing the causes of the <term>passions</term><note>original: "pathe." Distorted emotions or impulses like anger, greed, or lust that distract from God.</note>. When it enters the state **against nature**, it forgets the righteousness of God and fights with other people, believing it is being treated unjustly. But when it is led to the state **above nature**, it finds the fruits of the Holy Spirit, which the <term>Apostle</term><note>Refers to St. Paul in Galatians 5:22-23.</note> named: love, joy, peace, and so on. And it knows that if it prefers bodily cares, it cannot remain there. Anyone who departs from that state falls into sin and into the terrible consequences that follow it—if not immediately, then in due time, as the justice of God knows.

<margin>91.</margin> To the extent that each person’s knowledge is true, gentleness, humility, and love confirm it.

<margin>92.</margin> Everyone baptized in the orthodox manner has received all grace mystically. They are thereafter fully assured of this through the practice of the commandments.

<margin>93.</margin> A commandment of Christ performed according to conscience, in proportion to the magnitude of the heart's pains, grants consolation; yet each of these comes in its own time.

<margin>94.</margin> Have constant prayer in every matter, so as to perform nothing without God's help.

<margin>95.</margin> Nothing is more powerful in action than prayer; and for God's good pleasure, nothing is more beneficial.

<margin>96.</margin> All practice of the commandments is contained within prayer. For nothing is higher than the love of God.

<margin>97.</margin> Undistracted prayer is a sign of love

<column-break/>

for God in the one who persists in it. Neglect of it and distraction is a proof of love for pleasure.

<margin>98.</margin> He who keeps vigil, is long-suffering, and prays without being oppressed clearly becomes a partaker of the Holy Spirit. But he who is oppressed in these things, yet persists by his own will, also quickly receives assistance.

<margin>99.</margin> One commandment is proven to be more excellent than another. Therefore, one faith is found to be more firm than another.

<margin>100.</margin> There is "faith from hearing," according to the Apostle, and there is faith which is the "substance of things hoped for." <note>Mark is quoting Romans 10:17 and Hebrews 11:1.</note>

<margin>101.</margin> It is good to benefit those who ask through words; but it is better to cooperate with them through prayer and virtue. For he who offers himself to God through these things helps his neighbor as well through his own assistance.

<margin>102.</margin> If you wish to benefit a lover of learning with a brief word, point him toward prayer, right faith, and patience in what comes upon him. For all other good things are found through these.

<margin>103.</margin> Regarding things for which someone has hoped in God, he no longer fights with his neighbor about them.

<margin>104.</margin> If every involuntary event has its cause in voluntary actions, according to the Scripture, no one is so much an enemy to a person as they are to themselves.

<margin>105.</margin> Ignorance precedes all evils; and second after it is unbelief.

<margin>106.</margin> Flee temptation through patience and prayer. If you resist without these, it comes upon you more intensely.

<margin>107.</margin> He who is gentle according to God is wiser than the wise; and the humble in heart is stronger than the strong. For they bear the yoke of Christ according to knowledge.

<margin>108.</margin> Whatever we either say or do without prayer turns out later to be either faulty or harmful; and it rebukes us unknowingly through the events themselves.

<margin>109.</margin> From works, words, and thought, there is only one just man <note>Meaning Christ alone is perfectly just by his own nature.</note>. But from faith, grace, and repentance, there are many just men.

<margin>110.</margin> Just as it is alien for one who is repenting to be high-minded, so it is impossible for one who sins voluntarily to be humble-minded.

<margin>111.</margin> <margin>variant: of grace</margin> Humility is not the condemnation of the conscience; rather it is the * grace of God and the recognition of His compassion.

# OF THE HOLY MARK THE ASCETIC #

... [it is moved] by this rational <term>mind</term><note>original: "nous." The highest faculty of the human person, often called the "eye of the heart."</note> through divine grace; and as much as you cast out "matter," so much will grace enter of its own accord; and as much as you bring matter back in, so much will grace withdraw.

<margin>113.</margin> The "matter" of a house consists of its vessels and food. But the "matter" of the mind is <term>vanity</term><note>original: "kenodoxia." Literally "empty glory" or the desire for human praise.</note> and pleasure.

<margin>114.</margin> The spaciousness of the heart is hope in God. Its narrowness is bodily worry.

<margin>115.</margin> The grace of the Spirit is one and unchanging, but it acts in each person as it wills.

<margin>116.</margin> Just as rain falling on the earth gives plants their specific qualities—sweetness to the sweet and bitterness to the more bitter—so grace, falling unchangeably upon the hearts of the faithful, grants activities that harmonize with their specific virtues.

<margin>117.</margin> To the one who hungers for the sake of Christ, grace becomes food; to the thirsty, a most sweet drink; to the cold, clothing; to the weary, rest; to the one who prays, full assurance; and to the one who mourns, consolation.

<margin>118. 16. On [the Spirit]</margin> Therefore, when you hear the Scripture saying * about the Holy Spirit—that "it sat upon each one of the Apostles," or that it "leapt upon the Prophet," or that it "acts," or "is grieved," or "is quenched," or "is provoked"; and again, that some have "the first-fruits" while others are "full of the Holy Spirit"—do not imagine any division, change, or alteration within the Spirit. Instead, believe according to the way we have already described: that it is unchangeable, unaltered, and all-powerful. Therefore, in its activities, it remains what it is, and to each person, it preserves what is necessary in a manner worthy of God. For like the sun, it is poured out perfectly upon those who have been baptized, but each of us is enlightened in proportion to how we hate and remove the <term>passions</term><note>original: "pathe." Distorted or obsessive impulses like anger or greed that cloud the mind.</note> that darken us. But to the degree that one loves these passions * and dwells on them, one remains in darkness.
<margin>* it appears</margin>

<margin>119.</margin> He who hates the passions removes their causes. But he who dwells on the causes is attacked by the passions, even if he does not wish to be.

<margin>120.</margin> When we are influenced by evil thoughts, we should blame ourselves and not "ancestral sin" <note>Mark is emphasizing personal responsibility for current choices rather than blaming inherited human nature.</note>.

<margin>121.</margin> The roots of [evil] thoughts are the obvious vices, which we defend at every turn with our hands, feet, and mouths.

<margin>122.</margin> It is impossible to converse with a passion in the mind without loving the causes of that passion.

<margin>123.</margin> For who that despises shame can converse with vanity? Or who that loves being humbled is troubled by dishonor? And who that has a broken and humble heart can accept the pleasure of the flesh? Or who that trusts in Christ worries about temporary things or gets into fights over them?

<column-break/>

<margin>124.</margin> He who is rejected by someone, yet does not fight back against the one rejecting him—neither in word nor in thought—possesses true knowledge and demonstrates a firm faith in the Master.

<margin>125.</margin> The sons of men are false in the scales of injustice, while God preserves justice for everyone.

<margin>126.</margin> If there is neither an excess for the one who does wrong, nor a deficiency for the one who is wronged, then truly "man walks in an image" <note>A reference to Psalm 39:6, suggesting the futility of human striving against God's providence.</note> but is troubled in vain.

<margin>127.</margin> When you see someone suffering greatly from many dishonors, know that they were filled with thoughts of vanity, and now they are unpleasantly reaping the harvest of the seeds sown in their heart.

<margin>128.</margin> He who has enjoyed bodily pleasures beyond what is necessary will pay back the excess with a hundredfold of pains.

<margin>129.</margin> One in authority is obligated to tell a subordinate what is required; if the subordinate refuses to listen, the leader should forewarn them of the coming consequences of their actions.

<margin>130.</margin> He who is wronged by someone, and does not seek his "due" from the wrongdoer, puts his trust in that part of Christ; he receives a hundredfold in this age and shall inherit eternal life.

<margin>131.</margin> The "remembrance of God" is a labor of the heart performed for the sake of piety. But everyone who forgets God becomes a lover of pleasure and loses their spiritual sensitivity.

<margin>132.</margin> Do not say that the <term>dispassionate</term><note>original: "apathes." One who has reached a state of inner peace and freedom from the rule of the passions.</note> person cannot suffer. For even if they do not suffer for themselves, they are obligated to do so for their neighbor.

<margin>133.</margin> When the enemy holds many "debts" <note>Handwritten records of debt, used here as a metaphor for sins.</note> of sins committed in forgetfulness, he then forces the debtor to perform those same sins in his memory, rightly taking advantage of the "law of sin."

<margin>134.</margin> If you wish to remember God continually, do not reject hardships as if they were "unjust," but endure them as things coming to you justly. For endurance, through every circumstance, stirs the memory [of God]. But <margin>* in other manuscripts: "slackening"</margin> *avoidance diminishes the mind's spiritual resolve and, through ease, produces forgetfulness.

<margin>135.</margin> If you wish to be covered by the Lord...

<meta>This page continues the ascetic teachings of Mark the Hermit, shifting from the nature of grace to the practical discipline of the mind and the "recognition of truth." -># ON THOSE WHO THINK THEY ARE JUSTIFIED BY WORKS<-

...your sins; do not make them known to men if you possess <term>virtue</term><note>original: "aretē." In this context, it refers to spiritual strength or the habit of doing good.</note>. For whatever we do regarding our virtues [by keeping them hidden], God does the same regarding our sins.

<margin>136.</margin> If you have hidden your virtue, do not be puffed up as if you were fulfilling <term>righteousness</term><note>original: "dikaiosynē." Living in a way that is right and just before God.</note>. For righteousness consists not only in hiding good deeds, but also in entertaining no forbidden thoughts in the mind.

<margin>137.</margin> Do not rejoice when you do good to someone, but rather when you endure without malice the opposition that follows it. For just as nights follow days, so do vices follow good deeds.

<margin>138.</margin> <term>Vain-glory</term><note>original: "kenodoxia." The desire for empty praise or human recognition.</note>, the love of money, and the pursuit of pleasure do not allow a good deed to remain spotless, unless these three first fall away through the fear of God.

<margin>139.</margin> In involuntary sufferings, the mercy of God is hidden; it draws the one who endures toward <term>repentance</term><note>original: "metanoia." A fundamental change of mind and heart.</note> and delivers them from eternal punishment.

<margin>140.</margin> Some who fulfill the commandments expect them to balance out their sins in a scale; others, through these deeds, seek to win the favor of Him who died for our sins. One must ask: which of them has the correct mindset?

<margin>141.</margin> Fear of hell and the love of the Kingdom provide the strength to endure afflictions. And this does not come from ourselves, but from Him who knows our inner thoughts.

<margin>142.</margin> The one who believes in things to come spontaneously and without doubt abstains from the pleasures of this world. But the one who lacks faith becomes a lover of pleasure and insensitive to spiritual things.

<margin>143.</margin> Do not say, "How can a poor man live luxuriously if he lacks the means?" For a person can live even more wretchedly in luxury through their thoughts alone.

<margin>144.</margin> Knowledge of things is one thing, and the <term>recognition of truth</term><note>original: "epignosis." A deep, experiential realization of spiritual truth, as opposed to mere factual information.</note> is another. As much as the sun differs from the moon, so much is the second more profitable than the first.

<margin>145.</margin> Knowledge of things increases in proportion to how one practices the commandments; but the recognition of truth grows according to the measure of one's hope in Christ.

<margin>146.</margin> If you wish to be saved and to come to the recognition of truth, always strive to transcend <term>sensible things</term><note>original: "aisthēta." Things perceived through the physical senses, like sight and touch.</note>, and through hope alone cling to God. In this way, even when you are turned aside against your will, you will find spiritual "principalities and powers" <note>A reference to the spiritual hierarchy of demons mentioned in the New Testament (Ephesians 6:12).</note> waging war against you through their assaults. By conquering these through prayer and remaining hopeful, you will possess the grace of God, which rescues you from the wrath to come.

<column-break/>

<margin>147.</margin> He who understands what was mystically spoken by Holy Paul—that our struggle is against the "spiritual forces of wickedness"—will also understand the Lord’s parable, which said that we must always pray and not lose heart.

<margin>148.</margin> The law symbolically commands us to work for six days and to rest on the seventh. For the work of the soul is doing good through money or physical things. Its "rest" and cessation from work is to sell everything and give to the poor, according to the word of the Lord, and by ceasing through poverty, to rest in spiritual hope. It is into this rest that Paul urges us to enter with haste, saying: "Let us strive to enter into that rest."

<margin>149.</margin> We have said these things not to exclude future rewards, nor to define the universal recompense as happening only here; but rather that one must first have the grace of the Holy Spirit active in the heart, and thus enter into the Kingdom of Heaven in proportion to that grace. Making this clear, the Lord said: "The Kingdom of Heaven is within you." The Apostle also said: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for," and again: "Run in such a way that you may take hold," and again: "Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith; or do you not recognize that Jesus Christ dwells in you? Unless, of course, you fail the test."

<margin>150.</margin> The one who has recognized the truth does not resist painful circumstances. For he knows that they lead a person to the fear of God.

<margin>151.</margin> Past sins remembered in detail harm a man who has hope. For if they are recalled with sorrow, they drive away hope; but if they are visualized without sorrow, they deposit the old defilement back into the soul.

<margin>152.</margin> When the mind, through self-denial, takes hold of a single-minded hope, the enemy then uses the pretext of confession to depict previous evils. He does this so that he may rekindle the passions that were forgotten by the grace of God, and thus secretly harm the person. For even if a person is intense* and hates the passions, he will necessarily be darkened and confused by what was done. And if he is still clouded and a lover of pleasure, he will certainly linger on these thoughts and converse with the assaults of the enemy with passion, treating them as a prior habit.

<margin>* in other manuscripts: "cheerful."</margin>

<note>original Greek vocabulary provided in text: righteousness, virtue, good deeds, vain-glory, repentance, commandments, kingdom of heaven, faith, hope, grace.</note>

<summary>This page explores the relationship between hidden virtue, the practice of the commandments, and the experiential "recognition of truth." It warns that spiritual progress is maintained through hope and prayer rather than self-justification through works.</summary>

## OF SAINT MARK THE ASCETIC

<columns>

...[to be] found as such a memory, and not a confession.

<margin>153.</margin> If you wish to offer a blameless confession to God, do not remember your <term>transgressions</term><note>original: "paratropas" — literally "turnings aside" or deviations from the path.</note> in detail, but endure their consequences bravely.

<margin>154.</margin> Troubles come upon us because of past sins, bringing with them what is appropriate for every offense.

<margin>155.</margin> The <term>man of knowledge</term><note>original: "ho gnostikos." In this ascetic context, it refers to one who has deep spiritual insight into the nature of reality and God.</note> and he who knows the truth confesses to God not through the memory of past deeds, but through the endurance of what comes upon him.

<margin>156.</margin> Having rejected pain and dishonor, do not promise to repent through other virtues. For <term>vanity</term><note>original: "kenodoxia" — the desire for empty glory or human praise.</note> and a lack of feeling are accustomed to serving sin even through "right-hand" <note>This refers to good or virtuous deeds that are nevertheless performed with a selfish or prideful motive.</note> actions.

<margin>157.</margin> For just as pains and dishonors tend to give birth to virtues, so pleasures and vanity tend to give birth to vices.

<margin>158.</margin> Every bodily pleasure comes from a prior state of <term>indulgence</term><note>original: "anesis" — relaxation, ease, or the loosening of discipline.</note>. And indulgence is born from unbelief.

<margin>159.</margin> One who is under the power of sin cannot overcome the fleshly mindset alone, because he has an unceasing stimulation dwelling in his limbs.

<margin>160.</margin> While we are subject to <term>passions</term><note>original: "empatheis." In Eastern Christian thought, passions are disordered desires that enslave the soul.</note>, we must pray and be submissive. For it is difficult, even with help, to fight against our <term>predispositions</term><note>original: "prolepseis" — past habits or mental impressions that influence current behavior.</note>.

<margin>161.</margin> He who fights against his own will with submission and prayer is a skilled athlete; he clearly demonstrates his spiritual struggle through his abstinence from physical things.

<margin>162.</margin> He who does not surrender his own will to God is tripped up by his own pursuits and falls under the control of his adversaries.

<margin>163.</margin> When you see two wicked people having love for one another, know that one is helping the other satisfy his own will.

<margin>164.</margin> The proud man and the vain man readily associate with one another; for the proud man praises the vain one who submissively bows before him, while the vain one magnifies the proud one who is constantly praising him.

<margin>165.</margin> A God-loving listener gains benefit from both; being encouraged by the good, he becomes more eager; being rebuked for the bad, he is forced to repent. We must have a life consistent with our progress; and according to our life, we owe it to offer prayers to God.

<column-break/>

It is good to hold to the most essential commandment and not to worry about specific details, nor to pray for specific things, but only to seek the Kingdom and the Word of God. But if we still worry about every need, we must also pray for every need. For he who does or worries about anything without prayer does not succeed in the end of the matter. And this is what the Lord said: "Without me you can do nothing."
<margin>166.</margin>

Whoever ignores the commandment regarding prayer is followed by even more absurd acts of disobedience, passing him on like a prisoner from one to another.
<margin>167.</margin>

He who accepts present sorrows in expectation of future goods has found the knowledge of truth; and he will easily be delivered from anger and grief.
<margin>168.</margin>

He who chooses hardship and dishonor for the sake of truth walks the apostolic path, having taken up the cross and wearing the chain. But he who tries to pay attention to the heart without these things is led astray in his mind and falls into temptations and the snares of the devil.
<margin>169.</margin>

It is impossible ever to defeat evil thoughts without their <term>causes</term><note>original: "aitias." These are the underlying triggers or external stimuli that provoke a thought.</note>, or the causes without the thoughts. For when we reject one part alone, after a short while we are carried away by both through the other.
<margin>170.</margin>

He who fights with people out of fear of hardship or reproach either suffers even more through various afflictions here, or is punished mercilessly in the age to come.
<margin>171.</margin>

He who wishes to shut out every evil occurrence ought to surrender his affairs to God through prayer; he should hold fast to hope in Him with his mind, and as much as possible, ignore the worry of physical things.
<margin>172.</margin>

When the devil finds a man occupied with bodily things beyond what is necessary, he first snatches away the spoils of knowledge. Then, he cuts off hope in God, as if it were the head.
<margin>173.</margin>

If you ever reach a * strong place of pure prayer, do not accept the knowledge of things presented by the enemy at that time, lest you lose the greater thing. For it is better to strike him down with the arrows of prayer while he is shut out below, than to converse with him while he offers worthless things.
<margin>174.</margin>
<margin>in other versions: "a pure manner"</margin>

</columns>

He emphasizes that prayer is the only defense against the "snares of the devil" and the distractions of the flesh.</summary>

### ON THOSE WHO THINK THEY ARE JUSTIFIED BY WORKS 71

<columns>

...and [the devil] contrives to tear us away from our prayer to Him.

<margin>175.</margin> The knowledge of things benefits a person in a time of trial and <term>listlessness</term><note>original: "akedia" — a state of spiritual apathy, boredom, or "the noonday demon" that makes one feel restless in prayer.</note>; but in a time of prayer, it is accustomed to causing harm.

<margin>176.</margin> If you have been chosen to teach in the Lord and you are ignored, grieve inwardly, but do not be visibly disturbed. For if you are grieved, you will not be condemned alongside the one who ignores you; but if you are disturbed, you will be tempted by that very same thing.

<margin>177.</margin> In a time of explanation, do not hide the things that are fitting for those present; recount the honorable things clearly, and the harsh things enigmatically.

<margin>178.</margin> Do not bring a mistake to the face of someone who is not under your <term>authority</term><note>original: "hypotage" — literally "under-ordering," referring to the formal spiritual submission of a monk to his superior.</note>. For this belongs more to power than to counsel.

<margin>179.</margin> <margin>they are revealed</margin> Things said in the plural become beneficial to all, as each person's own circumstances are revealed to them according to their conscience.

<margin>180.</margin> He who speaks rightly ought to receive the words as if they were from God. For the truth does not belong to the speaker, but to the God who is at work.

<margin>181.</margin> Do not contend with those who oppose the truth if you do not have their pledge of obedience, lest you stir up hatred, according to the Scripture.

<margin>182.</margin> He who yields to a subordinate who contradicts him where he should not, leads that person astray in that matter and prepares him to disregard the agreements of obedience.

<margin>183.</margin> He who admonishes or disciplines a sinner in the fear of God acquires for himself the virtue that is opposite to that mistake. But he who bears a grudge and rebukes with ill-will falls into the same passion according to the spiritual law.

<margin>184.</margin> He who has learned the law well fears the Lawgiver. And fearing Him, he turns away from every evil.

<margin>185.</margin> Do not be double-tongued, being disposed one way in speech and another way in conscience. For the Scripture places such a person under a curse.

<margin>186.</margin> There is one who speaks the truth and is hated by fools, according to the <term>Apostle</term><note>A reference to St. Paul, likely Galatians 4:16: "Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?"</note>. And there is one who acts hypocritically and is loved for it. However, neither of these rewards lasts a long time, because the Lord, in His own time, gives to each what is due.

<column-break/>

<margin>187.</margin> He who wishes to remove future hardships ought to endure present ones gladly. For by exchanging one thing for another in his mind, he will escape great punishments through small pains.

<margin>188.</margin> Guard your speech from boasting and your thought from conceit, lest you be abandoned and do the opposite. For good is not brought to fulfillment by man alone, but by the all-seeing God.

<margin>189.</margin> The all-seeing God assigns worthy consequences to our thoughts and voluntary intentions, just as He does to our deeds.

<margin>190.</margin> Involuntary thoughts spring up from prior sin, but voluntary thoughts spring from our free will. Therefore, the latter are found to be the cause of the former.

<margin>191.</margin> Sorrow follows bad thoughts that occur against our intention; for this reason, they quickly disappear. But joy follows those that occur according to our intention; hence they become difficult to get rid of.

<margin>192.</margin> The pleasure-lover is grieved by censures and hardships, but the God-lover is grieved by praise and abundance.

<margin>193.</margin> He who does not know the judgments of God walks a path with cliffs on both sides in his mind, and is easily overturned by every wind. When praised, he becomes arrogant; when rebuked, he is embittered. When feasting, he becomes lewd; when suffering hardship, he laments. When he understands, he shows off; and when he does not understand, he pretends. When rich, he is boastful; and when poor, he acts hypocritically. Having been filled, he becomes bold; and when fasting, he is <term>vain</term><note>original: "kenodoxei" — seeks empty glory or human approval for his asceticism.</note>. He contends with those who correct him, and he looks upon those who forgive him as if they were fools.

<margin>194.</margin> Unless one acquires knowledge of the truth and the fear of God through the grace of Christ, he is wounded terribly not only by passions, but also by external circumstances.

<margin>195.</margin> When you want to solve a tangled matter, seek what is pleasing to God regarding it, and you will find its solution to be beneficial.

<margin>196.</margin> In whatever things God is well-pleased, all creation also serves. But in those things He turns away from, creation likewise sets itself in opposition.

<margin>197.</margin> He who sets himself in opposition to grim circumstances fights against the command of God without knowing it; but he who accepts them with true knowledge is "waiting for the Lord," according to the Scripture.

<margin>198.</margin> When temptation comes upon you, do not seek to know why...

</columns>

### OF THE HOLY MARK THE ASCETIC

<columns>

...or why it has come; but rather how you might endure it thankfully, without pain, and without bearing a grudge.

<margin>199.</margin> Another’s evil does not add sin to us, unless we ourselves welcome it with evil thoughts.

<margin>200.</margin> Since it is not easy to find someone who has pleased God outside of <term>temptations</term><note>original: "peirasmoi" — can mean trials, testings, or temptations to sin.</note>, one ought to give thanks to God for every occurrence.

<margin>201.</margin> If Peter had not failed in his night’s fishing, he would not have succeeded in the day’s catch. And if Paul had not been physically blinded, he would not have regained his spiritual sight. And if Stephen had not been slandered as a blasphemer, he would not have seen God while the Heavens were opened to him.

<margin>202.</margin> Just as work performed according to God’s will is called virtue, so too is an unexpected affliction named a temptation.

<margin>203.</margin> God tempted Abraham—that is, He afflicted him for his own benefit—not so that God might learn what kind of man he was (for He knew him, He who knows all things before they come to be), but so that He might provide him with opportunities for perfect faith.

<margin>204.</margin> Every affliction tests the <term>inclination of the will</term><note>original: "rhopen tou thelematos" — the "tilt" or weight of one's choice.</note>, whether it leans to the right or to the left. For this reason, an incidental affliction is called a temptation: it provides the one undergoing it with a <term>trial</term><note>original: "peiran" — a play on words with "peirasmos" (temptation), meaning an experimental knowledge or proof.</note> of their hidden desires.

<margin>205.</margin> The fear of God compels us to fight against wickedness; and as we fight, the grace of God * fights against it.

<margin>*alternate: abolishes it</margin>

<margin>206.</margin> Wisdom consists not only in knowing the truth through natural logic, but also in enduring the malice of those who do wrong as if it were one’s own. For those who stayed with the former were lifted up to pride; but those who reached the latter attained <term>humility</term><note>original: "tapeinophrosyne" — literally "lowliness of mind," a core monastic virtue.</note>.

<margin>207.</margin> If you wish not to be energized by evil thoughts, accept the humiliation of the soul and the affliction of the flesh. And do this not just occasionally, but in every time, place, and circumstance.

<margin>208.</margin> He who is voluntarily disciplined by painful things will not be mastered by <term>involuntary thoughts</term><note>original: "akousion logismon" — intrusive thoughts that occur without the person's intent.</note>; but he who does not accept the former is taken captive by the latter, even against his will.

<margin>209.</margin> When you are wronged and your vitals and heart are hardened, do not be grieved that the circumstance was set in motion by <term>divine providence</term><note>original: "oikonomikos" — referring to God's "economy" or management of the world for the soul's salvation.</note>; but rather, joyfully overturn the rising 

<column-break/>

thoughts. For you know that when these thoughts are destroyed at their first assault, the evil is naturally destroyed along with the impulse; but if the thoughts persist, the evil usually gains strength.

<margin>210.</margin> Without <term>contrition of heart</term><note>original: "syntrimmou kardias" — literally a "crushing" or "breaking" of the heart in repentance.</note>, it is entirely impossible to be rid of wickedness. And the heart is broken by a threefold self-control: I mean in sleep, in food, and in bodily comfort. For an excess of these brings on <term>sensuality</term><note>original: "hedypatheia" — literally "sweet-suffering," the state of being controlled by pleasure.</note>; and sensuality welcomes evil thoughts, while setting itself against prayer and proper service.

<margin>211.</margin> If you have been appointed to lead the brothers, keep your station, and do not remain silent about what is necessary because of those who speak against you. When they obey, you will have a reward for their virtue; when they disobey, you will certainly forgive them, and you will receive equal favor from Him who said: "Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you."

<margin>212.</margin> Every occurrence is like a <term>market-festival</term><note>original: "panegyrei" — a public gathering or fair where goods were traded.</note>. He who knows how to trade will gain much, but he who does not know will suffer loss.

<margin>213.</margin> If someone does not obey after a single word, do not force them with a spirit of contention; but rather, take for yourself the gain that the other person threw away. For your <term>forbearance</term><note>original: "anexikakia" — the quality of enduring evil without resentment.</note> will benefit you more than his correction would have.

<margin>214.</margin> When the harm of one person spreads to many others, then one must not be long-suffering, nor seek one's own benefit, but rather the benefit of the many so they may be saved. For the virtue that benefits many is more profitable than that which benefits only one.

<margin>215.</margin> If someone falls into any sin and is not grieved in proportion to the fault, they will easily fall into the same snare again.

<margin>216.</margin> Just as a lioness does not approach a heifer in friendship, so <term>shamelessness</term><note>original: "anaischyntia" — lack of healthy shame or conscience.</note> does not kindly receive "sorrow according to God."

<margin>217.</margin> Just as a wolf does not mate with a sheep to produce offspring, so <term>satiety</term><note>original: "koro" — fullness or over-eating.</note> does not mate with heart-felt pain to give birth to virtues.

<margin>218.</margin> No one can have pain and "sorrow according to God" unless they first love the causes of these.

<margin>219.</margin> Fear of God and rebuke lead to sorrow; while self-control and watchfulness are the companions of pain.

<margin>220.</margin> He who is not disciplined by the commandments and warnings of Scripture will be driven by "the whip of the horse and the goad of the ass." And if even these...

</columns>

### ON THOSE WHO IMAGINE THEY ARE JUSTIFIED BY WORKS

...he will reject; their jaws will be tightened with muzzle and bridle. <note>original: "en kēmō kai chalinō" — This is a reference to Psalm 32:9, suggesting that those who will not be led by God's spirit must be controlled like animals.</note>

<margin>221.</margin> One who is easily conquered by small things is, of necessity, already enslaved to the great. But the one who despises the small will, in the Lord, stand firm against the great.

<margin>222.</margin> Do not attempt to help someone who boasts of their virtues by rebuking them; for a person cannot be a lover of self-display and a lover of truth at the same time.

<margin>223.</margin> Every word of Christ reveals God’s mercy, righteousness, and wisdom; it strikes the power of these truths into the ears of those who listen gladly. Thus, the unmerciful and the unjust, hearing with displeasure, were unable to know the wisdom of God, and even crucified the Teacher. We should therefore consider whether we listen to Him gladly. For He Himself said: "He who loves me will keep my commandments, and he will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." <note>John 14:21-23</note> You see how He has hidden His own manifestation within the commandments? Of all the commandments, the most comprehensive is the love of God and neighbor; this love is established through <term>abstinence from material things</term><note>original: "hylōn apochēs" — releasing the soul's attachment to physical objects and worldly wealth.</note> and the <term>stillness of thoughts</term><note>original: "logismōn hēsychias" — the internal quietude of the mind.</note>.

<margin>224.</margin> Knowing this, the Lord commands us, saying: "Do not worry about tomorrow." <note>Matthew 6:34</note> And rightly so. For if one is not first freed from material things and the worry over them, how shall they be freed from evil thoughts? And if one is encompassed by thoughts, how can they see the sin hidden beneath them? This sin is like a darkness and a mist of the soul, taking its origin from evil notions and actions. The devil tests us through a <term>non-violent assault</term><note>original: "prosvolēs aviastou" — a suggestion or "flicker" of a thought that does not force the human will but invites it.</note>, pointing out the beginning of a sin; then man, through a love of pleasure and vanity, gladly enters into conversation with it. For even if one’s <term>discernment</term><note>original: "diakrisin" — the ability to distinguish between good and evil thoughts.</note> did not wish to sin, yet in practice, he was mastered by it and accepted it. If one has not glimpsed this "comprehensive sin," when will they pray concerning it to be purified? And if one is not purified, how shall they find the "place of pure nature"? And if one has not found this, how shall they see the inner house of Christ? For we are the house of God, according to the words of the prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles.

<column-break/>

<margin>225.</margin> Therefore, through the sequence of things mentioned above, we must seek to find that "house," and remain persistent in prayer, knocking so that—either here or at the moment of our departure—the Master may open to us, lest because of our negligence He says: "I do not know where you are from." <note>Luke 13:25</note> Not only ought we to ask and receive, but we must also guard what is given. For there are some who lost what they had even after receiving it. A bare knowledge or an accidental experience of these matters may perhaps be held by those who have learned late or are young; however, the patient and constant "work" is hardly found except among the most devout and experienced elders. These are the ones who, having often lost the way through inattention, sought it again through voluntary labors and found it. Let us also not cease from doing this until we possess that grace which cannot be taken away.

<margin>226.</margin> These are a few of the righteous requirements of the Spiritual Law that we have come to know out of many. The great Psalmist <note>Referring to King David</note> continually guides those who chant unceasingly to learn and practice these in the Lord Jesus. To Him be glory, power, and worship, now and forever. Amen.

according to the Gospel—a soul that conducts

can overcome the evils teeming within;
especially the passions mentioned above. For those
passions to which the soul has become habituated through
preconception and long custom
pull it down more forcefully;
one must therefore undertake a more diligent and unceasing
struggle against them, until one subdues
<margin>* In other manuscripts: "of wickedness"</margin> the carnal and irrational workings * of the heart.
The soul was previously subject to these and
pulled down by them; through the constant
reminder of thoughts and through evil meditation,
it was led away as a captive by the
internal consent to these ideas.
Since we have now been separated from your person
bodily for a short while—though not in heart—
being hidden in the desert among the true
workers and athletes of Christ,
so that we too, by struggling even a little
and contending alongside the brothers who strive
against opposing powers and
who nobly resist the passions,
might set aside our hesitation,
cast off our negligence,
and take up every diligence and care,
hastening to please God;
therefore, we have been eager to engrave a short
exhortation and soul-profiting admonition
through this letter to your Sincerity. <note>Another formal title for the recipient.</note>
Regarding the things I spoke to you in person,
may you reap spiritual benefit from them by reading
these few words in our modest letter of counsel
diligently, as if we were present with you.
Now, the very beginning of your profit according to God,
O child, you ought to make from this point:

<column-break/>

unceasingly, and as an ever-present memorial,
you must consider in your constant meditation
all the providences <note>original: "oikonomias" — God’s plan and "management" of human salvation.</note> of the man-loving God
that have happened and are happening to you,
and His benefits for the salvation of your soul.
You must not let these many and
great benefits of His be forgotten, hidden by the
forgetfulness of wickedness or the cause of laziness,
and thereby pass the remaining time
unprofitably and ungratefully.
For such unceasing memories,
piercing the heart like a sting, <note>original: "kentron" — a goad or sharp point used to drive oxen, here used as a metaphor for a spiritual stimulus.</note>
always move it
toward confession, toward humility,
toward thanksgiving with a contrite soul,
toward every good diligence, and a return
of good ways and character, and every
virtue according to God. Let the soul always meditate
with a clear conscience on the prophetic saying:
"What shall I give back to the Lord for all
He has given back to me?" <note>Psalm 116:12</note>
For when the soul considers the benefits
of the man-loving God from the time of birth,
or from how many dangers it was often rescued,
or how many evils it fell into,
having often slipped into voluntary transgressions,
yet was not handed over—as would be just—to the
deceiving spirits for destruction and death;
but instead, the man-loving Master,
overlooking the transgressions with long-suffering,
protected the soul, waiting for its
return. Even when it served the enemy and
evil spirits voluntarily through the passions,
He Himself nourished and sheltered it,
providing for it in every way.
And finally, by a good impulse,
He guided it to the way of salvation,
and placed a love for the ascetic life in the heart,
and gave it strength to leave the world
and all its deception of fleshly pleasures,
and adorned it with the angelic habit <note>original: "angelikō schēmati" — the formal clothing or "habit" of a monk, symbolizing a life like the angels.</note>
of the ascetic order;
and He prepared the way for it to be easily received
by holy men in a community of brothers.
Who, having a clear conscience
and considering these things,
would not always continue in contrition of heart?
Having so many pledges of
prior benefits—even though he himself had
done nothing good before—
would he not always take up a firm hope?
For he reasons this:
that if He did this when I had done nothing good,
but had even sinned much before Him,
living in impurities of the flesh
and in many other wickednesses,
He did not deal with me according to my sins,
nor according to my lawless acts...

</columns>

<header>### CONCERNING THOSE WHO THINK THEY ARE JUSTIFIED BY WORKS.</header>

<columns>

...[God] has repaid me, but instead has arranged so many gifts and graces for my salvation. If I give myself entirely from now on to serve Him in all pure conduct and the achievement of virtues—to how many good things and spiritual gifts will He then deem me worthy? Strengthening me, guiding me, and prospering me in every good work? Therefore, the person who always maintains such a **way of thinking** <note>original: "logismon" — in ascetic literature, this refers to the underlying thought-patterns or "internal dialogue" of the soul.</note>, and does not forget God's benefits, persuades and directs himself. He urges himself toward every good ascetic practice of virtue and every labor of righteousness, always eager, always ready to do the will of God.

Therefore, my beloved child, since you possess a natural intelligence by the grace of Christ, keep this **spiritual conversation** <note>original: "adoleschian" — literally "chatter" or "musing," used here to mean a constant internal meditation on God.</note> and good study always within yourself. Do not let yourself be covered by destructive forgetfulness, nor be hindered by **sloth** <note>original: "rhathymia" — a key ascetic term for spiritual apathy or "the noonday devil" that makes one want to give up.</note> which makes the mind empty and turns it away from life. Do not let your reasoning be darkened by ignorance, the cause of all evils, or be enticed by wicked negligence. Do not be dragged down by the pleasure of the flesh, nor defeated by gluttony. Do not let your mind be taken captive by desire, nor work defilement within yourself by consenting to **fornicating thoughts**; do not be conquered by anger, which gives birth to hatred of one's brother. 

Do not, for the sake of some pitiful and miserable excuse, cause grief or be grieved yourself, gathering memories of evil thoughts against your neighbor. This turns one away from pure prayer to God and enslaves the mind, making one look at a brother of the same soul with a beastly thought. By the irrational way of fleshly thinking, the conscience is bound, and one is handed over for a time to the discipline of the evil spirits to whom one yielded. This continues until the mind, utterly at a loss and swallowed up by grief and sloth—having lost its progress toward God for the reasons mentioned—begins again to take hold of the path of salvation through great humility. After laboring much in prayers and all-night vigils, and having undone the causes [of the fall] through humility and confession toward God and one’s neighbor, the person begins to be sober again. Being illumined by the light of **Evangelical knowledge** through divine grace, he comes to know this: that he who does not perfectly give himself over to the Cross...

<column-break/>

...in a spirit of humility and self-abasement—casting himself down beneath everyone to be trampled, devalued, despised, wronged, laughed at, and mocked, and to endure all these things with joy for the sake of the Lord, seeking no human things at all, whether glory or honor or praise, or the pleasure of food, drink, or clothing—such a person cannot become a true Christian.

Therefore, since such struggles, contests, and crowns lie before us, how long shall we be mocked by a mere outward form of piety? We serve the Lord with a "mask" on, appearing as one thing to men, but appearing as something else to Him who knows all secret things. For though we are considered holy by many, we are still far from being holy in our character; truly we have the **form of godliness** <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 3:5, "having a form of godliness but denying its power."</note>, but we do not possess its power before God. We are considered virgins and pure by many, but before Him who understands the secrets, we are defiled within by consenting to fornicating thoughts and are mired in the workings of the passions. And because of our outward, "staged" asceticism, we even become conceited by the praise of men, and our minds are blinded. 

How long, then, shall we walk in the vanity of the mind, failing to grasp the mindset of the Gospel? We do not recognize the way of life according to the conscience, so that we might pursue it diligently and find the **confidence** <note>original: "parrhesian" — a term meaning "boldness" or "freedom of speech" before God in prayer.</note> that comes from a clear conscience. Instead, we still lean only on the supposed righteousness of the "outward man" because we lack true knowledge. We deceive ourselves through outward practices alone, wishing to please men and hunting for the glory, honor, and praise that comes from them. 

The Judge who cannot be deceived will surely come—He who reveals the hidden things of darkness and makes manifest the counsels of the heart. He does not respect the rich man nor pity the poor; He will strip away the outward appearance and reveal the truth hidden within. He will crown the true contestants and athletes who lived according to their conscience in the presence of the Angels and before His own Father. But those who were merely "staged," who wrapped themselves in a form of godliness and showed only a public way of life to men...

<sig>11</sig>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual advice from St. Mark the Ascetic to his disciple Nicolas. It moves from a general call to gratitude into a stern warning about "internalized" sins—the passions that hide behind a mask of outward religious behavior—using the Parable of the Ten Virgins as a central metaphor.</meta>

# OF THE HOLY MARK THE ASCETIC

<columns>

...those who put on a show of virtue and vainly support themselves upon it, deceiving themselves. Before the church of the Saints on high and the entire heavenly host, He triumphs over them; and so, being terribly put to shame, He sends them away into the outer darkness, just like the foolish virgins. For those virgins preserved their outward virginity—indeed, they were not accused of any fault in that regard—and they even possessed a measure of "oil" in their vessels, meaning they shared in certain virtues and outward achievements, as well as some spiritual gifts. This is why their lamps remained lit for a time. 

However, through negligence, ignorance, and **sloth** <note>original: "rhathymia" — a state of spiritual apathy or listlessness often described as the "noonday devil."</note>, they failed to take forethought. They did not accurately recognize the hidden swarm of **passions** <note>original: "pathon" — in ascetic theology, these are disordered impulses or spiritual sicknesses like pride or anger.</note> within them, which are set in motion by evil spirits. Instead, their thoughts were corrupted by the workings of the adversary; they shared in these thoughts by consenting to them in their minds, being secretly lured away and defeated. 

They were overcome by the foulest envy, by "good-hating" jealousy, strife, contention, hatred, anger, bitterness, malice, hypocrisy, wrath, pride, vainglory, people-pleasing, self-satisfaction, love of money, **acedia** <note>original: "akedia" — spiritual weariness or lack of care for one's soul.</note>, and carnal desire (which produces a love of pleasure within one’s thoughts). They fell to unbelief, lack of the fear of God, cowardice, sorrow, argumentativeness, laxity, sleep, self-conceit, self-justification, haughtiness, arrogance, greed, profligacy, covetousness, and—most grievous of all—despair, along with the subtle workings of wickedness. 

These are the things that also corrupt the practice of good deeds or a "venerable way of life," even when people think they are performing them before others to reap their praise. Even if such people shared in some spiritual gifts, they "sold them off" to the spirits of vainglory and people-pleasing. By participating in these other passions, they mixed their good practices with wicked and carnal mindsets. Because of this, their works were rendered unacceptable and unclean, just like the sacrifice of Cain. Thus, they were deprived of the Bridegroom’s joy and shut out of the heavenly bridal chamber.

Therefore, as we consider, discern, and test these things, let us know and understand what state we are in. While we still have time for repentance and turning back, let us correct ourselves so that our good works may be performed purely. May they be true and clean, unmixed with a carnal mindset, so that they are not rejected...

<column-break/>

...as a blemished sacrifice due to a lack of fear, negligence, and a lack of true knowledge. We must take care lest we endure the labor of virginity, self-control, vigils, fasting, and hospitality, and consume our days in these tasks, only to find that because of the aforementioned passions, our supposed "righteous acts" are found to be a blemished sacrifice, unacceptable to Christ, our heavenly High Priest.

Therefore, my child, one who wishes to "take up the Cross" and follow Him must first and foremost take care to acquire knowledge and understanding. This is done through a continuous inner searching of one’s **thoughts** <note>original: "logismoi" — the internal suggestions or "inner dialogue" that lead toward or away from God.</note>, a deep concern for salvation, intelligence, great zeal toward God, and by questioning those servants of God who are of one soul and one mind and who are fighting the same struggle. This is so that one does not walk in darkness without the light of a lamp, ignorant of where and how he is walking.

For the **self-willed** <note>original: "idiorrythmos" — literally "following one’s own rhythm"; in a monastery, this refers to a monk who lives by his own rules rather than under a guide or common rule.</note> person who walks without the knowledge of the Gospel and without a guide stumbles often. He falls into many pits and traps of the evil one; he wanders much and falls into many dangers, not knowing what his end will be. Many, indeed, have passed through many labors, ascetic practices, and hardships, enduring much toil for God’s sake; yet their self-will, their lack of discernment, and their failure to seek help from their neighbor rendered all those great labors void and useless.

You, then, my beloved child—as I said at the beginning of this exhortation—must not forget the benefits bestowed upon you by the worshipful and man-loving God. Do not let them be stolen away by the "theft" of malice or pulled under by sloth. Instead, place before your eyes God’s benefits to you from your very birth until now, whether they be physical or spiritual. Meditate on them and "chatter" about them constantly, according to the scripture: *Do not forget all His rewards* <note>A reference to Psalm 103:2.</note>. 

Do this so that your heart may be easily moved toward the fear and love of God, so that you might repay Him, according to your power, with a precise life, a virtuous conduct, a pious conscience, graceful speech, right faith, a humble mind, and—to put it simply—to dedicate your whole self to God. Let yourself be compelled by the memory of the good things you have received from your good and man-loving Master, so that in a spontaneous way, through such a remembrance of His benefits...

<summary>This page warns that outward religious devotion is worthless if the heart is secretly harborning "passions" like pride and envy, comparing such people to the Foolish Virgins. It emphasizes that a "self-willed" spiritual life without guidance leads to failure, urging the monk to focus on gratitude to God as the primary motivator for true virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the letter from St. Mark the Ascetic to Nicolas. Having warned against the "hidden passions" on the previous page, Mark now reminds Nicolas of God’s personal intervention in his life—specifically a miraculous survival of a shipwreck—to motivate his commitment to a life of strict asceticism and spiritual renewal.</meta>

### LETTER TO NICOLAS THE MONK

->Rather, with the help of a divine inclination <note>original: "rhopēs" — a downward weight or turning of the scale, here meaning divine help or momentum</note> from above, your heart is wounded with love and longing. For those wonders which He did not perform for others who were much better than you, He performed for you, according to His own unutterable love for mankind. Therefore, strive to keep in unceasing memory all the good things that have happened to you from God. Especially remember without ceasing that great and wonderful grace and benefit which He granted you when you were sailing with your mother from the Holy Places <note>Jerusalem and the surrounding sites of Christ's life.</note> to Constantinople, as you related to us. It was when that fearful and uncontrollable storm arose, and a great wave moved in the night, and all those in the ship—along with the sailors and your mother herself—perished in the deep. Yet, by a paradoxical and divine power, you alone were thrown out with two others and saved. 

Consider how it was providently arranged for you to come to Ancyra <note>Modern-day Ankara, Turkey; a major city in the Byzantine Empire.</note> and be taken in with fatherly compassion by a certain noble man <margin>*In another [manuscript]: "by another"</margin>, and how you were joined in disposition to that most devout child, Epiphanius. This was so that both of you, guided by a holy man, might enter the path of salvation and be received by the holy servants of God as genuine children. For all these good things that have come to you from God, what worthy return can you make to Him who called your soul to eternal life? For the future, you ought no longer to live for yourself, as is just, but for Christ who died and rose for you. You must strive for every virtue of righteousness and the fulfillment of the commandments, always seeking what is the good, perfect, and acceptable will of God, pursuing this with all your strength. 

Furthermore, my child, subject your youth to the Word of God just as the Word itself demands: to present your body as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your rational worship. Every moisture of fleshly desire must be cooled and dried up through "scantiness of food," "scantiness of drink," and "all-night vigils," so that you may say from your heart: *I have become like a wineskin in the frost; I have not forgotten your statutes* <note>Psalm 119:83. The image of the "wineskin in the frost" refers to the drying out of the passions through ascetic discipline.</note>. Knowing that you belong to Christ, crucify your own flesh, according to the Apostolic voice <note>Galatians 5:24</note>, along with its passions and desires. Deaden your members that are upon the earth—not only the act of sexual immorality, but also the internal 

<column-break/>

impurity <note>original: "akatharsian"</note> worked in the flesh by evil spirits. And he who expects the crown of true, undefiled, and complete virginity does not stop his struggle there. Following the Apostolic teaching, he strives to deaden even the very impulse and movement of passion. Even then, he is not yet fully satisfied, for he expects to house angelic and stainless virginity within his own body through a vehement love <note>original: "erōti" — used here for divine or spiritual eros.</note>. He prays that even the mere thought of desire in the mind—even without the movement or action of a bodily passion—should vanish like a passing flicker of the mind. 

This is possible to achieve only through help from above, and the power and supply of the Spirit—if indeed there are some who are deemed worthy of this grace. Thus, he who expects the crown of pure, immaterial, and stainless virginity crucifies the flesh through ascetic labors. He deadens the members on the earth through the intensity and persistence of self-control <note>original: "enkrateias" — often translated as temperance or continence.</note>, wasting away the "outer man," thinning him, and making him shriveled and hardened. He does this so that, through faith and struggle and the working of grace, the "inner man" may be renewed, progressing toward the better day by day—increasing in love, adorned with meekness, gladdened by the joy of the spirit, governed by the peace of Christ, led by kindness, guarded by goodness, encompassed by the fear of God, enlightened by understanding and knowledge, brightened by wisdom, and guided by humility. 

The mind <note>original: "nous" — the highest faculty of the human soul, the "eye of the heart."</note>, being renewed by the Spirit through these and similar virtues, recognizes within itself the character of the God-like image. It perceives the intellectual and unutterable beauty of the Master’s likeness and grasps the wealth of the self-taught and self-learned wisdom of the internal law. Therefore, O child, thin the youthful flesh, and fatten the immortal soul with the things mentioned before; renew the mind with these virtues through the cooperation of the Spirit. For the flesh of youth, fattened by various foods and the drinking of wine, is like a pig ready for slaughter. In the heat of the body's pleasures, the soul is slaughtered; and in the boiling of evil desire, the mind is taken captive, unable to resist the pleasures of the flesh...

<summary>Mark the Ascetic recounts Nicolas's miraculous survival of a shipwreck that killed his mother, using this as motivation for Nicolas to commit to a rigorous life of fasting and prayer. He explains that the goal of asceticism is to "thin" the body to "fatten" the soul, allowing the Holy Spirit to renew the inner man in the image of God.</summary>

# OF THE HOLY MARK THE ASCETIC

...being able. For an influx of blood produces an outflow of the spirit <note>original: "pnevmatos" — referring here to the spiritual focus or the 'breath' of prayerful life, which the desert fathers believed was hindered by heavy digestion.</note>. Especially should a young person not even smell the consumption of wine, so that a double fire does not appear—one from the internal activity of the passions and the other from the wine poured in from the outside. Through these, the pleasure of the flesh might boil over and drive away the spiritual pleasure of the labor of compunction <term>Compunction: (katanyxis) A state of heart-felt sorrow for sins that leads to spiritual sweetness and clarity.</term> from itself, producing confusion and a hardening of the heart. Instead, out of spiritual desire, youth should not even indulge in a total fullness of water; for the lack of water contributes greatly to the cooperation of chastity <note>original: "sophrosynēs" — a multifaceted term for temperance, self-control, and purity of mind.</note>. Having tested this through action, you will receive the full assurance from experience itself. We do not legislate or define this as a yoke of necessity we wish to place upon you, but we lovingly advise and counsel it as a helpful strategy and method for the cooperation of true virginity and exact chastity, leaving it to your own free will to do as it wishes.

Come then, for the rest of our discourse, let us deal briefly with the irrational passion of anger. It desolates every soul, confusing and darkening it, and making a human being resemble a wild beast during the time of its movement and activity—especially one who is prone to slip and is sharply inclined toward it. This passion is particularly rooted in pride; it is strengthened by it and becomes indestructible. As long as the diabolical tree of bitterness, anger, and wrath is watered by the foul water of pride, it flourishes and thrives, bearing much fruit of iniquity. Thus, the building of the evil one becomes indestructible in the soul, having the foundations of pride as its support and strength. If, therefore, you want the tree of iniquity—I mean the passion of bitterness, anger, and wrath—to wither within you and become fruitless, so that the axe of the Spirit might come and cut it down and cast it into the fire, according to the Gospel voice, and take it away along with all malice; and if you want the house of iniquity, which the evil one builds wickedly in the soul—gathering various excuses, whether reasonable or irrational, like stones through material things or words in one’s thoughts, and constructing a building of malice in the soul, placing the thoughts of pride as support and strength

<column-break/>

—if, then, you want this house to be demolished and razed to the ground, keep the humility of the Lord unforgotten in your heart: Who He is, and what He became for our sake. Consider from what height of the revealed light of the Godhead—which is glorified in the Heavens by every rational nature, according to the power of the celestial beings: Angels, Archangels, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers, Cherubim, and Seraphim, and the unnameable intellectual Powers whose names have not reached us, according to the Apostle's enigma <note>A reference to St. Paul's mention of celestial hierarchies in his letters (e.g., Colossians 1:16), which the author calls an "enigma" because their full nature remains a mystery.</note>—to what depth of human humility He descended through His unutterable goodness. He became like us in every way, we who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, who had become captives through the transgression of Adam and were dominated by the enemy through the activity of the passions. While we were in such a harsh captivity and ruled by invisible and bitter death, the Lord of all creation, visible and invisible, was not ashamed. Instead, He humbled Himself and took upon Himself the man who had been condemned under the passions <margin>*of the | penalty, | and the | Master's | sen- | tence.</margin> of dishonor and desire and the Master's sentence. He became like us in all things except sin—that is, without the passions of dishonor. For the penalties brought upon man by the Master’s sentence because of the sin of transgression—death, toil, hunger, thirst, and the like—He took them all upon Himself, becoming what we are, so that we might become what He is. The Word became flesh, so that the flesh might become Word. Being rich, He became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich through His poverty. Through His great love for mankind, He was made like us, so that through every virtue we might be made like Him. For since Christ's dwelling among us, the human being who is truly according to the "image and likeness" is renewed through the grace and power of the Spirit. Such a person reaches the measure of perfect love, which casts out fear and can no longer fall; for "love never falls." For Love, says John, is God; and he who abides in love abides in God. The Apostles were deemed worthy of this measure, as were those who practiced virtue similarly to them and presented themselves perfect to the Lord, with perfect longing, throughout their entire lives...

He concludes by pointing to the "kenosis" or self-emptying humility of Christ as the only way to demolish the soul's internal house of malice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Mark the Ascetic's spiritual direction to the monk Nicolas. Having previously discussed physical temperance and the dangers of anger, Mark now provides a specific meditative practice: contemplating the "Humility of Christ" as a psychological tool to dismantle pride and resentment.</meta>

# LETTER TO NICOLAS THE MONK

->...having followed Christ. Therefore, if you always and unforgettingly reflect upon such great humility, which the Lord took up through His ineffable love for mankind <note>original: "philanthrōpia" — a term describing God's inherent benevolence toward humanity</note>—that is to say, the dwelling of the Word of God in the womb, the taking on of human nature, the birth from a woman, the gradual growth of His physical stature, the dishonors, the insults, the reproaches, the mockeries, the scourgings, the spitting, the ridicule, the taunting, the scarlet robe, the crown of thorns, the sentence passed against Him by the rulers, the shouting against Him by the lawless Jews (who were His own kin) saying, "Away with Him, away with Him, crucify Him!", the Cross, the nails, the spear, the drink of vinegar and gall, the triumph of the nations, the mockery of those passing by who said, "If you are the Son of God, come down from the Cross and we will believe you," and the rest of the sufferings which He endured for us: the crucifixion, death, the three-day burial in the tomb, the descent into Hades. Then, consider the fruits of these sufferings—what they are and of what kind: that is, the resurrection from the dead, the plundering of Hades and death, the souls that came out with the Lord, the ascension into Heaven, the sitting at the right hand of the Father, the honor and glory above every "principality and power and every name that is named," and the worship of all the Angels for the Firstborn of the dead, because of His sufferings. This is according to the voice of the Apostle which says: "Let this mind be in us, which was also in Christ Jesus; who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also has highly exalted Him, and given Him a name which is above every name; that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and those on earth, and those under the earth," and so forth. Behold the reasons for the aforementioned things according to the justice of God, into what glory and height they raised the Lordly humanity <note>original: "Kuriakon anthrōpon" — a theological term referring to the human nature assumed by Christ</note>. Therefore, if with desire and disposition you preserve these memories unforgettingly<-

<column-break/>

->in your heart, the passion of bitterness, rage, and anger will not rule over you. For when the foundations of the passion of pride are removed through the humility of Christ, which you are contemplating, the entire building of the lawlessness of rage, anger, and sorrow easily and automatically collapses. For what heart, however hard or stony, if it has continually in mind such great <margin>* Majesty</margin> Divinity* of the Only-begotten humbled for our sake, and the recounted memory of the aforementioned sufferings, will not be crushed? Will it not be moved to compunction? Will it not be humbled? Will it not voluntarily become "earth and ashes" and a footstool for all people according to the Scripture? And when the soul is thus humbled and crushed, looking toward the humility of Christ, what rage will be able to take hold of it? What anger? What bitterness can prevail? But, as it seems, the forgetfulness <term>Forgetfulness: (lēthē) In ascetic thought, this is not a simple lapse in memory, but a spiritual darkness that causes one to lose sight of God’s presence.</term> of these beneficial and life-giving thoughts—and its sister, listlessness <term>Listlessness: (rhathymia) A state of spiritual boredom or laziness often called the "noonday demon."</term>, and their coworker and companion, ignorance—prepare the heavier and more internal passions of the soul (which are difficult to discover and difficult to correct) to act and nest within it, like a terrible curiosity covering and darkening the soul. These things produce a lack of fear and a neglect of good things, providing an entrance and an operation for every passion, fearlessly and easily. For when the soul is covered by all-evil forgetfulness, and destructive listlessness, and the mother and nurse of all evils, ignorance, the wretched and blinded mind is easily bound by everything seen, thought, or heard. For example, if it sees the beauty of a woman, it is immediately wounded by fleshly desire; and thus, the memories thereafter take up what was passionately and pleasurably observed, or heard, or touched, and through the re-shaping of thoughts and evil meditation, they paint the images within. And so they defile the still-passionate and wretched mind through the energy of the spirits of fornication. For then, even the flesh—if it be well-fed, or youthful, or moist—is readily stirred to passion by such memories and acts out its own part, moving toward desire; sometimes in sleep, or in waking, working uncleanness, even if it did not physically commune with a woman.<-

<summary>Mark explains that meditating on the life and Passion of Christ is the primary cure for pride and anger. He warns that spiritual ignorance, forgetfulness, and listlessness are the "mothers of all evils" that allow sensory temptations to turn into internal mental fantasies and physical passions.</summary>

<keywords>humility, Passion of Christ, Philippians 2, pride, anger, forgetfulness, listlessness, ignorance, mental images, ascetic psychology</keywords>

...thought to be temperate, and a virgin, and pure by

attentively watches himself, and with little-need, and

associate with spiritual and experienced fathers,
and being eager to be with and be guided by
them. For it is dangerous to live alone, and
according to one's own rhythm <note>original: "idiorrythmon" — living by one's own rules rather than under a community or guide</note>, and without witnesses, and

so that even if he does not himself have the lamp of true
<margin>

<column-break/>

...through which the remaining passions of wickedness, creeping in, are active, live, and gain strength in the hearts of those who love pleasure and in the souls of the uneducated. But through much attentiveness and the supervision of the mind, combined with help from above, one finds those evils that remain unknown to others and are not even thought to exist—yet are more destructive than all other evils. By using the weapons of righteousness which are opposite to them—namely, a good memory (which I call the cause of all good things) and enlightened knowledge, through which the soul wakes up and drives the darkness of ignorance away from itself, and an excellent zeal that prepares and urges the soul toward salvation—one prevails. Having put on these weapons of virtue in the power of the Holy Spirit, through every prayer and petition, you shall nobly and courageously fight against those three previously mentioned giants of the spiritual <note>original: "noēton" — intellectual or spiritual, referring to the "perceived" enemies of the mind</note> foreigners. Through an excellent memory of God, you must always think on whatever is true, whatever is noble, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, if there is any virtue and if there is any praise <note>A quotation of Philippians 4:8</note>,

<column-break/>

thus driving away from yourself that most wicked forgetfulness. Through enlightened and heavenly knowledge, you shall vanish the destructive ignorance of darkness. And through all-virtuous and most beautiful zeal, you shall drive out that godless and innate sloth <note>original: "rhathy mian" — a state of spiritual laziness, indifference, or "acedia"</note> which works evil in the soul. You must acquire these virtues not from simple free will alone, but from the power of God and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, with much attentiveness 
<margin>attentiveness <note>The marginal note suggests a variant spelling or correction: "proseche" instead of "prosecheia".</note></margin>
and prayer; thus you will be able to be delivered from those three previously mentioned strong giants of the evil one. For the harmony of true knowledge, the memory of God’s words, and good zeal—when forced to stand together in the soul through active grace and guarded diligently—vanishes every trace of forgetfulness, ignorance, and sloth from the soul and reduces them to nothingness. Thus, grace reigns thereafter in the soul, in Christ Jesus our Lord; to whom be glory and power unto the ages of ages. Amen.

### BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
# O F  H E S Y C H I U S
### THE PRESBYTER

<image-desc>A smaller floral divider mirroring the one above.</image-desc>

Our Holy Father Hesychius, who became a Presbyter <note>a priest or elder</note> of the Church in Jerusalem, flourished during the time of Theodosius the Younger <note>Theodosius II, reigned 408–450 AD</note>, blossoming in the word of teaching. He died around the year four hundred and thirty-three. Although his writings are many, only this discourse, divided into two hundred and three chapters, was placed here; it is as useful as any other, being most beneficial for beginners regarding <term>nepsis</term> <note>spiritual watchfulness or sobriety of the soul</note>, the attention of the mind, and the guarding of the heart. Concerning him, the critic Photius <note>Photius the Great, 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note> says the following

<column-break/>

word for word, in Reading 198, page 267:
"And the twenty-second part <note>referring to a volume or chapter in a collection</note> contains the work of Hesychius, Presbyter of Jerusalem, in which the entire discourse of the book is completed. It is established as being as useful as any other work for those who practice their life for the inheritance of the Heavens. In its delivery, it possesses clarity; and in other respects, it is of such a kind as would be fitting for men who do not turn toward the struggle of words <note>dialectic or academic debate</note>, but who have accepted all labor and diligence for the sake of the practice of deeds <note>asceticism and moral action</note>."
