# HESYCHIUS
## THE PRESBYTER
### TO THEODOULOS
A SOUL-PROFITING AND SAVING DISCOURSE CONCERNING WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE, ARRANGED IN CHAPTERS.

->**The beginning of the soul’s illumination, and a true instruction. These are called the Refutative and Prayerful [texts].**<-

---

<margin>1.</margin> Watchfulness <note>original: "Nepsis"—a state of spiritual alertness, sobriety, and "keeping awake" to one's internal thoughts</note> is a spiritual method that, with God’s help, completely frees a person from passionate thoughts, words, and evil deeds, provided it is practiced over time and followed with zeal. To those who travel this path, it grants a secure knowledge of the incomprehensible God—as far as that is attainable—and the resolution of divine and hidden mysteries. It is the fulfillment of every commandment of God in both the Old and New Testaments, and the provider of every good thing in the age to come. This is, essentially, the purity of the heart; yet because of its great magnitude and beauty—or to speak more accurately, because of our own neglect—it is very rare today among Monks. It is this purity which Christ calls blessed, saying:
> Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. <note>Matthew 5:8</note>

Because it is of such value, it is bought at a high price. Watchfulness, when it dwells in a person for a long time, becomes a guide to a righteous and God-pleasing life. This is also the stepping stone to contemplation <note>original: "theoria"—the direct spiritual vision of God or divine truth</note>, and it teaches us how to move the three parts of the soul <note>The "tripartite" soul: the intelligent, the desiring, and the spirited/emotional parts</note> justly, and how to guard the senses securely. Daily, it increases the four general virtues in the person who participates in it.

<margin>2.</margin> The great lawgiver Moses—or rather, the Holy Spirit—shows the blameless, pure, encompassing, and elevating nature of such virtue. Teaching us how one must begin and complete it, he says: "Take heed to yourself, lest there be a hidden word in your heart—

<column-break/>

—an iniquity." <note>Deuteronomy 15:9</note> He calls the "hidden word" the single-thought appearance <note>original: "emphasis"—the first mental image or suggestion</note> of some evil thing hated by God. The Fathers also call this a "provocation" <note>original: "prosbōle"—the initial assault or suggestion of a thought from the outside</note> brought to the heart by the devil. Our thoughts follow this suggestion as soon as it appears to the mind, and they begin to converse with it in a passionate manner.

<margin>3.</margin> Watchfulness is the path of every virtue and commandment of God. It is also called "stillness of the heart" <note>original: "kardiakē hesychia"</note>; and when it is perfected without mental images, it is the same as the "guarding of the mind."

<margin>4.</margin> Just as one born blind does not see the light of the sun, so the person who does not walk in watchfulness does not see the rich flashes of grace from above. Neither will they be freed from evil works, words, and thoughts that are hateful to God. At the hour of their death, such people will not pass freely by the rulers of Tartarus <note>A reference to the "toll-houses" or demonic barriers believed to test the soul after death</note>.

<margin>5.</margin> Attention <note>original: "Prosoche"—closely related to watchfulness</note> is a continuous stillness of the heart from every thought. In this state, the soul always, perpetually, and without ceasing, "breathes" and calls upon Jesus Christ, the Son of God and God Himself. With Him, the soul bravely draws up its battle lines against its enemies, and to Him it confesses its sins—for He alone has the authority to forgive sins. The soul continually embraces Christ through this invocation, doing so secretly to Him alone who knows the hearts, attempting to hide its internal struggle and its sweetness from all men, lest the evil one secretly...

<meta>This page continues the discourse by Hesychius the Presbyter. On the previous page, he began defining watchfulness (nepsis) as a spiritual path toward purity of heart. # A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE CONCERNING WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE

...lest [neglect] should prosper vice and destroy this most beautiful work.

<margin>6.</margin>
Watchfulness <note>original: "Nepsis"—spiritual sobriety or alertness</note> is a constant fixing of the mind <note>original: "logismos"—the reasoning faculty or specific thoughts</note> and its stationing at the gate of the heart. From there, it watches the "thief" thoughts as they approach, listening to what these murderous forces say and seeing what they do. It observes the specific form being engraved and set up by the demons, attempting to deceive the mind through the use of the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"—here meaning mental imagery used as a lure</note>. If we are diligent in these things, they will show us, with great clarity and expertise, the true nature of this mental warfare, provided we are willing to see it.

<margin>7.</margin>
This vigilance is born from a twofold fear—the fear of God’s judgment and the fear of losing His presence—as well as from the times God seems to withdraw from us and the trials that serve to discipline us. It is a continuous, supervisory attention within the governing part of the human person <note>original: "hegemonikon"—the ruling part of the soul or intellect</note>, attempting to block the very spring of evil thoughts and actions. It is for this reason that such "desertions" and unexpected trials from God occur: to correct our way of life, especially for those who have tasted the rest of this beautiful work and then become negligent. Continuity in this practice creates a habit; the habit then creates a natural "density" or frequency of watchfulness; this in turn gradually gives birth to a contemplation <note>original: "theoria"—spiritual insight or vision</note> of the war itself. This is then succeeded by the persistent Prayer of Jesus <note>original: "Iesou euche"—the Jesus Prayer</note>, a sweet stillness of a mind free from images, and a stable state of soul established through Jesus.

<margin>8.</margin>
The intellect, standing and calling upon Christ against its enemies and fleeing to Him for refuge, is like a beast surrounded by many dogs that holds its ground within a fortress. From a distance, it mentally foresees the invisible ambushes of the unseen enemies; by constantly petitioning the Peacemaker, Jesus, against them, it remains unhurt by them.

<margin>9.</margin>
If you understand this, and if it has been granted to you to "stand in the morning" <note>a reference to Psalm 5:3</note> to be seen by God and to see Him, you know what I am saying. If not, be watchful and you shall receive.

<margin>10.</margin>
As the gathering of the seas makes much water, so too is the gathering and strengthening of watchfulness and sobriety <note>original: "nephaliodes"—the state of being sober-minded</note>. It creates a deep inner stillness of the soul, an abyss of wondrous and secret contemplations, discerning humility, uprightness, and love. This is the result of extreme watchfulness and the Prayer of Jesus Christ offered without distracting thoughts; <margin>is. intensely</margin> and this (*) must be done strictly, frequently, and without losing heart.

<margin>11.</margin>
"Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the Kingdom of

<column-break/>

Heaven," He says, "but he who does the will of my Father." <note>Matthew 7:21</note> And the will of His Father is this: "You who love the Lord, hate what is evil." <note>Psalm 97:10</note> Therefore, along with the Prayer of Jesus Christ, let us also hate evil thoughts; in doing so, behold, we have done the will of God.

<margin>12.</margin>
As a pattern for all virtue, as a model for the human race, and as a restoration of our ancient fall, our Master and God took flesh and set it before us. He painted the picture of an all-virtuous life in His own flesh. Among all the good things He showed us, after His baptism He went up into the wilderness and began a mental struggle <note>original: "noetes pales"—spiritual or intellectual wrestling</note> when the devil approached Him as if He were a mere man. By this method of victory, the Master taught even us, His unworthy servants, how we must conduct our struggle against the spirits of wickedness—namely, through humility, fasting, prayer, and watchfulness—even though He Himself, as God and the God of gods, had no need of such things.

<margin>13.</margin>
As for how many "ways" of watchfulness there are, which are able to gradually cleanse the mind from passionate thoughts, I will not hesitate to show them to you in simple and plain language. For in this discourse on the times of war, I did not think it right to hide the benefit behind complex words, especially for the sake of the simpler brothers. "But you, child Timothy," it says, "pay attention to what you read." <note>A traditional address to the reader, echoing St. Paul’s letters to Timothy</note>

<margin>14.</margin>
One way of watchfulness is to frequently examine the imagination, or rather the "attack" <note>original: "prosbole"—the first stage of a tempting thought entering the mind</note>, because Satan cannot create thoughts or present false deceptions to the mind without the use of mental imagery.

<margin>15.</margin>
A second way is to have a heart that is deeply silent at all times, resting in stillness <note>original: "hesychia"—the practice of inner quiet</note> from every thought, and to pray.

<margin>16.</margin>
Another way is to constantly call upon the Lord Jesus Christ for help in humility.

<margin>17.</margin>
A fourth way is to keep the remembrance of death unceasing in the soul.

<margin>18.</margin>
All these practices, beloved, block evil thoughts like gatekeepers. As for looking toward heaven and considering the earth as nothing—which is very effective when combined with the others—I will set that out more extensively in another place, God willing.

<margin>19.</margin>
If, having cut off the causes of the passions for a short time, we occupy ourselves with spiritual...

<sig>12</sig>

<vocab>Watchfulness, Virtue, Jesus Prayer, Thoughts/Reasonings, Imagination, Sobriety, Humility, Mental Warfare</vocab>

<summary>Hesychius defines watchfulness as a mental "gatekeeper" and outlines four practical methods for maintaining inner sobriety: monitoring mental images, practicing deep silence, frequent use of the Jesus Prayer, and the remembrance of death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual instructions of Hesychius the Presbyter. The previous page discussed the foundational nature of watchfulness (nepsis) as a guard at the gates of the heart. This page transitions from the general theory of contemplation to the practical, fourfold method of inner warfare and the necessity of the "Jesus Prayer" for spiritual victory.</meta>

### HESYCHIUS THE PRESBYTER TO THEODULUS

...in contemplations; but if we do not abide in them, making this our very task, we easily turn back again to the passions of the flesh. We reap nothing else from such a lapse but the total darkening of the mind and a turning away toward material things.

<margin>20.</margin> One who is a combatant in the inner life must, at every moment, possess these four things: humility, extreme attentiveness, refutation, and prayer. He needs humility because his struggle is against the proud demons, and he must have the help of Christ ready in the hand of his heart, for "the Lord hates the proud." <note>Proverbs 3:34 / James 4:6</note> He needs attentiveness so that he may always keep his heart free of any thought, even if that thought appears to be good. He needs refutation <note>original: "antirrhesis"—the practice of talking back to or contradicting a temptation as soon as it appears</note> so that as soon as he recognizes the intruder, he may immediately speak back to the evil one with anger. As it says: "And I will answer those who reproach me with evil" <note>Psalm 119:42</note> and "Shall not my soul be subject to God?" <note>Psalm 62:1</note> Finally, he needs prayer so that, immediately after the refutation, he may cry out to Christ with "groanings that cannot be uttered." <note>Romans 8:26</note> Only then will the combatant see the enemy dissolve or be driven away by the adorable name of Jesus, like dust before the wind or like smoke vanishing along with its mental imagery.

<margin>21.</margin> One who does not possess prayer that is pure of thoughts lacks a weapon for the war. By "prayer," I mean that which is unceasingly active in the inner sanctuary of the soul, so that by the invocation of Christ, the enemy who fights in secret may be scourged and scorched.

<margin>22.</margin> You ought to watch with a sharp and intense gaze of the mind so that you may perceive those thoughts that are entering. Once you recognize them, you must immediately crush the head of the serpent <note>A common patristic metaphor for destroying a sinful thought at its first appearance</note> through refutation. Along with this, cry out to Christ with a groan, and you will then experience divine, invisible assistance. Then you shall see clearly the uprightness of the heart.

<margin>23.</margin> Just as someone holding a mirror in his hand while standing in the midst of many people can see his own face and the faces of those looking into the mirror with him, so too the one who looks deeply into his own heart sees his own internal state, and he also sees the "black faces" of the <term>mental Ethiopians</term> <note>original: "noetōn Aithiopōn"—a common desert metaphor for demons, referencing their "dark" or "shadowy" nature in contrast to the light of the soul</note>.

<margin>24.</margin> But the mind cannot conquer a demonic <term>fantasy</term> <note>original: "phantasia"—a mental image or lure used by demons to stir the passions</note> by itself; let it never be so bold as to try. For the demons are crafty; they even pretend to be defeated to trip you up through vainglory.

<column-break/>

But at the invocation of Jesus Christ, they cannot endure to stand or to practice their deceits against you even for an hour.

<margin>25.</margin> Be careful that you do not become like Israel of old, or you too will be handed over to your mental enemies. For after Israel was delivered from the Egyptians by the God of all, they devised for themselves a molten idol as a helper. <note>Exodus 32; a warning against self-reliance in the spiritual life</note>

<margin>26.</margin> You should understand this "molten idol" to be our own weak mind. As long as the mind calls upon Jesus Christ against the spirits of wickedness, it easily pursues them and skillfully turns back the invisible, hostile powers of the enemy. But when the mind foolishly trusts entirely in itself, it falls with a great crash, like the so-called "swift-winged" bird. The scripture says: "In God my heart trusted, and I was helped, and my flesh has flourished again." <note>Psalm 28:7</note> And "Who but the Lord will stand up for me and join my battle against the countless evil thoughts?" <note>Reflecting Psalm 94:16</note> He who trusts in himself and not in God will suffer a most extraordinary fall.

<margin>27.</margin> O friend, if you wish to compete in the struggle, let the little creature, the spider, be your constant example for the form and order of <term>stillness of heart</term> <note>original: "kardiakē hesychia"—the state of inner quiet and peace</note>; otherwise, you have not yet practiced stillness in the mind as you ought. The spider hunts small flies; but if you practice stillness in this way, laboring within your own soul, you will never cease to "slaughter the Babylonian infants." <note>Reference to Psalm 137:9, allegorically meaning the destruction of evil thoughts while they are still "infants" or newly born in the mind</note> For such a slaughter, you are called blessed by the Holy Spirit through David.

<margin>28.</margin> Just as it is impossible for the Red Sea to be seen in the firmament among the stars, and just as it is impossible for a man walking on the earth not to breathe this air, so it is impossible to cleanse our heart from passionate thoughts and to drive out mental enemies from it without the frequent invocation of Jesus Christ.

<margin>29.</margin> If you always make your home in your heart with a humble spirit, the remembrance of death, self-reproach, refutation, and the invocation of Jesus Christ—and if you travel this narrow but joyful and pleasant path of the mind daily with these weapons, watching soberly—you will come to the holy contemplations of the "Holy of Holies." You will be enlightened by Christ regarding deep mysteries, for in Him are the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and in Him the "fullness of the Deity dwells bodily." <note>Colossians 2:9</note> For you shall perceive...

Hesychius uses the metaphors of a mirror, a spider, and the "Babylonian infants" to illustrate the vigilance required to maintain a pure heart.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual treatise of Hesychius of Sinai (often called Hesychius the Presbyter) addressed to Theodulus. The previous page established the fourfold method of inner warfare (humility, attentiveness, refutation, and prayer). This page expands on the role of the Holy Spirit, the tactics of demons who "hide" the war to induce complacency, the management of anger (thymos) within a monastic community, and the definition of the four cardinal virtues in the context of the soul's inner life.</meta>

# A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON SOBRIETY AND VIRTUE

...regarding Jesus, because the Holy Spirit has leapt into your soul; from Him, the mind of man is enlightened to see with an "unveiled face." <note>original: "anakelymmeno prosopo" - a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18, describing a direct, clear vision of God's glory.</note> No one, he says, can say "Jesus is Lord" except in the Holy Spirit <note>1 Corinthians 12:3</note>—plainly confirming the truth of the One who is sought in a mystical way.

<margin>30.</margin> However, those who love learning should also know this: the envious demons often hide and withdraw the mental war from us. These terrible foes begrudge us the benefit, the knowledge, and the ascent toward God that comes from this struggle. They do this so that, once we have become carefree, they might suddenly snatch our mind away and render our thoughts inattentive once again. Their unceasing aim and the struggle they plot is to prevent our heart from being attentive, for they know the great wealth that is gathered in the soul through such watchfulness. But at such times, let us stretch ourselves toward spiritual contemplations through the remembrance of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the war will return to the mind. Only let us do everything with the counsel—if I may put it this way—of the Lord Himself, and with great humility.

<margin>31.</margin> For those living in a monastic community <note>original: "koinobion" - a monastery where monks live and work together</note> it is necessary, with a voluntary choice and a willing heart, to cut off our every will before the superior. With God's help, we ourselves then become easy to lead and "will-less" <note>original: "athelitoi" - meaning one has surrendered their self-will to God</note> in a sense. It is proper to treat this as a craft, so that we are not disturbed by rage, nor move our spirited power <note>term: "thymikon" — the "spirited" or "incensive" part of the soul, often associated with anger or courage</note> irrationally and against nature. Otherwise, we will find ourselves without the confidence needed for the invisible war. For it is the nature of our will, when it is not cut off by us voluntarily, to become angry toward those who attempt to cut it off involuntarily. From this, our anger is moved to bark wickedly, and it destroys the knowledge of the struggle which was barely acquired through much labor. For anger is by nature destructive. If it is moved against demonic thoughts, it destroys and annihilates them; but if it is stirred up against men, it likewise destroys the good thoughts within us. Thus I see that anger is destructive to all kinds of thoughts, whether they be evil or even "on the right hand" <note>original: "dexion" - meaning thoughts that appear good or pious but might be distractions</note> if that should happen. For anger was provided to us by God as a weapon and a bow, but only if it is not held back in both cases <note>meaning: if it is not used correctly against the right targets</note>; yet if it acts indiscriminately, it is a cause of ruin. For I have known even

<column-break/>

a bold dog* that destroyed the sheep just as it did the wolves. <margin>* equal to.</margin>

<margin>32.</margin> In the same way, one must flee from unrestrained familiarity <note>term: "parresia" — in an ascetic context, this refers to a lack of restraint in speech or a chatty, over-familiar social behavior that breaks a monk's inner silence.</note> as if it were the venom of an asp, and avoid many social encounters as if they were snakes and the offspring of vipers. These things are capable of very quickly bringing about a total forgetfulness of the inner war, dragging the soul down from the high joy that comes from the purity of the heart. For cursed forgetfulness <note>original: "lethe"</note> is opposed to attention just as water is to fire; it is a powerful enemy to it at every hour. From forgetfulness we fall into negligence, and from negligence into contempt, sloth, and improper desires. Thus we return again to the things behind us, just as a dog returns to its own vomit. Let us therefore flee familiarity as a deadly venom; the evil possession of forgetfulness and its consequences are healed by a very strict guarding of the mind and the continuous invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ. For without Him, we can do nothing.

<margin>33.</margin> It is not possible—not even a little—to befriend a snake and carry it in one's bosom, nor is it possible to flatter, serve, and love the body in every way (beyond what is necessary and required) while also caring for heavenly virtue. For it is the nature of the snake to bite the one who warms it, and it is the nature of the body to defile with pleasure the one who serves it. When the body stumbles, let it be chastised unsparingly with the blows of the fist, like a runaway slave full of new wine; let it know the Lord as its master. This corruptible clay—this servant and creature of the night—must not play the merchant nor ignore its mistress, the incorruptible soul. Do not trust your flesh until your departure from this life. "The will of the flesh," it says, "is enmity against God, for it does not submit to the law of God." <note>Romans 8:7</note> And "the flesh desires against the spirit." <note>Galatians 5:17</note> "Those who live in the flesh cannot please God; but we are not in the flesh, but in the spirit." <note>Romans 8:8-9</note>

<margin>34.</margin> It is the work of Prudence to always move the spirited power toward the engagement of the inner battle and toward self-reproach. It is the work of Wisdom to move the rational power <note>term: "logistikon" — the reasoning faculty of the soul</note> toward strict and continuous sobriety and spiritual contemplation. It is the work of Justice to direct the desiring power <note>term: "epithymetikon" — the part of the soul associated with longing and appetites</note> toward both virtue and God. And it is the work of Fortitude to govern and restrain the five senses, so that the inner man (that is, the heart) and the outer man (the body) are not defiled through them.

<summary>This page describes the psychological and spiritual tactics of ascetic life, warning against the "forgetfulness" caused by social familiarity and explaining how the soul's faculties—anger, reason, and desire—must be redirected through the four cardinal virtues toward God.</summary>

<margin>35.</margin> *His majesty is over Israel* <note>original: "Epi ton Israel he megaloprepeia autou" - Psalm 68:34 (Septuagint 67:35).</note>; that is, over the mind that sees, as far as is possible, the beauty of the glory of God Himself. *And His power is in the clouds*; that is, in those luminous souls who gaze toward the morning light. Christ, who sits at the Father's right hand, shines upon them like the sun radiating through pure clouds, revealing Him as the Beloved.

<margin>36.</margin> Divine Scripture says that "one who sins will destroy much righteousness" <note>Ecclesiastes 9:18</note>. Likewise, a mind that sins loses the divine food and the immortal, heavenly drink described in the previous chapter.

<margin>37.</margin> We are not stronger than Samson, nor wiser than Solomon, nor more knowledgeable in divine things than the holy David; nor do we love God more than Peter, the chief of the Apostles. Let us therefore not trust in ourselves, for Scripture says: "He who trusts in himself shall fall a terrible fall."

<margin>38.</margin> Let us learn humility from Christ, lowliness from David, and how to weep over what happens to us from Peter. But let us not lose hope, as did Samson, Judas, and even the exceedingly wise Solomon.

<margin>39.</margin> For the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour <note>1 Peter 5:8</note>, along with his dark powers. Therefore, let the heart's constant attention, watchfulness <note>term: "nepsis" - a state of spiritual alertness and sobriety</note>, refutation of evil thoughts, and prayer to Christ Jesus our God never cease. For you will find no greater help in all your life than Jesus. He alone, as God, knows the deceits, the methods, and the traps of the demons.

<margin>40.</margin> Let the soul, then, trust in Christ and call upon Him, and let it not be afraid in the least. For it does not fight alone, but is accompanied by the awesome King, Jesus Christ, the Creator of all things—both those without bodies and those with bodies, that is, the visible and the invisible worlds.

<margin>41.</margin> Just as rain softens the earth the more it falls upon it, so too does the holy name of Christ gladden and cheer the earth of our heart the more we cry out to it and call upon it frequently.

<margin>42.</margin> It is good for those without experience to know this: we possess enemies who are bodiless, invisible, malicious, and clever at doing harm. They are agile, light, and have been experienced in war from the time of Adam until the present. We, on the other hand, are heavy in nature, weighed down toward the earth both in our bodies and in our 

<column-break/>

way of thinking. We have no other way to conquer them except through the unceasing watchfulness of the mind and the calling upon Jesus Christ, our God and Maker. For the inexperienced, let the prayer of Jesus Christ and the attempt to test it and know its goodness be their guide. For the experienced, the actual practice, the testing, and the peace that comes from this good work are the best methods and teachers.

<margin>43.</margin> Just as a small, innocent child is delighted when seeing a conjurer <note>original: "phantasiopoion" - someone who creates illusions or mental images</note> and follows him out of simple-heartedness, so too our soul—being simple and good, as it was created by its good Master—is delighted by the deceptive mental images <note>term: "phantasiai" - the "picture-shows" or mental images used by demons to tempt the soul</note> of the devil. Deceived, it runs toward the evil as if it were good, like a dove lured to the one who plots against her young. In this way, the soul mixes its own thoughts with the mental image of the demonic provocation—whether it be the face of a beautiful woman or something else entirely forbidden by the commandments of Christ. The soul then tries to find a way to bring that beautiful sight into reality. Having then reached the point of "consent," it finally carries out through the body the lawless deed it first saw in the mind, leading to its own condemnation.

<margin>44.</margin> This is the "art" of the evil one; with these arrows, he poisons every soul. For this reason, it is not safe to allow thoughts to enter our heart—especially in the beginning—before one has much experience in this mental warfare. This is because our soul still takes pleasure in demonic provocations, finds them sweet, and follows them. Instead, we should only notice them and immediately cut them off as soon as they emerge and strike. Once the mind has spent a long time in this wonderful work and has been trained and gained understanding—becoming habitually used to this war—it can then truly perceive these thoughts. As the Prophet says, it can then easily "seize the little foxes" <note>Song of Solomon 2:15</note>. Only then is it right to allow them in, so as to examine and rebuke them with expert knowledge.

<margin>45.</margin> Just as it is impossible for fire and water to pass through the same pipe at the same time, it is impossible for sin to enter the heart unless it first knocks at the door of the heart by means of the mental image of an evil provocation.

<margin>46.</margin> First comes the "provocation" <note>term: "prosbole" - the initial "hit" or suggestion of a thought</note>; second is "coupling," which is the mixing of our own thoughts...

<summary>Hesychius warns that even the wisest and strongest biblical figures fell when trusting themselves, urging the reader to use the name of Jesus and the "art" of watchfulness to cut off sinful thoughts at their first appearance. He explains the psychological process by which a simple mental image (phantasia) leads the soul from a "hit" to "consent" and finally to a sinful act.</summary>

...and the thoughts of evil demons; third is **consent**, <note>original: "synkatathesis" - the moment the will agrees to act upon a tempting thought.</note> which occurs when the two types of thoughts deliberate wickedly; and fourth is the **physical act**, that is, the sin itself. If, therefore, the mind remains attentive and watchful, and through contradiction and the calling upon the Lord Jesus it drives away the **assault** <note>original: "prosbolē" - the initial flickering of a thought or image in the mind.</note> as soon as it appears, the subsequent stages remain inactive. For the evil mind [the demon] is incorporeal and cannot deceive souls except through imagination and thoughts. Regarding the initial assault, David says: "In the mornings I destroyed [all the sinners of the land]" <note>Psalm 101:8 (Septuagint 100:8). In monastic thought, "mornings" refers to the very first moment a thought appears.</note>, and so on. And the great Moses says regarding consent: "And you shall not consent to them." <note>Deuteronomy 13:8.</note>

<margin>47.</margin> Mind invisibly entwines with mind in battle—the demonic mind against our own. For this reason, we must cry out to Christ from the depths of our being so that He may drive away the demonic mind and, as the Lover of Mankind, grant us the victory.

<margin>48.</margin> Let the image of your inner stillness <note>term: "hesychia" - a state of inner quiet and prayerful silence.</note> be like one who holds a mirror and gazes into it intently; then you will see the evil and the good things that are being intellectually inscribed upon your heart.

<margin>49.</margin> Always take care to have no thought in your heart, whether it seems irrational or reasonable, so that you may easily recognize the "aliens"—that is, the firstborn sons of the Egyptians. <note>An allegorical reference to the Exodus; here, the "firstborn of Egypt" represent the primary demonic thoughts that must be struck down.</note>

<margin>50.</margin> How good and delightful, how bright and sweet, how beautiful, radiant, and lovely is the virtue of **watchfulness**! <note>term: "nepsis" - spiritual sobriety or alertness.</note> Through You, O Christ God, it is made prosperous, and it is traveled by the human mind with great humility and wakefulness. For its branches extend even to the sea and the abyss of contemplations, and its shoots reach the rivers of delightful and divine mysteries. It waters the mind that has long been parched by impiety, by the saltiness of evil thoughts and spirits, and by the hostile wisdom of the flesh, which is death.

<margin>51.</margin> Watchfulness is like Jacob’s ladder, upon which God rests and the Angels ascend. It removes all evil from us, cutting off talkativeness, abuse, slander, and the entire catalog of sensory evils; for it cannot bear to be deprived of its own sweetness even for a moment.

<margin>52.</margin> My brothers, let us pursue this virtue with zeal. Flying in Christ Jesus with a pure mind in its divine heights, let us stir up

<column-break/>

the contemplation of our sins and our former life. Thus, being crushed and humbled by the memory of our sins, we may have the uninterrupted help of Jesus Christ our God in this invisible war. For if we are deprived of Jesus' help through pride, vainglory, or self-love, we will lose that purity of heart through which God is made known to man. For, as promised, the latter [purity] is the cause of the former [knowing God].

<margin>53.</margin> A mind that does not neglect its own secret internal work, along with the other good things it finds from the constant practice of "guarding the heart," will also find that the five senses of the body become idle regarding external evils. For by paying attention entirely to its own virtue and watchfulness, and wishing to delight in good thoughts, it does not allow itself to be robbed through the five senses when material and vain thoughts approach; instead, recognizing their deceptive nature, it pulls the senses back into itself.

<margin>54.</margin> Remain present in your intellect, and you will not grow weary in temptations; but if you depart from there, endure whatever comes upon you.

<margin>55.</margin> Just as bitter wormwood benefits those with a poor appetite, so it is beneficial for those of bad character to suffer hardships.

<margin>56.</margin> If you do not wish to suffer evil, do not wish to do evil; for the one follows the other inevitably. "For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap." <note>Galatians 6:7.</note> Therefore, when we sow wicked things voluntarily and reap them involuntarily, we ought to marvel at the justice of God.

<margin>57.</margin> The mind is blinded by these three passions: love of money, vainglory, and pleasure.

<margin>58.</margin> Knowledge and faith, the companions of our nature, have been blunted by nothing else but these three.

<margin>59.</margin> Fury, anger, wars, murders, and the entire catalog of remaining evils have gained great strength among men because of these.

<margin>60.</margin> One who does not know the truth cannot truly believe. For knowledge naturally precedes faith. The things said in Scripture were spoken not only that we might understand them, but that we might do them.

<meta>This page continues the spiritual instructions of Hesychius the Presbyter to his student Theodoulos. ->### HESYCHIUS THE PRESBYTER TO THEODOULOS<-

Hope in God, and firm faith, and inner knowledge, and deliverance from temptations, and the gifts of grace, and heartfelt confession, and constant tears, come to the faithful through prayer. Not only these, but also the endurance of oncoming afflictions, and the sincere forgiveness of one’s neighbor, and the recognition of the spiritual law, and the discovery of God's righteousness, and the visitation of the Holy Spirit, and the bestowing of spiritual treasures—indeed, everything God has promised to provide to faithful people both here and in the age to come. Simply put, it is impossible for the soul to appear in the image of God except through the grace of God and the faith of a person who remains in the mind with great humility and undistracted prayer.

<margin>62.</margin> We have learned from experience that it is a truly great good for one who wishes to cleanse his own heart to constantly call upon the Lord Jesus against the "noetic" enemies <note>original: "noētōn polemiōn" — referring to the invisible or mental enemies, specifically demons and sinful thoughts.</note>. Observe how the word I have spoken from experience is in harmony with the testimony of Scripture. It says, "Prepare, Israel, to call upon the name of the Lord your God." <note>Amos 4:12.</note> And the Apostle says, "Pray without ceasing." <note>1 Thessalonians 5:17.</note> Our Lord also says: "Without me you can do nothing. He who abides in me, and I in him, he bears much fruit." <note>John 15:5.</note> And again: "If anyone does not abide in me, he is cast out like a branch." <note>John 15:6.</note> Prayer is a great good, encompassing all things good, for it cleanses the heart in which God is seen by the faithful.

<margin>63.</margin> The virtue of humility, because it is by its nature "height-making" <note>original: "hypsopoion" — a paradoxical term meaning that by lowering oneself, one is actually exalted by God.</note>, beloved by God, and a destroyer of almost all the evils within us that God hates, is for these reasons difficult to acquire. You might easily find partial practices of many virtues in a single man, but if you look for the scent of humility in him, you will hardly find it. For <margin>*with diligence.</margin> this reason, much * diligence is needed to acquire this possession. Indeed, the Scripture calls even the devil "unclean" because from the beginning he rejected this good thing—the virtue of humility—and loved pride. Therefore, he is called an "unclean spirit" throughout all the Scriptures. For what sort of bodily uncleanness can a being work who is entirely incorporeal,

<column-break/>

without flesh, and without a fixed place, such that he should be called "unclean" for that reason? It is clear that he was called unclean because of his pride; and from being a pure and luminous angel, he was revealed to be profane. "Everyone who is proud in heart is an abomination to the Lord." <note>Proverbs 16:5.</note> For it is said that pride is the first sin. Thus the proud Pharaoh said, "I do not know your God, and I will not let Israel go." <note>Exodus 5:2.</note>

<margin>64.</margin> There are many activities of the mind that can provide us with the good gift of humility, if only we are not negligent of our salvation. These include the memory of sins in words, deeds, and thoughts, and many other things that contribute to humility when gathered by spiritual contemplation. True humility is also produced when one constantly revolves in one's mind the achievements of those nearby, magnifying other people's natural advantages while comparing one's own traits to theirs. When the mind sees its own worthlessness in this way, and how far it falls short of the perfection of the brothers, a person considers himself to be "earth and ashes" <note>Genesis 18:27.</note> and not even a human being, but a kind of dog, falling behind and falling short of all rational people on earth in every way.

<margin>65.</margin> The "Mouth of Christ," the pillar of the Church, our great father Basil says: a great good for not sinning, and for not falling into the same things on the following day, is for us to examine ourselves in our own conscience regarding the events of the day after it has been completed—what we have done wrong and what we have done right. Job also did this both for himself and for his children. For these daily accountings bring light to every hour.

<margin>66.</margin> And another of those wise in divine things said: the flower is the beginning of the fruit; and self-control <note>term: "enkrateia" — disciplined restraint of the appetites and passions.</note> is the beginning of practice. Therefore, let us practice self-control, and this with "measure and weight" as the Fathers teach. Let us pass the whole day of twelve hours in the "guarding of the mind" <note>term: "tērēsei noos" — the practice of keeping the mind focused and free from intrusive thoughts.</note>. By doing this, we shall be able, with God's help, to extinguish and diminish wickedness by a certain force. For the virtuous life is a "life of force," <note>original: "biastē" — referring to Matthew 11:12, suggesting the Kingdom is taken by effort and spiritual violence against one's own ego.</note> through which the Kingdom of Heaven is given.

<margin>67.</margin> The way to knowledge is "dispassion" <note>term: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but freedom from the compulsion of the passions.</note> and humility; without these, no one will see the Lord.

It explains that the devil is called "unclean" specifically because of pride and provides practical methods for cultivating lowliness of heart, such as evening self-examination and honoring the virtues of others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual instructions of Hesychius the Presbyter to his student Theodoulos. The previous page established that "watchfulness" (nepsis) and the invocation of Jesus are the primary defenses against mental distractions. ### A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE

<margin>68.</margin> One who constantly occupies himself with his inner life is sober-minded; not only that, but he also contemplates, speaks of God, and prays. This is what the Apostle means when he says: "Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh." <note>Galatians 5:16</note>

<margin>69.</margin> One who does not know how to walk the spiritual path takes no care for passionate thoughts <note>original: "empathōn noēmatōn" — thoughts triggered by underlying desires or compulsions.</note>; instead, he directs all his energy toward the flesh, and either gluttonizes and lives without restraint, or he becomes grieved, angry, and resentful. Consequently, he either darkens his mind or uses excessive ascetic practice and muddies his understanding.

<margin>70.</margin> One who has renounced worldly things—such as a wife, money, and the like—has made the "outer man" a monk, but not yet the "inner man." But one who has renounced the passionate thoughts of these things (that is, the mind) is a true Monk. It is easy for someone to make the outer man a monk if they wish; but it is no small struggle to make the inner man a monk.

<margin>71.</margin> Who is there, then, in this generation, who has been entirely freed from passionate thoughts and has been deemed worthy of pure and immaterial prayer at all times? This is the sign of the "inner monk."

<margin>72.</margin> Many passions are hidden in our souls; they are only exposed when their causes <note>The "causes" (aitia) refer to external triggers or objects of temptation.</note> appear.

<margin>73.</margin> Do not focus all your energy on the flesh; rather, appoint for it an ascetic practice according to its strength, and turn your whole mind to the inner life. For "bodily exercise profits a little, but godliness is profitable for all things." <note>1 Timothy 4:8. In this context, "bodily exercise" refers to physical fasting and vigils without the inner work of the heart.</note>

<margin>74.</margin> Pride occurs when the passions are inactive; this happens either because the triggers have been cut off or because the demons are retreating craftily <note>The author warns that a lack of temptation isn't always progress; it can be a trick by demons to make one feel superior.</note>.

<margin>75.</margin> Humility and suffering free a person from every sin; the former cuts off the passions of the soul, and the latter cuts off those of the body. For this reason the Lord says: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" <note>Matthew 5:8</note>—they see Him and the treasures within Him when they cleanse themselves through love and self-control, and they see more clearly the more they intensify their purification.

<margin>76.</margin> The "watchtower" for every word concerning virtue is the guarding of the mind, just as in the old days 

<column-break/>

the "goal" of David <note>A reference to Psalm 101:2 or similar themes of the "perfect heart."</note> prefigured the circumcision of the heart.

<margin>77.</margin> Just as we are harmed when we see things that are harmful to our physical senses, so it is also with the mind.

<margin>78.</margin> Just as one who wounds the heart of a plant withers the whole thing, so you should understand the human heart. One must pay attention at every moment, because the "thieves" <note>referring to demonic thoughts</note> are never idle.

<margin>79.</margin> The Lord, wishing to show that every commandment is a debt to be paid, while the status of "sonship" is gifted to humans by His own blood, says: "When you have done all those things which are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants, and we have only done what we were duty-bound to do." <note>Luke 17:10</note> Therefore, the Kingdom of Heaven is not a "wage" for works, but the grace of the Master prepared for faithful servants. A servant does not demand freedom as a wage, but gives thanks as a debtor and receives it by grace.

<margin>80.</margin> Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; and to those who serve Him well, He grants freedom. For He says: "Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord." <note>Matthew 25:21</note> He is not yet a faithful servant who relies on bare knowledge alone, but he who believes Christ through obedience to His commands.

<margin>81.</margin> One who honors the Master does what is commanded by Him. If he slips or is disobedient, he endures what follows as his own fault. If you love learning, be also a lover of labor; for bare knowledge puffs a person up. <note>Refers to 1 Corinthians 8:1.</note>

<margin>82.</margin> Temptations that happen to us unexpectedly teach us, by God's providence, to be lovers of labor.

<margin>83.</margin> The characteristic of a star is the light surrounding it; the characteristic of a god-fearing and God-worshiping person is lowliness and humility. Indeed, there is no other identifying or signifying mark of Christ's disciples than a humble mind and a lowly appearance. All four Gospels proclaim this. He who does not live this way—that is, living humbly—falls away from the side of Him who humbled Himself even to the cross and death, who is also the practical Lawgiver of the divine Gospels.

<margin>84.</margin> "Those who thirst," He says, "come to the water." <note>Isaiah 55:1</note> And you who thirst for God, come in purity of mind. Yet, for one who flies high through such purity, it is also necessary to look toward the earth of his own lowliness; for no one is [greater] than the humble... <note>Text cuts off at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>This page explores the distinction between the 'outer monk' who only performs external rituals and the 'inner monk' who guards the mind from passionate thoughts. It emphasizes that salvation and the Kingdom of Heaven are gifts of grace rather than wages earned through works, with humility being the defining characteristic of a true disciple of Christ.</summary>

### ON WATCHFULNESS AND HOLINESS

...higher. For just as when light is absent, everything is murky and dark, so too when humility is absent, all our efforts toward God are vain and stale.

<margin>85.</margin>
Hear the conclusion of the matter: Fear God and keep His commandments, both mentally and physically. For if you force yourself to keep them mentally <note>original: "noētōs" — refers to the inner focus of the mind or intellect</note>, you will rarely need to labor physically for them. For David says: "I desired to do your will and your law in the midst of my belly." <note>Psalm 40:8. The "midst of the belly" is a Hebrew idiom for the innermost part of a person, the heart or soul.</note>

<margin>86.</margin>
Unless a person performs the will and the law of God in the "midst of the belly"—that is, in the center of the heart—they cannot easily perform it outwardly. An unwatchful and indifferent person will say to God: "I do not want to know your ways." This is entirely due to a lack of divine illumination; however, those who participate in that light will not only be fully convinced but will become steadfast and capable in divine matters.

<margin>87.</margin>
Just as physical salt seasons bread and all food, and keeps certain meats from rotting and preserves them, so you must understand the mental sweetness and wondrous labor regarding the guarding of the mind. For it divinely seasons both the inner and outer man, drives away the stench of evil thoughts, and preserves us steadfast in good works.

<margin>88.</margin>
Many thoughts arise from an "assault" <note>term: "prosbolē" — the first stage of a temptation where a thought or image is presented to the mind before the person engages with it</note>, and from these come evil physical actions. But the one who immediately quenches the first thought through Jesus escapes what follows. Such a person will grow rich in sweet divine knowledge, through which they will find God who is everywhere. By fixing the mirror of the mind on Him, one is continually enlightened, like pure glass reflecting the physical sun. Then the mind, having reached the ultimate object of its desire, will rest from all other contemplation.

<margin>89.</margin>
Since every thought enters the heart through the imagination of physical things, the blessed light of the Divinity only shines upon the heart when it is completely empty of everything and becomes formless. Indeed, that brilliance appears to the pure mind when it is stripped of all mental images.

<margin>90.</margin>
The more intensely you pay attention to the mind, the more you will pray to Jesus with longing; and again, the more 

<column-break/>

neglectfully you examine the mind, the further you will be distanced from Jesus. And just as the former case intensely enlightens the air of the mind, so too turning away from watchfulness and the sweet invocation of Jesus naturally darkens the mind. This is simply the nature of the matter, as we have said, and it cannot be otherwise. You will learn this by experience through trial; for virtue—especially this delightful, light-bearing work—is not naturally learned except by experience <gloss>* in another: it is taught</gloss>.

<margin>91.</margin>
To call upon Jesus continuously with a longing full of sweetness and joy causes the "air" of the heart to be full of joy and stillness, thanks to extreme attention. But it is Jesus Christ, the Son of God and God Himself, who is the cause of the heart being perfectly purified—He who is the cause and maker of all good things. For He says: "I am God, making peace." <note>Isaiah 45:7</note>

<margin>92.</margin>
A soul that is benefited and sweetened by Jesus repays its benefactor with a certain exultation and love through confession. It gives thanks and calls upon the Peacemaker with gladness, seeing Him mentally in its midst, dissolving the fantasies of evil spirits.

<margin>93.</margin>
And because, as David says, "my mental eye has looked upon my mental enemies," and "my ear shall hear the wicked rising up against me," <note>Psalm 92:11</note> and I have seen the recompense of sinners from God happening within me; when there are no fantasies in the heart, the mind stands in its natural state. It is then ready to be moved toward every delightful, spiritual, and God-loving contemplation.

<margin>94.</margin>
So then, as I said, watchfulness and the Jesus Prayer are naturally constituted to support one another. For extreme attention supports continuous prayer, and prayer in turn supports extreme watchfulness and attention in the mind.

<margin>95.</margin>
The unforgetting memory of death is a good teacher for both the body and the soul. We should skip over everything in between and always look forward to that very bed where we shall lie in our death-agony, and all the rest.

<margin>96.</margin>
Brothers, it is impossible for one who wishes to remain awake at all times to take a nap; rather, one of two things must happen: either he falls and perishes, stripped of his virtues, or...

<summary>Hesychius explains that internal "watchfulness" (nepsis) and the Jesus Prayer are interdependent practices that purify the heart. He uses the metaphor of salt and light to describe how these practices season the soul and allow it to reflect the divine light once it is cleared of mental images.</summary>

### A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE

...to stand armed in the mind; for the enemy also always stands ready with his own battle-array.

<margin>107.</margin>
<margin>* to intercept.</margin>
A certain divine state arises in our mind from the constant remembrance and invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ, provided we do not neglect the continuous mental prayer to Him, diligent watchfulness <note>term: "nipsis" — a state of spiritual alertness and sobriety often described as the "guarding of the heart."</note>, and the work of supervision. Indeed, let us always have this as our work, performed in the same way: the invocation of Jesus Christ our Lord, crying out with a burning heart so as to * partake <note>original: "metalabhein" — the margin suggests "mesolabhein" (to intercept), perhaps referring to catching thoughts before they take root.</note> in the holy name of Jesus. For constancy is the mother of habit, both in virtue and in vice; and habit, once formed, rules like a second nature. When the mind enters such a state, it hunts for its enemies like a hunting dog seeking a hare in the thickets—but the dog seeks to devour, while the mind seeks to destroy the enemy's influence.

<margin>108.</margin>
<margin>* change/ distraction.</margin>
Whenever, therefore, evil thoughts happen to multiply within us, let us cast the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ into their midst. We shall then see them immediately dispersed like smoke in the air, as experience has taught. Once the mind is left alone again, let us return to our continuous attention and invocation. Whenever we suffer this by * temptation <note>original: "peirasmos" — a trial or a testing of the soul's resolve.</note>, let us act in this manner.

<margin>109.</margin>
Just as it is impossible for a naked body to enter into battle, or to sail a great sea while wearing heavy garments, or to live without breathing, so it is impossible without humility and continuous supplication to Christ to learn the noetic <note>term: "noētos" — relating to the intellect or the spiritual "eye" of the soul, as opposed to the physical senses.</note> and secret warfare, or to skillfully pursue and strike down the enemy.

<margin>110.</margin>
<margin>* change/ evil.</margin>
The great and most practical David says to the Lord: "I will guard my strength for You." <note>Psalm 59:9. Here, "strength" is interpreted as the spiritual energy of the heart.</note> Thus, the guarding of the strength of our inner and noetic stillness <note>term: "hesychia" — a state of inner silence and tranquility necessary for prayer.</note>—from which all virtues are born—comes to us through the help of the Lord. He both gave the commandments and drives away from us that * foul forgetfulness which is so destructive to the stillness of the heart, acting upon it like water upon fire. Therefore, Monk, do not fall into the sleep of death through negligence; rather, scourge the enemies with the name of Jesus. As a certain wise man has said: 

<column-break/>

"Let the name of Jesus cling to your breath," and then you shall know the profit of stillness.

<margin>111.</margin>
When we, though unworthy, are granted the awesome and terrifying privilege of the divine and spotless Mysteries <note>The "Mysteries" refers to the Holy Eucharist or Communion.</note> of Christ our God and King, then more than ever let us demonstrate watchfulness, the guarding of the mind, and strictness. We do this so that the divine fire—that is, the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ—may consume our sins and our small or great defilements. For as it enters into us, it immediately drives the evil spirits of wickedness from the heart and forgives the sins we committed previously; the mind is then left undisturbed by evil thoughts. If after this we strictly guard our mind and stand at the gate of our heart, when we are again deemed worthy of the Mysteries, the Divine Body will brighten the mind even more and make it star-like.

<margin>112.</margin>
Forgetfulness is known to extinguish the guarding of the mind, just as water extinguishes fire. But the continuous prayer of Jesus, combined with intense watchfulness, consumes forgetfulness from the heart. For prayer needs watchfulness just as a lamp needs a light.

<margin>113.</margin>
One must labor in the guarding of precious things; and truly precious are those things that guard us from every evil, both of the senses and of the mind. These are: the guarding of the mind along with the invocation of Jesus Christ; looking always into the depths of the heart; and maintaining a perpetual stillness of the intellect, so to speak, even from thoughts that appear to be "on the right" <note>This refers to thoughts that seem good or pious but act as distractions from pure prayer.</note>. We must strive to be found empty of thoughts so that thieves do not hide within us. Even if we suffer in the heart by remaining in this state, consolation is near.

<margin>114.</margin>
<margin>* coal.</margin>
The heart, when it is watched unceasingly and not permitted to receive the forms, images, and fantasies of dark and evil spirits, is naturally disposed to give birth to light-filled thoughts. For just as a * coal <note>original: "anthrax" — a burning ember or piece of charcoal.</note> generates a flame, so much more does God, who has dwelt in the heart since Holy Baptism, ignite our intellect toward contemplation <note>term: "theoria" — the spiritual "vision" or direct experience of God's presence.</note>, like a flame upon wax, provided He finds the air of our intellect clear of the winds of wickedness and protected by the guarding of the mind.

### OF HESYCHIUS THE PRESBYTER TO THEODOULOS

<margin>105.</margin>
For we must always revolve the name of Jesus Christ within the space of our heart, just as lightning flashes in the air of the firmament when rain is about to descend. Indeed, those who have experience of the mind and of the inner warfare know this accurately. Let us lead this mental war in an orderly fashion: first, attention <note>term: "prosoche" — a state of focused spiritual alertness</note>; then, having recognized the enemy thought as it approaches, let us strike it with words of cursing in the heart, combined with holy anger; the third stage is to pray immediately against it, concentrating the heart through the invocation of Jesus Christ, so that the demonic phantom may be instantly dissolved, and the mind might not follow the imagination like a child led astray by a clever performer.

<margin>106. * let [the throat] grow hoarse.</margin>
Let us labor as David did, crying out, "Lord Jesus Christ" <note>original: "Kyrie Iesou Christe"</note>; * let our throat grow hoarse, and let our mental eyes never fail from hoping in the Lord our God.

<margin>107.</margin>
Always remembering the parable of the unjust judge, which the Lord spoke to show that we must always pray and not lose heart, we shall find both our profit and our vindication.

<margin>108.</margin>
Just as it is impossible for one gazing at the Sun not to have their eyes richly illuminated, so the one who always stoops into the air of the heart cannot fail to be enlightened.

<margin>109.</margin>
As it is impossible to live this present life without eating and drinking, so it is impossible for the soul to reach anything spiritual and pleasing to God without the guarding of the mind and purity of heart—which is, and is called, watchfulness <note>term: "nipsis" — spiritual sobriety and alertness</note>—or to be freed from mental sin, even if one forces oneself not to sin out of fear of punishments.

<margin>110.</margin>
Nevertheless, those who refrain from outward sin by a certain force are blessed before God, angels, and men, because they are found to be "those who take by violence" the Kingdom of Heaven.

<margin>111.</margin>
This is the wonder of the mind's profit born of stillness <note>term: "hesychia" — inner silence and tranquility</note>: that while all sins first knock at the mind as mere thoughts, and only become sensible and "thick" sins if accepted by the intellect, the virtue of mental watchfulness cuts them all off. It does not allow them to enter our inner man or be led into evil deeds, through the assistance and

<column-break/>

protection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>112.</margin>
The Old Testament is an image of external and sensible bodily discipline <note>term: "askesis" — spiritual exercises or training</note>; but the Holy Gospel, which is the New Testament, is an image of attention, that is, of the purity of the heart. And just as the Old Testament did not bring perfection, nor did it fully satisfy the inner man in godliness—for "the law made nothing perfect," as the Apostle says—but only prevented the "thick" or outward sins (such as preventing one from knocking out the eye or tooth of a neighbor), so cutting off thoughts from the heart and evil intentions is the decree of the Gospel, which leads to a greater purity of soul. So it is with bodily righteousness and discipline—I mean fasting, self-control, sleeping on the ground, standing, vigils, and the rest which pertain to the body—they cause the passionate part of the body to be still from outward sin. As I said, these things are good, like the Old Testament; they are a training for our outer man and a guard against outward passions. However, they are not a guard against, or a prevention of, mental sins; they cannot, by themselves, deliver us (with God's help) from envy, anger, and the rest.

<margin>113.</margin>
But purity of heart—that is, the observation and guarding of the mind, of which the New Testament is the type—if it is kept by us as it should be, uproots and cuts off all passions and all evils from the heart. In their place, it introduces joy, good hope, compunction, mourning, tears, a true knowledge of * ourselves and our sins, the remembrance of death, true humility, infinite love for both God and men, and a divine yearning within the heart.
<margin>* variant: of our own selves.</margin>

<margin>114.</margin>
Just as it is impossible to walk upon the earth without cutting through this air, so it is impossible for the heart of man not to be constantly attacked by demons, or to be secretly influenced by them, even if one practices much bodily discipline.

<margin>115.</margin>
If you desire in the Lord not merely to *seem* to be a Monk, and good, and gentle, and always united to God, but you truly wish to *be* such a person, then pursue the virtue of attention with all your might. This is the guarding of the mind, the keeping of the spirit, and the heart's perfection of sweet stillness, free from mental images...

He contrasts the Old Testament as a symbol of physical discipline with the New Testament as the path to heart purity.</summary>

### A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE

...a blessed state of the soul; a thing not found among many.

<margin>116.</margin> For this is called intellectual philosophy <note>original: "noete philosophia" — here referring to the practical "philosophy" of the inner life and spiritual discipline</note>; and you must travel this path with much watchfulness <note>term: "nepsis" — a state of spiritual sobriety and alertness</note> and warm zeal, together with the prayer of Jesus, with humility, with constancy, and with silence of the lips—both the physical lips and those of the mind. Travel it with restraint in foods and drinks, and from every sinful thing. Travel this path in the way of the intellect, skillfully and with prudence; and this path shall teach you, with God’s help, things you did not know. It will make things known to you, and enlighten you, and give you understanding, and apprentice you to those very things which you were previously unable to take into your mind while walking in the darkness of passions and dark deeds, covered by the abyss of forgetfulness and confusion.

<margin>117.</margin> Just as the valleys abound in grain, so does this path multiply every good thing in your heart; or rather, our Lord Jesus Christ will provide these things to you, for without him we can do nothing. And first, you shall find this path to be a ladder, and then a book to be read. Then, as you progress, you shall find it to be the city of the Heavenly Jerusalem, and you shall clearly see with your mind Christ, the King of the powers of Israel, together with his co-essential Father and the Holy Spirit, who is to be worshipped.

<margin>118.</margin> It is through false imagination <note>term: "phantasia" — in this context, it refers to deceptive mental images or "pre-visualizations" of sin planted by demons</note> that the demons always lead us into sinning. Indeed, it was with the imagination of greed and profit that they prepared the wretched Judas to betray the Lord and God of all things. Through the lie of worthless physical rest, and honor, and profit, and glory, they placed a noose around him and brought about his eternal death; the miserable ones rewarded him with the exact opposite of their own imagination—of their "assault," I should say.

<margin>119.</margin> See how the enemies of our salvation cause us to fall through imagination, lies, and empty promises. Even Satan himself crashed down from the heights like lightning because he imagined an equality with God. And in this way, he again separated Adam from God by making him imagine a divine status. In this same way, the liar and treacherous enemy is accustomed to deceiving all those who sin.

<margin>120. and</margin> We are embittered in our heart <gloss>by</gloss> the venom of evil thoughts whenever we are led away by forgetfulness, neglecting attention <note>original: "prosoche"</note> and the prayer of Jesus for a long time; but we are sweetened again in

<column-break/>

perception and a certain sweetness of blessed joy, when we perform the aforementioned things strongly and eagerly in the workshop of the mind, with discipline and through divine love. For then, we are eager to walk in the stillness <note>term: "hesychia" — inner silence and tranquility</note> of the heart for no other reason than the sweet pleasure and delight it brings to the soul itself.

<margin>121.</margin> The science of sciences and the art of arts is the art of dealing with the villainous thoughts. Therefore, the best method and art against them is to see, in the Lord, the "imagination of the assault" <note>This refers to the "prosvole," the first flickers of a tempting thought appearing in the mind</note> and to guard the intellect. Just as we guard our physical eye and look sharply with it to avoid anything that might strike it by accident, and as much as we are able, we prevent every speck of dust from entering it.

<margin>122.</margin> Just as snow will not bear a flame, nor will water produce fire, nor a thorn bush produce figs—so the heart of any man shall not be freed from demonic thoughts, words, and deeds if he has not purified the interior and joined watchfulness with the prayer of Jesus, attaining humility and stillness of the soul, and pressing on with much zeal as he travels. Otherwise, the inattentive soul must necessarily be barren of every good and perfect thought, like a fruitless mule; for such a soul lacks the understanding of spiritual prudence. Truly, the sweet thing and name of Jesus is the peace of the soul, as is the emptying of passionate thoughts.

<margin>123.</margin> Whenever the soul enters into an evil agreement with the body, then both build a city of vanity and a tower of pride, along with the ungodly thoughts that dwell within them. But the Lord, by the fear of Hell, confuses their agreement and divides them, forcing the mistress soul to speak and to think things that are foreign and contrary to the body. From this <margin>* fear</margin> fear and division occur, because the "mind of the flesh" is an enmity toward God, and it does not submit to the law of God.

<margin>124.</margin> We must weigh our daily deeds every hour and pay attention; and as much as possible, we must necessarily make them light in the evening through repentance, if indeed we wish to overcome wickedness with Christ. And we must examine if we perform all our physical and visible deeds according to God, in the presence of God, and for God alone—so that we are not mindlessly robbed by our senses.

### HESYCHIUS THE PRESBYTER TO THEODOULOS

<margin>125.</margin> For if we gain something every day, with God’s help, from our watchfulness <note>term: "nepsis" — spiritual sobriety and alertness</note>, we ought not to wander about with indifference and suffer loss through many dangerous encounters. Instead, we must despise vain things for the sake of the lovely and sweet profit and beauty of virtue.

<margin>126.</margin> We ought to move the three parts of the soul <note>The "tripartite soul" is a traditional model: the rational (logistikon), the spirited/angry (thymikon), and the desiring (epithymetikon) parts.</note> rightly and according to the nature in which they were created by God. We should direct **anger** <note>original: "thymos"</note> against our "outer man" and against the serpent, Satan. "Be angry," it says, "against sin"—that is, be angry with yourselves and with the devil, so that you do not sin against God. We must move the **desiring part** toward God and toward virtue. Finally, let us set the **rational part** over both of these with wisdom and knowledge; let it arrange, admonish, punish, and rule as a king rules over servants. Then the reason within us governs these things according to God’s will, even if the passions rebel against reason. Let us appoint reason to lead them. For the Brother of the Lord <note>referring to the Apostle James</note> says: *If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body* [James 3:2], and so on. For to speak truly, every lawlessness and sin is carried out through these three parts, and every virtue and righteousness is likewise established through them.

<margin>127.</margin> The mind is darkened and remains fruitless whenever it speaks worldly words, or entertains them in the thoughts, or when the body and mind are vainly occupied with sensory things, or if the Monk gives himself over to vanities. For immediately and at once he loses his warmth, his contrition <note>original: "katanyxis" — a piercing of the heart by grace</note>, and his boldness and knowledge in God. For as much as we pay attention to the mind, we are enlightened; and as much as we do not pay attention, we are darkened.

<margin>128.</margin> He who seeks and pursues the peace and stillness <note>original: "hesychia"</note> of the mind every day will easily despise all sensory things so that he does not labor in vain. But if he deceives his own conscience, he will sleep the bitter death of forgetfulness—the very thing the divine David prays not to sleep. And the Apostle also says: *To him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin* [James 4:17].

<margin>129.</margin> Through neglect, the mind can return again to its own proper order and watchfulness, provided it meets with diligence once more, and if we again set the practical part of our mind in fervent zeal.

<column-break/>

<margin>130.</margin> A mill-donkey cannot go beyond the circle to which it is tethered; neither can a mind progress in perfecting virtue without first correcting its inner state. For it is always blind in its inner eyes, unable to see virtue and the light-flashing Jesus.

<margin>131.</margin> A bold and proud horse leaps joyfully when it receives a rider; and a mind that is delighted will find joy in the light of the Lord, entering into the first stages of insights <note>original: "noemata"</note> as it is set free. It will proceed from the power of the mind’s practical philosophy, renewing itself into an ineffable power capable of contemplating unspoken things and virtues. Receiving into the heart a depth of high, infinite, and divine thoughts, God—the God of Gods—will appear to the heart as far as is possible. The mind, struck with wonder, lovingly glorifies God—the One who is seen and who sees—and who, through both, saves the one who thus gazes upon Him.

<margin>132.</margin> A heart-stillness <note>original: "hesychia"</note> that is rightly achieved will behold a lofty depth through knowledge <note>original: "gnostikos"</note>; and the ear of a mind in stillness will hear extraordinary things from God.

<margin>133.</margin> A traveler who begins a long, difficult, and painful journey, fearing he might lose his way when returning, will set up certain markers and guides along his path to make his return home easier. So too, the man walking the path of watchfulness will set up "words" as pillars, fearing this very same thing.

<margin>134.</margin> But while for the traveler, returning to where he started is a cause for joy, for the watchful man, "turning back" is the ruin of the rational soul and a sign of apostasy from works, words, and thoughts pleasing to God. In times of a death-bearing sleep of the soul, he will have his thoughts like stings, waking him up by the memory of the great surfeit and laziness that came upon him through neglect.

<margin>135.</margin> When we fall into afflictions, despairs, and hopelessness, we ought to do as David did: pour out our hearts to God, and report our prayer and our affliction to the Lord just as it is. For we confess to God because He is able to wisely manage our affairs, and to turn our affliction—if it is for our benefit—into...
