# A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE

...to make it easy; and to rescue us from destructive and corrosive grief.

<margin>136.</margin> For anger directed against other people is contrary to our nature, and grief that is not according to God’s will, along with listlessness <note>term: "akedia" — a state of listlessness or spiritual sloth often described by monks as the "noonday demon"</note>, are equally destructive to both good and insightful thoughts. When the Lord scatters these through our confession, He creates joy within us.

<margin>137.</margin> The Prayer of Jesus <note>original: "Iesou euche" — the repetitive prayer "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me"</note> combined with watchfulness, arising from the depths of the mind’s reflection, is naturally suited to erase thoughts that have become fixed and established in the heart, even against our will.

<margin>138.</margin> We will find relief and joy when we are in the midst of the distress caused by many irrational thoughts if we rebuke ourselves in truth and without attachment—or by "reporting" everything to the Lord as if to a man. Through these two methods, we will certainly find rest from everything.

<margin>139.</margin> The lawgiver Moses is taken by the Church Fathers as an image of the Mind <note>original: "nous"</note>. He is the one who sees God in the burning bush, his face is glorified, and he is appointed as "God to Pharaoh" by the God of Gods. He scourges Egypt, leads Israel out, and gives the law. When these events are taken allegorically according to the spirit, they represent the activities and excellencies of the Mind.

<margin>140.</margin> Aaron, the brother of the lawgiver, is an image of the "outer man" <note>the physical or worldly aspect of a person</note>. Therefore, let us also bring accusations with anger—just as Moses did when Aaron stumbled—and say: "How has Israel wronged you, that you were so quick to turn them away from the Lord God, the living Almighty?"

<margin>141.</margin> <margin>* Or: "to exchange."</margin> The Lord showed us this, along with all other good things, when He was about to raise Lazarus from the dead: the act of restraining, through indignant rebuke, the effeminate and dispersive part of the soul. I mean that we should strive to rescue the soul from self-love, vanity, and pride through the habit of self-reproach, which He knows.

<margin>142.</margin> Just as it is impossible to cross the great expanse of the sea without a large ship, so it is impossible to drive out the assault of an evil thought without calling upon Jesus Christ.

<margin>143.</margin> Contradiction <note>original: "antirrhēsis" — the practice of speaking back to a temptation with scripture or rebuke</note> tends to muzzle thoughts, but calling upon the Name <note>original: "epiklēsis"</note> tends to drive them from the heart. For when an assault takes the form of an image of a sensory thing in the soul—such as the face of someone who has hurt us, or the phantom of a woman’s beauty, or of gold or silver—

<column-break/>

if any of these things appear in our intellect, immediately the thoughts of resentment, lust, or greed that are haunting the heart are exposed. And if our mind is experienced and trained, being in the habit of "guarding the mind" and seeing clearly in the bright air the seductive phantoms and deceptions of the demons, it easily and immediately extinguishes the "fiery darts of the devil." It does this through a prompt response, contradiction, and the Prayer of Jesus Christ. It does not allow the passionate phantom to stir the mind along with it, nor does it allow our thoughts to take the shape of that image passionately, or to converse with it in a friendly way, or to dwell on it, or to give consent to it. For evil deeds necessarily follow such things, just as night follows day.

<margin>144.</margin> <margin>* Or: "unlawful."</margin> But if our mind is inexperienced in the agility of watchfulness, it immediately mingles with whatever passionate image appears to it and enters into a dialogue, receiving sinful * inquiries and giving answers. Then our own thoughts become mixed with the demonic phantom. The phantom grows and multiplies even further so that it appears lovely, beautiful, and pleasing to the mind that has accepted it and is being plundered by it. The mind then suffers the same thing as a dog in an open field where there happen to be some innocent lambs. The lambs often run toward the dog when it is seen, as if toward their own mother, gaining nothing from their closeness to the dog except to take on its filth and stench. In the same way, our thoughts run unskilfully toward all the demonic phantoms in the mind. When they have become mixed together, as I said, one can see them both * <margin>* Or: "counseling."</margin> wishing to destroy the City of Ilium <note>original: "Ilioupolis" — Troy</note>, like Agamemnon and Menelaus. For so do these thoughts take counsel on what must be done to bring into physical action that which appeared beautiful and sweet to them through the deception of the demonic assault. And so, finally, the "falls" of the soul are crafted within; from that point on, it is necessary to bring into the outside world what was conceived inside the heart.

<margin>145.</margin> For the mind is a simple and innocent thing, easily following phantoms and difficult to restrain from unlawful images unless it has someone to stop it continually...

The author uses vivid metaphors, including the biblical Moses and Aaron and the classical siege of Troy, to describe the internal struggle for the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual instructions of Hesychius the Priest to Theodulus. # HESYCHIUS THE PRIEST TO THEODULUS

...and bridling the reasoning, which is the sovereign ruler over the passions.

<margin>146.</margin> Contemplation and knowledge are naturally the guides and sponsors of a precise way of life; for when the intellect is lifted up by these, it reaches a state of looking down upon pleasures and other sensory things—even the delights of this life—as being of little value.

<margin>147.</margin> An attentive life achieved in Christ Jesus, in turn, becomes the father of contemplation and knowledge. It is the progenitor of divine ascents and the wisest insights when it is joined to its "spouse," humility. As the divine Prophet Isaiah says: "Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall sprout wings and fly through the Lord." <note>original: "pterobolēsousi kai petasthēsontai" — Hesychius is paraphrasing Isaiah 40:31, emphasizing the soul's upward flight through divine strength.</note>

<margin>148.</margin> It appears hard and difficult for people to keep the soul quiet <note>term: "hesychazein" — the root of Hesychasm, referring to inner stillness or silence</note> from every thought. And indeed, it is truly laborious and painful. For it is not only burdensome for those uninitiated in this spiritual warfare to enclose and confine the incorporeal soul within the "bodily house," but also for those who have already gained experience in the internal, immaterial battle. However, he who has taken the Lord Jesus into his heart through constant prayer will not grow weary in following Him, according to the Prophet. Such a person will not desire the "day of man" <note>This likely refers to worldly fame or the temporary standards of human judgment.</note> because of the beauty, delight, and sweetness of Jesus. He will not be put to shame by the surrounding wicked demons—his enemies—when he speaks to them at the "gate of the heart," driving them back with the power of Jesus.

<margin>149.</margin> When a soul takes flight through death into the air, having Christ with it and on its side at the heavenly gates, it will not be put to shame by its enemies there. Instead, it will speak to them at the gates with the same boldness it has now. Only let the soul not grow weary of crying out to the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, day and night until the moment of its departure. He will surely grant the soul's vindication swiftly, according to His own truthful and divine promise which He spoke regarding the Unjust Judge: "Yes, I tell you, He will grant it," both in this present life and after the soul's departure from the body.

<margin>150.</margin> When sailing the mental sea, take courage in Jesus. For He calls out to you mystically within your heart: "Fear not, my child Jacob, few in number Israel; fear not, worm Is-

<column-break/>

-rael, I am your protector." <note>original: "skōlēx Israēl" — quoting Isaiah 41:14. The term "worm" is used biblically to denote humility or perceived helplessness before God's intervention.</note> If God is for us, what wicked power can be against us? For He has blessed the pure in heart and has decreed that the sweet Jesus—who alone is pure—should enter into pure hearts in a divine manner, desiring to dwell within them. Therefore, let us not cease training our minds in godliness, according to the divine Paul. For godliness was rightly said to be that which pulls out the seeds of the wicked one by the roots. This is godliness; this is the "way of the word," that is, the path of the rational faculty or the path of thought. In the Greek Attic dialect, the words *oimos* and *keleuthos* both mean "way," which here signifies the process of reasoning. <note>Hesychius is using a linguistic metaphor to explain that spiritual progress is a "path" (*oimos*) traveled by the "mind" (*logos*).</note>

<margin>151.</margin> A person will delight in the abundance of peace, according to David, if he does not show partiality to human faces while judging unrighteously in his heart. This means not accepting the "forms" or mental images of the wicked spirits. By entertaining these forms, one begins to "think" the sin, thereby judging poorly and passing sentence in the "land" of one's own heart, giving over what is right to sin. For the great and knowledgeable Fathers in some of their writings called both demons and thoughts "men," because of their rational-like nature <note>original: "logistikon" — the capacity for logic or reasoning</note>. An example of this is in the Gospel where the Lord says: "A wicked man has done this," referring to the one who mixed tares with the wheat. <note>referencing Matthew 13:24-30</note> There is no swift rebuttal from those who commit evil; for this very reason, we are consumed by our thoughts.

<margin>152.</margin> If we begin to live our lives with attentiveness of mind, and if we join humility to watchfulness <note>term: "nepsis" — spiritual sobriety or wakefulness</note> and link prayer to our rebuttal of thoughts, we will travel the path of <margin>* of the mind.</margin> repentance well. It is like carrying a lamp—the worshipful and holy Name of Jesus Christ—as we clean, sweep, decorate, and purify our heart's house from wickedness. But if we rely only on our own watchfulness or attention, we will quickly be shoved aside by our enemies; we will be overturned and fall. Those cunning and treacherous beings will cast us down, and we will become even more entangled in their nets of wicked thoughts—perhaps even easily slaughtered by them—since we do not possess the "mighty spear," the Name of Jesus Christ. For only this venerable sword, <margin>* revolving/frequently moving.</margin> when turned frequently within a single-minded heart, knows how to turn them back and cut them to pieces...

<summary>Hesychius emphasizes that the "Name of Jesus" acts as a spiritual weapon and lamp, essential for purifying the heart and protecting the soul during its "ascent" after death. He warns that watchfulness alone is insufficient without the power of Christ and the virtue of humility.</summary>

# SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE

...to contradict and to hide, like fire to straw.
<margin>153.
*in other [versions]:
work.</margin>
The definition of unceasing watchfulness <note>term: "nepsis" — a state of spiritual alertness or "sobriety" of the mind</note>—which is the great profit and gain of the soul—is to see immediately the images of thoughts <note>term: "logismoi" — spontaneous thoughts or "proposals" from the subconscious or spiritual enemies</note> as they are being formed in the mind. Rebuttal <note>original: "antirrhesis"</note> consists of exposing and rebuking the thought that tries to enter the "air" of our mind through the mental image of some sensory thing. But that which immediately extinguishes and dissolves every thought, every argument, every fantasy, every idol, and every evil pillar of the enemy, is the invocation of the Lord. For we ourselves see within our mind their total defeat through Jesus, our great God, and the vindication of us who are humble, lowly, and useless.
<margin>154.</margin>
Many of us are ignorant of the fact that all thoughts are nothing other than fantasies of sensory and worldly things. But if we persevere in watchful prayer, prayer strips the mind of every material fantasy of evil thoughts; it makes known to the mind the schemes of our enemies and the great benefit of prayer and watchfulness. "With your eyes you will perceive, and you will see the reward of spiritual sinners," says David, the divine singer of psalms. <note>A reference to Psalm 91:8, applied here to "intellectual" or "noetic" sinners—the demonic thoughts.</note>
<margin>155.</margin>
Let us remember death unceasingly, if possible. Through this remembrance, a setting aside of cares and all vanities is born within us, as well as the guarding of the mind and continuous prayer—detachment from the body and a hatred of sin. To tell the truth, almost every virtue flows from this source as if from a spring. Therefore, let us use this practice as we use our own breath, if possible.
<margin>156.
emptied.</margin>
A heart * emptied of fantasies will give birth within itself to divine and mysterious thoughts that leap about like fish and dolphins playing in a calm sea. The sea is stirred by a gentle breeze, but the abyss of the heart is stirred by the Holy Spirit. "Because you are sons," it says, "God has sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out: Abba, Father!" <note>original: "Abba ho Patēr" — quoting Galatians 4:6</note>
<margin>157.</margin>
Every Monk will be at a loss and in conflict if he tries to take up spiritual work before achieving watchfulness of the mind—either because he does not know its beauty, or, if he

<column-break/>

knows it, he is unable to do so because of negligence. But his doubt will undoubtedly be resolved once he enters into the "guarding of the mind," which is also called "intellectual philosophy" or "the practical philosophy of the mind." He will have found the way of Him who said: "I am the way, and the resurrection, and the life." <note>original: "egō eimi hē hodos, kai hē anastasis, kai hē zōē" — quoting John 14:6 and 11:25</note>
<margin>158.</margin>
Again, he will be at a loss when seeing the abyss of thoughts and the multitude of "Babylonian infants." But Christ also resolves this difficulty, provided we stand continually upon Him on the foundation of our intellect. We dash all these Babylonian infants against this Rock and shatter them, fulfilling our desire through them according to the scripture. <note>Hesychius is using a famous allegorical interpretation of Psalm 137:9. The "Babylonian infants" are the first small stirrings of sinful thoughts, which must be "dashed against the Rock," which is Christ, before they grow into mature passions.</note> For it says, "He who keeps the commandment will know no evil word"; and, "Without me," He said, "you can do nothing."
<margin>159.</margin>
This man is truly a Monk: the one who achieves watchfulness. And this man is truly watchful: the one who is a Monk in his heart.
<margin>160.</margin>
Human life extends and circles through years, months, weeks, days and nights, hours and moments. It is right, then, for us to extend our virtuous labors throughout these times—I mean watchfulness, prayer, and the sweetness of the heart—in rhythmic stillness <note>term: "hesychia" — inner silence or stillness</note> until our departure.
<margin>161.</margin>
The hour of death will come upon us—it will come, and it is impossible to escape. Oh, that the prince of the world and of the air <note>A reference to the demonic powers that, in this tradition, are said to encounter the soul after death.</note> might find our sins to be few and petty when he comes, so that he cannot justly convict us; for then we would weep in vain. "For that servant who knew his master's will and did not act like a servant shall be beaten with many blows," He says.
<margin>162.</margin>
"Woe to those who have lost their heart," it says; "and what will they do when the Lord visits them?" Therefore, brothers, we must be diligent.
<margin>163.</margin>
Passionate thoughts follow after thoughts that seem simple and dispassionate, as we have found through long experience and observation. The former become an entrance for the latter; dispassionate thoughts lead to passionate ones.
<margin>164.</margin>
Indeed, a person must be "cut in two" by their own will. One must divide oneself with the wisest intention, as I said, and truly become an unyielding enemy to oneself. Whatever disposition a person has toward someone who has terribly oppressed and wronged them—that is how...

# 98 HESYCHIUS THE PRIEST TO THEODULUS

...and much more, if indeed we wish to succeed in the great and first commandment. I mean, of course, the way of life of Christ—blessed humility, the life of God in the flesh. Wherefore the **Apostle** says: *Who will deliver me from this body of death?* <note>original: Romans 7:24</note> and *For it is not subject to the law of God.* <note>original: Romans 8:7</note> But showing that subjecting the body to the will of God is within our power, he said: *For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged; but being judged, we are disciplined by the **Lord**.* <note>original: 1 Corinthians 11:31-32. Hesychius suggests that through spiritual discipline, the body can be brought into harmony with God's will.</note>

<margin>165.</margin> The beginning of fruit-bearing is the flower; the beginning of the guarding of the mind is temperance in food and drink, the denial of all kinds of thoughts <note>term: "logismoi" — spontaneous, often distracting or intrusive thoughts</note>, the rejection of them, and the stillness of the heart.

<margin>166.</margin> For those being strengthened in **Christ Jesus**, and beginning to run with the security of watchfulness <note>term: "nepsis" — a state of spiritual alertness or "sobriety" of the mind</note>, it first appears in the mind like a lamp, held as it were by the hand of the mind and guiding us into the paths of understanding. Afterward, it circles in the firmament of the heart like a full-shining moon. Then it appears to us like a sun, with **Jesus** radiating the sunbeams of righteousness—clearly showing Himself and the utterly transparent lights of His contemplations <note>term: "theoria" — spiritual insights or visions of divine truths</note>.

<margin>167.</margin> For He reveals these things mystically to a mind that persists in His commandment which says: *And you shall circumcise the hardness of your heart.* <note>original: Deuteronomy 10:16</note> And as has been said, diligent watchfulness teaches a person extraordinary concepts. For the Divine does not show partiality. Wherefore the **Lord** says: *Hear me and understand; for to him who has, more shall be given and he shall have abundance; but from him who has not, even what he seems to have shall be taken away from him.* <note>original: Matthew 13:12</note> And *to those who love **God**, all things work together for good.* <note>original: Romans 8:28</note> Much more, then, will the virtues work together for him.

<margin>168.</margin> A ship will not travel many miles without water; and the guarding of the mind will not advance at all without watchfulness joined with humility, and the prayer of **Jesus Christ** continually.

<margin>169.</margin> The stones are the foundation of a house; but the foundations and the roof of this virtue is the adorable and holy name of **our Lord Jesus Christ**. A foolish captain will easily be shipwrecked in a time of storm if he drives away the sailors and throws the oars and sails into the sea while he himself sleeps; but more easily will a soul be drowned by demons if it neglects watchfulness and...

<column-break/>

<margin>170.</margin> ...calling upon the name of **Jesus Christ** when the assaults of thoughts begin.

What we know, we write and speak; and what we have seen while traveling the path, we testify to those who wish it, if indeed you are willing to receive what has been said. For He Himself has said: *If anyone does not remain in me, he is cast out like a branch and withers, and they gather them and throw them into the fire, and they are burned; but the one who remains in me, and I in him.* <note>original: John 15:5-6</note> For just as it is impossible for the sun to shine without light, so it is impossible for the heart to be cleansed from the filth of destructive thoughts without the prayer of the **Name of Jesus**. And if this is true—as I see it is—let us use it like our own breath. For the one is light, but the others are darkness; the one is **God** and Master, while the others <margin>*in other [versions]: are servants, and demons.</margin> are servants of demons.

<margin>171.</margin> Let the guardianship of the mind be called, aptly and truly, the "Bringer of Light," the "Bringer of Lightning," the "Radiator of Light," and the "Bringer of Fire." For it surpasses, to tell the truth, countless physical and many other virtues. For this reason, one should call this virtue by these honorable names because of the brilliant lights born from it. Those who have fallen in love with it—though they may have been sinners, useless, profane, ignorant, senseless, or unjust—can become righteous, useful, pure, holy, and wise through **Jesus Christ**. Not only this, but they can also behold mysteries and speak of God <note>term: "theologein" — to speak of God, often implying an experiential knowledge rather than just academic study</note>. Having become contemplative, they swim in this purest and infinite light, touching it with unspeakable touch, and they dwell and live with Him, since they have *tasted that the **Lord** is good.* <note>original: Psalm 34:8</note> Thus is clearly fulfilled in such "fore-angels" <note>Those living an angelic life on earth.</note> the word of the divine **David**: *Surely the righteous shall give thanks to your name, and the upright shall dwell with your presence.* <note>original: Psalm 140:13</note> For indeed, truly, these alone sincerely call upon and confess **God**, with whom they also love to converse at all times because they love Him.

<margin>172.</margin> Woe to the "inner man" because of the "outer man." For the inner man will be greatly grieved by the outer senses; and being grieved, he will use lashes against the outer senses. He who has practiced what is in the <margin>*in other [versions]: the deed.</margin> letter, has already recognized what is in the contemplation.

<margin>173.</margin> If our inner man is watchful according to the **Fathers**, he is also able to guard the outer man. Except that both we and the evil-working demons together...

# 99 A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE

...the sins; and some, in thoughts alone, or in fantastical paintings, form the sin in their minds as they wish. But we do so both through thoughts within and through deeds without. For the demons, lacking the density of bodies, produce punishment for themselves and for us through thoughts alone, and through craftiness and deceit. For if those wretches did not lack the density of a body, they would never cease from sinning even through deeds, for they always preserve a will ready for impiety.

<margin>174.</margin> But the single-worded prayer <note>original: "monologistos" — refers to the short, repetitive Jesus Prayer</note> kills and turns their deceits to ash. For when **Jesus**, the **God** and **Son of God**, is called upon by us continuously and untiringly, He does not permit them even the beginning of an entry—which they call "provocation" <note>term: "prosvole" — the first stage of a tempting thought entering the mind</note>—to show the mind any form in the mirror of the intellect, nor to speak any words to the heart. And if a demonic form does not enter the heart, it will be empty of thoughts, as we said; for it is their habit to secretly converse with the soul through thoughts and to teach it wickedness.

<margin>175.</margin> From continuous prayer, then, the air of the intellect is cleansed of dark clouds and the winds of the spirits of wickedness. When the air of the heart is cleansed, it is impossible for the divine light of **Jesus** not to shine in it—unless we are puffed up by vainglory, pride, and a desire for display, and are lifted up into <margin>\* the incomprehensible.</margin> \* the immovable, and find ourselves without help from **Jesus**; for **Christ** hates such things, He who is the teacher of humility.

<margin>176.</margin> Let us hold fast, therefore, to these two things: prayer and humility. Together with watchfulness <note>term: "nepsis"</note>, they arm us against demons like a flaming sword. For it is possible for us, by living thus daily and hourly, to celebrate joyfully in the heart and in a mystical way.

<margin>177.</margin> The eight generic thoughts of wickedness <note>term: "logismoi" — the eight capital sins in early monasticism: gluttony, lust, greed, anger, sorrow, sloth, vainglory, and pride</note>, in which every thought is contained and from which all have their birth—as according to the myths of the Greeks every polluted demon-god arose from Hera and Zeus—all these come up to the gate of the heart. Finding the mind unguarded, they enter one by one at their own time. Whichever of the eight thoughts ascends and enters the heart, it brings in a swarm of shameful thoughts; and having thus darkened the mind, it <meta>catchword: it</meta>

<column-break/>

calls upon the body, urging it toward the execution of shameful deeds.

<margin>178.</margin> Therefore, he who guards the "head of the serpent" <note>A metaphor for stopping a tempting thought at its very first appearance</note> and, through forceful rebuttal, uses words of holy anger to strike it down, has beaten back the war. For by crushing the head, he escapes many evil thoughts and the most wicked deeds. And then the intellect remains calm, as **God** accepts its vigilance over its thoughts. In return, He grants it the gift of knowing how to overcome its adversaries, and how the heart must be gradually cleansed of thoughts that "defile the inner man," as the **Lord Jesus** says: *For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications... these are what defile a person.* <note>original: Matthew 15:19-20</note>

<margin>179.</margin> Thus, the soul is able to stand in the **Lord** in its own beauty and loveliness and uprightness, just as it was created by **God** in the beginning, exceedingly good and upright. As the great servant of **God**, **Anthony**, says: "Virtue consists in the soul's intellectual part being in its natural state." And again he said: "For the soul to be upright is for its intellectual part to be in that natural state in which it was created." And a little later he says again: "Let us cleanse the intellect; for I believe that when it is purified on all sides and stands in its natural state, it is able to become clairvoyant and see more and further than the demons, having the **Lord** who reveals things to it." This is what the renowned **Anthony** says, as the great **Athanasius** records in the *Life of Anthony*.

<margin>180.</margin> Every thought creates an image of a sensible thing in the mind. For the "Assyrian" <note>A traditional monastic term for the Devil, based on the biblical enemies of Israel</note>, being himself a mind, is not able to deceive in any other way except by using the sensible and familiar things known to us.

<margin>181.</margin> Just as it is impossible for us, being human, to chase winged birds in the air or to fly like them—for our nature does not possess this—so it is impossible to overcome bodiless demonic thoughts without "watchful" <note>term: "neptikos"</note> and frequent prayer, or without the eye of the mind swimming steadily toward **God**. If you do not do this, you are "hunting the earth" <note>margin note: \* Or "acting in vain."</note>.

<margin>182.</margin> Truly then, if you wish to put your thoughts to shame, to be at peace in a kindly way, and to watch over your heart with ease, let the Jesus Prayer cling to your breath, and in a few days you will see this come to pass.

# HESYCHIUS THE PRIEST TO THEODOULOS

<margin>183.</margin> Just as it is impossible for letters to be written in the air—for they must be carved into some solid body so that they may be preserved permanently—so let us bind the prayer of **Jesus Christ** to our diligent watchfulness <term>watchfulness: "nepsis," a state of spiritual sobriety and alertness</term>. In this way, the all-beautiful virtue of sobriety may remain permanent with Him, and through Him, it may be kept for us forever, never to be taken away.

<margin>184.</margin> Roll your works upon the **Lord**, and you will find grace, as it is said. Let it not be said of us by the Prophet: "You are near, O **Lord**, to their mouths, but far from their hearts." <note>original: "nephron" — literally 'kidneys' or 'reins,' used biblically to refer to the innermost thoughts and emotions</note> No one else besides **Jesus** will firmly bring peace to your heart from the passions, except **Jesus Christ** Himself, who joined together things that were far apart.

<margin>185.</margin> Both darken the soul in equal measure: the internal conversations with distracting thoughts <note>original: "logismoi" — the intrusive thoughts that lead to temptation</note>, and external chance encounters and idle talk. To avoid harm to the mind, we must love to avoid both types of idle chatter—grieving both the thoughts and the people for a reason that is most pleasing to **God**—lest the mind, becoming darkened, grows slack in its watchfulness. For when we are darkened by forgetfulness, we lose the mind's clarity.

<margin>186.</margin> For he who guards the purity of his heart with all diligence will have its lawgiver, **Christ**, as a teacher, secretly speaking His will to him. "I will hear what the **Lord God** will speak in me," says David, revealing this very thing. Describing the mind's inspection of itself during spiritual warfare, and **God's** helpful protection, he said: "And a man will say, 'Surely there is a reward for the righteous.'" Then, showing the result of this inquiry, he says: "Surely it is **God** who judges them"—that is, the evil demons in the land of our heart. And elsewhere he says: "A man shall approach, and a deep heart, and **God** shall be exalted." And then their blows shall be accounted to us as the arrows of infants.

<margin>187.</margin> Let us always live with our hearts educated in wisdom, according to the Psalmist, constantly breathing **Christ Jesus**, who is the very power of **God the Father** and the wisdom of **God**. And if, by some circumstance, we grow slack and neglect this spiritual practice, the next morning let us again gird the loins of our mind <note>reference to 1 Peter 1:13</note> well, and firmly

<column-break/>

take up the work once again. We must know that there is no excuse for us, having known what is good, if we do not put it into practice.

<margin>188.</margin> Just as harmful foods, when recently cast into the body, cause distress—but if the one who ate them immediately senses the harm and quickly vomits them up by some medicinal draft, he remains unharmed—so it is with the mind. When it receives and swallows evil thoughts, and feels their bitterness, it can easily vomit them out and completely cast them away through the prayer of **Jesus** called out from the depths of the heart. This is what spiritual education and experience have taught those who practice watchfulness regarding the matter at hand.

<margin>189.</margin> With your every breath and your nostrils, unite watchfulness and the name of **Jesus**, or the unerring meditation on death and humility. For both are known to be of great benefit.

<margin>190.</margin> The **Lord** said: "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls."

<margin>191.</margin> The **Lord** said: "Whoever humbles himself like this child will be exalted; but he who exalts himself will be humbled." "Learn from me," He says. You see that humility is a matter of learning. For His commandment is eternal life, and this is humility. Therefore, he who is not humble has slipped away from life and will clearly be found in its opposite state.

<margin>192.</margin> For if every virtue is built through the soul and the body, and both the soul and the body are creations of **God**—through which, as I said, virtue is constituted—how are we not utterly insane to boast in the "decorations" of a soul and body that are not our own? Why do we seek vain glory and lean upon pride as if upon a reed staff? Why do we provoke our **God**, who surpasses us in infinite greatness, against our own heads—which is the most terrifying thing—because of our extreme lawlessness and folly? For the **Lord** opposes the proud. Instead of imitating the **Lord** in humility, we become friends with the **Lord's** enemy, the proud demon, through a vainglorious and proud mindset. For this reason, the Apostle said: "For what do you have that you did not receive?" Did you create yourself? If you received from **God** the body and the soul, from which and in which and through which every virtue consists, why do you boast as if you had not received them? For it is the **Lord** who grants these things to you.

<summary>Hesychius emphasizes the necessity of combining the Jesus Prayer with watchfulness (nepsis) to guard the heart, using a vivid analogy of vomiting to describe casting out evil thoughts. He concludes by teaching that humility is a learned virtue and that pride is irrational since all human faculties are gifts from God.</summary>
<keywords>watchfulness, nepsis, Jesus Prayer, logismoi, humility, pride, spiritual warfare, purity of heart, Hesychius of Sinai</keywords>

-># A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE ON WATCHFULNESS AND VIRTUE<-

<margin>193.</margin> In short, the purification of the heart—through which humility and every good gift descend upon us from above—is nothing other than refusing to allow intrusive thoughts <note>original: "logismoi" — the persistent, often tempting thoughts that stir the mind</note> to peek out and enter the soul.

<margin>194.</margin> For guarding the mind with **God's** help, and having stayed within the soul for **God's** sake alone, provides the governing part of the soul <term>governing part: "hegemonikon," the ruling faculty of the mind or reason</term> with prudence in its spiritual struggles. It grants a significant ability to the one who shares in it, allowing them to manage their deeds and words with sound judgment, in a way acceptable to the **Lord**.

<margin>195.</margin> The ornaments of the Priest in the Old Testament were clearly prototypes of a pure heart. We should therefore attend to the "plate" of the heart <note>original: "petallon" — referring to the golden plate worn on the High Priest's turban inscribed with "Holy to the Lord"</note>, lest it be blackened by sin, so that we may scrub it clean through tears, repentance, and prayer. For the mind is a nimble thing, difficult to restrain from unlawful imaginings; it easily follows both evil and good mental fantasies.

<margin>196.</margin> Truly blessed is the person who has so closely joined the prayer of **Jesus** to their intellect, crying out to Him unceasingly in the heart, just as the air is united to our bodies or a flame to wax. When the sun passes over the earth, it creates the day; so too, when the holy and venerable Name of the **Lord Jesus** shines continuously in the intellect, it generates countless sun-like insights.

<margin>197.</margin> When the clouds are scattered, the air is shown to be pure. Likewise, when the fantasies of the passions are scattered by **Jesus Christ**, the Sun of Righteousness, they naturally produce light-filled and star-like thoughts in the heart, for its inner atmosphere has been illuminated through **Jesus**. As the book of Wisdom says: "Those who trust in the **Lord** shall understand truth, and the faithful shall remain with Him in love." <note>original: "Ecclesiastes" — the author cites this, but the quote is actually from Wisdom of Solomon 3:9</note>

<margin>198.</margin> One of the Saints said: "Be vengeful only toward the demons, and remain an enemy to the body at all times." The flesh is a deceitful friend; the more it is pampered, the more it wages war. And again: "Acquire enmity toward the body, and battle against the belly."

<margin>199.</margin> In our previous words, in the first and second hundred chapters, we arranged the labors of holy stillness of the mind <term>stillness: "hesychia," a state of inner silence and tranquility</term>. These were not merely the cultivation of our own intellect, but the things which the divine words of the God-wise Fathers

<column-break/>

teach us concerning the purity of the mind. Now, having said a few more things to show the profit of guarding the mind, we shall cease our speaking.

<margin>200.</margin> Come now, follow me toward the continuity of this blessed guarding of the mind. Whoever you are that longs in spirit to see "good days," I will teach you in the **Lord** a seasoned labor and the lifestyle of the Noetic Powers <note>original: "noerōn Dynameōn" — the Angels</note>. For the Angels do not grow weary of hymning the **Creator**, nor does a mind that purely competes alongside them. And just as those immaterial beings do not worry about food, so too those who are material but becoming "immaterial" do not worry about it, if they truly enter the heaven of the mind's stillness.

<margin>201.</margin> Just as the Powers above do not worry about money or possessions, so too those who have cleansed the "eye of the soul" and have entered into the habit of virtue will not be anxious about the harassment of evil spirits. Just as the wealth of the Angels is their progress toward **God**, so too for such people is their manifest desire and love for **God**, their fixed gaze upon the Divine, and their ascent. Furthermore, stretching out with longing and insatiable hunger in this ascent—born from a taste of the Divine and an ecstatic yearning—they will not stop until they reach the Seraphim. Nor will they cease the watchfulness of the mind <term>watchfulness: "nepsis," spiritual sobriety</term> and their loving elevation until they become like Angels in **Christ Jesus** our **Lord**.

<margin>202.</margin> There is no venom greater than the venom of the asp or the basilisk, and there is no evil greater than self-love <term>self-love: "philautia," an excessive, egoistic attachment to oneself</term>. The offspring of self-love are these winged things: praise in the heart, self-satisfaction, gluttony, fornication, vainglory, envy, and the crown of them all—pride. This pride knows how to pull down not only humans but even Angels from the Heavens, wrapping them in gloom instead of light.

<margin>203.</margin> <margin>* In other manuscripts: "not our own."</margin> These things are for you, Theodoulos <note>the name means "Servant of God"</note>, from the one whose name means "stillness" <note>the author Hesychius, whose name means "Still" or "Quiet"</note>, even if he has failed in the practice of it. But perhaps * these things are not entirely mine, but what **God** has given—**God** who is praised and glorified in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by every rational nature, both Angels and humans, and by all creation which the ineffable Trinity has fashioned, the one **God**. May we also obtain His radiant Kingdom through the prayers of the most pure **Theotokos** <note>the Virgin Mary, Mother of God</note> and of our Holy Fathers. To this unsearchable **God** be eternal glory. Amen.

<vocab>purification of the heart, guarding of the mind, watchfulness, virtue, Jesus Prayer, stillness, self-love, Theodoulos</vocab>

It warns against the "venom" of self-love and pride while offering a final doxology and dedication to the disciple Theodoulos.</summary>

## BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
### OF OUR HOLY FATHER
# NILUS THE ASCETIC

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'N' set within a rectangular frame featuring floral patterns.</image-desc>

For the divinely inspired Father Nilus, Constantinople was his fatherland, and the divine Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), the Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquence.</note> was his teacher. The time in which he flourished was the year four hundred and forty-two. Blessed with noble birth and overflowing wealth, he served as the Prefect <term>Prefect: "Eparchos," the highest-ranking administrative official in the city of Constantinople.</term> of his homeland. Later, saying farewell to all worldly things and reaching Mount Sinai, he chose the ascetic life. Being deeply learned in both our Christian wisdom and secular <note>original: "thyrathen" — literally "the wisdom from outside," referring to classical Greek philosophy and rhetoric.</note> literature, he left behind various writings full of spiritual wisdom and unspeakable grace. From these, we have gathered—in the manner of a bee—the discourse on Prayer, which is divided into one hundred and fifty-three

<column-break/>

chapters, as well as the work entitled *The Ascetic Discourse*. With these, as if with honeycombs, we welcome those who encounter them; for they truly drip with honey and the nectar of ambrosia, and they promise an abundant harvest of spiritual profit. The most wise Photius <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893), Patriarch of Constantinople and author of the *Bibliotheca*, a massive summary of ancient and Byzantine books.</note> also mentions him in "Reading 201," on page 266, saying: "And a discourse by Nilus the Monk was read, divided into one hundred and fifty-three chapters; in these, the divine man unfolds the pattern of prayer. Many other noteworthy things of his were also read... attesting to his perfection in deeds and his power in words."

# NILUS THE ASCETIC
## PROLOGUE TO THE ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-THREE CHAPTERS ON PRAYER

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'P' set within a rectangular frame featuring floral motifs and stylized crosses at the corners.</image-desc>

While I was feverish with the heat of impure passions, you restored me, as is your custom, by the touch of your God-loving letters, comforting my mind—which was exhausted by shameful things—and blessedly imitating the great teacher and instructor. And it is no wonder. For the noble portion has always been your lot, just as it was for the blessed Jacob. For

<column-break/>

having served well for the sake of Rachel and having received Leah, you seek the beloved one as well, since you have surely completed your seven years for her too. <note>An allegory from Genesis 29; in mystical tradition, Leah represents the "active" life of labor and virtue, while Rachel represents the "contemplative" life or the direct vision of God.</note> As for me, I cannot deny that although I have toiled all night, I have caught nothing. Nevertheless, at your word, I have let down the nets and caught a great number of fish—not large ones, I think, but numbering one hundred and fifty-three nonetheless. <note>A reference to the miraculous catch of 153 fish in John 21:11, here symbolizing the 153 chapters on prayer that follow.</note> These I send to you in the basket of love, divided into an equal number of

# DISCOURSE ON PRAYER

...matters, having issued the command. I admire you and greatly envy your excellent purpose, as you are a lover of these chapters on prayer. For you do not simply love those that are held in the hands and have their being in ink upon paper, but those which are established in the mind <note>original: "nous" — the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the "eye of the heart."</note> through love and the forgetting of grievances.

<margin>* perhaps "therein"</margin>
But since all things are double, one set against the other according to the wise Jesus <note>A reference to Jesus son of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus 42:24): "All things come in pairs, one opposite the other."</note>, receive them according to the letter, and understand them according to the spirit, for the mind precedes every letter. For if the mind did not exist, neither would the letter. Therefore, the way of prayer is also twofold. One way is practical, and the other is theoretical <note>In this context, "practical" refers to the struggle for virtue, while "theoretical" (theoria) refers to the direct contemplation of God.</note>. In the same way, with numbers, that which is at hand is quantity, but that which is signified is quality. For having divided this discourse on prayer into one hundred and fifty-three chapters, we have sent you a Gospel-like portion <note>original: "opsonion" — a ration or provision. The number 153 refers to the "great fish" caught by the disciples in John 21:11.</note>, so that you might find the delight of symbolic numbers, and the shapes of the triangle and the hexagon. This signifies both a pious knowledge of the Trinity and a description of the order of this world. Indeed, the number one hundred by itself is a square. But the number fifty-three <note>The text likely refers to the remainder after 100, though mathematically 153 is the 17th triangular number.</note> is triangular and spherical. For twenty-eight is triangular, while twenty-five is spherical—for five times five is twenty-five. Therefore, you have the square shape, not only through the "fourfold" <term>Fourfold: "Tetraktys," a Pythagorean term here applied to the four cardinal virtues: courage, temperance, justice, and wisdom.</term> of the virtues, but also the wise knowledge of this age, which resembles the number twenty-five because of the spherical <note>original: "sphairikon" — In ancient mathematics, numbers like 5 and 6 were "spherical" because their squares end in the same digit, symbolizing the cyclical nature of time.</note> nature of time. For week moves upon week, month upon month, and time rolls from year to year, and season upon season, as we see in the movements of the sun, the moon, spring, summer, and the rest. The triangle, then, may signify to you the knowledge of the Holy Trinity. Or otherwise: if you consider the number one hundred and fifty-three as a triangle through its sum, understand it as representing Practice, Physics, and Theology; or Faith, Hope, and Love; or gold, silver, and precious stones. Such is the nature of the number. As for the humble nature of these chapters, you will overlook it, as one who knows both how to be full and how to be in want; and indeed, as one who remembers Him who did not reject the widow's two mites, but accepted them above the wealth of many others. Therefore, knowing how to preserve the fruit of goodwill and love for your true brothers, pray for him who is ill so that he may recover, and having picked up

<column-break/>

his bed for the future, he may walk, by the grace of Christ. Amen.

<margin>1.</margin>
If anyone wishes to prepare fragrant incense, he shall combine transparent frankincense, cassia, onycha, and stacte in equal parts according to the Law <note>A reference to the recipe for sacred incense in Exodus 30:34.</note>. These are the four virtues. For if they are complete and in equal proportion, the mind will not be betrayed.

<margin>2.</margin>
A soul purified through the fulfillment of the commandments prepares a stable condition for the mind, making it receptive to the state it seeks.

<margin>3.</margin>
Prayer is the conversation of the mind with God. What state, then, does the mind require so that it may be able to reach out toward its own Master without turning back, and to converse with Him without any mediator?

<margin>4.</margin>
If Moses was forbidden to approach the burning bush on earth until he had loosened the sandals from his feet, how can you—who wish to see Him who is beyond all sense and thought and to become His conversationalist—not loosen from yourself every passionate thought?

<margin>5.</margin>
First, pray for the gift of tears, so that through mourning you may soften the wildness dwelling in your soul; and having confessed your lawless deeds against yourself to the Lord, you may obtain forgiveness from Him.

<margin>6.</margin>
Employ tears for the success of every request. For the Master rejoices greatly when you pray with tears.

<margin>7.</margin>
If you pour out fountains of tears during your prayer, do not be at all exalted in yourself, as if you were above many others. For your prayer has received help so that you might be able to eagerly confess your sins and appease the Master through tears. Do not, therefore, turn the remedy for passions into a passion itself, lest you further provoke Him who gave the grace.

<margin>8.</margin>
Many, while weeping for their sins, forgot the purpose of tears and, becoming maddened, were led astray.

<margin>9.</margin>
Stand with effort and pray intensely, and turn away the intrusions of cares and reasonings. For they disturb and trouble you so that they may loosen your intensity.

<margin>10.</margin>
When the demons see you eager to pray truly, then they suggest thoughts of certain things that are supposedly neces- <note>The catchword at the bottom "anag-" leads to "anagkaion" or "necessary."</note>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NILUS THE ASCETIC

...burning [passions], and after a short time they take away the memory of them, moving the mind to seek them out; and when it does not find them, it becomes greatly discouraged and grieved. But when the mind stands for prayer, they remind it of those things it sought and remembered, so that the mind, being moved toward the knowledge of them, might lose the fruitful prayer.

<margin>11.</margin> Strive to keep your mind <note>original: "nous" — the intellect or the "eye of the heart," which the desert fathers believed should be clear of all images during prayer.</note> deaf and speechless during the time of prayer, and then you will be able to pray.

<margin>12.</margin> When a temptation meets you, or a dispute provokes you to move toward anger against your opponent or to break out in some unseemly cry, remember prayer and the judgment regarding it, and immediately the disorderly movement within you will grow calm.

<margin>13.</margin> Whatever you do to take revenge on a brother who has wronged you will all become a stumbling block to you at the time of prayer.

<margin>14.</margin> Prayer is the offspring of gentleness and the absence of anger.

<margin>15.</margin> Prayer is the manifestation of joy and thanksgiving.

<margin>16.</margin> Prayer is the remedy <note>original: "alexēma" — a defense or protection, like a medicinal ward.</note> for grief and discouragement.

<margin>17.</margin> "Go, sell your possessions and give to the poor," and taking up the cross, deny yourself, so that you may be able to pray without distraction.

<margin>18.</margin> If you wish to pray in a praiseworthy manner, deny yourself every hour, and though suffering many terrible things, practice philosophy <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to the ascetic life—the practical pursuit of wisdom through self-discipline.</note> for the sake of prayer.

<margin>19.</margin> Whatever hardship you endure while practicing this philosophy, you will find its fruit at the time of prayer.

<margin>20.</margin> Desiring to pray as you ought, do not grieve any soul; otherwise, you run in vain.

<margin>21.</margin> "Leave your gift," it says, "before the altar, and go first and be reconciled with your brother, and then come and you shall pray without disturbance." <note>A reference to Matthew 5:24.</note> For resentment <note>original: "mnessikakia" — literally "the remembering of wrongs."</note> clouds the ruling faculty of the one praying and darkens his prayers.

<margin>22.</margin> Those who heap up griefs and resentments for themselves are like those who draw water and pour it into a pierced jar.

<margin>23.</margin> If you are patient, you will always pray with joy.

<margin>24.</margin> When you are praying properly, such things will happen to you that it will seem entirely just

<column-break/>

to use anger. But there is no such thing as "just anger" against one's neighbor at all. For if you search, you will find that it is possible for a matter to be settled well even without anger. Therefore, use every device so as not to break out in anger.

<margin>25.</margin> See to it that while you seem to be healing another, you yourself do not become incurable and place an obstacle in the way of your prayer.

<margin>26.</margin> By sparing others from your anger, you will find mercy, and you will show yourself to be prudent, and you will be among those who truly pray.

<margin>27.</margin> He who arms himself against anger will never tolerate desire. For desire provides the fuel for anger, and anger troubles the intellectual eye, ruining the state of prayer.

<margin>28.</margin> Do not pray only with outward gestures, but urge your mind toward the awareness of spiritual prayer with much fear.

<margin>29.</margin> Sometimes, having immediately stood for prayer, you will pray well; at other times, though you labor greatly, you will not achieve your goal—this is so that you might seek it all the more, and having received it, you will hold the achievement as something that cannot be stolen.

<margin>30.</margin> When an Angel stands by, all those who trouble us suddenly withdraw, and the mind is found in great ease, praying healthily. But sometimes, when our usual warfare presses upon us, the mind struggles and is not permitted to look up; for it has been predisposed by various passions. Nevertheless, by seeking further, it will find; and to him who knocks, it shall be opened.

<margin>31.</margin> Do not pray for your own desires to be done, for they do not always agree with the will of God. Rather, pray as you were taught, saying: "Thy will be done in me." And in every matter, ask Him in this way, so that His will may be done. For He wills what is good and profitable for your soul, but you do not always seek this.

<margin>32.</margin> Often while praying, I have asked for something to happen which I thought was good, and I persisted in the request, unreasonably forcing the will of God—not leaving it to Him to arrange what He knows to be profitable. And yet, having received it, I was later very distressed that I had not rather asked for the will of God to be done. For the matter did not turn out to be what I thought it was.

->## DISCOURSE ON PRAYER<-

<margin>33.</margin> What is good, except for God? Therefore, let us surrender everything concerning ourselves to Him, and it will be well with us. For He who is good is certainly also the provider of good gifts.

<margin>34.</margin> Do not be distressed if you do not immediately receive from God the request you are asking for. For He wishes to benefit you even more by your persevering with Him in prayer. For what is higher than conversing with God and being drawn away by communion <note>original: "synousia" — literally a "being together" or "intimacy," often used for deep communion.</note> with Him?

<margin>35.</margin> Undistracted prayer is the highest intellection <note>original: "noēsis" — the activity of the nous or spiritual intellect.</note> of the mind.

<margin>36.</margin> Prayer is the ascent of the mind <note>original: "nous" — the spiritual "eye" of the soul, distinct from the analytical brain.</note> to God.

<margin>37.</margin> If you long to pray, renounce all things, so that you may inherit the All.

<margin>38.</margin> Pray first for the purification of the passions; second, to be rescued from ignorance and forgetfulness; and third, from every temptation and abandonment.

<margin>39.</margin> Seek only righteousness and the Kingdom in your prayer—that is, virtue and knowledge—and all other things shall be added to you.

<margin>40.</margin> It is right to pray not only for your own purification, but also for every one of your fellow kin, so that you may imitate the Angelic way.

<margin>41.</margin> See if you truly stand before God in your prayer, or if you are defeated by human praise and are eager to hunt for it, using the long duration of your prayer as a cover.

<margin>42.</margin> Whether you pray with brothers or alone, strive to pray not out of habit, but with feeling.

<margin>43.</margin> The "feeling" of prayer is mindfulness accompanied by reverence, and compunction <note>original: "katanysis" — a piercing of the heart that leads to repentance and spiritual sweetness.</note>, and pain of soul in the confession of faults with hidden sighs.

<margin>44.</margin> If your mind is still being stolen away at the peak of the time of prayer, it does not yet know that a Monk is praying, but is still worldly, beautifying the outer tent.

<margin>45.</margin> When praying, guard your memory with power, so that it does not present your own affairs to you, but move yourself toward the awareness of your standing [before God]. For the mind is very prone by nature to be plundered by memory during the time of prayer.

<margin>46.</margin> The memory brings to you fantasies of old things as you are praying, or new cares, or the face of one who has grieved you.

<column-break/>

The demon is very envious of a man who prays, and uses every device to ruin his purpose. He never stops moving the thoughts <note>original: "noēmata" — mental images or concepts.</note> of things through the memory, and stirring up all the passions through the flesh, so that he might be able to hinder his best course and his journey <note>original: "ekdēmia" — a "traveling abroad" or departure, suggesting the mind leaving the body behind to meet God.</note> toward God.

<margin>47.</margin> When the most evil demon, having done much, is unable to hinder the prayer of the righteous man, he gives way a little, and later takes revenge on him for having prayed. For either he sets him on fire with anger, thus destroying the excellent state created in him by the prayer, or he provokes him toward irrational pleasure and thereby insults the mind.

<margin>48.</margin> Having prayed as you ought, expect what you ought not, and stand manfully guarding your fruit. For this you were appointed from the beginning: to work and to guard. Therefore, do not leave what has been produced unguarded after working; otherwise, you have profited nothing by praying.

<margin>49.</margin> All the war that is waged between us and the unclean demons occurs over nothing else than spiritual prayer. For it is extremely hostile and most burdensome to them, but to us it is saving and most pleasant.

<margin>50.</margin> What do the demons wish to activate in us? Gluttony, fornication, greed, anger, and resentment, and the rest of the passions; so that the mind, having been thickened by them, cannot pray as it should. For the passions of the irrational part [of the soul], once they take charge, do not allow the mind to move rationally <note>original: "logikōs" — according to the Logos or reason; the proper, divine-aligned function of the mind.</note>.

<margin>51.</margin> We pursue the virtues for the sake of the inner principles <note>original: "logoi" — the spiritual "reasons" or essences of created things.</note> of created things, and we pursue these for the sake of the Word <note>original: "Logos" — Christ, the Divine Reason.</note> who gave them being; and He is accustomed to appear in the state of prayer.

<margin>52.</margin> The state of prayer is a dispassionate habit <note>original: "hexis" — a stable internal disposition.</note> which, by supreme love, snatches the wisdom-loving mind to the intellectual height.

<margin>53.</margin> He who truly wishes to pray must not only rule over anger and desire, but must also be free from every passionate thought.

<margin>54.</margin> He who loves God always converses with Him as with a Father, turning away from every passionate thought.

<margin>55.</margin> It is not the one who has attained dispassion <note>original: "apatheia" — a state of spiritual peace where the passions no longer disturb the soul.</note> who already prays truly. For he can still be occupied with bare thoughts or with histories...

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NILUS THE ASCETIC ###

...to be distracted by them, and to be far removed from God.

<margin>57.</margin> It is not when the mind <note>original: "nous" — the spiritual intellect or the "eye of the heart."</note> no longer lingers on the bare thoughts of things that it has already reached the place of prayer. For it can still be occupied with the contemplation of things and be busy with their principles <note>original: "logois" — the inner meanings or divine reasons behind created things.</note>. Even if these are just bare words, since they are contemplations of things, they still shape and form the mind and lead it far away from God.

<margin>58.</margin> Unless the mind goes beyond the contemplation of physical nature, it has not yet seen the perfect "place of God." For it can still be involved in the knowledge of intelligible things <note>original: "noētōn" — things grasped by the intellect rather than the senses.</note> and be distracted by them.

<margin>59.</margin> If you wish to pray, you have need of God, who gives prayer to the one who prays. Therefore, call upon Him, saying: "Hallowed be Thy Name, Thy Kingdom come"—that is, the Holy Spirit and Your Only-Begotten Son. For thus He taught, saying: "Worship the Father in Spirit and in Truth."

<margin>60.</margin> He who prays in spirit and truth no longer honors the Creator because of His creatures <note>i.e., by looking at the world around him</note>, but hymns Him out of Himself <note>meaning, from within the divine experience itself</note>.

<margin>61.</margin> If you are a theologian, you will pray truly; and if you pray truly, you are a theologian.

<margin>62.</margin> When your mind, through a great longing for God, gradually withdraws as it were from the flesh, and turns away from all thoughts arising from the senses, or memory, or bodily temperament, while being filled with both reverence and joy, then consider yourself to have approached the borders of prayer.

<margin>63.</margin> The Holy Spirit, sympathizing with our weakness, visits us even when we are impure; and if He finds the mind alone praying to Him with a love for truth, He enters into it and vanishes the entire army of thoughts and reflections surrounding it, urging it toward the love of spiritual prayer.

<margin>64.</margin> While others <note>meaning demons or external influences</note> produce thoughts, reflections, or contemplations in the mind by altering the state of the body, the Lord does the opposite: entering the mind itself, He puts into it the knowledge of whatever He wills, and through the mind, He calms the lack of self-control in the body.

<margin>65.</margin> No one who loves true prayer and yet is an-

<column-break/>

-gry or holds a grudge is beyond blame. For he is like someone who wishes for sharp vision but keeps poking his own eyes.

<margin>66.</margin> If you long to pray, do nothing that is contrary to prayer, so that God, drawing near, may journey with you.

<margin>67.</margin> Do not form an image of the Divine within yourself when you are praying, nor allow your mind to be impressed with any kind of form; rather, approach the Immaterial <note>God</note> in an immaterial way, and you will understand.

<margin>68.</margin> Guard yourself against the traps of the enemies. For it happens that while you are praying purely and calmly, a strange and alien form suddenly appears to you, in order to lead you into a sense of conceit by suggesting that the Divine is located there. This is to convince you that the object suddenly revealed to you is the Divine. But the Divine is without quantity and without form.

<margin>69.</margin> When the envious demon cannot stir the memory during prayer, he then forces the bodily temperament <note>original: "krasin" — the balance of humors or physical state</note> to produce some strange fantasy in the mind, and thus gives it a form. But one who is accustomed to dwelling in intellectual concepts is easily bent; and he who is striving for immaterial and formless knowledge is deceived, grasping smoke instead of light.

<margin>70.</margin> Stand on your guard, keeping your mind away from thoughts during the time of prayer, so that you may fulfill your request and stand in your own proper stillness. Then He who sympathizes with the ignorant will visit you, and you will receive the most glorious gift of prayer.

<margin>71.</margin> You will not be able to pray purely while entangled in material things and shaken by constant cares. For prayer is the laying aside of thoughts.

<margin>72.</margin> A man who is tied up cannot run. Neither can a mind enslaved to passion see the place of spiritual prayer. For it is dragged and tossed about by passionate thoughts and will have no steady station.

<margin>73.</margin> When the mind finally prays purely and without passion, the demons no longer attack it from the "left" <note>meaning through base passions or lusts</note>, but from the "right" <note>meaning through spiritual pride or "good" distractions</note>. They suggest to it a supposed "glory of God" and some kind of form pleasing to the senses, so that it thinks it has perfectly attained the goal of prayer. A man of knowledge <note>original: "gnostikos" — one who has deep spiritual insight</note> said that this happens because of the passion of vanity and by the demon who touches the area of the brain... <note>Text ends mid-word: "enkepha-" (brain).</note>

### A DISCOURSE ON PRAYER ###

...another place.

<margin>74.</margin> I believe that when the demon touches that aforementioned place <note>Evagrius often associates the "place of the mind" with the physical brain or a spiritual center where thoughts are formed.</note>, he twists the light around the mind <note>original: "nous" — the spiritual intellect.</note> however he wishes. In this way, the passion of vainglory is stirred into a thought, shaping the mind foolishly toward a mere guess of divine and essential knowledge. When such a person is not troubled by fleshly and impure passions, but appears to stand in a state of purity, they imagine that no contrary influence is working within them. Thus, they suspect that the vision occurring within is a divine manifestation—even though it is produced by a demon who uses great cunning to alter the light joined to the brain, shaping the mind as we said before.

<margin>75.</margin> When the Angel of God stands by us, with a word alone he stops all contrary energy from acting upon us and moves the light of the mind to act without error.

<margin>76.</margin> Regarding the statement in the Revelation <note>referring to Revelation 8:3-4</note> that the Angel brings incense to offer with the prayers of the Saints: I believe this is the grace which is worked through the Angel. For he imparts knowledge of true prayer, so that the mind may thereafter stand firm, free from all agitation, listlessness <note>original: "akēdias" — a state of spiritual boredom or exhaustion often called the "noonday demon."</note>, and neglect.

<margin>77.</margin> The bowls of incense are said to be the prayers of the Saints, which the twenty-four elders offered up. The "bowl" should be understood as friendship with God, or rather, perfect and spiritual love, in which prayer is enacted in spirit and in truth.

<margin>78.</margin> Whenever you think you have no need of tears for your sins during prayer, consider how far you have wandered from God—when you ought to be always in Him—and you will weep more fervently.

<margin>79.</margin> Indeed, if you recognize your true measure, you will mourn gladly, calling yourself wretched as Isaiah did: how is it that, being unclean and living in the midst of such a people—that is, among adversaries—you dare to stand before the Lord of Sabaoth <note>original: "Kyriō sabaōth" — the Lord of Hosts.</note>.

<margin>80.</margin> If you truly pray, you will find great certainty; and Angels will attend you as they did Daniel, and they will illuminate you regarding the meaning of the things that happen.

<margin>81.</margin> Know that the holy Angels encourage us toward prayer and stand beside us, rejoicing and praying

<column-break/>

on our behalf. Therefore, if we are negligent and accept contrary thoughts <note>original: "logismous" — intrusive or tempting thoughts.</note>, we provoke them greatly; for while they struggle so hard for us, we do not even wish to supplicate God for our own sakes. Instead, we treat our own ministry with contempt, and leaving behind their Master and God, we consort with impure demons.

<margin>82.</margin> Pray gently and calmly, and sing psalms with understanding and rhythm, and you shall be like an eaglet soaring in the heights.

<margin>83.</margin> Psalmody calms the passions and causes the lack of self-control in the body to grow still; prayer, however, prepares the mind to exercise its own proper activity.

<margin>84.</margin> Prayer is the activity that befits the dignity of the mind; or rather, it is the mind's best and purest use.

<margin>85.</margin> Psalmody belongs to "manifold wisdom" <note>referring to the various moral and natural lessons found in the Psalms.</note>; prayer, however, is the prelude to immaterial and manifold knowledge.

<margin>86.</margin> Knowledge is a most beautiful thing, for it is a co-worker with prayer, awakening the intellectual power of the mind for the contemplation of divine knowledge.

<margin>87.</margin> If you have not yet received the gift of prayer or psalmody, persevere, and you shall receive it.

<margin>88.</margin> "And He spoke a parable to them, that they must always pray and not lose heart" <note>Luke 18:1</note>. Therefore, do not lose heart for the time being, nor be discouraged because you have not received; for you shall receive later. And He added to the parable: "Even if I do not fear God and have no regard for man, yet because this woman bothers me, I will give her justice." So shall God also bring about the vindication of those who cry out to Him day and night, speedily. Be of good cheer, then, persisting with labor in holy prayer.

<margin>89.</margin> Do not wish for your affairs to turn out as they seem best to you, but as it pleases God; then you will be untroubled and thankful in your prayer.

<margin>90.</margin> Even if you think you are with God, guard yourself against the demon of sexual immorality. For he is very deceptive and most envious; he desires to be swifter than the movement and sobriety of your mind, so as to tear it away from God even while it stands before Him with reverence and fear.

<margin>91.</margin> If you care for prayer, prepare yourself for the attacks of demons, and endure their...

...endure the lashes. For like wild beasts they <note>original: "the demons"</note> will come upon you, and they will harm your whole body.

<margin>82.</margin> Prepare yourself like an experienced athlete, so that even if you suddenly see a vision, you are not shaken; even if you see a sword drawn against you, or a torch rushing across your eyes, do not be troubled; even if you see a hideous and bloody form, do not let your soul lose heart. But stand firm, making the "good confession," and you will look upon your enemies with greater ease.

<margin>83.</margin> He who endures painful things will also attain joyful things. By persisting through the unpleasant, he will not fail to share in the pleasant.

<margin>84.</margin> See to it that the evil demons do not deceive you with some kind of vision; instead, be mindful, turning to prayer and calling upon God. If the thought is from Him, He will enlighten you; but if not, He will quickly drive the deceiver away from you. Be bold, for these "dogs" will not stay if you employ fervent intercession toward God. For immediately, by God’s power, they will be lashed invisibly and driven far away.

<margin>85.</margin> It is right that you should not be ignorant of this trick: at times the demons divide themselves. If you seem to seek help against some, the others will enter in the guise of angels to drive away the first ones—this is done so that you may be deceived into thinking they are truly angels.

<margin>86.</margin> Take great care to have humility and courage, and no demonic assault will touch your soul; "no plague shall come near your dwelling," for He will command His angels concerning you to guard you. And they will invisibly drive away all opposing energy from you.

<margin>87.</margin> He who cares for pure prayer will hear noises, thuds, voices, and insults from demons; but he will not collapse, nor will he betray his reasoning. He shall say to God: 

> I will fear no evil, for You are with me;

and other such words.

<margin>88.</margin> In the time of such temptations, use a short and intense prayer.

<margin>89.</margin> If the demons threaten to appear suddenly from the air to terrify you and snatch away your mind, do not be frightened of them; do not care for their threat at all. For they terrify you as a way of testing

<column-break/>

you, to see if you pay attention to them, or if you have completely despised them.

<margin>100.</margin> If you stand before God the Almighty, the Creator and Provider of all, during prayer, why do you stand before Him so irrationally that you ignore His unsurpassable fear, yet are frightened by gnats and beetles? Or have you not heard the one who says: 

> You shall fear the Lord your God;

and again: 

> Before whose power all things shudder and tremble; 

and so on.

<margin>101.</margin> Just as bread is food for the body and virtue for the soul, so spiritual prayer is food for the mind.

<margin>102.</margin> Do not pray like the Pharisee, but like the Publican in the holy place of prayer, so that you too may be justified by the Lord. <note>Refers to the parable in Luke 18:9-14 regarding pride versus humility in prayer.</note>

<margin>103.</margin> Struggle not to pray against anyone in your prayer, so that you do not tear down what you are building, making your prayer an abomination.

<margin>104.</margin> Let the debtor of ten thousand talents <note>A reference to the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant in Matthew 18.</note> teach you: if you do not forgive your debtor, you will not obtain forgiveness yourself. For it says He delivered him to the torturers.

<margin>105.</margin> Set aside the needs of the body while standing at prayer, so that you are not distracted by the sting of a flea, a louse, a gnat, or a fly, and thus lose the greatest gain of your prayer.

<margin>106.</margin> It has come down to us that while one of the saints was praying, the evil one resisted him so much that as soon as the saint stretched out his hands, the demon transformed into a lion, raised his front paws, and drove his claws into both thighs of the athlete <note>original: "agonistou" — a common term for a monk as a spiritual contestant or athlete of God.</note>; yet the demon did not leave until the saint lowered his hands. But the man never lowered them until he had finished his usual prayers.

<margin>107.</margin> We also know of such a thing regarding John the Short <note>Saint John the Dwarf, a famous 4th-century Desert Father.</note> who lived in a pit; or rather, a very great Monk; who remained unmoved from his communion with God even when a demon in the form of a dragon coiled around him, chewing his flesh and vomiting on his face.

<margin>108.</margin> You have surely read the lives of the Tabennisiot Monks <note>Monks from the monastery founded by St. Pachomius at Tabennisi in Egypt.</note>, which say that while Abba Theodore was speaking a word to the brothers, two vipers came under his feet; but he, undisturbed, making his feet like an arch, kept them underneath until...
