### A DISCOURSE ON PRAYER ###

...He finished speaking these words; and then he showed these things to the brothers, explaining the matter.

<margin>109.</margin> We read again about another spiritual brother that while he was praying, a viper <note>original: "echidna"</note> came and fastened itself to his foot. Yet he did not lower his hands until he had finished his customary prayer; and he suffered no harm, for he loved God more than himself.

<margin>110.</margin> Keep your eye steady and undistracted during your prayer; and having denied your flesh and your soul, live according to the mind <note>The Greek "nous" refers to the highest faculty of the human soul, the "eye of the heart" that seeks direct communion with God.</note>.

<margin>111.</margin> Once, while another holy man was praying intensely, living in stillness in the desert, demons stood over him and for two weeks tossed him about like a ball and threw him into the air, catching him in his rush mat; yet they were not able at all to drag his mind down from its fiery prayer.

<margin>112.</margin> To another God-loving man who was practicing the mindfulness of prayer while walking in the desert, two angels appeared and walked on either side of him; but he paid them no attention at all, so that he might not lose the "greater thing" <note>meaning God Himself</note>; for he remembered the Apostolic word saying: *neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers, shall be able to separate us from the love of Christ.* <note>A reference to Romans 8:38-39.</note>

<margin>113.</margin> A Monk becomes equal to the angels through prayer, longing to see the face of the Father who is in heaven.

<margin>114.</margin> Do not seek at all to perceive any form or shape during the time of prayer.

<margin>115.</margin> Do not desire to see angels, or powers, or Christ through your physical senses, lest you become completely deranged by receiving a wolf instead of a shepherd and bowing down to your demonic enemies.

<margin>116.</margin> The beginning of the mind’s wandering is vanity; moved by this, the mind attempts to describe the Divine in shapes and forms.

<margin>117.</margin> I will say what is mine, which I have also said to the younger ones: blessed is the mind which, at the time of prayer, has attained complete formlessness.

<margin>118.</margin> Blessed is the mind which, praying without distraction, always experiences an even greater longing for God.

<margin>119.</margin> Blessed is the mind which, at the time of prayer, becomes immaterial and free from all possessions.

<margin>120.</margin> Blessed is the mind which, at the time of prayer, has attained complete "insensibility" <note>original: "anaisthesia" — here meaning a holy detachment from physical sensations and the material world.</note>.

<margin>121.</margin> Blessed is the Monk who considers all men 

<column-break/>

as God, after God.

<margin>122.</margin> Blessed is the Monk who looks upon the salvation and progress of everyone as his own, with all joy.

<margin>123.</margin> Blessed is the Monk who considers himself the "offscouring" <note>original: "peripsēma" — meaning the lowest of the low or the dust under everyone's feet.</note> of all.

<margin>124.</margin> A Monk is one who is separated from all and yet harmoniously joined to all.

<margin>125.</margin> A Monk is one who considers himself one with everyone, because he seems to see himself constantly in every person.

<margin>126.</margin> He truly fulfills his prayer who always offers all his foresight and care as fruit to God.

<margin>127.</margin> Avoid every lie and every oath as a Monk who desires to pray; otherwise, you merely wear a mask that does not fit you.

<margin>128.</margin> If you wish to pray in the spirit, draw nothing from the flesh; then you will not have a cloud casting a shadow over you during the time of prayer.

<margin>129.</margin> Entrust the needs of your body to God, and it will be clear that you also trust Him with the needs of your spirit.

<margin>130.</margin> If you attain the promises, you shall reign; therefore, looking toward these, you will gladly endure your present poverty.

<margin>131.</margin> Do not refuse poverty and affliction, for they are the fuel of unburdened prayer.

<margin>132.</margin> Let your bodily virtues serve the virtues of the soul; and let those of the soul serve the spiritual virtues; and let these, in turn, serve the immaterial and essential knowledge.

<margin>133.</margin> While praying against a thought, observe if it ceases easily; see where this comes from, lest you be caught in an ambush and, being deceived, surrender yourself.

<margin>134.</margin> There are times when the demons suggest thoughts to you and then provoke you, as it were, to pray against them or to argue with them—and then they retreat of their own accord. This is so that you may be deceived into thinking of yourself as one who has begun to conquer thoughts and terrify demons.

<margin>135.</margin> If you are praying against a passion or a demon that is troubling you, remember the one who said:

You shall say these things at the proper time, arming yourself with humility against your opponents.

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NILUS THE ASCETIC ###

...sin in a disciplined way and blamelessly, according to the divine Apostle.

<margin>137.</margin> If you help someone, you will be harmed by another; so that in being wronged, you might say or do something improper and scatter poorly what you gathered well. For this is the goal of the evil demons. Therefore, one must pay attention wisely.

<margin>138.</margin> Expect the sudden attacks of demons, while concerning yourself with how to escape their slavery.

<margin>139.</margin> By night, the evil demons seek to disturb the spiritual teacher by themselves; but by day they do so through other people, surrounding him with difficult circumstances, slanders, and dangers.

<margin>140.</margin> Do not reject the fullers <term>original: knapheis; workers who clean and thicken cloth by trampling and beating it</term>. For even if they beat you while treading upon you, and stretch and scrape you, nevertheless your garment becomes bright through these very actions.

<margin>141.</margin> As long as you have not renounced the passions, but your mind <note>original: "nous"</note> opposes virtue and truth, you will not find the fragrant incense of prayer in your bosom.

<margin>142.</margin> Do you desire to pray? Having departed from the things of this world, have your citizenship in heaven <note>A reference to Philippians 3:20</note> at all times—not simply in bare words, but in angelic action and divine knowledge.

<margin>143.</margin> If you only remember the Judge when things go poorly, acknowledging that He is fearsome and impartial, you have not yet learned to serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in Him with trembling <note>A reference to Psalm 2:11</note>. For you should know that even during spiritual comforts and feasts, one must serve Him with even greater reverence and awe.

<margin>144.</margin> A discerning man is one who, until he has achieved perfect repentance, does not allow himself to be free from the sorrowful memory of his sins and the just punishment they would receive in the eternal fire.

<margin>145.</margin> He who is caught in sins and outbursts of anger, and yet dares shamelessly to reach for the knowledge of divine things or to intrude upon immaterial prayer, let him receive the apostolic penalty: for it is not without danger for him to pray with a bare and uncovered head. For such a soul, he says, ought to have "authority" over her head because of the angels who are present <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:5-10, interpreted here as the soul needing the "covering" of humility and shame</note>, being clothed in the shame and humility that is proper to her.

<column-break/>

<margin>146.</margin> Just as an intense gaze at the sun at high noon does not benefit a person with diseased eyes, so also the mental image of awesome and supernatural prayer in spirit and truth would not benefit a passionate and impure mind at all; on the contrary, it stirs the Divine to indignation against him.

<margin>147.</margin> If the One who is self-sufficient and impartial did not accept the person coming to the altar with a gift until he was reconciled with his neighbor who was grieved with him <note>A reference to Matthew 5:23-24</note>, consider how much guard and discernment is needed so that we may offer acceptable incense to God at the spiritual altar.

<margin>148.</margin> Do not be a lover of words, nor a lover of glory; otherwise, the "sinners" <note>referring to demons</note> will work not only on your back, but on your very face; and you will be a laughingstock to them at the time of prayer, being drawn away and enticed by them into strange thoughts.

<margin>149.</margin> Attention seeking prayer will find prayer; for prayer follows attention more than anything else, and it is this that we must strive for.

<margin>150.</margin> Just as sight is the best of all the senses, so prayer is more divine than all the virtues.

<margin>151.</margin> The praise of prayer is not simply its quantity, but its quality. This is shown by the men who went up to the temple <note>The Pharisee and the Publican in Luke 18</note>, and by the saying: *When you pray, do not babble...* <note>Matthew 6:7</note> and so forth.

<margin>152.</margin> As long as you pay attention to the proportions of the body, and your mind dwells on the pleasant things of the "tent" <note>original: "skēnē," a common metaphor for the physical body</note>, you have not yet seen the place of prayer; rather, the blessed path to it is still far from you.

<margin>153.</margin> When you stand at prayer and rise above every other joy, then you have truly found prayer.

While the previous page (110) concluded a series of 143 numbered aphorisms on prayer and spiritual struggle, this page shifts to a formal prose treatise comparing true Christian philosophy with the flawed practices of pagan Greeks and certain Jewish sects. ->ASCETIC DISCOURSE.<-

### BY THE SAME
### HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER OF OURS
# NILUS THE ASCETIC
### AN ASCETIC DISCOURSE, MOST NECESSARY AND VERY PROFITABLE

Many among the Greeks <note>In this context, "Greeks" refers to the pagan philosophers of antiquity.</note> attempted to philosophize, and not a few among the Jews as well; but only the disciples of Christ have truly pursued the goal of authentic wisdom. This is because they alone possessed Wisdom itself as their teacher, demonstrating through their deeds the lifestyle that is proper to such a pursuit. For the former groups were like actors performing a drama on a stage, adorning themselves with a mask that did not belong to them; they took on an empty name while remaining destitute of true Philosophy. They showed off their "philosophy" through the rough cloak <term>original: tribon; a simple, coarse garment worn by philosophers to show their disdain for luxury</term>, the long beard, and the staff. Yet, they pampered their bodies and served their desires as if they were mistresses. They were slaves to the belly, accepting the pleasures of the gut as a work of nature. They were obedient to anger and fluttered with excitement for worldly glory. They leapt greedily at lavish tables like little dogs. They did not realize that, above all else, a philosopher must be free; one must flee from being a slave to the passions even more than one would flee from being a slave bought with silver or born into a household. For being a slave to men perhaps does nothing to harm one who has lived uprightly, but to serve pleasures while being mastered by the passions brings only shame and much laughter. Among them are those who have entirely neglected practical virtue, thinking instead that they have taken up "logical philosophy." These are mere "sky-talkers" <note>original: "meteo-roleschai"; those who babble about the heavens or lofty things without practical grounding</note> and explainers of things that cannot be proven. They claim to know the size of the heaven, the measurements of the sun, and the powers of the stars—sometimes they even attempt to speak of God! In these matters, truth is unattainable and guesswork is dangerous. Yet they live more dishonorably than pigs wallowing in the mire.

<margin>* But if.</margin>
* There are also some who became "practical" philosophers <note>Meaning those who practiced asceticism or self-discipline.</note>, but they became even worse than the others, for they sold their labors for the sake of reputation and praise. For the most part, these wretches practiced their discipline for no other reason than for 

<column-break/>

show and the love of glory; they exchanged their great hardships for something cheap and worthless. For to remain silent at all times, to feed on grass, to cover the body with hair rags, and to live shut up in a large jar <note>original: "pithos"; a reference to the Cynic philosopher Diogenes, who famously lived in a storage jar to show his rejection of society</note> while expecting no reward after death, is the very height of folly. It is to let the prizes of virtue vanish along with this life, setting up a struggle for oneself that has no season for crowning—a constant wrestling match deprived of trophies, and a racing pit that offers nothing more than sweat.

As for those among the Jews who honored this way of life, they are the descendants of Jonadab <note>Referencing the Rechabites mentioned in Jeremiah 35, known for their ascetic refusal to drink wine or live in houses.</note>. They lead all those who wish to live in the same way into this specific way of life: they live in tents at all times, abstaining from wine and everything that leads to a luxurious lifestyle. Their diet is cheap, and they keep the needs of the body measured. While they care greatly for their moral habits, they largely wait for contemplation <note>original: "theoria"</note>. Indeed, this is why they are called Essenes <note>A Jewish sect known for communal living and asceticism.</note>, as that is what the name signifies. Simply put, they succeed in the goal of philosophy, as their actions do not conflict with their profession. But what is the use of their struggles and their laborious discipline when they have rejected the Judge of the Games, Christ? <term>original: Agonothetes; the official who presided over the games and distributed prizes</term> For the reward of their labors has likewise vanished for them, since they denied the Giver of prizes and the Author of true life. For this reason, they have fallen away from true philosophy. For Philosophy is the establishment of character combined with true knowledge of 
<margin>the Being</margin>
* Reality <note>original: "ontos"; that which truly exists</note>. Both groups have fallen away from this—the Jews and the Greeks alike—having rejected the Wisdom that came down from heaven. And apart from...

<summary>St. Nilus contrasts the "true philosophy" of Christian disciples with the hypocrisy of pagan philosophers and the Christ-rejecting asceticism of the Essenes and Rechabites. He defines true philosophy as a combination of moral discipline and the correct knowledge of God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues St. Nilus the Ascetic’s "Ascetic Discourse." Having previously criticized the pagan philosophers for their hypocrisy, Nilus now contrasts them with the true "philosophy" established by Jesus Christ and the Apostles, before lamenting how the monks of his own day have fallen away from this high standard.</meta>

->OF OUR HOLY FATHER NILUS THE ASCETIC<-

...without Christ, those who attempted to philosophize failed, for He was the only one who demonstrated the true philosophy <note>In early Christian writing, "philosophy" refers not just to logic or ethics, but to the entire way of life dedicated to God, particularly the ascetic or monastic life.</note> through both His deeds and His words. For He was the first to cut the path of this life by His own conduct, showing a way of living that was pure. He constantly raised the soul above the passions of the body, and finally, He even showed contempt for the soul itself when the salvation of humanity—which He was managing—required His death. Through these actions, He taught that whoever chooses to philosophize correctly must deny all the pleasures of life, master both labors and passions well, and despise the body. Such a person should not even hold their own life as precious, but must be ready to give it up eagerly whenever it is necessary to lay it down for the sake of virtue.

The holy Apostles received this way of life and imitated it. As soon as they were called, they renounced the world and looked down upon their homelands, their families, and their possessions. They immediately transferred themselves to a hard and laborious life, passing through every difficulty: being afflicted, ill-treated, driven out, going naked, and lacking even basic necessities. Eventually, they even dared to face death, perfectly imitating the Teacher in all things and leaving behind an image of the best way of life.

But while Christians were obligated to model their own lives after this image, they either lacked the will or the strength for such imitation. Only a few were able to peer above the worldly disturbances and flee the storm-tossed life of the cities. Thus, getting outside the noise, they embraced the **monastic life**, making it a "wax mold" of Apostolic virtue. They preferred **poverty** <term>original: aktemosyne; the voluntary lack of possessions</term> over owning things for the sake of remaining undistracted. They chose simple, improvised food over seasoned delicacies to avoid the uprisings of the passions, fulfilling the body's needs with whatever food was at hand. They disregarded soft clothing and anything beyond what was necessary as the invention of human luxury, using a simple and unelaborated robe for the body's needs. They considered it unphilosophical to be preoccupied with things on the ground (which are provided spontaneously to the beasts) while they were supposed to be caring for heavenly things. They did not know the world, for they had moved beyond human passions. There was no one among them who was greedy or defrauded, no one who was a judge or was being

<column-break/>

judged. For each one had an unbribable judge: his own conscience. One man did not grow rich while another lived in poverty; nor did one waste away from hunger while another burst with satiety. Instead, the generosity of those who had an excess filled the needs of those who lacked. There was equality and "equal law" <note>Nilus uses the term *isonomia*, an ancient Greek political concept of equal rights, applying it here to the economic equality of early Christian communities.</note> because of the voluntary blending of those in higher positions with the lowlier, and thus inequality was cast out. 

Or rather, it was not even "equality" then; for even then a certain inequality was produced by the zeal of those striving to be *more* humble—just as today, inequality is produced by the madness of those fighting to be *more* glorified. Envy was cast out; jealousy was exiled; vanity was banished; pride was destroyed. All causes of civil strife were dissolved. Regarding the coarser passions, they were like dead men, totally insensitive. They did not even experience fantasies of such things in their dreams because they had turned away from the memory of them so thoroughly from the start. Through daily ascetic practice and persistence, they had ascended to such a state. 

To put it simply, they were lamps shining in the darkness, fixed stars illuminating the lightless night of this life, and harbor breakwaters that were themselves never touched by the storm. They proved to all that it is easy to escape the attacks of the passions unharmed.

But that exact way of life and that "citizenship in the heavens" <note>A reference to Philippians 3:20.</note>—like a painted image that is diminished little by little by the negligence of those who copy it over time—has reached the extreme of dissimilarity and has entirely abandoned the archetype. For we, who were supposed to be crucified to the world, who renounced this life, and denied our [merely] human status to strive for the nature of the **Bodiless Ones** <note>The "Bodiless Ones" (*Asomatoi*) is a standard term for the Angels.</note> through a similar state of **passionlessness** <term>original: apatheia; not a lack of feeling, but a state of being undisturbed by sinful desires</term>, have instead retreated backward. We cloud the precision of those who lived well with worldly business and shameful gains. We cause those who could have been glorified for the virtue of the wise to be blasphemed because of our own inattention. We hold the handle of the plow, keeping a solemn appearance, yet we are not fit for the Kingdom of Heaven because we have turned back <note>A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note> and forgotten our obligations, holding on to worldly things with much zeal. No longer is the cheap and improvised life sought among us, nor is quiet considered useful for being freed from the passions...

<summary>St. Nilus describes the "true philosophy" of Christ and the Apostles, characterized by renunciation and equality, but laments that contemporary monks have lost this original purity and returned to worldly concerns.</summary>
<keywords>Christian Philosophy, Apostolic Life, Monasticism, Poverty (Aktemosyne), Passionlessness (Apatheia), Equality, Spiritual Decline, St. Nilus the Ascetic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues St. Nilus the Ascetic’s "Ascetic Discourse." # ASCETIC DISCOURSE

...of the ancient defilements. Instead, a throng of worldly affairs, which brings only useless worry regarding our true goal, is now held in high esteem; and ambition for material wealth has conquered the saving exhortations of the Lord. For while the Lord turns us away from all earthly care and commands us to seek only the **Kingdom of Heaven**, we—as if eager to walk the opposite path—have ignored the Master’s commands. Having abandoned His divine care, we have placed our hopes in our own hands. For though He said: 
> Look at the birds of the heaven, that they do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. 

And again: 
> Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they do not toil, nor do they spin. 

Furthermore, He even forbade carrying a travel bag, a money belt, or a staff, commanding us to follow only His most truthful promise—the same promise He gave to the **Apostles** when He sent them out for the benefit of the rest of humanity, saying: 
> The laborer is worthy of his food. 
<note>Matthew 10:10. Nilus argues that God’s providence is more reliable than human effort.</note>
He knew that His providence was a more certain way to provide for our necessities than our own busy-ness. 

We, however, do not refuse to acquire as much land as we can. We buy flocks of sheep and plowing oxen—enviable in their form and size—and well-fed donkeys. We do this so that the sheep may provide wool in abundance for our needs, while the oxen, serving the requirements of agriculture, may provide food for us and fodder for themselves and the other animals. Meanwhile, the beasts of burden, carrying loads and bringing in imports from foreign lands to make up for what our own land lacks, supply our necessary food and increase our life of luxury. Not only this, but we also choose the most profitable of trades—those that leave absolutely no time for the remembrance of God, drawing all our leisure to themselves. We have, it seems, judged the weakness of our Caretaker, or perhaps our own previous profession <note>The "profession" (homologia) refers to the monastic vows or the baptismal promise to renounce the world.</note>. For even if we do not admit this in words, we are exposed by our actions. We rejoice in the conduct of worldly life when we practice the same things as worldlings; and perhaps we are even more worn down by bodily labors. As a result, the many now consider **piety** <note>original: "εὐσέβεια" (eusebeia), meaning religious devotion or godliness.</note> to be a means of profit. And for no 

<column-break/>

other reason is the formerly tranquil and blessed life pursued, than that through this feigned godliness we might flee from burdensome public duties. Having secured a license for enjoyment, we may then extend our impulses without restraint toward whatever we please. With great shamelessness, we behave boastfully toward simpler folk—and sometimes even toward those in high positions—as if we thought the virtuous life was a pretext for tyranny, rather than for humility and gentleness. Because of this, even by those 
<margin>belonging to a household</margin>
who ought to revere us, we are viewed as *household* servants; and we are mingled among the common throngs and the rabble of the marketplaces. We possess nothing distinctive from the rest of mankind, as we should; we wish to be recognized not by our way of life, but by our clothing. Avoiding the labors required for virtue, we madly crave the glory that follows them, making a mere stage-play out of what was once the truth. 

Today, someone who has taken up this venerable habit <note>The "habit" (schema) is the distinctive clothing of a monk.</note>, though he has not yet washed away the stains of his soul, nor erased the engraved patterns of old sins from his mind—but is perhaps still behaving lewdly in his imagination—and has not yet trained his character to suit his profession, nor even knows what the goal of **philosophy** <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to the ascetic or monastic life lived according to God's will.</note> according to God actually is, has already fashioned a **Pharisaic brow** <note>A "Pharisaic brow" (Pharisaïkēn ophryn) indicates a haughty, arrogant expression of religious superiority.</note>, thinking highly of himself because of his clothing. He goes about carrying the tools of a craft he has never learned. He professes a knowledge by his outward appearance that he has not even tasted with the tips of his lips. He is a reef instead of a harbor; a **whitewashed tomb** instead of a temple; and a wolf instead of a sheep, found in his outward appearance only for the destruction of those who are enticed by him. 

For when such men run away from the **monasteries** because they cannot endure the strictness of that life, they go revelling through the cities. Then, being brought low by the needs of their bellies, they carry around the form of piety like a bait to deceive the many. They endure doing anything that the needs of the body force upon them—for nothing is more compelling than natural necessity, which devises clever ways for those in want, especially when laziness is also present. These men, therefore, studiously attend to the doors of the rich, moving about even more craftily than **parasites**...

Here, he describes the scandalous behavior of materialistic monks who wander cities, behaving like gluttons and hypocrites, thereby bringing the monastic calling into disrepute and leading laypeople into the sin of greed.</meta>

# BY OUR HOLY FATHER NILUS THE ASCETIC

...not less [than the animals]. In the marketplaces, they run alongside people just like **slaves**, shoving aside those nearby. By pushing everyone out of the way, they scramble to make their own passage easy—and they do all this for the sake of a table, having never learned to restrain their appetite for gluttonous foods. Nor were they willing to follow **Moses** and carry "a digging-peg upon their belt for their necessity"; <note>Original: *passalon* (peg/trowel). This refers to Deuteronomy 23:13. Nilus uses this Mosaic hygiene law as a metaphor for spiritual self-discipline and "cleaning up" one's physical desires.</note> for had they possessed this understanding, they would have known that the limit of every culinary pleasure is hunger. Even the most ordinary things, when they satisfy the body’s lack, cover up the indecencies of untimely desire.

Because of this, the **Name of God is blasphemed**, and the once-renowned life has become an abomination. The lifestyle of those who truly live according to virtue is now considered a fraud. The cities are burdened by those who wander about aimlessly, and those in their homes are harassed. People feel sickened at the very sight of them, seeing them begging shamelessly and lingering at their doors. 

Many, having been welcomed into homes and pretending to be pious for a short while—hiding their villainous reputation behind a mask of hypocrisy—later robbed their hosts and fled, ensuring that this ill-repute spread across the whole of monastic life. Consequently, these men are driven out of cities like pests, though they were once meant to be instructors of self-control. They are hunted like the accursed, no less than those afflicted with **leprosy**. 

One would rather trust thieves and housebreakers than those who pursue the **monastic life**; for it is easier to guard against obvious villainy than against a manufactured "reliability" that lies in ambush. People reckon that these men have neither begun a life of godliness nor known the profit of **stillness** <note>Original: *hesychia* (quietness/stillness), the core goal of Eastern monasticism.</note>. Perhaps some, being recognized as needy, were forced into the monk’s life without proper judgment, viewing the vocation as a business venture to provide for their basic needs. I think they might have pursued this more honorably if they did not approach everyone’s doors, but instead used their [monastic] habit as a cloak for more substantial profits, pretending 

<margin>* [corrupt text] ...babbling ...delicate living ...softness/unsteadiness.</margin> 

they wanted to pay the necessary "tax" to their bodies. It is unclear whether this innovation of *luxury* came from the immeasurable desires of those who live in *delicacy*; and it is difficult to heal those who are incurably sick. For how could anyone explain the usefulness of health to those who have never

<column-break/>

<margin>* Phthisis: the name of a disease arising from the blood.</margin> 

experienced it, but have instead been raised from their very swaddling clothes with a *wasting disease*? They consider this natural misfortune to be a habit, thinking it does not clash with a healthy state of being. 

For every word of correction is superfluous when the listener’s zeal has leaned toward the worse and is set in opposition to the words of counsel. This is especially true when the hope of profit feeds their desire; the passion completely blocks their hearing to any advice, so that no warnings intended for self-control can find a way in, since the mind is turned toward a longing for profit—even if that profit is shameful. 

But we, **beloved**, who think we have renounced the world out of a longing for **virtue**, and have denied worldly desires and promised to follow **Christ**, why are we again entangled in the distractions of life? Why do we poorly rebuild what we previously tore down so well? Why do we enjoy the ill-counsel of those who do not pursue this vocation as they should, re-igniting the cravings of the weaker ones through our zeal for vain things? We have become a "path to greed" for the more innocent. 

For we have been commanded by the **Lord** to heal, not irritate, those who are prone to slipping, and to put their benefit before our own pleasure. We must not, by following our own uncritical impulses, cause many of the simpler folk to stumble, becoming for them a cause for worldly ambition. Why do we place so much value on **matter**, which we were taught to despise—clinging to money and possessions, and dividing our minds with many useless worries? Zeal for these things causes us to neglect the best and most necessary spiritual attendance, and to ignore the beauties of the soul. It leads those who gape at worldly things into a great pit; they think the height of good fortune is the enjoyment of **wealth**. They see those who profess to be "philosophers" <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to the monastic life, the "true philosophy" of seeking God.</note> and who boast of being above pleasures, yet who are more zealous for these things than they themselves are. 

Nothing leads so inevitably to punishment as making many people imitators of one’s own evils. For the destruction of those who imitate us becomes an added penalty for the teacher—and it is no small condemnation for those who did not reject such a shameful imitation.

<summary>Nilus denounces hypocritical monks whose greed and gluttony bring shame to the monastic life and lead laypeople into materialism. He argues that by seeking wealth and luxury, these monks act as "teachers of evil" and incur a double penalty for their bad example.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Nilus’s critique of monks who have abandoned their vows. Having previously described their gluttony and public misconduct, he now argues that the pursuit of private property is the root cause of their spiritual decline and public shame.</meta>

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE

...that they have become teachers of evils. Those who have used wise reasoning have fled from such learning, judging it to be shameful. Therefore, let no one be resentful toward these words; either correct the things being done wrongly through the indifference of the many—which result in the shaming of the **Name**—or else renounce the name itself. For if the goal is to live the **philosophical life**, <note>Original: *philosophia*. In early Christian texts, "philosophy" refers to the ascetic or monastic life of seeking divine wisdom.</note> then possessions are superfluous. Philosophy promises a detachment even from the body itself for the sake of the soul’s purity. But if acquiring things is the great ambition for some, along with enjoying the pleasures of this life, why do they honor "philosophy" with their words while in their deeds they have chosen a total separation from it? They perform actions completely alien to their profession, yet drape themselves in solemn titles. 

Is it not then shameful when we are mocked by those of lower status—whom we call "worldly" people—for violating the laws of the **Savior**? We end up being lectured on the very commandments we have ignored by the people who were supposed to be learning from us! For when we are fighting, they say to us: "A servant of the Lord must not fight, but be kind to everyone." <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:24.</note> And again, when monks quarrel over money or property, the laypeople say: "If someone takes your tunic, let him have your cloak as well." <note>A reference to Matthew 5:40.</note> What else are they doing but mocking and ridiculing us for the contradiction between our profession and our deeds? 

Is it not inevitable that those who claim property must fight, and do everything that the care of such things requires? If someone moves the boundary marker of a vineyard and adds it to their own land; or if someone’s livestock wanders in; or if another person diverts the water flowing to a garden—is it not then "necessary" to become enraged? One becomes worse than a madman, dealing out vengeance for all these things, and remains nailed to the law courts. The mind, which ought to be occupied with the **contemplation of reality**, must instead transform its contemplative power into worldly cunning, so that our abundance of useless things might prosper. Why do we claim these foreign things as our own, forging heavy shackles of matter for ourselves? We do not listen to the one who mourns such people: "Woe to him," says the prophet, "who gathers for himself what is not his, and loads himself down with a heavy collar." <note>A reference to Habakkuk 2:6.</note> For if those who pursue us are light, as the scripture says: "Those who pursued you were swifter 

<column-break/>

than the eagles of the sky," <note>A reference to Lamentations 4:19.</note> and we weigh ourselves down with worldly affairs, then clearly, moving more slowly in the race, we will be easily overtaken by our enemies. **Paul** taught us to flee from these enemies when he said: "Flee from greed." Even those who are unburdened when running for the prize, if they are not carried along by intense strength, fall far behind, while the pursuing enemies perhaps have swifter feet.

An attachment to worldly things is a great obstacle to those hurrying toward **virtue**; it often brings destruction to both soul and body. For what else destroyed **Naboth the Israelite**? Was it not an enviable vineyard that caused his death, stirring up his neighbor **Ahab** to envy against him? <note>Naboth was executed after refusing to sell his ancestral vineyard to King Ahab (1 Kings 21).</note> And what caused the two and a half tribes to remain outside the **Promised Land**, if not their multitude of livestock? <note>The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled east of the Jordan because the land was good for grazing (Numbers 32).</note> And what separated **Lot** from **Abraham**, if not the abundance of their flocks, which stirred up constant strife among their shepherds? In the end, it tore them away from each other completely. 

If, therefore, possessions provoke the envious to malice against those who have them, and shut out the owners from more serious pursuits, and cut through family ties, and turn friends into enemies—and if they have nothing in common with the future life and serve no great purpose for the life in the body—why do we abandon the service of **God** to become entirely devoted to vanity? For are we the ones who provide the necessities of our own lives? It is God who manages this. Human effort, if it does not meet with God’s help, inevitably misses its mark; but God’s management provides perfect goods even without human cooperation. 

What did their own effort profit those to whom God said: "You sowed much, but brought in little... and I blew it away from your hands"? <note>A reference to Haggai 1:6-9.</note> And what of the necessities of life was ever lacking for those who lived according to virtue, even though they took no thought for such things? Did not **Israel** feed itself for forty years in the desert, enjoying nothing from agriculture? They did not lack food; rather, the sea produced a miraculous nourishment, belching up the quail-mother, and the heaven brought down **Manna**, a strange and foreign rain. The rock, which had no moisture, split open and provided an abundant stream. Their clothes and shoes... <note>Nilus is concluding with the miracle of the Israelites' clothes not wearing out during the Exodus (Deuteronomy 29:5).</note>

<summary>Nilus argues that private property is the primary obstacle to the monastic life, leading to legal disputes, public mockery from laypeople, and spiritual ruin. He cites various Biblical figures to prove that wealth causes division, whereas God's providence sustains those who live virtuously without possessions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Nilus’s argument against monastic materialism. Having just mentioned the shame of monks being rebuked by laypeople for their greed, he now provides biblical examples of how God sustains those who prioritize the spirit over material provision.</meta>

## BY OUR HOLY FATHER NILUS THE ASCETIC

...served for all that time without wearing out. <note>Nilus refers here to the clothes and shoes of the Israelites in the desert, which according to Deuteronomy 29:5 did not wear out for forty years.</note> What kind of farming did Elijah do while he was being fed by the brook? Did not ravens bring him his food? When he went to Zarephath, did not a widow—who was herself lacking even the barest necessities—provide him with bread, snatching it from the very mouths of her own children? This was done to show that **virtue** is more precious even than natural instinct. These things are indeed miraculous, yet they are also consistent with reason; for it is possible for even one who does not eat to live, whenever God wills it. How else did Elijah complete a journey of forty days on the strength of a single meal? And how did Moses remain without a taste of human food for eighty days on the mountain while **philosophizing** with God? <note>Original: *prosphilosophon*. Again, Nilus uses "philosophy" to describe the intimate, ascetic communion between the soul and the Divine.</note> After forty days he came down, and being moved to anger by the making of the golden calf, he immediately smashed the tablets and ran back up the mountain. After spending another forty days there, he finally came down to the people carrying the second set of tablets. 

What human reasoning can present a logical explanation for such a miracle? How could the fluid nature of the body, being in constant motion, endure for so long when nothing was being added to replace the strength that evaporates day by day? The Divine Word solves this difficulty when it says: *“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”* Why then do we drag this **heavenly citizenship** down to earth by immersing ourselves in material miseries? Why do we "clothe ourselves in dung," we who were once "nursed in crimson"? <note>A reference to Lamentations 4:5. Nilus interprets "crimson" as high, fiery spiritual contemplations and "dung" as the mess of worldly business.</note> For when we rest upon bright and fiery thoughts, we are being nursed in crimson; but when we abandon such a state and become defiled by earthly affairs, we clothe ourselves in dung. Why do we withdraw our hope from God and support the "flesh of our arm," <note>A reference to Jeremiah 17:5, "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm."</note> attributing the Master's providence to our own hands? Job prayed that he might be counted as having committed a great sin if he had ever "put his hand to his mouth to kiss it" <note>Job 31:27. In the ancient world, kissing one's own hand was a gesture of self-adulation or pagan worship; Nilus applies it to those who take credit for their own prosperity.</note>; yet we do not fear doing this now. For it is the habit of the many to "kiss their hands," saying that they possess their wealth because of them. To these people, God speaks in riddles through the symbol of a name, saying: <margin>* In others: *the law*</margin> *“Whatever walks on its paws (hands) is unclean; and whatever walks on all fours continually is unclean.”* <note>A spiritual interpretation of the dietary laws in Leviticus 11:27.</note> He walks "on his hands" who

<column-break/>

leans upon his own works and places all his hope in them. He walks "on all fours" who trusts in sensory things and continually drags down the "ruling part" of his mind through preoccupation with them. He walks with "many feet" who is tightly gripped by bodily concerns. For this reason, the wise author of the Proverbs does not want the perfect man to have even two feet, but only one, and even then to move it only rarely toward bodily affairs, saying: *“Seldom set your foot in your neighbor’s house, lest he become weary of you and hate you.”* <note>Proverbs 25:17. Nilus interprets the "neighbor" or "friend" here as Christ.</note> For if one who only occasionally bothers Christ about the needs of the body—which is the goal of such "friends," as the Savior says to His disciples, *“You are my friends”*—if he does this too frequently, he becomes hateful. What then will happen to the man who is constantly occupied with these needs, and who is never raised up toward the **upright life**? 

Such a man remains low because he does not have "legs above his feet" to leap with them away from the earth. <note>Nilus refers to Leviticus 11:21, which permits eating leaping insects that have jointed legs above their feet to hop. He uses this as a metaphor for the soul's ability to "hop" back to God after attending to physical needs.</note> For just as legs, through their joints, first receive the whole weight of the body upon themselves, but when they approach the ground, they suddenly prepare the body to spring up into the air; so also the **reasoning mind**, which is capable of discerning the things of nature, after humbling itself to attend to the needs of the body, quickly sends its thoughts back up to the heights, lifting nothing of its "dusty" earthly concerns along with it. To have "straight legs" belongs to those who are not excessively indulgent or always lying on the ground, but it also belongs to the **holy powers** (the angels), because they have no need at all for bodily things nor do they require any leaning toward them. Signifying this, the great Ezekiel said that *“their legs were straight, and their feet were winged,”* <note>Ezekiel 1:7.</note> which reveals the unwavering nature of their will and the swiftness of that nature toward spiritual things. But for humans, it is enough to have "bending legs"—serving at one time the needs of the body, and at another time serving the upward-tending occupations of the soul. Because of the soul’s kinship with the powers above, it should spend most of its time soaring with them; but because of the body, it should spend only as much concern on the earth as necessity compels. To crawl continually in the pursuit of pleasures...

and finding her cleaning *wheat and nodding off, they slipped in unnoticed and killed Ish-bosheth, finding him asleep. For everything sleeps—the intellect, the soul, and the senses—whenever bodily concerns take control. For the doorkeeper cleaning wheat shows that the <term>discernment</term> <note>original: *dianoia*. In this context, it refers to the discursive or analytical part of the mind that acts as a gatekeeper.</note> has become busily preoccupied with bodily things; and not just in passing, but with a certain zeal, it pursues the "purity" of these material things. 

That the Scripture does not teach this merely as a historical event is clear from this: for how would a king have a woman as a doorkeeper, when he ought to be guarded by a multitude of soldiers and have all the pageantry of his rank around him? Or how was he so destitute as to have her cleaning wheat herself? Rather, the illogical is often mixed into the historical narrative for the sake of the truth of what is being signified. For the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: *nous*. The highest faculty of the human soul, meant for direct communion with God.</note> of each person, like a king, dwells within, having discernment as the doorkeeper of the senses. When this discernment hands itself over to bodily things—and cleaning wheat is a bodily thing—the plotters easily slip in unnoticed and put the intellect to death. For this reason, the great Abraham does not trust a woman to guard the door; for he knows how easily the senses are deceived, so that while the discernment is delighted by the sight of sensible things, it divides 

<column-break/>

the intellect, and persuades it to share in these delights with it, even if the sharing is clearly dangerous. Instead, Abraham himself sits by [the door], providing an open entrance for divine thoughts, but barring the door to worldly anxieties. For what do we gain for our life from this vain labor over such things? Is not "all labor," according to the <term>Preacher</term>, <note>original: *Ekklesiastes*. A reference to the book of Ecclesiastes 6:7.</note> "for one's mouth"? And food and covering are, according to the Apostle, enough for the support of this wretched flesh. Why then do we make our labors endless and "toil for the wind," as Solomon says? By our zeal for earthly things, we hinder the soul from the enjoyment of divine goods; and we attend to and cherish the flesh more than is right. We nourish it as an enemy and a foe from our own neighborhood, so that its battle is not only a matter of dispute, but it fights against the soul with such excessive strength that it lusts after honors and crowns. 

For what is the actual need of the body, that we should use it as an excuse to stretch our desire into an endless impasse? It is surely bread and water. Then, do not the springs provide their flow in abundance? And is not bread easily obtained by those who have hands? From such labors we are able to survive, by which the need of the body is fulfilled while the soul is distracted little or not at all. But does clothing provide much anxiety? Not even this, if we look only to the need and not to the vanity born of habit. For what spider-woven garments, what fine linen, or purple, or silk did the first man wear? Did not the Creator make him a garment from skins and command him to be nourished by the plants of the field? By setting these boundaries for the needs of the body and arranging things thus, He was restraining from afar the shame of man’s current way of life. 

And I do not say that He who feeds the birds of the heaven will not also surely nourish us now as we live piously; and He who clothed the lilies of the field with such glory will also clothe us. However, it is not yet possible to persuade those who are far removed from this faith. For who would not provide the necessities, along with supplications, to one who lives according to **virtue**? Once, a Prophet alone rebuked a king who had acted lawlessly, in the presence of his entire army. And when the rebuke stirred his anger, the king stretched out his hand against the prophet, but he could not seize him, nor was he able to pull his hand back to himself, for it had withered. It was a contest between virtue and royal power—and the victory belonged to virtue. The prophet did not fight, yet virtue routed the enemy; the contestant was still, and faith did the work. The king's own allies became the judges of the contest, and the hand remained frozen, witnessing the victory of virtue. They did these things because they judged it right to live for the soul alone, turning away from the body and the body's necessities. And their lack of need made them higher than everyone; for they preferred to leave the body and be released from life in the flesh rather than betray the dignity of virtue and, for the sake of a physical need, flatter one of the wealthy. We do not carefully study the conduct of the saints, whose virtue we supposedly set out to imitate. Naaman the commander of Syria came to Elisha, bringing many gifts with him. He did not even receive him into his sight, so that it would not be thought that he provided the healing for the sake of the gifts brought. These things are said not so that we might learn arrogance, but so that we do not flatter those who pursue the things we claim to despise, just for the sake of our needs. ...farming and trade? Is it such a great thing for God if we contribute our own effort, even if we grant that the care of farming is something fresh? Human diligence cuts the earth and casts down seeds; but God waters the seeds with successive rains, preparing the roots to stretch out into the tender depths <note>original: "lagosi". Literally "flanks" or "hollows" of the earth.</note> of the ground. He makes the sun rise to warm the earth, calling the plants upward with its heat. He sends forth gusts of wind, measured to the age of the growing crops—fanning the greening plain with soft breaths at the start, so that the sown crops are not scorched by being smoothed over by hot winds. Then, with steadier blasts of wind, He brings the milky grain within its husk to ripeness, providing a heat suitable for the threshing floor and favorable winds for the winnowing. 

If even one of these things fails, human labor is proven futile; and our diligence becomes idle when it is not sealed by the gifts of God. Often, though none of these things was lacking for the completion of the harvest, a heavy rain falling out of season—plentiful and sudden—has swept away the grain while it was still being threshed or after it had been piled up clean. Sometimes, even in the storehouse itself, the worm has destroyed it, snatching the ready table away from the very mouth, so to speak. Where then, and for what purpose, is our diligence useful, when God holds the rudders of affairs, bringing and carrying all things as He wills? 

But we will say that the body needs comfort in its weaknesses. Yet how much better is it to die than to do anything unbecoming of our profession? <note>In this context, "profession" refers to the monastic vow or the Christian calling.</note> Certainly, if God still wishes us to live, He either implants a balanced strength in the body so as to bear the pain of the illness, or He allows us to receive the crowns awarded for noble endurance; or He will devise a way to comfort the sufferer. For the spring of wisdom will never lack a device for comfort. It is good then, beloved—exceedingly good—to ascend to the ancient blessedness <note>The "ancient blessedness" refers to the state of humanity before the Fall, or the idealized life of the early desert monks.</note> and to take hold of the way of life of the ancients. For it will be easy for everyone, I believe, if they so desire. And even if some labor is involved, it will not be fruitless, for it possesses sufficient comfort: both the glory of those who have gone before us and the correction of those who follow. It will be no small gain...

<column-break/>

...for those who have begun such a way of life, and for those who later leave behind an image of the best conduct, which is the recovery of what was lost. Let us flee the ways of life in cities and villages, so that those in cities and villages may run toward us. Let us pursue the wilderness, so that we may draw to ourselves those who now flee from us—if this is at all dear to some. For indeed, it is written in praise of certain people that they left the cities and dwelt in the rocks, becoming like "fledgling doves." <note>A reference to Psalm 55:6-7 or Jeremiah 48:28, often used to describe those seeking monastic solitude.</note> 

And John the Baptist also lived in the wilderness, and all the cities came to him with their entire populations. Those clothed in silk garments hurried to the sight of his leather belt; those who had houses with golden roofs chose the hardship of the open air; and the rest upon the sand was preferred over reclining on beds inlaid with precious stones. All things were bearable to them, though they happened contrary to habit; for the desire to see the man cut short the perception of painful things, and the wonder at his virtue stole away the hardship of his rigorous discipline.

So much more precious is virtue than wealth, and a quiet life more illustrious than many riches. How many were wealthy at that time, priding themselves on their glory, yet they have been silenced; while the wonder of the man without worldly status is sung until now. The memory of the "citizen of the desert" <note>original: "erēmopolitou". A common title for famous ascetics who "colonized" the desert.</note> is cherished by all; for the fame of virtue is eternal, and it sends forth its renown as an Angel of its own inner beauty. 

Let us decline the breeding of cattle, so that we may take up the pastoral habit <note>This refers to spiritual leadership or the "shepherding" of souls rather than literal animals.</note>; let us leave behind shameful trade, so that we may acquire the "pearl of great price"; let us flee the farming of the earth, which brings up thorns and thistles, so that we may become workers and guardians of Paradise. Let us throw everything aside and choose the quiet life, so that we may put to shame those who now bring up the possession of property as a reproach against us. For nothing so shames those who attack us as a gentle correction regarding the things for which we are reproached; for a change in those being mocked becomes a reversal for those who mock. And I think this also is shameful—and it truly is shameful, for which reason we are rightly laughed at by everyone: when someone has just approached the monastic life and has only learned the outward habits of the discipline—how they pray and when, and what kind of...

...the conduct of one’s lifestyle. Such a person immediately becomes a teacher without having ever been a disciple. He goes forth dragging along a string of students, even though he himself is still in need of instruction. He considers the matter to be so great and yet so easy, not knowing that the **care of souls** is the most difficult of all tasks. Souls require, first of all, a cleansing of their old defilements, and then a great deal of attention to receive the impressions of the lessons of virtue. 

But if a man has imagined nothing beyond physical asceticism, how will he correct the character of those placed under him? How will he reshape those who are gripped by evil habits? How will he help those being warred upon by the **passions**, when he does not even know the nature of the war within the mind? Or how will he heal the wounds that occur in battle, when he himself is still lying down wounded and in need of bandages? 

Every art requires time and much instruction to be mastered; is the **art of arts** <note>A common term in early monastic writing for the guidance of souls.</note> the only one to be practiced without being a disciple? A man without experience would not dare to try farming, nor would someone uninitiated in medicine attempt medical works. For the one would be exposed for failing to benefit the sick—or even making the disease worse—while the other would be exposed for leaving the plowed land barren and foul. 

Yet, as if it were the easiest thing of all, people without any training dare to tackle **piety** <note>original: "theosebeia". This refers to the lived practice of a religious life.</note>. This difficult task is considered simple by the masses. Even **Paul** says he has not yet "attained" it, yet those who do not even know that they are ignorant confidently claim to have understood it perfectly. Because of this, the monastic life has become an object of contempt, and those who pursue it are mocked by everyone. For who would not laugh seeing a man who was a water-carrier in a tavern yesterday appearing today as a teacher of virtue, surrounded by a bodyguard of disciples? Or seeing a man who only recently retreated from worldly <note>original: "politikon". If they were clearly convinced of how much labor it takes to lead people to godliness, and if they accurately knew the danger that follows the task, they would certainly have declined the matter as something exceeding their strength. Instead, out of an inexperienced love for glory, they put their hand to a dangerous business. 

Regarding those who merely *seemed* to be teachers—the Pharisees—the Lord said: *Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! He intended that by paying attention to the "Woe," they might restrain themselves from the untimely desire for glory among men, fearing the condemnation even more.

They accept the healing of others when they have not yet healed their own passions, nor are they able to lead others to victory based on their own success.

Only then, from one’s own experience, can one suggest the methods of battle to others and make victory easier for them by foretelling the tactics used in the war. ...victory, because as if in a **night-battle**, he followed the engagements without the mind being aware of the enemies' ambushes. This was also done symbolically by Joshua <note>The Greek text uses "Jesus" (Ἰησοῦς), which is the same name as Joshua; in the context of the Jordan crossing, it refers to Joshua son of Nun.</note>, when the army crossed the Jordan at night. He commanded them to pull stones out of the river, and once outside the river, to set them up as pillars, plaster them, and write upon them how they crossed the Jordan. This signifies that one must bring the deep-seated thoughts of a **passionate life** <note>Life governed by the "passions," such as anger, greed, or lust.</note> into the light, and clearly expose them to public shame, and not begrudge others this knowledge. In this way, not only does the one who has already crossed know the manner of the passage, but those who choose to do the same may make their crossing easy through what they have learned. Thus, the experience of some becomes the instruction of others. 

But those [false teachers] do not do these things, nor do they listen to others who speak of them. Looking only toward their own self-assurance, they demand the service of slaves from their brothers, as if they were **slave-traders**. They place the whole of their glory in this: in presiding over a great many people. Their struggle is to drag along behind them a following no smaller than other brotherhoods during public processions, like a train of captives. They display the character of hucksters rather than teachers. For when they think it is easy to give orders in word—even if the commands are heavy—but refuse to teach by deed, they make their purpose clear to everyone: that they do not hurry to benefit those who come to them, but rather to achieve their own pleasure, and so they slip into this position of leadership.

Let these men learn, if they are willing, from Abimelech and Gideon, that it is not words, but **deeds** that lead subordinates toward imitation. For the one [Abimelech] made a bundle of wood, and after making it, he carried it and said: "In the manner you saw me doing, so you also do." This man introduced the work as something common, placing himself at the head of the labor and saying: "You shall watch me and do likewise." And the Apostle [Paul] says: "These hands have ministered to my needs and to those who were with me." And the Lord Himself first acted, and only then taught. Who could these examples fail to persuade that teaching through deeds is more trustworthy than teaching through words? Yet these men shut their eyes to such images; instead, they arrogantly put forward what others must do. And when they think they know

<column-break/>

something of these things by hearsay, they act like the shepherds denounced by the Prophet for their lack of experience: they carry a sword upon their arm. For this reason, because of the arm, their **right eye** is blinded. For when right action is neglected because of pride, it also extinguishes the brightness of **contemplation** <term>Theoria: the spiritual "vision" or deep understanding of divine truths</term> along with it. 

This is what happens to those who shepherd harshly and inhumanely, when they keep their power to punish ready at hand. For immediately, the contemplative thoughts on the right side are extinguished. Then again, their actions, being deprived of contemplation, wither away. They are able neither to act nor to see, having buckled the sword not to the thigh, but to the arm. Those who use the "cutting word" <note>Referring to sharp, discerning spiritual reasoning.</note> against their own passions wear the sword on their **thigh**; but those who have punishment ready at hand for the sins of others wear it on their **arm**. 

In the same way, Nahash the Ammonite—whose name translates as "Snake"—threatened the "discerning Israel" that he would gouge out every right eye, so that no "right thought" remaining within might guide the possessor toward "right action." He knew that this is the cause of great progress for those who move from contemplation to the **practical life** <term>Praxis: the active struggle against the passions and the performance of virtues</term>. For among such people, the deed performed becomes blameless, having been foreseen by the sharpest eyes of knowledge. 

It is clear from experience that it is easy for men who have no spiritual benefit of their own to take up the leadership of others. For no one who has tasted **stillness** <note>Hesychia: the state of inner quietude and focus on God.</note> and contemplation, having begun to have leisure for it, would choose to bind his mind with cares for physical things. He would not draw his mind away from knowledge—where it is raised high and travels far—only to be dragged down to earthly matters. This is even more evident from that famous parable which Jotham <note>The text says "Jonathan" (Ἰωνάθαν), but this refers to the Parable of the Trees told by Jotham in Judges 9:8-15.</note> put before the men of Shechem, saying: "The trees of the forest went forth to anoint a king over themselves. And they said to the vine, 'Reign over us.' And the vine said, 'Shall I leave my good fruit, which God and men have honored, to go and rule over the trees?'" Similarly, the fig tree refused because of its own sweetness, and the olive because of its own quality. But the bramble—a fruitless and thorny bush—accepted the rule over them, neither...

<summary>This page critiques prideful spiritual leaders who prioritize status over personal virtue, contrasting them with biblical figures who led by labor and example. It uses the allegory of the "blinded right eye" to explain how the loss of spiritual vision leads to harsh, ineffective leadership.</summary>

...having its own quality, nor of the trees subjected to it. For the parable said that it was not the trees of a paradise, but the trees of a thicket <note>Original: δρυμοῦ. Refers to Jotham's Parable in Judges 9, where the trees look for a king.</note> that required supervision. Just as the vine, the fig tree, and the olive tree refused to rule over the trees of the thicket—rejoicing more in their own fruit than in the dignity of high office—so too do those who see in themselves some fruit of virtue and feel the benefit of it. Even if many people try to force them into such a position of leadership, they refuse; they prefer their own spiritual profit over the honor given by the masses. 

But the curse that was laid upon the trees in that parable also happens to men who conduct themselves in the same way. For either fire, it says, will come out of the bramble and consume the trees of the thicket, or it will come out from the trees and consume the bramble. For when agreements become useless, danger must follow both those who subject themselves to an **unskilled teacher** and those who take up the mantle of leadership over negligent disciples. Indeed, the teacher's lack of skill destroys the students, and the students' negligence brings danger to the teacher—especially when they are lazy because of his own lack of knowledge. 

For nothing should escape a teacher's notice when it comes to the correction of those under him, nor should the students overlook any of the teacher's commands. For it is a heavy and dangerous thing both for students to commit a fault and for the teacher to overlook those who are failing. Let them not think the matter is an excuse for relaxation or enjoyment; for the **ruling of souls** <term>rule of souls: a technical term for spiritual direction (Greek: psychagogia)</term> is the most laborious of all tasks. Those who rule over irrational animals and cattle have herds that do not argue back, and because of this, their leadership often goes well. But for those who supervise humans, the variety of characters and the cunning arising from human reason make supervision much more difficult. Those who come to this task must "anoint themselves" as if for a painful struggle, so that they may bear the failings of everyone with great patience, and long-sufferingly teach those things that are hidden due to ignorance. 

For this reason, the oxen in the Temple carry the **basin** <note>The "Brazen Sea" in Solomon's Temple, a massive washbasin supported by twelve bronze oxen (1 Kings 7:25).</note>, while the **lampstand** <note>The Menorah.</note> was made entirely solid and of hammered work.

<column-break/>

The lampstand signifies that the one who proposes to enlighten others ought to be solid in all his parts and have nothing light-minded or hollow within him. All "excess" parts must be hammered away—those things which do not serve as an example of a **blameless life** <note>Original: πολιτείας ἀνεπιλήπτου.</note> to those who see him. 

Regarding the oxen under the basin: the person who has undertaken such a work should refuse none of the things that come upon him, but must bear both the weight and the filth of those who are lesser, as long as bearing it is not life-threatening. For certainly, if he intends to make the actions of those who approach him clean, he must necessarily experience some of their filth himself. For just as the basin, while cleaning the hands of those being washed, receives their filth itself, so it is impossible for one who discusses the **passions** <term>passions: in ascetic theology, these are disordered impulses like anger, lust, or pride</term> and cleanses such stains from others to pass through without being defiled. For the very memory of these things naturally soils the mind of the speaker. Even if you do not stamp the mind with the vivid colors of shameful things, nevertheless, the discourse stains the surface of the intellect, clouding it with "unclean colors" as the words flow forth. 

The leader must also be so knowledgeable that he is ignorant of none of the Enemy’s <note>The Devil.</note> schemes. He must strip bare the hidden maneuvers of those spiritual wrestling-matches. By foretelling the ambushes of the opponent, he awards victory to his students without them having to toil, leading them out of the struggle as "crowned victors." But such a person is rare and not easily found. The great Paul testifies this of himself, saying: 
> *For we are not ignorant of his designs.* <note>2 Corinthians 2:11</note> 
And the marvelous Job, wondering about such a person, says: 
> *Who will uncover the face of his garment? And who can enter into the folds of his breastplate? Who will open the gates of his face?* <note>Job 41:13-14 (Septuagint numbering). Neilus applies this description of the Leviathan to the Devil.</note> 
What he means is this: The face that appears on him is not his true one; for he covers his wickedness with many garments. He lures people with a deceptive appearance, while in secret he craftily builds their destruction. And so that Job does not count himself among those who are ignorant of the Enemy’s nature, he clearly states the evidence, knowing all the monster's supernatural tricks. He says: 
> *His eyes are like the sight of the Morning Star* <note>Original: Ἑωσφόρου (Lucifer). Here used as a metaphor for the devil’s dazzling but false light.</note> *and his innards are like shields.* 
He says these things to expose the Enemy’s villainy. For through the...

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE #

...mimicking the appearance of **Lucifer** <note>Original: Ἑωσφόρου (Heosphoros), the "Bringer of Light." The author suggests a false teacher puts on a show of holiness to hide a deadly interior.</note>, devising ways to draw onlookers to himself; but through the "vipers" within, he brings about death for those who approach. The proverb also exposes the danger of this matter, saying: *He who splits wood is endangered by it if the axe-head falls off.* <note>Referencing Ecclesiastes 10:9.</note> For the one who divides things through reason—separating what seems to be unified from its natural growth and wanting to show things as entirely foreign to one another, namely the truly good from those things that only seem to be so—is in danger among his listeners if his reasoning is not secured on every side. If the word loses its safety, it provides an occasion for a **stumbling block** <term>skandalon: a trap or an obstacle that causes a fall</term> to those who hear it.

Thus, one of those who studied under **Elisha** was cutting wood by the **Jordan**, and when the axe-head fell into the river, he sensed the danger and cried out to his teacher, saying: "Alas, my Lord, for it was borrowed!" <note>2 Kings 6:5. The "borrowed" axe-head represents knowledge taken from others rather than owned through personal experience.</note> This is what happens to those who attempt to teach from things they have merely heard, but are unable to reach the goal because they do not speak from their own **internal disposition** <term>hexis: a permanent state of character acquired through practice</term>. When they are caught saying something contrary to their purpose, they then confess their ignorance, being in danger because of the "borrowed" word they used. Therefore, the great Elisha, by throwing a piece of wood into the depths, made the lost item float; he clarified the meaning that was thought to be hidden in the depths and brought it before the eyes of the listeners.

Behold, the **Jordan** signifies the word of **repentance**; for there the Baptism of repentance was performed by **John**. But he who speaks about repentance without precision—and who, by exposing a hidden goodness, causes his listeners to fall into contempt—has "lost his axe-head" in the Jordan. It is well, then, that the wood which appeared brings the iron up from the deep and makes it float. For before the **Cross** <note>Original: Σταυροῦ (Staurou). The "wood" Elisha threw in is seen here as a prefiguration of the Cross of Christ.</note>, the word concerning repentance was hidden; therefore, anyone who wished to say something about it was quickly proven wrong for daring too much. But after the Cross, it became manifest to all, shown forth at the proper time through the Wood. I say these things not to discourage people from leadership, nor to prevent anyone from guiding the young toward **godliness** <note>Original: θεοσέβεια (theosebeia)</note>, but rather to urge them first to take up the habit of **virtue** <note>Original: ἀρετή (arete)</note> proportional to the greatness of the task, and not to...

<column-break/>

...readily hand themselves over to this goal. They might consider the pleasant things—the service they receive from disciples and the praise from outsiders—while ignoring the danger that follows. They must not make agricultural tools out of the "weapons of war" before a state of peace is reached. For only after subduing all the **passions** <term>pathe: unruly impulses like anger, greed, or lust</term>, and no longer being troubled by wars from any side, nor being forced to use defensive weapons, is it good to "farm" others. But as long as the passions act as tyrants, and the war of the flesh persists against the "mind of the flesh," one must not take their hands off their weapons, but must keep them ready without ceasing. This is so the plotters do not find our relaxation to be an opportunity for attack and overcome us without a struggle.

For to those who struggle well for virtue, and who through great humility do not yet think they have conquered, the Word says encouragingly: *Beat your swords into plowshares and your spears into pruning hooks.* <note>Isaiah 2:4 / Micah 4:3. Neilos applies this to the soul that has finished its internal combat and can now focus on "cultivating" the souls of others.</note> This exhorts them not to waste further time fighting enemies who are already defeated, but for the benefit of the many, to convert the powers of the soul from a "warring state" to "farming" those who are still running wild with the works of wickedness.

Conversely, to those who—before reaching such a state, whether through inexperience or arrogance—attempt tasks beyond their own strength, the Word advises the opposite, saying: *Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears.* <note>Joel 3:10. Neilos argues that if you are still at war with your own sins, you shouldn't be "farming" (teaching), but "fighting."</note> For what is the use of farming when war occupies the land? Such a harvest provides abundance to the enemies rather than to those who labored. This is perhaps why God did not allow the **Israelites** to attend to farming while they were still in the wilderness fighting various nations, so that it would not hinder their military training. But after the truce with their enemies, He advises them to use it, saying: "When you enter the **Promised Land**, you shall not plant..." <note>A reference to Leviticus 19:23, where new trees are not to be harvested for three years.</note> This is understood logically: for before perfection is reached, the things planted do not become firm, as the character of those who ought to be planting is still shifting in an unstable state. For order and sequence exist in the matters of godliness more than in anything else, and one must start from the...
