### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...to be brought near. For those who overlook the initial stages and are enticed by more gluttonous desires are eventually forced by necessity to follow the sequence of the proper order. Just as **Jacob**, drawn by the beauty of **Rachel**, overlooked the "weakness of **Leah’s** eyes," <note>Referring to Genesis 29. In the ascetic tradition, Leah (the first wife) represents the active life of labor and struggle, while Rachel (the second) represents the contemplative life of spiritual beauty.</note> yet he did not flee from the labor required to attain such virtue; for he also fulfilled the seven-year period for her. Therefore, the one who wishes to follow the **spiritual way of life** <term>politeia: a citizen's way of life, here referring to the disciplined life of a monk</term> according to the law must not descend from the end back to the beginning, but must progress from the beginning toward perfection. In this way, he will achieve what he strives for and will lead his acquaintances blamelessly toward the goal of virtue. 

However, many people, without having contributed any labor or achieved even a small or great work of **godliness** <term>theosebeia: literally 'fear of God' or 'true religion'</term>, rush toward the name of "Teacher" as if by chance, not considering this a danger. Not only do they not refuse when some encourage them toward the task, but they even go about the narrow streets, dragging in everyone they happen to meet, promising them every kind of care—much like those hiring laborers—and making agreements concerning food and clothing. 

It is necessary for those who love the matter in this way, and who wish to appear with a great multitude in public processions, to rest upon their guides and maintain the whole "stage-play" of leadership—like those who have taken up a role in a drama. To avoid being abandoned by those performing this service for them, they gratify their followers' pleasures and desires in many ways. They are carried unhindered toward the pits of destruction, like charioteers who have let go of the reins and surrendered the course to the horses’ own whims. As a result, they are carried over cliffs and into pits, stumbling over everything in their path because there is no one to check them or hinder their disordered impulses. 

But let such people listen to the blessed **Ezekiel**, who laments those who provide the material for the pleasures of others and who, by complying with each person's will, store up "woe" for themselves. For he says: 

> Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow and make veils for every head of every age, to destroy souls for the sake of a handful of barley and a piece of bread! <note>Ezekiel 13:18. Neilos interprets this as teachers making people "comfortable" in their sins for the sake of small rewards.</note>

In the same way, these men collect the needs of the body from contributions, 

<column-break/>

resting upon these provisions as if they were sewn together from rags. Those who ought to pray or prophesy with an "uncovered head" <note>Referencing 1 Corinthians 11:4-5.</note> are put to shame by these veils; they emasculate their manly state with these coverings and destroy souls that ought not to have died. Indeed, it would have been better if, obeying **Christ** the true Teacher, they had refused the guardianship of others with all their might. For He said to His own disciples: 

> Do not be called **Rabbi**. <note>Matthew 23:8. Original: Ῥαββί.</note>

If He exhorted **Peter** and **John** and the whole choir of the **Apostles** to stand far off from such a task and to consider themselves small in the face of such dignity, who then is he who imagines himself to be above them, judging himself worthy of a rank from which they were barred? Or perhaps, in saying "do not be called Rabbi," He forbids not the *being* so, but the *craving of the title*. 

If someone, by choice, should be compelled by the acceptance of one or two followers to lead even more, let him first examine himself strictly to see if he is able to teach what must be done through **deeds** rather than through **words**. Let him offer his own life as an image of every virtue to those who are learning, so that those "transcribing" from that model do not dull the beauty of virtue through the ugliness of his errors. 

Furthermore, let him know that he must agonize no less for those under his authority than for himself. For just as he will give an account for himself, so will he give an account for them once he has accepted the responsibility for their salvation. Indeed, it was a point of zeal for the **Saints** not to leave their disciples inferior to their own virtue, but to reshape them from their initial state into a better one. Thus, the **Apostle Paul** turned **Onesimus** from a runaway slave into a martyr; **Elijah** appointed **Elisha** a prophet from being a plowman; **Moses** adorned **Joshua** (who was younger than everyone) into something better; and **Eli** showed **Samuel** to be even greater than himself. 

Even if the zeal of these students cooperated with them in the acquisition of virtue, the cause of all their progress was finding teachers who were able to fan the smoldering spark of their eagerness through encouragement and make it shine forth. Because of this, those who ministered God's will to men became the "mouth of God," for they heard Him saying: [text continues...]

### ASCETIC DISCOURSE ###

-> “If you extract what is precious from what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth.” <note>Jeremiah 15:19</note><-

God also suggests the character of the teacher to **Ezekiel**, teaching him what kind of disciples should be fashioned from what materials:

> “Son of man,” He says, “take for yourself a brick and place it before your face; and you shall portray upon it the city of Jerusalem.” <note>Ezekiel 4:1</note>

This signifies that the Teacher works a holy Temple out of clay—that is, the disciple. The instruction "place it before your face" is also excellent; for improvement will be swift for the disciple if he is always in the Teacher’s sight. The continuous actions of good examples engrave similar images upon souls that are not entirely hard or rough. This is why **Gehazi** <note>The servant of the prophet Elisha who fell to greed</note> and **Judas** fell away—the former through theft, the latter through betrayal—because they withdrew themselves from the eyes of the Teacher. If they had remained with those who could discipline them, they would not have stumbled. That danger follows the teacher due to the negligence of the disciples is shown by what follows:

> “And you shall place an iron griddle between yourself and the brick; and it shall be an iron wall between you and it.” <note>Ezekiel 4:3</note>

For he who wishes not to share in the punishment of the slothful must, after having fashioned for him a city out of clay, recount the punishments threatened against those who relapse from such a state. In this way, these warnings become a "wall," separating the blameless teacher from the guilty disciple. God, commanding this of **Ezekiel**, says:

> “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; and if you see the sword coming and do not testify to them, and the sword takes someone from among them, I will require his soul from your hand.” <note>Ezekiel 33:7-8</note>

**Moses** also established such a wall for himself, saying to the Israelites:

> “Take heed to yourself, that you do not seek to follow them after they have been destroyed from before you.” <note>Deuteronomy 12:30</note>

For it happens to those who attend to their own minds too carelessly that after the **passions** <term>pathe: the disordered impulses or suffering of the soul</term> have been cut off, images of old fantasies begin to sprout like shoots. If someone allows these to fall continually into the **sovereign faculty** <term>hegemonikon: the ruling part of the soul or seat of reason</term> and does not block their entrance, he will house the passions once again, making his life a struggle even after victory. For it is possible for passions, even when tamed and taught to eat grass like oxen, through the negligence

<column-break/>

of the one taming them, to become wild again and resume their beastly ferocity. So that this does not happen, he says: "Do not seek to follow them after they have been destroyed from before you," so that the soul, by "seeking" them, does not acquire a habit of delighting in such fantasies and relapse into its ancient wickedness. The blessed **Jacob** knew these things happen—that such things cause more harm to the mind when they are observed and meditated upon continually, sealing the images of shameful fantasies clearly and distinctly—and so in **Shechem** he hid the "foreign gods." For the labor concerning the passions hides and destroys them, not just for a short time, but "until this very day"—that is, for all time; since "today" extends alongside the entire age, always signifying the present time.

**Shechem** is interpreted as "Shouldering" <note>original: ὤμιασις (omiasis), a Greek interpretation of the Hebrew name Shechem, often associated with the shoulder or bearing a burden</note>, which signifies the labor concerning the passions. Therefore, he gives Shechem to **Joseph** as a special portion, for he fought against the passions through the labor found within them. Indeed, Jacob, saying that he took Shechem with "sword and bow," shows that he mastered the passions through battle and labor, hiding them in the land of Shechem. It seems, however, somehow contradictory to hide the gods in Shechem and to "set up an idol in secret." For the one—hiding them in Shechem—is praiseworthy, while the other—setting up an idol in secret—is blameworthy. Thus, he placed this under a curse, saying:

> “Cursed is the man who sets up an idol in secret.” <note>Deuteronomy 27:15</note>

For hiding something in the earth for the purpose of total concealment is not the same as setting it up "in secret." That which is hidden in the earth and no longer appears to the senses is eventually abandoned by memory over time. But that which is "set up in secret" perhaps escapes the notice of those outside, yet being seen continually by the one who set it up, it renews the memory, being secretly carried like a shrine in the heart. For every shameful thought formed in the mind is a "hidden carved image." Truly, it is a shame to bring such thoughts into the open; therefore, it is dangerous to set up a carved image in secret, but even more dangerous to follow and seek out forms already vanished, as the mind easily leans back toward the cast-out passion, and the scale of pleasures...

<meta>This page continues St. Neilos the Ascetic’s instructions on spiritual discipline and the responsibilities of a teacher. Having previously discussed the formation of the disciple (the "clay brick"), Neilos now warns about the volatility of virtue and the psychological strategies used by demons to lead the soul from one passion to another.</meta>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...weighted down to the very ground. For such is the nature of the habit of virtue: it is exceedingly prone to shifting; if it is neglected, it swings toward the opposite. This, it seems, Scripture signifies to us through a symbol when it says: “The land into which you are entering is a moving land, amidst the movement of the nations.” <note>Original: γῆ... μετακινουμένη — likely a figurative interpretation of passages concerning the instability of the Promised Land when the people were unfaithful.</note> For as soon as the one who possesses the habit of virtue moves toward the opposite, virtue moves along with him; for it is a “moving land.” Therefore, one must not give the initial entrance into the mind to the fantasies of those thoughts which are naturally harmful. Nor should one allow the mind to go down into **Egypt**, for from there it is led down to the **Assyrians**. <note>In ascetic literature, Egypt often symbolizes the darkness of the passions or the "world," while Assyria symbolizes the captivity of the mind to those passions.</note> For if the mind descends into the darkness of impure thoughts—which is what “Egypt” is interpreted to mean—it is then dragged by force, even against its will, by the passions toward their execution. 

For this reason, the Lawgiver <note>Moses</note>, symbolically blocking the entrance of pleasure, commanded us to **watch the head of the serpent**, since the serpent also watches our heel. <note>A reference to Genesis 3:15. In ascetic thought, the "head" of the serpent is the first suggestion of a sinful thought, while the "heel" is the final action.</note> For the serpent’s aim is the outward action; if he cannot grasp that, he cannot easily inject his venom through the bite. But our effort must be to crush the very first assault of pleasure. For if this "head" is crushed, the outward action becomes weak.

Perhaps even **Samson** would not have burned the crops of the foreigners <note>The Philistines; Judges 15:4-5</note> if he had not turned the heads of the foxes away and tied their tails together. For the one who is able to perceive the ambush of crafty thoughts from the very beginning—ignoring their starts, for they devise ways to make themselves appear respectable so they can seize the end goal—will expose the absurdity of these thoughts by comparing their ends to one another. He "ties tail to tail" and places the "torch" of reproof in their midst. 

To make what is being said clearer, I will exercise this principle on two types of thoughts; this will serve as a true proof for all the rest. Often, the thought of **sexual immorality** <term>porneia: often translated as fornication or sexual impurity</term> comes from **vainglory** <term>kenodoxia: the desire for empty praise</term>. It shows the "gateways" of the roads leading to Hades as if they were majestic, but it hides the ruinous places through which it leads those who thoughtlessly follow it into the chambers of death. For it sometimes suggests the priesthood, or sometimes the perfect life of a Monk; it makes many people come to him for their benefit, and prepares him to imagine 

<column-break/>

his own success in both word and deed. And when it has sufficiently led him astray with these ideas and drawn him far away from his natural sobriety <term>nepsis: spiritual watchfulness or "sobriety" of the mind</term>, it then sketches out a meeting with a supposedly "respectable woman." From there, it brings him to consent to the foul deed, dragging the confidence of his conscience down into the deepest shame. 

Therefore, he who wishes to "tie the tails" together should take the ends of these thoughts: the punishment for vainglory and the dishonor of sexual immorality. When he sees them clearly opposing each other, let him consider that he has done what Samson did. 

Again, the thought of **gluttony** <term>gastrimargia: "belly-madness" or overindulgence</term> has sexual immorality as its end. The thought of sexual immorality has **sorrow** <term>lype: a dejected or worldly grief</term> as its end. For immediately, despondency and sorrow follow the one who has been defeated by such thoughts after he regains his sobriety. Let the one who is struggling, then, consider not the enjoyment of food, nor the smoothness of pleasure, but the ends of each. And when he finds that sorrow follows both, let him know he has "tied tail to tail" and has destroyed the "crops of the foreigners" with his reproof.

If, therefore, the war against the passions requires such great science and experience, let those who take on the leadership of others realize how much knowledge they need. They must guide their subordinates wisely toward the "prize of the upward call" <note>Philippians 3:14</note> and clearly teach them all the rules of the struggle. This way, they will not merely beat the air with their hands while mimicking victory, but in the actual battle against the opponent, they will deliver lethal blows. They must not throw their hands into the air in vain, but must strike the opponent himself. For this struggle is more difficult than the gymnastic games. In those games, the bodies of athletes fall, but they can easily be raised again; here, however, it is **souls** that fall, and once they are overturned, it is difficult to raise them up. 

If someone is still boxing against a life of passion and is defiled with blood, yet attempts to build a **Temple of God** out of rational souls, such a person will surely hear: "You shall not build a Temple for Me, for you are a man of blood." <note>1 Chronicles 22:8; God's words to King David</note> For it is from a state of peace that one must build a Temple to God. And **Moses**, when he took the Tabernacle and pitched it outside the camp, showed that the Teacher must be as far as possible from the turmoil of war and far from the defilement...

<summary>St. Neilos explains how to defeat sinful thoughts by comparing their eventual miserable results (the "tails") and warns that only those who have achieved inner peace may lead others.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual warfare, logismoi, vainglory, sexual immorality, gluttony, Samson's foxes, Temple of God, spiritual teacher, nepsis, watchfulness</keywords>

<meta>This page continues St. Neilos the Ascetic’s instructions on the spiritual life, moving from the internal struggle against thoughts to the external structure of the monastic life: the relationship between the teacher and the disciple. He emphasizes the total surrender of the will required for spiritual progress.</meta>

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE #

...having moved away from the encampment <note>original: στρατοπέδου — here referring to the "camp" of worldly life or spiritual warfare</note> to a peaceful life free from war. But when such teachers are found, they have need of disciples who have so denied themselves and their own wills that they differ in no way from a lifeless body or from material placed before a craftsman. This is so that, just as a soul acts within a body however it wishes without the body resisting, or as a craftsman displays his own skill upon the material without being hindered by the material in reaching his own goal, so the teacher may work the faith of virtue into his disciples, having them be obedient and contradicting nothing.

For to meddle in the teacher's management <note>original: οἰκονομίας (oikonomias) — refers to the way a superior directs the lives and tasks of those under them</note> and to wish to test the things commanded by him is to hinder one's own progress. For that which appears reasonable and persuasive to the inexperienced is not always truly reasonable. For the craftsman judges the matters of his craft in one way, and the unskilled person in another. For the one makes use of a rule based on knowledge <term>episteme: scientific or specialized knowledge</term>, while the other relies on what seems likely. That which "seems likely" rarely hits upon the truth, but for the most part fails to reach correctness, having a kinship with deception.

<margin>5</margin> For what seems less reasonable than when a ship is being carried sideways during what sailors call an "upright voyage" <note>likely referring to sailing close to the wind or against a heavy current</note>, the captain commands everyone to sit on the side that is dipping into the water, leaving the side that is raised up? This is even though the wind is pushing more against that raised side and threatening to overturn it onto the very side he ordered them to weigh down! Indeed, likelihood would suggest advising them to weigh down the side that is rising up, not to run toward the one already in danger. But nevertheless, those on board obey the captain rather than their own ideas. For necessity persuades them to be slaves to the skill of the one to whom authority has been entrusted, even if what is happening does not seem persuasive based on what is seen.

Therefore, let those who have entrusted their own salvation to others, setting aside what seems "likely" to them, yield to the skill of the one who knows, judging that person's knowledge to be more trustworthy than their own reasonings. And first, when they renounce the world, let them leave nothing behind, fearing the very heavy example of **Ananias**. <note>In Acts 5, Ananias and Sapphira held back part of the proceeds from a sale while pretending to give everything to the Apostles; they were struck dead for "lying to the Holy Spirit."</note> He thought he could hide his theft from men, but he received a condemnation from God for his theft. But just as they give themselves, so let them give 

<column-break/>

all their possessions. For they know well that whatever is left behind continuously drags the mind toward itself, distracting it for a long time from better things; and later, it will completely break it away from the brotherhood.

For this reason, the Holy Spirit wrote the lives of the ancients, so that He might lead each person practicing any way of life toward the truth through appropriate examples. How then did **Elisha**, when joining himself to his teacher, renounce the world? It says he was plowing with oxen, and twelve yoke of oxen were before him; and he slaughtered the oxen and boiled them using the wooden equipment of the oxen. <note>See 1 Kings 19:19-21. Elisha’s destruction of his tools symbolizes a point of no return.</note> This signifies the "heat of his zeal." For he did not say, "I will sell the equipment of the oxen and manage the money properly," nor did he calculate that if these things were sold, they would provide for a greater need. Being entirely possessed by the desire that was drawing him toward the company of his teacher, he looked down upon visible things. Rather, seeing them as distractions from his right purpose, he hastened to be rid of them, knowing that delay is often the cause of a change of heart.

How then did the Lord, when setting before the rich man the perfection of a life according to God, command him to sell his possessions and give to the poor, leaving nothing for himself, unless He knew that what is left behind becomes a cause of distraction just as much as the whole? I think also that **Moses**, by commanding those who wished to purify themselves in the "great vow" to shave their whole body, was commanding the complete laying aside of possessions. <note>Neilos interprets the laws of the Nazirites or the purification of Levites (Numbers 6 or 8) as a metaphor for spiritual poverty.</note>

Secondly, let them so forget their kinship and family relations that they are never troubled even by the memories of them. For if the Ark caused the cows yoked to the wagon to forget their nature—even though their calves were shut up at home and no one was forcing them, they completed the journey without fault, turning neither to the right nor to the left, nor showing through lowing the pain of being separated from their offspring; but though burdened by the weight of the Ark and struggling against the tyranny of nature, they walked as if on a straight rule without turning aside, overcome by the reverence for the Ark resting upon them—if, I say, those cows were so disposed, why should those who are about to carry the **spiritual Ark** not maintain the same? <note>Referring to 1 Samuel 6, where two cows left their nursing calves to carry the Ark of the Covenant back to the Israelites, a miraculous act contrary to animal instinct.</note>

<summary>Neilos argues for total obedience to a spiritual teacher, comparing it to the trust sailors place in a captain, and uses the examples of Elisha and the cows carrying the Ark to illustrate the necessity of abandoning all worldly ties and property.</summary>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...ought to be done; indeed, even more was required so that the rational nature, through its failure to perform those things by reason, is not put to shame and proven inferior to the irrational nature in necessary works, which the irrational animals perform by necessity. **Perhaps Joseph also** wanders through the wilderness for this reason: because he sought the boundary of perfection within the names of kinship. Therefore, the "man" who is truly an "agent of truth," <note>original: ὁ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν ἄνθρωπος — likely a reference to the anonymous man Joseph meets in Genesis 37:15, interpreted allegorically</note> after asking him the cause of his wandering and learning that it was a longing for his own kin—for he did not say he came to "feed" them, but to "shepherd" them, unless he had a mistaken judgment about the craft—says to him: "They have departed from here; for I heard them saying, 'Let us go to **Dothan**.'" Now, **Dothan** is interpreted as *sufficient failing* <note>original: ἔκλειψις ἱκανή (ekleipsis hikane). Early Christian writers often used symbolic etymologies; here, Dothan represents a "total eclipse" or "complete abandonment" of worldly ties</note>. This teaches the person still wandering among friends according to the body that it is not possible to attain perfection in any other way than by *sufficiently failing* in one's longing for the kin of the flesh. For even if one leaves **Haran**, which signifies the senses—for they are interpreted as *hollows* <note>original: τρώγλαι (troglai) — caves or holes</note>—and comes out from the valley of **Hebron**, meaning from lowly works; and even if one leaves the wilderness where the one seeking perfection goes astray; if he does <gloss>not</gloss> move his dwelling into that *sufficient failing*, there is no benefit to him from his vain hardship. This is because he misses the mark of perfection due to his affection for his kindred. Moreover, even the **Lord**, when He rebuked the **Theotokos Mary** <note>The "God-bearer" or Mother of God</note> as she sought Him among His kinsfolk—and when He judged the one who loves father or mother more than Him to be unworthy of Himself—He was firmly establishing this "failing" of the bonds of kinship. After achieving these things, one should advise those who have recently escaped from worldly turmoils to keep stillness <term>hesychia: a state of inner quietness and external silence</term>. They must not, through constant outings, reopen the wounds inflicted on the mind through the senses, nor introduce new forms to the old idols of their sins. Instead, they should turn away from the assault of new impressions and apply every effort to erase the old fantasies. For stillness is indeed laborious for those who have recently renounced the world. For then memory, having found the opportunity, stirs up all the inherent impurity; it was not free to do this before because of the multitude of distracting affairs. Yet, along with the labor, stillness also brings a benefit, deliver-

<column-break/>

ing the mind over time from the disturbance of foul thoughts. For if it is the goal to wash the soul and be purified of all things that defile it, they must withdraw entirely from the affairs through which filth increases. They must provide great tranquility to the reasoning faculty, stay far from those things that irritate it, and flee from the company of those who are most familiar, embracing solitude, the mother of philosophy <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to the monastic life and the pursuit of divine wisdom</note>. It is easy to fall back into the same nets from which they thought they had escaped whenever they eagerly seek to live among the confused crowds without fear. For it is useless for one who has moved toward virtue to delight in the same things which he fled after condemning them. For habit has a pulling force that is to be feared; they might renew the shameful practices and create memories of the evils they had forgotten, despite the stillness achieved through great effort. For the mind of those who have recently withdrawn from vice is like a body beginning to recover from a long illness. In such a state, any chance excuse becomes a cause for the disease to return, as the body has not yet been solidified into strong health. For the "mental nerves" <note>original: νοεροὶ τόνοι (noeroi tonoi) — the tension or strength of the intellect</note> of such a person are still fluid and shaking, and there is a fear that the passion might run back, being naturally stirred up by the distractions found among crowds. For this reason, **Moses** commanded those who wished to suffer nothing from the Destroyer to remain within their doorways, saying:
> "None of you shall go out the door of his house, so that the Destroyer might not touch you." <note>Exodus 12:22</note>
And **Jeremiah** also seems to command this when he says:
> "Go not forth into the field, and walk not in the ways, for the sword of the enemy dwells round about." <note>Jeremiah 6:25</note>
For it belongs to noble champions to engage the enemy hand-to-hand. But if there is someone who is not yet able to fight at all, let him remain safely at home without being harassed, providing for himself a danger-free security through stillness. Such a one was **Joshua the son of Nun**, about whom it is written: "But his servant **Joshua**, being a young man, did not depart from the tent." <note>Exodus 33:11</note> For he knew that those who go out into the plain are snatched away by the "brothers of the body" and "friends of the flesh" <note>Refers to physical desires or worldly associations</note> because of a premature struggle. He was educated by the history of **Abel**; and not least, one can learn this accurately from the story of **Dinah**, that it is truly a girlish and womanly—

<summary>St. Neilos explains that spiritual perfection requires a "sufficient failing" or total abandonment of family ties and worldly senses. He advocates for hesychia (stillness) as a necessary period of convalescence for the soul to prevent a relapse into old vices.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of St. Neilos the Ascetic. Having previously discussed the need to abandon family ties to reach spiritual perfection, the author now addresses the psychological state of the monk, specifically the dangers of pride and the necessity of complete mental withdrawal from worldly memories.</meta>

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE #

...is a sign of the intellect <note>original: διανοίας (dianoias)</note> to attempt things beyond one's own spiritual state, and to be deceived by the assumption that one is self-sufficient. For if the soul had not readily stripped for the contemplation of worldly affairs—believing itself capable and thinking it would not be seduced at all by their pleasure—the soul's power of judgment would not have been prematurely corrupted, lured away by the sensory imagination <note>original: φαντασίας (phantasias)</note>, before it had even conversed with the lawful and courageous Word. Knowing that this passion—I mean that of conceit—dwells among men, and wishing to uproot it from our very character, God said to **Moses**: "Make the sons of **Israel** reverent" <note>original: εὐλαβεῖς (eulabeis) – meaning cautious or God-fearing</note>. For to readily strip for struggles beyond one's strength is a character foreign to reverence. Therefore, we must not involve ourselves in worldly <note>original: πολιτικοῖς (politikois) – literally 'city-like' or 'civil'</note> turmoils before we have reached a stable spiritual state; rather, we must flee as far as possible, keeping the mind distant from the noises echoing around us. For there is no great benefit in withdrawing from things if we are still surrounded by the reports of them; or in leaving the city's activities only to sit by the gate, like **Lot**, becoming filled with the turmoil coming from within. Instead, one must withdraw far outside, according to the great **Moses**, so that not only the deeds but even the voices of these things may cease, as he says:

> When I go out of the city and spread my hands, the voices shall cease. <note>Refers to Exodus 9:29</note>

For true serenity <note>original: γαλήνη (galene)</note> exists when not only the actions but also the memories of them are at rest, providing time for the soul to be able to see the stamped impressions <note>original: τύπους (tupous) – the lingering mental images of past sins or worldly attachments</note> and to struggle against each one and cut it out of the mind. But when other forms keep entering, it is impossible to erase the previous impressions, as the reasoning faculty is preoccupied with those that are arriving; thus, the labor of cutting out the passions <note>original: πάθη (pathe) – the disordered impulses or emotions</note> necessarily becomes more difficult. They gain strength from gradual growth, and like a river with an unceasing flow, they flood the soul's power of discernment with inflowing imaginations. For just as those who wish to see the dry bed of a river—perhaps because some things worthy of study are lying there—gain nothing by pumping out the water in that spot where they think the object of their search lies, because the inflowing water immediately fills the emptied space; but when they

<column-break/>

stop the flow from above, the ground is revealed to them without effort. The remaining water recedes of its own accord, yielding the dry earth to them for the investigation of the things they desire. In the same way, the emptying of the forms that produce the passions becomes easy once the senses no longer supply things from the outside. But if the senses continue to send in sensory things like a stream, it is not only difficult but entirely impossible to cleanse the mind <note>original: νοῦν (noun)</note> of such a flood. Even if the passions do not trouble us through constant encounters—not finding an opportunity for movement—they nevertheless return secretly and grow more robust, gaining strength from the passage of time. Just as ground that is constantly trampled upon, even if it contains thorns, does not sprout them (for the friction of feet hinders nature), yet it extends its roots deep into the earth's bosom; then, when it finds a permitting season, it sprouts and grows lush. In this way, the passions, when hindered from appearing openly by constant social encounters, become more vigorous; and when they find the opportunity of stillness <note>original: ἡσυχίας (hesychias)</note>, they attack with great strength, making the war heavy and dangerous for those who were negligent at the start of their battle against them. For this reason, the prophet commands us to "destroy the seed from **Babylon**," advising us to vanish those forms while they are still in the storehouses of the senses, so that they do not fall into the soil of the mind and sprout. For if they are watered by the torrential and useless rains of constant meditation, they will bear the abundant fruit of wickedness. Another prophet also calls those blessed who do not wait for the peak of the passions, but destroy them while they are still clinging to the breast:

> Blessed is he, saying, who shall seize your infants and dash them against the rock. <note>Psalm 137:9. In ascetic theology, 'infants' represent the first stirrings of sinful thoughts.</note>

Perhaps even the great **Job**, philosophizing about his own circumstances, hints at something similar:

> He says that the **Papyrus** and the **Rush** <note>original: Πάπυρον καὶ Βούτομον</note> flourish in water;

but when deprived of the river, every herb withers. And the saying,

> The **Ant-lion** <note>original: Μυρμηκολέων (Myrmekoleon) – a legendary beast, half-lion and half-ant</note> perished because it had no prey,

seems to signify something similar. For wishing to show the predatory nature of passion, the great **Job** devised its name from the most daring **Lion** and the most lowly **Ant**.

<summary>St. Neilos explains that spiritual progress requires total withdrawal from worldly memories, not just physical distance. He uses the analogy of a riverbed and various biblical metaphors to show that passions must be uprooted while they are still "infants" or "seeds" before they grow uncontrollable.</summary>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...having composed the name. For the attacks of the passions begin from trivial fantasies, in the manner of an **Ant**, creeping in secretly; but in the end, they grow to a great and exceptional bulk, so as to present a danger no less than the pouncing of a **Lion** <note>Neilos is playing on the word 'Myrmekoleon' or Ant-Lion, a mythical creature from ancient bestiaries. He uses it to show how a small thought ('ant') can grow into a fierce obsession ('lion').</note> to anyone who happens to be there. Therefore, the spiritual wrestler must grapple with the passions when they approach like an **Ant**, putting forward their triviality as bait. For if they reach the point of attaining the strength of a **Lion**, they become difficult to overcome—unless one refuses to provide them with "food." Their food, as has already been said many times, is the images of sensory objects that enter through the senses; for these nourish the passions, successively arming each idol <note>original: εἴδωλον (eidolon) – here meaning a mental image or false representation</note> against the soul.

For this reason, the Lawgiver <note>Refers to Moses</note> constructed the lattice-work for the Temple, signaling that those who wish to keep their intellect pure for the Temple must be on guard. Just as there a screen <note>original: δικτύῳ (diktyo) – literally a net or lattice</note> was fashioned for the windows to prevent any unclean thing from creeping in, so also must one interweave the difficulties of the coming judgment as "logical restraints" <note>original: κωλύματα λογισμῶν (kolymata logismon)</note> for the senses, walling off the entrance to the incoming unclean forms.

And perhaps this is why **Ozias** <note>Usually identified as Ahaziah in 2 Kings 1:2, though Neilos writes 'Ozias' (Uzziah). Ahaziah fell through a lattice and became ill; Uzziah was struck with leprosy in the Temple.</note> became ill, because he fell from the lattice-work; for to fall from the lattice-work is to miscalculate the reasons for divine retribution at the time of temptation, having been cast down toward pleasures. What is more grievous than this illness? For illness of the body is to have the balance of the elements exist contrary to nature, when the dominance of one is turned toward an unnatural state; but illness of the soul is to deviate from right reason, having been defeated by disease-causing passions.

Solomon wove such "nets" for the sight of those capable of hearing, saying: *When your eyes see a strange woman, then your mouth will speak crooked things* <note>A paraphrase of Proverbs 23:33</note>. By "crooked things," he means the things that are destined to happen after the sin, at the time of retribution. For these things, when considered with the proper state of mind, bar any dangerous gazing of the eyes. He also describes what the state of one's reasoning ought to be at that time: *For you lie down,* he says, *as if in the heart of the sea, and like a pilot in a great surge.* For if one is able, at the time of a provoking sight,

<column-break/>

to fight back, he will make himself as intensely engaged against the threatened punishments as one who is tossed by a storm at sea. For he will overcome his wrestlers without effort, not feeling the blows being dealt to him; as if to say: *They struck me, and I felt no pain; they mocked me, and I did not know it* <note>Proverbs 23:35</note>. Those people, he says, were striking him and thought they were making sport of him, but I did not even feel the blows—for they were like the arrows of infants—nor did I turn toward their deceptions, pretending as if they were not even present.

So also **David**, despising such adversaries, said: *When the wicked one turned away from me, I did not know it* <note>Psalm 101:4 (LXX 100:4)</note>; he says he took no notice either when they approached or when they withdrew. But as for the man who does not even know this—that there is much commerce between the senses and sensory objects, and that deception easily arises from this commerce—and who does not suspect the harm coming from them, but is filled by them without being on guard: how will he recognize the plot at the time of the deception, if he has not been pre-educated in the discernment of these things?

That a battle occurs between the senses and sensory objects, and that sensory objects impose taxes upon the defeated senses, is clear from the war of the **Assyrians** against the **Sodomites**. For the History <note>Genesis 14</note> introduces the four kings of the Assyrian nation against the five kings around **Sodom**: first, there was an agreement, a treaty, and peace offerings at the Salt Sea; then, a period of slavery for the five kings lasting twelve years; then, in the thirteenth year, a rebellion; and in the fourteenth year, the four kings attacked the five and took them captive.

The historical account ends there; but we are instructed by this history regarding our own condition, and we are taught the war of the senses against sensory objects. For each of us, from birth until the age of twelve, not yet having a purified power of discernment, subjects the senses without examination to sensory objects, as if they were masters serving whatever is commanded: sight to visible things; hearing to sounds; taste to flavors; smell to vapors; and touch to the sensory objects naturally suited to move it. Because of infancy <note>original: νηπιότητα (nepioteta) – meaning both physical childhood and spiritual immaturity</note>, one is unable to find any hindrance to distinguish these perceptions. But when the reasoning <note>original: λογισμὸς (logismos)</note> is about to become bright, and the...

<meta>This page continues the discourse of St. Neilos the Ascetic. Having previously discussed how passions grow from small "ants" into "lions" through the senses, Neilos now explores the psychological mechanics of habit and the spiritual necessity of never looking back toward worldly attachments.</meta>

### AN ASCETIC DISCOURSE ###

...if he begins to perceive the harm, he immediately meditates on **revolt** <note>original: ἀποστασία (apostasia) – literally a standing away or rebellion</note> and flight from such slavery. And if, becoming strong in his **reasoning** <term>logismos: the faculty of thought or the specific "thoughts" that tempt the soul</term>, he confirms this resolve, he remains free forever, having escaped bitter masters. But if his judgment is too weak for the undertaking, he again betrays his senses into captivity, defeated by the dynasty of sensory things; thereafter, he endures a tyrannical slavery without any good hope. 

For this reason, the five kings in history <note>Refers to the Battle of Siddim in Genesis 14, where five kings were defeated by four.</note> who were defeated by the four are driven into **bitumen pits**; this is so that we may learn that those defeated by sensory things are swallowed up as if by abysses or pits, plunging into the specific sensory object that corresponds to each of their five senses. They no longer perceive anything beyond what is seen, because they have clothed their desire in earthly things and have loved the enjoyment of things here more than the things of the intellect. 

So also, the servant who has loved his own master, his wife, and his children, and refuses true freedom because of his kinship to bodily things, becomes an **eternal slave** after having his ear pierced with an awl <note>Referencing the law in Exodus 21:5-6 regarding Hebrew slaves who refuse manumission.</note>. This is done so that, failing to hear with the natural opening of the ear, he may never receive the **word of freedom**, but remain a slave perpetually, having loved present things. 

For this same reason, the Law commanded that the hand of the woman who seized the private parts of a man be cut off while two men were fighting <note>Referencing Deuteronomy 25:11-12.</note>. This is because, when there is a battle of thoughts concerning the choice between worldly and heavenly goods, she abandoned the choice of the heavenly and grabbed hold of the things of **generation and corruption** <note>Neilos allegorizes the reproductive organs as symbols of the material cycle of birth and decay.</note>; for through the reproductive organs, he signaled the affairs of material life. 

There is, therefore, no benefit in renouncing one's possessions if one does not persist in that judgment, but is instead dragged back and gives in to one's reasoning—proclaiming an attachment to those things by constantly turning back toward what was left behind, just like **Lot’s wife**. For she, having turned back, stands to this day as an example to the disobedient, having been transformed into a **pillar of salt**. For such is **habit** <term>synetheia: the force of customary behavior</term>, of which she is the symbol: it turns back toward itself those who wish to depart without turning around. 

What also of the Law which commands that the one entering the Temple, after completing the prayers, should not return through the same gate by which he entered, but

<column-break/>

should exit through the opposite gate, making his journey straight forward without turning back? <note>Referencing Ezekiel 46:9.</note> This signifies that one must not incline the intensity of the straight path toward virtue into wavering hesitations. For constant inclinations toward the things from which we have departed pull us completely backward by the force of habit; by weakening our forward momentum, they drag us away entirely and prepare us to return to our **ancient evils**. 

For habit is a terrible thing to hold one fast and not permit one to rise again toward the **original state** <term>hexis: a stable internal disposition or "habit of soul"</term> of virtue. For a **state** of soul arises from **habit**, and from that state, a **nature** is produced. It is difficult to displace or change a nature; for even if it is bent slightly by force, it quickly runs back to itself. While it may be shaken from its own boundaries, it does not change completely unless great labor prepares it to run the same course back again, so as to return from the habit to the state that was abandoned. 

Observe, then, the soul that follows its customs: how it sits upon **idols**, nailing itself to formless matter. When the **Word** <note>Here, "Logos" or Reason, personified as Laban searching for his household gods in Genesis 31.</note> wishes to lead it by the hand to higher things, the soul does not sit with Him but refuses the ascent, saying: "I cannot rise before you, for the custom of women is upon me." <note>Rachel's excuse to her father Laban in Genesis 31:35. Neilos interprets "the custom of women" as the soul's menstruation or "unclean habit" of worldly attachment.</note> For the soul that has rested in the affairs of life for a long time sits upon idols—things which are formless in themselves but receive a shape through human artifice. 

For are not wealth, glory, and the other affairs of life formless things? They have nothing clear or well-defined, but they cheat the truth with a deceptive likeness by receiving various changes from one moment to the next. We ourselves impose a "form" upon them when we mold fantasies of "usefulness" around things that serve no profitable end, doing so through our human reasonings. For when we expand the body's necessary requirements into an impossible luxury through our inventions—seasoning and dressing our food with ten thousand spices, and ambitiously variegating our garments for the sake of opulence and daintiness—we are then called to account for this vanity, as we have needlessly and in vain sought to fulfill a need that could have been satisfied by very little...

<summary>St. Neilos uses several Old Testament allegories to argue that spiritual progress is impossible if one remains psychologically attached to old habits. He warns that repeated behavior (habit) eventually becomes an unchangeable "nature" that traps the soul in material "idols" like wealth and luxury.</summary>
<keywords>habit, nature, asceticism, Lot's wife, Rachel's idols, five senses, spiritual freedom, slavery to passions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of St. Neilos the Ascetic. Having previously discussed the soul's descent into sensory slavery and the "ear-piercing" of habit, Neilos now focuses on the "sitting" of the soul in various states and the anatomical allegory of the passions—specifically how gluttony serves as the root of all other vices.</meta>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...boasting in [worldly] trimmings, we fashion defenses as if we were performing our duties. For what else are we doing but struggling to give form to formless matter? It was well said that such a soul **sits upon** these things; for one who has confirmed such judgments within herself regarding the aforementioned things is nailed to the affairs of this world, thereafter serving habit rather than truth. By these habits, she defiles her nature, as if by **monthly uncleanness** <note>original: ἐμμήνῳ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ (emmēnō akatharsia) — a reference to the ritual impurity associated with menstruation in Leviticus 15:19, here used as a metaphor for the lingering "stain" of bad habits.</note>. 

Scripture here uses the term "sitting" to mean idleness from good deeds and a love of pleasure. It refers to idleness when it says: *Those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron* <note>Psalm 107:10</note>. For darkness and chains are obstacles to work. It refers to the **love of pleasure** <term>philēdonia: the obsessive seeking of physical or sensory gratification</term> when it speaks of those whose hearts turned back toward Egypt and said to one another: *We remember when we sat by the fleshpots and ate meat to our fill* <note>Exodus 16:3</note>. 

Indeed, the lovers of pleasure "sit by fleshpots," for their appetites are set ablaze by a moist and ceaseless heat. **Gluttony** <term>gastrimargia: literally "stomach-madness," considered the first and most fundamental of the eight capital vices in ascetic theology</term> is the mother of this love of pleasure. For gluttony gives birth to pleasure, and perhaps to many of the other passions as well. From this, as from a root, the remaining passions spring up like lush branches; growing little by little from their mother-root, they form trunks of malice that reach toward the sky. 

The love of money, anger, and grief are the offspring and sprouts of gluttony. For the glutton first has need of money to fulfill his gaping desire, even if that desire is never actually filled. <margin>•</margin> Against those who hinder the acquisition of these things, the **irascible part** <term>thymikon: the "spirited" or "incensive" faculty of the soul, which produces anger or righteous indignation</term> is necessarily moved. **Grief** <note>original: λύπη (lypē) — specifically the sorrow or dejection that follows a frustrated desire.</note> follows of necessity when the anger cannot proceed to action due to weakness. 

Indeed, he who "walks upon his chest and belly" <note>An allegorical reference to the serpent in Genesis 3:14.</note>, when he possesses the materials that produce pleasures, walks upon the belly; but when he lacks these, he moves to the chest, where anger resides. For when lovers of pleasure are deprived of their pleasures, they become angry and embittered. This is why the great Moses places a **breastplate** <note>original: λογεῖον (logeion) — the High Priest's "breastplate of judgment" described in Exodus 28:15.</note> upon the chest of the priest. He demonstrates through symbols that one must secretly guide the impulses of the passionate, irascible part with **reason** <term>logismos: the faculty of logical thought and discernment</term>; for the "breastplate" is a breastplate of judgment. One who is still imperfect controls the passion through reason; but the "perfect" Moses removes the irascible part entirely. He does not merely wear a breastplate, but he...

<column-break/>

...removes the **breast-piece** <note>original: στηθύνιον (stēthunion) — referring to the priestly portion of a sacrifice in Leviticus 8:29.</note> itself. For it says: *Moses took the breast-piece and removed it as an offering before the Lord.* 

There are others who neither cut out anger entirely nor master the passion through reason, but overcome it through **toil** <note>original: πόνῳ (ponō) — physical labor or ascetic struggle.</note>. These are those who remove the breast-piece along with the **arm** <note>original: βραχίονι (brachioni) — or shoulder; in Leviticus 7:34, the breast and the right thigh/shoulder are given to the priests.</note>. For the arm is a sign of toil and labor. 

Similarly, the idea of "walking on the belly" as a symbol for pleasure is most true, for the belly is nearly the sole cause of pleasures. When the stomach is full, intense appetites for other pleasures arise; but when it is empty, they are quiet and more stable. Here, too, there is a difference between the "one making progress" and the "perfect" man. 

Moses, being perfect, completely rejected the pleasure of food and *washed the belly and the feet with water* <note>Leviticus 8:21</note>. By "belly" he hints at pleasure, and by "feet" he hints at the steps and progress of the soul. But the one making progress washes *the things inside* the belly, not the whole belly itself. There is a great difference between "he washed" and "they shall wash." One is a voluntary act; the other occurs by command. For the perfect man must move toward acts of virtue with self-commanded zeal, while the one making progress obeys the exhortation of his leader. 

Observe very carefully that while he removes the breast-piece entirely, he does not remove the belly, but only washes it. For the wise man is able to refuse and cut off all anger; but he is unable to "cut out" the stomach. Nature forces even the most self-controlled person to use necessary food. 

However, in the soul that does not follow right and stable reason, but has been corrupted by adulterous pleasures, the **belly swells** <note>A reference to the "Ordeal of the Bitter Water" in Numbers 5:27, used to test a woman accused of adultery.</note>. This is because even if the body's vessels are overfilled, the desire remains thirsty. Following the swelling of the belly, the **thigh falls away**. For the mind grows weak in the generation of good things when the stomach is inflamed by the luxury of foods, and it becomes paralyzed toward spiritual toils. The law's discourse hinted at these toils through the symbol of the "thigh." 

Therefore, the lover of pleasure "walks on his belly," sinking entirely into indulgent pleasures. The one beginning the virtuous life removes the **fat** <note>original: στέαρ (stear) — the fat of the sacrificial animal, here transcribed as "phtear" (well/pit), but likely meaning the fatty tissue.</note> of the belly, refusing the foods that fatten the body. The one making progress washes the things inside the belly; and the perfect man washes the whole thing.

<summary>St. Neilos uses allegories from the Levitical priesthood and the book of Numbers to explain the hierarchy of passions, identifying gluttony as the root of anger and greed, and explaining how different stages of asceticism handle these physical drives.</summary>
<keywords>gluttony, anger, Moses, asceticism, breastplate of judgment, belly, thigh, passions, spiritual progress, Leviticus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of St. Neilos the Ascetic on the struggle against the passions. Having established that "sitting" in bad habits defiles the soul, Neilos now explores the biological and spiritual link between gluttony and lust, using allegorical interpretations of the Old Testament to champion the ascetic life of the desert.</meta>

### AN ASCETIC DISCOURSE ###

...the stomach, completely casting away those things that exceed necessary needs. Very aptly, the phrase "you shall go" is attached to the breast and the stomach; for **pleasure** <term>hēdonē: in this context, sensory gratification that distracts from spiritual goals</term> does not belong to those who stand firm and are at rest, but to those who are in motion and full of turmoil. Rather, even before these things, the movement of sexual desire is closely related to **gluttony** <term>gastrimargia: literally "stomach-madness," the first of the capital vices</term>. Wherefore nature, wishing to show the kinship of these passions, placed the reproductive organs below the stomach, signifying their close relationship by their proximity. 

For if this passion of lust is weak, it is weak because of the lack of what lies above it <note>meaning: a lack of food in the stomach</note>; but if it is vigorous and stirred up, it draws its power from being supplied from there. Gluttony is not only the nurse and nourisher of these, but it is also by nature the destroyer of all good things. For when gluttony rules and holds the beginning, good things naturally fall and are destroyed: **self-control** <gloss>enkrateia</gloss>, **temperance** <gloss>sōphrosynē</gloss>, **courage** <gloss>andria</gloss>, **endurance** <gloss>karteria</gloss>, and all the remaining virtues. 

This was indicated enigmatically by **Jeremiah**, when he said: *The chief cook of the Babylonians tore down the wall of Jerusalem roundabout* <note>Jeremiah 52:12-14. Neilos is allegorizing Nebuzaradan, the "captain of the guard," whose title in the Septuagint Greek is "archimageiros" or "Chief Cook."</note>. He called the passion of gluttony the "chief cook." For just as a chief cook puts all his effort into serving the stomach and devises arts, crafting ten thousand pleasures, so gluttony moves every machine, serving the pleasure of the throat. The variety of foods tears down and levels the fortification of the virtues. For seasonings and condiments become like siege engines and **battering rams** <term>helepoleis: massive mobile siege towers used in ancient warfare</term> against a virtue already well-established, shaking and casting its firmness and stability to the ground. 

Just as luxury is destructive of virtues, so again **frugality** <term>euteleia: a simple, inexpensive way of life</term> is naturally able to dissolve the fortifications of vice. For just as the wall of Jerusalem—representing the peaceful soul—was torn down by the Babylonian chief cook, who broke through the pleasures of the flesh with the art of fine cooking; so also a *rolling barley loaf of the Israelites* threw down the tents of the Midianites <note>Judges 7:13; in Gideon's dream, a humble barley loaf destroys the enemy camp.</note>. For a simple diet, rolling and advancing for a long time, dissolves the passions of **fornication**. For the Midianites bear the symbol of the passions of lust; for they were the ones who brought sexual immorality upon Israel and deceived a great

<column-break/>

multitude of the young. Very aptly, the Scripture describes the Midianites as having **tents**, but Jerusalem as having a **wall**. For all things that encompass virtue are fixed and firm; but those things that hold vice together are a mere form and a tent, differing nothing from phantoms. 

Because of this, the saints fled the cities and avoided the company of the masses. Rather, they knew that living with corrupt men was a more destructive thing than a plague. Because of this, taking nothing for themselves, they left their possessions as sheep-pastures, refusing the distraction that comes from such things. Because of this, **Elijah**, leaving Judea, lived on Mount Carmel, which was a desert and full of wild beasts; and besides the trees, it had nothing for the consolation of food. He was satisfied, then, with the wild fruits of these trees, fulfilling the necessity of nature. 

**Elisha**, likewise, followed the same way of life, inheriting from his teacher—among other good things—a love for staying in the deserts. And **John**, dwelling in the desert of the Jordan, ate locusts and wild honey, showing the many how little the body truly needs, and reproaching them for their calculated pursuit of enjoyment. Perhaps also **Moses** sets such a law universally, commanding the Israelites concerning the **Manna**, to gather only each day's portion for that day. He was secretly commanding that human life should be "of the day" <note>ephemeral; focused on the present</note> and not preoccupied with hoarding. He believed it appropriate for a rational nature to be satisfied with what is at hand and to acknowledge God as the steward of all else. 

For those who make provision for the future only appear to distrust God's graces, as if the eternal gifts would not always rain down upon men. To say it briefly: because of this, all the saints, *of whom the world was not worthy*, left the inhabited world, wandering in deserts, and mountains, and caves, and the holes of the earth; and they *went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, tormented* <note>Hebrews 11:37-38</note>. They were fleeing the habitual vices of men and the strange things overflowing in the cities, so that they might not be carried away by the rush of the current—as if by the violence of a mountain stream—into the indifferent dissipation of the many; but rather, rejoicing...

<summary>Neilos provides an allegorical interpretation of gluttony as the "chief cook" who destroys the soul's defenses, while advocating for the "barley loaf" of frugality and the desert life of prophets like Elijah and John the Baptist.</summary>

<meta>This page continues St. Neilos the Ascetic’s discourse on the spiritual life. Having previously discussed how gluttony and physical passions weigh down the soul, Neilos now contrasts the treachery of human society with the simplicity of the desert. He uses the biblical figures of Daniel and the "wild donkey" from Job to advocate for a life of ascetic detachment.</meta>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...living with wild beasts, judging the harm from them to be less than the harm from men. They flee from men as conspirators, yet they trust the beasts as friends; for those beasts do not teach wickedness, and they stand in awe of and honor virtue. Thus, for instance, humans sought to destroy **Daniel**, but the lions preserved him. They protected the one who had been unjustly condemned out of envy; and while justice was subverted among men, the beasts themselves proclaimed the correct judgment concerning the one unjustly condemned. And so the man's virtue became a cause for envy and strife among men, but a reason for reverence and honor among the beasts. 

Therefore, let all in whom the desire for improvement has been sown emulate the virtues of the saints, and departing from the slavery of the body's commands, let us pursue **freedom** <gloss>eleutheria</gloss>. And concerning the **wild donkey** <note>original: "agrios onos" — a reference to Job 39:5-8, often used by desert fathers to symbolize the soul freed from worldly social constraints</note> left in the desert by the Creator, which does not hear the shouting of the tax collector and mocks the city's crowds—even if until now we have prepared it for burden-bearing by yoking it to passions and vices—let us now at least loose its bonds. And even if those who are not its masters by nature, but who have acquired lordship through habit <note>referring to the passions that take control of us through repetitive bad habits</note>, should object, let them hear us saying—not with the tongue alone and a bare voice, but with a settled disposition—that "the Lord has need of it" <note>Matthew 21:3. Neilos is allegorizing the donkey that carried Christ into Jerusalem as the human soul/body being reclaimed for God's use</note>. Immediately they will send it, so that, adorned with the **apostolic garments** <gloss>meaning: the teachings and virtues of the apostles</gloss>, it may become a vehicle for the **Word** <term>Logos: the Divine Reason or Christ himself</term>. Or, released into its ancient pasture, let it seek after "every green thing" <note>Job 39:8</note>; which means following the flourishing words of **Holy Scripture**, to be led into a blameless life, harvesting both nourishment and great delight at once. 

At the same time, we must also ask how the wild donkey, left by God in the desert, seeks after "every green thing" while living in the wilderness and having its dwelling in the salt-land—since the salt-land and the desert are, for the most part, not at all suitable for the growth of grass. Unless, perhaps, someone should say that the "desert of passions" is sufficient to seek the **contemplation** <term>theōria: the spiritual practice of "seeing" God through prayer and scripture</term> found in divine words, after the moisture of the passions has been consumed. Let us leave behind worldly affairs and look up toward the goods of the soul. How long shall we remain with these litigious playthings, never taking up a courageous mindset?

<column-break/>

How long shall we behave more weakly than those who are quite literally infants, not even being led by them by the hand toward progress in greater things? When those children change in age, they also change their attitude toward games, and they easily let go of their attachment to material things. For nuts, perhaps, and knucklebones, and balls are the materials of their play; and they are devoted to these as long as they have an incomplete understanding, and they consider these things precious. But if one progresses and becomes a man, he throws those things away and takes hold of serious business with great diligence. 

We, however, have remained in infancy, marveling at things worthy of play and mockery; and leaving aside the pursuit of better concerns and the adoption of a logic fitting for men, we trudge along in **earthly pleasures**, providing laughter to those who judge things according to the natural order. For just as it is shameful to see a grown man sitting in the ashes and drawing the delights of children in the dust, so it is shameful—and much more shameful—to see those who are negotiating for the enjoyment of **eternal goods** rolling in the ashes of earthly things, shaming the perfection of their calling by the unsuitability of their pursuits. 

The cause of this for us, it seems, is that we perceive nothing greater than what is seen; nor, by comparing the cheapness of present things, do we recognize the excellence of the goods there, before being blinded by the brilliance of those things here that seem precious and binding our desire to them. For always, by the absence of better things, the worse things are honored, inheriting the rank of the former. If we had a higher conception of the things to come, we would not continue staring open-mouthed at these present things. 

Let us begin, therefore, to withdraw from the present. Let us despise possessions and money, and all the things that drown the mind and pull it under the surface. Let us cast off the cargo, and the ship will rise up a little. While we are in the storm, let us even throw out most of the gear, so that the **pilot-mind** <gloss>kybernētēs nous: the intellect acting as the navigator of the soul</gloss> might be able to be saved along with the thoughts sailing within. For if those sailing the sea, when caught in a storm, despise their trade-goods and with their own hands throw the cargo into the sea, judging their possessions second to their life...

<summary>Neilos uses the story of Daniel and the allegory of the wild donkey to argue that the desert and its "beasts" are safer for the soul than human society. He calls for spiritual maturity, urging believers to cast off worldly possessions like a ship's captain jettisoning cargo during a storm to save the vessel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Ascetic Discourse" of St. Neilos the Ascetic. In the previous section, Neilos spoke of how desert-dwelling saints find more peace among wild beasts than among treacherous men. He now shifts to a metaphor of the spiritual life as a voyage and an athletic contest, emphasizing the necessity of "nakedness" (detachment from material possessions and worldly worries) to defeat the devil.</meta>

# THE ASCETIC DISCOURSE #

...and so that the ship, being overfilled, does not risk sinking under the weight of its cargo, they lighten it, perhaps casting even their most precious treasures into the depths. Why then do we not also, for the sake of the better life, despise those things that drag the soul down into the abyss? Why is the fear of God not as powerful as the fear of the sea? Those sailors, desiring this temporary life, do not consider the loss of their goods a great matter. But we, though we claim to strive for eternal life, do not despise even the most trivial things; rather, we choose to perish along with our heavy burden rather than be saved by being deprived of those things.

Let us strip off everything, I urge you; for our opponent stands naked. Do those who compete in the games do so while clothed? The law of the athlete brings them into the stadium naked. Whether it is hot or cold, they enter in this way, leaving their garments outside. If any of them refuses to be naked, he has also refused the contest. But we, who profess to be athletes and who struggle against opponents far more agile than any we can perceive with our senses, not only have we not stripped off, but we attempt to compete while carrying ten thousand burdens upon our shoulders, giving our opponents many handles against us. 

For how shall he box against "the spiritual forces of evil" <note>original: "pneumatika tēs ponērias" — a reference to Ephesians 6:12</note>, who strives for possessions and is easily struck from every side? How shall he wrestle the spirit of avarice who is girded with money? How shall he run against the demons—who are naked of every concern—when he is clothed in ten thousand worries? For the Divine Scripture says, "the naked man shall pursue on that day"; the naked man, not the one clothed in the heavy, patchwork rags of worldly affairs; the naked man, not the one whose path is blocked by the many-layered thoughts of possessions and money. For the naked man is difficult to catch, or even impossible to capture, by those who plot against him. Indeed, if the great **Joseph** <note>the biblical Joseph, son of Jacob</note> had been truly "naked" [in spirit], the Egyptian woman would not have found anything to grab hold of, as the Divine word says: "she caught hold of his garments, saying: 'Sleep with me.'" <note>Genesis 39:12</note> These garments represent physical things, by which pleasure takes hold and pulls us; and anyone who clings to these must necessarily be dragged around while fighting those who would take them away. This athlete of self-control <term>sophrosyne</term> <note>a Greek virtue meaning temperance or soundness of mind</note>, as...

<column-break/>

...he saw himself being pulled by force toward the fellowship and union of pleasure, even through the necessary needs of the body; having learned that he must live naked in the presence of the mistress who was able to seize and force him, he left his garments and fled. He went outside, just as if he were in Paradise, walking about in virtue while naked, in imitation of the first-created man [Adam]. Adam had received nakedness from God as a special gift of honor, until through disobedience he came to need clothing. As long as he fought against the opponents who advised him to break God's commandment, he stood naked, like an athlete in the arena <term>skamma</term> <note>the dug-up ground or pit where ancient Greek wrestlers and jumpers competed</note>. But having been defeated and becoming full of distress, he naturally put on clothes, laying aside his nakedness along with his athletic character. 

For this reason, the writer of Proverbs says to the trainer: "Take away his garment, for he has passed by." <note>Neilos adapts Proverbs 20:16 to his athletic metaphor: once a person enters the "arena" of spiritual life, they must be stripped of worldly attachments</note> For as long as he was outside the stadium, he rightly used the clothes of those who do not compete, hiding his athletic courage behind physical garments. But since he has entered the contest, "take away his garment," for one must compete naked. Or rather, not only naked, but also anointed with oil. Being naked makes the athlete untouchable to his opponent; and the oil, even if he should be grabbed, makes him slip out of the grip. 

For this reason, opponents strive to throw "dust" <term>konis</term> <note>sand or dust used in ancient wrestling to provide a grip on an oiled body</note> at their rivals, so that by roughening the smoothness of the oil with dust, they might make them easy to seize. What dust is in that context, earthly things are in our contest; and what oil is there, freedom from care <term>amerimnon</term> is here. And just as there the anointed man easily breaks the so-called "knots" (holds), but if he takes on dust, he can hardly escape the hand of his wrestler; so here, the one who has no cares is difficult for the devil to catch. But the one who worries, and who roughens the smoothness of his mind's lack of care with worries—as if with dust—can hardly <margin>* perhaps: "escape"</margin> * escape from his hand. Freedom from care belongs to the perfect soul; but being worn down by worries belongs to the imperfect. For it is said of the perfect soul that it is a "lily among thorns." <note>Song of Songs 2:2</note> This signifies the soul that lives without care in the midst of those who are full of many worries. For the "lily," even in the Gospel, [represents]...

<summary>St. Neilos uses metaphors of sailors lightening a ship and athletes stripping for a race to explain that spiritual victory requires "nakedness"—total detachment from material wealth and worldly anxieties. He cites Joseph’s escape from Potiphar’s wife and Adam’s original nakedness as biblical models for this ascetic ideal.</summary>
