<meta>This page continues the "Ascetic Discourse" of St. Neilos the Ascetic. In the previous section, Neilos compared the spiritual life to an athletic contest, urging the monk to "strip off" worldly possessions to avoid giving the devil a "handle" to grab during the struggle.</meta>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...indicates a carefree soul; for it does not labor, it says, nor does it spin, and yet it is clothed in a glory greater than Solomon's. <note>original: "Solomōntos" — Neilos is quoting Christ’s "Lilies of the Field" sermon from Matthew 6:28-29</note> But concerning those who have great anxiety for bodily things, the whole life of the ungodly is spent in worry. For it is truly impious to extend the care of bodily things throughout one's entire life, and to show no zeal regarding the things of the future; to consume all of one's time on the body, even though it does not require much attention; but for the soul, which has such a great length of progress to make that a whole lifetime is not enough to reach its perfection, to not even allot the chance moment. And if we do seem to allot any time to it, we provide it in an exhausted and sluggish manner, being lured away by the brilliance of visible things. We suffer the same fate as those hooked by the most hideous prostitutes, who, due to their lack of genuine beauty, create a counterfeit one to entrap those who look upon them, correcting their deformity through the clever use of cosmetics. For once we have been defeated by the vanity of present things, we are unable to see the shame of matter, being cheated by our own attachments. And for this reason, we do not stop at what is necessary; but having set up "satiety" <note>original: "koron" — the state of being overfilled or glutted</note> as the tyrant of our life, we rest upon all kinds of possessions. We do not see that the measure of possession is the **need of the body**. Whatever exceeds this is henceforth a disorder, and no longer a necessity. For just as a tunic that is measured to the body is both a necessity and an ornament, but one that flows everywhere, tangling the feet and dragging on the ground, becomes—besides being unseemly—an obstacle to every task; so too the possession that exceeds the body's need is both an obstacle to virtue and earns great condemnation among those who are able to investigate the nature of things. Therefore, one should neither listen to those deceived by sensory things, nor should one mindlessly follow those who have become attached to earthly things because they did not pay attention to the things of the mind. For it is the same as using the blind as judges of color, or the deaf as judges of musical notes, since they are deprived of the criteria for the things being judged. One should not trust these people, as if they had chosen the enjoyment of present things according to reason; for they are blind, having their reason <note>original: "logismon" — the faculty of rational judgment</note>, which is the most necessary criterion,

<column-break/>

filled [with darkness], by which we are naturally meant to judge between what is excellent and what is indifferent. One of these was Achar <note>original: "Achar" — In the Septuagint, the biblical Achan (Joshua 7) is called Achar. He stole forbidden spoils and hid them in his tent.</note>, the son of Charmi; he confessed to Joshua in the "tent of life" <note>original: "Iēsou" — The Greek name for Joshua and Jesus is identical; Neilos is referring to Joshua 7:19-21.</note> that he had hidden the stolen things under the earth, and beneath these, he had buried the silver. For the man who judges the various and bright things of matter to be superior, and buries his **reason** beneath them, is reasonably deceived like a mindless animal, yielding and giving in to the imagination of whatever pleases him. This happens because **reason** has been cast down from its ruling thrones and has been placed instead in the rank of the subject criminals. For if reason were established in its proper rank, and entrusted with the judgment of visible things, it would have brought forth a just and upright verdict, punishing the impulse that ran toward deceptive things. It is good, therefore, to remain within the limits of necessity, and to strive with all one's might not to exceed them. For if one is carried away even a little by desire toward the "sweet things" of life, no reason can henceforth stop the forward momentum. For there is no limit to that which is beyond necessity; rather, foolish zeal and endless vanity-labor increase the desire for such things perpetually, feeding the appetite just as a flame is fed by the addition of fuel. For once those who have passed the boundaries of natural necessity begin to progress toward a material life, they wish to add "sweet side-dishes" to their bread; and to their water, they add the wine they once needed, and from that, wine that is even more expensive. They cannot bear to follow the standard of necessary clothing, but first, they purchase "bright" wools, selecting the very flower of the fleece; then, they move from these to garments made of a mixture of linen and wool; then, they seek out silks. And these are plain at first, but later they are embroidered with battles, and wild beasts, and all kinds of histories. They also manufacture silver and gold-plated vessels, not only to serve at banquets, but even to extravagantly decorate their animals and beds. And why must I further set forth their untimely ambition, since they extend it even to the most dishonorable of needs? They do not even deign to have the vessels for their excrement fashioned from any other material, unless silver serves even this shameful duty. Such is the nature of...

<summary>St. Neilos warns that exceeding basic bodily necessity leads to a "slippery slope" of greed and vanity, using the biblical figure of Achan to show how material desire buries human reason. He satirizes the progression of luxury from simple food and wool to embroidered silks and even silver chamber pots.</summary>
<keywords>asceticism, luxury, reason (logismos), Achan/Achan, necessity (chreia), vanity, greed, early Christian ethics</keywords>

--- Page 147 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Ascetic Discourse" of St. Neilos the Ascetic. In the previous section, Neilos compared the spiritual life to an athletic contest, urging the monk to "strip off" worldly possessions to avoid giving the devil a "handle" to grab during the struggle.</meta>

### ASCETIC DISCOURSE ###

...pleasure; extending itself to the very extremes, and honoring shameful deeds through the extravagance of matter. To possess such things further is contrary to nature. For the way of life according to nature was defined as the same for both us and the animals by the Creator:

> "Behold," says God to man, "I have given to you every herb of the field; it shall be for food common to you and the wild beasts." <note>original: "idou gar dedōka..." — This is a paraphrase of Genesis 1:29-30, emphasizing a shared, simple diet between humans and animals in Paradise.</note>

Therefore, having received our diet alongside the irrational beasts, yet turning it toward wastefulness through our own inventions, how could we not reasonably be judged more irrational than them? For the beasts remain within the boundaries of nature, disturbing nothing of what was ordained by God. But we, who have been honored with reason, have entirely strayed from the ancient law. What "gourmet dishes" are found among the irrational animals? What bread-making or arts of cooks create pleasures for the miserable <term>gaster (belly)</term>? <note>The word "gaster" refers to the stomach, often used in ascetic texts to represent the passion of gluttony.</note> Do they not love the ancient simplicity, eating grass, sufficing with what is available, and using a little stream for drink—and that perhaps only rarely? Therefore, their carnal pleasures are diminished, as they do not inflame their appetites with any fatty food; nor do they even recognize the difference between male and female [outside of the mating season]. For there is one time of the year that provides them this sensation, when the law of nature found for them a meeting for the sowing of their own kind, for the preservation of the species. But for the rest of the time, they are so estranged from it that they completely forget such an appetite. But for humans, from the extravagance of food, an insatiable desire for <term>aphrodisiōn (sexual pleasures)</term> <note>Literally "the things of Aphrodite," referring to carnal or sexual desires.</note> sprouts up, sowing maddening cravings and allowing the passion no time for rest. Since, therefore, great harm follows from possessions, and it provides the starting point for all passions like a cause of disease, let us remove this cause, if indeed we care for the well-being of the soul. Let us heal the disease of **love of money** through <term>akthemosyne (non-possessiveness)</term>; let us flee the gatherings of useless men, embracing solitude. For living with one's own kin is harmful and destructive to a peaceful state. For just as those who find themselves in plague-ridden air will certainly fall ill, so those who live among indifferent men partake of their...

<column-break/>

...wickedness. For what do those who have renounced the world still have in common with the world? "No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please the one who enlisted him." <note>original: "oudeis gar strateuomenos..." — quoting 2 Timothy 2:4. St. Neilos uses this to argue that a monk must be as single-minded as a soldier.</note> For preoccupation with business hinders military exercises. And if we fight untrained against those experienced in war, how shall we stand? Or rather, if the truth must be told, we fight so sluggishly and loosely that we cannot even resist an enemy who is already down, and those standing are plotted against by the fallen. For we suffer what those in wars do because of a love of money—those who strip the dead, often being killed after the victory by those lying on the ground, and perishing after their triumphs for the sake of base gain. We suffer piteously when we approach an enemy who is lying down and breathing his last. For just as those men, searching the dead out of a desire for money, often approach someone half-dead and, while stripping him, receive a fatal blow in secret and fall, senselessly shaming their glory in victory; so we, when through **temperance** and **continence** we strike down the <note>The "barbarian" here is a metaphor for the Devil or a demonic passion.</note> barbarian—or seem to have struck him down—then, having fallen in love with his garments (which are the things honored by men: wealth, power, health, fame), we draw near to him, longing to take something of his, and thus we die, bringing ourselves to the slaughter. In this way the "five virgins" perished <note>referring to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25:1-13. In Patristic thought, the foolish virgins are often said to have "died" spiritually because they lacked mercy/almsgiving, even though they were chaste.</note>; they killed the enemy through their **purity**, but through a **lack of compassion** which the love of money generates, they pushed themselves onto the sword. The enemy, while lying down, was unable to kill those standing over him [until they reached for his goods]. Let us, therefore, desire nothing of his, lest along with his things we also lose our soul. For he [the devil] calls out for these things even now and encourages everyone, especially if he finds them to be persuasive. For if he called the Lord Himself, saying:

> "All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me" <note>original: "tauta soi panta dōsō..." — quoting the Devil's temptation of Jesus in Matthew 4:9.</note>

and attempted to deceive through the seemingly brilliant things in life Him who had no need of them, how will he not succeed in deceiving easily-captured men, who are already inclined toward the enjoyment of sensory things? Let us **train the mind for godliness**, if indeed bodily training has been set right. For "bodily training is of little pro..."

<summary>St. Neilos argues that human greed and gluttony violate the natural order observed even by animals, leading to uncontrollable carnal desires. He warns that even after a spiritual victory, a monk can be destroyed by "stripping the fallen enemy"—clinging to worldly honors or wealth.</summary>
<keywords>asceticism, nature, gluttony, greed, non-possessiveness, spiritual warfare, military metaphor, St. Neilos the Ascetic, Five Virgins, temptation of Christ</keywords>

--- Page 148 ---
<meta>This page continues St. Neilos the Ascetic’s "Ascetic Discourse." On the previous page, Neilos used the law of nature to argue for a simple diet, comparing human gluttony unfavorably to the natural moderation of animals.</meta>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER NEILOS THE ASCETIC ###

...profitable <note>original: "[ōphe]limos" — This is the conclusion of a quote from 1 Timothy 4:8: "For bodily exercise is profitable for a little."</note>, resembling childhood lessons; but **piety** is beneficial for all things, producing health in the soul for those who desire victory over the opposing passions. For just as it is fitting for athletes training in childhood exercises to discipline the body, to move the limbs continuously, to diligently care for their manly and athletic strength in a competitive spirit, and to be anointed for the sacred contests; so it is the care of those beginning the life of godliness to restrain their actions. For it is a thing to be cherished if they should overcome their passions, which are driven to frenzy by habitual pleasures; and because of habit, they are driven toward evils almost without choice.

But for those who have reached a state of **practical virtue** and are now concerned with the things of the mind, every effort must be made to guard their <term>logismos</term> <note>original: "logismon" — the inner train of thought or reasoning</note>, so that it does not move in a disordered way and fall toward something incomplete. Simply put: for some, the effort is to discipline bodily movements; for others, it is to fetter the impulses of the mind, so as to move rhythmically toward the <term>philosophical</term> <note>In this ascetic context, "philosophy" refers to the disciplined, spiritual way of life rather than academic study.</note> way of living alone, without any worldly imagination distracting the mind from more divine thoughts.

For the entire desire of the godly person must be stretched toward the Beloved, so that human thoughts find no time at all to enact their own passions. For if each passion, when it is moved in one who is overcome, holds the mind fettered, why should not the zeal for virtue also hold the intellect in a state of leisure from all other things? For what sensation of external things does the angry person receive, while fighting in his mind against the image of the one who grieved him? Or the one who desires money, when, snatched away by his imagination, he gazes at the materials for profit? And the immoral person, often while sitting with others, has his senses submerged; having captured the desired face, he converses with it, forgetting those present. He sits like a speechless statue, knowing nothing of what happens before his eyes or what is being said; having leaned toward what is within, he is entirely absorbed by his imagination. Such a soul the Law perhaps calls "sitting apart" <note>The Law (Leviticus 15) uses this term for ritual separation or uncleanness; here Neilos uses it to describe a soul "separated" from reality by its own fantasies.</note>, when, sitting far from the senses, it contracts its own activity, perceiving nothing at all of external things because of the foul imagination holding it captive. But if these things—

<column-break/>

—so master the mind through attachment and cause the senses to be idle, how much more will the love of **philosophy** make the mind renounce both sensible things and the senses themselves, snatching it upward and occupying it with the <term>theoria</term> <note>original: "theōria" — the contemplative vision or direct experience of divine truths.</note> of intelligible things?

For just as a mind that is being cut or burned would not be entered by any thought outside of the prevailing passion because of the dominant pain, so it is impossible for one thinking passionately about anything to have any other thought enter besides the passion holding the mind, which has made the whole mind take on its own quality. For pain does not admit labor; nor does grief admit joy; nor does gloom admit cheerfulness. Nor again does a dominant labor allow pleasure, nor does a prevailing grief have joy yoked with it, nor is gloom mixed with cheerfulness. Instead, opposite passions are intertwined against each other and would never come together in the same place; nor would they lean toward a friendly fellowship because of their naturally irreconcilable enmity and alienation.

Therefore, let not the purity of virtue be muddied by thoughts of worldly affairs, nor let the clarity of **contemplation** be disturbed by bodily cares; so that the image of true philosophy, shining with its own beauty, may no longer be blamed by the "bold-mouthed." Nor let it become a subject of mockery due to the lack of skill of the writers, but rather let it be praised—if not by men, then certainly by the powers above, or by the Master Christ himself, from whom the saints also sought praise. Like the great David, who trampled upon human glory and asked for acclaim from God, saying: *My praise is from You* <note>original: "para sou ho epainos mou" — Psalm 22:25</note>; and: *In the Lord shall my soul be praised.*

For men often slander good things through envy, but the **"theater above"** <note>A common patristic image of the angels and God as the true audience of the monk's life.</note> judges matters impartially and awards the vote to the truth of what is done. Therefore, let this theater be delighted—which must necessarily be delighted by the pleasantness of the works. As for men, who can neither grant rewards for a life well-lived nor punish those who are otherwise, there is not much concern. Even if they, out of envy or prejudice, overshadow the works of virtue with the names of vice, the life known to God and the Angels is not misled...

<summary>Neilos explains that just as passions can totally consume a person's attention, the love of God (spiritual philosophy) should occupy the mind so completely that worldly distractions and physical sensations are ignored. He emphasizes that the monk should seek praise only from the "heavenly theater" rather than from men.</summary>
<keywords>piety, athletes of Christ, logismos, passions, theoria, contemplation, divine praise, King David, heavenly theater, focus</keywords>

...slander with blasphemies; for surely, at the time of recompense, the reward of eternal blessings will follow for those who have lived well—not based on human opinion, but on the very truth of how they lived. Which may we all attain; by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit; now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

# A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## OF THE BLESSED
# DIADOCHOS
### BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal divider consisting of a stylized floral and vine pattern.</image-desc>

---

Our Father among the Saints, Diadochos, who served as the Bishop of Photiki in Old Epirus <note>A region in the northwest of the Greek peninsula and parts of modern Albania.</note> of Illyricum, was an ancient figure. That he lived before the seventh century can be concluded from the works of Saint Maximus <note>Saint Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD), a highly influential theologian.</note>, in which he mentions the chapters written by Diadochos. That he was also a wise man, shining in both **practice** <note>original: "praxis" — the active struggle to acquire virtue and discipline the body.</note> and **contemplation** <note>original: "theoria" — the spiritual vision or deep understanding of divine things.</note>, is clear to anyone who wishes to learn from this surviving discourse of his. Having pursued wisdom through long experience and having "set up ascents in his heart" <note>A reference to Psalm 83:6 in the Septuagint, describing the soul's progress toward God.</note>, he composed this work excellently. He divided it into one hundred chapters, revealing with total precision, so to speak, the deepest mysteries of the virtue of prayer. Indeed, he packed it with scriptural sayings and insights of precise knowledge, leaving behind for almost all the <term>watchful</term> <note>original: "neptikois" — refers to the practice of Nepsis, or spiritual sobriety and alertness of the mind.</note> and God-bearing fathers who came after him a kind of archetype for the teaching of sacred Watchfulness, composed of all the virtues. Because of this, you will find many of them looking frequently to these

<column-break/>

chapters as if at perfectly accurate maps, drawing from them their starting points and quoting their very words as testimony in their own hard-won works on watchfulness. Photius <note>A famous 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople known for his vast library and reviews of ancient books.</note> also mentions these, saying: *Reading 201 <note>original: "sa" — the Greek numeral for 201, referring to the entry in Photius's "Bibliotheca."</note>, page 269.* "To these (namely the ten definitions), the one hundred chapters are subjoined; and this discourse is composed in the best manner for those in training, and for those already practiced in the deeds that bring perfection, it presents no lack of clarity..." Furthermore, the Council <note>Refers to the 14th-century Hesychast councils which defended traditional prayer practices.</note> convened in the presence of Andronikos Palaiologos; Gregory of Thessalonica <note>Saint Gregory Palamas (1296–1357).</note>, Symeon of Thessalonica, Gregory of Sinai; the most holy Kallistos, and many others, bear witness to the blamelessness of these works.

Regarding the hundredth chapter, which Photius mentions as appearing perhaps objectionable <note>Some early readers were confused by Diadochos's descriptions of how grace and sin interact in the soul.</note>, the divine Maximus frees it from such concerns, unfolding its meaning toward the correct goal of piety; as is seen at the end of these works.

BY THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

# DEFINITIONS
## BY THE BLESSED
# DIADOCHOS
## BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' with ornate flourish and radial line patterns.</image-desc>
The definition of **faith** is a state of thinking about God that is free from passions. <note>original: "apathēs" — a state where the mind is not disturbed by worldly desires or emotional turmoil.</note>

<margin>2.</margin>
The definition of **hope** is the departure of the mind toward the things it expects.

<margin>3.</margin>
The definition of **patience** is to persevere unceasingly, seeing the invisible as if it were visible through the eyes of the intellect. <note>original: "dianoia" — the faculty of discursive thought or the mind's eye.</note>

<margin>4.</margin>
The definition of **freedom from greed** is to desire *not* to possess things as much as an ordinary person desires *to* possess them.

<margin>5.</margin>
<margin>* In another manuscript: "toward God."</margin>
The definition of **spiritual knowledge** is to be unaware of oneself while in a state of ecstasy <note>original: "ekstēnai" — literally "standing outside" oneself in a state of divine rapture.</note> toward God.

<column-break/>

<margin>6.</margin>
The definition of **humility** is the immediate forgetting of one's own virtuous achievements.

<margin>7.</margin>
The definition of **freedom from anger** is a great and constant desire not to become angry.

<margin>8.</margin>
The definition of **purity** is a spiritual sense that is always bonded to God.

<margin>9.</margin>
The definition of **love** is the growth of friendship toward those who insult you.

<margin>10.</margin>
The definition of **perfect transformation** in the delight of God is to consider the gloom of death as a thing of joy.

## BY THE SAME
## BLESSED
# DIADOCHOS
## BISHOP OF PHOTIKI
### OF OLD EPIRUS IN ILLYRICUM.

->ASCETIC DISCOURSE, DIVIDED INTO 100 PRACTICAL CHAPTERS OF KNOWLEDGE AND SPIRITUAL DISCERNMENT.<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Brothers, let **faith**, **hope**, and **love** lead every spiritual contemplation—but love most of all. For while the first two teach us how to rightly despise visible things, love joins the soul itself to the virtues of God, tracking the Invisible One with noetic <note>original: "noera" — relating to the 'nous' or the highest part of the human spirit capable of direct experience of God.</note> perception.

<margin>2.</margin>
God alone is good by nature. But

<column-break/>

man also becomes good through the cultivation of his character, by means of the One who is truly good. In this state, he remains unchanging when the soul, through the cultivation of what is beautiful, becomes established in God to the degree that its active power wills. For He says: "Become good and merciful, as your Father who is in heaven is." <note>A variation of Matthew 5:48 and Luke 6:36.</note>

<summary>This page presents ten concise definitions of Christian virtues by St. Diadochos and begins his "One Hundred Chapters," emphasizing that man becomes good by participating in God's goodness.</summary>
<keywords>Diadochos of Photiki, definitions of virtue, faith, hope, love, humility, asceticism, Epirus, spiritual knowledge, noetic perception, theosis</keywords>

--- Page 151 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Ascetic Discourse" of Saint Diadochos of Photiki. Having provided short definitions of virtues on the previous page, he now moves into deeper theological and psychological reflections on the nature of evil, the "image and likeness" of God, and the distinction between spiritual knowledge and wisdom. This text is foundational to the Philokalia and Eastern Christian asceticism.</meta>

-># ASCETIC DISCOURSE<-

<margin>3.</margin>
Evil does not exist in nature, nor is anyone evil by nature; for God did not create anything evil. But when someone, through the desire of the heart, gives form to that which has no actual substance, then it begins to exist exactly as the one doing so intends it to. Therefore, one ought to always disregard the habit of evil through the diligent remembrance of God. For the nature of the good is more powerful than the habit of evil, because the former truly exists, while the latter does not—except only when it is being practiced. <note>Diadochos argues that evil is not a "thing" created by God, but a "lack of being" or a choice made by human will. This is a common theme in early Christian philosophy known as the "privation of the good."</note>

<margin>4.</margin>
All humans are made in the **image** of God, but to be in the **likeness** of God belongs only to those who, through great love, have enslaved their own freedom to God. For when we are no longer our own, we become like Him who reconciled us to Himself through love. No one can achieve this unless they first persuade their soul not to be intimidated by the trivial glory of this life. <note>The "Image" is seen as the inherent human potential (rationality and free will), while the "Likeness" is the actualized state of holiness achieved through a life of virtue.</note>

<margin>5.</margin>
**Self-determination** <term>original: "autexousiotētos" — the power of free choice or self-governance</term> is the will of a rational soul, moving readily toward whatever it desires. Let us persuade it to move only toward the good, so that we may always consume the memory of evil with good <margin>* In another [manuscript]: "good thoughts" or "benevolences"</margin> * memories.

<margin>6.</margin>
The light of true knowledge is to discern without stumbling between good and evil. For then the path of righteousness, leading the mind toward God, the <margin>*Sun</margin> * of Righteousness, introduces it into an infinite illumination of knowledge, so that it may henceforth seek love with boldness. One must, therefore, snatch what is right with a calm anger from those who dare to insult it. For the zeal of piety proves its victory not by hating, but by correcting.

<margin>7.</margin>
Spiritual discourse <note>original: "logos" — can mean speech, reason, or a divine word.</note> satisfies the intellectual sense; for it is carried from God through the energy of love. Because of this, our mind remains untroubled in its theological movements. For it does not then suffer the poverty that brings about anxiety, since it is expanded by contemplations as much as the energy of love desires. It is good, therefore, to always wait in faith for the illumination to speak, through love being put into action; for nothing is poorer than a mind, apart from God, philosophizing on the things of God.

<margin>8.</margin>
Neither should one who is unillumined attempt spiritual contemplations, nor indeed should one who is richly illuminated by the kindness

<column-break/>

of the All-Holy Spirit come to the act of speaking. For where there is poverty, it brings ignorance; but where there is wealth, it does not permit one to speak. For then the soul, intoxicated with the love of God, wishes to enjoy the glory of the Lord with a silent voice. One must, therefore, observe the middle state of this spiritual energy before entering into divine speech. This measure grants a certain form of glorious words to the soul. The abundance of illumination nourishes faith, so that the one speaking in faith may be the first to taste the fruit through the love of knowledge. The laboring farmer must be the first to partake of the fruits. <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:6, suggesting that the teacher must experience the spiritual truths before sharing them with others.</note>

<margin>9.</margin>
Both **wisdom** and **knowledge** are gifts of the one Holy Spirit, as are all the divine gifts. Yet each of them has its own unique operation. Therefore, to one is given wisdom, and to another knowledge, according to the same Spirit, as the Apostle bears witness. <note>Refers to 1 Corinthians 12:8.</note> For knowledge joins a person to God through experience, without moving the soul to express the reasons for things. Because of this, some who practice the solitary life <note>original: "monērē bion" — the monastic or eremitic life.</note> are illuminated by it in their perception, yet they do not proceed to divine speech. **Wisdom**, however, if it is given to someone along with knowledge in fear (though this is rare), reveals the very inner workings of that knowledge in love. For the one usually illuminates through action, and the other through speech. Knowledge is brought by prayer and much stillness in complete freedom from care, while wisdom comes from the humble study of the Spirit's oracles—and above all, the grace of God who gives it.

<margin>10.</margin>
When the irascible part <note>original: "thymōdes" — the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, or drive.</note> of the soul is moved against the passions, one should know that it is a time for silence, for it is the hour of battle. But when one sees that disturbance brought into a calm, whether through prayer or through acts of mercy, let them be moved by the desire for words, securing the wings of the mind with the bond of humility. For unless one humbles oneself greatly through self-abasement, they cannot discourse on the majesty of God.

<margin>11.</margin>
Spiritual discourse always preserves the soul from vainglory. For by benefiting all its parts with the perception of light, it makes the soul have no need for honor from men. Therefore, it always keeps the intellect free from fantasies, as it transforms the whole mind into love...

<summary>This page explores the nature of evil as a non-substantial choice and details the psychological requirements for spiritual teaching, specifically distinguishing between experiential knowledge (gnosis) and the ability to express it (wisdom).</summary>
<keywords>evil as privation, image and likeness, free will, autexousiotetos, gnosis vs wisdom, stillness, irascible power, humility, spiritual discourse</keywords>

--- Page 152 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Ascetic Discourse" of Saint Diadochos of Photiki. On the previous page, Diadochos discussed the nature of free will and the distinction between the "image" and "likeness" of God. Here, he explores the transition from worldly wisdom to divine love, the necessity of humility, and the spiritual "perception" (aisthesis) of the heart.</meta>

-># OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI<-

...of God. But the word of the wisdom of the world always calls a person toward self-glory. For since it cannot provide benefit through the experience of spiritual perception, it grants a "friendship of praises" to its own followers, being a fabrication of vainglorious men. Therefore, we shall unerringly recognize such a disposition of the Word of God, if in carefree silence we spend the hours of not speaking, remaining in the warm remembrance of God.

<margin>12.</margin>
He who loves himself cannot love God; but he who does not love himself because of the surpassing wealth of the love of God, this person loves God. Therefore, such a person never seeks his own glory, but the glory of God. For he who loves himself seeks his own glory, but he who loves God loves the glory of Him who made him. For it is characteristic of a soul that is perceptive and God-loving to always seek the glory of God in all the commandments it performs, but to delight in its own humiliation. For glory is fitting for God because of His majesty, but humility is fitting for man, so that through it we may be made intimate with God. If we also do this, following the example of the Holy Baptist John, rejoicing in the glory of the Lord, let us begin to say unceasingly: <note>original: "ἐκεῖνον δεῖ ὑψοῦσθαι, ἡμᾶς δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι" — He must increase, but we must decrease (John 3:30).</note>

<margin>13.</margin>
<margin>alternately still mourning</margin>
I know someone who loves God so much and yearns for Him—though he feels he does not love Him as much as he wishes—that his soul is unceasingly in such a warm desire that God may be glorified in him, while he himself might be as if he did not even exist. This person neither knows what he is, nor does he delight in the praises of words. For through the great desire for humility, he does not even consider his own worth. Instead, he serves God as the law requires of priests, and with a great disposition of love for God, he "steals" from himself the memory of his own dignity. He hides the boast that comes from this in the depths of the love of God, in a spirit of humility; so that he always appears in his own mind as an "unprofitable servant." <note>A reference to Luke 17:10: "So you also, when you have done everything you were told to do, should say, 'We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.'"</note> He acts as if he were entirely a stranger to his own worth through the desire for humility. This we also must do, fleeing all honor and glory because of the surpassing wealth of the love of the Lord who so loves us.

<margin>14.</margin>
He who loves God with the perception of the heart is known by Him. For as much as 

<column-break/>

one receives the love of God in the perception of the soul, so much does one dwell in the love of God. Therefore, such a person will not cease reaching out for the illumination of knowledge with a certain intense passion, until he perceives even the strength of his bones being consumed. He no longer knows himself, but is entirely transformed by the love of God. Such a person is present in this life and yet is not in it. For while still residing in his own body, he departs from it through love by the movement of the soul unceasingly toward God. For henceforth, being unremittingly burned by the fire of love, his heart is joined to God by a certain necessity of longing. Having once stepped out of self-love for the love of God; as it says, <note>original: "εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν, Θεῷ, εἴτε σωφρονοῦμεν, ὑμῖν" — For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you (2 Corinthians 5:13).</note>

<margin>15.</margin>
When one begins to perceive the love of God abundantly, then one begins in the perception of the spirit to also love one's neighbor; for this is the love about which all the Holy Scriptures speak. For friendship according to the flesh is very easily dissolved when some slight cause is found, because it is not bound by the perception of the spirit. Because of this, even if some irritation occurs in a soul energized by God, the bond of love is not dissolved in it. For rekindling itself by the warmth of the love of God, the soul is immediately called back more quickly to the good, and with much joy it receives the love of the neighbor even if it has been greatly insulted or harmed by them; for in the sweetness of God it entirely consumes the bitterness of strife.

<margin>16.</margin>
No one can love God with all their heart without first having feared Him with the perception of the heart; for as the soul is purified and softened through the activity of fear, it comes to an active love. No one can come to the fear of God in the aforementioned way unless they become free of all worldly cares. For when the mind is in great stillness and freedom from care, then the fear of God "troubles" <note>Diadochos uses "troubles" or "disturbs" (ochlei) here in a positive sense, like a medicinal agitation that clears away spiritual lethargy.</note> it, purifying it with much perception from all earthly "density," so that it may lead it into a great love for the goodness of God. Thus fear belongs to the righteous who are still being purified with a moderate amount of love; but perfect love belongs to those already purified in...

<summary>This page explores the internal transformation from self-love to the "perception" of divine love, emphasizing that true love for God requires deep humility and the rejection of worldly glory. Diadochos also describes how spiritual love for God naturally extends to a resilient love for one's neighbor and identifies the fear of God as the necessary precursor to perfect love.</summary>

-># ASCETIC DISCOURSE<-

...in whom there is no fear; for **perfect love**, it says, **casts out fear**. <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ τελεία ἀγάπη, φησίν, ἔξω βάλλει τὸν φόβον" — 1 John 4:18.</note> Both, however, belong to the righteous alone, those who work out the virtues through the energy of the Holy Spirit. For this reason, in one place Scripture says, *fear the Lord, all you His saints,* <note>Psalm 34:9</note> and in another, *love the Lord, all you His holy ones,* <note>Psalm 31:23</note> so that we may clearly learn that the fear of God belongs to those righteous ones who are still being purified—accompanied by a moderate amount of love, as has been said—while perfect love belongs to those who have already been purified. In these latter ones, there is no longer any thought of fear, but an unceasing burning and a clinging of the soul to God through the energy of the Holy Spirit, according to the one who said: *my soul clings close behind you; your right hand has upheld me.* <note>Psalm 63:8</note>

<margin>17.</margin>
Just as wounds occurring on the body, when they have become calloused and neglected, do not feel the medicine applied to them by physicians; but once they have been cleaned, they feel the action of the medicine and thereby arrive at a complete healing; so also the soul, as long as it remains neglected and entirely covered by the leprosy of the love of pleasure, cannot feel the fear of God, even if someone should unceasingly proclaim to it the fearful and powerful judgment of God. However, when it begins to be purified through great attentiveness, it then feels the divine fear as a kind of medicine of life, burning it, as it were, through the energy of its rebukes in a fire of **dispassion** <term>apatheia: a state of holy detachment where the soul is no longer enslaved by turbulent passions</term>. From this point on, as it is purified part by part, it reaches the perfection of purification, increasing in love as much as it decreases in fear, so that it may thus arrive at perfect love, in which, as has been said, there is no fear, but total dispassion enacted through the glory of God. Let our unceasing "boast of boasts" be, first, the fear of God, and finally, love—the fulfillment of the law of perfection in Christ.

<margin>18.</margin>
A soul that has not been released from worldly cares will neither love God genuinely nor loathe the devil as he deserves. For it has, for a time, a burdensome veil: the anxiety of this life. Hence, in such people, the **mind** <term>nous: the "eye of the soul" or the faculty of spiritual perception</term> cannot recognize its own internal court of justice, so that it might judge with-

<column-break/>

-out error the votes of its own judgment. Therefore, withdrawal from all things is useful.

<margin>19.</margin>
The hallmarks of a pure soul are: abundant speech <note>Referring here to spiritual discourse or prayer</note>, innocent zeal, and an unceasing longing for the Lord of Glory. At that point, the mind also accurately adjusts its own scales, presiding over its own thoughts as if in a most pure court of justice.

<margin>20.</margin>
Faith without works and work without faith will be rejected in the same way. For the believer, in demonstrating faith, must offer his deeds to the Lord. For even to our father Abraham, faith was not reckoned as righteousness unless he had offered the fruit of it: his son.

<margin>21.</margin>
The one who loves God both believes genuinely and performs the works of faith holily. But the one who only believes and does not abide in love does not even possess the faith he thinks he has. For he believes with a certain lightness of mind, as one who is not energized by the weight of the glory of love. Therefore, **faith active through love** is the great summary of the virtues.

<margin>22.</margin>
The depth of faith, when searched out, becomes turbulent; but when viewed with a simple disposition, it becomes calm. For the "water of the forgetting of evils" <note>An allusion to the waters of baptism or spiritual peace</note> in the depths of faith does not allow itself to be viewed by meddling thoughts. Therefore, with simplicity of mind, let us sail upon these same waters, so that we may thus arrive at the harbor of the will of God.

<margin>23.</margin>
No one can love or believe genuinely unless he holds himself as his own accuser. For when our **conscience** <term>syneidesis: the internal moral awareness</term> disturbs itself with rebukes, the mind is no longer permitted to sense the fragrance of super-worldly goods, but is immediately divided by doubt. It yearns with a warm movement because of its previous experience of faith, but it is no longer able to grasp it in the perception of the heart through love, because of the frequent stings, as I said, of the rebuking conscience. Nevertheless, having purified ourselves with warmer attentiveness, we shall, after more experience in God, obtain the object of our desire.

<margin>24.</margin>
Just as the senses of the body are somehow forcibly urged toward things that appear beautiful to us, so also the senses of the mind are accustomed to be guided toward invisible goods when the mind tastes of the divine. For everything certainly yearns for its own kin: the soul, being incorporeal, yearns for the heavenly...

### OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

...of good things, while the body is like the dust of earthly luxury. Thus, we shall come to the experience of immaterial sensation <note>original: "αἰσθήσεως" (aisthesis) — here referring to a spiritual "sense" or direct perception of God</note> without error, if indeed we refine our physical nature through our ascetic labors.

<margin>25.</margin>
That there is but one natural sensation, the very action of holy knowledge <term>γνῶσις (gnosis): spiritual insight or experiential knowledge of God</term> teaches us. However, this sensation was later divided into two modes of operation because of Adam's disobedience. One mode is simple and occurs within the soul through the Holy Spirit. No one can know this mode except those who, for the sake of the hope of future goods, gladly distance themselves from the "good things" of this life and who, through self-control <term>ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia): mastery over one’s desires and bodily needs</term>, wither every appetite of the physical senses. For in these people alone is the mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the 'eye of the heart' in Eastern Christian tradition</note> able to move vigorously because it is free from worldly care, and it is thus able to perceive divine goodness in an inexpressible way. Then, according to the measure of its own progress, it shares its inherent joy even with the body, rejoicing with an infinite longing in the love of its confession to God. For regarding this it says:
> *My heart hoped in him, and I was helped; and my flesh flourished again, and with my will I shall give thanks to him.* <note>Psalm 28:7</note>
For the joy that then truly occurs in the soul and the body is a reliable reminder of the incorruptible life.

<margin>26.</margin>
Those who are struggling must always keep their understanding <note>original: "διάνοια" (dianoia) — the discursive or reasoning faculty of the mind</note> as calm as a sea without waves. In this way, the mind can distinguish between the thoughts that pass through it: it stores the good, God-sent thoughts in the treasuries of the memory, while it casts the sinister, demonic thoughts out from the storehouses of nature. For a calm sea allows those who hunt for fish to see all the way to its depths, so that almost nothing escapes them of the paths of the creatures moving there. But when the sea is disturbed by winds, it hides in the gloom of the storm that which it took pride in showing during the "smile" of the calm. In such times, we see that the skill of those who devise fishing-snares becomes useless. This is exactly what happens to the contemplative mind when the depths of the soul are disturbed, especially by unjust anger.

<margin>27.</margin>
It belongs to very few to accurately recognize all their own failings, and only to those whose minds are never snatched away from the memory of God. For just as our physical eyes, when they are

<column-break/>

healthy, can see everything—even gnats or mosquitoes flying in the air—but when they are clouded by discharge or covered by certain humors, they see large things only dimly and cannot perceive small things at all through the sense of sight; so it is with the soul. If, through careful attention, it thins out the blindness caused by "love of the world" <note>original: "φιλοκοσμία" (philokosmia) — an attachment to material existence and worldly values</note>, it considers even its very small failings to be exceedingly great, and it offers tear after tear with much gratitude and without ceasing. For it says:
> *The righteous shall give thanks to your name.* <note>Psalm 140:13</note>
But if the soul remains in a worldly state of mind, it only slightly perceives if it commits something murderous or something worthy of heavy punishment. Of its other failings, it can signal nothing; instead, it often considers its faults to be achievements. Therefore, the wretched soul is not ashamed to speak warmly in defense of them.

<margin>28.</margin>
To purify the mind is the work of the Holy Spirit alone. For unless "the strong man" <note>A reference to Matthew 12:29</note> enters and plunders and binds the thief, the loot will in no way be set free. Therefore, through all things—and even more through the peace of the soul—we must allow the Holy Spirit to rest within us, so that we may have the lamp of knowledge shining within ourselves at all times. For when it flashes unceasingly in the inner chambers of the soul, not only do the small and dark demonic attacks in the mind become visible, but they also become very weak when exposed by that holy and glorious light. For this reason, the Apostle says:
> *Do not quench the Spirit.* <note>1 Thessalonians 5:19</note>
This means: do not grieve the goodness of the Holy Spirit by doing evil or thinking evil, lest you be deprived of that protecting torch. For the eternal and life-giving Spirit is not literally "extinguished," but its grief—that is, its withdrawal—leaves the mind gloomy and without the light of knowledge.

<margin>29.</margin>
As I have said, we understand that there is one natural sensation of the soul. That it is split into five senses for the various needs of our body is what the all-holy and philanthropic Spirit of God teaches us. This sensation is divided along with the movements of the soul because of the "slip" <note>original: "ὄλισθον" (olisthon) — referring to the Fall of Man</note> that occurred in the mind through disobedience. Therefore, one part of it is carried away with the passionate part of the soul...

Diadochos emphasizes that only the Holy Spirit can truly purify the mind, allowing a person to recognize even their smallest failings.</summary>

...of the beauties of life. But the soul often rejoices with its own rational and intellectual movement; for our mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the 'eye of the heart'</note>, when we are self-controlled, runs toward and longs for heavenly beauties. Therefore, if we come into the habit of despising the beautiful things in the world, we shall be able to join the soul's earthly desire to its rational disposition, for the communion of the Holy Spirit governs this within us. For unless his own Divinity actively illuminates the storehouses of our heart, we would not be able to taste the Good in an undivided sensation—that is, in a complete and unified disposition.

<margin>30.</margin>
The sensation of the mind is a precise "tasting" of things being discerned. Just as through our physical sense of taste, when we are in a state of health, we distinguish good foods from bad without error and long for what is wholesome; so also our mind, when it begins to move vigorously and with great freedom from care, is able to perceive the divine consolation <term>παράκλησις (paraklesis): comfort or encouragement, often associated with the Holy Spirit as the "Comforter"</term> in abundance, and never be snatched away by its opposite. For just as the body, when tasting earthly delicacies, has an unerring experience of the sensation, so also the mind, when it triumphs over the "wisdom of the flesh," is able to taste the consolation of the Holy Spirit without error. For he says: *Taste and see that the Lord is good* <note>Psalm 33:9 (Septuagint) / 34:8 (KJV)</note>. And through the activity of love, the mind keeps the memory of this taste unforgotten, unerringly testing those things that differ, according to the words of the saint: *And this I pray, that your love may abound still more and more in knowledge and all sensation, so that you may discern the things that are excellent* <note>Philippians 1:9–10; "sensation" here translates "αἴσθησις" (aisthesis)</note>.

<margin>31.</margin>
When our mind begins to perceive the grace of the All-Holy Spirit, then Satan also begins to "comfort" the soul with a certain pleasant-looking sensation during the stillness of the night, at that moment when one falls into a very light state of sleep. If the mind is found holding the holy name of the Lord Jesus with a very fervent memory, and uses that all-holy and glorious name as a weapon against the deception, the deceiver of the trickery withdraws; but then he is kindled into an actual war against the soul. Wherefore the mind, precisely recognizing the

<column-break/>

deception of the evil one, makes further progress in the experience of discernment <term>διάκρισις (diakrisis): the spiritual gift of distinguishing between divine, human, and demonic impulses</term>.

<margin>32.</margin>
Good consolation comes either during bodily wakefulness or when one is about to fall into a state of sleep, provided one is in a fervent memory of God and is glued, as it were, to his love. But the consolation of deception always occurs, as I said, when the spiritual athlete enters a light sleep, while having only a moderate memory of God. For the consolation which is from God clearly desires to encourage the souls of the athletes of piety toward love in a great outpouring of the soul; but the other, since it is accustomed to fanning the soul with a certain "wind of deception," attempts to steal away the experience of the sensation of the healthy mind regarding the memory of God through the body's sleep. If, therefore, the mind is found—as I said—attentively remembering the Lord Jesus, it scatters that pleasant-looking breeze of the enemy, and rejoicing, it moves into the war against him, having as a "right-hand weapon" (alongside grace) the confidence born of experience.

<margin>33.</margin>
If the soul is kindled toward the love of God by an indubitable and non-imaginary movement, drawing even the body into the depth of that inexpressible love—whether in wakefulness, or in the manner I described, or when the one being acted upon by holy grace is entering sleep—and at that time perceives nothing else at all except that toward which it is moved: then one must know that this is the activity <term>ἐνέργεια (energeia): the active power or operation of God</term> of the Holy Spirit. For being entirely sweetened by that unspeakable sweetness, the soul can perceive nothing else at that moment, because it rejoices with a certain unyielding joy. But if the mind conceives any doubt at all, or any foul thought during this activity, even if it uses the holy name for defense against the evil and not rather for the love of God alone: one must realize that this consolation is from the Deceiver, through an appearance of joy. But that joy is "quality-less" and entirely lacks a steady disposition, for the enemy wishes to commit adultery with the soul when he sees the mind boasting precisely in the experience of its own sensation. Then, as I said, he calls to the soul with certain good-looking consolations so that, as the soul is distracted by that loose and watery sweetness, the mingling of the Deceiver might go unrecognized by it. From this, therefore, we shall know the spirit...

-># 146 OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS BISHOP OF PHOTIKI<-

...of truth, and the spirit of error. It is impossible, however, for someone to taste the divine goodness in sensation, or to experience the bitterness of the demons sensibly, unless they are fully convinced that grace has taken up residence in the depth of the mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the 'eye of the heart'</note>, while the evil spirits dwell around the limbs of the heart. The demons never want people to believe this, so that the mind, knowing this exactly, might not arm itself against them with the memory of God.

<margin>34.</margin>
There is one kind of love which is natural to the soul, and another which comes to it from the Holy Spirit. The first is moved in a balanced way from our own will when we desire it. Therefore, it is easily snatched away by evil spirits whenever we do not hold firmly to our own purpose. But the latter so inflames the soul with the love of God that all parts of the soul are joined to the ineffable goodness of divine desire in an infinite simplicity of disposition. For then the mind, becoming as it were pregnant by the spiritual activity, gushes forth a certain fountain of love and joy.

<margin>35.</margin>
Just as the sea, when it is tossed about, has a nature to yield to the oil poured upon it—the storm being overcome by the quality of the oil—so also our soul, when it is nourished by the goodness of the Holy Spirit, rests in a sweet calm. For it is overcome with joy, as the holy one says: *But be subject to God, O my soul* <note>Psalm 61:6 (Septuagint) / 62:5 (KJV)</note>, by that overshadowing dispassion <term>ἀπάθεια (apatheia): a state of being free from disordered passions; not 'apathy' in the modern sense, but spiritual peace</term> and ineffable goodness. For this reason, then, no matter what kind of provocations are contrived by the demons against the soul, it remains without anger and full of all joy. No one reaches or remains in this state unless they constantly soothe their soul with the fear of God. For to those who are struggling, the fear of the Lord Jesus brings a kind of purification. For he says: *The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever* <note>Psalm 18:10 (Septuagint) / 19:9 (KJV)</note>.

<margin>36.</margin>
Let no one who hears of the "sensation of the mind" expect that the glory of God will appear to them visibly. For we say that we "sense" it in the sense that the soul is purified in a certain ineffable taste of divine consolation <term>παράκλησις (paraklesis): divine comfort or encouragement</term>. But nothing of the invisible world appears to it. Since now we walk through

<column-break/>

faith and not through sight <note>original: "εἴδους" (eidous) — form or appearance</note>, as the blessed Paul says. Therefore, if light, or some fiery shape, or a voice should appear to anyone who is struggling, let them by no means accept such a vision. For it is a clear deception of the enemy, which many have suffered and, out of ignorance, were turned aside from the way of truth. But we know that as long as we dwell in this corruptible body, we are away from God—that is, we are not able to see either Him or any of His heavenly wonders visibly.

<margin>37.</margin>
The dreams that appear to the soul through the love of God are, in a way, unerring witnesses of a healthy soul. For they do not change from one form to another, nor do they terrify the senses, nor do they cause sudden laughter or gloom. Instead, they approach the soul with all gentleness, filling it with spiritual gladness. Therefore, even after the body has woken up, the soul seeks the joy of the dream with great longing. But the fantasies of the demons are entirely the opposite. For they do not stay in the same form, nor do they show an undisturbed appearance for long. For since they do not have what they have by choice, but only borrow it from their own deception, it cannot suffice them for very long. Moreover, they say great things and make many threats, often shaping themselves into the likeness of soldiers. Sometimes they even sing to the soul with a loud shout. Therefore, when the mind is pure, it recognizes them and wakes the body from the fantasy. Sometimes it even rejoices, having been able to recognize their trickery. For this reason, even within the dream itself, the mind often rebukes them, moving them to great anger. However, sometimes even good dreams do not bring joy to the soul, but produce in it a sweet sorrow and painless tears. This happens to those who have advanced into great humility <term>ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosyne): the virtue of lowliness of mind or humility</term>.

<margin>38.</margin>
We have spoken as we have heard from those who have had experience in the discernment of good and bad dreams. But let it be enough for us, as a great virtue, not to trust any fantasy at all. For dreams for the most part are nothing else but the idols of our thoughts, or again, as I said, the mockery of demons. Whenever even from God's...

He provides a guide for discerning between spiritual dreams that bring lasting peace and demonic fantasies that are unstable and frightening.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Ascetic Discourse" by Diadochos of Photiki. The previous page discussed the indwelling of grace in the mind (nous) versus the external presence of demons. ->### ASCETIC DISCOURSE<-

...if a vision should ever be sent to us by the divine goodness and we do not accept it, the much-longed-for Lord Jesus will not be angry with us for this. For He knows that we do this because of the deceits of the demons. The aforementioned discernment <note>original: "διάκρισις" (diakrisis) — the spiritual gift of being able to distinguish between divine, human, and demonic impulses</note> is indeed accurate. However, it sometimes happens that the soul, having been stained imperceptibly by a certain "snatching away"—a state from which I believe no one is found to be exempt—loses the track of accurate diagnosis and believes things that are not good to be good.

<margin>39</margin> Let us take as an example of this matter a servant called by his master at night after a long absence. Even if the servant hears the call before the walls of the house, if he does not recognize the voice with certainty, he may refuse to open the doors at all. He fears that the similarity of the voice might deceive him and make him a traitor to the things entrusted to him. Not only was his lord <note>original: "Κύριος" (Kyrios) — used here for the master in the analogy, mirroring the title of Christ</note> not angry with him when day came, but he even deemed him worthy of much praise, because he considered even his master’s voice to be a deception, wishing not to lose any of his property.

<margin>40</margin> No one should doubt that when the mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> begins to be frequently energized by the divine light, it becomes entirely transparent, so that it sees its own light abundantly. This happens entirely when the power of the soul gains mastery over the passions. However, that everything appearing to it in a shape—whether as light or as fire—comes from the evil artifice of the enemy, the divinely-inspired Paul clearly teaches us, saying that he [Satan] transforms himself into an angel of light. Therefore, no one should pursue the ascetic life with this hope, lest Satan find the soul ready to be snatched away. Instead, we should aim only to reach the point of loving God with every sensation and full assurance of heart. This consists in loving Him with "all the soul, and all the heart, and all the mind." For he who is energized toward this by the grace of God has departed from the world, even if he remains present in the world.

<margin>41</margin> Obedience <note>original: "ὑπακοή" (hypakoe) — literally 'attentive listening'</note> is known to be the first and best among all the introductory virtues, for it puts away self-conceit <note>original: "οἴησις" (oiesis) — a deluded sense of one's own importance or spiritual progress</note>. It gives birth to humility within us. Hence, it becomes an entrance and a door to the love for Christ for those who gladly cling to it. By rejecting this,

<column-break/>

Adam slid down into the deepest Tartarus <note>The Greek term for the underworld, used here to describe the depth of the fall</note>; but the Lord, loving this virtue according to the plan of His economy <note>original: "οἰκονομία" (oikonomia) — God's plan for the salvation of humanity</note>, was obedient to His own Father even unto the cross and death. And this He did though He was in no way inferior to His Father’s majesty, so that by dissolving the crime of human disobedience through His own obedience, He might lead those who have lived in obedience back to the blessed and eternal life. Therefore, those who take up the struggle against the pride of the devil must attend to this first. For as we progress, obedience will show us all the paths of the virtues without error.

<margin>42</margin> Self-control <note>original: "ἐγκράτεια" (enkrateia) — also translated as temperance or continence</note> is a name common to all the virtues. Therefore, the one who struggles must exercise self-control in everything. For just as when any of the smallest members of a man are removed, the whole man is made unsightly in form—even if what is missing is small—so also by neglecting one virtue, a person destroys the whole beauty of self-control without realizing it. We must, therefore, not only labor at the bodily virtues, but also at those which are able to purify our inner man. For what benefit will there be for one who keeps his body a virgin if his soul is being "adulterated" by the demon of disobedience? Or how shall he be crowned who refrains from gluttony and every bodily desire, but neglects to deal with self-conceit and vainglory? Nor can he endure even a brief affliction, which the balance of the scales of justice is destined to weigh against the light of righteousness for those who have performed the works of righteousness in a Spirit of humility.

<margin>43</margin> Those who struggle must hate all irrational desires in such a way that they acquire a habit of hatred toward them. But self-control regarding food should be maintained in such a way that one never comes to the abhorrence of any food. For such a thing is both accursed and entirely demonic. We do not abstain from foods because they are "vile"—heaven forbid—but so that by distancing ourselves from a variety of foods, we may moderately punish the inflamed members of the flesh. Furthermore, we do it so that our surplus might become a sufficient provision for those in poverty, which is the mark of sincere love.

### OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

...fights against perception; for all things are exceedingly good. But to abstain with pleasure from many pleasant things is a mark of greater discernment and spiritual knowledge. We could never gladly despise these present pleasures unless we were to taste the sweetness of God in all perception and full assurance.

<margin>45</margin> Just as the body, when weighed down by an abundance of food, makes the mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the "eye of the heart"</note> somewhat cowardly and sluggish, so too when the body is exhausted by excessive self-denial, it renders the contemplative part of the soul gloomy and averse to study. One must, therefore, adapt one’s diet to the movements of the body: so that when it is healthy, it may be properly disciplined, but when it is weak, it may be moderately nourished. For the spiritual athlete must not be physically exhausted, but must have enough strength for the contest, so that through the labors of the body, the soul also may be properly purified.

<margin>46</margin> Whenever vainglory <note>original: "κενοδοξία" (kenodoxia) — the desire for empty praise or human approval</note> greatly inflames us, finding an excuse for its own wickedness in the arrival of some brothers or any kind of stranger, it is good then to allow a moderate relaxation of our usual diet. By doing so, we shall send the demon away unsuccessful and grieving over his failed attempt; we shall properly fulfill the law of love; and through this concession, we shall keep the mystery of our self-control <note>original: "ἐγκράτεια" (enkrateia)</note> unexposed to display.

<margin>47</margin> Fasting has a boast in itself, but not toward God; for it is merely a tool, as it were, which brings those who desire it into a rhythm of self-control. Therefore, those who struggle for piety must not think highly of themselves because of it, but should only wait in faith for God to bring our purpose to its end. For those skilled in any art never boast of the result of their profession based on their tools alone; rather, each one waits for the completion of the work, so that from the finished product he may demonstrate the precision of his craft.

<margin>48</margin> Just as the earth, when moderately watered, brings forth the seed cast into it with a great increase, but when soaked by heavy rains produces only thorns and thistles; so too the soil of the heart, if we use wine in moderation, yields its natural seeds in purity, and those sown into it by the Holy Spirit spring up very lushly

<column-break/>

and bear much fruit. But if the heart becomes waterlogged through excessive drinking, its thoughts truly bring forth nothing but thorns and thistles.

<margin>49</margin> When our mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> is tossed about by the waves of excessive drinking, it not only looks passionately upon the images shaped by demons in sleep, but it even creates certain fair-seeming sights within itself, using its own fantasies as if they were real and burning with desire. For when the sexual organs are heated by the fervor of wine, the mind is forced to present to itself a pleasurable shadow of passion. We ought, therefore, by practicing moderation, to escape the harm that comes from excess. For when the mind does not have that pleasure which drags it down to paint pictures of sin, it remains entirely free of fantasies and better prepared for the struggle.

<margin>50</margin> All prepared drinks, which those skilled in such inventions call "aperitifs" <note>original: "προπόματα" (propomata) — drinks taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite</note>—seemingly because they lead a multitude of foods into the stomach—should not be sought by those who wish to discipline the bloated parts of the body. For not only does their quality become harmful to the bodies of athletes, but their very irrational mixture greatly wounds the <margin>In others: "God-bearing"</margin> * God-bearing conscience. For what is lacking in the nature of wine that its simplicity must be made effeminate by the mixture of various seasonings?

<margin>51</margin> Our Lord and Teacher of this sacred way of life, Jesus Christ, was given vinegar to drink during His Passion by those serving diabolical commands, in order (it seems to me) to leave us a clear model of the disposition of our sacred struggles. For He says that those struggling against sin must not use foods or drinks that provide pleasure, but rather must endure the bitterness of the battle with fortitude. <margin>In others: "of eating"</margin> Let hyssop also be added to the sponge * of insult, so that the form of our purification might be perfectly represented in this example. For bitterness is characteristic of the struggles, while the cleansing power of hyssop belongs entirely to perfection.

<margin>52</margin> One would not declare frequenting a bathhouse to be sinful or irrational; but to abstain even from this for the sake of self-control is what I call courageous and most prudent. For neither is our body made effeminate by pleasurable...

### ASCETIC DISCOURSE

...that moisture, nor do we come to a remembrance of the inglorious nakedness of Adam, so that we might worry over those leaves of his to cover the secondary excuse for shame. Rather, we who have recently leaped out of the ruin of worldly life must be united to the beauty of self-control <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne) — a core Greek virtue meaning excellence of mind, temperance, or chastity</note> through the purity of our own bodies.

<margin>53</margin> There is nothing to prevent one from calling for a physician in times of illness. Since the art of medicine was eventually to be gathered through human experience, the medicines themselves existed beforehand. However, one ought not to place their hope of healing in them, but in our true Savior and Physician, Jesus Christ. I say this to those in monasteries <note>original: "Κοινοβίοις" (Koinobiois) — communal religious houses where monks live together</note> or in cities who are succeeding in the goal of self-discipline <note>original: "ἐγκράτεια" (enkrateia) — inner power or self-mastery, especially over physical desires</note>, because they are unable, due to the circumstances they encounter, to have the continuous activity of faith through love. This is also to ensure they do not fall into vainglory and the temptation of the devil, for some of them boast among many people that they have no need of doctors. But if someone practices the solitary life <note>original: "ἀναχωρητικὸν βίον" (anachoretikon bion) — the life of an anchorite or hermit</note> in more desert-like places with only two or three brothers of like mind, let him approach the Lord in faith—the one who heals us of every disease and every infirmity—no matter what suffering he falls into. For after the Lord, such a person has the solitude of the desert as a sufficient consolation for illness; thus, such a person never becomes poor in the activity of faith. This is especially true because he finds no place to display the virtue gained from his endurance, being hidden by the beautiful veil of the desert; for this reason, the Lord "settles the solitary in a home" <note>A reference to Psalm 68:6</note>.

<margin>54</margin> Whenever we feel excessive hatred toward the physical imbalances that happen to us, we must know that our soul is still enslaved to the desires of the body. Because it longs for material prosperity, it does not want to depart from the "good things" of life, but instead considers it a great burden not to be able to enjoy the beauties of life because of illness. But if the soul accepts the distresses of illness with gratitude, it is recognized as being not far from the borders of dispassion <note>original: "ἀπαθεία" (apatheia) — not a lack of feeling, but a state of being undisturbed by passions or suffering</note>; hence, it then accepts death with joy, seeing it as a gateway to true life.

<margin>55</margin> The soul will never desire to be separated 

<column-break/>

from the body unless its disposition toward this "air" <note>referring to the worldly atmosphere or the physical realm</note> becomes indifferent. For all the senses of the body are opposed to faith; since the senses deal only with present things, while faith promises the richness of future goods. It is fitting, then, for the spiritual athlete never to dwell on thoughts of swaying or shady trees, or flowing springs, or varied and flowering meadows, or fine houses, or even visits with relatives. Nor should he remember, if it should happen, the honors of public festivals. Instead, he should use what is necessary with gratitude, but consider this life to be a kind of foreign road, abandoned by every fleshly disposition. For only in this way, by narrowing our intellect <note>original: "διάνοια" (dianoia) — the processing mind or discursive thought</note>, may we turn it entirely toward the tracks of the eternal path.

<margin>56</margin> That sight, taste, and the other senses dissipate the memory of the heart when we use them beyond measure is something that the first Eve tells us. For as long as she did not look at the tree, she remembered the Divine command with pleasure and care; therefore, she was still covered by the wings of Divine love, as it were, and was unaware of her own nakedness. But when she looked at the tree with pleasure and touched it with great desire, and finally tasted of its fruit with a certain active enjoyment, she was immediately enticed toward physical union. Having been joined to passion in her nakedness, she gave her whole desire over to the enjoyment of present things, mixing her own fall and that of Adam through the sweet appearance of the fruit. From then on, the human mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> can only with difficulty remember God or His commandments. We, therefore, by not looking always into the depths of our heart for the unceasing memory of God, pass through this deceptive life like the blind. For it is the special quality of truly spiritual philosophy to keep love always free from the influence of the eyes. The very experienced Job teaches us this, saying: "if my heart also followed my eye" <note>Job 31:7</note>; truly, this premise is a sign of the highest self-discipline.

<margin>57</margin> He who always dwells within his own heart is "away from home" regarding all the beauties of life. Spirit...
