### OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

...for one walking in the **Spirit** is unable to know the desires of the flesh; since, from then on, such a person takes his walks within the fortress of the virtues, having these very virtues as the gatekeepers of the city of purity. Consequently, the machines of the demons become idle and ineffective against him, even if the arrows of vulgar love <note>original: "πανδήμου ἔρωτος" (pandemou erotos) — referring to common, worldly, or physical lust as opposed to divine love</note> somehow reach as far as the windows of nature <note>original: "θυρίδων τῆς φύσεως" — likely referring to the physical senses</note>.

<margin>58.</margin> Whenever our soul no longer begins to desire the beauties of the earth, then a certain state of <term>listlessness <note>original: "ἀκηδιαστής" (akidiastes) — related to "akedia," a spiritual sloth or despondency that makes religious life feel burdensome</note></term> usually creeps into the mind. It neither allows the mind to serve the ministry of the Word with pleasure, nor does it leave the mind with a clear desire for the good things of the future. Instead, it excessively devalues this temporary life as if it held no work worthy of virtue, and even treats knowledge itself as worthless—either because it has already been granted to many others, or because it promises us nothing perfect. We shall escape this lukewarm and sluggish passion if we restrict our thinking within very narrow limits, looking only toward the **remembrance of God**. For only in this way can the mind return to its own warmth and be able to withdraw from that irrational dissipation.

<margin>59.</margin> The mind certainly demands a task from us when we block all its exits with the remembrance of God, an activity that ought to satisfy its natural agility. One should, therefore, give it nothing but the prayer "Lord Jesus" <note>original: "Κύριε Ἰησοῦ"</note> as its entire occupation for reaching this goal. For "no one," it says, "can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit" (1 Cor 12:3). Let the mind continually contemplate this saying within its own treasuries with such focus that it does not turn aside into any fantasies. For all those who meditate unceasingly on this holy and glorious name in the depths <margin>* alternatively: in the remembrance</margin> of the heart can eventually see the light of their own mind. For when the name is held by the thought with intense care, it consumes all the filth that surfaces on the soul with a powerful sensation. Indeed, "our God," it says, "is a consuming fire" (Heb 12:29), burning away wickedness. From this, the Lord then calls the soul to a great love of His glory. For when that glorious and much-desired name lingers through the remembrance of the mind in the warmth of the heart, it unfailingly produces in us the habit of loving His goodness,

<column-break/>

with nothing further remaining to act as an obstacle. For this is the "pearl of great price" (Matt 13:46) which a person can acquire by selling all their possessions, and in its discovery, they possess an unspeakable joy.

<margin>60.</margin> There is one kind of joy that belongs to beginners, and another that belongs to those reaching perfection. The former is not free from the influence of fantasies, while the latter possesses the power of humility. Between these two lies a "godly sorrow" and a <margin>* alternatively: active</margin> painless tear. For indeed, in the abundance of wisdom is an abundance of knowledge, and "he who increases knowledge increases pain" (Eccl 1:18). Therefore, the soul must first be called to the struggle by the introductory joy, but then it must be rebuked and tested by the truth of the Holy Spirit regarding the evils it has committed or the distractions it still indulges in. For it says, "With rebukes You chasten a man for iniquity, and You make his soul melt away like a spider" (Ps 39:11). Thus, after the divine rebuke has tested the soul as if in a <term>furnace <note>original: "χωνευτηρίῳ" (choneuterio) — a crucible or smelting pot used to purify precious metals</note></term>, it may then receive the activity of a joy that is free from fantasy, in the warm remembrance of God.

<margin>61.</margin> When the soul is troubled by anger, or muddied by the effects of excess, or vexed by a harsh despondency, the mind is unable to hold fast to the remembrance of God, no matter how much it forces itself. Being entirely darkened by the intensity of the passions, it becomes completely estranged from its own proper perception. Therefore, the desire has nowhere to imprint its seal, so that the mind might carry the form of its meditation unforgotten; for the memory of the intellect has been hardened by the cruelty of the passions. But if the mind is free from these things, even if what is desired is stolen away for a brief moment by forgetfulness, the mind immediately uses its own natural agility and warmly seizes that much-desired and saving "prey." For it then possesses Grace itself, which meditates along with the soul and cries out with it, "**Lord Jesus Christ**," just as a mother might teach her child and meditate along with him on the name "Father," until she leads him to the habit of calling clearly upon his Father, even in his sleep, instead of any other infant-like babble. This is why the Apostle says: "Likewise the Spirit also helps in our weaknesses. For we do not know what we should pray for as...

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE

...what we should [pray for]. We do not know, but the **Spirit** himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered <note>original: "στεναγμοῖς ἀλαλήτοις" (stenagmois alaletois) — a reference to Romans 8:26, describing a deep, spiritual prayer that transcends human words</note>. Since we are like infants in relation to the perfection of virtue, we absolutely require his help; so that, by his unutterable sweetness, while all our thoughts are held together and delighted, we might be moved with our whole disposition toward the remembrance and love of our God and Father. Therefore, in him—as the divine Paul says again—we cry out, when we are attuned by him to call God our Father unceasingly: "Abba, Father."

<margin>62.</margin> **Anger** <term>Anger <note>original: "θυμός" (thymos) — in Greek philosophy and asceticism, this is the "incensive" or "spirited" part of the soul. While it can lead to the passion of rage, Diadochos argues it is naturally intended to be a source of spiritual energy and zeal against evil.</note></term> usually disturbs and confuses the soul more than other passions, yet there are times when it benefits it greatly. For when we use it calmly against the ungodly, or against those who act wantonly in any way—doing so so that they might either be saved or be put to shame—we provide the soul with an increase in gentleness. For in this way, we certainly run alongside the purpose of God’s justice and goodness. Moreover, we often "make manly" <note>original: "ἀπαρρενοῦμεν" (aparrenoumen) — meaning to strengthen or make courageous, contrasting it with spiritual "softness" or "effeminacy" (θηλυδρῶδες)</note> the soul’s softness by becoming severely angry against sin. We should not doubt that we even rage against the spirit of corruption itself; when we are in deep despondency, we should feel superior to the boasting of death. To teach us this, the Lord—having twice groaned in spirit at Hades and having "troubled himself" <note>reference to Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus in John 11:33-38</note>, even though he performs everything he wishes with an untroubled will—thus restored the soul of Lazarus to his body. So it seems to me that a "sober anger" was provided to our nature by God our Creator as a weapon of righteousness. If Eve had used it against the serpent, she would not have been acted upon by that passionate pleasure. Thus, it seems to me that the one who uses anger soberly out of zeal for piety will certainly be found more approved in the scales of recompense than the one whose mind, due to a lack of movement, is not moved to anger at all. For the latter appears to have the "charioteer" of human thoughts untrained, while the former becomes a competitor upon the horses of virtue and is carried into the midst of the demonic ranks, always exercising the four-horse chariot of self-control in the fear of God. This is the "Chariot of Israel" mentioned in Scripture regarding the ascension of the divine Elijah; since it appears that God spoke to the first Jews in various ways concerning the four 

<column-break/>

virtues. Therefore, this great and distinguished foster-child of wisdom was taken up entirely upon a chariot of fire, having used his own virtues like horses—so it seems to me—in the Spirit that snatched him away in a fiery breeze.

<margin>63.</margin> One who has partaken of holy knowledge and tasted the sweetness of God ought never to judge, nor to initiate a lawsuit against anyone at all, even if someone takes away the very clothes they are wearing. For the justice of the rulers of this world is entirely defeated by the justice of God. Rather, it is nothing compared to the justice of God. For what difference is there between the children of God and the men of this age, unless the justice of the latter appeared imperfect compared to the righteousness of the former? Thus, one is called human justice, and the other divine righteousness. In this way, our Lord, when he was reviled, did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but even endured the stripping of his clothes in silence and was in agony for our salvation. And what is greater: he made a request to the Father on behalf of those who were doing him evil. But the people of this world will not stop litigating unless they recover their property with interest, sometimes receiving the interest even before the debt itself, so that their "justice" often becomes the beginning of a great injustice.

<margin>64.</margin> "We must not," I have heard some pious people say, "allow just anyone to plunder the things we have for our own management or for the relief of the poor, lest we become the cause of sin for those who wrong us by our patient endurance—especially if we suffer this at the hands of Christians." But this is nothing other than wanting to hold onto one's possessions for oneself under a senseless pretext. For if I abandon prayer and attention to my own heart to begin pleading cases little by little against those who wish to wrong me, and if I sit in the courtyards of the courtrooms, it is clear that I consider the things being defended more important than my own salvation—not to say, more important than the saving commandment itself. For how will I follow the Gospel command at all, which orders me: "From him who takes away your goods, do not demand them back" <note>Luke 6:30</note>; unless I endure it with joy, according to the Apostolic...

### BY THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

...as a saying <note>original: "λόγιον" (logion) — likely referring to a scriptural principle or a spiritual maxim</note>, the plundering of my possessions; since no one, by going to law and recovering what was taken by force, frees the greedy man from his sin; because earthly courts cannot determine the incorruptible judgment of God. For the perpetrator fulfills those laws by which he must also offer a defense for the cause of his action. Therefore, it is good to bear the violence of those who wish to wrong us, and to pray for them, so that through repentance—and not through the returning of what they snatched from us—they might be released from the crime of greed. For this is what the justice of God desires: that we might one day win back the greedy man himself through his repentance, and not merely the objects of his greed, making him free from sin.

<margin>65.</margin> It is extremely fitting and profitable in every way that, once we have recognized the way of piety <term>piety <note>original: "εὐσεβείας" (eusebeias) — a term encompassing both right belief and right living toward God</note></term>, we should immediately sell all our possessions and distribute the money according to the Lord’s command. We should not, under the pretext of wishing to perform commandments continually <note>i.e., by holding onto wealth to give it away slowly over time</note>, disobey the saving command to give it all at once. For from this we will gain, first of all, a beautiful freedom from care, and thereafter a poverty that is safe from plots—a poverty which thinks itself above every injustice and every lawsuit, because we no longer possess the "fuel" that ignites the fire of the greedy. Moreover, **humility** will embrace us more than all other virtues, and will rest us in her own bosom as though we were naked. Just as a mother takes her own child into her arms and warms it when, in its childlike simplicity, it has stripped off and thrown away its garment; for it delights more in its nakedness due to its great innocence than in the variety of its clothing. For it says: "The Lord preserves the simple; I was brought low, and He saved me" <note>Psalm 116:6 (114:6 in the Septuagint)</note>.

<margin>66.</margin> The Lord will certainly demand an account from us regarding almsgiving according to what we have, not according to what we do not have. If, therefore, I spend in a short time out of fear of God—and by a good and fervent command—what I might have had to give over many years, for what will I, who now have nothing, be accused? But someone will say: "How then will the poor, who were accustomed to being supported little by little from our means, be shown mercy in the future?" Let such a person learn not to reproach

<column-break/>

God under the pretext of his own love of money. For God will not fail to provide for His own creation, as He has since the beginning. For before this or that person was moved to almsgiving, the poor were not deprived of food or shelter. It is good, therefore, at the very moment of one's recognition of the truth, to cast away—along with good service to others—that irrational pride and boasting that comes from wealth, hating one's own desires, which is to "hate one's own soul" <note>cf. John 12:25</note>. Thus, no longer finding joy in the distribution of money, we may humble our souls greatly, as if we were achieving nothing good. For as long as we have an abundance of money, we rejoice greatly (if the energy of the Good is in us) in its scattering, as we cheerfully serve the divine command. But when we have exhausted everything, a boundless sorrow and humility enter in, as we feel we are doing nothing worthy of righteousness. From that point on, the soul turns back upon itself in great humility, so that what it cannot acquire daily through almsgiving, it may provide for itself through labored prayer, endurance, and lowliness of mind. For it says: "The poor and the needy shall praise your name, O Lord" <note>Psalm 74:21</note>. Furthermore, the gift of **theology** <term>theology <note>original: "θεολογίας" (theologias) — in the early Church, this did not mean academic study, but the highest form of prayer and the direct, mystical contemplation of God</note></term> is not prepared for anyone by God unless that person prepares himself by divesting himself of all his belongings for the sake of the glory of the Gospel of God; so that in a poverty beloved by God, he may preach the wealth of the Kingdom of God. For He who said, "In your goodness, O God, you have provided for the poor," and added, "The Lord will give the word to those who preach with great power" <note>Psalm 68:10-11</note>, clearly signifies this.

<margin>67.</margin> All the gifts of our God are very good and providers of all goodness. But nothing so inflames us and moves the heart to the love of His goodness as **theology**. For being the firstborn offspring of God's goodness, it grants the soul its first and greatest gifts. First, it prepares us to rejoice in despising all the friendships of this life, since we possess the words of God as an unspeakable wealth instead of corruptible desires. Then, it illuminates our mind with the fire of transformation, making it a companion of the ministering spirits <note>i.e., the angels</note>. Those who truly enter into this...

### ASCETIC DISCOURSE. 153

...having been prepared, let us walk, beloved, toward virtue—the beautiful, the all-beholding, the provider of all freedom from care, which in the dawn of unutterable light feeds the mind with the words of God. To put it briefly, virtue joins the rational soul to God the Word <note>original: "Θεῷ λόγῳ" (Theō Logō) — referring to Christ as the Logos</note> through the holy prophets in an inseparable communion; so that even among men—O, the wonder!—the divine guide of the bride <note>original: "νυμφαγωγός" (numphagōgos) — a "bridesmaid" or "escort" who leads the bride to the groom; here, a metaphor for the divine grace or virtue leading the soul to God</note>, having harmonized the divine sounds <note>variant: "the God-singing sounds... singing clearly the mighty acts of God."</note>, clearly sings the mighty acts of the Lord.

<margin>68.</margin> Our mind <term>mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — in Eastern Christian thought, the "eye of the heart" or the faculty of direct spiritual perception</note></term> often feels burdened regarding prayer, because of the extreme narrowness and restraint of the virtue of petition. Yet, it gives itself over to theology <note>original: "θεολογίαν" (theologian) — here meaning the mystical contemplation of God rather than academic study</note> with joy, because of the breadth and freedom of divine contemplations. Therefore, so that we do not give the mind a path for much speaking, or allow it to "take wing" beyond measure, let us yield to joy but devote most of our time to prayer, the singing of psalms, and the reading of the Scriptures. We should not overlook the contemplations of learned men whose faith is made known through their words. By doing this, we do not prepare our own words to mix with the words of grace, nor do we permit the mind to be dragged down by vainglory or dissipated through excessive joy and much speaking. Instead, we shall keep it free from all imagination <note>original: "φαντασίας" (phantasias) — mental images or distractions that interfere with pure prayer</note> during the time of contemplation, and we will provide it with almost entirely tearful thoughts from this practice. For when the mind rests in times of stillness <term>stillness <note>original: "ἡσυχίας" (hesychias) — the state of inner silence and tranquility sought by monks</note></term>, and is sweetened especially by the delight of prayer, it not only escapes the aforementioned pitfalls but is also renewed to strike more sharply and without labor upon divine contemplations, while also progressing in the contemplation of discernment with great humility. However, one must know that there is a prayer that is above all "breadth"; this belongs only to those who are filled with holy grace in all perception and assurance.

<margin>69.</margin> Grace <term>grace <note>original: "χάρις" (charis)</note></term> at first is accustomed to illuminate the soul with its own light in great perception. But as the struggles proceed, it works its own mysteries within the God-contemplating soul, for the most part, in an unknown way—so that it may first set us 

<column-break/>

rejoicing upon the track of divine contemplations, as those being called from ignorance to knowledge; but in the midst of our struggles, it keeps our knowledge free from vainglory. It is necessary, then, that we feel a proportionate grief as though we have been abandoned, so that we may be further humbled and submit to the glory of the Lord, while also rejoicing at the proper time, taking wing through good hope. For just as excessive grief brings the soul into despair and unbelief, so also excessive joy invites it to presumption—I speak here of those who are still "infants" <note>spiritually immature or beginners in the ascetic life</note>. For the middle point between illumination and abandonment is "trial"; and the middle point between grief and joy is "hope." For he says, *Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he inclined to me*, and again, *According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your comforts delighted my soul* <note>Quotes from Psalm 40:1 and Psalm 94:19</note>.

<margin>70.</margin> Just as the doors of bathhouses, when opened continuously, quickly push the internal heat to the outside, so also the soul, when it desires to converse much—even if it says all good things—dissipates its own memory through the "vocal gate." From then on, the mind is deprived of timely <margin>* variant: "Lordly"</margin> thoughts, and it discusses whatever happens to come its way in a kind of troublesome "clashing of words" <margin>* variant: "clashing of reasonings"</note>. Since it no longer possesses the Holy Spirit to keep its thoughts free from imagination—for the Good always flees from "much speaking," as it is a stranger to all turmoil and imagination—timely silence is therefore a good thing. It is nothing other than the mother of the wisest thoughts.

<margin>71.</margin> Now, the word of knowledge <term>knowledge <note>original: "γνῶσεως" (gnōseōs) — spiritual insight or experiential knowledge of God</note></term> teaches us that many passions <term>passions <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē) — disordered impulses such as anger, greed, or pride</note></term> initially disturb the God-contemplating soul; and more than all others, anger and hatred. The soul suffers this not so much because of the demons who stir these things up, but because of its own progress. For as long as the soul is carried away by the mindset of the world, even if it sees justice being trampled by some people, it remains unmoved and untroubled. For being concerned with its own desires, it does not look toward the justice of God. But when it begins to rise above its own passions <margin>* variant: "desires"</margin> through both the contempt of present things and the love of God, it cannot bear to see justice set aside either in itself or in another, but it becomes incensed against...

<summary>Diadochos explains the delicate balance between prayer and theological contemplation, advising "timely silence" to preserve the soul's inner heat. He describes how spiritual progress paradoxically makes a person more sensitive to injustice, leading to a holy indignation that replaces worldly indifference.</summary>

For while natural love is a sign of a nature that is healthy through self-control, it cannot lead the mind to passionlessness as Spiritual love can.

For this is the light of true knowledge.

<margin>76.</margin>
Some have supposed that grace and sin—that is, the Spirit of Truth and the spirit of error—are both hidden at the same time in the mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) — the intellect or "eye of the heart"</note> of those who are baptized. For this reason, they say, one presence encourages the mind toward good things, while the other immediately pulls it toward the opposite. But I have understood from the Divine Scriptures and from the very perception of the mind itself, that before holy baptism, grace encourages the soul toward good things from the *outside*, while Satan lurks in the soul's very depths, attempting to block all the mind's right-hand passages. But from the very hour in which we are reborn, the demon is cast outside, and grace enters within. Hence we find that, just as error once ruled the soul, so after baptism, Truth rules it. Nevertheless, even after this, Satan still acts upon the soul just as before, and often even more severely—not as if he were present alongside grace (heaven forbid!), but by "smoking" the mind, as it were, through the moisture of the body and the sweetness of irrational pleasures. This happens by God's permission, so that by passing through the storm, the fire, and the trial, a person may come to the enjoyment of the good. For it says: "We went through fire and water, and You brought us out into a place of refreshment." <note>Psalm 66:12</note>

<margin>77.</margin>
Grace, as I said, is hidden in the very depths of the mind from the moment we are baptized, concealing its own presence from the soul's own perception. But when someone begins to love God with their whole purpose, then in an ineffable way, grace speaks to the soul through the mind's perception, sharing a portion of its own goods. From then on, the person who wishes to hold fast to this discovery comes to the desire of giving up all present goods with great joy, so that they may truly acquire the field in which they found the treasure of life hidden. For when one gives up all worldly wealth, then they find

<column-break/>

the place where the grace of God is hidden. For according to the soul's progress, the divine gift reveals its own goodness in the mind. However, the Lord then permits the soul to be troubled even more by demons, so that He may properly teach it discernment <term>discernment <note>original: "διάκρισιν" (diakrisin) — the ability to distinguish between divine, natural, and demonic impulses</note></term> between good and evil, and to make the soul more humble; for when the soul is being purified, it feels great shame from the foulness of demonic thoughts.

<margin>78.</margin>
We are "in the image" of God through the intellectual movement of the soul; for the body is like its dwelling place. Since, therefore, through Adam’s transgression, not only were the lines of the soul's character stained, but our body also fell into corruption, for this reason the holy Word of God became flesh. As God, He granted us the water of salvation through His own baptism for our rebirth. For we are reborn through water by the energy of the Holy and Life-giving Spirit. Thus, we are immediately cleansed in both soul and body, if we approach God with our whole disposition; the Holy Spirit makes His home in us, and sin is driven out by Him. For it is impossible for two "persons" to be present in the soul—as some have thought—since the character of the soul is single and simple. When divine grace joins itself through holy baptism in an infinite love to the lines of the "image" as a pledge of the "likeness," where can the presence of the evil one find a place? Especially since there is no fellowship of light with darkness! We who are runners in the sacred contests believe, therefore, that the multi-formed serpent <note>original: "πολύμορφον ὄφιν" (polymorphon ophin) — a common patristic metaphor for the devil's varied deceptions</note> is cast out from the storehouses of the mind through the washing of incorruption. Do not wonder why, after baptism, we still think of wicked things alongside the good. For the washing of holiness removes the stain from sin, but it does not yet change the "double-ness" of our will, nor does it prevent the demons from warring against us or speaking words of deceit to us. This is so that those things we failed to guard while in our natural state, we might now keep through the power of God, having taken up the weapons of righteousness.

...from the soul through holy baptism. However, he <note>the demon/Satan</note> is permitted, for the reasons previously mentioned, to exert influence upon it through the body. For the grace of God makes its dwelling in the very depths of the soul—that is, in the mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) — the intellect or "eye of the heart"</note>. For it says, "All the glory of the daughter of the King is within" (Psalm 45:13), hidden from the demons. Therefore, from the very depths of our heart, we feel a divine longing welling up like a spring whenever we warmly remember God. But the evil spirits then leap upon the senses of the body and lurk there, acting through the ease of the flesh upon those who are still infants in the soul. Thus, our mind always delights in the law of the Spirit, according to the divine Apostle Paul, but the sensory organs of the flesh wish to be led away by the smoothness of pleasures. Consequently, grace gladdens the body with an inexpressible joy through the perception of the mind in those advancing in knowledge <note>original: "γνώσει" (gnōsei)</note>. But the demons, through the senses of the body, whenever they find us running the course of piety in a particularly negligent and careless way, take the soul captive, violently dragging it, murderers that they are, toward things it does not want.

<margin>80.</margin> Those who say that the two "persons"—that of grace and that of sin—appear together in the hearts of the faithful, wish to establish their own suspicion by quoting the Evangelist: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it" (John 1:5). They claim that the divine radiance is in no way defiled by its association with the evil one, even if the divine light draws near the darkness of the demon in the soul. But they are proven to think outside the Holy Scriptures by this very evangelical saying. For since the Word of God, the true light, saw fit to appear to creation in his own flesh—lighting among us the light of holy knowledge through his immeasurable love for humanity—the "mindset of the world" did not "overcome" (that is, did not grasp) the counsel of God. For the "mindset of the flesh is enmity against God" (Romans 8:7). This is why the theologian <note>Diadochus uses "theologian" as a specific title for John the Evangelist</note> used such a word. Indeed, after saying a few things in between, the divine man adds: "He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world"—meaning he guides and gives life—"he was in the world, and

<column-break/>

the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name" (John 1:9-12). And the most wise Paul also says, interpreting the phrase "did not overcome": "Not that I have already obtained it, or am already perfected; but I press on, if I may also overcome <note>original: "καταλάβω" (katalabō) — here meaning to seize or grasp the prize</note>, because I also was overcome by Jesus Christ" (Philippians 3:12). So, the Evangelist does not say that Satan failed to "overcome" the true light from the beginning, for Satan is a stranger to it, since it does not even shine in him. Rather, the Word, through his saying, declares those men unworthy who hear of the power and wonders of God but do not wish to draw near to the light of his knowledge because of their darkened hearts.

<margin>81.</margin> Reason teaches us that there are, as it were, two kinds of knowledge regarding evil spirits: for some of them are "finer" or more subtle, while others are more material <note>original: "ὑλωδέστερα" (hylōdestera) — literally "more woody" or matter-bound</note>. The more subtle ones war against the soul, while the others are accustomed to take the flesh captive through certain oily <note>original: "λιπαρῶν" (liparōn) — suggesting slick, fatty, or indulgent physical comforts</note> comforts. Therefore, the demons who wrestle with the soul and those who wrestle with the body are opposed to one another, even if they have the same intention of harming humans. So, when grace does not dwell in a person, they lurk in the depths of the heart like snakes, not allowing the soul to look up toward the desire for the good at all. But when grace is hidden in the mind, they then run through the parts of the heart like dark clouds, turning toward the passions of sin or transforming into various distractions, so that by distracting the mind through memory, they might tear it away from its conversation with grace. When, therefore, we are set on fire by the demons who disturb the soul toward psychological passions—and especially toward pride <term>pride <note>original: "οἴησιν" (oiēsin) — a specific type of self-conceit or imaginary self-importance</note></term>, which is the mother of all evils—let us consider the dissolution of our body, and we shall put to shame the swelling of our vanity. We must do the same when the demons wrestling with the body prepare our heart to boil over with shameful desires. For this thought alone <note>the remembrance of death</note> is able to nullify all the various kinds of evil spirits in...

This page further explores how the "law of sin" operates in the flesh versus the "law of the mind," using the writings of St. Paul and the imagery of spiritual warfare to explain the mechanics of temptation.</meta>

...by the remembrance of God. But if, because of this recollection, the demons of the soul again suggest to us an infinite worthlessness of human nature—claiming the flesh is of no value through their reasoning—(for they love to do this when someone wishes to test them with such a thought), let us then contemplate the honor and glory of the heavenly kingdom, while not overlooking the bitterness and gloom of the judgment. We do this so that, by the former, we may comfort our despondency, and by the latter, we may brace the ease and laxity of our hearts.

<margin>82.</margin> Our Lord teaches in the Gospels that when Satan returns and finds his house swept and unoccupied—that is, the heart that bears no fruit—he then takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, enters into it, and settles there, making the last state of that person worse than the first. From this we must understand that as long as the Holy Spirit is within us, Satan cannot enter and remain in the depths of the soul. But the divine Paul also clearly teaches us the meaning of this contemplation. For having observed the form of this struggle from his own experience in the spiritual contest, he says: "For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. But I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind, and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members" (Romans 7:22-23). And regarding perfection, he says: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh... for the law of the Spirit of life has set me free from the law of sin and death" (Romans 8:1-2). He says elsewhere, to teach us again that Satan wars against the soul (which participates in the Holy Spirit) from the vantage point of the body: "Stand therefore, having girded your waist with truth; and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet with the preparation of the Gospel of peace; above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked one, and receive the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Ephesians 6:14-17). Now, being "taken captive" is one thing, and "wrestling" is another. For the former signifies a forced removal, while the 

<column-break/>

latter indicates an equal struggle. Therefore, the Apostle says that the devil attacks Christ-bearing souls with "fiery darts." For one who has no power over his opponent certainly makes use of darts against him, so that by the flight of the arrows he might be able to hunt down the one fighting him from a distance. In this same way, since Satan cannot—due to the presence of grace—lurk within the mind <note>original: "νοΐ" (noï) — the intellect or the spiritual center of the person</note> of those who are struggling as he did before, he hovers over the moisture <note>original: "ὑγρότητι" (hygrotēti) — likely referring to the bodily fluids or "humors" associated with laxity and physical pleasure in ancient medicine</note> of the body as if lurking in the flesh, so that through the body's ease he may entice the soul. Therefore, we must moderately waste away the body, so that through its moisture the mind does not slide into the smooth path of pleasures. We should be convinced by that very Apostolic saying that the mind of those who are struggling is energized by the divine light; therefore, it serves and delights in the divine law. But the flesh, because of its ease, gladly admits the wicked spirits. Therefore, it sometimes chooses to serve their wickedness. From this, it is most clear that the mind is not a common dwelling place for both God and the devil. For how could I "serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh" (Romans 7:25), unless my mind stood in total freedom for the battle against the demons, gladly serving the goodness of grace, while the body admitted the scent of irrational pleasures? This is because, as I said, in those who are struggling, the evil spirits are permitted to lurk within the body. "For I know," he says, "that in me, that is, in my flesh, nothing good dwells" (Romans 7:18). So, for those who resist sin in the midst of their struggles—for the Apostle is not saying this about himself personally <note>Diadochos argues Paul is describing the general state of the Christian struggle, not his own perfected state</note>—the demons fight against the mind, but they attempt to weaken the flesh with seductive appeals toward the smoothness of pleasures. For they are permitted, by a just judgment, to linger in the depths of the body even in those who are intensely struggling against sin. This is so that the free will of the human mind may always be put to the test. If someone is able to "die" while still living through their labors <note>referring to ascetic practices like fasting and vigil</note>, then they become entirely a house of the Holy Spirit. For such a person has already "risen" before they have died. This was the case for the blessed Paul himself, and for all those who have struggled or are struggling perfectly against sin.

<meta>This page continues Diadochos of Photiki’s discourse on the relationship between grace and the human soul. Having previously established that grace dwells in the depths of the mind while sin operates through the "law of the members" (the body), Diadochos now addresses how thoughts from both sources appear to arise from the same heart and why the soul often mistakes demonic suggestions for its own impulses.</meta>

### OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI

The heart produces thoughts from within itself, both good and bad. However, it does not produce evil thoughts by its very nature. Rather, having once been accustomed to the memory of evil through the first deception <note>Referring to the Fall of Adam and Eve in Eden</note>, the heart conceives most of its wicked thoughts from the bitterness of demons. We perceive all of these as if they proceed from the heart itself. Because of this, some have mistakenly supposed that sin dwells in the mind alongside grace. They argue that the Lord said: <note>original: "τὰ δὲ ἐξερχόμενα ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ἐκ τῆς καρδίας ἐξέρχονται"</note> “But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this is what defiles a person. For out of the heart come evil thoughts, sexual immorality,” and so on. But they do not realize that our mind <term>nous (the spiritual intellect)</term>, possessing a power of extremely subtle perception, makes the thoughts suggested by evil spirits its own. This happens through the activity of the flesh, to which the soul is joined in a way we do not fully understand, because the flesh is prone to such things. Since the flesh always loves being flattered by deception beyond measure, the thoughts sown in the soul by demons seem to proceed from the heart. We make them our own only when we choose to take pleasure in them. The Lord used the phrase mentioned above to rebuke this very tendency, as the divine word reveals. For whoever takes pleasure in the thoughts suggested by the malice of Satan, and "writes" the memory of them in his own heart, clearly begins to bear fruit from his own inner disposition from then on.

<margin>83.</margin> In the Gospels, the Lord says that the "strong man" cannot be cast out of his house unless a "stronger man" binds him, plunders his goods, and casts him out. How then can he who was cast out with such shame enter again and dwell with the true Master of the house, resting in his own home as he wishes? For no king, after defeating a tyrant who opposed him, would ever think of allowing that tyrant to remain with him in the royal palace. Instead, he would either slay him immediately or bind him for long-term punishment and hand him over to his armies to face a most wretched death.

<margin>84.</margin> If anyone supposes that because we think both good and

<column-break/>

evil at the same time, both the Holy Spirit and the devil dwell together in the mind, let them learn that this is because we have not yet "tasted and seen that Christ is the Lord." For as I said above, at first, grace hides its presence within those who are baptized, waiting for the soul's resolve. But when a person turns entirely toward the Lord, grace then reveals its presence to the heart with an ineffable perception. It again waits for the soul's movement, yet it allows demonic "arrows" to reach the depths of its perception so that the person may seek God with a more fervent resolve and a humble disposition. If, then, a person begins to advance in the keeping of the commandments and unceasingly calls upon the Lord Jesus, the fire of holy grace spreads even to the outer senses of the heart, convincingly burning up the "weeds" of the human earth. Consequently, the demonic plans only reach that place from a distance, now merely poking at the passible part of the soul <note>The "passible" part of the soul is the seat of emotions and desires</note>. But when the person of the struggle girds himself with all the virtues—especially total <term>unclutteredness (freedom from possessions)</term>—then grace illumines his entire nature with a deeper perception, warming him into a great love for God. Therefore, the demonic arrows are then extinguished outside the physical senses. For the breeze of the Holy Spirit, moving the heart with winds of peace, extinguishes the arrows of the fire-bearing demon while they are still being carried through the air. Nevertheless, God sometimes allows the malice of demons to affect even one who has reached this measure, leaving his mind unlit for a time, so that our free will <term>autexousion</term> is not entirely bound by the bond of grace. This is not only so that sin might be defeated through struggle, but also so that the person might still progress in spiritual experience. For what the student considers "perfection" is still "imperfect" compared to the riches of the God who teaches in love—even if one is able to ascend the whole of Jacob’s ladder <note>Genesis 28:10-19; a metaphor for the stages of spiritual ascent</note> through the progress of their labors.

<margin>85.</margin> The Lord Himself says that Satan fell from...

<summary>Diadochos explains that while evil thoughts feel as though they originate in the heart, they are actually demonic suggestions that the mind "claims" through pleasure. He argues that grace and sin do not inhabit the mind simultaneously, using the progression of spiritual maturity to show how grace eventually purifies even the outer senses.</summary>

->### ASCETIC DISCOURSE<-

...fallen from heaven, so that the foul-looking one <note>referring to Satan</note> might not gaze upon the dwellings of the holy Angels. How then can he, who is not even deemed worthy of the fellowship of good servants, have the human mind as a common dwelling place with God? But even if they claim this happens by "concession" <note>original: παραχώρησιν (parachōrēsin) – a term for God's providential "stepping back" or allowing a trial to occur</note>, they add nothing to their argument. For educational abandonment does not in any way deprive the soul of the divine light; instead, grace merely hides its presence from the mind for a time, as I have said, so that the soul may be driven by the bitterness of the demons. This is done so that the soul, recognizing the malice of its enemy little by little, might seek out help from God with all fear and much humility. This is the same way a mother might briefly push away from her arms a nursing infant who is misbehaving against the rules of suckling; she does this so that the child, being terrified by some foul-looking men or wild beasts standing around, might return with great fear and tears to its mother’s bosom. On the other hand, abandonment through rejection <note>original: κατὰ ἀποστροφὴν (kata apostrophēn) – a withdrawal of grace caused by the soul's persistent turning away from God</note> hands the soul over to the demons as a prisoner, since it does not wish to have God. But we are not children of shrinking back—may it never be!—but we believe ourselves to be true infants of God’s grace, being nursed by it through small concessions and frequent consolations. Through this kindness, we hope to reach the "mature man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." <note>A reference to the New Testament, Ephesians 4:13</note>

<margin>86.</margin>
Educational abandonment brings much grief, humility, and a measured sense of despair to the soul, so that the part of the soul that is boastful and easily agitated might be properly brought to humility. Immediately, it also brings to the heart a great desire for the beauty of silence. However, abandonment caused by God’s rejection allows the soul to be filled with despair, unbelief, pride, and anger all at once. We, therefore, who have experienced both types of abandonment, should approach God according to the character of each. In the first case, we owe Him thanks along with a defense for our failings, as if He were a good Father punishing the lawlessness of our will with the bitterness of the trial. In this way, He teaches us the difference between virtue and vice...

<column-break/>

...like a good Father. In the second case <note>abandonment by rejection</note>, we must offer unceasing confession of sins, constant tears, and greater withdrawal from the world. Thus, by increasing our labors, we may be able to prevail upon God to look upon our hearts as He did before. However, one must know that when the battle between the soul and Satan occurs during an "essential encounter"—I am speaking here of educational abandonment—grace hides itself, as I have already said, but it assists the soul with an unknown help. It does this so that it may demonstrate to the soul’s enemies that the victory belongs solely to the soul.

<margin>87.</margin>
Consider someone standing in an open place during the winter season at the break of day, looking toward the east. While all his front parts are warmed by the sun, his back remains entirely devoid of heat because the sun is not yet directly overhead. In the same way, those who are at the beginning of spiritual activity have their hearts warmed only partially by holy grace. Because of this, their mind <term>nous (the faculty of spiritual perception)</term> begins to bear spiritual thoughts; yet parts of the person remain preoccupied with "thinking according to the flesh," because all the members of the heart are not yet illuminated by the deep perception of the Holy Light of grace. Some people, failing to understand this, have mistakenly believed that two distinct substances <note>referring to a "good" and "evil" soul or mind</note> dwell within the minds of those who are struggling. They think it is as if two opposing powers coexist there. This is why the soul happens to think both good and bad things at the same moment. It is like the man in my example who, at the same touch of the air, both shivers and feels warmth. Ever since our mind slipped into the "doubling of knowledge" <note>Referring to the Fall of Adam and Eve and the resulting knowledge of both good and evil</note>, it has the necessity, even if it does not wish it, to carry both good and bad thoughts at the same moment—especially in those who are attaining a subtle degree of discernment. For as soon as the mind hastens to think of the good, it immediately remembers the evil. This is because human memory was split into a kind of double-thought following Adam’s disobedience. However, if we begin to fulfill the commandments of God with warm zeal, grace will illuminate all our senses with a deep perception, burning up our worldly thoughts and sweetening our heart with the peace of an unyielding friendship. It brings forth thoughts that are spiritual and no longer...

He also uses the analogy of morning sun in winter to explain how a believer can experience both spiritual and worldly thoughts simultaneously during their early progress.</summary>

# OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI #

...causes us to reason according to the flesh; this happens very frequently even to those approaching perfection, who possess the unceasing memory of the Lord in their heart.

<margin>88.</margin>
Holy grace bestows two good things upon us through the baptism of regeneration, one of which infinitely surpasses the other. The first is granted immediately: for grace renews us in the very water of baptism and brightens all the features of the soul—that is, the "image of God" <note>original: τὸ κατ' εἰκόνα (to kat' eikona) – the inherent human capacity for God given at creation</note>—by washing away every wrinkle of our sin. The second good, however, grace waits to work out in cooperation with us: this is the "likeness of God" <note>original: τὸ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν (to kath' homoiōsin) – the actual realization of godliness through virtue</note>. Thus, when the mind begins to taste the goodness of the All-Holy Spirit with a deep sense of perception, we should know that grace is beginning, as it were, to paint the "likeness" over the "image." Just as painters first sketch the figure of a person in a single color, and then little by little add various hues until they preserve the very likeness of the subject down to the hair; in the same way, the holy grace of God first restores the "image" through baptism to what it was when man was first created. But when grace sees us desiring the beauty of the "likeness" with all our purpose, and standing naked and undaunted in its workshop, it then adds virtue upon virtue, raising the form of the soul from glory to glory, and bestows upon it the character of the "likeness." Therefore, while our spiritual perception <note>original: αἴσθησις (aisthesis) – a key term for Diadochos meaning a conscious, felt experience of God's presence</note> shows us that we are being formed into the likeness, we shall only know the perfection of this likeness through enlightenment. For the mind receives all the virtues through perception, advancing according to a certain measure and inexpressible rhythm; but no one can acquire spiritual love unless they are enlightened with full assurance by the Holy Spirit. For if the mind does not perfectly receive the "likeness" through divine light, it may possess almost all the virtues, yet it still remains without a share in perfect love. For when a person is made like the virtue of God (as far as a human can be said to be like God), then they also carry the likeness of divine love. Just as in a portrait, when the brightest

<column-break/>

color is added to the image, it preserves the likeness of the subject even to the point of capturing their smile; in the same way, for those being painted into the divine likeness by divine grace, the addition of the enlightenment of love reveals that the "image" has attained the full beauty of the "likeness." For no other virtue can provide the soul with dispassion <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia) – not a lack of feeling, but freedom from the grip of disordered passions</note> except love alone; for love is the fulfillment of the law. Thus, our inner man is renewed day by day in the tasting of love, and is made full in love's perfection.

<margin>89.</margin>
At the beginning of one's progress—if we warmly love the virtue of God—the All-Holy Spirit gives the soul a taste of God's sweetness with full perception and assurance, so that the mind may know with precise knowledge the ultimate prize for its God-loving labors. However, for a long time thereafter, the Spirit hides the richness of this life-giving gift. He does this so that, even if we practice all the other virtues, we might not think ourselves to be anything at all, because we do not yet possess holy love as an established habit <note>original: ἕξιν (hexin) – a permanent state or disposition of the soul</note>. During such times, the demon of hatred disturbs the souls of those who are struggling, to the point that he even slanders those who love them, inciting feelings of hatred and bringing the destructive energy of spite almost to the very point of a kiss. Because of this, the soul suffers greatly, for it carries the memory of spiritual love but is unable to possess it in felt perception because it lacks the most perfect of labors. Therefore, one must work at love by force <note>original: ἐκ βίας (ek bias) – an ascetic principle of "forcing" oneself toward the good when feelings are absent</note> for a time, so that we may arrive at the taste of it in all perception and assurance. For no one living in this flesh is able to acquire the perfection of love, except for those saints who have reached the point of martyrdom and perfect confession. For whoever has attained this is entirely changed, and does not even easily desire food. For what desire for the world's goods will remain in one who is nourished by divine love? For this reason, the most wise Paul—the great vessel of knowledge—preaching to us from his own assurance regarding the future delight of the righteous, says: "The Kingdom of Heaven is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and..." <note>The text concludes with a quote from Romans 14:17.</note>

<summary>Diadochos explains the theological distinction between the "image of God" (restored at baptism) and the "likeness of God" (achieved through spiritual growth and love). He describes how grace fluctuates between giving a "taste" of sweetness and hiding itself to prevent pride and foster true virtue.</summary>

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE #

...joy in the Holy Spirit; which are the fruits of perfect love. Thus, those who are progressing toward perfection are able to taste this joy here continuously. But no one can possess it perfectly, except when mortality is perfectly swallowed up by life.

<margin>91.</margin> Let someone from among those who love God with an insatiable mind tell me: when I desired to truly know the love of God, the Good One <note>A common title for God the Father or Christ in ascetic literature.</note> granted this to me in great perception and certainty. Such a person says: "I felt this operation <note>original: ἐνέργεια (energeia) – the active power or 'working' of God within the person</note> so intensely that my soul was urged with an unspeakable joy and love to depart from the body and go to the Lord, and it became almost ignorant of the nature of this temporary life." 

The person who has experienced this love, even if he is insulted ten thousand times or suffers financial loss—for it happens that such a person must still endure such trials—does not get angry against the offender. Instead, he remains, as it were, "glued" to the soul of the one who insulted or harmed him. He is only set aflame against those who mistreat the poor, or who (as the Scripture says) speak injustice against God, or who otherwise live wickedly. For the one who loves God more than himself—or rather, the one who no longer loves himself but only God—no longer defends his own honor. Rather, he wishes only for righteousness to be honored by the One who honored him with eternal honor. This is no longer the result of a small effort of will; rather, he possesses such a disposition as a habit, due to his extensive experience of God’s love. 

Furthermore, one must know that the person energized by God into such love rises even above faith during the time of such an operation. For through this great love, he holds in the perception of his heart the very One who is usually honored through faith. This is what **Saint Paul** clearly signifies to us when he says: 
> "And now abide these three: faith, hope, love; but the greatest of these is love." <note>1 Corinthians 13:13</note>
For the one who holds God in the wealth of love, as I said, is then much greater than his own faith, for he exists entirely within longing.

<margin>92.</margin> The middle stage of the working of holy knowledge <note>original: γνῶσις (gnosis) – spiritual insight or direct experience of God</note> causes us to feel no small grief

<column-break/>

when, through some provocation, we have insulted someone and made him an enemy to us. Therefore, our conscience never stops pricking us until, through much apology, we restore the person we insulted to his former disposition. 

The highest opening of the mind occurs even when someone of this world is unjustly angry against us. This causes us to meditate and worry greatly; for if we become a stumbling block to anyone at all in this current age, our mind then becomes idle regarding theology <note>original: θεολογία – in this context, it refers not to academic study, but to the direct contemplation of and communion with God.</note>. For the Word of knowledge, being entirely love, does not allow the intellect to expand toward the grasping of divine contemplations unless we first recover the person who is angry with us in vain back into love. 

If that person does not wish for this to happen, or has moved away from our company, it is proper for us to keep the image of his face in our soul’s disposition, adding it to a boundless <margin>form / pouring out</margin> * pouring out <note>The translator notes a textual variation in the margin: "schema" (form/shape) versus "chyma" (pouring out/flow). Diadochos likely means an overflowing of love.</note> of the soul. Thus, in the depths of the heart, we fulfill the law of love. For it is said that those who wish to have the knowledge of God must look upon the faces of those who are angry without cause with a mind free of bitterness. When this happens, not only will our mind move without stumbling in its contemplation of God, but it will also ascend with much boldness into the love of God, pressing on unhindered from the second step to the first.

<margin>93.</margin> The path of virtue appears rough and gloomy to those who are just beginning to love piety. This is not because the path itself is like that, but because human nature is accustomed from the womb to the "broad way" of pleasures. However, to those who are able to pass the middle of the path, it is shown to be entirely pleasant and easy. For when the bad habit is subjected to the good through the operation of the good, the memory of irrational pleasures perishes. From then on, the soul joyfully traverses all the paths of virtue. 

For this reason, the Lord, leading us into the path of salvation, says: 
> "For narrow and constrained is the path that leads to life, and few are those who enter through it." <note>Matthew 7:14</note>
But to those who wish to approach the keeping of His holy commandments with great resolve, He says: 
> "For my yoke is easy, and..." <note>Matthew 11:30</note>

<summary>This page discusses the transformative power of divine love (agape), which can lead a person to value God's honor above their own and even temporarily transcend faith through direct experience. It also emphasizes that spiritual contemplation (theology) is blocked by conflict with others, requiring reconciliation or at least internal love for one's enemies to proceed.</summary>

# OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI #

...my burden is light <note>original: "τὸ φορτίον μου ἐλαφρόν ἐστι" — a reference to Matthew 11:30</note>. Therefore, at the beginning of the struggle, one must work out the holy commandments of God with a certain forced will. This is so that our good Lord, seeing our purpose and our labor, may send down His own "ready will"—an effortless desire—to those who so sweetly serve His glorious purposes. For it is then that a "will" is prepared by the Lord, so that we may do what is good unceasingly and with great joy. At that point, we will truly perceive that "it is God who works in us both to will and to work for His good pleasure" <note>original: "ὁ Θεός ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ θέλειν, καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας" — quoting Philippians 2:13</note>.

<margin>94.</margin> Just as wax that has not been warmed or softened for a long time cannot receive the seal placed upon it, so also a human being, unless tested through labors and infirmities, cannot contain the seal of God’s virtue. For this reason, the Lord says to the divine Paul: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is perfected in weakness." And the Apostle himself boasts, saying: "Most gladly, therefore, I will rather boast in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me" <note>2 Corinthians 12:9</note>. But it is also written in the Proverbs: "For whom the Lord loves He disciplines, and He scourges every son whom He receives" <note>Proverbs 3:12</note>. Now, the Apostle calls "weaknesses" the uprisings of the enemies of the cross, which continually happened to him and to all the saints of that time, so that they would not become prideful—as he himself says—due to the "abundance of revelations." Instead, through these frequent humiliations, they remained in the form of perfection through humility, guarding the divine gift in a holy manner. 

However, for us today, let us call "weaknesses" both evil thoughts <term>logismoi: intrusive or obsessive thoughts that tempt the soul</term> and bodily ailments. For back then, because the bodies of the saints struggling against sin were handed over to deadly tortures and various other afflictions, they were far above the passions that entered human nature through sin. But now, since "peace abounds" for the churches through the Lord, it is necessary for the bodies of those struggling for piety to be tested by continuous ailments, and for their souls to be tested by evil thoughts. This is especially true for those in whom spiritual knowledge <note>original: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note> operates with full perception and certainty. This happens so that they may remain free from all vanity and conceit, and be able to contain—as I

<column-break/>

said—the seal of divine beauty in their hearts through great humility, according to the saint who said: "The light of Your countenance, O Lord, has been signed upon us" <note>Psalm 4:6</note>. We must, therefore, endure the counsel of the Lord with thanksgiving. For then the continuity of illnesses and the battle against demonic thoughts will be reckoned to us as a "second martyrdom." For the one who then told the holy martyrs, through those lawless rulers, to deny Christ and to desire worldly glories, is the same one who now stands before the servants of God, saying the same things incessantly to them. He who then caused pain to the bodies of the righteous and utterly insulted the honorable teachers through those who served those devilish mindsets, is the very same one who now brings various sufferings upon the confessors of piety, along with many insults and humiliations. This happens especially when they help the oppressed poor with great power for the glory of the Lord. Because of this, we ought to work out the "martyrdom of our conscience" before God with security and patience. For as the scripture says: "I waited patiently for the Lord, and He inclined to me" <note>Psalm 40:1</note>.

<margin>95.</margin> Humility is a thing difficult to acquire. The greater it is, the more it must be achieved through many struggles. It comes to those who partake in holy knowledge <note>gnosis</note> in two ways: When the spiritual striver is in the middle of his spiritual experience, his mindset is somewhat humbler either because of bodily weakness, or because of those who are pointlessly hostile to those who care for righteousness, or because of evil thoughts. But when the mind <note>original: νοῦς (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul</note> is illuminated by holy grace in great perception and certainty, then the soul possesses humility as if it were its very nature. For, being nourished by divine goodness, it can no longer be lifted up by the swelling of ambition, even if it were to carry out the commandments of God unceasingly. Rather, the soul considers itself lowlier than everyone else because of its communion with divine gentleness. That first kind of humility often involves grief and dejection; but this second kind involves joy with an all-wise sense of awe. Therefore, the first comes to those who are in the middle of their struggles, as I said, but the second comes to those who are drawing near to perfection.

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE #

...is sent down. For this reason, that former grace <note>The "educational" grace mentioned on the previous page</note> is often reproached by the successes of worldly life. But this latter grace, even if one were to offer it all the kingdoms of the world, is neither terrified nor does it feel the terrible arrows of sin at all; for being entirely spiritual, it is completely ignorant of bodily glories. It was necessary for the spiritual combatant to pass through the former state in every way to reach this one. For if grace does not first soften our free will through that imposition of educational trials <note>original: "παιδευτικῶν παθῶν"—referring to the suffering or "passions" used by God for training</note>, it would not grant us the richness of this higher state.

<margin>96</margin> Those who are friends of the pleasures of the present life proceed from thoughts to actual transgressions. For being carried away by an undiscerning mind, they desire to bring almost all their passionate thoughts into unlawful words and unholy deeds. But those attempting to succeed in the ascetic life go from transgressions to more wicked thoughts, or into certain wicked and harmful words. For if the demons see such people either gladly enduring insults, or speaking idly and at the wrong time, or laughing improperly, or getting immoderately angry, or desiring empty and vain glory, then they arm themselves against them with one accord. For they take <term>vainglory</term> <note>original: "φιλοδοξίαν"—literally "love of glory" or ambition</note> especially as a pretext for their own wickedness; jumping through it as if through a dark window, they plunder the soul. Therefore, those who wish to live among the multitude of virtues should neither desire glory, nor meet with many people, nor make frequent outings, nor insult anyone, even if those insulted deserve it. Nor should they speak much, even if they are able to say all things well. For much speaking <note>original: "πολυλογία"</note> immoderately scatters the mind, and not only makes it idle regarding spiritual work, but also hands it over to the demon of <term>listlessness</term> <note>original: "ἀκηδείας"—Akedia is a state of spiritual despondency or boredom, often called the "noonday demon"</note>. This demon, after weakening the mind excessively, hands it over to the demon of sorrow, and finally to the demon of anger. Therefore, the mind must always be occupied with the keeping of the holy commandments and with the deep memory of the Lord of Glory. For "he who keeps a commandment," it says, "will know no evil word" <note>original: "ῥῆμα πονηρόν"—quoting Ecclesiastes 8:5</note>; that is, he will not be turned aside into base thoughts or words.

<margin>97</margin> When the heart receives the arrows of the demons with a certain burning pain, so that the one under attack feels he is actually bearing the arrows, the soul hates the passions with labor, as it is in the beginning of being purified. For if one does not grieve greatly over the shamelessness of sin, one could not rejoice richly in the goodness of righteousness. Therefore, he who wishes to purify his heart should set it on fire continuously with the memory of the Lord Jesus <note>An early reference to the practice that became the Jesus Prayer</note>, having this as his only meditation and unceasing work. For those who wish to cast off their internal corruption must not pray only at certain times and not others, but must always be at leisure for prayer through the guarding of the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦς"—the "eye of the soul" or the intellect in a spiritual sense</note>, even if they happen to be walking outside of houses of prayer. For just as he who wishes to purify gold, if he lets the fire go out in the furnace for even a short time, causes the material being purified to harden again; so also he who remembers God at one time but not another, loses through his leisure what he thinks he gained through prayer. It is the mark of a virtue-loving man to always consume the earthly nature of the heart with the memory of God, so that little by little, as evil is consumed by the fire of good memory, the soul may perfectly return to its natural brilliance with greater glory.

<column-break/>

<margin>98</margin> <term>Dispassion</term> <note>original: "Ἀπάθεια"—Apatheia is not a lack of feeling, but a state where the passions (urges like anger or lust) no longer control the person</note> is not simply to not be attacked by demons—for then we would have to have departed from the world, as the Apostle says <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 5:10</note>—but it is to remain "un-fought" while being attacked by them. Just as armored soldiers are shot at by their opponents and hear the sound of the archery, and even see the arrows sent at them, yet they are not struck because of the strength of their military garments. But while those men, protected by iron, have their invulnerability while being attacked, we—armed with the panoply of the holy light and the helmet of salvation through all good works—shall cut through the dark ranks of the demons. For purity is brought about not only by no longer practicing evil, but by the forceful rejection of evil through the diligent pursuit of good.

# OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKI #

...to please God in some way. But the enemy moves the body toward the desire for sexual union <note>original: "συνουσίας" — refers to sexual intercourse</note> through a certain fiery activity. This happens to the body, first because this pleasure is natural to our constitution—intended for the procreation of children—and therefore easily surrendered to; and secondly, it happens by the permission of God. For when the Lord sees one of His spiritual combatants flourishing greatly in the abundance of virtues, He sometimes allows him to be sullied by such a demon, so that he may consider himself more lowly than all other people in this life. Indeed, the disturbance of this passion either follows after great achievements or even anticipates them, so that by either the onset or the assault of the passion, the soul might appear useless to itself, no matter how great its achievements may be. But against the one <note>The temptation following virtue</note> we shall fight with great humility and love; and against the other <note>The temptation anticipating virtue</note> with self-control, a lack of anger, and a deep meditation on death. Thus, by unceasingly perceiving the activity of the Holy Spirit, we may rise above these passions in the Lord.

<margin>100</margin>
All of us who share in holy knowledge will certainly give an account even for involuntary distractions <note>original: "μετεωρισμῶν" — literally "loftiness" or "drifting thoughts," referring here to the mind wandering during prayer</note>. For as the divine Job says: "I have marked even if I have transgressed involuntarily," <note>Job 31:33 (Septuagint variant)</note> and rightly so. For if one does not devote oneself to always remembering God and does not neglect His holy commandments, one would not fall into either involuntary or voluntary sin. Therefore, one must immediately offer an intense confession to the Master even for involuntary sins—that is, a labor beyond one's usual spiritual rule. For it is not possible for a human being not to commit human errors, until our conscience is fully assured through tears of love regarding their forgiveness. For it says: *If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.* <note>1 John 1:9</note> We must, therefore, pay attention unceasingly to the feeling of confession, lest our conscience deceive itself, thinking it has confessed sufficiently to God. For God's judgment is far better than our own conscience, even if one is not aware of any fault in themselves with full certainty, just as the most wise Paul teaches us, saying: *I do not even judge myself. For I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not*

<column-break/>

*thereby justified. It is the Lord who judges me.* <note>1 Corinthians 4:3-4</note> For if we do not confess properly even concerning these things, we shall find a certain hidden dread within ourselves at the time of our departure <note>meaning the hour of death</note>. It is necessary for us who love the Lord to pray that we be found outside of all fear at that time. For he who is found in fear then will not freely pass by the rulers of Tartarus <note>original: "ταρταρέους ἄρχοντας" — referring to demonic authorities or "toll-houses" believed to challenge the soul after death</note>. For those rulers take the soul's own dread as an advocate for their own wickedness. But the soul that rejoices in the love of God, at the hour of its release, is carried above all the dark ranks with the angels of peace. For it is as if it has grown wings through spiritual love, having the love which is the unceasing fulfillment of the law. Therefore, at the coming of the Lord, those who depart this life with such boldness will be caught up together with all the Saints. But those who feel even a little dread at the time of death will be left behind in the multitude of all other men to be judged, as being under judgment. This is so that, having been tested through the <term>fire of judgment</term> <note>original: "πυρὸς τῆς κρίσεως" — a purifying trial after death</note>, they may receive the lots owed to them according to their deeds from our good God and King, Jesus Christ. For He is the God of justice, and upon us who love Him is the wealth of the goodness of His kingdom, forever and unto all the ages of ages. Amen.

->* * *<-

### Interpretation of the saying in this present 100th Chapter which says: "so that, having been tested through the fire of judgment," which was asked by some; an interpretation by Saint Maximus. ###

<margin>Response</margin>
Those who have acquired the perfection of love toward God, and have raised the wing of the soul through virtues, are—according to the Apostle—caught up in the clouds and do not come into judgment. But those who have not entirely acquired perfection, but possess both sins and achievements, these come into the court of judgment. And there, through the counter-examination of their good and bad deeds, being as it were "fired" <note>tested by fire</note>, if the scale <note>original: "πλάστιγξ" — the tray of a balance scale</note> of good deeds weighs more heavily, they are cleansed of punishment.

...gazing at creation for God's sake, he called to mind the angels and all the invisible powers, and descended even to the earth; he did not exclude the wild beasts, the cattle, the birds, or the reptiles; for he considered it his duty to worship the Creator and lead a hymn of praise arising from these things. Just as the fire surrounded the bush but did not burn it, so it is for those who have received the gift of dispassion <note>term: "dispassion" (Greek: *apatheia*) — not a lack of feeling, but a state of being free from the control of disordered passions and compulsions</note>.
