<margin>4.</margin>
The moon, in its waxing and waning, reveals the human condition: sometimes a person does what is good, and at other times he falls into sin; then, through repentance, he runs back to a life of virtue. Therefore, the intellect <note>term: "intellect" (Greek: *nous*) — in Orthodox theology, the "eye of the soul" or the faculty that perceives God, distinct from the discursive reason</note> of the one who has stumbled is not lost, as some among you believe. Just as the body of the moon does not diminish, but only its light, so too does a person regain his proper radiance through repentance, just as the moon, after it has waned, clothes itself in its own light once more. For "the one who believes in Christ, even if he dies, shall live"; and he shall know, it says, "that I, the Lord, have spoken, and I will do it."

<margin>5. Likely concerning foul thoughts</margin>
If, when a swarm of *enemy formations* <note>original: "ἐχθρῶν σχηματισμῶν" — a military metaphor for demonic suggestions or intrusive thoughts</note> rises up against your mind, you give in and are defeated, know that you have been separated for a time from divine grace. Because of this, you were delivered into the hands of your downfall by a just judgment. Therefore, struggle never to be left behind by grace through negligence, not even for a moment. But if you are able to become stronger than the slip and leap over the wall of passionate thoughts and the successive, filthy assaults of the enemies' many-mindedness, do not be ignorant of the gift given to you from above. For the Apostle says: "It was not I, but the grace of God which is with me" that achieved such a victory. And from the foul thoughts rising up against me, He lifted me up; and from the "unjust man"—meaning the devil—

<column-break/>

and from the "old man" He rescued me. Hence, lightened by the wing of the Spirit and released from the weight of the body, I was able to fly above the hunting demons, who ensnare the human intellect through the love of pleasure, which they offer with forceful and violent persuasion. He, then, who led me out of the land of Egypt—that is, from the soul-destroying ways of the world—is the same one who, fighting for me with a hidden hand, struck down Amalek <note>Amalek was the biblical enemy of the Israelites; in ascetic literature, he represents the passions that attack the soul during its journey to the "Promised Land" of holiness</note>. And He has given me hope that the Lord will also destroy the rest of the nations of unholy passions from before our face. This God of ours will give wisdom and power. For some have received wisdom, yet not the power of the Spirit to conquer their enemies. He will lift your head above your enemies and give you wings like a dove, and having flown, you shall find rest in God. The Lord will make your arms a bow of bronze, showing you to be firm, ready, and vigorous against the adversary, and trampling under your feet all who stand against you. Ascribe, therefore, the grace of purity to the Lord, because He did not shut you up in the hands of the desires of your flesh and blood, or those of the corrupting and unclean spirits that follow them; instead, He secured you with His own right hand. Build an altar to Him, just as Moses did after turning back Amalek. For this reason, I will confess and praise You, Lord, and I will sing to Your name, magnifying Your mighty deeds; for You have redeemed my life from corruption and snatched me from the snares and nets of this easily-besetting, many-formed, and worn-out wickedness.

<margin>6.</margin>
The wicked demons rekindle, renew, uplift, and multiply our foul passions; but the visitations of the Divine Word—and especially those that come through the shedding of tears—deaden the passions, even if they happen to be long-standing, and dissolve them. Little by little, they bring the destructive, sinful workings of the soul and body into non-existence. Only let us not grow weary of waiting upon the Lord through prayer and through unyielding, "shameless" <note>original: "ἀναιδοῦς" — likely referring to the "persistent widow" or the friend at midnight in the Gospels, suggesting a bold, insistent type of prayer</note> hope.

...demons strive to defile; but neither in this shall they break or weaken the one who is accustomed to bearing everything with endurance and nobility. <margin>19.</margin> The enemies fight against our character and zeal, buffeting the soul with various and unspeakable temptations. <margin>20.</margin> Nothing is so naturally prone to making virtue vanish as <term>buffoonery</term> <note>original: "εὐτραπελία" (eutrapelia) — while it can mean "wit," in monastic literature it refers to coarse jesting or frivolous talk that distracts from spiritual focus.</note>, playing the fool, and idle talk. <margin>21.</margin> It is most fitting and profitable for the soul to stoutly bear every affliction, whether brought by men or by <term>demons</term>. <margin>22.</margin> There are times when a person is moved from the "seat on the right"—even if he is a diligent seeker—when temptations abound and he is displaced from his own spiritual rank. But you must hope to be restored to your former beautiful state once the evil one has been cast away from you by divine command. <margin>23.</margin> Man is a great thing when he grows within and is magnified by the virtues. Yet, this great person still fears sin as an elephant fears a mouse, lest after preaching to others, he himself should be disqualified.

<margin>24.</margin> Not only near the end of the world will the devil "speak words against the Most High," as Daniel says, but even now, through our thoughts, he sometimes sends out heavy blasphemies into heaven itself, slandering the Most High, His creatures, and the holy mysteries of Christ. <margin>25.</margin> Fighting and reproaching with boldness, the enemy comes upon the soul as it departs from the body, becoming a bitter and fearsome accuser regarding its failings. Against Him we have sinned, and to Him we shall give account, having as a pledge of His compassion and salvation toward us His precious Cross. But you—flee far from us, destroyer! You have nothing in common with the servants of Christ." As the soul says these things with courage, the devil finally turns his back, wailing and wailing, unable to withstand the name of Christ. Finding itself above him, the soul flies over the enemy, buffeting him, just as the one called O- <note>The text breaks off here; likely a reference to a specific bird or a biblical figure like Othniel.</note>

<margin>26.</margin> ...as a swift-winged hawk <note>original: "ξυπτέρυξ" (xypteryx) — likely a variation of "oxypteryx," meaning sharp or swift-winged, used here to describe a bird of prey chasing a crow.</note> pursues the Crow. After these things, the soul is conveyed by the divine angels, rejoicing, to the places appointed for her, according to her spiritual state.

Know that even by a small temptation, through God’s permission, the diligent seeker is sometimes hindered from making progress. Let the <term>Echeneis</term> <note>original: "Ἐχενηΐς" — the Remora or "stay-ship" fish. In antiquity, it was believed this tiny fish could stop a massive ship simply by attaching itself to the hull.</note> convince you of this—that tiniest of fish which, by its touch alone, <margin>*or: renders useless</margin> brings a ten-thousand-ton merchant ship to a halt and prevents the hindered vessel from moving forward. And remember certainly the one who said: *“I, Paul, great as I am, desired to come to you once and twice, and Satan hindered us.”* <note>A reference to 1 Thessalonians 2:18.</note> But do not be troubled by this; rather, fight back through endurance, and you will attain grace.

<margin>27.</margin> The one who is thriving greatly in the virtues, if through negligence he should turn away from what is proper, the "sons of the evil East" come up against him—Amalek, and especially Midian, the power that loves <term>fornication</term> <note>Midian is often used in monastic literature as a symbol of sensory or sexual temptation.</note>. They come with their camels—that is, with their passionate memories, which are without number—and they destroy all the produce of the land, which is to say, all excellent practice and spiritual disposition. Then, finally, the "Israel" <note>Here, Israel represents the monk or the soul of the believer.</note> becomes impoverished and loses heart entirely, and is forced to cry out to the Lord. In this way, a good thought is sent from heaven, imitating Gideon, through much faith and humility. For he says, *“my thousand is the humblest in Manasseh,”* <note>A quote from Judges 6:15.</note> so as to draw up a battle line against such great multitudes with only three hundred weak men, and to wondrously set up trophies of victory against the adversaries through the alliance of grace.

<margin>28.</margin> You will not be able to "tread upon the Asp and the Basilisk" <note>A reference to Psalm 91:13.</note> and the rest, unless by much supplication you entreat God and receive defending angels to lift you up with their own hands, raising you above your miry thoughts.

<margin>29.</margin> When someone who is boxing <note>The author uses "πυκτεύων" (pukteuon), referring to the sport of boxing, as a metaphor for spiritual combat.</note> vigorously is defeated, let him not lose heart at all, nor grow weary. Instead, let him be restored by the words of Isaiah and take courage, chanting such charms as these: *“Though you have grown strong, you shall be defeated, O evil demons; for even if you grow strong again, you shall be defeated again. And whatever counsel you take, the Lord will scatter it, for God is with us.”* <note>A paraphrase of Isaiah 8:9-10.</note> It is God who raises up those who have been shattered,

<column-break/>

and who prepares our enemies to be beaten whenever we repent.

<margin>30.</margin> It is impossible for one who is being disciplined by temptations to pass through them without grief. But afterward, such people are filled with great joy, sweet tears, and divine thoughts—all those who have cultivated toil and affliction in their hearts.

<margin>31.</margin> If Isaac willed it, and Esau once ran toward the desire for the blessing, yet they were disappointed—since it is God who shows mercy, and blesses, and anoints with the Spirit—we must realize He does so not necessarily to the one we might have willed, but to the one whom God predestined for service before he was even formed. Therefore, let us not be troubled at all, nor let us feel envy when we see certain brothers who are wretched and "the least" making progress in virtue. You have also heard the Lord saying: *“Give this man your place, so that he may sit higher up.”* <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 14:8-10.</note> Rather, I marvel at the Judge in these matters, who has anointed wisely and ineffably; that he should make that "least" and "last" person to be first and to lead, while making us—who were first in asceticism and in time—to be last. For as the Lord has distributed to each man, so shall we walk; if indeed "we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit," as it is written.

<margin>32.</margin> Never accept it when a person under your obedience says to you: "Grant me a period of time for virtue," or "Let me test this or that matter, and in that way I will succeed." For the one who speaks this way clearly fulfills his own will and sets aside the conditions of the most excellent obedience.

<margin>33.</margin> The sufferings of the flesh and of the soul, as you know, will vanish in time and by the divine nod, even if they have been greatly increased. But the mercy of Christ shall in no way perish; for the mercy of the Lord is from this age and unto the age to come upon those who fear Him.

<margin>34.</margin> Royal treasuries shall be filled with gold, and the minds of true Monks shall be filled with knowledge.

<margin>35.</margin> There are times when a teacher is handed over to dishonor, undergoing temptations for the sake of those who have been spiritually benefited. *“For we,”* he says, *“are without honor, and are dishonored by the thorn, and are weak; but you have become glorious and strong in Christ.”* <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 4:10, where Paul discusses the "folly" and weakness of the Apostles for the sake of the Church.</note>

<meta>This page continues the "Consolatory Chapters" by St. John of Karpathos. It transitions from general metaphors of the soul's journey to specific ascetic advice on dealing with "logismoi" (thoughts), the restoration of the soul through dispassion, and the necessity of humility regardless of one's progress in the spiritual life.</meta>

-># OF OUR HOLY FATHER JOHN OF KARPATHOS<-

<margin>36.</margin>
The source and foundation of the corruption of the flesh is the **passionate thought** <note>original: "ἐμπαθὴς λογισμός" (empathis logismos) — in monastic literature, a "thought" is not just an idea, but a suggestion or impulse from the ego or the demonic that can lead to sin.</note>. The person who remains watchful after a fall expels this thought from the soul through **repentance**. For it is better that you have mourned, so that the evil and unholy thought—which urged the commission of such an act—might be removed from your midst. Therefore, spiritual mourning is the very opposite of the "spirit of corruption."

<margin>37.</margin>
Who will announce to the person crushed by dishonor and the weakness of their virtues that they shall see Jesus? They shall see Him not only in the future, but even now, coming to them with power and great glory through **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias) — a state of being "passionless," not as in "without feeling," but as in being free from the control of disordered desires or "passions."</note>. This is so that the soul, having grown old in its "barrenness" like Sarah, yet unexpectedly bearing a son of righteousness, might say: *“God has brought me laughter”* <note>Genesis 21:6</note>. This means He has granted the greatest joy to the one who was grieved for many years by many passions. Or, as another translator rendered it: *“God has made me delicate”*—that is, my youth has been renewed like an eagle's. For though I was previously grown old in sins and shameful passions, I have now been reborn; I return to my youth and grow tender, I who was formerly hardened by material things. Now, at last, I look upon the things of this world with a "smooth" or clear gaze, having recovered my natural simplicity and lack of complexity, for my mind has been healed by God’s great mercy. And my flesh has become like that of **Naaman the Syrian** <note>original: "Σύρου Νεεμάν" (Syrou Neeman) — referring to the general healed of leprosy in 2 Kings 5.</note>, like the flesh of a little child, because I have been washed in the "Jordan of knowledge." I am now "single-minded" <note>original: "μονότροπος" (monotropos) — often used to mean "monastic," but literally "single-turning" or "undivided."</note> by the grace of God, delivered from the serpent’s cunning and from the crowd of "material" and complex thoughts of malice which I had previously acquired against my true nature.

<margin>38.</margin>
Imagine the Lord saying to you: "At a certain time I took away from you this or that gift of grace, in which you thought your mind found fulfillment and rest; but in their place, I have given you another gift as a counterbalance." But you, thinking only of what was taken away and not perceiving what was given in their stead, become gloomy and suffer, wounded by grief. Yet, you actually please me by your sorrow when it comes from Me; for I cause grief for your own benefit, seeking to save rather than destroy the one I consider my <margin>* perhaps: son</margin> **son**.

<margin>39.</margin>
Consider this: command yourself not to eat fish, and observe how after this the enemy <note>the devil</note> relentlessly drives you toward a desire for fish. And you, in turn, feel a frantic urgency for that which you did not even want, so that you might learn by a small example what happened to **Adam**. For having heard "do not eat of this one thing," he ran toward that forbidden thing alone with great desire.

<column-break/>

<margin>40.</margin>
God saves one person through knowledge, and another through **innocence** and guilelessness. For you ought to know that God will never reject the innocent person.

<margin>41.</margin>
Those who make use of prayer most intensely are the ones besieged by the most terrifying and savage temptations.

<margin>42.</margin>
If you have chosen to clothe yourself in **dispassion**, do not be indifferent, but strive with all your might to attain it. For we "groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling," so that—not only physically after the end of the age, but even now intellectually through the "earnest money" <note>original: "ἀρραβῶνα" (arrhavona) — a down-payment or guarantee of a future inheritance.</note>—what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. For "death is swallowed up in victory," and all the "Egyptians" <note>symbolizing the passions or demons</note> who oppress us and pursue us shall be swallowed up in the waves by the power sent down to us from heaven.

<margin>43.</margin>
Do not forget the one who said, *“I fear lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified,”* and, *“Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall,”* and *“You who are spiritual, consider yourself, lest you also be tempted.”* If you forget the turning away and lawlessness of **Solomon** after he received such great grace; if you consign to oblivion the unexpected denial of the great **Peter**, then you will grow over-confident in your knowledge. You will boast of your way of life, take pride in the length of your ascetic practice, and give place to pride. But do not be careless, O brother; rather, be fearful as long as you draw breath, even if you have reached the number of Moses' years. Pray, saying: *“O Lord, do not cast me off in the time of my old age; when my strength fails, do not forsake me. O God, my Savior, my praise is in You continually.”* <note>Psalm 71:9</note>

<margin>44.</margin>
The Lord says to you, as He did to **Matthew**: *“Follow me.”* If you, then, are pursuing your much-desired Master with eagerness, but along the road of life you should strike your foot against a stone of passion and fall...

It also warns that even advanced practitioners must remain humble and vigilant, as temptations increase with prayer and no one is immune to falling.</summary>

# CONSOLATORY CHAPTERS

...sin unexpectedly, or as often happens in muddy places, you have slipped and fallen against your will; as many times as you happen to fall and bruise your body, so many times rise up with the same zeal and pursue your own Lord until you catch Him. Thus I appeared to you in the Holy Thought, to see the power and glory that saves me; and in your name, O Lord, I will lift up my hands and receive. I shall be filled as if with marrow and fatness, and my lips shall rejoice as they sing to you <note>These phrases are drawn from Psalm 63 (62 in the Septuagint), a morning prayer expressing the soul’s thirst for God.</note>. For it is a great thing for me that I have been named a **Christian**, just as the Lord says to me through Isaiah: *“It is a great thing for you to be called my servant.”* <note>cf. Isaiah 49:6.</note>

<margin>45.</margin> On the one hand, He says that the Father will give good things to those who ask Him; on the other, that He will give the **Holy Spirit** to those who pray. By these words, we understand that God's petitioners receive not only the forgiveness of their failings but also the distribution of heavenly gifts, being strengthened by such an understanding. For the Lord promises such good things not to the righteous, but to sinners. For if you, He says, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him? <note>Luke 11:13.</note> Therefore, ask without ceasing and with an unwavering mind, even if you are lowly in your virtuous life and very weak beyond what is worthy, and you shall receive great things.

<margin>46.</margin> How can the unbeliever or the person of little faith be convinced that an ant grows wings, and a certain worm in turn becomes a bird, and that many other things happen paradoxically in creation? Let them observe this so that, having set aside the disease of unbelief and hopelessness, they may finally grow wings and flourish like a tree in the all-praiseworthy knowledge. For I am, says the Lord, He who makes the dry wood flourish and gives life to dried-up bones <note>A reference to the vision of the valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37.</note>.

<margin>47.</margin> By no means should we wish to be consumed by anxieties for the needs of the body. Rather, let us trust God with our whole soul, just as a certain good man once said: *“Trust in the Lord, and you shall be trusted.”* And as the blessed **Peter the Apostle** writes: *“Be sober and watch in prayers, and cast all your care upon God, because He cares for you.”* <note>1 Peter 5:7-8.</note>

<column-break/>

If you still hesitate and disbelieve that He truly intends to care for you and nourish you, look at the **spider**, and consider how much a human differs from a spider. I speak of the spider, than which nothing is weaker or more powerless. Having no possessions, making no journeys across the sea, not going to law, not getting angry, and possessing no storehouses, it lives out its life in complete gentleness, self-control, and the utmost stillness <note>original: "ἡσυχίᾳ" (hesychia) — a technical term in Eastern Christianity for "stillness" or "quietness," often referring to a specific style of meditative prayer.</note>. It does not meddle at all in the affairs of its neighbors but only does its own work in a kind of rest; it maintains an undisturbed state, almost giving a voice to those who are ambitious in their laziness. For *“let every man who wishes to be idle not even wish to eat.”* <note>cf. 2 Thessalonians 3:10.</note> It remains so silent that it surpasses and defeats **Pythagoras**, whom the Greeks admire above all philosophers for practicing the restraint of the tongue.

Pythagoras, then, even if he did not speak to everyone, at least spoke secretly from time to time with those men who were most dear to him. He even spoke ambitiously to bulls and eagles on many occasions—certain nonsense and delusions. And while he abstained entirely from wine, he made use of water. But this creature [the spider], by its exceeding and extreme speechlessness, has surpassed Pythagoras's restraint of the tongue. It has spat upon not only the drinking of wine but also the drinking of water. 

In such a quiet state, therefore, does the weak and humble spider dwell; it does not allow itself to walk outside anywhere, nor to wander here and there in fantasy, nor to labor and toil endlessly. The Lord, who dwells on high and looks upon the humble (for nothing is humbler than the spider), extends His **providence** <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia) — God's caring and purposeful guidance of the universe.</note> even to it. He sends it its daily little bit of food, preparing the small insects it needs for its life to fall into its nets near its little tent.

<margin>48.</margin> But perhaps someone enslaved to gluttony will say: "I eat very much, and because I have many expenses, it is necessary for me to be entangled in the myriad affairs of life." But let even such a person consider the great **whales** that feed in the **Atlantic** sea; they are nourished abundantly by God and never experience hunger...

<summary>St. John of Karpathos encourages persistent repentance after spiritual falls and argues that God's providence sustains even the lowliest creatures, like the spider, and the largest, like the whales of the Atlantic.</summary>

...received. For each of those beasts swallows an animal so large that not even a populous city could consume that much in a single day. For "all things," it says, "look to You to give them their food in due season" <note>Psalm 104:27. John uses the vast appetite of wild animals as a metaphor for God's infinite capacity to provide.</note>. Therefore, it is God who feeds both the one who eats much and the one who lives on a meager diet. Having heard these things, even you who possess a "wide and spacious belly" <note>A humorous or pointed reference to those struggling with gluttony or physical needs.</note>, entrust yourself entirely from now on to God and to faith. Shake off every kind of worldly distraction and a mind burdened with many cares, and be no longer unbelieving, but believing.

<margin>49.</margin> If we truly wish to please God and to be befriended by that most blessed friendship, let us present our mind "naked" to God. We must drag along nothing of the present age—no craft, no conceit, no sophistry, no self-justification—even if we are educated in all the wisdom of the world. For the Divine turns away from those who approach Him with a conceited manner, who are fed by vainglory, and who are puffed up. For some of the interpreters have well rendered "empty conceit" as a "feeding-trough" and a "bellows" <note>original: "σιτιστήριον καὶ φύσαν." The image is of someone being fattened on pride like an animal or puffed up with air.</note>.

<margin>50.</margin> How could we be able to wrestle down the sin that has already taken hold of us? There is a need for force. For a man, it says, "labors in pains" <note>Proverbs 16:26 (Septuagint).</note> and forces himself away from his own destruction, contending always from above for the holiness of his own thoughts. To dissolve force with force is not forbidden by the laws. If, then, we bring the force of some zeal—even if it is very weak—and we wait for the power that is to come upon us from on high while "sitting in Jerusalem" (that is, in unceasing prayer and the other virtues), when will that mighty force come to us? For it does not work anything weak according to our own measure of force. Rather, it is a force that cannot be described by lips of flesh, winning by its great strength and struggling against both the worst habits and the malice of the demons. It wins over the inclination toward the worse in our souls, and it wins over the unseemly movements of the body. For "there was," it says, "a sound from heaven like a rushing mighty wind" <note>Acts 2:2. The Greek word for "mighty" (biaia) also means "violent" or "forceful." John argues that we must use spiritual "force" to counter the "force" of sin.</note>, so that it might force out the evil that is always forcing us toward the worse.

<margin>51.</margin> The enemy lies in wait "like a lion in his den" <note>Psalm 10:9.</note>

<column-break/>

and hides traps and snares for us, consisting of impure and impious thoughts. But we too, if we do not slumber, will be able to set greater and more difficult traps, snares, and ambushes for him. For prayer and psalmody, watchfulness, humility, service to neighbors, mercy, thanksgiving, and the hearing of divine oracles—these become an ambush for the enemy, and a trap, a pit, scourges, a noose, and snares.

<margin>52.</margin> Having advanced very far in age, the divine David, thanking God who chose him, says near the end of his blessing: "Now your servant has found his heart to pray this prayer" <note>2 Samuel 7:27. In the Greek Bible, "found his heart" implies finding the inner focus or courage to truly communicate with God.</note>. This is said so that we may learn that there is need of much struggle and time in prayer, so that we may eventually find that undisturbed state of the mind—a certain other "inner heaven" where Christ dwells. As the Apostle says: "Do you not realize that Jesus Christ dwells in you?" <note>2 Corinthians 13:5.</note>

<margin>53.</margin> If Christ has become for us "righteousness and wisdom" and so forth, it is clear that He is also "rest." For "Come to me," He says, "all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" <note>Matthew 11:28.</note>. It is well said, then, that the Sabbath—that is, rest—was made for man. For in Christ alone will the human race find true rest.

<margin>54.</margin> Just as there is a "cup of falling" and a "chalice of wrath" <note>Isaiah 51:17.</note>, so there is also a "cup of weakness." The Lord, having taken this from us at the fitting time, gives it into the hands of our enemies, so that henceforth not we, but the demons may be weak and fall.

<margin>55.</margin> Just as in external affairs there are money-changers, weavers, bird-catchers, warriors, and builders, so also consider the internal things: that there are, within our reasonings, gamblers, sorcerers, pirates, hunters, defilers, and murderers. One must quickly shut these out through pious contradiction and prayer, especially the "defilers" <note>original: "κοινωτάς." These are thoughts that make the holy "common" or "unclean."</note>, so that they do not defile the holy place and profane the man of God.

<margin>56.</margin> Not only with the tongue is the Lord robbed...

...towards salvation, just as with the thief crying out from the cross, but also through silent reasoning. For it says that the woman with the flow of blood said within herself: "If I only touch the hem of His garments, I shall be saved." <note>Matthew 9:21. The author emphasizes that God hears the internal disposition of the heart, not just spoken words.</note> Likewise, the servant of Abraham spoke to God in his mind concerning Rebecca.

<margin>57.</margin> This very sin almost drives the repentant person toward God, as they become sensible of its foul stench, its weight, and its madness. But for the person who does not wish to turn toward repentance, it does not drive them toward God; rather, holding them in its power, it binds them with unbreakable chains, making their desires for destruction even more intense and sharp thereafter.

<margin>58.</margin> Guard yourself against the potions of Jezebel, <note>In the Byzantine tradition, Jezebel often symbolizes the "spirit of fornication" or "false teachings" that seduce the soul into pride.</note> chief among which are the thoughts of arrogance and vainglory. You will be able to overcome these by the grace of God, by treating your soul as nothing and humbling it, and by throwing yourself before the Lord, calling upon Him to help you, and recognizing that gifts are heavenly in origin. For this reason, it says: "No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven." <note>John 3:27.</note>

<margin>59.</margin> The Law says: "If witnesses are brought against him and he does not destroy the thing, he shall pay." <note>A paraphrase of Mosaic laws concerning restitution and responsibility.</note> There are times at a banquet when a vainglorious thought leaps forward, wishing to speak out of season. But angelic thoughts bear witness to you, prompting you to destroy that talkative and ill-timed thought. If, therefore, you do not destroy it with noble silence, but instead allow it to go forth into the open—being softened by arrogance—then you shall pay the debt. This great sin is handed over to justice, resulting either in heavy physical pains, or in severe clashes with the brothers, or in punishment in the age to come. For indeed, we shall give an account for every idle and vainglorious word because of the lack of discipline of the tongue. Therefore, we must keep watch over our tongue with sobriety.

<margin>60.</margin> All those who are tested by pleasures, by anger, by vainglory, and the like, are said to be burned by the sun by day and by the moon by night. Pray, therefore, to be sheltered by the divine, dew-bearing cloud, <note>The "dew-bearing cloud" refers to the presence of the Holy Spirit, which refreshed the Three Holy Children in the furnace and protects the monk from the "heat" of passions.</note> so that you may escape the scorching heat of the enemies.

<margin>61.</margin> By no means give any freedom of speech to the

<column-break/>

shield-bearers of excessive wine-drinking and the slaves of the disordered table. Do not grant it to those who wish to speak with you shamelessly, even if they have grey hair on their faces, and even if they have spent a long time in the monastic life—lest, according to the Scripture, "rottenness covers you," and you are led away with the unclean and those uncircumcised in heart.

<margin>62.</margin> First, Peter is entrusted with the keys, then he is permitted to fall into denial, so that his pride might be tempered by the fall. <note>Matthew 16:19 and 26:69-75. The author suggests that God allows even great saints to fail to prevent them from becoming arrogant about their spiritual gifts.</note> You, therefore, if you have received the key of knowledge and yet fall into various thoughts, do not be surprised. Glorify our only wise Lord, who bridles with such occurrences the conceit that rises up against divine knowledge. For temptations act as a bridle, able to restrain human puffiness through the providence of God.

<margin>63.</margin> If the Lord often takes away good things from us, just as He took the wealth of Job—for "The Lord gave, and the Lord took away"—then surely He will also take away from our hands the evils which He brought upon us. For "good things and bad come from the Lord," <note>Sirach 11:14.</note> and He who brought the bad upon us will Himself bring us eternal joy with eternal glory. For "Just as I watched over them," says the Lord, "to pluck up and to break down... so I will watch over them to build and to plant." <note>Jeremiah 31:28.</note> Let the common proverb be silent which says: "Where there is evil, there is no good." For the Lord who changed circumstances for the worse is certainly able to transform them back to a more radiant state unexpectedly.

<margin>64.</margin> He who attacks the demons more forcefully and contentiously, whether through self-control, prayer, or any virtue, will receive deeper wounds from them in return—to the point that he might even fall into a state of despair, seeing the sentence of spiritual death in his own soul. This leads him to say: "Who will deliver me from this body of death?" <note>Romans 7:24.</note> For I am forced, against my will, to bow down to the laws of the adversary.

<margin>65.</margin> It was not without reason written that some said to themselves: "Arise, and let us go against a people that dwells securely in hope and is at rest." And again: "Come, let us go up and speak to them with a deceitful, mental tongue, and turn—"

# OF THE BLESSED DIADOCHOS, BISHOP OF PHOTIKE

...drive them from us and away from the truth. For the terrible demons are accustomed, throughout the entire life of those who have chosen the life of stillness <note>original: "ἡσύχιον βίον" (hesychion bion) – a life of "hesychia" or inner silence and contemplation, a cornerstone of Eastern monasticism.</note>, to sharpen the swords of temptation. They wage war even more manically against the more devout and God-fearing, pushing them toward the very act of sin through unbearable conflicts. They do this perhaps so that they might be able to cause those under attack to fall away from faith in Christ, from prayer, and from good hope. 

But we, as David says, "shall not depart from You" <note>Psalm 80:18 (Septuagint 79:19).</note> until You have mercy on us, and until those who swallow us up are far removed from us. We shall not depart from You until You command those who tempt us to leave us, and we are brought to life through endurance and firm dispassion <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias) – not a lack of feeling, but a state where the soul is no longer controlled by disordered passions or impulses.</note>. For the life of man is a place of trial <note>A reference to Job 7:1: "Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?"</note>; and for a set time, one is often prepared by the Judge of the contest to fall under the feet of "strangers" <note>Demonic forces or intrusive thoughts.</note>. Yet it is the mark of a great-natured and noble soul not to despair in the midst of calamities.

<margin>66.</margin>
If a demon has such power that, even against a person's will, he can reshape them and carry them toward his own impulse—causing them to depart from their natural, good condition—how much more power does an Angel have? When an Angel receives God's command at the appointed time, is he not able to lead the whole disposition of a person toward what is better? 

If the freezing North wind has enough power to transform the most tender nature of water into the hardness of stone, what might the warmest South wind do? If air that is deeply chilled can make everything yield to it and conform to its state—for "who can stand before the face of His cold?" <note>Psalm 147:17.</note>—how could warmth not transform all things toward itself? For who can stand before the face of heat? Let us believe, therefore, that the cold and black coal of our intellect shall, sooner or later, become warm and light-filled through the touch of the most divine fire.

<margin>67.</margin>
There is also a certain state in the present life which serves as a witness and a sign of dispassion for our "inner Joseph." <note>A metaphor for the soul or the intellect, referencing Joseph’s purity in Egypt.</note> In this state, the mind, having departed from "Egypt," stands aloof from passionate attachments and the most shameful slavery of the "basket" <note>A reference to the labor of the Israelites in Egypt (Psalm 81:6).</note>. It then hears a "language it did not know" <note>Psalm 81:5.</note>: no longer the filthy language of demons which destroys right thinking, but the holy language 

<column-break/>

of the light-bearing Angels, who reshape the mind from the bodily to the incorporeal; a language that brings illumination to the soul that receives it.

<margin>68.</margin>
I have heard some brothers, who were incessantly ill in body and unable to practice fasting, say to me: "How can we be delivered from the devil and the passions without fasting?" To them, it must be said: you will be able to wear down and cast out both evil things and the "suggestors" of evil, not only through abstinence from food, but also through the cry of the heart. 

For it says, "They cried to the Lord in their trouble, and He delivered them." <note>Psalm 107:6.</note> And again it is written: "Out of the belly of Hades I cried; You heard my voice... and let my life rise up from corruption." <note>Jonah 2:2, 6.</note> Therefore, until lawlessness passes away—that is, the harassment of sin—I will "cry out to God Most High" <note>Psalm 57:2.</note> so that, granting a supreme blessing, He may vanish the very assault of sin by His own authority. May He erase the "idols" of the passion-driven mind and show our weaknesses—which are currently <margin>Perhaps: "the Athens among us that is filled with idols"</margin> <note>This marginal note plays on Acts 17:16, where St. Paul sees Athens full of idols. It suggests the inner state of a person can be like a pagan city before it is cleared by prayer.</note> filled with idols—to be free of them. 

If, therefore, you have not received the gift of self-control <note>Specifically referring here to the physical strength for ascetic fasting.</note>, know that the Lord wishes to hear you as you pray in hope. Knowing the judgment of the Master, do not be discouraged by your inability to practice asceticism. Rather, make it your work to be delivered from the enemy through prayer and grateful endurance. If, then, thoughts of weakness and misery "persecute you from the city" of fasting, flee to the other: that is, to prayer and thanksgiving.

<margin>69.</margin>
It says that Pharaoh, when he entreated, asked that "God might take away this death from me," and he was heard. <note>Exodus 10:17.</note> Likewise, the demons, when they pleaded with the Lord that they might not be sent into the abyss, obtained their request. <note>Luke 8:31-32.</note> How much more will a Christian be heard when he prays to receive freedom from "spiritual death"?

<margin>70.</margin>
A person who is for a time enlightened and given rest by divine grace, but who, after grace is withdrawn, falls into wanderings and grumbles because of this—failing to act manfully to call back that saving "assurance" <note>original: "πληροφορίαν" (plerophorian) – a technical term for the conscious, certain experience of God's presence or grace.</note> through supplication, but instead becoming despondent—is like...

<summary>Diadochos encourages those facing intense demonic temptation, using natural analogies to show that God's grace is more powerful than evil. He specifically provides pastoral comfort to the sick, explaining that the "cry of the heart" (prayer) is as effective as physical fasting for spiritual liberation.</summary>
<keywords>hesychia, spiritual warfare, dispassion, fasting, prayer, inner Joseph, Athens of the mind, plerophoria, endurance, Diadochos of Photike</keywords>

# CONSOLATORY CHAPTERS

Like a poor man who received alms from the palace, but was distressed because he did not go inside to dine with the king.

<margin>71.</margin> "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" <note>John 20:29</note>, just as those are blessed who, through the withdrawal of grace, find no consolation within themselves. Instead, they see only a prolonging of sorrowful things and a deep darkness, yet they do not despair. Rather, they are strengthened by faith, considering that they see the "Invisible One" <note>Hebrews 11:27</note> and so they endure nobly.

<margin>72.</margin> Humility that is given from heaven by the grace of God in its own time—after many struggles, grief, and tears—to those who seek it, is exceedingly stronger and greater than the humility that comes to those who have merely fallen away from virtue. Those deemed worthy of this former humility are truly perfect men, and they remain unharmed by the assaults of the enemy.

<margin>73.</margin> When the devil left the Lord, then the Angels came and ministered to Him <note>Matthew 4:11</note>. It should be known, therefore, that just as it is not written that the Angels were present while He was being tempted, so it is with us when we are tempted: for a certain time, the Angels of God withdraw to a short distance. Then, after the departure of the tempters, they come to us, ministering divine thoughts, support, illumination, contrition, comfort, patience, sweetness, and everything that saves, strengthens, and restores a weary soul. For it was said to Nathanael: "You shall see the Angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man" <note>John 1:51</note>. This means that upon the human race, the ministry and help of the Angels shall be poured out richly.

<margin>74.</margin> Remember that High Priest <note>Joshua (or Jesus) the High Priest in Zechariah 3:1</note>, at whose right hand the devil stood to oppose him in every right thought, word, and deed, so that you might not be struck with awe or confusion at the things that happen to you.

<margin>75.</margin> It is proper for the Monk to understand: what is "weakness"? It is according to the saying, "Have mercy on me, for I am weak" <note>Psalm 6:2</note>. And what is "apostasy" <note>original: "ἀποστασία" (apostasia) – a total falling away or rebellion</note> from God? This latter thing is the "sickness" of the devil and his Angels.

<margin>76.</margin> In the same way that contact with fire makes iron impossible to touch, so frequent prayers prepare the mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) – the "nous," the highest faculty of the soul or the "eye of the heart"</note> to be stronger for the war against the enemy. Therefore, with all their power, the enemies strive to instill sluggishness in us regarding the persistence of prayer, knowing

<column-break/>

that prayer is a plot against themselves, but a champion for the mind.

<margin>77.</margin> David accepted the zeal of those who had gone out with him from Ziklag against the foreigners, even if they grew faint and remained behind at the brook Besor <note>1 Samuel 30:9-25</note>. For when he returned to them after his victory over the barbarians, he heard some saying that a portion of the spoils should not be given to those who sat by the brook due to exhaustion. While those men were ashamed and said nothing, the most excellent David defended them, saying: "They sat by the supplies and guarded them." Therefore, he assigned them an equal portion— <margin>equal to that given</margin> —to that given to the brave and stout-hearted warriors. Consider, therefore, if in the case of a brother who showed warmth at the beginning but later sank down a little, his "supplies of salvation" might be understood as: faith, repentance, humility, weeping, patience, hope, long-suffering, and the rest. If a person who is weak in his way of life sits by these things and perseveres in the expectation of Christ, he will likely obtain some eternal gift.

<margin>78.</margin> Those who have dedicated themselves entirely to God in both action and contemplation <note>original: "πράξει καὶ θεωρίᾳ" (praxei kai theoria) – the two stages of monastic life: ascetic practice and spiritual vision</note> are called "Levites" and "Priests." But those who are not strong enough to follow in the tracks of the passions <note>The author likely means "to track down and defeat the passions"</note> yet still crave virtue and are zealous for it as much as possible—longing for it continually even if they often fail because they have been unnerved by wickedness—these are called the "beasts of the Levites." It is likely that in the proper time, these too will receive the gift of dispassion <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" (apatheias)</note> through the sole loving-kindness of God; "for the Lord has heard the desire of the poor" <note>Psalm 10:17</note>.

<margin>79.</margin> The outrages which the enemy brings upon us, whether visibly or invisibly, we often perceive and see. But the torments and pains which he suffers from us—whenever we succeed in virtues, or repent for our sins, or show long-suffering and endure in our misfortunes, or pray and practice the rest—by which he is sawed asunder, punished, wails, and beats his breast: all these things we do not see, by divine economy <note>original: "κατ' οἰκονομοίαν" (kat' oikonomian) – God's purposeful arrangement or management</note>, so that we do not become conceited or slack.

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER JOHN OF KARPATHOS

For it is just, he says, in the sight of God, to repay with affliction those who afflict us. <note>original: "δίκαιον γάρ, φησὶ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ἀνταποδοῦναι τοῖς θλίβουσιν ἡμᾶς θλῖψιν" — a quote from 2 Thessalonians 1:6.</note>

<margin>80.</margin> If a stump that has grown old in the earth and died in the rock buds again at the scent of water, blooming like a new plant, it is likely that we too, being raised up by the power of the Holy Spirit, shall blossom with the incorruption that we received by nature. <note>John refers here to the original state of humanity before the Fall.</note> Thus we may produce a harvest like a new plant, even if we have fallen down into the "old man." <note>term: "old man" (παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον) — a Pauline term for the unregenerate self prone to sin.</note>

<margin>81.</margin> To the soul that has despaired of itself because of an excess of temptations and a swarm of sins, saying, "Our hope is lost," we declare: it has been said by God, who does not despair of our salvation, "You shall live, and you shall know that I am the Lord." <note>Ezekiel 37:6</note> And to the soul that wonders how it can possibly give birth to Christ through great virtues, it has been said: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you." <note>Luke 1:35</note> Where the Holy Spirit is present, do not look for the usual sequence of nature or habit or law. For the adorable and Holy Spirit is all-powerful; He brings into existence for you even things that did not exist, so that you may be struck with wonder. Furthermore, He shows the <term>nous</term><note>The "intellect" or "eye of the soul," the faculty that perceives God.</note> to be a conqueror now, though it was previously conquered. For the <term>Paraclete</term><note>The "Comforter" or "Advocate," a title for the Holy Spirit.</note> who comes upon us from above out of compassion is above all things; for He sets you above all natural movements and demonic passions.

<margin>82.</margin> Struggle to keep the radiance in your <term>hegemonikon</term><note>The "ruling faculty" or "governing part" of the soul.</note> pure and unblemished. If you begin to look at things with passion, the Lord has darkened you and "sent a muzzle upon your face," <note>referencing Psalm 31:9 or Job 41:13</note> and the light of your eyes is no longer with you. But even if things are this way, do not grow weary or faint, but intercede alongside Holy David, saying: "Send out your light and your truth." <note>Psalm 42:3</note> To me who am gloomy, He is "the salvation of my countenance and my God." For "You will send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and You will renew the face of the earth." <note>Psalm 103:30</note>

<margin>83.</margin> Blessed is the one who greedily eats and drinks prayers and psalms here night and day, and strengthens himself with the glorious reading of the Scriptures. For such a participation will yield to the soul undiminished joy in the age to come.

<margin>84.</margin> With all your power, ensure that you do not fall. For falling is not fitting for a strong ath-

<column-break/>

lete. But if it should happen that you fall, jump up immediately and stand again for the "good fight." <note>2 Timothy 4:7</note> Even if this happens ten thousand times because of the withdrawal of grace, let there be ten thousand risings—that is, the act of getting up—right until your death. For it is written: "If a righteous man falls seven times"—meaning throughout his whole life—"seven times he shall rise again." <note>Proverbs 24:16</note> As long as you hold the weapon of the <term>holy schema</term>,<note>The monastic habit, symbolizing the monk's vows and way of life.</note> along with tears and supplication to God, you are counted among those who stand, even if you have fallen many times. As long as you remain among the monks, like a brave soldier you receive wounds from the front; for these you will be highly praised, because even when struck, you did not endure to give in or desert. But if you depart from the monks, you will be struck in the back as a fugitive, a coward, a deserter, and one who has lost all boldness before God.

<margin>85.</margin> To despair is more grievous than to sin. For Judas the betrayer was faint-hearted and inexperienced in spiritual warfare, and because of this, when he despaired, the enemy rushed upon him and "fastened a noose around him." <note>Matthew 27:5</note> But Peter, the solid rock, though he suffered a terrible fall, as one experienced in warfare he did not lose heart or despair in his distress. Instead, leaping up, he offered the bitterest tears from a soul that was afflicted and humbled. And immediately our enemy, witnessing this, was burned as if by the fiercest flames in his eyes, and he leapt away, fleeing far off and howling terribly.

<margin>86.</margin> Against these three things especially, the monk ought to wage an unceasing war: against gluttony, against useless glory <note>vain-glory</note>, and against the love of money, which is idolatry.

<margin>87.</margin> A certain Israelite king overcame the nation of the "troglodytes" <note>cave-dwellers</note> and other barbarians through psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, using the words and instruments of David. You also have "barbarian troglodytes"—the demons who dwell in your senses and your limbs, punishing your flesh through burning lust. They prepare you to look, hear, and smell passionately, and to speak unseemly words, and to have "eyes full of adultery," <note>2 Peter 2:14</note> and to be thrown into confusion within and without, as in the Babylonian furnace. Therefore, take care yourself with great faith and psal-

...with psalms, and hymns, and spiritual songs, to utterly destroy those cave-dwellers who work evil. <note>original: "τρογλυδύτας" — literally "troglodytes." St. John uses this term metaphorically for demons or base passions that hide in the dark, "underground" recesses of the human psyche.</note>

**Left Column:**

<margin>88.</margin> Just as the Lord wills for man to be saved through man, so too Satan hastens for man to be destroyed through man. Therefore, one must not be joined to a man who is contemptuous, malicious, or fails to guard his tongue, lest you depart into punishment along with him. For even by drawing near to a righteous man, one barely finds salvation. But if someone associates with a wicked person without being on their guard, they will find a ready shipwreck, just like a plague or leprosy. And who, then, will have mercy on the one who cheerfully approaches a dragon? Flee, therefore, from those who are uneducated in the use of the tongue, those who are prone to strife, and those who are disturbed in their inner and outer members.

<margin>89.</margin> Who is wise, and understanding, and desires to be called a friend of God? Let such a person strive to present their soul to the Lord just as they received it from Him: pure, unscarred, and entirely blameless, so that for this they may be crowned in the heavens and be blessed by the Angels.

<margin>90.</margin> A single good word made that once-defiled thief pure and holy, and brought him into Paradise. And a single unseemly word barred Moses from the Promised Land. Let us not, therefore, consider "tongue-aching" <note>term: "γλωσσαλγία" (tongue-aching) — refers here to talkativeness, complaining, or the lack of restraint in speech.</note> to be a small disease. For those who love slander and babbling shut the kingdom of heaven against themselves. For a talkative man, even if he succeeds here on earth, shall not be directed rightly there <note>referring to the afterlife</note>; rather, he shall be tripped up, and evils shall hunt him into corruption. Thus, a certain wise man said well: "It is better to fall from a height to the ground than to fall by the tongue." <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Sirach 20:18.</note> We must, therefore, believe the Apostle James when he writes: "Let every man be quick to hear, and slow to speak." <note>James 1:19</note>

<margin>91.</margin> So that we may not be distracted or deceived by the senses regarding vanity, it is good to heed the one who says: "Go, my people, enter into the inner chamber of your heart," <note>An adaptation of Isaiah 26:20.</note> which is hidden from every sensory thought—that imageless dwelling <note>term: "ἀνείδωλον ἐνδιαίτημα" — a key concept in Hesychasm (the practice of inner stillness), referring to a state of prayer where the mind is free from mental images or distractions.</note> which is illuminated by both dispassion and the overshadowing of holy grace. Shut your door to all visible things; hide yourself for a little while—for all

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**

human life is short—and after this he says: "Until the wrath of the Lord passes." Just as another used to say, "until iniquity passes away." <note>Psalm 57:1</note> For the wrath of the Lord and iniquity are, perhaps, the demons, the passions, and sins; just as Isaiah says to God: "Behold, You were angry, and we sinned." <note>Isaiah 64:5</note> A man escapes this wrath by continually attending to the heart in prayer, and by struggling to get inside the "holy of holies." <note>original: "ἀδύτων" — the innermost, inaccessible parts of a temple; here used for the depths of the heart.</note> For he says, "Draw wisdom from the innermost parts." <note>Job 28:18 (Septuagint translation).</note> Because "all the glory of the king's daughter is from within." <note>Psalm 45:13</note> "I labor until I enter the sanctuary of God." <note>Psalm 73:17</note> And "into the mountain of inheritance," he says, "into the prepared dwelling, which You have fashioned, O Lord, a sanctuary which Your hands have prepared." <note>Exodus 15:17</note>

<margin>92.</margin> Let the one who truly wishes to renounce the world imitate the blessed prophet Elisha, keeping nothing for himself, through a great and fire-burning love for God. Let him distribute all his possessions to the needy, and thus, having taken up the cross of the Lord, let him hasten with purpose toward a voluntary death <note>meaning a death to worldly desires</note>, which becomes the mediator of the eternal <margin>or: life</margin> kingdom.

<margin>93.</margin> When you come to realize that the "Amorite" <note>A biblical reference to the enemies of Israel, used here allegorically for a persistent sin or demonic influence.</note> is strong within you like an oak, pray to the Lord fervently, so that He may dry up his fruit from above—that is, the practice of sin—and his roots from below—that is, the impure thoughts. And pray that the Lord may remove the Amorite from your presence. <note>Referencing Amos 2:9.</note>

<margin>94.</margin> One must not be surprised whenever you see those who are unable to keep stillness mocking our stillness <note>term: "ἡσυχία" (hesychia) — the practice of silence and inner stillness.</note>; rather, sing psalms against them, yet without bearing a grudge. Oppose them with your more intense submission to God, crying out in your singing: "Nevertheless, be subject to God, O my soul." <note>Psalm 62:5</note> For "instead of loving me, they slandered me, but I gave myself to prayer," <note>Psalm 109:4</note> for the sake of my own healing and theirs.

<margin>95.</margin> If a harsh wind does not blow on the sea, no wave will appear. And if a demon does not visit us, the soul will not be stormed by passions, nor will the body.

<margin>96.</margin> If you are always warmed by prayer and divine grace, the Holy Scripture says to you, as to one clothed in the armor of light, "your garment is warm." <note>Job 37:17</note> For your enemies...

<margin>100.</margin> If, according to John, God is love, then the one who loves remains in God, and God in him. Therefore, whoever hates one of the same race exists in a state of distance from God; for if God is love, and the one remaining in love remains in God and God in him. # BY THE SAME
# HOLY FATHER
# **JOHN**
## **OF KARPATHOS**
### AN ASCETIC AND HIGHLY CONSOLATORY DISCOURSE ADDRESSED TO THE MONKS FROM INDIA WHO REQUESTED IT, COMPLETING THE NUMBER OF ONE HUNDRED CHAPTERS

Never desire to bless a worldly person more than a Monk—one who has a wife and children and is cheerful because he does much good, performs charity abundantly, and is not tempted by demons at all—thinking yourself to be less than him in pleasing God. Do not lament yourself as if you were perishing. For I do not say that you live blamelessly by persevering among Monks; but even if you happen to be a great sinner, the affliction of your soul and your hardship are more precious to God than the surpassing virtue of a man of the world. Your great grief, your despondency, your sighs, your distress, your tears, the torment of your conscience, the uncertainty of 

<column-break/>

thought, the judgment in your mind, the beating of the breast, the mourning of the intellect, the wailing of the heart, the brokenness, the misery, the gloom, and the sense of being nothing—all these and such things, which often happen to those cast into the iron furnace of temptations, are more precious and exceedingly more acceptable than the "pleasing life" of the worldly man. Take care, then, that you do not fall under the reproach of the Divine Scripture speaking of you: *What profit did we gain as suppliants going before the Lord and spending time in His house always?* <note>A paraphrasing of Malachi 3:14, expressing the frustration of those who feel their religious devotion brings only hardship.</note> Clearly, every servant who stays close to the Master of the house sometimes receives lashes, and blows, and reproaches, and insults. But those who are outside are, for a time, far away...

It argues that the internal suffering and "holy misery" of a struggling monk are more spiritually valuable than the easy virtues of a comfortable person in the world.</summary>

# ASCETIC DISCOURSE

...of the wounds as if they were strangers, or neglected. "What benefit have we," one might say, "we who fall into distressing things in soul and body, who always pray and sing psalms? While those who neither pray nor keep watch rejoice, and are glad, and prosper, and pass their lives cheerfully?" And as the Prophet says, "Behold, houses of strangers are built up, and we call the strangers blessed?" <note>The author echoes a common spiritual struggle found in Psalm 73 and Malachi 3:15, where the believer envies the apparent peace of the ungodly.</note> And he continues, saying: "These things were spoken by the servants of God, those who possess knowledge." But nevertheless, one must know that those who are afflicted and grieved in various ways suffer nothing strange, for they are enduring the same as their Master through many trials. For they heard Him saying in the Gospels: "Truly I say to you, you who are near me shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice. But in a little while, I will visit you through the Comforter, <note>The "Comforter" or "Paraclete" is the Holy Spirit (John 14:26).</note> and I will drive away your despondency, and I will restore you with thoughts of heavenly life and rest, and with sweet tears, of which you were deprived for a few days while being tested. And I will give you the breast of my grace, just as a mother to a whimpering infant, and I will strengthen you with power from above, you who have become weak in being at war. And I will sweeten you who have been embittered, as Jeremiah says in the Lamentations regarding your hidden Jerusalem; <note>Jerusalem is often used in ascetic literature as a symbol for the soul or the "peaceful" state of the heart.</note> but I will see you, and your heart shall rejoice through the hidden visitation, and your sorrow shall be turned into joy. And your joy no one shall be able to take away." Therefore, let us not be shortsighted. Nor let us be blind, calling those in the world more blessed than ourselves; but knowing the difference between the legitimate sons and the bastards, <note>original: "νόθων" — a reference to Hebrews 12:8, which suggests that those who avoid God's discipline are not true children.</note> let us rather embrace the supposed misery and intense exhaustion of the Monks. The end of this results in eternal life, and in the unfading crown of the Lord's glory. Let us therefore embrace the hardship of those who seem to be sinful ascetics—not to say the righteous—and the being "cast aside" in the house of God, that is, in the rank of those serving Christ unceasingly; and not to dwell in the tents of sinners, or to associate with people of the world, even if they perform great acts of righteousness. For your Heavenly Father says to you, O Monk, He who loves you exceedingly, and afflicts you,

<column-break/>

<margin>
In other copies: "Father," or "Every panther."
</margin>

...and wears you down in various trials: "Know well, wretched Monk, that just as I spoke through the Prophet, I will be your instructor, and I will meet you on the way to Egypt, <note>In monastic thought, "Egypt" represents the world of passions or the initial state of the soul before its exodus toward God.</note> training you through distressing things. And I will hedge up your blameworthy ways with the thorns of my own providence, <note>original: "σκόλοψι" — literally "thorns" or "splinters," referring to the divine obstacles God places in a person's path to prevent them from sinning.</note> piercing you with unexpected misfortunes and hindering you, so that you do not carry out into action whatever you wish in your foolish heart. And I will shut up the sea of your passions with the gates of my own mercies. And I will be to you like a * **panther**, consuming you with thoughts of self-blame, and condemnation, and repentance in the awareness of the things you have done in ignorance. All these distressing things are the greatest grace of God. And not only a panther, but I will also be a goad to you, wounding you with thoughts of compunction, <note term="compunction">original: "κατάνυξις" (katanyxis) — a piercing of the heart by sorrow for sins, which paradoxically leads to spiritual joy.</note> and with pains of the heart; and pain shall not cease from your house—that is, from the soul and the body, which are being hosted well and profitably by the truly sweet and honey-dripping punishments of God." But the end of these punishments, and of the pains, and of the turmoil, and of the shame, and of the fears, and of the despairs that are accustomed to happen to those who have set out to practice the ascetic life—the end of all these gloomy things is heavenly joy, and uninterpretable delight, and unutterable glory, and unceasing exultation. "For because of this I afflicted you," He says, "so that they might feed on the manna of knowledge; and I made you go hungry, so that I might do good to you in the end, and lead you into the kingdom above." For then you shall leap, you humble Monks, like calves released from their bonds, <note>This imagery is taken from Malachi 4:2, describing the freedom and joy of the saved.</note> from the passions of the flesh and the trials of the enemies. And then you shall trample down the lawless demons who now trample upon you. And they shall be ashes under your feet. For if you are god-fearing and humble-minded, not being puffed up with vain arrogance, nor being headstrong, but being pricked in the heart, and considering yourself to be an unprofitable servant, and being broken in spirit—if you are such a humble-minded person, your failing, O Monk, is of more value than the righteousness of the worldlings. And your filth is more necessary than the great cleansing of those involved in worldly affairs. For what is it that causes you distress? Certainly, it is some blemish that has occurred. But look at...

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER JOHN OF KARPATHOS

...a person whose hands are stained, cleansed by a little oil. <note>original: "δι’ ὀλίγου ἐλαίου" - oil was often used as a solvent for cleaning in the ancient world.</note> How much more can you be cleansed by the mercy of God. For just as it is not difficult for you to wash your garment, so it is much less difficult for the Lord to wash you from every blemish, even if temptation should necessarily arise every day, as is likely. For when you say, "I have sinned against the Lord," the answer is given: "Your sins are forgiven." "I am the one who wipes them out, and I will not remember them." "For as far as the east is from the west, I have removed your sins from you"; and "as a father has compassion on his children, so I have compassion on you." <note>John is weaving together several scriptural passages here: 2 Samuel 12:13, Isaiah 43:25, and Psalm 103:12-13.</note>

Only do not turn away or leap away from the One who chose you to sing psalms and to pray. But cling to Him throughout your whole life, whether through pure confidence or through a <term>godly boldness</term> <note>original: "ἀναισχυντίας θεοσεβοῦς" - literally 'godly shamelessness,' meaning a persistent, humble boldness in prayer that refuses to let go of God.</note> and a firm confession to Him. And He Himself cleanses you by His own will. For what God cleanses by His own will, not even the great Apostle Peter himself would be able to make common, or <margin>*alternatively: to condemn.</margin>* to sentence. For it was said to him: "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." <note>Acts 10:15</note> For if it is God who, by His own love for humanity, has justified us, who will be the one to condemn us? <note>Romans 8:33-34</note> For as we call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, our conscience is easily cleansed. And there is no distinction between us and the prophets or the other saints. For God did not appoint us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us. So that whether we are awake in virtues, or sleep due to some circumstance—as is likely in certain failings—we may live together with Christ. Looking toward Him with great groaning and lamenting unceasingly, and breathing Him in.

Let us, therefore, put on the breastplate of faith and have the helmet of the hope of salvation, so that the arrows of despair and hopelessness find no way to slip in. But you yourself say, "I am angry when I see worldly people not being tempted at all, and I am terribly distressed." But know, beloved, that Satan has no need to tempt those who are already self-tempted, and who are always dragged down to the earth by the affairs of life. Know this too: that for those who are being tempted, the prizes

<column-break/>

...and the crowns are set aside. They are not for those who do not care about God, nor for those worldly people who lie on their backs and snore. But "I," someone says, "am tempted very much. And my loins are filled with mockings," as the prophet says. "And there is misery and bowing down, and there is no healing in my flesh, nor care for my bones." <note>Psalm 38:3-7</note> And yet, near at hand stands the great Physician of the suffering, who bore our infirmities and by whose stripes we were and are healed. He is present even now, applying the saving medicines. "For I," He says, "have struck through abandonment, and I will heal." Do not be afraid; for when the anger of my wrath has dripped away, I will heal you again. For just as a woman will not forget to have mercy on the offspring of her womb, so "neither will I forget you," says the Lord. <note>Isaiah 49:15</note> For if the entrails <note>The "entrails" or "inward parts" were considered the seat of emotion and compassion in ancient physiology.</note> of a bird are poured out upon its chicks, and every hour it visits them, calls to them, and gives food into their mouths, how much more are my compassions poured out upon my creatures?

And much more are my own inner mercies poured out upon you, and I visit you secretly. And they converse within your mind. And I put food into your intellect as it gapes open like a little swallow. For I supply you with the food of the greater fear, and the food of heavenly longing, and the food of the groans of consolation, and the food of <term>compunction</term> <note>original: "κατανύξεως" - a spiritual state of heart-piercing sorrow for sin mixed with joy in God's mercy.</note>, and the food of melody, and the food of deeper knowledge, and the food of certain divine mysteries. If I am lying while speaking these things to you, I your Master and Father, then convict me, and I will endure it. These are the things the Lord always speaks to us in our thoughts.

Now I know that I have exceeded the limit by writing so much; but you urged me to do this. We have extended the discourse for the sake of strengthening those who are in danger of falling due to discouragement. For there were found among you in **India**—as you wrote to me—certain brothers who, contrary to expectation, were very heavily burdened by temptations, and were renouncing both the life and the conduct of the **Monks**. They were saying that it is a stifling life, full of ten thousand dangers. And they clearly called worldly people blessed, and cursed the day they took the <term>habit</term> <note>original: "σχῆμα" - the Schema, the distinctive clothing and lifestyle of a monk.</note>. For this reason, I too was forced to make [my discourse] longer...

ASCETIC DISCOURSE

<margin>* alternatively: many.</margin>
...this present discourse, and through *smooth words <note>original: "λείων ῥημάτων" - simple or accessible language intended for a general audience.</note>, so that even the layman and the unlettered might understand what is said. # A SHORT BIOGRAPHY
## OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER
# T H E O D O R E
### THE GREAT ASCETIC
## AND BISHOP OF EDESSA

<image-desc>Ornamental divider identical to the one above, featuring central floral motifs and horizontal vine scrolls.</image-desc>

Theodore, our Father among the Saints, lived during the reigns of <note>Emperor</note> Heraclius and Constantine the "Bearded" <note>original: "Πωγωνάτου" (Pogonatos) - a nickname for Emperor Constantine IV.</note>, around the year six hundred and sixty. He first undertook the ascetic life of struggle at the monastery of Saint Sabbas <note>A famous monastery in the Judean desert known for its strict discipline and liturgical influence.</note>. Later, by a divine vote, he was elevated to the Episcopal throne of the city of Edessa. Having become a worker of many miracles while still living, and even after death, and having revealed many martyrs and those being saved through his divine teachings, he departed to the eternal mansions on the nineteenth of July, just as his life was recorded in the book called the *Kalokairine* <note>original: "Καλοκαιρινῇ" - literally "The Summer Book," a collection of hagiographies for the summer months.</note>. As for his other writings, if he

<column-break/>

left any, we are not able to speak of them clearly. However, the present hundred chapters, having been laboured over by him, were admitted into the catalog of the other <term>watchful fathers</term> <note>original: "νηπτικῶν" (neptikōn) - referring to the tradition of "nepsis" or spiritual sobriety and alertness of the heart.</note>. For these chapters put forth an abundant fruit of <term>Holy Watchfulness</term> <note>original: "Ἱερᾶς Νήψεως" (Hieras Nēpseōs) - the practice of guarding the mind from distracting thoughts to maintain focus on God.</note> and spiritual benefit to those who read with precision, and those who long for their own salvation. Come and harvest most transitionally.

At the end of these present chapters, this "contemplation" attributed to Theodore was also added. Seeing that it possesses the same "watchful" character as the chapters and follows the same style of speech, we have concluded from certain likely signs and marks that it is a genuine offspring of the same Theodore.

## OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER
# T H E O D O R E
### THE GREAT ASCETIC,
### AND BISHOP OF EDESSA
### 100 HIGHLY PROFITABLE CHAPTERS FOR THE SOUL.

---

<margin>1.</margin> Since, by the grace of our good God, we have renounced Satan and his works and have aligned ourselves with Christ—both in the **washing of rebirth** <note>original: "λουτρῷ τῆς παλιγγενεσίας" - a reference to Holy Baptism.</note> and now once again through the **monastic profession** <note>original: "μοναχικοῦ ἐπαγγέλματος" - the vows taken by a monk upon entering a monastery.</note>—let us keep His commandments. For this is required of us not only by our double vow, but also by our natural debt. According to this debt, having been created by God as "very good" in the beginning, we ought to remain so. For even if sin crept in through our negligence and introduced things **contrary to nature** <note>The Church Fathers often taught that sin is an "unnatural" state, whereas virtue is the "natural" state for which humans were designed.</note>, we were called back again through the abundance of our God’s mercy and were renewed by the suffering of the One who is beyond suffering. We were bought at a price by the blood of Christ, having been ransomed from the ancient, ancestral transgression. Therefore, if we become righteous, it is no great thing; rather, it is falling away from righteousness that is pitiful and worthy of condemnation.

<margin>2.</margin> Just as a good work, when done without right faith, is entirely dead and ineffective, so too **faith alone**, without works of righteousness, does not rescue us from the eternal fire. "For he who loves me," says the Lord, "will keep my commandments." If, therefore, we love the Lord and believe in Him, let us strive for the practice of His commandments so that we may attain eternal life. But if we neglect the keeping of His commands—which even the rest of creation obeys once and for all—how can we call ourselves believers? We have been honored above all creation, yet we alone among all things are shown to be disobedient to the commands of our Creator

<column-break/>

and ungrateful toward our Benefactor?

<margin>3.</margin> By keeping the commandments of Christ, we provide nothing to Him, for He is without need and the giver of all good things. Instead, we benefit ourselves, securing for ourselves eternal life and the enjoyment of unspeakable goods.

<margin>4.</margin> Anyone who opposes us in the fulfillment of God’s commandments—even if it be a father, or a mother, or whoever it may be—let them be detestable to us and hated, so that we might not hear it said that "he who loves father or mother more than me, or anyone else at all, is not worthy of me."

<margin>5.</margin> Indeed, with all our strength, let us bind ourselves to the practice of the Lord's commandments, so that we are not bound by the unbreakable chains of evil desires and soul-destroying pleasures. Otherwise, the sentence regarding the **barren fig tree** will be spoken of us as well: "Cut it down," it says, "why should it even waste the ground?" For every tree, He says, that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

<margin>6.</margin> One who is defeated by desires and pleasures, and who turns back to the world, will quickly fall into the nets of sin. Once sin is committed, it is like **fire in stubble** <note>original: "πῦρ κατὰ καλάμης" - a common metaphor for sin's rapid and destructive spread.</note>, or a stone rolling down a steep slope, or a gully that widens its outlets; these are the things commonly said of it, and in every way, it works the destruction of the one who possesses it.

<margin>7.</margin> As long as the soul remains in an "unnatural" state, hardened and overgrown with the thorns of pleasures, it is a dwelling place for strange beasts, according to the saying: "There the **onocentaurs** <note>original: "ὀνοκένταυροι" - mythical creatures (half-donkey, half-man) mentioned in the Greek Septuagint version of Isaiah 13:22 to describe a desolate, cursed place.</note> shall rest, and there they have made their nests."

<summary>This page introduces 100 chapters on spiritual life by St. Theodore of Edessa, emphasizing that keeping God's commandments is a "natural debt" owed by humans as creatures and redeemed souls. He warns that faith without works is dead and that sin, if left unchecked, turns the soul into a wilderness for demonic passions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "One Hundred Chapters" of St. Theodore of Edessa. The previous page ended with Chapter 2, discussing the necessity of both faith and works.
