->### PROFITABLE CHAPTERS FOR THE SOUL<-

...the hedgehog, and demons shall meet with **centaurs** <note>original: "ὀνοκενταύροις" - literally "donkey-centaurs," a mythological hybrid used in the Septuagint translation of Isaiah 34:14 to describe desolate, spiritually haunted places.</note>; these are the various passions of dishonor. But when the soul recalls itself to its **natural state** <note>The "natural state" (κατὰ φύσιν) refers to the soul's original purity before the fall into sin.</note>—which it can do whenever it wishes as long as it is joined to this small body—and tames itself through diligent labor and lives according to the law of God, then the wild beasts that previously nested there will flee. Our Guardian Angels then arrive, making the day of the soul's return a day of gladness; and the grace of the All-Holy Spirit dwells within it, teaching it the knowledge of how to remain in the good and progress toward even greater things.

<margin>8.</margin> The spiritual fathers define **prayer** as a spiritual weapon, and it is impossible to go out to war without it, lest we be taken captive and led away into the land of our enemies. It is not possible to acquire pure prayer without persisting with God in an upright heart; for He is the one who gives prayer to the one who prays, and who teaches humanity knowledge.

<margin>9.</margin> That the passions should trouble the soul and assault it for battle is not within our power to prevent. However, to allow their **thoughts** <note>original: "ἐννοίας" - refers here to the mental images or suggestions that precede an action.</note> to linger within us and to stir up the passions—this *is* within our power. The first case is without sin, since it is not up to us; but in the second case, if we fight back bravely, we shall win crowns of victory. If, however, we are defeated through laziness and cowardice, we bring about our own punishment.

<margin>10.</margin> There are three most general passions from which all others are born: **love of pleasure, love of money, and love of glory.** <note>original: "φιληδονία, φιλαργυρία, καὶ φιλοδοξία" - these are considered the "three giants" or root vices in Eastern Christian asceticism.</note> Five other spirits of wickedness follow these, and from them a great swarm of passions and forms of diverse evil are produced. Therefore, the one who conquers the three leaders and commanders has also brought down the five, and thereafter subdues all the passions.

<margin>11.</margin> Whatever we have done out of passion, the memories of those things also tyrannize the soul with passion. But when the passionate thoughts are entirely erased from the heart so that they no longer even assault it, then a sign appears of the forgiveness of former sins. For as long as the soul is moved by passion, the dominion of sin is recognized as still being within it.

<margin>12.</margin> Physical and material passions are naturally diminished and withered through the hardships of the body; but the passions of the soul,

<column-break/>

and those which are invisible, are destroyed through humility, gentleness, and love.

<margin>13.</margin> Passionate desire is withered by self-control combined with humility; a flaming temper is calmed by love; and a wandering **thought** <note>original: "λογισμὸν" - often translated as "inner reasoning" or "intrusive thought."</note> is gathered back by intense prayer alongside the remembrance of God. In this way, the three parts of the soul are purified. This is what the divine Apostle was setting right when he said: *Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.* <note>Hebrews 12:14</note>

<margin>14.</margin> Some have been at a loss, asking whether the thought stirs the passions or the passions stir the thought—some saying one thing and some the other. But I say that thoughts are moved by the passions; for if the passions were not in the soul, their thoughts would not trouble it.

<margin>15.</margin> It is the custom of the demons who always war against us to hinder those virtues which are possible and appropriate for us, while suggesting a strong path toward those which are impossible or untimely. For those progressing in **obedience** <note>original: "ὑποταγῇ" - refers to monks living under a superior in a community.</note>, they force them to perform the works of **solitaries** <note>original: "ἡσυχαστῶν" - Hesychasts, or those practicing a life of silence and solitude.</note>; but for solitaries and hermits, they instill a desire for the communal rule. They use this method with every virtue. But let us not be ignorant of their designs, knowing that all things are good in their proper time and measure, while those things that are beyond measure and untimely are entirely harmful.

<margin>16.</margin> For those living in the world and near the "matter" of the passions, the demons wage war through outward actions and physical wrestling. But for those in the deserts, because of the scarcity of physical things, they trouble them through thoughts. This second war is far more difficult than the first. The war through physical things requires time, place, and opportunity; but the war of the mind is swift and difficult to restrain. Pure prayer has been given to us as the opponent of this bodiless wrestling; therefore, it has been commanded to be practiced unceasingly. It prepares the mind to be strong for the contest, as it can be performed even without the body.

<margin>17.</margin> Indicating the perfect death of the passions, the divine Apostle says: *And those who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.* <note>Galatians 5:24</note> For when we kill the passions and cause the desires to disappear...

<summary>St. Theodore outlines the internal spiritual battle, identifying the three root passions (pleasure, money, and glory) and emphasizing that while initial thoughts are unavoidable, dwelling on them is a choice. He highlights prayer as the primary weapon for the mind, especially for those in solitude who face mental rather than physical temptations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "One Hundred Chapters" of St. Theodore of Edessa, following the discussion of spiritual warfare and prayer. This page begins with the conclusion of Chapter 17 and covers Chapters 18 through 26, focusing on the mastery of the flesh, the progression of sinful thoughts, the structure of the soul according to Gregory the Theologian, and the ladder of virtues leading to love.</meta>

# OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THEODORE

...indeed, and let us subdue the **mind of the flesh** <note>original: "φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς" — a term used by St. Paul to describe a mindset governed by physical impulses rather than spiritual ones.</note> to the Spirit, then we take up the cross and follow Christ; for withdrawal from the world is nothing else than the putting to death of the passions and the revelation of the life that is hidden in Christ.

<margin>18.</margin> Those who are troubled by the rebellion of this "body of death" <note>A reference to Romans 7:24, referring to the fallen human condition.</note> and who lose heart in the face of the hourly war it wages, should blame themselves and not the flesh. For if they had not given it strength by "making provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts," they would not have suffered so much from it. Do they not see those who have **crucified themselves** with its passions and desires, and who carry the death of Jesus in their mortal flesh, so that they possess the body as a co-worker toward what is good rather than an opponent? Instead, the body yields and is led by the law of God. Let these troubled souls do the same, and they shall enjoy a similar rest.

<margin>19.</margin> Every consent of a thought toward some forbidden desire—that is, a pleasurable inclination of the mind—is a sin for a Monk. For first, the thought begins to darken the mind through the "passionate" part of the soul; then the soul inclines toward the pleasure, failing to endure the struggle. This is then called "consent," which, as has been said, is a sin. If this consent lingers, it stirs up what is called a "passion"; then, by degrees, it leads to the actual commission of the sin in deed. For this reason, the prophet calls "blessed" those who dash the **Babylonian infants** <note>A reference to Psalm 137:9. In the spiritual tradition, "Babylonian infants" are interpreted as the very first stirrings of evil thoughts, which should be destroyed against the "rock" (Christ) before they grow into mature sins.</note> against the rock. The meaning of this is clear to those who are prudent and wise.

<margin>20.</margin> Since the Angels are servants of love and peace, they rejoice at our repentance and our progress in virtue; therefore, they strive to fill us with spiritual contemplations and cooperate with us toward every good thing. Conversely, the demons—being the creators of anger and malice—rejoice when virtue decreases and make it their business to divert our souls toward shameful fantasies.

<margin>21.</margin> Faith is a well-disposed good; it gives birth in us to the fear of God. The fear of God teaches the keeping of the commandments, which is called **practice** <note>original: "πρακτική" (praktiki) — the active stage of the spiritual life involving the struggle against passions and the cultivation of virtues.</note>. From this practice, the precious state of **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπάθεια" (apatheia) — not a lack of feeling, but a state of freedom from being controlled by disordered passions.</note> blossoms. The offspring of dispassion is love, which is the fulfillment 

<column-break/>

of all the commandments, binding and holding them all together.

<margin>22.</margin> Just as the physical senses, when healthy, perceive whatever illness possesses the body—whereas one who does not perceive it is sick with "insensibility"—so it is with the mind. As long as it preserves its own proper activity, it recognizes its own powers and knows from which direction the passions enter more tyrannically to assault it; it then directs its strong battle toward that area. It is a wretched thing if, through insensibility, one wastes his days like a man fighting in the dark, unable to see the thoughts of the war.

<margin>23.</margin> When our **rational faculty** <note>original: "λογιστικόν" — the governing, reasoning part of the human soul.</note> applies itself without yielding to the contemplation of virtues, and the **appetitive faculty** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμητικόν" — the part of the soul associated with desire and longing.</note> is stretched toward this alone and toward Christ its giver, and the **irascible faculty** <note>original: "θυμικόν" — the part of the soul associated with "spiritedness," righteous anger, or drive.</note> is armed against the demons, then our powers are functioning **according to nature** <note>original: "κατὰ φύσιν" — acting in the way God originally intended for humanity before the fall.</note>.

<margin>24.</margin> Every rational soul is tripartite <note>Divided into three parts: the rational, the irascible, and the appetitive. This was a standard psychological model in ancient Greek philosophy and Christian asceticism.</note> according to **Gregory the Theologian** <note>St. Gregory Nazianzen (4th century), one of the most influential Church Fathers.</note>. The virtue that resides in the rational part he called prudence, understanding, and wisdom. That in the irascible part, he called courage and patience. That in the appetitive part, he called love, temperance, and self-control. **Justice** (or Righteousness) is sown throughout all of these, preparing them to act harmoniously: through prudence, fighting against opposing powers and championing the virtues; through temperance, looking upon things without passion; through love, persuading one to love all people as oneself; through self-control, cutting off every pleasure; and through courage and patience, arming oneself for the invisible wars. This is the harmony of the sweet-sounding instrument of the soul.

<margin>25.</margin> He who cares for temperance and longs for blessed purity—which one would not be wrong to call "dispassion"—let him bruise and enslave his flesh with a humble mind, calling upon divine grace, and he will achieve what he desires. But he who nourishes the body with an excess of food will be tormented by the spirit of fornication. Just as much water extinguishes a flame, so do hunger and self-control, combined with humility of soul, vanish the burning of the flesh and shameful fantasies.

<margin>26.</margin> The passion of bearing a grudge... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

# SOUL-PROFITING CHAPTERS

...let it be far from your soul, O lover of Christ; do not give any place to enmity. For just as fire is hidden in stalks of flax <note>original: "λινοκαλάμῳ"</note>, so is the **bearing of a grudge** <note>original: "μνησικακία" — the spiritual sickness of holding onto past wrongs</note> nested in the heart. Rather, pray warmly for the one who has grieved you, and do good to him as far as your hand is able, so that you may rescue your soul from death and not be without boldness <note>original: "ἀπαρρησίαστος" — meaning lacking the confidence to speak freely before God</note> in the time of your prayer.

<margin>27.</margin> The Lord rests in the souls of the humble, but in the hearts of the proud, shameful passions dwell. For nothing empowers these passions against us so much as arrogant thoughts; and nothing uproots the "evil weeds" of the soul like blessed **humility**. For this reason, it is rightly called the "passion-killer" <note>original: "παθοκτόνος"</note>.

<margin>28.</margin> Let your soul be pure of evil memories, and let it be guided by the best thoughts. Always keep in mind the saying: "A pleasure-loving heart is a prison and a chain at the time of one's departure from this life, but a **labor-loving** <note>original: "φιλόπονος" — referring to someone dedicated to the 'toil' of spiritual discipline</note> heart is an open door." For indeed, Angels lead pure souls as they exit the body, guiding them by the hand toward the blessed life; but demons—alas!—will seize those that are defiled and unrepentant.

<margin>29.</margin> A head adorned with a precious diadem, glistening with Indian stones and pearls, is beautiful. But incomparably more beautiful is a soul rich in the knowledge of God and illumined by the most radiant **contemplations** <note>original: "θεωρίαις" — the spiritual "vision" or deep perception of divine truths</note>, having the All-Holy Spirit dwelling within it. And who can worthily describe the beauty of such a blessed soul?

<margin>30.</margin> Do not allow fury and anger to lodge within you; for it is said, "A wrathful man is not decorous" <note>original: "εὐσχήμων" — meaning dignified or respectable</note>. Wisdom rests in the hearts of the gentle. But if the passion of anger masters your soul, those living in the secular world will be found better than you, and you will be put to shame, having become an "unapproved" monk.

<margin>31.</margin> In every temptation and every war, keep prayer as your invincible weapon, and you shall conquer by the grace of Christ. But let this prayer be pure, just as our wise Teacher <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Timothy 2:8.</note> suggests to us: "I desire," he says, "that men pray in every place, lifting up holy hands, without anger and doubting thoughts." However, he who neglects such prayer will be handed over to temptations and passions.

<margin>32.</margin> It is written that "wine gladdens the heart of man" <note>original: "Οἶνος εὐφραίνει καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου" — a quote from Psalm 103:15</note>. But you, who have promised to mourn and weep, 

<column-break/>

shun such "gladness," and you will be gladdened by spiritual gifts. If you find your joy in wine, you will live alongside shameful thoughts and be pierced by many sorrows.

<margin>33.</margin> Do not intend to celebrate the feast days with wine-drinking, but with the renewal of the mind and purity of soul. By stuffing your belly and drinking wine, you will only provoke the One who presides over the festival to anger.

<margin>34.</margin> We are commanded to keep **vigil** <note>original: "Ἀγρυπνεῖν" — staying awake for prayer</note> with the singing of psalms, prayers, and reading at all times, but especially during feasts. For a wakeful Monk thins his intellect for soul-profiting contemplations. Much sleep, however, thickens the mind. But when you are awake, do not give yourself over to empty stories or evil thoughts. For it is better to sleep than to stay awake for vain words and reasoning.

<margin>35.</margin> He who nurses a snake in his bosom and an evil thought in his heart will be put to death. The first is struck in the body by a venomous sting; the second deposits deadly venom in the soul. Let us quickly kill these "offspring of vipers" and not go into labor with evil thoughts in the heart, lest we suffer bitter pain.

<margin>36.</margin> A pure soul may rightly be called a "chosen vessel," an "enclosed garden," a "sealed fountain," and a "throne of perception" <note>References to various biblical images, particularly from the Song of Songs, used here to describe the sanctity of the soul.</note>. But the soul defiled by unclean stains is filled with the stench of filth.

<margin>37.</margin> I have heard from experienced and practical elders that evil thoughts are born in the soul through the adornment of clothes, the filling of the belly, and harmful social encounters.

<margin>38.</margin> Let the desire for money not lodge in the souls of ascetics. For a monk with many possessions is like a waterlogged ship, tossed by waves of worry and sinking into the depths of sorrow. The evil of **love of money** <note>original: "φιλαργυρία" — literally 'silver-love'</note> is the parent of many passions, rightly called the "root of all evils" <note>Reference to 1 Timothy 6:10.</note>.

<margin>39.</margin> **Non-possession** <note>original: "Ἀκτημοσύνη" — the monastic virtue of owning nothing</note> and silence are a treasure hidden in the field of the monastic life. Go, then, sell what you have and give to the poor, and acquire this field; and digging up the treasure, guard it for yourself as something that cannot be stolen, so that you may possess a wealth that is never emptied.

<margin>40.</margin> If you have come to live with a spiritual father and have felt benefit from him, let no one...

# OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THEODORE

<margin>40.</margin> ...root of his love and companionship. Do not judge him in any matter, and do not speak ill of him when you are rebuked or even struck. Do not lend your ear to anyone who slanders him, nor join sides with one who reviles him, so that the Lord does not become angry with you and strike you out of the book of the living.

<margin>41.</margin> The prize of **obedience** <note>original: "ὑποταγῆς" — referring to the monk's submission to a spiritual elder</note> is perfected through **renunciation** <note>original: "ἀποταγῆς" — the act of giving up worldly possessions and one's own will</note>, as we have learned. Let the one who pursues this be fenced about with three weapons: I mean faith, hope, and most venerable and divine love. Walled in by these, he may fight the good fight and receive the crowns of righteousness.

<margin>42.</margin> Do not be a judge of your spiritual father's actions, but rather a fulfiller of his commands. For it is the habit of demons to point out his failings to you, so that they may deafen your ears to his words. In doing so, they either drive you away from the "wrestling ring" as a weak and cowardly soldier, or they dissolve your resolve with thoughts of unbelief and make you slack toward every form of virtue.

<margin>43.</margin> He who disregards the commands of his father is found to be a transgressor of his exceptional covenant and promises. But he who embraces obedience, having slaughtered his own will with the **sword of humility**, has fulfilled—at least as far as it concerns him—those things which he promised to Christ before many witnesses.

<margin>44.</margin> Having observed closely, we have recognized and clearly learned that the demons, those enemies of our life, feel great envy toward those practicing under the obedience of spiritual fathers. They gnash their teeth against them and devise all sorts of machines. What do they not do? What do they not suggest? All this is done to separate the monks from the paternal embrace. They show pretexts that seem "reasonable," they engineer provocations, and they stir up hatred toward the father. They make his admonitions look like insults and his rebukes feel like sharpened arrows. "Why," the demon says, "being a free man, have you become a slave—and a slave to a pitiless master? How long will you be worn down by the yoke of slavery and never see the light of freedom?" Then, they suggest that the monk should perform "good works" like hospitality, visiting the sick, or caring for the poor instead. Then they over-praise the prize of extreme **stillness** <note>original: "ἡσυχίας" — hesychia, or quiet contemplative prayer</note> and solitude, sowing every kind of evil weed in the heart of the soldier of piety, so that they might only

<column-break/>

cast him out of the spiritual sheepfold. Having loosened him from that wave-less harbor, they throw him back toward the sea that rages with soul-destroying surges. Then, having taken him as a prisoner into their own power, they use him according to their own evil wills.

<margin>45.</margin> But for you who are under the obedience of a father, let the deceit of these enemies and foes not go unnoticed. Do not forget your promise and your vow to God; do not be defeated by insults, nor fear rebukes, mockeries, or sneers. Do not yield to the excesses of evil thoughts, nor flee from your father's austerity. Do not dishonor the good yoke of humility with the boldness of self-satisfaction and arrogance. Instead, placing in your heart the Master’s saying—that *he who endures to the end will be saved*—run with patience the race set before you, looking toward Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith.

<margin>46.</margin> Just as a goldsmith puts gold into a crucible to make it purer, so a novice monk, giving himself over as an athlete of obedience, is "fired" by all the painful trials of a life lived according to God's will. By learning obedience through toil and much patience, his character is "re-smelted." He learns humility and is restored to a bright state, becoming worthy of heavenly treasures and that indestructible way of life—the blessed end where pain and sighing have fled, and where joy and continuous gladness are planted.

<margin>47.</margin> Right and heartfelt faith gives birth to the fear of God. The fear of God, in turn, teaches us the keeping of the commandments. For it is said: "The keeping of commandments is the fear of God." From the keeping of the commandments, <term>practical virtue</term> <note>original: "πρακτικὴ ἀρετὴ" — the active struggle against the passions</note> is established, which is the beginning of <term>contemplative virtue</term> <note>original: "θεωρητικῆς" — the higher stage of spiritual vision</note>. The fruit of these is <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "ἀπάθεια" — a state of soul where one is no longer moved by sinful impulses</note>. Through dispassion, love is born in us. And concerning love, the beloved disciple says: *God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him.*

<margin>48.</margin> How truly beautiful and good is the way of life of Monks! How truly beautiful and good it is, if it is lived according to the boundaries and laws which its leaders and guides—taught by the Holy Spirit—established. For the soldier of Christ is imma-

### SOUL-PROFITING CHAPTERS

...should be, and free from every worldly thought and action, as the Apostle says:
> No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him. <note>original: 2 Timothy 2:4</note>

<margin>49.</margin> Therefore, the <term>Monk</term> <note>original: Μοναχὸς (Monachos) — literally "one who lives alone," referring to a consecrated religious person</note> must be immaterial, beyond passion, and free from every evil desire. He should not be a lover of luxury, nor a heavy drinker, nor sluggish, nor lazy. He must not be a lover of money, pleasure, or vainglory. For unless a person removes themselves from these things, they will not be able to succeed in this "angelic way of life." But for those who do succeed properly, the "yoke is easy" and the "burden is light," because divine hope makes everything easier. Such a life is sweet, its practice is delightful, and its portion is good—a portion that shall not be taken away from the soul that possesses it.

<margin>50.</margin> You who have renounced worldly cares and put on the armor of the **ascetic** <note>original: ἀσκητικῶν (asketikon) — referring to the disciplined training of a spiritual athlete</note> struggle: do not desire to possess wealth even for the sake of giving to the poor. For this too is a deception of the Evil One that leads to vainglory, intended to throw the mind into a state of busybody-ness. Even if you have only bread, or even just water, you can still earn the reward of **hospitality** <note>original: φιλοξενίας (philoxenias) — literally "love of strangers"</note> through them. And even if you have neither of these, but you welcome a stranger with a good intention and give them a word of comfort, you can still obtain that same reward. You have the example of the widow in the Gospel, testified to by the Lord, who surpassed the intent and power of the wealthy with only two copper mites.

<margin>51.</margin> These things are said to those dwelling in stillness. But those who are under **obedience** <note>original: ὑποταγῇ (hypotage) — submission to a spiritual elder</note> to a father should have only one thing in mind: to never fall away from their father’s command in any way. By succeeding in this, they have succeeded in everything. Conversely, if they fail in such precision and lifestyle, they will be found worthless in every form of virtue and spiritual life.

<margin>52.</margin> Take this advice of mine as well, you who love Christ: love **exile** <note>original: ξενιτείαν (xeniteian) — the practice of living as a stranger or pilgrim far from one's home</note>, freeing yourself from the circumstances of your own country. Do not be carried away by cares for parents or friendships with relatives. Flee from the pastimes of the city and persevere in the wilderness, saying with the Prophet: "Behold, I have fled far away, and I have lodged in the desert." <note>original: Psalm 55:7</note>

<margin>53.</margin> Seek out places that are secluded and removed from the

<column-break/>

world. Even if there is a scarcity and shortage of necessary things there, do not be afraid. If enemies surround you like bees or wicked drones, attacking you with all kinds of warfare and disturbing you with various thoughts, do not be terrified. Do not give them a listening ear, and do not flee from the arena of the contest. Rather, endure with patience, chanting to yourself and saying:
> I waited patiently for the Lord, and He inclined to me, and heard my prayer. <note>original: Psalm 40:1</note>

And then you will see the greatness of God—His help, His guardianship, and all His other providential care for your salvation.

<margin>54.</margin> You must have friends, O lover of Christ, who are helpful and who contribute to your way of life. For "let men of peace," it is said, "be your friends." These are spiritual brothers and holy fathers, concerning whom our Lord said:
> These are my mother and my brothers: those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven. <note>original: Matthew 12:48-50</note>

<margin>55.</margin> Do not be a craver of varied and expensive foods, or of deadly luxuries. For "she who lives in pleasure," it says, "is dead while she lives." <note>original: 1 Timothy 5:6</note> Even with foods that are easily obtained, avoid satiety if possible. For it is written: "Do not be deceived by the filling of the belly."

<margin>56.</margin> If you have chosen to practice stillness, you should avoid spending time continually outside of your cell. For this is very harmful; it takes away grace, darkens the mind, and withers one's longing for God. Because of this, it is said:
> The wandering of desire undermines the innocent mind. <note>original: Wisdom of Solomon 4:12</note>

Therefore, cut off your relationships with the many, lest your mind becomes distracted and shatters your way of <term>stillness</term> <note>original: ἡσυχίας (hesychia) — the practice of inner silence and prayer</note>.

<margin>57.</margin> While sitting in your cell, do not make your work mindless or full of idleness. For "the one who travels without a goal," it is said, "will labor in vain." Instead, acquire a good spiritual task. Collect your mind; keep always before your eyes the final hour of death. Remember the vanity of the world—how deceptive it is, how weak, how worthless. Meditate on the tragedy of the **dread reckoning** <note>original: λογοθεσίου (logothesiou) — the final judgment or "accounting" of the soul</note>, and how the bitter **tax collectors** <note>original: φορολόγοι (phorologoi) — a metaphor for demons who "inspect" the soul's sins after death</note> will present each of our actions, words, and thoughts—those which they themselves suggested, and which we accepted. Remember also the punishments in Hades, and how those shut up there...

# OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THEODORE

...once your souls have been purified, remember also that great and fearful day—I mean the common resurrection—and the standing before God, the final sentence of the Judge who cannot be deceived. Consider the punishment that will overtake sinners: the shame, the rebuke of the conscience, the being cast out from God, and being thrown into the eternal fire, into the worm that never ends, into the darkness where there is no light, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. Reflecting on all these other punishments, do not cease to drench your cheeks, your clothes, and the place where you sit with drops of tears. For by these thoughts, I have seen many gain a great abundance of tears and wonderfully cleanse all the powers of the soul. <note>The original Greek text contains a printer's repetition here, repeating the phrase "drench your cheeks... by these thoughts" twice; I have smoothed this for readability.</note>

<margin>58.</margin>
But also consider the good things laid up for the righteous: the standing at the right hand of Christ, the blessed voice of the Master, the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, the gift that is beyond understanding, that sweetest light, the joy that has no end, the gladness never interrupted by sorrow, those heavenly dwellings, life with the Angels, and all the other things promised to those who fear the Lord.

<margin>59.</margin>
Let these thoughts live with you, sleep with you, and rise with you. See that you never forget them; but wherever you may be, do not let your mind depart from the memory of these things, so that evil thoughts may flee and you may be filled with divine consolation. The soul that is not fortified by these thoughts cannot achieve **stillness** <term>Hesychia: a state of inner quiet and focused prayer</term>. For a spring that has no water bears its name in vain.

<margin>60.</margin>
And this way of life has been commanded for those succeeding in stillness: fasting as much as you are able, vigils, sleeping on the ground, and every other kind of hardship for the sake of the rest to come.

> For I consider, it says, that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. <note>original: Romans 8:18</note>

And especially pure prayer, which one might say is almost unceasing and uninterrupted. This is a secure wall, a calm harbor, a guardian of

<column-break/>

virtues, the destruction of passions, the vigor of the soul, the purifier of the mind, rest for those who are weary, and consolation for those who mourn. Prayer is conversation with God, the contemplation of invisible things, the assurance of those things we desire, the conduct of Angels, the encouragement of good things, the substance of things hoped for. Seize hold of this queen of virtues, O **ascetic** <note>original: ἀσκητά (asketa) — one who practices disciplined spiritual training</note>, with all your might. Pray by day and by night, in despondency and in cheerfulness. Pray with fear and trembling, and with a sober and wakeful mind, so that your prayer may be acceptable to the Lord;

> For the eyes of the Lord, it says, are upon the righteous, and His ears are open to their prayer. <note>original: Psalm 33:16 / 1 Peter 3:12</note>

<margin>61.</margin>
It was aptly and very accurately said by one of the ancients that, among the demons who oppose us, the first in the battle are those entrusted with the appetites of **gluttony** <note>original: γαστριμαργίας (gastrimargias)</note>, those who suggest **avarice** <note>original: φιλαργυρίαν (philargyrian)</note> to us, and those who call us toward **vainglory** <note>original: κενοδοξίαν (kenodoxian)</note>. All the others, walking behind these, take over those who have already been wounded by them.

<margin>62.</margin>
And indeed, by observing, we have come to know that it is not possible for a person to fall into sin or any passion without first being wounded by one of these three. This is why the Devil brought these three thoughts to the Savior at that time. When our Lord showed Himself superior to them, He commanded the Devil to retreat, giving us the victory over him. As a good and man-loving Master, He clothed Himself in a body like ours in all things except sin, and showed us the unerring path of sinlessness. Walking in this path, we reshape within ourselves the "New Man," who is renewed according to the image of the One who created him.

<margin>63.</margin>
The word of David teaches us to hate the demons with a "perfect hatred," since they are the enemies of our salvation; and this is very helpful for the work of virtue. Who, then, is the one who hates his enemies with a perfect hatred? It is the one who no longer sins, whether in action or in thought. But as long as the "vessels of their friendship"—that is, the causes of the passions—are within us, how can perfect hatred for them be achieved? For a heart that loves pleasure has no strength to nurture this hatred within itself.

<margin>64.</margin>
The "wedding garment" is **dispassion** <term>Apatheia: not a lack of feeling, but a state of soul where one is no longer dominated by disordered passions</term> of the rational soul, which has been separated from worldly pleasures and has renounced all improper...

...desires, but instead occupies itself with God-loving thoughts and the purest meditation on divine contemplations. However, through the passions of dishonor and the idle chatter associated with them, the soul strips off this "garment of temperance" and makes itself useless, clothed instead in torn and filthy rags. This is made clear in the Gospels, where the man who was bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness had woven his garment from such thoughts and actions; for this reason, the Word <note>original: ὁ λόγος (ho logos); referring here to the Divine Word or the scriptural reasoning</note> declared him unworthy of the divine and incorruptible wedding feast.

<margin>65.</margin> A certain wise man once spoke rightly about self-love <note>original: φιλαυτία (philautia), often defined in this tradition as an excessive or disordered love for the body</note>, which hates everyone. For this terrible war of self-love is the first of all the "thoughts" <note>original: λογισμῶν (logismon); in monastic literature, these are intrusive, suggestive thoughts that lead to sin</note>, acting like a tyrant; it is the leader of the group through which "the three and the five" <note>Likely referring to the three powers of the soul (rational, spirited, and appetitive) and the five senses, which the passions use to seize the mind.</note> take your mind captive.

<margin>66.</margin> I would be surprised if someone who sates himself with food could ever attain dispassion <term>apatheia: a state of being free from the disturbance of the passions, not to be confused with modern "apathy" or indifference</term>. By dispassion, I do not mean merely abstaining from the outward act of sin—for that is called self-control <term>enkrateia: the initial stage of discipline where one actively resists sinful impulses</term>. Rather, I mean the state that uproots passionate thoughts from the very depths of the mind; this state is also called "purity of heart."

<margin>67.</margin> It is easier to cleanse an impure soul than it is to restore to health a soul that was once cleansed but has been wounded again. For those who have only recently renounced the confusion of the world, whatever faults they happen to fall into, it is easier for them to take hold of dispassion. But for those who have already tasted the good words of God and walked the path of salvation, and then run back toward sin, dispassion becomes somehow difficult to achieve. This is partly due to a "bad state" <note>original: κακὴν ἕξιν (kaken hexin); referring to a deeply ingrained habit or character trait</note> and evil custom, and partly because the "demon of sorrow" <note>original: λύπης (lypes); in this context, the specific spiritual despondency or regret that paralyzes the soul</note> is always fixing itself upon the pupils of their eyes, bringing before them the phantom image of their sin. Nevertheless, a diligent and hardworking soul can successfully overcome even this difficulty through the cooperation of divine grace. This grace acts toward us with patient love, calling us to repentance <term>metanoia: literally a "change of mind" or inner transformation</term> and receiving those who return with an unspeakable heart of compassion, just as we were taught in the Gospels through the parable of the Prodigal Son.

<margin>68.</margin> None of us can overcome the methods and crafts of the Evil One by our own strength, but only by the invincible power

<column-break/>

of Christ. Therefore, those who are puffed up by their own ascetic practices and by their own "free will" <note>original: αὐτεξουσίου (autexousiou)</note> are wandering in vain, claiming they can abolish sin—which can only be abolished through the grace of God. Sin was, in fact, put to death through the mystery of the Cross. For this reason, the Great Light of the Church, John Chrysostom <note>The 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople, famous for his eloquence</note>, says that human zeal is not enough unless one also enjoys help from above. And conversely, we gain nothing from help from above if there is no human zeal. Both of these points are proven by the cases of Judas and Peter. The former, though he enjoyed much help, gained nothing because he was unwilling and did not contribute his own effort. Peter, on the other hand, although he was eager, fell because he did not enjoy any [divine] help at that moment. Virtue is woven together from these two elements. "Therefore," he says, "I urge you neither to sleep as if God does everything, nor to think that by your own labors you can achieve everything while you are striving."

<margin>69.</margin> God does not want us to be idle; for this reason, He does not perform the whole work Himself. Nor does He want us to be arrogant; for this reason, He did not give the whole power to us. Instead, by removing what is harmful from both sides, He left us what is useful. The Psalmist also teaches this well, saying, "Unless the Lord builds the house, the watchman and the laborer wake in vain." <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 127:1.</note> For it is impossible to "step upon the asp and the basilisk and trample the lion and the dragon" <note>References to Psalm 91:13, symbols of demonic powers.</note> unless a person first cleanses himself as much as possible and is then strengthened by Him who said to the Apostles: "Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." <note>Luke 10:19.</note> This is also why we were commanded to beg the Master in our prayer "not to lead us into temptation, but to deliver us from the evil one." For if we are not delivered from the "fiery arrows of the evil one" through the power and help of Christ, and if we are not deemed worthy to attain dispassion, we labor in vain, thinking we are achieving something by our own strength or zeal. Therefore, whoever wishes to stand against the methods of the devil, to make them ineffective, and to become a sharer in divine glory, must use tears, groans, and an insatiable desire with a burning soul, night and...

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of divine grace working alongside human effort (synergy) to overcome the passions and the devil. It distinguishes between outward self-control and inner dispassion, emphasizing that true purity of heart is a gift from Christ rather than a product of mere human will.</summary>
<keywords>dispassion, self-control, self-love, grace, free will, John Chrysostom, repentance, spiritual warfare, synergy, purity of heart</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Soul-profiting Chapters" of St. Theodore of Edessa. The previous page discussed the danger of self-love and the "garment of temperance." This page begins mid-sentence, continuing the advice on how to invite the divine presence into the soul through purity and the constant watchfulness over one's thoughts.</meta>

->### OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THEODORE<-

...by day to seek God's help and divine assistance. For whoever wishes to share in this help must make their soul pure from every worldly pleasure and from contrary passions and desires. For concerning such souls, God says:
> I will dwell in them and walk among them.
And the Lord said to His disciples:
> If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.

<margin>70.</margin> A certain one of the ancients spoke a very wise and easily understood word regarding "thoughts" <note>original: λογισμοὺς (logismous); in this context, these are intrusive or tempting thoughts that lead to sin</note>: judge your thoughts at the judgment seat <term>bema: a raised platform for an orator or judge; here, the "judgment seat of the heart"</term> of your heart, determining whether they are ours or belong to the enemy. Place those that are our own and good into the inner treasury of the soul, keeping them as an inviolable treasure. As for the opposing thoughts, punish them with the whips of a rational mind and exile them, giving them neither a place nor a home within the borders of your soul. Or, to speak more fittingly, slaughter them completely with the sword of prayer and divine meditation, so that when these "thieves" are destroyed, the "chief thief" <note>referring to the devil</note> may be afraid. For indeed, he who is a strict examiner of his thoughts is also a true lover of the commandments.

<margin>71.</margin> Let him who fights to cut off the things that war against and trouble him enlist many soldiers as allies in the battle. I mean, specifically, humility of soul, bodily labor, and every other hardship of ascetic practice—along with prayer from a contrite heart accompanied by many tears. As David sings:
> Look upon my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins, and do not be silent at my tears.
And again:
> My tears have been my bread day and night, and I mingled my drink with weeping.

<margin>72.</margin> The devil, the adversary of our life, uses many thoughts to make our sins appear small; often he covers them with forgetfulness so that we, giving in to the weariness of our labors, might not take into account the mourning due for our stumbles. But we, brothers, should not forget our failings, even if we believe they have been forgiven through repentance. Rather, let us always remember our sins and never cease to mourn over them, so that by making humility our good companion,

<column-break/>

we may escape the snares of vanity and pride.

<margin>73.</margin> Let no one think that they endure labors and achieve virtue through their own strength. For God is the cause of all good things for us, just as the deceptive demon of our souls is the cause of evil. Therefore, whatever good things you accomplish, offer the thanksgiving to the Cause; and whatever evils trouble you, cast them upon the author of those things.

<margin>74.</margin> He who joins practical life <note>original: πρακτικὴν (praktiken); the active life of virtues and discipline</note> with knowledge <note>original: γνώσει (gnosei); spiritual insight or contemplation</note> is a praiseworthy farmer, watering the field of the soul from two very clear springs. For the spring of knowledge gives wings to the youthful essence through the contemplation of higher things, while the practical spring puts to death the members that are upon the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, and evil desire. When these are put to death, the flowers of the virtues blossom beautifully, bearing the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. And then, finally, this wise farmer, having crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, will say along with the God-bearing herald <note>St. Paul</note>:
> It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me.

<margin>75.</margin> And do not let this escape you, O lover of Christ: that if a single passion finds a place in you and becomes rooted as a habit, it will bring others into the same fold. For even if the passions and the demons who create them oppose one another, they all seek our destruction with one accord.

<margin>76.</margin> He who withers the "flower of the flesh" through asceticism and cuts off its every will, carries the marks of Christ in his mortal flesh.

<margin>77.</margin> The labors of asceticism end in the rest of dispassion <term>apatheia: a state of being free from the disturbance of the passions</term>, but the ways of luxury result in the passions of dishonor.

<margin>78.</margin> Do not allow yourself to count the many yearly cycles of your monastic life, nor be captured by boasting in your endurance of the desert and the hardness of your struggles. Instead, keep in mind the Master's saying:
> I am an unworthy servant, and have not yet fulfilled the commandment.
For in truth, as long as we are in this present life, we have not yet been called back from our exile.

<summary>St. Theodore provides practical and psychological advice for the monastic life, emphasizing the "judgment of thoughts" (logismoi), the necessity of humility to combat pride, and the synergy between active discipline and spiritual knowledge.</summary>

# SOUL-PROFITING CHAPTERS

...but even now we sit by the river of Babylon <note>original: ποταμὸν Βαβυλῶνος; a reference to Psalm 137, symbolizing the soul's exile from its true spiritual home</note>, even now we suffer under the Egyptian brick-making <note>original: Αἰγύπτιον πλινθουργίαν; referring to the Israelites' slavery in Exodus, a metaphor for being enslaved to worldly passions</note>, having not yet glimpsed the Land of Promise. This is because we have not yet stripped off the "old man," who is corrupted according to the desires of deceit; we have not yet worn the image of the Heavenly One, for we still carry the image of the one made of dust. Therefore, we have no cause for boasting, but rather we ought to weep, begging the One who is able to save us from the wretched slavery of the most bitter Pharaoh <note>here, a symbol for the Devil</note>, to deliver us from this terrible tyranny, and to lead us into the good Land of Promise, to find rest in the sanctuary of God and be found at the right hand of the Majesty of the Most High. To attain these good things, which are beyond human comprehension, is not a result of our own works—those which we think we perform in righteousness—but is by the immeasurable mercy of God. Therefore, let us not cease pouring out tears day and night, according to the one who said: *I have grown weary with my groaning; every night I will wash my bed and soak my couch with my tears.* For those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.

<margin>79.</margin> Drive far away from you the talkative spirit <note>original: πολύρρημον Πνεῦμα; literally "the many-worded spirit"</note>, for within it lie terrible passions: from it comes lying, from there comes boldness <note>original: παρρησία (parrhesia); in monastic contexts, this refers to an inappropriate "boldness" or lack of healthy boundaries/respect</note>, from another side comes coarse jesting, filthiness, and foolish talk; and to summarize it with the well-known saying: *from talkativeness, sin shall not be escaped.* But the silent man is a throne of perception. Moreover, the Lord said that we shall give an account for every idle word; thus, silence is altogether necessary and beneficial.

<margin>80.</margin> We have been commanded not to return insults or abuse to those who revile and insult us, or who mistreat us in any other way, but rather to speak well of them and bless them. For as long as we are at peace with men, we are at war with the demons; but when we hold grudges against our brothers and fight with them, we are at peace with the demons—those whom we have been taught to hate with a perfect hatred and to maintain an unyielding war against.

<margin>81.</margin> Flee from tripping up your neighbor with a deceitful tongue, lest you yourself be tripped up by the Destroyer; for I have heard the Prophet crying out: *The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit.* And may the Lord destroy all

<column-break/>

deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks proud things. Likewise, flee from mocking the stumble of your brother, lest you fall away from kindness and love. For he who does not have kindness and love toward his brother has not known God; for "God is love," as cries out John, the "Son of Thunder" and the beloved disciple of Christ. For if Christ, he says, the Savior of all, laid down His life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.

<margin>82.</margin> It is with good reason that love has been called the "metropolis" <term>metropolis: literally the "mother-city" or capital; the central virtue from which all others flow</term> of the virtues, and the sum of the Law and the Prophets. Therefore, let us show every effort until we attain to holy love; through it, let us shake off the tyranny of the passions and be raised up into the heavens, lightened by the wings of the virtues, and we shall see God, as far as is possible for human nature.

<margin>83.</margin> If God is love, he who has love has God within himself. But if love is absent, we have no benefit at all, nor can we even say that we love God. For if someone says, "I love God," and hates his brother, he is a liar. And again it says: *No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us.* From this it is clear that love is the most comprehensive and the highest of all the good things spoken of through Holy Scripture. There is no form of virtue through which a person is made intimate with God and joined to Him that does not depend upon love and is not encompassed by it, held together and guarded by an ineffable reason.

<margin>84.</margin> When we receive brothers who visit us, let us not consider this a disturbance or an interruption of our stillness <note>original: ἡσυχίας (hesychias); the state of inward silence and prayer</note>, lest we fall away from the law of love. Nor should we welcome them as if we were doing them a favor, but rather as if we are the ones receiving a favor; being indebted by the encounter, let us show hospitality with entreaty and cheerfulness, just as the Patriarch Abraham showed us. For this reason, the Theologian <note>refers to St. John the Evangelist</note> teaches us again, saying: *Little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth, and by this we know that you are of the truth.*

<margin>85.</margin> The Patriarch <note>Abraham</note>, possessing hospitality as his primary labor, used to sit before his tent...

### OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THEODORE

...calling out to those passing by, he spread the table for all—both the ungodly and the barbarians—without distinction. Because of this, he was deemed worthy of that wondrous feast, entertaining Angels and the Lord of all. <note>The author refers to the hospitality of Abraham in Genesis 18.</note> Let us also, therefore, attend to hospitality with great zeal and readiness, so that we may receive not only Angels, but God Himself. For the Lord says, "Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me." <note>original: ἐποιήσατε ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἐλαχίστων, ἐμοὶ ἐποιήσατε; quoting Matthew 25:40</note> It is good to do good to all, but especially to those who are unable to repay you.

<margin>86.</margin>
The one whose heart does not condemn him regarding a commandment of God—whether by rejection, or negligence, or the acceptance of a contrary thought—this person would be "pure in heart" and worthy to hear: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.*

<margin>87.</margin>
Let us strive to discipline our senses by reason <note>original: Λόγῳ (Logos); here meaning the rational faculty or the Word of God acting as a guide</note>, and especially the eyes, the ears, and the tongue. We should permit them to see, hear, and speak not according to passion, but for our own benefit. For none of these organs is more prone to slip into sin than when it is not disciplined by reason. Conversely, nothing is more ready for their salvation than when reason acts as their charioteer, regulating them and leading them toward what is necessary and desired. For when the senses are disorderly, even the sense of smell becomes effeminate, the touch reaches out brashly, and a swarm of countless passions enters in. But when they are arranged in an orderly way by reason, a great peace and steady calm is revealed from every side.

<margin>88.</margin>
Just as precious ointment, even if it is shut in a vessel, spreads its own fragrance through the air and fills not only those standing near but also those all around with pleasure; so too the fragrance of a virtuous and God-loving soul, being given off through all the senses of the body, reveals to those who see it the virtue stored within. For who—seeing a tongue that speaks nothing harsh or discordant, but only what is good and useful to the hearers; eyes that are modest; hearing that receives none of the improper songs or words; feet that walk decorously; and a face not dissolved in laughter, but

<column-break/>

rather prepared for tears and mourning—will not recognize that a great fragrance of virtues is stored within? Therefore the Savior also says: *Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.*

<margin>89.</margin>
That which Christ our God called the "narrow way" in the Gospels, He again called a "kind yoke" and a "light burden." <note>Referencing Matthew 7:14 and 11:30</note> How then can both be reckoned together, since they seem to be opposites? It is because that path is entirely harsh and steep by its nature, but by the choice <note>original: προαιρέσει (proairesis); a technical term for the moral will or disposition</note> of those who succeed in it and by their good hopes, it is desirable and lovely, bringing pleasure rather than affliction to virtue-loving souls. Therefore, one may see those who have chosen the narrow and difficult way traveling it with more readiness than those on the broad and spacious one. Listen, for instance, to the blessed Luke saying that the Apostles, after being scourged, "departed from the presence of the council rejoicing." <note>Acts 5:41</note> And yet, such is not the nature of scourging; for it is not accustomed to produce pleasure and joy, but rather anguish and pain. But if scourgings produced pleasure for the sake of Christ, what wonder is it if the rest of the hardships and the "buffeting of the body" <note>original: ὑπωπιασμὸς τοῦ σώματος; referencing 1 Corinthians 9:27</note> produce the same for His sake?

<margin>90.</margin>
When we are tyrannized and held captive by the passions, we often wonder to ourselves: why do we suffer these things? One must therefore know that such captivities happen to us because we are distracted from the contemplation <term>theoria: spiritual perception or "seeing" God</term> of God. If someone would fix his mind without distraction upon our Master and God, the Savior of all Himself is faithful to rescue such a soul from every passionate captivity, just as the prophet says: *I foresaw the Lord before me always, for He is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken.* <note>Psalm 16:8</note> What is sweeter or safer than always having the Lord at one's right hand, sheltering and guarding, and not allowing one to be shaken? To achieve this is within our power.

<margin>91.</margin>
The Fathers said well and indisputably: a man finds no rest in any other way, unless he acquires this disposition in his mind—that only he and

While the previous page focused on hospitality and the discipline of the senses, this page (193) shifts toward the internal psychological battle. It specifically addresses the "mother of all evils"—self-love—and outlines the progression from active virtue to the heights of prayer and divine contemplation. ### SOUL-PROFITING CHAPTERS

...to be with God: in the world, not letting the mind wander at all, but longing for Him and clung to Him alone. Such a person will find true rest and freedom from the tyranny of the passions;
> for it says, "My soul clung behind you; your right hand supported me." <note>original: ἐκολλήθη γάρ, φησιν, ἡ ψυχή μου ὀπίσω σου; quoting Psalm 63:8 (LXX 62:9). This implies a soul following God so closely it "sticks" to His path.</note>

<margin>402.</margin>
<term>Self-love</term> <note>original: φιλαυτία (philautia); an excessive or disordered love of oneself, often cited by Greek Fathers as the root of all sin.</note>, the love of pleasure, and the love of glory drive the memory of God out of the soul. Self-love is the mother of unimaginable evils. When the memory of God fails, the turmoil of the passions finds a place to grow within us.

<margin>403.</margin>
The person who eagerly uproots self-love from his own heart will easily master all the other passions as well, with the Lord’s help. For from self-love, anger, grief, malice, the love of pleasure, and <term>impertinence</term> <note>original: παρρησία (parresia); usually meaning "boldness," but in an ascetic context, it often refers to a lack of respectful restraint or "cheekiness" toward others.</note> are naturally born. He who is defeated by self-love is subject to all the other passions. We define self-love as a passionate disposition and friendship toward the body, and the fulfillment of fleshly desires.

<margin>404.</margin>
Whatever a person loves, he desires to be with constantly and without ceasing, and he turns away from everything that hinders him from greeting and dwelling with his beloved. It is clear, then, that the one who loves God longs to encounter and converse with Him always. This comes to us through <term>pure prayer</term>. We must attend to this with all our power, for it is the nature of prayer to make us intimate with the Master. Such a person was he who said:
> "O God, my God, I rise early for you; my soul thirsted for you." <note>original: ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Θεός μου, πρὸς σὲ ὀρθρίζω, ἐδίψησέ σε ἡ ψυχή μου; quoting Psalm 63:1 (LXX 62:2).</note>
For he rises early for God who has distanced his mind from every evil and is wounded by divine love without distraction.

<margin>405.</margin>
We have learned that <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia); not "apathy" in the modern sense, but a state of being "passionless" or calm, where one is no longer controlled by impulsive desires or anger.</note> is born from self-control and humility. From faith, knowledge is born. From these, the soul progresses to discernment and love. Having embraced divine love, the soul ascends on the wings of pure prayer toward its heights without ceasing, until it arrives at the "knowledge of the Son of God," as the Apostle says, "to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." <note>Quoting Ephesians 4:13.</note>

<margin>406.</margin>
Through <term>practical virtue</term> <note>original: πρακτικῆς ἀρετῆς; the active struggle to do good and avoid sin.</note>, desire is enslaved and anger is bridled. Through knowledge and <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: θεωρίας (theoria); the spiritual "seeing" or direct experience of God's presence.</note>, the mind takes flight,

<column-break/>

and being lifted above material things, it journeys toward God, attaining true blessedness.

<margin>407.</margin>
This is our first struggle: to diminish the passions and conquer them by force. The second contest is to acquire the virtues and not leave our soul empty or idle. The third "lap" of the spiritual race is to soberly guard the fruits of our virtues and our labors. For we are commanded not only to work laboriously but also to guard vigilantly.

<margin>408.</margin>
> "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,"
says the Lord. <note>Quoting Luke 12:35.</note> Now, a good belt for the loins—by which we can become nimble and light—is self-control joined with humility of heart. By self-control, I mean the abstaining from all passions. The light-bearer for the spiritual lamp is pure prayer and perfect love. Those who have prepared themselves in this way are truly like people waiting for their Lord, so that when He comes and knocks, they will open immediately. Having entered, He—with the Father and the Holy Spirit—will make His home with them. Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when He comes, will find doing so.

<margin>409.</margin>
A Monk must love God with his whole heart and his whole mind as a son; as a servant, he must revere and obey Him, and work out His commandments with fear and trembling. He must be fervent in spirit, clothed in the full armor of the Holy Spirit, to attain the enjoyment of eternal life. He must perform all that is commanded without falling short, being sober and guarding the heart from evil thoughts. He must carry out divine meditation unceasingly with good thoughts, examining himself every day regarding his evil thoughts and actions to fill in what is lacking. He must not be puffed up by his successes, but call himself an "unprofitable servant" who falls far short of fulfilling his obligations. He should give thanks to Holy God and attribute the grace of his successes to Him, doing nothing at all for vainglory or to please people, but doing everything in secret and seeking only praise from God. Above all things and in all things, he must remain in the Orthodox faith...

<meta>This page concludes a set of "chapters" or spiritual aphorisms by St. Theodore and begins a new, more advanced work entitled "Theoretikon" (A Contemplative Work). The text transitions from practical obedience to the internal anatomy of the soul's purification.</meta>

<page-num>194</page-num>
<header>OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THEODORE</header>

...to be fenced in within the soul according to the divine dogmas of the Catholic <note>The word "Catholic" here refers to the "universal" or "whole" Church as defined by the early Ecumenical Councils.</note> Church, handed down by the God-proclaiming Apostles and the holy fathers. For those who live their lives in this way, there is a great recompense: life without end and an indestructible dwelling-place with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the **consubstantial** <note>original: ὁμοουσίῳ (homoousios); the theological term meaning "of the same essence," used to describe the relationship between the persons of the Trinity.</note> and **tri-hypostatic** <note>original: τρισυποστάτῳ (trisyponstatos); existing in three distinct persons or "hypostases."</note> Godhead.

<margin>100.</margin>
"The end of the matter; hear all," said the **Preacher** <note>original: ἐκκλησιαστής (Ekklesiastes); referring to King Solomon as the author of the book of Ecclesiastes. This quote is from Eccl. 12:13.</note>: "Fear God and keep His commandments; for this is the whole man." I show you, he says, a summary and more excellent way of salvation: fear God and keep His commandments. This "fear" is not the "introductory" kind felt because of the threat of punishments, but the **perfect** and **perfecting** fear which we ought to have out of love for the One who gave the command. For if we only avoid sins because of the dread of punishment, it is clear that if no punishment were proposed, we would have committed them, possessing a will that loves sin. But if we abstain from these things not because of the threat of punishment, but because we hate the evil itself, then we practice the virtues out of friendship toward the Master,

<column-break/>

fearing only that we might fall away. For in fearing lest we betray any of the things commanded, this fear proves to be **pure** <note>original: ἁγνὸς (hagnos); a reference to Psalm 19:9, "The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever."</note>, existing for the sake of the Good itself. It purifies our souls, being equal in power to perfect love. The person who has this fear and keeps the commandments is the "whole man"—meaning the perfect and complete man. Having recognized these things, let us fear God and observe His commandments so that we may be perfect and fully equipped in the virtues. Let us keep a humble mind and a contrite heart, and unceasingly sing to the Lord the prayer spoken by the divine and great **Arsenius**:
> *My God, do not forsake me; I have done nothing good in Your sight, but grant me, through Your compassion, to make a beginning.* <note>St. Arsenius the Great (c. 350–445 AD) was a famous Desert Father whose life was defined by silence and tears of repentance.</note>
For the whole of our salvation lies in the mercies and the love for mankind of God. To Him be glory, power, and worship—to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and forever and unto the ages. Amen.

## A CONTEMPLATIVE WORK

How much greater is the struggle to break this iron bond [of the world], to be freed from the service of matter, and to acquire the habit of good things! Truly, the soul needs to be noble and courageous for the flight from matter. The object of our zeal is not merely the purification of the passions; for that is not virtue in and of itself, but rather the **preparation** for virtue. One must, in addition to the purification of wicked habits, also work toward the acquisition of the virtues. Purification of the soul consists of the following: for the **rational** part <note>original: λογιστικοῦ (logistikon); the part of the soul responsible for thought and reason.</note>, it is the removal of "lower" and "wandering" characters—

<column-break/>

according to the **Theologian’s** voice <note>original: θεολόγον φωνήν; likely referring to St. Gregory Nazianzen (the Theologian), who frequently wrote about the soul's ascent from worldly "noises."</note>—I mean the cares and turmoils of this life, and the riddance and total erasure of wicked inclinations or absurd preconceptions. For the **desiring** part <note>original: ἐπιθυμητικοῦ (epithymetikon); the seat of longing and physical appetite.</note>, it is to rush toward nothing material, nor to look toward the senses, but to become obedient to reason. Consequently, for the **spirited** part <note>original: θυμοειδοῦς (thymoeides); the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and "heat."</note>, it is to be disturbed by nothing that happens. After this purification, then...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous practical exhortations into a more philosophical and systematic treatise titled "Theoretikon." It explores the psychological faculties of the soul—Mind, Will, and Spirit—and how they participate in the process of deification. It also introduces a key distinction between "natural" and "supernatural" knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>195</page-num>
<header>### THEORETIKON</header>
<note>The Greek title "Theoretikon" refers to a work focused on "theoria" or divine contemplation, rather than just practical action.</note>

the mortification of the most shameful powers, or their regulation, is necessary for both the ascent and **deification**; <note>original: θεώσεως (theosis). This is the Eastern Christian concept of a human being becoming "partaker of the divine nature" through grace.</note> for it is necessary, in turning away from evil, to do good. Furthermore, one must first deny oneself and, having thus taken up the cross, follow the Master toward the highest state of deification.

And what is the ascent and deification? Of the **mind**, <note>original: νοῦς (nous); often translated as "intellect," the highest faculty of the soul capable of direct experience of God.</note> it is the ultimate knowledge of all beings and of the One who is beyond all beings, as far as is attainable by human nature. Of the **will**, it is the complete and continuous stretching and movement toward the "First Beauty" <note>A traditional philosophical name for God.</note>. Of the **spirited faculty**, <note>original: θυμοειδοῦς (thymoeidos); the part of the soul associated with courage, drive, or righteous anger.</note> it is the most energetic and practical movement toward the object of desire, unflagging and unyielding, not cut short by any distressing circumstances that may arise, but journeying with intense passion and without turning back.

The soul’s movement toward what is beautiful must be as much more vehement than its movement toward what is base, as the beauties of the mind surpass the beauties of the senses. One must pay only as much attention to the flesh as suffices for the care and provision of what is necessary for its existence, so that the living creature is not violently destroyed. To state these things is very easy, but to put them into practice is more laborious. For it is not without toil that those hard-to-move habits can be uprooted from the soul; nor indeed is the possession of knowledge acquired without sweat.

Furthermore, looking fixedly at the Blessed Nature and stretching toward it comes about through many labors and over a long time, until the faculty of the will, following such an impulse, attains a permanent state. Great resistance of the mind is needed against the senses, which pull it downward; and this is the struggle and battle against the body. This battle is unceasing until death, even if it seems to have lessened through the withering of anger and desire, and the enslavement of the senses under the surpassing knowledge of the mind.

However, one thing must be noted: that an unilluminated soul—since it is not naturally inclined to be helped by God—can neither be genuinely purified nor be led up to the Divine Light as has been described. For one must consider that what has been said applies only to the faithful. For the sake of greater clarity, we must briefly distinguish the differences in **knowledge**. Of the types of knowledge found here, one is according to nature, and the other is supernatural. The second will become clear from the first.

<column-break/>

We call "natural knowledge" that which the soul is able to receive through research and inquiry, using its natural parts and powers, concerning creation and the Cause of creation—obviously, as much as is attainable by a soul bound to matter. For it has been said in the treatise *On Sensation, Imagination, and Mind* that the energy of the mind is blunted by its connection and intermingling with the body. Consequently, it cannot come into direct contact with purely intellectual forms, but requires **imagination** <note>original: φαντασίας (phantasias); in this context, the faculty that creates mental images from sensory data.</note> for its thinking, which is of an image-like nature and possesses material extension and thickness. Therefore, the mind within the flesh requires forms proportionate to itself so that it might be able to grasp them.

Thus, whatever knowledge a mind in this state receives according to its own natural method, we call "natural knowledge." But **supernatural knowledge** is that which is produced in the mind beyond its own method and power; that is, when the things being understood exceed the proportions of a mind joined with flesh, so that the knowledge is proper to a mind existing without a body. This comes about by God alone, whenever He finds such a mind thoroughly purified from every material attachment and possessed by divine love.

Not only is knowledge divided in this way, but **virtue** is as well. For there is one kind which does not exceed nature, which would reasonably be called natural; and there is another which is energized by the First Beauty alone, being beyond natural power and condition, which should appropriately be called supernatural. Thus, with these things distinguished, even an unilluminated person might perhaps possess natural knowledge and virtue, but the supernatural, by no means. For how could they, being without a share in the Acting Cause? But the illuminated person can have both; or rather, they could not acquire supernatural virtue at all without first acquiring the natural kind. Yet there is nothing to prevent one from participating in supernatural knowledge without the natural kind.

One must know this, however: that just as irrational animals possess sensation and imagination, and man also possesses these powers but in a much better and higher way, so it is with natural virtues and types of knowledge; both are said to have them, but the human is far superior...
