The enlightened man holds these virtues more highly than the one who is unenlightened. Furthermore, regarding the "natural knowledge" already mentioned—that which deals with virtues and their opposite habits—this also seems to be twofold. One type is "bare" knowledge; this occurs when the one seeking wisdom <note>original: ὁ φιλοσοφῶν (ho philosophon). In monastic texts, "philosophy" often refers to the ascetic life of seeking true wisdom in God.</note> has not yet experienced these states of being, and thus he sometimes wavers in his conviction. The other type is "practical" and, so to speak, "living"; this is when knowledge is confirmed through the actual experience of such states. This second kind is clear and certain, admitting no doubt or hesitation whatsoever.

Since things are so, there seem to be four things that oppose the **intellect** <term>original: νοῦς (nous); the highest faculty of the human soul, intended for direct contemplation of God</term> in its quest to acquire virtue. First is the "preconception" of opposite habits, which we have mentioned; through long-standing custom, it tries to persuade the soul to be dragged down toward earthly things. Second is the activity of **sense perception**, which shows itself in the beauties of the sensory world and drags the intellect along with it. Third is the dullness of the intellect’s own power, which it suffers because of its entanglement with the body. For the intellect does not relate to the "intelligible" <note>The "intelligible" (noeta) refers to spiritual realities that can only be understood by the mind, not the physical eyes.</note> in the same way that sight relates to the visible, or to put it simply, as the senses relate to the sensory world—at least, I mean the intellect while the soul is still in the flesh. For the immaterial **Minds** <note>original: Νόες (Noes); referring here to the Angels, who perceive spiritual truth directly.</note> strike upon spiritual realities more energetically than sight strikes upon visible objects. But just as a diseased eye cannot perceive things meant to be seen clearly or plainly, but instead receives blurred and indistinct images, so too the intellect within us perceives spiritual things. Being unable to gaze clearly upon the "intelligible beauties," it is simultaneously unable to desire them—for the measure of one's desire follows the measure of one's knowledge—and is at the same time dragged down toward sensory beauties, which strike it more clearly. For it is inevitable that the soul be occupied with whatever beauty is currently appearing to it, whether that beauty is real or not.

Finally, beyond these, there is the assault of the impure and "man-hating" spirits. One cannot describe how many and what kind of traps they set everywhere along the path—alas!—fixing them to souls in many shapes and ways: through the senses, through speech, through the mind, and through almost everything that exists. If He who took the wandering sheep upon His shoulders <note>A reference to Christ as the Good Shepherd (Luke 15:4-7).</note> did not, with his infinite care, keep those who look to Him in a higher state, no soul could ever escape. To escape all these things, then, we need these three remedies: the first and greatest is to look toward God with the whole soul 

<column-break/>

and to ask for the hand of help from Him, placing all hope in Him, as those who are truly convinced. For unless He helps us, we will inevitably be carried away by those forces dragging us back. 

The second remedy—which I believe leads to the first—is the continuous nourishment of the intellect through **knowledge**. <term>original: ἐπιστήμη (episteme); here meaning a systematic, spiritual understanding of the cosmos.</term> By "knowledge," I mean the understanding of all things, both sensory and spiritual: whether they exist in themselves, how they relate to the First Principle <note>God as the origin of all existence.</note>, how they come from there to here, and the contemplation (as far as is attainable) of the Cause of all beings based on the things surrounding Him. For investigating the nature of beings is most cleansing; it frees the soul from passionate attachment to them and from the deception surrounding them, and it is the most effective way to lead the soul back to the Principle of all. From things that are beautiful, wonderful, and great, the soul is granted a reflection of that which is Most Beautiful, Most Wonderful, and Greatest—or rather, that which is *beyond* beauty, wonder, and greatness. When the mind is always occupied with these things, it is impossible for it not to desire the Truly Good; for if it is drawn toward what is foreign to it, how much more will it be drawn toward what is its own? Once the soul has fallen in love with these things, what could induce it to attend to the things below, or to those things which naturally pull it away from its Beloved? Might it even grow frustrated with life in the flesh, seeing it as a hindrance to these beautiful things? For even if it is said that the intellect in "matter" <note>The physical body.</note> perceives spiritual beauty only dimly, yet these spiritual goods are so great and of such a kind that even a tiny trickle or a faint reflection of that overflowing Beauty is enough to persuade the intellect to fly above all non-spiritual things and be carried toward those alone. It would never again endure departing from that delight, even if some painful thing should happen.

The third remedy that must be present is the **mortification** <term>original: νέκρωσις (nekrosis); the practice of "putting to death" selfish impulses or bodily comforts to focus on the spirit.</term> of the "yoked" body. Otherwise, it is impossible to receive those reflections clearly and plainly. The flesh is mortified through fasting, vigils, sleeping on the ground, wearing rough clothing when necessary, and through toil and labor. In this way, the flesh is mortified—or rather, it is "crucified with Christ." It becomes refined and purified; and having become light and agile, it follows the movements of the intellect easily, without resisting, and is lifted up together with that which is high. For without this, all effort is proven to be in vain. This is the...

The venerable triad <note>Likely referring to the three remedies or faculties discussed on the previous page that realign the soul.</note>, whenever it harmonizes with itself, generates the choir of blessed virtues within the soul. For it is impossible to find a trace of vice, or for any of the virtues to be absent, in those who are adorned by this triple grace. But perhaps the speech is troubled by the casting away of possessions and the rejection of glory, for as long as the soul is bound to these, it is pierced by many passions. I, for my part, strongly maintain that it is impossible for a soul nailed to wealth and glory to take flight. However, I do not say it is possible for a soul to remain devoted to these things once it has struggled sufficiently in the aforementioned three areas so as to reach a state of habit <term>original: ἕξις (hexis); a stable internal disposition or "second nature" acquired through practice</term> in them. For if the soul truly knows nothing as "beautiful" except that which is above all things, and is convinced that among other things, that which is more like the First Beauty is the more beautiful—and holds this conviction unto the very end—how could it ever love or accept silver, or gold, or any other thing dragged down here below? Let these things also be said by me concerning glory.

But not even that most persistent thing—I mean anxieties <note>original: φροντίδας (phrontidas); the worldly cares or "distractions" that weigh down the mind</note>—can withstand this reasoning. For what will he be anxious about, who is neither affected by nor turned toward anything here? For the "cloud of anxieties" is composed from the "exhalation," so to speak, of the most generic passions: I mean the love of pleasure, the love of money, and the love of glory. Thus, he who is free from these is also a stranger to anxiety. Nor is prudence <term>original: φρόνησις (phronesis); practical wisdom or the ability to apply spiritual principles to life</term> believed to be anything other than a form of wisdom; and being the most powerful of the things that carry us toward the heights, it is not lacking in the things we have mentioned. For in the knowledge of the virtues is also included the most accurate discernment of both the good and its opposite. Prudence has need of these as its primary tools. Experience and the struggle against the body will teach the methods of use and the "wrestling" involved. 

The matter of fear is not left out of this account either. For the greater the love <note>original: ἔρως (eros); used here in the sense of intense, longing desire for God</note>, the more fear increases along with it. For regarding the Good, the more hope one has of attaining it, the more it knows how to "sting" those who are wounded by it—more so than the threats of ten thousand punishments. For just as attaining it is most blessed, the fear of failing to attain it is equally great, which is the most wretched state. But so that our discourse may proceed in an orderly fashion, we must begin from the "End" <term>original: τέλος (telos); the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing</term>. For it seems that everything that comes into being receives the distinction of its parts and their order from its own proper end. Therefore, the end of our life is blessedness, which one might also call the 

<column-break/>

Kingdom of Heaven, or of God. This is not only to see the most sovereign Trinity, but also, in addition to this, to receive the divine influence and, as it were, to experience deification <term>original: θέωσιν (theosis); the transformative process of becoming like God through participation in His grace</term>. It is for that which is needy and imperfect within us to be filled up and perfected by this divine influence. And this is the "food of the intellectual beings" <note>intellectual beings (noerōn): referring to angels and the human intellect (nous)</note>: the filling up of what is lacking through that divine influence. 

And there is a certain eternal circle, beginning from the same and ending at the same. For as much as the soul understands <note>original: νοεῖ (noei)</note>, it also desires. And as much as it desires, it enjoys. And as much as it enjoys, it is strengthened again toward understanding, and begins once more its "motionless motion"—or if you prefer, its "motionless stillness." Such, then, is the End, as far as it is attainable for us. We must now consider how one must travel toward this same end. For rational souls, being intellectual substances and falling only a little short of the intellects of the Angels, the life here—the life in the flesh—is a prize-fight <note>original: ἆθλον (athlon); the labor of a contest</note> and a struggle <note>original: ἀγὼν (agon)</note> that has been granted to us. The "prize" is the aforementioned state: a gift of divine goodness and, at the same time, worthy of His justice. On the one hand, it is a gift because we seem to obtain these goods from our own "sweat" (labors). On the other hand, it is because the Power that is infinite in its giving surpasses every labor; and further, because the very ability to desire and to do good is itself His gift. 

What then is the struggle here? The rational soul is yoked to a beast-like body, which has its existence from the earth and is weighed down toward the things below. It is so blended with it that the two—the soul and the body, though they are most opposite—become one. Let it not be thought that this involves a "turning" or a confusion of the parts—far from it!—but from two things that move according to their own natures, one person <term>original: ὑπόστασιν (hypostasin); the underlying reality or individual personhood</term> comes to be in two perfect natures. Thus, this "mixed animal" called man, having become dual-natured, is designed to enact the properties of each nature in turn. To the body, it is natural to desire things similar to itself; for this love for similar things is natural to all beings, as existence is seemingly preserved by the company of similar things, and the enjoyment of them through sense-perception. Furthermore, to that which is heavy, rest is dear. To the beast-like nature, these things are natural and lovely. But to the rational soul, insofar as it is an intellectual substance, those things that are "intelligible" <note>spiritual or mental realities</note> are more natural and desirable; and it enjoys these in its own proper way. But before all things and above all things, the love for God is naturally rooted within it. And it wills...

# OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THEODORE

...to enjoy Him and the other **intelligible things** <note>original: νοητῶν (noētōn); spiritual realities perceived by the intellect rather than the physical senses</note>, but he is now unable to do this without hindrance. The first man, however, was able to perceive and enjoy them without hindrance—just as he perceived **sensible things** <note>original: αἰσθητῶν (aisthētōn); physical objects perceived by the five senses</note> through his senses, so he could perceive the intelligible through his mind. It was necessary for him to occupy himself not with the lesser things, but with the better. For having the capacity for both, it was up to him whether to be present with the intelligible through the mind, or the sensible through the senses. I do not mean that Adam was not supposed to use his senses—for his body was not bestowed upon him in vain—but that he was not meant to revel in sensible things alone. Instead, by perceiving the beauty of created things, he ought to have run back to their Cause; and from that point, he should have reveled in wonder. Thus, he would have had a double motivation for marveling at the Creator. Certainly, he was not meant to be glued to sensible things and to marvel at them rather than the One who made them, letting go of the beauty of the mind. 

Adam, then, was in this state. But since he used his senses wrongly and marveled at sensible beauty—the fruit appearing to him as "beautiful to the eyes and good for food"—by tasting it, he let go of the enjoyment of intelligible things. From that point, the Just Judge, having deemed Adam unworthy of the **contemplation** <note>original: θεωρίας (theōrias); the direct vision or spiritual experience of God</note> of God and of true beings—which Adam himself had despised—withdrew it from him. He "made darkness His secret place" <note>A reference to Psalm 18:11/17:11</note> between Himself and immaterial essences. For it was not right for holy things to be laid open to the profane. To the things Adam loved, God allowed him their enjoyment: permitting him to live by the senses and by the faint traces of the mind. From this, our **struggle** <note>original: ἀγὼν (agōn); an athletic or military contest, often used for the spiritual life</note> toward the things here has become more burdensome. For we no longer have the power to enjoy intelligible things as easily as we enjoy sensible things through the senses, as has been said. Even if we are helped greatly through baptism, being purified and lifted up, yet it is necessary for us to occupy ourselves with these intelligible things as far as possible, and not with the sensible. We must marvel at and desire those higher things. One should not marvel at any sensible thing for its own sake, nor desire to enjoy it. For in truth, physical beauty seems to have no proportion to intelligible beauty. As much as one essence surpasses another, so much more marvelous is the beauty of the higher essence. To desire the uglier instead of the more beautiful, and the more dishonorable instead of the more precious—what kind of extreme madness is that? These things, then, concern both sensible and intelligible creations.

<column-break/>

And what can you say about the One who is above all these, when we prefer even formless and unlovely matter over Him? This, then, is the struggle: to attend to ourselves with precision, so that we may always enjoy the intelligible. By stretching our mind and our desire toward those higher things, may we never be stolen away by these sensible things, being dragged down toward them through the senses so as to marvel at them for their own sake. But if it is necessary to use the senses at all, they should be used for this: so that from the created things we may grasp the Creator. We should see Him in them, as one sees the sun in the reflection of water. For images exist in created beings of the First Cause of all, according to what they can contain. 

This, then, is the **achievement** <note>original: κατόρθωμα (katorthōma); a successful spiritual feat or righteous deed</note>. We must consider how it is to be achieved. For it has been said that the body longs to enjoy its own things through the senses. This is contrary to the purpose of the soul; and the stronger the body is, the more it desires them. Therefore, the soul has taken care to place a bridle on all the senses, so that we do not revel in sensible things, as has been said. But since the body, when it is robust, rushes headlong and becomes difficult to restrain in its impulses, the soul has sought its **mortification** <note>original: νέκρωσις (nekrōsis); literally "putting to death" or disciplining the body's passions</note> through fasting, vigils, standing, sleeping on the ground, abstaining from bathing, and every other kind of hardship. Thus, by withering the body’s power, the soul may have it well-reined and obedient for its own intellectual activities. For this was the goal set for achievement. 

Since these things are easy to pray for but difficult to do—and failures are many times more frequent than successes, even if one is very attentive, because the senses are constantly stealing us away—a third remedy has been devised: **prayer** and **tears**. For prayer contains thanksgiving for the good things given, a request for the forgiveness of failures, and a plea for strengthening power for the future. For without the divine inclination, as was said before, the soul would achieve nothing. Furthermore, prayer brings about union with the Beloved, enjoyment, and a total turning of the power of the will toward Him. This was the most excellent part of the achievement: to persuade the will to want these things as much as possible. As for tears, they have great power. For they both propitiate the Master on behalf of our failures and wash away the sensible pleasures that have attached themselves to us...

# THEORETICAL [WORKS]

...cleanses every stain, and gives wings to the desire for things above; these things are so. Therefore, the ultimate **success** <note>original: κατόρθωμα (katorthōma); a righteous deed or spiritual achievement</note> is the **contemplation** <note>original: θεωρία (theōria); spiritual vision or direct insight into divine truths</note> and complete longing for **intelligible things** <note>original: νοητῶν (noētōn); spiritual realities perceived by the intellect rather than the physical senses</note>. Through this comes the discipline of the flesh, which includes parts such as fasting, temperance, and others. All these are practiced for the sake of something else. Through these, and alongside them, comes prayer. Each of these is divided into several parts. For just as they exist for the sake of other things, so too do other things exist for their sake. 

Let no one think that **ambition** <note>original: φιλοδοξία (philodoxia); literally "love of glory" or "vainglory"</note> and the **love of money** <note>original: φιλαργυρία (philargyria)</note> belong to the body; for only the **love of pleasure** <note>original: φιληδονία (philēdonia)</note> belongs to the body alone, which finds its suitable remedy in the affliction of the body. But the two aforementioned vices are the offspring of **ignorance**. For through a lack of experience with truly beautiful things, and a lack of knowledge regarding the intelligible, the soul has adopted these "bastard" impulses. Through wealth, the soul thinks it can comfort its own neediness. At the same time, wealth is pursued because of a love for pleasure, because of ambition, and for its own sake as if it were some other kind of "good." Regarding this, we say that this happens through ignorance of the things that are truly good. 

As for ambition, it does not exist because of a bodily lack, for it comforts nothing regarding the body. It arises from a lack of experience and ignorance of the **First Good** and of true glory. To speak briefly, ignorance is the natural root of all evils. For one has not grasped the nature of things as they ought to be: from where each thing proceeded, and where it ends. Then, having disregarded one's own proper **end** <note>original: τέλους (telous); the final goal or purpose of human life</note>, one is carried down toward earthly things. For the soul does not naturally crave the "apparent" good. If it is tyrannized by habit, it certainly has the power to master that habit. However, when the habit did not yet exist,

<column-break/>

the soul was deceived by ignorance. Therefore, one must first of all strive to hold right opinions about the nature of beings, and then subsequently give wings to the **will** <note>original: βούλησιν (boulēsin)</note> toward the First Good. One must look down upon all present things, condemning their great vanity. For what do they contribute toward our proper end? 

To summarize the whole matter briefly: there is only one task for the rational soul while in a body, and that is to strive for its own proper end. Since the activity of the will is immobile without **intellection** <note>original: νοήσεως (noēseōs); the act of the mind or intellect</note>, we must also take up intellectual activity. This is either for the sake of willing that we might understand, or for the sake of understanding itself and for the sake of the will—which seems more likely. For even **blessedness** <note>original: μακαριότης (makariotēs)</note>, for which the life of the virtuous person here is not only a herald but also a pattern, possesses both activities: intellection and pleasure. Whether both activities are primary, or whether one is more sovereign, let those who wish to philosophize about it do so; but for the present, we set down both activities. One we call **contemplation** <note>original: θεωρίαν (theōrian)</note> and the other **practice** <note>original: πρᾶξιν (praxin)</note>. 

It is impossible for one to be found without the other at these highest levels of activity. However, in the lower levels, and those following after them, it is possible. Whatever things hinder these activities, or look toward their opposites, we call **vices**. Whatever things are helpful, or deliver us from hindrances, we call **virtues**. Activities stemming from the virtues we call successes; those from their opposites, we call failures and sins. The defining form of every activity—whether toward the worse or toward the better—is the ultimate **goal** <note>original: σκοπός (skopos)</note>, which we know to be a composite activity of both intellection and will.

# A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS
# MAXIMUS
### THE CONFESSOR

Our Father among the Saints, Maximus the Confessor, lived during the reign of Constantine Pogonatus <note>Constantine IV (r. 668–685 AD), known as "the Bearded" (Pogonatos).</note>, around the year 670 AD. He was the primary overthrower of the evil-minded heresy of the **Monothelites** <note>A 7th-century heresy teaching that Christ had two natures but only one will (the divine will), which the Orthodox Church rejected, insisting He had both a human and divine will.</note>. Having previously distinguished himself in the imperial courts and being honored with the dignity of **Protasekretis** <note>original: Πρωτασηκρήτου (Protasekretou); the chief secretary of the Byzantine Empire, a position of great political and intellectual influence.</note>, he later abandoned his worldly offices to strip for the struggles of the ascetic life. Approaching the fountain of wisdom with his mouth, and being constantly watered by the life-flowing streams of the Divine Scriptures, he truly poured forth from his heart rivers of divine **dogmas** <note>essential religious doctrines</note> and writings that flooded all the ends of the inhabited world. We have channeled the sweet and resurrection-bringing water of these works into this book through these present chapters, setting them before those who are gripped by a noble thirst for wisdom, so that by drinking abundantly from it, they may never thirst again. For within these pages, the knowledge and practice of sacred and **deifying love** <note>original: θεοποιοῦ ἀγάπης (theopoiou agapēs); love that transforms the human person into the likeness of God.</note> are explored philosophically; the unerring glory of high **Theology** <note>In this context, *Theology* refers specifically to the study of the nature of God and the Trinity.</note>

<column-break/>

is strengthened; the mystery regarding the **Economy of the Word** <note>original: οἰκονομίας τοῦ λόγου (oikonomias tou logou); the divine plan of salvation through the Incarnation of Jesus Christ.</note> is piously unfolded; the practical **contemplation** <note>original: θεωρία (theōria); spiritual vision or insight.</note> of the god-like virtues is clearly and skillfully explained; and the loathsome gang of vices and passions that oppose them is denounced. To put it briefly: within these works, the adornment of moral character shines forth, and the treasures of many different soul-profiting themes are stored up. Through these, one might easily be freed from every vice, become habituated in the virtues, gain the strength to become a citizen of heaven, and attain divine glory. Furthermore, this Father's explanatory unfolding of the "Our Father" <note>The Lord's Prayer.</note>—which is far superior to many others and promises great benefit to those who read it—has been added to these chapters. The wise **Photius** <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893 AD), Patriarch of Constantinople and a famous scholar who reviewed hundreds of books in his *Bibliotheca*.</note> also mentions this divine Father in reading 191, page 251. He notes that his style is "extended in its periods, fond of **hyperbaton** <note>a literary device where the natural order of words is disrupted for emphasis or style.</note>, and flourishing in its use of periphrasis, not striving for plain speech..." Nevertheless, if anyone delights in unrolling the mind through **anagoge** <note>a method of spiritual interpretation that "leads upward" from the literal text to mystical realities.</note> and contemplation, he could not encounter works more varied or more diligently crafted than these.

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER

# MAXIMUS

### THE CONFESSOR

#### PROLOGUE

## O N  L O V E

##### TO ELPIDIUS THE PRIEST <note>original: Πρεσβύτερον (Presbyteron); a title for a priest or an elder in the church.</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap "I" decorated with vine-like scrollwork and topped with a small cross, flanked by two larger decorative crosses in the margins.</image-desc>
Behold, along with the discourse on the **ascetic life** <note>The disciplined spiritual life of self-denial and prayer.</note>, I have also sent the discourse on love to your Holiness, Father Elpidius. It is arranged in sets of one hundred chapters <note>original: ἑκατοντάσιν (hekatontasin); these "Centuries" were a popular literary form in Byzantine spirituality, consisting of groups of 100 short, pithy sayings.</note> to match the number of the four Holy Gospels. It contains nothing that is perhaps worthy of your expectations, but it is certainly not less than the best of my own strength. However, let your Holiness know that even these thoughts are not the products of my own intellect. Rather, after going through the writings of the **Holy Fathers** <note>The influential early theologians of the Christian tradition.</note> and collecting from them the concepts that contribute to our subject, I have condensed many things into a few short chapters so that they might be easy to survey and remember. I send them now to your Holiness, asking that you read them with a fair mind and seek only the spiritual benefit within them, while overlooking the unrefined style of the language. I also ask that you pray for my insignificance, as I am devoid of all spiritual benefit. I also ask this: do not consider

<column-break/>

what has been said as a nuisance. For I have simply fulfilled a command. I say this because there are many of us today who trouble others with words, but those who teach—or are taught—by deeds are very few. Instead, pay close attention to each of the chapters. For I do not think that everything is easy for everyone to grasp; indeed, most of them require much investigation by most people, even if they seem to have been expressed simply. For perhaps something useful to the soul might be revealed as it is uncovered through them; and it will certainly be revealed, by the grace of God, to the one who reads with an uncomplicated mind, with the fear of God, and with love. But for the one who does not read for the sake of spiritual benefit—whether it be this work or any other—but rather to "hunt for words" in order to criticize the author (so that he might represent himself, in his own conceit, as wiser than the writer), nothing beneficial will ever be revealed to him from any source.

->OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS<-

# THE FIRST CENTURY
## OF THE CHAPTERS
### ON LOVE

<margin>1.</margin> Love is a good disposition of the soul, according to which it prefers nothing among existing things to the knowledge of God. It is impossible to arrive at the steady habit of this love if one has an attachment to any earthly thing.

<margin>2.</margin> Love is born from **dispassion** <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia); in the Orthodox tradition, this is not a lack of feeling, but a state of being "passionless" or free from disordered urges and compulsions.</note>. Dispassion is born from hope in God; hope from patience and long-suffering; and these from all-encompassing self-control. Self-control is born from the fear of God, and fear from faith in the Lord.

<margin>3.</margin> The one who believes in the Lord fears punishment. The one who fears punishment practices self-control over the **passions** <note>In this context, "passions" refer to internal spiritual sicknesses like pride, anger, or greed.</note>. The one who practices self-control over the passions patiently endures tribulations. The one who patiently endures tribulations will have hope in God. Hope in God separates the mind from every earthly attachment. When the mind is separated from these, it will possess love for God.

<margin>4.</margin> The one who loves God prefers the knowledge of Him over all things created by Him, and through longing, he constantly perseveres in this knowledge.

<margin>5.</margin> If all things exist through God and for God, and God is better than the things created by Him, then the person who abandons God and occupies himself with inferior things shows that he prefers the things created by God over God Himself.

<margin>6.</margin> The one who keeps his mind fixed on the love of God despises all visible things and even his own body as if it were something belonging to another.

<margin>7.</margin> If the soul is better than the body, and God is incomparably better than the world He created, then the one who prefers the body over the soul, and the world over God the Creator, is no different from those who worship idols.

<margin>8.</margin> The one who has separated his mind from love for God and from waiting upon Him, and has it bound to some 

<column-break/>

sensible thing <note>A thing perceived by the physical senses rather than the intellect.</note>, is the one who prefers the body over the soul and the things created over God the Creator.

<margin>9.</margin> If the life of the mind is the illumination of knowledge, and it is love for God that gives birth to this illumination, then it is rightly said that nothing is greater than divine love.

<margin>10.</margin> When the mind travels abroad in the longing of love for God, then it no longer senses any existing thing at all. For being illuminated by the divine and infinite light, it becomes insensible to all things created by Him, just as the eye no longer sees the stars when the sun rises.

<margin>11.</margin> All the virtues cooperate with the mind toward divine longing, but more than all of them, pure prayer does so. For through this, the mind takes wing toward God and moves outside of all existing things.

<margin>12.</margin> When, through love, the mind is snatched away by divine knowledge and, going outside of created things, perceives the divine infinity, then—according to the divine **Isaiah** <note>Refers to Isaiah 6:5.</note>—coming into a state of wonder and a realization of its own lowliness, it says with deep feeling the words of the prophet:

> Woe is me, for I am pierced to the heart; for being a man, and having unclean lips, I dwell in the midst of a people with unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth.

<margin>13.</margin> The one who loves God cannot help but also love every human being as himself, even though he is displeased by the passions of those who are not yet purified. Therefore, when he sees their correction, he rejoices with a joy that is immeasurable and beyond words.

<margin>14.</margin> A soul is "unclean" when it is filled with intrusive thoughts, lust, and hatred.

<margin>15.</margin> The one who sees even a trace of hatred in his own heart for any fault whatsoever toward any person at all is entirely a stranger to the love of God. For love ...

<summary>This page introduces the definition of divine love as the highest disposition of the soul, outlining a chain of virtues—from faith and fear to dispassion—that leads to it. Maximus emphasizes that true love for God requires detaching the mind from created things to focus entirely on the Creator.</summary>
<keywords>love (agape), dispassion (apatheia), knowledge (gnosis), self-control, fear of God, prayer, Isaiah, purification, mind (nous)</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "First Century on Love" by Maximus the Confessor, starting from the conclusion of the 15th aphorism. It contains a series of short spiritual instructions (numbered 16 through 39) focusing on the relationship between love for God and love for one's neighbor, and the nature of "dispassion."</meta>

->FIRST CENTURY<-

...love for God does not tolerate hatred toward man at all.

<margin>16.</margin> "The one who loves me," says the Lord, "will keep my commandments; and this is my commandment: that you love one another." Therefore, the one who does not love his neighbor does not keep the commandment; and the one who does not keep the commandment is unable to love even the Lord.

<margin>17.</margin> Blessed is the person who is able to love every person equally.

<margin>18.</margin> Blessed is the person who is not attached to any corruptible or temporary thing.

<margin>19.</margin> Blessed is the **mind** <note>original: νοῦς (nous); in this tradition, the "nous" is the "eye of the soul" or the highest faculty of the human person, capable of direct experience of God.</note> that has passed beyond all created things and unceasingly delights in divine beauty.

<margin>20.</margin> The one who makes provision for the flesh to satisfy its desires, and who holds a grudge against his neighbor for the sake of temporary things—such a person serves the creation rather than the Creator.

<margin>21.</margin> The one who keeps the body free from pleasure and disease holds it as a fellow-servant for the service of higher things.

<margin>22.</margin> The one who flees all worldly desires sets himself above all worldly matter.

<margin>23.</margin> The one who loves God certainly also loves his neighbor. Such a person cannot hoard money, but manages it in a godly way, providing for each of those in need.

<margin>24.</margin> The one who practices almsgiving in imitation of God knows no difference between the evil and the good, the just and the unjust, regarding the necessities of the body. Instead, he distributes to all equally according to their need, even if he prefers the virtuous person over the wicked because of their good will.

<margin>25.</margin> Just as God, being good and **dispassionate** <note>original: ἀπαθής (apathes); meaning free from the "passions" or disordered impulses like anger and greed.</note> by nature, loves all equally as His own works—yet He honors the virtuous one as someone who has made God's knowledge his own, while in His goodness He has mercy on the wicked and corrects him through discipline in this age—so too the person who is good and dispassionate in their will loves all people equally. He loves the virtuous person because of both their shared nature and the person's good will; but he loves the wicked person because of their shared nature, showing mercy as one would for a fool who is walking in darkness.

<margin>26.</margin> The disposition of love is recognized not only through the giving of money, but much more through the sharing of the word and bodily service.

<margin>27.</margin> The one who has sin-

<column-break/>

-cerely renounced the things of the world and serves his neighbor without hypocrisy through love is quickly freed from every passion, and becomes a partaker of divine love and knowledge.

<margin>28.</margin> The one who has acquired divine love within himself does not grow weary of "following after the Lord his God," as the divine Jeremiah says <note>original: Ἱερεμίαν; a reference to Jeremiah 17:16.</note>. Rather, he bears every labor, reproach, and insult nobly, thinking no evil at all toward anyone.

<margin>29.</margin> When you are insulted by someone or belittled in some way, then watch out for thoughts of anger; do not let them separate you from love through the pain they cause, nor establish you in the region of hatred.

<margin>30.</margin> When you suffer because of an insult or dishonor, know that you have been greatly benefited, for **vainglory** <note>original: κενοδοξία (kenodoxia); the vice of seeking empty praise or worldly reputation.</note> has been driven out of you through that dishonor.

<margin>31.</margin> Just as the memory of fire does not warm the body, so faith without love does not bring the illumination of knowledge into the soul.

<margin>32.</margin> Just as the light of the sun attracts a healthy eye to itself, so the knowledge of God naturally draws a pure mind to itself through love.

<margin>33.</margin> A pure mind is one that has been separated from ignorance and is illuminated by divine light.

<margin>34.</margin> A pure soul is one that has been freed from the passions and is unceasingly gladdened by divine love.

<margin>35.</margin> A **passion** <note>original: Πάθος (pathos); here defined technically.</note> is a blameworthy movement of the soul that is contrary to nature.

<margin>36.</margin> **Dispassion** is a peaceful state of the soul in which the soul becomes difficult to move toward wickedness.

<margin>37.</margin> The one who has diligently acquired the fruits of love does not turn away from it, even if he suffers ten thousand evils. Let Stephen, the disciple of Christ, and those like him, persuade you; he even prayed for those who were killing him and asked for God's forgiveness for them because they did not know what they were doing.

<margin>38.</margin> If it is the nature of love to be long-suffering and kind, then the one who fights with anger or acts wickedly is clearly a stranger to love. And the one who is a stranger to love is a stranger to God, since "God is love."

<margin>39.</margin> "Do not say," says the divine Jeremiah, "that you are the temple of the Lord." And you should not say that...

<summary>This page defines the inseparable link between loving God and loving one's neighbor, emphasizing that true love treats all people equally regardless of their merit. It also provides technical definitions for "passion," "dispassion," and the "pure mind" in the context of Christian asceticism.</summary>
<keywords>love, commandments, mind (nous), dispassion (apatheia), almsgiving, Jeremiah, Stephen the Protomartyr, passions, vainglory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "First Century on Love" by Maximus the Confessor. The previous page ended with aphorism 24; this page picks up at aphorism 40. The numbering follows the traditional division of Maximus's centuries (chapters of 100 sayings each).</meta>

# ->OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS<-

<margin>40.</margin>
"Mere faith" <note>original: ψιλὴ πίστις (psili pistis); "bare" or "naked" faith refers to an intellectual belief that is not yet lived out or animated by love.</note> in our Lord Jesus Christ can save me. This is impossible, unless you also acquire love for Him through your works. For as for "merely" believing, even the demons believe—and they tremble.

<margin>41.</margin>
The "work of love" consists in doing good to one’s neighbor from a sincere heart, as well as in long-suffering, patience, and using things according to right reason.

<margin>42.</margin>
The one who loves God neither causes grief nor is grieved by anyone over temporary things. Such a person experiences and causes only one kind of grief: the "salutary" or "saving" grief <note>original: σωτήριον (soterion); a sorrow that leads to repentance and spiritual growth.</note> which the blessed Paul both felt and caused for the Corinthians.

<margin>43.</margin>
The one who loves God lives an **angelic life** on earth, fasting and keeping vigil, singing psalms and praying, and always thinking well of every human being.

<margin>44.</margin>
If anyone desires something, they struggle to obtain it. Of all things good and desirable, the Divine is incomparably better and more desirable. How much zeal, then, ought we to show so that we may obtain that which is by nature good and desirable?

<margin>45.</margin>
Do not defile your flesh with shameful deeds, and do not stain your soul with evil thoughts; then the peace of God will come upon you, bringing love with it.

<margin>46.</margin>
Discipline your flesh with fasting and vigils, and occupy yourself tirelessly with psalmody and prayer; then the sanctification of **self-control** <note>original: σωφροσύνης (sophrosynes); often translated as temperance or "soundness of mind," it implies a balanced mastery over one's impulses.</note> will come upon you, bringing love with it.

<margin>47.</margin>
The one who has been deemed worthy of divine knowledge, and has acquired its illumination through love, will never be tossed about by the spirit of **Vainglory**. But the one not yet deemed worthy is easily carried away by it. If such a person looks toward God in everything they do, acting solely for His sake, they will easily escape it with God's help.

<margin>48.</margin>
The one who has not yet obtained divine knowledge—which is made active through love—is proud of what they have achieved for God. But the one deemed worthy of this knowledge says, with deep sincerity, the words of the Patriarch Abraham when he was granted a divine appearance: "I am but earth and ashes."

The one who fears the Lord always has **humility** as a companion, and through its 

<column-break/>

reflections, comes to divine love and thanksgiving. For such a person remembers their former way of life in the world, their various failings, and the temptations that have befallen them since youth—and how the Lord rescued them from all those things, transferring them from a life of passion to a life according to God. Thus, along with fear, they also receive love, always giving thanks with great humility to the Benefactor and Pilot of our life.

<margin>49.</margin>
Do not soil your mind by entertaining thoughts of desire and anger, lest you fall away from pure prayer and stumble into the spirit of **listlessness**. <note>original: ἀκηδίας (akedias); also known as acedia, this is a state of spiritual apathy, boredom, or "the noonday demon" that makes spiritual tasks feel burdensome.</note>

<margin>50.</margin>
The mind falls away from its "boldness" before God whenever it consorts with evil or foul thoughts.

<margin>51.</margin>
The foolish person is led by the passions. When moved by anger, they are troubled and hasten to flee from their brothers without reason. When warmed by desire, they change their mind again and run back to meet them. The wise person does the opposite in both cases: in the face of anger, they cut off the causes of the trouble and free themselves from grief toward their brothers; in the face of desire, they restrain their irrational impulses and social interactions.

<margin>52.</margin>
In a time of trials, do not abandon your monastery. Instead, endure the waves of your thoughts bravely, especially those of grief and listlessness. For if you are tested through these afflictions by divine providence, you will have a firm hope in God. But if you abandon your post, you will be found unproven, cowardly, and unstable.

<margin>53.</margin>
If you wish not to fall away from the love of God, do not let your brother go to sleep while grieving against you, nor go to sleep yourself while grieving against him. Be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer to Christ the "gift of love" with a clear conscience through earnest prayer.

<margin>54.</margin>
If the one who has all the gifts of the Spirit but lacks love gains nothing—according to the divine Apostle—how much zeal ought we to show in order to acquire it?

<margin>55.</margin>
If love does no evil to one's neighbor, then the one who envies his brother, and is grieved...

<meta>This page continues St. Maximus the Confessor's "First Century on Love." While the previous page ended at aphorism 46, this page begins with the conclusion of aphorism 55 and continues through aphorism 69. Maximus is exploring how external behaviors—like slander and grudges—reveal the internal state of the soul.</meta>

### ->FIRST HUNDRED<-

[...grieving] <note>This sentence fragment concludes aphorism 55, discussing the person who lacks love.</note> at his success, and staining his reputation with mockery, or plotting against him with some malice—how does such a person not make himself a stranger to love, and liable to eternal Judgment?

<margin>56.</margin>
If love is the fulfillment of the law, then the one who bears a grudge against his brother, devises snares against him, prays against him, or rejoices at his fall—how is he not a lawbreaker and worthy of eternal punishment?

<margin>57.</margin>
If the one who speaks against a brother and judges a brother speaks against the law and judges the law, and the "law of Christ" is love, how does the slanderer not fall away from the love of Christ and become the cause of his own eternal punishment?

<margin>58.</margin>
Do not lend your ear to the tongue of the slanderer, nor your tongue to the ear of the person who loves fault-finding, by speaking or hearing with pleasure against your neighbor; do not do this lest you fall away from divine love and be found a stranger to eternal life.

<margin>59.</margin>
Do not accept insults against your father, nor encourage the one who dishonors him, lest the Lord be angry at your deeds and destroy you from the land of the living.

<margin>60.</margin>
Silence the slanderer who speaks into your ears, so that you do not commit a double sin with him: habituating yourself to a destructive passion <note>original: πάθει (pathei); in this context, an uncontrolled or harmful impulse of the soul.</note>, and failing to stop him from babbling against his neighbor.

<margin>61.</margin>
"But I say to you" (says the Lord) "love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, pray for those who ill-treat you." <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 5:44.</note> Why did He command these things? So that He might free you from hatred, grief, anger, and grudge-bearing, and make you worthy of the greatest possession: perfect love. It is impossible to have this love if one does not love all people equally in imitation of God, who loves all people equally and "wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth."

<margin>62.</margin>
"But I say to you, do not resist the evil person; but whoever slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And to him who wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also. And whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two." Why? So that He might keep you free from anger, untroubled, and without grief, and that He might instruct the other through your forbearance <note>original: ἀνεξικακίας (anexikakias); the quality of enduring evil without bitterness.</note>,

<column-break/>

and lead both, as a good Father, under the yoke of love.

<margin>63.</margin>
Toward whatever things we have once been affected by, we also carry around their mental impressions <note>original: φαντασίας (phantasias); mental images or memories stored in the mind.</note> in a passionate way. Therefore, the one who overcomes passionate impressions surely despises the actual things of which they are memories. For the war against memories is as much harder than the war against physical things as sinning in one's thoughts is easier than sinning in action.

<margin>64.</margin>
Of the passions, some are physical and some are psychological. The physical ones find their starting points in the body; the psychological ones arise from external things. Both, however, are cut short by love and self-control <note>original: ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia); ascetic discipline or temperance.</note>: love cuts off the psychological passions, and self-control the physical ones.

<margin>65.</margin>
Some passions belong to the incensive <note>original: θυμικοῦ (thymikou); the "spirited" part of the soul, associated with anger and drive.</note> part of the soul, and others to the appetitive <note>original: ἐπιθυμητικοῦ (epithymetikou); the part of the soul associated with desires and cravings.</note> part. Both are moved through the senses, and they are stirred up when the soul is found lacking in love and self-control.

<margin>66.</margin>
The passions of the incensive part of the soul are harder to combat than those of the appetitive part. Therefore, the commandment of love was given by the Lord as a greater remedy against that part.

<margin>67.</margin>
All other passions touch either only the incensive part of the soul, or the appetitive, or even the rational part—such as forgetfulness and ignorance. But listlessness <note>original: ἀκηδία (akedia); a state of spiritual apathy, boredom, or "weariness of heart."</note>, by grasping all the powers of the soul, sets almost all the passions in motion together. Therefore, it is the heaviest of all the passions. Thus, the Lord has beautifully given the remedy against it, saying: "In your patience <note>original: ὑπομονῇ (hypomone); endurance or steadfastness.</note> possess your souls."

<margin>68.</margin>
Never strike any of the brothers, especially without cause, lest he depart unable to bear the affliction; for then you will never escape the reproach of conscience, which will always cause you grief during the time of prayer and drive the mind away from divine confidence <note>original: παρρησίας (parresias); boldness or intimacy in speaking with God.</note>.

<margin>69.</margin>
Do not tolerate suspicions or people who bring you scandals <note>original: σκάνδαλα (skandala); literally "stumbling blocks" or causes for offense.</note> against others. For those who accept scandals in any way—whether from things that happen by choice or against one's will—do not know the "way of peace," which leads those who love it through love to the knowledge of God.

<summary>This page continues Maximus the Confessor’s teachings on love, focusing on the psychological and spiritual dangers of slander, grudges, and listlessness (akedia). He emphasizes that perfect love requires treating all people equally and overcoming passionate memories to achieve the knowledge of God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "First Century on Love" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The previous page (ending at aphorism 61) discussed the dangers of slandering others and how such behavior isolates a person from divine love. This page moves from identifying obstacles to love toward defining the nature of "perfect love"—an impartial, Christ-like affection for all people regardless of their character—and the spiritual disciplines required to attain it.</meta>

# OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

<margin>70.</margin> He does not yet possess perfect love who is still influenced by the changing moods of men—for instance, loving one person while hating another, or even loving and then hating the same person for the very same reasons.

<margin>71.</margin> Perfect love does not divide the single nature of all humanity based on their various dispositions; rather, always looking toward that common nature, it loves all people equally. It loves the virtuous as friends, and it loves the wicked as enemies <note>The sense here is loving those who act as enemies</note> by doing good to them, showing long-suffering, and enduring what they inflict. It does not take account of evil at all, but even suffers on their behalf if the occasion calls for it, in order to make them friends as well, if possible. But even if this is not possible, such love does not fall away from its own state, always demonstrating the fruits of love equally to all people. For this reason, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, demonstrating His own love for us, suffered for the sake of all humanity and granted the hope of resurrection equally to all—even if each person makes themselves worthy either of glory or of punishment.

<margin>72.</margin> He who does not despise glory and dishonor, wealth and poverty, pleasure and pain, has not yet acquired perfect love. For perfect love despises not only these things, but even this temporary life itself and death.

<margin>73.</margin> Listen to what those who were deemed worthy of perfect love have to say:
> Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written: “For Your sake we are killed all day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.” Yet in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. <note>original: Romans 8:35-39</note>

<margin>74.</margin> Regarding love for one's neighbor, listen again to what they say:
> I tell the truth in Christ, I am not lying, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual grief in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my countrymen according to the flesh, who are Israelites... <note>original: Romans 9:1-4</note> and so on.

In the same way, Moses and the rest of the saints spoke.

<column-break/>

<margin>75.</margin> He who does not despise glory and pleasure, and the love of money <term>philargyria; literally 'love of silver'</term> which increases them and is sustained by them, cannot cut away the excuses for anger. And he who does not cut these away cannot attain perfect love.

<margin>76.</margin> Humility and the endurance of hardship free a person from every sin—the former by cutting off the passions of the soul, and the latter the passions of the body. The blessed David did this, as seen in his prayer to God:
> Look upon my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins. <note>original: Psalm 24:18 (Septuagint numbering); Psalm 25:18 in modern Bibles.</note>

<margin>77.</margin> Through the commandments, the Lord makes those who practice them <term>apatheis; often translated as 'dispassionate,' meaning free from the control of harmful impulses</term>. Through the divine doctrines, He grants them the illumination of knowledge.

<margin>78.</margin> All doctrines concern either God, or things visible and invisible, or the providence and judgment regarding them.

<margin>79.</margin> Almsgiving <note>original: ἐλεημοσύνη (eleemosyne); acts of mercy or charity</note> heals the irascible <note>original: θυμικὸν (thymikon); the part of the soul associated with anger and righteous indignation</note> part of the soul; fasting withers away desire; and prayer purifies the mind and prepares it for the contemplation of created things. For the Lord granted us the commandments in accordance with the powers of the soul.

<margin>80.</margin> “Learn from Me,” He says, “for I am meek and humble in heart,” <note>original: Matthew 11:29</note> and so on. Meekness keeps the temper undisturbed, while humility frees the mind from pride and vainglory.

<margin>81.</margin> The fear of God is twofold. One kind is generated in us from the threat of punishment; from this arises self-control, hope in God, and dispassion, from which love eventually follows in due order. The other kind is joined to love itself, always producing reverence in the soul, so that it does not come to despise God because of the boldness of love.

<margin>82.</margin> Perfect love casts the first kind of fear out of the soul that possesses it, for such a soul no longer fears punishment. But it always possesses the second kind of fear joined to itself, as was said. To the first fear, the following applies:
> By the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil; <note>original: Proverbs 16:6</note> and, The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. <note>original: Psalm 111:10</note>

<summary>This page defines perfect love as an impartial state that treats all people with kindness regardless of their character, modeled on Christ's sacrifice. Maximus explains that such love is achieved by mastering the soul's impulses through humility, almsgiving, and a specific "reverent" fear of God.</summary>
<keywords>perfect love, impartiality, dispassion, apatheia, humility, almsgiving, fasting, fear of God, St. Paul, King David, irascible soul</keywords>

# THE FIRST CENTURY

...and to the second, this: "There is no want to those who fear Him." <note>A reference to Psalm 34:9</note>

<margin>83.</margin> "Put to death therefore your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness," and so forth. <note>A quotation from Colossians 3:5</note> By "earth," he refers to the "mind of the flesh" <note>original: "φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός" — the orientation of the mind toward material self-gratification</note>. By "fornication," he means the sin committed in actual deed. By "uncleanness," he names the internal consent to sin. By "passion," he refers to the "impassioned thought" <note>original: "ἐμπαθῆ λογισμὸν"</note>. By "evil desire," he means the simple acceptance of a thought or a longing. And by "covetousness," he names the "matter" that generates and increases the passion. The divine Apostle commanded us to put all these to death, as they are the "members" of the carnal mind.

<margin>84.</margin> First, memory brings a simple thought to the mind. When this thought lingers, passion is stirred. If the passion is not removed, it bends the mind toward "consent." Once consent occurs, it finally leads to the sin committed in action. Therefore, the all-wise Apostle, writing to those from the nations <note>the Gentiles</note>, commands them to first remove the end-result of sin, and then, moving backward in order, to arrive at the cause. The cause is covetousness—which, as previously stated, generates and increases passion. I believe that here he means "gluttony" <note>original: "γαστριμαργίαν"</note>, for it is the mother and nourisher of fornication. For covetousness is an evil not only regarding money, but also regarding food; just as self-control is necessary not only regarding food, but also regarding money.

<margin>85.</margin> Just as a small bird with its foot tied begins to fly but is pulled back down to the earth by the string, so too the mind that has not yet acquired "dispassion" <note><term>dispassion</term>: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but a state where one is no longer enslaved by reactive or harmful passions</note> may fly toward the knowledge of heavenly things, but it is pulled back down to earth, dragged by the passions.

<margin>86.</margin> When the mind is perfectly liberated from the passions, then it journeys without turning back toward the "contemplation of beings" <note><term>contemplation</term>: "theoria" — the spiritual perception of the inner meaning of created things</note>, making its way toward the knowledge of the Holy Trinity.

<margin>87.</margin> When the mind is pure, it takes up the "concepts" of things and is moved through them toward spiritual contemplation. But when it has become impure through "negligence" <note>original: "ῥᾳθυμίας"</note>, it imagines the concepts of other things as simple ideas, but when it receives those involving human affairs, it is turned toward

<column-break/>

shameful or evil thoughts.

<margin>88.</margin> When, during the time of prayer, no worldly thoughts disturb the mind, then know that you are not outside the borders of dispassion.

<margin>89.</margin> When the soul begins to perceive its own health, it also begins to see the images in its dreams as simple and undisturbed.

<margin>90.</margin> Just as the beauty of visible things attracts the physical eye, so too does the knowledge of invisible things draw the pure mind to itself. By "invisible," I mean "incorporeal" things <note>realities without physical bodies, such as angels or the soul</note>.

<margin>91.</margin> It is a great thing not to be affected by physical objects, but it is a much greater thing to remain "dispassionate" toward the mental images of them. For the war the demons wage against us through "thoughts" <note><term>thoughts</term>: "logismos" — refers to intrusive, suggestive, or tempting thoughts</note> is more severe than the war waged through physical things.

<margin>92.</margin> One who has achieved the virtues and is enriched with knowledge, seeing things as they naturally are, does and speaks everything according to "right reason" <note>original: "ὀρθὸν λόγον"</note>, without being turned aside at all. For it is through the "unreasonable" use of things that we become either virtuous or wicked.

<margin>93.</margin> A sign of perfect dispassion is when only "bare thoughts" <note>concepts stripped of emotional or sinful charge</note> of things always rise up in the heart, both when the body is awake and during sleep.

<margin>94.</margin> Through the practice of the commandments, the mind strips off the passions. Through the spiritual contemplation of visible things, it strips off the "impassioned" thoughts of things. Through the knowledge of invisible things, it strips off the contemplation of visible things. And this, in turn, it strips off through the knowledge of the Holy Trinity.

<margin>95.</margin> Just as the sun, when it rises and lights up the world, reveals both itself and the things it illuminates, so too the "Sun of Righteousness" <note>A title for Christ</note> rising in the pure mind reveals both Himself and the "inner principles" <note><term>inner principles</term>: "logoi" — the divine purposes or "blueprints" behind everything God has made</note> of all things that have been and shall be brought into being by Him.

<margin>96.</margin> We do not know God from His essence, but from His magnificent works and His providence for all beings. Through these, as through mirrors, we perceive His infinite goodness, wisdom, and power.

<margin>97.</margin> The pure mind is either occupied with bare thoughts... <note>The text continues on the next page</note>

# BY THE SAME AUTHOR
## THE SECOND CENTURY

<margin>1.</margin> He who loves God genuinely also prays entirely without distraction; and he who prays entirely without distraction also loves God genuinely. But one whose mind is nailed to any earthly thing cannot pray without distraction.

<margin>2.</margin> A mind that lingers upon a sensory object certainly has a passion for it—such as desire, or grief, or anger, or resentment. Unless it comes to despise that object, it cannot be freed from that passion.

<margin>3.</margin> <margin>down</margin> When the passions control the mind, they bind it to material objects; and having separated it from God, they make it occupy itself with those things. But when the love of God takes control, it looses the mind from its bonds, persuading it to disregard not only sensory objects but even our own temporary life.

<margin>4.</margin> The work of the commandments is to make the thoughts of things "bare" <note>meaning thoughts stripped of emotional attachment or "passion"</note>; the work of reading and contemplation is to make the mind immaterial and formless. From this, it follows that one can pray without distraction.

<margin>5.</margin> The "practical method" <note>the active struggle for virtue and self-control</note> is not enough to perfectly free the mind from passions so that it can pray without distraction, unless various

<column-break/>

burning with desire, yet it finds no consolation from the things "according to Him" (for this is impossible and unattainable for every created nature equally). Instead, it finds consolation from the things "around Him." I mean the things concerning His eternity, His infinity and boundlessness, His goodness, wisdom, and power, and His creative, providential, and judicial care of all beings. This alone is entirely comprehensible about Him: His infinity, and the very fact of knowing nothing <note>This refers to "apophatic theology," the idea that God’s essence is so far beyond us that we know Him best by realizing He is beyond all human concepts</note>; just as the great theologians have said—Gregory and Dionysius. <note>Referring to St. Gregory of Nazianzus and Dionysius the Areopagite</note>

spiritual contemplations succeed it. For the former only frees the mind from a lack of self-control and from hatred, but the latter also rid it of forgetfulness and ignorance. Only then will it be able to pray as it ought.

<margin>6.</margin> There are two highest states of pure prayer: one belongs to those in the "practical" life, and the other to those in the "contemplative" life. The first is born in the soul from the fear of God and a good hope; the second from divine love and the highest state of purification. The marks of the first measure are when one gathers the mind away from all worldly thoughts and makes prayers without distraction or disturbance, as if God Himself were standing present (as indeed He is). The mark of the second is when, in the very surge of prayer, the mind is snatched up by the divine and infinite light and loses all sensation of itself or of any other being, except for Him alone who, through love, works such an illumination within. Then, even when moving among the principles concerning God, the mind receives clear and distinct impressions of Him.

<margin>7.</margin> Whatever a person loves, they surely cling to; and they despise all things that hinder them from it, so that they may not be deprived of it. So too, the one who loves God cares for pure prayer, and every passion which

It distinguishes between the "practical" struggle against passions and the "contemplative" heights of divine illumination.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor's chapters on love. The previous page ended with aphorism 7, discussing how the mind frees itself from earthly attachments. This page picks up at the end of that thought and moves into the psychological roots of the "passions"—a technical term for disordered or unhealthy attachments—and the nature of true love.</meta>

...whatever is hindering it, he casts out from himself.

<margin>8</margin> He who has cast out self-love—the mother of the <term>passions</term> <note>original: "παθῶν" (pathe) — in this context, passions are not just strong emotions, but disordered attachments or spiritual sicknesses that cloud judgment.</note>—will also easily, with God’s help, lay aside the rest, such as anger, grief, resentment, and so on. But he who is mastered by the first [self-love] is wounded by the others, even if he does not wish it. Self-love is defined as a passionate attachment to the body.

<margin>9</margin> For these five reasons, people love one another, whether in a praiseworthy or a blameworthy way:
1. For the sake of God—as the virtuous man loves everyone, and as one who is not yet virtuous loves the virtuous man.
2. By nature—as parents love their children and vice versa.
3. Out of vainglory—as one who is honored loves the person who honors him.
4. Out of greed—as one loves a rich man for the sake of financial gain.
5. Out of self-indulgence—as one who pampers the belly and what lies beneath it.
The first is praiseworthy; the second is neutral; the others are <term>passionate</term> <note>meaning driven by disordered desire rather than reason.</note>.

<margin>10</margin> If you hate some people, and others you neither love nor hate, while others you love but only moderately, and yet others you love intensely—from this inequality, know that you are far from perfect love, which assumes that one loves every person equally.

<margin>11</margin> "Turn away from evil and do good" <note>A reference to Psalm 34:14.</note>. That is, fight your enemies to diminish the passions, then be watchful so they do not increase. And again, fight to acquire the virtues, and afterward be watchful to preserve them. This is what is meant by the biblical command "to work and to keep" <note>A reference to Genesis 2:15, where Adam is told to work and keep the Garden of Eden.</note>.

<margin>12</margin> Those who tempt us by God's permission <note>Theologians often distinguish between God's "will" and His "permission" (concession) for trials to occur.</note> either inflame the desiring part of the soul, or disturb the spirited part, or darken the reasoning part, or afflict the body with pains, or snatch away physical possessions.

<margin>13</margin> Either the demons tempt us by themselves, or they arm those who do not fear the Lord against us. They act by themselves when we are apart from other people, as they tempted the Lord in the desert. They act through other people when we associate with others, as they tempted the Lord through the Pharisees. But let us, looking to our Example [Christ], repel them from both sides.

<margin>14</margin> When the mind begins to progress in the love of God, then the demon of blasphemy also begins to tempt hi- <column-break/> m, and suggests such thoughts to him as no man—but only the devil, the craftsman of these things—ever invents. He does this because he envies the lover of God, so that the person, falling into despair for having thought such things, might no longer dare to fly up to God through habitual prayer. But the destroyer gains nothing from this toward his own purpose; rather, he makes us more steadfast. For being fought and fighting back, we are found to be more tested and more genuine in the love of God. "May his sword enter into his own heart, and may his bows be broken" <note>Quoting Psalm 37:15.</note>.

<margin>15</margin> The mind, when applying itself to visible things, naturally perceives things through the medium of the senses. Neither the mind is evil, nor is natural perception, nor the objects themselves, nor the senses. For these are the works of God. What, then, is evil? Clearly, it is the <term>passion</term> [disordered attachment] that accompanies the natural thought, which can be avoided in the use of thoughts if the mind is watchful.

<margin>16</margin> Passion is a movement of the soul contrary to nature, directed either toward irrational affection or toward uncritical hatred, either for something sensory or because of something sensory. For example: irrational affection for foods, or for a woman, or for money, or for passing glory, or some other sensory thing. Hatred is similarly uncritical when directed at any of the aforementioned things, or at someone because of them.

<margin>17</margin> Or again, vice is the mistaken judgment of thoughts, followed by the misuse of things. For example, regarding a woman: the right judgment of sexual intercourse is that its purpose is procreation. Therefore, he who looks only toward pleasure has erred in judgment, considering what is not good to be good. Such a person misuses a woman in intercourse. It is the same for all other things and thoughts.

<margin>18</margin> When the demons, having driven your mind out of <term>self-control</term> <note>original: "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne) — a term for temperance or wholeness of mind.</note>, surround you with thoughts of fornication, then with tears say to the Master: "Having cast me out now, they have surrounded me; O my joy, deliver me from those who surround me," and you shall be saved.

<margin>19</margin> The demon of fornication is heavy, and he attacks fiercely those who struggle against the passion, and especially during the neglect of...
