<meta>This page continues the "Second Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor’s *Four Hundred Chapters on Love*. The previous page (specifically aphorism 19) was discussing the ways the mind is distracted by external stimuli. This page begins mid-sentence, concluding the thought on how even casual interactions can later disturb the soul's peace.</meta>

->### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS<-

...diet, and in associations with women. For [the mind] is secretly robbed by the smoothness of pleasure; later, it attacks the person while they are at rest through memory, setting the body on fire and presenting various images to the mind. Therefore, the mind is even accused of consenting to the sin. If you do not wish these things to linger in you, take up fasting, labor, vigils, and <term>blessed stillness</term> <note>original: "καλὴν ἡσυχίαν" (kalēn hēsychian) — 'Hesychia' refers to an inner stillness and silence essential for deep prayer.</note> along with intense prayer.

<margin>20.</margin> Those who are always seeking after our soul seek it through <term>passionate thoughts</term> <note>original: "ἐμπαθῶν λογισμῶν" (empathōn logismōn) — in this tradition, 'logismoi' are not just neutral thoughts, but intrusive, tempting suggestions that lead toward disordered desires.</note>, so that they may cast it into sin either in the mind or in actual practice. Therefore, when they find that the mind does not accept them, they will be shamed and disgraced; but when they find the mind occupied with spiritual <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "θεωρίᾳ" (theoria) — the spiritual "vision" or deep insight into divine truths.</note>, they will be turned back and greatly shamed in an instant.

<margin>21.</margin> He who prepares the mind for the sacred struggles and drives out passionate thoughts from it holds the rank of a **Deacon**. He who enlightens the mind with the knowledge of created things and destroys "knowledge falsely so-called" holds the rank of a **Priest**. And he who perfects the mind with the <term>holy chrism</term> <note>original: "ἁγίῳ μύρῳ" — a reference to the oil used in the sacrament of Chrismation (Confirmation), symbolizing the sealing of the Holy Spirit.</note> of knowledge and the worship of the Holy Trinity holds the rank of a **Bishop**.

<margin>22.</margin> The demons grow weak when the passions within us are diminished through the keeping of the commandments. They perish entirely when, through **dispassion**, the passions disappear and they no longer find the means by which they entered the soul to wage war against it. This is the meaning of the scripture: "They shall weaken and perish from your presence." <note>A reference to Psalm 9:3.</note>

<margin>23.</margin> Some people abstain from the passions out of human fear. Others do so out of vainglory. Still others do so out of self-control. But there are others who are freed from the passions by the divine judgments of God.

<margin>24.</margin> All the words of the Lord contain these four things: commandments, dogmas, threats, and promises. It is for the sake of these that we endure every hardship—such as fasting, vigils, sleeping on the ground, labors and toils in service, insults, dishonor, tortures, death, and the like. For as the scripture says: "Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways." <note>A reference to Psalm 17:4 (Septuagint 16:4).</note>

<margin>25.</margin> The reward of self-control is **dispassion**; the reward of faith is **knowledge**. Dispassion gives birth to discernment, and knowledge gives birth to the love for God.

<column-break/>

<margin>26.</margin> When the mind succeeds in <term>practice</term> <note>original: "Πρακτικὴν" (praktikēn) — the active struggle to acquire virtue and overcome vices.</note>, it advances in prudence; when it succeeds in contemplation, it advances in knowledge. For the former leads the combatant to the discernment of virtue and vice, while the latter leads the participant to the inner principles of both incorporeal and corporeal things. Then, one is deemed worthy of the grace of **theology** when—having soared above all these things on the wings of love and being found in contemplation—one examines the truth concerning God through the Spirit, as far as it is possible for the human mind.

<margin>27.</margin> When you are about to speak of God, do not seek the principles of His essence, for the human mind will not find them—nor will the mind of any other being after God. Rather, examine as far as possible the things *around* Him: such as His eternity, infinity, and limitlessness; His goodness, wisdom, and power; and His creative, providential, and judicial care for all beings. For among men, he is a great theologian who discovers the principles of these things even to a small degree.

<margin>28.</margin> A powerful man is one who has joined **practice** with **knowledge**. For through practice, he withers his desire and tames his anger; and through knowledge, he gives wings to his mind and departs to dwell with God.

<margin>29.</margin> When the Lord says, "I and the Father are one," He signifies the identity of their **essence** <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousias).</note>. But when He says again, "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me," He shows the inseparability of their **persons** <note>original: "ὑποστάσεων" (hypostaseōn) — the technical term for the three distinct Persons of the Trinity.</note>. Those "tritheists" <note>Those who wrongly believe in three separate Gods.</note> who separate the Son from the Father fall into a precipice on both sides: for if they say the Son is co-eternal with the Father but separate Him from Him, they are forced to say He was not born of the Father, and thus they fall into saying there are three Gods and three beginnings. Or, if they say He was born of the Father but separate Him, they are forced to say He is not co-eternal with the Father, making the Lord of Time subject to time. We must, as the Great <term>Gregory</term> <note>referring to St. Gregory of Nazianzus (the Theologian), a primary authority on Trinitarian dogma.</note> says, both preserve the one God and confess the three Persons, each with its own property. For the Godhead is divided, but undividedly (according to the same author), and is joined together, but distinctly. Thus, both the division and the union are paradoxical. For what would be paradoxical if the Son were united to and separated from the Father just as one human is from another, and nothing more?

<margin>30.</margin> He who is perfect in love, even if he has not reached the height of dispassion, knows the difference...

<summary>This page outlines the psychological and spiritual ascent of the monk, moving from the struggle against intrusive thoughts and passions (practice) to the heights of spiritual vision and Trinitarian theology (contemplation). Maximus emphasizes that while God's essence remains unknowable, His attributes and the mystery of the Trinity can be glimpsed through a life of disciplined love.</summary>

## SECOND HUNDRED CHAPTERS

...of one’s own and another’s, or of a believer and an unbeliever, or of a slave and a free person, or generally of male and female. But having become superior to the tyranny of the passions, and looking toward the single nature of all human beings, he considers everyone equally and is disposed toward all in the same way. For in such a person there is neither Greek nor Jew, nor male and female, nor slave and free person, but Christ is all and in all. <note>The author is paraphrasing Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11 to describe the "perfected" state of a soul that sees the image of God in every human being regardless of social or biological status.</note>

<margin>31.</margin> From the passions underlying the soul, the demons take the opportunity to stir up in us **passionate thoughts** <note>original: "ἐμπαθεῖς λογισμούς" (empathēis logismous) — intrusive, emotionally charged thoughts that pull the mind away from peace.</note>; then, using these to wage war on the mind, they force it to give its consent to sin. Once the mind is defeated, they lead it to sin in the imagination; and once this is complete, they then bring the person captive into the physical act. After this, those who have desolated the soul through these thoughts withdraw, taking the thoughts with them. There remains in the mind only the **idol of sin**, concerning which the Lord says: *“When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, let the reader understand.”* <note>Matthew 24:15.</note> Understand then that the "holy place" and "temple of God" is the human mind, in which the demons—having desolated the soul through passionate thoughts—set up the idol of sin. That these things have already occurred in history, no one who has read the works of Josephus <note>original: "Ἰωσήππεια" (Iosēppeia) — referring to Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century historian who chronicled the Roman destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 70 AD.</note>, I think, can doubt. However, some say these things will also happen in the time of the Antichrist.

<margin>32.</margin> There are three things that move us toward what is good: natural seeds, the holy powers, and a good **deliberate choice** <note>original: "προαίρεσις" (proairesis) — a technical term for the faculty of the will that makes moral decisions.</note>. The "natural seeds" are like when we do for others what we wish they would do for us, or when we see someone in distress or in need and naturally feel mercy. The "holy powers" <note>This refers to angelic or divine assistance.</note> are when, being moved toward a good deed, we find helpful cooperation and are guided to success. "Good deliberate choice" is when, discerning good from evil, we choose the good.

<margin>33.</margin> Conversely, there are three things that move us toward evil: the passions, the demons, and an evil deliberate choice. The "passions" are active when we desire a thing contrary to reason—such as food outside the proper time or beyond our actual need, or a woman outside the purpose of 

<column-break/>

procreation and outside what is lawful. And again, [passions are active] when we are angry or enraged beyond what is fitting, such as against someone who has dishonored or harmed us. The "demons" watch for an opportunity during our negligence and attack us, suddenly stirring up the aforementioned passions and similar ones with great intensity. "Evil deliberate choice" is when, even with knowledge of what is good, we choose the evil instead.

<margin>34.</margin> The rewards for the labors of virtue are **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπάθεια" (apatheia) — in the Orthodox tradition, this is not a lack of feeling, but a state of soul where one is no longer controlled by disordered impulses or "passions."</note> and **spiritual knowledge** <note>original: "γνῶσις" (gnōsis).</note>. For these become the mediators of the Kingdom of Heaven, just as passions and ignorance lead to eternal punishment. Therefore, he who seeks these rewards for the sake of human glory, and not for the sake of the good itself, hears from the Scripture: *“You ask and you do not receive, because you ask wrongly.”* <note>James 4:3.</note>

<margin>35.</margin> There are many things naturally good done by people, but they become "not good" because of the reason they are done. For example: fasting and vigils, prayer and psalm-singing, almsgiving and hospitality are naturally good works; but when they are done for the sake of vainglory, they are no longer good.

<margin>36.</margin> In all things done by us, God looks for the **intent**—whether we do it for His sake or for some other reason.

<margin>37.</margin> When you hear the Scripture saying, *“You will render to each according to his works,”* <note>Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6.</note> understand that God does not reward as "good" those things done without a right intent, even if they seem good. He rewards only those done with a right purpose. For the judgment of God does not look upon the outward actions, but upon the **intent** of those actions.

<margin>38.</margin> The demon of **pride** <note>original: "ὑπερηφανίας" (hyperēphanias).</note> has a double wickedness: either it persuades the monk to attribute his successes to himself and not to God—the Giver of all good things and the helper toward achievement—or, if he is not persuaded by this, it suggests that he should despise those brothers who are still less perfect than himself. This person does not realize that he is being tricked into denying the help of God. For if he despises others for being unable to succeed, he is presenting himself as having succeeded by his own power—which is impossible, since the Lord said: *“Apart from me you can do nothing.”* <note>John 15:5.</note> For when our weakness is moved toward good things, it cannot bring them to completion without the Giver of good things.

<summary>This page discusses the psychology of temptation, emphasizing that God judges the internal intent (proairesis) behind actions rather than just the actions themselves. It also warns against the "demon of pride," which tricks the soul into taking credit for spiritual progress that actually comes from divine grace.</summary>
<keywords>dispassion (apatheia), spiritual knowledge (gnosis), passions, demons, deliberate choice (proairesis), abomination of desolation, pride, monk, Josephus</keywords>

### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

<margin>39.</margin> One who has come to know the weakness of human nature has gained experience of divine power. Such a person, having achieved some things through this power and striving to achieve others, never looks down on any human being. For he knows that just as God helped him and freed him from many difficult **passions** <note>original: "παθῶν" (pathōn) — in this context, "passions" refers to disordered desires or emotional disturbances like anger, greed, or pride that "happen" to the soul.</note>, so too is God able to help everyone when He wills, especially those who are struggling for His sake. Even if, by certain judgments, God does not deliver all people from their passions at once, He nevertheless heals each of those who strive, specifically as a good and philanthropic physician.

<margin>40.</margin> When the passions become inactive, pride often follows, either because the causes of the passions have been cut off or because the demons have craftily withdrawn.

<margin>41.</margin> Almost every sin is committed for the sake of pleasure; and its removal comes through hardship and grief—either voluntary, through repentance, or through a providential circumstance brought about by **Divine Providence** <note>original: "προνοίας" (pronoias) — the traditional Christian concept of God's caring and purposeful guidance of the universe.</note>. For "if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged; but being judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world." <note>A quotation of 1 Corinthians 11:31-32.</note>

<margin>42.</margin> When a temptation <note>original: "πειρασμός" (peirasmos) — can mean a trial, a test, or an enticement to sin.</note> comes upon you unexpectedly, do not blame the person through whom it came, but seek the *reason why* it came, and you will find correction. For whether through that person or through another, you were destined to drink the wormwood <note>Wormwood is a proverbially bitter herb, used here to represent the "bitter medicine" of God's corrective discipline.</note> of God's judgments.

<margin>43.</margin> As one who is prone to evil, do not refuse to suffer hardship, so that by being humbled through it, you may "vomit out" your pride.

<margin>44.</margin> Some temptations bring pleasures to people, some bring griefs, and others bring bodily pains. For according to the underlying cause of the passions in the soul, the Physician of souls applies the medicine through His judgments.

<margin>45.</margin> The onset of temptations is brought upon some for the removal of sins already committed, and upon others for the removal of those currently being practiced. For others, they are brought to cut off sins that are about to be practiced—this is in addition to the trials that occur for the sake of testing, as in the case of Job.

<margin>46.</margin> The person of sound mind, considering the healing nature of divine judgments, bears the misfortunes that happen through them with gratitude, considering no one else the cause of these things except his own sins. But the foolish person, being ignorant of God's most wise providence, when he sins and is disciplined, considers either

<column-break/>

God or other people to be the causes of his own evils.

<margin>47.</margin> There are certain things that stop the movement of the passions and do not allow them to grow; and there are other things that diminish them and lead to their reduction. For example: fasting, physical labor, and vigils <note>original: "ἀγρυπνία" (agrypnia) — the practice of staying awake for prayer during the night.</note> do not allow desire to grow. But withdrawal, contemplation, prayer, and **eros for God** <note>original: "ἔρως εἰς Θεόν" — Maximus uses the word 'eros' (passionate longing) to describe the highest, most intense form of love for the Divine.</note> diminish it and lead to its disappearance. The same applies to anger: for example, long-suffering, the forgetting of grievances, and gentleness stop it and do not allow it to grow; but love, almsgiving, kindness, and philanthropy lead to its reduction.

<margin>48.</margin> He whose **mind** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the "eye of the heart" in Eastern Christian tradition.</note> is continually directed toward God has his desire increased beyond measure into divine eros, and his entire anger is transformed into divine love. For through long participation in the divine illumination, having become entirely light-like, and having bound his passionate part to himself, he has turned it—as was said—into incomprehensible divine eros and unceasing love, moving entirely from earthly things to the divine.

<margin>49.</margin> It is not necessarily the case that one who does not envy, or is not angry, or does not hold a grudge against one who has grieved him, already possesses love for that person. For it is possible, even without yet loving, not to return evil for evil because of the commandment; but it is not at all possible to return good for evil spontaneously without effort. To do good to those who hate us from the heart’s disposition belongs to perfect spiritual love alone.

<margin>50.</margin> One who does not love someone does not necessarily hate them; and again, one who does not hate someone does not necessarily love them. Rather, one can be in a middle state toward another—that is, neither loving nor hating. For the disposition of love is naturally produced only by the five ways mentioned in the ninth chapter of this hundred: some of which are praiseworthy, one is middle, and others are blameworthy.

<margin>51.</margin> When you see your mind occupied with material things with pleasure, and lingering affectionately in the thoughts of them, know that you love these things more than God. For "where your treasure is," says the Lord, "there also your heart will be." <note>Matthew 6:21.</note>

<margin>52.</margin> A mind united to God and lingering with Him through prayer and love becomes wise, good, powerful, philanthropic, merciful, and long-suffer—

<summary>This page contains a series of ascetic aphorisms regarding the nature of the "passions," the purpose of trials (temptations) as divine medicine, and the transformation of the human intellect (nous) through intense longing for God.</summary>

### SECOND CENTURY

->**[Section 52 continued]**<-
...and to put it simply, he carries almost all the divine attributes within himself. But by departing from this state, he becomes either animal-like—having become a lover of pleasure—or beast-like, because he fights against other men for the sake of these things.

<margin>53.</margin> Scripture calls "the world" <note>original: "Κόσμον" (Kosmon) — here meaning the material realm and the attachments to it rather than the physical universe itself.</note> material things; and "worldly" are those who occupy their mind with these things. It is to these people that Scripture speaks more reprovingly: "Do not love the world, nor the things in the world. For the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not from God, but is from the world," and so forth. <note>A reference to 1 John 2:15-16.</note>

<margin>54.</margin> A **monk** is one who has withdrawn his mind from material things and, through self-control, love, the singing of psalms, and prayer, perseveres in his devotion to God.

<margin>55.</margin> A "cattle-breeder" in a spiritual sense is the one who practices the **active life** <note>original: "ὁ πρακτικός" (ho praktikos) — the first stage of the spiritual life, focused on the struggle for virtue and the purging of the passions.</note>. For moral achievements take the place of cattle. Therefore, Jacob said, "Your servants are cattle-breeders." <note>Genesis 46:32.</note> However, a "shepherd of sheep" is the one who possesses **knowledge** <note>original: "ὁ γνωστικός" (ho gnostikos) — the second stage of the spiritual life, focused on the contemplation of God and the inner meanings of creation.</note>. For thoughts take the place of sheep; they are shepherded by the mind onto the mountains of divine contemplations. This is why "every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians"—that is, to the opposing powers.

<margin>56.</margin> When the body is moved through the senses toward its own desires and pleasures, the base mind follows along and consents to its fantasies and impulses. But the virtuous mind practices self-control; it restrains itself from **passionate** <note>original: "ἐμπαθῶν" (empathōn) — referring to thoughts or impulses driven by disordered emotions or desires.</note> fantasies and impulses, and instead chooses to philosophize on how to make these movements of the soul better.

<margin>57.</margin> Among the virtues, some are physical and some are spiritual. The physical virtues include things like fasting, vigils, sleeping on the ground, service to others, and manual labor—either to avoid being a burden or to share with those in need. The spiritual virtues are things like love, patience, gentleness, self-control, prayer, and the like. If, due to some necessity or physical circumstance—such as illness or something similar—it happens that we are unable to perform the aforementioned physical virtues, we find forgiveness from the Lord, who knows the reasons. But if we do not perform the spiritual virtues, we have not a single excuse, for they are not subject to physical necessity.

<margin>58.</margin> Love for God persuades the one who shares in it to look down upon every passing pleasure, every pain, and every grief. Let all the saints persuade you, who suffered so much for Christ's sake.

<column-break/>

<margin>59.</margin> Guard yourself against the mother of evils, which is **self-love** <note>original: "φιλαυτίας" (philautias) — in Maximus's theology, this is the root of all sin; an irrational, selfish attachment to the body.</note>; this is an irrational love for the body. From this, with a display of logic, are born the three primary and most general passionate and mad thoughts: I mean gluttony, greed, and vainglory. These take their starting points from the supposedly "necessary" needs of the body; and from these three, the entire catalog of evils is born. It is therefore necessary, as has been said, to be on guard and to fight against self-love with great **watchfulness** <note>original: "νήψεως" (nēpseōs) — also known as "sobriety of soul," a state of spiritual alertness and mental clarity.</note>. For when self-love is destroyed, all the evils that spring from it are destroyed along with it.

<margin>60.</margin> The passion of self-love suggests to the **Monk** that he should take pity on his body and indulge it more than is proper in matters of food—supposedly for the sake of "management" and "governance"—so that, being gradually dragged away, he might fall into the pit of pleasure-seeking. To the **layperson** <note>original: "κοσμικῷ" (kosmikō) — literally "one of the world."</note>, self-love suggests making provision for the flesh to fulfill its desires.

<margin>61.</margin> They say that the highest state of prayer is this: when the mind goes outside the flesh and the world, and becomes entirely immaterial and without form while praying. The one who keeps this state unharmed is truly praying without ceasing.

<margin>62.</margin> Just as the body, when it dies, is entirely separated from the things of the world, so too the soul, when it meditates on that highest state of prayer and "dies" to the world, is separated from all worldly thoughts. For if one does not die such a death, he cannot be found with God and live.

<margin>63.</margin> Let no one deceive you, Monk, into thinking you can be saved while being a slave to pleasure and vainglory.

<margin>64.</margin> Just as the body commits sin through physical objects and has the physical virtues for its training so that it may be disciplined, so also the mind commits sin through passionate thoughts and likewise has the spiritual virtues for its training, so that by seeing things purely and without passion, it may be disciplined.

<margin>65.</margin> Just as nights follow days and winters follow summers, so also griefs and pains follow vainglory and pleasure—whether...

<meta>catchword: whether (εἴτε)</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Maximus defines the spiritual roles of the monk and the layperson, identifying self-love (philautia) as the root of all vice. He distinguishes between physical and spiritual virtues, noting that while physical acts like fasting can be excused by illness, spiritual virtues like love and prayer are always required.</summary>

...in the present, or in the future.

<margin>66.</margin>
It is not possible for one who has sinned to escape the future judgment without either voluntary labors here <note>meaning ascetic practices like fasting or vigils</note>, or involuntary afflictions <note>meaning trials or suffering that happen to us against our will</note>.

<margin>67.</margin>
For five reasons, he says, we are permitted by God to be fought by demons. The first, they say, is so that by being attacked and counter-attacking, we might come to a clear distinction between **virtue** and **vice**. Second, so that by acquiring virtue through war and labor, we might hold it firm and unchangeable. Third, so that as we progress in virtue, we do not become high-minded, but learn to be humble-minded. Fourth, so that having been tested by vice, we might hate it with a perfect hatred. And fifth, above all these, so that having become **dispassionate** <note>original: "ἀπαθεῖς" (apatheis) — a state of being free from disordered passions or emotional attachments, not a lack of feeling</note>, we do not forget our own weakness, nor the power of the One who helped us.

<margin>68.</margin>
Just as the mind of a hungry person imagines bread, and that of a thirsty person water, so also the mind of a glutton imagines a variety of foods; and the lover of pleasure imagines the forms of women; and the vainglorious person imagines honors from men; and the lover of money imagines profits; and the person who remembers wrongs imagines vengeance on the one who grieved him; and the envious person imagines the misfortune of the one he envies; and so it is with the other **passions** <note>original: "παθῶν" (pathon) — disordered impulses or suffering caused by attachment to worldly things</note>. For the mind, when troubled by the passions, receives these passionate thoughts both while the body is awake and during sleep.

<margin>69.</margin>
When **desire** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμία" (epithymia)</note> increases the materials that produce pleasures, the mind imagines them in sleep. But when **anger** <note>original: "θυμός" (thymos) — often translated as the "incensive power" or the "spirited" part of the soul</note> increases, it sees things that produce fears. However, the impure demons increase these passions by taking our negligence as their co-worker and stirring them up; but the holy **Angels** diminish them by moving us toward the practice of the virtues.

<margin>70.</margin>
The desiring part of the soul, when frequently provoked, implants a habit of pleasure-loving in the soul that is difficult to move. But the anger, when continually disturbed, makes it cowardly and unmanly. These are healed: the former by intense asceticism, fasting, vigils, and prayer; the latter by kindness, love for humanity, affection, and mercy.

<margin>71.</margin>
The demons fight us either through actual things, or through the passionate thoughts <note>original: "νοημάτων" (noematon) — mental concepts or representations</note> regarding those things. They fight through things against those who are in the midst of worldly affairs; and through

<column-break/>

thoughts against those who have withdrawn from things.

<margin>72.</margin>
To the degree that it is easier to sin in the mind than in action, to that same degree the war through thoughts is heavier than the war through things.

<margin>73.</margin>
Things are outside of the mind, but the thoughts of these things are formed within it. It is therefore within the mind's power to use these thoughts well or ill. For the misuse of things follows the mistaken use of thoughts.

<margin>74.</margin>
The mind receives passionate thoughts through these three: through sense-perception, through the body's **constitution** <note>original: "κράσεως" (kraseos) — the physical temperament or biological makeup of the body</note>, and through memory. Through sense-perception, when things that strike us—toward which we already possess passions—move the mind toward passionate reasonings. Through the body's constitution, when the makeup of the body is altered by an undisciplined diet, or by the operation of demons, or by some illness, and moves the mind again toward passionate reasonings, such as toward sexual immorality. And through memory, when the memory brings back the thoughts of things toward which we were affected, and moves the mind similarly toward passionate reasonings.

<margin>75.</margin>
Of the things given to us by God for our use, some are found in the soul, some in the body, and some around the body. For example, in the soul are its powers; in the body are the sense organs and the other limbs; and around the body are foods, possessions, money, and so forth. Therefore, using these things well or ill—or using the circumstances surrounding them—renders us either virtuous or wicked.

<margin>76.</margin>
Of the circumstances surrounding things, some belong to the soul, some to the body, and some to the things around the body. Of those in the soul, for example, are knowledge and ignorance, forgetfulness and memory, love and hatred, sorrow and joy, and so forth. Of those in the body, for example, are pleasure and pain, sensation and its loss, health and disease, life and death, and such like. Of those around the body, for example, are having children or being childless, wealth and poverty, fame and obscurity, and so forth. Some of these are considered good and some bad by men; however, none of them are bad in their own nature, but according to the...

<header>SECOND CENTURY</header>

...use, whether they are found to be essentially evil or good.

<margin>77.</margin> Knowledge is good by nature, and health is likewise; but for many, the opposite of these has been more beneficial. For to those who are wicked, knowledge does not result in good, even if it is naturally good (as has been said). Similarly, neither health, nor wealth, nor joy are beneficial to them, for they do not use these things in a profitable way. Is it then the case that the opposites of these things are beneficial? <note>Maximus is arguing that things like poverty or sickness might be better for a person if they prevent them from sinning.</note> Therefore, those opposites are not evil in their own right, even if they seem to be evil.

<margin>78.</margin> Do not misuse your **thoughts** <note>original: "νοήμασιν" (noēmasin) — the mental concepts or images we hold in our minds</note>, lest you are forced to misuse actual things as well. <margin>* perhaps one might sin.</margin> For if a person does not first sin in his mind <insert>perhaps one might sin</insert>, he will never sin in action.

<margin>79.</margin> The "image of the earthly man" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:49</note> consists of the general **vices**: namely, foolishness, cowardice, lack of restraint, and injustice. The "image of the heavenly man" consists of the general **virtues**: namely, prudence, courage, self-control, and justice. But just as we have worn the image of the earthly, let us also wear the image of the heavenly.

<margin>80.</margin> If you wish to find the Way that leads to life, seek it in the Way itself, and there you will find it—in the One who said: *I am the Way, and the Door, and the Truth, and the Life.* <note>Maximus combines John 14:6 and John 10:9. He teaches that Christ is not just the goal, but the very path of virtue we walk.</note> However, seek with great effort, because there are few who find it, lest you be left behind by the few and found among the many.

<margin>81.</margin> For these five reasons, the soul is restrained from sins: either through fear of men, or through fear of judgment, or because of the future reward, or through the love of God, or finally, because of a stinging conscience.

<margin>82.</margin> Some say that evil would not exist in the world unless there were some other power drawing us toward it. But this power is nothing other than our own **negligence** <note>original: "ἀμέλεια" (ameleia)</note> of the natural activities of the mind. Therefore, those who take care for these activities always do good, and never do evil. If you also wish it, drive away negligence and you will simultaneously drive away **vice**, which is the mistaken use of thoughts, followed by the misuse of things.

<margin>83.</margin> It is according to nature for the rational part within us to be subject to the Divine Word <note>original: "Λόγῳ" (Logō) — referring both to reason and to Christ as the Logos</note> and to rule over the irrational part within us.

<column-break/>

Let this order, then, be preserved in all things, and then neither will evil exist among beings, nor will anything be found drawing us toward it.

<margin>84.</margin> Some **inner thoughts** <note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismōn) — often refers to persistent or intrusive thoughts that can lead to temptation</note> are simple, while others are composite. Simple thoughts are those that are **dispassionate** <note>original: "ἀπαθεῖς" (apatheis) — neutral thoughts without emotional attachment</note>. Composite thoughts are those that are **passionate**, being composed of a passion and a mental image. Given this, many simple thoughts can be seen following composite ones, once the composite ones begin to move toward sin in the mind. For example, regarding gold: a passionate thought of gold rises in someone’s memory, and they move in their mind toward stealing it, thus completing the sin in the mind. Following the memory of the gold come memories of a purse, a money-box, a private chamber, and so on. Now, the memory of the gold was composite (for it contained the passion of greed), but the memory of the purse, the money-box, and the rest was simple, for the mind had no passion toward them. The same applies to every thought—to vainglory, to women, and the rest. For not all thoughts that follow a passionate thought are themselves passionate, as this reasoning has shown. From this, we can know which mental images are passionate and which are not.

<margin>85.</margin> Some say that the demons, by touching the parts of the body during sleep, stir up the passion of lust. Then, once the passion is stirred, it brings the form of a woman into the mind through the memory. Others say that they appear to the mind in the form of a woman, and by touching the parts of the body, they stir up desire, and thus the fantasies occur. Still others say that the passion prevailing in the approaching demon stirs the passion in the person; and so the soul is set on fire toward these thoughts, bringing up the forms through the memory. The same applies to other passionate fantasies; some say they happen one way, some another. However, in none of the ways mentioned can the demons stir any passion whatsoever if **love** and **self-control** <note>original: "ἐγκρατείας" (egkrateias)</note> are present in the soul, whether the person is awake or asleep.

<margin>86.</margin> Some of the commandments of the Law must be kept both bodily and spiritually. Others, spiritually only. For example, "You shall not commit adultery," "You shall not murder," "You shall not steal," and similar ones, must be kept both bodily and spiritu...

<summary>This page discusses the moral importance of how we use our thoughts and physical health, defining evil as the negligence of the mind's natural functions. It also provides a psychological analysis of how "passionate" thoughts develop and how the soul can remain protected through love and self-control.</summary>

<margin>87.</margin> There are three general moral states among monks. The first is to commit no sin in action. The second is for the soul not to linger on **passionate thoughts** <term>logismoi: obsessive or intrusive thoughts driven by ego or desire</term>. The third is to look upon the forms of women and those who have caused us grief with **dispassion** <term>apatheia: a state of inner peace where one is no longer controlled by reactive emotions</term> in one's mind.

<margin>88.</margin> A person without possessions is one who has renounced everything they own and possesses nothing at all on earth except their body; and even having broken their attachment to the body, they have entrusted their own provision to God and to the pious.

<margin>89.</margin> Among those who possess things, some possess them dispassionately; therefore, when they are deprived of them, they do not grieve, like those who "accepted the seizure of their possessions with joy." <note>A reference to Hebrews 10:34.</note> Others possess things with passion; for this reason, when they are about to lose them, they become deeply sorrowful—like the rich man in the Gospel who "went away grieving"—and if they are actually deprived of them, they grieve even unto death. Therefore, the loss of a thing reveals the inner disposition of both the dispassionate and the passionate person.

<margin>90.</margin> The demons wage war against those who pray with great intensity so that they might not even perceive the simple concepts of physical things. They fight against those seeking knowledge <note>original: "γνωστικούς" (gnostikous) — those pursuing deep spiritual insight</note> so that passionate thoughts might linger within them. And they fight against those struggling in the life of action to persuade them to commit sins in practice. In every way, the wretched ones fight against all people, seeking to separate them from God.

<margin>91.</margin> Those who are trained in piety by Divine Providence during this life are tested by these three temptations: either by the giving of pleasant things, such as health, beauty, fine children, money, fame, and the like; or by the onset of grievous things, such as the loss of children, money, or fame; or by things that cause pain to the body, such as illnesses, tortures, and so on. To those in the first group, the Lord says: *If anyone does not renounce all his possessions, he cannot be my disciple.* To those in the second and third groups, He says: *In

your patience, possess your souls.* <note>Luke 14:33 and Luke 21:19.</note>

<margin>92.</margin> They say that these four things change the temperament <term>krasis: the "mixture" or balance of humors in the body</term> of the body and, through it, give thoughts to the mind—whether passionate or dispassionate: namely, the **Angels**, the **demons**, the **air** (environment), and **diet**. It is said that the Angels change it by word; the demons by touch; the air by its changes; and the diet by the qualities of the foods, as well as by their excess or deficiency. Beyond these are the changes that happen to the body through memory, hearing, and sight—when the soul first experiences grief or joy from what happens to it. When the soul suffers from these things, it changes the temperament of the body; and when the temperament is changed by the aforementioned things, it provides thoughts to the mind.

<margin>93.</margin> Death is properly the separation from God, and "the sting of death is sin." <note>1 Corinthians 15:56.</note> Adam, having received it, became an exile from the tree of life, from paradise, and from God; and the death of the body followed from necessity. But Life is properly the One who said: *I am the Life.* <note>John 14:6.</note> He, having entered into death, led the one who had died back into Life.

<margin>94.</margin> A person who writes treatises does so either for their own reminder, or for the benefit of others, or for both; or for the harm of some, or for display, or out of necessity.

<margin>95.</margin> The "place of green pastures" is **practical virtue**; the "water of rest" is the **knowledge of created things**. <note>Maximus is interpreting the imagery of Psalm 23.</note>

<margin>96.</margin> The "shadow of death" is human life. If anyone is with God, and God is with them, they are able to say with power: *Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me.* <note>Psalm 23:4.</note>

<margin>97.</margin> A pure mind sees things rightly. Trained speech brings what has been seen before the eyes of others. A clear ear receives them. But the one who is deprived of these three mocks the speaker.

<margin>98.</margin> One who is "with God" is the one who knows the Holy Trinity, its creation, and its providence, and who possesses a soul whose emotional part has been made dispassionate.

## BY THE SAME AUTHOR
# THIRD HUNDRED [ON LOVE]

<margin>1.</margin> The reasonable use of thoughts and things is productive of **self-control** <term>sophrosyne: a state of temperance or soundness of mind</term> and knowledge; but their irrational use leads to **lack of restraint** <term>akolasia: a lack of discipline or indulgence in pleasures</term>, hatred, and ignorance.

<margin>2.</margin> *Thou hast prepared a table before me,* and so forth. <note>Quoting Psalm 23:5.</note> Here, the "table" signifies **practical virtue** <term>praktike: the active stage of the spiritual life focused on purifying the heart from passions</term>. For this was prepared by Christ against those who afflict us. The "oil" that anoints the mind is the contemplation of created things. The "cup" of God is the **knowledge of God**. His "mercy" is His Word and God <note>original: "λόγον αὐτοῦ, καὶ Θεόν" (His Word, and God). Maximus identifies God's mercy with the Logos, the Second Person of the Trinity.</note>; for He, through His incarnation, pursues us all our days until He overtakes all who are to be saved, just as He did with Paul. The "house" is the Kingdom in which all the Saints are restored; and "length of days" is eternal life.

<margin>3.</margin> Vices happen to us through the **misuse** <term>parachrēsis: using a natural faculty for a purpose other than what God intended</term> of the soul's powers—namely, the desiring, the incensive <note>The "incensive" or "spirited" power is the faculty of the soul used for courage or righteous anger.</note>, and the rational powers. The misuse of the rational power is ignorance and folly. Of the incensive and desiring powers, it is hatred and lack of restraint. The proper use of these is knowledge and prudence, love and self-control. If this is so, then nothing created and brought into being by God is evil.

<margin>4.</margin> It is not food that is evil, but **gluttony** <term>gasterimargia: literally "belly-madness"</term>. Nor is childbearing evil, but fornication. Nor is money evil, but the love of money. Nor is glory evil, but **vainglory**. If this is so, there is nothing evil among existing things except for misuse, which happens from the mind’s neglect of its natural cultivation.

<margin>5.</margin> The evil found in **demons** <note>In the Byzantine tradition, demons are fallen angels whose "evil" is not an essential part of their nature, but a corruption of their will.</note>, as the Blessed Dionysius <note>Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian theologian whom Maximus deeply admired.</note> says, is this: irrational anger, mindless desire, and rash imagination. But "irrationality," "mindlessness," and "rashness" in

<column-break/>

rational beings are privations of reason, mind, and foresight. Now, privations are secondary to the states they lack. There was, therefore, a time when reason, mind, and devout foresight existed in them. If this is so, not even the demons are evil by nature; rather, they have become evil through the misuse of their natural powers.

<margin>6.</margin> Some passions produce lack of restraint; some produce hatred; and others produce both lack of restraint and hatred.

<margin>7.</margin> Talkativeness and <gloss>perhaps "gluttony" <note>original: "ἡδυφαγία" (sweet-eating). The margin suggests "ἀδηφαγία" (gluttony/excessive eating).</note></gloss> are the causes of a lack of restraint. Love of money and vainglory are the causes of hatred toward one's neighbor. But the mother of both is **self-love** <term>philautia: excessive or ego-driven love of self, considered the root of all sins</term>.

<margin>8.</margin> Self-love is a passionate and irrational love for the body, which is opposed by love and self-discipline. Clearly, the one who has self-love possesses all the passions.

<margin>9.</margin> *No one* (says the Apostle) *ever hated his own flesh* <note>Quoting Ephesians 5:29.</note>, but he surely "batters it and makes it his slave," <note>Quoting 1 Corinthians 9:27.</note> providing nothing more than food and clothing, and only those things necessary for living. In this way, a person loves the body **dispassionately** <term>apatheia: a state of inner freedom where one is not ruled by reactive emotions</term>, nurturing and cherishing it as a servant of divine things, fulfilling only its actual needs.

<margin>10.</margin> Whomever one loves, one surely hastens to serve. If, therefore, someone loves God, they surely hasten to do what is pleasing to Him. But if they love the flesh, they do what delights the flesh.

<margin>11.</margin> Love, self-control, contemplation, and prayer are pleasing to God. To the flesh, however, gluttony, lack of restraint, and those things that increase them are pleasing. For this reason, *those who are in the flesh cannot please God.* <note>Quoting Romans 8:8.</note> But those who belong to Christ...

<summary>Maximus begins his Third Century by defining evil not as a substance, but as the "misuse" of God-given faculties. He interprets Psalm 23 allegorically and identifies "self-love" (philautia) as the root cause of all spiritual disorders.</summary>
<keywords>misuse of faculties, Psalm 23, self-love, gluttony, Dionysius the Areopagite, demons, practical virtue, self-control</keywords>

[of Chri]st, "have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." <note>Maximus is completing a sentence from the previous page, quoting Galatians 5:24.</note>

<margin>12.</margin>
**The mind**, if it inclines toward God, keeps the body as its servant and provides it with nothing more than the necessities of life. But if it inclines toward the flesh, it becomes enslaved to the passions, always looking after the body’s desires.

<margin>13.</margin>
**If you wish** to overcome your thoughts, attend to the **passions** <term>passions: disordered impulses like greed or lust that cloud the mind</term>, and you will easily drive the thoughts from your mind. For example: regarding **sexual immorality**, fast, keep vigil, work hard, and seek solitude. Regarding **anger and sorrow**, despise reputation, dishonor, and material things. Regarding **resentment**, pray for the one who has grieved you, and you will be delivered.

<margin>14.</margin>
**Do not measure yourself** against those who are weaker than you; rather, stretch yourself toward the commandment of love. For by measuring yourself against the weak, you fall into the pit of **self-conceit** <note>original: "oiēseōs" — a sense of inflated self-importance</note>; but by stretching toward love, you advance toward the height of **humility**.

<margin>15.</margin>
**If you truly** keep the commandment of love for your neighbor, you will never show the bitterness of grief toward him. Is it not clear that by preferring temporary things and fighting for them, you go to war against your brother?

<margin>16.</margin>
**It is not because of need** that gold has become so sought after by men, but because it allows the majority to serve their pleasures.

<margin>17.</margin>
**There are three** causes for the love of money: **love of pleasure, vanity, and lack of faith**; but the most dangerous of these is lack of faith.

<margin>18.</margin>
**The lover of pleasure** loves silver so that he may live in luxury; **the vain man** loves it so that he may be glorified; but **the faithless man** loves it so that he may hide and keep it, fearing famine, or old age, or disease, or exile. He places his hope in money rather than in God, the Creator and Provider of all creation, down to the last and smallest of living things.

<margin>19.</margin>
**There are four** types of people who acquire money: the three mentioned above, and the **steward** <term>oikonomikos: one who manages resources for the benefit of others</term>. Only the steward acquires it rightly, so that he may never cease providing for the needs of everyone.

<margin>20.</margin>
**All passionate thoughts** either provoke the **desiring** faculty of the soul, or disturb the **incensive** <term>incensive: the "thymos" or spirited part of the soul, often associated with anger or courage</term> faculty, or the **rational** faculty. And

<column-break/>

as a result, the mind becomes "clouded" <note>literally "suffering from ophthalmia," an eye inflammation, used here as a metaphor for spiritual blindness</note> toward **spiritual contemplation** and the departure toward prayer. For this reason, the Monk—and especially the one practicing **stillness** <term>hesychast: a monk who seeks God through silence and inner quiet</term>—must pay close attention to his thoughts and both recognize and cut off their causes. He recognizes them in this way: for example, the desiring part of the soul is provoked by passionate memories of women. The cause of these is the lack of restraint in food and drink, and frequent or irrational conversation with those women. Hunger, thirst, vigil, and withdrawal cut these off. Again, passionate memories of those who have grieved us disturb the incensive part of the soul. The cause of this is love of pleasure, vanity, and the love of material things; for the passionate man is grieved because he was either deprived of these or failed to obtain them. Despising and devaluing these things for the sake of the love of God cuts off these memories.

<margin>21.</margin>
**God knows Himself**, and He also knows the things created by Him. The **holy powers** <term>holy powers: the angelic ranks</term> also know God, and they know the things created by God; but the holy powers do not know God and His creations in the same way that God knows Himself and His creations.

<margin>22.</margin>
**God knows Himself** from His own blessed essence. He knows the things created by Him from His wisdom, through which and in which He made all things. But the holy powers know God by **participation** <term>metochē: the way a creature shares in the life of God without becoming God by nature</term>, though He is beyond participation; and they know the things created by Him by perceiving the spiritual concepts within them.

<margin>23.</margin>
**Created things are outside the mind**; but the mind receives the contemplation of them within itself. This is not the case with God, who is eternal, infinite, and undefined, and who has granted to all beings their existence, their well-being, and their eternal being.

<margin>24.</margin>
**The rational and intellectual essence** participates in the Holy God by its very existence, by its capacity for well-being—that is, for goodness and wisdom—and by the grace of eternal being. In this way, it knows God. It knows the things created by Him by perceiving the "artistic" wisdom found in created things, which is an abstract and non-substantial concept formed in the mind.

<margin>25.</margin>
**Four of the divine attributes**, which hold together, guard, and preserve all beings, have been shared by God through His extreme goodness...

<meta>This page continues the "Third Hundred" chapters on love by Maximus the Confessor. The previous page discussed the practical disciplines of the soul—fasting, prayer, and humility—to overcome the passions. This page shifts toward "theology" in the classical sense: the study of God's nature and the ontological structure of the created world.</meta>

<page-num>219</page-num>
<header>THE THIRD HUNDRED</header>
<sig>29</sig>

**God**, the Being who is always Being, brought into existence the rational and intellectual essence out of His goodness and wisdom. Two of these—existence and eternal existence—He granted to their very nature; the other two—goodness and wisdom—He granted to the **disposition of their will** <term>disposition: the Greek term 'gnome' refers to the capacity for choice and the inclination of the heart</term>. He did this so that what He is by nature, the creature might become by **participation** <note>original: "metousian" — the idea that humans don't become gods by their own power, but by sharing in God's life</note>. Because of this, the creature is said to have been made according to the "image and likeness" of God. It is "according to the image" insofar as it is a being created by Being, and an eternal being created by the Eternal Being (even if it has a beginning, it has no end). It is "according to the likeness" insofar as it becomes good like the Good One and wise like the Wise One—the one who is so by grace reflecting the One who is so by nature. Every rational nature is made in the image of God; but only the good and the wise are made in His likeness.

<margin>26.</margin>
**All rational and intellectual essence** is divided into two: that is, the **Angelic** and the **human** nature. Furthermore, the entire Angelic nature is divided into two general dispositions and "herds": the holy and the accursed—that is, the holy powers and the unclean demons. All human nature is likewise divided into only two general dispositions: I mean the pious and the impious.

<margin>27.</margin>
<margin><insert>perhaps "having" is missing</insert></margin>
**God**, being self-existence, self-goodness, and self-wisdom—or rather, to speak more truly, being beyond all these things—has absolutely no opposite. But created things all have existence through participation and grace. The rational and intellectual ones also have an aptitude for goodness and wisdom. For these, the opposite of "being" is "non-being." The opposite of the aptitude for goodness and wisdom is **wickedness** and **ignorance**. Whether these things exist forever or cease to exist is in the power of the Creator; but whether they participate in His goodness and wisdom or not depends on the will of the rational beings themselves.

<margin>28.</margin>
<margin><insert>perhaps "to be" is missing</insert></margin>
**The Greeks** <note>original: "Hellēnes" — here referring to pagan philosophers, likely Neoplatonists</note> say that the essence of all things has co-existed with God from eternity, and that only the qualities of things come from Him. They claim that "essence" itself has no opposite, and that opposition exists only in the qualities. But we say that only the Divine Essence has no opposite, as it is eternal and infinite, and the giver of eternity to others. For the essence of created things, "non-being" is the opposite. It remains in the power of Him who truly Is whether they exist forever or not. 

<column-break/>

But His gifts are **without regret** <note>a reference to Romans 11:29</note>; and for this reason, they always exist and shall exist, held together by His almighty power—even if they have an opposite in "non-being," as was said, having been brought from non-being into being, and having their existence or non-existence dependent upon His will.

<margin>29.</margin>
**Just as evil** is the privation of good, and ignorance is the privation of knowledge, so also non-being is the privation of being—not the privation of the One who truly Is (for He has no opposite), but of that which exists by participation. The first two types of privation depend on the choice of the creatures; the latter depends on the will of the Creator, who, out of His goodness, always wills for beings to exist and to be forever blessed by Him.

<margin>30.</margin>
**Of all created things**, some are rational and intellectual and are capable of receiving opposites—such as virtue and vice, or knowledge and ignorance. Others are various bodies composed of opposites, namely: earth, air, fire, and water. Some are entirely incorporeal and immaterial, even if some of these are joined to bodies; others are composed only of matter and form.

<margin>31.</margin>
**All bodies** are by nature motionless; they are moved by the soul—some by a rational soul, some by an irrational soul, and some by a soul without sensation <note>referring to the "soul" of plants, which governs growth but not feeling</note>.

<margin>32.</margin>
**Of the powers of the soul**, one is nutritive, another is imaginative and impulsive, and another is cognitive and intellectual. Plants participate in the first one only. Irrational animals participate in the second one as well as the first. Humans participate in the third, in addition to the first two. The first two powers are perishable, but the third is shown to be imperishable and immortal.

<margin>33.</margin>
**The holy powers** <note>meaning the angels</note> pass on illumination to one another. They also pass on to human nature either their own virtue or their knowledge. Regarding virtue, they share a goodness that imitates God; through this, they do good to themselves, to each other, and to those beneath them, making them "god-like." Regarding knowledge, they share either the higher truth about God—for as it says, "You, O Lord, are on high forever" <note>Psalm 92:8</note>—or a deeper understanding of incorporeal things, or more accurate facts about bodies, or a clearer view of Providence, or a more distinct understanding of Judgment.

<margin>34.</margin>
**Impurity of the mind** consists first in having false knowledge; second, in being ignorant...

<summary>Maximus explores the metaphysical distinction between God (who has no opposite) and creatures (whose opposite is non-existence). He classifies the different types of souls—nutritive, sensitive, and rational—and explains how angels share divine light with humanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Third Hundred" chapters on love by Maximus the Confessor. The previous page discussed the nature of rational beings (Angels and humans) and their creation in the "image and likeness" of God. This page moves into the psychological and ascetical mechanics of the spiritual life—how the mind interacts with objects, thoughts, and passions.</meta>

<page-num>220</page-num>
<header>OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS</header>

...anything universal, as I speak in terms of the human mind. For it is the property of an Angel to be ignorant of nothing in the particular. Third, to have impassioned thoughts. Fourth, to give consent to sin.

<margin>35.</margin> Impurity of the soul is the failure to act according to nature. For from this, impassioned thoughts are born in the mind. For the soul acts according to nature when its **affective powers** <term>affective powers: the "passible" parts of the soul, divided into 'thymos' (incensive/anger) and 'epithymia' (desire)</term>—I mean **anger** and **desire**—remain **impassible** <note>original: "apatheis" — a state of being undisturbed by disordered passions</note> when confronted by things and the mental representations of them.

<margin>36.</margin> Impurity of the body is sin committed in actual deed.

<margin>37.</margin> He who is not affected by the things of the world loves **stillness** <note>original: "hesychian" — a state of inner quiet and focused prayer</note>; and he who loves nothing human loves all people; and he who is not offended by anyone, whether because of their failings or because of suspicious thoughts, has knowledge of God and of divine things.

<margin>38.</margin> It is a great thing not to be affected by **things**; but it is a much greater thing to remain impassible toward the **mental representations** of them.

<margin>39.</margin> Love and self-control keep the mind impassible, both toward things and toward the mental representations of them.

<margin>40.</margin> The mind of the one who loves God does not wage war against things, nor against the mental representations of them, but against the **passions** <term>passions: "pathe" — disordered impulses or emotions that cloud judgment</term> that are joined to those representations. For example, he does not fight against a woman, nor against someone who has grieved him, nor against the mental images of them, but against the passions joined to those images.

<margin>41.</margin> The entire war of the **Monk** is against the demons, so that he may separate the passions from his mental representations. For otherwise, he cannot look upon things without being affected by passion.

<margin>42.</margin> A **thing** is one thing, a **mental representation** is another, and a **passion** is another still. A **thing** is, for example, a man, a woman, gold, and so forth; a **mental representation** is a bare memory of one of the aforementioned; and a **passion** is an irrational love or an uncritical hatred for one of these things. Therefore, the Monk’s battle is against the passion.

<margin>43.</margin> An **impassioned thought** is a composite reasoning, made of a passion and a mental representation. Let us separate the passion from the representation, and the bare reasoning remains. We can separate them through spiritual love and self-control, if we so will.

<column-break/>

<margin>44.</margin> The **virtues** separate the mind from the passions; **spiritual contemplations** <term>contemplations: "theoriai" — the practice of seeing the divine principles behind created things</term> separate it from bare mental representations; and **pure prayer** presents the mind to God Himself.

<margin>45.</margin> The virtues exist for the sake of the knowledge of created things; knowledge exists for the sake of the knower; and the knower exists for the sake of the One who is known unknowingly and who knows beyond all knowledge.

<margin>46.</margin> God, being more than full, did not bring created things into being because He lacked anything; but rather so that they might receive His life by participating in Him in proportion to their nature, and that He might rejoice in His works, seeing them rejoicing and ever-satisfied by the One who can never be exhausted.

<margin>47.</margin> The world has many who are "poor in spirit," but not in the proper way; and many who "mourn," but because of the loss of money or the death of children; and many who are "meek," but toward unclean passions; and many who "hunger and thirst," but to seize the property of others and to profit from injustice; and many who are "merciful," but only toward the body and the things of the body; and "pure in heart," but for the sake of vainglory; and "peacemakers," who yet subject the soul to the flesh; and many who are "persecuted," but as lawbreakers; and many who are "reviled," but for shameful sins. Only those are **blessed** who do and suffer these things for the sake of **Christ**. Why? Because theirs is the kingdom of heaven, and they shall see God, and so forth. Thus, it is not because they do and suffer these things that they are blessed (for those mentioned above do the same), but because they do and suffer them **for the sake of Christ**.

<margin>48.</margin> In everything we do, the **intention** <note>original: "skopos" — the aim or goal of an action</note> is what is sought by God (as has been said many times), whether we do it for His sake or for some other reason. Therefore, whenever we wish to do something good, let us have God as our aim, not the desire to please people, so that by always looking to Him, we may do everything for His sake, lest we undergo the labor and yet lose the reward.

<margin>49.</margin> Cast out from your mind at the time of prayer both the bare mental representations of human affairs and the contemplations of all created things; so that the lesser...

<summary>Maximus defines the psychological mechanics of spiritual life, distinguishing between physical objects, our mental memories of them, and the "passions" (disordered emotions) that link the two. He emphasizes that true blessedness depends entirely on one's inner intention and doing all things for the sake of Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Third Century (set of one hundred chapters) on Love by Maximus the Confessor. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing the danger of forming material mental images of the Divine. This page explores the psychological origins of sin, the nature of judgment, and "self-love" (philautia) as the root of all spiritual ailments.</meta>

<page-num>221</page-num>
<header>THIRD HUNDRED</header>

...imagining Him as something material, you fall away from Him who is incomparably better than all existing things.

<margin>50.</margin> If we love God sincerely, we cast out the **passions** <note>original: "pathe" — disordered emotions or impulses that distract the soul from God</note> through that very love. Love for Him consists in preferring Him over the world, and the soul over the flesh. This is achieved by despising worldly things and devoting oneself to Him constantly through self-control, love, prayer, psalmody, and the like.

<margin>51.</margin> If, by devoting ourselves to God for a long time, we take care of the **passible part** <term>passible part: the "pathetikon," the part of the soul capable of feeling emotion or desire, which must be purified</term> of the soul, we no longer run aground against the attacks of intrusive thoughts. Instead, by understanding their causes more accurately and cutting them off, we become more discerning. Thus, the scripture is fulfilled in us: *My eye has looked down upon my enemies, and my ear shall hear of the wicked who rise up against me.* <note>Reference to Psalm 91:12 (LXX) / Psalm 92:11 (NRSV)</note>

<margin>52.</margin> When you see your mind moving with piety and justice among the **concepts** <note>original: "noemasi" — the mental representations of things</note> of the world, know that your body also remains pure and without sin. But when you see your mind occupied with sins in its thoughts and you do not restrain it, know that your body will not be long in falling into those very same things.

<margin>53.</margin> Just as the body has the world of **material things** <note>original: "pragmata"</note>, so the mind has its own world of **concepts**. And just as the body commits adultery with the body of a woman, so the mind commits adultery with the concept of a woman through the imagination of its own body. For in its thoughts, it sees the form of its own body mingling with the form of the woman. Likewise, it takes revenge on the form of one who has caused grief through the form of its own body. This applies to other sins as well. For whatever the body does in actual deed in the world of things, the mind also does in the world of concepts.

<margin>54.</margin> Is it not a cause for shuddering, amazement, and mental ecstasy that while God the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, the Son cries out: *Judge not, that you be not judged; condemn not, that you be not condemned*? The Apostle likewise says: *Judge nothing before the time, until the Lord*

<column-break/>

*comes;* and *in the judgment you use to judge another, you condemn yourself.* Yet men, neglecting to weep for their own sins, have snatched the judgment away from the Son. As if they themselves were sinless, they judge and condemn one another. At this, heaven was astonished and the earth shuddered, yet they are not ashamed in their lack of perception.

<margin>55.</margin> He who busies himself with the sins of others, or judges his brother based on suspicion, has not yet begun to repent. He has not sought to know his own sins, which are in truth heavier than a great weight of lead; nor does he know why a man becomes "heavy-hearted," loving vanity and seeking lies. Therefore, like a fool walking in darkness, he neglects his own sins and imagines those of others, whether they truly exist or are merely assumed through suspicion.

<margin>56.</margin> **Self-love** <note>original: "philautia" — the excessive or irrational love of the self/body</note> (as has been said many times) is established as the cause of all passionate thoughts. For from it are born the three most generic thoughts of desire: **gluttony**, **greed** <note>original: "philargyria" — literally "love of silver"</note>, and **vainglory**. From gluttony, fornication is born; from vainglory, **pride** is born. All others follow each of these three: anger, grief, resentment, envy, slander, and the rest. These passions, then, bind the mind to material things and drag it down to the earth, weighing upon it like a very heavy stone, even though the mind is by nature lighter and swifter than fire.

<margin>57.</margin> The beginning of all passions is self-love; the end is pride. Self-love is an irrational affection for the body. He who cuts this off, cuts off all the passions that arise from it.

<margin>58.</margin> Just as parents of bodies feel affection for their own offspring, so the mind is naturally attached to its own **reasonings** <note>original: "logois"</note>. And just as their children seem the most decent and beautiful of all to their passion-driven parents—even if they are the most ridiculous in every way—so to the foolish mind its own reasonings appear the wisest of all, even if they are the most wretched. This is not so for the wise man regarding his own reasonings. Rather, even when he seems certain that they are true and good, then he especially does not...

<summary>Maximus explains how the mind functions like an internal world where sins are committed through thoughts just as they are in the physical world. He identifies "self-love" (philautia) as the foundational vice that leads to gluttony, greed, and pride, and warns against the spiritual danger of judging others while ignoring one's own faults.</summary>
<keywords>self-love, philautia, judgment, passions, mental representations, gluttony, pride, repentance, asceticism</keywords>

<page-num>222</page-num>
<header>OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS</header>

...[does not] trust his own judgment; but appoints others, wise men, as judges of his own words and thoughts, lest he "run in vain, or has run," and through them he receives confirmation. <note>Refers to Galatians 2:2. St. Maximus is likely finishing a thought on humility in spiritual direction.</note>

<margin>59.</margin> When you conquer one of the lower **passions** <note>original: "pathe" — disordered impulses</note>, such as gluttony, or sexual immorality, or anger, or greed, the thought of **vainglory** <term>vainglory: "kenodoxia," the desire for empty praise or human recognition</term> immediately flies upon you. If you conquer this one, the thought of **pride** <term>pride: "hyperephania," a deeper arrogance that sets oneself above others or even God</term> succeeds it.

<margin>60.</margin> All the lower passions, while they rule the soul, drive the thought of vainglory out of it; but when all the aforementioned passions are defeated, they give way to it.

<margin>61.</margin> Vainglory—sometimes being destroyed, sometimes remaining—gives birth to pride. When it is being destroyed, it produces self-conceit; when it remains, it produces boastfulness. Vainglory is destroyed by **hidden labor** <note>original: "krypte ergasia" — spiritual practices performed in secret to avoid being seen by others</note>; but pride is destroyed by ascribing one's successes to God.

<margin>62.</margin> He who has been deemed worthy of the knowledge of God, and has truly enjoyed the pleasure that comes from it, despises all the pleasures born of the **desiring part** <note>original: "epithymetikon" — the faculty of the soul associated with appetite and longing</note> of the soul.

<margin>63.</margin> He who desires earthly things either desires food, or things that serve the belly, or human glory, or money, or something else that follows these. And unless the mind finds something better than these, toward which it might transfer its desire, it could never be persuaded to despise them completely. But the knowledge of God and of divine things is incomparably better than these.

<margin>64.</margin> Those who despise pleasures do so either out of fear, or hope, or knowledge, or even out of love for God.

<margin>65.</margin> Knowledge of divine things without **passionlessness** <note>original: "apatheia" — a state of being undisturbed by the passions</note> does not persuade the mind to fully despise material things, but is like a mere mental concept of a physical object. Because of this, one can find many people who have much knowledge, yet roll in the passions of the flesh like pigs in the mud. For having been cleansed for a short time through diligence and having attained knowledge, they later grew negligent; they became like **Saul**, who was deemed worthy of the kingdom, but after living unworthily, was cast out from it with terrible wrath. <note>Reference to 1 Samuel 15:23-26</note>

<margin>66.</margin> Just as a mere thought of human affairs does not force the mind to despise divine things, so also mere knowledge of divine things does not fully persuade it to despise

<column-break/>

human things. This is because the truth now exists in shadows and conjectures; therefore, the mind needs the blessed passion of **holy love**, which binds the mind to spiritual **contemplations** <term>contemplations: "theoriai," the deep spiritual seeing of divine truths</term> and persuades it to prefer the immaterial to the material, and the spiritual and divine to the sensible.

<margin>67.</margin> He who has cut off the passions and made his thoughts simple has not necessarily turned them toward the divine; rather, he might feel nothing toward either human or divine things. This happens to those involved in the **practical life** <note>original: "praktikon" — the stage of active ascetic discipline</note> alone, who have not yet been deemed worthy of knowledge. They abstain from passions out of fear of punishment or hope for the Kingdom.

<margin>68.</margin> We walk by faith, not by sight; and we possess virtue through "mirrors" and "enigmas." <note>Reference to 2 Corinthians 5:7 and 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly..."</note> Because of this, we need much dedication to these things, so that through long-term practice and persistence, we might make the habit of these contemplations difficult to break.

<margin>69.</margin> If, after cutting off the causes of the passions for a short time, we occupy ourselves with spiritual contemplations but do not always dwell in them as our primary work, we easily turn back again to the passions of the flesh. We harvest nothing from our effort but mere knowledge mixed with conceit; the end of which is the gradual darkening of knowledge itself and the total turning away of the mind toward material things.

<margin>70.</margin> A blameworthy passion of love occupies the mind with material things; a praiseworthy passion of love binds it to the divine. For the mind is accustomed to expand in whatever things it spends its time; and wherever it expands, it turns its desire and love—whether toward divine, familiar, and spiritual things, or toward the things and passions of the flesh.

<margin>71.</margin> God created the invisible world and the visible world; and He clearly made both the soul and the body. If the visible world is so beautiful, what then must the invisible be like? And if that is better than this, how much greater than both is God, their Creator? If, therefore, the Creator of all beautiful things is better than all His works, for what reason does the mind leave what is better than all and occupy itself with the worst of all? I mean, with the passions of the flesh. Or is it not clear that, because it has lived with these and been accustomed to them from birth...

<summary>Maximus explores the psychological transition from conquering physical passions to facing the spiritual traps of vainglory and pride. He argues that only a deep, love-anchored knowledge of God can prevent the mind from relapsing into material desires.</summary>
