<page-num>223</page-num>
<header>THE THIRD CENTURY</header>

...[the soul has not yet] received perfect experience of that which is better than all and above all things. If, therefore, through long-term practice of self-control regarding pleasures and through the meditation on divine things, we gradually break the soul away from such a worldly attachment, it expands as it makes little by little progress in divine matters. It then recognizes its own dignity and its final goal, and it transfers its entire desire toward the Divine.

<margin>72.</margin> One who speaks dispassionately <note>original: "apathos" — without being driven by a disordered emotion like anger or spite</note> about a brother’s sins does so for two reasons: either to correct him, or to benefit another. If he speaks for any other reason—whether to the person himself or to someone else—he does so to reproach or to mock him. Such a person will not escape divine abandonment; rather, he will certainly fall into the same sin or another, and being rebuked and reproached by others, he will be put to shame.

<margin>73.</margin> There is not just one single account for those who commit the same sin in outward action, but various ones. For instance: it is one thing to sin out of a habit, and another to sin by being suddenly carried away <note>original: "synarpagen" — a sudden impulse or lapse of judgment</note>. In the latter case, the person had no such thought before the sin, nor does he hold onto it after the sin; rather, he grieves deeply over what happened. But the one who sins out of habit is the opposite: even before the act, he did not stop sinning in his mind, and after the act, he remains in the same disposition.

<margin>74.</margin> He who pursues the virtues for the sake of **vainglory** <term>vainglory: "kenodoxia," the seeking of empty praise from others</term> clearly pursues knowledge for vainglory as well. Such a person obviously does not do or say anything for the sake of spiritual edification, but in everything he hunts for the glory of those who see or hear him. This **passion** <term>passion: "pathos," a disordered or unhealthy impulse of the soul</term> is exposed when others criticize his works or his words. He becomes deeply grieved by this—not because they are not being edified (for that was not his goal anyway), but because he himself has been belittled.

<margin>75.</margin> The passion of **greed** <note>original: "philargyria" — literally "love of silver"</note> is exposed in this: when one receives with joy but gives with grief. Such a person cannot be a good steward.

<margin>76.</margin> A person endures suffering for these reasons: for the love of God, or for the hope of reward, or for the fear of punishment, or for the fear of men, or by nature, or for pleasure, or for profit, or for vainglory, or out of necessity.

<margin>77.</margin> It is one thing to be rid of thoughts, and

<column-break/>

another to be freed from the passions. Often someone is rid of thoughts when the objects toward which he feels a passion are not present. But the passions remain hidden in the soul and are exposed when the objects reappear. Therefore, one must guard the mind in the presence of things and recognize which thing he feels a passion toward.

<margin>78.</margin> That person is a genuine friend who, in a time of trial, shares in the afflictions, necessities, and misfortunes of his neighbor as if they were his own, doing so calmly and without disturbance.

<margin>79.</margin> Do not dishonor your conscience, for it always gives you the best advice. It suggests to you the divine and angelic will; it frees you from the hidden defilements of the heart, and it grants you confidence before God at the time of your departure.

<margin>80.</margin> If you wish to become discerning and moderate, and not be a slave to the passion of self-conceit, always seek to find what is hidden within existing things <note>original: "en tois ousi" — in the nature of beings/reality</note> regarding knowledge. When you find many various things that escape your understanding, you will marvel at your own ignorance and restrain your pride. By knowing yourself, you will understand many great and wonderful things; for to think that one knows prevents one from progressing toward knowing.

<margin>81.</margin> That person truly wishes to be saved who does not resist medical drugs. These "drugs" are the pains and sorrows brought upon us by various circumstances. He who resists them does not know what is being negotiated here, nor what he will gain when he departs from this life.

<margin>82.</margin> Vainglory and greed are parents to one another. Those who seek vainglory seek to be rich, and those who are rich seek vainglory—but this is how it is for people of the world. For the monk, being without possessions, he is more prone to vainglory; if he has money, he hides it, being ashamed as if he possesses something unsuited to his monastic habit.

<margin>83.</margin> It is characteristic of a monk’s vainglory to be boastful about virtue and its consequences. It is characteristic of his pride to be lifted up by his successes, to belittle others, and to attribute these successes to himself rather than to God. But for the person of the world, it is characteristic of vainglory and pride to be boastful about beauty, wealth, power, and worldly wisdom.

<margin>84.</margin> The successes of worldly people are fall- <note>The word is cut off here by the page break: "ptomata," likely meaning "the falls" or "ruins" of others.</note>

<summary>This page outlines the psychology of sin and virtue, distinguishing between habitual and accidental sins, and defining the different manifestations of vainglory in monks versus laypeople. It emphasizes that true knowledge begins with the humility of recognizing one's own ignorance.</summary>

<page-num>224</page-num>
<header>OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS</header>

...these belong to the Monks. And the achievements <note>original: "katorthomata" — successes or righteous deeds</note> of Monks are the failures of those in the world. For example: the achievements of those in the world are wealth, and glory, and power, and luxury, and many children, and things following these. If a Monk pursues these, he is destroyed. But the achievements of a Monk are poverty <note>original: "aktēmosynē" — literally "the state of possessing nothing"</note>, lack of glory, lack of power, self-control, suffering for the sake of virtue, and things following these. If a lover of the world falls into these against his intention, he considers it a great failure, and often risks even using a noose <note>a reference to suicide by hanging</note>; and indeed, some have used one.

<margin>85.</margin> Foods were created for two reasons: for nourishment and for healing. Therefore, those who partake of them for any other reason—as if misusing <note>original: "parachrōmenoi"</note> the things given by God for our use—are condemned as lovers of luxury. And in all matters, the misuse of a thing is the sin.

<margin>86.</margin> Humility <note>original: "tapeinophrosunē" — literally "lowliness of mind"</note> is continuous prayer with tears and labors. For by always calling upon God for help, it does not allow a person to foolishly trust in their own power and wisdom, nor to exalt themselves over others. These are the severe diseases of the passion of pride.

<margin>87.</margin> It is one thing to fight against a bare thought <note>original: "psilō logismō" — a neutral mental image or concept without emotional charge</note> so that it does not stir up a passion. It is another thing to fight against a passionate thought so that there is no consent to it. Both ways, however, do not allow the thoughts to linger.

<margin>88.</margin> Sorrow is yoked to resentment <note>original: "mnēsikakia" — literally "remembering wrongs" or holding a grudge</note>. When the mind looks upon the face of a brother with sorrow, it is clear that it holds resentment toward him. The "ways of the resentful lead to death," because every resentful person is a lawbreaker.

<margin>89.</margin> If you hold a grudge against someone, pray for him, and you will stop the movement of the passion; by separating the sorrow from the memory of the evil he did to you through prayer, you will become loving and kind, and you will completely vanish the passion from the soul. But if someone else holds a grudge against you, be generous toward him, be humble, live well with him, and you will deliver him from the passion.

<margin>90.</margin> You will stop the sorrow of the envious person with effort. For he considers your success to be his own misfortune. It is not possible to stop it otherwise unless you hide the success. But if the success benefits many,

<column-break/>

yet causes him sorrow, which side will you disregard? It is necessary, then, to seek the benefit of the many, but as much as possible, do not neglect the envious person. Do not be carried away by the wickedness of the passion, as if to take vengeance not on the passion, but on the one suffering from it. Rather, through humility, consider him superior to yourself, and in every time, place, and matter, prefer him. You can stop your own envy if you rejoice with the one you envy in the things he rejoices in, and if you are saddened in the things he is saddened by, fulfilling the word of the Apostle: 
> *To rejoice with those who rejoice, and to weep with those who weep.* <note>Romans 12:15</note>

<margin>91.</margin> Our mind <note>original: "nous" — the highest faculty of the human soul, the "eye of the heart"</note> is in the middle of two things, each performing its own work: one toward virtue and the other toward vice—that is, an Angel and a demon. The mind has the authority and power to choose which it wishes to follow or to resist.

<margin>92.</margin> The holy powers urge us toward what is good; our natural seeds of virtue and a good will also help us. But the attacks of the demons are supported by the passions and a wicked will.

<margin>93.</margin> Sometimes God Himself, dwelling within, teaches the pure mind; sometimes the holy powers suggest good things; and sometimes it is the nature of things when they are rightly contemplated.

<margin>94.</margin> The mind that has been deemed worthy of knowledge <note>original: "gnōseōs"</note> must keep its thoughts regarding things dispassionate, its contemplations <note>original: "theōrēmata"</note> secure, and its state of prayer unclouded <note>original: "atholōton" — literally "not muddy" or clear</note>. It cannot, however, always keep these from the physical vapors of the flesh when it is smoked by the plots of the demons.

<margin>95.</margin> We are not angry for all the same things that make us sorrowful. For the things that produce sorrow are more numerous than those that produce anger. For example: this thing was broken, that thing was lost; so-and-so died. For such things we only feel sorrow. But for the rest, we feel both sorrow and anger, when we are in an unphilosophical state.

<margin>96.</margin> When the mind receives thoughts of things, it is naturally reshaped according to each thought. When it contemplates these things spiritually, it is diversely transformed according to each contemplation. But when it comes to be in God, it becomes entirely formless and without shape. For by contemplating the One who is of a single form <note>original: "monoeidē" — uniform or simple</note>, the mind itself becomes of a single form and entirely light-like <note>original: "phōtoeidēs"</note>.

<margin>97.</margin> A soul is perfect when its passionate power...

<header>THE FOURTH CENTURY</header>

<margin>98.</margin>
...power has leaned entirely toward God. That Mind <note>original: "Nous" — the highest faculty of the human soul, often translated as "intellect" or "spiritual eye"</note> is perfect which, through true faith, has come to know the Beyond-Known <note>original: "hyperagnōston" — referring to God’s essence which surpasses all human understanding</note> in a beyond-known way, and has gazed upon His creations in their entirety, and has received from God a comprehensive knowledge of the providence and judgment within them—as much, I say, as is possible for human beings.

# BY THE SAME AUTHOR
## THE FOURTH CENTURY

<margin>1.</margin>
First, the Mind wonders when it considers the divine infinity in all its aspects, and that unfathomable and much-desired sea. Second, it is struck with amazement at how He brought the existence of all beings into being out of nothing. But just as there is no limit to His greatness, so there is no finding out of His wisdom.

<margin>2.</margin>
For how could one not wonder while beholding that boundless sea of goodness, a sea beyond all amazement? Or how could one not be ecstatic when considering how and from where both the rational and intellectual essence <note>original: "ousia" — substance or being</note> came to be, as well as the four elements from which bodies are made, since no matter pre-existed their birth? What kind of power was that which, being moved into action, brought these things into existence? But the children of the Greeks <note>original: "Hellēnōn paides" — a common patristic reference to pagan philosophers, particularly Neoplatonists</note> do not accept this, being ignorant of that all-powerful goodness and its effective wisdom and knowledge which is beyond the mind.

<margin>3.</margin>
Since God exists as the Creator from eternity, He creates when He wills, by His co-essential <note>original: "homoousiō" — of the same substance; a term usually applied to the Trinity</note> Word and Spirit, through His infinite goodness. And do not ask: "For what reason did He create now, if He has always been good?" For I tell you that the unsearchable wisdom of the infinite essence does not fall under human knowledge.

<margin>4.</margin>
The Creator of all things, when He willed, gave essence to and brought forth the knowledge of beings which pre-existed in Himself from eternity. For it is absurd to doubt concerning the Almighty God whether He is able to give essence to something whenever He wills.

<margin>5.</margin>
Seek the cause for which God created; for that is a matter of knowledge. But as for the *how* and *why*

<column-break/>

<margin>99.</margin>
Time is divided into three parts. Faith extends along all three divisions <note>Faith relates to the past (creation), present (grace), and future (the promise)</note>; hope extends to one <note>Hope is directed solely toward the future fulfillment</note>; and love extends to two. Faith and hope last until a certain point; but love, being united to the Beyond-Infinite One into the infinite ages, remains and ever increases. For this reason, love is the greatest of all.

<insert>5. (continued)</insert> only recently, do not seek it; for this does not fall under your mind’s grasp. For of divine things, some are comprehensible and others are incomprehensible to humans. For unbridled contemplation <note>original: "theōria"</note> might perhaps push one over a precipice, as one of the saints has said.

<margin>6.</margin>
Some say that created things co-existed with God from eternity, which is impossible. For how can things that are in every way finite co-exist from eternity with Him who is in every way infinite? Or how are they truly "creations" if they are co-eternal with the Creator? This, however, is the argument of the Greeks, who introduce God as the creator of qualities only, and not of essences. But we, who have known the Almighty God, say that He is the Creator not of qualities, but of essences endowed with qualities. If this is so, then creations have not co-existed with God from eternity.

<margin>7.</margin>
In one sense the Divine and divine things are known, and in another sense they are unknown. They are known by the contemplations surrounding Him <note>referring to God's activities or "energies" in the world</note>, but unknown in the things that pertain to His very self <note>referring to the Divine Essence</note>.

<margin>8.</margin>
Do not seek "habits" or "aptitudes" <note>technical terms in ancient philosophy for acquired traits or capacities</note> in the simple and infinite essence of the Holy Trinity, lest you make it composite like created things; which is an absurd and unlawful thing to imagine concerning God.

<margin>9.</margin>
Only the infinite essence—all-powerful and the creator of all—is simple, of a single form, without quality, peaceful, and without conflict. But all of creation is composite, consisting of essence and accident <note>original: "symbebekotos" — a philosophical term for properties that are not part of the essential nature, such as color or size</note>, and

<summary>This page concludes the Third Century with a meditation on the supremacy of Love over Faith and Hope, then begins the Fourth Century by defending the doctrine of creation from nothing against pagan philosophical views. Maximus emphasizes that while we can know God through His works, His essence and the "why" of creation's timing remain beyond human comprehension.</summary>

<margin>10.</margin> Every intellectual <note>original: "noera" — relating to the Nous or spiritual intellect</note> essence, and every sensory essence, having been brought into being, received powers from God for the perception of existing things. To the intellectual essence, He gave the power of thoughts; to the sensory essence, He gave the senses.

<margin>11.</margin> God is only participated in <note>He is the source that others share in, but He does not need to participate in anything else</note>; but the creation both participates and transmits. It participates in "being," and it transmits "being" alone—though it is one way for the bodily essence and another way for the incorporeal <note>spiritual or immaterial</note> essence.

<margin>12.</margin> The incorporeal essence, through speaking, acting, and being contemplated, transmits "well-being" <note>original: "eu einai" — a technical term in Maximus's philosophy referring to a life of virtue and grace, as opposed to mere existence</note>; but the bodily essence transmits "being" only by being contemplated.

<margin>13.</margin> To always exist <note>original: "aei einai"</note>, or not to exist, regarding the intellectual and rational essence, depends on the will of Him who created all things "very good"; but to be either good or bad by choice depends on the will of the creatures themselves.

<margin>14.</margin> Evil is not observed in the essence <note>the nature or substance</note> of created things, but in their mistaken and irrational movement.

<margin>15.</margin> The soul moves reasonably <note>or "rationally"</note> when its desiring faculty <note>term: "epithymetikon" — the part of the soul responsible for hunger, desire, and yearning</note> is flavored by self-control; when its incensive faculty <note>term: "thymikon" — the part of the soul associated with "spirit," courage, or anger</note> holds fast to love, turning away from hatred; and when its rational faculty <note>term: "logistikon" — the highest part of the human soul that reasons and thinks</note> lives for God through prayer and spiritual contemplation.

<margin>16.</margin> He does not yet possess perfect love, nor a deep knowledge of divine providence, who in a time of trial does not show long-suffering toward the painful things that happen, but rather cuts himself off from the love of his spiritual brothers.

<margin>17.</margin> The goal of divine providence is to unify those who have been scattered in many ways by vice, through right faith and spiritual love. Indeed, the Savior suffered for this: that He might gather into one the children of God who were scattered. Therefore, he who does not endure troublesome things, nor bears painful things, nor waits through distressing things, walks outside of divine love and the goal of providence.

<margin>20.</margin> Do not despise the commandment of love, because through it you will be a son of God; but by transgressing it, you will be found a son of Gehenna <note>a reference to the place of spiritual punishment or "hell"</note>.

<margin>21.</margin> These are the things that separate the love of friends: envying or being envied, causing loss or suffering loss, dishonoring or being dishonored, and thoughts born of suspicion. <margin>26.</margin> Do not judge the man who was a spiritual and virtuous brother yesterday as evil and wicked today, because of the hatred produced in you today through the influence of the evil one. <margin>28.</margin> Do not ruin your usual praise of a brother because of a hidden resentment <note>original: "lypē" — literally "sorrow" or "grief," but in this context, it refers to the pain of a perceived offense or resentment</note> still dwelling within you, by subtly mixing blame into your words during a conversation with other brothers. Instead, use pure praise in the conversation and pray sincerely for him as you would for yourself, so that you may quickly be delivered from destructive hatred.

<margin>29.</margin> Do not say, "I do not hate my brother," while you are actually turning away from the memory of him. Rather, listen to Moses saying: *Do not hate your brother in your mind; you shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.* <note>Quoting Leviticus 19:17</note>

<margin>30.</margin> If a brother happens to be under trial and persists in speaking ill of you, do not be shaken from your state of love, even though the same evil demon is troubling your own mind. You will not be shaken from this state if, when you are insulted, you bless; and when you are slandered, you think kindly of him. This is the way of philosophy according to Christ <note>original: "kata Christon philosophia" — a common Patristic term referring to the lived experience of the Christian life and ascetic discipline rather than academic study</note>; and he who does not walk this path does not dwell with Him.

<margin>31.</margin> Do not consider those who bring you reports that create resentment and hatred toward a brother as being well-intentioned, even if they seem to be telling the truth. Rather, turn away from such people as if they were deadly snakes, so that you may stop them from speaking ill and deliver your own soul from malice.

<margin>32.</margin> Do not wound your brother with words of hidden meaning <note>original: "di' ainigmatōn" — through riddles or insinuations</note>, lest by receiving the same in return from him, you drive the disposition of love away from both of you. Instead, go with loving boldness and rebuke him, so that by resolving the causes of the resentment, you may deliver both of you from turmoil and grief.

<margin>33.</margin> Examine your conscience with all exactness, lest it be your own fault that your brother has not been reconciled. Do not deceive your conscience, for it knows your secrets; it will accuse you at the time of your departure <note>referring to the moment of death</note> and will become a stumbling block to you at the time of prayer.

<margin>34.</margin> In a time of peace, do not remember the things said by a brother during a time of resentment—whether the painful things were said to your face or to someone else about you and you later heard them—lest by entertaining

<margin>35.</margin> A rational soul that nurtures hatred toward a human being cannot be at peace with God, the Giver of the commandments. For He says: *If you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your heavenly Father forgive your trespasses.* <note>Quoting Matthew 6:15</note> If that person does not wish to be at peace, you at least must guard yourself from hatred, praying for him sincerely and not speaking ill of him to anyone.

<margin>36.</margin> The supreme peace of the Holy Angels is maintained by these two dispositions: love toward God and love toward one another. Likewise, this is true for all the saints from the beginning of time. Therefore, it is most beautifully said that *on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.* <note>Quoting Matthew 22:40</note>

<margin>37.</margin> Do not be self-satisfied, and you will not be a hater of your brother; do not be a lover of self <note>original: "philautos" — a technical term in Maximus's thought for "self-love," which he considers the root of all sin</note>, and you will be a lover of God.

<margin>38.</margin> Having chosen to live with spiritual brothers, renounce your own will from the very start. For in no other way will you be able to be at peace, either with God or with those living with you.

<margin>39.</margin> He who has been able to acquire perfect love, and has regulated his whole life according to it, is the one who truly says, "Lord Jesus," in the Holy Spirit.

<margin>40.</margin> Love for God always loves to give wings to the mind for divine conversation; love for neighbor prepares one always to think well of him.

<margin>41.</margin> It belongs to the person who still loves empty glory, or who is attached to some material thing, to be grieved with people over temporary things, or to bear them a grudge, or to have hatred toward them, or to be a slave to shameful thoughts. To a soul that loves God, such things are entirely foreign.

<margin>42.</margin> When you say nothing and do nothing shameful in your mind, and when you bear no grudge against one who has caused you loss or spoke ill of you, and when at the time of prayer you always keep your mind immaterial and formless <note>original: "aylon kai aneideon" — referring to a state of prayer where the mind is not distracted by sensory images or concepts</note>, then know that you have reached the measure of dispassion <note>original: "apatheia" — not "apathy," but a state of being unmoved by disordered passions</note> and of perfect love.

<header>OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS</header>

...of the soul. A sign of deliverance <note>from resentment</note> is no longer bearing a grudge <note>original: "mnesikakein" — literally "remembering evil" or nursing a grievance</note> against the one who has spoken ill or is currently speaking ill of you.

<margin>44.</margin> If you wish to be just, render to each of the parts within you what is worthily due: I mean to the soul and to the body. To the reasoning part <note>original: "logistikon"</note> of the soul, give spiritual readings, contemplations, and prayer; to the spirited part <note>original: "thymikon" — the seat of anger or intense emotion</note>, give spiritual love, which stands opposed to hatred; to the desiring part <note>original: "epithymetikon"</note>, give temperance and self-control; and to the flesh, give food and clothing, only those things which are most necessary.

<margin>45.</margin> The mind acts according to its nature when it keeps the passions <note>original: "pathe" — disordered impulses or attachments</note> in subjection, contemplates the inner principles <note>term: "logoi" — the divine blueprints or reasons for the existence of all created things</note> of beings, and dwells with God.

<margin>46.</margin> Just as health and disease are observed in the body of a living being, and light and darkness in the eye, so virtue and vice are observed in the soul, and knowledge and ignorance in the mind.

<margin>47.</margin> The Christian practices philosophy <note>original: "philosophei" — here meaning the lived ascetic and spiritual discipline rather than academic study</note> in these three areas: in the commandments, in the dogmas, and in faith. The commandments separate the mind from the passions; the dogmas lead it into the knowledge of beings; and faith leads it into the contemplation of the Holy Trinity.

<margin>48.</margin> Some of those who are struggling merely repel passionate thoughts, while others actually cut off the passions themselves. One repels them, for instance, through psalmody, or prayer, or by raising the mind <note>to God</note>, or some other timely distraction; but one cuts off the passions by holding in contempt those very things for which he holds a passionate attachment.

<margin>49.</margin> The things for which we hold passionate attachments are these: for example, a woman, money, gifts, and so forth. One is able to hold a woman in contempt when, after withdrawing <note>from the world</note>, he withers the body as is necessary through self-control. One despises money when he persuades his reason to be content with self-sufficiency in all things. One despises glory when he loves the hidden practice of the virtues, which is visible to God alone. It is the same with other things. The one who holds these things in contempt never falls into hating anyone.

<margin>50.</margin> The one who has renounced physical things—such as a wife, money, and the like—has made the "outer man" a Monk, but not yet the "inner man." But the one who has renounced the passionate thoughts of these things has made the "inner man" a Monk, which

<column-break/>

is the mind. Anyone can easily make the outer man a Monk, if only they wish to; but it is no small struggle to make the inner man a Monk.

<margin>51.</margin> Who then, in this generation, is entirely delivered from passionate thoughts and has been deemed worthy of pure and immaterial prayer—which is the sign of the "inner monk"?

<margin>52.</margin> Many passions are hidden in our souls, but they are only exposed when the objects of those passions appear.

<margin>53.</margin> Someone may not be troubled by passions when the objects are absent, having attained a partial dispassion <note>original: "apatheia" — a state of stillness where one is no longer driven by disordered impulses</note>; but if the objects appear, the passions immediately distract the mind.

<margin>54.</margin> Do not think you possess perfect dispassion when the object is not present. But when the object appears and you remain unmoved—both toward the thing itself and the subsequent memory of it—then know yourself to have stepped within its boundaries. Even so, do not become complacent; for virtue, when practiced over time, puts the passions to death, but when neglected, it rouses them again.

<margin>55.</margin> The one who loves Christ certainly imitates Him to the best of his power. For instance, Christ did not cease from doing good to people; when they were ungrateful and blasphemed Him, He was long-suffering; and when He was beaten and murdered by them, He endured it, reckoning no evil against anyone at all. These three things are the works of love toward one's neighbor. Without them, the one who says he loves Christ or will attain His Kingdom deceives himself. For He says: *Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father.* <note>Quoting Matthew 7:21</note> And again: *The one who loves me will keep my commandments,* <note>Quoting John 14:15</note> and so forth.

<margin>56.</margin> The whole purpose of the Savior's commandments is to free the mind from lack of self-control and from hatred, and to lead it to the love of Him and of one's neighbor; from these is born the light of holy, active knowledge.

<margin>57.</margin> When you have been deemed worthy of some partial knowledge from God, do not neglect love and self-control. For these, by cleansing the passionate part of the soul, always prepare the way to knowledge for you.

<margin>58.</margin> The way to knowledge is dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"</note> and humility; without these, no one will see the Lord.

<summary>This page defines the "inner monk" as one who has renounced passionate thoughts in the mind, rather than just physical possessions. Maximus explains that true spiritual health requires balancing the soul's reasoning, emotional, and desiring parts through the imitation of Christ's long-suffering love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Fourth Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor’s Chapters on Love. Following the previous page, which outlined the tripartite nature of the soul and the balance between the mind and the flesh, Maximus now focuses on the necessity of uniting knowledge with love to avoid the pitfalls of spiritual pride.</meta>

### THE FOURTH CENTURY

<margin>59.</margin> Since "knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" <note>quoting 1 Corinthians 8:1</note>, join love to knowledge, and you will be free of pride <note>original: "atyphos" — literally "without smoke" or vanity</note> and a spiritual builder, building up both yourself and all who draw near to you.

<margin>60.</margin> Love follows from this: because it does not envy, it is not embittered toward those who are envious; it does not boastfully display what is envied, nor does it think it has already reached the goal; and it admits its ignorance of things it does not know without blushing. In this way, love makes the mind humble and prepares it to always progress in knowledge.

<margin>61.</margin> It is natural for conceit <note>original: "oiesis" — a high opinion of oneself or self-delusion</note> and envy to accompany knowledge, especially at the beginning. Conceit arises only from within; but envy arises both from within and from without. It is internal toward those who possess knowledge, and external from those who are ignorant of it. Therefore, love overturns all three: conceit, because it is not puffed up; internal envy, because it is not jealous; and external envy, because it is long-suffering and kind. It is necessary, then, for one who has knowledge to also acquire love, so that he may keep his mind unhurt in all circumstances.

<margin>62.</margin> He who has been deemed worthy of the gift of knowledge, yet holds grief, or a grudge, or hatred against any person, is like one who pierces his own eyes with thorns and briars. For this reason, knowledge absolutely requires love.

<margin>63.</margin> Do not direct your whole effort <note>original: "cholēn" — literally "gall" or "bile," used here metaphorically for one's intense focus or "whole heart"</note> toward the flesh, but define for it a discipline according to its strength, and turn your whole mind toward inner things. For "bodily exercise is of little profit, but godliness is profitable for all things" <note>quoting 1 Timothy 4:8</note>, and so forth.

<margin>64.</margin> He who unceasingly occupies himself with inner things becomes self-controlled, long-suffering, kind, and humble. Not only this, but he also contemplates, speaks of God <note>original: "theologei"</note>, and prays. And this is what the Apostle means by "walk by the Spirit" <note>quoting Galatians 5:16</note>, and so forth.

<margin>65.</margin> He who does not know how to travel the spiritual path takes no care for passionate thoughts, but directs his whole effort toward the flesh. He either gluttonizes and lives wantonly, or he is grieved and angered and bears grudges—and from these things his mind is darkened; or else he practices asceticism immoderately and muddies his own understanding.

<column-break/>

<margin>66.</margin> Scripture does not abolish anything given to us by God for our use; rather, it restrains immoderation and corrects irrationality. For example, it does not forbid eating, nor the procreation of children, nor the possession of money and its proper management; but it does forbid gluttony, fornication, and the like. It does not even forbid the thinking of these things, for they were created for this purpose; rather, it forbids the thinking of them with passion <note>term: "empathōs" — thinking with a disordered emotional attachment or lust</note>.

<margin>67.</margin> Some of the things we do for God's sake are done according to commandment, while others are not by commandment but are, so to speak, a voluntary offering. For example, according to commandment, we are to love God and our neighbor, to love our enemies, not to commit adultery, nor to murder, and the rest; if we transgress these, we are condemned. But not by commandment are virginity, celibacy <note>original: "agamia"</note>, voluntary poverty <note>original: "aktemosyne"</note>, withdrawal <note>original: "anachoresis" — the act of a hermit retreating from the world</note>, and so forth. These are gifts, so that if we are unable to fulfill some of Christ's commandments due to weakness, we may appease our good Master through these offerings.

<margin>68.</margin> He who honors celibacy or virginity must necessarily have his "loins girt" and his "lamp burning" <note>alluding to Luke 12:35</note>: the loins through self-control, and the lamp through prayer, contemplation, and spiritual love.

<margin>69.</margin> Some of the brethren think they are devoid of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Because of their negligence in practicing the commandments, they do not realize that he who has unadulterated faith in Christ possesses all the divine gifts within himself in summary. But since we are far from an active love for Him because of our laziness—the very thing that would reveal to us the divine treasures within—we naturally think ourselves devoid of divine gifts.

<margin>70.</margin> If Christ dwells in our hearts through faith, according to the divine Apostle, and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Him <note>referencing Ephesians 3:17 and Colossians 2:3</note>, then all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in our hearts. They are revealed to the heart in proportion to each person's purification through the commandments.

<margin>71.</margin> This is the treasure hidden in the field of your heart <note>referencing Matthew 13:44</note>, which you have not yet found because of your laziness. For if you had found it, surely you would...

<summary>Maximus explains that knowledge without love leads to conceit and envy, while spiritual treasures (wisdom and Christ Himself) are already hidden within the heart, waiting to be revealed through the active practice of the commandments and purification of the passions.</summary>
<keywords>knowledge vs love, conceit, envy, asceticism, commandments vs voluntary gifts, inner treasure, indwelling of Christ, purification</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Fourth Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor’s Chapters on Love. It follows a passage discussing how the misuse of knowledge can be like blinding oneself with thorns, distracting the believer from the "field" of spiritual labor.</meta>

### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...you have sold everything and bought this field <note>a reference to the Parable of the Pearl of Great Price in Matthew 13:44-46</note>; but now, leaving the field, you attend to things around the field, in which nothing else is found except thorns and thistles.

<margin>72.</margin> For this reason the Savior says: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* <note>Matthew 5:8</note> They will see Him and the treasures within Him then, when they have purified themselves through love and self-control <note>original: "egkrateia" — disciplined restraint over one's impulses</note>; and they will see Him all the more as they intensify their purification.

<margin>73.</margin> For this reason He says again: *Sell your possessions and give alms, and behold, all things will be clean for you.* <note>Luke 11:41</note> This is for those who no longer spend their time on matters concerning the body, but hasten to purify the mind—which the Lord calls the "heart"—from hatred and lack of restraint. For these things defile the mind and do not allow it to see Christ, who dwells in it through the grace of Holy Baptism.

<margin>74.</margin> Scripture calls the virtues "ways"; and love is established as the greatest of all virtues. For this reason the Apostle <note>St. Paul the Apostle</note> said: *And yet I show you a still more excellent way* <note>1 Corinthians 12:31</note>, as a way that persuades one to look down upon material things and to prefer nothing transitory over things eternal.

<margin>75.</margin> Love for God opposes desire <note>original: "epithymia" — often translated as lust or misplaced craving</note>, for it persuades the mind to exercise self-control over pleasures. Love for one's neighbor opposes anger <note>original: "thymos" — the "spirited" or "incensive" faculty of the soul</note>, for it causes one to look down upon fame and money. And these are the "two denarii" <note>silver coins</note> which the Savior gave to the innkeeper <note>in the Parable of the Good Samaritan, Luke 10:35</note> so that he might take care of you. But do not appear ungrateful by joining with the robbers <note>the passions or demons</note>, lest you be beaten again, and found not merely half-dead, but fully dead.

<margin>76.</margin> Purify your mind from anger, the bearing of grudges, and shameful thoughts; only then will you be able to know the indwelling of God.

<margin>77.</margin> Who enlightened you into the faith of the Holy, Consubstantial, and Adorable Trinity? Or who made known to you the incarnate plan <note>original: "oikonomia" — God's "household management" or plan for salvation</note> of the One of the Holy Trinity? Who taught you the reasons for incorporeal beings <note>angels and souls</note>? Or the truths concerning the origin and the end of the visible world? Or the resurrection from the dead and eternal life? Or the glory of the Kingdom of Heaven and the fearful Judgment? Was it not the grace of Christ dwelling within you?

<column-break/>

This grace is the "pledge" <note>original: "arrhabon" — a down payment or guarantee</note> of the Holy Spirit. What is greater than this grace? What is better than this wisdom and knowledge? What is higher than these promises? If we are idle and negligent, and do not purify ourselves from the passions that defile us and blind our minds—preventing us from seeing the truth of these things more clearly than the sun—let us blame ourselves and not deny the indwelling of grace.

<margin>78.</margin> God, who promised you eternal blessings and gave the pledge of the Spirit in your heart, commanded you to take care of your way of life, so that the "inner man," being freed from the passions, might begin even now to enjoy the blessings to come.

<margin>79.</margin> Having been deemed worthy of these divine and sublime contemplations, take great care of love and self-control, so that by keeping the emotional part of the soul undisturbed, you may have the light of your soul shine without failing.

<margin>80.</margin> Bridle the spirited part <note>anger/energy</note> of the soul with love; wither the desiring part <note>appetite/craving</note> with self-control; and give wings to the rational part with prayer. Thus the light of the mind will never be darkened.

<margin>81.</margin> These are the things that dissolve love: dishonor, financial loss, slander against one's faith or one's life, beatings, wounds, and so forth—whether these happen to the person himself or to any of his relatives or friends. He who dissolves love because of such things has not yet understood the purpose of the commandments of Christ.

<margin>82.</margin> Strive as much as you can to love every person. If you cannot yet do this, at least hate no one. But you cannot even do this unless you look down upon the things of the world.

<margin>83.</margin> Has someone spoken ill of you? Do not hate that person, but hate the slander and the demon that prompted him to speak. If you hate the one who slandered you, you have hated a human being and broken the commandment. What he did in word, you now do in deed. But if you keep the commandment, show the works of love: help him in any way you can, so that you might deliver him from the evil.

<margin>84.</margin> Christ does not want you to hold any hatred toward any person, nor grief, nor anger, nor a grudge in any way whatsoever, for any reason.

<vocab>Maximus the Confessor, love (agape), self-control (egkrateia), mind (nous), grace (charis), commandments, purification, Trinity, pledge/earnest (arrhabon)</vocab>

<summary>In this passage, Maximus the Confessor explains that spiritual knowledge requires a pure heart, achievable only through the balance of love and self-control. He uses the Parable of the Good Samaritan to illustrate how love for God and neighbor protects the soul from the "robbers" of passion and resentment.</summary>
<keywords>love, self-control, purification of the mind, Holy Trinity, Baptismal grace, Good Samaritan allegory, forgiveness, passions, inner man</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Fourth Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor’s Chapters on Love. It transitions from discussing the purification of the mind to the practical and spiritual challenges of maintaining love amidst slander, trials, and the mystery of God's providence.</meta>

<page-num>231</page-num>
->### THE FOURTH CENTURY<-

<margin>85.</margin> Many of us are talkers, but few are doers. Nevertheless, no one should distort the word of God through their own negligence. Instead, one should confess their own weakness while not concealing God’s truth. We must do this so that we do not become' liable twice over—once for breaking the commandments, and again for misinterpreting the word of God.

<margin>86.</margin> Love and self-control <note>original: "egkrateia" — the disciplined mastery over one's impulses and desires</note> free the soul from the passions <note>irrational or harmful impulses that cloud the mind</note>. Reading and spiritual contemplation <note>original: "theoria" — the focused gaze of the mind on divine truths</note> deliver the mind from ignorance. Finally, the state of prayer presents the mind to God Himself.

<margin>87.</margin> When the demons see us despising the things of this world—so that we do not come to hate people for the sake of material things and thus fall away from love—they then stir up slanders against us. They do this so that, being unable to bear the grief of the false accusations, we might be provoked into hating those who slandered us.

<margin>88.</margin> There is no pain of the soul heavier than slander, whether one is slandered regarding their faith or their conduct of life. No one can look down upon this except the person who looks to God alone. Such a person is like Susanna <note>The heroine from the biblical Book of Susanna, who was falsely accused of adultery and faced death before being vindicated by God</note>, who found in God the only power able to rescue her from distress, just as He rescued her then. God is able both to convince people of the truth—as He did for her—and to comfort the soul with hope.

<margin>89.</margin> To the extent that you pray from your soul for the one who slandered you, to that same extent God will reassure those who were scandalized by the rumors.

<margin>90.</margin> By nature, God alone is good; and by choice <note>original: "gnome" — the faculty of will or intention</note>, only the one who imitates God is good. For it is the aim of Him who is good by nature to unite the wicked to Himself so that they may become good. For this reason, when He is reviled by them, He blesses; when persecuted, He endures; when slandered, He encourages; when murdered, He prays for them. He does everything so that He does not fall away from the goal of love—which is God Himself.

<margin>91.</margin> The commandments of the Lord teach us to use "middle things" <note>original: "mesois pragmasin" — things like wealth, health, or reputation which are morally neutral in themselves and depend on how they are used</note> with right reason. The reasonable use of these middle things purifies the state of the soul; a pure state of soul gives birth to dispassion <note>original: "apatheia" — a state of inner peace and freedom from the control of the passions</note>; and from dispassion is born perfect love.

<margin>92.</margin> A person does not yet possess dispassion if they are unable to overlook the fault of a friend—whether it is a real fault or only

<column-break/>

one that seems to be real—during a time of trial or conflict. For when the passions lying deep in the soul are stirred up, they blind the intellect and do not allow it to see the rays of truth, nor to distinguish the better from the worse. Therefore, such a person has not yet acquired perfect love, which "casts out the fear" of judgment.

<margin>93.</margin> There is no price high enough for a faithful friend, because he considers his friend's misfortunes as his own and suffers with him even unto death, sharing in his hardships.

<margin>94.</margin> Many are the friends who stand by in times of prosperity; but in times of trial, you will find barely one.

<margin>95.</margin> We must love every person from the depths of the soul, but we must place our hope in God alone and serve Him with all our strength. For as long as He preserves us, all our friends cherish us and all our enemies are powerless against us. But when He abandons us, all our friends turn away from us and all our enemies prevail against us.

<margin>96.</margin> There are four general ways in which God "abandons" or withdraws from us: 
1. The "providential" abandonment <note>original: "oikonomike" — related to the "economy" or divine plan of salvation</note>, as happened with the Lord, so that through His apparent abandonment the abandoned ones might be saved. 
2. For the purpose of testing, as with Job and Joseph, so that one might be revealed as a pillar of courage and the other as a pillar of self-restraint. 
3. For paternal correction, as with the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note>, so that by remaining humble he might preserve the excellence of grace. 
4. By way of rejection, as with the Jews, so that by being punished they might be moved toward repentance. 
All these ways are for our salvation and are full of divine goodness and love for humanity.

<margin>97.</margin> Only those who are strict keepers of the commandments and true initiates into the mysteries of God’s judgments do not abandon their friends when those friends are being tested by God's permission. Those who despise the commandments and are uninitiated into divine judgments enjoy their friend's company in times of prosperity, but when that friend suffers in a time of trial, they abandon him. Sometimes they even take the side of his enemies.

<margin>98.</margin> The friends of Christ love everyone sincerely, yet they are not loved by everyone. The friends of the world, however, are not loved by everyone either. The friends of Christ maintain the continuity of love until the end; but the friends of the world only until...

<summary>This page explores the nature of true friendship and love, emphasizing that slander and trials are tests that reveal the soul's state. Maximus details how dispassion (apatheia) leads to perfect love and explains the four ways God seemingly withdraws from humans to facilitate their spiritual growth.</summary>

<margin>99.</margin> A faithful friend is a strong shelter; for when a friend is prospering, he is a good counselor and a soul-mate <note>original: "sympsychos" — sharing the same soul or mind</note> coworker; and when a friend is suffering, he is a most genuine helper and a most sympathetic protector.

### MAXIMUS
## THE CONFESSOR
#### ON THEOLOGY AND THE INCARNATE DISPENSATION <note>original: "oikonomia" — the plan or "management" of God for the salvation of humanity</note> OF THE SON OF GOD, TO THALASSIUS. 200 CHAPTERS.

### THE FIRST CENTURY <note>A "century" is a collection of 100 spiritual or theological aphorisms.</note>

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "O" featuring floral and scroll patterns.</image-desc> One God, without beginning, incomprehensible, possessing the whole power of being entirely; pushing away every thought of *when* or *how* He is; as He is inaccessible to all and known to none of the things that exist by way of natural manifestation.

<margin>2.</margin> God is not, in Himself, as it is possible for us to know; neither a beginning, nor a middle, nor an end, nor any other thing at all of those that are naturally observed with them; for He is indefinite, and unmoved, and infinite, as being infinitely beyond all essence <term>original: "ousia" — the fundamental substance or "being" of a thing</term>, and power, and energy <term>original: "energeia" — the active operation or manifestation of a thing's nature</term>.

<margin>3.</margin> Every essence, introducing its own limit, is by nature the beginning of the motion observed within it according to its power; but every natural motion toward activity, being conceived after the

<column-break/>

essence, but conceived before the energy, is a middle, as being naturally divided in the middle of both; and every energy, being naturally circumscribed by its own principle <note>original: "logos" — the inner reason or defining purpose</note>, is the end of the movement of the essence that was conceived before it.

<margin>4.</margin> God is not essence, according to the way essence is simply or specifically spoken of, so that He might also be a beginning; nor is He power according to energy simply or specifically spoken of, so that He might also be the end of the movement of the essence conceived before it; but He is an essence-making and super-essential <note>original: "hypereousios" — "above being"; emphasizing that God's nature is beyond all categories of existence</note> Being, and a power-making and beyond-power Foundation; and the active and never-ending habit of all energy; and to speak briefly, the Maker of every essence, and power, and energy, and beginning, and middle, and end.

<meta>Institutional stamp from the University of Crete (ΠΑΝΕΠΙΣΤΗΜΙΟ ΚΡΗΤΗΣ) in the bottom right corner.</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the Chapters on Love with a final exhortation on the nature of Christian love and begins a new work on theology. Maximus defines God as a "super-essential" being who exists beyond the philosophical categories of essence, power, and movement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "First Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor’s "Chapters on Theology and the Incarnate Dispensation." Having introduced the work on the previous page, Maximus here explores the relationship between God, time, eternity, and the human soul.</meta>

<page-num>233</page-num>
<header>THE FIRST CENTURY</header>

<margin>5.</margin> Beginning, middle, and end are the distinguishing marks of divisible periods of time. One might also say, if speaking truly, that they belong even to those things perceived within eternity <note>original: "aion" — refers to the "everlasting" realm or age beyond linear time, yet still created</note>. For while time has its movement measured by number, eternity—having its very existence characterized by a "once" <note>The idea that even the "eternal" realm had a beginning in God's will</note>—undergoes a kind of extension, having received a beginning to its being. If, then, both time and eternity are not without a beginning, much more so are the things contained within them.

<margin>6.</margin> God is uniquely and alone, by his very nature, Truly Being <note>original: "Kyrios estin" — He who sovereignly exists</note>, enclosing within himself the whole of what it means "to be" in every way, as he is even superior to "Being" itself. If this is so, then nothing else that is said "to be" possesses "True Being" in its totality. Therefore, nothing whatsoever is perceived as co-eternal with him that is different in essence—not eternity, not time, nor anything dwelling within them. For "True Being" and "Not-True Being" can never coincide with one another.

<margin>7.</margin> Every beginning, middle, and end has not altogether escaped the category of relationship. But since God is infinitely and endlessly superior to every relationship, he is naturally neither a beginning, nor a middle, nor an end. Nor is he anything else at all among those things where a category of relationship or of "being toward something" can be perceived.

<margin>8.</margin> All created beings are called "intelligible things" <note>original: "noumena" — things grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note>, for they have the principles of the knowledge concerning them as something demonstrable. But God is not named as an "intelligible thing"; rather, he is believed to exist only through the things that are understood. For this reason, nothing of the intelligible world can be compared to him in any way.

<margin>9.</margin> The various forms of knowledge regarding created things have their own natural principles linked to demonstration, by which they naturally undergo limitation. But God is believed to exist only through the principles found in created things. To the pious, he grants a confession and faith that he "Truly Is" as something more certain than any proof. For faith is true knowledge that possesses its principles beyond the need for proof, since it is the very foundation <note>original: "hypostasis" — the underlying reality or substance</note> of things that are beyond mind and reason.

<margin>10.</margin> God is the beginning, middle, and end of all beings, in the sense that he acts upon them but is not acted upon <note>He is the "unmoved mover"</note>; just as with all other names we give him. For he is the beginning as Creator; he is the middle as Provider; and he is the end as the Conclusion. For "from him,"

<column-break/>

it says, "and through him, and to him are all things." <note>A reference to Romans 11:36</note>

<margin>11.</margin> No rational soul is more honorable than another rational soul by its essence. For God, being good, created every soul "in his own image" <note>Genesis 1:27</note> and brought it into being as something self-moving. Each soul, however, according to its own intention, either chooses honor or voluntarily brings dishonor upon itself through its deeds.

<margin>12.</margin> God is the "Sun of Righteousness," as it is written <note>Malachi 4:2</note>, shining the rays of his goodness upon all people simply and without distinction. The soul, however, by its own disposition, is like either wax or clay. If it loves God, it is like wax; if it loves matter, it is like clay. Just as clay is naturally hardened by the sun, while wax is naturally softened, so every soul that loves matter and the world is hardened by God’s admonition, and like Pharaoh, drives itself toward its own destruction. But every soul that loves God is softened like wax, and receiving the divine impressions and characters, it becomes a "dwelling place of God in the spirit." <note>Ephesians 2:22</note>

<margin>13.</margin> The person who has occupied their mind with divine thoughts, and has accustomed their speech to honor the Creator unceasingly with divine hymns, and has sanctified their senses with pure perceptions—such a person has added to the natural beauty of "the image" the goodness of "the likeness" produced by choice <note>The Greek Fathers distinguished "image" (nature) from "likeness" (virtue attained by will)</note>.

<margin>14.</margin> One keeps their soul spotless for God if they compel their intellect to think only of God and his virtues; if they appoint their speech to be a righteous interpreter and announcer of his virtues; and if they teach their senses to perceive the visible world and everything in it with piety, announcing to the soul the majesty of the principles within them.

<margin>15.</margin> God, who freed us from the bitter slavery of the tyrannical demons, granted us humility as the compassionate "yoke of piety." Through humility, every power of the devil is tamed; and every good thing is produced and kept safe from corruption for those who choose it.

<margin>16.</margin> The one who believes, fears; and the one who fears, is humbled; and the one who is humbled, becomes gentle, having acquired a state of stillness from the unnatural movements of anger and desire. The gentle person keeps the commandments; and the...

<meta>Library stamp: ΠΑΝΕΠΙΣΤΗΜΙΟ ΚΡΗΤΗΣ (University of Crete) at bottom right.</meta>

<summary>This page explores the transcendence of God over time and eternity, defining Him as the ultimate source and end of all things. Maximus then discusses how the human soul, though created equal in nature, distinguishes itself through its free choice to either be hardened by "the sun" of God's goodness like clay or softened like wax.</summary>

While the previous page (233) dealt with the nature of God, time, and eternity, this section (starting mid-thought and continuing through aphorisms 17–26) shifts toward the "ascesis" or spiritual discipline required to attain true knowledge, using various Biblical metaphors to illustrate the pitfalls of pride and hypocrisy.</meta>

<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS</header>

...by keeping the commandments, one is purified; the one who is purified is illumined; and the one who is illumined is deemed worthy in the chamber of the Mysteries to rest with the Bridegroom Word <note>original: "nymphios logos" — referring to the mystical union between the soul and Christ, the Word of God</note>.

<margin>17.</margin> Just as a farmer, looking for a suitable place to transplant wild trees, happens upon an unexpected treasure; so too every ascetic who is humble-minded, simple, and whose soul is smooth <note>original: "leios" — a soul free from the "roughness" or "hairiness" of material attachments</note> of material coarseness—like the most blessed Jacob—when asked by the Father about the manner of his knowledge, "How is it that you found it so quickly, my son?" <note>A reference to Genesis 27:20</note> answers by saying: "Because the Lord God delivered it to me." For whenever God delivers to us the wise contemplations of his own wisdom without our own labor, when we did not expect it, let us understand that we have suddenly found a spiritual treasure. For the proven ascetic is a spiritual farmer, transplanting the contemplation of visible things (which is like a wild tree) toward the realm of the intelligible; and finding treasure, he finds the revelation of the wisdom within existing things, granted according to grace.

<margin>18.</margin> When the knowledge of divine contemplations falls suddenly upon the ascetic who did not expect it because of his humility, it breaks the reasoning of the one who seeks this knowledge with labor and pain for the sake of display and does not find it. It generates in the foolish man a vain envy toward his brother, a meditation on murder, and grief for himself, because he does not possess the puffed-up pride that comes from praise.

<margin>19.</margin> Those who seek knowledge with pain and fail to find it, fail either because of unbelief, or perhaps because they are naturally unfit and intend to use it contentiously to exalt themselves against those who do know—just as the people of old did against Moses. To them the Law rightfully says, "certain ones, having forced their way, went up into the mountain, and the Amorite dwelling in that mountain came out and wounded them" <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 1:41-44</note>. For it is necessary that those who put on a pretense of virtue for the sake of display should not only fail while they falsify piety, but should also be wounded by their own conscience.

<margin>20.</margin> He who desires knowledge for display and fails should neither envy his neighbor nor be grieved; but let him make his preparation in one of the neighboring areas, as has been commanded—that is, through practice <note>original: "praxis" — the active life of virtue and labor</note>, first laboring with the body to provide the soul with the readiness for knowledge.

<margin>21.</margin> Those who correctly and with piety approach existing

<column-break/>

beings, and who devise no way of love-for-display, will find the all-bright contemplations of beings coming to meet them, producing in them a most accurate comprehension of themselves. To these the Law says: "Having entered, you shall inherit great and beautiful cities, and houses full of all good things, which you did not build; and hewn cisterns which you did not dig; and vineyards and olive groves which you did not plant" <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 6:10-11</note>. For he who lives not for himself but for God becomes full of all the gifts of grace—which were previously not appearing because of the pressing disturbance of the passions.

<margin>22.</margin> Just as sensation is spoken of in two ways—one according to habit <term>Habit (*hexis*): a stable internal state or disposition that exists even when not being used, like the ability to see while one is asleep</term>, which belongs to us even while we sleep and does not perceive any underlying objects, and is of no use if it does not reach toward activity; the other according to activity <term>Activity (*energeia*): the active exercise of a faculty or power</term>, through which we perceive sensible things—so too knowledge is twofold. One is scientific, collecting the principles <note>original: "logous" — the underlying reasons or inner essences of things</note> of beings according to habit alone; this is of no use if it does not extend toward the activity of the commandments. The other is practical activity, which considers the comprehension itself to be true through the experience of beings.

<margin>23.</margin> The hypocrite, as long as he thinks he is hidden, remains quiet, hunting for the glory that comes from appearing righteous; but when he is caught, he puts forward death-dealing words, thinking to cover his own unseemliness with slanders against others. The Word, having likened such a man to the "brood of vipers" <note>A reference to Matthew 3:7</note> because of his duplicity, commanded him to produce "fruits worthy of repentance." That is, to reshape the hidden disposition of the heart to match the outward ways that are seen.

<margin>24.</margin> Some say that every creature is a "beast" if it is not judged clean by the law of animals in the air, the earth, and the sea, even if it seems to be mild in character; the Word addresses each man according to his own particular passion.

<margin>25.</margin> He who feigns friendship for the purpose of harming his neighbor is a wolf hiding his own wickedness in a sheepskin; whenever he finds a bare character, or a word spoken or done simply according to Christ, he seizes and destroys it—pouring out ten thousand blames upon the words or characters he attacks, acting like a spy upon the freedom of the brothers in Christ.

<margin>26.</margin> He who feigns silence for the sake of villainy, [ga-...]

<summary>In this selection, Maximus the Confessor distinguishes between true spiritual knowledge (gnosis) given by grace to the humble and the "theatrical" knowledge sought by the proud. He uses the Aristotelian distinction between "habit" and "activity" to argue that spiritual knowledge is useless unless it is put into practice through the commandments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "First Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor’s theological chapters. The previous page (234) concluded with a discussion on the ascetic as a "spiritual farmer" and the sudden gift of divine wisdom. This page (numbered 285 in this manuscript) continues these aphorisms, moving from the social conduct of the seeker to the mystical heights of divine illumination and the hierarchy of the spiritual life.</meta>

<page-num>285</page-num>
<header>FIRST CENTURY</header>

...[befo]re <note>The text begins mid-sentence from the previous page.</note>, he crafts a plot against his neighbor; failing in this, he departs, adding further pain to his own existing passion. But he who is silent for the sake of being helpful increases friendship, and he shall depart rejoicing as one who has received a light that dissolves the darkness.

<margin>27.</margin> The one who, in a Council <note>original: "Synedrion" — here referring to a formal gathering or spiritual assembly</note>, rashly interrupts the hearing of words, does not hide the fact that he is sick with a love of glory <note>original: "philodoxia" — a technical term in asceticism for the craving for human approval or vanity</note>. Being captured by this vanity, he puts forward countless courses and detours of arguments, wishing to break the flow of what is being said.

<margin>28.</margin> The wise person, whether teaching or being taught, only wishes to learn and to teach those things that are beneficial. But the person who only *thinks* they are wise, whether asking or being asked, puts forward only the most meddlesome and superfluous matters.

<margin>29.</margin> Whatever good things someone participates in according to the grace of God, they are a debtor to share these generously with others. For He says, "Freely you received, freely give" <note>Matthew 10:8</note>. For the one who hides the gift slanders the Lord as if He were a hard master, using a "sparing of the flesh" to drain away virtue. But the one who sells the truth to enemies, later being caught in his own vanity and unable to bear the shame, hangs himself <note>An allusion to Judas Iscariot</note>.

<margin>30.</margin> Those who still shrink back from the war against the passions, and who fear the sudden attack of invisible enemies, ought to remain silent. That is to say, they should not yet employ the method of "contradiction" <note>original: "antirrhetikos" — the ascetic practice of speaking back to or arguing against demonic thoughts</note> for the sake of virtue. Instead, they should hand over the care of themselves to God through prayer. To such people it is said in the Book of Exodus:
> The Lord will fight for you, and you will be silent. <note>Exodus 14:14</note>
But those who have already seen the destruction of their pursuers <note>A metaphor for the passions, likened to the Egyptians in the Red Sea</note>, and who seek the ways of the virtues for the sake of grateful learning, need only have the ear of their intellect opened. To these He says:
> Hear, O Israel. <note>Deuteronomy 6:4</note>
And finally, for the one who, through purification, intensely desires divine knowledge, a reverent boldness is appropriate; to such a one it will be said:
> Why do you cry out to me? <note>Exodus 14:15</note>
Therefore, for the one to whom silence is commanded because of fear, taking refuge in God is most profitable. For the one commanded to listen, a readiness for the obedience of the commandments is fitting. But for the gnostic <note>original: "gnostikos" — one who has attained spiritual knowledge</note>, it is necessary to cry out unceasingly through petition, both for the turning away of evils and for thanksgiving in the participation of good things.

<margin>31.</margin> A soul can never be extended toward the knowledge of God unless God Himself, employing a "condescension" <note>original: "synkatabasis" — God stooping down to the human level</note>, touches it and leads it up to Himself. For the human mind would never have

<column-break/>

had the strength to run upward so far as to take hold of any divine illumination, if God Himself had not drawn it up—as far as it was possible for a human mind to be drawn up—and enlightened it with divine rays.

<margin>32.</margin> The one who imitates the disciples of the Lord does not refuse, for the sake of the Pharisees, to make a path on the Sabbath through the grain-fields and to pluck the ears of corn. Rather, after "practice" <note>original: "praktike" — the first stage of spiritual life focusing on the virtues</note>, having come to reside in "dispassion" <note>original: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but a state where the passions no longer control the soul</note>, such a one gathers the inner meanings <note>original: "logoi" — the divine blueprints or reasons behind created things</note> of created things, piously nourishing themselves on the divine science of all that exists.

<margin>33.</margin> The one who is merely "faithful" according to the Gospel moves the mountain of his own wickedness through action <note>original: "praxis"</note>, pushing away the former disposition he had toward sensible things which kept him in a state of unstable wandering. But the one who is able to be a "disciple," receiving from the Word the fragments of the "gnostic loaves" with his own hands, feeds thousands. He shows through his actions that the power of the Word is multiplied. And the one who has the strength to be an "Apostle" heals every disease and infirmity, casting out demons—that is, he puts to flight the activity of the passions. He heals the sick by leading those deprived of piety back to the habit of it through hope, and he strengthens those made weak by sluggishness with the word of judgment. For having been commanded to "tread upon snakes and scorpions" <note>Luke 10:19</note>, he wipes out the beginning and the end of sin.

<margin>34.</margin> The Apostle and the Disciple are, of course, also "faithful" (believers). But the Disciple is not necessarily an Apostle, though he is certainly a believer. And the one who is only a "faithful" believer is neither a Disciple nor an Apostle. Nevertheless, through their way of life and through "contemplation" <note>original: "theoria"</note>, the third can be transferred to the rank and dignity of the second, and the second to that of the first.

<margin>35.</margin> Whatever things are created in time and according to time stay still once they are completed, ceasing from their natural growth. But whatever things are worked out in the science of God according to virtue, even when completed, they move again toward further growth. For their ends become the beginnings of other things. For he who has ceased within himself, through the virtues, from the "subsistence of things that perish" during his practical action, has already begun other, more divine formations. For God never ceases from good things, since He has no beginning of them. For just as it is the nature of light to illuminate, so it is the nature of God to do good. Therefore, while the law provides a limit in time for the composition of things in birth and decay...

Following the previous page’s advice on humility and sharing spiritual gifts, Maximus now turns to an allegorical interpretation of Jewish law—specifically the Sabbath, circumcision, and the harvest—viewing them as stages of the soul's journey toward God. This reflects his "mystical exegesis," where physical laws of the Old Testament are revealed as spiritual blueprints for the Christian life.</meta>
