->### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS ###<-

...narrating, the Sabbath is honored through inactivity; but by the Gospel, which introduces the state of the things of the mind <note>original: "noēton" — refers to the "intelligible" realm, things understood by the intellect rather than the senses</note>, it is made radiant through the doing of good works. This is true even if those who do not yet know that the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath, and that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath, become indignant.

<margin>36.</margin>
In the Law and the Prophets, there is "Sabbath," "Sabbaths," and "Sabbath of Sabbaths." Just as there is "circumcision" and "circumcision of circumcision"; and "harvest" and "harvest of harvests," according to the saying: "when you reap your harvest" <note>Leviticus 23:10</note>. The first of these is the completion of practical, natural, and theological philosophy <note>These are the three stages of the spiritual life in Maximus’s system: Ethics (Praktike), Contemplation of Nature (Physike), and Theology/Union (Theologia)</note>. The second is the contribution and enjoyment of "becoming" <note>original: "genesis" — the world of change and creation</note> and the inner principles <note>term: "logoi" — the divine blueprints or reasons for created things</note> according to that becoming. This happens in a threefold way for each of the things mentioned, so that the person of knowledge <note>term: "gnostikos" — here meaning a mature spiritual seeker, not a member of the Gnostic sect</note> may know the principles by which Moses died while observing the Sabbath outside the holy land, while Joshua the son of Nun performed circumcision after crossing the Jordan. Those who inherit the good land offer to God the contribution of the "double harvest," which surpasses all else.

<margin>37.</margin>
Sabbath is the dispassion <note>term: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but freedom from the grip of destructive passions</note> of the rational soul, when it has completely cast off the scars of sin through the practical life.

<margin>38.</margin>
Sabbaths are the freedom of the rational soul, when it has set aside even its natural activity toward the senses through the spiritual contemplation of nature.

<margin>39.</margin>
Sabbath of Sabbaths is the spiritual stillness <note>term: "hesychia" — inner silence or tranquility</note> of the rational soul, when it has withdrawn the mind even from all the more divine principles found in existing things. Through a state of loving ecstasy <note>original: "erotiken ekstasin" — a longing so intense it carries the soul out of its self-centeredness</note>, it has clothed itself entirely in God alone, and through mystical theology has made the mind completely immovable in God.

<margin>40.</margin>
Circumcision is the casting off of the passionate disposition of the soul toward the world of "becoming."

<margin>41.</margin>
Circumcision of circumcision is the complete casting off and removal of even the natural movements of the soul toward "becoming."

<margin>42.</margin>
Harvest is the collection and recognition—performed with true knowledge—of the more spiritual principles regarding virtue and the nature of existing things.

<margin>43.</margin>
Harvest of harvests is the incomprehensible contemplation of God that takes place unknowingly in the mind after 

<column-break/>

the mystical contemplation of things understood by the intellect. This is properly offered by the one who worthily honors the Creator through both visible and invisible creatures.

<margin>44.</margin>
There is also another more spiritual harvest, said to be of God himself; and another more mystical circumcision; and another more hidden Sabbath, in which God, "sabbathing" from his own works, gives rest. This is according to the saying, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few" <note>Matthew 9:37</note>; and "circumcision of the heart in the spirit" <note>Romans 2:29</note>; and "God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works which God began to do" <note>Genesis 2:3</note>.

<margin>45.</margin>
The harvest of God is the dwelling and establishment of the worthy within Him, which takes place at the completion of the ages.

<margin>46.</margin>
Circumcision of the heart in the spirit is the complete removal of natural activities regarding sensory and intellectual things. This occurs through the presence of the Spirit, which immediately and entirely transforms both body and soul toward what is more divine.

<margin>47.</margin>
The Sabbath-rest of God is the return of all created things to Him. At this point, He rests from His natural activity toward them, while inexpressibly performing His own most divine activity. For God ceases from the natural activity within each of the beings—the way each being is naturally moved—whenever each being, having laid hold of divine activity in a proportional way, limits its own natural activity around God Himself.

<margin>48.</margin>
The diligent must investigate what is fitting to understand as the works which God "began" to create, and again those which He did "not begin." For if He rested from all the works which He *began* to do, it is clear He did not rest from those which He did *not begin* to do. Perhaps, then, the works of God which began to exist in time are all existing things that "participate" <note>This is a Platonic/Christian concept where creatures exist only because they share in God's existence</note>—such as the various essences of beings. For they have "non-existence" as something older than their existence. There was once a time when these participating beings did not exist. But the works of God which perhaps did not begin to exist in time are those things that are "participated in," which beings participate in by grace—such as Goodness, and everything that is contained within the principle of Goodness. # FIRST CENTURY #

...all life, and immortality, and simplicity, and immutability, and infinity, and all those things that are contemplated as belonging to His essence. These are also the works of God, yet they did not begin in time. For there was never a "time" when virtue was not; nor any of the other things mentioned. Even if the things that participate in them <note>The "participants" are created beings like humans or angels who possess these qualities by God's gift.</note> have, in themselves, begun to exist in time. For every virtue is without beginning, having no time older than itself, since it has God alone as its eternal progenitor.

<margin>49. Perhaps He is set apart above all.</margin> From all things that exist, both those that participate and those that are participated in, God is set apart infinitely and in an infinite way. For everything that has the "reason of being" <note>original: "logon tou einai" — the fundamental principle of its existence</note> predicated of it is a work of God. Even if one thing has begun to exist in time according to its birth, while another has been implanted in created things by grace—like an innate power that loudly proclaims God, who is present in all things.

<margin>50.</margin> All immortal things, and immortality itself; all living things, and life itself; all holy things, and holiness itself; all virtuous things, and virtue itself; all good things, and goodness itself; and all beings, and being itself—all these are clearly the works of God. But some of these began to exist in time; for there was once a time when virtue, and goodness, and holiness, and immortality did not exist <note>Maximus refers here to these qualities as they exist within the created order; in God, they are eternal, but as created "habits" or "states" in us, they have a beginning.</note>. The things that began in time exist and are named through their participation in those things that did not begin in time. For God is the Creator of all life, immortality, holiness, and virtue; for He is set apart beyond the essence of all things that can be thought or spoken.

<margin>51.</margin> The sixth day, according to the Scriptures, signifies the completion of those things that are under the law of nature. The seventh day describes the limit of the movement of time’s unique character. But the eighth day indicates the manner of a state that is beyond nature and time.

<margin>52.</margin> He who keeps the sixth day according to the Law, fleeing the dominion of the passions that crush the soul in its activity, passes through the sea into the wilderness without fear. He keeps the Sabbath by resting from the passions alone. But he who has crossed the Jordan <note>The crossing of the Jordan represents a deeper spiritual transition than the crossing of the Red Sea; it is the entry into the "Promised Land" of the virtues.</note> and has left behind that state of merely resting from the passions, has entered into the inheritance of the virtues.

<margin>53.</margin> He who keeps the sixth day according to the Gospel, having first put to death the initial movements of sin, attains through the virtues a state of <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but a state where the emotions are no longer disordered by sin</note>, which is a wilderness to all malice. He keeps the Sabbath in his mind, resting even from the bare mental images of the passions. But he who has crossed the Jordan is translated into the region of spiritual knowledge, in which the mind—the temple mystically built by "Peace"—becomes a dwelling place of God in the spirit.

<column-break/>

<margin>54.</margin> He who has completed the sixth day in a divine manner, along with his fitting works and thoughts, and has himself—with God—brought his own works to a good conclusion, has crossed over in his understanding beyond the whole substance of things under nature and time. He has been translated into the mystical contemplation of the ages and eternal things. He keeps the Sabbath in his mind in an unknowable way, through the total abandonment and transcendence of all created things. But he who is also deemed worthy of the eighth day has risen from the dead—that is, from all things after God, I mean both sensible and intelligible things, and words and concepts. He lives the blessed life of God, who alone is truly and properly called and is "Life," since he himself has become God by <term>deification</term> <note>original: "theosis" — the process of becoming "divine" by grace, united with God's own life.</note>.

<margin>55.</margin> The sixth day is the complete fulfillment of the practical activities concerning virtue according to nature. The seventh day is the conclusion and rest of all natural concepts regarding the ineffable knowledge of contemplation. The eighth day is the translation and passage of those who are worthy toward deification. And perhaps, showing this seventh and eighth day more mystically, the Lord called them the "day and hour of completion" <note>Matthew 24:36</note>, as they circumscribe the mysteries and the inner principles of all things. None of the powers of heaven or earth can know these at all before the experience of suffering <note>original: "pathein" — also meaning "to undergo" or "to experience" the transition</note>, except for the blessed Godhead itself who performs them.

<margin>56.</margin> The sixth day signifies the <term>reason of being</term> <note>original: "logos tou einai"</note> of things that exist. The seventh day indicates the manner of the <term>well-being</term> <note>original: "eu einai"</note> of things that exist. But the eighth day suggests the ineffable mystery of the <term>eternal well-being</term> <note>original: "aei eu einai"</note> of things that exist.

<margin>57.</margin> Knowing that the sixth day is a symbol of practical activity, let us fulfill on it every debt of the works of virtue; so that it may be said of us also, "And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good."

<margin>58.</margin> He fulfills the debt of the praised...

# OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS #

...of a good work for God, he who through the body labors for the soul creates the beautiful variety of virtues.

<margin>59.</margin> He who has completed the preparation of the works of righteousness has crossed over to the rest of spiritual contemplation <note>original: "gnostikes theorias" — the stage of spiritual life where one contemplates the inner principles of creation</note>. In this state, having embraced the inner principles of all beings in a manner worthy of God, he rests from the mind's movement regarding those things.

<margin>60.</margin> He who has participated in the seven-fold rest of God <note>The "Seventh Day" or Sabbath rest from labor.</note>—which He took for our sake—will also participate in His "eight-fold" activity through deification <note>term: "theosis" — the process by which a human being becomes united with God's grace, described as the "Eighth Day" of eternal life</note>, which is a mystical rest. From this rest, he himself sees the linen cloths and the napkin that was upon the head lying in the tomb. When anyone like Peter and John <note>A reference to the disciples running to the empty tomb in John 20:3-8.</note> beholds these things, they believe that the Lord has risen.

<margin>61.</margin> Perhaps the "tomb of the Lord" is either this world or the heart of each of the faithful. The "linen cloths" are the inner principles <note>original: "logoi" — the divine blueprints or reasons behind created things</note> of sensible objects together with the various modes of virtue. The "napkin" is the simple and uniform knowledge of intelligible things, along with the theological understanding that is possible for us. Through these things, the Word <note>original: "Logos" — Christ, the Second Person of the Trinity</note> was previously known, for without them, the grasp of what is beyond these things is entirely beyond our capacity.

<margin>62.</margin> Those who bury the Lord honorably will also behold Him risen in glory; but to all those who do not act this way, He remains invisible. For He is no longer able to be "captured" by those who plot against Him, since He no longer possesses the outward veils through which He appeared to allow Himself to be caught by those who wished, and through which He endured suffering for the salvation of all.

<margin>63.</margin> He who buries the Lord honorably is held in respect by all who love God. For he has rightfully rescued the Lord from triumph and reproach, leaving no occasion for blasphemy to the unfaithful regarding His being nailed to the wood <note>The Cross.</note>. But those who placed seals upon the tomb and stationed soldiers there are hateful for their attempt. These are the ones who slander the risen Word as having been stolen—bribing them with money, just as they did the false disciple for his betrayal. I am speaking here of the "showy" or "vainglorious" way of practicing virtue. Thus they buy the soldiers to slander the risen Savior. The spiritual man <note>original: "ho gnostikos" — one who possesses true spiritual knowledge</note> knows the deeper meaning of these sayings. He is not ignorant of how and in how many ways the Lord is crucified, buried, and rises—as if putting to death the passionate 

<column-break/>

thoughts that sit beside the heart <note>Maximus compares the guards at the tomb to the distracting or sinful thoughts that "guard" the heart against spiritual progress.</note> prompted by demons. These are the thoughts that divide the garments of moral beauty as if they were spoils in times of temptation. And he rises by leaping over the "seals" placed upon the soul—the patterns of sins committed through habit or preconception.

<margin>64.</margin> Every lover of money who hypocritically pretends to virtue out of "piety," as soon as he finds the material gain he desires, denies the way of life by which he was previously thought to be a disciple of the Word.

<margin>65.</margin> When you see certain proud people who cannot bear to see their betters praised, and who devise ways to keep the spoken truth from being proclaimed—obstructing it with a thousand temptations and unlawful slanders—consider that the Lord is being crucified and buried by them again. And He is guarded by soldiers and seals. But the Word, turning these obstacles back upon them, rises; appearing more clearly because He was fought against. For He is sharpened, as it were, toward passionlessness through His sufferings. For He is stronger than all things, both being and being called "Truth."

<margin>66.</margin> The mystery of the embodiment <note>original: "ensomatoseos" — the Incarnation of God into a human body</note> of the Word contains the power of all the riddles and types in the Scripture, and the science of all visible creations. He who knows the mystery of the Cross and the Burial knows the inner principles of the things mentioned above. But he who has been initiated into the ineffable power of the Resurrection knows the purpose for which God fundamentally established all things.

<margin>67.</margin> All visible things require a "cross"—that is, a state that holds back the habitual attachment to things acted upon through the senses. And all intelligible things <note>Non-physical concepts or spiritual realities.</note> need a "burial"—that is, the total stillness of the mind's activity regarding them. For when the attachment and the natural activity and movement regarding all things are removed, the Word alone appears, existing in Himself. He appears as if risen from the dead, containing all that comes from Him, yet with nothing having a natural attachment or kinship to Him. For the salvation of those who are saved is by grace, not by nature.

<margin>68.</margin> Ages, times, and places belong to the category of "relative things," without which nothing that is conceived with them can exist. But God is not among "relative things," for He has nothing at all that is conceived alongside Him. If, therefore, the...

<meta>This page continues the "First Century of Various Chapters" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The previous page discussed how the person who labors for God creates a variety of virtues and begins to move from active work to spiritual contemplation. This page explores the final "end" of the soul in God, the symbolic meaning of figures in the Passion of Christ, and the spiritual stages of the ascetic life.</meta>

### FIRST CENTURY ###

...the inheritance of those who are worthy is God Himself. He who is deemed worthy of this grace will be beyond all ages, and times, and places, having God Himself as his place, according to that which is written: *Be to me a God who protects, and a fortified place to save me.* <note>Psalm 71:3 (Septuagint 70:3). Maximus interprets "place" not as a physical location but as the divine presence itself.</note>

<margin>69.</margin> The "end" <note>term: "telos" — the final goal or purpose of a thing's existence</note> has absolutely nothing in common with the "middle" <note>term: "mesotes" — the intermediate state or the process of moving toward a goal</note>; otherwise, it would not be the end. The "middle" consists of everything that comes after the beginning but falls short of the end. If, therefore, all ages, times, and places—along with everything that can be conceived alongside them—exist after God (who is the Beginning without a beginning), and if they fall far behind Him, then they are no different from the "middle" state. Since God is the "end" of those who are saved, those who reach this ultimate "end" will see nothing of the "middle" state remaining in their contemplation.

<margin>70.</margin> The entire world, being bounded by its own inner principles <note>term: "logoi" — the divine blueprints or reasons inherent in created things</note>, is called both "place" and "age" for those who dwell within it. It possesses modes of contemplation suited to its nature, which are capable of instilling in us a partial understanding of the all-encompassing wisdom of God. As long as people use these things for understanding, they cannot be without the "middle" or without partial comprehension. But when that which is "in part" is abolished by the appearance of "perfection," then all "mirrors" and "riddles" pass away <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:10-12.</note>. When the Truth arrives "face to face," the one who is being saved and perfected according to God will exist beyond all worlds, ages, and places in which he was previously disciplined like a child.

<margin>71.</margin> Pilate is a type of the natural law; the crowd of Jews represents the written law. Therefore, the person who does not rise above these two laws through faith cannot receive the Truth that is beyond nature and <margin>\* perhaps: law</margin> reason. Instead, such a person will inevitably crucify the Word—either as a Jew, considering the Gospel a "stumbling block," or as a Greek, considering it "foolishness." <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 1:23. "Greek" here refers to the "natural law" of the philosophers.</note>

<margin>72.</margin> When you see Herod and Pilate becoming friends with one another for the sake of killing Jesus, understand this to be the convergence of the demon of fornication and the demon of vainglory. They agree with each other to put to death the "word of virtue and knowledge." For the vainglorious demon, by feigning spiritual knowledge, passes the person <margin>\* perhaps: purity</margin> over to the demon of fornication; and the demon of fornication, by feigning \* purity,

<column-break/>

passes the person back to the demon of vainglory. This is why it says that Herod, having dressed Jesus in a "splendid robe," sent Him back to Pilate. <note>Luke 23:11-12. Maximus sees the "splendid robe" as the outward show of false virtue or vainglory.</note>

<margin>73.</margin> It is good not to allow the mind to attend to the flesh and its passions. For it says, "they do not gather figs from thorns"—that is, virtue from the passions—"nor grapes from a bramble bush"—that is, the joy of spiritual knowledge from the flesh. <note>Matthew 7:16.</note>

<margin>74.</margin> The ascetic who is tested through the endurance of temptations, purified through bodily discipline, and perfected through the diligent study of high contemplations, is deemed worthy of divine consolation. For it says: *The Lord has come from Sinai*—that is, from temptations; *and He appeared to us from Seir*—that is, from bodily labors; *and He hastened from Mount Paran with ten thousands of Kadesh*—that is, from the "mountain of faith" with ten thousands of "holy knowledges." <note>Deuteronomy 33:2. Maximus provides an allegorical interpretation of these place names: Sinai (trials), Seir (labor), and Paran/Kadesh (faith and holiness).</note>

<margin>75.</margin> Herod represents the mindset of the flesh; Pilate represents sense-perception; Caesar represents the objects of the senses; and the Jews represent the thoughts of the soul. Whenever the soul, through ignorance, attaches itself to sensible objects, it betrays the Word to "sense-perception" to be put to death. It confirms the kingdom of corruptible things over itself by its own confession. For the Jews said: *We have no king but Caesar.* <note>John 19:15.</note>

<margin>76.</margin> In another sense, Herod occupies the place of the "activity of the passions"; Pilate represents the "deceptive habit" <note>original: "hexis" — a settled disposition or state of mind</note> regarding them; Caesar represents the "dark ruler of this world"; and the Jews represent the soul. Therefore, when the soul bows down to the passions and hands over virtue to the power of a "habit of wickedness," it clearly denies the kingdom of God and transfers itself to the destructive tyranny of the devil.

<margin>77.</margin> The subjugation of the passions is not enough for the soul to reach spiritual joy unless it also acquires the virtues through the fulfillment of the commandments. For it says: *Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you*—that is, the operations of the passions—*but that your names are written in heaven* <note>Luke 10:20.</note>—having been transferred to the state of "dispassion" <note>term: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but a state of being free from the control of disordered passions</note> through the grace of adoption found in the virtues.

<margin>78.</margin> The wealth of virtues acquired through practice is absolutely necessary for the person of knowledge <note>original: "gnostikos" — one who seeks or possesses deep spiritual knowledge</note>. For he says: *He who has a purse*—that is, spiritual knowledge...

<meta>This page continues the spiritual teachings of St. Maximus the Confessor, moving from general advice on the spiritual life to specific allegorical interpretations of the Gospels. It explores the symbolic meaning of numbers—specifically 30 and 38—and concludes with a philosophical reflection on the limitations of human thought when approaching the simplicity of God.</meta>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS #

...spiritual; let him likewise take a knapsack; that is, the abundance of virtues that richly nourishes the soul. He who does not have a purse and knapsack—clearly meaning spiritual knowledge <note>term: "gnosis" — direct, experiential knowledge of divine things</note> and virtue—let him sell his garment and buy a sword: let him eagerly give up, he says, his own flesh to the labors of the virtues, and let him wisely wield, for the sake of the peace of God, the war against the passions and the demons; or rather, the habit that discerns, through the Word of God, the worse from the better.

<margin>109.</margin> The Lord appears when he is thirty years old, teaching those who can see through this number the hidden mysteries concerning Himself. For the number thirty, when understood mystically, introduces the Lord as the Creator and Provider of time, of nature, and of the intelligible things <note>term: "noeta" — things perceived by the mind or spirit rather than the physical senses</note> that are beyond visible nature. He is the Creator of time through the number seven (for time is measured by the week); of nature through the number five (for nature is divided fivefold through the senses); of the intelligibles through the number eight (for the origin of the intelligibles is beyond the measured cycle of time); and He is the Provider through the number ten—both because of the holy ten commandments which lead men toward the good, and because the Lord's name <note>The Greek letter Iota, the first letter of "Iesous" (Jesus), represents the number 10.</note> mystically begins with this letter since He became man. Thus, by joining five, seven, eight, and ten, He fulfills the number thirty. Therefore, the one who knows how to follow the Lord well as his leader will not be ignorant of the principle <note>term: "logos" — the underlying reason or divine purpose</note> by which he himself will appear as "thirty years old," being able to preach the Gospel of the Kingdom. For when he has blamelessly created a world of active virtues like a visible nature, and has kept the cycle of his soul (like time) from being altered by the occurrence of opposites, and has harvested knowledge through contemplation without stumbling, and has been able to providently instill this same habit in others—then he himself, whatever his physical age may be, is thirty years old in the spirit, manifesting the energy of his own goodness in others.

<margin>80.</margin> The one who is paralyzed by the pleasures of the body is neither active toward virtue nor easily moved toward knowledge. Therefore, he has "no man"—that is, no wise reasoning—to cast him into the pool <note>A reference to the Paralytic at Bethesda in John 5:1-9.</note> when the water is stirred. This "pool" is the virtue that is receptive to knowledge, which heals every disease; unless, perhaps, through laziness, the sick man delays and is preceded by someone else who prevents his healing. For this reason, he lies down in his sickness for thirty-eight years. For the one who does not behold the visible creation for the glory of God, and does not piously raise his mind to the intelligible nature, naturally remains sick for the number of years mentioned. For the number thirty, when taken naturally, signifies sensible nature <note>term: "aisthete physis" — the world perceived by the physical senses</note>; just as when viewed practically, it signifies active virtue. The number eight, when understood mystically, indicates the intelligible nature of incorporeal beings; just as when viewed through knowledge, it signifies all-wise theology. If one is not moved toward God by these, he remains paralyzed, until the Word comes and teaches him the shortcut to healing, saying: *Rise, take up your bed and walk.* <note>John 5:8. Maximus interprets this as a command to transcend the flesh.</note> This means: raise the mind from the pleasure that holds it, carry the body on the shoulders of the virtues, and go to the "house"—clearly meaning heaven. For it is better for the worse part (the body) to be carried toward virtue on the shoulders of action by the better part (the mind), than for the better part to be carried toward pleasure by the worse part through self-indulgence.

<column-break/>

<margin>81.</margin> Until we have purely transcended both our own essence <note>term: "ousia" — the fundamental nature or "being" of a person</note> and the essence of all things that exist after God in our thinking, we have not yet attained the habit of immutability in virtue. But when this dignity is achieved by us through love, then we shall know the power of the divine promise. For we must believe that the steadfast settlement of those who are worthy is there, where the mind, having gone ahead through love, has rooted its own power. For the one who has not gone out of himself and out of all things that can be conceived in any way, and has not established himself in the silence that is beyond intellection <note>term: "noesis" — the act of mental or spiritual perception</note>, cannot be entirely free from change.

<margin>82.</margin> Every intellection implies multiplicity, or at the very least, a duality. For it is a relationship between certain extremes, joining together the one who thinks and that which is thought. Neither of these is able to preserve absolute simplicity. For the one who thinks is a subject, certainly possessing the power of thinking alongside it. And that which is thought is also a subject...

<summary>Maximus uses biblical numerology (the numbers 30 and 38) to explain stages of spiritual maturity and the healing of the soul. He argues that true stability in virtue requires the mind to transcend all created things and enter a state of divine silence beyond human thought.</summary>
<keywords>thirty years old, numerology, paralytic, Bethesda, virtue, knowledge, transcendence, simplicity, intellection, Maximus the Confessor</keywords>

<page-num>241</page-num>

-> # FIRST HUNDRED # <-

...what everything is, either having the power of being understood conceived along with it in a subject, or having the essence of which it is a power existing beforehand. For none of the things that exist is in its entirety a simple essence or intellection <note>term: "noesis" — the act of the mind or intellect</note> in and of itself, such that it is also an indivisible unity. But whether we call God "essence," He does not naturally have the power of being understood conceived along with Him (lest He be composite); or whether we call Him "intellection," He does not naturally have an underlying essence capable of receiving that intellection. Rather, God is Himself intellection according to essence; He is entirely intellection, and He alone is essence according to that intellection, and entirely essence, and that alone. He is entirely beyond essence, because He is also an indivisible, impartible, and simple unity <note>term: "monad" — a single, indivisible unit</note>. Therefore, whoever possesses intellection in any way has not yet departed from duality <note>term: "dyad" — the number two, representing the split between the thinker and the object of thought</note>; but he who has utterly left this behind has come to be, in a certain measure, in the unity, having transcendently set aside the power of thinking.

<margin>83.</margin> In the many, there is otherness, unlikeness, and difference; but in God, who is properly one and alone, there is identity. There is only simplicity and likeness. It is not safe, therefore, to embark upon contemplations concerning God before one has come to be outside of the "many." Moses demonstrates this by pitching the tabernacle of his mind outside the camp, and only then conversing with God. For to attempt to speak of the Unspeakable with the spoken word <note>note: original "logos prophorikos" — the external, uttered word</note> is dangerous, because the spoken word is a duality, or even more. But to contemplate "That Which Is" with the soul alone, without voice, is the most powerful way; for it stands according to the indivisible unity, and not among the many. For the High Priest, who was commanded to enter the Holy of Holies within the veil only once a year, teaches that only the one who has passed through the material world and the "Holy Places"—and has come within the Holy of Holies—should approach the perceptions of God. That is to say, the one who has passed beyond the entire nature of both sensible and intelligible things, and has become pure, unclad, and naked of every characteristic of created existence, should apply his mind to the conceptions of God.

<margin>84.</margin> The great Moses, having pitched his own tabernacle outside the camp—that is, having established his will and his mind outside of visible things—begins to worship God; and entering into the dark cloud <note>note: original "gnophos" — the divine darkness where God dwells, signifying His unknowability</note>, the formless and immaterial place of knowledge, he is initiated there into the most sacred rites.

<column-break/>

<margin>85.</margin> <margin>Perhaps "in the body" is missing.</margin> The "dark cloud" is the formless, immaterial, and bodiless state; or rather, it is the knowledge that contains the archetypes <note>term: "paradeigmata" — the original patterns or blueprints of all created things</note> of all beings. The one who comes within this, like another Moses, understands immortal things while [in a] mortal <insert>body</insert> <note>original: "physei thneto" — by mortal nature</note> by nature. Through this state, having painted the beauty of divine virtues within himself—like a painting that faithfully imitates the image of the archetypal beauty—he descends, offering himself as a model for those who wish to imitate virtue. In this, he demonstrates the philanthropy and ungrudging nature of the grace he has received.

<margin>86.</margin> Those who pursue the philosophy according to God without blemish find a very great profit from the science found within it: that the will no longer changes along with circumstances, but with stable firmness, they eagerly set their hand to all things that harmonize with the reason of virtue.

<margin>87.</margin> Having been baptized in Christ through the Spirit, we receive a first incorruptibility according to the flesh; but we expect the final incorruptibility according to Him in the Spirit through the increase of good works and the death of our own will—provided we keep the first one spotless. In this state, no one who possesses these attained goods fears their loss.

<margin>88.</margin> God, wishing to send down grace from heaven to those on earth because of His mercy toward us, symbolically fashioned the sacred tabernacle and everything in it, which is an image, a type, and an imitation of Wisdom.

<margin>89.</margin> The grace of the New Covenant is mystically hidden in the letter of the Old. Therefore, the Apostle says that the Law is spiritual. The Law, then, according to the letter, grows old and ages as it is set aside; but according to the spirit, it is always new and active. For grace is entirely ageless.

<margin>90.</margin> The Law has a shadow of the Gospel; but the Gospel is an image of the future goods. For the one prohibits the activities of evil, while the other sets forth the practice of good deeds.

<margin>91.</margin> We say that the whole of Holy Scripture is divided into flesh and spirit, as if it were a kind of spiritual human being. For he who says the literal text of Scripture is the "flesh," and its meaning is the "Spirit" or the "soul," will not miss the truth. But the wise...

<meta>This page continues the "Chapters on Knowledge" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The previous page discussed the transcendence of God as a simple Unity (Monad) beyond human intellection. This page transitions into the relationship between the stages of spiritual life—represented by the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel—and the different ways the Divine Word (Logos) reveals Himself to the soul.</meta>

-> ### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS ### <-

...clearly, he who has let go of what is corruptible, having become entirely belonging to the incorruptible.

<margin>92.</margin> The Law is the "flesh" of the spiritual person described in Holy Scripture; the Prophets are the "senses"; and the Gospel is the "rational soul." The Gospel acts through the "flesh" of the Law and the "senses" of the Prophets, and it reveals its own power through these activities.

<margin>93.</margin> The Law contained a shadow, and the Prophets contained an image, of the divine and spiritual blessings found in the Gospel. But the Gospel itself has shown us the truth as being present through actual events—the truth that was once overshadowed by the Law and prefigured by the Prophets.

<margin>94.</margin> He who fulfills the Law through his way of life and conduct only ceases from the actual results of vice, sacrificing the activity of his irrational passions to God. In this way, he is satisfied with salvation, due to the spiritual "infancy" <note>Maximus refers to the "infancy" of those who follow the Law literally without yet grasping its deeper spiritual meaning.</note> within him.

<margin>95.</margin> He who is tutored by the prophetic word, in addition to discarding the outward activity of the passions, also rids himself of the internal consents formed in the soul. This is so that he does not, while appearing to abstain from vice in the "inferior" part (the flesh), secretly practice it abundantly in the "superior" part (the soul).

<margin>96.</margin> He who genuinely embraces the life of the Gospel cuts off both the beginning and the end of vice. He pursues every virtue in word and deed, offering a "sacrifice of praise and confession." He is delivered from the disturbance of active passions and is free from the mental battle against them; he possesses only the hope of future blessings as an insatiable pleasure that directs his soul.

<margin>97.</margin> To the more diligent students of the Divine Scriptures, the Word <note>term: "Logos" — the Divine Reason or Word of God, incarnate as Christ.</note> of the Lord appears in two forms. The first is common and more public, visible to many, of which it is said: *We saw him and he had no form nor beauty* <note>original: "εἴδομεν αὐτὸν καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος, οὐδὲ κάλλος" — quoting Isaiah 53:2.</note>. The other is more hidden and reachable only by a few—those who have already become like the Holy Apostles Peter and John, before whom the Lord was transfigured into a glory that overcomes the senses. In this form, he is *fair in beauty beyond the sons of men* <note>original: "ὡραῖος κάλλει παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων" — quoting Psalm 45:2.</note>. Of these two forms, the former is suited for beginners,

<column-break/>

while the second is suited for those who have been perfected in knowledge <note>term: "gnosis" — spiritual knowledge or insight into divine mysteries.</note> as far as is possible. The first is an image of the Lord’s first coming, where the literal text of the Gospel must be placed, which purifies those in the "practical" life <note>term: "praktikos" — the stage of spiritual life focused on the struggle for virtue and the purging of passions.</note> through sufferings. The second is a prefiguration of the second and glorious coming, where the "spirit" of the text is understood, transforming the "gnostics" <note>term: "gnostikos" — those who have moved beyond simple faith to a deeper, contemplative understanding of God.</note> through wisdom toward deification <note>term: "theosis" — the process of becoming like God through union with Him.</note>. From the transformation of the Word within them, they behold the glory of the Lord with an "unveiled face."

<margin>98.</margin> He who steadfastly endures hardships for the sake of virtue experiences the "first coming" of the Word acting upon him, cleansing him of every stain. But he who has raised his mind to the state of the Angels through contemplation <note>term: "theoria" — the direct perception or vision of God and the inner meanings of creation.</note> possesses the power of the "second coming," which works in him a state of passionlessness and incorruptibility.

<margin>99.</margin> Sensation follows the "practical" person, who achieves virtues through toils. But "insensibility" <note>meaning: a holy indifference to worldly stimuli or physical pain.</note> follows the "gnostic" who has withdrawn his mind from the flesh and the world toward God. For the one, struggling through practice to loosen the soul’s natural bond to the flesh, finds his will constantly flagging under the weight of toils. But he who has loosened the "nails" of this relationship through contemplation is not held back at all; he has already become pure of the capacity to suffer or be controlled by those who wish to seize him.

<margin>100.</margin> The Manna given to Israel in the desert is the Word of God, which suffices as every spiritual pleasure for those who eat it. It is adapted to every taste according to the specific desire of the one eating, for it possesses the quality of every spiritual food. Therefore, to those born from above of "incorruptible seed" through the Spirit, it becomes "pure rational milk." To the weak, it is a "vegetable," comforting the suffering power of the soul. But to those who, through habit, have the senses of the soul trained to distinguish good and evil, it provides "solid food." The Word of God also has other infinite powers, not contained here; but if someone is released from this life and becomes worthy to be set over many things, or over all, he will receive those powers of the Word in their entirety, or in part...

# BY THE SAME AUTHOR

## SECOND CENTURY

<margin>1.</margin>
**G**od is one, because there is one Godhead: without beginning, simple, beyond essence <note>original: *hyperousios*; this suggests God does not just "exist" as a thing among other things, but is the source of existence itself</note>, indivisible, and inseparable. The same is both Unity and Trinity; the same is entirely Unity, and the same is entirely Trinity. It is entirely Unity according to its essence <note>original: *ousia*, the shared divine nature</note>, and entirely Trinity according to the Persons <note>original: *hypostases*, the distinct realities of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>. For the Godhead is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and the Godhead is in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The same is whole in the whole Father, and the Father is whole in the same whole Godhead. The same is whole in the whole Son, and the Son is whole in the same whole Godhead. The same is whole in the whole Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is whole in the same whole Godhead. The whole Godhead is the Father, and it is in the whole Father, and the Father is whole in the whole Godhead, and the whole Godhead is the whole Father. And the Son is whole in the same whole Godhead, and the same Godhead is whole in the whole Son, and the Son is both the whole Godhead and in the whole same Godhead. And the same Godhead is whole as the Holy Spirit, and it is in the whole Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit is the whole Godhead, and the Holy Spirit is whole in the same whole Godhead. For the Godhead is not in the Father by parts, nor is the Father a "part" of God; nor is the Godhead in the Son by parts, nor is the Son a part of God; nor is the Godhead in the Holy Spirit by parts, nor is the Holy Spirit a part of God. For the Godhead is not divisible, nor is the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit an "incomplete" God. Rather, the same whole Godhead is perfectly perfect in the perfect Father; the same is whole and perfect in the perfect Son; and the same is whole and perfect in the perfect Holy Spirit. For the Father is whole and perfect in the whole Son and the Spirit; and the Son is whole and perfect in the whole Father and the Spirit; and the Holy Spirit is whole and perfect in the whole Father and the Son. Therefore, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.

<column-break/>

For there is one and the same essence, power, and activity <note>original: *energeia*, the way God acts in the world</note> of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, none of whom exists or is even conceived of without the others.

<margin>2.</margin>
Every act of intellection <note>original: *noesis*, the activity of the mind or intellect</note> belongs to those who think and to the things being thought. But God is neither among those who think nor among the things being thought, for He is beyond these. If He were not, He would be limited by the relationship of a thought—as if He were a thinker in need of an object, or an object of thought naturally falling under the power of a thinker. It remains, then, for us to understand that God neither thinks nor is thought of in a human way, but is beyond both thinking and being thought of. For thinking and being thought of belong naturally to those beings that come after Him.

<margin>3.</margin>
Every act of intellection is situated within an essence as a quality, and its movement is directed toward a "qualified" essence <note>i.e., a thing that has specific characteristics</note>. It is impossible for the mind to grasp something that is entirely free, simple, and self-subsisting, unless that mind itself were free and simple. But God is entirely simple in both ways: He is Essence without a subject <note>original: *hypokeimenon*, meaning He is not a "thing" that possesses "properties"</note>. Since an act of intellection always requires some subject, God is not among the things that can be thought of, as He clearly exists beyond essence and intellection.

<margin>4.</margin>
Just as in the center of a circle, where the positions of the lines extending straight out from it are seen as completely undivided, so too the person deemed worthy to be in God will know all the inner principles <note>original: *logoi*, the divine blueprints or reasons for created things</note> of created things that pre-exist in Him, according to a certain simple and undivided knowledge.

<margin>5.</margin>
When the mind takes the shape of the things it thinks about, a single thought becomes many thoughts, taking form according to each species of the objects being thought. But when the mind passes beyond the multitude of sensible and intelligible things that give it shape and becomes entirely "formless," then the Word <note>original: *Logos*</note> who is beyond intellection makes the mind His own, bringing it to rest from the things that change it...

<note>original: *Theos* (God), *theotes* (Godhead), *anarchos* (without beginning), *haple* (simple), *hyperousios* (beyond essence), *adiairetos* (indivisible), *monas* (unity), *trias* (trinity), *hypostaseis* (persons), *Pater* (Father), *Yios* (Son), *Pneuma Hagion* (Holy Spirit), *ousia* (essence), *dynamis* (power), *energeia* (activity/energy), *noesis* (intellection), *nooumenon* (the object of thought)</note>

<summary>This page marks the beginning of the Second Century of Maximus the Confessor's theological chapters, focusing on the absolute unity and co-equality of the Holy Trinity and God's existence beyond human thought and essence. He uses the analogy of a circle's center to describe how the soul, when united with God, perceives the underlying principles of all creation in a single, simple act of knowing.</summary>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...it according to the forms of the thoughts <note>original: *noemata*; refers to the conceptual shapes or mental images that the mind uses to understand reality</note> naturally occurring; he who has experienced this has himself rested from his works, just as God rested from His own.

<margin>6.</margin> He who has reached the perfection that is awesome to men in this life, bears fruit for God: love, joy, peace, and patience. Regarding the future, he bears incorruptibility, eternity, and things similar to these. Perhaps the first group belongs to the one who has completed the "practical" life <note>original: *praktike*; the stage of spiritual life focused on purifying the soul through the practice of the virtues</note>; the second group belongs to the one who, through true knowledge <note>original: *gnosis*</note>, has gone out from created things.

<margin>7.</margin> Just as the proper work of disobedience is sin, so the proper work of obedience is virtue. And just as transgression of the commandments and separation from the Lawgiver follows disobedience, so the keeping of the commandments and union with the Lawgiver follows obedience. Therefore, he who has kept a commandment through obedience has both worked righteousness and has not separated himself from the union of love with the Lawgiver.

<margin>8.</margin> He who is being gathered together from the division caused by transgression first separates himself from the passions, then from passionate thoughts, then from nature and the principles <note>original: *logoi*; the inner blueprints or reasons for being</note> concerning nature, then from mental concepts and the knowledge concerning them. Finally, having passed through the variety of principles concerning providence, he arrives unknowingly at the principle of the Unity <note>original: *monas*; the absolute oneness of God</note> itself. In this state, the mind—having contemplated only its own unchangeability—rejoices with an inexpressible joy, as one who has received the "peace of God which surpasses all understanding" and which continually guards the one deemed worthy of it from falling.

<margin>9.</margin> The fear of hell <note>original: *geenna*</note> prepares those being initiated to flee vice; but the desire for the reward of good things grants to those who are progressing a readiness for the activity of the virtues. However, the mystery of love transcends all created things, making the mind "blind" to everything that comes after God. For the Lord makes wise only those who have become blind to all things after God, showing them more divine realities.

<margin>10.</margin> The Word <note>original: *Logos*</note> of God, being like a grain of mustard seed, seems very small before it is cultivated. But when it is properly cultivated, it shows itself to be so great that the high-natured principles <note>original: *logoi*</note> of both sensible and intelligible creations rest upon it like birds. For the principles of all things are 

<column-break/>

contained within Him, yet He is contained by no being. Because of this, the Lord said that the one who has faith like a grain of mustard seed can move a mountain by a word; that is, he can drive away the power of the devil that is against us and move it from its foundation.

<margin>11.</margin> The Lord is the "grain of mustard seed," sown according to faith by the Spirit in the hearts of those who receive Him. He who diligently cultivates this seed through the virtues moves the "mountain" of earthly mindedness, pushing away the stubborn habit of vice by his authority. He then gives rest to the principles of the commandments and the ways of virtue—or even the divine powers—as if they were the "birds of heaven."

<margin>12.</margin> Building upon the Lord as upon a foundation of faith, let us place the height of good things: gold, silver, and precious stones. By this I mean pure and unadulterated theology <note>original: *theologia*; in this context, the direct knowledge of God as Trinity</note>, a life that is transparent and bright, and divine reflections and pearl-like thoughts. Let us not use wood, nor grass, nor stubble—that is, let us not use idolatry (the trembling obsession with sensible things), nor an irrational life, nor passionate thoughts which are deprived of the insight of wisdom like ears of corn without grain.

<margin>13.</margin> Let the one who desires knowledge fix the foundations of his soul immovably in the Lord, as God said to Moses: 
> "But as for you, stand here with me." <note>Exodus 33:21</note>
It should be known, however, that even among those who stand with the Lord, there is a difference. This is not to be read casually by those who love learning, as it is written: 
> "There are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God come in power." <note>Matthew 16:28; Mark 9:1</note>
For the Lord does not always appear in glory to everyone standing with Him. To the beginners, He comes in the "form of a servant" <note>Philippians 2:7</note>; but to those who are able to follow Him as He ascends the high mountain of His Transfiguration <note>original: *metamorphosis*</note>, He appears in the "form of God," in which He existed before the world began. It is possible, therefore, that the same Lord does not appear in the same way to everyone who happens to be with Him, but to some in one way and to others in another, according to the measure of faith in each.

<margin>14.</margin> When the Word of God becomes manifest and bright within us, and his face...

He interprets the Parable of the Mustard Seed and the Transfiguration as metaphors for the soul's growth and varying capacities to perceive divine glory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Century on Theology" by Maximus the Confessor. It specifically deals with the mystical interpretation of the Transfiguration of Christ on Mount Tabor and the stages of spiritual ascent (praxis, contemplation, and theology) as represented by the figures of Moses and Elijah.</meta>

-> SECOND CENTURY 245 <-

...[his face] shines like the sun, then his garments also appear white; that is, the words of the Holy Scripture of the Gospels become clear, plain, and have nothing hidden. Moreover, Moses and Elijah appear with Him; that is, the more spiritual meanings <note>original: "logoi"; the inner reasons or spiritual principles behind things</note> of the Law and the Prophets.

<margin>15.</margin> Just as the Son of Man comes, as it is written, with His angels in the glory of the Father, so at every stage of progress in virtue, the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> of God is transfigured for those who are worthy. He comes with His angels in the glory of the Father. For the more spiritual meanings in the Law and the Prophets—whom Moses and Elijah represent by appearing with the Lord during the Transfiguration of God—maintain the proportion of the glory within them, revealing to the worthy a power that they are currently able to contain.

<margin>16.</margin> Anyone who has been initiated into the teaching regarding the Monad <note>original: "Monas"; the divine Unity or Oneness of God</note> also surely recognizes the principles <note>original: "logoi"</note> concerning Providence and Judgment that dwell with it. Therefore, according to the vision of Saint Peter, he decides it is good for "three tabernacles" to be made within himself. These represent the three states of salvation: I mean that of virtue, that of knowledge, and that of theology <note>original: "theologia"; here meaning the highest mystical knowledge of God</note>. The first requires courage and self-control in action, of which the blessed Elijah was the type; the second requires justice in the contemplation of nature, which the great Moses indicated through himself; and the third requires the pure perfection of wisdom, which the Lord revealed. They were called "tabernacles" <note>or "tents"</note> because there are other more excellent and splendid dwellings that will receive the worthy in the future state.

<margin>17.</margin> The "practical" person <note>one focused on the active life of virtue</note> is said to dwell in the flesh, since they cut off the soul's attachment to the flesh through the virtues and strip away the deception of material things. But the "gnostic" <note>original: "gnostikos"; one who possesses spiritual knowledge</note> is said to dwell within virtue itself, as if seeing the truth "in a mirror" * and "in riddles." 
<margin>* perhaps: "still."</margin>
For the substantial forms of good things have not yet been seen by him as they truly are, through "face to face" enjoyment. For every saint walks "in an image" of the good things to come, crying out: "I am a stranger 

<column-break/>

and a pilgrim, just as all my fathers were."

<margin>18.</margin> One who prays must never stop the high ascent that leads to God. For just as one must make ascents from "strength to strength" in the practical progress of the virtues, and an ascent from "glory to glory" in the spiritual knowledge of contemplation, and a transition from the literal text of Holy Scripture to the spirit, so must those who find themselves in the place of prayer. They must lift the mind away from human things and the disposition of the soul toward more divine things. This is so the mind may be able to follow Jesus, the Son of God, who has "passed through the heavens." He is everywhere and passes through all things for our sake according to His "economy" <note>original: "oikonomia"; the divine plan for salvation and the Incarnation</note>, so that we, by following Him, may pass through all things that come after Him and reach Him. This happens if we perceive Him not according to the smallness of His condescension in the "economy," but according to the majesty of His natural infinity.

<margin>19.</margin> It is always good to be at leisure and to seek God as we have been commanded. For even if in this present life we are unable to reach the very end of the depth of God while seeking Him, perhaps by reaching even a little of His depth, we see things "holier than the holy" and "more spiritual than the spiritual." This is shown figuratively by the High Priest, who enters from the holy things of the courtyard into the "holy of holies" * among the holier things.
<margin>* perhaps: "of the holier saints."</margin>

<margin>20.</margin> Every Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> of God is neither "many-worded" nor "much-speaking." Rather, it is one thing composed of various contemplations <note>original: "theoremata"</note>, each of which is a part of the Word. Therefore, he who speaks on behalf of the truth—even if he is able to speak so as to leave out nothing concerning the matter being sought—has spoken the "one Word" of God.

<margin>21.</margin> In Christ, who is God and the Word of the Father, "all the fullness of the deity dwells bodily" according to His essence. In us, however, the fullness of the deity dwells according to grace, whenever we gather within ourselves every virtue and wisdom. In this way, as far as is possible for a human being, nothing is lacking for a true imitation of the Archetype. For it is not unlikely that, according to the principle of "adoption" <note>original: "thesis"; the state of becoming a child of God by grace</note>, the fullness of the deity—which is composed of various spiritual contemplations—should also dwell in us.

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS #

<margin>22.</margin> Just as the word <note>original: "logos"</note> among us proceeds naturally from the mind <note>original: "nous"</note> and is the Messenger <note>original: "Angelos"</note> of the hidden movements of the mind; so the Word of God <note>original: "Logos tou Theou"</note>, who knows the Father by essence just as a word knows the mind that generated it, reveals the Father whom He knows as His natural Word. No created being can approach the Father without Him; for this reason, He is called the "Messenger of Great Counsel." <note>This title comes from the Septuagint Greek version of Isaiah 9:6, traditionally applied to Christ as the one who announces God's plan.</note>

<margin>23.</margin> The "Great Counsel" of God the Father is the silent and unknown mystery of the Dispensation <note>original: "oikonomia"; the divine plan for humanity’s salvation through Christ</note>. The only-begotten Son fulfilled this mystery through His incarnation and revealed it, becoming the Messenger of the Great Counsel of God the Father that existed before all ages. Furthermore, anyone who understands the inner principle of this mystery becomes a "messenger of the great counsel of God." Through both deed and word, such a person is raised up incomprehensibly through all things until they reach the One who descended so far for their sake.

<margin>24.</margin> If for our sake the Word of God descended through the Dispensation into the lower parts of the earth, and yet—being entirely unmovable by nature—also ascended above all the heavens; and if in Himself He pre-enacted as a man what is to come, then let the one who loves the friendship of knowledge look on with mystical joy at the nature of the promised end for those who love the Lord.

<margin>25.</margin> If the God-Word of God the Father became a man and a son of man for this reason: so that He might make humans gods <note>This refers to "theosis" or deification, the central Eastern Christian idea that humans are invited to share in God's life by grace.</note> and sons of God, let us believe that we shall be where Christ Himself is now. He is the head of the whole body, having become the forerunner for our sake before the Father. For God will stand in the "assembly of gods"—that is, those who are being saved—standing in their midst and distributing the honors of the blessedness found there, without being separated from those worthy of Him by any distance of space.

<margin>26.</margin> He who is still fulfilling the passionate desires of the flesh dwells in the land of the Chaldeans <note>A biblical region often used as a symbol for a state of spiritual confusion or attachment to the material world.</note> as an idolater and a maker of idols. But when he distinguishes things a little and gains a sense of the ways of nature that are fitting, leaving the land of the Chaldeans, he comes to Haran in Mesopotamia. I mean by this a state that is the midpoint between virtue and vice; a state not yet cleansed of the error that comes through the senses—for this is what "Haran" signifies. But if he rises above even that balanced 

<column-break/>

understanding of the beautiful which is gained through the senses, he will hasten toward the "good land." That is to say, he enters a state free from all vice and ignorance, which the God who does not lie reveals and promises to give as a prize of virtue to those who love Him.

<margin>27.</margin> If the Word of God was crucified for us out of weakness and was raised by the power of God, it is clear that He is always doing and suffering this spiritually for our sake, becoming all things so that He might save all. Therefore, the divine Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> rightly decided to know nothing among the Corinthians who were "weak" except Jesus Christ and Him crucified <note>1 Corinthians 2:2</note>. Yet to the Ephesians, who were "perfect," he writes: "God raised us up and seated us with Him in the heavenly places in Christ" <note>Ephesians 2:6</note>. By this, Paul says that the Word of God becomes according to the capacity of each person. He is crucified for those who are just being introduced to the practical life of piety, nailing their passionate activities with divine fear. But He rises and ascends into the heavens for those who have entirely "stripped off the old man," who is corrupted by deceitful desires, and have "put on the new man," created through the Spirit according to the image of God <note>Colossians 3:9-10</note>. For these people, the grace within them reaches the Father and is "above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named," whether in this age or the one to come <note>Ephesians 1:21</note>. For all things after God—whether things, names, or honors—will be beneath the person who, through grace, has come to be in God.

<margin>28.</margin> Just as the Word of God dwelt intellectually among the Patriarchs and Prophets before His visible appearance in the flesh, prefiguring the mysteries of His presence; so also after this dwelling among us, He comes not only to those who are still "infants," nourishing them spiritually and leading them toward the maturity of perfection in God, but also to the "perfect," secretly sketching for them the features of His future coming as if in an image.

<margin>29.</margin> Just as the words of the Law and the Prophets were forerunners of the Word’s coming in the flesh, training souls for Christ, so also the glorified Word of God Himself, having become flesh, is the forerunner of His spiritual presence...

-> SECOND CENTURY <-

...dispensation has occurred; <note>This sentence continues from the previous page's discussion on the Word's work.</note> educating souls through His own words toward the reception of His manifest divine presence. This presence He always makes manifest by transforming those who are worthy from the flesh toward the spirit through virtue. He will also do this at the end of the age, openly revealing things that have until now been kept secret from all.

<margin>30.</margin>
Insofar as I am imperfect and unsubmissive, not obeying God through the practice of the commandments, nor becoming perfect in my mind <note>original: "phresin"</note> according to knowledge, Christ—as far as it concerns my state—is also considered imperfect and unsubmissive because of me. For I diminish Him and cut Him short by not growing together with Him in the spirit, since I happen to be the body of Christ and "members in part." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:27, suggesting the mystical union where the believer's lack of growth reflects on the "stature" of Christ within them.</note>

<margin>31.</margin>
"The sun rises and the sun sets," says the Scripture <note>Ecclesiastes 1:5</note>. So too does the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>; at one time He is thought to be "above," and at another "below"—clearly according to the worthiness, the reason, or the manner of those who pursue virtue and move toward divine knowledge. Blessed is the one who, like Joshua son of Nun <note>original: "Iesous ton Naue"</note>, holds the Sun of Righteousness <note>Malachi 4:2</note> within himself so that it does not set throughout the whole measure of this present life's day—a day that is not circumscribed by the evening of malice or ignorance—so that he may be able to lawfully put to flight the wicked demons who rise up against him.

<margin>32.</margin>
When the Word of God is lifted up in us through practice <note>original: "praxis"</note> and contemplation <note>original: "theoria"</note>, He draws all things to Himself: our thoughts and words concerning the flesh, the soul, and the nature of beings. He even draws the very members of the body and the senses, sanctifying them according to virtue and knowledge and bringing them under His own yoke. Therefore, let the spectator of divine things ascend with haste, following the Word until he reaches the "place" where He is. For He draws there, as the Preacher <note>original: "Ekklesiastes"</note> says: "and he draws to his place" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:5</note>—clearly drawing those who follow Him as the Great High Priest who leads them into the Holy of Holies, where He Himself has entered as a forerunner on our behalf <margin>perhaps "concerning us."</margin> and for our sake.

<margin>33.</margin>
He who pursues the philosophy of piety and stands in battle-array against the invisible powers should pray that both natural discernment remain with him—possessing a balanced light—and the illuminating grace of the Spirit. For the former educates the flesh toward virtue through practice, while the latter guides the mind to prefer the companionship of wisdom above all else—

<column-break/>

through which he accomplishes the destruction of the strongholds of malice and "every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God" <note>2 Corinthians 10:5</note>. This is shown through the prayer of Joshua son of Nun <note>original: "Iesous tou Naue"</note> when he asked for the sun to stand still over Gibeon—that is, for the light of the knowledge of God to be kept for him without setting upon the "mountain" of mental contemplation—and for the moon to stand over the Valley—that is, for natural discernment, which rests upon the weakness of the flesh, to remain unchangeable from virtue.

<margin>34.</margin>
Gibeon is the high mind <note>original: "nous"</note>. The Valley is the flesh that has been humbled by death. The sun is the Word <note>original: "logos"</note> who illuminates the mind and supplies it with the power of contemplations, freeing it from all ignorance. The moon is the law of nature, which persuades the flesh to be lawfully submissive to the spirit so as to receive the yoke of the commandments. The moon is a symbol of nature because of its changeable quality, but in the saints it remains unchangeable through their immutable habit of virtue.

<margin>35.</margin>
The Lord should not be sought outside of those who seek Him; rather, those who seek Him must seek Him within themselves through faith made active in works. For it says, "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" <note>Romans 10:8</note>; that is, the word of faith, since Christ Himself is the Word being sought.

<margin>36.</margin>
Let us neither despair of God's love for mankind because we contemplate the height of divine infinity—as if it could not reach us due to that height—nor should we lose faith that a resurrection of the virtue that has died within us can occur when we consider the infinite depth of our fall through sin. For both are possible for God: both to descend and illuminate our mind through knowledge, and to raise up virtue in us again and exalt it with Himself through the works of righteousness. For it says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?' (that is, to bring Christ down) or 'Who will descend into the abyss?' (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead)" <note>Romans 10:6-7</note>. Perhaps, according to another interpretation, the "abyss" refers to all things after God, in which the Word of God becomes present in His entirety to the whole of creation through His providence, like life visiting those who are dead. For all things that live by participation in life are otherwise dead. But "heaven"...

# OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...the natural hiddenness of God, according to which He is incomprehensible to all. If someone should again take "heaven" to be the discourse of theology <note>original: "theologia" — for Maximus, this refers specifically to the study of God in His own internal nature</note>, and the "abyss" to be the mystery of the dispensation <note>original: "oikonomia" — the "economy" or plan of God's action in the world, especially the Incarnation</note>, he would not be speaking unreasonably, according to my view. For both are difficult to approach for those who attempt to seek them through logical demonstration; or rather, they are entirely inaccessible when searched for without faith.

<margin>37.</margin>
In the practical life <note>original: "praktiko" — the stage of active purification through the virtues</note>, the Word becomes "flesh" by being thickened through the various modes of the virtues; but in the contemplative life <note>original: "theoretiko" — the stage of spiritual vision</note>, being refined by spiritual insights, He becomes what He was in the beginning: God the Word with the Father.

<margin>38.</margin>
He makes the Word "flesh" who, using examples and thicker, simpler words because of the proportionate capacity of his hearers, makes the teaching of the Word an ethical one. Conversely, he makes the Word "spirit" who sets forth mystical theology through lofty contemplations.

<margin>39.</margin>
The one who theologizes through affirmations <note>original: "kataphatikos" — Cataphatic theology describes what God is (e.g., God is Love, God is Light)</note> makes the Word "flesh"; for he has no other way to know God as Cause except from things seen and touched. But the one who theologizes through negations <note>original: "apophatikos" — Apophatic theology describes what God is not, recognizing His transcendence</note> from abstractions makes the Word "spirit," as being God "in the beginning." From absolutely nothing that can be known, he rightly knows the One who is beyond all knowledge.

<margin>40.</margin>
The one who has learned to "dig"—following the examples of the Patriarchs—the wells of virtue and knowledge within himself through practice and contemplation, will find Christ within as the fountain of life. From this, Wisdom exhorts us to drink, saying: "Drink waters from your own vessels and from the spring of your own wells" <note>Proverbs 5:15</note>. By doing this, we shall find that Her treasures are already within us.

<margin>41.</margin>
Those who live in a beast-like manner, attending only to the senses, dangerously make the Word "flesh" for themselves. They misuse God's creatures to serve their passions; they do not perceive the "word" of wisdom manifest in all things so as to know and glorify God from His works. Nor do they understand where we come from, what we are, for what purpose we exist, or where we are being carried through this visible world. Instead, they pass through this age in darkness, groping with both hands only at ignorance concerning God.

<margin>42.</margin>
Those who sit only by the literal text <note>original: "rheto" — the "letter" of the law</note> of the Holy Scripture, and bind the dignity of the soul to the bodily service of the 

<column-break/>

Law <note>A reference to Jewish ritual law or literalism that ignores the spiritual intent</note>, blamefully make the Word "flesh" for themselves. They imagine that God is well-pleased with the sacrifices of unreasoning animals. For such people, great care is given to the body with external purifications, but the beauty of the soul is neglected, spotted with the stains of passions—the soul for which the whole power of visible things was created, and for which every divine word and law was given.

<margin>43.</margin>
The Holy Gospel says that the Lord is set for the "fall and resurrection of many in Israel" <note>Luke 2:34</note>. Therefore, let us consider if He is set for the "fall" of those who look upon the visible creation with the senses alone, and those who follow only the letter of the Holy Scripture, as they are unable to cross over to the "new spirit" of grace because of their folly. But He is the "resurrection" of those who spiritually contemplate and hear both the creatures of God and His words, and who care for the divine image in the soul in the proper ways.

<margin>44.</margin>
The Lord being set for the "fall and resurrection of many in Israel" can also be understood in a purely positive sense. For "fall" can be understood as the falling away of the passions and evil thoughts in each of the believers; and "resurrection" as the rising of the virtues and every thought dear to God.

<margin>45.</margin>
The one who thinks the Lord is only the Creator of things that are born and die <note>original: "genesei kai phthora" — the world of change and decay</note> misidentifies Him as a "gardener," just as Mary Magdalene did <note>John 20:15</note>. Therefore, for the benefit of such a person, the Master flees from their touch; since He has not yet been able to "ascend to the Father" in that person's mind, He says: "Do not touch Me" <note>John 20:17</note>. For He knows that the one who approaches Him with such a lowly, physical preconception is harmed.

<margin>46.</margin>
Those who, through fear of the "Jews," have shut the doors and sit in the upper room in Galilee—that is, those who, through fear of the spirits of wickedness, have safely ascended to the height of divine contemplations in the "land of Revelations," having closed their senses like doors—receive the Word of God as God. He comes to them unknowingly, appearing without the operation of the senses. He grants them dispassion <note>original: "apatheian"</note> through His peace, and the distribution of the Holy Spirit through His breathing upon them, and [power] against the spirits of...

<summary>Maximus explains how the Divine Word (Logos) is perceived differently based on a person's spiritual maturity—appearing as "flesh" to the literal-minded or those beginning their practice, and as "spirit" to those capable of mystical, apophatic contemplation.</summary>
