# SECOND CENTURY

...granting authority over the wicked powers, and revealing the symbols of His own mysteries.

<margin>47.</margin> To those who search for the word about God according to the flesh, the Lord does not "ascend to the Father"; but to those who seek Him according to the Spirit through lofty contemplations <term>theoria: the spiritual vision of divine truths</term>, He does ascend to the Father. Let us not, therefore, always keep Him "below"—He who became "below" for our sake out of His love for mankind—but let us rise with Him to the Father, leaving behind the earth and earthly things. We do this so He might not say to us what was said to the unrepentant Jews: "Where I go, you cannot come." For without the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>, it is impossible to reach the Father of the Word.

<margin>48.</margin> <margin>perhaps: "mode"</margin> The "land of the Chaldeans" represents the life of the passions, in which the idols of sin are manufactured and worshipped. The "land between the rivers" <note>Mesopotamia</note> represents a state that wavers between opposing ways of life. The "Promised Land" is the state of soul filled with every good thing. Thus, anyone who neglects this state of being—as the ancient Israelites did—is dragged back into the slavery of the passions and stripped of the freedom they were given.

<margin>49.</margin> It should be noted that none of the Saints appear to have gone down into Babylon <note>a symbol of exile and spiritual confusion</note> of their own will. For it is not right, nor is it consistent with rational understanding, for those who love God to choose the worse over the better. If some of them were led there by force along with the people, we understand this to refer to those who—not by preference but by circumstance—leave the higher word of knowledge to handle the teaching concerning the passions for the sake of those needing guidance. This is why the great Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> judged it more useful to remain "in the flesh"—that is, in ethical teaching—for the sake of his students, even though he had a total desire to be released from ethical teaching and to be with God through a supernatural and simple contemplation of the mind.

<margin>50.</margin> Just as the blessed David would play the harp and soothe Saul when he was being choked by the evil spirit, so every spiritual word, sweetened by insights of knowledge, soothes the mind when it is seized by fits, freeing it from the evil conscience that chokes it.

<column-break/>

<margin>51.</margin> One who is "ruddy with beautiful eyes" <note>referring to the description of David in 1 Samuel 16:12</note>, according to the blessed David, is the person who has the word of knowledge shining alongside the radiance of a life lived according to God. In such a person, practice and contemplation stand together: the one is made bright by the modes of the virtues, and the other is enlightened by divine thoughts.

<margin>52.</margin> The kingdom of Saul is an image of the physical worship of the Law, which the Lord abolished because it "perfected nothing"; for the Scripture says the Law made nothing perfect. But the kingdom of the great David is a prefiguration of the worship of the Gospel, for it perfectly contains the heartfelt desires of God.

<margin>53.</margin> Saul represents the natural law, which was originally given by the Lord to rule over nature. But because he transgressed the commandment through disobedience by sparing Agag, the king of Amalek <note>Amalek often represents the flesh or base passions in patristic thought</note>—that is, by sparing the body and sliding toward the passions—he is cast out of the kingdom. This happens so that David might take over Israel—that is, the law of the Spirit, which gives birth to the peace that visibly builds for God the temple of contemplation.

<margin>54.</margin> The name "Saul" is interpreted as "Obedience of God." Therefore, as long as the "word of obedience" acts as a priest within us, even if "Saul" should spare Agag—that is, the earthly mindset—the "priest-word" <note>referring to Samuel</note> will zealously kill it, striking and shaming the sin-loving mind for being a transgressor of divine decrees.

<margin>55.</margin> When the mind becomes arrogant and stops asking the word of teaching—which anointed it to fight the passions—about what should and should not be done, it is inevitably captured by the passions through ignorance. Separating itself bit by bit from God, it falls into involuntary circumstances, "making a god of the belly" <note>seeking comfort in demons or physical appetites</note> and trying to find comfort for its pressures there. Let Saul convince you of this: by not taking Samuel as his counselor in all things, he was forced to turn to idolatry and stooped to asking a medium <note>the Witch of Endor</note> for advice as if she were a god.

<margin>56.</margin> The person who prays to receive the "daily bread" <term>epiousios: often interpreted as "bread for existence" or "supersubstantial bread"</term> does not necessarily receive it all exactly as the Bread is, but according to how the receiver is able to take it. For the Bread of Life gives Himself to all who ask, as...

<summary>Maximus uses the biblical stories of David and Saul as allegories for the soul's struggle between the "natural law" and the "law of the spirit," warning that neglecting spiritual growth leads to a return to the "Babylon" of the passions. He emphasizes that Christ (the Bread of Life) is received by the believer according to their individual capacity for spiritual contemplation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Century on Theology" by St. Maximus the Confessor. Following the previous page’s discussion on the soul's journey from the passions (Chaldea) to spiritual knowledge, these aphorisms (numbered 56–64) explore how the Divine Word (Logos) reveals Himself differently to individuals based on their spiritual maturity, moving from the "flesh" of the literal scriptural letter to the "spirit" of mystical vision.</meta>

->### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS<-

...the Lover of mankind. However, He is not the same to everyone; rather, to those who have performed great works of righteousness, He is present more fully; to those who are lesser in these things, He is present less so; to each according to the capacity of the mind to receive Him.

<margin>57.</margin> The Lord is sometimes "away from home" and sometimes "at home." According to the vision of "face to face," He is at home; according to the vision through "a mirror and in riddles," He is away from home.

<margin>58.</margin> To the person of <term>praxis: the life of active virtue and self-discipline</term>, the Lord is "at home" through the virtues; but from the one who takes no account of virtue, He is "away from home." And again, to the person of <term>theoria: the contemplative life of spiritual vision</term>, He is "at home" through true knowledge of created things; but from the one who trips up in this knowledge in some way, He is "away from home."

<margin>59.</margin> He "journeys away" from the flesh, as one who has moved from the practical state to the cognitive state; being caught up as if "in the clouds" by higher thoughts into the transparent air of mystical contemplation, according to which he will be able to be "always with the Lord." But he is "away from the Lord" who is not yet able to contemplate thoughts with a pure mind, as far as is possible, apart from the activities of the senses, and who cannot yet contain the simple Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> concerning the Lord without riddles.

<margin>60.</margin> The Word of God is called "flesh" not only because He became incarnate, but also because the Word—who is God and is understood simply "in the beginning with God and the Father," having the clear and naked archetypes of the truth concerning all things—does not contain parables, riddles, or histories needing allegory. But when He visits humans who are unable to approach naked intelligible things with a naked mind, He speaks to them from their own familiar things. By being composed through a variety of histories, riddles, parables, and obscure words, He "becomes flesh." For at our first encounter, our mind does not meet the naked Word, but the Word-made-flesh, namely, through the variety of the words. He is Word by nature, but "flesh" in appearance; so that to the many He seems to be flesh and not the Word, even if in truth He is the Word. For the meaning of Scripture is not what it appears to be to the

<margin>* perhaps: "toward flesh only without the 'of which'"</margin> many, but something other than what it seems. For the Word "becomes flesh" through each of the recorded sayings.

<margin>61.</margin> The beginning of the instruction toward piety for men <gloss>*</gloss> is not naturally meant to be "toward the flesh." 

<column-break/>

For we converse with the "letter" and not the "spirit" during our first encounter with godliness. But as we progress bit by bit toward the spirit, and scrape away the thickness of the words with more subtle contemplations, we come to be purely in the pure Christ, as far as is possible for humans. This is so that we may be able to say, according to the great Apostle,

> Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him so no longer;

this is because of the mind's approach to the Word, simply and without the veils that were over Him; having progressed from knowing the Word as "flesh" to His glory as "the Only-begotten from the Father."

<margin>62.</margin> He who has lived the life in Christ has surpassed the righteousness of both the law and nature. This is what the divine Apostle indicates when he says,

> For in Christ Jesus, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything.

By "circumcision," he indicates the righteousness of the Law; and by "uncircumcision," he hints at natural equality before the law.

<margin>63.</margin> Some are reborn through water and Spirit; others receive baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire. By these four—I mean the water, the spirit, the fire, and the Holy Spirit—I understand the one and the same Spirit of God. To some, the Holy Spirit is "water," as a cleanser of the external defilements regarding the body. To others, He is "Spirit," as an activator of the goods of virtue. To others, He is "fire," as a purifier of the internal stains deep within the soul. And to others, according to the great Daniel, He is "Holy Spirit," as the provider of wisdom and knowledge. For from His diverse activity upon the subject, the one and the same Spirit receives various names.

<margin>64.</margin> The Law gave the Sabbath so that, it says,

> your beast of burden and your servant may rest.

Both of these terms, through riddles, indicate the body. For the body is the "beast of burden" for the mind of *praxis*, being forced to carry by weight the habits of the virtues during action. But it is the "servant" of the contemplative mind, as it is now reasoned with by contemplations, and serves the cognitive commands of the mind in a rational way. The Sabbath is for both of them the end of the good things worked by them in action and contemplation, providing the rest that is appropriate for each.

<summary>St. Maximus explains how the Word (Logos) adapts Himself to human understanding by appearing as "flesh" (the literal letter of Scripture) before being revealed as "spirit" to the mature. He also provides an allegorical interpretation of baptismal elements and the Sabbath as stages of spiritual growth.</summary>

# SECOND CENTURY

<margin>65.</margin> The one who accomplishes virtue with the proper knowledge makes a beast of burden of the body, driving it by reason toward the performance of duties. He makes a "servant" of the method of action used in virtue—that is, the specific way in which virtue is naturally practiced—as if it were bought with the silver of discerning thoughts. The "Sabbath" is the dispassionate and peaceful state of both soul and body according to virtue; in other words, an unchanging <term>hexis: a stable internal disposition or habit</term>.

<margin>66.</margin> To those who still focus most of their care on the bodily forms of virtue, the Word of God <note>original: "Logos"</note> becomes "chaff" and "grass," nourishing the <term>passionate part: the part of the soul associated with emotions and desires</term> for the service of the virtues. But to those who have been raised up by the <term>theoria: contemplative vision</term> of true divine understanding, He is "bread," nourishing the intellectual part of their soul toward a god-like perfection. Therefore, we find the Patriarchs providing themselves with food for the journey: both bread for themselves and fodder for their donkeys. <note>This refers to the sons of Jacob traveling to Egypt in Genesis 42:25–27.</note> Likewise, the Levite in the Book of Judges says to the old man who hosted him in Gibeah: "We have both bread for ourselves and straw for our donkeys, and there is no lack of anything for your servants." <note>See Judges 19:19.</note>

<margin>67.</margin> The Word of God is called and truly is "dew," "water," "spring," and "river," according to the capacity of those who receive Him. To some, He is dew, as He quenches the burning and activity of the passions that press upon the body from without. To those whose depths are being eaten away by the venom of wickedness, He is water—not only as a destroyer of the opposition through a contrary force, but as a giver of vital power for "well-being." He is a spring to those who possess the habit of contemplation perpetually bubbling up, acting as a provider of wisdom. He is a river to those who pour forth godly, straight, and saving teaching like a flood, abundantly watering humans, cattle, wild beasts, and plants. He does this so that humans may achieve <term>theosis: the process of being united with God and becoming "gods" by grace</term>, being raised up by the meanings of the things spoken; and that those who have become "beastly" through the passions might, through the precise demonstration of the ways of virtue, become "humanized" and regain their natural rationality. And those who have become "wild beasts" through evil habits and wicked deeds might, through gentle and soothing

<column-break/>

exhortation, be tamed and return to the natural gentleness of their kind. Finally, those who, like plants, are insensitive to what is good, might be softened by the Word's passage into their depths, gaining a sense for fruit-bearing and the power of the Word's quality which nourishes them.

<margin>68.</margin> The Word of God is a "Way" for those who run the race of virtue well and vigorously according to <term>praxis: active spiritual discipline</term>, swerving neither to the right through vainglory nor to the left through a leaning toward the passions, but directing their steps according to God. King Asa of Judah, because he did not guard this "Way" until the end, is said to have suffered in his feet in his old age, as he had grown weak in the race of a life according to God. <note>Referencing 1 Kings 15:23 and 2 Chronicles 16:12.</note>

<margin>69.</margin> The Word of God is called a "Door" for those who have well completed the entire way of the virtues through the blameless race of action, leading them into knowledge and showing them, like light, the many-shining treasures of wisdom. For He Himself is the Way, the Door, the Key, and the Kingdom: the Way as a guide; the Key as the one who opens (and is opened to) those worthy of divine things; the Door as the one who introduces us; and the Kingdom as the one who is inherited and who exists in all things by participation.

<margin>70.</margin> The Lord is called "Light," "Life," "Resurrection," and "Truth." He is Light as the brightness of souls, the chaser of the darkness of ignorance, the one who illuminates the mind to understand unspoken things, and the one who reveals mysteries visible only to the pure. He is Life as providing the movement fitting for souls who love the Lord in divine things. He is Resurrection as raising the mind from its dead attachment to material things, making it pure of all corruption and death. And He is Truth as granting an unchangeable habit of good things to those who are worthy.

<margin>71.</margin> The God-Word of God the Father is mystically present in each of His commandments. And God the Father is entirely inseparable from His own Word by nature. Therefore, the one who receives a divine commandment and carries it out receives the Word of God within it; and the one who has received the Word through the commandments has also received through Him the Spirit who is naturally in Him.

> "Truly, truly, I say to you," He says, "the one who receives whomever I send receives me; and the one who receives me receives the one who sent

# OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...me." <note>This likely completes a quote from John 14:23: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him."</note> Therefore, the one who receives a commandment and carries it out, having received it, possesses the Holy Trinity mystically.

<margin>72.</margin> It is not the one who honors God with words alone who glorifies God in himself, but the one who, for God's sake, endures the suffering of labors on behalf of virtue. Such a person is glorified in return by God with the glory that is in God, receiving as a prize for virtue the grace of <term>apatheia: a state of holy detachment or freedom from passions</term> through participation in Him. For everyone who glorifies God in himself through the sufferings for virtue that follow the <term>praktike: the stage of active spiritual struggle and ascetic practice</term>, is himself also glorified in God through the dispassionate <term>theoria: contemplative vision</term> of divine illuminations. For the Lord says as He approaches His passion: "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him; and if God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him at once." <note>John 13:31-32</note> From this it is clear that divine gifts of grace follow the sufferings endured for the sake of virtue.

<margin>73.</margin> As long as we see the Word of God <note>original: "Logos"</note> in the literal text of the Holy Scripture, "clothed in the flesh" in various ways through enigmas, we have not yet intellectually contemplated the Father as the incorporeal, simple, unified, and solitary one, within the incorporeal, simple, unified, and solitary Son. This is according to the saying: "He who has seen me has seen the Father; and I am in the Father and the Father is in me." <note>John 14:9–10</note> Therefore, there is a great need for knowledge, so that having first pierced through the veils of the words surrounding the Word, we may thus behold with a naked mind the Word Himself standing pure by Himself—revealing the Father clearly within Himself, as far as is reachable for human beings. Because of this, it is necessary for the one who seeks God piously not to be held captive by any literal expression, lest he receive the things *around* God instead of God—that is, lest he dangerously cherish the literal words of the Scripture instead of the Word, while the Word escapes the mind which thinks it holds the incorporeal Word by grasping His outer coverings. This is like the Egyptian woman <note>Potiphar's wife, from Genesis 39</note> who did not catch Joseph himself, but only took hold of his garments; or like the men of old who, remaining only in the outward beauty of visible things, unknowingly "worshiped the creature rather than the Creator." <note>Romans 1:25</note>

<margin>74.</margin> The Word of the Holy Scripture, in its higher meanings, strips off the composition of the words that were shaped for it in a bodily way. It shows itself to the more discerning mind as a "still small breeze" <note>1 Kings 19:12</note> because of the extreme abandonment of natural 

<column-break/>

activities—a mind that was only able to receive a perception of the simplicity that indicates the Word in some measure, just as the great Elijah was granted this vision in the cave of Horeb. "Horeb" is interpreted as "renewal" <note>original: "neoma"</note>; which is the stable disposition (<term>hexis</term>) of virtues in the new spirit of grace. The "cave" is the hiddenness of wisdom in the mind, in which the one who enters will mystically perceive the knowledge that is beyond sense-perception, where God is said to be. Therefore, everyone who truly seeks God like the great Elijah will not only be in Horeb—that is, as an active practitioner in the habit of the virtues—but also in the cave that is in Horeb—that is, as a contemplative in the hiddenness of wisdom, which exists only in the stable habit of the virtues.

<margin>75.</margin> When the mind shakes off the many opinions about existing things that weigh upon it, then the Word of truth appears clearly to it, giving it the instructions of true knowledge. It pushes away the former preconceptions as if they were "scales" from its visual powers, according to the divine and great Apostle Paul. <note>Acts 9:18</note> For scales are truly laid upon the discerning part of the soul, blocking the passage to the pure Word of truth; these scales are both the literal interpretations of the Scripture and the sensory, passionate contemplations of visible things.

<margin>76.</margin> The divine Apostle Paul said that he "knew in part" <note>1 Corinthians 13:12</note> the knowledge of the Word. But the great Evangelist John says that he "beheld His glory"; for he says, "We beheld His glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." <note>John 1:14</note> Perhaps Saint Paul said he knew "in part" the knowledge of the Word as God, for He is known only in some measure from His activities (<term>energeiai</term>). For the knowledge of Him according to His essence and person (<term>hypostasis</term>) stands as inaccessible to all alike, both Angels and men, being known by no one. But Saint John, having been initiated into the perfect meaning—as far as is possible among men—of the Word's becoming human (<term>enanthropesis</term>), said that he beheld the 

<margin>Perhaps: "the Word according to the flesh."</margin>

glory of the Word as flesh. That is, he beheld the Word—or rather, the purpose for which God became man, "full of grace and truth." For the Only-begotten is not "filled with grace" insofar as He is God by essence and co-essential with God the Father; but insofar as...

->### SECOND CENTURY<-

...by nature, according to the <term>economy: the divine plan for salvation</term>, He became man, and for our sake was made of the same essence as us. He has been set apart for those who need grace; and from His fullness, we always receive grace according to our own <term>progress: spiritual advancement (prokope)</term>. Thus, the one who has kept the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> perfect and undefiled within himself will receive the glory of the Word of God who was incarnate for us—the glory full of grace and truth. He will receive the glory of the One who glorified and sanctified Himself for us, in our likeness, according to His presence. For it says: "When He is revealed, we shall be like Him." <note>1 John 3:2</note>

<margin>77.</margin>
Until the soul makes its transition from strength to strength, and from glory to glory—that is, from virtue to a greater progress in virtue, and from knowledge to a higher ascent of knowledge—it does not cease being a "sojourner," according to what is written: *My soul has long been a sojourner.* <note>Psalm 120:6</note> For great is the distance and many are the levels of knowledge that must be traversed by the soul, until it passes into the "place of the wonderful tabernacle," even to the "house of God," with the voice of exultation and the sound of one keeping festival. <note>Psalm 42:4</note> It adds voice upon voice—spiritual voice upon spiritual voice—to its progress in divine <term>contemplations: theoria</term>, along with the mental exultation, or joy, over what has been contemplated, and the corresponding thanksgiving. For all those who have received the Spirit of grace in their hearts celebrate such festivals, crying out: **Abba Father**.

<margin>78.</margin>
The "place of the wonderful tabernacle" is the dispassionate and painless habit of the virtues, in which the Word of God, as He comes to be within us, adorns the soul with various beauties of virtue, as if it were a tabernacle. And the "house of God" is the knowledge composed of many and various contemplations, through which God, dwelling in the soul, fills it from the "chalice of wisdom." The "voice of exultation" is the soul's leaping for joy over the wealth of the virtues. The "voice of thanksgiving" is the gratitude for the glory of the banquet of wisdom. And the "sound" is the perpetual, mystical doxology arising from the blend of both exultation and thanksgiving.

<margin>79.</margin>
He who has nobly wrestled down the passions of the body, and has fought sufficiently against the unclean spirits, and has expelled their thoughts from the territory of his soul,

<column-break/>

let him pray for a clean heart to be given to him and a right spirit to be renewed in his inward parts <note>Psalm 51:10</note>; that is, to be perfectly emptied of evil thoughts and filled with divine concepts through grace. This is so that he may become a mental world of God, radiant and great, composed of moral, physical, and theological <term>insights: contemplations (theoremeta)</term>.

<margin>80.</margin>
He who has made his heart clean will not only know the principles of those things that are beneath or after God, but after passing through all things, he even sees God Himself in a certain way—which is the highest end of all goods. When God comes to be in such a heart, He deigns to engrave His own letters there through the Spirit, as if on Mosaic tablets; to the extent that the heart has given itself over to <term>practice: praktike</term> and <term>contemplation: theoria</term>, according to the mystical commandment that bids us to "increase."

<margin>81.</margin>
Perhaps a "clean heart" is said to be that which possesses no natural movement toward anything else in any way whatsoever. In such a heart, as if on a writing tablet smoothed well through extreme simplicity, God comes to be and writes His own laws.

<margin>82.</margin>
A heart is clean when it presents its memory to God as entirely formless and without shape, ready to be marked only by His impressions, through which He is naturally made manifest.

<margin>83.</margin>
The "Mind of Christ," which the saints receive according to the saying, *But we have the mind of Christ* <note>1 Corinthians 2:16</note>, does not come to us through the loss of our own mental power, nor as a supplementary addition to our mind. Nor does it transition essentially or personally into our mind. Rather, it is that the Mind of Christ, by its own quality, illumines the power of our mind and brings our mind's activity into alignment with its own. For I believe that to "have the mind of Christ" is to think according to Him, and to think of Him through all things.

<margin>84.</margin>
We are said to be the "Body of Christ" according to the passage: *Now you are the body of Christ and members in particular.* <note>1 Corinthians 12:27</note> We do not become that Body by losing our own bodies, nor does Christ transition personally into us or get divided member by member. Rather, it is that we shake off the corruption of sin in likeness to the Lord’s flesh. For just as Christ was sinless by nature in both flesh and soul (insofar as He is understood as man),

Maximus clarifies that "having the mind of Christ" means aligning one's intellect with divine activity rather than losing one's human identity.</summary>

->### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS<-

...just as He was, so we too who have believed in Him are able to be without sin.

<margin>85.</margin>
There are, according to the Scriptures, ages of time; these encompass the "consummation of other ages," according to the verse: *But now once at the consummation of the ages* <note>Hebrews 9:26</note> and so forth. And there are, again, other ages free from a temporal nature, coming after this present temporal age at the consummation of the ages; according to the verse: *That He might show in the ages to come the surpassing riches* <note>Ephesians 2:7</note> and so forth. We find in the Scriptures a multitude of ages—past, present, and future. We also find "ages of ages," and a specific "age of the age," and "eternal times," and "generations joined to ages." But lest we now extend our discourse too far beyond our current subject by explaining what is meant by "temporal ages," and what by "eternal times" and "generations"—or what is meant simply by "ages," or "ages of ages," or the "age of the age"—we shall leave the investigation of these matters to those who love learning, and return to the purpose for which we brought these things forward.

<margin>86.</margin>
We know what the Scripture calls "beyond-the-ages" <note>original: "hyper-aionion"</note>; it signifies that such a state exists, but does not give it a specific name. This is seen in the verse: *The Lord reigning for the age, and beyond the age, and still further.* <note>Exodus 15:18 or Psalm 145:13</note> Therefore, there is something above the ages: the pure <term>Kingdom of God: the eternal realm of divine presence</term>. For it is not permitted to say that the Kingdom of God began or was manifested within ages or times. We believe this Kingdom to be the inheritance, the dwelling, and the place of the saved; as true doctrine hands down to us, it is the <term>goal: (telos) the final completion of a journey</term> for those who are moved by desire toward the ultimate Object of longing. Once they reach this goal, they receive a rest from all movement whatsoever, as there is no longer any time or age for them to pass through. For having passed through all things, they have arrived at God, who exists before all ages, and whom the nature of the ages cannot reach.

<margin>87.</margin>
For as long as someone is in this life, even if he has reached the goal according to the state of things here—both in action and <term>contemplation: (theoria) spiritual vision or insight</term>—he still possesses knowledge, prophecy, and the "pledge of the Holy Spirit" <note>2 Corinthians 1:22</note> only "in part," but not the fullness itself. One day, after the completion of the ages, he will come to

<column-break/>

the perfect lot, which shows the Truth standing by itself, face to face, to those who are worthy. Then, he will no longer have just a "part" of the <term>fullness: (pleroma) the total presence of divine grace</term>, but will receive the entire fullness of grace through <term>participation: (methexis) the soul's sharing in God's life</term>. For the divine Apostle says that all those who are saved will attain to a "perfect man," to the "measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ," <note>Ephesians 4:13</note> in whom are the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge. When these treasures are revealed, that which is "in part" shall be done away with.

<margin>88.</margin>
Some ask: what will be the state of those deemed worthy of perfection in the Kingdom of God? Will it be a state of <term>progress: (prokope) moving forward</term> and transition, or a state of identity in "standing still"? And how should we conceive of the souls and bodies then? To this, one might say by way of conjecture: just as in physical life there are two reasons for food—one for growth and the other for the preservation of those being fed. For until we reach the goal of physical maturity, we are fed for growth; but once the body stops increasing in size, it is no longer fed for growth but for preservation. In the same way, there are two reasons for the soul's nourishment. It is fed while it is progressing in virtues and spiritual insights, until it passes beyond all created things and reaches the "measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." Once it arrives there, it stops all progress through intermediaries that lead to increase and growth. Instead, it is fed directly in a way that is "beyond understanding." Perhaps, therefore, this form of "incorruptible food" is not for growth, but for the preservation of the <term>godlike perfection: (theoeidous) having the form or character of God</term> given to it, and for the manifestation of the infinite splendors of that nourishment. Through this, the soul receives the quality of "always being well" <note>original: "aei eu einai"</note> dwelling within it, and it becomes "god" through the participation in divine grace. The soul ceases from all its own natural activities of mind and sense, and it causes the natural activities of the body to cease along with it, as the body is <term>deified: (theothentos) transformed by divine grace (theosis)</term> along with the soul according to its own proportional participation. Thus, God alone shines through the soul and the body, their natural characteristics having been surpassed by the abundance of glory.

<margin>89.</margin>
Some of those who love learning ask: in what manner will the eternal dwellings be...

<meta>This page continues the "Second Century on Theology" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The previous page ended while discussing the nature of the "mansions" or "abodes" promised in the afterlife. St. Maximus is exploring whether these are physical locations or spiritual states of being.</meta>

### SECOND CENTURY

...and the difference of the promises: whether they exist as a physical location <note>original: "hypostasin topikēn"</note>, or as a conceptual understanding of the spiritual quality and quantity unique to each dwelling <note>Greek: "monē", often translated as 'mansion' or 'abode' in the Father's house</note>? To some, the first seems true; to others, the second. But he who knows what it means that "the kingdom of God is within you" and what "many mansions with the Father" means, will favor the second view.

<margin>90.</margin>
Some ask what difference there is between the "Kingdom of God" and the "Kingdom of the Heavens": whether they differ in substance or only in concept. To them it must be said: they do not differ in substance, but in concept. For the Kingdom of the Heavens is the clear comprehension of the nature of beings according to their own inner principles <note>Greek: "logoi", the divine blueprints or reasons for things</note> as they pre-existed eternally in God. But the Kingdom of God is the communication by grace of those good things that belong to God by nature. The first relates to the ultimate purpose of all beings; the second is conceptually what exists after that ultimate purpose is reached.

<margin>91.</margin>
The phrase "the Kingdom of the Heavens is at hand" <note>Matthew 3:2</note> does not, in my opinion, refer to a shortening of chronological time. For "it does not come with observation," nor will they say, "look here" or "look there" <note>Luke 17:20-21</note>, but it refers to the internal relationship of those who are worthy of it toward that state. For "the Kingdom of God," it says, "is within you."

<margin>92.</margin>
The Kingdom of God the Father is potentially <note>original: "dynamei"</note> present in all who believe, but it is present in actuality <note>original: "energeia"</note> in those who have entirely laid aside the whole life of the soul and body according to nature, and have acquired the life of the spirit alone, being able to say: "I no longer live, but Christ lives in me." <note>Galatians 2:20</note>

<margin>93.</margin>
Some say the Kingdom of the Heavens is the way of life of the worthy in the heavens. Others say it is the condition of those being saved which is like that of the Angels. Still others say it is the very form of the divine beauty for those who have worn "the image of the heavenly." <note>1 Corinthians 15:49</note> In my view, all three opinions are in harmony with the truth. For to everyone is given future grace according to the proportion of the quality and quantity of righteousness within them.

<margin>94.</margin>
As long as someone, following practical philosophy <note>The stage of active spiritual struggle and discipline</note>, manfully goes through the divine contests, they hold within themselves the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> who came out

<column-break/>

from the Father into the world through the commandments. But when they leave behind the wrestling of practice against the passions—having been revealed as a victor over passions and demons—and move toward the contemplative <note>original: "gnōstikēn"</note> philosophy through spiritual vision <note>original: "theoria"</note>, they allow the Word mystically to "leave the world again and go to the Father." Therefore the Lord says to the disciples: "Because you have loved me and have believed that I came out from God; I came out from the Father and have come into the world; again, I leave the world and go to the Father." <note>John 16:27-28</note> By "world," He perhaps meant the laborious work of practicing the virtues; and by "Father," the state beyond the world and free from all material thinking, in which the Word of God comes to be in us, ceasing from the battle against passions and demons.

<margin>95.</margin>
He who has been able to put to death the "members upon the earth" <note>Colossians 3:5</note> through action, and to conquer the world of passions within himself through the word of the commandments, will have no further tribulation. He has already left the "world" and has come to be in Christ—who conquered the world of passions and is the Giver of all peace. For he who does not leave behind his attachment to material things will always have tribulation; as things change by their nature, his mind changes along with them. But he who is in Christ will in no way feel any material change. Therefore the Lord says, "I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, I have conquered the world." <note>John 16:33</note> That is: in me, the Word of virtue, you have peace, being delivered from the whirlwind and turmoil of material passions and things; but in the "world"—that is, in the attachment to material things—you have tribulation because of their constant change. For both have tribulation: the one practicing virtue because of the toil joined to it, and the one loving the world because of the failure of material things. But the one has a saving tribulation, the other a destructive and deadly one. The Lord is the rest for both: for the former, by ceasing the toils of virtue within Himself through contemplation and dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"</note>; for the latter, by taking away through repentance the attachment to things that perish.

<summary>St. Maximus discusses the difference between the Kingdom of Heaven and the Kingdom of God, defining them as internal spiritual states rather than physical locations. He explains the transition from the "practical" life of virtue to the "contemplative" life of peace in Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Kingdom of God, Kingdom of Heaven, practical philosophy, contemplation, Logos, passions, dispassion, repentance, Maximus the Confessor</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the Second Century of "Various Chapters on Theology and Economy" and begins the Third Century. The text continues Maximus’s exploration of how the spiritual life is divided into three stages: practical (ethics), natural (contemplation of creation), and theological (mystical union with God).</meta>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

<margin>96.</margin> The inscription written on the title-board of the Savior <note>This refers to the "INRI" sign placed on the Cross</note> clearly taught that the one who was crucified is King and Lord of practical, natural, and theological philosophy. For it says the word was written in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. I understand that by "Latin," it signifies practical philosophy—since the Roman Empire was defined by Daniel as being the most courageous of all the kingdoms on earth; and if anything is characteristic of the practical life, it is courage. By "Greek," it signifies natural contemplation, since the Greek nation, more than any other people, devoted themselves to natural philosophy. By "Hebrew," it signifies theological initiation into the mysteries, since this nation was clearly dedicated to God from the beginning for the sake of the fathers.

<margin>97.</margin> We must not only be the slayers of bodily passions, but also the destroyers of those thoughts which are influenced by the passions in the soul. This is according to the saint who says: "In the mornings I destroyed all the sinners of the land, to blot out from the city of the Lord all those who work iniquity" <note>Psalm 101:8 (Septuagint numbering). Maximus interprets the "city" as the soul and "sinners" as intrusive thoughts.</note>; that is, the passions of the body and the lawless thoughts of the soul.

<margin>98.</margin> He who has kept the path of the virtues unblemished, without leaning toward either side <note>avoiding extremes of excess or deficiency</note>, and has done so with a pious and right

<column-break/>

knowledge, will know the presence of God that comes to him through dispassion <term>apatheia: a state of being where one is no longer driven by reactive, selfish emotions</term>. For the Psalmist says: "I will sing and understand in a blameless way; when will You come to me?" <note>Psalm 101:2</note>. For the "Psalm" signifies virtuous practice, while "understanding" signifies the cognitive science based on virtue, through which one perceives the divine presence. And he who waits for his Lord through the watchfulness of the virtues would be faithful and good.

<margin>99.</margin> One who is being introduced to piety should not be led toward the practice of the commandments through kindness alone, but should also be made to struggle more frequently through the memory of divine judgments and severity. This is so that he might not only love the divine things through desire, but also abstain from evil through fear. For "I will sing of mercy and judgment to You, O Lord" <note>Psalm 101:1</note>; so that he may sing to God while being delighted by desire, and yet remain firm in the song while being tempered by fear.

<margin>100.</margin> He who has harmonized the body to the soul through virtue and knowledge has become a lyre, a temple, and a flute of God. He is a lyre, because he has preserved the harmony of the virtues; he is a flute, because he receives the inspiration of the Spirit through divine contemplations; and he is a temple, because through the purity of his mind, he has become a dwelling place for the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>.

### BY THE SAME AUTHOR

## THE THIRD HUNDRED

### VARIOUS CHAPTERS ON THEOLOGY AND ECONOMY,
### AND ON VIRTUE AND VICE.

<margin>1.</margin> There is one Good, beyond all beginning and beyond all being <note>original: "hyperousion"</note>: the Holy Trinity, a Unity in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It is an infinite union of three infinites. It possesses a nature entirely inaccessible to created beings—its "how," "what," and "of what kind" are beyond us. For it escapes every perception of those who think, never departing from the hidden interiority of its nature; and it infinitely extends beyond the knowledge of all possible knowledge.

<column-break/>

<margin>2.</margin> That which is "Good" in its essence and in the primary sense is that which has no beginning, no end, no cause for its being, and no movement of any kind toward any cause regarding its existence. But that which is not like this is not "being" in the primary sense—it has a beginning, an end, a cause for its being, and a movement toward some cause regarding its existence. Thus, that which is not "being" in the primary sense, even if it is said to "be," exists and is named so only by participation and by the will of the One who Truly Is.

<summary>This page concludes the Second Century of Maximus's theological chapters with an allegory of the Cross's inscription representing the three stages of spiritual life, and begins the Third Century by defining the nature of the Trinity as the only "True Being."</summary>

<meta>This page begins the "Third Hundred" (also known as the Third Century) of Maximus the Confessor’s "Chapters on Theology and the Incarnate Dispensation of the Son of God." # THIRD HUNDRED

<margin>3.</margin> If the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> leads the way in the beginning of all created things, then there never was, is, not will be any word or reason higher than this Word. This Word is not without mind, nor is it without life; rather, it possesses mind and life, for it has the Father—who exists substantially—as the Mind who begets Him, and it has the Holy Spirit—who also exists substantially—co-existing as Life.

<margin>4.</margin> There is one God: the Father, who is the Begetter of one Son and the Source of the Holy Spirit; an unconfused Unity and an indivisible Trinity. He is the Mind without beginning; the sole Begetter of the only, substantially existing, and beginningless Word; and the Source of the only eternal Life, that is, the Holy Spirit.

<margin>5.</margin> There is one God because there is one divinity: a Unity without beginning, simple, beyond essence <term>beyond essence: "hyperousios," meaning God's nature is above the very category of being or existence as we understand it</term>, impartible, and indivisible. The same is both Unity and Trinity, and so forth.

<margin>6.</margin> If every participation is conceived of as existing before those who participate in it, then clearly the Cause of all things—pre-existing by nature and conceived of before all beings—stands incomparably above all things in every way. He does not exist as an "essence" that possesses "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "essence" is what a thing is, and "accidents" are its properties (like color or size). Maximus argues God is not a "thing" with properties.</note>; for if He did, the Divine would be shown to be a composite being, requiring the existence of other things to complete His own being. Rather, He is "beyond essence" in relation to essence. For if human arts invented the shapes of the things they made, and if nature in general produced the forms of the things under it, then how much more did God bring the very essences of beings into existence out of non-existence! As One who is beyond essence—and even beyond the very concept of being "beyond essence"—He is infinitely set apart. It is He who joined knowledge to the arts for the invention of shapes, gave nature the power to produce forms, and established the very existence of all essences as they are.

<margin>7.</margin> He who cannot be participated in by His essence, yet wishes to be participated in by those who are able through some other way, never departs from the total hiddenness of His essence. Even the very way in which He is participated in (as He wills and according to what He alone knows) remains forever unmanifest to all. Thus, by His will, He brought into existence those things that participate in Him, according to the reason <note>Logos</note> which He alone knows, through the surpassing power of His goodness. Therefore, that which came to be by the will of the Creator can never be co-eternal with the One who willed it to exist.

<margin>8.</margin> The Word of God, having been born once according to the flesh, is always willing to be born spiritually

<column-break/>

through His love for mankind in those who desire Him. He becomes an infant, forming Himself within them through the virtues. He reveals Himself only as much as He knows the receiver can hold; He does not diminish the manifestation of His own greatness out of jealousy, but measures it according to the capacity of those who long to see Him. In this way, the Word of God is always being revealed to us through the various ways we participate in Him, yet He remains forever unseen to all because of the supreme nature of His mystery. For this reason, the divine Apostle, wisely considering the power of this mystery, says: "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever" <note>Hebrews 13:8</note>; for he knew that the mystery is always new and never grows old by being fully grasped by the mind.

<margin>9.</margin> Christ God is born, becoming man by taking on flesh with a rational soul—He who provided the beginning of existence to all things out of non-existence. The Virgin, giving birth in a way that transcends nature, did not break any of the evidence of her virginity. For just as He became man without altering His nature or changing His power, so too He made her who bore Him a Mother while still preserving her as a virgin. He interprets one miracle by another, while simultaneously hiding one with the other. Since God, in Himself, is always a mystery by His very essence, the more He brings Himself out of His natural hiddenness through revelation, the more hidden He actually becomes. Thus, by making the Virgin a mother through child-bearing, <margin>* perhaps as much as through the birth the [bonds] of</margin> *He made the bonds of her virginity even more unbreakable.

<margin>10.</margin> Natures are made new, and God becomes man. Not only did the divine nature—stable and unmoved—move toward the shifting and unstable nature of man so that it might stop man’s wandering; and not only did human nature, without seed, produce flesh for the Word in a way beyond nature; but a star also appeared from the east in the daytime, guiding the **Magi** to the place where the Word was made flesh. This was to show mystically that the Word found in the Law and the Prophets <note>The Old Testament scriptures</term> triumphs over the senses and guides the nations toward the great light of knowledge. For the word of the Law and the Prophets, when understood with piety, acts like a star to guide those called by grace toward the full knowledge of the incarnate Word.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of the Trinity and the relationship between God's hidden essence and His manifestation in creation. It concludes with a theological reflection on the Nativity, describing how the Logos is continually born in the souls of believers and how the Incarnation fulfills the Law and the Prophets.</summary>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

<margin>11.</margin> Since I, as a human being, willfully transgressed the divine commandment, the devil was able to lure the stability of my nature toward pleasure by baiting me with the hope of becoming a god. Through this pleasure, he gained a foothold for death and took delight in it, feasting upon the corruption of our nature. Because of this, God becomes a perfect human being, setting aside nothing of our nature except for sin—since sin was not originally part of our nature. He did this so that, by baiting the "insatiable dragon" <note>A common early Christian metaphor for the devil, often referencing the Leviathan of the Old Testament.</note> with the lure of His flesh, He might provoke the dragon to gape wide and swallow it. This flesh became a poison to the devil, completely destroying him by the power of the divinity within it; but to human nature, it became a remedy <note>original: "alexeterion," a protective medicine or antidote</note> that calls us back to our original grace through that same divine power. Just as the devil poured the venom of his malice into the Tree of Knowledge and corrupted our nature when we tasted it, so too, when he desired to consume the flesh of the Master, he was destroyed by the power of the divinity dwelling within that flesh.

<margin>12.</margin> The great mystery of the Incarnation <note>The act of God taking on human flesh.</note> always remains a mystery. This is not only because it is revealed to those being saved by Him in a way that is proportional to their own capacity, always leaving more to be seen than what has already been glimpsed; it is also because the revelation itself remains entirely hidden. It cannot be understood by any rational explanation as it truly is. And let what I say not seem like a paradox: for God is beyond essence <term>beyond essence: "hyperousios," meaning God exists above the very category of "being" or "existence" as humans understand it</term>, and having risen above all essence, He willed to enter into essence. Thus, He was given an essence in a way that is beyond essence. Therefore, as a lover of mankind, He truly became a man from the essence of men, yet He was a man beyond the level of men. The manner in which He became man remains forever unmanifest, for He became man in a way that surpasses the human condition.

<margin>13.</margin> Let us faithfully consider the mystery of the divine Incarnation, and let us simply glorify—without prying curiosity—the One who was pleased to do this for our sake. For who, relying on the power of logical demonstration, can explain how the Word of God is conceived? How there is a beginning of flesh without seed? How there is a birth without the loss of virginity? How she who remained a Virgin after birth is yet a Mother? How He who is beyond all perfection progressed in age? How He who is pure was baptized? How He who was hungry provided nourishment? How He who grew weary bestowed strength? How He who suffered granted healing? How He who died gave life? And, to speak of the first and the last things: how does God become man? And what is even more

<column-break/>

mysterious: how is the Word substantially present in the flesh according to His person <term>person: "hypostasis," the specific, individual existence of the Word as one of the Trinity</term>, while according to His essence He remains entirely and personally present in the Father? How is He simultaneously both fully God by nature and fully man by nature, having denied neither nature in any way—neither the divine nature by which He is God, nor our nature by which He became man? Faith alone can contain these mysteries, for faith is the foundation <note>original: "hypostasis," here meaning the underlying reality or substance of things hoped for (referencing Hebrews 11:1).</note> of things that exist beyond the mind and reason.

<margin>13.</margin> <note>The original manuscript repeats the numbering '13' (ιγ') for this paragraph, though it is the 14th chapter in the sequence.</note> Through his disobedience, Adam taught us that the beginning of our nature’s generation comes from pleasure; the Lord, casting this pleasure out of our nature, did not accept a conception from seed. Through her transgression of the commandment, the woman showed that the beginning of our nature’s birth comes through pain; the Lord, shaking this pain off from our nature by His birth, did not allow the woman who bore Him to undergo corruption. He did this to remove from my nature both voluntary pleasure and the involuntary pain that follows it. He became the destroyer of that which He did not create <note>i.e., God did not create sin or death; He created nature. He "destroyed" the corruption that had attached itself to nature.</note>, and He secretly taught us to make a beginning of another life according to the will—a life that perhaps begins with pain and labor, but which ends certainly in divine pleasure and unending joy. For this reason, He who made man becomes man and is born as a man, so that He might save man. Having healed our passions by His own sufferings, He proved Himself to be a "passion" Himself <note>Maximus is using a wordplay: Christ took on "passibility" (the ability to suffer) to heal our "passions" (sinful impulses).</note>, renewing our spiritual state through His loving-kindness and His own physical deprivation.

<margin>15.</margin> The one who, through divine longing, has conquered the soul’s attachment to the body has become uncircumscribed <term>uncircumscribed: "aperigraphos," meaning not limited or defined by physical boundaries or earthly constraints</term>, even while remaining in a body. For God, who draws the desire of the one who loves Him, is incomparably higher than all things, and He does not allow the lover to fix his desire upon anything that comes after God. Let us, therefore, love God with all the power of our nature, and let us make our will unshakeable by all bodily things. Let us, in our inner disposition, rise above all things—both those sensed by the body and those understood by the mind—and let our will lose nothing to the limitations of our physical nature as we strive to be with God, who is by nature beyond all limits.

<margin>16.</margin> The hardship of the saints is a contest between envy and virtue. On the one hand, envy seeks to prevail...

<summary>Maximus explains the Incarnation as a divine "bait" used to destroy death and the devil, while emphasizing that the union of God and man remains an incomprehensible mystery accessible only through faith. He contrasts the fallen birth of Adam (rooted in pleasure and pain) with the Virgin Birth of Christ, which initiates a new, spiritual life for humanity.</summary>

...one who strives for vice through the punishment of those who do right; and the other, who strives to ensure that the good remain undefeated even when they have the greater share of misfortunes.

<margin>17.</margin>
The prize of virtue is to struggle through labors; the trophy of victory for those who endure is the soul's <term>apatheia</term> <note>original: "apatheia." In early Christian thought, this is not "apathy" in the modern sense of indifference, but a state of being "passionless"—freedom from the disordered desires and emotional disturbances that pull a person away from God.</note>. Through this dispassion, the soul is united to God through love, and is separated in its disposition from the body and the world. Indeed, for those who endure, the mistreatment of the body is the strengthening of the soul.

<margin>18.</margin>
<margin>* perhaps "of pleasure"</margin>
Having been robbed of our original state by the deception of pleasure, we chose the death of the true life instead. Therefore, let us gratefully endure the body's labor, which is the "slayer" of that pleasure; let this labor's death to pleasure cancel out the * death that occurred <note>original: "the death that occurred through [pleasure]." The marginal note suggest adding the word "pleasure" to the sentence for clarity.</note> within itself. In this way, we may receive back that life which was sold away for pleasure, now bought back by the small labors of the flesh.

<margin>19.</margin>
If the power of sin is usually fattened when the flesh is in comfort, it is clear that when the flesh suffers, the power of virtue naturally flourishes. Let us, then, nobly endure the suffering of the flesh, for it cleanses the soul’s defilements and brings about the glory that is to come. For "the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." <note>A quotation from St. Paul's Letter to the Romans 8:18.</note>

<margin>20.</margin>
Just as physicians who treat the body do not offer one and the same medicine to everyone, so God, when healing the diseases of souls, does not know only one mode of treatment suitable for all. Instead, by assigning to each soul what is fitting, He works His healings. Let us, therefore, give thanks while being treated, even if the process involves some torment. For the end result is blessed.

<margin>21.</margin>
Nothing tests the soul's disposition quite like the uprisings of bodily suffering. If the soul gives in to these, it proves that it loves the flesh more than God. But if it remains unshaken by these tremors, it shows that it honors virtue more than the flesh. Through this virtue, the soul receives God as a resident—the God who, for the soul's sake, endured suffering just as we do, and who cried out long ago to His disciples: "Take heart, I have overcome the world." <note>John 16:33.</note>

<margin>22.</margin>
If all the saints have participated in <term>paideia</term> <note>original: "paideia." This refers to divine discipline, education, or training through trials, much like an athlete's training or a child's upbringing.</note>, let us also give thanks as we are disciplined with them, so that we may be deemed worthy to share in their glory. For "the one whom the Lord loves,

<column-break/>

He disciplines; and He scourges every son whom He receives." <note>Hebrews 12:6.</note>

<margin>23.</margin>
<margin>* perhaps "opened up"</margin>
Adam, by accepting the "side" <note>A reference to Eve, who was taken from Adam's side, and the subsequent temptation in Eden.</note> when it offered pleasure, cast the human race out of Paradise. But the Lord, by allowing His side to be * pierced by a spear in pain, brought the thief into Paradise. Let us, then, love the labor of the flesh and hate its pleasure; for the former leads us in and restores us to good things, while the latter leads us out and separates us from them.

<margin>24.</margin>
If God suffers in the flesh by becoming human, who that suffers would not rejoice, having God as a partner in suffering? For to suffer with Him becomes a means to the Kingdom. For he who said this is true: "If we suffer with Him, it is so that we may also be glorified with Him." <note>Romans 8:17.</note>

<margin>25.</margin>
If it is necessary for everyone to labor because of the pleasure that was mixed into our nature through our first ancestor, let us nobly endure temporary labors. These labors both blunt the sting of pleasure within us and deliver us from the eternal punishments that come because of it.

<margin>26.</margin>
Love is the goal of all good things, for it leads, introduces, and unites those who walk in it to God—the highest of all goods and the cause of every good. Love remains faithful and unfailing. For **faith** is the foundation of the virtues that follow it (I mean hope and love), giving a firm existence to the truth. **Hope** is the strength of the extremes (I mean love and faith), revealing through itself that which is faithful and beloved to both, and teaching us how to direct our course toward it. But **love** is the fulfillment of these, being the final object of desire; it embraces the whole of the others entirely, providing a rest from the movement toward the goal. In place of "believing that it exists" and "hoping that it will be present," love introduces the "enjoyment of it as present" through itself.

<margin>27.</margin>
The most perfect work of love, and the end-goal of its activity, is to make the unique qualities of each (God and human) shine forth in the other through a relative exchange of their connected properties. It makes the human a god and makes God appear and be called human, because of the single and unchanging will and movement of both toward the same purpose. <note>This refers to theosis (deification), where the human person is so united to God that they share in divine attributes by grace, just as God shared in human attributes by nature.</note>

<margin>28.</margin>
If we were made entirely "according to the image of God," let us become [an image] of ourselves and of God; or rather...

<meta>This page continues the "Third Hundred" chapters by Maximus the Confessor. The previous page discussed the soul's detachment from the body and the "labor" required to reclaim the life lost to pleasure. Here, Maximus transitions into his famous discourse on the triad of evils—ignorance, self-love, and tyranny—and how the virtue of love (agape) restores the fragmented human nature to unity with God.</meta>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...of the only and whole God, and being ourselves whole, bearing nothing earthly in ourselves, so that we may draw near to God and become gods, receiving the state of being gods from God <note>original: "theoi genōmetha." This refers to the concept of **theosis** or deification, the process by which a person becomes united with God's grace so thoroughly that they "become by grace what God is by nature."</note>. For in this way the divine gifts are honored, and the presence of divine peace is welcomed.

<margin>29.</margin> Love is a great good, the first and most excellent of all goods, since through itself it joins God and men together around the one who possesses it. It even prepares the Creator of men to appear as a man, because of the unchanging likeness of the deified person toward God—a likeness achieved through the Good, as far as is possible for a human. I understand the practice of this likeness to be loving the Lord God with all one's heart, soul, and strength, and one's neighbor as oneself.

<margin>30.</margin> It is necessary to know that the devil, having deceived us with a calculated and wicked trickery through <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "philautia." In Maximus’s thought, self-love is the "mother of all passions," a disordered attachment to the body and its sensations.</note> and the assault of pleasure, has separated us from God and from one another in our will. He has distorted what is straight and divided our nature according to this manner of living, cutting it up into many opinions and fantasies.

<margin>31.</margin> There are three things that are the greatest and primary sources of evil, the parents of all vice: I mean ignorance, self-love, and tyranny. These are dependent on one another and supported by one another. For from ignorance of God comes self-love, and from self-love comes tyranny over those of the same race. No argument can deny that the Evil One established these within us by the misuse of our own natural powers—namely, our <term>reason</term>, <term>desire</term>, and <term>spiritedness</term>.

<margin>32.</margin> Instead of ignorance, we ought to be moved by **reason** toward God through a singular search for knowledge. Through **desire**, we ought to be driven by longing for God alone, purified of the passion of self-love. And with **spiritedness** <note>original: "thymos." Often translated as "anger," in this context it refers to the "drive" or "intensity" of the soul, which should be used to fight for virtue rather than against other people.</note> separated from tyranny, we should struggle only to attain God. Thus, through these powers, we may produce a divine and blessed love that joins the lover of God to God and reveals them to be a god.

<margin>33.</margin> Since self-love is the beginning, as I said, and the mother of evils <gloss>* perhaps "being plucked out"</gloss>, it is customary for everything born from it and after it to be plucked out along with it. For when self-love is gone, no trace or form of vice can possibly exist at all.

<column-break/>

<margin>34.</margin> It is necessary for us to hold fast to ourselves and to one another to the same extent that Christ Himself demonstrated beforehand, when He submitted to suffering on our behalf.

<margin>35.</margin> For the sake of love, all the saints resisted sin, making no account of this present life. They endured various forms of death so that they might be gathered to themselves and to God away from the world, and so that they might heal within themselves the "fissures" of nature. For this is the true and blameless <term>divine wisdom</term> <note>original: "theosophia." Here, it refers to the practical wisdom of living in God, rather than the modern esoteric movement.</note> of the faithful; its end is the Good and the Truth. The Good is seen in love for humanity, and the Truth in a God-loving faith—these are the hallmarks of love. For love joins humans to God and to one another, and because of this, it possesses a permanence of goods that never fails.

<margin>36.</margin> The activity and proof of perfect love toward God is a genuine disposition of voluntary goodwill toward one's neighbor. "For he who does not love his brother whom he has seen," says the divine John, "cannot love the God whom he has not seen."

<margin>37.</margin> The way of truth is love. The Word of God, having named Himself this way, presents those walking in it to God the Father, after they have become pure from all things.

<margin>38.</margin> This is the door through which the one who enters into the Holy of Holies becomes a witness of the "Holy of Holies" and is established as a spectator of the unapproachable beauty of the holy and royal Trinity.

<margin>39.</margin> It is truly fearful, and beyond all judgment, to voluntarily kill the life given to us by God through the gift of the Holy Spirit, by loving things that perish. Those who have practiced preferring the truth over self-love will certainly heal this fear.

<margin>40.</margin> Let us use peace as we ought. Having cast off the friendship with the world and the "ruler of the world" <note>original: "kosmokrator," referring to the devil.</note> which wrongly existed within us, let us finally end the war against God that is conducted through the passions. Having made an unbreakable treaty of peace with Him by the "abolition of the body of sin," let us cease our enmity toward Him.

<margin>41.</margin> It is impossible for us to be reconciled with God while we are rebelling against Him through the passions, and while [serving] the evil tyrant and murderer of...

<summary>This page outlines Maximus the Confessor's theology of love as the remedy for the three primary evils: ignorance, self-love, and tyranny. He emphasizes that love for God is proven through love for neighbor and that this path leads to theosis (becoming "gods by grace") and the vision of the Trinity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Third Hundred" chapters of Maximus the Confessor’s work on love. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing the soul’s liberation from the devil. Here, Maximus explores the "fragmentation" of human nature caused by sin and how the virtue of love (agape) restores humanity to its original unity and to God.</meta>

# THE THIRD HUNDRED

...souls who endure paying tribute to the devil through vice, not having previously declared total war against the evil one. For until that time, we remain his enemies and opponents—even if we wrap ourselves in the title of "the faithful"—as long as we choose to be enslaved to shameful passions. And no benefit will come to us from worldly peace thereafter, while the soul is in a bad state, rebelling against its own Creator and refusing to come under His kingdom; still being sold to ten thousand cruel masters <note>Maximus refers here to the "passions" or disordered desires as slave-masters of the soul.</note> who drive it toward vice and the road leading to destruction, making it deceptively choose that path rather than the one that saves.

<margin>42.</margin>
God made us for this: that we might become "partakers of the divine nature" <note>original: "theias koinōnoi physeōs" - a direct quote from the New Testament (2 Peter 1:4).</note> and sharers in His eternity, and that we might appear like Him through <term>deification</term> <note>original: "theosis." The process of becoming "god-like" through union with God's grace.</note> by grace. It is for this purpose that all things that exist were brought together and are sustained, and it is for this that things that did not exist were produced and brought into being.

<margin>43.</margin>
If we desire to be called "of God" and truly to be so, let us struggle not to betray the Word <note>original: "Logos." This refers both to Christ and to the "reason" or "principle" of virtue within us.</note> to the passions, like Judas; nor to deny Him, like Peter. For the refusal to do good out of fear is a denial of the Word; but the intentional act of sin and the impulse toward it is a betrayal.

<margin>44.</margin>
The end of every affliction is joy; the end of every labor is rest; and the end of every dishonor is glory. Simply put: the end of all the painful things endured for the sake of virtue is to be with God, to remain with Him forever, and to enjoy eternal and never-ending refreshment.

<margin>45.</margin>
God, wishing to unite us to one another in both nature and knowledge, and as a Good Father pushing the whole human race toward this goal, lovingly etched for us the saving commandments. For this reason, He commanded us to show mercy and ordained that we should simply be shown mercy.

<margin>46.</margin>
Human <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "philautia." Maximus views this as the root of all sin—a selfish attachment to the body over the soul.</note> and confusion, having either pushed away or cleverly subverted the law and each other, have cut our single nature into many parts. It has introduced the "insensitivity" that now prevails and has armed our nature against itself through our <term>will</term> <note>original: "gnome." This refers to our personal faculty of choice or "deliberative will," which Maximus believes is the source of human division.</note>. For this reason, anyone who, by a sober logic and 

<column-break/>

a nobility of wisdom, has been able to dissolve this "unevenness" of nature, has shown mercy to himself before all others. He has fashioned his will according to nature and has approached God by his will for the sake of nature. He has demonstrated in himself what the character of the "image" <note>Referring to the "Image of God" in which humanity was created (Genesis 1:26).</note> is, and how God, in the beginning, created our nature to be appropriately like Himself—a clear reflection of His own goodness. He established it to be entirely at one with itself: peaceful, without conflict, and without rebellion, bound to God and to itself through love. By this love, we hold fast to God with desire, and to one another with compassion.

<margin>47.</margin>
The God who loves mankind became man for this reason: to gather human nature to Himself and to stop it from being driven wickedly toward itself—or rather, from rebelling against itself and being divided, having no stability because of the unstable movement of each person’s individual will.

<margin>48.</margin>
Nothing after God is more precious to those who have understanding—or rather, nothing is more dear to God—than perfect love <note>original: "agape."</note>. It gathers those who are divided into one, and it is able to create a single, unwavering identity of will among many, or among all. For it is the specific property of love to produce a single will among those who seek it.

<margin>49.</margin>
If "the Good" is by nature something that unites those who are divided and holds them together, then "the Evil" is clearly that which divides and destroys those who were united. For by its very nature, evil is scattered, unstable, multiform, and divisive.

<margin>50.</margin>
The riddance of all evils and the short road to salvation is the true love of God according to knowledge, and the total denial of the soul's affection for both the body and this world. By this denial, we cast off the desire for pleasure and the fear of pain, and we are freed from "bad self-love," being lifted up toward the knowledge of the Creator. Having exchanged a wicked self-love for a good, intellectual self-love—one that is separated from bodily affection—we do not cease worshiping God through this "good self-love," always seeking from God the preservation of our soul.

<summary>Maximus explains that sin has fragmented human nature into many conflicting wills, but God became man to restore this unity. The key to this restoration is "agape" (perfect love), which overcomes "philautia" (selfish self-love) and reunites the soul with God and others.</summary>

<keywords>theosis, deification, philautia, self-love, agape, unity of nature, will, gnome, restoration, mercy, salvation</keywords>
