<meta>This page continues St. Maximus the Confessor’s "Third Hundred" chapters on love and virtue. The previous page discussed the soul's liberation from the devil and the beginning of the journey toward deification. On this page, Maximus transitions to the psychological and spiritual mechanics of how "self-love" (philautia) enslaves the soul through the cycle of pleasure and pain, and how the "Logos" (Reason/Word) restores the soul to its natural state.</meta>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...for this is true worship, and truly pleasing to God: the meticulous care of the soul through the virtues.

<margin>51.</margin> One who does not crave bodily pleasure, and is entirely unafraid of pain, has reached <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "apathes." In the tradition of Maximus, this is not "apathy" or a lack of feeling, but a state where the soul is no longer controlled by impulsive or disordered desires.</note>. For along with <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "philautia." Maximus identifies "self-love"—an obsessive attachment to the body’s comfort—as the root of all sin.</note>, which gave birth to them, such a person has simultaneously put to death all the passions that arise from and because of them, together with ignorance—the chief commander of all evils. Such a person becomes entirely devoted to the Beauty that is fixed, remains constant, and is always the same by nature. They remain forever unmoved within that Beauty, reflecting the glory of God with an "unveiled face," and beholding the divine and unapproachable glory from the light-filled radiance within themselves.

<margin>52.</margin> Let us deny the pleasure and the pain of this present life with all our might, and let us be completely delivered from every device of the passions and every demonic trickery. For it is because of pleasure that we love the passions, and because of pain that we flee from virtue.

<margin>53.</margin> Since every vice is naturally destroyed along with the methods that sustain it, a person finds through experience that pain always follows every pleasure. Toward pleasure, they direct their entire impulse; from pain, they direct their entire flight. They struggle for the one with all their might, and they fight against the other with all their zeal. They imagine—though it is impossible—that through such a maneuver they can keep these two apart. They hope to possess self-love joined only to pleasure, entirely free from pain. But it seems they are blinded by passion, failing to realize that it is never possible for pleasure to exist without pain. For the sting of pain is mixed into pleasure, even if it seems hidden to those who possess it because of the dominance of the pleasure-passion. Since whatever is dominant naturally overshadows everything else, it masks the perception of what lies beside it. Therefore, by claiming pleasure because of self-love, and by striving to flee pain for that same reason, we give birth to the countless forms of the soul-destroying passions.

<margin>54.</margin> One becomes ignorant of the experience of sensory pleasure and pain when they bind—or rather, glue—the mind (the <term>nous</term>) <note>The "nous" is the "eye of the heart" or the highest faculty of the human soul, capable of direct communion with God.</note> to God, the one who is truly beloved, desired, and sought after, having become free from bodily attachment.

<margin>55.</margin> Just as one cannot worship God

<column-break/>

purely without thoroughly cleansing the soul, so one cannot "worship" creation without looking after the body. It is through the body that a person performs a destructive kind of "worship" <note>Maximus plays on the word "latreia" (worship/service), contrasting the service of God with the "service" of the material world through the senses.</note> and, becoming self-loving, experiences an unceasing activity of pleasure and pain. Such a person is forever eating from the "tree of disobedience"—that is, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—possessing through experience a knowledge where both are mixed together within the senses. One would not be far from the truth to say that the "tree of the knowledge of good and evil" is the visible creation itself; for by its nature, the partaking of it produces both pleasure and pain.

<margin>56.</margin> Where Reason <note>original: "Logos." This refers to both human rationality and the Divine Reason that should govern it.</note> does not rule, the power of the senses naturally prevails. Within this sensory power, the strength of sin is somehow entangled, dragging the soul down through pleasure out of a misplaced pity for its own flesh. Having handed over the care of the flesh to the soul as if it were its natural task, the soul is persuaded by this "love of natural life" to become the creator of non-substantial evil.

<margin>57.</margin> Vice is a sickness of the rational soul; it is the forgetting of those things that are naturally good. This forgetfulness arises from an impassioned attachment to the flesh and the world. But the Reason (Logos), acting as a general according to spiritual knowledge, destroys this attachment. It searches into the nature of the world and the flesh and drives the soul toward its kindred region of intelligible things <note>The "intelligible" or "noetic" realm refers to the spiritual world that is perceived by the mind rather than the physical senses.</note>. The "law of sin" has no passage to that region, for it no longer has the senses acting as a bridge to transport it to the mind. The connection between the soul and the senses has been dissolved, and the senses are left behind among the objects of sight, while the mind, having passed beyond their nature and attachment, no longer perceives them.

<margin>58.</margin> Just as Reason, when it masters the passions, turns the senses into instruments of virtue; so also the passions, when they master Reason, shape the senses toward sin. One must soberly observe and meditate on how the soul might make a beautiful and proper reversal, using those very things through which it previously sinned to instead bring about the birth and existence of the virtues.

<margin>59.</margin> The Holy Gospel introduces the denial of the carnal life and the confession of the spiritual life. I speak of those who always live according to the human way—I mean the human life in the flesh in this present age...

<meta>Institutional stamp from the University of Crete at bottom right.</meta>

<summary>Maximus explains how self-love traps the soul in a cycle of pleasure and pain, identifying the "Tree of Knowledge" with the visible world when it is used without reason. He argues that the mind must transcend sensory attachment to return to its natural state of virtue and communion with God.</summary>

### THIRD HUNDRED

...those who are dying to the world, but living according to God in the spirit alone—following the divine Apostle and those with him. They live no life of their own, but have Christ living in them, possessing Him in their soul alone. Thus, those who for God’s sake are dead in the flesh in this age are judged; they endure many tribulations, torments, and hardships, along with persecutions and ten thousand kinds of temptations, which they undergo with joy.

<margin>60.</margin> Every <term>passion</term> <note>original: "pathos." In Maximus’s thought, a passion is an irrational, disordered movement of the soul that replaces true love for God with a love for material things.</note> is formed through a combination of some sensible object, a sense perception, and a natural power—I mean, for example, <term>anger</term> <note>original: "thymos," the spirited or incensive power of the soul.</note> or <term>desire</term> <note>original: "epithymia," the appetitive power.</note>—whenever what is natural is perverted. If, therefore, the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "nous," the highest faculty of the human soul, meant for direct contemplation of God.</note> observes the composite end resulting from the sensible object, the sense perception, and the natural power associated with it, it can restore each of these to its own natural <term>principle</term> <note>original: "logos," here meaning the divine purpose or inner reason of a thing.</note> by distinguishing them. It considers the sensible object in itself, without its relation to the sense perception, and the sense perception apart from its familiarity with the sensible object. It likewise considers desire (or any other natural power) apart from its passionate disposition toward the sense and the object. As the movement of the passion prepares this kind of contemplation, it scatters and thins the composition of whatever passion occurs—just like the ancient calf of Israel <note>A reference to Exodus 32:20, where Moses ground the golden calf into powder and scattered it in water.</note>—and sows it under the water of knowledge. This completely vanishes even the bare imagination of the passions through the restoration of the things that naturally constitute it back to themselves.

<margin>61.</margin> A life stained by the failings of fleshly passions is a "spotted garment." For just as people are naturally revealed by their clothing, so too they are revealed by their conduct in life—whether they are just or unjust. One has a clean garment in a life of virtue; the other possesses a life stained by evil deeds. Or rather, the "spotted garment of the flesh" <note>A reference to Jude 1:23.</note> is the habit and disposition that forms the soul through the memory of the flesh's evil movements and activities according to the conscience. Seeing this habit always around itself like a garment, the soul is filled with the stench of the passions. For just as a garment of incorruption is woven for the soul from the Spirit through the virtues being reasonably interwoven with one another,

<column-break/>

which, when the soul puts it on, makes it beautiful and glorious—so also from the flesh, as the passions are woven together in proportion to one another, a kind of unclean and spotted garment is made. This reveals the soul by its own appearance, bestowing upon it another form and image instead of the divine.

<margin>62.</margin> The Incarnation of God is the surest proof of the hope of <term>deification</term> <note>original: "ektheosis" or "theosis." The core concept that "God became man so that man might become god" by grace.</note> for human nature, making man a "god" to the same extent that He Himself became man. For it is clear that He who became man without sin deified nature without changing it into the divinity; and He will raise man up for His own sake to the same degree that He lowered Himself for man's sake. Teaching this mystically, the great Apostle says that in the ages to come, the "surpassing wealth" of God’s kindness toward us will be shown <note>Ephesians 2:7</note>.

<margin>63.</margin> When Reason presides over anger and desire, it produces the virtues. When the intellect applies itself to the principles of created things, it gathers unerring knowledge. Therefore, when Reason finds the "naturally beloved" after discarding all opposites, and when the intellect—after crossing through the realm of things that can be known—grasps the Cause that is beyond essence, knowledge, and all beings, then the "passion" of deification by grace occurs. This draws Reason away from natural distinction (where there is no longer anything to be distinguished) and brings the intellect to rest from natural thinking (where there is no longer anything to be known). In the identity of this "rest" <note>original: "stasis." In Maximus's triad of "Motion-Genesis-Rest," the soul finally finds rest in God.</note>, it makes the one deemed worthy of divine participation a "god."

<margin>64.</margin> Pain cleanses the soul that has been rusted by the filth of pleasure, and it completely "un-nails" the soul’s attachment to material things, once it has learned through loss that friendship with them is harmful. For this reason, God permits the devil, by a righteous judgment, to oppress men with torments.

<margin>65.</margin> Pleasure and grief, desire and fear, and the things that follow them, were not originally created with human nature; otherwise, they would be part of the definition of that nature. I say this having learned from the great <term>Gregory of Nyssa</term> <note>A 4th-century theologian who argued that certain emotional states were "accidental" to human nature, added as a result of the Fall.</note> that these things were introduced through our fall from perfection, having become attached to the more irrational part of our nature; through which, instead...

<summary>Maximus explains how the intellect can dismantle sinful passions by analyzing them into their natural components and describes the Incarnation as the mechanism for human deification. He also uses the metaphor of a 'spotted garment' to describe a soul stained by fleshly habits.</summary>

### [OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS]

...Immediately upon the transgression of the blessed and divine image, the likeness to irrational animals became transparent and manifest in man. For it was right that, once the dignity of reason was veiled, human nature should be justly punished by the characteristics of irrationality it had drawn upon itself; God wisely providently leading man to a realization of his rational greatness.

<margin>66.</margin>
Even the **passions** <note>original: "pathe." Feelings or impulses that, when disordered, lead away from God.</note> become good in the diligent, whenever they wisely detach them from bodily things and use them for the acquisition of heavenly things. For example, when we make **desire** <note>original: "epithymia."</note> an appetitive movement for the intellectual longing for divine things; **pleasure**, the painless joy of the mind’s willing activity in divine gifts; **fear**, a precautionary care against future punishment for offenses; and **grief**, a corrective repentance for a present evil. To put it briefly, like wise physicians who remove a current or intended blight from a decaying body using the venom of a viper, we use these passions to destroy present or expected vice, and to acquire and preserve both virtue and knowledge.

<margin>67.</margin>
The law of the first covenant <note>Referring to the Old Testament.</note>, through **practical philosophy** <note>The stage of spiritual life focused on purifying the soul from passions through the practice of virtues.</note>, purifies nature from every defilement; while the law of the new covenant, through **contemplative initiation**, cognitively raises the mind from bodily things to the kindred sights of the intelligible realm.

<margin>68.</margin>
Holy Scripture calls those who are being introduced, and who happen to be at the gateways of the divine court of virtues, "those who fear." Those who have acquired a proportionate habit of the principles and ways of virtue, it designates as "those making progress." Those who, through virtue, have already cognitively reached the <unclear>summit of the manifest truth</unclear> <note>This section is partially obscured by an ink blot in the original manuscript.</note> of the virtues, it addresses as "the perfect." Therefore, he who has turned away from his old way of life in the passions, and has surrendered his whole disposition to divine things through fear, lacks nothing of the beauty appropriate to those being introduced; even if he has not yet acquired the habit of the virtues or become a sharer in the wisdom spoken of among the perfect. But neither does the one making progress fall short of any of the beauties assigned to his rank, 

<column-break/>

even if he has not yet acquired that same knowledge of divine things that surpasses the perfect. For the perfect, having already been mystically granted **contemplative theology**, and having established their mind pure of every material imagination, and bearing the full imitation of the <gloss>divine image</gloss> <margin>perhaps "image" (eikona)</margin> of divine beauty without lack, appear to have taken divine love into their very hearts.

<margin>69.</margin>
Fear is twofold: one is pure, the other is not pure. The fear which arises pre-eminently from punishment for offenses, having sin as the cause of its own birth, is not pure; nor will it exist forever, as it disappears along with sin through repentance. But the fear which always exists apart from the grief over offenses—this is **pure fear**, and it will never cease to be. For it is somehow essentially implanted by God in creation, making manifest to all His natural awesomeness, which transcends every kingdom and power.

<margin>70.</margin>
He who does not fear God as a judge, but stands in awe of Him because of the surpassing excellence of His infinite power, is rightly without lack, being perfect in love—loving God with awe and appropriate reverence. And this is the one who has acquired the fear that "remains forever and ever" (Psalm 19:9), and for him there is no lack at all.

<margin>71.</margin>
From the things that exist, we know the Cause of existing things; and from the difference between existing things, we are taught the self-subsistent **Wisdom** of the Existent; and from their <gloss>truly natural movement</gloss> <margin>perhaps "of the existing things"</margin>, we learn the self-subsistent **Life** of the Existent—the life-giving power of existing things, the **Holy Spirit**.

<margin>72.</margin>
The **Holy Spirit** is absent from nothing that exists, and especially from those who have shared in reason in any way. For He sustains the knowledge of each thing, because He is God and the Spirit of God, providently passing through all things by His power, stirring the natural principle <note>original: "logos." The divine blueprint or inner purpose within every created thing.</note> in each, and through it leading the one who perceives it to a realization of things done wrongly against the law of nature; and having a will ready for the reception of naturally correct thoughts. Therefore, we find many even among the most barbarian and nomadic peoples who lay claim to goodness and nobility...

<summary>Maximus explains how human passions can be redirected toward spiritual growth and distinguishes between 'slavish' fear of punishment and the 'pure' fear of divine awe. He concludes by discussing the Holy Spirit's presence in all of creation as a providential guide for reason and conscience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues St. Maximus the Confessor’s "Third Century" of theological chapters. The previous page ended with a discussion on how the New Covenant leads the mind from physical things to the inner principles (logoi) of creation.</meta>

### ->THIRD CENTURY<-

...and those who from of old held sway in them, rejecting their beastly laws.

<margin>73.</margin>
The Holy Spirit is, in a simple sense, in all things, insofar as He sustains all things and stirs the natural seeds within them. But He is present in a specific way in all those under the Law, insofar as He points out the transgression of the commandments and illuminates the promise regarding Christ. In all those who live according to Christ, He is present not only in the ways already mentioned, but also as the Spirit of **adoption** <note>original: "uioithetikon." The process by which a believer becomes a child of God by grace.</note>. However, as the author of **wisdom**, He is not simply in all the aforementioned, but only in those who understand and have made themselves worthy of His deifying indwelling through a **godly way of life** <note>original: "entheou politeias." Literally, a "divinely-inspired citizenship" or conduct.</note>. For everyone who does not perform the divine will, even if he is a believer, has an uncomprehending heart—a workshop of evil thoughts—and a body burdened with debt to sin, being continually held fast by the defilements of the passions.

<margin>74.</margin>
God, who desires the salvation of all people and hungers for their **deification** <note>original: "ektheosin." The process of being united with God and transformed by His grace.</note>, dries up their self-conceit like the "fruitless fig tree." He does this so that they might prefer truly *being* righteous over merely *seeming* to be so. Thus, stripping off the garment of moral display worn for hypocrisy, and pursuing an unadulterated life of virtue as the Divine Word wills, they may spend their lives in piety, demonstrating the disposition of the soul to God rather than showing off an external fashioning of character to men.

<margin>75.</margin>
The principle of *doing* is one thing, and the principle of *undergoing* is another. The principle of *doing* is the natural power for the activity of the virtues; but the principle of *undergoing* is either the grace of things above nature, or the occurrence of things contrary to nature. For just as we have no natural power for that which is **transcendent** <note>original: "hyperontos." That which exists beyond being; God.</note>, so we have no natural power for that which does not exist. We "undergo," then, the deification which is above nature by grace, but we do not "do" it; for we do not possess a natural power capable of achieving deification. Again, we "undergo" the occurrence of evil as something contrary to nature by our own choice; for we do not have a natural power for the production of evil. Therefore, in the first case, being natural beings, we "do" the virtues because we have the natural power to do them. But in the second case, we "undergo" deification in the future, receiving the grace that enables this experience as a gift.

<margin>76.</margin>
We "do" as long as we have the natural, rational power to produce the 

<column-break/>

virtues in our activity, and as long as we have the intellectual power to receive all knowledge—a power that transcends the nature of all things that are and are known, leaving all the ages behind it. But we "undergo" when, having completely passed beyond the inner principles of beings, we come unknowingly to the **Cause** <note>Referring to God as the source of all existence.</note> of all things. There, we bring our own powers to rest along with all naturally limited things, becoming that which is by no means an achievement of our natural power. For nature does not possess a power capable of grasping what is above nature. Nothing created is by nature capable of producing **deification** <note>original: "theoseos."</note>, because it cannot grasp God. For it is the property of divine grace alone to bestow deification upon beings in due proportion; grace which illumines nature with a light above nature and places nature above its own limits through the abundance of glory.

<margin>77.</margin>
When we do the virtues, we cease doing them after this life; but we never cease "undergoing" the deification that comes through grace on their account. For the experience that is above nature is infinite, because it is also effective; but that which is contrary to nature is non-existent and ineffective.

<margin>78.</margin>
The modes of virtue and the **inner principles** <note>original: "logoi." The divine patterns or reasons inherent in created things.</note> of beings are types of divine goods. Through these, God always becomes man. As a body, He possesses the modes of the virtues; as a soul, He possesses the principles of knowledge in the Spirit, through which He deifies those who are worthy. He grants a substantial character to virtue and bestows a real, essential existence to unerring knowledge.

<margin>79.</margin>
The believer, according to Saint Peter, is the **practical intellect** <note>original: "praktikos nous." The mind engaged in the active struggle for virtue.</note>. When he is held by Herod—meaning the "law of the skin," for "Herod" is interpreted as "leathern," which is the "mindset of the flesh"—he is shut up by two guards and one iron gate. He is attacked by the activity of the passions and by the mental consent to those passions. Having passed through these as if through prisons or jails by means of the word of **practical philosophy** <note>The discipline of purifying the soul's passions.</note>, as if by an angel, he comes to the iron gate that leads to the city. I mean by this the rigid, sharp, and hard-to-overcome attachment of the senses to the things of the world. The word of natural **contemplation** <note>original: "theoria." Spiritual insight into the nature of reality.</note> in the Spirit opens this gate, automatically leading the mind toward things of its own kind...

It also provides an allegorical interpretation of St. Peter's escape from prison as the mind's liberation from the flesh and the senses.</summary>

### ->OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS<-

...the mind then fearlessly passes into **intelligible** <note>original: "noēta." In Maximus's thought, these are spiritual realities perceived by the intellect rather than the physical senses.</note> things, being free from the madness of Herod.

<margin>80.</margin>
The devil is both an enemy of God and an avenger. He is an enemy when, as if out of hatred for God, he seems to possess a kind of destructive "love" for us humans, persuading our **will** <note>original: "proairesin." Our faculty of choice or moral disposition.</note> through the methods of voluntary passions and pleasure to prefer temporary things over eternal blessings. Through these means, he steals the soul's entire desire and completely separates us from divine love, making us voluntary enemies of the One who created us. But he is an avenger when he strips away his mask of "love" and reveals his hatred toward us; once we have become subject to him through sin, he demands our punishment. For nothing is so dear to the devil as a human being being punished. When he is granted this permission, he blows upon us successive waves of involuntary sufferings, falling upon those over whom he has received authority by God's concession like a violent storm. He does this not because he wishes to fulfill the divine command, but because he desires to feed his own passion of hatred toward us. His goal is that the soul, collapsing out of weakness under the heavy weight of painful calamities, might cut off its own power of divine hope—making the onset of these painful events a cause for **atheism** <note>original: "atheïas." Not necessarily a formal denial of God, but a practical loss of faith in God's care or existence due to suffering.</note> rather than for correction.

<margin>81.</margin>
When those who have acquired the habit of practice and theoretical knowledge use these for the sake of human glory—sketching out the character of the virtues only in appearance, and speaking words of wisdom and knowledge only with the tongue, while lacking works of justice—and when they display to others a pride based on their supposed virtue and knowledge, they are quite rightly handed over to fitting labors. Through suffering, they learn the **humility** <note>original: "tapeinophrosunēn." The "lowliness of mind" that Maximus considers essential for true spiritual progress.</note> they had ignored because of their vain conceit.

<margin>82.</margin>
Each of the demons carries out his service according to the specific disposition that lies within him, bringing about this or that temptation. For one is the producer of one vice, and another of another; and one is clearly more foul than another, being more suited to a particular form of evil.

<margin>83.</margin>
Without divine permission, even the demons themselves are unable to serve the devil in any way. For God Himself knows

<column-break/>

how, with the necessary love for humanity and good providence, He permits the devil to carry out various punishments through his servants. The account of **Job** <note>The biblical figure who suffered extreme loss and physical ailment as a test of faith.</note> clearly demonstrates this, recording that the devil was completely unable to approach Job without the divine will.

<margin>84.</margin>
**Hypostatic faith** <note>original: "Enupostatos pistis." Faith that is not just an idea, but has a "subsistent" or concrete reality in the person's life through action.</note> is that which is evident and active. Through such faith, the Word of God is shown in those who practice it, becoming "embodied" in the commandments. Through these commandments, as the Word returning to the Father in whom He naturally exists, He leads back those who perform them.

<margin>85.</margin>
The mystery of the New Testament proclaims a change of life, an angelic way of service, a voluntary estrangement of the soul from the body, and the birth of a divine transformation in the spirit. The Word knows how to call the cutting away of the soul's passionate relationship with the body "spiritual circumcision."

<margin>* perhaps regarding</margin>
Because God is good and wishes to root out the seed of evil within us—namely, **pleasure**, which has plundered the mind of divine love—He permits the devil to bring pains and punishments upon us. By this, He scrapes away the poison of previous pleasure through the pains of the soul. He wishes to create in us a hatred and complete detachment from present things which only entice the senses—seeing as they have brought nothing more than punishment as a * profit in their use. Thus, He makes the devil's punishing and misanthropic power a circumstantial cause for the return to virtue for those who had voluntarily slipped away from it.

<margin>86.</margin>
It is fitting and just for those who gladly accepted the devil's evil suggestions of voluntary sins to be punished by him. For the devil is both the sower of pleasure through voluntary passions and the bringer of pain through involuntary trials.

<margin>87.</margin>
The theoretical and **gnostic** <note>original: "gnōstikos." Referring to one who possesses spiritual knowledge (gnosis) of divine mysteries.</note> mind is often handed over to the devil for punishment for this reason: the devil brings labors and calamities upon it justly, so that through suffering it may learn to philosophize more about endurance and the patience of labors, rather than vainly and pridefully exulting in things that are not real.

<margin>88.</margin>
One who suffers on account of a broken divine commandment, if he recognizes the reason for the divine providence that is healing him, accepts the calamity with gratitude and joy, and for the sake of that commandment...

<summary>St. Maximus explains the relationship between human will, divine providence, and the devil's role as a "punisher." He argues that God permits suffering to purge the soul of the "poison" of pleasure and to lead the proud back to humility.</summary>

### ->THIRD CENTURY<-

...is disciplined and corrects his fault. But he who is insensible to this healing is justly led away from the grace that was given to him, and is handed over to the confusion of the **passions** <note>original: "pathōn." In this context, these are the disordered impulses or irrational emotions that cloud the soul's judgment.</note>, being left to fulfill the actions of those things for which he had an internal desire.

<margin>700</margin>
Every person who, out of an awareness of their past deeds, willingly accepts the painful onset of involuntary temptations with the necessary gratitude, does not become an exile from the state of virtue and grace. Such a person has willingly come under the yoke of the **King of Babylon** <note>original: "Basileōs Babylōnos." A reference to the biblical account where the Israelites were told to submit to Nebuchadnezzar as a divine discipline. Maximus uses this as an allegory for accepting earthly trials as a means of spiritual debt-repayment.</note> and accepts the onset of these torments as a debt being paid. While remaining in these trials, he pays a debt to the King of Babylon—namely, the violent pains arising from the "passionate" part of his nature and the mental consent to them, which he owes because of his previous faults. To God, however, he offers the correction of his past negligences through true worship—that is, through a humble disposition.

<margin>701</margin>
He who does not gratefully accept the calamity brought upon him through involuntary temptations for his correction—and who, thinking himself to be righteous, does not put away his conceit—resists the divine decrees of the just judgments of God. By refusing to willingly come under the yoke of the King of Babylon according to the divine command, he is handed over to a real captivity: to collars, chains, plague, death, the sword, and complete exile from his own land. For he who is exiled from the state of virtue and knowledge as if from his "own land" suffers all these things and more. Because of his pride and vain conceit, he refuses to satisfy the penalties for his faults by being well-pleased in tribulations, necessities, and distresses, as the **Divine Apostle** <note>original: "theion Apostolon." Referring to St. Paul, specifically his words in 2 Corinthians 12:10.</note> says. For the great Apostle knew that the outward humility of the body through labors preserves the divine treasures within the soul. Therefore, he loved and endured these things for his own sake and for those to whom he served as a model of virtue and faith; so that even if they suffer as "guilty" ones (like the rebuked **Corinthian** <note>original: "Korinthion." Likely a reference to the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 and later restored.</note>), they might find consolation and a pattern of endurance in the one suffering while "not guilty."

<column-break/>

<margin>702</margin>
He who does not remain fixed on the outward forms of visible things through his senses, but instead searches with his mind for their **inner principles** <note>original: "logous." The divine reasons or blueprints behind created things.</note> as types of intelligible realities, or who contemplates the principles within created things, is taught that nothing in the visible world is "unclean." For all things are, by nature, very good.

<margin>703</margin>
He who is not changed by the movement of sensory things practices the virtues in a pure way. He who does not allow his mind to be shaped by their outward forms has received a true understanding of beings. And he who, as an excellent **theologian**, passes beyond the very essence of beings with his intellect, has reached the **Monad** <note>original: "monadi." The "One" or the Unity of God.</note> in a state beyond knowledge.

<margin>704</margin>
Every contemplative mind that possesses the "sword of the Spirit," which is the Word of God, and kills within itself the movement toward visible creation, has succeeded in virtue. By cutting away the imagination of sensory forms, it finds the truth within the principles of beings, in which natural contemplation consists. By rising above the essence of beings, it receives the illumination of the divine and **unoriginate** Monad, in which the mystery of true theology is established.

<margin>705</margin>
God appears to each person according to the "opinion" they hold regarding Him. To those who possess an integrated material composition and whose soul-powers are equal to one another in a single, ever-moving motion toward God, He appears as **Monad** and **Triad** <note>original: "monas kai trias." The Unity and Trinity of God.</note>, so that He might demonstrate His own existence and mystically teach the "manner" of that existence. But to those whose desire is moved only toward material things, and whose soul-powers are disconnected from each other, He appears not as He is, but as they are—showing that they have grasped with both hands the "material duality" from which the physical world of matter and form is composed.

<margin>706</margin>
The Divine Apostle calls the various energies of the Holy Spirit "different gifts," though they are worked by one and the same Spirit. If, therefore, the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each according to the measure of their faith through the participation in such a gift, then clearly each of the faithful receives according to the proportion of their faith and the underlying...

<margin>107</margin> Just as one person receives the word of wisdom, another the word of knowledge, another faith, and another some other of the gifts of the Spirit enumerated by the Great Apostle <note>A reference to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 12:8-10.</note>; so too, one person receives through the Spirit the gift of perfect and direct love toward God, which contains nothing material, according to the proportion of their faith. Another receives, through the same Spirit, the gift of perfect love toward their neighbor. Yet another receives something else, according to the same Spirit—each one, as I said, having their own gift activated within them. For the Apostle says that every habit of a commandment being put into action is a gift of the Spirit.

<margin>108</margin> The Lord’s **Baptism** is the complete death of our **will** <note>original: "proaireseōs." This refers to our faculty of choice or moral intentionality.</note> toward the sensible <note>Meaning "perceivable by the senses."</note> world. The **Cup**, however, is the denial of even our present life for the sake of the truth.

<column-break/>

<margin>109</margin> The Lord’s **Baptism** is a type <note>In this context, a "type" is a symbolic foreshadowing or a spiritual pattern.</note> of our own voluntary labors for the sake of virtue. Through these, we wash away the stains upon our conscience and accept a voluntary death of our will toward appearances. The **Cup** is a type of the involuntary temptations that rise up against us by circumstance for the sake of the truth. Through these, by preferring the divine desire even over our own nature, we willingly undergo the circumstantial death of nature.

<margin>110</margin> This is the difference between Baptism and the Cup: Baptism makes the will dead to the pleasures of life for the sake of virtue, while the Cup <note>original: "potērion." # FOURTH CENTURY

<margin>1</margin> He placed the Cup before Baptism because virtue exists for the sake of the truth, but truth does not exist for the sake of virtue. Therefore, he who practices virtue for the sake of the truth is not wounded by the arrows of **vainglory** <note>original: "kenodoxia." A technical term in ascetic theology for the desire for human praise or empty pride.</note>. But he who pursues the truth for the sake of virtue has the conceit of vainglory as his companion.

<margin>2</margin> He says that Truth is divine knowledge, while virtue consists of the struggles of those who desire it for the sake of truth. Therefore, he who undergoes the labors of virtue <margin>* perhaps: "virtues."</margin> for the sake of knowledge does not become vainglorious, for he knows that the truth is by nature ungraspable through labors alone. For that which is primary is not by nature circumscribed by that which is secondary. But he who pursues knowledge because of his struggles for it is certainly vainglorious, as he seems to have taken the crowns before the sweat. He does not know that labors are for the sake of the crowns, not crowns for the sake of the labors. For by nature, every method becomes unpracticed 

<column-break/>

once that for which it naturally exists is accomplished, or is thought to be accomplished.

<margin>3</margin> He who pursues only the form of knowledge—which is bare speech—and only the image of virtue—which is bare character—is himself a "Jew" <note>Maximus uses "Jew" here allegorically to refer to anyone who follows the "letter" of a law or the outward appearance of religion without its spiritual "spirit" or "truth."</note>, becoming puffed up by the mere types of the truth.

<margin>4</margin> He who does not look at the entire visible worship of the Law according to the senses, but who examines each of the visible symbols with the approaches of the mind, learns the God-perfecting **Reason** <note>original: "Logon." The underlying divine purpose or the presence of the Word/Christ hidden within the Old Testament law.</note> hidden in each one. Such a person finds God in the Law, searching well through his intellectual power—as if in a pile of refuse—through the matter of the legal decrees, to see if he might find the **Pearl of the Word** <note>original: "margaritēn logon." A reference to the Pearl of Great Price, signifying the hidden divine truth that escapes sensory perception.</note> hidden somewhere in the flesh of the Law, which completely escapes the senses.

# FOURTH CENTURY

...the mind, wisely searching for the principle <note>original: "logon." In the theology of St. Maximus, the *logoi* are the divine "blueprints" or intentions of God for every created thing.</note> within each creature, finds God from the manifest majesty of all things, thus being taught the very Cause of all that exists.

<margin>6.</margin> Since discernment is the characteristic of one who searches <note>original: "pselaphontos," literally "groping" or "feeling around," like someone searching in the dark.</note>, the person who approaches the symbols of the Law with spiritual knowledge and contemplates the visible nature of things scientifically <note>original: "epistemonikos." In this context, it refers to a rigorous, spiritual understanding rather than modern empirical science.</note>, distinguishes between Scripture, creation, and himself. He divides Scripture into **letter** and **spirit**; creation into **principle** <note>original: "logon"</note> and **appearance**; and himself into **mind** <note>original: "noun"</note> and **sense**. By taking the spirit of Scripture, the principle of creation, and the mind of himself, and uniting them indissolubly to one another, he finds God. Thus, he recognizes God as he ought—and as far as is possible—as being in Mind, Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>, and Spirit. He is freed from all things that mislead and drag one down into ten thousand opinions—namely, the letter, appearance, and 

<margin>* equality or specific movement of quantity</margin> 

sense, in which diverse **quantity** <note>original: "posotetos." Maximus often associates quantity and division with the fallen material state, as opposed to the absolute unity of God.</note> exists, which is the opposite of the Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the absolute unity and oneness of God.</note>. But if someone entangles and confuses the letter of the law, the appearance of visible things, and his own senses with one another, he is "blind and shortsighted," suffering from ignorance of the Cause of all things.

<margin>7.</margin> The divine and great Apostle, in defining what faith is, says: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." <note>Quoting Hebrews 11:1.</note> If someone were also to define it as an inherent good, or as true knowledge that demonstrates unutterable blessings, they would not miss the truth.

<margin>8.</margin> **Faith** is a relational power, or an active relationship that brings about the supernatural, immediate, and perfect union of the believer with the God in whom they believe.

<margin>9.</margin> Since a human being consists of soul and body, they are moved by two laws: that of the **flesh** and that of the **Spirit**. The law of the flesh has its activity according to the senses, while the law of the Spirit has its activity according to the mind. The law of the flesh naturally binds one to matter when acting through the senses; but the law of the Spirit, acting through the mind, creates an immediate union with God. Thus, the person who does not "doubt in his heart"—that is, in his mind—does not divide or cut through the immediate union with God achieved through faith. As one who is beyond passion, or rather, as one who has already become "god" <note>original: "theos." This refers to *theosis* or deification, where the human participates in God's life by grace.</note> through the

<column-break/>

union of faith, he will say to **this mountain**, "Move from here," and it will move. By saying "**this**," he points specifically to the mindset and the law of the flesh. This "mountain" is truly heavy and difficult to shift; and as far as natural power is concerned, it is entirely immobile and unshakable.

<margin>10.</margin> The power of irrationality is so deeply rooted in human nature through the senses that most people believe a human being is nothing more than flesh, possessing the senses only for the enjoyment of this present life.

<margin>11.</margin> "All things," He says, "are possible to him who believes" <note>Mark 9:23.</note> and does not doubt. This means not being divided from the union with God achieved through the mind and faith, despite the soul's relationship to the body via the senses. For such things of the world and the flesh alienate the mind from God. Faith, however, makes the mind belong to God, having been perfected by virtuous achievements. This is what must be understood by the phrase, "all things are possible to the believer."

<margin>12.</margin> **Faith** is unproven knowledge. If it is unproven knowledge, then faith is a relationship that transcends nature, through which we are united to God in a way that is beyond understanding—a union that is unknown in a worldly sense, rather than one based on logical demonstration.

<margin>13.</margin> Having attained immediate union with God, the mind finds its power of thinking and being thought completely at rest. Therefore, whenever the mind breaks this union by thinking about anything "after" <note>Meaning anything lower than or separate from God.</note> God, it becomes divided. It cuts through that union which is beyond understanding—the union in which it was joined to God and had become "god" by participation through a supernatural state. Like an immovable mountain, such a mind shifts the very law of its own nature.

<margin>14.</margin> The person being introduced to piety, who is being taught the works of righteousness, carries out the practice only with total obedience and faith. It is as if they are eating the "**flesh**" of the virtues—that is, the visible aspect of moral training. But they leave the **principles** <note>original: "logous"</note> of the commandments, in which the knowledge of the perfect resides, to God through faith, being unable as yet to stretch themselves out to the full length of faith.

<margin>15.</margin> The perfect person has run through not only the rank of the beginner but also that of those making progress. He is not ignorant of the principles of what he does according to the commandments; instead, having first "drunk" those principles in the spirit, he then eats all the "**flesh**" of the virtues through his actions...

<summary>This page defines faith as a supernatural union with God that transcends sensory perception and logical proof. St. Maximus explains that by aligning the mind with the "Spirit" and the "Logos," a believer can overcome the heavy "mountain" of the fleshly law and achieve deification.</summary>

### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...of things, elevating the movement of those things perceived by the senses toward the knowledge that is according to the mind <note>original: "noun." In Eastern Christian thought, the *nous* is the "eye of the soul" or the highest faculty of the human person, capable of direct experience of God.</note>.

<margin>16.</margin> The Lord said, "Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness" (Matthew 6:33). This means that before all else, we must seek the recognition of the truth, and then the practice of the appropriate ways of life. He clearly showed that those who believe must seek only for divine knowledge and the virtue that adorns it through our actions.

<margin>17.</margin> Since there are many things required for the believers to reach the knowledge of God and virtue—such as the release from passions <note>disordered impulses or attachments</note>, the endurance of trials, the principles of virtues, the active ways of living, the stripping away of the soul’s disposition toward the flesh, the distancing of the senses from their attachment to physical things, and the mind’s complete withdrawal from all created things—and simply ten thousand other things for the turning away from vice and ignorance and the achievement of knowledge and virtue. Therefore, the Lord rightly said, "Whatever you ask in faith, you shall receive" (Matthew 21:22). He meant that the pious must seek and ask, with understanding and faith, only for those things that contribute to the recognition of God and virtue. For all these things are beneficial, and the Lord certainly gives them to those who ask.

<margin>18.</margin> Therefore, the person who seeks everything that leads to union for the sake of faith alone—that is, the immediate union with God—will certainly receive them. But he who seeks these things, or even the things mentioned before, for any other reason, will not receive them. For he does not truly believe, but like an unbeliever, he pursues his own glory through divine matters.

<margin>19.</margin> He who is pure in his will from the corruption of sin destroys the very corruption that is natural to things that decay. For the incorruptibility of the will naturally preserves the corruption of nature as incorrupt, according to God's providence, through the grace of the Spirit within it, not allowing the nature to be destroyed by opposing qualities.

<margin>20.</margin> Since the principle of nature and the principle of grace are not one and the same, it is not a cause for bewilderment why some of the saints at times rose above passions, but at other times fell under them. We should understand that the miracle was the work of grace, while the passion belonged to their human nature.

<column-break/>

<margin>21.</margin> He who keeps the memory of the saints' lives through imitation puts away the deadness of the passions and receives the life of the virtues.

<margin>22.</margin> In whatever way God—who defined the life of each person before the ages—wills, He leads each person toward their own proper end of life, whether they be just or unjust.

<margin>23.</margin> Regarding the dark storm that happened to the blessed Paul (Acts 28), I judge it to be the weight of involuntary trials. The island represents the firm and unshakable state of divine hope. The fire represents the state of spiritual knowledge. The brushwood represents the nature of visible things; Paul gathered these with his "hand"—by which I mean the grasping power of the mind in contemplation—nourishing the state of knowledge with thoughts derived from these things. This heals the gloom rubbed into the intellect by the storm of trials. The viper is the evil and destructive power hidden secretly in the nature of physical things. It bit the hand—that is, the active grasping power of the mind’s contemplation—but it did not harm the discerning mind, for the mind immediately destroyed it with the light of knowledge as if in a fire. This destructive power, which attaches itself to the mind's practical movement through the contemplation of physical things, was thus neutralized.

<margin>24.</margin> The Apostle was an "aroma from life to life" (2 Corinthians 2:16) insofar as he prepared believers, through his own example, to move through action toward the fragrance of the virtues. Or, as a herald, he led those who obeyed the word of grace from a life centered on the senses to a life in the spirit. Yet he was an "aroma of death to death" for those who moved from the death of ignorance into the death of unbelief, giving them a sense of their future judgment. Or again, he is an "aroma from life to life" for those being led from practice to contemplation; and an "aroma of death to death" for those who, after putting to death their earthly members through idleness toward sin, move toward the praiseworthy "deadness" <note>This refers to *apatheia*, or a state where the person is "dead" to the influence of sinful thoughts.</note> regarding passionate thoughts and fantasies.

<margin>25.</margin> There are three powers of the soul: reason, anger <note>original: "thymos." In this context, it refers to the "spirited" or "incensive" power used for courage and righteous indignation.</note>, and desire. Through reason, we seek; through desire, we long for...

### FOURTH CENTURY

...the good that is sought, and through the "incensive power" <note>original: "thymos." In ancient psychology, this is the "spirited" or "furious" part of the soul that provides drive and energy.</note> we fight for it. Those who love God remain within these powers through the divine Word of virtue and knowledge. Through one power, they seek; through another, they long for; and through the third, they fight for the good. Thus, they receive incorruptible nourishment: the knowledge of created things that strengthens the mind.

<margin>26. (perhaps 26 in knowledge)</margin>
Human nature had become dead to the knowledge given to it. The Word of God, by becoming man, filled that nature with knowledge once again. He sharpened it toward "unchangeableness"—not by changing its essential nature, but by its quality—and He deified it <note>original: "etheosen." This refers to "theosis" or deification, the process of becoming like God through grace.</note>. He marked it without lack with His own Spirit, just as water is mixed with the quality of wine to give it strength. For this reason, He truly becomes man: so that He might make us gods by grace.

<margin>27.</margin>
God, who created human nature, gave it existence by His will alone, and He also joined to it a power capable of doing what is necessary. By "power," I mean the movement toward the activity of virtues that is sown essentially within our nature. However, according to our "gnomic" will <note>original: "gnomikos." This refers to the "deliberative will"—the personal way an individual chooses to use their natural powers.</note>, this power is revealed according to how the owner chooses to use it.

<margin>28.</margin>
We possess a natural criterion: the law of nature. This law teaches us that before we seek the wisdom found in all things, our desire should be moved toward the initiation into the mysteries of the Creator of all.

<margin>29.</margin>
Jacob’s well is the Scripture. The water is the knowledge found within the Scripture. The depth is the difficult-to-navigate arrangement of the riddles of the text. The "bucket" <note>original: "antlema." The vessel used to draw water.</note> is the learning of the divine Word through the "letter" (the written text), which the Lord did not have—for He is Himself the Word. He does not give the knowledge that comes from study and practice to those who believe, but rather the ever-flowing wisdom that comes from spiritual grace. He grants this wisdom, which never fails, to those who are worthy. For the "bucket"—that is, formal learning—takes only a tiny portion of knowledge and leaves the whole behind, as it cannot be contained by any human logic. But the knowledge according to grace possesses the whole, even without study, and it is the wisdom attainable by humans, sprouting in various ways according to their needs.

<margin>30.</margin>
The Tree of Life, and that which is not of its kind, are named separately for a reason. One is called the Tree of Life; the other is not "life," but only

<column-break/>

the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. There is a great and inexpressible difference between them. For the Tree of Life is certainly the producer of life. That which is not the Tree of Life is clearly the producer of death. For that which is not productive of life—by the very fact that it is not called the "Tree of Life"—must clearly be productive of death. For nothing else stands in direct opposition to life.

<margin>31.</margin>
The Tree of Life, being Wisdom, has a vast difference from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, which is neither wisdom nor called such. For the characteristics of Wisdom are Mind <note>original: "nous"</note> and Reason <note>original: "logos"</note>. But the characteristics of the state that stands in opposition to Wisdom are "unreason" <note>original: "alogia"</note> and "sensation" <note>original: "aisthesis," referring to the raw data of the senses without spiritual interpretation.</note>.

<margin>32.</margin>
Since man came into being as a composite of an intellectual soul and a sensible body, let us say that in one sense, the Tree of Life is the "Mind" of the soul, in which the treasure of Wisdom resides. The Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil is the "Sensation" of the body, in which the movement of unreason clearly exists. Man received the divine command not to touch this tree through actual experience, but he did not keep it.

<margin>33.</margin>
Both trees, according to the Scripture, characterize certain things: namely, the Mind and Sensation. For the Mind has a "discriminative power" <note>the ability to tell things apart</note> between intelligible and sensible things, between temporary and eternal things. More specifically, as a power of the soul, it persuades the soul to hold onto the eternal and to rise above the temporary. But Sensation has a discriminative power between the pleasure and pain of bodies. Rather, as it is a power of living and sensing bodies, it persuades them to be drawn toward pleasure and to reject pain.

<margin>34.</margin>
If a man makes his distinction solely according to the sensation of bodies—pleasure and pain—he transgresses the divine command and eats from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. That is, he chooses the unreason of the senses. He possesses only that distinction which sustains the body, according to which he holds onto pleasure as "good" and avoids pain as "evil." But if he makes his distinction entirely through the intellectual power that separates the eternal from the temporary, he keeps the divine command and eats from the Tree of Life. I mean the Wisdom that is established according to the Mind; for he possesses only that distinction which sustains the soul...

He argues that the Incarnation of the Word restores human nature’s ability to choose divine wisdom over sensory pleasure, enabling deification by grace.</summary>

->### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS<-

...judgment; through which, as a "good," one holds fast to the glory of eternal things, but as an "evil," one abstains from the corruption of temporal things.

<margin>35.</margin> A good of the mind is a dispassionate <note>original: "apathes." In this context, it refers to a state of being undisturbed by worldly desires or emotions, allowing for spiritual focus.</note> disposition toward the spirit; but an evil is a passionate relationship with sense-perception. A good of sense-perception is a passionate movement toward the body according to pleasure; but an evil is the state that follows when this pleasure is taken away.

<margin>36.</margin> One who has convinced their own conscience that the worst things are "naturally good" when they are committed, has—like a hand—extended their practical power and wrongly taken from the tree of life, believing that which is naturally worst to be immortal. For this reason, God naturally implanted in man a sense of "accusation" within the conscience against evil, and separated him from "life" <note>This refers to the expulsion from Eden and the loss of access to the Tree of Life.</note> because he had become evil by his own choice. This was done so that, while doing evil, he would not be able to convince his own conscience that the worst things are naturally good.

<margin>37.</margin> The vine produces wine; wine produces intoxication; and intoxication produces ecstasy. Therefore, natural reason—which is the "vine"—when cultivated by the virtues, gives birth to knowledge. Knowledge, in turn, gives birth to a "good ecstasy," which lifts the mind out of its relationship with sense-perception.

<margin>38.</margin> The Evil One is accustomed to maliciously mixing the forms and shapes of sensible things <note>Physical things we can see and touch.</note> with our thoughts of those things. Through these forms, the passions are naturally crafted around the appearance of visible objects. This happens when our rational energy, which should be focused on spiritual things, is brought to a standstill by the "middle ground" of our senses. Because of this, the Evil One is strong enough to plunder the soul and drag it down into a confusion of passions.

<margin>39.</margin> The Word of God is simultaneously both a lamp and a light: a light as it illuminates the natural thoughts of the faithful, and a lamp as it burns away those thoughts that are against nature. It is a light as it dissolves the darkness of a life lived only for the senses for those who hasten through the commandments toward the life they hope for; and it is a lamp as it punishes with the "fire of judgment" those who, in this dark night of life, deliberately hold onto the flesh out of love for it.

<margin>40.</margin> It is said that one who has not first been led back to themselves by casting off passions that are "against nature" cannot be led back to their own Cause—that is, to God—through the acquisition of "supernatural" <note>original: "hyper physin." Things that are beyond the capacity of human nature and granted by God's grace.</note> blessings by grace. For one who is truly being gathered to God must be separated in their mind from all created things.

<column-break/>

<margin>41.</margin> The work of the Written Law is the removal of the passions. The work of the Natural Law is "equity"—treating all people with equal honor. But the perfection of the Spiritual Law is "likeness to God," as far as that is possible for a human being.

<margin>42.</margin> The power of the mind is naturally capable of receiving knowledge about bodies and incorporeal things. However, regarding the Holy Trinity, the mind receives only the "impressions" that God exists, and this through grace alone. It receives this by believing only *that* He is, but it does not dare to define *what* He is in His essence, as a demonic mind might arrogantly do. For one who is without knowledge can never understand the way virtue cleanses us of vice.

<margin>43.</margin> One who loves falsehood is handed over to it for their own destruction. This is so that they may learn through suffering the very thing they chose to embrace, and discover through experience how they were unknowingly hugging death instead of life.

<margin>44.</margin> God alone has the knowledge of the Good, as He is the nature and the knowledge of the Good by His very essence. He has an "ignorance" of evil, as He possesses an inability for it. For those things that He has the power to do naturally, of those things He possesses the knowledge essentially.

<margin>45.</margin> The "breast" mentioned in the Book of Leviticus <note>Referencing Leviticus 7:30–34, regarding the portions of the sacrifice given to the priests.</note> signifies the better and higher contemplation <note>original: "theoria." Spiritual vision or insight into the meaning of things.</note>. The "arm" signifies action—that is, the habit and energy of the intellect, or virtue and knowledge. Knowledge leads the mind directly to God, while virtue, through action, separates the mind from the knowledge of created things. The Word has set these portions apart for the "priests"—those who have acquired God alone as their inheritance through all things and possess nothing earthly at all.

<margin>46.</margin> Since those who are entirely persuaded by the Spirit through knowledge and virtue make the hearts of others receptive to piety and faith through their teaching, they take away their "practical habit" and "power" from the pursuits of corruptible nature and transfer them to the activity of supernatural, incorruptible blessings. For this reason, the Word commanded that the "breast of the offering"—meaning the heart of those being brought to God—and the "arm"—meaning their actions—be dedicated to the priests.

<margin>47.</margin> All righteousness in this present life, when compared to the righteousness to come, is merely like a mirror...

He also provides an allegorical interpretation of the priestly portions in Leviticus as symbols of spiritual contemplation and virtuous action.</summary>

# FOURTH CENTURY

...it holds the image of archetypal realities, but it does not possess the realities themselves as they exist in their own form. For all knowledge here, when compared to the knowledge to come, is a riddle <note>original: "aenigma." Referring to 1 Corinthians 13:12, "For now we see through a glass, darkly [in a riddle]."</note>; it possesses an impression of the truth, but it does not possess that truth itself which is destined to be revealed.

<margin>48.</margin> Since divine things are held together by virtue and knowledge, the **mirror** is indicative of the prototypes according to virtue, and the **riddle** is expressive of the archetypes according to knowledge.

<margin>49.</margin> The one who has pleased God through practice <note>original: "praxis," the active life of cultivating virtues.</note>, transfers the mind through contemplation <note>original: "theoria," the spiritual perception of divine truths.</note> to the realm of intelligible things; this is so that they might not, through some fantasy, behold the "death" that exists within the passions through the senses, as if they were being completely found by no one who wishes to seize them.

<margin>50.</margin> The one who has seen the beauty of future goods with the clear eye of faith, is ready to obey and depart from their "land," their "kindred," and their "father's house" <note>An allusion to Abraham in Genesis 12:1.</note>—leaving behind the flesh, the senses, and sensible things, along with all worldly relations and attachments. Such a person becomes higher than nature in times of trial and struggle, preferring the **Cause** of nature—as the great **Abraham** preferred God over his son **Isaac**.

<margin>51.</margin> One who seeks to pursue virtue or the study of divine words—not for the sake of glory, nor under the pretext of greed, nor for the sake of flattery, or to please men, or for outward display—but doing, saying, and thinking everything for the sake of God, this person walks in the way of truth with knowledge. For the Divine Word does not naturally love to dwell in paths that are not straight, even if he finds the "way" itself ready for his entrance.

<margin>52.</margin> Suppose someone fasts and abstains from the diet that ignites the passions, and does all other things that can contribute to the removal of wickedness; such a person has "prepared the way." But if they practice these ways for the sake of vainglory, greed, flattery, or any other reason besides pleasing God, they have not "made his paths straight." Such a person has endured the labor of preparing the way, but they do not have God walking within their paths.

<margin>53.</margin> "Every valley shall be filled" <note>An allusion to Isaiah 40:4 and Luke 3:5.</note>; not simply every valley, nor those of everyone. For it does not refer to those who have not prepared the way of the Lord and made 

<column-break/>

his paths straight. Therefore, whenever a "valley"—that is, the flesh or the soul—of those who have "prepared the way of the Lord" (as I said) and made his paths straight, is filled with knowledge and virtue through the presence of the Word of God walking in them through the commandments, then all the spirits of "knowledge falsely so-called" <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:20.</note> and of wickedness are humbled. The Word tramples and subordinates them, casting down the evil power that exalts itself against human nature, and, as it were, undermining the magnitude and height of the "mountains" and "hills," and leading them to the filling of the valleys. For the rejection of passions that are contrary to nature, and the application of virtues that are according to nature, refills the "valley-like" soul and humbles the <gloss>*</gloss> mountainous <margin><gloss>*</gloss> perhaps "limited/defined"</margin> dominion of the evil spirits.

<margin>54.</margin> The "rough ways"—that is, the attacks of involuntary temptations—shall become "smooth ways." This happens especially when the mind, rejoicing and being glad, is well-pleased in weaknesses, in distresses, and in necessities, through these involuntary labors stripping away the entire dominion of the voluntary passions. For he has called the occurrences of involuntary temptations "rough," which are transformed into "smooth ways" through the patience found in thanksgiving.

<margin>55.</margin> The one who desires the true life, knowing that every labor—whether voluntary <note>Such as fasting or asceticism.</note> or involuntary <note>Such as illness or external persecution.</note>—becomes the death of pleasure (the "mother of death"), will receive all the rough attacks of involuntary temptations with joy and gladness. Through patience, they make these afflictions easy and smooth ways, which lead them without error toward the prize of the "upward calling," as they piously make their divine race through them. For indeed, **pleasure** is the mother of death, and **pain** is the death of pleasure—whether that pain is chosen by will or comes against the will.

<margin>56.</margin> Therefore, everyone who has dissolved through self-control that winding and complex pleasure—which is intertwined in many ways with all sensible things at once—has "made the crooked ways straight." And the one who has trampled the difficult and rough attack of pains through patience has "made the rough ways into smooth ways." Hence, as a prize for virtue and the labors on its behalf—as those who have competed well and lawfully—

...having conquered pleasure through the longing for virtue, and having trampled upon pain by the love of knowledge <note>original: "gnosis," referring to spiritual insight rather than just data.</note>, and having nobly endured the divine contests through both, such a person shall see, according to what is written, the salvation of God.

<margin>57.</margin> The one who loves virtue withers the furnace of pleasures by their own will. The one whose mind is seasoned with the knowledge of truth is not held back by involuntary pains, because of the "ever-moving motion" <note>A classic Maximian term describing the soul's dynamic rest in God.</note> of their desire which carries them toward God.

<margin>58.</margin> The one who has straightened the "crookedness" of voluntary passions—that is, the impulses of pleasure—through self-control, and has smoothed the "roughness" of involuntary trials—that is, the ways of pain—through patience, and has set them into "level paths," such a person will rightly see the salvation of God, having become pure in heart. In this heart, through the virtues and through godly contemplations <note>original: "theoria."</note>, they behold God at the finish line of their struggles, according to the saying: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* In exchange for the labors of virtue, they receive the grace of <term>impassibility</term> <note>original: "apatheia," a state of being undisturbed by the passions, not a lack of feeling.</note>, and nothing reveals God to those who possess it more than this.

<margin>59.</margin> Scripture calls "cisterns" those hearts which are receptive to the heavenly gifts of holy knowledge. These are carved out by the sturdy Word of the commandments, casting out—like <insert>calloused stones</insert> <margin>*perhaps "mounds of earth."</margin>—both the love of pleasure toward the passions and the attachment to the sensory things of nature. They are then filled with the knowledge of the Spirit, which flows from above, cleansing the passions and giving life and nourishment to the virtues.

<margin>60.</margin> The Lord hews "cisterns" in the desert—I mean in the world and in human nature—clearing out the hearts of the worthy and purifying them from the material weight and worldly mindset. He makes them spacious enough to receive the divine rains of wisdom and knowledge, so that they may water "Christ’s cattle"—I mean those who are still bound by the infancy of the soul—with moral instruction.

<margin>61.</margin> Scripture calls the high spiritual contemplation of nature the "mountainous region." This is cultivated by those who have moved beyond the fantasies of the senses and have crossed over, by means of the virtues, to the spiritual principles <note>original: "logoi," the inner divine blueprints of things.</note> within those senses.

<margin>62.</margin> As long as the mind has within itself a living

<column-break/>

memory of God, it seeks the Lord through contemplation—not simply, but "in the fear of the Lord," which is to say, through the practice of the commandments. For the one who seeks the Lord through contemplation without practice <note>original: "praxis."</note> does not find Him; for they have not sought the Lord in the fear of the Lord. And so, "the Lord prospered him." For the Lord prospers everyone who acts with knowledge, both by teaching the ways of the commandments and by revealing the true principles of all things.

<margin>63.</margin> The high discourse concerning the Godhead is a "tower" in the soul, fortified by the activity of the commandments. This is what it means when it says that *Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem.* For the one who is successfully prospered in seeking the Lord through contemplation, along with the <insert>appropriate</insert> <margin>*perhaps "applied" or "fitting."</margin> fear—that is, the practice of the commandments—builds towers in Jerusalem. This means that in the simple and peaceful state of the soul, they raise up high discourses concerning the Godhead.

<margin>64.</margin> The principles <note>logoi</note> of particular things, when they advance toward the universal, create the unification of things that were divided. This is because the more universal principles encompass the more particular ones in a single form; the particulars naturally refer back to them. Furthermore, between the mind and the senses, heaven and earth, the visible and the intelligible, and nature and reason, there is a certain spiritual principle that relates them and gives them a union with one another.

<margin>65.</margin> The one who is able to "nail down" the senses so they are no longer subject to the passions, and who has separated the soul from its attachment to those senses, has succeeded in walling off the entry of the devil into the mind. Therefore, in the "desert"—I mean in the contemplation of nature—they have built, as it were, "secure towers": pious opinions concerning all that exists. Anyone who takes refuge in these towers does not fear the demons who rob in this desert—meaning the nature of visible things—who lead the mind astray through the senses and drag it down into the gloom of ignorance. They do not fear the demons who use appearances to lead people astray.

<margin>66.</margin> Every mind that has strength for contemplation is a true "farmer," guarding the divine seeds of good things from weeds through its own zeal and care, until it has...
