### FOURTH CENTURY

...the memory of God. For it says, *and he sought the Lord in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the fear of the Lord.* The Word knows that "Zechariah," when translated into the Greek tongue, means "Memory of God" <note>original: "Theou mnēmēn." St. Maximus uses the etymology of Hebrew names to draw out spiritual meanings.</note>. Therefore, let us always pray to the Lord that the memory of His salvation be preserved in us, so that success itself does not corrupt the soul by lifting it up to pride—causing it to dare things beyond its nature, just as Uzziah did <note>Referencing King Uzziah (Ozias), who was successful until his pride led him to overstep his religious authority, resulting in leprosy (2 Chronicles 26).</note>.

<margin>67.</margin> The unwavering contemplation <note>original: "theoria."</note> of created things requires a soul that has been set free from the passions. Such a soul is called "Jerusalem," both because of its perfect virtue and its immaterial knowledge <note>original: "gnosis."</note>. This state comes about not only through the absence of passions, but also through the absence of worldly or sensory fantasies.

<margin>68.</margin> Without faith, hope, and love, nothing evil is ever completely abolished, nor is anything good ever fully achieved. Faith persuades the mind to approach God when it is under attack, becoming a complete supply of spiritual weapons and a source of courage. Hope stands as the most truthful guarantor of divine help, promising the destruction of opposing powers. But love makes the mind difficult to move—or rather, entirely immovable—keeping it fixed in divine affection even when under attack, pinning the entire power of its nature to divine desire.

<margin>69.</margin> Faith comforts the mind when it is at war by strengthening it with the hope of help. Hope, by bringing the promised help before the eyes as if it were already present, repels the assault of the enemies. Love makes the attack of the enemies "dead" to the God-loving mind, for the assault is entirely eclipsed by the mind's intense longing for God.

<margin>70.</margin> The first and only "son" of the truly divine portion—that is, of true knowledge—is the "word of resurrection" within us according to faith. This comes with the necessary management of the will, or <term>discernment</term> <note>original: "diakrisis," the ability to distinguish between spiritual impulses.</note>, which properly handles the uprisings of voluntary temptations. For the first resurrection of God—who was "dead" within us through our ignorance—is faith, which is properly managed through the practice of the commandments.

<margin>71.</margin> Turning toward God clearly reveals through itself the fullest meaning of divine hope. Without hope, it is not in the nature of anything to incline toward God in any way whatsoever.

<column-break/>

For it is the unique property of hope to bring future things before the eyes as if they were present. It convinces those being attacked by the opposing power that the God who shields them is never absent—the God for whose sake and through whom the saints wage their war. For without some expectation of either a difficult or an easy outcome, no one's turning toward the good can naturally occur.

<margin>72.</margin> Truly, nothing gathers those who have been scattered as love does; it creates a single will in them, held together by a shared spirit. The hallmark of this love is the beauty of equality. Therefore, love is the offspring of the gathering and union of the soul’s powers—that is, the **rational**, the **spirited**, and the **desiring** powers—toward the same divine goal. Through this love, those who have already received "equality" with God through grace engrave the beauty of divine splendor upon their memory. They possess an unforgetting desire for divine love, which records and imprints that undefiled beauty upon the ruling part of the soul.

<margin>73.</margin> Every mind girded with divine strength possesses "elders" and "rulers," so to speak: the **rational power**, from which the faith of knowledge is naturally born (by which it is wordlessly taught that God is always present, and by which it joins with future things through hope as if they were present); and the **desiring power**, through which divine love is established. Because of this love, the mind voluntarily pins itself to the longing for the undefiled Godhead and holds an unbreakable desire for the One it loves. It also possesses the **spirited power**, through which it clings tightly to divine peace, directing the movement of desire toward divine eros. Every mind has these powers working together for the destruction of evil and for the establishment and preservation of virtue.

<margin>74.</margin> Without the rational power, there is no scientific knowledge. Without knowledge, faith is not established. From faith proceeds that beautiful offspring, hope, through which the believer joins with future things as if they were present. Without the desiring power, there is no longing, the end of which is love—for to love something is the specific work of desire. And without the spirited power <note>original: "thymos," often translated as "anger," but here referring to the soul's "nerve" or "drive."</note> to provide muscle to the desire for union with what is pleasant, peace can never naturally occur. For truly...

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...truth, peace is the undisturbed and complete possession of what is desired.

<margin>75.</margin> One who has not first been purified from the passions <note>original: "pathōn." In this context, passions are not just "feelings," but disordered impulses or compulsive attachments that cloud the mind.</note> must not touch "natural contemplation." This is because the images of sensory things have the power to imprint themselves upon the mind of one who is not yet perfectly liberated from these passions, leading to further disturbance. For the mind that lingers upon the outward surfaces of sensory things through the imagination becomes a creator of impure passions, as it is unable to cross over through contemplation toward those spiritual realities that are its true kin.

<margin>76.</margin> One who, at the time of an uprising of the passions, bravely closes the senses and completely thrusts away both the imagination and the memory of sensory things—restraining every natural movement of the mind toward the investigation of external things—has shamed and defeated the evil and tyrannical power rising against him, doing so by the help of the divine hand.

<margin>77.</margin> When reason becomes mindless, when anger becomes headlong, and when desire becomes irrational—and when ignorance, tyranny, and licentiousness hold sway over the soul—then the habit of vice is naturally put into practice, having become entangled with the various pleasures of the senses.

<margin>78.</margin> The mind that knows how to escape invisible entanglements through spiritual knowledge <note>original: "gnōstikōs." Referring to the "Gnostic" or the one who possesses deep, experiential knowledge of God.</note> must not pursue natural contemplation, nor do anything else during an attack by evil powers, except to pray and to subdue the body with labors. It must, with all diligence, bring about the destruction of the "earthly mindset" <note>original: "choïkou phronēmatos." This refers to the part of our thinking bound to material and worldly concerns.</note> and guard the "walls of the city." By this, I mean the virtues that protect the soul—or rather, the methods that guard those virtues: specifically, self-control and patience. This is done lest the enemy, deceiving us through "things on the right" <note>A common ascetic phrase meaning "spiritual-sounding deceptions" or "excessive zeal."</note>, steals away our yearning and turns us from God. Such an enemy pours a murky confusion over the soul, and through things that are merely *perceived* to be good, he drags down the mind—which seeks the good—toward what is worse.

<margin>79.</margin> He who bravely closes his senses through reasoned and comprehensive self-control and patience, and who walls off the entrances of sensory forms into the mind through the powers of the soul, easily destroys the devil's evil machines. He makes the devil return in shame by the same way he came. The "way" by which the devil comes is the material things that seem necessary for the maintenance of the body.

<column-break/>

<margin>80.</margin> When the Mind <note>original: "nous." The highest faculty of the human person, meant for direct communion with God.</note> has naturally joined the senses to itself through the mediation of Reason, it gathers true knowledge from the contemplation of nature.

<margin>81.</margin> There are springs outside the "city"—that is, outside the soul—which King Hezekiah blocked; these are all the things of the senses. The "waters" of these springs are the sensory thoughts <note>original: "noēmata."</note>. However, there is a river that flows through the middle of the city: this is the knowledge gathered from sensory thoughts through natural contemplation. It passes through the middle of the soul, acting as a boundary between the Mind and the senses. For the knowledge of sensory things is neither entirely alienated from the power of the mind, nor is it wholly assigned to the activity of the senses. Rather, standing in the middle, it facilitates the union of the Mind with the senses and the senses with the Mind. In relation to the senses, it is shaped by the forms of sensory things; in relation to the Mind, it translates those forms into rational principles <note>original: "logous." Maximus teaches that every created thing contains a "logos" or divine blueprint.</note>. Therefore, the knowledge of visible things is rightly called a "river dividing the middle of the city," as it is the frontier between the two extremes of Mind and sensation.

<margin>82.</margin> He who, during a time of rising temptations, abstains from natural contemplation and instead holds fast to prayer—withdrawing the mind from all things toward itself and toward God—kills the habit that produces vice. He turns away the devil in shame, for the devil relies on that habit and comes to the soul with his characteristic arrogance, exalting himself against the truth through proud thoughts. The Great David likely knew this through his own experience and actions; he was the one most practiced in the ranks of spiritual warfare. He said: *While the sinner stood before me, I was dumb, and was humbled, and I held my peace even from good things* <note>original: Psalm 38:2-3 (Septuagint numbering); Psalm 39:1-2 in modern Bibles.</note>. After him, the divine Jeremiah commanded the people not to go out of the city, because of the sword of the enemies dwelling round about <note>Referencing Jeremiah 6:25.</note>.

<margin>83.</margin> Even the blessed Abel would have been safe if he had guarded himself and not gone out with Cain into the "field"—that is, into the vastness of natural contemplation—before he had reached a state of impassibility <note>original: "apatheia." A state of soul where one is no longer driven by disordered impulses.</note>. Had he stayed, Cain would not have risen up and killed him with guile, stealing his yearning through the contemplation of created things...

<meta>Institutional library stamp at bottom right: UNIVERSITY OF CRETE</meta>

<summary>St. Maximus warns that natural contemplation (studying God through creation) is dangerous for those not yet purified of passions, as the devil uses sensory images to deceive. He provides an allegorical interpretation of King Hezekiah and the figures of Abel and Cain to emphasize the need for inner prayer and self-control over outward investigation.</summary>

<keywords>St. Maximus the Confessor, Mind (Nous), Passions, Natural Contemplation (Theoria), Reason (Logos), Senses, Self-control, Patience, Hezekiah, David, Jeremiah, Abel and Cain, Impassibility (Apatheia)</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Fourth Century on Theology" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The previous page discussed how the mind must avoid "natural contemplation" (finding God through nature) when it is still being attacked by disordered passions, lest it be overwhelmed by sensory images.</meta>

### FOURTH CENTURY

<margin>84.</margin> Before one reaches a state of perfect spiritual stability, the "law of the flesh" <note>original: "ho tēs sarkos nomos." This refers to the instinctive, material impulses that conflict with the spirit.</note> is both called and acts as "Cain" <note>Maximus allegorizes Cain, the first murderer, as the rebellious impulse of the body.</note>.

<margin>85.</margin> Likewise, Dinah, the daughter of the Great Jacob, would not have been "humbled" <note>In the biblical context of Genesis 34, "humbled" refers to the violation of Dinah.</note> by Shechem the son of Hamor if she had not gone out among the "daughters of the land"—that is, among the sensory fantasies of the mind.

<margin>86.</margin> It is good for us not to touch **natural contemplation** <note>original: "physikēs theōrias." This is the practice of seeking the spiritual principles (logoi) within created things.</note> before we have attained a stable spiritual state. Otherwise, while seeking spiritual meanings in visible creations, we may unknowingly collect passions. For in those who are still spiritually immature, the outward forms of what they see exert a greater power over the senses than the hidden **inner principles** <term>logoi: the divine intentions or blueprints behind every created thing</term> of those objects exert over the soul. Indeed, those who bind their intellect to the "letter" of things in a **literalistic manner** <note>original: "Ioudaikōs," literally "Jewishly." In this tradition, it refers to a material or surface-level interpretation of reality and scripture.</note> expect the promises of incorruptible goods to happen in this current age, remaining ignorant of the goods that are natural to the soul.

<margin>87.</margin> He who has "borne the image of the heavenly" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:49.</note> strives to follow the spirit of Holy Scripture in all things; in this spirit, the soul is preserved through virtue and knowledge. But he who bears the image of the earthly follows only the letter; in this, the worship of the body according to the senses consists, which only serves to create the passions.

<margin>88.</margin> **God's power** is established as the virtue that destroys the passions and guards godly thoughts. This power is born from the **practice of the commandments** <note>original: "praxis." The active life of doing good and resisting vice.</note>, through which we—with the cooperation of God, or rather by the power of God alone—destroy the powers of evil that oppose the good. **God's height** is the knowledge of the truth. This is born from the labor of contemplating created things and from the "sweat" of practicing the virtues, which becomes the father of such labor. Through this knowledge, we completely vanish the power of falsehood that opposes the truth, humbling and casting down every "high thing" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 10:5.</note> of the evil spirits that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. For just as practice gives birth to virtue, so contemplation gives birth to knowledge.

That knowledge which is "unforgetting" possesses a movement of the mind that is beyond ordinary understanding; because it moves toward the divine infinity, it is itself "unlimited." Through this lack of limit, it mirrors the infinite glory of the Truth. Furthermore, the voluntary imitation of God's wise and providential goodness brings to the mind a distinct honor: a likeness to God, as far as that is possible, within one's inner disposition.

<column-break/>

<margin>89.</margin> The **tongue** is a symbol of the soul's capacity for spiritual knowledge; the **throat**, however, is a sign of that natural self-love directed toward the body. Therefore, the person who blameworthily "glues" these two together cannot remember the state of peace found in virtue and knowledge, for he delights in the confusion caused by his eagerness for bodily passions.

<margin>90.</margin> Natural desires and pleasures do not bring reproach upon those who possess them, as they are a necessary consequence of our physical nature. For even against our will, a natural pleasure is produced by basic food when it comforts a prior hunger, or by drink when it drives away the distress of thirst, or by sleep when it renews the strength spent during wakefulness. These, and other natural functions of ours, are necessary for the constitution of our nature. For the diligent person, they are even useful for the acquisition of virtue. These natural functions accompany every mind that flees the confusion of sin, so that the mind is not held in slavery by those "against-nature" passions <note>original: "para physin pathōn." These are disordered attachments (like gluttony or lust) that exceed the body's natural needs.</note>—passions which are within our control and are blameworthy. These unnatural passions have no place in us except through the movement of our natural functions, yet they are not of a nature to cross over with us into the immortal and everlasting life.

<margin>91.</margin> The words of God, when they are spoken merely as bare sounds, are not truly "heard," for they lack the "voice" that comes from the **practice** of those who speak them. But if they are "spoken" through the practice of the commandments, they cause the demons to melt away by that voice, and they lead men to build the divine temple of the heart through their progress in the works of righteousness.

<margin>92.</margin> Just as God is not subject to our knowledge in His essence, so also His Word cannot be fully grasped by our knowledge. For though the word of Holy Scripture can be "circumscribed" (limited) according to the letter—since it ends within the time-frame of the historical events it records—according to the spirit, it remains forever uncircumscribed in the various contemplations of its inner meanings.

<margin>93.</margin> One who approaches Holy Scripture "gnostically" <note>original: "gnōstikōs." Meaning with spiritual insight or deep experiential knowledge.</note> for the sake of the soul must laboriously practice the interpretation of names. From this, he will be able to clarify the entire meaning of what is written, provided he cares for an accurate understanding of the text. But he must not [interpret] **Jewishly**... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "Iou-" at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Maximus explains the danger of literalism and sensory distraction (Dinah/Cain), emphasizing that while natural needs are blameless, spiritual maturity requires moving from the "letter" of things to their spiritual "inner principles" (logoi) through both practice and contemplation.</summary>
<keywords>Cain, Dinah, natural contemplation, literalism, praxis, theoria, logoi, passions, spiritual knowledge, Maximus the Confessor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Fourth Century on Theology" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The text concludes a warning against interpreting spiritual promises through a purely material or "literalistic" lens before moving into definitions of prayer and the allegorical significance of King Hezekiah and Jerusalem.</meta>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...nor to drag down the height of the Spirit to the body and the earth in a **literalistic manner** <note>original: "Ioudaikōs." In this context, it refers to a "Jewish" or surface-level interpretation of scripture that focuses only on physical fulfillment rather than spiritual truth.</note>, nor to limit the divine and incorruptible promises of spiritual blessings within the decay of transient things.

<margin>94.</margin> Just as a **vow** <note>original: "euchē." Here used in the sense of a promise or offering made to God.</note> is a promise of good things offered to God by human beings according to their commitment, so **prayer** <note>original: "proseuchē." Distinguished here as the act of asking for God's help.</note> is clearly, by the same logic, a request for the good things supplied by God to humanity for their salvation—a request that brings a return for the good disposition of those who preceded it. A **cry** <note>original: "boē," a shout or loud call.</note> is the offering and increase of virtuous ways in **practice** <term>praxis: the active struggle to acquire virtues and overcome passions</term> and of insightful principles in **contemplation** <term>theoria: the spiritual perception of divine truths and the inner meanings of creation</term>. This occurs during the time of the uprising of evil demons; God hears this "cry" naturally, more than any other thing, as if it were a "great voice"—recognizing the inner disposition of those who care for virtue and knowledge.

<margin>95.</margin> The evil and destructive kingdom of the devil—prefigured by the kingdom of the **Assyrians** <note>In the Bible, the Assyrians are often seen as the enemies of God's people; Maximus uses them to symbolize the forces of the devil.</note>—has gathered a war against virtue and knowledge, and tries to overthrow the soul through its own innate powers. First, it irritates **desire**, provoking it toward an appetite for things contrary to nature and persuading it to prefer sensory things over spiritual ones. Then, it rouses **anger** to fight on behalf of what desire has chosen. Finally, it teaches **reason** <note>original: "to logikon," the rational faculty of the soul.</note> to invent ways to achieve these sensory pleasures.

<margin>96.</margin> It is a characteristic of Supreme Goodness that not only the divine and incorporeal essences of **spiritual beings** <term>intelligible: things perceived by the mind or spirit rather than the physical senses</term> were made to be images of His unspoken and divine glory—receiving as much of the unthinkable beauty of that unapproachable splendor as is permitted—but He also mixed echoes of His own majesty into **sensible things** <note>original: "aisthētois," things perceptible by the physical senses.</note>, even though they fall far short of spiritual essences. These echoes are able to carry the human mind, as if riding upon them, toward God without error, becoming higher than all visible things by stepping into that supreme blessedness.

<margin>97.</margin> Every mind crowned with virtue and knowledge is like the **Great Hezekiah** <note>A righteous King of Judah (reigned c. 715–686 BC) known for his reforms and his trust in God during the Assyrian siege.</note>, having been granted the privilege of reigning over Jerusalem; that is, 

<column-break/>

over the state that sees only peace, or rather, a condition stripped of all kinds of **passions** <note>original: "pathōn." In ascetic theology, passions are disordered or obsessive impulses like pride, greed, or lust.</note>. For "Jerusalem" is interpreted as the **"vision of peace."** Such a mind has all of creation under its hand, through the various forms that complete it. To God, the mind offers the spiritual principles of knowledge like gifts; to itself, it provides the ways of virtue that exist within it according to the natural law as if they were offerings. Through both of these, the mind welcomes the One who is able to grant success in both—I mean the **philosophical mind** <note>In this context, a "philosopher" is not an academic, but someone who truly loves and pursues the wisdom of God through life and action.</note> which has been perfected through reason and life, and through practice and contemplation.

<margin>98.</margin> One who has achieved virtue and knowledge to the highest degree through practice and contemplation is naturally raised above all fleshly and slandered passions. Such a person rises above physical bodies in their **practice**, by which I mean things subject to birth and decay. To put it simply, by means of **contemplation**, they have intellectually passed through all the spiritual principles within sensory forms, and such a person has led their mind up toward things that are kindred and divine.

<margin>99.</margin> One who has been granted the privilege of inhabiting **impassibility** <term>apatheia: not a lack of feeling, but a state of soul where one is no longer dominated by disordered desires</term>—as if it were Jerusalem—through the labors of practical struggle, is freed from all the disturbance of sin. Such a person acts, speaks, hears, and thinks only peace. After receiving the nature of visible things through **natural contemplation**, they offer the more divine principles within that nature to the Lord as gifts. They bring the laws within nature to Him as if to a King. Such a person is "exalted in the eyes of all nations" <note>A reference to 2 Chronicles 32:23, where Hezekiah is honored by all nations.</note>, becoming higher than all things—specifically higher than the passions of the flesh through practice, and higher than physical bodies and all sensory forms through contemplation, having crossed through the spiritual principles and ways within them.

<margin>100.</margin> **Practical philosophy** makes the practitioner higher than the passions. **Contemplation**, however, places the one who knows higher than visible things, raising the mind toward kindred spiritual realities.

<meta>This page begins the "Fifth Century" (or fifth set of one hundred chapters) of St. Maximus the Confessor's theological reflections. It follows the conclusion of the fourth century, which discussed the spiritual interpretation of the Old Testament and the struggle against the "Assyrians" (symbolizing demonic forces). This page focuses on the relationship between spiritual practice (praxis) and contemplation (theoria), the nature of passions, and how God uses creation and "wrath" to educate the soul.</meta>

# BY THE SAME AUTHOR
## FIFTH CENTURY

<margin>1.</margin> He who knows through **practice** <term>praxis: the active struggle to acquire virtues and overcome passions</term> and acts through **knowledge** <term>gnosis: spiritual insight or understanding of divine truths</term> is a throne and a footstool of God. He is a throne because of his knowledge, and a footstool because of his practice. If someone were to say that the human mind is "heaven" when it is cleansed of every material fantasy and occupied with divine, intelligible concepts—or rather, when it is adorned by these divine **principles** <note>original: "logois." In Maximus’s thought, "logoi" are the inner purposes or blueprints of things created by God.</note>—it seems to me they would not be far from the truth.

<margin>2.</margin> Every philosopher—meaning every pious person—who is guarded by virtue and knowledge, or by practice and **contemplation** <term>theoria: the spiritual perception of the inner meaning of reality</term>, has a single help for the destruction of evils when he sees an evil power rising against him through the passions (just as King Hezekiah saw the King of the Assyrians). That help is God, whom he appeases by crying out wordlessly through an intense increase in virtue and knowledge. He then receives an Angel for an ally—or rather, for salvation. This "Angel" is a greater principle of wisdom and knowledge that wipes out every "mighty man," "warrior," "leader," and "captain" in the enemy camp <note>Maximus is allegorizing the biblical account where an angel destroys the Assyrian army (2 Chronicles 32:21).</note>.

<margin>3.</margin> Every passion is naturally ruled by its corresponding **sensible object** <note>original: "aisthēton." A physical thing that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>. For without some underlying object that moves the powers of the soul toward itself through one of the senses, a passion could never be formed. Without a sensible thing, a passion does not take shape: if there is no woman, there is no sexual immorality; if there is no food, there is no gluttony; if there is no gold, there is no love of money. Therefore, the sensible object—or rather, the demon using it to provoke the soul toward sin—rules every passionate movement of our natural powers.

<margin>4.</margin> "Rubbing" refers to the outward action, but "rubbing out" <note>original: "tripsis" vs "ektripsis." A play on words in Greek where the prefix 'ek-' denotes total removal or blotting out.</note> vanishes even the memory of the vice. For "rubbing" is merely the cancellation of the outward act of passion; but "rubbing out" is the complete disappearance of even the evil movements within the mind.

<margin>5.</margin> Sensible things and **intelligible things** <note>original: "noēta." Things perceived by the intellect/mind rather than the physical senses, such as concepts or spiritual realities.</note> are intermediaries between God and humanity. The human mind rises above these as it

<column-break/>

travels toward God. It does so by not being enslaved to sensible things through practice, and by not being held back at all by intelligible things during contemplation.

<margin>6.</margin> Creation acts as an accuser of ungodly people. Through the principles (logoi) within it, creation heralds its own Creator; and through the natural laws found within each of its species, it acts as a tutor leading humanity toward virtue. These "principles" are recognized in the stability of each species' continuity, while the "laws" are seen in the consistency of the natural activity of each species. By failing to apply our intellectual power to these things, we have remained ignorant of the Cause of all beings and have become stuck in all passions that are contrary to nature.

<margin>7.</margin> The Word commands that gifts be offered to God by us in order to demonstrate the infinity of the Divine Goodness. Since God needs nothing, He accepts the things given to us by Him as if they were "gifts" from us, crediting the entire contribution to us. This shows that God's goodness toward us is vast and inexpressible: He accepts His own things as ours when we offer them to Him, and He acknowledges a debt for them as if they belonged to someone else.

<margin>8.</margin> By understanding the spiritual principles of visible things, a person is taught that there is a Creator of all things seen. As for the concept of *what* He is like, the person leaves that unexamined as something unattainable. For visible creation provides a clear grasp of the fact *that* He is the Creator, but not *what kind* of Being the Creator is.

<margin>9.</margin> The "wrath of God" is the painful sensation experienced by those being disciplined. This painful sensation consists of the infliction of involuntary hardships, through which God often leads the mind—which has become puffed up by its virtue and knowledge—toward restraint and humility. In this way, God allows the person to become aware of themselves and a witness to their own weakness. Being thus educated, the person sets aside the vain swelling of the heart.

<margin>10.</margin> The "wrath of the Lord" is the suspension of the supply of divine gifts. This suspension is often helpful...

<vocab>practice (praxis), knowledge (gnosis), contemplation (theoria), virtue, mind (nous), passion (pathos), creation (ktisis), Creator, personal weaknesses, Hezekiah</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces the 'Fifth Century' of Maximus’s theology, focusing on how spiritual practice and mental contemplation allow a person to transcend the material world. It explains that passions rely on physical objects and that true spiritual progress requires 'rubbing out' even the mental memory of sin.</summary>

# OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS
## [FIFTH CENTURY, CONTINUED]

...rightly happens to every high and lofty mind; it also happens to a mind that boasts of the good things given to it by God as if they were its own personal achievements.

<margin>11.</margin> Every <term>gnostic</term> <note>original: "gnostikos." In the tradition of Maximus, this refers to someone who has attained true spiritual knowledge or "insight," rather than the heretical movement of Gnosticism.</note> and philosophical mind possesses both a "Judah" and a "Jerusalem." It possesses Judah as <term>practical philosophy</term> <note>original: "praktiken philosophian." This refers to "praxis," the active struggle to purify the soul and acquire virtues.</note>, and Jerusalem as <term>contemplative initiation</term> <note>original: "theoretiken mystagogian." This refers to "theoria," the spiritual vision of divine mysteries.</note>. Whenever, therefore, the God-loving mind—having through divine grace struck down every power opposed to virtue and knowledge in both its active and contemplative life—attains a complete victory over the "spirits of wickedness" but fails to offer the proper thanks to God, the Cause of that victory; and if it instead becomes uplifted in heart, considering itself the cause of all its success; then, because it has not repaid God in proportion to the gift He bestowed, it receives upon itself the wrath of <term>abandonment</term> <note>original: "egkataleipseis." A technical term in ascetic theology referring to God withdrawing the "feeling" of His presence so that the person learns humility or tests their resolve.</note>. Not only is the mind itself affected, but so are "Judah" and "Jerusalem"—meaning the habit of action and the state of contemplation. By God’s permission, shameful passions immediately rise up against the soul's practice, defiling the conscience that was previously pure; and false concepts become entangled with the contemplation of reality, distorting the previously correct glory of its knowledge. For shameful passions follow the one who is prideful in action, while righteous judgment allows the one who is puffed up in knowledge to stumble in true contemplation.

<margin>12.</margin> A truly divine limit and law exists within all things according to <term>providence</term> <note>original: "pronoia." God's purposeful care and guidance of the universe.</note>. This law allows those who have proven ungrateful for better things to be disciplined by their opposites, leading them back to a sense of gratitude. It uses the experience of opposing forces to create a recognition of the divine power that achieves all that is good. This is done so that we might not be allowed by Providence to maintain an unshakeable <term>conceit</term> <note>original: "oiesin." An over-inflated sense of one's own spiritual status or "spiritual ego."</note> regarding our improvements, which would cause us to slide into the anti-divine disposition of arrogance—believing that our possession of virtue and knowledge is ours by nature rather than something acquired through grace. If we did this, we would find ourselves using what is good to give birth to what is evil; and those things that should have strengthened the divine knowledge within us to remain unshaken would instead, God forbid, become the very means by which we fall ill with ignorance of that knowledge.

<margin>13.</margin> We recognize that a divine limit and law exists within all

<column-break/>

things: it is the providence that holds all beings together. According to a righteous judgment, this providence disciplines through the "lack of good things" those who, amidst an abundance of goods, proved ungrateful toward the Giver. It leads them toward an awareness and recognition of Him who bestows all goodness by making them experience the opposites. For <term>conceit</term> regarding one's virtue, if left undisciplined, naturally gives birth to the disease of arrogance—a disposition that sets itself in opposition to God.

<margin>14.</margin> He who thinks he has grasped the "end" or goal of virtue will no longer seek the Fountainhead and Cause of all good things. He has limited the power of his own desire to himself, and thus he robs himself of the very Definition of salvation—by which I mean, he loses God. But he who is conscious of his own "natural poverty" regarding what is good never ceases to run forward, seeking the One who is able to fill his deficiency.

<margin>15.</margin> He who recognizes the "infinitude" of virtue never stops his race along its path. He does this so that he might not lose the very Beginning and End of virtue—which is God—by fixing the movement of his desire upon himself. He avoids the delusion of thinking he has reached perfection, for such a delusion would mean falling away from the "Truly Existing One" toward whom every effort of the serious person is directed.

<margin>16.</margin> "Wrath"—that is, the "abandonment" mentioned before—justly falls upon the high-minded soul. This is the permission given to demons to trouble the mind during contemplation. The purpose is for the mind to gain an awareness of its own natural weakness, and to recognize the divine power and grace that formerly shielded it and achieved every good thing. Thus, the soul is <term>humbled</term> <note>original: "tapeinothe." To be brought to "tapeinosis" or humility, the foundational virtue in Maximus’s system.</note> and casts far away that strange and unnatural loftiness. This prevents the "other wrath" from coming upon it—the total removal of the spiritual gifts—once it has been humbled and brought back to a conscious awareness of the One who provides all that is good.

<margin>17.</margin> If someone is not corrected by the first kind of wrath (abandonment) and brought to humility, seeing it as a teacher of proper gratitude, they clearly receive the second kind of wrath. This "other wrath" comes upon them and strips away the gifts...

<summary>Maximus explains how spiritual pride leads to "divine abandonment," a pedagogical state where God allows passions and false thoughts to trouble the soul to teach it humility. He argues that virtue and knowledge are infinite because they lead to God, and thus one must never think they have "finished" their spiritual journey.</summary>
<keywords>praxis, theoria, Judah and Jerusalem, pride vs humility, divine providence, abandonment, spiritual discipline, Maximus the Confessor</keywords>

# FIFTH CENTURY
## [CONTINUED]

...activity, and making it a desert, stripped of the power that previously guarded it. "For I will take away," He says, speaking of the ungrateful Israel, "its hedge, and it shall be for plunder; and I will pull down its wall, and it shall be for trampling; and I will let my vineyard go, and it shall not be pruned or dug; and thorns shall grow up in it as in a wasteland, and I will command the clouds not to rain on it." <note>original: Isaiah 5:5-6. Maximus uses this Old Testament imagery of a ruined vineyard to describe a soul that has lost divine protection due to pride.</note>

<margin>18.</margin> Furthermore, a slippery path toward impiety is established by an insensitivity regarding the loss of virtues. For he who has accustomed himself, for the sake of the pleasures of the flesh, to disobey God, will also deny God Himself when a pretext arises; preferring the life of the flesh to God—the pleasures of which he has held to be superior to the divine wills.

<margin>19.</margin> Whenever we perceive the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "nous." In Eastern Christian thought, the *nous* is the "eye of the soul," the faculty of direct spiritual perception, distinct from the discursive reason.</note> to have suffered in any way, let us believe that in such a mind, both its <term>practical</term> <note>original: "praktiken." The active struggle to acquire virtue and purify the heart.</note> and <term>contemplative</term> <note>original: "theoretiken." The spiritual vision or "theoria" of divine truths.</note> powers have suffered along with it according to their natural principles. For it is not possible for the "subject" to suffer without the things "in the subject" also suffering. I call the mind the "subject," as it is receptive of virtue and knowledge; and "in the subject" are practice and contemplation, which hold the status of accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that exists in a subject but is not part of its essential definition.</note> in relation to the mind. Therefore, they suffer with it in every way when it suffers, having the mind’s specific movement as the beginning of their own alteration.

<margin>20.</margin> Every God-loving and virtuous man—like Hezekiah <note>referring to King Hezekiah’s victory over the Assyrians and his subsequent illness and recovery, often used as a type for the soul's struggle.</note>—who has knowledgeably girt himself with power against the <term>demons</term>, should any assault of evil spirits occur (engaging him invisibly in battle within the mind), and who through prayer receives an Angel sent from God—by which I mean a greater <term>word of wisdom</term>—and having crushed and scattered the phalanx of the devil; if such a man does not credit God as the cause of such victory and salvation, but attributes the whole victory to himself, he has not "repaid God according to His gift." He has failed to equal the magnitude of the salvation with the abundance of his thanksgiving, nor has he measured his own disposition against the benefit bestowed by the One who saved him.

<margin>21.</margin> Let us enlighten the mind with divine thoughts, and let us brighten the body with the ways of the more divine

<column-break/>

words we have contemplated, making the body a rational workshop of virtue through the rejection of the <term>passions</term> <note>original: "pathe." These are disordered impulses or attachments—like greed, anger, or pride—that cloud spiritual vision.</note>. For the innate passions of the body, when governed by reason, are not blameworthy; but when moved without reason, they bring reproach. He says, therefore, that a rejection must occur of those things whose movement is innate, but whose use often becomes contrary to nature when not governed by reason.

<margin>22.</margin> Everyone who has lifted up his heart because of the gifts he received—becoming high-minded as if he had not "received" them <note>cf. 1 Corinthians 4:7: "What do you have that you did not receive?"</note>—justly receives the wrath that comes upon him. This happens by God allowing the devil to engage him intellectually, shaking his methods of <term>practice</term> regarding virtue and clouding the clear principles of <term>contemplation</term> regarding knowledge. This occurs so that, having learned his own weakness, he may recognize the only Power that subdues the passions within us. Thus he may be humbled, repenting and casting off the weight of conceit, and may appease God, turning away the wrath that comes upon those who do not repent—the wrath that takes away the grace guarding the soul and leaves the ungrateful mind a desert.

<margin>23.</margin> A "saving wrath" is the divine permission for the high-minded mind to be warred upon by the passions through the demons. This is so that he may know, while suffering dishonorably despite boasting of his virtues, who is the true Giver of these; or that he may be stripped of those "foreign things" <note>The virtues are "foreign" or "other's things" in the sense that they belong to God, not the ego.</note> which he thought he possessed as his own.

<margin>24.</margin> Blessed indeed is that mind which has died laudably to all existing things: to sensible things, by the laying aside of sensory activity; and to intelligible things, by the cessation of intellectual movement. Note that he calls the "laudable death of the mind" the volitional departure from all created beings, after which it is naturally suited to receive the life of divine grace; receiving, instead of created things, the Cause of all things in a way beyond conception.

<margin>25.</margin> Blessed is he who has joined practice to that which is naturally good, and contemplation to that which is naturally true. For all practice is naturally meant to occur for the sake of the good, and all contemplation seeks only the truth through knowledge. Once these are accomplished, there will be nothing at all to strike the practical part of the soul, nor to scrape the contemplative part... <gloss>Perhaps it should read: "nor to scrape away the sharp contemplative part of the soul."</gloss> <note>The Greek text here is slightly fragmented or contains a variant reading in the margin regarding how the contemplative part of the soul is "sharpened" or "scraped."</note>

<vocab>Israel, God, Hezekiah, mind (nous), practical (praxis), contemplative (theoria), virtue, knowledge, passions, demons, angel, thanksgiving.</vocab>

<summary>This page explores the necessity of humility, warning that pride in one's spiritual progress leads to "divine abandonment" or a "saving wrath" where God allows demons to attack the soul to remind it of its dependence on grace. It concludes by defining the "blessed death" of the mind as a state where it transcends both sensory and intellectual concepts to unite with God.</summary>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...having moved beyond both being and that which is thought, and having entered into God Himself, who alone is good and true, and who exists beyond all <term>essence</term> <note>original: "ousian." In this context, it refers to the fundamental nature or substance of things. Maximus argues God is "beyond essence" (super-essential).</note> and thought.

<margin>26.</margin>
The goal of <term>practical virtue</term> <note>original: "praktikes aretes." The stage of spiritual life focused on purifying the passions and acting rightly.</note>, they say, is "the good." This is the fulfillment of divine activity, toward which the rational part of the soul leads us, using <term>anger</term> and <term>desire</term> <note>Maximus often refers to the three parts of the soul: the rational, the spirited (anger), and the appetitive (desire). When used "according to nature," these powers fuel the pursuit of God.</note> according to their true nature; in this state, the beauty of being "in the likeness" of God naturally shines forth. Furthermore, they say the goal of <term>contemplative philosophy</term> <note>original: "theoretikes philosophias." The stage of spiritual life focused on the direct vision of divine truths.</note> is "the truth." This is the simple, unified knowledge of all things pertaining to God, toward which the pure <term>mind</term> <note>original: "nous." The highest faculty of the soul, capable of direct spiritual intuition.</note> is carried, having completely extinguished its judgment based on the senses. In this knowledge, the unadulterated dignity of the "divine image" is clearly demonstrated.

<margin>27.</margin>
No one is able to truly bless God without having first sanctified the body with virtues and enlightened the soul with forms of knowledge. For the disposition achieved through virtue is like the "face" of the contemplative mind, lifted toward the height of true knowledge as if toward heaven.

<margin>28.</margin>
Blessed is the one who knows in truth that God performs every action and contemplation within us—as if we were His instruments—including virtue, knowledge, victory, wisdom, goodness, and truth. We contribute nothing at all to these things, except for a disposition that wills what is good. The great <term>Zerubbabel</term> <note>A leader of the Jewish people who oversaw the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem. Maximus is referencing a famous story from the book of 1 Esdras (3 Esdras) where Zerubbabel wins a debate by arguing that "Truth" is the strongest thing in the world.</note> possessed this disposition, and in addition to the things already mentioned, he said to God: "Blessed are You, who gave me wisdom, and I give thanks to You, O Lord of our Fathers; from You is victory, and from You is wisdom, and Yours is the glory, and I am Your servant." <note>original: 1 Esdras 4:59-60.</note> Like a truly grateful servant, he attributed everything to God, the Giver of all. Having received wisdom from God, he confessed to Him—the Lord of the Fathers—the power of those graced gifts, which are the union of victory and wisdom, of virtue and knowledge, of action and contemplation, of goodness and truth. For when these things are united with one another, they radiate the single glory and brightness of God.

<margin>29.</margin>
All the successes of the saints were clearly gifts from God. No one possesses anything at all that was not given as a good thing from the Lord God, measured out in proportion to the gratitude and goodwill of the receiver. One possesses only those things which are presented by the Master who bestows them.

<column-break/>

<margin>30.</margin>
The mind that presides over virtue and knowledge, wishing for the soul to be liberated from the evil slavery of the passions, says: "Women are very strong, but truth overcomes all things." <note>original: 1 Esdras 3:12. In the biblical story, three bodyguards debate what is strongest: wine, the king, women, or truth. Zerubbabel argues for truth.</note> By "women," he means the deifying virtues, from which is formed that love which unifies humans with God and with one another. This love snatches the soul away from all things subject to birth and decay, and even from those intellectual essences above them, entwining the soul with God Himself through a kind of erotic union—as far as is possible for human nature—and mystically bringing about an unstained and divine life together. By "truth," he means the sole and unique Cause of all beings: the Beginning, the Kingdom, the Power, and the Glory, from which and through which all things have come to be and continue to be, and by which and through which they are held together in existence. It is for the sake of this Truth that all those who love God direct their every effort and movement.

<margin>31.</margin>
Through the "women," he indicated the goal of the virtues, which is love—the unceasing pleasure and indivisible union of those who participate in the One who is Good by nature. Through "truth," he signaled the limit of all knowledge and of all things known. Into this Truth, as the beginning and end of all beings, the natural movements of the soul are drawn by a general principle. For Truth naturally conquers all things, being the source and cause of beings, drawing the movement of all created things toward itself.

<margin>32.</margin>
By a "transcendent privation" <note>Maximus is using "apophatic" language here—describing God by what He is not. Truth is "one" because it lacks the "manyness" of created things.</note> of the many, Truth naturally appears as one and alone, overshadowing the cognitive powers of everything capable of thinking or being thought. This is because Truth exists "super-essentially" beyond both the thinker and the thought. With infinite power, Truth marks the boundaries of the beginning and the end of all things, drawing every movement of all creatures toward itself. To some, it provides a clear knowledge of the grace they had lacked; to others, it grants an inexpressible perception of the goodness they desired, making their recognition manifest through actual participation.

<margin>33.</margin>
The mind, he says, is an instrument of wisdom; the word (reason) is an instrument of knowledge. The natural assurance of both is found in the faith that consists of both. And the natural love for humanity is the instrument of the gift of healings. For every divine gift...

<summary>This page explores the ultimate goals of spiritual life—the "Good" for the active life and "Truth" for the contemplative life—using the biblical figure of Zerubbabel to illustrate that all human virtue is a gift from God. Maximus allegorizes the "strength of women and truth" from the book of Esdras to describe the deifying power of love and the transcendent nature of divine Truth.</summary>

### FIFTH CENTURY

...possesses something <term>divine</term> <note>original: "theion." The OCR "deion" is a common transcription error for "theion."</note> and natural within us—like a power, a habit, or a disposition—acting as a receptive instrument. For example: he who has made his mind pure of every sensory imagination receives wisdom; he who has made <term>reason</term> <note>original: "logos." Here referring to the rational faculty that governs behavior.</note> the master of the innate passions—I mean anger and desire—receives knowledge; he who possesses an unshakable assurance according to mind and reason concerning divine things receives the faith that can do all things; and he who has perfected natural philanthropy, after the complete destruction of <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "philautia." In patristic theology, this is considered the root of all sin.</note>, receives gifts of healing.

<margin>34.</margin>
Each of us possesses the manifest activity of the Spirit according to the proportion of the faith within us. Thus, each person is the steward of his own grace. No one who is of sound mind would ever envy another who excels in spiritual gifts, since the disposition that receives divine blessings lies within his own power.

<margin>35. Scholia</margin>
The cause (he says) of the permanence of divine blessings is the measure of each person’s faith. For as we believe, so we also have the increase of eagerness for action. He who acts according to the proportion of his action demonstrates the measure of his faith, receiving the measure of grace just as he believed. But he who does not act according to that proportion demonstrates the measure of his unbelief, receiving the deprivation of grace just as he disbelieved. Therefore, the envious person does wrong in begrudging those who succeed, for the choice to believe and act—and to receive grace according to the measure of faith—clearly lies within his own choice, and not in another’s.

<margin>36.</margin>
The lover of what is good, through the providence of the words of wisdom, willingly hastens toward the grace of <term>deification</term> <note>original: "theosis." The process of becoming like God through union with Him.</note>. But the one who does not love these things is led away from vice unwillingly through the methods of discipline and just judgment. The former is deified through providence as a lover of God; the latter, as a lover of matter, is not permitted to fall into condemnation through judgment. For God, being good, heals those who are willing through the words of wisdom, but cures those difficult to move toward virtue through the methods of discipline.

<margin>37.</margin>
True faith is a truth that is both cohesive and constitutive, containing no falsehood. A good conscience carries with it the power of love, as it has not a single transgression of the commandments.

<column-break/>

<margin>38.</margin>
And there shall rest upon him, it says, seven spirits: the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of understanding, the spirit of knowledge, the spirit of science, the spirit of counsel, the spirit of might, and the spirit of the fear of God. It is characteristic of these spiritual gifts that: fear brings the rejection of evils; might brings the practice of good things; counsel brings the discernment of opposites; science brings the unadulterated knowledge of duties; knowledge brings the active comprehension of the <term>divine principles</term> <note>original: "logoi." The underlying blueprints or spiritual meanings within created things and virtues.</note> within the virtues; understanding brings the soul’s total disposition toward what has been known; and wisdom brings the indiscernible union with God, through which the desire of the worthy becomes enjoyment. This makes the participant a god by participation, and establishes him as an interpreter of divine blessedness through the eternal, unbroadcast <margin>* perhaps: "proffering" or "projection"</margin> approach and outflow toward those in need of divine mysteries.

<margin>39.</margin>
The spirit of the fear of God is the abstention from evils in action. The spirit of might is the eager impulse and movement toward the activity and practice of the commandments. The spirit of counsel is the habit of discernment, by which we rationally perform the divine commandments and distinguish better things from worse. The spirit of science is the unerring knowledge of the ways of acting according to virtue, whereby in our actions we never fall away from the right judgment of reason. The spirit of knowledge is the comprehension of the commandments and the principles within them, which constitute the ways of the virtues. The spirit of understanding is the assent to the ways and principles of the virtues, or to speak more accurately, a transformation by which a blending occurs of the natural powers with the ways and principles of the commandments. Finally, the spirit of wisdom is the ascent to and union with the cause of the more spiritual things within the commandments; through this, we are initiated into the principles of beings—as they exist in God—in a way that is unknown yet permitted to humans. From the heart, like some gushing spring, we then offer the truth found in all things in various ways to other people.

<margin>40.</margin>
From the last things of God, which are closest to us, we ascend in order and sequence toward the first things, which are far from us but close to God. For from the idleness...

<summary>This page outlines how the Holy Spirit's gifts are received according to a person's faith and action, specifically detailing the "seven spirits" (from Isaiah) as stages of spiritual growth. Maximus explains that these gifts lead the believer from the fear of God and practical virtue to a final, deifying union with the Divine Wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Spirit, seven spirits, deification, theosis, faith, grace, wisdom, discernment, logoi, Maximus the Confessor</keywords>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

**18**

...from the avoidance of evils through fear, we come to the practice of virtues through strength; from the practice of virtues, to the discernment of the divine will; from discernment, to the habit of virtues, that is, to <term>science</term> <note>original: "epistēmēn." In this context, it refers to a stable, certain spiritual knowledge.</note>; from the habit of virtues, to the knowledge of the <term>inner meanings</term> <note>original: "logōn." These are the divine principles or "blueprints" that God placed within created things and virtues.</note> within those very virtues; from this, to the transformative habit toward the known principles of the virtues—I mean, <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "synesin."</note>; and from this, to the simple and precise contemplation of the truth in all things. Setting out from this, we will offer many and varied pious discourses concerning the truth, drawn from the wise contemplation of the essences of beings, both sensible and intelligible.

<margin>41.</margin>
That which is first in activity for us—the good which is fear—the word of Scripture has listed last as the beginning of wisdom. Moving from fear toward the goal of wisdom, we ascend to understanding, after which we become close to God himself, having wisdom alone as the mediator of our union with him. For it is impossible to lay hold of wisdom without first having shaken off the plague of ignorance and the dust of wickedness through fear and the other intermediate gifts. For this reason, the scriptural order placed wisdom close to God and fear close to us, so that we might learn the boundary and law of good order.

<margin>42.</margin>
Ascending through these eyes of faith—that is, through enlightenments—we are gathered toward the divine <term>unity</term> <note>original: "monada."</note> of wisdom. We bring back the division of gifts that occurred for our sake to the Cause of those gifts through the gradual increase in virtues, omitting nothing mentioned above through the cooperation of God. This is so that we do not, by neglecting things bit by bit, make our faith blind and eyeless, lacking the enlightenments that come through the works of the Spirit, and be justly punished for endless ages—having, as far as it was up to us, blinded the divine eyes within us through our lack of faith.

<margin>43.</margin>
Everyone who has dug out such eyes of faith within himself through the idleness of the commandments is entirely condemned, no longer having God looking upon him. For if the Word <note>original: "logos." Refers here to the teaching of Scripture.</note> calls the activities of the Spirit the "eyes of the Lord," then he who does not

<column-break/>

open these through the practice of the commandments does not have God looking upon him. For it is not natural for God to oversee those on earth through any other eyes, since the enlightenment we gain through virtue is the very ray of divine vision.

<margin>44.</margin>
Wisdom is a <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monas." An indivisible unit.</note>, seen without being divided in the various virtues that proceed from it. It is conceived of in a single form through their activities, and is again demonstrated to be a simple monad by the restoration of the virtues to it—when we, for whose sake it makes its progression according to the birth of each virtue, are gathered back to it through each virtue by our upward striving.

<margin>45.</margin>
He who does not work the divine commands according to faith has blind faith. For if God’s commands are light, it is clear that he who does not perform them is without divine light; he carries around the divine name as a bare title, but not in truth.

<margin>46.</margin>
No one who sins can have the weakness of the flesh as an advocate for his sin. For the union with the God-Word <note>The Incarnation of Christ.</note> strengthened the whole of nature by the undoing of the curse, making our disposition's attachment to the passions inexcusable. For the divinity of the Word, always present by grace to those who believe in him, withers away the law of sin in the flesh.

<margin>47.</margin>
He who has conquered the irrational desires—or rather, movements—of the passions contrary to nature through faith in God and love, also moves outside the law of nature itself. He is transferred entirely into the region of <term>intelligible things</term> <note>The realm of spiritual realities perceived by the mind rather than the senses.</note>, and he casts out his natural kinship along with the foreign slavery that had been added to him.

<margin>48.</margin>
Knowledge not bridled by divine fear during practice produces <term>pride</term> <note>original: "typhon." A delusional self-inflation or vanity.</note>, persuading the one puffed up by it to present what is borrowed as his own, turning the <gloss>contribution</gloss> <note>original: "eranon." A metaphor for a shared feast or collection of gifts.</note> of the Word into his own praise. But practice <note>original: "praxis."</note>, increasing along with divine longing, does not grasp for knowledge beyond what should be done; it makes the practitioner humble-minded, as he withdraws into himself before the principles that are beyond his own power.

<margin>49.</margin>
A heavenly dwelling is the <term>dispassionate habit</term> <note>original: "apathēs hexis." A state of soul, also known as apatheia, where one is no longer controlled by disordered impulses.</note> according to virtue, and the knowledge that has no thought of error warring against it.

<margin>50.</margin>
Just as the end of a monad that has been moved is...

Maximus argues that faith without action is spiritual blindness and that through Christ, human nature is empowered to overcome all fleshly excuses for sin.</summary>

### FIFTH CENTURY

The myriad <note>A "myriad" is the number 10,000, but in this philosophical context, it represents the full expansion of multiplicity.</note> and the beginning of a myriad that has not yet moved is the monad <note>The "monad" is the number one or "unity," representing the starting point and the simple source of all things.</note>. For the beginning of every end is established clearly as the immobility inherent to it; and the end of every beginning is the completion of the movement inherent to it. So too is **faith**, being by nature the beginning of virtues, it has as its end the completion of the good achieved through them. And the good according to nature, as the end of virtues, having faith as its beginning, is interiorly gathered back to it. For faith is an interior good, and the good is faith put into action. 

God is by nature faithful and good: the one as the first good, the other as the ultimate object of desire. These are established as being the same as each other in every way, separated from one another by no reason except for that of mental conception, entirely because of the movement of those things starting from Him and ending in Him. Therefore the myriad, bearing the type of the ultimate object of desire, describes the perfect yearning of those moving toward it; and the monad, bearing the symbol of the first good, brings with it a perfect basis for those moving from it.

<margin>51. In another version: 'nature'.</margin> The **first dispassion** <note>original: "apatheia." This is the goal of the first stage of spiritual life—not a lack of feeling, but a state where the soul is no longer disturbed or controlled by disordered passions.</note> is the complete abstinence from evil actions, seen in those who are being introduced to the spiritual life. The **second** is the complete rejection of thoughts <note>original: "logismōn." In this tradition, these are the "seeds" of temptation that enter the mind before an action is taken.</note> in the intellect regarding consent to evil, occurring in those who pursue virtue with reason. The **third** is the complete immobility of desire regarding the passions, in those who intellectually contemplate the inner meanings <note>original: "logous." The divine principles or reasons behind created things.</note> of visible things through their outward forms. The **fourth dispassion** is the complete cleansing of even the bare imagination itself, established in those who, through knowledge and contemplation, have made the ruling part of the soul <note>original: "hēgemonikon." The "command center" or highest faculty of the human person.</note> a pure and transparent mirror of God. 

Therefore, the one who has cleansed himself of the activity of passions, and has been freed from the intellectual consent to them, and has brought to a standstill the movement of desire concerning them, and has established the mind as unstained by their bare imagination, possessing the four general types of dispassion, goes out from matter and material things, and hastens toward the intellectual and divine and peaceful inheritance of intelligible realities.

<margin>52. Scholion.</margin> He says that the **first dispassion** is the movement that remains untouched by the sin of the body in actual practice. The **second** is the complete rejection of passionate thoughts in the soul, through which the movement toward the first dispassion is distanced from the passions,

<column-break/>

not having passionate thoughts to ignite it toward action. He says the **third** is the complete immobility of desire regarding the passions, through which the second is naturally produced, being established by the purity of thoughts. He says the **fourth dispassion** is the complete laying aside of all sensory imaginations in the intellect, from which the third took its birth, not having the imaginations of sensory things giving form to the images of the passions within it.

<margin>53.</margin> For every person of practice, reason and intellect labor like a servant boy and a servant girl, both devising and creating the modes of action according to virtue, and as it were, having all their power set in opposition against the spirits of wickedness that resist practice. When they have fulfilled **practical philosophy** <note>This refers to the active struggle for virtue and the purging of the passions.</note>, which the number of years outside the Sabbath indicated—for it is said that the number **six** signifies practical philosophy—they are released into spiritual freedom, clearly approaching the contemplation of the related inner meanings <note>original: "logōn."</note> in existing things: both the reason and the intellect.

<margin>54.</margin> The "foreign servant boy and girl" are **anger** <note>original: "thymos." The spirited or incensive power of the soul, which should be used for courage.</note> and **desire** <note>original: "epithymia." The desiring power, which should be directed toward God.</note>. These the contemplative mind always yokes to the lordship of reason for the service of the virtues, through courage and temperance, not giving them total release into freedom until the law of nature is completely swallowed up by the law of the spirit—just as the death of the wretched flesh is swallowed by infinite life—and the **image of the beginningless kingdom** is clearly shown, having the whole form of the archetype through imitation. When the contemplative mind attains this, it makes both anger and desire free: transforming the latter into the incorruptible pleasure of divine love and stainless enchantment; and transferring the former into spiritual fervor, a white-hot perpetual motion, and a **sober madness** <note>original: "sōphrona manian." A classic mystical term for a love of God so intense it appears like madness to the world, yet is perfectly ordered.</note>.

<margin>55.</margin> The **image of the beginningless kingdom** is the immutability of the mind regarding true knowledge, and the incorruptibility of the senses regarding virtue—when soul and body are bound to one another by the divine law of the spirit alone, according to the transformation of the senses toward the mind in the spirit...

<summary>This page outlines the progression of spiritual growth through four levels of dispassion (apatheia), moving from external behavior to the complete purification of the imagination. It also explains how the soul's natural powers of anger and desire are transformed into divine love and spiritual fervor as the person enters the 'Beginningless Kingdom.'</summary>
<keywords>dispassion, apatheia, monad, myriad, faith, practical philosophy, anger, desire, sober madness, image of the kingdom, purification of the mind</keywords>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS
<meta>Institutional stamp: UNIVERSITY OF CRETE</meta>

...they possess the ever-moving and living activity of the Word <note>original: "Logos." In Christian theology, the Word is the second person of the Trinity, through whom all things were created.</note> being shown through all things; in this activity, every unsuitability toward the divine is entirely absent.

<margin>56.</margin>
They say that **pleasure** is "activated desire," occurring when a perceived good is present, according to its own definition. Conversely, **desire** is "unactivated pleasure," regarding a future good. They define **anger** <note>original: "thymos." This refers to the "spirited" or "incensive" power of the soul, which can manifest as righteous indignation or sinful rage.</note> as the "meditated movement of madness," and **madness** as "activated anger." Therefore, the person who subjects these powers to **Reason** <note>original: "Logos." Here referring to both human rationality and the Divine Word.</note> will find that desire becomes a spiritual pleasure for him—through the soul's stainless union with the divine by grace. Anger becomes a "pure fervor," acting as a guardian for that divine pleasure. It becomes a **sober madness** <note>original: "sophrona manian." A paradoxical term used by the Fathers to describe a spiritual ecstasy where the soul is "carried out" of itself by love for God, yet remains disciplined.</note>, according to the soul's longing and its power of attraction, which draws it away from created things and makes it completely ecstatic toward God. Therefore, as long as "the world" lives in us—that is, the soul's voluntary attachment to material things—we must not give freedom to these powers. Otherwise, they might mix with the objects of the senses as if they were of the same kind, wage war against the soul, and lead it away as a prisoner of war to the passions, just as the Babylonians once did to Jerusalem. For the "age" <note>The "aeon" or period of time.</note> in which the Law commanded that the "children of the foreigners" should be enslaved, the Word used to signify the soul's dispositional attachment to this world, or rather to this present life, using historical events to demonstrate spiritual concepts.

<margin>57.</margin>
He calls **evil** "begun," for it has its beginning in our own "contrary-to-nature" movement. But he says **good** is "not begun," for by nature the good exists before every age and every time. He calls the good "intelligible," as it is the only thing one ought to think upon; but evil is "not intelligible," for it is the only thing one ought *not* to think upon. He calls the good "speakable," for it alone should be spoken of. He also calls the good "becoming," for though it is by nature "un-become" <note>Meaning eternal and uncreated.</note>, it allows itself to "become" in us by grace through God’s love for humanity, according to the capacity of us who act and speak. For we "make" the good, which is the only thing that ought to come into being. We do not "make" evil, which is the only thing that ought not to come into being. He calls **evil** "perishable," for the nature of evil is corruption, having no actual existence in any way. But **good** is "imperishable," as it is always existing, never ceasing to be, and is the protector of all things in which it dwells. Therefore, we seek this Good with our **rational faculty**; we long for it with our **desiring faculty**; 

<column-break/>

we guard it as something sacred with our **spirited faculty**; through our **perceptive faculty**, we distinguish it from its opposites according to true knowledge; through our **vocal faculty**, we make it manifest to those who are ignorant of it by speaking of it; and through our **generative faculty**, we multiply it—or rather, to speak more truly, we ourselves are multiplied according to it.

<margin>58.</margin>
The contemplative mind <note>original: "nous." The highest faculty of the human soul, intended for direct intuition of God.</note>, while it reigns over the concepts and sights found in created things and over its own movements, must maintain a "barren habit" toward vice. This means it must neither conceive nor give birth to evil at all. The mind must be carried along while moved in contemplation, lest while making a spiritual investigation of beings, it should secretly fall into one of the evil spirits that are prone to corrupt the pure investigation of the heart through the medium of the senses.

<margin>59.</margin>
The person who is wounded by **vainglory** <note>original: "kenodoxia," or empty glory/pride.</note> because of his virtue or knowledge—vainly nourishing his "hair" like **Absalom** <note>A reference to 2 Samuel 14-18. Absalom’s long hair, which was his pride, eventually led to his death when it got caught in a tree.</note>—displays an ethical way of life that is artificial and mixed, like a **mule**, intended to deceive those who see him. Suspended upon this mule of pride, he thinks he can overcome the Father <note>Referring to both God and the spiritual teacher who gave birth to him through instruction.</note> who "begot" him through the teaching of the Word. In his pride, he wishes to tyranically drag to himself all the glory of virtue and knowledge that belongs to the Father from God. But such a person, when he goes out into the "broad space" of natural contemplation in the spirit to engage in the rational war for truth, is caught by the "thicket of the oak" <note>Referencing the tree that caught Absalom.</note> of material sights because of his living attachment to the senses. He possesses "empty pride" which binds him to death and hangs him between heaven and earth. For the vainglorious man has no knowledge to pull him up toward heaven (away from the pride that drags him down), nor does he have "earth"—I mean the firm foundation of action in **humility**—to pull him down from the conceit that puffs him up. His teacher, who begot him, being a lover of God, mourns him even when he is dead out of love for humanity; in imitation of God, he does not wish for the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live.

<margin>60.</margin>
**Wisdom** is the beginning and the end of the salvation of each person. In the beginning, it produces **fear**, and later it perfects...

The previous page discussed the transformation of natural powers like desire and anger when directed toward God.
