# FIFTH CENTURY

...perfected and consisting; or rather, it is fear in the beginning, occurring for our sake by divine arrangement <note>original: "oikonomikos," referring to God's "economy" or management of human salvation</note>, so that it may stop the lover of vice from his ways; and later it is found to be desire for its own sake at the end, so that it may fill with spiritual laughter <note>A Patristic term for the deep, inner joy of the soul in God</note> those who have exchanged the company of all other things for its own.

<margin>61.</margin>
Wisdom is fear insofar as it becomes a state of deprivation <note>avoidance of worldly things</note> for those who do not yet yearn for it; and it is desire insofar as it is found to be a habit of enjoyable activity for those who love it. For wisdom, by freeing the soul from passions through the hope of escaping punishment, creates fear; yet it also works desire by habituating the mind to look toward future blessings through the acquisition of the virtues.

<margin>62.</margin>
Every kind of **confession** <note>original: "exomologesis," which means both admitting sins and declaring God's praise</note> humbles the soul. One kind of confession humbles the soul because it has been made righteous by the grace of God; the other kind humbles the soul by teaching it that it is held accountable for crimes through the negligence of its own will.

<margin>63.</margin>
The discourse of confession is twofold: one part is made in **thanksgiving** for the good things that have been granted; the other is spoken in **rebuke** and scrutiny of the evil things that have been committed. For "confession" is the term used both for the grateful numbering of divine benefits by those who have been treated well, and for the admission of bad deeds by those who are guilty. Both are productive of humility. For both the one who gives thanks for good things and the one who is scrutinized for his crimes are humbled—the former judging himself unworthy of the good things given to him, and the latter begging to receive forgiveness for his transgressions.

<margin>64.</margin>
The passion of **pride** <note>term: <term>Hyperphania</term> (Pride) - in this tradition, it is viewed as a cognitive error, a failure to recognize the source of one's strength</note> consists of two ignorances; and when these two ignorances come together into one, they produce a single, confused state of mind. For only that person is proud who is ignorant of both divine help and human weakness. Therefore, pride is the deprivation of both divine and human knowledge. For by the denial of these two true extremes, a single, false affirmation is created.

<margin>65.</margin>
**Vainglory** is a departure from the goal that is according to God, and a transition toward another goal other than the divine one. For a vainglorious person is one who practices virtue for the sake of his own glory rather than God's, purchasing empty praises from men through his own labors.

<margin>66.</margin>
The **man-pleaser** <note>one who acts solely to be seen and approved by other people</note> cares only for the outward appearance of his character, and indeed for the words of a 

<column-break/>

flatterer; he does this so that he may seize the sight of some and the hearing of others—those who are pleased only by, or even struck with awe by, what is seen and heard, and who define virtue solely by the senses. We say, therefore, that man-pleasing is the display of manners and words for the sake of virtue performed for the benefit of a human audience.

<margin>67.</margin>
**Hypocrisy** is a pretense of friendship; or hatred disguised in the form of friendship; or enmity operating through goodwill; or envy mimicking the character of love; or a life that possesses a veneer of order in the fiction of virtue, but not in the reality of it; or a pretense of righteousness maintained by the appearance of being so; or a deception having the form of truth. Those who mimic the serpent in the crookedness of their character practice this.

<margin>68.</margin>
God is the Cause of all things that exist, and of the good things that are within them. Therefore, the person who is puffed up concerning virtue or knowledge, and who does not extend his awareness of his own weakness to match the measure of his progress in virtue through grace, has not escaped the evil of pride. He who practices what is good for the sake of his own glory has preferred himself to God, being pierced by the nail of vainglory. He who acts or speaks of virtue in order to be seen by men has placed human approval far above divine approval, being diseased with the passion of man-pleasing. And he who merely paints his character with the dignity of virtue for the sake of deception, covering the wicked disposition of his will with the outward form of piety, purchases "virtue" through the fraud of hypocrisy. Such a person, therefore, has diverted his goal to things other than the Cause <note>God</note> of each of these virtues.

<margin>69.</margin>
None of the wicked demons ever hinders the zeal of the virtuous man; rather, they deceitfully trim away the "shortcomings" of the virtues and suggest "intensifications," acting as if they are zealous alongside the contestants. They do this so that they may make the entire thought of the practitioner their own, having destroyed the equal balance of the **middle way** <note>the "royal path" or moderate mean between extremes</note>, and secretly lead the soul toward a different resting place than the one it intended.

<margin>70.</margin>
The demons neither hate self-control, nor do they loathe fasting, nor the distribution of money, nor hospitality, nor the singing of psalms, nor the leisure of reading, nor stillness, nor...

<vocab>wisdom, fear, confession, humility, pride, vainglory, man-pleasing, hypocrisy, demons</vocab>

It emphasizes that demons often attack not by stopping virtue, but by pushing it toward immoderate extremes.</summary>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

<margin>71.</margin>
...the highest of disciplines, nor sleeping on the ground, nor vigils, nor all the rest by which the life according to God is characterized, so long as the goal and the cause of what is being done is directed toward them.

The ascetic might quickly cast down other demons and easily escape the harm they cause. But as for those who seem to cooperate in the race for virtue, and who wish, as it were, to help build the temple for the Lord—what mind, even among the most exalted, could grasp them? Only the active and living Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> that passes through all things can do so, "reaching even to the division of soul and spirit" <note>A reference to Hebrews 4:12. Maximus uses this to distinguish between human effort and divine grace.</note>. This means distinguishing which works or thoughts are "soulish"—that is, the natural forms or movements of virtue—and which happen to be "spiritual"—that is, those that are supernatural and characterize God, given to nature by grace. It involves knowing the "joints and marrow"—the fitting or entirely unfitting union <note>original: "syneusin"</note> of the modes of virtue with spiritual principles—judging the deliberations and thoughts of the heart. By this, I mean the hidden dispositions in the depths of these matters and the invisible causes within the soul, before whom no creature is hidden within us, even those things that seem to be secret. Indeed, all things that have happened or been thought, as well as those yet to happen or be thought by us, are open to Him.

<margin>72. Scholion</margin>
The "division of soul and spirit," he says, is the difference in how virtues arise: those whose principles <note>original: "logoi"</note> we possess naturally, and those in the Spirit whose grace we receive as a gift. The Word makes a clear distinction and judgment between these.

<margin>73.</margin>
The "deliberations" and "intentions" which the Word is able to discern, he says, are the soul's dispositions toward both divine principles and thoughts, and the causes of these very dispositions. For **deliberation** stirs the memory, which is where disposition dwells; and **intention** looks toward a goal, which characterizes the cause.

<margin>74.</margin>
If God is, in His essence, **Knowledge**, and if the mind clearly precedes all knowledge (since knowledge is something the mind naturally grasps), then God is surely beyond knowledge—just as He is infinitely beyond every mind—since knowledge by its nature is something grasped by the mind.

<margin>75.</margin>
Who, if they do not have the Word of God dwelling in them, can bow down the hidden traps of the demons' hypocrisy against us, stand entirely alone without any mixture, and build the temple of the Lord? This follows the example of the Great Zerubbabel and Jesus <note>original: "Iesous," referring to Joshua son of Jozadak, the High Priest in the book of Ezra</note>, and the leaders of the ancestral houses. They said clearly and with a loud voice to the deceivers of pride, vainglory, man-pleasing, and hypocrisy: "It is not for us and you together to build the house for the Lord our God; for we alone will build for the Lord of Israel." <note>Quoting Ezra 4:3. In Maximus's allegory, the "enemies" who want to help build are the subtle vices like pride that latch onto good works.</note> They knew that any mixture with these vices causes the ruin and destruction of the entire building, and silences the grace of the beauty of the divine offerings.

<column-break/>

<margin>76.</margin>
No one who has one of the aforementioned demons participating in their virtue can build for the Lord. For such a person does not have God as the "end" <note>term: "telos" — the ultimate purpose or goal</note> of their actions, even if they perform them visibly; rather, they serve the passion which is established through that action.

<margin>77.</margin>
Those who fight against us by way of **deficiency** in virtue are the demons who teach lust, drunkenness, greed, and envy. But those who fight by way of **excess** are those who teach conceit, vainglory, and pride; they secretly wound us from the "right side" using "left-handed" means <note>A common ascetic metaphor: sins of the 'left' are obvious vices; sins of the 'right' are virtues performed with a prideful or wrong intent.</note>.

<margin>78.</margin>
May it be that we also always say to those spirits of wickedness who invisibly attack us with a pretense of spiritual friendship, wishing secretly to bring about the "death of sin" through what is good, and who say: "We will build the temple for your Lord with you." [We should reply]: "It is not for us and you together to build the house for the Lord our God; for we alone will build for the Lord of Israel." We say "alone" because, having been freed from the spirits that fight us through deficiency in virtue—from which we have already departed—we do not wish to be lifted up again by "excesses" and fall into a ruin that is far more grievous than the first. For in the first case <note>falling through weakness</note>, there was an easy hope of recovery for those forgiven due to weakness; but in the latter <note>falling through pride</note>, there is either no hope or it is very difficult, for they are hated because of their pride and for making something else "more right" than what is truly right. And we say "alone" not only because we have the Holy Angels as helpers in good things, but rather because we have God Himself, who reveals Himself to us through...

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "good things" (καλῶν), which will likely begin the next page.</meta>

<summary>Maximus analyzes the psychological "division of soul and spirit," distinguishing between natural human virtues and those granted by divine grace. He warns against "demons of excess" (like pride and vainglory) that attempt to "help" a person perform virtues only to corrupt the soul's ultimate goal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Fifth Century" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The previous text (Margin 71-72) concluded with a discussion on the Word of God as a judge of the heart’s hidden dispositions, comparing the spiritual life to the building of a temple.</meta>

### FIFTH CENTURY

...works of righteousness, and building us as a holy temple for Himself, and free from every passion.

<margin>79.</margin> The definition of virtue is the union of human weakness, through its own recognition, with divine power. Therefore, he who defines himself only by the weakness of his nature has not yet reached the boundary of virtue; for this reason, he falls into error, having not yet received the power that strengthens what is weak. On the other hand, he who arrogantly presents his own weakness as if it were strength in opposition to divine power has overstepped the boundary of virtue. Because of this, when he falls into error, he does not recognize it—as if what is inferior has become superior within him—for he considers his very transgression to be virtue. Thus, the person who defines himself by his natural weakness is more excusable than the one who falls from virtue into passions through laziness. Or rather, the one who presents his own weakness as strength against divine power in the performance of duties has fallen from virtue more through self-will <note>original: "authadeia," a sense of stubborn self-pleasing or arrogance</note>.

<margin>80.</margin> Since it has been said that "the effective prayer of a righteous man carries great power," <note>A reference to James 5:16.</note> I know of two ways this is made effective. First, when the one approaching God offers this prayer along with works performed according to the commandments. In this way, the prayer does not fall idle or without substance, sounding only in bare words and the empty noise of the tongue, but is active and living, being "ensouled" <note>original: "psychoumenēn," given life or a soul</note> by the works of the commandments. For the substance of prayer and petition is clearly the fulfillment of the commandments through virtues; by this, the righteous man possesses a prayer that is strong and all-powerful, made effective by the commandments. The second way is when the person who stands in need of the righteous man's prayer performs the works of prayer himself, both by correcting his former life and by making the righteous man’s prayer powerful through his own good conduct.

<margin>81.</margin> There is no benefit in the prayer of a righteous man for someone who needs it if that person takes more pleasure in transgressions than in virtues. For even the Great Samuel once mourned for Saul when he sinned, but he was unable to move God to mercy, because he did not have as an ally in his mourning the necessary correction from the one who had sinned. Therefore, putting an end to the senseless

<column-break/>

mourning of His servant, God said to him: "How long will you mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him from reigning over Israel?" <note>1 Samuel 16:1</note>

<margin>82.</margin> And again Jeremiah, most compassionate of men, was not heard when praying for the people of the Jews who were raving in the delusion of demons; his prayer had no power because there was no turning back from the delusion of the godless Jews. Thus, God, leading him away from praying in vain, said: "As for you, do not pray for this people, and do not ask for them to be pitied, and do not pray, and do not come to me further concerning them, for I will not listen." <note>Jeremiah 7:16</note>

<margin>83.</margin> It is truly a mark of great stupidity—not to say madness—to seek salvation through the prayers of the righteous while still delighting in one's own disposition, and to ask for forgiveness for those very things in which one boasts while being stained by purposeful action. One who needs the prayer of a righteous man—if he truly hates evil—ought not to allow that prayer to remain idle and motionless. Instead, he should make it active and strong, "giving it wings" <note>original: "pteroumenēn," to be feathered or winged for flight</note> with his own virtues, so that it might reach the One who is able to grant forgiveness for transgressions.

<margin>84.</margin> The prayer of the righteous man is very powerful when it is made effective, whether by the righteous person who offers it, or by the one asking the righteous person for it. For when it is made effective by the righteous man, it gives him confidence <note>original: "parrhēsian," boldness or freedom of speech</note> before the One who is able to grant the requests of the righteous. And when it is made effective by the one asking for it, it draws him away from his former malice, changing his inner disposition toward virtue.

<margin>85.</margin>
<margin>Question</margin> Since the Apostle said: "In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials," <note>1 Peter 1:6</note> how can someone who is grieving in trials also rejoice in the very thing that causes grief?

<margin>86.</margin>
<margin>Answer</margin> The word of truth recognizes two types of grief. One is established invisibly in the soul, the other visibly in the senses. The former encompasses the whole depth of the soul, being tormented by the scourge of conscience. The latter defines the entire range of the senses, being contracted by the weight of painful things and the loss of natural expansion. One is the end of sensory pleasure, the other is the end of spiritual joy...

<summary>Maximus discusses the nature of virtue as a balance of human weakness and divine power, and explores why the prayers of the righteous require the active cooperation and repentance of those being prayed for. He concludes with a psychological distinction between spiritual and sensory grief.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, divine power, prayer of the righteous, Samuel, Saul, Jeremiah, repentance, effective prayer, trials, joy and grief</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Fifth Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor’s "Chapters on Knowledge." The previous page (Margin 79-80) discussed the definition of virtue as the union of human weakness with divine power and the effectiveness of prayer when joined with active commandments.</meta>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...existing; or rather the one belongs to those judgments <note>original: "gnōmikōn," relating to the personal will or disposition</note> based on the senses, while the other occurs as a perversion of judgment <note>original: "paragnōmēn," an error or deviation in will</note> resulting from the passions.

<margin>87.</margin> Sorrow, to put it in my own words, is a state deprived of pleasures. Now, the deprivation of pleasures constitutes the onset of pains. Pain is clearly a lack or a withdrawal of a natural state. A lack of a natural state is a suffering <note>original: "pathos," which can mean both "passion" and "suffering" or "undergoing" something</note> of the power that underlies that natural state. The suffering of that natural power is the mode of the misuse of natural energy. Misuse of the mode of energy is the movement of a power toward something for which it was not naturally intended.

<margin>88.</margin> He says that sorrow in the soul is the end of sensory pleasure. For it is from the latter that sorrow of the soul is composed. Just as, conversely, the end of spiritual pleasure is sorrow according to the flesh. For the gladness of the soul becomes the sorrow of the flesh.

<margin>89.</margin> He says there are two kinds of sorrow: one concerning the senses, which is composed of the deprivation of bodily pleasures; and the other concerning the mind, which occurs through the deprivation of the goods of the soul. He also says there are two kinds of temptations: the voluntary and the involuntary. The voluntary ones are the fathers of sensory, bodily pleasure, but they are the procreators of sorrow in the soul. For sin, when committed alone, grieves the soul. The involuntary temptations—which are manifested in pains that go against our will—are the fathers of spiritual pleasure, but the procreators of sensory, bodily sorrow.

<margin>90.</margin> Just as the Word <note>original: "ho logos," likely referring here to the rational principle or the teaching of Scripture</note> knows sorrow to be twofold, as I said, so it also understands the manner of temptations to be twofold. One is according to choice <note>original: "kata gnōmēn"</note>, and the other is against choice <note>original: "para gnōmēn"</note>. One is the creator of voluntary pleasures, and the other is the bringer of involuntary pains. For the temptation according to choice clearly establishes the voluntary pleasures of our preference. But the temptation against choice obviously imposes involuntary pains contrary to our preference. The former is the cause of sorrow in the soul, while the latter is the cause of sorrow in the senses.

<margin>91.</margin> Temptation according to choice establishes sorrow in the soul, but clearly creates pleasure in the senses. On the other hand, temptation against

<column-break/>

choice produces pleasure in the soul, but sorrow in the flesh.

<margin>92.</margin> I believe our Lord and God, when teaching His own disciples how to pray, told them to pray against the form of temptation that is according to choice, saying: *And lead us not into temptation.* <note>Matthew 6:13.</note> That is, we should pray not to be abandoned to experience those pleasurable, willful, and voluntary temptations. However, the Great James, who is called the brother of the Lord, teaches those struggling for the sake of the truth not to shrink back from the form of involuntary temptations, saying: *Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet various trials* <note>James 1:2.</note>—meaning, obviously, those involuntary trials that go against our choice and produce pain. This is shown clearly: in the first instance, the Lord adds, *But deliver us from the evil one*; while here, the Great James says, *Knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience; but let patience have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.* <note>James 1:3-4.</note>

<margin>93.</margin> The Lord teaches us to pray against voluntary temptations, as they produce pleasure for the flesh but pain for the soul. The Great James, however, exhorts us to rejoice in involuntary temptations, as they take away the pleasure of the flesh and the pain of the soul.

<margin>94.</margin> A person is perfect who fights voluntary temptations through self-control <note>original: "enkrateia"</note> and endures involuntary temptations through patience <note>original: "hypomonē"</note>. And a person is complete who carries out action <note>original: "praxin"</note> with knowledge and does not leave contemplation <note>original: "theōrian"</note> inactive.

<margin>95.</margin> Since sorrow and pleasure are divided between the soul and the senses, the person who secures the pleasure of the soul while accepting the sorrow of the senses with patience becomes approved, perfect, and complete. Approved, because of the experience of sensory opposites; perfect, because they fight unyieldingly against sensory pleasure and sorrow through self-control and patience; and complete, because they preserve their states of being—even though these states are opposed to sensory conditions—unharmed in the stability of the identity found in reason. I am speaking of action and contemplation, which are held together with one another, neither being separated from the other; rather, action...

<summary>In this passage, St. Maximus the Confessor analyzes the psychological and spiritual relationship between pleasure, sorrow, and temptation. He distinguishes between voluntary temptations (which cause bodily pleasure but spiritual grief) and involuntary trials (which cause bodily pain but spiritual joy), harmonizing the Lord's Prayer with the Epistle of James.</summary>

**FIFTH CENTURY**

...of contemplation, revealing knowledge through its various modes; and contemplation, no less than the Word <note>original: "logou," referring to the Divine Reason or teaching</note>, has the virtue of action as its armor.

<margin>96.</margin> One who has experienced the sorrow and pleasure of the flesh might be called "tested" <note>original: "dokimos," a term for a person or coin that has been tried and proved genuine</note>, as one who has undergone both the ease and difficulty of bodily affairs. But the "perfect" person is the one who, by the power of reason, has wrestled down the pleasure and the pain of the flesh. And the "complete" person is the one who has maintained the habits of practice and contemplation unchanged through his intense longing for the Divine.

<margin>97.</margin> There are two ways in which sorrow affects the soul: one arises from our own failings, and the other from the failings of others. The cause of such sorrow is clearly the sensory pleasure <note>original: "hēdonē"</note> of the one who is grieving, or of those for whom he grieves. For according to strict logic, almost no sin exists among humans that does not have its origin in an irrational relationship between the soul and the senses for the sake of pleasure. On the other hand, the cause of pleasure in the soul is clearly the sensory sorrow felt by one who delights in his own or another's virtues. For strictly speaking, almost no virtue exists among humans that does not have its origin in the soul's reasoned detachment from the senses.

<margin>98.</margin> Without the soul’s passionate relationship with the senses, there is absolutely no sin among humans; and for every sorrow that forms in the soul, a pleasure of the flesh has come before it.

<margin>99.</margin> The true birth of virtue is the soul’s voluntary detachment <note>original: "allotriōsis," meaning estrangement or alienation</note> from the flesh. He who subdues the flesh with voluntary labors gladdens the soul spiritually.

<margin>100.</margin> When the soul has acquired a detachment from the senses for the sake of virtue, the senses will necessarily experience pain. This is because the senses no longer possess the soul's power, which was previously linked to them by a disposition of the will <note>original: "gnōmikēn schesin"</note> to pursue pleasures. On the contrary, the soul manfully strikes away the uprising of sensory pleasures through self-control. Regarding the onset of unnatural and involuntary pains, the soul remains entirely unyielding through endurance. It does not fall away from the God-befitting dignity and glory of virtue for the sake of unstable pleasure, nor does it fall from the heights of virtue out of a desire to avoid the pain felt by the flesh. The cause of sensory sorrow is the soul's total lack of concern for things that are natural to it; whereas sensory pleasure clearly arises from the soul’s unnatural activity, which can have no other basis for its existence than the soul’s abandonment of what is natural.

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...of things that are naturally good, it is not the power that invents the mode of sensory pleasure.

<margin>4.</margin> Where reason <note>original: "logos"</note> leads the way for the senses in the contemplation <note>original: "theoria"</note> of visible things, the flesh is deprived of all its natural pleasure. It no longer has its desires running wild, released from the bonds of reason, to serve its own pleasures. Consequently, when the reason within us necessarily holds dominion, the flesh—enslaved to reason for the sake of virtue—is put to the test.

<margin>5.</margin> When the intellect <note>original: "nous"</note> regards its own natural power as being the same as the senses, it becomes entangled in the outward appearances of sensory things and devises fleshly pleasures. It becomes unable to pass beyond the nature of visible things because it is held captive by its passionate relationship with the senses.

<margin>6.</margin> If it is not possible for the intellect to pass over to the intelligible things <note>intellectual or spiritual realities</note> that are akin to it without the contemplation of the sensory things placed in between, and if this contemplation is utterly impossible without the senses (which are connected to the intellect but naturally akin to sensory things), then a choice follows. If the intellect, upon approaching visible things, gets stuck in their outward appearances—thinking that the senses it is joined with are its only natural activity—it falls away from natural, intelligible realities. It then takes hold of bodies "with both hands," as the saying goes, which are contrary to nature. By acting through these bodies against reason, because the senses have triumphed over them, the intellect becomes the father of sorrow in the soul, tormented by frequent lashes of conscience. Yet, it clearly becomes the maker of sensory pleasure, growing fat on the inventions of ways to provide for the flesh. But if, at the very moment it approaches visible things, the intellect cuts through the outward appearance toward the senses and beholds the spiritual, pure, and formless principles <note>original: "logous," the underlying divine reasons or blueprints of creation</note> of the intelligible things, it achieves the pleasure of the soul, for it is not held captive by any of the sensory things it contemplates. Meanwhile, it establishes sorrow in the senses, as they are deprived of all natural sensory things.

<margin>7.</margin> Since sensory pleasure produces sorrow in the soul—that is to say, pain (for these two are the same)—it is natural that pleasure in the soul produces sorrow in the senses, or pain. Rightly then, the one who yearns for the life of God

<column-break/>

and our Savior Jesus Christ—which comes through the Resurrection of the dead into an inheritance that is "incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven" <note>A reference to 1 Peter 1:4</note>—possesses exultation and unspeakable joy in the soul, continually gladdened by the hope of future goods. But in the flesh and the senses, such a person possesses sorrow: the pains that come upon it from various trials and the sufferings associated with them. For every virtue is accompanied by pleasure and pain: pain of the flesh, which is deprived of its agreeable and smooth sensations, and pleasure of the soul, which feasts purely upon the spiritual principles <note>original: "logois"</note> of every sensory thing.

<margin>8.</margin> In this present life—for this is what "the now" means to me—the intellect must grieve according to the flesh because of the many pains of the trials brought upon it for the sake of virtue. Yet it must always rejoice according to the soul and take pleasure in the hope of eternal goods, even if the senses are being worn down. "For the sufferings of this present time," says the divine Apostle, "are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed in us" <note>Romans 8:18</note>.

<margin>9.</margin> The flesh belongs to the soul, but the soul does not belong to the flesh. For the lesser, he says, belongs to the greater, not the greater to the lesser. Therefore, since the law of sin <note>original: "nomos tēs hamartias"</note>—which is sensory pleasure—was mixed into the flesh because of the Fall, death was devised to be the condemnation of that sin through the pains of the flesh, in order to abolish the law of the flesh. One who recognizes that death entered in because of sin for the purpose of its own destruction always keeps the soul joyful; through various pains, such a person beholds the law of sin being removed from their own flesh, preparing them to receive the blessed life in the spirit. There is no other way to obtain this life unless the law of sin is first emptied out from the "vessel" of the flesh in this present life, specifically in the soul's disposition toward the flesh.

<margin>10.</margin> He who grieves according to the flesh for the sake of virtue because of pains, rejoices in that very virtue according to the soul, beholding the beauty of future things as if they were present. For the sake of this beauty, as Great David <note>King David of the Psalms</note> says, he dies every day by the putting away of the fleshly will, and is continually renewed according to the birth of the soul in the spirit.

<summary>Maximus explores the dialectic between the soul and the senses, arguing that the pursuit of spiritual "logoi" (divine principles) naturally causes pain to the sensory flesh while bringing divine joy to the soul. He frames the trials of the virtuous life as a necessary purging of the "law of sin" to prepare the believer for eternal life.</summary>

For by "sorrow," we do not mean that irrational kind which tortures the soul over the loss of passions or material things—an experience where one's impulses are directed contrary to nature toward what is forbidden, or where one flees from what should be embraced. Instead, we mean that rational sorrow approved by those wise in divine matters, which signifies a present evil. For they say that sorrow is a "present evil" <note>In Stoic and Patristic thought, sorrow/grief was defined as the soul's reaction to a perceived present evil.</note> that takes root in the soul when sensory pleasure overcomes rational discernment. Yet, it is experienced through the senses when the soul's progress toward virtue is achieved without hindrance; this brings labor and pain to the senses only in proportion to the pleasure and joy it creates in the soul, as the soul is led toward God through the kinship of illumination found in virtue and knowledge.

<margin>11. Scholion <note>A "scholion" is an explanatory note or commentary on the main text.</note></margin> By "salutary pleasure," he means the joy the soul feels in virtue. By "beneficial sorrow," he means the suffering the flesh undergoes for the sake of virtue. Therefore, the person who is stuck in passions and material things directs his impulses toward what is forbidden. And the person who does not welcome the circumstances that cause the loss of passions and material things flees from what he should not flee.

<margin>12.</margin> Neither does divine grace work the illumination of knowledge without a faculty capable of receiving that illumination according to its natural power; nor, indeed, does the receptive faculty work the illumination of knowledge apart from the grace that bestows it.

<margin>13.</margin> Neither does the grace of the All-Holy Spirit work wisdom in the saints without an intellect <term>nous; the "eye of the soul" or the faculty of direct spiritual perception</term> capable of receiving it; nor does it work knowledge without a power of reason capable of receiving the word; nor faith without a rational and mental assurance regarding the things of the future which are yet hidden to all; nor the gifts of healing without a natural love for humanity; nor any other of the remaining spiritual gifts without a receptive habit and power in each individual. Furthermore, a human being cannot acquire any of the things listed through natural power alone without the divine power that bestows them. All the saints clearly demonstrate this because, after receiving divine revelations, they seek the <term>logoi; the inner principles or divine "reasons" behind created things</term> of what has been revealed.

<margin>14.</margin> The one who asks without passion receives the grace of being able to act in accordance with virtue. And the one who seeks dispassionately finds, through natural contemplation <term>theoria; the spiritual perception of God's presence in creation</term>, the truth in

existing things. And the one who knocks dispassionately at the door of knowledge will enter without hindrance into the hidden grace of mystical theology.

<margin>15.</margin> The one who seeks divine things dispassionately will certainly receive what is sought. But the one who seeks with some passion will fail to obtain it. For it says: "You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly." <note>A reference to James 4:3.</note>

<margin>16.</margin> The Holy Spirit seeks and searches for the knowledge of all things within us. But it does not seek what is sought for its own sake—for it is God and is beyond all knowledge. Just as the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> becomes flesh not for its own sake, but for us, accomplishing the mystery through the flesh. For just as the Word could not perform the things of the flesh in a manner befitting God without a rationally-enlightened flesh, so the Holy Spirit does not work the knowledge of mysteries in the saints without the natural power that seeks and searches for knowledge.

<margin>17.</margin> Just as it is impossible for the eye to perceive sensory things without the light of the sun, so the human intellect could never receive spiritual contemplation <note>original: "theoria"</note> without spiritual light. For sensory light naturally illuminates the senses for the perception of bodily things, but spiritual light illumines the intellect for the understanding of things that are beyond the senses.

<margin>18.</margin> Human nature possesses the powers for seeking and searching out divine things as something essential, implanted by the Creator at its very entry into being. However, the revelations of divine things are performed by the power of the All-Holy Spirit coming upon us according to grace. But because in the beginning, through sin, the Evil One pinned these powers to the nature of visible things, there was no one who understood or sought out God. While everyone shared in human nature, they held their intellectual and rational power confined to the outward appearance of sensory things, possessing no concept of what is beyond the senses. Quite rightly, then, the grace of the All-Holy Spirit—acting upon those who did not willfully remain under the power of deception—unpinned their power from material things and restored it to its original state. # 294 OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...they sought and searched, and thus they "sought out and searched out" <note>original: "ἐζήτησαν καὶ ἠρεύνησαν... ἐξεζήτησαν καὶ ἐξηρεύνησαν" — Maximus is likely referencing 1 Peter 1:10, emphasizing the intensity of the spiritual search.</note>; namely, through the same grace of the Spirit.

<margin>19.</margin> Salvation of souls is, properly speaking, the goal of faith. The goal of faith is the true revelation of that which has been believed. The true revelation of that which has been believed is the unutterable <term>interpenetration</term> <note>original: "περιχώρησις" (perichoresis). This term usually describes the mutual indwelling of the Persons of the Trinity, but here Maximus applies it to the union between the believer and God.</note> of the one believed, according to the proportion of faith in each person. The interpenetration of the one believed constitutes the return of those who have believed to their Beginning at the very End. The return of those who have believed to their own Beginning at the End is the fulfillment of desire for those who are moving toward God. The fulfillment of desire is the ever-moving rest of those who desire around the Object of their desire. Ever-moving rest around the Object of desire is the constant and uninterrupted enjoyment of that Object. The constant and uninterrupted enjoyment of the Object of desire is the participation in the divine things that are above nature. Participation in the divine things above nature is the <term>likeness</term> of the participants to that which they participate in. The likeness of the participants to that which they participate in is the actual identity of the participants with the participated through similarity. The possible identity of the participants through similarity is the <term>deification</term> <note>original: "θέωσις" (theosis). The process of becoming like God or being "divinized" through His grace.</note> of those deemed worthy of deification. Deification is, to provide a summary definition, the encompassing and the limit of all times and ages, and of all things within time and age. The encompassing and the limit of times and ages, and of all things within them, is the unity of the pure and proper Beginning with the proper and pure End in those who are being saved. The uninterrupted unity of the pure Beginning and End in those who are being saved is the departure from those things that are naturally measured by a beginning and an end—a departure toward that which is superior to them. The departure from those things defined by nature, by a beginning, and by an end, is the immediate, infinite, and endlessly understood (in those deemed worthy of this superior departure from nature) all-powerful and beyond-mighty energy of God. The immediate, infinite, and endlessly all-powerful and beyond-mighty energy of God is the unutterable and

<column-break/>

beyond-unutterable pleasure and joy of those who are acted upon <note>The Greek "ενεργουμένων" implies that the soul is now the recipient of God's direct action or energy.</note> according to this unburnt and beyond-comprehension union; of which it is impossible to find a principle, a concept, or a description within the nature of created things.

<margin>20.</margin> Nature does not possess the principles of things that are above nature, just as it does not possess the laws of things that are contrary to nature. By "above nature," I mean the divine and inconceivable pleasure which God naturally produces when He is united by grace to those who are worthy. By "contrary to nature," I mean the unutterable pain resulting from the deprivation of this pleasure, which God naturally produces when He is united—contrary to grace—to those who are unworthy. For according to the underlying quality of each person's disposition, God, in a way known only to Himself, provides a sense of Himself to all, just as each person has shaped himself to receive Him who will be united to all things at the end of the ages.

<margin>21.</margin> The Holy Spirit guides those who seek the spiritual principles and methods of this salvation toward understanding, not allowing the power by which they naturally seek divine things to remain motionless or inactive.

<margin>22.</margin> First, one seeks by <term>deliberate choice</term> <note>original: "προαιρέσει" (proairesis) — the faculty of moral choice or the will.</note> to put sin to death, and to put the will to death with respect to sin. And thus one "searches" for how and in what way these must be put to death in relation to each other. And again, after the perfect death of these in relation to each other, one seeks the life of the choice according to virtue, and the life of virtue according to the choice. And thus one searches for how and in what way to create this life in them. We may therefore define "seeking" as the longing for something desired, and "searching" as the effective method of reaching that longing for the desired thing.

<margin>23.</margin> Truly, the one who is to be saved must not only put sin to death by his choice, but also the choice itself with respect to sin. He must not only raise the choice to virtue, but also virtue to the choice; so that the choice, having been separated from all sin (as the dead from the dead), may no longer perceive it, and being alive (as the living to the living), may perceive the whole of virtue through an uninterrupted union. For he who has put his choice to death with respect to sin has become united to the likeness of the death of Christ; and he who has raised it up to righteousness has become united also to His resurrection.

<summary>This page presents a logical chain of definitions (a sorites) explaining how faith leads to "theosis" or deification, described as an "ever-moving rest" and a union with God's energy. Maximus also explains that God's presence will be experienced as either infinite pleasure or unutterable pain depending on the individual's moral disposition.</summary>

### THE SIXTH CENTURY

<margin>24.</margin> When sin and the **will** <note>original: "προαίρεσις" (proairesis) — often translated as "deliberate choice" or "moral disposition."</note> are dead to each other, they possess a double insensitivity toward one another. Likewise, when righteousness and the will share life with each other, they possess a double perception.

<margin>25.</margin> Christ, being God by nature and becoming man, is inherited by us as God through grace—according to an ineffable <term>participation</term> <note>original: "μέθεξιν" (methexis) — the central Platonic and Christian idea that creatures "share" in the life of God without becoming God by essence.</note> that is beyond nature. Yet, for our sake, in a form like ours, He identifies with us as a man and inherits Himself along with us, according to His inconceivable <term>condescension</term> <note>original: "συγκατάβασιν" (synkatabasis) — God's "stooping down" to meet human limitations.</note>. The saints, having mystically foreseen this in the Spirit, were taught how the sufferings that lead the way in this present life for the sake of virtue must precede the glory in Christ that will be revealed in the future because of that virtue.

<margin>26.</margin> The **mind** (*nous*), moving toward the Cause of all beings <note>i.e., God</note> solely by desire and in a way beyond known limits, seeks only Him. But **reason** (*logos*), approaching the truths found within created beings in various ways, searches out the inner principles <note>original: "λόγους" (logoi) — the divine blueprints or intentions behind every created thing.</note> of those beings.

<margin>27.</margin> **Seeking** is the first and simple movement of the mind toward its own Cause, accompanied by desire. **Searching** is the first and simple discernment of reason concerning its own Cause, involving a certain mental conception. Furthermore, **diligent seeking** is the mind's movement toward its own Cause according to specialized knowledge, accompanied by a burning desire. **Diligent searching** is the discernment of reason regarding its own Cause through the actual practice of the virtues, occurring alongside a prudent and wise mental conception.

<margin>28.</margin> The holy and divine **Prophets**, having "diligently sought and searched" <note>quoting 1 Peter 1:10</note> concerning the salvation of souls, possessed a fiery and burning movement of the mind toward God with knowledge and desire, as well as a prudent and wise discernment of reason through the practice of divine things. Those who imitate them also seek out the salvation of their souls with knowledge, and searching with prudence and wisdom, they pursue discernment in divine works.

<margin>29.</margin> Reason recognizes that the **knowledge of divine things** is twofold. One kind is **relative**, existing in words and concepts alone; it does not possess the actual perception of what is known through experience. It is through this kind of knowledge that we manage our affairs in this present life. The other kind is **proper and true**, based solely on experience; it occurs through actual practice without the need for words or concepts, providing a full perception of the

<column-break/>

one known through a participation in grace. Through this latter knowledge, we receive that deification (*theosis*) which is above nature and which operates unceasingly in the future state. They say that relative knowledge, because it consists of words and concepts, serves to stir up the desire for knowledge through actual participation. However, actual knowledge—which provides participation in the one known through experience—removes the need for knowledge that consists merely of words and concepts.

<margin>30.</margin> He says that knowledge is twofold: one resides in words and divine concepts, not yet possessing the "form-giving" perception of the things understood; the other resides in action alone, possessing the "form-giving" enjoyment of truths without words or concepts. For since the Word <note>or "Reason"</note> naturally signifies what is to be known through knowledge, it moves the desire of those who are moved by it toward the enjoyment of the thing signified.

<margin>31.</margin> The wise say it is impossible for the **rational account** of God to coexist with the **experience** of God, or for the **conceptualization** of God to coexist with the **perception** of Him. By "rational account" of God, I mean the analogy drawn from created beings for the sake of theoretical knowledge. By "perception," I mean the experience of goods that are above nature through participation. By "conceptualization," I mean the simple and unified knowledge of Him derived from created beings. Perhaps this is recognized in all other matters as well: the experience of a thing puts an end to the rational description of it, and the perception of a thing makes the idle conceptualization of it cease. By "experience," I mean the actual knowledge itself that comes after all rational description. By "perception," I mean the very participation in the one known, which appears after every concept. Perhaps it was this that the **Great Apostle** <note>St. Paul</note> was teaching mystically when he said: "Whether there are prophecies, they will fail; whether there are tongues, they will cease; whether there is knowledge, it will vanish away" <note>1 Corinthians 13:8</note>, clearly speaking about the knowledge that resides in words and concepts.

<margin>32.</margin> It was truly fitting that the Creator of the essence of beings by nature should also become the Author of the **deification** of those created beings by grace—so that the Giver of "being" might also appear as the Bestower of "eternally well-being." Since none of the beings knows at all what it is in its own essence, it follows naturally that none of the things to come...

# OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

No being possesses foreknowledge of existing things by its own nature, except for God, who is beyond all being. He alone knows Himself—what He is according to His **essence** <term>essence</term> <note>original: "ousia" — the fundamental nature of what something is in itself, which for God remains unknowable to creatures.</note>—and He foreknew the existence of all things created by Him even before they came to be. In His grace, He intends to generously grant to created beings a knowledge of what they and others are according to their essence, and to reveal the inner **principles** <term>principles</term> <note>original: "logoi" — the divine blueprints or intentions behind every created thing.</note> of their coming-into-being, which pre-existed in Him in a unified way.

<margin>33.</margin>
The Word of God, who created human nature, did not create sensory pleasure or pain along with it. Rather, He implanted in the mind a certain capacity for pleasure, through which it would be able to enjoy Him in an ineffable way. However, at the very moment of his creation, the first man gave this capacity—by which I mean the natural desire of the mind for God—over to the senses. Through these senses, he experienced a pleasure that was **contrary to nature** <note>original: "para physin" — a key concept in Maximus: sin is not a "thing" but a movement of natural powers toward the wrong goal.</note>. Consequently, God, in His care for our salvation, implanted pain as a kind of punishing power. Thus, the law of death was wisely rooted in the nature of the body, setting a limit to the madness of the mind as its desire moved unnaturally toward sensory things.

<margin>34.</margin>
Pleasure and pain were not co-created with the nature of the flesh. Instead, the transgression devised pleasure to corrupt the **will** <note>original: "proairesis" — the faculty of choice or moral disposition.</note>, while it condemned the nature to dissolution through pain. This happened so that pleasure might produce the voluntary death of the soul—which is sin—and pain might produce the dissolution of the flesh through its breakdown into its constituent parts. For in His providence, God gave nature involuntary pain and the death that follows it as a punishment for voluntary pleasure.

<margin>35.</margin>
Because of the irrational pleasure that came upon our nature, a rational pain entered in its place through many sufferings. It is in and through these sufferings that death occurs, bringing about the removal of unnatural pleasure. However, this does not mean the total destruction of the grace of divine pleasure, which is naturally meant to be revealed to the mind.

<margin>36.</margin>
The practice of voluntary labors and the endurance of involuntary trials take away pleasure and stop its active movement; yet they do not destroy the capacity for it that lies within our nature like a law of 

<column-break/>

becoming. For the philosophy of virtue is naturally meant to produce **dispassion** <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but a state where the passions no longer control the person’s choices.</note> of the **disposition** <note>original: "gnome" — the personal, deliberative will.</note>, rather than of the nature itself. It is precisely through this dispassion of the disposition that the grace of divine pleasure is experienced by the mind.

<margin>37.</margin>
Every pain has a preceding active pleasure as the cause of its own birth. Therefore, pain is a "debt" that is naturally paid by all who participate in human nature. For physical pain always follows unnatural pleasure in all those whose birth was preceded by the law of pleasure without cause. By "without cause," I mean the pleasure arising from the transgression, which clearly did not follow as a successor to any prior pain.

<margin>38.</margin>
It was utterly impossible for our nature, which had been subjected to both voluntary pleasure and involuntary pain, to be recalled to its original life unless the Creator became man. He accepted the pain—which had been devised as a punishment for nature's voluntary pleasure—by His own choice, even though His own birth was not preceded by the pleasure that comes from sexual union. He did this to free nature from the birth that leads to condemnation, by accepting a birth that did not have pleasure as its beginning.

<margin>39.</margin>
Since the transgression, all humans have had pleasure preceding their own natural birth. Not one person was entirely free from this natural birth rooted in passionate pleasure. Instead, everyone paid the "debt" of suffering and the death that follows it as a natural obligation. The way to freedom was completely blocked for those held captive by unjust pleasure and naturally subject to just sufferings and the most just death. It was necessary, therefore, to destroy this most unjust pleasure and the just sufferings caused by it—sufferings by which man was miserably torn apart, having the beginning of his life in the corruption of pleasure and the end of his life in the corruption of death. To restore our suffering nature, it was necessary to devise a pain and a death that were simultaneously "unjust" and "causeless." "Causeless" in the sense that they were not preceded by pleasure as the cause of birth; and "unjust" in the sense that they were not the consequence of a passionate life. Thus, by being placed between unjust pleasure and pain...

<summary>Maximus explains how the Fall trapped humanity in a cycle where pleasure in the senses leads to a "debt" of pain and death. He argues that Christ broke this cycle through a "causeless" birth (without sexual pleasure) and an "unjust" death (without sin), thereby liberating human nature.</summary>

# SIXTH CENTURY

...and of a most just death, [so that] pain and a most unjust death might entirely abolish that most unjust beginning that comes from pleasure, as well as the most just end of nature through death which follows it. Thus, the human race might again become free of pleasure and pain, with nature recovering its original state of blessing—a state unpolluted by any of the traits found in things subject to birth and decay. For this reason, the **Word** <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Logos" — the second person of the Trinity through whom all things were created.</note> of God, being perfect God by nature, becomes a perfect man, composed of a **rational soul** <term>rational soul</term> <note>original: "psyche noera" — the intellectual part of the human person that distinguishes us from animals.</note> and a **passible body** <term>passible body</term> <note>original: "soma patheton" — a body capable of suffering, hunger, and fatigue.</note> similar to ours, except for sin alone. He did not possess at all that pleasure arising from disobedience, which normally precedes birth from a woman in time. However, through His love for mankind, He willingly accepted the pain resulting from that pleasure—the pain which serves as nature's end—so that by suffering unjustly, He might abolish the tyranny of pleasure-based birth that rules over nature. Since the Lord’s death was not a debt He owed for Himself like other men, it was instead a weapon wielded against that tyranny. He wiped out the "just" end of nature (death) because He did not possess the lawless pleasure for which death was the punishment.

<margin>40.</margin>
It was truly necessary for the Lord, being wise, just, and powerful by nature, to act as follows: as wise, not to be ignorant of the method of healing; as just, not to save man (who had been captured by sin through his own will) through mere tyranny; and as all-powerful, not to fail in completing the healing.

<margin>41.</margin>
The wisdom of God is shown in His truly becoming our nature; His justice in His taking on the passibility of our nature in His birth just like us; and His power in His creating an eternal life and unchanging **freedom from passion** <term>freedom from passion</term> <note>original: "apatheia" — not a lack of feeling, but a state where the soul is no longer driven by disordered impulses.</note> for nature through His sufferings and death.

<margin>42.</margin>

He showed the equality of His justice in the greatness of His **condescension** <term>condescension</term> <note>original: "synkatabasis" — God's voluntary stooping down to the human level.</note>, by willingly submitting to the condemnation of our passible nature and making that

It was in this passibility that the power of sin and death resided, along with the tyranny of sin through pleasure and the lordship of death through pain. For the power of pleasure and pain is clearly present in the passible part of our nature. Indeed, we often try to comfort ourselves against pain through pleasure, which only *increases* the penalty of nature.

## OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...[death] having clearly become most unjust, since He [Christ] did not have as the beginning of His own birth that most unjust pleasure of the **Forefather** <term>Forefather</term> <note>original: "Propator" — referring to Adam, the first man.</note> arising from disobedience. By abolishing both—I mean the beginning and the end of human birth according to Adam—He brought about their destruction, since they were not originally from God. Thus, He set free from this same guilt all those who are spiritually reborn from Him.

<margin>45.</margin>
The Lord removed the pleasure that comes from the **law of sin** <term>law of sin</term> <note>original: "nomos tes hamartias" — St. Paul's term for the compulsive drive toward sin in human nature.</note> to set aside the birth according to the flesh for those being born in Him by grace through the **Spirit** <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "Pneuma" — the Holy Spirit.</note>. He allows them to receive death—which was previously the condemnation of nature—as the condemnation of sin. They no longer possess the pleasure of birth from Adam, but only the pain through Adam working in them. This is not a debt for sin, but by a **divine plan** <term>divine plan</term> <note>original: "oikonomia" — the "stewardship" or arrangement of God's salvation in history.</note> because of our natural condition, serving as a death against sin. Just as when death does not have pleasure as its mother (from which it naturally becomes a punisher), it clearly becomes the Father of eternal life. For as the life of Adam according to pleasure became the mother of death and corruption, so also the death of the Lord through Adam—being free from Adam’s pleasure—becomes the progenitor of eternal life.

<margin>46.</margin>
After the transgression, human nature had as the beginning of its own birth a conception through pleasure from seed, and a birth through **corruption** <term>corruption</term> <note>original: "rheusin" — literally "flow" or "flux," referring to the unstable, decaying nature of mortal life.</note>; and as its end, death through corruption according to pain. But the Lord, not having this beginning of birth according to the flesh, was not subject to its end—that is, death. <note>Maximus means that while Christ died, He was not "held" or conquered by death because He did not inherit the "guilt" of the pleasure-based birth.</note>

<margin>47.</margin>
In the beginning, sin enticed Adam and persuaded him to transgress the divine commandment. By establishing pleasure through that transgression, and nailing itself through pleasure into the very depth of our nature, sin condemned the whole of nature to death, pushing our nature toward the undoing of existence through death. For this was engineered by the sower of sin and father of evil, the wicked devil. Because of his pride, he made himself an exile from divine glory, and through envy toward us and God, he expelled Adam from **Paradise**

<column-break/>

to destroy the works of God and to dissolve the things composed for birth.

<margin>48.</margin>
Envying both God and us, the devil deceitfully persuaded man that he was envied by God, and so prepared him to transgress the commandment. He envied God so that His all-praised power that **deifies** <term>deifies</term> <note>original: "theourgousa" — "divinely working" or "making divine."</note> man might not be manifest in action; and he envied man so that he might not become a participant in divine glory through virtue. For that most foul one envies not only our glory from God through virtue, but also God’s all-praised power over us through salvation.

<margin>49.</margin>
Just as in Adam death was the condemnation of nature (since nature had pleasure as the beginning of its own birth), so death in Christ became the condemnation of sin, because in Christ nature recovered a birth pure of pleasure.

<margin>50.</margin>
If we, who have been deemed worthy to become the house of God by grace through the Spirit, ought to show such endurance of suffering for the sake of righteousness to condemn sin—and as good people, readily undergo shameful death as if we were evildoers—what will be the end of those who disobey the **Gospel** <term>Gospel</term> <note>original: "Euangelion" — the "Good News" of Christ.</note> of God? That is, what will be the end or the condemnation of those who have not only pursued until the end the pleasure-based birth of Adam (which prevails over nature), but have also not accepted God the Father calling them through the incarnate Son? Nor have they accepted the Son Himself, the mediator who intercedes with the Father, who by the Father's will and His own choice offered Himself to death for us. He did this for our reconciliation with the Father, so that through Himself He might glorify us as much as He accepted to be dishonored by our sufferings for our sake, brightening us with the beauty of His own divinity.

<margin>51.</margin>
Since for all the saved, God will be an uncircumscribed, immediate, and infinite place, becoming all things to all people according to the proportion of their righteousness—or rather, according to the measure of the sufferings endured here for the sake of righteousness with knowledge—He gives Himself to each member, according to the...

<summary>Maximus explains that Christ broke the cycle of human corruption by being born without the "pleasure" of the Fall, thereby turning death into a means of destroying sin rather than punishing nature. He contrasts the devil’s envy with God's desire to deify humanity through virtuous suffering and the grace of the Spirit.</summary>

### HUNDRED AND SIXTH CHAPTER

...manifesting the power dwelling in each member as it acts within itself, and through itself holding the members together toward **being** <term>being</term> <note>original: "einai" — simple existence as a gift from God.</note>, held together for life. Where then shall the ungodly and the sinner appear if they are deprived of this grace? For if one is unable to receive the presence of God acting according to **well-being** <term>well-being</term> <note>original: "eu einai" — not just existing, but existing in a state of virtue and grace.</note>, where shall he appear when he has suffered the fall from the divine life that is beyond age, time, and place?

<margin>52.</margin> He who does not have God sustaining his life toward **well-being**—God who is to become the "place" for all who are worthy—how shall he exist? How can he be, if he does not have God Himself as his "place" according to the rest and established dwelling of those who possess **well-being** in God? And if "the righteous is saved with much difficulty," what shall become of, or what shall be suffered by the one who has made no account of piety and virtue during this present life?

<margin>53.</margin> God, according to the single, infinitely powerful will of His goodness, will hold all things together—both Angels and humans, both the good and the evil. But these will not all participate in God equally (for He is partitioned among them without being affected Himself), but rather each according to their own proportion.

<margin>54.</margin> Those who, by their nature, have kept their **disposition** <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "gnome" — the personal will or "inclination" of an individual.</note> governed by a law equal to all, and have made their disposition capable of receiving the principles of nature according to the full account of **well-being**, will participate entirely in God’s goodness. This is because their disposition is in harmony with the divine will, and they will receive the divine life shining upon them as it does in Angels or in holy men. But those who, by their nature, have made their disposition unequal and lawless, and have proven their disposition to be scattered away from the principles of nature regarding the full account of **well-being**, will fall away from the whole of goodness. This is because of the hostility of their disposition toward the divine will. They will experience
<margin>* perhaps: opposition or alienation</margin>
an **affinity** <note>The marginal note suggests an alternative reading: "opposition" or "alienation." This changes the meaning from a "warped affinity" to a direct "hostility."</note> of their disposition toward **well-being**; in this state, such people will experience a separation from God. They do not possess the principle of **well-being** as a life-giving force in their actions, which is the state through which divine life is meant to shine.

<margin>55.</margin> The principle of nature shall be the "scale" of each person’s disposition during the Judgment, testing its movement toward "alas!" or toward "well done!" This movement determines whether the participation or non-participation in the divine life occurs. For according to **being** and **ever-being** <term>ever-being</term> <note>original: "aei einai" — eternal existence, which Maximus argues is given to everyone, even the lost.</note>, God is present to hold all things together; but according to **ever-well-being** <term>ever-well-being</term> <note>original: "aei eu einai" — eternal happiness in God.</note>, He is present only to the Saints, both Angels and humans. As for **ever-ill-being** <note>original: "aei pheu einai" — literally "ever-alas-being," a play on words with "ever-well-being."</note>, He leaves this as a judged fruit of the disposition for those who are not holy.

<column-break/>

God is present to all to sustain them in existence and eternal existence; but in regard to **eternal well-being**, He is present in a unique way only to the Saints, both Angels and men. He leaves **eternal ill-being** to those who are not such, as the judged fruit of their own will.

<margin>56.</margin> The mystery of the divine **Incarnation** <term>Incarnation</term> <note>original: "sarkosis" — the becoming-flesh of God.</note> does not mean that because the elements from which Christ was composed are different by nature, there is also a difference in His **Person** <term>Person</term> <note>original: "hypostasis" — the distinct "who" of Christ, which remains one.</note>. The first point ensures that no "addition" is made to the mystery of the Trinity <note>i.e., Christ is not a fourth person added to the three.</note>; the second point ensures that nothing in the Godhead is considered to be of the same nature or essence as the flesh. For the union of the two natures occurred into one **Person**, not into a single nature. Thus, the "oneness" of the Person is shown to be composed of the natures that came together in the union, while the "difference" of the things that came together into an unbreakable union is preserved in their natural properties, remaining entirely without change or confusion.

<margin>57.</margin> We do not speak of a "difference of persons" in Christ, because the Trinity remained the Trinity even when the **Word** <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Logos" — the second person of the Trinity.</note> became flesh; no "addition of a person" occurred in the Holy Trinity because of the Incarnation. But we do speak of a "difference of natures," so that we do not mistakenly claim that the flesh is of the same essence as the Word.

<margin>58.</margin> He who does not speak of a "difference of nature" has no way to prove the confession that "the Word became flesh" without change; for he does not recognize that both the One who assumed and that which was assumed are preserved according to their nature in the one Person of the one Christ and God the Savior after the union.

<margin>59.</margin> If there is a difference according to nature between the flesh and the Godhead in Christ after the union—for the Godhead and the flesh are never the same in essence—then the union of the things that came together was not to produce one nature, but rather one Person. In this Person, we find no difference in Christ of any kind. For the Word is the same as His own flesh according to Person. In whatever way Christ might have a "difference," He cannot be one in every respect; but in whatever way He admits no difference at all, in that respect "The One" is always piously affirmed and named of Him.

<margin>60.</margin> **Faith** through **hope** makes **love** for God perfect. A good conscience establishes love for one’s neighbor through the keeping of the commandments. For...

### OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...a good conscience has no accuser for a transgressed commandment; the heart alone is naturally suited to be trusted with these things by those who long for true salvation.

<margin>61.</margin>
Nothing is swifter than believing, and nothing is easier than confessing the grace of what has been believed through the mouth. For the former manifests the ensouled **love** <term>love</term> <note>original: "agapē" — the highest form of Christian love.</note> of the believer toward the Creator; the latter manifests a god-loving **disposition** <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "diathesis" — an inner state or orientation of the soul.</note> toward one's neighbor. Love and a genuine disposition—that is, faith and a good conscience—are clearly the work of the heart’s internal movement, requiring absolutely no external matter for their birth.

<margin>62.</margin>
He who suffers from a total lack of movement toward what is good is certainly mobile toward what is evil. For it is impossible to be immobile in both directions. Hence, Scripture knows to call the soul’s laziness regarding good things "stones," as it is insensible to virtues; and "wood," the eagerness regarding evil things. But the movement according to the senses, when joined to the **activity of the mind** <term>activity of the mind</term> <note>original: "kata noun energeia" — the focused operation of the intellect.</note>, produces virtue accompanied by knowledge.

<margin>63.</margin>
The "middle wall," I believe, refers to the natural law of the body; the "partition" refers to the attachment to the **passions** <term>passions</term> <note>original: "pathē" — disordered or irrational impulses of the soul, often translated as "sufferings" or "afflictions."</note> within the law of the flesh—that is, sin. For only the attachment to the passions of dishonor becomes a partition of the natural law—that is, of the **passible part of nature** <term>passible part of nature</term> <note>original: "pathetikon meros" — the part of human nature capable of feeling or suffering.</note>—walling off the body from the soul and not allowing the **reason** <term>reason</term> <note>original: "logos" — here meaning the divine principle or rationale that guides virtuous action.</note> of the virtues to pass through the soul into the flesh in practice. But when the Word arrived and wrestled down the law of nature—that is, the passible part of nature—He abolished the attachment to the unnatural passions within it.

<margin>64.</margin>
Whenever the Evil One, by a deceptive trick, plunders the innate knowledge of God from nature and claims it for himself, he is a "thief," attempting to transfer worship to himself away from God. This he does, obviously, by leading the mind's contemplation away from the **spiritual principles** <term>spiritual principles</term> <note>original: "pneumatikoi logoi" — the inner meanings and divine purposes embedded in created things.</note> within created things, and confining the intellectual power solely to the outward appearance of sensible objects. And whenever he sophistically drags down the practical power from natural movements to those that are against nature, and through seemingly "good" things persuasively pins the soul's **desire** <term>desire</term> <note>original: "ephesis" — the soul's natural reaching out toward an object.</note> to the

<column-break/>

worse things, he "swears falsely by the name of the Lord," leading the persuaded soul toward things other than what was promised. He is a "thief" in that he plunders the knowledge of nature for himself, and a "perjurer" in that he persuades the soul’s practical power to labor in vain for things contrary to nature.

<margin>65.</margin>
Or again, a "thief" is one who, to deceive his listeners, professes to practice divine words whose power he has not recognized through his actions; he makes the bare utterance a business for gaining glory and hunts for the praise of being considered righteous by his audience through the words of his tongue. Simply put, he whose life is discordant with his speech, and whose soul's disposition is opposed to his knowledge, is a "thief," appearing improperly in the light of borrowed goods. To him, the Word rightly says: "But to the sinner God said, 'Why do you declare my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth?'" <note>This is a quote from Psalm 50:16 (LXX numbering: Psalm 49:16).</note>

<margin>66.</margin>
Likewise, a "thief" is also one who, by visible manners and habits, covers up the invisible malice of the soul, masking the internal disposition with a pretense of decency. Just as the former person steals the intellect of his listeners with the utterance of words of knowledge, so this person steals the perception of those watching him with the mask of his habits. To him, it shall similarly be said: "Be ashamed, you who are clothed in strange garments," <note>Reference to Zephaniah 1:8.</note> and "the Lord will reveal their form in that day." For every day, in the secret workshop of the heart, as I say these things, I seem to hear God declaring "the day," as I am explicitly condemned in both respects.

<margin>67.</margin>
A "perjurer"—that is, one who swears falsely in the name of the Lord—is one who promises a life of virtue to God but practices things foreign to the promise of his own profession, and who breaks the covenant of the confession of a holy life through the idleness of the commandments. To put it briefly, he who has chosen to live according to God, but is not completely dead to this present life, is a liar and a perjurer; for he swore to God—that is, he promised—an blameless course in the divine struggles...

He uses the metaphors of the "thief" and the "perjurer" to describe those who possess spiritual knowledge or outward decency without corresponding internal transformation or action.</summary>
