### SIXTH CENTURY

...and not fulfilling it, and for this reason being in no way praised. For "everyone who swears by Him shall be praised" <note>A reference to Psalm 63:11 (Septuagint 62:12).</note>, that is, everyone who promises a certain way of life to God, and through the truth of works of **righteousness** <term>righteousness</term> <note>original: "dikaiosynē" — often implying both justice and moral rectitude.</note> fulfills the oaths of that good promise.

<margin>68.</margin> He who pretends to have knowledge through the mere utterance of words steals the mind of his listeners for his own glory. And he who pretends to have virtue in his habits for his own glory steals the vision of those who behold him. Through such deceit, both are thieves and lead others astray: the one misleads the **intellect** <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "dianoia" — the discursive or reasoning mind.</note> of the soul of his listeners, while the other misleads the bodily senses of those who watch him.

<margin>69.</margin> If the one who fulfills his own promises receives praise, as one who swears by God and speaks the truth, then it is clear that he who becomes a transgressor of his own agreements will have blame and dishonor, as one who swore by God and lied.

<margin>70.</margin> Not every human being coming into this world is necessarily enlightened by the Word <note>The "Logos" or Christ.</note>; for many remain unenlightened and have no part in the light of true knowledge. However, it is clear that every human being, according to their own choice, who enters the true "world" of the virtues [is enlightened]. For everyone who truly enters into this world through a voluntary birth is indeed enlightened by the Word, receiving an unshakeable **disposition** <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "hexis" — a stable habit or state of being.</note> toward virtue and an unfailing science of true knowledge.

<margin>71.</margin> Not all things that have the same sounding name are to be understood in one and the same way. Rather, each thing said must be understood according to the underlying power of the manner of Holy Scripture, if we intend to correctly hit the mark of the purpose of what has been written.

<margin>72.</margin> None of the persons, places, times, or other things—whether animate or inanimate, sensible or intelligible—recorded in Scripture always have the same meaning throughout their **history** <term>history</term> <note>original: "historia" — the literal or factual level of the text.</note> or **contemplation** <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "theoria" — the deeper, spiritual, or allegorical insight.</note>. Therefore, he who practices the divine knowledge of Scripture without stumbling must interpret each of the things listed differently, according to the differences of the events or sayings, and must wait for the contemplation that properly fits the manner or the time.

<column-break/>

<margin>73.</margin> It is necessary to teach all those in the whole world to live and conduct themselves by the Word alone, and to have only so much care for their bodies as to sever the soul's attachment to them through great effort, giving no "imagination of matter" whatsoever to the soul. This is because the soul's original attachment to the senses—which pushed aside the Word and accepted the irrationality of pleasure like a creeping vision—has now been extinguished by the Word. It was against this [sensory attachment] that death was justly decreed, so that it might cease providing the devil with an entrance to the soul.

<margin>74.</margin> Although the senses are one in genus, they are fivefold in species. Through the perceptive activity of each species, they persuade the wandering soul to cherish the corresponding "sensible thing" instead of God. Therefore, he who wisely follows the Word, before the forced and involuntary death [of the body], voluntarily passes a sentence of death upon the flesh, effecting a total separation of the will from the senses.

<margin>75.</margin> When the senses take the mind captive, they teach a kind of "polytheism" through each sense-organ, serving the corresponding sensible thing as if it were divine through their slavery to the passions.

<margin>76.</margin> He who sits only by the "letter" of Scripture has only his senses ruling his nature, through which only the soul's attachment to the flesh is naturally manifested. The letter, if not understood spiritually, has only the senses to define its utterance, and does not allow the power of what is written to pass through to the mind. If the letter is related only to the senses, then everyone who receives the letter according to the history alone, in the **Jewish manner** <note>original: "Ioudaïkōs" — in Patristic Greek, this often refers to a literalist or "fleshly" interpretation of the Law, rather than a spiritual one.</note>, lives according to the flesh. Such a person dies the death of sin daily in their will because of the "living" senses, being unable to put to death the deeds of the body by the **spirit** <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "pneuma".</note> so that they might live the blessed life in the spirit. "For if you live according to the flesh, you will die," says the divine **Apostle** <note>St. Paul, in Romans 8:13.</note>; "but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live."

<margin>77.</margin> Therefore, let us not take the divine lamp—that is, the enlightening word of knowledge—which we light through contemplation and practice, and put it under a bushel, lest we be condemned for restricting the uncircumscribed [wisdom] to the letter of wisdom... <note>Text cuts off mid-sentence: "uncircumscribed" (aperigrapton).</note>

<summary>St. Maximus discusses the spiritual pitfalls of hypocrisy and literalism, arguing that true enlightenment comes from choosing a life of virtue and interpreting Scripture spiritually rather than through the "fleshly" senses. He emphasizes that the "letter" of the Law can lead to spiritual death if it is not transcended through the Spirit.</summary>
<keywords>hypocrisy, virtue, illumination, Word/Logos, hermeneutics, history vs. contemplation, senses, asceticism, literalism, Apostle Paul</keywords>

### OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...prehensible power; but upon the lampstand—I mean the **Holy Church**—at the height of true **contemplation** <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "theōria" — the spiritual perception of divine truths beyond the literal sense.</note>, providing the light of divine torches to all.

<margin>78.</margin> He who bears the assaults of involuntary temptations with an unshaken mind, like the **Blessed Job** and the noble martyrs, is a strong lamp, himself keeping the light of salvation unquenchable. This light is preserved in the manner of his courageous endurance, for he possesses the Lord as strong and unquenchable. Moreover, he who knows the schemes of the evil one, and is not ignorant of the entanglements of invisible warfare, is also illuminated by the light of knowledge and appears as another lamp, speaking appropriately with the **Great Apostle**: "For we are not ignorant of his designs." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 2:11.</note>

<margin>79.</margin> The **Holy Spirit** performs purification for those worthy of the purity of the virtues through fear, piety, and knowledge. He grants the illumination of the knowledge of beings—according to the inner principles by which they exist—through strength, counsel, and understanding to those worthy of light. Finally, He grants perfection through all-radiant, simple, and complete wisdom to those worthy of **theosis** <term>theosis</term> <note>original: "theōsis" — the process of being united with God or "deification."</note>. This wisdom leads them directly to the Cause of all beings, in every way possible for a human being, so that they are known only by the divine characteristics of goodness. In this state, they know themselves from God, and they know God from themselves, with no barrier standing between them. For there is nothing in the middle between wisdom and God. They shall possess an unchangeable stability, for all "middles" have been completely crossed—those things in which there was once a danger of falling into error regarding knowledge. By "middles," he means the essence of **intelligible** <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "noētos" — things perceived by the mind or spirit.</note> and **sensible** <term>sensible</term> <note>original: "aisthētos" — things perceived by the physical senses.</note> things, through which the human mind is naturally led to God as the Cause of all that exists.

<margin>80.</margin> Fear, piety, and knowledge produce **practical philosophy** <note>The stage of moral purification and the practice of virtues.</note>. Strength, counsel, and understanding achieve **natural contemplation** in the Spirit. Only divine wisdom grants **mystical theology**.

<margin>81.</margin> Just as it is impossible for a lamp to be kept burning without oil, so it is impossible for the light of the divine **gifts** <term>gifts</term> <note>original: "charismata" — spiritual graces or talents given by God.</note> to be kept unquenchable without a **habit** <term>habit</term> <note>original: "hexis" — a stable internal disposition or state of being.</note> that nourishes good things with appropriate words, ways, manners, thoughts, and reflections. 

<column-break/>

For every spiritual gift requires a corresponding habit, which unceasingly pours into it the "intellectual matter," just as oil is poured into a lamp, so that it remains sustained according to the disposition of the one who receives it.

<margin>82.</margin> Just as it is impossible to find genuine oil in nature without an olive tree, and impossible for the oil to be held without a vessel to receive it, and just as the light of a lamp is surely extinguished if not nourished by oil—so too, without the **Holy Scriptures**, there is no truly God-befitting power of thought. Without a "habit," acting as a vessel capable of receiving thoughts, a divine thought could never be established. And if the light of knowledge within the spiritual gifts is not nourished by divine thoughts, it is not preserved unquenchable for those who possess it.

<margin>83.</margin> I take the **Old Testament** to be signified by the olive tree on the left, as it provides more for "practical philosophy." The olive tree on the right is the **New Testament**, as the teacher of a new mystery and the producer of the "contemplative habit" in each of the faithful. For the one provides the ways of virtue, while the other provides the principles of knowledge to those who practice divine philosophy. The one, snatching the mind away from the mist of visible things, leads it up to what is kindred to it, once it has become pure of every material imagination. The other cleanses the mind from material attachment by the tension of courage—striking out, as if with a hammer, the nails that bind the will's disposition to the body.

<margin>84.</margin> The **Old Testament**, being reckoned as the "body" in relation to the "soul," raises the mind through the middle way of the virtues, preventing the mind from being dragged down toward the body. The **New Testament** raises the mind toward God, set on fire by the fire of love. The one makes the body move in harmony with the mind in its outward orientation; the other makes the mind identical to God through the "habit of grace," giving it such a likeness to God that God is known through the mind—He who by nature is otherwise entirely unknowable to anyone—just as an archetype is known from an image.

<margin>85.</margin> The **Old Testament**, being a symbol of the practice of virtue, prepares the body to agree with the mind in its movement. The **New Testament**, being the producer of contemplation and knowledge, illuminates the mind that mystically clings to it with divine thoughts, and...

<vocab>Maximus the Confessor, Holy Church, contemplation, Blessed Job, Holy Spirit, theology, Old Testament, New Testament, mind, knowledge</vocab>

<summary>Maximus explains the progression of the spiritual life from purification to deification, using the Holy Spirit's gifts and the allegory of the two Testaments as olive trees. He emphasizes that spiritual knowledge requires a stable internal disposition (habit) and the nourishment of Scripture to remain "lit" within the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Sixth Century" of the "Chapters on Knowledge" by St. Maximus the Confessor. It develops the relationship between the Old and New Testaments, the synergy of spiritual practice and divine contemplation, and the interpretation of biblical imagery regarding the soul's ascent and the struggle against evil.</meta>

### SIXTH CENTURY

...with spiritual gifts. And while the Old Testament provides the **modes of the virtues** to the one seeking knowledge <note>original: "gnōstikō" — the 'gnostic' or person of spiritual insight</note>, the New Testament grants the **principles of true knowledge** <note>original: "logous" — the underlying divine reasons or purposes</note> to the one engaged in practice.

<margin>86.</margin> God is said to be—and indeed becomes—**Father** by grace to those whose birth in the spirit is based solely on a volitional choice for virtue. In this birth, the "face" of the soul reflects the character of God who begat it through the virtues. By their transformed way of life, such people lead those who observe them to glorify God; they offer their own lives as an exceptional **exemplar** <note>original: "examplarion" — a model or pattern to be copied</note> of virtue for imitation. For God is not naturally glorified by mere words, but by works of righteousness that shout the divine majesty much louder than any speech.

<margin>87.</margin> The **natural law** is "on the left" because of its relationship to the senses; it introduces the modes of the virtues to reason and produces an active knowledge. The **spiritual law**, however, is "on the right" because of its relationship to the mind; it mixes the spiritual principles found in all things with the senses and produces a reasoned, intentional practice.

<margin>88.</margin> He who shows knowledge being "embodied" through practice, and practice being "ensouled" by knowledge, has found the exact method of true **theurgy** <term>theurgy</term> <note>original: "theourgias" — literally 'God-working'; here it refers to the cooperation between human effort and divine action.</note>. But he who keeps these two separated has either made his knowledge into a ghost-like fantasy without substance, or he has reduced his practice to a hollow **idol**. For knowledge without practice does not differ from a fantasy, since it lacks the practice that gives it a concrete existence; and practice without reason is like an idol, since it lacks the knowledge that should give it a soul.

<margin>89.</margin> The mystery of our salvation makes life a demonstration of the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>, and makes the Word the glory of our life. It makes practice into an "active contemplation" and contemplation into a "mystical practice." To put it briefly: it works to make virtue the manifestation of knowledge, and knowledge the power that preserves virtue. Through both—I mean virtue and knowledge—it shows a single **wisdom** being established. This is so we may know that the **Two Testaments** agree with each other in everything according to grace; they harmonize more toward the completion of a single mystery than even the soul and body do toward the birth of a single human being.

<margin>90.</margin> Just as soul and body together form a human being through their union, so practice and contemplation 

<column-break/>

complete a single **gnostic wisdom** <note>Knowledge-filled wisdom</note> through their meeting. And the Old and New Testaments work together to produce one single mystery. Only God is **Good by nature**, from whom all things are enlightened and made good through participation—at least those things capable of receiving nature’s light and goodness.

<margin>91.</margin> He who understands the visible world contemplates the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world</term> <note>original: "kosmos noētos" — the realm of spiritual realities perceived by the mind rather than the eyes.</note>. For by using the senses, he forms images of spiritual things, and in his mind, he gives shape to the divine principles he has glimpsed. He transfers the structure of the spiritual world into the variety of the senses, and he transfers the complex composition of the sensory world into the mind. In the spiritual realm, he understands the sensory world by bringing the senses to the mind through their underlying principles; in the sensory realm, he understands the spiritual world by skillfully clothing the mind in symbolic types for the sake of the senses.

<margin>92.</margin> The Prophet <note>Likely referring to the imagery in Habakkuk 3.</note> named the primary principle of the **Unity** <note>original: "monados" — the Monad</note>—which is the beginning of every virtue—the "**Head**," as in: *My head went into the clefts of the mountains.* He called the thoughts of the spirits of wickedness the "**clefts of the mountains**," by which our mind was swallowed up through the original transgression. The "**lowest earth**" refers to a state that feels no divine knowledge or any movement of life according to virtue. The "**abyss**" is the ignorance that weighs upon the habit of vice, upon which the seas of wickedness rest like solid ground. Or he meant that the "earth" is the fixed habit of vice, and the "**eternal bars**" are the passionate attachments to material things that hold that wretched habit in place.

<margin>93.</margin> The **endurance of the saints** consumes the power of evil when it attacks. It persuades them to find beauty in the labors they suffer for the sake of truth, and it teaches them to expand more in their sufferings than in their comforts. For those who care too much for life in the flesh, the natural weakness of the flesh regarding suffering becomes a foundation for a spiritual power that surpasses them. For see how the natural weakness of the saints is the foundation for an exceedingly divine power, through which the Lord showed the proud **Devil** to be inferior and defeated.

<margin>94.</margin> The **Word of grace** came to human nature—that is, the Church of the nations—through many temptations, just as **Jonah** passed through many tribulations to reach Nineveh, the great city.

<summary>This page explores the inseparable union of spiritual practice (praxis) and contemplation (theoria), asserting that the Old and New Testaments function like the body and soul of a single divine mystery. Maximus also provides an allegorical interpretation of the "Head" and the "Abyss," illustrating how divine power is perfected in human weakness during the struggle against vice.</summary>

304 OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...convinced the **reigning law of nature** to rise from its throne—that is, to move away from its former habit of following evil through the senses—and to take off its robe. By this, I mean setting aside the vanity and pride of worldly glory. He then put on sackcloth, which represents mourning and the difficult, harsh discipline of self-denial <note>original: "kakopatheias" — literally "suffering of evil," referring here to ascetic labor</note>, and a way of life that is fitting for God. He sat upon ashes; and "ashes" are the **poverty of spirit**, upon which sits everyone who is taught to live piously and who possesses the scourge of conscience to discipline themselves for their transgressions.

<margin>95. Scholion * perhaps "assault" or "clothing."</margin> Note how he calls the **king** the "natural law"; the **throne** the "passionate habit of the senses"; the **robe** the "assault of empty vanity"; the **sackcloth** the "mourning of repentance"; the **ashes** "humility"; the **men** those [faculties] concerning "desire"; the **oxen** those concerning "anger"; and the **sheep** those who stumble in the "contemplation of visible things."

<margin>96.</margin> He who, through the virtue of the law, forgets the passions of the flesh as things "on the left," and who, through unerring knowledge, is not captured by the sickness of spiritual conceit <note>original: "phusiōseōs oiēseōs" — an inflated sense of one's own importance or spiritual status</note> as if it were "on the right" because of his achievements—such a person has become a true man. He does not know his **right hand**, for he does not love fleeting glory; nor does he know his **left hand**, for he is not provoked by the passions of the flesh. The Word, it seems, calls the vainglory one feels over supposed successes the "right hand," and the lack of restraint regarding shameful passions the "left hand." For the principle of virtue knows no sin of the flesh (the left), and the principle of knowledge knows no vice of the soul (the right).

<margin>87.</margin> The rational knowledge of the virtues—that is, the true recognition of the cause of virtues through active practice—is designed to produce a complete **ignorance** of both the "right" and "left." These represent the excess and the deficiency that lie on either side of the "middle way" of the virtues. For if nothing irrational exists within Reason <note>original: "Logō" — here meaning both the divine Word and the faculty of human reason</note>, then clearly the one who has been led up to the Reason of the virtues will in no way

<column-break/>

recognize the position of irrational things. For it is not possible to look at two opposing things at the same time, nor to know one while the other is simultaneously appearing.

<margin>98.</margin> If there is no logic for unbelief within faith, and if light is not by nature the cause of darkness, and if the devil cannot be shown to coexist with Christ—then it is clear that the **irrational** cannot coexist at all with **Reason** <note>original: "Logō"</note>. If the irrational cannot be present with Reason, then the one who has been led up to the Reason of the virtues will in no way recognize the position of irrational things. He knows virtue only as it truly is, and not as it is merely thought to be; therefore, he knows neither a "right hand" through excess, nor a "left hand" through deficiency. For in both cases, the irrational is clearly observed.

<margin>99. Scholion</margin> He calls **unbelief** the "denial of the commandments," and **faith** the "assent to them." **Darkness** is "ignorance of the good," and **light** is the "discernment of the good." He has called **Christ** the "essence and the substance of the good," and the **devil** the "vile habit that generates all evils."

<margin>100.</margin> If Reason <note>original: "Logos"</note> is the limit and the measure of all beings, then it is equally irrational to move beyond the limit and measure, or to fall short of the limit and measure. Both movements equally cause a fall away from truly **Being**. The first (the "right") makes the movement of their course unclear and undefined; they do not have God as their goal because of an immoderate mind, as they imagine a "right" that is more "right" than the truth <note>original: "dexiou dexiōteron" — a play on words suggesting a person trying to be 'more right than right,' leading to spiritual pride</note>. The second (the "left") moves beside the goal, persuading them to move only toward the senses because of a weakness of mind; they think that which is defined by the senses is the pre-ordained end. The one who does not suffer these things remains ignorant of them; he is joined to the Reason of virtue alone, and he has limited every movement of his own mental power to that Reason. Therefore, he is unable to think of anything beyond Reason or beside Reason.

<meta>This page transitions from the "Sixth Century" to the "Seventh Century" of St. Maximus the Confessor's "Chapters on Knowledge." The previous page concluded the discussion on the repentance of Nineveh, using it as an allegory for the "natural law" governing the soul. 305 SEVENTH CENTURY

## BY THE SAME AUTHOR

# SEVENTH CENTURY

---

<margin>1.</margin>
**Natural Reason** <note>original: "Logos" — the underlying principle or logic of a thing</note>, through the medium of the virtues, is naturally designed to lead the person who is diligent in practice back to the **mind**. The mind, in turn, introduces the seeker of knowledge to **wisdom** through **contemplation** <note>original: "theoria" — the spiritual perception of divine truths</note>. On the other hand, irrational passion persuades the one who neglects the commandments to be dragged down toward **sensation**; the ultimate end of this is for the mind to be nailed to **pleasure**.

<margin>2. Scholion</margin>
He calls "virtue" the most dispassionate and stable habit regarding the Good, on either side of which nothing else stands, as it bears the character of God—to whom nothing is opposite. The cause of the virtues is God; the "active knowledge" of God is the transformation of the person who has truly recognized God into the Spirit, according to their inner state.

<margin>3.</margin>
If Reason defined how the birth of each thing naturally occurs, nothing that exists has naturally exceeded or fallen short of itself. Therefore, the "boundary" of existing things is the recognition of their **Cause** <note>meaning God as the source of all being</note> through desire; and the "measure" is the achievable imitation of the Cause through action. To move beyond the boundary and the measure of things in motion makes the race foolish, as they do not reach God—in whom the movement of all things according to desire comes to rest, receiving as an unfailing <note>original: "anupostaton" — literally "without a separate substance," meaning the end is found entirely within God</note> end the enjoyment of God. Conversely, to move contrary to the boundary and the measure of things in motion makes the race foolish, reaching toward sensation instead of God, where the insubstantial enjoyment of the passions occurs according to pleasure.

<margin>4.</margin>
The **mind** that is stretched out toward the Cause of all things without attachment will exist in a state of complete "ignorance," beholding no "reason" <note>original: "logon" — here meaning a defined concept or category</note> in God, who exists by His essence above every reason and beyond every cause. Having withdrawn to Him from all existing things, the mind knows no principle of the things from which it departed, beholding only—in an uninterpretable way—the One to whom it has come by grace. For even the principles of incorporeal beings are left behind by the mind that has run up to God in **ecstasy** <note>original: "ekstasin" — literally "standing outside" oneself or the world</note>. For nothing that comes after God is naturally able to be contemplated at the same time as God.

<column-break/>

<margin>5.</margin>
**Pride** <note>original: "typhos" — a sense of being "puffed up" or delusional</note> is truly a cursed passion, composed of two evils: I mean **arrogance** <note>original: "hyperephania" — looking down on others/God</note> and **vain-glory** <note>original: "kenodoxia" — seeking empty praise</note>. Arrogance denies the Cause of virtue and nature; vain-glory makes both nature and virtue itself illegitimate. For nothing is accomplished according to God by the arrogant person, and nothing proceeds according to nature for the vain-glorious person.

<margin>6.</margin>
It is characteristic of **arrogance** to deny that God is the generator of virtue and nature. It is characteristic of **vain-glory** to divide nature toward degradation. From these, pride is naturally born, being a composite habit of vice that involves a voluntary denial of God and an ignorance of the natural "equality of honor" <note>the fundamental dignity shared by all humans</note>.

<margin>7.</margin>
Pride is a mixture of arrogance and vain-glory. Toward God, it holds contempt, through which it naturally slanders **Providence** blasphemously. Toward nature, it possesses alienation, through which it handles all natural things contrary to nature, by way of misuse, corrupting the proper beauty of nature.

<margin>8.</margin>
The "spirit of the burning heat" <note>original: "pneumatos tou kausōnos" — referring to the scorching east wind or Sirocco</note> signifies not only temptations, but also the abandonment by God which takes away from the Jews the provision of divine gifts. But kinship through the **Spirit** dissolves the soul's attachment to the choices of the flesh, and persuades <margin>perhaps: "persuades" (missing in text)</margin> it to run toward God, fixed there by desire.

<margin>9.</margin>
When the **natural law** does not have sensation prevailing over reason, it teaches us, without being told, to embrace all who are our kin and of the same race. It uses nature itself as a teacher for helping those in need, wanting for everyone exactly what each person considers desirable when done to themselves by others. Teaching this, the Lord says: "Whatever you wish..."

It introduces the "natural law" as the basis for the Golden Rule.</summary>

# OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS

...wish that men should do to you, do likewise to them. <note>A reference to the "Golden Rule" from Luke 6:31.</note>

<margin>10. Scholion</margin>
He says that it is the work of the **natural law** to create a single-minded relationship of all people toward one another according to their **disposition** <note>original: "gnomē" — the personal will or inclination</note>. For among those where nature is governed by **reason** <note>original: "logos"</note>, a single disposition naturally exists. Where the disposition is the same, the character of their morals and the course of their lives is clearly designed to be one. Where the character of morals and the course of life are the same, there is obviously one and the same bond of relationship according to their will, leading everyone toward the one principle of nature. In this state, the division of nature that currently prevails through **self-love** <note>original: "philautia" — often considered the root of all sin in Maximus’s thought</note> is completely absent. 

The **written law**, however, restrains the disordered impulses of the more foolish through the fear of punishment. It habituates them by teaching them to look only toward the preservation of equality. Through this, the power of justice is confirmed over time and passes into nature, turning fear into a disposition that is gently and gradually blended with a will for the Good. This habit cleanses the mind through the forgetting of former things and gives birth to a love for one's fellow man.

<margin>11. Scholion</margin>
The written law, he says, by preventing injustice through fear, habituates one toward what is just. Over time, this habit creates a "justice-loving" disposition, from which a stable state of virtue arises, bringing about a forgetfulness of previous wickedness.

<margin>12.</margin>
The **law of grace** directly teaches those who are led by it to imitate God himself. He loved us so much—more than himself, if it is permitted to say so—and that while we were still enemies through sin, that he came into our essence without change, though he is beyond all essence. He accepted a nature in a way that transcends nature, becoming a man and choosing to be called one of us. He did not refuse to make our condemnation his own. He **deified** <note>original: "etheose" — from theosis, the process of becoming like God</note> us by grace to the same extent that he became man by his **economy** <note>term: "economy" (oikonomia) — the way God manages the salvation of the world, specifically through the Incarnation</note>. He did this so that we might learn not only to hold onto one another naturally and to love one another spiritually as ourselves, but also to care for one another divinely, even above ourselves. The proof of this love for one another is to choose willingly and eagerly to die for one another for the sake of virtue. For there is no 

<column-break/>

greater love than this, it says, that someone should lay down his life for his friend. <note>Quoting John 15:13.</note>

<margin>13.</margin>
The **natural law** is, to speak briefly, a natural reason that has brought sensation under its control for the removal of **irrationality** <note>the state of being ruled by animal instinct rather than reason</note>; it is through irrationality that the division of things naturally joined occurs. The **written law** is natural reason which, after the removal of irrationality according to sensation, has also taken on a spiritual longing that holds together our kinship with one another. The **law of grace** is a reason that stands above nature; it transforms nature without changing its essence, leading it toward **deification** <note>term: "theosis" — the transformative process whose goal is likeness to or union with God</note>. It shows to the nature of men, as if in an image, the Archetype that is beyond essence and nature, providing the permanence of "ever-well-being."

<margin>14.</margin>
To hold one's neighbor as oneself belongs only to the care of life according to "being" <note>simple existence</note>; this is the standard of the natural law. To love one's neighbor as oneself is to provide for the neighbor’s "well-being" according to virtue; this is what the written law commands. But to love one's neighbor *more* than oneself is the unique characteristic of the law of grace.

<margin>15.</margin>
He who is restrained from the impulses toward bodily pleasure learns the principles of **providence**, which holds back the flammable material of the passions. But he who receives the lashes of bodily pain is taught the principles of **judgment**, which cleanses him through involuntary sufferings from previous defilements.

<margin>16.</margin>
The word of Scripture introduces the Prophet <note>Jonah</note> grieving for the booth and the gourd—by which I mean the flesh and the pleasure of the flesh—while God holds fast to Nineveh. This makes it clear that while some things are dear to men, <margin>* Perhaps the "but" is redundant</margin> that which appears beloved to God is far better and more precious than all existing things. This is especially true compared to things that do not truly exist, but seem to exist only through a false judgment; such things have no principle of existence at all, but are only a fantasy deceiving the mind, providing a hollow form <margin>* perhaps: "but not a substance"</margin> but a substance to the passion.

<margin>17.</margin>
The accurate knowledge of the oracles of the Spirit is naturally revealed only to those worthy of the Spirit. These are the ones who, through great care for the virtues, have cleansed their minds of the soot of the passions, like a pure and transparent mirror. At the same...

<summary>This page defines and compares the three laws of spiritual life: the Natural Law (reason over instinct), the Written Law (habitual justice and equality), and the Law of Grace (sacrificial love and deification). It emphasizes that the highest form of love is to value others above oneself, imitating Christ's Incarnation.</summary>

### SEVENTH CENTURY

...striking them like a face being imprinted, they receive the knowledge of divine things. But for those whose lives are stained <margin>* perhaps: "with stains"</margin> by passions, it is barely possible even through likely conjectures to find evidence for the knowledge of divine things, let alone to have the audacity to think or speak of it with precision.

<margin>18.</margin> The mind that has received the form of knowledge through the virtues in the Holy Spirit is said to "suffer" <note>original: "pathein" — in this context, it means to "undergo" or "experience" God's action rather than initiating it oneself.</note> divine things, because it did not acquire this by its own nature or existence, but by grace through participation. But one who has not received knowledge through grace, even if he says something "insightful," does not know the power of what is said through experience. For mere learning does not grant knowledge that has become a habit <note>original: "hexis" — a stable, permanent disposition of the soul.</note>.

<margin>19.</margin> A mind purified to the highest degree through the virtues is naturally able to judge the principles <note>original: "logoi" — the inner purposes or divine intentions behind things.</note> of the virtues, making the knowledge that has been divinely characterized by them its own "face." For in itself, every mind is formless and without character, possessing only an acquired form—either the knowledge that subsists through the virtues in the Spirit, or the ignorance that results from the passions.

<margin>20.</margin> Everyone who has fallen away from divine love has the "law in the flesh" reigning through pleasure, being neither able nor willing to keep any divine commandment. For having preferred a pleasure-loving life over the life and kingdom conducted according to virtue in the Spirit of God, he has drawn ignorance upon himself instead of knowledge.

<margin>21.</margin> He who does not cross over in his mind toward the inner divine beauty of the legal "letter" <note>Referring to the literal text of the Old Testament Law.</note> in the Spirit, naturally gives birth to a pleasure-loving disposition of the will—that is, worldly attachment and a love for the world—stemming only from the outward recitation of learning in words.

<margin>22.</margin> "Shame of the mouth" <note>A phrase often used in ascetic literature to describe the disgrace of worldly or sinful thoughts that find expression.</note> is the worldly meditation of thoughts in the mind, and the love of the body. <margin>* perhaps: "for the excess"</margin> For in this state, the "world" naturally comes to be through the bodily formation appearing in the letter of the law, according to the disposition of the will—that is, the condition that loves the world and the pleasure-loving meditation of thoughts in the mind. For toward whatever we are relationally disposed, toward that we also possess meditation in our mind.

<margin>23.</margin> Or again, "shame of the mouth" is the 

<column-break/>

movement of the mind that brings form to the passions and shapes a beauty according to pleasure for the senses. For without the mind’s inventive power to shape a form, a passion is never brought to action. Or, it is a dedicated offering <note>original: "anathema" — something set apart, often in a negative sense of being cursed or excluded.</note>, and the material, ugly, and unformed movement of the passions. But "shame of the mouth" is the movement that gives form to the passion for the sake of the senses, providing the passion with a material suited to its invention.

<margin>24.</margin> He who believes that sacrifices, festivals, sabbaths, and new moons were ordained by God according to the Law for the sake of bodily luxury and rest, will completely and utterly fall under the guilt of the activity of the passions and the shame of the filth of the shameful thoughts associated with them. He will be under the corruptible world and the body-loving meditation in his thoughts; he will be under the matter and form of the passions, able to hold nothing precious except things that perish.

<margin>25.</margin> He who is convinced that it is a divine ordinance to feast bodily according to the law, accepts gluttony as a gift from God to live with in joy; from this, he gives birth to ways of life that defile the activity of the senses through misuse.

<margin>26.</margin> When the contemplative part of the soul embraces luxury according to the letter of the law as if it were divine because of the commandment, it pursues a use of the senses that is contrary to nature, allowing no natural use of their activity to shine through. For it gives birth both to the habit and the activity of the passions, and installs gluttony as something divine, for the purpose of generating ways of life that defile the senses through misuse, leading to the destruction of the natural principles <note>original: "logoi"</note> and seeds within created things.

<margin>27.</margin> No one who clings only to the bodily worship of the law could ever accept a natural principle or reasoning, because symbols are not by nature the same as the things they represent. For he who remains within the symbols of the law cannot see the nature of things according to reason, nor can he acquire the principles <margin>* principles</margin> placed substantially by the Creator within existing things, because of the difference between symbols and the nature of beings.

<margin>28.</margin> He who considers his belly to be God, and takes pride in his shame as if it were glory, only...

->### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS<-

<column-break/>

...knows how to cling to divine things through diligence, fleeing the dishonor of the passions. For this reason, such a person cares only for the things of time—that is, matter and form—and the five-fold operation of the senses used improperly. For when sensory perception is entwined with matter and form through a mixture, it is the nature of this union to produce passion, and to kill and destroy the natural principles <note>original: "logoi" — the inner divine purposes or "blueprints" behind created things.</note>. For passion and nature, according to the principle of being, can in no way coexist with one another. It is not the nature of the principle of nature to appear at all alongside passion, just as passion is not naturally born alongside nature at its beginning.

<margin>29.</margin> One who does not believe that Scripture is spiritual does not perceive his own poverty of knowledge, but is destroyed by famine. For famine is truly the absence of those good things known through experience, and a total lack and scarcity of the spiritual foods that sustain the soul. For how could anyone not consider it a famine or a loss when things he has never known at all are taken away?

<margin>30.</margin> Truly, the people of the faithful and those who have recognized the truth suffer famine; so too does the soul of the individual whenever it abandons spiritual contemplation <note>original: "theoria" — the visionary experience of divine truth beyond mere logic.</note> in grace and falls into the slavery of the literal "type" <note>original: "typikes" — referring to the Old Testament symbols or the literal, physical meaning of the text as a "shadow."</note> in the written word. Such a soul does not nourish the mind with the greatness of spiritual concepts, but instead fills the senses with passionate imagination through the physical descriptions of the scriptural symbols.

<margin>31.</margin> Everyone who does not accept the spiritual contemplation of Holy Scripture has, like the Jews, rejected both the natural law and the written law; such a person is ignorant of the law in grace, according to which contemplation is given to those led by it. Therefore, he who takes the written law in a bodily sense does not nourish the soul with virtues. He who does not apply himself to the principles of created things does not feast the mind generously on the manifold wisdom of God. And he who does not know the great mystery of the new grace does not rejoice in the hope of future deification <note>original: "theosis" — the process of being united with God's life and nature.</note>. Consequently, the lack of contemplation according to the written law brings with it the poverty of the manifold wisdom of God understood according to natural law; this in turn results in ignorance of the deification

<column-break/>

to be given by grace to all.

<margin>32.</margin> Every mind that is discerning according to Christ and strong in its vision always desires and seeks the "Face of the Lord." The Face of the Lord is established as the true contemplation and knowledge of divine things through virtue. By seeking this, the mind is taught the cause of its own lack and poverty. For just as the face is the characteristic of each individual, so spiritual knowledge vividly characterizes the Divine. He who seeks this knowledge is said to seek the Face of the Lord. But he who becomes "enfleshed" according to the letter of the law through bloody sacrifices possesses a self-chosen ignorance; he accepts the commandment only for the sake of bodily pleasure and clings physically to the matter of the written word only through the senses.

<margin>33.</margin> He who worships in a bodily way according to the law generates sin in action as if it were "matter," and he is shaped materially by the "form" of his legalistic consent to the corresponding pleasures of the senses. But he who receives Scripture spiritually puts to death the action as matter and the consent to sin as form—along with those ways the senses are misused for pleasure—doing so through natural reasonings in the height of contemplation.

<margin>34.</margin> Matter and form, and the five ways the five senses are misused regarding matter and form—by which I mean the passionate and unnatural entanglement of the senses with sensible things, namely things subject to time and flux—are handed over to be put to death by the higher principles and reasonings of natural contemplation. This is done by the spiritual law, or the mind, after the passing away of bodily worship according to the letter of the law and the crossing over from ignorance. The goal is to abolish and kill the most universal relationship with things under time—which exists in symbols for the sake of the senses and the body—once one has reached the height of the law of spiritual contemplation.

<margin>35.</margin> Without natural contemplation, no one can discern the dissonance <note>original: "apemphasin" — the unsuitability or lack of fit between a physical symbol and the divine reality it points to.</note> between legal symbols and divine things. For if one does not first naturally examine the dissonance of divine and intelligible things within the symbols, it is impossible for him to desire to come entirely outside of the senses in his mind toward the...

<summary>Maximus explains that a literal, "fleshly" interpretation of Scripture leads to spiritual famine and passion, while "spiritual contemplation" (theoria) allows the mind to see through symbols to the divine principles (logoi) and achieve deification (theosis).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Seventh Century of Theological Chapters" by St. Maximus the Confessor. The previous page discussed the soul's struggle against passions and the danger of remaining stuck in a literal or "bodily" understanding of reality, which leads to a spiritual famine.</meta>

...the beauty of intelligible things, it is absolutely impossible for one to be released from the bodily variety found in physical places. As long as a person stays attached to this "letter" of the Law, they naturally fail to find relief from the poverty caused by a famine of knowledge. Such a person has condemned themselves to "eat the earth"—that is, the body—just like the deceptive serpent. They do not live according to Christ, who is the "heaven," or rather the spirit of Scripture and the soul. To eat Christ is to consume the "heavenly and angelic bread." By this, I mean being nourished by the spiritual contemplation <note>original: "theoria" — the deep, visionary insight into the spiritual meaning behind physical symbols.</note> and knowledge of the Scriptures in Christ. This is the knowledge that God provides abundantly to those who love Him, as it is written: *"He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of Angels."* <note>A reference to Psalm 78:24-25.</note>

<margin>36.</margin>
We must recognize that a sensory and bodily interpretation of Scripture clearly gives birth to passions and a mindset attached to things that are temporary and fleeting. This is an "impassioned activity" of the senses toward sensible objects. Like the children and descendants of Saul, these interpretations must be done away with through "natural contemplation" on the mountain—that is, by the spiritual lifting up <note>original: "anagoge" — the process of interpreting a text to find its highest spiritual or mystical meaning.</note> of the divine oracles. We must do this if we desire to be filled with divine grace.

<margin>37.</margin>
The truth is wronged both by the Law when it is understood only according to the "letter," and by those who follow it in that way. Anyone who imitates that mindset limits the power of the Law to the literal text alone. Such a person refuses to accept "natural contemplation" as the means to reveal the knowledge hidden mystically within the letter. This contemplation stands in the middle, between "types" <note>original: "typoi" — symbols or prefigurations in the Old Testament.</note> and the "truth." It leads people away from symbols and guides them toward the truth. One who denies this is excluded from the divine initiation into the mysteries. Therefore, those who care for divine visions must use natural contemplation to "kill" this bodily and temporary interpretation of the Law, treating it as something subject to time and decay, and they must do this on the "mountain" of high knowledge.

<margin>38.</margin>
The "bodily mind" of Scripture is completely abolished by the person who, through natural contemplation, puts to death the soul's pleasure-loving and body-loving relationship with unstable and flowing matter—a relationship born from the written Law. By blocking out the "earthbound" meaning of the Law as if they were the children and descendants of Saul, and by using natural contemplation as if 

<column-break/>

standing on the mountain of the heights of knowledge, one makes their former bodily interpretation of the Law manifest before the Lord through confession. For those who love learning, "exposing them to the sun before the Lord" <note>original: "exheliasai" — a reference to 2 Samuel 21:6, where Saul’s sons are "exposed" or "hanged" before the Lord. Maximus treats this as a metaphor for bringing hidden literalisms into the light of spiritual knowledge.</note> can be understood as bringing the prejudices shaped by the "letter" into the light of knowledge. This means revealing, from the height of contemplation, that the letter of the Law is "dead" when compared to knowledge in the spirit.

<margin>39.</margin>
The Scripture says, *"The letter kills, but the spirit gives life."* <note>2 Corinthians 3:6.</note> Therefore, that which is meant to be killed must be put to death by the life-giving Spirit. It is absolutely impossible for the bodily aspect of the Law and the divine aspect—that is, the letter and the spirit—to coexist and be active in the same person at the same time. That which is capable of taking away life cannot, by its nature, agree with that which provides life.

<margin>40.</margin>
The spirit is the provider of life; the letter is the taker of life. Therefore, the letter and the spirit cannot act at the same time, just as that which gives life cannot coexist with that which brings corruption.

<margin>41.</margin>
Mystical circumcision is the complete removal of the mind's passionate relationship with the world of "becoming" <note>original: "genesis" — the realm of changing, created things as opposed to the eternal.</note> which has been forced upon us. If we look at things according to nature, we know that perfection does not consist in the removal of something God created as naturally complete. Nature is not made perfect by being mutilated by human craft or by an intentional "design" to discard what God gave it according to the principle of creation. If that were the case, we would be suggesting that human craft is more powerful than God in establishing righteousness, and that we are "fixing" a deficiency in nature that God supposedly left behind. Rather, from the physical location of the circumcised member, we are taught to perform a circumcision of the "will" <note>original: "gnome" — the faculty of choice or intention.</note> regarding the passionate disposition of the soul. In this way, the will is harmonized with nature by correcting the passionate "law" we have acquired through our involvement with the world of change.

<margin>42.</margin>
Uncircumcision is natural. Everything natural is a work of divine creation and is "very good," according to the voice that says, *"And God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good."* <note>Genesis 1:31.</note> But the Law, by commanding uncircumcision to be removed through circumcision as if it were "unclean," would seem to imply that God is correcting His own work through human skill—if one were to think...

He allegorizes the execution of Saul’s descendants to represent the soul's need to "kill" literalist prejudices to reach the heights of divine knowledge.</summary>

...most impious. Therefore, the one who approaches the symbols of the law in a natural way knows that God does not correct nature through artifice. Instead, God commands that the "passion-prone" part of the soul—the part that ought to be obedient to reason—be circumcised. This is what is symbolically shown through the physical part of the body. This "circumcision" is something that spiritual knowledge <note>original: "gnosis"</note>, through the courage found in active practice, is naturally meant to strip away from our inner disposition. For the Priest who performs the circumcision represents this spiritual knowledge; he wields the courage of the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> in action like a blade of iron against the passions. Indeed, the tradition of the Law vanishes when the spirit triumphs over the literal letter.

<margin>43.</margin>
The Sabbath is a rest from the passions and from the mind's preoccupation with the nature of created things. It is either the complete "non-action" of the passions, or the total pause of the mind’s movement regarding created things and its perfect transition toward the Divine. In this state, the person who has arrived at what is divinely permitted through virtue and knowledge must not "gather wood"—that is, they must not dwell on any material thoughts that ignite the passions. Nor should they even collect the "reasons" of nature <note>The inner principles or "logoi" that define how things work.</note>, so that we do not end up defining God according to the limits of nature, as the Greeks <note>Maximus refers here to pagan philosophers who limited the divine to the laws of the physical cosmos.</note> do. God is proclaimed only by a perfect silence, and He is made present through a total, transcendent "unknowing" <note>original: "agnosia" — a state of mystical union where God is known to be beyond all human concepts.</note>.

<margin>44.</margin>
A "crown of goodness" is pure faith, adorned like precious stones with the lofty heights of doctrine and spiritual words and insights, encircling the God-loving mind like a head. Or rather, the "crown of goodness" is the Word of God Himself. By the variety of His ways in providence and judgment—that is, through our self-control in voluntary passions and our endurance in involuntary ones—He encircles the mind as its head. By the participation in the grace of deification <note>original: "theosis" — the process of becoming like God.</note>, He makes the mind even more beautiful than it is in itself.

<margin>45.</margin>
Here he says that self-control is a work of Providence, as it cleanses the passions of our will. He says that endurance is an achievement of Judgment, as it stands against involuntary temptations. These are symbols of "practical philosophy," leading those held captive by sin toward virtue, just as the people were led out of Egypt.

<margin>46.</margin>
It was not because God wanted days to be honored by men that He commanded the Sabbath, the new moons, and the 

<column-break/>

feasts to be honored. For if that were the case, He would have established a dogma of "worshipping the creation rather than the Creator" by the Law's command, leading people to think that days are holy in themselves and therefore worthy of worship. Instead, He indicated symbolically that He Himself is to be honored through these days. For He Himself is the Sabbath, as the rest from the soul’s labors in the flesh and the cessation of the toils of righteousness. He is the Passover <note>original: "Pascha"</note> as the Liberator of those held in the bitter slavery of sin. He is Pentecost as the beginning and the end of all things—and the Word <note>Logos</note> by whom all things naturally consist. Consider how the Law "kills" those who understand it in a bodily <note>meaning: literal or physical</note> way, by persuading them to worship the creation instead of the Creator, and to believe that things made for their sake are holy by nature, while remaining ignorant of the One for whose sake they themselves were made.

<margin>47.</margin>
The world is a limited place and a circumscribed state of "standing still." Time, on the other hand, is a circumscribed movement. From this, a certain "changeability" exists within it—the movement according to life. But when nature passes through place and time, both in action and in thought—that is, when it passes through the "necessities" of limited rest and movement—and is joined immediately to Providence, it finds Providence as its "Reason" <note>Logos</note>. This Reason is simple and stable by nature, possessing no circumscription, and therefore, absolutely no movement.

<margin>48.</margin>
While nature exists within the world in a temporal way, its movement is subject to change because of the world’s limited stability and the passing flow of time. But when nature comes to be in God, it will have an "unmoving movement" and a "stable ever-movement" <note>A classic Maximian paradox: the soul is at rest because it has reached its goal, but "moves" in an eternal deepening of its relationship with God.</note> because of the natural unity of the One in whom it has come to be. This movement happens eternally around the Same, the One, and the Only. This, as the Word knows, is the immediate and permanent establishment of created things around the First Cause.

<margin>49.</margin>
The mystery of Pentecost is the immediate union of those being cared for with Providence. That is, it is the union of nature with the Word <note>Logos</note> according to the plan of Providence, in which there is no longer any appearance of time or "becoming." Again, our "Trumpet" is the Word, as He sounds within us the divine and inexpressible knowledge. He is our "Propitiation," as He became like us and, in Himself, dissolves the charges against us. And by the gift...

<meta>This page continues St. Maximus the Confessor’s "Seventh Century of Theological Chapters." ### SEVENTH CENTURY

...by the gift of grace in the Spirit, deifying <term>theopoion: the process of becoming like God</term> the nature that had sinned. And the "Feast of Tabernacles" <margin>perhaps: toward immortality</margin> is the practice of remaining unchangeable in what is beautiful, according to our God-imitating habit; it is the cohesive bond of our transformation into immortality.

<margin>50.</margin> He who delights only in literal, bloody sacrifices prepares those who offer them to be preoccupied with the passions, as if God Himself were subject to passion. For the one who worships sincerely loves to delight in the same things that the Object of his worship delights in. Therefore, the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> recognizes "sacrifice" as being, instead, the slaughter of the passions and the offering up of our natural powers. Of these, the ram is a type of reason; the bull carries the symbol of the spirited <term>thymos: the "high-spirited" or "angry" part of the soul</term> power; and the goat is a clear representation of desire.

<margin>51.</margin> We recognize that spiritual sacrifices are not only the "killing" of the passions—slain by the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God—and the emptying or pouring out of all life in the flesh (like blood) according to one's spiritual purpose, but also the offering of a philosophical character. It is the offering of all natural powers, consecrated to God and consumed as a whole-burnt offering by the fire of grace in the Spirit, leading toward the divine destiny.

<margin>52.</margin> The earthly mind <note>original: "choikos nous"</note> of the Scripture, when it takes hold of the soul, casts out natural reasonings, making them vanish through the misuse of natural powers. For this mind, while alive, truly accomplishes, pursues, and destroys, confining the Law to the flesh alone. It honors the "natural" words and thoughts as if they were divine, yet they are actually passions of dishonor. These natural reasonings, when they receive permission from the "law of the spirit," kill and put to death both the passion and the fleshly mind at once.

<margin>53.</margin> As soon as someone rationally pursues the philosophy of the virtues <margin>*perhaps "pursues" or "pursued"</margin>, they simultaneously transfer the reception of the Scriptures toward the spirit in a natural way. They serve God in the "newness of the spirit" through high contemplations <note>original: "theoria"</note> expressed in action, rather than in the "oldness of the letter." They avoid the low, bodily acceptance of the Law through the senses, which—as it was for the Jews—makes one a nourisher of passions and a servant of sin.

<margin>54.</margin> As soon as a person stops receiving the Scripture according to the senses and the "body" of the text, they simultaneously run back toward the Spirit and the Mind through the mediation of nature. They perform spiritually

<column-break/>

those things which the Jew, by performing them only bodily, causes God to be angry.

<margin>55.</margin> Every mind that is high and elevated according to God, in that very state, slays the energy of the passions and the unseemly movement of thoughts. Furthermore, it slays the unrestrained ways of using the energy of the senses. For the passions are destroyed by the high reasonings of nature, being triumphed over through high contemplation.

<margin>56.</margin> The power of sin—that is, the "mind of the flesh"—is naturally abolished by the grace of Holy Baptism. Then, the active obedience to the divine commandments kills it with the "sword of the Spirit," which is the word of divine knowledge in the spirit. This grace cries out mystically to the passion of sin, just as the Great Samuel cried out to Agag: "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women today." <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 15:33. Maximus uses this violent imagery to describe the soul's total destruction of sinful habits.</note>

<margin>57.</margin> The passion of gluttony <note>original: "gastrimargia" (stomach-madness)</note> has made many virtues "childless" using the smooth reasoning of pleasure as its sword. Through lack of restraint, it kills the seeds of self-control; through greed, it corrupts the equality of justice; through self-love, it cuts through the natural continuity of love for mankind. To put it briefly: the passion of gluttony is the destroyer of every offspring of virtue.

<margin>58.</margin> While the passion of gluttony kills all the divine offspring of the virtues, it is itself killed by the grace of faith and the obedience to the divine commandments, through the word that accords with knowledge.

<margin>59.</margin> Our Lord is truly the "Light of the Gentiles," revealing to them through true recognition the eyes of the mind which had been closed by the gloom of ignorance. He prepared Himself again for the faithful people as a beautiful "exemplar" of virtue, becoming for them a sketch and a pattern of a virtuous person. Looking to Him as the "Captain of our salvation," we successfully achieve the virtues through action, imitating Him as much as is possible for us.

<margin>60.</margin> Everyone who hates because of envy, and who maliciously spreads rumors with slanders against those who are in the midst of the struggles...

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...of the virtues, and being more powerful through the abundance of the word of spiritual knowledge, he is like Saul, being choked by an evil spirit. He cannot bear the glory of the happiness found in the virtue and knowledge of one who is better than him. For this reason, he rages even more, because he cannot overcome his benefactor. Often, he even bitterly sends away his beloved Jonathan—by which I mean the innate reasoning of the conscience—who rebukes his unjust hatred and truthfully recounts the achievements of the one he hates.

<margin>61.</margin>
<margin>* perhaps: "the"</margin>
Let us also call upon the spiritual <term>noetos: "intelligible" or perceived by the mind rather than the senses</term> David to play the harp of spiritual contemplation and knowledge. May he strike a chord for our mind, which is currently seized by material things, and drive away * the evil of our material entanglement with the senses. Let us do this so we may be able to understand the Law spiritually, find the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> hidden within it in a mystical way, and make it a lasting possession—a provision for eternal life.

<margin>62.</margin>
Everyone who loves salvation clings entirely to either practice <note>original: "praxis"</note> or contemplation <note>original: "theoria"</note>. For without virtue and knowledge, no one has ever been able to obtain salvation. Virtue consists in ordering the movement of the body, skillfully reining it in with right reason as if with a bridle when it rushes toward impropriety. Contemplation consists in wisely choosing to guard those things that have been rightly understood and judged.

<margin>63.</margin>
Since that which thinks is intellectual <term>noeron: the subject or capacity for thought</term>, and that which is thought of is intelligible <term>noeton: the object of thought</term>, the object of thought serves as the nourishment and, so to speak, the very constitution of the thinker. It is fitting, then, that since God is the object of thought for the bodiless powers <note>meaning: the angels</note>, He—being understood by them as far as they can reach—shines upon them from within the mind that thinks and is nourished.

<margin>64.</margin>
The "intelligible" is one thing, and the "intellectual" is another. For the intelligible, as has been said, is a kind of nourishment for the intellectual. The object of thought (the intelligible) is greater than and precedes the thinker (the intellectual). For those things are called "intellectual" which, because they are minds, think upon the higher "intelligibles." For the intelligible is the thing being thought, which is also the food of the intellectual, or rather, the thinker.

<margin>65.</margin>
It must be understood that effects <term>aitiata: things that are caused</term> contain the images of their causes insofar as they are able to receive them. For all things brought into creation are effects, while the things that brought them forth are the causes. Yet there is no direct likeness to one another between causes and effects <note>meaning: the Creator is fundamentally different from His creation</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>
66. 
This 
chapter 
is taken 
word-for-
word 
from the 
writings 
of 
Dionysius 
the 
Areopagite.
</margin>
* It is necessary to know that our mind has, on one hand, a power for thinking through which it sees the "intelligibles"; on the other hand, it has a "union" that surpasses the nature of the mind, through which it is joined to those things that are beyond itself. It is according to this union that we must understand divine things, not according to our own standard. Rather, we must go entirely out of ourselves, being no longer our own, and becoming entirely God’s. For it is better to belong to God than to ourselves. In this way, divine things will be granted to those who have come to be with God.

<margin>
67. 
A com-
mentary 
on the 
above.
</margin>
* When the mind wishes to think, it descends from its own height into specific thoughts. For thoughts are lower than the thinker, since they are being thought and grasped; naturally, this causes a scattering and division of the mind's own unity. For while the mind is simple and undivided, thoughts are numerous and scattered, serving as the "forms" of the mind. For this reason, intellectual things—that is, those that think—are "lesser" than the intelligibles—that is, the things being thought. He speaks of a "union" of the mind (as he says more clearly in the following sections) through which it stretches upward toward things beyond itself; that is, it applies itself to the contemplation of God. This happens by "standing outside" <term>ekstasis: the act of going out of oneself to reach God</term> of all things perceived by the senses and the mind, and even beyond its own movement. Only then can it receive the ray of divine knowledge.

<margin>68.</margin>
If the intellectual being moves intellectually in a way consistent with itself, it certainly thinks. If it thinks, it certainly loves what it has thought. If it loves, it certainly undergoes an "ecstasy" <note>original: "ekstasis"</note> toward that which is loved. If it undergoes this, it is clear that it also hastens toward it. If it hastens, it certainly intensifies the intensity of its movement. If it intensifies its movement forcefully, it does not stop until it is entirely within the Beloved, and is willingly encompassed as a whole by the Whole. In this way, it accepts a "saving circumscription" through its own choice, so that the whole being may be qualified by the Whole that encompasses it. The result is that the one encompassed no longer wishes to be known at all by itself, but only by the One that encompasses it—just as air is completely illuminated by light, or as iron is entirely glowing with fire, or any other such example.

<margin>69.</margin>
There is no exact likeness between effects and causes. Rather, while effects possess the images of their causes as far as they are able, the causes themselves are set apart from their effects and are established above them according to the principle of their own origin. For the characteristics of the effects exist beforehand in the causes in a surpassing and essential way.

<summary>Maximus explores the philosophical relationship between the thinker and the object of thought, arguing that true union with God requires an "ecstasy" where the mind goes beyond its own nature to be entirely encompassed by the Divine. He draws heavily on the Neo-Platonic language of Pseudo-Dionysius to explain how the human mind reaches its ultimate end in God.</summary>

# THE SEVENTH CENTURY

<margin>70.</margin>
All things brought into existence within creation are effects; whether they are in heaven or on earth. The causes, however, are those who brought them into being—namely, the three persons <term>hypostases: the individual realities of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term> of the Holy Trinity. It is therefore evident that there is no likeness between these two groups—I mean between the causes and the effects.

---

<margin>71.</margin>
There is a great relationship between the thinkers and the things thought <term>nooumena: things understood by the mind</term>, and between the perceivers and the things perceived by the senses. But man, being composed of a soul and a sensory body, exists through a natural relationship and specific character that alternates between each of the two divisions of creation. Thus, he is both limited and he limits: he is limited in his essence, but he limits by his power. For he is naturally limited by the things of the mind and the senses because he is soul and body, yet he is naturally suited to limit these things by his power, insofar as he thinks and perceives. But God is simply and infinitely beyond all existing things, both those that contain and those that are contained, as He is entirely unrelated <note>original: "aschetos"—meaning God is not bound by the same relationships or dependencies as created things</note> to all things.

---

<margin>72.</margin>
Every forbidden pleasure is naturally produced from passion through the medium of sensation toward something perceived by the senses. For pleasure is nothing other than a form of sensation, shaped in the perceiving subject by some sensible object; or it is a mode of sensory activity established according to irrational desire. For desire, when added to sensation, turns into pleasure, bringing its own form upon it; and sensation, when moved according to desire, produces pleasure once it has taken hold of the sensible object. Therefore, the saints—knowing that the soul, when moved unnaturally toward matter through the medium of the flesh, puts on an "earthly form"—chose instead to move naturally toward God through the medium of the soul. They intended to bring even the flesh into a proper relationship with God, beautifying it as much as possible with divine reflections through the practice of the virtues.

---

<margin>73.</margin>
In a magnificent way, the saints crossed through this present age of struggle according to the true and unerring path of natural movement. They united the senses— <margin>* perhaps: "this seems redundant"</margin> * having captured them through the medium of reason <note>original: "logos"</note>—to the mind <note>original: "nous"</note> which holds the inner principles of all beings. They then presented this mind to God, once it was purely released from movement toward all created things and had come to rest even from its own natural activity. In this state, having been gathered entirely toward God, they were deemed worthy to be blended with the whole of God through the Spirit. They bore the image of the heavenly One as far as is

<column-break/>

possible for humans, and they drew so much of the divine reflection that— <margin>* perhaps: "they were dedicated/offered up"</margin> if it is permitted to say so—they were * placed within God, having been tested by Him.

---

<margin>74.</margin>
They say that God and man are paradigms <note>examples or models</note> of one another. To the same extent that God is "humanized" for man's sake through His love for mankind, man is "deified" <term>theosis: the process of becoming like God or being united with Him</term> for God’s sake through love. And man is snatched up by God in his mind toward the unknown to the same extent that man has made the naturally invisible God manifest through his virtues.

---

<margin>75.</margin>
Everyone who has put to death his "earthly members" and has extinguished the entire "mindset of the flesh," shaking off all relationship to it (through which the love we owe to God alone is divided), and who has denied all the identifying marks of the flesh and the world for the sake of divine grace—such a person is able to say with the blessed Apostle Paul, <term>Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?</term> and so on. Such a man has become "without father, without mother, and without genealogy" like the Great Melchizedek. He no longer has anything by which he might be held back by the flesh or nature, because of the union that has taken place with the Spirit.

---

<margin>76.</margin>
I do not believe it is right to call the end of this present life "death," but rather a release from death, a separation from corruption, a freedom from slavery, a cessation of disturbance, an end to wars, a retreat of darkness, a rest from labors, a calming of agitation, a covering of shame, an escape from passions, and—to put it briefly—the boundary of all evils. The saints achieved these things through voluntary mortification, presenting themselves as strangers and sojourners in this life. They fought bravely against both the world and the body and the rebellions arising from them. Having suffocated the deception that arises from the entanglement of the senses with sensible things, they kept the dignity of the soul enslaved to no one.

---

<margin>77.</margin>
Nature itself provides no small proof that the knowledge of Providence is naturally sown within us. Whenever it pushes us, as if untaught, toward God through prayers during sudden circumstances, it prepares us to seek salvation from Him. For when we are suddenly seized by necessity against our will...
