# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...before we think, let us look to God; so that His providence might draw us to Himself, even without our own reasoning, and so that the speed of His divine help might overcome the power of our own intellect <term>noera: relating to the mind or intellect</term>, showing His assistance to be stronger than all else. For nature would not lead us against our will to become something that is beyond our nature. It is clear to everyone that everything which follows naturally from something else carries a powerful and invincible proof of the truth's power.

<margin>78.</margin>
Since among existing things, some are good and others are bad, and these are either present or future: a good thing that is expected is called **desire**; a good thing that is present is **pleasure**. Conversely, an evil thing that is expected is called **fear**; an evil thing that is present is **sorrow**. Thus, pleasure and desire are observed in relation to "good" things—whether they are truly good or merely thought to be so—while sorrow and fear are observed in relation to bad things. Indeed, when desire attains its object, it produces pleasure; when it fails, it produces sorrow.

<margin>79.</margin>
They say that all **sorrow** is evil by its very nature. For even if the earnest man <term>spoudaios: a person dedicated to virtue</term> feels sorrow over the misfortunes of others out of mercy, he does not do so as his primary intent, but as a result of the circumstances. However, the contemplative <term>theoretikos: one who practices spiritual "seeing" or contemplation</term> remains dispassionate even in these things, having joined himself to God and detached himself from all things here.

<margin><unclear>80.</unclear></margin>
All the saints, having truly grasped the divine and unerring Word <term>Logos</term>, passed through this age without leaving the soul’s footprint upon any of its delights. For they rightfully soared with their minds toward the highest reaches of what humans can grasp concerning God—I mean His goodness and love. They were taught that it was by these that God was "moved" both to give being to all things and to grant them "well-being." This is true if it is even permissible to speak of "motion" in God, who alone is unmoved; perhaps it is better to call it His **Will**, which moves all things, brings them into being, and sustains them, while He Himself is never moved in any way.

<margin>81.</margin>
The soul, being an intellectual and rational essence, both thinks and reasons. It possesses the **intellect** <term>nous</term> as its power, **thinking** <term>noesis</term> as its motion, and the **thought** <term>noema</term> as its activity. For the "thought" is the limit of the thinking process between the one who thinks and the object being thought, acting as the boundary of the relationship between these two extremes.

<column-break/>

For when the soul thinks, it stops its process of thinking about that specific object once it has been grasped. That which has been truly understood once does not call upon the soul's power to be understood again. Thus, every single "thought" receives a point of rest from the specific act of thinking that was directed toward it.

<margin>82.</margin>
Just as ignorance divides those who are lost, so the presence of the **intellectual light** <note>original: "noetou photos"—the light of the mind or divine understanding</note> is a gathering and unifying force for those being enlightened. it is perfecting and leads them back toward "True Being," turning them away from many opinions and gathering their various sights—or more accurately, their fantasies—into a single, true, pure, and uniform knowledge, filling them with a single, unifying light.

<margin>83.</margin>
The **Beautiful** and the **Good** are the same, because all things, for every reason, seek the Beautiful and the Good. There is nothing in existence that does not participate in them. For the Beautiful and the Good are to all things truly admirable, desirable, lovely, pleasing, and worth choosing. Note how the **Divine Eros** <term>Eros: intense, longing love</term>, pre-existing in the Good, gave birth to the "good eros" within us, through which we long for the Beautiful and the Good, according to the one who said: *I became a lover of her beauty* <note>original: "Erastes egenomen tou kallous autes" — a quote from the Wisdom of Solomon 8:2</note>. And again: *Love her, and she shall keep thee; embrace her, and she shall exalt thee.* <note>A reference to Proverbs 4:8</note>

<margin>84.</margin>
Theologians sometimes call the Divine "Eros," sometimes "Love" <term>Agape</term>, and sometimes "the Beloved." Therefore, as Eros and Love, He moves; as the Beloved, He moves all things capable of eros and love toward Himself. To speak more clearly: He moves by creating a well-disposed relationship of love in those capable of it, and He moves them by naturally drawing the longing of those who move toward Him. And again, He moves and is moved, as one who **thirsts to be thirsted for**, who loves to be loved, and who cherishes being cherished.

<margin>85.</margin>
<margin>This current passage is taken word-for-word from the same Areopagite <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note>.</margin>
Divine Eros is also **ecstatic**, not allowing lovers to belong to themselves, but to the objects of their love. This is shown as the higher things [God's providence] care for the lower, as equals maintain a bond with one another, and as the lower things turn back toward the more divine first principles. This is why the Great Paul, having come under the "possession" of the Divine...

### SEVENTH CENTURY

<margin>
86. Likewise the present section
</margin>
...having partaken of **love** and the **ecstatic power** <term>ekstatike dynamis: the power to "stand outside" oneself in longing for another</term>, he speaks with a divinely inspired mouth. *I no longer live,* he says, *but Christ lives in me* <note>original: "Ζῷ ἐγὼ, φησιν, οὐκ ἔτι, ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ Χριστός" — Galatians 2:20</note>, like a true lover. He is "beside himself," as he says, for the sake of God; he lives not his own life, but the life of the Beloved, which is exceedingly dear to him. We must also dare to say this for the sake of truth: that the very Cause of all things, through the beautiful and good love <term>eros: intense, yearning love</term> for all things, and through the abundance of His loving goodness, comes to be **outside of Himself**. Through His providence for all existing things, He is as it were charmed by goodness, affection, and love. From His state above all things and set apart from all, He is drawn down to what is in all things, according to an ecstatic, supernatural power that yet never leaves His own nature. Therefore, those skilled in divine things call Him "Zealous" <note>original: "ζηλωτὴν" — referring to the "Jealous God" of Exodus 20:5, interpreted here as intensely loving</note>, because His good love for all beings is great and awakens a zeal for His loving desire. He shows Himself to be zealous because the things He desires are themselves objects of zeal, and because the beings He provides for are zealous for Him.

<margin>
87.
</margin>
They say that God Himself is the "sender forth" and "begetter" of **affection** <term>agape</term> and **love** <term>eros</term>. For He, having these within Himself, brought them forth into the external world—that is, toward His creations. And according to this it is said, *God is love* <note>1 John 4:8</note>. And again, He is called "sweetness" and "desire," which is *eros*. He is the Beloved and the truly Lovable. Because the "loving eros" pours out from Him, He who begat it is said to "be moved." Yet because He is the truly Lovable, the Beloved, the desired, and the chosen, He "moves" those who look toward Him—and He moves each according to their capacity for desire.

<margin>
88.
</margin>
Understand God to be the "matchmaker" <note>original: "προαγωγικὸν" — proagogos usually meant a procurer or pimp in secular Greek, but Maximus reclaims it here</note> and the "mover" toward a spiritual, loving union. That is, He is the mediator of this union and the one who joins us to it, so that He might be loved by His own creations. He is called "moving" because He moves each thing according to its own inner principle <term>logos</term> to return to Him. Although the name "matchmaker" signifies something unholy among those outside the faith, here it refers to the mediation that brings about union in God.

<margin>
89.
</margin>
The loving movement of the Good, pre-existing in the Good, being simple and self-moving, and proceeding from the Good, returns again to the same. It is without end

<column-break/>

and without beginning. This signifies our own ever-moving desire and union toward the Divine. For the loving union toward God is set apart from and transcends every other union.

<margin>
90.
Literally from the words of Hierotheus.
</margin>
Whether we speak of **love** <term>eros</term> as divine, or angelic, or intellectual, or psychic, or natural, let us understand it as a certain **unifying and binding power**. It moves superior beings to provide for those below them; it moves those of equal rank into a social bond with one another; and finally, it moves the lower beings to turn back toward those who are better and superior to them.

<margin>
91.
Literally from the words of Dionysius.
</margin>
If knowledge unites those who know, and ignorance is always the cause of change and the separation of the ignorant person from themselves, then nothing shall move the one who has truly believed according to the sacred Word from the hearth of true faith. Upon this hearth, one possesses the permanence of unmoving and unchangeable identity. For the one who is united to the Truth knows well that it is well with them, even if the many should admonish them as if they were **ecstatic** <note>In the sense of being "out of one's mind" or "mad."</note>. For it naturally escapes the notice of the many that he has "departed" from error toward the truth of real faith. But he truly knows himself not to be mad—as they say—but rather to be liberated from the unstable and shifting corruption found in the various forms of error, through the simple Truth that is always the same and remains as it is.

<margin>
92.
Perhaps: to have.
</margin>
The saints have become good, lovers of humanity, kind-hearted, and merciful. They possess a single disposition of love toward the entire human race. Through this love, they have held fast throughout their lives to that most excellent form of all goods—I mean **humility**. This humility is the guardian of good things and the destroyer of their opposites. Thus, the saints have not been captured by any of the troubling temptations, whether they be voluntary (within our power of reason) or involuntary (beyond our control). They wither the uprisings of the former through self-control <term>enkrateia</term>, and they shake off the attacks of the latter through patience <term>hypomone</term>.

<margin>
93.
</margin>
Right faith and pure fear of God produce the **perfect practice** of virtue. A firm hope and an uncorrupted understanding produce **natural contemplation** <term>physike theoria</term>, which is the stumble-free ascent of the mind. Finally, perfect love and a mind entirely and voluntarily filled with the things that are—by way of transcendence—produce **deification** <term>theosis</term> during the soul's assumption.

<page-num>316</page-num>
<header>OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS</header>

...yes, they say, to establish the mind <term>nous: the highest faculty of the human soul, meant for direct contemplation of God</term> as pure from every passionate imagination. In terms of natural contemplation <term>theoria: spiritual insight into the inner meaning of creation</term>, one must show the mind to be a knowledgeable master of the true understanding of all things according to the cause by which they exist. Finally, through theological mystagogy <note>original: "θεολογικῆς μυσταγωγίας" — instruction into the divine mysteries</note>, one is made like unto God and His equal, as far as is attainable by grace, so that one no longer perceives anything at all that comes after God, due to His surpassing excellence.

<margin>95.</margin>
What aether—that is, the element of fire—is in the world of the senses, prudence <term>phronesis: practical wisdom or discernment</term> is in the world of the mind. It is an illuminating habit, demonstrating the specific spiritual principles <note>original: "λόγων" (logoi) — the divine blueprints or inner essences of things</note> of each being, revealing through them the unerring Cause within all things, and drawing the soul’s desire toward the Divine. And what air is in the sensible world, courage is in the world of the mind; it is a habit of movement, both sustaining and activating the innate life according to the spirit, and strengthening the soul's perpetual movement toward the Divine. What water is in the sensible world, temperance <term>sophrosyne: self-control or "sound-mindedness"</term> is in the world of the mind; it is a habit that produces vital fertility in the spirit and generates that unsparing, erotic enchantment for divine desire. And what earth is in the sensible world, justice is in the world of the mind; it is a habit that generates the forms of all the principles in existing things, distributing to each its equal share of vital life in the spirit, and serving as the unshakeable foundation for one's proper place in the Good.

<margin>96.</margin>
Just as when the flesh is healthy and grows fat, the soul is tormented and darkened—since the habit of the virtues and the illumination of knowledge withdraw—so also when the soul is guarded and made radiant by the divine beauty of the virtues and the illumination of knowledge, the "outer man" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:16</note> is wasted away, as the flesh loses its natural vigor because of the desire of the Word <term>Logos: both the Divine Reason and the Person of Christ</term>.

<margin>97.</margin>
It was not possible for a man to be shown as a Son of God and a "god" according to deification <term>theosis: the process of becoming like God through union with Him</term> by grace, without first

<column-break/>

being born in the spirit by his own choice, through the self-moving and free power naturally present in him. This is a certain god-making, divine, and immaterial birth. But the first man, by preferring sensory pleasure and what is currently obvious over the intelligible and as-yet-unseen goods, neglected this birth; he was consequently condemned to have a material and perishable birth from bodies, which is outside of one's own choice.

<margin>98.</margin>
Man is now moved either by the irrational imaginations of the passions through the deception of pleasure; or by the principles of the arts and crafts out of the necessity of circumstance; or by the natural laws of nature for the sake of learning. None of these things originally drew man by necessity, for he was rightly placed above them all. For it was fitting that the man from the beginning should not be distracted by anything at all that came after him, or around him, or within him; rather, for his perfection, he needed only one thing: an unhindered movement of his entire power of love toward the One who was above him—I mean, toward God.

<margin>99.</margin>
The first man had nothing placed between God and himself for the sake of knowledge, nothing to hinder that kinship which was to be achieved through the self-chosen movement of love toward God. For being dispassionate <term>apathes: free from the compulsive grip of the passions</term> by grace, he was not led away by the deception of passionate imagination through pleasure; and being without need, he was free from the situational necessity of the arts and crafts; and being wise in the contemplation of nature, he stood above it through knowledge.

<margin>100.</margin>
God, who established all nature with wisdom and secretly placed the knowledge of Himself within the power of every rational being, also gave to us humans—as a most generous Master—a natural longing and love <term>eros</term> for Him. He naturally joined to this the power of reason <term>logos</term>, so that we might be able to know with ease the ways to fulfill that longing, and that we might not stumble and miss the goal for which we struggle. Moved according to this longing, we are led to seek and to manage our lives so that we might obtain that One for whose sake we received the longing in the first place.

#### A BRIEF EXPLANATION ADDRESSED TO A CERTAIN LOVER OF CHRIST

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'A' at the beginning of the text, flanked by four small star-shaped decorative elements.</image-desc>

I have received my God-guarded master himself, arriving through his most laudable letters; he who is always present, and is by no means able to be absent in spirit. Nevertheless, through an abundance of virtue, you have sought in a God-like manner to be with your own servants, and you do not reject the opportunity which God has given to our nature. Therefore, marvelling at the greatness of his condescension <note>original: "συγκαταβάσεως" (synkatabasis) — a term often used for God’s "stooping down" to human level, here applied to the patron's humility</note>, I have fashioned my fear toward him as something mixed with longing. And from both of these, fear and longing, I have established a single love, composed of reverence and goodwill. This was done so that fear, stripped of longing, might not become hatred, nor longing, without the attachment of sober fear, become contempt. Instead, let love be shown to be a law, indwelling in affection, making its own everything that is naturally related. Through goodwill, it masters hatred; through reverence, it puts contempt far away. This very fear, which I say is most of all the constitutive element of divine love, the blessed David recognized when he said: **"The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever."** <note>original: "Ὁ φόβος Κυρίου ἁγνὸς διαμένων εἰς αἰῶνα αἰῶνος" — Psalm 18:10 in the Septuagint / 19:9 in English Bibles</note> He clearly knew this fear to be different from the fear established by the dread of punishment for crimes. For the latter is cast out, completely vanishing by the presence of love, as the great Evangelist John shows in his own words, saying: **"Love casts out fear."** <note>1 John 4:18</note> But the former fear naturally characterizes the law of true affection; in reverence it preserves for the ages 
<margin>*perhaps: for the saints.</margin>
the * saints, and toward God and one another, it keeps the ordinance and manner of love

<column-break/>

completely indifferent <note>original: "ἀδιάφορον" — here meaning impartial or unchanging</note>. Therefore, having also myself mixed fear with longing, as I said, I have established this law of love toward my master until today. By reverence I was prevented from writing, lest contempt find a place. But by goodwill I was pushed toward writing, lest the complete refusal to write be considered hatred. I write this because I am commanded to do so, not as much as I myself reason, but as much as God wills, and gives by grace for the 
<margin>*perhaps: knowledge</margin>
emergence of * what is profitable. "For the counsel of the Lord," says David, "remains forever, the thoughts of His heart to generation and generation." <note>Psalm 32:11 Septuagint / 33:11 English</note> He perhaps calls "counsel" of God the Father the ineffable emptying <term>kenosis: the self-emptying of Christ in the Incarnation</term> of the only-begotten Son for the divinization <term>theosis: the process of a human being becoming "god-like" through union with God's grace</term> of our nature, according to which He holds the limit of all the ages circumscribed. And he calls "thoughts of His heart" the principles of providence and of judgment <note>original: "προνοίας, καὶ τῆς κρίσεως λόγους" — the divine logic behind God's care for the world (providence) and His right ordering of it (judgment)</note>; according to these, He wisely conducts both our present life and the future, as if they were different generations, assigning to each the fitting manner of activity accordingly. If, then, the work of the divine counsel is the divinization of our nature, and the goal of the divine thoughts is the conduction of the requirements of our life toward the end, then it is surely profitable to know and to practice—and thus duly to write—the power of the Lord's Prayer. <header>OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS</header>

...Lord. May He open my mind to understand the mysteries contained within [the Prayer], and grant me a word proportionate to the clarity of the things understood. For the Prayer possesses, in its very description, the entire mystical purpose hidden within it; or, to speak more precisely, it is openly proclaimed to those who are strong in mind. For everything that the Word of God—having emptied Himself <note>A reference to "kenosis," the doctrine of Christ "emptying" Himself of divine status to become human (Philippians 2:7).</note>—achieved in the flesh, the word of the Prayer contains as a petition. It teaches us to seek after those goods of which God the Father alone is the provider, through the Son acting naturally as mediator in the Holy Spirit. For indeed, according to the divine Apostle, the Lord Jesus is the "mediator between God and men." To men, He makes the unknown Father manifest through the flesh; to the Father, He brings men—now reconciled—through the Spirit in Himself. For their sake and on their behalf, He became man without change, becoming the author and teacher of new mysteries so numerous and great that no word has yet been able to encompass their measure. Out of these, He has clearly gifted seven general mysteries to humanity by a special act of generosity. The purpose of the Prayer mystically contains the power of these seven, as I have said: **theology**, **adoption** by grace, **equality of honor** with the Angels, **participation** in eternal life, the **restoration** of a nature that inclines passionlessly toward itself, the **abolition** of the law of sin, and the **overthrow** of the tyranny of the evil one who mastered us through deception. Let us, therefore, consider the truth of what has been said. For the Word of God, in becoming flesh, teaches **theology** <note>original: "θεολογίαν" — In early Christian writing, "theology" specifically meant the knowledge of the Holy Trinity (the inner life of God), distinct from "economy" (God’s actions in history).</note>, as He reveals in Himself both the Father and the Holy Spirit. For the whole Father and the whole Holy Spirit were essentially and perfectly in the whole Son, even when He was made flesh. They were not themselves made flesh, but the Father gave His good pleasure and the Spirit cooperated as the Son Himself brought about the incarnation—if indeed the Word remained mindful and living, contained essentially by no other at all except the Father and the Spirit, while forming a union according to His person with the flesh out of His love for mankind. He grants **adoption** by bestowing from above that supernatural birth in grace through the Spirit, and **divinization** <note>original: "σύνθεωσιν" (syntheosis) — the process of a human being becoming "god-like" through union with God.</note>. The protection and preservation of this state in God depends on the **will** <note>original: "προαίρεσις" (proairesis) — deliberate choice or moral disposition.</note> of those who are born...

<column-break/>

...loving the grace given with a genuine disposition, and through the practice of the commandments, carefully beautifying the loveliness given by grace. One is transformed into divinity <note>original: "θεότητος" — refers to theosis, the goal of the Christian life.</note> by the emptying out of the passions to the same degree that the Word of God, through His own will, economically emptied Himself of His own pure glory and, becoming truly man, was so named. He has made men **equal in honor with the Angels**, not only because He "made peace through the blood of His cross between things in heaven and things on earth," and abolished the opposing powers that filled the space between heaven and earth—thereby revealing a single festival for the preservation of divine gifts for both earthly and heavenly powers, as human nature resounds together with the powers above in the glory of God with one and the same will—but also because, after the completion of the divine plan for us, He was taken up with the body He had assumed. He united heaven and earth through Himself, joined sensible things to intelligible things, and showed that created nature is one, bound to itself at its furthest reaches through virtue and the knowledge of the First Cause. He shows, I believe, through the mysteries He performed, that the **Logos** <note>original: "λόγος" — the Divine Reason or Word of God.</note> is the union of things that are divided, while **unreason** <note>original: "ἀλογία" (alogia) — literally "without-logos," meaning folly or the lack of divine reason.</note> is the division of things that are united. Let us, then, learn to be transformed by the Logos through our actions, so that we may be united not only with the Angels through virtue, but also with God through the knowledge that comes from stripping away created things. He grants **participation in divine life** by making Himself edible—as He Himself knows, and as those who have received such a mental perception from Him know—so that by the taste of this food, they may truly know through experience that "Christ is the Lord," mixing those who eat with His divine quality for the sake of divinization, since He clearly is and is called the Bread of life and power. He **restores nature** to itself, not only because in becoming man He kept His will passionless and undisturbed toward nature—even toward those who crucified Him, not allowing His natural foundation to be shaken at all, but rather choosing death for their sake instead of life—just as the voluntariness of His passion...

He explains that Christ's incarnation serves as the mechanism for humans to achieve equality with angels and union with God (theosis).</summary>

<page-num>319</page-num>
<header>ON THE PRAYER OF THE OUR FATHER</header>

...is shown by the compassionate disposition of the One who suffered, being confirmed. Not only that, but He also abolished the enmity, nailing the record of sin to the cross, through which nature was at a relentless war with itself. He called those who were "far off" and those who were "near"—meaning those under the Law and those outside the Law—and He broke down the middle wall of the fence, clarifying the law of the commandments through His teachings. Thus, He created the two into one new man, making peace and reconciling us through Himself to the Father and to one another; our will no longer stands in opposition to the principle of our nature, but just as our nature is unchanging, so too our will remains steadfast in good.

He establishes our nature as pure from the law of sin, for He did not allow pleasure to precede His incarnation for our sake. For His conception was miraculously without seed, and His birth was incorruptible, beyond the laws of nature. Indeed, the God who was born tightened the bonds of His mother’s virginity through the birth even more than nature would allow. In this way, He frees all of nature from the power of the law that had mastered it, at least in those who are willing—those who imitate His own voluntary death through the mortification of their earthly members according to the senses. For the mystery of salvation belongs to those who *will* it, not to those who are forced by tyranny.

He brings about the destruction of the tyranny of the evil one, who mastered us through deception. He took the very flesh that was defeated in Adam and put it forward as a weapon against the enemy, thereby conquering him. He did this to show that the flesh, which had previously been led toward death, could now capture the one who had captured it, destroying his life through a natural death. This death became a <note>The image here is that Christ's humanity acts as a "bait" on the "hook" of His divinity, poisoning the devil when he tries to swallow Him.</note> poison to the enemy, forcing him to vomit out all those whom he had the power to swallow because he held the dominion of death. Yet to the human race, this death became life, pushing the whole of nature toward the resurrection of life, like a lump of dough. It was for this purpose above all that the Word, being God, became man (a truly strange thing to see and hear!) and willingly accepted the death of the flesh.

The text of the Prayer, as I have said, will be found to contain a petition for all these things. For it speaks of a "Father," and the "Name" of the Father, and a "Kingdom." It presents the one who prays as a "Son" of this Father by grace. It seeks that the will of the heavenly and earthly beings should become one.

<column-break/>

It commands us to ask for <term>daily bread</term> <note>original: "epiousios." In Greek, this term refers to bread that is "sufficient for existence" or "supersubstantial," pointing toward the Eucharist.</note>. It legislates reconciliation among men, and by the act of "forgiving and being forgiven," it binds nature back to itself, so that it is no longer severed by a divided will. It teaches us to pray against entering into temptation, which is the "law of sin," and it exhorts us to be delivered from the evil one. 

For it was necessary that the Author and Giver of all good things should also be the Teacher. To those who believe in Him as disciples and who imitate His conduct in the flesh, He provides the words of this prayer as instructions for life. Through these words, He revealed the "hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge" <note>A reference to Colossians 2:3.</note> that exist within Him, driving the desire of those who ask toward the actual enjoyment of those treasures.

For this reason, I believe the Word has called this teaching a "prayer," as it contains a petition for the gifts given to men by God according to grace. Our divinely inspired fathers have defined "prayer" in this way, stating that <term>prayer</term> <note>original: "proseuche."</note> is a petition for those things which God is naturally inclined to grant to men in a fitting manner. In the same way, they defined a <term>vow</term> <note>original: "euche." In the original Greek, this word carries a double meaning of "prayer" and "solemn promise."</note> as a pledge or a promise of things which men offer to God while worshiping Him sincerely. They presented Scripture as a witness to this distinction in many ways, such as: "Make vows and pay them to the Lord our God," and "I will pay to the Lord the vows I have made." These refer to the "vow." 

Regarding "prayer," they cite: "And Hannah prayed to the Lord, saying: 'O Lord <term>Adonai</term>, <term>Eloi</term> <term>Sabaoth</term> <note>Maximus retains the Hebrew names for God found in the Greek Bible: Lord, My God, of Hosts.</note>, if You will indeed look upon Your maidservant and give me the fruit of my womb.'" Also, "Hezekiah the king of Judah and Isaiah the son of Amoz the prophet prayed to the Lord," and the verse spoken by the Lord to His disciples: "When you pray, say: 'Our Father who art in the heavens.'"

Thus, a **vow** is the keeping of the commandments, confirmed by the resolve of the one who made the vow. **Prayer**, on the other hand, is a petition for the transformation of the one who kept the commandments into the likeness of the good things he has preserved. Or rather: the vow is the *contest* of virtue, which God receives most lovingly when it is offered; but prayer is the *prize* of virtue, which God gives in return with great joy. Therefore, since it has been shown that the Prayer is a petition for the goods provided by the Word made flesh, let us look to the Word Himself...

<summary>Maximus explains how Christ's incarnation and death reconciled human nature and liberated the will from the "tyrant" of sin. He then defines the Lord's Prayer as a petition for these divine gifts, distinguishing between a "vow" (man's effort to keep commandments) and "prayer" (man's request for God's grace).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Maximus the Confessor's theological exposition of the Lord's Prayer. Having established Christ's role in reconciling human nature, Maximus now begins a phrase-by-phrase commentary on the prayer itself, focusing on the first three petitions: the invocation of the Father, the hallowing of the Name, and the coming of the Kingdom.</meta>

<page-num>320</page-num>
<header>BY OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS</header>

Having established the Teacher of the word of prayer, let us approach with confidence, diligently exercising the meaning of each phrase through <term>contemplation<note>original: "theoria" — a deep, spiritual insight or vision that looks beyond the literal surface of the text to its divine reality.</note></term> as far as we are able, just as the Word himself is accustomed to provide what is beneficial and grants power to the mind of the speaker.

<margin>The Text.</margin>
> "Our Father who art in heaven;
> hallowed be thy name;
> thy kingdom come."

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
The Lord immediately teaches those who approach him to begin with <term>theology<note>In this historical context, "theology" specifically refers to the knowledge of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—rather than religious study in general.</note></term> as is fitting. He initiates them into the mystery of how the creative Cause of all things exists, being himself the essential Cause of all beings. For the words of the prayer contain a revelation of the Father, the Name of the Father, and the Kingdom of the Father. Thus, from the very beginning, we are taught to revere, invoke, and worship the <term>Monadic Trinity<note>The concept that God is one single Essence (Monad) existing as three Persons (Trinity).</note></term>. For the Name of God the Father, existing in essence, is the Only-begotten Son. And the Kingdom of God the Father, existing in essence, is the Holy Spirit. Indeed, what Matthew calls the "Kingdom" here, another of the Evangelists elsewhere calls the "Holy Spirit," saying, "Let thy Holy Spirit come and cleanse us." For the Father does not possess the Name as something acquired, nor do we perceive the Kingdom as a dignity merely attributed to him. He did not begin to exist such that he only then began to be "Father" or "King"; rather, as he is eternal, he is eternally Father and King, never having begun to exist, nor ever having begun to be Father or King. But if he is eternally Father and King, then the Son and the Holy Spirit have always co-existed essentially with the Father; they are from him and naturally in him, beyond cause and reason, but not *after* him as if they were created later for some reason. For the relationship between them carries a power of mutual indication; the relations by which they are known do not allow them to be perceived as coming one after another. Having <margin>In others it is read [thus].</margin> begun the prayer with this, we are urged to honor the <term>consubstantial<note>Sharing the same "substance" or "essence"; a core concept of the Nicene Creed.</note></term> and beyond-essential Trinity as the creative cause of our own coming-into-being. Moreover, we are taught to proclaim the grace of adoption granted to us, as we are deemed worthy to call our Creator by nature "Father" by grace. This is so that, out of reverence for the title of our Begetter by grace, we may strive to imprint the characteristics 

<column-break/>

of the one who begot us upon our lives. By hallowing his name on earth and acting as our Father does, we show ourselves to be his children through our deeds, magnifying the Son—the Father’s natural Son who is the author of this adoption—through everything we think or do. We "hallow" the name of our Father-by-grace who is in heaven by putting to death our earth-bound desires and cleansing ourselves of soul-destroying passions. For "hallowing" (sanctification) is the total stillness and death of the desires of the senses. Once we have reached this state, we soothe the unseemly <margin>* Perhaps: "not having."</margin> barking of our <term>anger<note>original: "thymos" — the "incensive" or spirited part of the soul, often associated with righteous indignation or, when disordered, with rage.</note></term>; we no longer have * anything to stir it up, for desire—which used to persuade anger to fight on behalf of its own pleasures—has already been put to death by the holiness according to the Word. By nature, anger acts as the "avenger" of desire, and it naturally ceases its madness whenever it sees that desire has been killed. It is logical, then, that through the rejection of anger and desire, the power of the Kingdom of God the Father follows in the prayer for those who have been deemed worthy to say,

<margin>Text.</margin>
> "Thy kingdom come."

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
That is to say, "Let the Holy Spirit come." For those who have been made into a temple for God through the Spirit by the reason and way of "meekness" have already become such a kingdom. For upon whom, He says, shall I rest? "But upon the one who is meek and humble, and who trembles at my words." From this it is clear that the Kingdom of God the Father belongs to the humble and the meek. For "Blessed are the meek," He says, "for they shall inherit the earth." God did not promise that those who love him would inherit this physical earth which occupies the center of the universe by nature—if it is true that he says, "For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven." And "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." And elsewhere to another who served with good will, "Enter into the joy of your Lord." And after him, the divine Apostle says: "For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead in Christ shall rise first incorruptible; then we who are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." These things being so...

<summary>Maximus explains that the opening of the Lord's Prayer is an initiation into the mystery of the Trinity, where "Name" refers to the Son and "Kingdom" to the Holy Spirit. He argues that hallowing God's name requires the moral purification of the soul, specifically the "mortification" of desire and anger to make room for the Holy Spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Theology, Trinity, Lord's Prayer, Holy Spirit, Adoption, Sanctification, Meekness, Exegesis, Maximus the Confessor</keywords>

--- Page 331 ---
<meta>This page continues Maximus the Confessor’s commentary on the Lord’s Prayer, specifically examining the petition "Thy kingdom come." He is transitioning from the theological definition of the Kingdom as the Holy Spirit to the practical and ethical implications of how a believer "inherits the earth."</meta>

<page-num>321</page-num>
<header>ON THE PRAYER OF THE OUR FATHER</header>

...promised to those who love the Lord. Who, by fixing the mind only on the literal word of the scripture, would say that heaven—the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world, the joy of the Lord hidden in mystery, and the perpetual, completely inseparable dwelling and establishment of the worthy with the Lord—is the same as the "earth," if they were moved by reason and desired to be a servant of the Word? 

But now, I think "earth" refers to the stable and completely unchangeable <term>habit<note>original: "hexis" — a settled state of character or a permanent disposition of the soul acquired through practice.</note></term> and power of the <term>meek<note>original: "praeis" — those possessing "praotes" or meekness, which in Greek philosophy and theology is the middle point between excessive anger and passivity.</note></term>, which remains unshaken from the Good. This state exists forever with the Lord, possessing unfailing joy, taking hold of the kingdom prepared from the beginning, and being deemed worthy of the station and rank found in heaven. This "earth" occupies a middle position within the whole scheme of virtue; for the meek person, standing in the middle between praise and blame, remains <term>impassible<note>original: "apathes" — not "unfeeling," but free from the control of reactive passions like rage or pride.</note></term>, neither puffed up by praises nor saddened by insults. 

For the Word, being naturally free, has set aside its craving; it does not feel these things when they disturb with their attacks, having brought itself to rest from the storm of such things, and having moved the entire power of the soul toward divine and tranquil freedom. Desiring to share this with his own disciples, the Lord says:

> Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.

By "rest," he means the power of the Divine Kingdom, which provides sovereign mastery to the worthy, having been freed from all slavery. If the indestructible power of the pure Kingdom is given to the humble and the meek, who would be so unloving and so entirely without desire for divine goods as not to long for the heights of humility and meekness, so that they might become, as far as is possible for a human, the "imprint" of the Divine Kingdom? By carrying within themselves the likeness of Christ, the truly great King by nature and essence, they receive through grace the unchanging form of the Spirit. In this state, says the divine Apostle:

> There is neither male nor female.

That is to say, there is no longer <term>anger<note>original: "thymos" — the "incensive" or spirited part of the soul often associated with masculine aggression.</note></term> or <term>desire<note>original: "epithymia" — the "appetitive" part of the soul associated with feminine longing or physical want.</note></term>. The former (anger) tyrannically carries away the reason and drives the intellect outside the law of nature. The latter (desire) makes things that are secondary to the one and only Desirable and Impassible Cause appear more 

<column-break/>

lovely, and because of this, sets the flesh as more precious than the spirit, making the enjoyment of visible things more delightful than the glory and splendor of the intelligible. Through the smoothness of sensory pleasure, it bars the mind from its kindred divine perception of spiritual realities. 

But when reason is solitary—stripped of affection and disposition even for the most extreme, yet natural, needs of the body through the abundance of virtue—the spirit completely conquers nature. It persuades the mind to cease from <term>moral philosophy<note>In Maximus's scheme, "moral philosophy" is the first stage of the spiritual life (practicé), which eventually gives way to higher "contemplation" (theoria).</note></term> when it is necessary to be with the <term>Supersubstantial Word<note>original: "hyperousios Logos" — the Word who exists beyond all categories of being or essence.</note></term> through simple and indivisible contemplation. Even if the mind is naturally suited to help navigate the easy honor and passage through things that flow with time, it is not reasonable, once these things have been passed, for a person who has been declared unrestrained by sensory things to be "clothed" in the moral way of life, as if with a <term>sheepskin<note>original: "melote" — a rough cloak of sheepskin, the traditional garment of prophets like Elijah, symbolizing asceticism and the mortification of the flesh.</note></term>.

Elijah the Great clearly shows this, demonstrating this mystery through his actions as a type. I speak of the "sheepskin" as the mortification of the flesh, in which the magnificence of moral decency is fixed. In his "ascent," he gave this to Elisha as an ally of the Spirit against every opposing power, and as a weapon to strike the unstable and flowing nature—of which the Jordan was a type—so that the disciple would not be held back from the passage to the Holy Land, being washed away by the muddy and slippery attachment to material things. 

Elijah himself, however, proceeds toward God, unhindered and held by no relationship to any existing thing at all. Simple in his desire and uncompounded in his judgment, he makes his dwelling with the One who is simple by nature, through the interconnected general virtues which are joined to one another through knowledge like "horses of fire." For he knew that the disciple of Christ must strip away those unequal dispositions whose differences prove a state of alienation. For the longing of desire is a "dilating" of the blood around the heart, while the incensive power (anger) clearly causes a "boiling" of the blood. Having already arrived at a state of living and moving and being in Christ, he put off the birth of unequal and strange dispositions within himself. He no longer carries within himself "male and female"—the contrary dispositions of these passions, as I said—so that the Word might not be enslaved, being altered by their unstable changes.

He uses the figures of Elijah and Elisha to illustrate how the believer must transcend the "male and female" passions of anger and desire to achieve spiritual freedom.</summary>

<page-num>322</page-num>
<header>OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, MAXIMUS</header>

Naturally, the reverence for the divine image has been blended into us, persuading the soul to be reshaped according to its <term>disposition<note>original: "gnome" — the deliberate choice or intent of the soul, which Maximus sees as central to our transformation.</note></term> toward the divine likeness. Thus, it becomes a radiant dwelling of the Holy Spirit—the great kingdom that essentially co-exists with God and the Father of all things—receiving, if it is permissible to say, the whole authority of knowledge of the divine nature as far as is possible. By this knowledge, the birth of worse things naturally ceases, and the existence of better things begins; the soul becomes equal to God through the grace of its calling, keeping within itself the <term>subsistence<note>original: "hypostasis" — the concrete reality or personhood of the spiritual gifts.</note></term> of the beautiful gifts bestowed upon it, never to be plundered. In this soul, Christ is always willing to be born mystically, becoming incarnate through those who are being saved. He makes the soul that gives birth to Him a Virgin Mother, which—to speak briefly—does not possess, in terms of its relationship, the characteristics of a nature subject to corruption and birth, such as "male and female." Let no one be startled to hear "corruption" associated with "birth" <note>Maximus is arguing that physical birth is tied to our fallen, corruptible state, whereas spiritual birth is beyond these categories.</note>. For if one examines the nature of things that come into being and pass away dispassionately and with right reason, they will clearly find that birth begins from corruption and ends in corruption. Christ does not possess the defining <term>passions<note>original: "pathe" — reactive states or sufferings inherent to physical, mortal life.</note></term> of such a birth; or rather, neither the life nor the word of Christ, and those who live according to Christ, possess them. For he who speaks is true: "In Christ Jesus, there is neither male nor female" <note>A reference to Galatians 3:28.</note>, meaning he is showing the signs and the passions of a nature subject to corruption and birth. Instead, there is only the godlike <term>Reason<note>original: "Logos."</note></term> shaped by divine knowledge, and the single movement of a will that chooses virtue alone. Neither is there "Greek and Jew," by which the differing—or more truly, the opposing—definitions of the glory of God are signified. The one [the Greek] profusely introduces a "rule by many" <note>original: "polyarchia" — polytheism.</note>, dividing the single Principle into opposing activities and powers, and fashioning a polytheistic worship that is both factious because of the multitude of those worshipped and ridiculous because of the differing ways they are worshipped. The other [the Jew] introduces a single principle, but one that is narrow, incomplete, and almost <term>without subsistence<note>original: "anypostaton" — lacking a personal reality.</note></term>, as if it were deserted by Reason and Life. Through these opposites, this view falls into an evil equal to the first: atheism. It circumscribes the single Principle within a single person, existing either without Reason <note>The "Word" or "Logos".</note> and Spirit, or merely being qualified by Reason and Spirit <note>i.e., treating the Word and Spirit as attributes rather than distinct Persons.</note>. Such a view fails to see that...

<column-break/>

...what kind of God would be deprived of these? Or how could He be God if He shared in them in a manner similar to created and rational beings, as if He were allotted these things as <term>accidents<note>original: "symbebekoton" — in philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing may or may not have, without losing its core identity. Maximus argues the Word and Spirit are not just "properties" of God.</note></term>? None of these things, as I said, exist at all in Christ. There is only the word of true godliness and the stable decree of mystical Theology, which rejects the "expansion" <note>The polytheistic scattering of the divine.</note> of the godhead in the first view, and does not accept the "contraction" <note>The unitarian reduction of the divine.</note> of the second. This is so that the faith is not turbulent due to a "natural multiplicity"—for that is the Greek way—nor is it <term>passive<note>original: "patheton."</note></term> due to a "personal singularity"—for that is the Jewish way, since it is either deprived of Reason and Spirit or merely "qualified" by them. But the Divine is revered as being Mind, Reason, and Spirit. It teaches us, who have been adopted through the calling of grace by faith into the full knowledge of the truth, to know one nature and power of the Godhead: that is, one God contemplated in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is the only uncaused Mind, existing essentially, the only Begetter of the essentially existing, beginningless Reason, and the Source of the only eternal, essentially existing Life, which is the Holy Spirit. There is a Trinity in Unity and a Unity in Trinity—not "one and another" <margin>* perhaps: in another</margin>. For the Trinity is not an "accident" within the Unity as if in a substance; nor, conversely, is the Unity in the Trinity. For He is without quality. Nor is it as "one thing and another" [of different kinds]. For the Unity does not differ from the Trinity by a difference of nature, since it happens to be a simple and single nature. Nor is it as "one alongside another." For the Trinity is not distinguished from the Unity, nor the Unity from the Trinity, by a decrease in power. Nor is it as something common and "general" <note>Like the category "Human" compared to individual people.</note> that is only contemplated in the mind as being above its "particular" parts. For the Unity is a truly self-subsistent essence and a truly self-powerful strength. Nor is it as "one through another." For the Trinity is not by derivation from a Unity, but exists unbegotten and self-manifesting. Rather, the very same is truly called and understood as both Unity and Trinity: the former according to the definition of its essence, the latter according to its mode of existence. The very same is a whole Unity, not divided by the <term>Persons<note>original: "hypostases."</note></term>, and the very same is a whole Trinity, not confused with the Unity. This is so that "polytheism" is not introduced by division, nor "atheism" by confusion. Fleeing these, the word according to Christ shines forth—and by the "word of Christ," I mean the new proclamation of the truth, in which there is no male and...

# ON THE PRAYER OF THE OUR FATHER

...female—I mean the signs and passions of a nature subject to corruption and birth. There is neither **Greek nor Jew**, which are opposing arguments regarding divinity. There is no **circumcision and uncircumcision**; these are the corresponding forms of worship. The one, through the symbols of the Law, speaks ill of visible creation and slanders the Creator as a maker of evils; the other, through its passions, treats creation as a god and sets the creature against its Creator. Both, in equal measure, gather divine insults against one another. There is no **Barbarian and Scythian**—that is, the internal rebellion of a single nature caused by a fragmented <term>will<note>original: "gnome"—referring to the personal, deliberative will that often deviates from the natural purpose of humanity.</note></term>, through which the unnatural law of mutual slaughter was introduced to humans. Nor is there **slave and free**, which is a division of the same nature occurring against our true purpose, treating as dishonorable one who is of equal honor by nature. This division relies on a law that supports the tyrants who trample the dignity of the divine image through their domineering <term>disposition<note>original: "diathesis"—the inward state or attitude of the masters.</note></term>. Instead, **Christ is all and in all**, creating—through things that transcend nature and law—a formation in the Spirit of the beginningless kingdom. As has been demonstrated, this kingdom is naturally characterized by **humility of heart and gentleness**. The union of these two reveals the perfect person who is being created according to Christ. For every humble-minded person is certainly also gentle, and every gentle person is certainly also humble-minded. One is humble-minded because they realize their very existence is "borrowed." One is gentle because they have discerned how to use the powers given to them according to nature. Such a person offers the service of these powers to the <term>Word<note>original: "Logos"—the divine Reason or Christ Himself.</note></term> for the production of virtue, while completely restraining the activity of the senses. Because of this, while their mind is constantly moving toward God, they do not experience the painful things that happen to the body. They are not moved by them, nor do they leave a trace of grief in the soul that might change its joyful state. Such a person does not consider physical pain to be a deprivation of pleasure. For they know only one pleasure: the soul’s <term>living together<note>original: "symbiosis"—a deep, shared life or union.</note></term> with the Word. To be deprived of this is unending punishment, which naturally encompasses all ages. Therefore, leaving behind the body and all things belonging to the body, they are carried swiftly toward that divine union. They consider it the only loss—even if they were to rule over everything on

<column-break/>

earth—to fail to achieve the expected <term>deification<note>original: "theosis"—the process of becoming like God through grace.</note></term> by grace. Let us, therefore, cleanse ourselves of every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that we may hallow the divine name. We must quench that desire which unbecomingly torments us with passions, and through reason, let us subdue that anger which rages in a disordered way after pleasures. Thus, through gentleness, we may receive the coming of the kingdom of God the Father, and we may join the next words of the prayer to the preceding ones, saying: **“Thy will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.”**

<margin>
Text.
Exposition.
</margin>

The person who offers worship to God through the <term>rational power<note>original: "logike dynamis"—the faculty of the soul responsible for reason and spiritual perception.</note></term> alone—mysteriously separated from both desire and anger—has fulfilled the divine will on earth just as the ranks of Angels do in heaven. Through all things, such a person becomes a fellow-worshiper and companion to the Angels, just as the Great Apostle says: ***But our citizenship is in heaven***. Among the Angels, there is no desire that dissolves the spiritual strength through pleasure, nor is there a raging anger that snarls at its own kind. Instead, there is only the <term>Word<note>original: "Logos"</note></term>, which naturally leads rational beings toward the First Word. This is the only thing God delights in and asks of us, His servants. He revealed this to the Great David, saying: ***For what do I have in heaven, and what have I desired from You upon the earth?*** Nothing is offered to God in heaven by the Holy Angels except this rational worship; this is exactly what He seeks from us, teaching us to say when we pray: *Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.* Therefore, let our reason be moved to seek God, let our power of desire be moved toward longing for Him, and let our <term>incensive power<note>original: "thymikon"—the faculty of the soul often associated with anger, which Maximus believes should be redirected as a protective force for virtue.</note></term> struggle to guard Him. Or rather, to speak more precisely, let the whole mind be stretched toward God, strengthened as if by a certain tension by the "incensive" faculty, and set on fire by the longing of the highest desire. In this way, by imitating the Angels in heaven, we shall be found always worshiping God, displaying the same way of life as the Angels while on earth. For just like them, we will have a mind that is not moved at all toward anything other than God. For if we live this way, we shall receive through our prayers "daily bread"...

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...and life-giving for the nourishment of our souls, and the preservation of the well-being of the good things granted to us, the Word who said, *“I am the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world,”* becomes everything in proportion to us who are nourished through virtue and wisdom. He is embodied in various ways in each of those being saved—as He alone knows—while we still exist in this present age, according to the power of the phrase in the prayer which says:

<margin>Text</margin>
<margin>Explanation</margin>
“**Give us today our <term>daily bread<note>original: "epiousios"—a famously difficult Greek word. While often translated as "daily," Maximus and other Church Fathers often interpreted it as "bread for the essence" or "super-substantial bread," referring to spiritual or sacramental nourishment.</note>.**”** For I believe this present age is signified by the word “today.” As if someone, interpreting it more clearly, were to say: "In this place of prayer, give us today—while we are in this present mortal life—our bread, which You prepared at the beginning for the immortality of our nature." This is so that the nourishment of the bread of life and knowledge might conquer the death of sin. The first man was not allowed to partake of this knowledge because he transgressed the divine commandment; yet if he had been filled with this divine food, he would not have been captured by the death of sin. (However, the one who prays to receive this daily bread does not necessarily receive it in its entirety as the bread is in itself, but according to the capacity of the one receiving it. For the Bread of Life, in His love for mankind, gives to all who ask, but not to everyone in the same way. To those who have performed great deeds, He gives more; to those who have done less, He gives less. To each, then, according to what their <term>intellectual<note>original: "kata noun"—referring to the "nous" or the highest part of the human soul/mind.</note></term> worthiness is able to receive.) I was led to this understanding of the present passage by the Savior Himself, who explicitly commanded His disciples not to take any account of physical food at all, saying: *“Do not worry about your soul, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. For the nations of the world seek after all these things. But seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”* How then does He teach us to pray for things which

<margin>* perhaps: do not seek</margin>
He previously commanded us not to seek? For it is clear that He did not command us to ask through prayer for those things which He advised us not to seek through commandment. For only that which is to be sought by commandment is to be asked for through prayer. Therefore, whatever we were not permitted to seek by commandment, it is likely

<column-break/>

not permissible to ask for through prayer. Since the Savior commanded us to seek only the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, He rightly prompted those who desire divine gifts to ask for this through prayer as well. Thus, by confirming the grace of those things naturally sought through prayer, He might unite the will of those who ask with the will of the One providing the grace, making them the same through a relational union. But if we are indeed commanded to ask through prayer for that "ephemeral" bread by which our present life is naturally sustained, let us not overstep the boundaries of the prayer by greedily looking toward many cycles of years. Let us not forget that we are mortal and that our life passes by like a shadow. Instead, let us ask through prayer for bread for the day without worry, and let us show that we lead a life that is a "meditation on death" <note>Maximus refers to the ancient philosophical idea (melete thanatou) adapted for Christian asceticism: living each day as if it were one's last to remain focused on God.</note> in a way that is philosophical according to Christ. Let us anticipate nature with our will, and before death actually arrives, let us cut off the soul from the care of bodily things. This is so that the soul might not be nailed to corruptible things by turning the use of its natural desire toward matter, and so that it might not learn a greed that deprives it of the abundance of divine goods. Let us flee, as much as we are able, from the love of matter, and let us wash away its relationship like dust from our intellectual eyes. Let us be satisfied with only those things that sustain us, and not those that merely provide pleasure to our present life. Let us entreat God for these things, as we were taught, so that we may be able to keep the soul unenslaved, not being held captive at all by any of the things loved for the sake of the body. Let us be shown to eat for the sake of living, rather than being convicted of living for the sake of eating. The former is characteristic of a rational nature, while the latter is clearly the property of an irrational one. Let us be strict guardians of this prayer, showing through our very actions that we hold fast to one thing alone: the things belonging to the Spirit of life. It is clear that we make use of the present life for the sake of acquiring that Spirit, and for this reason we cherish the use of this life only so far as we do not refuse to support it with bread alone, and to preserve its natural health as much as it is within our power to keep it incorrupt. This is not so that we may simply live, but so that we may live for God—rendering the body a rational messenger of the soul through the virtues, and...

...making a herald of this by a stability fixed in goodness; and naturally confining this bread to a single day, not daring to extend the request for it to a second day because of the Giver of the prayer. And such a person knows only one pain: the failure to attain these things, of which the devil is the instigator, but of which every person is the actual worker who, through a weakness of <term>disposition<note>original: "gnome"—often translated as the "gnomic will," referring to the personal, deliberative aspect of the human will in Maximus's theology.</note>, is worn away, not guarding what is precious by a loving disposition of the mind. Having a choice that does not lean at all toward visible things, and therefore not being brought low by the painful things that happen to him bodily, such a person truly forgives those who sin against him. For no one can at all seize the good that he eagerly desires, since it is believed to be incorruptible by nature. Thus, he presents himself as an <term>exemplar<note>original: "exomplarion"—a Greek transliteration of the Latin "exemplarium."</note> of virtue to God—if it is even lawful to say this—commanding the Unimitation to come to the imitation of himself, saying: **"Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors."** He asks God to be toward him as he himself has been toward his neighbors. For if he wishes to be forgiven by God just as he has forgiven those who sinned against him, then clearly, just as God forgives dispassionately those whom He forgives, so he too, remaining dispassionate toward the things that happen to him, forgives those who have offended, not allowing his mind to be shaped by any memory of past sorrows. This is so that he might not be found standing apart from any human being while being human himself, thereby cutting through nature by his personal disposition. For only when the personal disposition is united with the <term>principle of nature<note>original: "logos tēs physeos"—the fundamental, God-given purpose and structure of a thing.</note> does God’s

It is not possible for the divine and ineffable <term>condescension<note>original: "synkatabasis"—God's act of "stepping down" to meet human capacity.</note> to be received in any other way while the personal disposition is at odds with itself. Perhaps for this reason, God wants us first to make reconciliations with one another—not so that He may learn from us how to be reconciled with sinners and forgive the payment for many and terrible crimes, but so that He might cleanse us of passions and show that the disposition of those being forgiven is in harmony with the state of grace. It has become clearly evident that once the disposition is united to the principle of nature, the choice of those who have achieved this will be without conflict toward God; for nothing irrational is naturally observed in the principle of nature, which is both a natural and divine law, when it receives the movement of the disposition working in accordance with itself. If there is nothing irrational in the principle of nature, then reasonably, the disposition moving according to the principle of nature will have its activity in harmony with God in all things. This is a practical disposition, characterized by the grace of the naturally Beautiful toward the birth of virtue. Thus is disposed the one who asks for the <term>gnostic bread<note>original: "gnostikon arton"—the "bread of knowledge" or spiritual insight.</note> while praying. After him, the one who seeks only the ephemeral bread because of the necessity of nature will be disposed in the same way, having forgiven his debtors their debts. He does this because he knows he is mortal by nature, and henceforth, expecting what is natural to happen each day because of uncertainty, he anticipates nature through his disposition, becoming a voluntary corpse to the world, according to the saying:

and because of this, he is at peace with all, so that he may carry with him no mark of the wickedness of this present age as he departs for the ageless life, and may receive from the Ruler of all the equal recompense of what he heralded here. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the "Our Father," moving from the petition for forgiveness to "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." Maximus interprets these as the final steps toward the goal of the Christian life: deification.</meta>

<page-num>326</page-num>
# OF OUR HOLY FATHER MAXIMUS

...completely forgiving those who stumble, and presenting to God a heart pure of grief, brightened by the light of reconciliation with one's neighbor, such a person will fail to obtain the grace of the good things prayed for <note>if they do not forgive</note>; and by a just judgment, they will be handed over to temptation and the evil one; so that they may learn to be purged of their offenses by having their own grievances against others removed. By **temptation**, he now means the law of sin, which the first man did not have when he came into being. By **the evil one**, he means the devil who infected human nature with this law and who, through deception, persuaded man to transfer the soul's desire from what was permitted to what was forbidden, and to turn toward the transgression of the divine commandment. The result of this was the laying aside of the incorruptibility given by grace. Or again, he says **temptation** is the soul's voluntary disposition toward the passions of the flesh, while **the evil one** is the active way of fulfilling that passionate disposition. From neither of these does the Just Judge exempt the one who does not forgive their debtors. Even if such a person asks for this purely through prayer, God permits such a person to be defiled by the law of sin and to be ruled by the evil one. He abandons the person who is hard and harsh in their <term>disposition<note>original: "gnome"—referring here to the deliberative or personal will.</note>; as they have preferred the passions of dishonor, of which the devil is the sower, over nature, of which God is the Creator. Indeed, He does not prevent such a person from voluntarily being disposed toward the passions of the flesh, nor does He rescue them from the active way of fulfilling that disposition. This is because such a person, considering nature inferior to the non-existent passions, ignored the <term>rational principle<note>original: "logos"—the underlying purpose or divine blueprint of a thing.</note> of nature through their zeal for these passions. According to this principle, one ought to have been moved to know what is the law of nature and what is the tyranny of the passions which arises according to choice through the <term>disposition<note>original: "gnomikos"—relating to the personal, choosing will rather than natural instinct.</note> but not naturally. One should then acquire the former, being preserved by natural activities, but drive the latter far from the disposition, and preserve nature through reason, standing by itself pure and blameless. Blameless, without hatred or division, and once again making the disposition a fellow-traveler with nature, bringing in absolutely nothing that the rational principle of nature does not provide; and because of this, to remove all hatred and every division from those who are kin by nature, so that when saying this...

<column-break/>

...prayer, they may be heard and receive a double grace from God instead of a single one: both the forgiveness of past offenses and protection and deliverance regarding future ones. Thus, they are not permitted to enter into temptation and are not left to be enslaved to the evil one, for the sake of one thing: readily forgiving the debts of their neighbors. Therefore, we too—to briefly go over the power of what has been said by retracing my steps a little—if we do not wish to be delivered to the evil one or to enter into temptation, let us believe in God and forgive the debts of our debtors. For He says, "If you do not forgive men their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you." This is so that we might not only receive forgiveness for what we have done wrong, but also conquer the law of sin, not being abandoned to enter into the experience of it, and so that we may trample upon the "evil serpent," its parent, from whom we pray to be delivered. For our General is Christ, who conquered the world, arming us with the laws of the commandments, and in a lawful way, through the laying aside of the passions, binding nature to itself through love. He moves our appetite insatiably toward Himself, who is the Bread of Life, Wisdom, Knowledge, and Righteousness. By the fulfillment of the Father’s will, He makes us fellow-worshippers with the Angels, manifesting through our way of life the heavenly pleasure in a way that imitates it well. From there, He leads us back again to the highest of divine ascents, to the Father of Lights, and makes us "partakers of the divine nature" through the participation in the Spirit by grace. By this grace, we are called **children of God**, carrying within us—entirely and without limit or stain—the very Author of this grace, who is the Son of the Father by nature. From Him, through Him, and in Him we have and shall have our being, our movement, and our life. Let the goal of our prayer be looking toward this <term>mystery of deification<note>original: "theosis"—the process of being made divine or union with God.</note>, so that we may know for what sort of things the <term>emptying<note>original: "kenosis"—the self-emptying of Christ in the Incarnation.</note> of the Only-begotten through the flesh has worked for us; and from where to where He has raised us up by the power of His man-loving hand—we who had taken the lowest place in the universe, into which the weight of sin had thrust us. And let us love even more the One who so wisely [gave] us this...

<summary>Maximus explains that forgiving others is the prerequisite for escaping the "law of sin" and the "evil one." The ultimate purpose of the Lord's Prayer is the "mystery of deification," where Christ leads the believer to become a child of God and a partaker of the divine nature.</summary>
<keywords>Maximus the Confessor, Lord's Prayer, temptation, theosis, deification, kenosis, forgiveness, law of sin, gnome, disposition</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes St. Maximus the Confessor’s commentary on the Lord’s Prayer, specifically focusing on the distinction between voluntary and involuntary temptation. It then transitions into a brief biographical sketch of St. Thalassius the Libyan, whose works often accompany those of Maximus in the manuscript tradition.</meta>

<page-num>327</page-num>
# ON THE PRAYER OF THE OUR FATHER

...having prepared salvation. And through our actions, let us show the prayer being fulfilled, and let us appear as those who herald God as truly being our Father by grace. Let us not, through the passions of dishonor, clearly prove ourselves to have the evil one as the father of our life—he who always attempts to rule over human nature like a tyrant. Let us not find ourselves secretly bartering away life for death, since each of these <term>principles<note>original: "proson"—referring to the inherent qualities or natures of God versus the devil.</note> is by nature inclined to share itself with those who approach it. For the one <note>God</note> provides eternal life to those who love Him, while the other <note>the devil</note> produces death in those who draw near, by suggesting voluntary temptations. For according to the Scriptures, the character of temptation is twofold. One kind is **pleasurable**, and the other is **painful**; one is **voluntary**, and the other is **involuntary**. The first is the progenitor of sin, and we are commanded to pray that we do not enter into it, according to the Lord’s teaching, when we say: **And lead us not into temptation**, and, **Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation**. The second kind is the punisher of sin, chastising the sin-loving <term>disposition<note>original: "diathesis"—the internal state or orientation of the soul.</note> by the infliction of involuntary labors. If anyone endures this second kind—especially one who is not already pierced by the nails of vice—he will hear the Great James loudly proclaiming: **Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, for the testing of your**

<column-break/>

**faith produces patience. And let patience have its perfect work.** The evil one craftily manages both of these temptations, the voluntary and the involuntary. In the first, he plots to distance the soul’s desire from divine love by sowing and stirring up the soul with the pleasures of the body. In the second, he "sophistically" <note>This refers to the devil asking God for permission to test someone, much like the Accuser in the Book of Job.</note> asks for permission to inflict pain, wishing to destroy our nature. He hopes to force the soul, when it is beaten down by the exhaustion of its labors, to turn its thoughts toward a slander of the Creator. But since we have recognized the designs of the evil one, let us shun voluntary temptation so that we do not distance our desire from divine love; and let us bravely endure involuntary temptation when it comes by God’s permission, so that we may appear to have preferred the Creator of nature over nature itself. May it be granted that all of us who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be delivered from the present pleasures of the evil one and be freed from the future pains, through the participation in the <term>reality<note>original: "hypostasis"—the underlying substance or actualization of the promised blessings.</note> of the future goods, as it has been revealed to us in Christ Himself our Lord; to Him alone, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory from all creation. Amen.

# A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
### OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER
# THALASSIUS
### THE LIBYAN AND AFRICAN

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial "T" (Theta) enclosed in a rectangular border with classical motifs.</image-desc>
Thalassius, our Holy Father, who was also a Priest and an Abbot, lived during the reign of Constantine Pogonatus <note>Constantine IV, who reigned from 668–685 AD. "Pogonatus" means "the Bearded."</note> around the year 660. He was a contemporary of Saint Maximus, who also addressed to him a collection of scriptural difficulties

<column-break/>

and their solutions. The present **four hundred chapters** <note>original: "Kephalaia"—this refers to the common Byzantine literary form of "Centuries," which are sets of 100 short aphorisms on the spiritual life.</note> which he diligently composed have been arranged here with the others, as they are a source of great spiritual benefit to those who read them.
