# OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER
# THALASSIUS
## THE LIBYAN AND AFRICAN
### ON LOVE, SELF-CONTROL, AND THE DISCIPLINE OF THE INTELLECT,
### TO PAUL THE PRESBYTER.

---

## THE FIRST CENTURY
### OF WHICH THE ACROSTIC IS AS FOLLOWS: <note>A "century" is a literary form consisting of 100 short chapters or aphorisms. In this case, the first letters of each chapter originally spelled out a dedicatory message in Greek.</note>

->TO MY SPIRITUAL BROTHER AND BELOVED LORD PAUL, FROM THALASSIUS.<-
->TO ONE WHO APPEARS TO BE A HESYCHAST, BUT IS IN TRUTH<-
->A MERCHANT OF VAINGLORY.<-
<note>Thalassius uses "Hesychast" to mean one who pursues inner stillness. Calling himself a "merchant of vainglory" is a traditional expression of monastic humility.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative rectangular frame around the drop-cap letter Pi (Π). The letter is stylized with floral or scroll-like ornamentation inside it and surrounding it. There are small cross-like symbols to the left and right of the bottom of the letter.</image-desc>

<margin>1.</margin>
Desire directed entirely toward God binds those who possess such desire to God and to one another.

<margin>2.</margin>
An intellect <note>original: "nous"—the highest faculty of the soul, through which one experiences God.</note> that has acquired spiritual love does not entertain thoughts about its neighbor that are unbecoming to love.

<margin>3.</margin>
He who blesses with his mouth but despises in his heart hides hypocrisy behind a pretense of love.

<margin>4.</margin>
One who has acquired love endures without disturbance the painful and laborious trials brought upon him by enemies.

<margin>5.</margin>
Love alone joins the creation to God, and joins individuals to one another in harmony.

<margin>6.</margin>
He has acquired true love who does not tolerate suspicions or negative words against his neighbor.

<margin>7.</margin>
He is honorable before God and men who does nothing intended to cause the dissolution of love.

<margin>8.</margin>
A true word proceeding from a good conscience is the characteristic of unfeigned love.

<column-break/>

<margin>9.</margin>
He who brings criticisms of a brother from a third party hides envy under the guise of goodwill.

<margin>10.</margin>
Just as bodily virtues attract the glory of men, so do spiritual virtues attract the glory of God.

<margin>11.</margin>
Love and self-control <note>original: "enkrateia"—mastery over one's impulses and desires.</note> purify the soul, while pure prayer illumines the intellect.

<margin>12.</margin>
That man is powerful who drives away wickedness through both practical action and spiritual knowledge.

<margin>13.</margin>
He has found grace before God who has acquired dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"—a state of being free from the control of destructive passions.</note> and spiritual knowledge.

<margin>14.</margin>
If you wish to overcome passionate thoughts, acquire self-control and love for your neighbor.

<margin>15.</margin>
Guard yourself from a lack of self-control and from hatred, and you will not find any stumbling block at the time of your prayer.

<margin>16.</margin>
Just as one cannot find perfumes in mud, so one cannot find the fragrance of love in the soul of one who bears a grudge.

<margin>17.</margin>
Master your anger and your desire with noble strength.

These aphorisms focus on the primary importance of love, self-control, and the purification of the intellect as the foundations of the spiritual life.</summary>

...and you will quickly be rid of evil thoughts.

<margin>18.</margin> Hidden labor <note>Spiritual work performed in secret, such as private prayer or fasting.</note> destroys vainglory, while not looking down on anyone drives away pride.

<margin>19.</margin> The characteristics of vainglory are hypocrisy and lying; the characteristics of pride are self-conceit and envy.

<margin>20.</margin> A true ruler is one who has ruled over himself, and has subjected both soul and body to the Word <note>original: "logos"—referring both to reason and to Christ, the Divine Word.</note>.

<margin>21.</margin> The sincerity of a friend is shown during a trial, when he becomes a sharer in one's distress.

<margin>22.</margin> Secure your senses through the practice of stillness <note>original: "hesychia"—a state of inner and outer quietness used to find God.</note>, and judge the thoughts that stand before your heart.

<margin>23.</margin> Toward thoughts that cause sorrow, be entirely without resentment; but toward those that seek pleasure, maintain a hostile disposition.

<margin>24.</margin> Stillness, prayer, love, and self-control are a four-horse chariot leading the intellect <note>original: "nous"</note> up toward the heavens.

<margin>25.</margin> Wither your body through fasting and vigils, and you will drive away the thought that is the executioner of pleasure.

<margin>26.</margin> As wax melts before the face of fire, so is an impure thought melted by the fear of God.

<margin>27.</margin> It is a terrible loss for an intelligent soul to let the intellect linger upon a blameworthy passion.

<margin>28.</margin> Endure the onset of sorrows and pains; for through these, the providence of God purifies you.

<margin>29.</margin> Having cast away material things and renounced the world, renounce thereafter your evil thoughts as well.

<margin>30.</margin> The proper work of the intellect is to always be at leisure in the words of God.

<margin>31.</margin> Just as it is the work of God to govern the world, so it is the work of the soul to govern the body.

<margin>32.</margin> With what hope shall we meet Christ, if we remain enslaved to the pleasures of the flesh until now?

<margin>33.</margin> Suffering and sorrow—whether voluntary or brought upon us by providence—destroy pleasure.

<margin>34.</margin> The love of money happens to be the "matter" of the passions, as it increases the pleasure that grips us.

<margin>35.</margin> The failure to obtain pleasure gives birth to sorrow, and pleasure is linked to every passion.

<margin>36.</margin> With whatever measure you measure out for your body, it shall be measured back to you in reverse by God.

<margin>37.</margin> Divine judgments consist of the just rewards for things done through the body.

<column-break/>

<margin>38.</margin> Virtue and knowledge <note>original: "gnosis"—spiritual insight or experiential knowledge of God.</note> give birth to immortality; the deprivation of these has become the mother of death.

<margin>39.</margin> Sorrow according to God <note>referring to "godly sorrow," a healthy repentance described in 2 Corinthians 7:10.</note> destroys pleasure; and the destruction of pleasure is the resurrection of the soul.

<margin>40.</margin> Dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"—not a lack of feeling, but a state where the soul is no longer controlled by disordered passions or "gut reactions."</note> is the soul's immovability toward evil; it is impossible to attain this without the mercy of Christ.

<margin>41.</margin> Christ is the Savior of soul and body, and he who follows in His footsteps is liberated from evil.

<margin>42.</margin> If you wish to attain salvation, renounce pleasure, and take up self-control and love, along with earnest prayer.

<margin>43.</margin> The characteristic of dispassion is true discernment; according to which one acts <gloss>perhaps: "it acts"</gloss> in all things with measure and rule.

<margin>44.</margin> Our Lord and God is Jesus the Christ; and the intellect that follows Him shall not remain in darkness.

<margin>45.</margin> Collect your intellect and guard your thoughts; and whichever ones you find to be passionate, wage war against them.

<margin>46.</margin> There are three things from which you receive thoughts: the senses, the memory, and the temperament of the body. Those arising from the memory are the most difficult.

<margin>47.</margin> He to whom wisdom has been given has known the inner principles <note>original: "logous"</note> of bodiless beings, and what the beginning and the end of the world are.

<margin>48.</margin> Do not neglect practical virtue, and your intellect will be illuminated. He says, "I will secretly open invisible treasures to you."

<margin>49.</margin> He who has been liberated from passions has found the grace of God; and he who has been deemed worthy of knowledge has found great mercy.

<margin>50.</margin> An intellect liberated from passions becomes light-like, being unceasingly illuminated by the contemplation of created things.

<margin>51.</margin> The light of the soul is holy knowledge. The fool who is deprived of it walks as if in darkness.

<margin>52.</margin> A fool is one who lives in darkness, and the darkness of ignorance succeeds him.

<margin>53.</margin> He who loves Jesus will be liberated from evil; and he who follows Him will see true knowledge.

<margin>54.</margin> An intellect liberated from passions sees concepts in their purity, both while the body is awake and during sleep.

<margin>55.</margin> An intellect purified to the highest degree is hemmed in by created things, and desires to always be beyond all things that have come into being.

<margin>56.</margin> Blessed is he who has reached the infinite...

...infinity; but that One has reached the end, who has passed beyond all finite things.

<margin>57.</margin> He who reveres God searches out the words of God; and he who is a lover of truth finds them.

<margin>58.</margin> An intellect <note>original: "nous"—the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the "eye of the heart" in Eastern Christian writing.</note> moved by rectitude finds the truth; but one moved by some passion will fail to reach it.

<margin>59.</margin> Just as God is unknown in His essence, so also is He infinite in His majesty.

<margin>60.</margin> An essence that has no beginning and no end cannot have its nature discovered by searching.

<margin>61.</margin> The salvation of all creation is the supremely good providence of the Creator over it.

<margin>62.</margin> In His mercies, the Lord supports all those who are falling, and He raises up all who have been broken down.

<margin>63.</margin> Christ is Lord of the living and the dead, and the just rewarder of every person's deeds.

<margin>64.</margin> Begin, if you wish, to rule over the soul and the body; anticipate the causes of the passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to disordered or compulsive impulses like greed, anger, or lust.</note> and cut them off.

<margin>65.</margin> Yoke the powers of the soul to the virtues, and they will surely be separated from the tyranny of the passions.

<margin>66.</margin> Bridle the impulses of desire with self-control, and those of anger with spiritual love.

<margin>67.</margin> Stillness <note>original: "hesychia"—the practice of inner quiet and withdrawal from distraction.</note> and prayer are the greatest weapons of virtue. For by purifying the intellect, they make it clear-sighted.

<margin>68.</margin> Social interaction is only beneficial if it is spiritual; but above all other kinds, stillness is to be preferred.

<margin>69.</margin> Of the five ways of conversation <note>Thalassius likely refers to a classical division of speech: questioning, answering, commanding, entreating, and declaring. He advises caution in how we use our words.</note>, choose three; do not frequent the fourth; and stay away from the fifth.

<margin>70.</margin> He who does not suffer for the things of the world loves stillness; and he who loves nothing human loves all people.

<margin>71.</margin> Conscience is a true teacher; he who obeys it remains without stumbling.

<margin>72.</margin> Only those who have reached the peak of virtue—or the peak of vice—are not judged by their conscience. <note>In the first case, the conscience is at peace; in the second, it has been "seared" or silenced by persistent wrongdoing.</note>

<margin>73.</margin> Extreme dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"—not a lack of feeling, but a state of freedom from the control of the passions.</note> makes thoughts "bare" <note>Simple and without emotional charge or temptation.</note>. Extreme knowledge stands one before the Supremely-Unknown.

<margin>74.</margin> Sorrow is a thing to be fled, for it is the failure to attain pleasures. He who despises pleasures remains free of sorrow.

<margin>75.</margin> Sorrow is entirely a deprivation of plea-

<column-break/>

-sure, whether you consider it "according to God" <note>Sorrow for sins (repentance).</note> or "according to the world" <note>Sorrow over lost material things or ego.</note>.

<margin>76.</margin> The Kingdom of God is goodness and wisdom; he who attains them lives as a citizen of the heavens.

<margin>77.</margin> That man is wretched who, by his deeds, prefers the body to the soul, and the world to God.

<margin>78.</margin> He possesses equal love for all who does not envy the diligent and pities the wicked.

<margin>79.</margin> He truly ought to rule who has legislated the ways of virtue for both his soul and his body.

<margin>80.</margin> He is a spiritual merchant who, for the sake of the future, detaches himself equally from the pleasant and the sorrowful things of this life.

<margin>81.</margin> Love and self-control strengthen the soul, while pure prayer and spiritual contemplation <note>original: "theoria"—the direct perception of divine truths.</note> strengthen the intellect.

<margin>82.</margin> When hearing a beneficial word, do not judge the speaker, lest you deprive yourself of the useful admonition.

<margin>83.</margin> An evil disposition thinks evil things, and misinterprets the successes of the neighbor as defects.

<margin>84.</margin> Do not trust a thought that judges your neighbor; for because it possesses an evil treasure, it thinks evil things.

<margin>85.</margin> A good heart brings forth good thoughts; for its inner reasonings are in accordance with its treasure.

<margin>86.</margin> Guard your thoughts and flee from vice, lest the intellect be darkened and see things other than what they truly are.

<margin>87.</margin> Consider the Jews and protect yourself: blinded by envy, they misinterpreted the Lord and God as Beelzebub.

<margin>88.</margin> Evil suspicion darkens the mind and makes it see things alongside the path instead of the path itself.

<margin>89.</margin> Vices are fastened alongside all the virtues; for this reason, the wicked misinterpret virtues as vices.

<margin>90.</margin> An intellect that lingers in pleasure or sorrow quickly falls into the passion of listlessness <note>original: "akedia"—a state of spiritual apathy, boredom, or "the noonday demon."</note>.

<margin>91.</margin> A clean conscience rouses the soul, but a filthy thought brings it down to the earth.

<margin>92.</margin> When the passions are active, they drive away vainglory; but when they are destroyed, it returns. <note>A warning that one may feel humble while struggling with sins, but may become proud of their progress once those sins are conquered.</note>

->BY THE SAME AUTHOR<-

# SECOND CENTURY

->THE ACROSTIC <note>An acrostic is a poem where the first letter of each line or section spells out a hidden message. The Greek letters of the following phrases likely correspond to the numbered points below.</note> OF WHICH IS AS FOLLOWS:<-

->PRAY FOR ME, BROTHER MOST HONORABLE, FOR I EXPECT GREAT EVILS,<-
->WORTHY OF MY OWN CHOICE; SORROWS TO THE SOUL<-
->AND PAINS TO THE BODY.<-

<margin>1.</margin> If you wish to be rid of every evil, renounce the mother of evils: self-love. <note>original: "philautia"—specifically an obsessive or disordered love of the self.</note>

<margin>2.</margin> The health of the soul is dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"—a state of being undisturbed by the passions.</note> and knowledge, which is impossible for one who is a slave to pleasures to obtain.

<margin>3.</margin> Self-control joined with patience, and love joined with long-suffering, dry up the pleasures of both the body and the soul.

<margin>4.</margin> Self-love has become the beginning of all evils for the soul; and self-love is defined as friendship toward the body.

<margin>5.</margin> It is the proper nature of the rational being to be subject to the Word <note>original: "logos"—referring both to the Divine Word and to the faculty of reason.</note>, and to subdue and enslave the body.

<margin>6.</margin> It is an insult to the rational nature to be subject to the irrational, and to provide for it in service of shameful desires.

<margin>7.</margin> It is an evil work of the rational soul to abandon the Creator and to worship the body.

<margin>8.</margin> You were commanded to have the body as a servant, but 

<column-break/>

not to be a slave to its pleasures against nature.

<margin>9.</margin> Break the bonds of friendship toward the body, and provide nothing for that servant except what is absolutely necessary.

<margin>10.</margin> Shut up your senses in the fortress of stillness <note>original: "hesychia"—the practice of inner and outer quiet.</note>, so that they do not distract the intellect toward their own desires.

<margin>11.</margin> The greatest weapons for one who practices stillness with patience are self-control, love, attentiveness, and spiritual reading.

<margin>12.</margin> The intellect does not stop circling around pleasures until it has enslaved the flesh and devoted itself to contemplation. <note>original: "theoria"—spiritual vision or the contemplation of divine truths.</note>

<margin>13.</margin> Let us struggle for the sake of the commandments, so that we may be freed from the passions; and for the sake of divine dogmas, so that we may be deemed worthy of knowledge.

<margin>14.</margin> The immortality of the soul is dispassion and knowledge; it is impossible for one who is a slave to pleasures to obtain it.

<header>OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THALASSIUS</header>

<margin>15.</margin> Bring the body into subjection by stripping away its pleasures, and deliver it from its wretched slavery.
<margin>16.</margin> Having been created free, and called to a state of freedom, do not allow yourself to be a slave to the buildup of impurity.
<margin>17.</margin> Through sorrows and pleasures, desires and fears, the demons bind the intellect <note>original: "nous"—the spiritual center of a person, often called the "eye of the soul."</note> to the things of the senses.
<margin>18.</margin> Fear of the Lord holds desires in check, and a "sorrow according to God" <note>A technical term for repentance or "godly grief" that leads to spiritual health rather than despair.</note> drives away worldly pleasure.
<margin>19.</margin> The desire for wisdom looks down upon fear, and the pleasure of spiritual knowledge puts sorrow to flight.
<margin>20.</margin> The Scriptures contain these four things: commandments, dogmas, threats, and promises.
<margin>21.</margin> Self-control and hard labor bring desire to a halt, while stillness <note>original: "hesychia"—a state of inner quiet and external silence.</note> and divine love cause it to diminish.
<margin>22.</margin> Do not sting your brother with words full of riddles <note>implying sarcastic or passive-aggressive remarks</note>; otherwise, you will not be able to bear it when you receive the same in return.
<margin>23.</margin> Patient endurance and the forgetting of wrongs bring anger to a halt, while love and compassion cause it to diminish.
<margin>24.</margin> To the one who has been given knowledge, an intellectual light has been given. But the one who receives it and then treats it with contempt will see only darkness.
<margin>25.</margin> The keeping of God’s commandments gives birth to dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"—not a lack of feeling, but freedom from the control of disordered impulses.</note>. This dispassion of the soul, in turn, preserves spiritual knowledge.
<margin>26.</margin> Lead the things of the senses up toward spiritual contemplation, and you will pull your perception above the realm of the physical.
<margin>27.</margin> The "sensory woman" <note>In this context, an allegory for the "practical" or lower part of the soul that deals with the physical world.</note> signifies the practical soul; if the intellect unites with her in the wrong way, it puts the virtues to death.
<margin>28.</margin> The searching of God's words teaches the knowledge of God to the one who seeks in truth, longing, and reverence.
<margin>29.</margin> Just as light is to those who see and to the things seen, so God is to those who understand and to the things understood.
<margin>30.</margin> The physical firmament signifies the firmament of faith, in which all the saints shine like stars.
<margin>31.</margin> Jerusalem is the heavenly knowledge of the bodiless beings <note>The angels.</note>; for within it is beheld the "vision of peace."
<margin>32.</margin> Do not neglect practical action, otherwise your knowledge will diminish; and if a "famine" occurs, you will find yourself "descending into Egypt." <note>An allegory: Egypt represents the world of passions and material attachment; the famine is a lack of spiritual grace.</note>
<margin>33.</margin> Spiritual freedom is the 

<column-break/>

release from the passions, which no one can achieve without the mercy of Christ.
<margin>34.</margin> The "Land of Promise" is the Kingdom of Heaven, which is brought about by dispassion and spiritual knowledge.
<margin>35.</margin> Spiritual "Egypt" is the darkening of the passions, into which no one descends unless they have fallen into a famine of virtue.
<margin>36.</margin> Let your ear frequently attend to spiritual words, and your intellect will move away from impure thoughts.
<margin>37.</margin> God alone is good and wise by His very nature. However, the human intellect can also become so through participation, if it makes the effort.
<margin>38.</margin> Exercise control over the belly, sleep, anger, and the tongue, and you will not "strike your foot against a stone." <note>A reference to Psalm 91:12.</note>
<margin>39.</margin> Struggle to love every person equally, and you will drive out all your passions at once.
<margin>40.</margin> The contemplation of sensory things is shared by both the intellect and the senses; but the knowledge of spiritual things belongs to the intellect alone.
<margin>41.</margin> It is impossible for the intellect to be at leisure for spiritual things unless it cuts off its attachment to the senses and the physical world.
<margin>42.</margin> Senses have a natural attraction to sensory things, and they drag the intellect along with them as they are pulled toward those things.
<margin>43.</margin> Incline your senses toward the service of the intellect, and do not give them the opportunity to distract it.
<margin>44.</margin> When the intellect happens to be occupied with physical things, pull the senses back by bringing the things at hand toward the intellect.
<margin>45.</margin> A sign that the intellect is focused on spiritual things is when it despises all things that try to flatter the senses.
<margin>46.</margin> When the intellect is opened to the contemplation of spiritual things, it finds the pleasure found within them difficult to leave.
<margin>47.</margin> When the intellect grows rich in the knowledge of the Unity <note>original: "monados"—the Monad or the Oneness of God.</note>, it then holds the senses in complete subjection.
<margin>48.</margin> Prevent your intellect from wandering through sensory things, so that it does not harvest pleasures and pains from them.
<margin>49.</margin> For those whose intellect dwells always in divine things, even the passionate part of their soul <note>original: "pathetikon meros"—the part of the soul associated with emotions and drives.</note> becomes a divine weapon.
<margin>50.</margin> It is impossible for the intellect to be shaped by spiritual knowledge unless it first drives out the vices from itself through their corresponding virtues.

It uses biblical allegories, such as Egypt and Jerusalem, to describe the movement between the life of the passions and the life of divine contemplation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Century" of aphorisms by St. Thalassius the Libyan. The previous page established the groundwork for how the intellect (nous) relates to the senses and the struggle against the passions. This section further explores the path to becoming "children of God" through the purification of the mind and the heart, emphasizing the roles of self-control, godly sorrow, and "hesychia" (inner stillness).</meta>

### ON LOVE AND SELF-CONTROL

<margin>51.</margin> The mind <note>original: "nous"—the highest faculty of the human soul, often described as the 'eye' through which one perceives God.</note> becomes a stranger to the things of this world only when it completely severs its attachment to the senses.
<margin>52.</margin> It is the nature of the rational part of the soul to devote itself to the knowledge of God; but it is the nature of its "passionate" part <note>The "passionate part" (pathetikon) refers to the aspects of the soul that experience desire and anger, which must be directed toward virtue.</note> to practice love and self-control.
<margin>53.</margin> It is impossible for the mind to truly dwell on any sensory object unless it possesses a passion for it.
<margin>54.</margin> A mind is perfect when it is fully convinced by spiritual knowledge; a soul is perfect when it has been thoroughly permeated by the virtues.
<margin>55.</margin> The mind's attachment to the senses makes it a slave to the pleasures of the body.
<margin>56.</margin> The mind is shaken from its place of spiritual knowledge whenever the passionate part of the soul is moved away from its proper virtues.
<margin>57.</margin> We have received the power to become children of God; yet we do not actually become so unless we strip away the passions.
<margin>58.</margin> Let no one think they have become a child of God in practice if they have not yet acquired the divine characteristics within themselves.
<margin>59.</margin> Our habitual likeness to either good or evil determines whether we are made into sons of God or sons of Satan.
<margin>60.</margin> A prudent man is one who watches himself closely and hastens to separate himself from every defilement.
<margin>61.</margin> A hardened soul does not feel it when it is disciplined, and it refuses to come to a realization of its Benefactor.
<margin>62.</margin> Filthy garments <note>A metaphor for a soul stained by sin.</note> lead to being cast out from the divine wedding and being made a companion of the outer darkness.
<margin>63.</margin> He who fears God takes care of his own soul and frees himself from evil company.
<margin>64.</margin> It is impossible to obtain God's mercy if one has abandoned Him and remains a slave to pleasures.
<margin>65.</margin> It is Jesus who says—even if we are unwilling to believe it—that no one can serve two masters.
<margin>66.</margin> A soul defiled by passions becomes hardened; without "incisions and cauteries" <note>Metaphorical language for severe divine discipline or trials intended to heal the soul.</note>, it refuses to believe.
<margin>67.</margin> Fearful trials await those who are hard-hearted; for without great pains, they do not allow themselves to be softened.
<margin>68.</margin> A prudent man takes care of himself, and through voluntary pains <note>Refers to ascetic practices like fasting or vigils chosen by the person.</note>, he escapes involuntary ones <note>Refers to suffering or punishments that come upon a person against their will.</note>.
<margin>69.</margin> Care for the soul consists of enduring hardship and humility; through these, God forgives all sins.

<column-break/>

<margin>70.</margin> Just as desires and anger multiply sins, so self-control and humility wipe them away.
<margin>71.</margin> A "sorrow according to God" <note>Metanoia or godly repentance.</note> crushes the heart, and the fear of punishment gives birth to this sorrow.
<margin>72.</margin> Godly sorrow cleanses the heart and drives the defilements of pleasure far away from it.
<margin>73.</margin> Patience is the soul's love of labor; and where there is a love of labor, the love of pleasure is exiled.
<margin>74.</margin> Every sin occurs because of pleasure, and every forgiveness comes through hardship and sorrow.
<margin>75.</margin> Involuntary pains fall upon a person by divine providence if they refuse to repent through voluntary pains.
<margin>76.</margin> Christ is the Savior of the entire world, and He granted repentance to humanity as the means to salvation.
<margin>77.</margin> Keeping the commandments gives birth to repentance, and keeping the commandments brings about the purification of the soul.
<margin>78.</margin> The purification of the soul is the riddance of the passions; and the riddance of the passions gives birth to love.
<margin>79.</margin> A soul is pure when it loves God; and a mind is pure when it is separated from ignorance.
<margin>80.</margin> Struggle for the commandments of Christ even unto death; for being cleansed through them, you shall enter into life.
<margin>81.</margin> Use the body as a servant of the commandments, keeping it—as much as you are able—free from pleasure and disease.
<margin>82.</margin> The rebellion of the flesh arises from the neglect of prayer, diet, and "good stillness" <note>original: "hesychia"—a state of inner quiet and outer silence necessary for prayer.</note>.
<margin>83.</margin> Good stillness brings forth good offspring: self-control, love, and pure prayer.
<margin>84.</margin> Spiritual reading and prayer cleanse the mind; love and self-control cleanse the passionate part of the soul.
<margin>85.</margin> Keep your self-control consistent at all times, so that you do not fall into extremes through irregularity.
<margin>86.</margin> He who sets rules for himself should not violate them; for he who cheats himself deceives himself.
<margin>87.</margin> There are "spiritual sunsets"—these are souls filled with passion; for upon such souls, the "Sun of Righteousness" has set.
<margin>88.</margin> A son of God is one who has become like God through the goodness of wisdom, power, and justice.
<margin>89.</margin> The sickness of the soul is the habit of vice; its death is sin put into action.

<summary>This page contains a series of ascetic aphorisms regarding the purification of the soul (psyche) and the intellect (nous). It emphasizes that spiritual progress requires transforming the "passionate" part of the soul through self-control, godly sorrow, and the keeping of Christ's commandments.</summary>

# OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THALASSIUS

<margin>90.</margin> True detachment from possessions is of the intellect; it is a state of total dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"—a state of being "passionless," not as in "indifferent," but as in being free from the control of reactive emotions or disordered desires.</note>. When the mind reaches this state, it withdraws from the things of this world.
<margin>91.</margin> Keep the virtues of the soul in harmony with one another, for from this harmony the fruit of righteousness is born.
<margin>92.</margin> They say that the contemplation of intelligible things <note>The "intelligible" (noeton) refers to things grasped by the mind/spirit rather than the physical senses.</note> is incorporeal, as it is entirely free from matter and form.
<margin>93.</margin> Just as the four elements consist of matter and form, so also the bodies made from them are composed of the same.
<margin>94.</margin> The Word <note>original: "Logos"—referring to the second person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ.</note>, having become flesh through His love for mankind, neither changed what He was, nor altered what He became.
<margin>95.</margin> Just as He is from both divinity and humanity,

<margin>1.</margin> Concerning Him who is good by nature <note>i.e., God</note>, think good thoughts. And concerning every human being, think honorable reflections.
<margin>2.</margin> We will be required by God to give an defense for our words, deeds, and thoughts on the Day of Judgment.

<margin>5.</margin> An evil thought is preceded by a passion. The cause of the passion is established by the senses. And the cause of the misuse of the sense itself is, clearly, the mind.
<margin>6.</margin> Shut out the senses and make war against <term>preconception</term> <note>original: "prolepsin"—a preconceived idea or mental trigger that leads to a reactive passion.</note>. And with the weapons of the commandments, put your passions to death.

and exists in divinity and humanity, so also we speak of the one Christ as being from two natures and in two natures.

<margin>97.</margin> We glorify the one indivisible hypostasis of Christ, and we confess the unconfused union of His natures.

<margin>99.</margin> Unique to the three hypostases are Fatherhood, Sonship, and Procession. Common to the three hypostases are the essence, the nature, the divinity, and the goodness.

<header>ON LOVE AND SELF-CONTROL</header>

<margin>7.</margin> Self-control is like every height that is raised up, as are contemplation and prayer.
<margin>14.</margin> The labors of asceticism produce a clean conscience: such as fasting, vigils, endurance, and long-suffering.
<margin>15.</margin> He who endures the onset of involuntary temptations <note>original: "peirasmon"—trials or tests that come upon a person without their choosing, such as illness or misfortune.</note> becomes humble, hopeful, and proven.
<margin>16.</margin> Endurance is the soul's love of labor; it consists of voluntary labors and involuntary temptations.
<margin>17.</margin> The patient bearing of terrors melts away vice, and endurance until the end destroys it completely.
<margin>18.</margin> The onset of labors causes pain to the senses, and the infliction of sorrow takes away pleasure.
<margin>19.</margin> There are four most general passions <note>In this context, "passions" (pathe) refers to disordered impulses or reactive emotions like anger, lust, fear, and grief.</note>, which Providence has wisely used against one another.
<margin>20.</margin> For the infliction of sorrow constricts pleasure, and the fear of punishments withers desire.
<margin>21.</margin> A prudent mind <note>original: "nous"—the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the "eye of the heart."</note> trains its soul and habituates its body to every kind of asceticism.
<margin>22.</margin> Make haste to receive the monk not just as the outward man, but also the inward one, freeing him from the passions.
<margin>+ 23.</margin> The first renunciation is the letting go of possessions; the second and third are the letting go of passions and of ignorance.
<margin>24.</margin> One who wishes can easily let go of possessions, but not without great effort can one let go of the *thoughts* <note>original: "noemata"—mental images or concepts associated with objects that can trigger desire.</note> regarding them.
<margin>25.</margin> By controlling desire, you will master anger; for desire is the cause of the outburst of anger.
<margin>26.</margin> So then, have we been freed from passionate thoughts and received pure and immaterial prayer, or not yet?
<margin>27.</margin> Great is the mind that has been freed from the passions, separated from created things, and dwells in God.
<margin>28.</margin> He who is progressing practices philosophy in these three: in the commandments, in the dogmas, and in faith in the Holy Trinity.
<margin>29.</margin> A mind freed from passions is found in these: in bare thoughts <note>Meaning thoughts that are simple concepts, free from emotional attachment or "charge."</note>, in the contemplation of beings, and in its own light.
<margin>30.</margin> The worst passions are hidden in our souls; they appear when things are put to the test.
<margin>31.</margin> Sometimes the mind remains undisturbed, having achieved a partial dispassion <note>original: "apatheia"—a state of being free from the control of reactive emotions.</note>; yet it is unproven because of the absence of the things [that tempt it].
<margin>32.</margin> The passions are moved through these three—

<column-break/>

—through memory, and through the temperament <note>original: "krasis"—the physical constitution or 'mixture' of the body's humors which was believed to affect one's mood and health.</note>, and through the senses, as has been said before.
<margin>33.</margin> The mind, having shut out the senses and balanced the temperament, has a war only against memory.
<margin>34.</margin> The passions are moved by the senses whenever self-control and spiritual love are not present.
<margin>35.</margin> Moderate fasting, vigils, and the chanting of psalms are naturally suited to balance the temperament of the body.
<margin>36.</margin> These three things clearly alter the temperament for the worse: disorder in diet, change in the air, and the touch of demons.
<margin>37.</margin> Passionate memories are stripped away through these: through prayer, reading, self-control, and love.
<margin>38.</margin> First shut out the senses through silence <note>original: "hesychia"—inner and outer stillness or quietude.</note>, and then fight against memories with the weapons of the virtues.
<margin>39.</margin> Vice in the intellect is the misuse of thoughts. Sin in action is the misuse of things.
<margin>40.</margin> The misuse of thoughts and things is to fail to use both piously and justly.
<margin>41.</margin> Blameworthy passions are the bonds of the mind, holding it fast in sensory things.
<margin>42.</margin> That person has perfect dispassion who is affected neither by things nor by the memories of them.
<margin>43.</margin> A good soul does good to its neighbor, and even when treated ungratefully, it is long-suffering; when suffering, it endures what comes from him.
<margin>44.</margin> Evil possessions are wicked thoughts; he who does not renounce them will not be disciplined in knowledge.
<margin>45.</margin> He who hears Christ enlightens himself, and he who imitates Him corrects himself.
<margin>46.</margin> The bearing of a grudge <note>original: "mnesikakia"—literally "remembering wrongs" or nursing resentment.</note> is a leprosy of the soul; it happens to the soul from dishonor, loss, or suspicious thoughts.
<margin>47.</margin> The Lord blinds an envious mind because it grieves unjustly at the good things of its neighbor.
<margin>48.</margin> A soul that speaks against others has a tongue like a briar; for it harms itself, the one who hears, and sometimes the one being spoken against.
<margin>49.</margin> He is free of grudges who prays for the one who grieved him. And he is delivered from the bearing of grudges who is not stingy with gifts.

<meta>This page continues the "Third Century" of aphorisms by St. Thalassius the Libyan. The previous page ended with an instruction on how to receive a monk. The text continues with numbered proverbs on spiritual life, moving through the themes of listlessness, gluttony, and the internal source of thoughts.</meta>

### 336 OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THALASSIUS

<margin>50.</margin> The death of the soul is hatred toward one’s neighbor. For the soul of the slanderer possesses this hatred and acts upon it.
<margin>51.</margin> Listlessness <note>original: "akedia"—a state of spiritual apathy, boredom, or "the noonday demon" that makes a monk feel restless and dissatisfied with his life.</note> is a disregard of the soul. A soul falls into such disregard when it is sick with a love of pleasure.
<margin>52.</margin> He who loves Jesus trains himself through labors; and the endurance of labors drives away listlessness.
<margin>53.</margin> The soul is strengthened through the labors of ascetic practice, and by doing all things in moderation <note>original: "metro"—measure or balance.</note>, it drives away listlessness.
<margin>54.</margin> He who controls his stomach withers his desire; and his mind <note>original: "nous"—the spiritual intellect or "eye of the soul."</note> does not become a slave to thoughts of sexual immorality.
<margin>55.</margin> The mind of a self-controlled man is a temple of the Holy Spirit. But the mind of a glutton is a dwelling place of ravens <note>original: "korakon"—in this context, ravens or crows symbolize dark, scavenging thoughts or demonic influences.</note>.
<margin>56.</margin> From a variety of foods, satiety produces desire. But a lack of food makes even plain bread sweet.
<margin>57.</margin> He is delivered from envy who rejoices in secret with the one being envied. And he delivers another from envy who keeps the envied person hidden.
<margin>58.</margin> Keep yourself far from the one who lives negligently, even if he has acquired a great name among many.
<margin>59.</margin> Gain a hardworking man as a friend, and you will find a protection for your eyes.
<margin>60.</margin> The negligent man has been sold to many masters, and as they lead him, so he spends his life.
<margin>61.</margin> Such a person is well-disposed toward you as a friend in a time of peace; but in a time of temptation <note>original: "peirasmos"—a trial or testing of character.</note>, he fights you like an enemy.
<margin>62.</margin> He offers his life for you before the passions are stirred, but when they are moved, he captures your life.
<margin>63.</margin> Just as fallow land is filled with thorns, so the negligent soul is filled with impure passions.
<margin>64.</margin> A prudent mind bridles its soul, beats the body into submission, and makes a slave of the passions.
<margin>65.</margin> Outward movements are a sign of what is within, just as the fruit that is brought forth reveals unknown trees.
<margin>66.</margin> Words and deeds expose a hypocrite, and they bring the hidden false prophet into the light.
<margin>67.</margin> A mind that has strayed does not discipline its soul; it distances the soul from love and self-control.
<margin>68.</margin> The cause of wicked thoughts is a base habit, established by pride and arrogance.
<margin>69.</margin> The characteristics of the aforementioned things are hypocrisy, deceit, cunning, pretense <note>original: "eironeia"—feigned ignorance or dissimulation.</note>, and every kind of base lie.

<column-break/>

Envy, strife, anger, sorrow, and resentment are slaves to those things mentioned above.
<margin>70.</margin> This is the path of those who live in negligence, and this is the "treasure" of those hidden within me.
<margin>71.</margin> Hardship and humility save the soul, and they deliver it from the passions mentioned above.
<margin>72.</margin> It is the characteristic of a wise thought to offer helpful speech, and of a good soul to offer virtuous action.
<margin>73.</margin> An illumined mind brings forth words of wisdom, and a pure soul cultivates divine thoughts.
<margin>74.</margin> Diligent thoughts meditate on wisdom, and the words of such a person enlighten those who hear them.
<margin>75.</margin> When virtues are established in the soul, it cultivates good thoughts. But when vices are established, it gives birth to base ideas.
<margin>76.</margin> The soul of a passionate person is a workshop of wicked thoughts; out of its own treasure, it brings forth evil.
<margin>77.</margin> The "good treasure" is the habit of the virtues; and the good mind brings forth good things from this habit.
<margin>78.</margin> A mind energized by divine love cultivates good thoughts about God. But when energized by self-love <note>original: "philautia"—an excessive or narcissistic love of self.</note>, it does the opposite.
<margin>79.</margin> A mind moved by love for one's neighbor thinks well of him at all times. But conversely, it suspects evil when moved by the opposite.
<margin>80.</margin> The virtues are the causes of good thoughts; the commandments are the cause of the virtues; and the practice of these commandments is caused by the free will <note>original: "proairesis"—deliberate choice or moral disposition.</note>.
<margin>81.</margin> As virtues and vices come and go, they dispose the soul for better or worse, moving it toward corresponding thoughts.
<margin>82.</margin> Vices are the causes of wicked thoughts; disobedience is the cause of vices; the deception of the senses is the cause of disobedience; and the mind’s negligence regarding its own safety is the cause of this deception.
<margin>83.</margin> In those who are progressing, their dispositions toward opposites become fixed. In those who are perfect, these habits become difficult to move in both directions.
<margin>84.</margin> The strength of the soul is an immovable habit of virtue; he who has reached this point says as one who cannot be conquered: *Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?* and so on.
<margin>86.</margin> Self-love precedes all the passions, while pride follows last of all.

<summary>This page contains a series of ethical and spiritual aphorisms focusing on the origins of thoughts, the dangers of negligence and self-love, and the importance of ascetic labor. St. Thalassius emphasizes that the "mind" (nous) is either a temple or a workshop depending on whether it is governed by virtues or passions.</summary>

### 337
# ON LOVE AND SELF-CONTROL

<margin>87.</margin> The three most general thoughts <note>original: "logismoi"—these are not just random thoughts, but impulsive patterns or "temptations" that lead to sin.</note> of desire have their origin in the passion of self-love <note>original: "philautia"—often considered the "mother of all vices" in Eastern Christian asceticism.</note>.

<margin>88.</margin> You surely recognize these as the thoughts of gluttony, vainglory, and greed. All other passionate thoughts follow these, though not all follow them in the same way.

<margin>89.</margin> From the thought of gluttony follows sexual immorality. From vainglory follows pride. The rest of the vices follow all three in common.

<margin>90.</margin> Sorrow, anger, resentment, envy, listlessness <note>original: "akedia"—the spiritual apathy or "noonday demon."</note>, and the rest follow all three general categories of thought.

->A Prayer<-

<margin>91.</margin> Christ, Master of all things, free us from all of these: both the destructive passions and the thoughts born from them.

<margin>92.</margin> We were created for your sake, so that we might enjoy the delights of Paradise, having been placed there by your hand.

<margin>93.</margin> But we have brought this current dishonor upon ourselves,

<column-break/>

preferring destructive pleasure over that blessed delight.

<margin>94.</margin> We have received the wages for this within ourselves, having exchanged eternal life for death.

<margin>95.</margin> Now therefore, O Master, as you have looked upon us in the past, look upon us until the end; just as you became human for us, save us all.

<margin>96.</margin> For you came to save us who were lost. Do not separate us from the portion of those who are being saved.

<margin>97.</margin> Raise up our souls and save our bodies; cleanse us all from every defilement.

<margin>98.</margin> Break the bonds of the passions that hold us fast, O You who broke the ranks of the unclean demons.

<margin>99.</margin> And deliver us from their tyranny, so that we may serve You alone, the eternal light.

<margin>100.</margin> May we rise from the dead and dance with the Angels—that blessed, eternal, and indestructible dance. Amen.

<margin>1.</margin> He who has separated his mind <note>original: "nous"—the spiritual intellect or the "eye of the heart."</note> from friendship and flattery toward the flesh has, through the life-giving Spirit, put to death the deeds of the body.

<margin>2.</margin> Do not think you have been separated from an attachment to the flesh if you still keep your mind occupied with the concerns of the flesh.

<margin>3.</margin> Just as the senses and

<column-break/>

<margin>4.</margin> Withdraw the soul from the perception of sensible things, and the mind will find itself in God and in the realm of intelligible realities.

<margin>5.</margin> Intelligent natures are akin to the Godhead and are grasped by the mind alone. But the senses and sensible things were created to serve the mind.

### 338
# OF OUR HOLY AND GOD-BEARING FATHER THALASSIUS

<margin>6.</margin> Let your sensory perception and the things you perceive serve spiritual contemplation; do not let them work in reverse, turning your senses toward the desires of the flesh.

<margin>7.</margin> You were commanded to "put to death the deeds of the body" <note>A reference to Romans 8:13. Thalassius suggests that physical discipline revives the soul that has been "killed" by pursuit of pleasure.</note> so that you might raise the soul, which had been deadened by pleasures, through your labors.

<margin>8.</margin> Be ruled by God and you will rule over your senses; do not give the authority of the superior <note>The "superior" part is the intellect or soul.</note> over to the inferior <note>The "inferior" part is the physical senses or bodily impulses.</note>.

<margin>9.</margin> God is eternal, infinite, and undefined; and He has promised eternal, infinite, and inexpressible blessings to those who obey Him.

<margin>10.</margin> It is the nature of the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "nous"—in Eastern Christian thought, this refers to the "eye of the soul," the faculty that perceives God directly.</note> to dwell in God, to contemplate Him, His providence, and His awesome judgments.

<margin>11.</margin> You have the power to lean in either direction; choose the better side and subdue the worse.

<margin>12.</margin> Sensation is good and the things perceived by the senses are good, for they are the works of the good God. However, they cannot be compared at all to the intellect and the <term>intelligible</term> things <note>original: "noeta"—realities perceived by the mind or spirit rather than the physical eyes, such as virtues or divine truths.</note>.

<margin>13.</margin> The Master created the rational and intelligent essence to be capable of receiving everything and of knowing Him; but He brought sensation and the sensible world into existence for the soul's use.

<margin>14.</margin> Just as it is absurd to subject a good master to a wicked slave, so it is absurd to enslave a rational intellect to a corruptible body.

<margin>15.</margin> An intellect that does not preside over the senses falls into evils through them; for being deceived by the pleasure of sensory things, it gives birth to wickedness within itself.

<margin>16.</margin> While controlling your senses, secure your memory as well. For the impressions <note>original: "prolepseis"—preconceptions or mental images formed by past experiences.</note> gathered through the senses revive the passions.

<margin>17.</margin> Chastise the body and be constantly attentive; in this way, you will very quickly be rid of the thoughts that arise from past impressions.

<margin>18.</margin> Devote yourself unceasingly to divine words; for diligence in studying them consumes the passions.

<margin>19.</margin> Reading, vigils, prayer, and the singing of psalms stop the intellect from wandering into the delusions of the passions.

<margin>20.</margin> Just as the spring moves plants to sprout, so too <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "apatheia"—not a lack of feeling, but a state of being free from the control of sinful passions.</note> moves the intellect toward the knowledge of all things.

<margin>21.</margin> Keep the commandments and you will find peace; you will love God and achieve true knowledge.

<column-break/>

With toil, labor, and the sweat of your brow, you were condemned to eat the bread of knowledge. <margin>22.</margin> <note>A play on the curse of Adam in Genesis 3:19. Thalassius suggests that spiritual knowledge now requires the same hard labor Adam faced in the fields.</note>

Negligence led the Forefather <note>Adam.</note> into transgression, and in place of the delights of Paradise, it condemned him to death. <margin>23.</margin>

You too must control "Eve" <note>Symbolically, the lower or more vulnerable part of the human psyche that is prone to temptation.</note>; watch out for the serpent, lest being deceived, she shares the fruit of the tree with you. <margin>24.</margin>

Just as the soul naturally gives life to the body, so virtue and knowledge give life to the soul. <margin>25.</margin>

The clouded intellect is a "waterless cloud," <note>A reference to Jude 1:12.</note> carried away by the spirits of vainglory and pride. <margin>26.</margin>

While controlling vainglory, be on your guard against sexual immorality. Lest while fleeing honors, you fall into dishonor. <margin>27.</margin>

When avoiding vainglory, look toward God. If you do not, you will certainly fall into the <term>delusion</term> <note>original: "oiese"—self-conceit or a false sense of one's own holiness.</note> of immorality. <margin>28.</margin>

The hallmark of vainglory is ostentatious behavior. The hallmark of pride is despising others and becoming angry. <margin>29.</margin>

When fleeing gluttony, guard against people-pleasing—specifically, the desire to show off a pale face to others. <margin>31.</margin> <note>Monks were often warned not to "advertise" their fasting by making themselves look sickly or pale just to get praise for their holiness.</note>

A beautiful fast is to eat little with joy, keeping to simple food and fleeing the praise of men. <margin>34.</margin>

When fasting until late in the day, do not eat until you are stuffed, lest you rebuild the very things you are trying to tear down. <margin>35.</margin>

If you do not drink wine, do not fill yourself with water; otherwise, you provide the same fuel for sexual immorality. <margin>36.</margin>

Pride causes one to depart from divine help, to trust in oneself, and to exalt oneself over other people. <margin>37.</margin>

There are two things set against pride; if a person does not accept them, they will face a third thing which is extremely bitter. <margin>38.</margin> <note>The "two things" usually refer to voluntary humility and prayer; the "third thing" refers to involuntary suffering or humiliation sent by God to break the pride.</note>

Pride is destroyed by prayer with tears, by not despising anyone, and by involuntary afflictions. <margin>39.</margin>

Discipline through temptations is an "intellectual rod," teaching humility to the one who exalts himself in foolishness. <margin>40.</margin>

The proper work of the intellect is to refuse to tolerate a thought that secretly slanders one’s neighbor. <margin>41.</margin>

Just as a gardener who does not pull out the weeds chokes the vegetables, so also the <unclear>...</unclear> <margin>42.</margin>

An <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "nous"—the "eye of the heart" or the faculty used to perceive spiritual realities.</note> that does not purify its thoughts loses the benefit of its labors.

<margin>40.</margin> A wise man is one who accepts counsel, and especially the guidance offered by a spiritual father.

<margin>41.</margin> One who has been deadened by the passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to disordered or selfish impulses like anger, greed, or lust.</note> does not perceive counsel; he simply cannot endure spiritual discipline at all.

<margin>42.</margin> He who does not accept counsel cannot set his paths straight, but is always carried toward cliffs and ravines.

<margin>43.</margin> A monk is an intellect that has renounced the world of the senses, and cannot endure to look even upon a thought of pleasure.

<margin>44.</margin> A physician is an intellect that has healed itself, and then heals others using the same remedies by which it was cured.

<margin>45.</margin> Seek virtue and do not let yourself be deprived of it, so that you do not live shamefully and die a pitiful death.

<margin>46.</margin> Our Lord Jesus granted light to everyone, but those who do not obey Him cast themselves into darkness.

<margin>47.</margin> Do not consider the loss of virtue to be a small thing, for it was through this loss that death entered the world.

<margin>48.</margin> Obedience to the commandment is the resurrection of the dead; for life follows virtue as a natural consequence.

<margin>49.</margin> Once the intellect was deadened by the transgression of your commandment, the death of the body followed by necessity.

<margin>50.</margin> Just as Adam fell under the power of death by his transgression, so the Savior, through His obedience, put death to death.

<margin>51.</margin> Put wickedness to death so that you do not "rise dead," passing from a small death into a great one. <note>The "small death" refers to physical death, while the "great death" refers to eternal separation from God.</note>

<margin>52.</margin> Because of Adam's transgression, the Savior became human, so that by undoing the condemnation He might raise all people up.

<margin>53.</margin> He passes from life to life who has put the passions to death and has separated himself from ignorance.

<margin>54.</margin> Search the Scriptures and you will find the commandments; do what they say, and you will be delivered from the passions.

<margin>55.</margin> Obedience to a commandment brings about the purification of the soul; and the purification of the soul brings about a participation in the Light.

<margin>56.</margin> The "Tree of Life" <note>A reference to the tree in the Garden of Eden, here interpreted allegorically.</note> is the knowledge of God; the pure person who participates in it remains immortal.

<column-break/>

The beginning of the practical life is faith in Christ, and its end is the love of Christ. <margin>57.</margin>

Jesus is the Christ, our Lord and God, who granted us faith in Him as a path to life. <margin>58.</margin>

He appeared to us with a soul, a body, and divinity, so that as God He might redeem both soul and body from death. <margin>59.</margin>

Let us acquire faith so that we may reach love, from which the illumination of knowledge is born. <margin>60.</margin>

To the possession of faith, these things follow in order: fear of God, self-control regarding pleasures, patience in labors, hope in God, <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "apatheia"—not a lack of feeling, but a state of being "passion-less," where one is no longer controlled by impulsive desires.</note>, and love. <margin>61.</margin>

From sincere love, a natural knowledge is born; this is then succeeded by the ultimate object of desire: the grace of <term>theology</term>. <note>In the early Church, "theology" did not mean academic study, but the highest state of prayer and direct union with God.</note> <margin>62.</margin>

An intellect that masters the passions certainly does so out of fear, believing God regarding the things it has hoped for and the things He has promised. <margin>63.</margin>

From the one to whom faith was given, self-control is demanded; when this endures over time, it gives birth to patience, which is a habit born of much labor. <margin>64.</margin>

The sign of patience is a love of labors; trusting in these, the intellect hopes to obtain what was promised and to escape what was threatened. <margin>65.</margin>

The expectation of future blessings joins the intellect to the things it expects; dwelling among them, it forgets the present world. <margin>66.</margin>

He who has tasted the things hoped for casts aside the things of the present; for he has poured out all his desire into those future blessings. <margin>67.</margin>

God is the one who promised future blessings; the person of self-control, believing Him, desires the future as if it were already present. <margin>68.</margin>

The sign that the intellect is dwelling among the hoped-for blessings is this: a total forgetfulness of things here on earth, and its expansion in the knowledge of the things to come. <margin>69.</margin>

Good is the dispassion which God teaches through truth, providing full assurance to the God-loving soul even from this life. <margin>70.</margin>

Beyond time, before every age, and beyond intellect and speech, are the blessings laid up for the heirs of the promise. <margin>71.</margin>

Let us regulate ourselves by the rules of piety, so that we do not fall away from our hope by being diverted into passions. <margin>72.</margin>

Jesus is the Christ who is one of the Tri— <margin>73.</margin> <note>The text breaks off here mid-word; likely "Trinity."</note>

It frames Christ's incarnation and obedience as the corrective to Adam's fall, offering a path for the soul to return to the "Tree of Life."</summary>

<margin>74.</margin> ...give, of which you are also to be an heir. He who has been taught the knowledge of created things by God does not doubt the Scriptures concerning the things previously mentioned.

<margin>75.</margin> When the Holy Spirit finds an <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "nous"—the spiritual faculty of the soul, often called the "eye of the heart."</note> stripped of passions, He initiates it proportionally into all the things we hope for.

<margin>76.</margin> The soul is granted knowledge of the divine words in proportion to the purification of its intellect.

<margin>77.</margin> He who has disciplined his body and dwells in spiritual knowledge is further purified by that very knowledge.

<margin>78.</margin> An intellect beginning to <term>philosophize</term> <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to the pursuit of divine wisdom and the ascetic life, rather than secular logic.</note> about divine things starts from faith, and passing through the intermediate stages, ends again in the highest form of faith.

<margin>79.</margin> At the beginning of this journey, fear is seen following behind; but at the end, love leads the way.

<margin>80.</margin> The intellect, starting from immediate faith, ends in a "theology" that is beyond all intellect; they define this as "unforgetting faith" and the contemplation of things that are invisible.

<margin>81.</margin> Discourses about God are contemplated by the saints not based on what He is in His essence, but from the things "around Him" <note>This refers to God's "energies" or attributes (like goodness and power) which we can perceive, as opposed to His "essence," which remains totally hidden.</note>.

<margin>82.</margin> Understand that those discourses "around God" are all described in two ways: some by <term>affirmation</term> <note>original: "thesin"—kataphatic theology, or saying what God IS (e.g., God is Good).</note> and some by <term>negation</term> <note>original: "aphairesin"—apophatic theology, or saying what God IS NOT (e.g., God is Infinite/not-finite).</note>.

<margin>83.</margin> Essence, deity, and goodness are said affirmatively; while being without beginning, infinite, and undefined are said negatively, by "removal" of human limits.

<margin>84.</margin> While the Holy Trinity is one essence beyond intellect, word, and hidden deity, the things contemplated "around" the Trinity are the ones mentioned above and others like them.

<margin>85.</margin> Just as they speak of one deity of the Holy Trinity, they also glorify the three <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: "hypostaseis"—the distinct persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit who share one divine nature.</note> of the one deity.

<margin>86.</margin> They understand the affirmations and negations mentioned before as being common to the Holy and <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "homoousios"—meaning "of the very same substance" or "one in being."</note> Trinity, excluding the unique personal properties.

<margin>87.</margin> They call the unique properties of the divine persons these: Fatherhood, Sonship, and Procession <note>The Holy Spirit "proceeds" from the Father.</note>, along with whatever else is said specifically of each.

<margin>88.</margin> They define a <term>hypostasis</term> as "essence with unique properties." Therefore, each person has both

<column-break/>

the common nature of the essence and the particular identity of the person.

<margin>89.</margin> They judge those things said commonly about the Holy Trinity by negation to be more accurate; however, this is not the case for the unique properties, for they say some of those are affirmative and some are negative, as mentioned before. Examples include "begotten" and "unbegotten." For "unbegottenness" differs from "begetting" only in what they signify: the first means the Father is not begotten, and the second means the Son is begotten.

<margin>90.</margin> One uses human words and names only for the sake of clarity regarding the discourses contemplated "around" the essence of the Holy Trinity. For these realities are unknown and ineffable to every mind and word, and are known only to the Holy Trinity itself.

<margin>91.</margin> Just as they call the one essence of the deity "three-personed," so they also confess the Holy Trinity to be of one substance.

<margin>92.</margin> The Father is seen as both "without beginning" and as the "Beginning." He is without beginning as He is unbegotten; but He is the Beginning as He is the begetter and sender-forth of those who come from Him according to essence, and who exist eternally in Him—namely, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

<margin>93.</margin> The <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Unity" or the "One."</note> moving from itself into a Trinity remains a Monad; and the Trinity, gathered back into a Monad, remains a Trinity—which is a great paradox.

<margin>94.</margin> They understand the Son and the Spirit as being both "without beginning" and "eternal." They are not "without beginning" in terms of their source (since they are referred back to the Father as their source), but they are eternal because they exist eternally with the Father—the one by being begotten, the other by proceeding.

<margin>95.</margin> They preserve the one deity of the Trinity as indivisible, and they maintain the three persons of the one deity as distinct and unconfused.

<margin>96.</margin> As for unique properties: they say "without beginning" and "unbegotten" belong to the Father; "being in the beginning" and "begotten" belong to the Son; "being with the beginning" and "proceeding" belong to the Holy Spirit. They do not call the "beginning" of the Son and the Spirit a temporal one—for how could it be? Rather, they indicate the Cause from which, like light from the sun, they have their existence eternally. They are from the Cause according to essence, even if they are not "after" the Cause in time.

<summary>This page contains a series of theological maxims by St. Thalassius defining the relationship between the one Essence and the three Persons of the Holy Trinity. He explains that God is understood both through what we can affirm (Goodness) and what we must negate (Infinitedness), emphasizing that the Persons of the Trinity are distinct but indivisible.</summary>

<page-num>341</page-num>
<header>ON LOVE AND SELF-CONTROL</header>

<margin>97.</margin> The distinctness <term>particularity</term> <note>original: "idiotes"</note> of the <term>persons</term> <note>original: "hypostases"—the three individual realities of the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> is preserved among them as immovable and unchangeable; and the commonality of the <term>essence</term> <note>original: "ousia"—the divine nature shared by the Trinity</note>, that is, the Godhead, is indivisible.

<margin>98.</margin> They confess a Unity in Trinity, and a Trinity in Unity, divided undividedly and joined together with distinction <note>original: "dieiremenos"—meaning they are distinct as persons but never separated in essence.</note>.

<margin>99.</margin> They know one Principle <note>original: "Arche"—meaning the source or origin of all existence.</note> of all things: the Father. He is the begetter of the Son and the source of the Spirit, as the eternal and co-eternal, infinite, and boundless source, <term>of one essence</term> <note>original: "homoousion"—having the same nature or substance.</note> and inseparable. Of created things, He is the Creator, Provider, and Judge; acting through the Son, clearly, in the Holy Spirit. For "from Him," it says, "and through Him, and to Him are all things; to Him be glory forever. Amen."

<column-break/>

<margin>100.</margin> Again, they say that the Son and the Holy Spirit are co-eternal with the Father, yet not "without source" <note>original: "synanarcha"—literally "without a beginning-principle."</note>. They are co-eternal as co-existing with the Father from infinity; but they are not "without source" in the sense of being without a cause, for they are from Him—even if they are not *after* Him—just as light comes from the sun, as was said before. They also call them "without beginning" <note>original: "anarcha"</note> when the term refers to a beginning in time, so that those things from which time itself originates are not thought to be subject to time. Thus, they are not "without beginning" in relation to their Cause <note>The Father</note>, but they are "without beginning" in relation to time, existing before all time and every age, and beyond age and time, through whom every age and time exist—both the things in ages and the things in time—and as co-eternal with the Father, as was said before. With whom be glory and power to Him, unto the ages of ages. Amen.

# A SHORT BIOGRAPHY
## OF OUR HOLY FATHER
# JOHN OF DAMASCUS

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' featuring stylized floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
Our Father among the Saints, John of Damascus—who, because of the gold-shining grace of his teaching, was nicknamed "Golden-flowing" <note>original: "Chrysorrhoas"—a title likening his eloquence to a river of gold.</note>—flourished during the reign of Leo the Isaurian <note>A Byzantine Emperor (reigned 717–741) known for his policy of Iconoclasm, which John strongly opposed.</note> around the year 730. Having served as a sacred Muse for the Church of Christ, he left behind many writings for her, dripping with unspeakable pleasure and spiritual grace. Among these, we have placed here the present discourse, as it contributes greatly to the subject of this book and is highly necessary for those who desire to

<column-break/>

know the knowledge of virtues and vices, which remains hidden from many. For he teaches clearly what they are, how many they are, and into how many types and kinds they are divided, and how one might come to possess the former and be rid of the latter. In short, this work is a "Lydian stone" <note>A touchstone used since antiquity to test the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves.</note>, scientifically distinguishing the proven gold of the virtues from the copper-adulterated <note>Imitation or fake gold.</note> nature of the vices. Thus, whoever accurately stores this knowledge in his breast will become, in a short time, an expert in all the virtues and passions without exception.

---

# BY OUR HOLY FATHER
## JOHN OF DAMASCUS

->A SOUL-PROFITING AND WONDERFUL DISCOURSE.<-

---

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'I' begins the text, set within a rectangular decorative frame featuring floral patterns, scrollwork, and small crosses at the cardinal points.</image-desc>

It should be known that man is twofold, composed of soul and body; he also has twofold senses, and twofold virtues for these. There are five senses of the soul and five of the body. The senses of the soul—which the wise also call "powers"—are these: <term>mind</term> <note>original: "nous"—the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the "eye of the heart."</note>, intellect, opinion, imagination, and sensation. The bodily senses are these: sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch. Thus, the virtues of these are twofold, as are the vices. Therefore, it is necessary for every person to know clearly how many are the virtues of the soul and how many are of the body, and likewise which are the passions of the soul and which are of the body.

We say that the primary virtues of the soul are these four most general ones: <term>courage</term> <note>original: "andreia"</note>, <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "phronesis"</note>, <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "sophrosyne"</note>, and **justice**. From these are born the other soul-virtues: faith, hope, love, prayer, humility, gentleness, long-suffering, forbearance, kindness, freedom from anger, divine knowledge, cheerfulness, simplicity, tranquility, sincerity, lack of vanity, lack of pride, lack of envy, guilelessness, freedom from the love of money, compassion, mercifulness, generosity, fearlessness, freedom from sorrow, remorse, modesty, piety, the desire for future blessings, the longing for the Kingdom of God, and the desire for adoption as sons of God.

The bodily virtues are these—or rather, they are the tools of virtue when practiced with knowledge and according to God's will, free from all hypocrisy and people-pleasing, leading a person toward progress in humility and <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "apatheia"—not a lack of feeling, but a state of soul where one is no longer controlled by disordered desires.</note>: self-control, fasting, hunger, thirst, vigil, standing all night in prayer, frequent kneeling <note>original: "kampsis gonaton"—prostrations.</note>, forgoing bathing, wearing only one tunic, eating dry foods, eating slowly, drinking only water, sleeping on the ground, poverty, lack of possessions, being unkempt, 

<column-break/>

neglecting appearance, lack of self-love, solitude, silence, not going out, being in want, self-sufficiency, quietness, practicing manual labor with one’s own hands, and every kind of hardship and bodily training. All these are most necessary and most profitable when the body is healthy and bothered by carnal passions. But if the body is weak, and with God’s help it has overcome these passions, these practices are not as necessary as holy humility and thanksgiving, which fulfill all things.

We must also speak of the vices of the soul and body, that is, the passions. The passions of the soul are these: forgetfulness, laziness, and ignorance. By these three, the eye of the soul—that is, the <term>mind</term>—is darkened and becomes dominated by all the other passions, which are: impiety, false belief <note>original: "kakodoxia"—specifically referring to heresy or wrong teaching.</note> or every kind of heresy, blasphemy, wrath, anger, bitterness, quick-temperedness, hatred of humanity, resentment, slander, condemnation, irrational sorrow, fear, cowardice, strife, jealousy, envy, vainglory, pride, hypocrisy, falsehood, unbelief, greed, love of material things, attachment, obsession with earthly matters, <term>listlessness</term> <note>original: "akedia"—a state of spiritual apathy or "the noonday demon."</note>, faint-heartedness, ingratitude, grumbling, vanity, conceit, pomposity, boastfulness, love of power, people-pleasing, deceit, shamelessness, insensitivity, flattery, craftiness, irony, double-mindedness, consenting to sins arising from the passionate part of the soul and constant meditation upon them, wandering of thoughts, self-love (the mother of all evils), and the root of all evils, the love of money, along with malice and wickedness.

The bodily passions are: gluttony, greediness, luxury, drunkenness, secret eating, various forms of love of pleasure, fornication, adultery, licentiousness, uncleanness, incest, the corruption of children, bestiality, evil desires, and all the shameful passions contrary to nature; thievery... <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "kleps..." (theft).</note>
