...sacrilege, robbery, murder, every kind of bodily ease, and the indulgence of the desires of the flesh—especially when the body is in good health; divinations, sorcery, omens, interpreting bird-signs, love of the world, ostentation, foolishness, vanity, face-painting, the blameworthy vice of idleness, light-mindedness, gambling, and the passionate misuse of the world's pleasures. The "flesh-loving" life, which thickens the mind and makes it earthly and beast-like, never allows it to look up toward God or the practice of the virtues. The roots of all these passions—and one might call them the primary causes—are <term>love of pleasure</term> <note>original: "philēdonia"</note>, <term>love of glory</term> <note>original: "philodoxia"</note>, and <term>love of money</term> <note>original: "philargyria"</note>, from which every evil is born. Indeed, a person does not commit any single sin unless these "mighty giants" first prevail and take mastery over them—as the most wise among ascetics, Mark, says—namely: <term>forgetfulness</term> <note>original: "lēthē"</note>, <term>sloth</term> <note>original: "rhathymia"</note>, and <term>ignorance</term> <note>original: "agnoia"</note>. These, in turn, are given birth by pleasure and ease, and by loving the glory of men and being distracted by them. But the primary cause of all these, and the "wicked mother" of them as has been said before, is <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "philautia"</note>, which is an irrational love for the body and a passionate attachment to it. Furthermore, the scattering and loosening of the mind through jesting and foul language are the sponsors of many evils and falls, as are <term>boldness</term> <note>original: "parrhēsia"—here meaning a lack of healthy boundaries or irreverence</note> and laughter. In addition to all these, one must know that passionate love of pleasure is diverse and multi-faceted, and many are the pleasures that deceive the soul when it is not sober toward God, strengthened by divine fear and the love of Christ, and diligent in the work of the virtues. For ten thousand pleasures are brought forth to drag the eyes of the soul toward themselves: <unclear>those</unclear> of bodies, of money, of luxury, of glory, of sloth, of anger, of power, of greed, and of avarice. Through deception, these appear to have bright and lovely faces, capable of drawing in those who are startled by such things and who do not love virtue intensely or endure its hardships. Every earthly attachment and passionate connection to material things creates pleasure and delight for the one who is attached; it reveals the soul’s faculty of desire as being irrationally and harmfully obsessed with these things. Because of this, when deprived of the thing desired, the one who is defeated by it is subjected to wrath, anger, grief, and malice.

<column-break/>

If, alongside this passionate attachment, a small habit gains the upper hand, it—alas!—imperceptibly and incurably prepares the captive to cling to that irrational attachment until the end, because of the pleasure hidden within it. For the pleasure of desire is many-sided, as was said before; it is fulfilled not only in fornication and other bodily enjoyments, but in all other passions as well. For <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "sophrosyne"—literally "sound-mindedness" or self-control</note> is not only abstaining from fornication and the pleasures of the belly, but also being free from all other pleasures. Therefore, the one who loves money, silver, or gain is "incontinent." For just as the former loves bodies, the latter loves money. In fact, the latter is even more "incontinent," inasmuch as he does not even have the force of nature pushing him toward it. Truly, that man would be called an unskilled charioteer who cannot restrain a gentle and compliant horse, rather than one who fails to hold back a harsh and difficult one. It is clear from every angle that the desire for money is superfluous and "unnatural," since it does not have its force from nature, but from a wicked choice; therefore, the person who is willingly defeated by it sins without excuse. Thus, we must clearly recognize that "love of pleasure" is not defined only by luxury and bodily enjoyment, but by every manner, thing, and choice of the soul that is loved with passionate attachment. So that the passions may be even more clearly distinguished according to the <term>tripartite soul</term> <note>The Platonic and Patristic model dividing the soul into three parts: Rational, Irascible (Spirited), and Desiring.</note>, we have decided to add these points in summary. The soul is divided into three: the **Rational**, the **Irascible**, and the **Desiring**. These are the sins of the **Rational** part: unbelief, heresy, foolishness, blasphemy, ingratitude, and the consenting to sins which arise from the passionate part of the soul. The healing and cure for these evils is unwavering faith in God, and the true, unerring, and orthodox dogmas of piety; the constant study of the oracles of the Spirit; pure and unceasing prayer, and thanksgiving to God. The sins of the **Irascible** part are these: cruelty, heartless hatred, malice, envy, murder, and constant...

# BY OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, JOHN OF DAMASCENUS

...continuous study of such things. But the healing and treatment for these <note>referring to the "irascible" or spirited part of the soul mentioned previously</note> is love for mankind, love, gentleness, brotherly love, compassion, patience, and kindness. 

The sins of the **desiring part** of the soul are these: gluttony, greediness, drunkenness, fornication, adultery, impurity, licentiousness, love of money, the desire for empty glory, for gold and wealth, and for fleshly pleasures. Their healing and treatment is fasting, self-control, enduring hardship, voluntary poverty, the scattering of wealth to the poor, a longing for those future immortal goods, the yearning for the Kingdom of God, and the desire for adoption as a child of God. 

It is necessary, therefore, for you to also understand the diagnosis of the **passionate thoughts** <note>original: "empathōn logismōn"</note>, through which every sin is performed. There are eight primary thoughts that encompass all wickedness:
1. Gluttony
2. Fornication
3. Love of money
4. Anger
5. Sadness <note>Specifically, worldly grief that leads to despair.</note>
6. Listlessness <note>original: "akēdia" – a state of spiritual apathy or "the noonday demon."</note>
7. Vainglory
8. Pride

Whether these eight thoughts bother us or not is not within our power; but whether they remain in us or not, and whether they stir up the passions or not, is within our power. Furthermore, there is a difference between a **provocation**, **coupling**, **struggle**, **passion**, **assent** (which draws near to and resembles the actual deed), **action**, and **captivity**. 

**Provocation** <note>original: "prosbolē"</note> is simply a suggestion made by the enemy <note>the devil</note>, such as, "Do this or that," just as it happened with our Lord and God when the tempter said, "Tell these stones to become bread." As has been said, this is not within our power to prevent. 

**Coupling** <note>original: "syndyasmos"</note> is the acceptance of the thought suggested by the enemy; it is like meditating on it and having a pleasurable conversation with it by our own choice. 

**Passion** <note>original: "pathos"</note> is the habit that arises from "coupling" with the thought suggested by the enemy—a constant meditation and imagination of it. 

**Struggle** <note>original: "palē"</note> is the resistance to the thought, either to destroy the passion within the thought, or to give in to it, as the Apostle says: "For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other." 

**Captivity** <note>original: "aichmalōsia"</note> is the forced and involuntary leading away of the heart, dominated by a prior prejudice and long-standing

<column-break/>

habit. **Assent** <note>original: "synkatathesis"</note> is the "nodding yes" to the passion within the thought. **Action** <note>original: "energeia"</note> is the performance of the deed itself that was agreed upon in the assent. 

Therefore, the person who deals with the first stage—the **provocation**—without passion, or who sends it away with a sharp rebuke from the very first moment, cuts off all the following stages at once.

The destruction of the eight passions should happen as follows:
* **Gluttony** is destroyed by self-control.
* **Fornication** by divine longing and the desire for future goods.
* **Love of money** by compassion for the poor.
* **Anger** by love for all and by goodness.
* **Worldly sadness** by spiritual joy.
* **Listlessness** by patience, endurance, and gratitude toward God.
* **Vainglory** by doing virtuous works in secret and by constant prayer with a broken heart.
* **Pride** by not judging anyone or looking down on them like the boastful Pharisee, but by considering oneself the least of all.

In this way, the mind, having been freed from the aforementioned passions and lifted up to God, lives the blessed life from that moment on, receiving the "pledge" of the Holy Spirit. When such a person departs this life with freedom from passion and true knowledge, they stand before the light of the Holy Trinity, shining alongside the divine angels for endless ages.

As previously shown, the soul has three parts: **Reason**, **Spirit**, and **Desire**. 
* If there is love and kindness in the **Spirit** <note>original: "thymikon" – the part of the soul associated with courage or anger</note>, and purity and self-control in the **Desire**, the **Reason** is enlightened. 
* If there is hatred for man in the **Spirit**, and lack of restraint in the **Desire**, the **Reason** is darkened. 

**Reason** is healthy, self-controlled, and enlightened when it keeps the passions in subjection, contemplates the inner meanings of God’s creations spiritually, and is led up toward the Blessed and Holy Trinity. **Spirit** moves according to its nature when it loves all people and holds no sadness or grudge against anyone. **Desire** is healthy when it has killed the passions through humility, self-control, and voluntary poverty—that is, when it moves past the pleasure of the flesh, money, and fleeting glory, and turns toward the...

# A SOUL-PROFITING DISCOURSE

...divine and immortal love. For desire <note>original: "epithymia"</note> moves toward three things: either toward the pleasure of the flesh, or toward empty glory, or toward the acquisition of money. Because of this irrational longing, a person despises God and His divine commandments; they forget their divine nobility, become wild like a beast toward their neighbor, darken their reason, and are not permitted to look up toward the truth. 

However, the person who has acquired a higher mindset from that point forward—as was said before—receives the Kingdom of Heaven and the blessed life, through the expectation of the blessedness that lies in store for those who love God. May we also be deemed worthy of this through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

One must also know this: it is not possible to reach the measure of any virtue whatsoever except through painstaking diligence <note>original: "philoponia" — literally, a love of labor or spiritual effort</note> to acquire it, striving with all one's power throughout one's whole life through practical care. Take, for example, almsgiving, or self-control, or prayer, or love, or any of the general virtues. 

Each person pursues virtue in a partial way. For instance, someone might practice almsgiving for a time; but because they only do it occasionally, we cannot strictly call them "merciful"—especially when what is done is not performed well and in a way pleasing to God. For even the good is not truly good when it is not done well. It is truly good only if it does not lose its reward because of this or that—perhaps seeking to please men for the sake of reputation, or hunting for glory, or acting out of greed and injustice. 

For God does not look only at the things being done, even if they appear good, but at the **aim** <note>original: "skopos" — the intention or target</note> for which they are done. For the God-bearing Fathers <note>A traditional term for the early Saints and theologians of the Church.</note> also say that whenever the mind forgets the goal of piety, then the visible work of virtue becomes useless. For things done without discernment and without a goal not only offer no benefit, even if they are good, but they even cause harm. 

The opposite is also true for things that appear to be bad, but are done for a godly purpose according to God's will; such as someone who enters a brothel to pull a prostitute out of her destruction. From this it is clear that a person is not "merciful" for giving alms only once, nor "self-controlled" for practicing self-control occasionally. Rather, the name belongs to the one who pursues virtue wholly, for the greatest part and through his entire life, with unfailing **discernment** <note>original: "diakrisis" — the ability to distinguish between spirits and intentions</note>. For discernment is greater than all the virtues,

<column-break/>

being like a queen and the "virtue of virtues." 

In the same way, regarding the opposite vices, we do not call someone a fornicator, or a drunkard, or a liar if they have slipped into one of these once. Rather, we use these names for the one who falls into such things most of the time and remains uncorrected.

Furthermore, it is necessary to know this in addition to what has been said—and it is most essential for all who are eager to master virtue and striving to avoid wickedness: Just as the soul is incomparably better than the body, and is in many great ways more distinct and honorable, so too the **virtues of the soul** (especially those that imitate God and bear His name) are superior to the virtues of the body. 

Conversely, one should understand that the **vices of the soul** are different from the passions of the body, both in their activities and in the payment of their punishments. Yet, I do not know how, but this escapes the notice of the many. They are cautious and flee from—or punish—drunkenness, fornication, adultery, theft, and similar things because they appear loathsome to the public. 

But as for the passions of the soul, which are much worse and heavier than these, and which lead to a demonic state and the eternal punishment laid up for them—toward these, they remain unfeeling if they hold onto them without correction. I am speaking of envy, malice, wickedness, callousness, and the root of all evils: **the love of money** <note>original: "philargyria" — literally, the love of silver.</note>, according to the Apostle, and things similar to these.

But these things we have set forth simply, according to our lack of learning, sketching a clear and concise discourse concerning virtues and passions. We have done this so that one may easily distinguish and recognize their division and difference through this detailed clarity. For this very reason, we have set out each one in its various and many-sided forms, so that no type of virtue or vice, if possible, remains unknown. 

We do this so that we might cheerfully draw the virtues toward ourselves—the virtues of the soul especially, through which we draw near to God—and so that we might flee and escape from the vices with great speed. For truly blessed is the one who seeks virtue and pursues it, and who diligently searches out what virtue is; for through it, he draws near to God and is joined to Him intellectually. For to such a person belong, in the true sense, prudence and courage, wisdom and true knowledge, and...

...is wealth that cannot be taken away: to be led through <term>practical virtue</term> <note>original: "praktikes aretes" — the active practice of the commandments</note> toward the <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "theoria" — spiritual insight or vision</note> of the Creator. It is called **Virtue**, because it is chosen <note>The author makes a wordplay between the Greek words "Arete" (virtue) and "haireisthai" (to choose)</note>. It is desirable and willed because we do good by our own choice and self-will, not involuntarily or by necessity. And it is called **Prudence**, as it means "carrying benefits within the mind." If you wish, let us add to this simple discourse, like a golden seal, a small word concerning what it means to be in the **image** and **likeness**, the most precious of all God’s creatures. Man alone, out of all things, is a mindful and rational living being created in the **image** and **likeness** of God. Every human being is said to be "in the image" according to the dignity of the mind and the soul—that is, its quality of being incomprehensible, invisible, immortal, and possessing free will. Indeed, it also includes the power of authority, procreation, and the ability to build. But "in the likeness" refers to the principle of virtue, and these actions which are named after God and imitate Him—

<column-break/>

—namely, in being kindly disposed toward those of the same race, to have compassion, to show mercy, and to love one’s fellow servant, and to demonstrate every kind of tender-heartedness and sympathy. For He says, Christ our God:
> **Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful.**

And while every human being possesses being "in the image"—for the gifts of God are irrevocable—the "likeness" is possessed by only a few: the virtuous and the holy, who imitate the goodness of God as far as is possible for humans. May we also be deemed worthy of His exceedingly good love for mankind, having pleased Him through good works and becoming imitators of those who have pleased Christ from the beginning of time. For to Him belongs mercy, and to Him is due all glory, honor, and worship, together with His Father who is without beginning, and His all-holy, good, and life-giving Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

# A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## CONCERNING ABBA
# PHILEMON

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter P (Φ) featuring ornate floral and strapwork patterns.</image-desc>
Philemon, our most holy Father, was among the <term>God-bearing Fathers</term> the most <term>watchful</term> <note>original: "neptikos" — referring to "nepsis," a state of spiritual sobriety and alertness</note> and also the most mournful. History has not revealed to us the exact times in which he flourished. However, it is set before those who wish to see in this present account that he stood out as much as any of the elders as most reverent, highly experienced, a lover of stillness, and a most genuine imitator of <term>Arsenius the Great</term> <note>A famous 4th-5th century desert father known for his silence and gift of tears</note>.
For persisting in prayers and petitions night and day in his ascetic hut, as if in some upper room of life,

<column-break/>

and washing himself ever more in the ever-flowing springs of tears and most sweet weeping, he did not merely surpass anything of the "evil party," but even those of the "better portion." He transcended all things at once—both the sensible and the intelligible—in a way pleasing to God. He stood before God "deaf and dumb," as it is written <note>A reference to Psalm 38:13, describing a state of total inner silence</note>, and he obtained the illumination of His divine and most beautiful grace. From this grace, as if from a solar disc, this celebrated man was abundantly enriched with the power to examine, to discern, to see clearly, and to foresee, all through the highest <term>stillness</term> <note>original: "hesychia" — a state of inner quietude and contemplative silence</note> and silence. This present discourse of his is a reliable witness to what has been said.

### CONCERNING ABBA
# PHILEMON
### A VERY PROFITABLE DISCOURSE.

<image-desc>Decorative scroll divider between the top text and the new chapter title. A decorative initial letter 'E' at the beginning of the text, surrounded by an ornate woodcut frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>

They used to say about Abba Philemon the **Hermit** <term>anachorete</term> <note>one who has withdrawn from the world for religious reasons</note> that he shut himself in a certain cave a short distance from the <term>Laura</term> <note>a type of monastery consisting of a cluster of individual cells for hermits</note> called "of the Romans." There he held fast to the struggles of asceticism, chanting to his own mind that which they say the **Great Arsenius** <note>Saint Arsenius the Great (c. 350–445 AD), a famous Desert Father known for his silence</note> used to say to himself: "Philemon, why did you come out?" He persevered in the cave for a sufficient time, working at making rope and weaving baskets, which he gave to the steward in exchange for a small amount of bread for nourishment. For he ate nothing except bread and salt, and even those only every few days. Consequently, he took no care for the flesh at all, but devoting himself to contemplation, he existed within the divine illumination. From that state, being initiated into the unutterable sacred mysteries, he lived in joy. When he went to the church on Saturdays and Sundays, he walked alone and deep in thought, allowing no one to approach him, so that his mind might not be interrupted from its work. In the church, he stood in a corner, pressing his face toward the ground, letting flow fountains of tears; he maintained unceasing mourning, the memory of death, and the example of the Holy Fathers—especially the Great Arsenius, whose footsteps he strove to follow.

<column-break/>

When a heresy arose in **Alexandria** and its surrounding area, he withdrew and went to the Laura of Nikanor nearby. There, the most God-beloved Paulinos received him, and having dedicated his own private place to him, established him in total **stillness** <term>hesychia</term> <note>original: "hesychia" — a central practice in Eastern Christian monasticism involving inner silence and the cessation of worldly concerns</note>. Indeed, for a whole year, he did not allow anyone at all to meet with him; in fact, Paulinos himself did not disturb him in the least, except only at the time when he provided him with the bread he required. When the Holy Resurrection of Christ [Easter] arrived, they met together, and during their conversation, the subject of the desert life was raised. Realizing that this goal was the preferred choice of this most devout brother, Philemon sowed in him ascetic, scriptural, and patristic words, demonstrating through all of them that without perfect stillness, it is impossible to please God. As it was also philosophized by the divinely-inspired Father **Moses** <note>likely referring to Abba Moses the Black, a prominent Desert Father</note>: "Stillness gives birth to asceticism; asceticism gives birth to weeping; weeping gives birth to fear; fear gives birth to humility; humility gives birth to foresight; foresight gives birth to love; and love makes the soul healthy and passionless. And then a person knows that they are not far from God." He said to him then: "You must completely purify the mind through stillness, and give to it

### CONCERNING ABBA PHILEMON

...unceasing spiritual labor. For just as the eye gazes upon sensible objects and is filled with wonder at the sight, so too the pure **mind** <term>nous</term> <note>original: "nous" — the highest faculty of the human soul, often called the "eye of the heart," capable of direct spiritual perception</note> gazes upon spiritual realities and is enraptured by spiritual **contemplation** <term>theoria</term> <note>original: "theoria" — the direct vision or insight into divine truths</note>, becoming difficult to draw away. And the more it is stripped of passions and purified through **stillness** <term>hesychia</term> <note>original: "hesychia" — a state of inner silence and tranquility essential for prayer</note>, the more it is deemed worthy of knowledge. The mind is perfect when it transcends essential knowledge and is united with God. Thus, possessing the royal dignity, it no longer tolerates being impoverished, nor is it carried away by lower desires, even if you were to offer it all the kingdoms of the world. 

If, therefore, you wish to attain all these virtues, be free from care regarding every man. Fleeing, flee the world, and walk eagerly on the path of the saints. Keep a neglected appearance, a soiled garment, humble clothing, a simple character, a plain word, a gait without vanity, an unaffected voice, living in poverty, being despised by all, and above all, maintain the guarding of the mind and **watchfulness** <term>nepsis</term> <note>original: "nepsis" — spiritual sobriety or alertness</note>. Practice endurance in all the narrowest circumstances, and keep all the good things you possess intact and unshaken. Pay strict attention to yourself, so as not to admit any of the intrusive pleasures. For the passions of the soul are stilled by silence; but when irritated and provoked, they naturally grow more wild and force those who possess them to sin further—just as physical wounds become difficult to heal when rubbed and scratched. Therefore, even an idle word can separate the mind from the memory of God, as the demons press toward this end and the senses obey them. For a great struggle and fear can guard the soul. You must, therefore, be separated from the entire world, and tear the soul away from sympathy for the body, becoming a man without a city, without a home, without personal property, without love of money, possessing nothing, without business, without contracts, ignorant of human affairs, humble-minded, compassionate, good, gentle, quiet, ready to receive in the heart the impressions born of divine knowledge. For it is impossible to write on wax without first smoothing away the characters previously inscribed there. This is what **Basil the Great** <note>St. Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), one of the most influential Fathers of the early Church</note> teaches us. Such was the 

<column-break/>

**choir of saints**, entirely separated from the conduct of the world, keeping the heavenly mindset unclouded within themselves; they shone brightly through the divine laws. Through both pious deeds and flashing words, they put to death their earthly members through self-control, and the fear and love of God. For through unceasing prayer and the study of the **Divine Scriptures** <note>The Bible, particularly the New Testament and the Psalms</note>, the spiritual eyes of the soul are opened, and they see the King of powers. Then great joy and a sharp desire are kindled in the soul, and as the flesh is also lifted up by the Spirit, the human being becomes entirely spiritual. These are the workers of blessed stillness and the narrowest way of life, who, having separated themselves from all human consolation, converse purely **alone to the alone** <note>original: "monoi pros mono" — a classic phrase describing the soul's direct intimacy with God in the heights of prayer</note> with the Master in the heavens.

When a certain God-loving brother heard these things and was wounded in his soul by divine desire, he went with him to **Skete** <note>A famous monastic settlement in the Egyptian desert</note>, where the greatest of the holy fathers finished the race of piety. They dwelt in the **Lavra** <term>lavra</term> <note>original: "laura" — a type of monastery consisting of a cluster of individual cells or caves for hermits</note> of **Saint John the Dwarf** <note>original: "Ioannou tou Kolobou" — a famous 4th-century Egyptian desert father known for his humility and obedience</note>, entrusting their care to the steward of the Lavra because they wished to live in stillness. By the grace of God, they lived in total stillness, making their way to the services without offense on Saturdays and Sundays; but for the remaining days of the week, they persevered, each performing their prayers and liturgies. This was the liturgy of the Holy Elder: at night, he would chant the entire **Psalter** <note>The Book of Psalms</note> and the odes quietly, and read one section of the **Gospel** <note>original: "megaleiou" — here referring to the "great" or "magnificent" words of the Gospel</note>. Then he would sit by himself, saying:

->**Lord have mercy**<-
<note>original: "Kyrie eleison" — the foundational phrase of the "Jesus Prayer"</note>

intently and for such a long time that he was no longer able to speak the words aloud. Then he would take some sleep, and so again around dawn, he would chant the First Hour and sit in his chair facing the east, chanting alternately; and again reciting from memory the **Apostle** <note>The Epistles of the New Testament, typically St. Paul</note> and the Gospel. Thus he spent every day, unceasingly chanting and praying, and being nourished by the contemplation of heavenly things, so that his mind was often raised up to contemplation and he did not know if he was still upon the earth. # A TRULY BENEFICIAL DISCOURSE

...the elder was so unyieldingly intent upon the **divine services** <term>leitourgiai</term> <note>original: "leitourgiai" — here referring to the prescribed cycle of prayer and worship</note>, and so completely transformed by divine thoughts, that a disciple said to him: “You labor so, Father, in such old age, chastening your body and bringing it into subjection?” But he answered and said: “Believe me, child; God has placed such zeal and longing for the service in my soul that I am able to fulfill its intensity. For longing for God and the hope of future blessings overcomes bodily weakness.” Thus he kept his whole longing taking wing toward heaven in his **mind** <term>nous</term>; and not only at other times, but even at the time of the table. Once, a certain brother living with him asked him: “What might be the mystery of **contemplation** <term>theoria</term>?” And when he saw that the brother was eager to learn and persistent, he said to him: “I tell you truly, child: if a person’s mind is purified to the highest degree, God reveals to them the contemplations of the very **liturgical powers** <note>This likely refers to the angelic ranks who serve in the heavenly liturgy</note> and orders.” He also asked him this: “Why, Father, do you find such sweetness in the **Psalter** <note>The Book of Psalms</note> above all other Holy Scripture? And why, when chanting softly, do you recite the words as if conversing with someone?” He said to him: “I tell you, child, God has imprinted the power of the psalms in my humble soul just as He did for the Prophet David; and I cannot be separated from the sweetness of the various contemplations within them. For they contain all of Holy Scripture.” And after being much pressed, he confessed these things with great humility for the sake of the brother's benefit.

A certain brother named John, coming from the coastal regions, approached this Saint and Great Father Philemon, and taking hold of his feet, said to him: “What shall I do, Father, to be saved? For I see that my mind is led about and wanders here and there, into things it should not.” The elder, after a short pause, said: “This is a passion of those outside <note>i.e., those still living in the world or not yet advanced in the spiritual life</note>, and it remains because you do not yet have perfect longing for God. For the warmth of longing and knowledge of Him has not yet come into you.” The brother says: “And what shall I do, Father?” He says to him: “Go, for now, and have a **hidden meditation** <term>krypte melete</term> in your heart, which can purify your mind from these things.” The brother, being uninitiated

<column-break/>

in what was being said, says to the Elder: “What is this hidden meditation, Father?” And he says to him: “Go, be **watchful** <term>nephe</term> <note>original: "nephe" — to be spiritually sober, alert, and attentive to one's thoughts</note> in your heart, and in your soul, with watchfulness and with fear and trembling, say:
> Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.
For the Blessed **Diadochos** <note>Diadochos of Photiki (c. 400–485), a spiritual writer whose works are included in the Philokalia</note> also passes this down to beginners.” Having gone away then, and by the cooperation of God and the prayers of the Father, having entered into **stillness** <term>hesychia</term>, he was sweetened by this meditation for a short time. But when it suddenly left him, and he was no longer able to practice it with watchfulness and to pray, he came again to the Elder and reported what happened to him. The Elder says to him: “Behold, for now you have known a trace of stillness and labor, and you have tasted the sweetness that comes from it. Keep this, then, in your heart always. Whether you eat, or drink, or find yourself in the company of others, or are outside your cell, or on a journey, let it not pass from you; with a watchful soul and an unwavering mind, pray this prayer, and chant, and meditate on prayers and psalms. Even in your necessary tasks, let your mind not be idle, meditating and praying in secret. For thus you can understand the depths of Holy Scripture and the power hidden within it, and give unceasing work to the mind, so that you fulfill the apostolic saying which commands:
> Pray without ceasing.
Attend closely, then, and guard your heart from receiving evil thoughts, or any vain and useless ones, but always—both when sleeping and rising, eating and drinking, and conversing—let your heart secretly in its soul sometimes meditate on the psalms, and sometimes pray:
> Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.
And again, when you chant with your tongue, take care not to say one thing with your mouth while your soul wanders in other things.” And again the brother asked: “In my sleep I see many vain fantasies.” The Elder said to him: “Do not be hesitant or discouraged; but before you sleep, make many prayers in your heart, and resist your thoughts, so as not to be led about by the desires of the devil, that God may receive you. As much as you have strength, take care to fall asleep after the psalms and mindful meditation.”

### CONCERNING ABBA PHILEMON

...and do not be negligent and permit your **mind** <term>nous</term> <note>In this tradition, the "nous" is the "eye of the soul" or the faculty that perceives God directly, distinct from the discursive reason.</note> to entertain distracting thoughts. Instead, lie down to sleep while meditating on the very things you were praying for, so that these thoughts may remain with you while you sleep and speak to you when you wake. Recite also the **Holy Symbol of the Orthodox Faith** <note>The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, the foundational statement of Christian belief</note> before you fall asleep. For holding the correct glory concerning God is the source and the guardian of all good things.

Again, a brother asked him, saying: "Out of love, Father, tell me: what is the inner work of your mind? Teach me, so that I too might be saved." But the Elder said: "Why do you wish to be so inquisitive about these things?" But the brother stood up, held the feet of the Saint, and kissed them, begging him to tell him. After many hours, the Elder said: "You are not yet able to bear it; for it belongs to a man who has become established in the habits of righteousness to assign to each sense its proper task. Indeed, it is not possible for someone who is not completely purified from the vain thoughts of the world to be deemed worthy of such a gift. Therefore, if you desire such things, maintain **secret meditation** <note>This refers to the practice of repeating a short prayer or scripture internally throughout the day</note> in a pure heart. For if your prayer and the meditation on the Scriptures remain unceasing, the noetic eyes of the soul will be opened, and a great joy occurs within it, along with a certain inexpressible and sharp longing, as even the flesh is set on fire by the Spirit, so that the whole person becomes spiritual. 

Whether in the night or in the day, if God should grant you to pray with a pure mind without distraction, do not strictly adhere to your personal rule of prayer; instead, as much as you are able, stretch yourself out by clinging to God, and He Himself will enlighten your heart regarding the spiritual work you should undertake." And he added this: "Once a certain elder visited me, and when I asked him about the state of his mind, he said: 'For two years I remained entreating God with my whole heart, asking unceasingly that He might grant the prayer which He himself delivered to his own disciples to be imprinted continually and without distraction in my heart.' And seeing my labor and my endurance, the Great-Giver Lord granted my request." He also said this: "The thoughts that arise in the mind concerning vain things are the sicknesses of an idle and sluggish soul. It is necessary then, according to what is written, to guard our own mind with all watchfulness, and to chant with understanding and pray with a pure mind without distraction..."

<column-break/>

"...Therefore, brothers, God wants us to show our zeal toward Him first through labors, then through love and unceasing prayer, and He Himself provides the way of salvation. It is clear that there is no other path leading up to heaven except for **perfect stillness** <term>hesychia</term> <note>original: "hesychia" — a state of inner quietness and cessation of worldly thoughts</note>, the flight from all evils, the acquisition of good things, perfect love toward Him, and communion with God in holiness and righteousness. If anyone achieves these things, they will very quickly run up to the heavenly realm. But it is absolutely necessary for the one desiring to ascend to this height to **mortify their members that are on the earth** <note>A reference to Colossians 3:5, meaning to put to death worldly impulses</note>. 

For when our soul is delighted by the **contemplation** <term>theoria</term> of the truly Good, it does not turn back toward any of the passions driven by pleasure. Instead, turning away from all bodily indulgence, it receives the manifestation of God with a pure and undefiled mind. We therefore need much watchfulness, bodily labors, and purification of the soul, so that we may house God in our hearts, so that from now on we may fulfill His divine commandments without wandering. He Himself will then teach us to keep His laws securely, sending out His own energies like sunbeams through the grace of the Spirit placed within us. 

For through labors and trials we must purify the Image according to which we were made rational, capable of all understanding, and possessed of a likeness to God. We must keep our senses free from every stain, being reforged as it were through the furnace of trials, and being transformed into the royal dignity. For God created human nature to be a partaker of every good, able to perceive noetically the choirs of angels, the glories of the Dominions, the Powers, the Principalities, the Authorities, the **unapproachable light** <note>original: "phos to aprositon" — a reference to 1 Timothy 6:16 regarding the nature of God's presence</note>, and the glory that flashes beyond all things. When you achieve virtue, do not let your thought be lifted up against your brother, as if you have succeeded and he has been negligent; for this is the beginning of pride. With all your power, guard yourself from doing anything to please people. And if you struggle against a passion, do not grow weary or lose heart if the war persists; but standing up, throw yourself before God with your whole heart, saying with the Prophet: 'Judge, O Lord...'"

<summary>Abba Philemon instructs a disciple on the necessity of "secret meditation" and the purification of the mind to achieve a state of unceasing prayer. He emphasizes that spiritual progress requires stillness (hesychia), humility, and the endurance of trials to restore the divine image within the soul.</summary>

...those who do me wrong; for I am not able to stand against them. And He, seeing your **humility**, will quickly send you His help. When you are walking with someone on the road, do not engage in empty conversation; instead, let the **mind** <term>nous</term> <note>The "nous" is considered the highest faculty of the human person, the "eye of the heart" that communes with God.</note> hold onto whatever spiritual work it had, so that it may develop a good habit, a forgetfulness of the world's pleasures, and arrive at the harbors of **dispassion** <term>apatheia</term> <note>Apatheia does not mean "apathy" in the modern sense, but a state of being free from the control of disordered passions and impulses.</note>.

With these and many more words, he instructed the brother and let him go. After a short time, the brother returned to him again, and beginning his questioning, he said: "What shall I do, Father? For during my nightly **liturgy** <note>In this context, "liturgy" refers to the monk’s private rule of prayer and psalm-chanting during the night.</note>, sleep weighs heavily on me and does not allow me to pray with **watchfulness** <term>nepsis</term> <note>Nepsis is a key term in Eastern Christian spirituality, meaning a state of spiritual sobriety and alertness.</note>; nor can I keep a longer vigil. Should I attempt some **handiwork** <note>original: "ergocheiron" — monks often performed manual labor like weaving baskets or ropes while praying to stay awake.</note> while I chant the Psalms?"

The Elder said: "When you are able to pray with watchfulness, do not touch handiwork. But if you are seized by **listlessness** <term>akedia</term> <note>Often called the "noonday devil," akedia is a state of spiritual boredom, restlessness, or exhaustion.</note>, move yourself a little, threatening your thoughts, and take up the handiwork." The brother spoke to him again: "Do you yourself, Master, not get weighed down by sleep during your liturgy?" He said to him: "Hardly ever; however, if it should ever happen to come upon me a little, I move and I recite from the beginning of the **Gospel according to John** <note>The "Prologue" of John (In the beginning was the Word...) was often used as a powerful meditative tool to refocus the mind on Christ.</note>, stretching the eye of my understanding toward God, and immediately the sleep vanishes. I use the same method regarding **thoughts** <note>original: "logismoi" — these are intrusive, tempting thoughts or "seeds" of temptation.</note>; for when one attacks, I meet it like fire with tears, and it vanishes. But you are not yet able to arm yourself in this way; instead, always maintain **secret meditation** <note>A short, repeated prayer used to keep the mind focused on God throughout the day.</note> and the daily prayers established by the Holy Fathers. I mean specifically the **third, sixth, and ninth hours**, as well as the evening and the nightly liturgies—strive to complete these. Guard yourself with all your might to do nothing for the sake of **human praise** <note>original: "anthropareskeia" — the vice of doing good deeds just to be seen and liked by others.</note>, nor ever hold any enmity against your brother, lest you separate yourself from your brother, and thus separate yourself from your God.

Strive to keep your mind from wandering, keeping it diligently focused on your inner thoughts. When you are in the church and you are about to partake of the **Divine Mysteries of Christ** <note>The Holy Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, do not leave until you have received the 'perfect peace.' Standing in one place, do not move from there until the dismissal. Consider yourself to be standing in **heaven**, and meeting God along with the Holy Angels, and receiving Him...

<column-break/>

...into your heart. Therefore, prepare yourself with **fear and much trembling**, so that you do not partake of the Holy Powers unworthily." Having well-armed the brother with these words in the Lord and having entrusted him to the Spirit of His grace, he let him go.

In addition to these things, the brother who lived with him also related this: "Once, while I was sitting near him, I asked him if he had been tested by the schemes of **demons** while living in the deserts." He replied: "Forgive me, brother; if God should permit the temptations I endured from the **devil** to come upon you, I do not think you could bear their bitterness. This is my seventieth year, or even more, that I have spent enduring temptations, living in various deserts in the highest **stillness** <term>hesychia</term> <note>Hesychia refers to a life of silence, solitude, and inner prayer.</note>. I have been so tested and have suffered such things from them that it is not profitable to describe their bitterness to those who have not yet experienced the life of stillness.

But I always did this in my temptations: I placed all my hope in God, to whom I made my **vows of renunciation** <note>The commitment a monk makes to "renounce" the world and its distractions.</note>. And He immediately rescued me from every necessity. Therefore, brother, I no longer take thought for myself. For I know that He cares for me, and I bear the temptations brought upon me more lightly. I offer only this one thing from my own side: **unceasing prayer**. For I know that the more the terrors intensify, the more the crowns are prepared for the one who endures. These are like 'exchanges' before the **Righteous Judge**.

Knowing these things, brother, do not fall into negligence, knowing that you stand in the middle of a war, struggling, and that those fighting for us against the enemy of God are very many. For how could we ever dare to face such a terrifying opponent of our race if the mighty right hand of **God the Word** <note>original: "Theou Logou" — referring to Jesus Christ as the Eternal Word.</note> did not hold us together, tending and sheltering us? How could human nature withstand his schemes? For who, as it says, 'shall uncover the face of his garment? And who can enter into the folds of his breastplate? From his mouth proceed burning lamps, and sparks of fire are cast abroad. From his nostrils proceeds smoke of a burning furnace, kindled with the fire of coals. His breath is coals, and a flame goes out of his mouth; and in his neck...' <note>A quote from the Book of Job (41:13-22), using the imagery of the Leviathan to describe the terrifying nature of the devil.</note>"

->### ON ABBA PHILEMON ###<-

...power dwells. Destruction runs before him; his heart is hardened; it stands like a stone, and like an **immovable anvil**. He makes the abyss boil like a copper pot; he considers the sea like a jar of ointment, and the underworld <note>original: "tartaron" — the deep pit of judgment</note> of the abyss as a prisoner. He looks upon everything high, for he is the king of all that are in the waters. Against this one, brother, is our struggle. The Word <note>referring to Scripture, specifically the description of Leviathan in Job 41</note> has described such a great and terrible **tyrant**.

But victory over him comes easily to those who have lawfully taken up the **monastic life** <term>monērē bion</term> <note>Literally the "solitary life" or "singular life" of a monk.</note>, because they possess nothing of his—through the renunciation of the world and the courageous practice of the virtues, and because we have the One who fights on our behalf. For tell me, who has ever approached the Lord and taken His fear into his **mind** <term>nous</term> without being transformed in nature? And by brightening himself with divine laws and deeds, has he not made his soul most radiant? And has he not prepared himself to flash forth with divine insights and thoughts? He does not leave the soul idle; for he has God rousing the mind to desire the light insatiably. Such a soul, being frequently energized, is not allowed by the Spirit to grow soft in the **passions**. Rather, like a king, breathing sharp and fearsome fire against his adversaries, cutting them down without mercy and never turning back, he achieves victory in the war through the **practical life** <term>praktikē</term> <note>The active stage of the spiritual life focusing on the purification of the heart and the acquisition of virtues.</note> by raising his hands to heaven, and through the **prayer of the mind**.

The same brother related this again: that in addition to his other virtues, Philemon possessed this one: he could never bear to hear an idle word. If someone, through a lack of attention, described a matter that did not contribute to the benefit of the soul, he would not answer at all. Furthermore, whenever I left to perform some **service** <note>original: "diakonian" — likely a communal chore or errand for the monastery</note>, he never asked, "Why are you leaving?" Or when I returned, he never said, "Where were you?" or "How or what did you do?" Once, for instance, when I had sailed to **Alexandria** for a necessary need, and from there went up to the **Queen of Cities** <note>original: "basilida tōn poleōn" — a traditional title for Constantinople</note> on account of a church matter; and indeed, having spent time with the most devout brothers there, I returned without having sent any word to the servant of God. Having spent a considerable time there, I came back to him in the **Skete** <note>A "skete" is a small, secluded community of monks in the Egyptian desert.</note>. When he saw me, he was filled with joy and greeted me,

<column-break/>

and after saying a prayer, he sat down without asking me anything at all, but remained focused on **contemplation** <term>theoria</term> <note>Theoria is the "vision" or "contemplation" of God, the highest stage of spiritual development in this tradition.</note>. Once, wishing to test him, I remained for several days without giving him bread to eat. He did not seek it, nor did he say anything. Afterward, I made a **prostration** <note>original: "metanoian" — a physical bow to the ground as a gesture of repentance or respect</note> to him and said, "Have charity, Father, and tell me: were you not grieved that I did not bring you food according to the custom?" And he said, "Forgive me, brother; even if you did not give me bread to eat for twenty days, I would not ask it of you. For as long as I endure in my soul, so I do in my body." So much was he focused on the contemplation of the truly Good. 

He used to say: "Since the time I came to the Skete, I have not allowed my **thought** <term>logismos</term> <note>Logismos refers to a thought or mental image, often one that suggests a temptation.</note> to go outside my cell; nor have I accepted any other thought into my mind except the fear of God and the judgments of the age to come. I contemplate the judgment threatened against sinners, the eternal fire, and the outer darkness; I think of how the souls of sinners and the righteous live, and the good things stored up for the righteous. Each one receives his own reward according to his own labor: one for the increase of his toils, another for **almsgiving** and unfeigned love, another for **poverty** <term>aktēmosynē</term> <note>The voluntary state of owning no possessions.</note> and the renunciation of the whole world; another for humility and the highest **stillness** <term>hesychia</term>; another for extreme obedience; another for **living as a stranger** <term>xeniteia</term>. Meditating on all these things, I do not allow another thought to be active in me, nor can I any longer be with men, or occupy my mind with them, lest I be separated from more divine thoughts."

He also added the story of a certain monk, saying that he had reached **dispassion** <term>apatheia</term> and used to receive his bread for food from the hand of an angel; but through negligence, he was deprived of this honor. For when the soul relaxes the intensity and tension of the mind, night takes hold of the soul. For where God does not shine, all things are poured out as if in gloom, and the soul cannot look toward God alone and tremble at His words. "For I am a God at hand," says the Lord, "and not a God far off. Can a man hide himself in secret, and I shall not see him? Do I not [fill] the heaven and the [earth]?" <note>A quotation from the Prophet Jeremiah 23:23-24.</note>

<summary>Abba Philemon describes the intense spiritual battle against the "tyrant" of the abyss and emphasizes the necessity of constant contemplation (theoria). He shares personal anecdotes about his own practice of unceasing prayer and the rewards awaiting those who cultivate specific virtues.</summary>

<keywords>Abba Philemon, spiritual warfare, Leviathan, theoria, hesychia, apatheia, Skete, monastic virtues, noetic prayer</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual dialogue concerning Abba Philemon. Having discussed the spiritual warfare against the "tyrant" of the passions, the text now explores the necessity of constant vigilance, the example of Solomon’s fall, and the specific ladder of virtues—from physical labor to the direct contemplation of God.</meta>

<page-num>353</page-num>
->## A HIGHLY BENEFICIAL DISCOURSE ##<-

“Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.” <note>Jeremiah 23:24</note> And he mentioned many others who had suffered similar things. In addition to these, he brought forward the fall of Solomon, saying: though he had received such great wisdom and was glorified by all—for he rose like the **morning star** <note>original: "heōsphoros" — the bringer of dawn, often used to describe great brilliance</note> in the morning, illuminating everyone with the brightness of his wisdom—yet for a small pleasure, he lost his glory. Therefore, it is a fearful thing to be negligent. One must pray without ceasing, so that no other thought might come and separate us from God, or anything else take its place beside our **mind** <term>nous</term> <note>In Eastern Christian thought, the 'nous' is the eye of the soul or the faculty of direct spiritual perception.</note>. For the pure heart, having become entirely receptive of the Holy Spirit, reflects God Himself clearly as in a mirror.

As I heard these things, he says, I understood by his very deeds that the passions of the flesh were completely inactive in him; he was entirely a lover of better things, so that he was always seen being transformed by the Divine Spirit, groaning with “unutterable groans” <note>Romans 8:26</note>. He was gathered into himself, weighing his own soul, and agonizing lest some impurity might cloud the purity of his intellect by entering in, or some hidden blemish might attach itself to him.

Seeing these things, says the brother who lived with him, and being stirred as if to a zeal for similar achievements, I continually pressed him and made frequent inquiries of him, saying: “How can I, like you, acquire a pure mind?” But he would say: “Go, labor; for there is need of toil and a **pain of heart** <note>original: "ponou kardias" — a technical term for the intense, focused effort in prayer</note>. For things worthy of effort and toil do not come to us while we are sleeping or relaxed. While the goods of the earth may come to some without labor, whoever wishes to come to spiritual progress must, before all things, renounce their own wills and acquire at all times **poverty** <term>aktēmosynēn</term> <note>literally "non-possession," the monastic vow of owning nothing</note> and mourning. One should not pay attention to the sins of others, but to their own alone, and weep for them day and night. And one should not have friendship with any man. For a soul deeply pained by misfortunes, and pierced by the memory of past sins, becomes dead to the world, and the world is made dead to it—that is, the passions of the flesh become inactive, and the person becomes inactive toward the passions. For he who renounces the world and joins himself to Christ, devoting himself to **stillness** <term>hēsychia</term> <note>the state of inner quiet and external silence sought by desert monks</note>, loves God and pre-

<column-break/>

-serves the **Image**, and grows rich in the **Likeness** <note>Refers to the Genesis 1:26 concept of being made in the image and likeness of God</note>. For he receives from above the provision of the Spirit and becomes a house of God, and not of demons. He understands righteous works for God’s sake; and a soul cleansed of this life’s affairs, free from the stains of the flesh, having "no spot or wrinkle," <note>Ephesians 5:27</note> shall be crowned with the crown of righteousness, outshining all in the beauty of virtue.

For where there is no mourning in the heart at the beginning of one’s renunciation, nor spiritual tears, nor memory of the endless punishment, nor true stillness, nor persistent prayer, nor psalmody and the study of the Divine Scriptures—where one has not become habituated to these things so as to be compelled by the endurance of the heart to do them through the mind, even when one does not wish to—then the fear of God does not flourish in that person's intellect. Such a person still rests in the friendship of the world and cannot acquire a pure mind in prayer. For piety and the fear of God cleanse the soul from the passions and prepare the mind to become free; they lead it to **natural contemplation** <term>physike theōria</term> <note>contemplating God through his creation</note> and enable it to touch upon **theology** <term>theologia</term> <note>In this context, not academic study, but the direct experiential knowledge of God</note>, which it receives in the form of blessedness, providing a "pledge" to those who pursue it here, and keeping the soul unshakable.

Therefore, with all our power, let us take care of **active work** <term>praxis</term> <note>the practice of virtues and asceticism</note>, through which we are led up to piety. This is the purity according to the intellect, whose fruit is natural and theological contemplation. For "action is the stepping stone to contemplation," as the resonant and **most theological mind** <note>A common title for St. Gregory of Nazianzus</note> says. If, therefore, we neglect action, we will be destitute of all philosophy. For even if someone should drive toward the very peak of virtue, he still needs the labor of asceticism to bridle the disorderly impulses of the body and to maintain the guard over his thoughts. Only thus might we barely attain the indwelling of Christ. For as much as righteousness abounds in us, so much does spiritual courage increase; and the perfected mind is entirely mingled with God and illuminated by the divine light, and the secrets of the mysteries are revealed. Then it truly learns where there is wisdom, where there is strength, where there is understanding to know all things, where there is length of days and life, and where there is the light of the eyes and peace.

<summary>This page describes the rigorous path toward spiritual purity, emphasizing that "action" (ascetic labor) is the necessary foundation for "contemplation" (direct knowledge of God). It uses the fall of Solomon as a cautionary tale against spiritual negligence and defines the pure heart as a vessel for the Holy Spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Abba Philemon, Solomon, pure mind, praxis, theoria, hesychia, asceticism, Holy Spirit, Gregory of Nazianzus, mourning, spiritual warfare</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on Abba Philemon, following the previous page’s warnings about spiritual negligence and the example of Solomon's fall. The focus shifts here from the struggle against passions to the state of peace and the overwhelming beauty of divine contemplation.</meta>

<page-num>254</page-num>
->### CONCERNING ABBA PHILEMON ###<-

...peace. For as long as one is occupied in the battle of the passions, they will not yet have the opportunity to enjoy these things. For both virtues and vices can make the **mind** <term>nous</term> <note>The 'nous' refers to the "eye of the heart," the faculty of direct spiritual perception rather than just logical reasoning.</note> blind: vices so that it cannot see the virtues, and virtues so that it does not look upon the vices. But when the mind receives a respite from war and is deemed worthy of spiritual gifts, then it becomes entirely light-like, being intensely energized by grace. It stands unswerving in the **contemplation** <term>theoria</term> <note>original: "theōrian" — the direct vision or experience of God's presence.</note> of spiritual realities. Such a person is no longer bound to the things of this world, but has "passed from death to life." <note>John 5:24</note> Therefore, those who embrace this zealous life and approach God must have a pure heart and a clean mouth, so that the word proceeding from the mouth may be pure and able to worthily hymn God. For the soul that is glued to God converses with Him continually. Let us desire, then, brothers, to reach that summit of the virtues, and let us not remain pinned to the earth by our passions. For the one who struggles and succeeds in drawing near to God—becoming a partaker of the holy light and being "wounded" by desire for Him—enjoys a certain spiritual and incomprehensible gladness from the Lord, just as the divine Psalm says:

> Delight in the Lord, and He will give you the requests of your heart; and He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your judgment as the noonday. <note>Psalm 37:4, 6 (LXX 36)</note>

For what desire of the soul is so sharp and unbearable as that which God implants in a soul purified from all malice? A soul that says from a true heart:

> I am wounded by love! <note>Song of Songs 2:5 or 5:8. Wounded here suggests a soul overcome by the intensity of divine love.</note>

The flashes of divine beauty are utterly ineffable and beyond description; words cannot represent them, nor can the ear receive them. Even if you speak of the rays of the **morning star** <note>original: "heōsphoros" — the bringer of dawn.</note>, or the brightness of the moon, or the light of the sun—all are worthless for an illustration of that glory, falling further short when compared to the true light than the deepest night or a gloomy, moonless darkness falls short of the clearest noon. For this is what Basil, the divinely inspired among teachers, having received it by experience and been taught, handed down to us.

<column-break/>

These things, and even more than these, the brother who lived with him related. But who would not also wonder at this other proof of his great humility? For although he had long been deemed worthy of the rank of **priest** <note>original: "presbyterion" — the office of an elder or priest.</note> and had touched heavenly things through his way of life and knowledge, he so shunned the "weight" of the Divine Liturgies <note>Meaning he avoided the honor and heavy responsibility of officiating at the altar out of extreme reverence.</note> that throughout the many years of his spiritual struggles, he could hardly bring himself to approach the sacred table. Even regarding the reception of the Divine Mysteries <note>Holy Communion</note>, he lived with such strictness that whenever he had social interactions with men, he would not partake—even though he never spoke of earthly things, but only held conversations for the benefit of those who sought him out. When he was about to partake of the Divine Mysteries, he would entreat God with prayers, psalmody, and confessions. He trembled at the voice of the priest when he called out, saying:

> The Holy things for the Holy. <note>A central cry in the Divine Liturgy before Communion.</note>

For he said that the whole Church was filled with holy Angels, and that the King of Powers Himself was mystically sacrificing, being transformed in our hearts into Body and Blood. Therefore, he would say: "We must dare to partake of the holy communion of the stainless Mysteries of Christ purely and cleanly—as if we were outside the flesh—without any doubt or hesitation, so that we may become partakers of the illumination that comes from them." For many of the Holy Fathers saw the Angels guarding them; therefore, they kept themselves in silence, not conversing with anyone. He also said this: that if he had need to sell his own **manual labor** <term>ergocheiron</term>, he would stand there pretending to be a **fool** <note>original: "salos" — a 'Holy Fool' who acts mad to hide his piety or avoid social traps.</note> so that he might not fall into some form of sin, such as a lie, an oath, idle talk, or any other kind, by speaking and answering. And anyone who wished to buy would take from him and give whatever they wanted. He worked at making what is called **woven baskets** <note>original: "malakion" — likely a type of soft basket or woven craft made from palm leaves or flax.</note>. He would receive what was given to him gratefully, saying nothing at all—this truly philosophical man.

# BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## OF OUR HOLY FATHER
# THEOGNOSTUS

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'O' with floral and architectural elements.</image-desc>
Whether the Holy Theognostus, the Father of these present chapters, is the same man as the Alexandrian commentator mentioned by Photius <note>Photius (c. 810–893 AD) was the Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar. His 'Bibliotheca' (or 'Myriobiblos') contains summaries of hundreds of books, including a entry on a 3rd-century writer named Theognostus of Alexandria.</note> in his "Readings," codex 106, page 151, or if he is someone else, or during which era he flourished, we cannot say with absolute certainty. However, as a tree is known by its fruit, we can see that this man was one of those who excelled in both **practice** <term>praxis</term> <note>original: "praxei" — the active struggle to purify the soul through discipline and the virtues.</note> and **knowledge** <term>gnosis</term> <note>original: "gnōsei" — spiritual insight or direct experiential knowledge of God.</note>. Because of the purity of his life, he was a dwelling place for the grace of the Spirit. His mind was illuminated by those divine radiances that naturally reveal all things, and he was inspired by the Spirit’s life-giving breezes like a musical instru-

<column-break/>

-ment. Like a perfectly tuned and sacred melody, he sang out these present chapters. Through the grace within them and their spiritual insights, he charms both the hearing and the intellect of his readers, stirring them toward a practical zeal for righteous living. For in these writings, he provides an excellent guide for the **active life** <term>praktikē</term>, and the ascent to **contemplation** <term>theoria</term> <note>original: "theōrias" — the state of spiritual "seeing" or experiencing the presence of God.</note> is taught without error. From these pages, one may also learn with precision what sort of person one honored with the **Priesthood** <term>Hierosyne</term> ought to be, and how he should conduct himself. In short, these chapters provide a wealth of moral benefit and soul-saving **watchfulness** <term>nepsis</term> <note>original: "nēpseōs" — a state of spiritual sobriety, alertness, and guarding the heart against negative thoughts.</note> for those who study them with diligence.

# ON PRACTICE AND CONTEMPLATION
## AND ON THE PRIESTHOOD

->THIS IS THE ACROSTIC.<-

->TO THE MOST HOLY FATHERS LAZARUS AND BARLAAM. THEOGNOSTUS<-
->THE MOST HUMBLE AND UNWORTHY OF ALL THE WORLD.<-

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'T' containing a smaller 'O' within a decorative border of scrolls and foliage.</image-desc>
Consider yourself to possess true virtue only when you have completely despised all things upon the earth, keeping your heart ready at all times, through a pure conscience, to depart to the Lord. If you wish to be known by God, remain unknown to men as much as you possibly can.

<margin>2.</margin>
Watch out for the excessive comforts of the body and withdraw from them, lest 

<column-break/>

they take away something of the fruit of your labors. This is because, in the preliminary struggles before one reaches the state of **dispassion** <term>apatheia</term> <note>original: "apatheias" — not a lack of feeling, but a state of freedom from the mastery of the passions/vices.</note>, any ease that creeps in from these comforts causes a loss. Consider it a loss not when you are deprived of pleasures, but when, through the enjoyment of them, you fall away from the greater things of the spirit.

<margin>3.</margin>
In all your senses, consider yourself to be like an ant or a worm, so that you may become a "God-fashioned" human being. For if that first humble state does not come first, this second state will not follow. And as much as...

The text begins with his "chapters" on the spiritual life, focusing on humility, the rejection of earthly praise, and the dangers of bodily comfort.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the writings of St. Theognostus, moving from the general introduction of his character into his specific "Chapters" or spiritual maxims. These teachings focus on the ladder of humility, the necessity of purification before attempting "theology," and the relationship between prayer and the virtues.</meta>

<page-num>356</page-num>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER THEOGNOSTUS

<margin>4.</margin> To the degree that you descend [in humility], you shall ascend. When you consider yourself as nothing before the Lord, according to the Psalmist, then you secretly become great from being small. At the moment you suspect you possess and know nothing, that is when you are truly rich in both **practice** <term>praxis</term> <note>The active struggle to live virtuously and discipline the body.</note> and **knowledge** <term>gnosis</term> that is praiseworthy in the Lord.

"Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked" <note>A reference to Psalm 10:15.</note>—I mean the arm of pleasure and malice, from which every vice is born. Break it through self-control and the innocence that comes from humility. Do this so that even if your sin is sought out during the investigation of your past deeds, nothing may be found. For our transgressions are blotted out when we hate the causes that brought them to completion and wage war against them, reclaiming our first defeat with a final victory.

<margin>5.</margin> Nothing is better than pure prayer, from which virtues flow as if from a spring: understanding, gentleness, love, self-control, and the divine help and consolation that come through tears. The beauty of this prayer lies in the mind being focused only on what is being said and thought, with an insatiable desire for divine success. This occurs when the mind, tracking its own Master through the contemplation of created things, seeks with burning desire to find and see the Unseen. Or, seeing the "darkness of His concealment" <note>A common mystical theme: God is so bright He appears as darkness to the limited human mind.</note>, the mind turns back to itself in reverent contraction, satisfied for now with the contemplation revealed for its benefit. It remains full of hope that it will one day grasp the desired goal, when the <unclear>manifestations</unclear> <note>original: "ekphaseōn" — this word is struck through in the manuscript.</note> are dissolved, and the imagination in shadows (as in a mirror and in riddles) <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12.</note> is gone, and a pure, face-to-face vision shall be its perpetual state.

<margin>6.</margin> Draw back from the highest contemplations unless you have reached the peak of **dispassion** <term>apatheia</term> <note>A state of being where one is no longer controlled by impulsive passions or desires.</note>. Do not run after the unattainable, desiring things beyond you. For if you wish, it is said, to become both a theologian and a contemplative, ascend through your way of life and through **purification** <term>katharsis</term>; acquire that which is pure. Since I mentioned **theology** <term>theologia</term> <note>In this context, "theology" means the direct experience and "speaking" of God, rather than just academic study.</note>, watch that you do not extend your reach to its infinite height. Consider that it is not lawful for us, who are still being fed the "milk" of the virtues, to try to fly toward this, lest we lose our feathers like immature chicks—even if

<column-break/>

the honey of knowledge forces our desire. When we are purified by temperance and tears, and are lifted from the earth like Elijah <note>Who was taken to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11).</note> or Habakkuk <note>Referring to the tradition where an angel carried Habakkuk by his hair to Babylon (Bel and the Dragon 1:36).</note>, then we begin the "abduction in the clouds." In pure, contemplative, and undistracted prayer, being outside the senses, we seek God; then perhaps we will touch theology to some extent.

<margin>7.</margin> If you desire to be deemed worthy of a divine vision and an appearance within your mind, first embrace a peaceful and quiet life. Having found leisure, know both yourself and God. If you do this, nothing prevents you from seeing the One who is invisible to all within your mind—as if in a gentle breeze, in a state that is pure and undisturbed by any passion—announcing salvation to you through a more distinct knowledge of Himself.

<margin>8.</margin> Just as when lightning flashes, thunder is immediately expected, so too where divine mercy has shone, the storm of passions grows calm. Where this state dwells with the one who has acquired it, there also is the "earnest money" <note>A "down payment" or "pledge" (arrhabōn) of future salvation.</note> of the blessedness of the world to come. But there is no divine mercy, or hope of dispassion, in a soul that loves the world more than the Creator, or is passionately attached to visible things and clings entirely to fleshly pleasures and enjoyments.

<margin>9.</margin> Do not seek with the mind what the Divine is or where it is; for it is beyond being and not contained by place, as it is above all. Only mirror God the Word as far as possible, who radiates with divine nature and is "located" by our thoughts everywhere because of the uncircumscribed nature of the Godhead. However, only to the extent you are purified will you be deemed worthy of this illumination.

<margin>10.</margin> If you love true knowledge and the assurance of unwavering salvation, first seek the wisdom to break the passionate bonds of the soul to the body. Stripped of attachment to material things, descend into the abyss of humility, and you will find the precious pearl of your salvation, hidden in divine knowledge like a shell, foretelling the brightness of the Kingdom of God.

<margin>11.</margin> For the one who has achieved spiritual obedience and subjected the flesh to the spirit, there is no need for human obedience; for he is subject to the Word and Law of God as a grateful subject. In

Theognostus warns against premature attempts at high contemplation, comparing the spiritual seeker to a chick that must mature before it can fly.</summary>
