<meta>This page continues the spiritual instructions of St. Theognostus. Having previously discussed the foundations of humility and prayer, the author now turns to the inner struggle of the soul and the immense responsibility of those called to the priesthood.</meta>

<page-num>357</page-num>

### ON PRACTICE AND CONTEMPLATION, AND ON THE PRIESTHOOD.

<margin>12.</margin> For those who experience a battle and war of the body against the soul, it is necessary to submit and to acquire a general and a pilot—one who steers with skill and arms the soul excellently—lest we be consumed by our spiritual enemies or swallowed up by the passions due to our lack of experience.

<margin>13.</margin> When you are no longer troubled by any passion, and divine desire grows within your heart; and when, regarding death as if it were a mere sleep, you do not fear it but rather long for your departure <note>original: ἀνάλυσιν (analysin) - a "loosening" or "departure," often used by St. Paul to refer to death as a release into the presence of God.</note>, then you have truly acquired the "earnest money" of salvation as you ought. You carry the Kingdom of Heaven within you, rejoicing with unspeakable joy.

->On the Priesthood.<-

<margin>14.</margin> Having been deemed worthy of the divine and venerable priesthood, you are first of all indebted to hold yourself as one sacrificed to the death of passions and pleasures. Only then should you dare to touch the life-giving and awesome sacrifice, unless you wish to be consumed by the divine fire like dry wood. For if the Seraphim <note>A reference to the vision in Isaiah 6:6, where a high-ranking angel uses tongs to touch a coal from the altar.</note> did not dare to touch the divine coal without tongs, how will you touch it without **impassibility** <term>apatheia</term> <note>A state of spiritual stillness where one is no longer controlled by emotional or physical compulsions.</note>? Through this state, you shall have your tongue sanctified, your lips purified, your soul kept holy along with your body, and your very hands made brighter than any gold, acting as servants of the transcendent fire and sacrifice.

Grasp firmly the power of these words: every day you look upon the salvation of God—that very thing which the aged Simeon <note>Luke 2:25–35; Simeon was the elder who held the infant Christ in the Temple.</note> saw but once and was struck with awe, praying for his release. And if you have not been instructed by the Holy Spirit to be an acceptable mediator between God and men, like an equal to the angels, do not recklessly dare to perform the awesome and most pure sacred rites, which even angels revere. Many of the saints withdrew in total piety from such purity, fearing they might be destroyed like that man, Uzzah <note>original: Ζᾶν (Zan). This refers to Uzzah from 2 Samuel 6:6-7, who was struck dead for touching the Ark of the Covenant without authorization.</note>, by the mere appearance of doing something good.

<margin>15.</margin> "Take heed to yourself," as the saying goes, so that if anything remains in you that is perhaps filthy due to weakness, it may be consumed by the divine fire. Offer the sacrifice first for your own sins at all times. In this way, like a useful vessel of election—pure and worthy of such a sacrifice—you might have the power to be transformed into the nature of silver or even gold,

<column-break/>

even if you were previously something wooden or earthen <note>Refers to 2 Timothy 2:20-21 regarding "vessels of honor" and "vessels of dishonor."</note>, provided only that you possess a confidence that calls upon the Divine. For where God is ready to listen, there is nothing to prevent the transformation that comes from Him.

<margin>16.</margin> Behold, then, the angelic honor of which you have been deemed worthy, and strive to remain untouched [by sin] in the rank to which you were called, through every virtue and purity. For you know from what state Lucifer <note>original: ἑωσφόρον (heosphoron) - the "Light-Bringer" or Morning Star; the angel who fell through pride.</note> fell and what he became because of his arrogance. May you not suffer the same by imagining great things for yourself. Rather, hold yourself as earth and ashes and refuse, and mourn constantly that you are at all deemed worthy to be called into divine communion and kinship through the handling of the holy things in the awesome sacred rite—all through the unutterable love for mankind and the unspeakable goodness of God.

<margin>17.</margin> One who is a priest must be pure from all passions, and especially from sexual immorality and the remembrance of wrongs <note>Resentment or holding a grudge.</note>. He must not even have a bare mental image of such things; otherwise, he will be loathsome and abominable—like one who is disfigured or has his face smeared with soot—as he touches the Royal Body.

<margin>18.</margin> Being first made whiter than snow by streams of tears, and thus with a conscience made white through purity, touch the holy things as a holy person. With your outward angel-like white robes, show forth the inner beauty of your soul. See that you are not filled with certainty in the divine rites merely by human traditions, but let grace also be with you secretly and mystically, giving you understanding of the higher things.

<margin>19.</margin> Being a lover of incorruption and immortality, approach the life-giving and incorruptible mysteries with reverence and pious faith. Long even for your departure from this world, as one who has been perfected through faith. If you fear death, you have not yet been blended with Christ through love—He whom you were deemed worthy to sacrifice with your own hands and whose flesh you are filled with. For if you were, you would hasten to go where the Beloved is, making no further account of this life or the flesh.

<margin>20.</margin> Having become a sacrificer of the flesh of God and a communicant through partaking of it, you are indebted to become conformed to the likeness of His death. You should no longer live for yourself, according to the Apostle <note>St. Paul (cf. 2 Corinthians 5:15 and Romans 6:5).</note>, but for the One who was crucified and died for you. But if you live for the flesh and the world in a passionate way, prepare yourself...

...through death, toward eternal punishment, unless you voluntarily stand [aright] before the end of the bloodless sacrifice <note>The "bloodless sacrifice" refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>. Yet many who served unworthily in this life, having been snatched away by sudden death, were sent to the judgments in the world beyond.

<margin>21.</margin>
For there was a certain priest here who was also a monk, possessing a reputation for piety and considered honorable by many for his outward appearance; however, inwardly he was secretly lustful and defiled. While performing the divine and sacred liturgy, when he approached the singing of the Cherubic Hymn <note>The Cherubic Hymn is a central chant in the Eastern Orthodox Liturgy, marking the transition to the most solemn part of the service.</note>, he bowed his neck as is customary before the holy table. While reading the prayer "No one is worthy..." <note>original: οὐδεὶς ἄξιος (oudeis axios) - the opening words of the priest's private prayer acknowledging his unworthiness before the Great Entrance.</note>, he was suddenly found dead, his soul having left him while he was in that very posture.

<margin>22.</margin>
Nothing is more vital than right reason and spiritual knowledge. For from these arises the fear and love of God; the former purifies through reverence and restraint, while the latter brings perfection through a state of illumination and discernment. This makes the mind soar through high contemplation and ascent. It is impossible, however, without fear, to be transported toward divine love, and through it to take flight and find rest in the things for which we hope.

<margin>23.</margin>
Come now, listen to me, you who fervently and unswervingly long for salvation: run until you attain it, seeking laboriously, asking unceasingly, and knocking patiently until you succeed, having fixed a firm foundation of faith and humility. You will know you have attained the <gloss>* the desired goal</gloss> not merely when you obtain forgiveness of sins, but when you no longer feel terror or fear the uprising of any passion, departing from the flesh fearlessly and with confidence.

<margin>24.</margin>
Seek to receive full assurance <note>original: πληροφορίαν (plerophorian) - a state of total certainty or spiritual conviction.</note> with many tears—but not long before your end, if you are humble-minded, lest you become complacent and later grow negligent. Rather, seek to find it near the moment of departure, yet in a way that remains hidden from your own pride, so that you do not lose what you desire by falling into the mockery of self-conceit. When that hoped-for time arrives, where will you go, O wretched one, without the "earnest money" <note>original: ἀρραβῶνος (arrabon) - a legal term for a down payment or pledge, here referring to the Holy Spirit as a guarantee of future salvation.</note> and the saving, unwavering assurance given through the Spirit?

<margin>25.</margin>

<column-break/>

only useless toil. A person possesses dispassion not when they are occasionally troubled by passions and occasionally at rest, but when they continually delight in a state of calm. Even when the causes of the passions are present, they remain unmoved—and especially when they no longer suffer even from the mere thoughts of these things.

<margin>26.</margin>
Fighting and reproaching, the enemy attacks the soul with audacity as it exits the body, acting as a bitter and terrifying accuser regarding its failings. But one can then see the God-loving soul—even if it had been wounded many times by sins before—not at all terrified by his attacks and threats. Instead, it is strengthened in the Lord, taking wing with joy, emboldened by the holy powers that guide it, and walled in by the light of faith. It cries out with great confidence against the evil one: "What are you to us, you fugitive from heaven and wicked slave? You have no authority over us. Christ, the Son of God, has authority over us and over all; against Him we have sinned, and to Him we shall give account, having the pledge of His mercy and salvation: His precious Cross. Flee far from us, you bringer of ruin! You have nothing to do with the servants of Christ." As the soul says these things with courage, the devil finally turns his back, wailing aloud, unable to withstand the name of Christ. Being above him, the soul flies over the enemy, striking him as a hawk strikes a crow. After this, it is tested by the divine angels and led rejoicing into the places appointed for it according to its state.

A desire for fleeting things will not drag you down to the earth if you keep your mind on heavenly things. Therefore, possess all things but consider them as refuse <note>A reference to Philippians 3:8.</note> in the hope of better things. When the time calls, shake off even this little body and follow the Angel of God who draws you forth.

# ON PRACTICE, CONTEMPLATION, AND THE PRIESTHOOD #

It is impossible, without right knowledge and dispassion <term>dispassion: *apatheia*, a state of spiritual freedom where one is no longer enslaved by impulsive emotions or sinful desires</term>, to receive the pledge <note>original: ἀρραβῶνα (*arrabōn*) - a down-payment or earnest money signifying a future full delivery</note> of the blessedness in the life to come, to depart from this world with confidence, to possess the full assurance of the things for which we hope, and to be numbered among the elect. By "knowledge," I do not mean worldly wisdom, but rather the unerring understanding of God and of divine things. Through this knowledge, the lover of God is lifted up by the grace of the Spirit toward "deification" <term>deification: *theosis*, the process of becoming like God through union with Him</term>, never being dragged down again by the passions.

<margin>29.</margin> Even if you follow the entire path of practical virtue, do not be so confident in yourself as to believe you are naturally suited for dispassion, nor should you dwell carelessly in the world. Otherwise, you may pick up the imprints of the passions once again and find it difficult to retreat from them. Instead, always be guided by fear, and take care of your changeable and shifting nature. In your wisdom, keep a great distance from the causes of the passions. For a dispassion that is truly unshakeable and absolute belongs only to those who have reached perfect love; through constant contemplation, they have been raised above all sensible things and have transcended the body of their humiliation. The flame of the passions no longer touches them, for it has been cut off by the voice of the Lord, because they have already been transformed toward incorruptibility.

<margin>30.</margin> Do not fall in love with dispassion before the proper time, lest you suffer what the first-formed man <note>referring to Adam</note> suffered by partaking prematurely of the tree of knowledge. Instead, work with patience through all-encompassing self-restraint and intense prayer. By guarding what you have achieved through self-reproach and extreme humility, wait for the grace of dispassion to come at the appropriate time—the harbor of rest after much storm and turmoil. For God is not unjust; He will not close the gate of dispassion to those who walk the path correctly when the time is right.

<margin>31.</margin> Go to the ant in your lowliness and insignificance, O sluggish and untried soul, and learn from me that God—who is all-sufficient and overflowing—has no need of our good deeds. Rather, He generously bestows His benefits and saves by grace those who are willing and grateful, even if He also lovingly accepts our work according to our strength. If you labor as a debtor in return for the good things He has already given you, you do well, and divine mercy is near. But if you think you have made God your debtor because of the good works you think you are doing, you have wandered from the straight path. For how can the Benefactor be a debtor? Nevertheless, even in this state,

<column-break/>

run like a hired servant, and by progressing little by little, you shall attain what you seek by the mercy of God.

<margin>32.</margin> Shall I show you another way to salvation—or rather, to dispassion? Compel the Creator in your prayers with all your might so that you do not miss your goal. Constantly put forward all the heavenly powers and all the saints together as mediators to Him, along with the all-pure Mother of God. Do not seek dispassion directly, as if you were unworthy of such a gift; instead, ask for salvation with great labor, and along with it, you shall also receive dispassion. For the one is like silver, but the other is like pure gold. Also, maintain a secret practice of serving God as much as possible, as well as certain hidden "mysteries" of prayer to Him—words that make you god-like—in which the Divine both delights and is moved to compassion.

<margin>33.</margin> Struggle to receive the pledge of salvation secretly within your heart with unwavering assurance, so that you do not find alarm or unexpected terror at the time of your departure <note>meaning the moment of death</note>. You will know you have received it when your heart no longer condemns you for your failings and your conscience no longer strikes you for having provoked God; when the wildness of the beast-like passions has been tamed in you by divine grace; when the tears of consolation flow freely; and when the mind prays purely and without distraction. Then you will be able to await that death—which is shunned by the many and yet is so fearful—with a gentle and prepared heart.

<margin>34.</margin> The "words of eternal life" <note>original: Ῥήματα ζωῆς αἰωνίου (*Rhēmata zōēs aiōniou*) - a reference to Peter's words to Jesus in John 6:68</note>, which the Chief of the Apostles testified that God the Word possesses, are the inner meanings of the things He has done. He who is initiated into these mysteries as a holy person has already acquired eternal life from this point onward, along with the pledge of the Spirit and the hope of salvation that does not disappoint. However, someone who prefers the flesh over the soul and has an attachment and a relationship to earthly things is not considered worthy of these gifts.

<margin>35.</margin> A rational being is not simply one who possesses the power of speech—for every human has this—but rather one who, through the use of reason, seeks and tracks down the discovery of God. Will he ever find what the "Supra-essential" <note>original: ὑπερούσιος (*hyperousios*) - a theological term for God's nature being beyond all categories of being</note> is in His essence? By no means; for this is impossible for any created nature. But he finds Him through the creative wisdom of all things—through His providence, His administration, His holding of all things together, and His governance.

...creation and preservation alike, in which the master craftsman is found and, as it were, perceived, in the same way as a builder is seen through the work of his own hands.

<margin>36.</margin> You will not achieve non-possession <term>non-possession: *aktimosyni*, the voluntary poverty or freedom from material attachments practiced by monks</term> as you ought without dispassion, nor dispassion without love, nor love without fear and pure prayer; nor can you have these without faith and freedom from anxiety, through which the mind taking wing, casts off earthly thoughts and flies to the heights, seeking its own Master.

<margin>37.</margin> Embrace purity as the apple of your eye, so that you may become a temple of God and a beloved home; for it is impossible to be brought near to God without self-control. These things are born of divine longing, detachment, and flight from the world; they are preserved by humility together with temperance, unceasing prayer, spiritual contemplation, and, along with a lack of anger, fervent tears. Without dispassion, you will not attain the beauty of discrimination <term>discrimination: *diakrisis*, the spiritual gift of being able to distinguish between good and evil impulses or thoughts</term>.

<margin>38.</margin> Let no one deceive you, brother: except through sanctification, as the Apostle says, is God seen <note>original: πλὴν ἁγιασμοῦ... καθορᾶται Θεός. A reference to Hebrews 12:14: "Holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord."</note>. For the Lord, who is supremely holy and beyond all purity, does not deign to appear to the impure. Just as he who loves father or mother, or again daughter and son, more than Him is unworthy of Him <note>original: ὁ πατέρα καὶ μητέρα ὑπὲρ τοῦτον φιλῶν... A reference to Matthew 10:37.</note>, so it is with anything temporary or material. And much more so for the one who prefers loathsome and foul-smelling sin to the love of the Lord; for God turns away in disgust from the one who does not turn away from filth, because corruption does not inherit incorruption.

<margin>39.</margin> You will not be deemed worthy of divine love without knowledge; nor of knowledge without faith—and by faith I mean not simply bare belief, but that which comes from the practice of the virtues. You will achieve true contrition <term>contrition: *katanyxis*, a state of spiritual piercing or deep repentance that softens the heart</term> when, through temperance, wakefulness, prayer, and humility, you have withered the innate pleasure of the flesh and are crucified with Jesus, no longer living according to the passions, but living and walking in the Holy Spirit with the hope of the portion above.

<margin>40.</margin> "By this I know that You have favored me," <note>original: Ἐν τούτῳ ἔγνων, ὅτι τεθέληκάς με. Quoting Psalm 41:11 (LXX 40:12).</note> cry out to God, "that my enemy shall not triumph over me," tyrannizing me through the passions and bruising me until the end. But so that You may snatch me from his hand before my death and, having deemed me worthy to live spiritually according to what is well-pleasing to You, through a good end, You might present me saved before Your judgment seat; receiving there the pledge of salvation through Your mercy and the unwavering assurance—lest, being troubled and found unprepared at the time of my departure, I consider the unbearable sorrow of both death and punishment to be more bitter and worse.

<margin>41.</margin> Faith and hope are not simply bare or ordinary things. Rather, faith requires a firm soul, and hope requires a straight mind and heart. For how can someone easily believe in things unseen without grace? And how can one hope for the unknown future unless one has some experience of the Lord's gifts through uprightness? Through these experiences, one receives assurance of those future things as if they were already present. Therefore, in both, there is a need for virtue and for God's inclination and help; if these are not present with us, we labor in vain.

<margin>42.</margin> The offspring of true virtue is knowledge, or dispassion, or both. If these are not present, then our labor is in vain, and the virtue we seem to have is not pure. For if it were, it would flourish with fruit, not leaves only; but as it is, by courting the favor of men, or self-satisfaction, or anything else that does not please God, it is counterfeit and not beloved of God. But if we correct the underlying cause, we will undoubtedly achieve what is profitable, receiving—when and to the extent it is needed—both knowledge and dispassion from the grace of our good God.

<margin>43.</margin> Discern the thoughts of the enemy through the illumination of grace, and throwing yourself before God with weeping, declare your weakness, considering yourself to be nothing—even if the deceiver tries to persuade you that you are someone important. Do not ask for the bestowing of gifts unless they lead to salvation and preserve humility. Seek the knowledge that does not puff up <note>original: φυσιοῦσαν (*physiousan*) - a reference to 1 Corinthians 8:1: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up."</note>, as it is the cause of the knowledge of God; and seek not to be dominated until the end by the passions like tyrants, but rather to be released from the flesh in dispassion, or—what is humbler—with the forgiveness of failings.

### ON PRACTICE AND CONTEMPLATION AND ON THE PRIESTHOOD ###

<margin>45.</margin> ...from there comes unwavering assurance. This assurance <term>assurance: *plerophoria*, a state of certain conviction and full spiritual confidence</term> arises either from extreme humility or from the grace of the Holy Spirit in those who are perfectly reconciled to God. In such people, dispassion is present entirely, or at least in part, according to their reconciliation and purification. But if people depart from the body in any other state—as if still in the "winter" of passions or on a "Sabbath" (meaning they are idle and lacking in virtues)—they are subject to judgment and examination, being held accountable at the time of recompense.

If you are saved freely, give thanks to God the Savior. If you also wish to offer gifts, offer the "two mites" from your widowed soul with gratitude: I mean humility and love. I know well that He accepts these more than a multitude of virtues cast into the treasury of salvation by many others. And if, like Lazarus, you need to be brought back to life after being killed by the passions, put forward these two virtues as your own true sisters to mediate with Him, and you will certainly obtain what you seek. <note>The author uses the story of the widow's mites (Luke 21:1-4) and the sisters of Lazarus, Martha and Mary (John 11), as metaphors for the essential virtues of humility and love.</note>

<margin>46.</margin> Even if you succeed in the practical life <term>the practical life: *praktiki*, the active struggle to acquire virtues and overcome vices</term>, you will not be able to approach dispassion through it alone, so as to pray purely and without distraction, unless spiritual contemplations also take over the mind. These include both illuminating knowledge and the understanding of created beings. Borne on the wings of these and enlightened by them, the mind is raised up by a total longing for true prayer toward the kindred lights of the heavenly, immaterial ranks. From there, as far as is possible, it is carried toward the great and three-sunned light of the Thearchic Trinity.

<margin>47.</margin> We shall not be punished in the future because we sinned, nor shall we be condemned for that reason—since we were allotted a changeable and shifting nature—but because, having sinned, we did not repent nor turn from the evil way toward the Lord, having received the authority and the time for repentance. We must show that the Good, which is the Divine, is not the opposite—that is, something subject to passion, such as being vengeful or angry. For the Divine is outside of all passion and all vengeance, even if it is said to be "shaped" by our deeds and dispositions, like a mirror, providing to each a reflection according to the worth of how they have lived.

<column-break/>

<margin>48.</margin> If you are shaken from your better standing, do not be troubled, but set it right, running back quickly to your former state with sorrow, gloom, and intense self-reproach; but also with a sufficient outpouring of tears and a contrite spirit. Through these, emerging from your accidental slip, you will come into the valley of saving joy, making yourself secure for the future with all your might. This is so that you do not provoke the Judge again and require tears and destruction as an atonement—for if this is not done here, it will certainly lead to punishment in the future.

->On the Priesthood<-

<margin>49.</margin> Once again our discourse is about the revered priesthood. It requires an angelic rank and purity, and even greater security and self-control afterward than before. For if that which was defiled can somehow become pure, how then can that which is pure be profaned? We must not mix darkness with light or a foul stench with perfume, lest we inherit the "woe" and destruction as temple-robbers, just like Ananias and Sapphira. <note>Ananias and Sapphira: A couple in the New Testament (Acts 5) who were struck dead for lying to the Holy Spirit regarding a financial gift to the Church.</note>

<margin>50.</margin> From a vessel that was lost and useless, even if you think you are perhaps worthy to enter the angelic and heavenly priesthood because of a small amount of purification, you have become a "vessel of election" <note>original: σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς. A title given to St. Paul in Acts 9:15, meaning a chosen instrument.</note> and useful to the Lord. Therefore, keep the honor you have been granted stainless, guarding the divine gift like the apple of your eye, lest by becoming defiled through heedlessness, you be cast down from the heights into the pit, finding it difficult to return.

<margin>51.</margin> Understand as a wise person that if God justifies, no one can condemn. If you have been called into the supernatural grace of the divine priesthood, do not worry about your past life, even if it was perhaps stained; for through God, a person is purified again through correction. But let your concern and watchfulness be for the time afterward, so as not to dim the grace. Thus, even if someone foolishly judges you for your priestly service because of your past, let them hear the divine voice echoing: "What God has cleansed, do not you call common." <note>original: ἃ ὁ Θεὸς ἐκαθάρισε, σὺ μὴ κοίνου. This quotes Acts 10:15, where Peter is told not to judge what God has purified.</note>

<margin>52.</margin> The dignity of the priesthood is light and its yoke is good, as long as it is carried according to divine law and directed rightly. The grace of the Holy Spirit is not for sale; but whenever human ambition and perishable gifts are used to trade for that which cannot be sold, and the calling is not...

...from above, the burden is indeed very heavy, as it is carried by one who is unworthy and beyond their strength. The yoke is exceedingly hard, wearing away both the neck and the strength of the one who pulls it, unless it is lightened; otherwise, it will continue until it utterly exhausts and consumes them.

<margin>53.</margin> Having boldly come under the yoke of the priesthood, set your paths straight and **rightly divide the word of truth** <note>original: "ὀρθοτόμει τὸν τῆς ἀληθείας λόγον" — a reference to 2 Timothy 2:15, meaning to teach the faith accurately and clearly</note> with fear and trembling, working out your own salvation through it. For **our God is a consuming fire**; and if you touch this fire as gold or silver, do not fear the burning, just as the children in Babylon did not fear the furnace. But if you are like grass or a reed—made of the more flammable material of an earthly mind—tremble lest you be burned up by the heavenly fire, unless you flee from the wrath like Lot by abstaining from these most awesome rites. I do not know if there might be some very small failings, born of weakness, that are consumed by this divine fire during the most holy service; in such a case, you might remain unburnt and unharmed within the fire, like that fragile bush in the desert. <note>The author compares the priest to the Burning Bush (Exodus 3:2), which burned but was not consumed, suggesting that only the pure or the truly repentant can survive contact with the Divine.</note>

<margin>54.</margin> Since you are unable to tear yourself away from the habit of passion—like one suffering from a chronic discharge—and because of long-standing habit, how do you dare to touch things that even angels cannot touch, you wretched soul? Either shudder and abstain from now on from the divine priestly service, and in this way appease the Divine; or, if you remain unfeeling and uncorrected, expect to fall into the hands of the living God in His wrath. He will not spare you out of loving-kindness, but will punish you without pity for your shameless daring in approaching the royal wedding with a defiled soul and garment—being unworthy even to enter, let alone to recline at the table.

<margin>55.</margin> I myself knew a certain priest who dared to perform the divine rites unworthily because he had fallen into the passion of sexual sin. First, he fell into an incurable and grievous disease and was already drawing near to death. Since every physician <term>physician: *paion*, a poetic term for a healer</term> achieved nothing toward curing the ill, and indeed the evil only grew worse, he eventually came to his senses. Realizing he was being put to death for ministering unworthily, he immediately renounced the holy Liturgy with an oath. Healing followed instantly upon his heels, so that not even a trace of the disease remained in him.

<margin>56.</margin> The dignity and the vestment of the priesthood are brilliant, but only as long as the soul within is also

<column-break/>

shining along with them through purity. But when the soul is stained by carelessness, and the conscience—which bears witness to the shame—is ignored, then the light becomes darkness, and the cause of eternal darkness and fire. Unless, perhaps, we leave this path as being too steep and precipitous, and turn to the other path of virtue and humility, which leads without danger into the Kingdom of God.

<margin>57.</margin> The attainment of salvation comes through lowliness and virtue, not through the glorious priesthood, which requires a way of life equal to the angels. Therefore, either become dispassionate like the angels, being outside the world and the flesh in your mindset, and so ascend this heavenly ladder; or, acknowledging your own weakness, fear the height, as it leads to a great fall for those who do not succeed. Choose the way of life loved by the many (the common life of virtue); it brings one no less close to God than the other. In this path, even if you happen to fall, rising again is easy through repentance, by the mercy and grace of God.

<margin>58.</margin> **Flesh and blood cannot inherit the Kingdom of God.** How then can you, who participate in the Flesh and Blood of God, fail to become "of one body" with Him and be mingled with His blood? How can you not already possess the Kingdom of Heaven within you? Are you still besieged by the passions of flesh and blood? I fear lest the Spirit of God will not remain in you because you are "fleshly," and you will then be **cut in two** at the time of judgment. Then, the venerable priesthood will be taken from you as one unworthy of such grace, and you will be sent away to eternal punishment.

<margin>59.</margin> Because there is no fear of God before your eyes, you think that ministering unworthily is a trivial matter, being deceived by self-love and imagining that the Divine is merely "good" (and therefore indulgent). This is what Dathan and Abiram suffered long ago, until the earth swallowed them up. Fearing this yourself, and truly dreading Him who is to be feared, understand the magnitude of the matter. Either handle the business of the divine priesthood worthily and purely—I might even say, like an angel—or, like a wise man, stand back from the awesome service. Do not, by holding it in contempt and deceiving your own rebuking conscience, have to say in the midst of painful condemnation when all things are judged and set right: "Fear

The author suggests that a humble life of virtue as a layman or simple monk is safer than the "steep precipice" of an unworthy priesthood.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual exhortations of St. Theognostos, specifically moving from the responsibilities of the priesthood to the preparation for death, the nature of the soul's departure, and the supreme value of humility.</meta>

<header>ON PRACTICE AND CONTEMPLATION AND ON THE PRIESTHOOD</header>

"The thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me." <note>original: "ἐν ἐφοβούμην ἦλθέ μοι..." — a quote from the Book of Job 3:25</note>

<margin>60.</margin>
With sobriety and through hard labor, offer first for yourself—with a broken heart and with tears—the world-saving and holy sacrifice <note>The author refers here to the Divine Liturgy/Eucharist</note> as an atonement. For who else will you have to labor for you in the same way, or to make offerings on your behalf after death? Therefore, like a person of keen mind, anticipate the end: entomb yourself even now and remember yourself beforehand in your mediation for salvation. Place the holy gifts themselves upon the holy table before God, and through them, remind Him of His own voluntary and man-loving slaughter <note>The "voluntary slaughter" refers to the Crucifixion of Christ, re-presented in the Eucharist</note>.

<margin>61.</margin>
The pleasure of a soul departing from the body in full assurance is unutterable and beyond expression; it strips off the body as if it were a garment. Because it has already attained the things it hoped for, it lays the body aside without pain, proceeding in peace toward the bright and joyful Angel who has come from on high. Together with the Angel, the soul passes through the air without hindrance, completely unharmed by the spirits of wickedness <note>The "spirits of wickedness in the air" refers to a common Byzantine belief in "toll-houses" or spiritual obstacles the soul faces after death</note>. Instead, it ascends in joy with boldness and cries of thanksgiving, until it arrives to worship the Creator. There, it receives the decree to be ranked with those like itself, equal in virtue, until the general resurrection.

<margin>62.</margin>
I tell you a strange word, and do not be surprised: even if you do not attain <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: "ἀπάθεια" (apatheia) — not a lack of feeling, but a state of being free from the "passions" or disordered desires like anger and pride</note> because of perhaps some tyrannical habits or predispositions, if you are found at the time of your departure in the abyss of humility, you will be raised up above the clouds no less than the dispassionate man. For even if the treasure of the dispassionate is gathered from every virtue, the precious stone of humility is more valuable than all of them. It does not only bring about atonement for its possessor before God, but also grants entrance with the chosen into the bridal chamber of His kingdom.

<margin>63.</margin>
When you receive atonement from God for your failings, glorify Him who is both "forgetful of evil" and "long-suffering," protecting yourself against voluntary sins with all your might. For while there is forgiveness for daily failings until the very end, you appear ungrateful if you easily sin with full knowledge. Nevertheless, if you drive away the "dog of despair" with the stone of hope, and always persistently and shamelessly ask for mercy, your many sins will be forgiven; so that you, being a debtor,

<column-break/>

may love the compassionate and supremely good One greatly in the age to come.

<margin>64.</margin>
When, being moved by divine grace, you find yourself before God with tears in prayer, roll yourself on the ground, spreading yourself out in the shape of a cross and striking your head. Seek from that state your release, as a freedom from corruption and an alienation from alien temptations. Yet, let it not be according to your own will, but as it seems best to God. And when and where—even if you are already desiring your departure and love it—if you have gone out to the Lord with tears in the abyss of humility, so that you might stand there without the anxiety of the burning heat of desire and petition; nevertheless, endure the delay for the present, as God has foreseen something better. But seek the unexpected with force and as if with an oath—doing everything, saying everything, contemplating and busying yourself with everything—so that you do not fall away from God.

<margin>65.</margin>
While you are still bearing the flesh, do not try to search out <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "νοητὰ" (noeta) — refers to spiritual realities that are grasped by the mind/spirit rather than the physical senses</note> things as they truly are, even if the intellectual part of the soul is drawn toward them through purity. For unless that which is incorporeal—currently held by breath and blood—is released from its density and comes to be with the intelligible beings, it will not have the power to contemplate and understand these things as it should. Therefore, preparing yourself to go out from matter, as if from a second dark maternal womb, toward those things that are immaterial and filled with light, be of good cheer and glorify the Benefactor who ferries us through death toward the things we hope for. Be sober at all times because of the ungodly demons who walk in a circle, always plotting against our good favor and craftily watching our "heel"—the conclusion of our life. Tremble until the very exit because of the uncertainty of the future, since you were created as a changeable and alterable being through your free will.

<margin>66.</margin>
At that time, the enemy meets us with fierce and fearful temptations, when he perceives the soul embracing great measures of virtue. He finds evidence for this from the words of prayer and the soul's ascent above the "material duality" of the flesh and the senses. The hater of mankind tempts so enviously then, that we may even despair of life itself; but the vain one does not realize how many blessings he actually brings to us, making us "proven" <note>original: "δοκίμους" (dokimous) — tested and found genuine like refined gold</note> from then on...

...working through patience, and weaving for us more radiant crowns.

<margin>67.</margin> There is no other struggle greater than that for **Chastity** <note>original: Σωφροσύνης — temperance or sound-mindedness, often specifically used for sexual purity</note> and virginity; for even by the Angels themselves is he wondered at, who honors the unwed life, and he is crowned no less than the athletes <note>In early Christian writing, monks and martyrs were often called "athletes of Christ"</note> of the faith. For someone bound to flesh and blood to strive always to imitate the immateriality of the bodiless ones through purity—how many labors and sweats does this require? And in truth, the achievement is so great and lofty that it almost seems impossible, as if above nature, unless God from above takes hold and helps, strengthening the weakness of nature and propping up what is decayed, and in a certain way, lifting one up from the earth through divine love and the hope of the rewards laid up for us.

<margin>68.</margin> Flesh made moist by much drinking and much sleep is a great obstacle to chastity. True chastity remains unmoved even in the phantasms of sleep; for the mind's running toward these [images] is a sign that it still carries the sickness of passion in its depths. But if through grace it should be deemed worthy, even apart from the body, to converse with God in sleep, it remains untouched itself, a wakeful guardian of soul and body while they rest—like a watchdog, sober and unplundered by the treacherous wolves.

<margin>69.</margin> I tell you a paradoxical word, and do not wonder: there is a certain mystery performed secretly between God and the soul. This belongs to the highest measures, to perfect purification, love, and faith. When a person, having been reconciled to the utmost, is united to God through intimacy, prayer, and unceasing contemplation <term>theoria: spiritual vision or contemplation of God</term>, in this state, Elijah shuts the heaven with a drought and ignites the sacrifice with heavenly fire. Moses cuts the sea, and by the stretching out of his hands puts Amalek to flight, and Jonah is saved from the whale and the deep. For he who is deemed worthy of this, even if he still lives in the flesh, leads God—who is most man-loving—by force wherever he wills. Though he remains in the flesh, he has surpassed the measure of corruption and mortality, expecting death as a common sleep, which sweetly sends him on toward the things hoped for.

### On the Priesthood.

<sig>6.</sig> <margin>70.</margin> Reverencing the Master's passions <note>The sufferings of Christ</note>, and the emptying <term>kenosis: the 'self-emptying' or radical humility of God becoming human</term> of the Word of God for our sake,

<column-break/>

and also the sacrifice and the intermingling in us of the life-giving and divine Body and Blood—of which we have been deemed worthy not only of participation, but also of the priestly service <note>original: ἱερουργίας — the performance of the sacred rites/liturgy</note>—humble yourself like a sheep for the slaughter, truly considering all others to be above you, and strive not to strike anyone’s conscience. Especially without reason and without holiness, do not dare to touch the holy things, lest you be consumed like grass by the divine fire, and like melted wax, be destroyed.

<margin>71.</margin> Truly indeed, if you handle the terrifying ritual of the divine and venerable priestly service as you ought, and your conscience does not condemn you in anything at all, expect salvation from this. For beyond every work and contemplation, the benefit that comes to you from here is great. But if not so, you yourself will see; it is certainly better to abstain—through acknowledgment of one's own weakness—from the height of the priesthood, rather than having laid hold of this imperfectly and unclearly. Though one may seem to the many to be exalted, such a one lies in a fall worthy of weeping due to unworthiness.

<margin>72.</margin> The worship of the venerable priesthood, and the propitiation and entreaty toward the Divine, surpasses all psalmody and prayer as much as the sun surpasses the stars. For we sacrifice that very Only-begotten One, and we set Him forth and offer Him as an appeal—He who was slaughtered freely for sinners through His love for mankind—not only for the forgiveness of sins, but for whatever we need for our benefit, provided the conscience is not defiled. And that which is united to the Divinity, like a coal <note>A reference to the "burning coal" from Isaiah 6, a common metaphor for the Eucharist</note>, burns all the matter of lawlessness and enlightens the hearts of those who approach with faith. Likewise, the divine and precious Blood washes and cleanses beyond all hyssop every stain and spot of those who, with all their power, dare to approach the holy things purely and not unclearly, should any stain be left behind by chance.

<margin>73.</margin> It is not the body that was taken up of the Word of God, as one of the saints said, that descends from heaven to be sacrificed, but the bread and the wine themselves are changed into the Body and Blood of Christ—through faith, fear, longing, and piety—being consecrated by those deemed worthy of the divine priesthood. receiving the transformation from the one into the other, by the active power and visitation of the All-Holy Spirit. He does not become a different body from that of the Lord, but is changed into it, being made incorruptible, not perishing. How much purity and holiness, then, does the priest require, since he touches the divine body? And what kind of boldness <note>original: παρρησίας — a term for "freedom of speech" or "confidence" before God</note>, since he becomes a mediator between God and men, and enlists as fellow-intercessors the All-Pure Mother of God <note>original: Πανάγνῳ καὶ Θεομήτορι</note>, all the heavenly powers of the Angels, and the saints of every age? It seems to me that he needs a purity equal to the angelic or archangelic dignity, and a similar intimacy with God.

<margin>74.</margin> You should note, O Pisenios, that this is why the holy gifts lie uncovered upon the holy table after the Creed, as they are about to be sanctified: so that they may, in a sense, intercede on behalf of those offering them, and cry out with wordless voices to Him who dwells in the heavens. For He, seeing them, does not look away; and beholding them, He does not ignore them, remembering His voluntary emptying <note>original: κένωσιν (kenosis) — the theological concept of Christ "emptying" himself to become human</note> for the sake of sinners, His ineffable condescension, and His sacrifice for the love of mankind. For it was not because we were justified that He granted us the ransom and salvation through His suffering, He who is

<column-break/>

both good and long-suffering, but He had mercy on us while we were still offending Him, and He called us back.

<margin>75.</margin> Even if you are diligent in pure prayer, which unites the immaterial mind to God in an immaterial way, and you have reached the point of seeing, as in a mirror, the lot that awaits you after the end of this life—having received the "earnest" <note>A biblical term (Greek: arrabon) meaning a down-payment or pledge of what is to come</note> of the Spirit and possessing the Kingdom of Heaven within you with all perception and assurance—do not endure to be released from the flesh without a foreknowledge of death. Instead, pray fervently for this, and be hopeful of obtaining it near your departure, if it be for your benefit. Prepare yourself for this departure continually, casting away all fear so that, having passed through the air <note>In Eastern Christian thought, the "air" is the realm where souls encounter spiritual obstacles after death</note> and escaped the spirits of wickedness, you may enter boldly and without terror within the heavenly arches. There you shall be ranked with the angelic orders, joined to the elect and the righteous of every age, and behold the Divine as far as is possible. If not that, then at least you shall contemplate the good things under Him and the Word of God, who radiates through the super-heavenly realms, worshipped with a single act of prostration alongside His immaculate flesh, together with the Father and the Spirit, by all the heavenly host and all the saints. Amen.

# A BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
### OF OUR HOLY FATHER
# PHILOTHEOS
### THE SINAITE

---

<image-desc>Decorative frame with ornamental flourishes containing the letter P.</image-desc>
Philotheos, our most holy Father, served as the Abbot <note>original: Ἡγούμενος (Hegumen) — the head of a monastery</note> of the rational flock <note>A common metaphor for a community of monks</note> at Sinai, and for this reason is called "the Sinaite." It is unclear in what period he flourished and when he died. However, this present discourse, divided into forty chapters, was most excellently and laboriously

<column-break/>

composed by him. It is filled with so much spiritual wisdom and benefit for the soul—more than one can say—that it did not seem right for him to be separated from the choir of the other "Watchful Fathers" <note>original: Νηπτικῶν (Niptic) — from 'nepsis', referring to the practice of mental stillness and watchfulness</note>. Far from it. Indeed, if someone were to call him an exact rule of watchfulness, the guarding of the mind, and the purity of the heart, they would not stray from the truth.

<page-num>366</page-num>

# OF OUR HOLY FATHER
## PHILOTHEOS
### THE SINAITE
#### 40 CHAPTERS ON WATCHFULNESS <note>original: ΝΗΠΤΙΚΑ (Neptika) — refers to "nipsis," the practice of spiritual sobriety or watchfulness over one's thoughts.</note>

---

<margin>1.</margin>
There is within us an intellectual <note>original: νοητὸς (noetos) — often translated as "noetic," referring to the spiritual intellect or the eye of the soul</note> war that is more difficult than the war of the senses. A worker of piety must run and pursue his goal in the mind, so as to treasure the perfect remembrance of God in the heart like a pearl or a precious stone. We must be willing to give up everything—even our bodies and the contempt of this present life—so that we may possess God alone in our hearts. For, as the divine Chrysostom said, the vision of God <note>original: θεοπτία (theoptia) — the direct experience or seeing of God</note> in the mind is sufficient to destroy the wicked ones.

<margin>2.</margin>
Therefore, with all their strength, those who struggle intellectually <note>meaning: those fighting the internal battle against intrusive thoughts</note> should select spiritual labors from the divine scriptures and apply them to the mind like healing plasters. From early morning, he says, with an exact remembrance of God and unceasing prayer to Jesus Christ in the soul, one must stand bravely and sharply at the gate of the heart. One must kill all "the sinners of the earth" <note>a reference to Psalm 101:8, interpreted here as sinful thoughts</note> through intellectual guarding, and through the intensity of faith and the remembrance of God, cut off the "heads of the powerful" <note>referring to the primary or most dangerous demonic thoughts</note> for the sake of the Lord. For we know that even in these intellectual labors, there is a divine way of working and an order. One must struggle in this way until the time for the feast <note>referring to mealtime or spiritual refreshment</note> arrives. Afterward, having given thanks to the Lord—who, through His philanthropy alone, fills us doubly with food for both the spirit and the body—one should spend time in the remembrance and meditation of death. On the following day, one must again hold firmly to the morning's work. By doing this daily, we may barely manage, in the Lord, to escape the nets of the intellectual enemy. If these practices endure in us, they give birth to these three: faith, hope, and love. Faith truly

<column-break/>

prepares us to fear God. Hope, leaping over the fear felt by a servant, joins a person to the love of God, for "hope does not disappoint," since it knows how to give birth to that twofold love <note>love for God and love for neighbor</note> upon which "hang the law and the prophets." Love never fails; it is the cause for its partaker to fulfill the divine laws both in this age and in the one to come.

<margin>3.</margin>
It is very rare to find those who practice stillness <note>original: ἡσυχάζοντας (hesychazontas) — those practicing Hesychasm, or inner silence</note> in their reasoning faculty. These are only the ones who, through this practice, devise ways for divine grace and consolation to draw near to them. If, therefore, we wish to walk the path of intellectual labor—the "philosophy according to Christ"—in the guarding of the mind and watchfulness <note>term: νῆψις (nipsis) — spiritual sobriety and alertness against temptation</note>, we must first begin this way by abstaining from many foods, taking food and drink by weight and measure as much as we are able. Watchfulness is rightly called a way leading to the Kingdom—both the one within us and the one to come. It is an intellectual labor that cleanses and whitens the mind's state, changing it from a passionate state to a state of dispassion. For it is like a luminous window through which God leans down and reveals Himself to the mind.

<margin>4.</margin>
Where there is humility, the remembrance of God through watchfulness and attention, and frequent prayer arrayed against enemies, there is the "place of God." This is the "heaven of the heart" in which the demonic ranks fear to linger because God dwells in that place.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nothing is more confusing than talkativeness, and nothing is more base than an unrestrained tongue, which is capable of destroying the soul's stability. For what we build up day by day, the soul destroys through talkativeness, tearing down what we have gathered without effort.

<summary>St. Philotheos of Sinai outlines the "intellectual war" of the monk, emphasizing the need for unceasing prayer (the Jesus Prayer) and "nipsis" (watchfulness) to guard the heart from sinful thoughts. He describes the spiritual progression from faith and hope to the ultimate goal of divine love and the "heaven of the heart."</summary>

# NOETIC CHAPTERS <note>original: ΝΗΠΤΙΚΑ ΚΕΦΑΛΑΙΑ (Neptika Kephalaia) — chapters concerning "nipsis," the practice of spiritual sobriety or watchfulness.</note>

...scatters [the soul's wealth], for what is worse than it? It is an uncontrollable evil. One must therefore set a limit for it, and apply force, and "throttle" it, so to speak, so that it serves only what is necessary. For who could fully describe the entire spiritual loss that comes from the tongue?

<margin>6.</margin> The first gate leading into the spiritual <note>original: νοητὴν (noeten) — often translated as "noetic," referring to the spiritual intellect</note> Jerusalem—which is the watchfulness of the mind—is the silence of the mouth practiced with knowledge, even if the mind is not yet at rest. The second is a measured temperance <note>original: ἐγκράτεια (egkrateia) — self-control or fasting</note> in food and drink. The third, which purifies both mind and body, is the unceasing remembrance and meditation on death. I myself, having seen the beauty of this [remembrance] just once, was wounded and delighted in spirit rather than in eye; I desired to gain it as my lifelong companion, having fallen in love with its grace and dignity. How humble it is, "sorrow-joyful" <note>original: χαρμολυπουμένη (charmolypoumene) — a classic ascetic term describing the state of mourning for sins while simultaneously rejoicing in God's mercy</note>, contemplative, and fearful of the coming just judgment, dreading the delays of this life! From its physical eyes, a living, healing water naturally drips; and from its spiritual eyes, it releases a spring of the wisest thoughts, which, flowing and leaping, gladdens the mind. This "daughter of Adam," I mean the remembrance of death—as I said—I always thirsted to have as a spouse, to sleep with her and converse with her, and to discuss what will happen after the body is laid aside. But that filthy Forgetfulness—the darkened daughter of the devil—has often prevented me.

<margin>7.</margin> For there is a war in secret waged by the spirits of wickedness, clashing with the soul by means of thoughts <note>original: λογισμῶν (logismon) — specifically "intrusive thoughts" or "temptations" that lead to sin</note>. Since the soul is invisible, these evil powers offer their attacks in a way that matches her nature, through this invisible war. One can see between them and the soul weapons, battle lines, deceitful traps, a fearsome war, a fighting encounter, and victories and defeats on both sides. However, this spiritual war we are describing lacks one thing that physical war has: a set time for the conflict to end. While physical war has its seasons and sets its own order, this one attacks suddenly, without warning, in the very center of the heart, lying in wait to deal the soul a fatal blow through sin. Why and for what reason does this struggle and wrestling stand against us? It is so that the 

<column-break/>

will of God—which we pray for when we say "Thy will be done in us"—might not be fulfilled through us. This "will" is the commandments of God. And if someone, through the Lord, were to subtly and soberly station their mind against deception and accurately observe the demons' attacks and the entanglements that arise from fantasies, they would find this to be true through experience. Therefore, the Lord also directed his aim against the wretched demons; as God, he foresaw their thoughts and, in opposition to their aim, he established his commandments with a threat to those who transgress them.

<margin>8.</margin> When we come into a certain habit of temperance—I mean the abstaining from visible evils that act through the five senses—we will then be able to guard the heart with Jesus, to be enlightened by him within it, and to taste through the mind a certain warm desire for his goodness. For we did not receive the law to purify the heart for any other reason than this: that once the clouds of wickedness have departed from the air of the heart and been scattered by continuous attention <note>original: προσοχῆς (prosochēs) — watchfulness or spiritual concentration</note>, we may be able to see clearly, as in fair weather, the Sun of Righteousness, Jesus, and be somewhat illumined by the words of his majesty in the mind. For these things are not meant to be revealed to everyone, but only to those who purify their intellect <note>original: διάνοιαν (dianoian)</note>.

<margin>9.</margin> Thus we must prepare ourselves daily to be such as we ought to appear before God. For the Prophet Hosea says: "Keep mercy and judgment, and draw near to your God always." And again, Malachi says in the person of God: "A son honors his father, and a servant his master; if then I am a Father, where is my glory? and if I am a Master, where is my fear? says the Lord Almighty." And the Apostle [Paul] says: "Let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit." And Wisdom [Proverbs] again: "With all watchfulness guard your heart, for from these are the outgoings of life." And the Lord Jesus Christ said: "Cleanse the inside of the cup, so that the outside may also be clean."

<margin>10.</margin> Untimely conversations sometimes produce hatred toward us from those listening; at other times, they lead to insults and laughter as they condemn the foolishness of our words; others cause a defilement of conscience, and others...

It details the "invisible war" fought against demonic thoughts in the heart and the necessity of purification to see the "Sun of Righteousness."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Forty Chapters on Watchfulness" by St. Philotheos of Sinai. The previous page discussed the three "gates" to guarding the mind: silence, temperance, and the remembrance of death. ### OF OUR HOLY FATHER PHILOTHEOS

...condemnation from God, and the grieving of the Holy Spirit, which is more terrifying than all other things.

<margin>11.</margin> He who cleanses his heart and uproots sin in the Lord, and who labors for the sake of a more divine knowledge <note>original: γνώσεως (gnoseos) — spiritual insight or experiential knowledge of God</note>, seeing in his mind things invisible to the many, must not for this reason exalt himself over anyone. For nothing among created things is purer than the incorporeal, and nothing is more gifted with knowledge than an angel; yet by becoming exalted, he was cast down from heaven like a lightning bolt. Thus, high-mindedness <note>original: ὑψηλοφροσύνη (hypselophrosyne) — the state of being "puffed up" or arrogant</note> was reckoned as impurity before God. Those who dig for gold are clearly visible to all.

<margin>12.</margin> The Apostle says: *Everyone who competes in the games exercises self-control in all things.* It is not possible for those bound to this wretched flesh—which always desires against the spirit—to be marshaled against the principalities, against the unseen and malevolent powers, while being glutted with food. For the Kingdom of God is not food and drink. The "mind of the flesh" is enmity toward God; for it does not submit to the law of God, nor indeed can it. It is clear that it cannot do so because, being earthly and mixed with humors, blood, and phlegm, it always falls downward, always clings to earthly things, and finds pleasure in the fleeting <note>original: ἰλλυμέναις (illymenais) — literally "twisting" or "rolling," referring to the unstable nature of worldly pleasures</note> delights of this present age. For the mind of the flesh is death; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

<margin>13.</margin> We have need of great humility as we attend to the guarding of the mind in the Lord—first toward God, then toward men. We ought to crush the heart in every way and from every side, practicing everything that humbles us. The heart knows how to be crushed and humbled through the memory of our former life in the world, if we remember it accurately. Also, the memory of all sins since childhood, reviewed in the mind one by one (except for carnal sins, for the recollection of these is harmful <note>Philotheos warns that dwelling on the details of past sexual sins can re-awaken the temptation</note>). This memory knows how to humble us, produce tears, and move us wholeheartedly toward thanksgiving to God, just as the perpetual and vivid memory of death does. This same memory of death gives birth to a mourning <note>original: πένθος (penthos) — a technical term for spiritual grief over one's distance from God</note> accompanied by a certain sweetness and joy, and produces watchfulness <note>original: νῆψιν (nepsin) — spiritual sobriety or "nipsis"</note> of the mind. Furthermore, the memory of the sufferings of our Lord Jesus Christ powerfully humbles one’s pride and makes one look toward the earth, as these sufferings are recounted

<column-break/>

and remembered one by one; these, too, provide tears. In addition to these, the many blessings of God, when counted and reviewed one by one, truly humble the soul, since our struggle is against proud demons.

<margin>14.</margin> Do not, O man, reject such life-saving medicines for the soul out of self-love; for if you do, you are no longer a disciple of Christ, nor even an imitator of Paul, who says: *I am not worthy to be called an Apostle*; and again: *I who was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man.* Do you see, O proud one, how the saint was not forgetful of his former life? Indeed, all the saints from the beginning of creation until now have clothed themselves in this last, holy, "double-cloak" <note>original: διπλοΐδα (diploid) — a garment folded double; here used metaphorically as a garment of protection or virtue</note> of God. For even our Lord Jesus Christ himself, being God incomprehensible, unknown, and ineffable, wishing to show the way of eternal life and holiness, clothed himself in humility with his entire fleshly being. Thus, holy humility ought rightly to be called a divine virtue, a master’s command, and a garment. Even the angels and all those bright and divine powers practice and preserve this virtue, knowing from what a fall Satan fell through pride. As an example of the fear of falling for both angels and men, the evil one lies in the abyss, shown by God to be more dishonored than all the rest of creation because of his own pride. We also know the fall by which Adam fell through pride. Therefore, having so many examples of this soul-profiting virtue, let us always be humbled in every way. To the best of our ability, let us use these means to be humbled in soul, body, mind, will, words, thoughts, and appearance, both outwardly and inwardly. This is what we must seek most of all, so that we do not have Jesus Christ—the Son of God and God who suffered for us—against us. For the *Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble*; and *everyone who is high-hearted is an impurity before the Lord*; and *he who humbles himself will be exalted*. And *Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.* Therefore, let us take heed.

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of humility and the "memory of death" as essential tools for spiritual watchfulness. St. Philotheos warns that even those with great spiritual knowledge must guard against pride, citing the falls of Satan and Adam as warnings, and the humility of Christ as the ultimate model for the believer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Chapters on Watchfulness" by St. Philotheos of Sinai. Having previously discussed the general need for self-control, the author now begins a detailed analysis of the "tripartite soul"—the reasoning, irascible, and desiring parts—and how the devil attacks each one to lead the monk away from the commandments of Christ.</meta>

# CHAPTERS ON WATCHFULNESS

<margin>15.</margin>
"Take heed," says our Savior, "lest your hearts be weighed down," and so forth <note>original: Luke 21:34</note>. And he who competes in the games exercises self-control in all things. Knowing, therefore, that all these things were spoken to us in the Holy Scriptures, let us lead our lives with self-control. Above all, let us train the body by habit and orderly virtue to abstain from excessive food, providing it with nourishment only in due measure. For in this way, the stirrings of the **desiring part** <note>original: ἐπιθυμητικοῦ (epithymetikou) — the part of the soul associated with physical appetites and needs</note> are more easily calmed and brought into subjection to the **ruling reason**; and, if one must speak persuasively and truly, the same applies to the stirrings of **anger** <note>original: θυμοῦ (thymou) — the "spirited" or irascible part of the soul</note>. Furthermore, we can then easily abstain from other failings. For those who have experienced virtue judge this to be "comprehensive self-control"—that is, to abstain from every form of evil. For the primary cause of purity is God, the cause and giver of all good things; but the secondary cause is the consistent and measured self-control from excessive food practiced every day.

<margin>16.</margin>
Just as Satan sets himself against God, attempting to prevent God’s will—which is expressed in the commandments—from being fulfilled, and tries to destroy that will through us (thereby warring against God), so in turn, God wishes His all-holy will to be accomplished through us. This will, as I have said, consists of the divine and life-giving commandments. Through us and through His own divine influence, God strikes down the deadly aim of the evil one. For the useless will of the enemy, which seems to oppose God by causing His commandments to be transgressed, is in turn overturned by God through human weakness. And see if this is not the case: All the commandments of the holy Gospel appear to legislate for the **three-fold nature of the soul** and to make it healthy through what they prescribe. Rather, they do not merely "appear" to do so, but they truly do heal it. It is evident that the devil also fights against this three-fold nature of the soul night and day. If Satan fights against the three-fold nature, he clearly fights against the commandments of Christ; for Christ legislates for the three-fold nature of the soul through the commandments. These parts are: the **irascible**, the **desiring**, and the **reasoning** <note>term: tripartite soul — a psychological model from Greek philosophy used by early Christians to explain how human emotions (desire and anger) should be governed by the mind (reason)</note>. Consider this: "Whoever is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment," and the subsequent commands; behold the healing of **anger**. But the enemy, in turn, tries to destroy this commandment and those related to it through thoughts of contention,

<column-break/>

resentment, and envy within the mind. For the adversary himself knows that **reason** <note>original: λογιστικόν (logistikon)</note> is the leader of the **irascible part** <note>original: θυμικοῦ (thymikou)</note>. By shooting at the reason through thoughts—as I said—using suspicions of envy, contention, strife, deceit, and vanity, he persuades the reasoning faculty to abandon its proper authority, to hand over the reins to anger, and to leave the soul pilotless. Then anger, having cast off its "pilot," brings out through the mouth in words the things previously laid up in the heart—things which were stored there through the enemy's suggestions and the mind's neglect. One can then see that the heart, instead of being filled with the Divine Spirit and divine thoughts, is overflowing with malice, just as the Lord said: "Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" <note>original: Matthew 12:34</note>. For if the evil one has the power to bring out through a single word the things meditated upon within, then the brother who has been caught will say not only "Raca" <note>note: an ancient Aramaic term of contempt meaning "empty-headed"</note> to his brother, and not only "fool," but will often fall into insulting speech and even murder. The evil one employs these tactics because God gave a commandment not to be angry without cause—things which would not have broken out into insulting words and their consequences if, at the very first assault, they had been driven out of the heart through prayer and internal attentiveness. Thus the Destroyer achieves his own aim, if he finds that the things he cast into the heart through thoughts have succeeded in breaking a divine commandment.

<margin>17.</margin>
And what has been commanded to the **desiring part** <note>original: ἐπιθυμητικῷ (epithymetikou)</note> by the Master’s divine commandment? "Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart" <note>original: Matthew 5:28</note>. When the evildoer sees that this commandment has been given, he weaves a sort of snare within the person to use against the commandment. Having moved the war away from the external "material" that causes provocation, he sets it up within the mind. One can then see him painting sexual images, forms, and figures in the mind; and one can hear words that provoke passion, and other such things known to those who have experience of the mind.

<margin>18.</margin>
And what is the commandment that counsels the **reasoning part** <note>original: λογιστικῷ (logistikon)</note>? "But I say to you, do not swear at all; let your word be 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no'" <note>original: Matthew 5:34-37</note>; and, "He who does not renounce all and follow me is not worthy of me" <note>original: Luke 14:33</note>; and, "Enter through the narrow gate" <note>original: Matthew 7:13</note>. These are the instructions for the reasoning faculty. So again the enemy, wishing to overpower this faculty like a master general...

It emphasizes that self-control and mental watchfulness are necessary to prevent internal thoughts from turning into sinful actions.</summary>
