<meta>This page continues the discourse on spiritual warfare. Previously, St. Philotheos discussed the need for physical self-control to calm the soul's passions. Here, he moves deeper into the internal structure of the human person, describing how the devil attempts to overthrow the "ruling reason" and how the four cardinal virtues can restore order to the tripartite soul. He also introduces the "remembrance of death" as a vital tool for mental clarity.</meta>

### OF OUR HOLY FATHER PHILOTHEOS

...to guard, which is the **reasoning part** <note>original: λογιστικόν (logistikon) — the faculty of the soul responsible for logic and discernment</note>, having driven it out of its senses and its ruling position through thoughts of gluttony and indifference. Having mocked the mind as if it were a drunken general, the serpent <note>meaning: the devil</note> uses the **desiring part** and the **spirited part** <note>original: ἐπιθυμητικόν and θυμικόν — the faculties of appetite and anger</note> as servants for his own will. These powers, once released from the control of the reasoning part, use our five senses as assistants to commit sins openly. These are the "falls." At such times, the eyes become inquisitive because they do not have the mind within to bind them; the hearing loves to listen to vanities; the sense of smell becomes softened by luxury; the mouth becomes uncontrolled; and the hands touch what they should not. What follows these is injustice instead of righteousness, folly instead of prudence, licentiousness instead of self-restraint, and slavery instead of courage.

For these are the four general virtues: **Righteousness, Prudence, Self-restraint, and Courage** <note>original: δικαιοσύνη, φρόνησις, σωφροσύνη, ἀνδρεία — the "Cardinal Virtues" of classical philosophy adopted by Christian writers</note>. When these are healthy, they govern the **tripartite soul** <note>original: τριμερὲς (trimeres) — the soul divided into reason, anger, and desire</note>. When the tripartite soul is guided well, it keeps the senses away from improper things. Then the mind (the *nous*) enjoys a great stillness, as its powers are divinely governed and obedient, and it easily acts with bravery in the **noetic war** <note>original: νοητῷ πολέμῳ (noeto polemo) — the "war of the mind" or spiritual struggle against demonic thoughts</note>. But if it confuses its own powers through lack of attention, being defeated by the attacks of the evil one, it transgresses the divine commandments. Following this transgression, there must either be a proportional repentance or punishment in the life to come. It is good, therefore, for the mind to always practice **watchfulness** <note>original: νήφειν (nephein) — the state of spiritual sobriety and alertness</note>, through which a person stands in their natural state and becomes a true guardian of the divine commands.

<margin>19.</margin> The soul has been besieged and fenced in by the spirits of wickedness, and it is bound with chains of darkness. Because of the darkness surrounding it, it is unable to pray as it wishes; for it is bound in secret, being blinded in its inner eyes. When, therefore, it begins to pray to God and to practice watchfulness through prayer, it will then be released from that darkness through prayer; for otherwise, it is impossible to be released. Only then can the soul recognize that there is another struggle inside the heart, another hidden opposition, and another war of thoughts provoked by the spirits of wickedness. As the Holy Scriptures testify, saying: "If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place" <note>original: Ecclesiastes 10:4</note>. The "place" of the mind is its firm standing in virtue and its watchfulness; for there is a standing both in 

<column-break/>

virtue and in vice. For it says: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners" <note>original: Psalm 1:1</note>; and the Apostle says: "Stand therefore, having girded your waist with truth" <note>original: Ephesians 6:14</note>.

<margin>20.</margin> Let us hold fast to Christ with great strength, because of those who struggle to take Him from our souls continuously. We must do this so that Jesus does not "slip away" because of the "crowd" of thoughts present in the place of the soul <note>an allusion to John 5:13</note>. It is not possible to hold Him firmly without the labor of the soul. Let us also contemplate His life in the flesh, so that we may lead our own lives with humility; and let us hold onto His passions, so that we may endure distressing things by imitating Him. Let us taste His ineffable and condescending **economy** <note>original: οἰκονομίαν (oikonomian) — God's plan for the salvation of humanity</note> performed for our sake, so that from the sweet tasting of the soul, we may know that "the Lord is Christ." Above all these things, or even before all things, let us believe in Him without doubting in what He says. Let us expect His providence toward us daily, and however it may arrive, let us receive it with gratitude, welcome it, and accept it eagerly, so that we may learn to look only toward God, who governs all things by the words of His divine wisdom. When we have done all these things, then we are not far from God; for "piety is an unfinished perfection," as one of the **God-bearing men** <note>original: θεοφόρων ἀνδρῶν — a term for saints who are believed to carry the presence of God</note> said, who was perfect in the spirit.

<margin>21.</margin> For the one who redeems his own life well, being refined in thought and devoted to the **remembrance of death** <note>original: μνήμῃ θανάτου (mneme thanatou) — the spiritual practice of reflecting on one's mortality to spur repentance</note>, and who wisely steals his mind away from the passions—such a person is naturally able to see the hourly presence of demonic attacks more sharply than someone who chooses to live without the remembrance of death. The latter tries to purify his heart for the sake of knowledge alone, but does not preserve it throughout with a mournful mindset. Sometimes, while such a person thinks he has mastery over everything, he is bound without knowing it by a single one of the most destructive passions through his own cleverness. He may even fall, apart from God, into **high-mindedness** <note>original: ὑψηλοφροσύνῃ (hypselophrosyne) — pride or arrogance</note>. Such a person needs to be very watchful so that he does not become conceited and lose his mind in the abyss. For it is natural, as Paul says, for souls who gather knowledge from here and there to be puffed up against those they consider inferior, because the spark of the "love that builds up" does not exist within them <note>original: 1 Corinthians 8:1</note>. But the one who remembers death as a constant study is sharper than the other in spotting the raids of the demons...

<summary>This page describes the psychological and spiritual mechanics of sin, explaining how the devil displaces reason to stir the passions. St. Philotheos emphasizes the "four cardinal virtues" and the "remembrance of death" as essential practices for maintaining spiritual watchfulness and humility.</summary>
<keywords>tripartite soul, reasoning part, cardinal virtues, watchfulness, nepsis, noetic war, remembrance of death, pride, spiritual warfare, Philotheos of Sinai</keywords>

On the previous page, he described how the soul's faculties—reason, desire, and spirit—can be thrown into disorder by the devil. ### CHAPTERS ON WATCHFULNESS 371

...seeing it in a poor state, he drives it out and strikes it.

<margin>22.</margin> The delightful remembrance of God—that is, Jesus—when joined with the heart's indignation and a bitterness that brings salvation, is naturally able to dissolve all the sorcery of thoughts, all notions, words, fantasies, dark images, and simply put, everything with which the Destroyer <note>original: ὁ πανώλης (ho panoles) — meaning the "utterly destructive one," a title for the devil</note> arrays himself and acts with youthful arrogance. He gropes about, seeking to swallow our souls, but when Jesus is called upon, He easily burns everything to ashes. For there is no salvation for us in anyone else except in Jesus Christ. As the Savior Himself said: "Without me, you can do nothing."

<margin>23.</margin> Therefore, with every guard, let us keep our heart at every hour and for every single moment. Let us keep the **soul-mirror** <note>original: ψυχικὸν ἔσοπτρον (psychikon esoptron) — an image suggesting the soul reflects either God or the darkness of the world</note> from being clouded by thoughts. It is in this mirror that Jesus Christ, the wisdom and power of God the Father, is naturally formed and "light-written." Within the heart, let us unceasingly seek the Kingdom of Heaven—the grain of mustard seed, the pearl, and the leaven. We shall find all these things mystically within ourselves if we purify the eye of the mind. This is why our Lord Jesus Christ said: "The Kingdom of Heaven is within you," indicating that the Divinity remains deep inside the heart.

<margin>24.</margin> **Watchfulness** <note>original: νῆψις (nepsis) — the practice of inner alertness and spiritual sobriety</note> clearly purifies the conscience. Once purified, the conscience shines out like a hidden light and drives away great darkness. When that darkness is driven away by frequent and genuine watchfulness, the conscience again reveals things that were hidden. Through the mind, it teaches us by means of watchfulness about the **invisible wrestling** <note>original: ἀόρατον πάλην (aoraton palin)</note> and the logical battle: how we must hurl spears in this single combat, and how to strike with well-aimed "javelins of thought" without the mind itself being struck. Instead of harmful darkness, the mind—hidden in Christ—longs for the Light. He who has tasted this understands what I mean. This taste of Light does not satisfy the soul’s hunger but rather starves it <note>meaning: the more the soul "eats" of this light, the more its spiritual hunger grows</note>; the soul is never filled, but the more it eats, the more it hungers. This Light draws the mind toward it like the sun draws the eyes. It is unexplainable, yet interpreted not by words but by the experience of those who have suffered or, more truly, been "wounded" by it. This experience commands me to be silent, even as my mind wishes to delight in speaking about these things. "Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord." For the sake of acquiring love and 

<column-break/>

purity—for these are peace and holiness.

<margin>25.</margin> We must arm our **anger** <note>original: θυμός (thymos) — the "spirited" or "incensive" faculty of the soul</note> only against the demons, who are hostile to our reasoning faculty, and be indignant against them. Hear now the method for the hourly war within us, and do it: join **watchfulness** with **prayer**. Watchfulness purifies prayer, and prayer purifies watchfulness. Watchfulness, seeing things unceasingly, perceives the thoughts that are entering; it blocks their entrance for a moment and calls upon the Lord Jesus Christ to drive out these wicked enemies. **Attention** <note>original: προσοχή (prosochi)</note> blocks them by speaking against them, and when Jesus is called, He drives out the demons along with their fantasies.

<margin>26.</margin> Be very precise in guarding your mind. When you recognize a thought, speak against it. Then immediately and quickly call upon Christ for vengeance. The sweet Jesus, while you are still speaking, will say: "Behold, I am here to grant you help." Once all these enemies have been calmed by prayer, focus your mind again. Behold, more waves will come, larger than the first, a continuous surge in which the soul swims. But behold, Jesus again arises when called by the disciple and rebukes the wicked winds as God. Having found a moment of peace for an hour or perhaps just a second, glorify the one who saved you and meditate on **death**.

<margin>27.</margin> Let us travel with all attention of the heart and with a spiritual sense. For attention and prayer, when yoked together daily, become like the **fiery chariot of Elijah**, lifting their participant into the heights of heaven. And what more can I say? For the one who achieves watchfulness, or strives to achieve it, a blessed heart is prepared—a **noetic heaven** <note>original: νοητὸς οὐρανὸς (noetos ouranos) — a "heaven of the mind" or "intellectual heaven"</note> with its own sun, moon, and stars. It becomes a container for the uncontainable God, through mystical contemplation and ascent. Therefore, let whoever seeks the praise of divine virtue strive to bring forth the Lord with a turning of the heart, and turn words into deeds with eagerness. By using a kind of force to restrain the "five-fold" senses <note>the five physical senses</note> through which the soul is known to be harmed, he will find the inner struggle and war easier for his mind. Restrain everything external through various spiritual strategies, and fight the thoughts born from them within the soul using "bodiless divine methods." Through the labor of **vigils** <note>original: ἀγρυπνία (agrypnia) — staying awake for prayer</note>, drive away pleasures...

<summary>This page describes "nepsis" (watchfulness) as a method of purifying the heart to see the Light of Christ within. It outlines a practical spiritual strategy: using the "Jesus Prayer" and righteous anger to repel intrusive thoughts while maintaining a constant inner focus on God.</summary>

### PAGE 372

...resort; and concerning food and drink, remain temperate, and thin the body sufficiently, so that you may easily prepare for yourself a light heart for the internal war. By doing this, you benefit yourself and no other. Punish the soul with the thought of death, and gather your scattered mind through the remembrance of Jesus Christ. For in the nights, the mind is especially accustomed to be illuminated by the bright contemplations <term>theoria: the act of spiritual seeing or divine vision</term> of God and of divine things.

<margin>28.</margin> Let us not reject the labors of physical disciplines. For just as grain grows from the earth, spiritual joy and the experience of good things sprout from such labors. Let us not deceive our conscience when it speaks to us of the things that save and the things we must do; it speaks incessantly of what is necessary and what is owed, especially if it happens to be purified through an active, practical, and refined **watchfulness** <term>nepsis: a state of sober alertness and vigilance over one's thoughts</term> of the mind. For then, because of its purity, the conscience is accustomed to bring forth appropriate and indisputable concise judgments. Therefore, we must not deceive it, for it announces within us a life pleasing to God. By sharply rebuking the soul when the mind is weighed down by sin, it shows the way to correct the fault, advising the stumbling heart to repent and pointing out the cure with a delightful suggestion.

<margin>29.</margin> Smoke rising from wood is heavy on the eyes, but it eventually reveals the light to them and delights those it previously grieved. Likewise, unceasing attention <note>original: προσοχὴ (prosochē) — focused spiritual concentration</note> brings a burden at first, but when Jesus arrives and is called upon in prayer, He illuminates the heart. For the remembrance of Him provides, along with that radiance, the very best of all good things.

<margin>30.</margin> Our enemy is naturally inclined to pry the mind away from its purpose; he eats "dust" and desires that we do the same with him. He wants the one made in the image of God to walk "upon his belly" <note>This is a reference to the curse of the serpent in Genesis 3:14</note>. For this reason, God says, "I will put enmity between you and him." Because of this, we must always **breathe God** <note>original: τὸν Θεὸν ἀεὶ ἀναπνέειν (ton Theon aei anapneein) — a famous ascetic phrase meaning to pray as naturally and constantly as one breathes</note>, so that by this, we may pass through each day unhurt by the devil's "fiery arrows." God says: "I will protect him because he has known my name," and "His salvation is near those who fear Him."

<margin>31.</margin> The blessed Apostle, the "Vessel of Election," who speaks in Christ and who had much experience of the unseen and intellectual war within us, wrote to the Ephesians,

<column-break/>

saying:
> Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

And the Apostle Peter says:
> Be sober, be vigilant, because your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, steadfast in the faith.

And our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking about the different dispositions of those who hear the words of the Gospel, said: "Then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts"—that is, performing the theft through a wicked forgetfulness—"lest they should believe and be saved." And again the Apostle says:
> For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, but I see another law warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive.

They have said these things to teach us and to make known that which is hidden.

<margin>32.</margin> Knowledge is naturally prone to puff itself up, imagining itself to be superior to many, if it is deprived of self-reproach and humility. Therefore, for those of us who have the recognition of our own weakness, let us hold this mindset, hearing him who says:
> Brothers, I do not count myself to have apprehended; but one thing I do: forgetting those things which are behind and reaching forward to those things which are ahead, I press toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ.

And again:
> I run thus: not with uncertainty. I fight thus: not as one who beats the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified.

Do you see such humility and, at the same time, such a race toward virtue? Do you see the humility of the great and holy Paul? "Christ," he says, "came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first." Is it not therefore necessary for us to be humble, since we possess the lowliness of nature? For what is lowlier than clay? And we must remember God, since we were created for this very purpose; but we must also practice temperance, so that we may run lightly in our Lord.

<margin>33.</margin> It is impossible for one who has given himself over to evil thoughts to be pure from sins in the "outer man." And it is not possible for those who do not uproot evil thoughts from the heart to keep them from being brought forth into evil deeds. And...

Here, the text shifts to the "mechanics" of how a thought becomes a sin and the importance of inner vigilance over outward appearance.</meta>

# CHAPTERS ON WATCHFULNESS

Looking lustfully is caused by the inner eye being "adulterated" <note>original: παραμοιχευθῆναι (paramoicheuthenai) - to be corrupted or led into adultery</note> and darkened. Likewise, the desire to hear shameful things is caused by hearing with the ears of the soul the foul demons within, as they whisper against us. Therefore, we ought to cleanse ourselves in the Lord, both inside and out. Each of us must guard our own senses and cleanse them from passionate activities and sins. Just as before, in our ignorance when we lived in the world following the vanity of our minds, we served the deception of sin with our whole mind and senses—so now, having transitioned to a life according to God, we must serve the living and true God, His righteousness, and His will with our whole mind and senses.

<margin>34.</margin> First, there is the **provocation** <term>prosvole: the initial suggestion or "flicker" of a thought</term>; then **coupling**; then **assent**; then **captivity**; then **passion**, which is formed through habit and repetition. Behold, this is how victory is won in the struggle against us. This is how the Holy Fathers define it.

<margin>35.</margin> They say that **provocation** is a bare thought, or an image of a thing that has newly appeared in the heart and presented itself to the mind. **Coupling** <term>syndyasmos: literally "joining together"</term> is to converse with that which appeared, whether with passion or without it. **Assent** <term>synkatathesis: consent</term> is the pleasurable leaning of the soul toward what was seen. **Captivity** <term>aichmalosia: being taken prisoner</term> is the violent and involuntary abduction of the heart, or a persistent dwelling with the thought that destroys our best spiritual state. They say **passion** <term>pathos: a deep-seated spiritual sickness</term> is properly that which has nested within the soul for a long time through passionate habit. Of all these, the first (provocation) is sinless; the second is not entirely so; the third is judged according to the state of the one struggling. This combat leads either to crowns of victory or to punishments.

<margin>36.</margin> For captivity is one thing during the time of prayer, and another thing outside of it. Passion, beyond doubt, is subject either to a corresponding repentance or to future punishment. Therefore, he who resists the first stage—that is, the provocation—or rejects it without obedience, has cut off all shameful things at once. This struggle against the evil demons belongs to both Monks and those who are not Monks; it results in both defeat and victory, as we have said. And from victory come crowns, or from failure, punishments for those who stumble and do not repent.

<column-break/>

Let us therefore struggle intellectually against them, so that we do not bring their evil counsels into sinful outward deeds. But by cutting off sin from the heart, we shall find the Kingdom of Heaven within ourselves. Let us guard the purity of our heart and a constant state of compunction <note>original: κατάνυξιν (katanyxin) - a sense of "piercing" sorrow for sins that leads to spiritual joy</note> before God through such "beautiful work" <note>a technical term for the practice of inner watchfulness</note>.

<margin>37.</margin> Many Monks do not know the wandering of the mind which it suffers from the demons. They are occupied with outward practice <note>monastic labors like fasting or labor</note> but take no care for the mind. Being simple and guileless, they sail through life, I believe, without tasting purity of heart, being entirely ignorant of the darkness of the passions within. Those who do not know the struggle of which Paul speaks—perhaps never having been shaped by the experience of what is good—judge only the sins committed in action as "falls." They do not account for defeats and victories in the realm of thought. Since these things are hidden, the physical eye cannot see them; they are known only to God, the judge of the contest, and to the conscience of the one struggling. To such people, I think that scripture applies: *And they said, "Peace," but there was no peace.* Because of their simplicity, one should be among such brothers to pray for them and teach them as much as possible to abstain from evil deeds. But for those who have a divine desire for the "seeing" part of the soul to be cleansed, there is another "practice of Christ" and another mystery.

<margin>38.</margin> Truly, the vivid **remembrance of death** <term>mneme thanatou: the spiritual practice of keeping one's mortality in mind</term> is a container of many virtues. it is the parent of grief; an exhortation to be temperate in all things; a reminder of hell; the mother of prayer and tears; the guard of the heart; detachment from the "clay" <note>the physical body</note> as something made of earth; and a fountain of quick-wittedness joined with discernment. The children of these are the two-fold fear of God and the cleansing of passionate thoughts from the heart. It encompasses many of the Lord's commandments. In it, one observes the hourly struggle—the most difficult to fight—which is the chief concern of Christ's athletes.

<margin>39.</margin> An unexpected circumstance or disaster that comes upon us damages the attention of the mind in no small way. By knocking the mind out of its better, virtuous, and beautiful state, it turns it toward sinful contentions and strife. The cause of this ruin for us is always being found unprepared for such occurrences.

<margin>40.</margin> Nothing will damage us, nor will any of the daily annoyances grieve us, if they fall upon us [while we...]

<summary>Philotheos outlines the five stages of how a thought becomes a sinful passion and emphasizes that true spiritual warfare happens in the mind before it ever reaches physical action. He highlights the "remembrance of death" as a vital tool for maintaining purity of heart and spiritual alertness.</summary>

# BRIEF BIOGRAPHY
## ELIAS
### PRESBYTER AND DEFENDER <note>original: Ἔκδικος (Ekdikos) — an ecclesiastical office in the Byzantine Church; a legal official or "defender" of the Church's rights.</note>

---

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' (Ἠ) with floral and scroll motifs inside a square border.</image-desc>Elias, this divine Father, who is also surnamed the Defender—whether he is that Elias of Crete, who was also a commentator <note>original: σχολιαστής (scholiastēs) — a scholar who writes explanatory notes or "scholia" on ancient texts.</note> on the theological discourses of Gregory the Theologian <note>Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, one of the Great Cappadocian Fathers.</note>, or someone else, is unclear to us. However, as far as can be gathered from these present chapters—judging the creator by the results of his work—he was a man who, if anyone else ever did, reached the very pinnacle of wisdom, both "external" <note>original: θύραθεν (thyrathen) — literally "from outside," referring to secular classical Greek philosophy and rhetoric.</note> wisdom, and much more so our own superior, divine wisdom. For a critical man might easily discern in these writings the power of his words and the surpassing fame of his virtue. We ourselves, having observed these things and having admired the abundant fruit of his moral and cognitive teaching—and indeed,
<column-break/>
having delighted in the graces of his metaphors and expressions, which provide a sort of leafy cover and a timely beauty to the fruit (I mean the beauty of his language with which their Father has most excellently graced them), we offer these to those who love reading. We invite them to enter in love this flowery and fragrant "Meadow" <note>The author uses the metaphor of a "meadow" (leimon), a common title for Byzantine spiritual anthologies.</note>, as it is so titled. It is thick with many tall trees of spiritual sayings and is watered by the sweetest streams of divine wisdom. Sit beneath its shade, so that you yourselves may not only enjoy the currents of practice <term>praxis: the active life of purifying the soul through discipline</term> but also, to speak in the language of the Song of Songs, may feast like temple-servants upon the fruits of contemplation <term>theoria: the mystical vision or direct experience of God</term>.

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring intricate leaf and vine motifs within a rectangular frame.</image-desc> It is necessary for every Christian who rightly believes in God not to be carefree, but always to expect and await trial <note>original: πειρασμόν (peirasmon) — often translated as "temptation," but in this context refers to trials or testing of one's faith.</note>; so that when it comes, he is not taken by surprise or troubled, but may gratefully endure the labor of affliction, and understand what he says when chanting with the Prophet:
> Test me, O Lord, and try me; and he did not say that your discipline destroyed me, but that it set me upright to the end. <note>original: Δοκίμασόν με Κύριε... — a reference to Psalm 26:2 (25:2 in the Septuagint), though the second half is a paraphrased interpretation of the benefit of divine discipline.</note>

<margin>2.</margin>
The beginning of good things is the fear of God; the end is the love <note>original: πόθος (pothos) — a strong desire or yearning love.</note> for Him.

<margin>3.</margin>
The beginning of every good is the effective word <note>original: λόγος (logos) — meaning reason, word, or discourse.</note> and reasoned action; therefore, neither is action good without the word, nor is the word that comes forth good without action.

<margin>4.</margin>
Action <note>original: Πρᾶξις (Praxis) — refers to the active life of virtue and ascetic discipline.</note> consists of, for the body: fasting and vigils; for the mouth: psalmody, prayer, and a silence more precious than speech; for the hands: the work performed by them without grumbling; and for the feet: that which is accomplished by them at the first prompting.

<margin>5.</margin>
Preceding all these are mercy and truth; their outpouring is humility, and from this comes the discernment <note>original: διάκρισις (diakrisis) — the spiritual gift of being able to distinguish between good and evil impulses.</note> according to the Fathers; without which, no other virtue will be able to see its own completion. For action that dishonors the yoke of reason is found wandering here and there regarding useless things, like a certain heifer; while the word that rejects the honorable garments of practice,

<column-break/>

is not graceful, even if it somehow styles itself to appear so.

<margin>6.</margin>
The courageous soul, like a woman throughout her whole life, holding the two burning lamps of practice and contemplation, performs what is required; the soul surrendered to pleasures, however, does the opposite.

<margin>7.</margin>
Voluntary hardship <note>original: κακοπάθεια (kakopatheia) — ascetic labor or "suffering of hardship."</note> is not sufficient for the soul for a perfect release from vice, unless it is also refined through involuntary hardship without being dissolved. For the soul is like a certain blade: unless it passes through fire and water—that is, voluntary and involuntary labors—it is not preserved unbroken against the resistances of those things that befall it.

<margin>8.</margin>
Just as there are three more general causes of voluntary trials—health, wealth, and fame—so there are also three for involuntary ones: losses, insults, and illnesses. These happen to some for edification, but to others for destruction.

<margin>9.</margin>
Attaching themselves to the soul are desire and grief; and to the body, pleasure and pain. For wanting to escape the painful sensation of agony, we flee toward pleasure; and from grief, we flee toward desire.

<margin>10.</margin>
The virtuous man possesses goodness as an internal disposition, while the vainglorious man possesses it only in his thoughts. The diligent man has evil on the surface, but the pleasure-lover has it in his depths.

<margin>11.</margin>
The action of the soul is self-control in simpli...

<margin>12.</margin>
The action of the mind <note>original: Νοῦ (Nous) — the "eye of the soul" or the highest faculty of the human person in Eastern Christian thought.</note> is prayer within contemplation, and contemplation within prayer.

<margin>13.</margin>
One who hates evil is rarely and carelessly found near it; but one who is attached to the causes of evil is found there more often and more attentively.

<margin>14.</margin>
For those whose intention is not to repent, sinning is continuous; but for those whose intention is not to sin, repentance <note>original: μετάνοια (metanoia) — a change of mind or heart.</note> is fully assured, and the cause of their sin is not frequent.

<margin>15.</margin>
Let sensation and conscience work together with the spoken word, so that the peaceful and divine Word <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note> is not ashamed to be found in their midst through the rashness or the immoderation of what is said.

<margin>16.</margin>
It is not the case that he who does not wrong his soul by his deeds has also preserved it unstained by his words; nor has he who guards it in these ways already kept it from defilements. For sin is established as threefold <note>In deed, word, and thought.</note>.

<margin>17.</margin>
You will not be able to look upon the face of virtue while you still look upon the face of vice with pleasure; the latter will appear hateful to you only when, as a lover of spiritual delight, you estrange your taste from it and your sight from such a form.

<margin>18.</margin>
The demons war against the soul primarily through thoughts <note>original: λογισμῶν (logismoi) — provocative or intrusive thoughts.</note>, not through things; for things by themselves war against themselves. Of things, hearing and sight are the causes; but of thoughts, habit and the demons are the causes.

<margin>19.</margin>
We find that the sinful part of the soul is threefold: in deeds, in words, and in thoughts. But the beauty of sinlessness is sixfold: for one must preserve the five senses and the spoken word without stumbling. He who does not stumble in these is a perfect man, able to bridle the remaining parts of the soul.

<margin>20.</margin>
The irrational part of the soul is divided six-fold: into the five senses and into the spoken word. This word is preserved inseparably with the part that experiences emotion <note>original: τῷ πάσχοντι (to paschonti) — the "passible" or emotional part of the soul.</note>, while being itself beyond emotion; yet it takes on the imprint of its vice when it is found in an emotional state.

<margin>21.</margin>
Neither can the body be purified without fasting and vigils, nor the soul without mercy and truth; nor is the mind <note>original: νοῦς (nous)</note> purified without commun-

<column-break/>

ion and the contemplation <note>original: θεωρίας (theoria)</note> of God. For these pairings are most distinguished in these matters.

<margin>22.</margin>
When the soul is surrounded by these aforementioned virtues, it makes its fortress—which is patience <note>original: ὑπομονή (hypomone) — endurance or steadfastness.</note>—unshakable by temptations. For the Word says: "In your patience possess your souls." <note>Luke 21:19</note> But if it were otherwise, the soul would be like an unwalled city that is accustomed to being shaken by the bars of cowardice, even by noises from afar.

<margin>23.</margin>
Not everyone who is wise in matters of reason is also wise in matters of thought; nor will those who are wise in matters of thought necessarily be found wise in matters of outward sensation. For even if sensation holds all things as subjects, they do not all pay tribute to it equally; for many, out of simplicity, do not know how to honor sensation in its own realm as it requires.

<margin>24.</margin>
Though prudence <note>original: φρόνησις (phronesis) — practical wisdom or discernment.</note> is by nature indivisible, it is cut into various sections; for to one more of it is given, and to another less, until practical virtue has increased. When it has the general virtues running alongside it, it fulfills the potential good in each; for many, according to the deficiency of their practical life, have also inherited their measure of wisdom.

<margin>25.</margin>
In matters according to nature, few wise men will be found; but in matters contrary to nature, many. For out of fear regarding these things, having emptied out all their natural prudence, they have little wisdom there; but they have the most in things that are superfluous and not praiseworthy by nature.

<margin>26.</margin>
For those who practice reasonable silence, time and measure are fellow-guests; and truth becomes a banquet for such a person, according to which the father of lies <note>A traditional title for the Devil, from John 8:44.</note>, coming to a soul that is departing, finds none of the things he seeks.

<margin>27.</margin>
+ The truly merciful man is not the one who voluntarily provides from his surplus, but he who concedes necessities to those who seize them.

<margin>28.</margin>
Some acquire the immaterial wealth of mercy through material riches; others, through the immaterial, lose the material, becoming aware of that which never fails.

<margin>29.</margin>
To be rich in good things is dear to everyone; but it is a cause of grief to one who has become divinely wealthy if he is not permitted to enjoy it for a very long time.

# GNOMIC ANTHOLOGY

->**THE GNOMIC ANTHOLOGY**<-

...and if it is given that the sickness of the soul is naturally hidden in the depths of sensation, and if that sickness must be brought to light from the outside by the "harvesting" of reproofs, while health must clearly be established from within by the renewal of the mind <note>original: νοός (noos) — the highest faculty of the soul, often called the "intellect" or "inner eye."</note>, then he is a fool who shakes off corrections and is not ashamed to lie forever in the hospital of insensitivity.

<margin>31.</margin>
Do not be embittered toward the one who has "performed surgery" <note>original: χειρουργήσαντος — literally "worked by hand," here used as a metaphor for a person whose sharp words of correction act like a surgeon's knife.</note> on you involuntarily. Instead, looking at the disgusting thing that was emptied out, consider yourself wretched, but call the one who caused this benefit for you "blessed" by the providence of God.

<margin>32.</margin>
Do not despair over any terrible aspect of your sickness, but through the more effective medicines of diligence, distance yourself from it—you who care for the health of the soul.

<margin>33.</margin>
Do not shrink from the one who strikes you at the right moment; rather, approach him, and he will show you how great a good it is to have your perception cleansed. Then you shall eat the sweet food of health, after the discarded bitterness has been consumed.

<margin>34.</margin>
To the extent that you feel pain, to that same extent welcome the one who points out these things to you through reproofs; for he becomes the cause of your perfect purification. Without this, the mind cannot exist in the "clean place" of prayer.

<margin>35.</margin>
When being reproved, one must either be silent or respond mildly to the accuser—not so that the one being reproved can justify his own actions, but perhaps to restore the one who is reproving in ignorance, should he have been offended.

<margin>36.</margin>
The one who repents before being called out by someone he has justly grieved has lost nothing of what is fitting. But the one who repents after being called out gains half of the "good harvest." Truly, the one who is never found "cast out of the assembly" <note>original: ἀποσυνάγωγος — meaning excommunicated or separated from the community due to resentment.</note> because of grief gains the whole amount previously paid; and the one who places the blame upon himself in everything adds a further reward for himself.

<margin>37.</margin>
Neither does the high-minded man recognize his own defects, nor does the humble-minded man recognize his own good deeds. For a wicked folly covers the former, while a God-pleasing "folly" <note>original: ἄνοια (anoia) — Elias uses this term ironically; the humble man is "unaware" of his virtues because he looks only to God.</note> covers the latter.

<margin>38.</margin>
The proud man does not wish to be compared to his equals in good things; but in bad things, when compared to his superiors, he considers

<column-break/>

his own fault to be bearable.

<margin>39.</margin>
Censure makes the soul firm, but praise makes it dissolute and more sluggish toward good deeds.

<margin>40.</margin>
Gold is the substance of wealth; humility is the substance of virtue. Therefore, just as he who lacks gold is poor, even if he does not appear so to those outside, so without humility, the one struggling <note>original: ἀγωνιζόμενος — a term for an ascetic "athlete" or spiritual practitioner.</note> will not be virtuous.

<margin>41.</margin>
Just as a merchant is not a merchant without gold, even if he is very skilled at trade, so without humility, the practitioner will not be found in possession of the delights of virtue, even if he trusts greatly in his own prudence.

<margin>42.</margin>
The one who ascends through humility becomes lower in his own estimation; but the one without it becomes higher, to the point that he refuses to be compared even to the least of men. And for this reason, he shows his resentment at the "first places" <note>The seats of honor at a banquet or gathering.</note>.

<margin>43.</margin>
It is good for the "spiritual athlete" to think of his work as less than it is, but to act more bravely than his fear. In this way, he is found to be respected by men and a worker for God who has no need to be ashamed.

<margin>44.</margin>
One must either be successful in all the commandments of God, or at least lay claim to the one virtue of humility, if one fears being seen as a stranger to those reclining in the bridal chamber <note>A metaphor for the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>.

<margin>45.</margin>
Join self-control with simplicity, and unite truth with humility, and you will be seen as a guest of justice; at her table, every other virtue loves to gather.

<margin>46.</margin>
Truth is blind without humility, and for this reason, it uses "contradiction" <note>Argumentativeness or the spirit of dispute.</note> as its guide—relying on it when it struggles, yet finding nothing but the fortress of resentment.

<margin>47.</margin>
A good character testifies to the beauty of virtue, while a steady composure of the limbs testifies to a peaceful soul.

<margin>48.</margin>
First, it is good to stumble in no part; second, it is good not to hide one's fault out of shame, nor to retreat into it; rather, one should humble oneself, join in the accusation against oneself, and gladly accept the penance <note>original: ἐπιτίμιον (epitimion) — a corrective spiritual discipline or punishment.</note>. If this does not happen, everything offered to God is powerless.

<summary>A collection of ascetic maxims focusing on the necessity of humility and the healing power of reproof. The author argues that without humility, no virtue is valid, comparing it to gold for a merchant.</summary>

--- Page 388 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Gnomic Anthology" of Elias the Presbyter, following directly from maxim 48. The text transitions into practical ascetic advice regarding the body, the control of speech versus food, and the psychological nuances of spiritual discipline.</meta>

# OF ELIAS THE PRESBYTER

<margin>49.</margin> In addition to voluntary hardship <note>original: κακοπαθείᾳ (kakopatheia) — referring to self-imposed ascetic practices like fasting or vigils.</note>, one must also accept involuntary hardship—I mean that which comes from demons, losses, and illnesses. He who does not accept these but is disgruntled is like one who wants to eat his bread with honey alone rather than salt. Such a person does not always have pleasure as a companion, but he always has satiety <note>original: κόρον (koron) — a sense of "too much" or being overfilled, implying that pleasure without the "salt" of struggle leads to a spiritual sickness or boredom.</note> as a neighbor.

<margin>50.</margin> A master who appears clothed in the form of a servant is seen in the one who washes the torn garment of a neighbor with godly words, or mends it with charitable gifts. But let the one doing this take care never to lose both the reward and the dignity of his authority through vainglory, by failing to perform this service with the heart of a servant.

<margin>51.</margin> Just as faith is naturally the "substance of things hoped for," <note>A direct reference to Hebrews 11:1.</note> so prudence is the substance of the soul, and humility the substance of virtue. It is a wonder how things that are complete in themselves appear incomplete without their accompanying attributes.

<margin>52.</margin> "The Lord shall guard your coming in and your going out," it says <note>Psalm 121:8</note>; clearly, this refers to the "coming in" of food and the "going out" of words through self-control. For the one who is disciplined regarding the entry of food and the exit of words escapes the desire that arises from the eyes and calms the anger that arises from agitation <note>original: ἀπνοίας (apnoias) — literally "breathlessness," used here to describe the physical state of being enraged.</note>. The spiritual athlete must care for these things above all and strive in every way; for in these matters, the practical life is strengthened and the contemplative life is established.

<margin>53.</margin> Some take great care regarding the entry of food, but are careless regarding the exit of words. Such people do not know how to "remove anger from the heart and desire from the flesh," according to the Preacher <note>Ecclesiastes 11:10</note>. It is through these disciplines that a pure heart is usually created by the renewing Spirit.

<margin>54.</margin> Simplicity in food will be found in the lesser quality of nourishment; blamelessness in words will be found in the superior quality of silence.

<margin>55.</margin> Purify your kidneys <note>original: νεφρούς (nephrous) — in biblical and Greek thought, the kidneys were considered the seat of the emotions and hidden impulses.</note> by fasting from food, and test your heart by self-control in words; then you will have both your desire and your anger at the service of good things.

<margin>56.</margin> The pleasure of the belly fades in those who practice asceticism as the body

<column-break/>

declines; but the pleasure of the throat <note>original: φάρυγγος (pharyngos) — distinguishing between the physical hunger of the stomach and the sensory craving of the palate/throat.</note> remains for the one who has not managed to punish it justly. One must strive, therefore, to wipe away the reproach of the effect by dealing with its cause, so that you are not found a stranger to the virtue of self-control in the next life and clothed in shame.

<margin>57.</margin> It is necessary for the ascetic to know when and with what foods he should feed the body as an enemy, when to encourage it as a friend, and when to comfort it as if it were sick. This is so he does not mistakenly give the enemy's portion to the friend, or the friend's portion to the enemy, or give their portions to the sick man; for having offended them both, he will find them warring against him in times of temptation.

<margin>58.</margin> When the one being nourished begins to value the food of hardship <note>original: τῆς τρυφῆς τὴν τροφὴν — a play on words between 'luxury' (tryphe) and 'nourishment' (trophe).</note> over luxury, then the grace of tears visits him and begins to comfort him. He forgets every other sweetness, as his soul is already swallowed up by the incomparable sweetness of these tears.

<margin>59.</margin> Tears are withheld from the one who takes the broad path; but they are poured out for the one who loves the narrow way.

<margin>60.</margin> No one is without sorrow, neither the sinner nor the righteous man; the former because he has not entirely left evil behind, the latter because he has not yet reached perfection.

<margin>61.</margin> Among the things within our power are the virtues of prayer and silence; but fasting and vigils <note>original: ἀγρυπνία (agrypnia) — the practice of staying awake for prayer during the night.</note> are often not entirely within our power, but depend on the constitution of the body. Therefore, the athlete should pursue whatever is easier for him to grasp.

<margin>62.</margin> Patience is the "house" of the soul, for the soul is contained within it; humility is its "wealth," for the soul is nourished by it.

<margin>63.</margin> If you do not endure labors, you will not be honored with praises. By looking at the pain before the pleasure, you will escape the sorrow that follows pleasure.

<margin>64.</margin> Do not be bound by a small fault, and you will not become a slave to a greater one; for a greater evil is not naturally formed before a smaller one.

<margin>65.</margin> By looking toward greater things, you will be formidable to lesser ones; but you will appear contemptible to the lesser if you have given up on the greater.

<margin>66.</margin> You will not be able to reach the greater virtues if you have not first attained the peak of those virtues that are within your power.

<margin>67.</margin> Wherever mercy and truth prevail, there is everything pleasing to God; for the one...

<summary>This page contains a collection of ascetic maxims (49-67) emphasizing the balance between physical discipline—such as fasting and silence—and the psychological state of the monk. It notably discusses the body as a fluctuating entity that must be treated alternately as an enemy, friend, or patient.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Gnomic Anthology" of Elias the Presbyter. The numbering in the margin transitions from the 60s to the 80s, continuing his structured advice on the purification of the soul, the nature of the "passions," and the practice of prayer.</meta>

# GNOMIC ANTHOLOGY

... judges no one without mercy; while the other shows love for humanity in nothing except through truth.

<margin>68.</margin> By mixing simplicity with <term>self-control</term> <note>original: ἐγκράτειαν (enkrateia) — the discipline of bodily and mental impulses, particularly regarding food and desire.</note>, you will come to encompass the blessedness of the world beyond.

<margin>69.</margin> You will certainly not see the <term>passions</term> <note>original: πάθη (pathe) — internal impulses or "sicknesses" of the soul like anger, greed, or lust that war against reason.</note> that make war against you unless you first leave the "earth" from which they were nourished unplowed.

<margin>70.</margin> Some hasten to purify only the matter of the body; others, that of the soul as well. For some have gained the strength to resist the memory of sin in its active expression; others have gained it against the "passion" itself; but those who have gained it against the "desire" are very few indeed.

<margin>71.</margin> The "evil matter" of the body is <term>passion</term> <note>original: ἐμπάθεια (empatheia) — a state of being dominated by worldly feelings.</note>; that of the soul is indulgence; that of the mind is <term>attachment</term> <note>original: προσπάθεια (prospatheia) — a "leaning toward" or mental clinginess to created things.</note>. The first is accused by the sense of touch; the second, by the rest of the senses; and the last, by a contrary disposition of the heart.

<margin>72.</margin> The indulgent person is close to being passionate; the attached person is close to being indulgent; but the <term>dispassionate</term> <note>original: ἀπαθής (apathes) — one who has reached "apatheia," a state of spiritual freedom where the passions no longer disturb the soul’s peace.</note> person is far from both.

<margin>73.</margin> A "passionate" person is one who has the sinful part of their reasoning acting with violence, even if for a time they do not sin outwardly. An "indulgent" person is one who has the activity of sin within their reasoning, even if they suffer internally. An "attached" person is one who leans more toward freedom or slavery regarding "middle things" <note>original: μέσων (meson) — things that are morally neutral in themselves, like wealth or health, which can be used for good or evil.</note>. And a "dispassionate" person would be one who is ignorant of the very difference between all these things.

<margin>74.</margin> Passion is destroyed from the soul through fasting and prayer; indulgence through vigils and silence; and attachment through stillness <note>original: ἡσυχίας (hesychias) — often referring to "Hesychasm," the practice of inner silence and focused prayer.</note> and attention. Dispassion, however, is established by the remembrance of God.

<margin>75.</margin> From the lips of dispassion, like honeycombs of honey, words of eternal life drip forth. Who then might be deemed worthy to touch their own lips to hers, to dwell between her breasts, and to partake of the sweet fragrance of her garments? That is, to be delighted by the laws of the virtues, which, it is said, are "above all the spices" of sensory perception.

<margin>76.</margin> Many, perhaps, are stripped of the garment of <term>self-love</term> <note>original: φιλαυτίας (philautias) — regarded by many Greek fathers as the root of all sin.</note>; but few are stripped of the love of the world. As for the garment of vainglory, which is called the "last garment," you will find only the dispassionate to be stripped of it.

<margin>77.</margin> Every soul will be stripped of the visible body; but only the soul that has enjoyed few pleasures here will be stripped of the "body of sin."

<column-break/>

<margin>78.</margin> All will appear as "dead" to those who are living; but only those who have hated sin from their very disposition will truly "die to sin."

<margin>79.</margin> Who might see themselves naked of sin before the common death of the body? And who is the one who has known themselves, and what their own nature is like, before that future stripping?

->A soul wounded by bridal love,<-
->Prayer knows how to join to the Bridegroom.<-

<margin>80.</margin> The rational soul lies on the border between the light of the senses and the light of the intellect. Through the former, it was permitted to perform the tasks of the body; through the latter, the tasks of the Spirit. But since the latter has been darkened for the soul, and the former has become clear through ancient habit, the soul cannot gaze fully at divine things unless it resides entirely with the intellect in prayer. It is necessary, then, for the soul to be in the "no-man's-land" between darkness and light, turning about according to its relation to the one and its imagination of the other.

<margin>81.</margin> A passionate mind cannot enter inside the "narrow gate" of prayer before it leaves behind the care of worldly relations; it will spend its time in pain, busying itself only around the outer curtains of that gate.

<margin>82.</margin> Let prayer remain with the mind like a sunbeam in the sun. Without it, the cares of the senses, like certain waterless clouds flying about, bar the mind from its own proper brilliance.

<margin>83.</margin> The power of prayer is a voluntary hunger for food; and the power of hunger is to neither hear nor see anything of worldly things unless it is an absolute necessity. He who does not take care for these things has not made the building of fasting firm, and he has caused the building of prayer to collapse upon itself.

<margin>84.</margin> Unless the mind becomes uncluttered from all things of the senses, it cannot be carried upward and recognize its own proper dignity.

<margin>85.</margin> Fasting is a symbol of the day because it is manifest; prayer is a symbol of the night because it is unseen. He who pursues each of these in its proper place will arrive at the city of his goal, where "pain, sorrow, and sighing have fled away." <note>A quote from the Orthodox funeral service and Isaiah 35:10.</note>

<margin>86.</margin> Spiritual labor is naturally constituted even without laborious physical work. Blessed, therefore, is he who [chooses] the better [labor] than the material...

<summary>This page explores the psychological and spiritual nuances of the "passions"—attachment, indulgence, and self-love—and provides a hierarchy of ascetic practices (fasting, silence, and prayer) to overcome them. It concludes by emphasizing prayer as the "narrow gate" that requires a mind stripped of sensory distractions to reach divine light.</summary>
<keywords>passions, dispassion, apatheia, fasting, prayer, hesychia, self-love, vainglory, the mind, spiritual labor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Gnomic Anthology" of Elias the Presbyter, picking up from the end of the previous discussion on spiritual labor and the hidden life. The numbering continues from 87 to 105, focusing heavily on the theology and practice of prayer (euchē).</meta>

# BY ELIAS THE PRESBYTER

...having considered it an immaterial labor, for through it he fulfilled the lack of work, living the hidden life of prayer, and manifest to God.

<margin>87.</margin> The divine Apostle exhorts us to endure in faith, to rejoice in hope, and to persevere in prayer, so that the beauty of joy remains with us. If this is so, then one who does not endure is unfaithful; and one who does not rejoice lacks hope, for they cast away prayer—the cause of joy—by not persevering in it.

<margin>88.</margin> If the <term>mind</term> <note>original: νοῦς (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul, often described as the "eye of the heart" or the intellect that perceives God.</note>, having been involved from the start with worldly thoughts, acquired such a friendship with them, how much more intimacy would it have in constant prayer? For in whatever things the mind lingers, in those it is also accustomed to expand.

<margin>89.</margin> Just as the mind, long ago separated from its own dwelling, forgot the brilliance of that place, so it must again, becoming forgetful of things here, run back to that brilliance through prayer.

<margin>90.</margin> Like an infant toward the cold breasts of a mother, the mind will be found toward a prayer that is unable to comfort it; but toward a prayer that is different, it is like a child falling asleep with pleasure in her arms.

<margin>91.</margin> There, he says—clearly in the mournful bed of the virtuous life, according to the Song of Songs—the bride-prayer might also say to her lover: "I will give my breasts to you, if you are wholly dedicated to me." <note>A mystical interpretation of the Song of Songs 7:12, where the act of prayer is personified as the Bride seeking union with the Divine.</note>

<margin>92.</margin> One who has not renounced all material things cannot have friendship with prayer.

<margin>93.</margin> Except for life and breath, be outside of all other things during prayer, if you wish to be alone with the mind.

<margin>94.</margin> The evidence of a God-loving mind is <term>single-thoughted prayer</term> <note>original: εὐχὴ μονόλογιστος (euchē monologistos) — prayer consisting of a single thought or phrase, used to focus the mind and prevent it from wandering.</note>, a timely word from a prudent thought, and a uniform "taste" of the free senses. In these three, the health of the soul's faculties is recognized.

<margin>95.</margin> The nature of the one who prays must be well-smoothed and softened like that of children, so that, according to their nature, his own nature may easily receive the unfolding that is established through prayer; therefore, let him who loves to be joined to it not be negligent.

<margin>96.</margin> Not everyone has the same goal in prayer; one has this goal, another has that. One 

<column-break/>

prays, if possible, for his heart to be always with the prayer; another, to transcend the prayer itself; another, so as not to be cut off by distracting thoughts during prayer. But everyone prays either to be preserved in good things or not to be carried away by evils.

<margin>97.</margin> If no one comes away from prayer without humility (for the one praying is truly crushed in humility), then the one who is arrogant on the outside does not actually pray in humility.

<margin>98.</margin> Looking at the widow who moved the cruel judge to justice, the one who prays will never grow weary because of the delay of the "good promises." <note>A reference to the Parable of the Unjust Judge in Luke 18:1-8, encouraging persistence in prayer.</note>

<margin>99.</margin> Prayer will not remain with you if you linger on things reasoned within or spoken without; but that same prayer will be seen returning to the one who cuts away the majority of distractions for its sake.

<margin>100.</margin> If the words of prayer do not penetrate the "flanks" of the soul, tears will not be permitted to wash around the cheeks of the face.

<margin>101.</margin> Sheaves arise for a farmer not merely by the sight of seeds thrown into the earth. For a monk, tears will well up not without labor for the one who pursues the words of prayer.

<margin>102.</margin> The key to the kingdom of heaven is prayer. The one who holds it as they should sees the good things stored therein for its friends; but the one who has not gained confidence in prayer only looks around at complaints.

<margin>103.</margin> The mind cannot speak with confidence to God during prayer, saying, "You have broken my bonds; I will offer to You a sacrifice of praise," <note>original: Διέῤῥηξας τοὺς δεσμούς μου... (Psalm 116:16-17)</note> unless the stumbling caused by cowardice, sloth, excessive sleep, and gluttony is broken off by a desire for better things.

<margin>104.</margin> He who wanders in thought during prayer stands outside the "first veil." He who accomplishes it with a single thought enters within. But only he has peered into the "Holy of Holies" who, with the peace of natural thoughts, contemplates those things surpassing all understanding, and is deemed worthy of a <term>theophany</term> <note>original: θεοφανείας (theophaneia) — a manifestation or direct appearance of God to the soul.</note> from there.

<margin>105.</margin> Whenever the soul, having found rest from external things, is joined to prayer, then like a flame surrounding it, prayer makes the soul into a fired substance, just as fire does to iron. The soul remains the same, yet it is not...

<summary>This page presents a series of aphorisms on the spiritual technology of prayer, describing it as a discipline that requires the renunciation of material attachments to achieve a "single-thoughted" state of union with God. It concludes with a powerful metaphor of the soul being transformed like iron in a forge when it enters the highest stages of contemplative prayer.</summary>
<keywords>prayer, Nous, single-thoughted prayer, theophany, humility, asceticism, Song of Songs, spiritual transformation</keywords>

# GNOMIC ANTHOLOGY

...and yet it remains untouched; for not even red-hot iron is affected by external touches <note>The author is likely comparing the soul's inner state to iron in a forge—transformed by divine fire but no longer susceptible to the "touch" of worldly distractions.</note>.
<margin>106.</margin> Blessed is the one who, in this life, is deemed worthy to be seen in this way—beholding his own statue, clay by nature, become fiery by grace.
<margin>107.</margin> For those being introduced to the spiritual life, the law of prayer lies upon them like a heavy master. But for those who have made progress, it is like love, driving the hungry soul toward a lavish feast.
<margin>108.</margin> For those who well pursue the **practical life**, sometimes prayer is like a cloud casting a shadow, barring the burning <term>reasonings</term> <note>original: λογισμούς (logismoi) — intrusive or passionate thoughts that "burn" the soul's peace.</note> from them; at other times, sprinkling these thoughts with drops like tears, it reveals spiritual contemplations.

<column-break/>

<margin>109.</margin> The sweet seasoning of a harp being struck by someone from without will be found; but the soul—unless the mystical address in the Spirit sounds within it during prayer—is not naturally inclined to become <term>compunctious</term> <note>original: εὐκατάνυκτος (eukatanuktos) — a state of spiritual "piercing" or tender sorrow and devotion.</note>. For the saying, "we do not know what we should pray for as we ought" <note>A reference to Romans 8:26.</note> and the rest, leads the one who prays into this very state.

## GNOSTIC CHAPTERS

-> THE MIND IS ENLIGHTENED BY GNOSTIC CONTEMPLATION, <-
-> RAISED TO THE HEIGHT, ENCOUNTERING THE FOUR LOGOI. <-
-> BUT IT IS DARKENED AGAIN, ROLLED INTO PASSION. <-

<margin>1.</margin> **I**t is necessary for the <term>gnostic</term> <note>original: γνωστικόν (gnostikon) — here meaning a person of spiritual knowledge, an advanced practitioner of the contemplative life.</note> to know when his <term>mind</term> <note>original: νοῦς (nous) — the highest faculty of the human soul, the "intellect" or "eye of the heart."</note> is in the region of <term>concepts</term> <note>original: νοημάτων (noēmata) — pure spiritual insights or thoughts of divine things.</note>, and when it is in the region of reasonings, and when it is in the region of sense-perception. And in this last state, he must know if he is found in things that are timely, or rather in things that are untimely.
<margin>2.</margin> When the mind is not engaged in concepts, it is certainly in reasonings. When it is in reasonings, it is not in concepts. But when it enters into sense-perception, it is with all of them together.
<margin>3.</margin> Through the concept, the mind passes toward <term>intelligible things</term> <note>original: νοητά (noēta) — spiritual realities that can only be perceived by the intellect, not the physical eyes.</note>; through reasoning, the reason (*logos*) passes toward logical things; and toward practical things, sense-perception passes through the imagination.
<margin>4.</margin> When the mind is gathered into itself, it contemplates nothing of what belongs to sense-perception, nor what belongs to reasoning. Instead, it sees "naked minds" and divine rays pouring forth peace and joy.
<margin>5.</margin> The mind of a thing is one thing, the mind itself is another, and the object brought under sense-perception is yet another. One is substance, another is an accident, and the third is either the difference of the subject.
<margin>6.</margin> Opening many paths, the mind shows itself to be insatiable. But when gathered into the single path

<column-break/>

of prayer, before reaching perfection, it appears constrained, begging the one who shares in it to be released back to the things from which it came <note>This describes the difficulty of focusing the mind in deep prayer; it feels "trapped" by the silence and longs for the distraction of its old habits.</note>.
<margin>7.</margin> The mind that has been led from above will not run back there again unless it achieves a perfect contempt for things below through leisure concerning divine things.
<margin>8.</margin> If you are not able to make your soul stay alone with only the reasonings concerning itself, at least force your body to be solitary, thinking always of the wretchedness surrounding it. For thus in time, by the mercy of God, you will be able to run back to the first dignity of your high birth <note>Referring to the "noble" state of the soul before it became enslaved to the passions.</note>.
<margin>9.</margin> The practical man is able to subject the mind easily to prayer, but the theoretical man subjects prayer to the mind. The former withdraws sense-perception from visible forms; the latter transfers the soul to the <term>logoi</term> <note>original: λόγους (logoi) — the inner "reasons" or divine principles underlying created things.</note> hidden within those forms. And while the one persuades the mind to ignore the reasons of bodies, the other understands the reasons of bodiless things. And bodiless things are the "reasons" of bodies, their qualities, and their substances.
<margin>10.</margin> When you [cut off] your mind from the [nature] of bodies...

# ELIAS THE PRESBYTER

...and when you free yourself from the indulgence of both wealth and food, then whatever gift you may offer will be considered pure by God. In return, it will be granted to you that the eyes of your heart be opened, so that you may clearly meditate on the words of God written within it. These words will be accounted as sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to your spiritual throat, because of the sweetness they pour forth.

<margin>11.</margin> You will not be able to make the mind superior to the desire for bodies, wealth, and unnecessary foods, unless you lead it into the "pure land of the righteous." In that place, the memory of death and the memory of God well up and wash away every towering structure of desire from the earthly heart.

<margin>12.</margin> Nothing is more fearsome than the thought of death, and nothing more wonderful than the memory of God. For the former brings about a <term>salutary sorrow</term> <note>original: λύπης σωτηριώδους — a "godly sorrow" that leads to repentance rather than despair.</note>, while the latter bestows gladness. "I remembered God," says the Prophet, "and I was glad." <note>A reference to Psalm 77:3 (76:4 in the Septuagint).</note> And the wise man says: "In all your works remember your last end, and you shall never sin." <note>A reference to Sirach 7:36.</note> It is impossible for anyone to take hold of the second state (gladness) without first experiencing the bitterness of the first (the thought of death).

<margin>13.</margin> Until the mind sees the glory of God with an "unveiled face," the soul cannot truly feel and say, "I will exult in the Lord; I will delight in His salvation." For the veil of <term>self-love</term> <note>original: φιλαυτίας (philautia) — often considered the "root of all passions" in Eastern Christian asceticism.</note> lies over its heart, preventing the "foundations of the world" from being revealed to it—which are the inner meanings of created things. This veil is not removed from the soul without both voluntary labors and involuntary trials.

<margin>14.</margin> It is not immediately after the flight from Egypt (which represents active sin), nor even after crossing the sea (the state of being a slave to habits), but after dwelling in the desert—situated between the outward acts of vice and the inner movements of malice—that the leader of the people <note>An allegorical reference to the mind leading the soul's faculties, just as Moses led Israel.</note> can spy out the "Land of Promise," which is <term>dispassion</term> <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia) — a state of being "un-passioned" or having mastery over one's impulses, rather than being cold or unfeeling.</note>. He does this by sending out his power of observation and spiritual vision.

<margin>15.</margin> Those sitting in the desert—that is, in a state where the passions are inactive—possess the goods of that blessed land by hearing alone. Those who have spied out its wonders have attained a "bare insight" into the 

<column-break/>

contemplation of visible things. But those deemed worthy to enter it have been filled, with their whole perception, by that which flows from it like "milk and honey"—I mean the inner meanings of the first and second <term>contemplations</term> <note>original: θεωρίας (theoria) — the spiritual "vision" or understanding of God's presence in nature and in His own nature.</note>.

<margin>16.</margin> One who still experiences the natural movements of the flesh has not yet been "crucified with Christ"; nor has one who is still dragged along by the imaginations of the soul been "buried" with Him. How then can such a person "rise with Him" to live in "newness of life"? <note>References to Romans 6:4-6.</note>

<margin>17.</margin> Since there are three virtues that encompass the soul—fasting, prayer, and silence—it is necessary that the one who finishes prayer should rest in a certain "natural contemplation"; the one who finishes silence should transition to "moral discourse"; and the one who fasts should move to a second, "favored" kind of food. <note>The author suggests that spiritual disciplines should transition into higher forms of thought rather than simply returning to mundane habits.</note>

<margin>18.</margin> As long as the mind exists in divine things, it preserves the "likeness" of God, being found good and compassionate. But when it enters into things of the senses, if it descends at the right time and in a proper way—giving and receiving experience—it returns to itself healthy once more. However, if it descends out of season or without need, it will be found like a reckless general, losing much of his power while in the thick of the fight.

<margin>19.</margin> The "Paradise of Dispassion" hidden within us is an image of the future Paradise that will receive the righteous. However, not all will be excluded from that future Paradise who were unable to enter this inner one.

<margin>20.</margin> The physical sun sends its rays from without into a closed house. But the spiritual Sun will not touch with His sweet rays the soul that expects Him but does not keep its senses closed off from visible things.

<margin>21.</margin> A <term>Gnostic</term> <note>original: Γνωστικός (Gnostikos) — in this context, not the ancient heretic, but the "person of spiritual knowledge" who has advanced in contemplation.</note> is one who manages his descents into worldly affairs with magnificence, but the ascents of his soul with humility.

<margin>22.</margin> A bee, wandering through meadows, gathers there the materials for its honey. A soul, wandering through the various "ages" <note>original: αἰῶνας (aionas) — refers to the various stages of God's providence throughout time and eternity.</note>, draws from them a sweetness into its intellect.

<margin>23.</margin> Just as the deer that has eaten snakes <note>Based on a medieval folk belief that deer ate snakes and then sought water to neutralize the venom.</note> runs to the springs of water to quench the poison, so the soul wounded by divine arrows feels an unceasing love for the One who wounded it.

<margin>24.</margin> Bare thoughts rush upon the "monadic" life (the solitary life), but "added reflections" rush upon the "dyadic" life (life in the world); to the...
