# ANTHOLOGION GNOMIKON
<note>original: ΑΝΘΟΛΟΓΙΟΝ ΓΝΩΜΙΚΟΝ — A collection of wise sayings or maxims, often compiled for the moral and spiritual instruction of monks.</note>

...to the multifaceted soul, distracting <term>thoughts</term> <note>original: λογισμοὶ (logismoi) — in ascetic tradition, these are not just random thoughts, but persistent suggestions or provocations that can lead the soul toward virtue or vice.</note> are driven away; but bare minds, stripped of bodies, approaching it, reveal the reasons concerning providence and judgment, appearing to it like someone uncovering the foundations of the earth.

<margin>25.</margin>
In the "dual life" <note>likely referring to the current earthly life where divisions exist.</note>, male and female are not meant to be seen simply as they are; for this will be found in the "monadic" or unified life. In that state, the difference between male and female—because of the "likeness" <note>A reference to being made in the image and likeness of God.</note>—will not be known in Christ Jesus. <note>A paraphrase of Galatians 3:28: "There is neither male nor female... for you are all one in Christ Jesus."</note>

<margin>26.</margin>
Thoughts belong neither to the irrational part of the soul (for there is no "thought" in unreasoning animals) nor to the intellectual part (since they are not in the Angels). Being the offspring of the rational faculty, and using <term>imagination</term> <note>original: φαντασίᾳ (phantasia) — the faculty that creates mental images.</note> as a ladder, they ascend to the mind from the senses, reporting the things of the senses to it; and they descend to the senses from the mind, suggesting the mind's concerns to them.

<margin>27.</margin>
Like people being pulled up from the depths and trying to catch hold of someone for help, so evil thoughts will be found when vice is in danger of sinking, as if in a shipwreck, amidst a flood of tears.

<margin>28.</margin>
Depending on the underlying quality of the soul, the thoughts that gather around it act either as pirates to sink it or as rowers to help it in its danger. Some drag the ship toward a sea of improper thoughts, while others, choosing the shore, run the ship aground toward peaceful coasts.

<margin>29.</margin>
The seventh thought is that of <term>vainglory</term> <note>original: κενοδοξία (kenodoxia).</note>. The soul that desires to cast it off as the last one will not be able to put on the eighth thought after them if it does not first strip off those that came before it. This eighth state the Divine Apostle knows how to call a "heavenly dwelling." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 5:2.</note> It can be put on through groans by those who, through these very groans, strip themselves of material things.

<margin>30.</margin>
Angelic thoughts are naturally present in perfect prayer; spiritual thoughts in "middle" prayer; and "natural" thoughts <note>original: φυσιολογικοί (physiologikoi) — thoughts concerning the nature of created things.</note> in introductory prayer.

<margin>31.</margin>
Just as the nobility of the grain is shown through the ear, so the purity of <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: θεωρίας (theoria) — the spiritual "vision" or deep understanding of God and creation.</note> is usually revealed through prayer. One person possesses the surrounding stalks like spears to ward off "seed-picking birds" <note>likely representing distracting or demonic thoughts.</note>, while the other possesses thoughts that "philosophize" during temptations in order to destroy them.

<margin>32.</margin>
The visible aspects of the soul through <term>practice</term> <note>original: πρᾶξιν (praxin) — the active struggle for virtue.</note> are like the "silvered wings of a dove." But the intelligible aspects—I mean the "back" of the soul—through contemplation, are established as if in the "yellowness of gold." <note>A reference to Psalm 68:13 (67:14 in the Septuagint): "the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold." In this tradition, silver represents active virtue and gold represents higher spiritual knowledge.</note> For the soul that has not been beautified cannot fly and rest where the dwelling of all those who rejoice is located.

<column-break/>

## BY THE SAME AUTHOR: ON PRACTICE AND CONTEMPLATION.

->A meadow here, full of fruits.<-
->Of spiritual practice and contemplation.<-

<margin>33.</margin>
The ancients were commanded of old to offer the firstfruits of the threshing floor and the winepress in the Temple. But now we must offer to God the firstfruits of "practice"—namely, self-control and truth—and of "contemplative virtue"—namely, love and prayer. Through the former, one cuts off the impulses of irrational desire and anger. Through the latter, one cuts off empty notions and the plots of one's neighbor.

<margin>34.</margin>
The beginning of practice is self-control and truth. Its middle is temperance and humility. Its end is the peace of thoughts and the sanctification of the body.

<margin>35.</margin>
"Practice" is not simply being able to do good things, but doing them *as they ought to be done*. The doer must bring along the right time and the right measure to the actions.

<margin>36.</margin>
"Contemplation" is not just seeing bodies as they are, but also perceiving their inner "reasons" <note>original: λόγους (logous) — the divine blueprints or purposes behind created things.</note> and what they look toward.

<margin>37.</margin>
There is no safe practice without contemplation, nor is there true contemplation without practice. For practice must be guided by reason, and contemplation must be put into action. Thus, through the former, vice is found to be powerless, and through the latter, virtue is made powerful in the good favor of kindness.

<margin>38.</margin>
The limit of "practical" things is the death of the passions. The end of "gnostic" (knowing) things is the contemplation of the virtues.

<margin>39.</margin>
As matter is to form, so practice is to contemplation; and as the eye is to the face, so contemplation will be seen in relation to practice.

<margin>40.</margin>
In the stadium of practical virtue, many run. But only one receives the prize: the one who desires to reach the end of practice through contemplation.

<margin>41.</margin>
The "practical" man drinks the drink of <term>compunction</term> <note>original: Κατανύξεως (katanyxeos) — a state of "godly sorrow" or piercing of the heart that leads to repentance.</note> during prayer; but the "contemplative" man is intoxicated by the best cup. The former, in those things according to nature...

Elias uses vivid metaphors—shipwrecks, dove wings, and threshing floors—to describe how a soul achieves peace and unity in Christ.</summary>

# OF ELIAS THE PRESBYTER
<note>Elias the Presbyter (likely Elias Ekdikos, c. 11th-12th century) was a prominent writer in the Philokalia tradition. His "Gnostic Chapters" are maxims intended to guide the monk from the active life of discipline to the contemplative life of mystical union.</note>

...philosophizing, while the other is even ignorant of himself while praying.

<margin>42.</margin>
The <term>practical man</term> <note>original: πρακτικὸς (praktikos) — one who focuses on "praxis," the active discipline of the body and soul to overcome passions and acquire virtues.</note> is not permitted to persist for long in spiritual <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: θεωρίαν (theorian) — "theoria," the direct spiritual "seeing" or vision of divine truths.</note>, for he is found to be like a guest in another’s house, quickly departing from it.

<margin>43.</margin>
The practical ones enter into the gates of the commandments of God through prayer, while the contemplative ones enter the courts of the virtues with hymns. The former give thanks because they have been released from their bonds; the latter because they have also taken captive those who were at war with them.

<margin>44.</margin>
The strength of one’s practice must be found to match the strength of one’s contemplation. Otherwise, like a ship carrying sails that do not fit, it may either suffer danger from the violence of the winds because the sails are too large, or suffer a loss of the spirit's breeze because they are too small for the vessel.

<margin>45.</margin>
Consider the pious <term>thoughts</term> <note>original: λογισμούς (logismous) — specific patterns of thought or mental suggestions.</note> as the oarsmen of the spiritual ship. The oars are the vital powers of the soul: anger and desire, will and choice. The practical man always has need of these, but the contemplative man does not. For at the time of prayer, having said "farewell" to all things, he seats himself at the rudders of discernment and stays awake through the whole night of contemplation, offering praises to the Upholder of all. And perhaps, taking up some <term>erotic melody</term> <note>original: μέλος ἐρωτικὸν — here "erotic" refers to *eros* in the mystical sense: an intense, yearning love for God.</note>, he sings to his own soul, observing the surges and rushing movements of the salty sea <note>A metaphor for the turbulent world or the passions.</note>, struck with awe by the divine judgments and decrees.

<margin>46.</margin>
He who holds the middle ground between practice and contemplation makes his voyage neither entirely with oars like sailors, nor entirely with spiritual sails, but works through both for the sake of a prosperous journey. He gladly bears the labors of practice because of the measure of contemplation he possesses, and he bears the words of incomplete contemplation because he is being helped by his practice.

<margin>47.</margin>
The contemplative man, having nature running alongside his will, makes the voyage effortlessly like a current; but the practical man, finding his disposition opposed to his choice, undergoes a great storm of thoughts, and risks coming nearly to despair because of the weight.

<margin>48.</margin>
Neither is a field that has not been well-worked accustomed to giving back seed to the sower in abundance and purity, 

<column-break/>

nor will the one pursuing the practical life see the fruit of prayer in abundance and purity unless he pursues it diligently and without ostentation.

<margin>49.</margin>
A mind worn by the constant footprints of prayer is like ground frequently trodden upon; for the latter will be smooth and the former straight for receiving—the ground receiving tender feet, and the mind receiving pure prayers.

<margin>50.</margin>
In matters of material things, the mind has <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: λογισμόν — here used as the faculty of discursive, logical thinking.</note> as a helper; but in immaterial things, unless the mind dismisses reasoning, it will have it like a thorn that buffets it.

<margin>51.</margin>
The practical man has a veil over his heart during prayer—the knowledge of sensible things—which cannot be lifted because of his attachment to them; but only the contemplative man, because of his detachment, is able to see "in part" the glory of God with an "unveiled face." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18 and 13:12.</note>

<margin>52.</margin>
Prayer combined with spiritual contemplation is the "Promised Land"; in which the knowledge of the principles of God’s providence and judgment flows like milk and honey. Prayer with a degree of "natural" contemplation is "Egypt"; in which a memory of the coarser desires arises in those who pray. But "simple" prayer is the "Manna" in the desert; which, because of its uniformity, shuts out the goods promised through desire for the impatient, but for those who endure such a narrow diet, it provides a better and lasting taste.

<margin>53.</margin>
Practice with contemplation shall be considered as a body with a guiding spirit; but without contemplation, it shall be considered as flesh with a spirit of mere impulse.

<margin>54.</margin>
Of the rational soul, the "court" is the senses, the "temple" is the intellect, and the "high priest" is the mind. In the court stands the mind that is cut off by untimely thoughts; in the temple, the one occupied by timely thoughts; but he who is deemed worthy to enter the divine sanctuary is occupied by neither of these.

<margin>55.</margin>
Lamentation and song and "woe" are found in the house of the practical soul because of its labor, but the voice of exultation and confession is heard in the house of the contemplative soul because of its knowledge.

<margin>56.</margin>
The practical man desires to "depart" <note>To die/be released from the body.</note> because of his labors and to be with Christ, but the contemplative man is more willing to remain in the flesh, both because of the joy he receives from prayer and because of the benefit that comes to his neighbor.

It emphasizes that while the practical life involves struggle and labor, contemplation brings a joyous, effortless intimacy with God.</summary>

-> ### ANTHOLOGY OF MAXIMS <-

<margin>57.</margin> In the case of more rational souls, <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: θεωρία (theoria) — the spiritual "vision" or insight into divine things.</note> precedes <term>practice</term> <note>original: πράξεως (praxeos) — "praxis," the active work of virtue and self-discipline.</note>; but for those who are more unrefined, practice precedes contemplation. Both, however, end in a single good goal, though this goal will be seen more quickly by those for whom contemplation leads the way for practice.

<margin>58.</margin> Paradise is the contemplation of intelligible things. In this paradise, the man of <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: γνωστικός (gnostikos) — an advanced practitioner who has attained spiritual insight.</note> enters through prayer as if into his own home. The <term>practical man</term>, however, will be seen as a passer-by; he desires to peek inside, but is not permitted to do so because the "fence" of his spiritual maturity has been raised too high.

<margin>59.</margin> Bodily passions are like wild beasts, while the passions of the soul are like birds. The practical man walls off the beasts from the rational vineyard, but he cannot yet do the same for the birds unless he enters into spiritual contemplation—no matter how much effort he puts into guarding the inner reaches.

<margin>60.</margin> No one can become a practical man, excelling in moral beauty, unless he himself—like the Patriarch Abraham—goes out from his own land (which is the natural law) and from his kindred (which is the life he shared with his peers). For in this way, he will receive as a seal the removal of general pleasure, through which the "veil" covering him from birth—which does not allow perfect freedom to be granted <unclear>to her</unclear>—is stripped away.

<margin>61.</margin> Just as a colt in springtime cannot bear to stay inside the manger and eat its fodder, so too a mind newly initiated into spiritual life cannot endure for long the <unclear>restriction</unclear> of prayer. Instead, it prefers to go out into the breadth of "natural contemplation," which is found through the chanting of psalms and reading.

<margin>62.</margin> Practice keeps its loins girded by fasting and vigils, which are its vital powers; meanwhile, the virtue of contemplation sets up "burning lamps" through silence and prayer, which are its powers of knowledge. To the former, the mind acts as a schoolmaster; to the latter, the "internal word" acts as a friend of the bridegroom.

<margin>63.</margin> An incomplete <term>mind</term> <note>original: Νοῦς (Nous) — the "eye of the soul" or the highest faculty of the human person.</note> is not permitted to enter the fruitful vineyard of prayer. Rather, as a poor man seeking gleanings, it can only with difficulty reach the bare echoes of the psalms.

<margin>64.</margin> Just as not everyone who comes to speak with a King

<column-break/>

is able to dine with him, so too those who reach the success of prayer will not necessarily be seen in the contemplation that belongs to it.

<margin>65.</margin> The bridle of anger is timely silence; the bridle of irrational desire is moderate eating; and the bridle of an unstable <term>thought</term> <note>original: λογισμοῦ (logismou) — specifically a "distracting" or "tempting" thought.</note> is "single-worded" prayer.

<margin>66.</margin> Both the one who dives into the deep sea for a physical pearl and the one who dives into the depth of knowledge for an "intelligible" pearl will fail to find what they seek unless they strip—the former of his clothes, the latter of his sensory perceptions.

<margin>67.</margin> The mind that comes to be inside its own understanding during prayer will be found like a bridegroom talking with a bride in the bridal chamber. But the one who is not permitted to enter stands outside, groaning and crying out: "Who will lead me into the fortified city? Or who will guide me so that I do not look upon vanities and false madness while I pray?"

<margin>68.</margin> Just as food is judged by the throat to be tasteless without salt, so too the prayer that passes through the mind will be judged to be without value if it lacks <term>compunction</term> <note>original: κατανύξεως (katanyxeos) — a state of "pierced" heart or spiritual sorrow/tears.</note>.

<margin>69.</margin> The soul that is still "chasing after" prayer is like a woman in labor; but the soul that has "caught" it is like a woman who has given birth and is filled with joy because of the child.

<margin>70.</margin> Long ago, the Amorite dwelling on the mountain used to wound those who tried to pass through by force. Now, an "evil forgetfulness" chases those who try to ascend to the higher prayer of simplicity before they have achieved <term>purity</term> <note>original: ἁγνείας (agneias) — chastity or moral spotlessness.</note>.

<margin>71.</margin> Demons are by nature in great enmity with pure prayer. They are not terrified by a great number of psalms (as an army might terrify external enemies), but rather by the "harmony of three": the mind with the word, and the word with the sense.

<margin>72.</margin> Bare prayer appears like bread to those who pray, strengthening them; prayer with a degree of contemplation is like oil, making them fat; but "formless" prayer is like fragrant wine, by which those who drink greedily are caught up in ecstasy.

<margin>73.</margin> A wild donkey is said to mock the crowd of the city, and a "monokeros" <note>original: μονόκερως (monokerōs) — often translated as "unicorn" or "rhinoceros" in biblical contexts; a symbol of untamable strength.</note> cannot be bound by anyone. So too the mind that has mastered its natural state and conquered thoughts that are contrary to nature: it mocks the vanity of thoughts while praying, and by no one...

<summary>This page outlines the distinction between the "practical" and "contemplative" lives, using vivid metaphors such as the vineyard, the diver seeking pearls, and the bridechamber to describe the soul's progress toward pure prayer. It emphasizes that true spiritual vision requires a stripping away of sensory distractions and a harmony between the mind, word, and senses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Gnomic Anthology" (or "Gnostic Chapters") by Elias the Presbyter, likely from the Philokalia. It follows the previous discussion on the distinction between the "practical" life of moral discipline and the "contemplative" life of spiritual vision. This section focuses heavily on the transition from discursive thought to the stillness of pure prayer.</meta>

<page-num>386</page-num>
<header>ELIAS THE PRESBYTER</header>

<margin>74.</margin> ...is able to be mastered by the senses. 
A man who shakes a rod at dogs only makes them more fierce against himself; so too does the man who tries to force demons away without pure prayer. <note>original: "καθαρῶς ἐκβιαζόμενος εὔχεσθαι" — suggests that purely "forcing" the issue through willpower is less effective than the "force" of pure prayer.</note>

<margin>75.</margin> The spiritual athlete must contract his senses into a "singular" diet <note>original: μονοειδῆ συστέλλειν τροφήν — meaning a simple, uniform diet to avoid stimulating the passions.</note> and contract his mind into <term>single-phrase prayer</term> <note>original: μονολόγιστον προσευχήν (monologiston proseuchen) — the practice of repeating a short, single prayer (like the Jesus Prayer) to focus the mind.</note>. For having become unattached to the passions in this way, he will reach the state of being "caught up" to the Lord while praying.

<margin>76.</margin> Those who seek pleasure while praying—being still caught up in material things—have <term>thoughts</term> <note>original: λογισμοὺς (logismoi) — specifically intrusive or distracting thoughts.</note> like croaking frogs distracting them. Those who have moderated their passions have <term>contemplations</term> <note>original: θεωρίας (theorias) — spiritual visions or insights.</note> like nightingales delighting them, flitting from branch to branch—that is, moving from one spiritual insight to another. But for the dispassionate, there is silence and great stillness from all thoughts and concepts during prayer.

<margin>77.</margin> In ancient times, Miriam, the sister of Moses, took up the timbrel and led the women in songs of victory after seeing the fall of the enemy. Today, to celebrate the soul that has conquered the passions, a higher <term>Love</term> <note>original: ἀγάπη (agape)</note> is awakened in virtue; taking up the "lyre" of contemplation with a song, she never ceases to praise God in joy along with the powers surrounding her, celebrating the wealth of beauty won through her previous labors.

<margin>78.</margin> Whenever the words of the Psalms are poured into the heart of the one praying with constancy, then the "earth" (the soul) begins to bring forth fruit spontaneously like a good field: as roses, the contemplation of <term>incorporeal beings</term> <note>original: ἀσωμάτων — angels or spiritual realities.</note>; as lilies, the clear radiance of created bodies; and as violets, the various and difficult-to-behold "judgments" of God.

<margin>79.</margin> A flame bound to wood becomes a source of light. A soul released from matter is found to be a "God-bearer." The flame is naturally inclined to rise as far as its fuel allows, but the soul rises until it reaches the perfection of Divine Love.

<margin>80.</margin> The soul that has perfectly denied itself and has been totally extended toward prayer does not come back "down" whenever it wishes, for it finds itself above the created world. Rather, it returns when it seems right to Him who directs our affairs with weight and measure.

<margin>81.</margin> When <term>listlessness</term> <note>original: ἀκηδία (acedia) — the "noonday demon" of spiritual sloth or despondency.</note> is driven from the soul and wickedness is shaken out of the mind, then the mind becomes "naked" in its simplicity. Living 

<column-break/>

an artless life, stripped of every veil of shame, it sings a "new song" to God. It strikes the notes of a melody of thanksgiving in gladness, celebrating the "dedication festival" <note>original: ἐγκαίνια (enkainia) — a festival of renewal or dedication.</note> of the life to come.

<margin>82.</margin> When the praying soul begins to be energized by more divine things, then it too—like the Bride in the Song of Songs—calls out to those of like mind: "My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my heart was moved for him." <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 5:4.</note>

<margin>83.</margin> A soldier returning from war puts away the weight of his armor; so too does the man of action put away his thoughts when he enters into contemplation. For just as the soldier has no need of weapons except in battle, the contemplative has no need of discursive thoughts unless he is descending back to the level of the senses.

<margin>84.</margin> Those in the "active life" see bodies according to their position; those in the "contemplative life" see them according to their nature; but only the "men of knowledge" <note>original: γνωστικοί (gnostikoi) — those possessing deep spiritual insight.</note> see the <term>inner principles</term> <note>original: λόγους (logous) — the divine blueprints or "logoi" underlying all creation.</note> of both.

<margin>85.</margin> In the inner principles of bodies, incorporeal things are known. In the incorporeal, one finds the "Supra-essential Word" <note>original: λόγος ὁ ὑπερούσιος — the Logos/Christ who is beyond being.</note>, toward whom every diligent soul hastens to return.

<margin>86.</margin> The inner principles of incorporeal things are like "bones" covered by the flesh of sensory things. No one can see them who has not moved "outside" of their attachment to the senses.

<margin>87.</margin> A soldier lays down his weapons when leaving the war; a contemplative lays down his thoughts when returning to the Lord.

<margin>88.</margin> A general is dejected if he misses the spoils of war; a man of action is dejected if he misses spiritual contemplation during prayer.

<margin>89.</margin> A deer runs to physical springs of water when bitten by a beast; a soul wounded by the "sweet arrow" of prayer runs to the rays of the incorporeal.

<margin>90.</margin> Just as the physical eye cannot see the inner grain of wheat, the "active" mind cannot see its own nature unless the eye is stripped of its husk and the mind of the attachments that veil it.

<margin>91.</margin> Stars are hidden by the rising sun; thoughts fail when the mind returns to its own kingdom.

<margin>92.</margin> After the end of the active life, spiritual contemplations pour over the mind like sunbeams rising from the horizon...

Elias uses metaphors of soldiers, nature (flowers and deer), and the Song of Songs to illustrate how the soul eventually transcends discursive thought to encounter the divine Logoi.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Gnomic Anthology" (Gnostic Chapters) by Elias the Presbyter. It transitions from the previous discussion on the stillness of prayer into a beautiful, allegorical exploration of the soul as a bride seeking her divine bridegroom (God), drawing heavily on the imagery of the Song of Songs. <page-num>387</page-num>
<header>GNOMIC ANTHOLOGY</header>

...peeking over, they seem to strike him from the outside, even though they are of his own household, and they embrace him because of his purity.

<margin>403.</margin>
The **contemplative mind** <note>original: "νοῦς θεωρητικὸς" (nous theoretikos) — the aspect of the mind capable of direct spiritual vision of God.</note> is able to speak of such things when it descends from above, out of heaven, yielding to the necessities of nature. Just as the one who proclaims: "What is more wonderful than divine beauty? And what thought is more delightful than the majesty of God? What longing is so sharp and unbearable as that which is produced by God in a soul purified from all evil?" And from a disposition that says:
> **"I am wounded by love."** <note>A quote from Song of Songs 2:5, signifying the soul’s intense desire for God.</note>

<margin>404.</margin>
It belongs to such a person to say:
> **"My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall flame out,"** <note>Psalm 38:4 (LXX) / Psalm 39:3.</note>

This belongs to the one who does not grow weary of following after God through prayer, nor of a man desiring to behold Him.

<margin>405.</margin>
Let the **practical soul** <note>original: "ψυχὴ πρακτικὴ" (psyche praktike) — the soul currently engaged in the "active life" of moral struggle and the purging of the passions.</note> also speak, after putting away evils—as it says in the *Song of Songs*—when evil demons and thoughts try to force her back to look upon vanities and false madness:
> **"I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?"** <note>Song of Songs 5:3.</note>

<margin>406.</margin>
It is the daring of a God-loving soul to say to God:
> **"Tell me, O good shepherd, where do you pasture your sheep? And where do you rest your lambs at noon? Lest, following after them, I should become like one who wanders among the flocks of your companions."** <note>Song of Songs 1:7.</note>

<margin>407.</margin>
The practical soul, seeking to master the **word of prayer** <note>original: "εὐχῆς λόγον" (euches logon) — the inner rationale or consistent state of prayer.</note> and failing to do so, also cries out like the bride in the *Song of Songs*:
> **"On my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him. I called him, but he did not answer me. I will rise up now through more laborious prayer and go about the city, in the streets and in the marketplaces; I will seek him whom I love."** Perhaps He who is in everything and yet outside of everything will be found by me; I shall be satisfied when His glory appears to me.

<margin>409.</margin>
When the soul begins to be entirely made of tears from the joy of prayer, then she also speaks with boldness, as a bride to her own bridegroom, crying out:
> **"Let my beloved come down into his garden, and let him eat of my tears, as if they were choice fruits, this hard-won consolation."**

When the practical soul, from the magnitude

<column-break/>

and beauty of created things, begins to wonder at the Creator and to delight in the pleasure derived from them, she also cries out in amazement:
> **"How beautiful you have become, O bridegroom, the paradise of your Father! A flower of the child, and his cedar like the cedars of Lebanon. I desired to sit under his shadow, and his fruit was sweet in my throat."** <note>A paraphrase combining Song of Songs 2:3 and other imagery to describe Christ as the beautiful "fruit" of God.</note>

<margin>100.</margin>
If a king, receiving someone into his own chamber, is found to be so illustrious, so admired, and so full of every joy, how much more will the soul be who has received the **King of Kings** into herself after being purified? According to His unerring promise, such a soul ought to secure herself with great reverence, casting out everything that does not seem to lead to His rest, and bringing in everything that leads to His pleasure.

<margin>101.</margin>
A person who expects to be called by the king tomorrow—what else will be on his mind? Will it not be the study of words that happen to please him? A soul that keeps this in mind will not be found unprepared for the judgment from the other side.

<margin>102.</margin>
Blessed is the soul that expects its Lord to come **today**, considering the entire labor of the day as nothing—nor that of the night—because He is to appear immediately in the morning.

<margin>103.</margin>
God sees all people, but those who see God are those who **see nothing** while praying. <note>This refers to the "apophatic" tradition: the mind is so focused on the formless God that it lets go of all created images and sensory thoughts.</note> And as many as "see" God and are heard, do not actually "see" Him [as an object], but blessed is the one who believes he is seen by God; for his foot shall not be shaken while he remains in His favor.

<margin>104.</margin>
The good things of the Kingdom that is within us—which the eye that loves beauty has not seen, and the ear that loves honor has not heard, and which have not entered the heart that is empty of the **Holy Spirit**—are the pledges <note>original: "ἀρραβῶνες" (arrhabones) — a legal term for a down-payment or earnest money.</note> of the future goods to be given to the righteous in the coming Kingdom of God. And he who does not delight in these—which are the fruits of the Spirit—cannot come into the enjoyment of those future things.

<margin>105.</margin>
The thoughts of those in the "practical" life are like deer. For just as deer are sometimes high up in the mountains because of the fear of hunters, and sometimes down in the valleys because of their desire for what is in them, so are these thoughts. They cannot always be in **spiritual contemplation** because of their own lowliness, nor can they always be in...

<vocab>Gnomic Anthology, soul, God, prayer, King, Holy Spirit, spiritual contemplation, Song of Songs, thoughts</vocab>

<summary>This page uses the erotic and pastoral imagery of the Song of Songs to describe the mystical union between the soul and God. It emphasizes that the soul must be purified through "practical" discipline before it can achieve the "contemplative" vision of the King of Kings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Gnomic Anthology" of Elias the Presbyter, likely from a collection of the Philokalia. It transitions from the previous page's discussion on the "practical soul" and the "contemplative mind" into a series of numbered aphorisms regarding prayer, the nature of the mind (nous), and the struggle against passions. <page-num>388</page-num>
<header>ELIAS THE PRESBYTER</header>

...to nature, because it does not always pursue rest; however, among those who are contemplative, they become overlookers of earth-bound <note>original: "περιπεζίων" (peripeziōn) — literally "walking around on foot" or "pedestrian" contemplations.</note> contemplations.

<margin>106.</margin> Drops of dew intoxicate the furrows of the earth; but the dispositions of the soul in prayer are the moistening sighs sent up from the heart.

<margin>107.</margin> No one will be seen in the contemplation of the **Godhead** understood in the Trinity if they have not first risen above the material duality and its neighboring monad; nor will they become higher than this duality if they have not made their own **mind** <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) — the spiritual intellect or the highest faculty of the human soul.</note> monadic <note>original: "μοναδικὸν" — single, unified, or simple.</note> among things understood by the intellect.

<margin>108.</margin> It will not be found so difficult to block the path of a river so that it does not flow downward, as it is to check the rush of the mind so that it is not scattered among visible things, but rather is gathered toward things above and its own kin whenever the one who prays desires it—even if the former is according to nature, and the latter has been established as contrary to nature.

<margin>109.</margin> Those who are being purified, sending their **mind** beyond visible things, are filled with such awe and such joy that they can no longer contain any earthly thing, not even if all the things men fight for were to flow toward them.

<margin>110.</margin> The stated laws of nature alone are sufficient to be greatly admired; but when understood, they are found to be flowering meadows, as if from heavenly nectar, abounding with pure blossoms—the sweetness of the spiritual banquet.

<margin>111.</margin> Among the dewy flowers of the meadows, the bees surround the queen of the swarm; but in the soul that has attained unceasing **compunction** <note>original: "κατανύξει" (katanyxei) — a state of heart-felt sorrow and spiritual longing.</note>, the intellectual powers <note>original: "νοεραὶ δυνάμεις" — the higher faculties of the soul or perhaps angelic forces.</note> encircle her as their own, working together to achieve her desires.

<margin>112.</margin> In the visible world, man is seen as if he were another world; but in the world of the intellect, it is **reason** <note>original: "λογισμὸς" (logismos) — the discursive or rational faculty of thought.</note>. For while man is the herald of heaven, earth, and the things in between, reason is the interpreter of the mind, the senses, and the things concerning them; without which, both worlds would have been struck deaf.

<margin>113.</margin> A captive released after a long time does not travel with such joy as the mind, freed from attachment, travels toward heavenly things as toward its own home, with a leaping foot.

<margin>114.</margin> To the one who does not pray with attention, but is distracted, the psalm will be considered foreign <note>original: "βάρβαρος" (barbaros) — unintelligible or "barbarian."</note>; and he himself will be like a foreigner to the psalm, and both will be as if driven mad by demons.

<margin>115.</margin> It is not the same thing for those to whom the world has been **crucified**, and those who have been **crucified to the world** <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul in Galatians 6:14.</note>. For to the former, the nails are fasting and vigils; but to the latter, they are poverty and abasement.

<column-break/>

Without the second group, the labors of the first are useless.

<margin>116.</margin> No one is able to pray purely who is gripped by a passion for beauty or a passion for honor. For attachments concerning these things, and the thoughts of vanity that hold an affinity for them, become like ropes entwined around him; they drag down the mind—like a bound sparrow trying to fly away—at the time of prayer.

<margin>117.</margin> It is impossible for the mind to become peaceful at the time of prayer if it has not acquired beloved **self-control** <note>original: "ἐγκράτειαν" (enkrateian).</note> and **love**. For the former strives to destroy the enmity of the body against the soul, while the latter strives to destroy enmity toward one's neighbor for the sake of God; and from this, the peace that surpasses all understanding, taking up its residence, promises to make an abode with the one who has thus become peaceful.

<margin>118.</margin> It is necessary for the one striving to enter the Kingdom of God to abound in good things—his work of righteousness—both in acts of mercy through giving from one’s own lack, and in labors for the sake of peace, through the decree of patience in the Lord.

<margin>119.</margin> Neither the one who is deficient in virtue through negligence, nor the one who is excessive through conceit, will be found within the harbor of **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπάθειαν" (apatheian) — a state of freedom from the passions, a goal of the ascetic life.</note>; for neither has come to the enjoyment of the goods of righteousness, since they are found with a middle ground of deficiency and excess.

<margin>120.</margin> Just as the earth cannot make the farmer rich if it does not grant him many times the seed sown, but only provides the seed itself or some small addition; so too, what is achieved by the man of action cannot make him righteous, unless his zeal toward God is found to be greater than his own initial choice.

<margin>121.</margin> Not all who do not love their neighbor are able to hate him, nor can those who do not hate him love him. It is one thing to envy another's progress, and another not to be a firm support for his progress. But the level of extreme malice will be found to be not only feeling the sting of another's excellence, but also slandering his good deeds as if they were not such.

<meta>This page continues the "Gnomic Anthology" of Elias the Presbyter. It follows the previous discussion on the purification of the mind and moves into a detailed classification of the "passions" (spiritual and physical impulses) and the psychological stages of temptation. The numbering continues from the previous section.</meta>

<page-num>389</page-num>
<header>GNOMIC ANTHOLOGY</header>

<margin>162.</margin> Some passions <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē) — in this context, "passions" refers to disordered medicinal or psychological impulses rather than simple "feelings."</note> are of the body, and others are of the soul. Some are according to nature, and others are contrary to nature. A person who pushes away the former but takes no care for the latter is like a man who builds a high, thick fence against wild beasts, yet stands by happily as birds eat the truly magnificent grapes of his **rational vineyard.** <note>The "rational vineyard" is a common metaphor for the human soul or the intellect (nous), which should produce spiritual fruit.</note>

<margin>163.</margin> First, the soul enters into an **imagination** of evil; then into **desire**; then into **pleasure** or **distress**; then into **sensation**; and after this, into **touch**, whether visible or invisible. In all these stages, thoughts <note>original: "λογισμῶν" (logismōn) — technical term for "thought-provocations" or internal suggestions that lead to sin.</note> follow along—except for the very first movement. If that first movement is not accepted, every evil that follows it will be found powerless.

<margin>164.</margin> Those who are approaching **dispassion** <note>original: "ἀπαθείᾳ" (apatheia) — the state of being free from the control of the passions.</note> are shaken only by imaginations. Those with **moderate passions** <note>original: "μετριοπαθεῖς" (metriopatheis) — those who have balanced their emotions but are not yet fully free.</note> are shaken by desires. Those who misuse the things they need are caught in the sensation of evil and are distressed by it; but those who join themselves to it without distress are in the stage of "touch."

<margin>165.</margin> Pleasure is established in all the members of the body, but it does not appear to disturb them all in the same way. Rather, it affects some more in the **desiring** part of the soul, others in the **spirited** <note>original: "θυμικόν" (thymikon) — the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, or "heat."</note> part, and others in the **rational** part; this happens through gluttony, quick-temperedness, and wickedness—the cause of all unholy passions.

<margin>166.</margin> It is necessary for the senses to open like the gates of a city; but it is also necessary not to allow "nations" that desire war and cause strife to enter through that opening of necessary gates.

<margin>167.</margin> Pleasure is the mother of desire; quick-temperedness is the mother of anger; and wickedness becomes the mother of envy. He who does not struggle against the "rulers" <note>Referring to the primary or "root" passions.</note> cannot be at peace with those at the bottom. Nor can anyone enter the harbor of **moderation** if they pursue the commandments by force alone.

<margin>168.</margin> Those who strike back against the first "attacks" <note>original: "προσβολὰς" (prosbolas) — the initial moment a tempting thought hits the mind.</note> do not allow thoughts to enter the **rational vineyard** like wild beasts to cause ruin. Others "link up" with the thoughts but do not take pleasure in them; they simply allow them to enter, provided they touch nothing within. Still others converse with the passions through their thoughts with pleasure, yet do not come to a full "consent" of the will. These are like people who let a wild boar inside

<column-break/>

the field and past the fence, but do not allow it to gorge itself on the clusters of grapes in the vineyard. However, they soon find that the beast is stronger than their own power, and they often find themselves falling into a consent to the passions.

<margin>169.</margin> A person who still requires the care of the "fence" of self-control <note>original: "ἐγκράτειαν" (enkrateian).</note> has not yet reached **simplicity**. For it is said that the "perfect" person does not merely practice self-control, but rather it is the one who is still struggling who does so. Such a person is like someone who owns a vineyard or a plot of land that is not in the middle of many other vineyards, but off in a corner somewhere; for this reason, it requires much guarding and watchfulness. But for the one who has reached simplicity, the vineyard remains untouched from every side; just as the mere report of a king or some other terrifying ruler makes thieves and vagabonds tremble at the very thought of an attempt.

<margin>170.</margin> Many ascend the cross of hardship, but few also accept its nails. For while many are obedient to voluntary labors and afflictions, only those who have died completely to this world and its comforts can endure those trials that come against their will.

<margin>171.</margin> Many have stripped off all the **garments of skins** <note>original: "δερματίνους χιτῶνας" — a theological term referring to the mortality and fallen state of humanity after Eden.</note>, but only those who have come to loathe the mother of vainglory—which is **self-sufficiency** <note>original: "αὐτάρσκειαν" (autarkeian) — here used in the sense of self-satisfaction or being pleased with oneself.</note>—have stripped off the very last garment: vainglory itself.

<margin>172.</margin> He who accepts the praise of men and the comfort of the body has not yet stripped off this last garment of vainglory. But he who has become naked of it is deemed worthy, from this moment on, to be clothed in the brilliance of the heavenly dwelling sought after with many sighs.

<margin>173.</margin> **Activity** is one thing, and the **effect** is another. The latter indicates a completed sin; the former indicates that the pleasure is only being active within, but not yet without. This is like people who do not move from their own land, yet still pay tribute to the tyrants what they demand.

<margin>174.</margin> While taste <note>i.e., the sense of taste or gluttony.</note> holds dominion in pleasures, it is impossible for all the other senses not to follow. Even if the lower belly seems to be at peace in those who are older (because they do not suffer the "burning" of youth due to the body's wasting away), the barren woman who commits adultery in her mind will not be judged **temperate** <note>original: "Σώφρων" (Sōphrōn) — meaning "self-controlled," "chaste," or "sane."</note> simply because she cannot give birth. Tempe-

...we might say that everything [is perceived rightly] by the person who is not suffering from within, nor rolled down by what they see.

<margin>135.</margin>
In foods, in forms, and in sounds, the **desiring faculty** <term>desiring faculty: "epithymetikon," the part of the soul responsible for physical cravings and appetites</term> of the soul is tested to see what it is like. Through things that are attractive and through those that are otherwise—whether in knowledge, sight, or hearing—it is revealed whether the soul uses these things properly, misuses them, or finds itself in a middle state between the two.

<margin>136.</margin>
In those for whom **fear** <note>In this ascetic context, "fear" usually refers to "fear of God"—a reverent awe that keeps a person from straying into harmful behavior.</note> does not lead the way, the thoughts <note>original: "logismoi" — the internal suggestions or provocations toward certain actions.</note> will be found in a state of confusion, like sheep that have no shepherd. But they are found in good order and within the fold of lawfulness when fear follows or leads them.

<margin>137.</margin>
**Fear** is the son of **Faith**; and fear is the shepherd of the commandments. He who has not acquired the "mother" of fear [Faith] will not be deemed worthy to be seen as a sheep in the Lord’s pasture.

<margin>138.</margin>
Some possess only the beginnings of good things, others the middle stages as well, and others their ends. Without these, a man will be found like a soldier without armor, or an officer without his rations, and because of

<column-break/>

this, he is like one who can only guard his own house from those attempting to break in and insult it. Such a man is not found in the honor that is proper to him in whatever assembly he may join.

<margin>139.</margin>
Those who urge us to indulge in the pleasures of the throat <note>A reference to gluttony or physical overindulgence.</note> while we are still spiritually immature act like people who urge the reopening of wounds that have already begun to heal for the sake of "warmth." It is like scratching a scab because the itching feels "pleasant," or eating things that kindle a fever. It is like breaking down the wall of a vineyard and allowing the **mindset of the flesh** to enter like a **wild boar** <note>original: "monion agrion" — a scriptural metaphor from the Psalms for a destructive force that ravages the soul's progress.</note> to devour good thoughts as if they were clusters of grapes. 

One must not obey such suggestions, nor bend to the untimely flatteries of men or of the passions. Rather, one must fortify the fence through **self-control** <term>self-control: "enkrateia," the virtue of discipline over one's impulses and appetites</term> until the "beasts"—the fleshly passions—cease their howling. And like birds, vain thoughts must not be allowed to descend and plunder the vineyard of the soul, which is guided toward the right path by **contemplations** <term>contemplations: "theoria," the spiritual practice of seeing the divine presence in all things</term> in Christ Jesus our Lord; to whom be glory forever. Amen.

# THE WRETCHED MONK NAMED THEOPHANES
## I SET FORTH A LADDER OF DIVINE GRACES
### WHICH EXPERIENCE HAS MADE KNOWN TO THE GOD-BEARERS

First is most pure prayer.
From which proceeds a certain warmth of the heart.
After which is an energy <term>energy: "energeia," meaning the active, felt presence or operation of God's grace</term> both strange and holy.
Then divine tears of the heart.
Upon which follows a peace from thoughts of all kinds. <note>original: "logismoi" — the intrusive, often distracting or tempting thoughts that cloud the mind.</note>
From which gushes forth the purification of the mind.
And the contemplation <term>contemplation: "theoria," the spiritual "seeing" or direct experience of divine truths</term> of the mysteries above.
After which is a strange illumination in an ineffable manner.
From which comes an unspeakable enlightenment of the heart.
And from there again, an incomplete perfection. <note>The author uses the paradox "incomplete perfection" to suggest that in the spiritual life, one never stops growing closer to God; it is a "perfection" that always has more room to expand.</note>
The step has indeed an infinite width,
Even if it is concluded here in a single line.
Immediately, the bottom step of the ladder
Describes only pure prayer.
But its forms are very many indeed,
And if we wished to list them all now,
It would extend our discourse to great length.
Understand the same from me, my friend:
Experience is the teacher of these things, not words.
A ladder stretching toward the heavens in a strange way.
A decade of steps, a strange quickening of the soul.
A decade of steps, it proclaims the life of the soul.
And as one of the God-bearers says somewhere:
> He who does not hasten to acquire life here,
> Let him not deceive himself with the vain hopes of the soul,
> That he shall receive it there in the hereafter.
A decade of steps, divine philosophy.
A decade of steps, the fruit of all books.
A decade of steps, it shows the perfect state.
A decade of steps, it leads up to the heavens.
A decade of steps, it makes one know God.
The ladder appears very short in its length,
But if one takes it by experience within the heart,
He will find wealth uncontainable by the world,
And a divine fountain flowing with a strange life.
This ladder is the best teacher
For each to know clearly their own measure.
Seeing the ladder of ten divine graces,
If you think you stand firmly upon it,
Tell me, on which of these steps are you,
For the benefit of us who are sluggish?
If you wish, friend, to learn anything of these,
Become free from all kinds of worldly affairs.

<meta>This page concludes the poetic description of the spiritual ladder by the monk Theophanes and transitions into a personal reflection of humility and self-warning. The author expresses fear that those who speak of high spiritual states without experiencing them will face dread at the hour of death. It follows the previous page's list of the ten stages of the soul's ascent.</meta>

<page-num>392</page-num>

From irrational things, and what seems rational.
For you shall learn nothing without freedom from care; <term>freedom from care: "amerimnia," a state of inner stillness and detachment from worldly anxieties necessary for deep prayer.</term>
By experience are these things known, not by word.
I say this to you only as a reminder,
For the word belongs to the Holy God-bearers. <term>God-bearers: "Theophoroi," saints believed to be so filled with the Holy Spirit that they "carry God" within them.</term>
Even if it enters the ear harshly
To one who is not found upon one of the steps,
Or who does not always meditate on such matters,
In the completion of life, and at the hour of death,
He shall truly have great fear and trembling,
And an immeasurable cowardice that will not depart.
The verses have ended upon a fearful note,
But it has happened thus for great profit.
For those who are more hard-hearted—of whom I am the first—
Do not seek repentance and goodness, <term>goodness: "kalokagathia," an ancient Greek ideal of nobility where outward beauty and inward virtue are perfectly combined.</term>
Except that by fearful things, they may instill dread.
He who has ears to hear, let him hear;
Listen and understand, you who have written these things:
How did you dare to say such things,
A man who possesses absolutely nothing of them?
How did you not shudder to teach about these?
Have you not heard what happened to Uzzah? <note>original: "Zan" (Ζὰν). This refers to Uzzah from the Old Testament (2 Samuel 6), who was struck dead for touching the Ark of the Covenant to steady it, despite his good intentions. The author uses it as a warning against handling holy mysteries without being worthy.</note>
Wishing to set right the Divine Ark?
Do not think that I say these things as one teaching,
But so that I may expose <note>original: "stēliteusō," literally to post someone's name on a public pillar (stēle) for shaming.</note> myself in these matters,
Seeing the prizes of those who struggle,
And my own fruitlessness in all things.
